16.7 ADVERTISING COMMUNICATIONS: BASIC
CONCEPTS
16.7.1 Information Processing Model (IPM)
In the 1640s, William McGuire prepared this model and connected it to the concept of persuasion in ad effectiveness. IPM essentially discusses the behaviour and attitudinal changes in response to persuasive communication. Let us have a look at the outline of the model: The above diagram explains information processing in five steps. * Exposure: All market players simultaneously expose customers randomly to brand-related information through various media and non- media activities. The objective is to inform them about the product attributes. * Attention: Customers choose their ad message based on their interests. Here, marketers face the challenge of attracting T.G.'s attention in a limited period.

* Comprehension: Customers will develop an understanding of the brand Advertising Literacy based on selective attention and interest areas. This is the stage at which T.G. is curious about the brand and wants to know more about it. * Acceptance: Out of the various shortlisted choices, customers accept a particular brand and reject another. This acceptance does not ensure that the decision will remain so forever, and such scepticism can change their decision. * Retention: In this phase, disbelief strengthens belief, and customers adhere to their decisions. Consumers are more determined to continue with the shortlisted brand. Most importantly, when information travels through these five stages, various stimuli, generally marketer--and advertiser-dominated, must reach through them to create a long-term memory. Memory plays an important role, especially at stages two, three, and four.
16.7.2 AIDA and DAGMAR Models
AIDA and DAGMAR are two models of consumer response to advertising and marketing activities. The AIDA model organises the response into four stages, namely: * Attention: Here, advertisers encourage the audience to hear the main idea of the advertisement. This is the first step to response; consumers' attention must be captured by emphasising the product's strong features, a genuine solution to the problem, the promise of savings through discounts, etc. and by providing any common angle that can attract consumer attention. E.g. Lifebuoy hand wash advertisement. * Interest: Once the attention is captured, further interest is generated in the customer's mind, and a more detailed picture of the message is painted--for example, the MamyPoko pants advertisement. * Desire: It helps customers embrace the central idea by explaining how the change will benefit them--E.g. Fortune Rice Bran Oil advertisement. * Action: The advertisement suggests the action advertisers want consumers to take--for example, the Fair and Lovely fairness cream and face wash advertisement featuring Yami Gautam. In 1661, Russel Colley proposed the DAGMAR model. It is expanded to define advertising goals for measured advertising results. As per this model, consumers' purchase decision goes through four stages, namely: * Awareness: Consumers must first know the brand and company's existence and availability. Once this awareness is attained, companies must use it immediately--for example, JustDial.com endorsements by Amitabh Bachchan. * Comprehension: Here, advertisers must focus on product benefits and give a deeper understanding of the product. For example, in the Colgate Super Flexi advertisement, * Conviction: At this stage, ads must build confidence in the customers' minds so they are compelled to buy the product--E.g. Sugarfree Natura

Participation in * Action: In this, the focus is on buying, and therefore, ads emphasise the
Interactive Media
benefits of customers' purchases--for example, Godrej Ezee's advertisement.
16.7.3 Push and Pull Strategy
These are two main types of promotional strategy. In the push strategy, the producer lures wholesalers and retailers in the form of trade shows, direct selling, subsidies, high commission rates, POP displays and others to stock their products and push them towards the customer, as explained in the figure below: Customers may not experience the push strategy as it is directed towards distributors, whereas the pull strategy aims at the end customer. Through various promotional strategies such as advertising, word of mouth, etc., the product is pulled through the channel by customer demand, as explained below: The push strategy is comparatively more interactive and works best in impulse-buying product categories. Companies generally combine both strategies to increase sales.
16.7.4 What is a Brand?
A positive brand image is a valuable asset of the company. Brands are the product's visual identity in the form of logo, colour, labelling, name, tagline, shapes, and graphics. It helps customers identify brand 'A' versus brand 'B'. The branding process is creating a unique brand name and position in the market through advertising and marketing campaigns. A good brand name must be unique, easy to pronounce, identifiable, have recall value, talk about the product's qualities and benefits, have legal protection, and not have wrong meanings associated with that word, especially when extending to another market.
16.7.5 Slogans, Jingles, Trademarks, Logo, and Mascot
These are important ingredients of the branding process and distinguish a company from its competition. A well-designed logo enhances brand value, gives a unique identity to the product, must be easily recognisable, builds trust, makes the product look more professional, and helps consumers associate the brand with the company. A slogan is a watchword, short, catchy phrase or motto used in advertising,

generally along with the logo. It is one of the most appealing tools to be used Advertising Literacy in the branding process and is often called the brand's fingerprint. It connects consumers with the brand and can change their perception. Slogans may change depending on the campaign. For Coca-Cola, its slogans are quite often changing. In the 2000s, their 'Thanda Matlab Coca-Cola' campaign with Amir Khan was worth noticing. In 2012, they launched their 'Open Happiness' campaign with Coke. In between, they had three more slogans, namely 'Piyo Sar Uthake', 'Jo Chaheho Jaye Coca-Cola Enjoy' and 'Burrrrrr'. Slogans are sometimes paired with jingles, a short tune used in advertising. Like slogans, jingles must be catchy and memorable and create familiarity and desire for the product. Many of us hear a jingle on the radio or television, and it gets into our heads, and the effect is long-lasting. Jingles are one of the classic examples of sound branding. Many times, companies also use mascots in advertising campaigns. Mascots are a highly visible part of the brand and can take the advertising campaign to the next level. They give the brand a personality. While designing mascots, one has to ensure that the image is associated with the brand image. The most important legal shield for brands is trademarks. These can be symbols, logos, words, or slogans. Companies register them and create ownership and exclusive rights to use them. Companies may extend trademark protection to packaging, colours, numerals, shape of goods, smell, sound, movement, and holograms. It is anything that distinguishes one company's goods from another. Anybody who infringes them can be taken to court.
16.7.6 USP
Unique Selling Proposition or Unique Selling Point is a marketing concept which Rosser Reeves introduced. It can be a real or perceived benefit that customers seek from the product more than that of its competitor. The purpose of having a USP is that the target audience must be convinced of the reason to buy a product. This proposition must be something other marketers have not yet claimed; only your product is offered or claimed to be offered first. Generally, the advertising campaign is built around USP. 16.8 THE ADVERTISING MANAGEMENT
PROCESS
16.8.1 Advertising Strategy
A company's advertising strategy should always support its marketing strategy and the company plans. When doing strategic planning, advertisers need to be creative and flexible. A rigid strategy may often lead to loss of market share. One may use push or pull techniques to set the strategies depending on the business's goals. Strategic planning goes through the following steps:
16.8.1.1 Setting Objectives
The first and foremost step in strategic planning is setting objectives. Objectives are statements that explain what needs to be attained by taking advantage of opportunities and overcoming any barriers. When setting objectives, advertisers need to understand the goal of the campaign. Depending on the company's goals, objectives can be short-term or long- term. Short-term objectives focus on customers' actions, i.e., on the purchase, and long-term objectives focus on change in brand attitude. These objectives are further classified as direct and indirect. Direct objectives focus on increased sales, new distribution channel development, and profitability, whereas indirect objectives focus on changing attitudes and increasing awareness.

16.8.1.2 Formulating Budget Advertising
Literacy The advertising budget is one of the important components of the marketing budget. Advertisers must first analyse the expected results and only invest in any campaign. Campaign goals and objectives must be first determined, and the budget should be set accordingly. A well-planned budget helps in the effective utilisation of funds and avoids wastage. There are different techniques for setting the ad budget, which are discussed below: * Based on previous years' expenditure on advertising. * Percentage of sales technique: here, advertisers assess the annual sales and then set a budget. * The advertisers set an equal budget at par with the competition, meaning whatever the competition spends is equal to the advertisers' budget. * In an objective-based budget, advertisers first consider the available funds and cut the number of objectives or prioritise them according to the existing funds.
16.8.1.3 Creating Advertising Messages
Designing an advertising message is considered the most creative part of the campaign. Creativity has no limitations; therefore, messages can be designed in multiple ways beyond imagination. One has to take cues from the objectives to write a precise message.
16.8.1.4 Selecting Media and Vehicles
Selecting media and vehicles is also known as 'media scheduling'. It is a strategic process where media planners do a lot of research before making final decisions. The key here is to choose the most cost-effective media to reach the focused target audience. Media planners make a 'media mix' as their customised recipes when needs arise. Media mix simply means the right combination of each medium to reach its target audiences. The choice of media can be from print (newspapers, magazines and direct mail) and electronic media (radio, television, and Internet). While preparing media mix, one has to check these simple tips: * Optimum utilisation of your resources: Try to make a mix that will reach as large an audience as possible while reducing wastage. * Reach with high frequency: Constantly making your presence felt will have a high register and recall value. * Know your customer: Understand his/her media consumption for better reach. * Do your homework: Research well before going on the floor. The duration and timing of the advertising campaign need to be strategically planned for campaign success. Check reach and coverage, the cost of the media vehicles, the nature of your product, business goals, campaign goals, and your audience profile.

Participation in * More money spent will not always ensure the success of the advertising
Interactive Media
campaign. * Negotiate with media houses for competitive prices.
16.8.2 Strategy Implementation
Once an effective plan is made, it needs to be carefully executed, and that is when strategic implementation comes into the picture. Any organisation is people-oriented, and any strategy cannot be executed without the active involvement of the organisation's employees. The second step is to assess the budget requirements and match them with strategy implementation. Then, assign roles and responsibilities to designated people and, most importantly, give them deadlines. Put simply, have a meticulous communication plan ready before implementation.
16.8.3 Assessing Advertising Effectiveness
Measuring and evaluating advertising effectiveness is extremely important not only for the current campaign but also gives direction for all future campaigns. The ultimate goal of any advertising is to assist the sales team in increasing sales or help the marketing team increase brand awareness. This is measured by calculating R3: Reach, resonance and reaction. Reach is the penetration of your advertisement amongst your target audience. Resonance will tell you how effectively and qualitatively you have reached them. Reaction is how your target responds to your message. Brief Note on the Format of Units
Dr. Kiron Bansal
While writing a Unit in Self Learning Material (SLM) format, the Course writers may like to keep the following points in mind:
Word Limit
The length of each Unit is 5000 - 6000 words or approximately 25 word-processed A-4 size pages in view of the considerations of pedagogy, uniformity and printing. Style The units have to be written by the course writers in their own words in conversational style in simple English. The use of personal pronouns such as 'you', 'we' builds interactivity in the learning material to give the feel as if the teacher is speaking to the learner through his/her writing.
Unit Structure
The unit structure is a detailed itemization of the content broken into sections and subsections. It displays structural relations within the content to help the learners overview the text and locate relevant parts efficiently (Annexure 1). Introduction A brief introduction introduces the subject matter and the scheme of contents. It establishes the connections of the unit with the previous as well as the next unit. Objectives The objectives of each unit have to be stated clearly in behavioural terms so that they are observable and measurable. Some examples of behavioural verbs are: define, describe, explain, list, select, state, compare, differentiate, identify, distinguish, summarise, illustrate, outline etc. (Annexure 2)
Main Body of the Unit
The main body of the unit includes the content in the form of sections and subsections with suitable headings and sub-headings. Usually each section relates to a different objective of the unit, presents at least one new point and helps the learner to move from one point to another. These points are followed by self check questions given at the end of each section. The content may be interspersed with examples, illustrations and case studies to explain the concepts/issues discussed in the unit. Case studies can be given separately in appendix.
Self Check Questions
Self check questions are related to the objectives of a unit and serve pedagogic functions as they break monotony and motivate the learner to participate in learning. These are, however, not sent to the University for assessment. Possible answers of the questions are given at the end of the unit to provide feedback to the learners and indicate that they are on the right path. Answers are based on what has been discussed and do not fall outside the scope of the unit.

Activities Some activities also need to be given in the unit to involve the learner. These activities may be based on the subject matter of the unit, further readings and sources. The learners can also be asked to read/write or view/listen or analyse a report/news item (Annexure 3). Graphics Graphics such as line drawings, diagrams, charts, graphs, flow charts, cartoons etc. have to be indicated in the text. For any such requirement, appropriate art work can be arranged by the University. Summary In summary, important issues discussed in the unit are recapitulated at the end for reinforcement. Glossary/Key words The keywords, new concepts, difficult terms and technical expressions discussed in the unit which need elaboration may be included in glossary (Annexure 4).
Citations, References & Further Readings
Since we do not follow the system of footnotes, a brief list of references may be provided at the end of the unit. Whenever an authority is quoted the source need to be properly cited. The books recommended for Further Readings should be easily available at reasonable prices. The name of the author, year of publication, title of the book, publisher, place of publication and chapter needs to be mentioned. References of the relevant websites may also be given. If the course writer feels that a published article or chapter from existing material should be made available to the learners as additional readings, the same may be indicated with complete references so that we may obtain copyright of the material and send it to our students.
Copyright Issues
Care needs to be taken while quoting from published or unpublished material - a maximum of 100 words may be quoted giving complete references and citations of the quoted work. If the quoted text, however, is more than 100 words, the course writer may either take written permission from the author or inform the Programme Coordinator giving complete references of the work so that we may obtain written permission to use the material otherwise it can fall under plagiarism. Similarly, if an already published map/photograph/news clipping/report/writing etc. needs to be included in the course material; a photocopy of the same with complete reference may be sent to us. We shall obtain requisite copyright permissions and get proper art work made for any such requirement.
Block Introduction
The Course Writer writing all the units of a block needs to prepare the Block Introduction in which various units of the block have to be briefly introduced and their linkages with each other as well as the next block established (Annexure 5).

Annexure 4
4.8 Key Words
Behaviourists : A school of thought in psychology that viewed animals and human behaviour in terms of external process only (stimulus-response theory). Language was believed to be a matter of habit formation and imitation and errors were seen as bad habits. Multilingualism : The use of more than two languages by an individual or a community Reinforcement : This is a stimulus which leads to a response either occurring or not occurring again. Structuralists : A school of thought in linguistics which stressed the importance of language as a system where units such as sounds, words, sentences were viewed as structured within the system. L1 : Usually your mother tongue/ first language which you acquire. L2 : Language which is learnt as a second language like English in India.

BLOCK 2 DATA COLLECTION METHODS
This block will focus on different methods of digital data collection that are available to journalists today. From digital sources and methods, to tools and ethics, the contents of this unit will help guide the learners on how they can use the digital sources abundantly available to us today to fulfill their responsibilities as journalists.
Unit 5 Managing Sources of Information, throws light on the practicalities of managing sources in the
digital age. You will learn about the different digital sources a journalists has at their disposal, the tools they can use to manage their research material, and the workflow they can develop to churn out well- crafted, source-backed stories. In Unit 6 Data Collection Methods, we will introduce you to the different methods digital journalists use to collect data today. You will be instructed on how to plan the data collection process for yourself and how to master the requisite skills for data collection in a rapidly changing digital media environment, including the ethical considerations intrinsic to the process.
Unit 7 Online Surveys, deals with one of the most simple but highly popular data collection tools used
today, online survey. You will learn about its construction and design principles, and also distribution and interpretation. Used optimally, the survey can be a valuable tool in the hands of a journalist, especially in its digital avatar. In Unit 8 Online Interviews, we delve into the art of conducting internet-mediated interviews, which are a boon in this time and age. You will learn about best practices to plan and conduct interviews, the technical considerations and contingencies you must be prepared for, and the optimal data management and analysis procedures that can help make an ordinary interview into an extraordinary one. This block dealt with how a journalist can use simple digital sources, tools and procedures to craft compelling stories that foster public trust. In the next block, we will focus on big data, data mining, and how the collection, collating and interpretation of data aid journalists to fulfill their duties as public watchdogs.

BLOCK 3 DATA HANDLING
This block is centered on how journalists handle data in the course of everyday news-making. The goal is to familiarise learners with important concepts such as big data and data mining, which have become fundamental to digital journalism today, determining which stories are told to the public and how.
Unit 9 Big Data: Meaning and Interpretation, introduces the concept of big data, the collection of
different kinds of digital actions and interactions that plays a big role in our lives today. You will understand its history, concepts and technicalities, but most importantly, how it has altered the very nature of media and new-making today. In Unit 10 Introduction to Data Mining, we will discuss data mining or the process of 'mining' of knowledge from the data available with us. You will learn to distinguish it from other stages in the data handling process, and about its applications in digital journalism, which though advantageous, must always be counter-balanced by an ethical compass.
Unit 11 Tools of Data Mining, will be a continuation of the previous unit but will go deeper to make you
familiar with the technical aspects of data mining. You will learn about the tools, skills and ethical frameworks involved in the process in the context of digital media, and how large amounts of data can be transformed into uncompromising news-making. This will bring you to the end of the third block wherein you will have learnt about key technical aspects of digital journalism, specifically pertaining to big data. In the final block coming up ahead, you will learn about some important processes involved in the analysis of data, which lies at the heart of digital journalism.

This block picks up after different data-related activities we discussed in previous units, specifically those related to data collection and data handling. Unit 12 Understanding Numbers, helps you understand how to work with numbers as a
journalist. You will learn that rather than being afraid of numbers, you can interpret them critically and frame compelling narratives based on them. This unit provides you the tools to do that.

We are in the midst of technological and cultural changes, and it is our duty as journalists to use our pens and keyboards to tell the stories of these digital times in a clear, ethical and humane manner.

COURSE INTRODUCTION
Writing is the backbone of Mass Communication. Combined with technology and skill-set, it can create a wide scope of professional opportunities if mastered properly. Journalistic writing concerns itself with all forms of factual and opinions writing that suit both traditional and online media platforms. The course BNM-025 Types of Journalistic Writings will provide you with the background context of writings for the media. While it deep dives into feature writing and imparts the skills required for ideation, features and new trends, it also spells out the nuances of political writing and the power-state- politics relationship in a democratic set up. This course also enlightens the learner about development perspectives in the countries of the global south and public policy formulation. Block 1 Feature writing This block consists of four units. Unit 1 introduces the idea of feature writing to the learner. It talks about the aspects of feature writing and the qualities of a feature writer. Unit 2 focuses on differentiating between news and feature writing, their key elements, techniques and teaches the art of writing engaging features. Unit 3 explains the different types of features, specialised features and new trends of feature writing. Unit 4 highlights the subjects, treatment and throws light on topic selection for feature writing and sources of information. Block 2 Political Reporting This block consists of four units. Unit 5 explains the relationship between state, politics and power and the importance of political writing. Unit 6 discusses the approaches and views on representative democracy while critically examining democracy - election interface and vital issues linked with it and political writing. Unit 7 deals with types and levels of participation and the role of dissent in democracy. Unit 8 teaches the techniques of various forms of political writing like editorial, opinion and long form journalism. Block 3 Development Journalism
Unit 9 explains the basic concepts and approaches to development. Unit 10
discusses how development issues are covered by various mass media with the help of case studies. Unit 11 tries to look at the international perspective of development in countries and its goals. Unit 12 focuses on content structuring and techniques of different types of development communication writing. Unit 13 explains the various aspects of solutions based journalism.
Block 4 Public Policy and Media
Unit 14 introduces the concepts, characteristics and types of public policy.
Unit 15 describes the various models of public policy in detail. Unit 16 talks
about the stages of public policy process, formulation of public policy and it's implementation. Unit 17 examines the connect between political ideology and public policy and its effect on public policy.

The course is designed to give a clear, yet concise idea about the different types of journalistic writings to suit the disciplines of mass communication and impart a skill set that will be useful in professional fields of interests. On completion of this course, you will be able to: * write features and differentiate between their types; * analyse the interplay of state, politics and power in a democracy and develop insightful perspectives to write about them; * develop the skills for need identification, content structuring and providing solutions to development problems in developing societies; and * comprehend and describe public policy and political ideology and how the two affect each other. The knowledge that you gather from this course and the skill set that you develop after a thorough understanding and practice of the course components will make it easier to navigate through the media text that you come across later in this programme and also when you start working in the media industry.

BLOCK 1
FEATURE WRITING

BLOCK 1 INTRODUCTION
The purpose of the first block is two-pronged: one, it introduces you to an engaging style of light writing - feature writing. Two, it introduces you to how other forms of writing are different from feature writing. The concepts explained in this block are helpful in building the base of journalistic writing.
Unit 1 What is Feature Writing looks at what a feature is and how it is
useful. It teaches you the various aspects of a feature and familiarizes you with the necessary qualities of a feature writer like researching, language, style and more.
Unit 2 News and Feature throws light on news writing - its principles and
elements, the characteristics of feature writing and also brings out a comparison between feature and other journalistic forms of writing.
Unit 3 Types of Feature discusses the types of feature and specialized
feature. It also teaches the new trends in feature writing. It encourages you to apply what you learn to create new feature stories.
Unit 4 Subjects and their Treatment focuses more on doable aspects like
how to choose a topic for feature writing and how to find sources for writing a feature. Other than these aspects, this unit also explains how to edit a feature after writing it. With this, you would come to the end of the first block in types of journalistic writing. Further blocks would help you build an understanding of other important aspects like the societal context and policy making, vis-a-vis journalistic writings.

1.0 INTRODUCTION
The main goals of feature writing are to engage, excite, and provoke readers. Not only are facts presented in this kind of narrative essential, but questions about "why" and, yes, "how" are also asked. You will learn about the creative world of feature writing in this lesson. This is a discipline that blends journalism and art. We will start by looking at what makes feature writing distinct that appears every day, why it is such a significant part of monthly publications, and how it may be financially and socially satisfying. You will learn the technique of writing attention-grabbing features, from taking concepts to creating your unique voice. Ready to turn your words into something more than just news? Let's dive in!

Feature Writing 1.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
This unit will introduce you to feature writing in general and discuss with the help of some examples, how a feature differs from other items printed in newspapers and magazines. At the end of this unit you should be able to * discuss the role of print media * differentiate between features and other items published in periodicals and newspapers a identify the desirable characteristics of a feature * list the various types of features, and, by extension, * describe what makes a good feature writer. The 'activities' you find interspersed are meant to be attempted in the blank spaces given. Aids to answers are provided at the end of the unit but we strongly advise you against reading the answers beforehand. In most cases, they are only hints or model answers and an not the one perfect answer to any question
1.2 ROLE OF PRINT MEDIA
If you read articles in magazines or newspapers, you would have come across the terms "print media", "journalism", and "feature articles". you would do well to first understand what is meant by such terms in case you are interested in achieving publication. The term Media (plural of medium) refers to a "channel, method or system of communication, information or entertainment ... whether magazine, newspaper, radio, television, or public platform." The term Print media would, of course, refer to magazines and newspapers. The term Electronic media refers to radio and television. A Journalist is a person who collects, edits and presents facts or events, in a popular way, without any attempt at interpretation. He has an important role to play in the print media. Apart from the news items he presents, the print media also carries other pieces of writing which are creative and interpretative, in addition to being factual. Such writing is covered by the terms "feature" or "feature article". A feature article, even if it is factual, differs from a straight news article in three ways. It (1) gives background and analysis (2) has a strong emotional or human interest appeal and (3) carries the stamp, both creative and interpretative, of the writer. The print media, then, has the following roles to play: It a) collects news b) reports events c) presents factual articles on various subjects d) publishes human interest features, and

e) suggests measures to improve existing evils in society in general. What is Feature Writing The print media, therefore, presents the world to the common man, at an affordable price, in a 'portable' way. Unlike the electronic media where an item is gone forever after it has been transmitted (unless of course one tapes it), the newspaper or the journal can be read and reread, at one's leisure, and stored as it is. Feature Writing 1.3 WHAT IS A FEATURE? If you are to write a feature for the newspaper, remember that * it should be written in the form of a story * its subject should be of specific interest * it should express feelings and emotions more than facts (and opinions) * it should be written in an informal style * any statistical details should come after the main story, and * it should be in an area where you yourself have some level of expertise. The definitions given below will make clear to you what a feature is.
1.3.1 Definitions
One way of deciding what is a feature is to decide what it is not. a. Feature is not a news report. A feature article may frequently examine a topic in greater detail than a news article or it may take a different approach when examining an ongoing subject. Compared to a news article, a feature is a longer piece of writing. Features are commonly utilised in periodicals, newspapers, and internet content and come in a variety of forms. (The Hindu, September 1, 2024)

b. Feature is not a news item. What is Feature Writing c. Feature is not an editorial.

1.4.1 Subject Matter
Naturally, you would start by observing what would be interesting to write a feature on. They couldn't possibly be beneficial to my lungs." After that, you consider writing a letter to the editor of your neighbourhood daily newspaper, but ultimately you decide to turn it into an article. Of course, the goal is to put your thoughts into perspective. Linking the feature to your readership is one of the things you would need to remember. To put it another way, you would need to consider the social environment. We use the term "social context" to mean that you should tie the feature you write to the topics that your readers are currently thinking about, their social status (class, region, age group, etc.), and anything else that is "concerned with the mutual relations of (classes of) human beings" Activity -3 Original Lines: "In New York City, dining alone is no longer seen as a sign of loneliness. 1.4.4 Writer's Perspective
Everybody views each given topic from a different angle. A person's viewpoint is how they view the world. Do you recall the poem about the blind men who went to see the elephant? Their perceptions of what an elephant was like were radically varied, depending on where they had touched the animal. That is to say, your writing style will influence the articles you write. Consider the phenomenon of brain drain. This problem may be seen from two angles: that of the bright but dissatisfied young scientist, and that of his elderly parents, who have high expectations that he would settle down with a kind girl who will take care of them when they are old. 1) Will you do it or not? (enquiring)
2) Could you please do it? (request)
3) If you don't do it, you will regret it. (threatening)
4) I beg of you, please do it. (supplicating)

1.5 WHO IS A GOOD FEATURE WRITER
Having come this far, you would by now have understood that there is more to being a feature writer than just taking up a pen on the spur of the moment and dashing off a feature that will make people sit up and take notice of you! Obviously you will have to consciously cultivate some qualities in yourself if you wish to succeed.
1.5.1 Expertise
Do not attempt to write features in areas which require specialist knowledge unless you have the expertise i.e. "special skill or knowledge that is acquired by training, study or practice." You would remember, of course, that a feature is "the subjective rather than the objective material" in a periodical. It contains "opinion, assessment and advice". So, for instance, if you feel that

the budget presented by a Minister is inflationary and potentially disastrous, What is Feature Writing do not rush in with an opinion alone. Make an assessment of the background, the overall situation under which such a budget was drafted, the facts and figures. Finally, on the basis of this assessment, offer advice. However, if you happen to be only deeply involved as a citizen who will be paying crippling taxes perhaps you would do better to seek another way of expressing an opinion.
1.5.2 Deep Research
We have talked, above, on acquiring background knowledge. This needs intensive research into the topic, even if you intend only to write a semi- humorous, light-hearted piece. When you do research, you collect and analyse facts and information and try to gain new knowledge or new understanding. Of course, your study is detailed and exhaustive. You may find that, during the course of your research, you have collected more materials than you will need for the time being. You might find it useful to maintain a file of clippings. Always indicate where you got the information from, on the clipping itself, in case you wish
1.5.3 Objectivity
You will immediately react to "objectivity" by saying, just now we were told that a feature contains "opinion, assessment and advice" and now we are told to be objective. Perhaps we should have used the word "perspective". To be objective means that what you say is based on facts and things that can be seen or measured. For instance, you may feel that a book reviewed by you is very popular. Perhaps all your friends have read it or heard about it. What would make your statement objective would be to collect information from a wider cross-section of potential readers. After all, your friends would necessarily be of your background, your temperament, your educational level, etc. Try even asking your fellow commuters in the bus, or your neighbour who is an avid reader of books and an executive by profession. Such a procedure would make your feature objective,
1.5.4 Personal Viewpoint
After you have researched well and collected enough material you would need to say it your way. You may have enough data about the budget, (discussed earlier). You would have found out what the budgets for the preceding five years were, what was the balance of payments position, what was the deficit financing status. Then you would have to confront the question "So what?" And this would indicate your personal viewpoint. This is true of any topic you choose to write on-environment, spots, cultural shows, whatsoever. And this, therefore, is a quality you should consciously cultivate a personal viewpoint which should emerge in any feature you write.
1.5.5 Precision in Language
Look at the work of any professional writer. Notice constantly how he is moving from the general and the abstract to the concrete example, the facts and figures, the illustrations. It is, no doubt, possible to be too concrete, too

Feature Writing illustrative and too precise, but few inexperienced writers need to worry about this get rid of obvious padding: Call a fool a fool Beware of pat expressions Take care of words loaded with associated meanings Avoid abstractions Read the example given below. This is a quotation from a writer who pared his work down to the absolute minimum: "You do not understand. This is a clean and pleasant cafe. It is well lighted. The light is very good and also, now, there are shadows of the leaves." This is in answer to a waiter urging another to close up since there are other cafe's open all night long. The beauty of the description lies in the precision. Do not be afraid to commit yourself once you have your facts straight. If you are sure that there is injustice done to one set of people because of any reason whatsoever, have your statistics straight and feel strongly about the issue, then say so. Anything you say will have to be essentially in your own way. This is what style means: choice of words, the way the sentences are structured, the use of punctuation etc. You must cultivate a style that is essentially your own and that reflects your own personality and viewpoint. If you read reports on the Republic Day celebrations you will be amazed at how differently the same thing can be described. Most feature-writers will give background information, scenic descriptions and proceed from the beginning of the parade to the end. 1.7 KEYWORDS

Feature Writing 2.2 NEWS WRITING
It is believed that it is difficult to define news. Nonetheless, news will always be something that surprises readers, listeners, and viewers. For any information to be appropriately referred to as the "News," it must be true, fresh, and captivating. News cannot exist without facts, hence there must be facts to report. It is crucial that the observer, listener, and reader are all unfamiliar with these facts. Once more, news is anything that is released online, on radio, aired on television networks, and published on the news sections of newspapers and magazines. News also covers the lives, relationships, and scandals involving the wealthy, well-known, and infamous. The news adage that is even somewhat significant is that negative news tends to sell more newspapers than positive news. What news would there be today, then? In light of the constraints of time, space, and resources, what should be included, what should be excluded, and what should be prioritised? And in the age of Internet, infinity, who's to say what's news, asks Wyford Hicks. Thus, it will not be an exaggeration to say that there are almost as many definitions of the news as there are reporters/journalists. Most news reporters will of course agree that every occurrence or event in itself is not and cannot be the 'news'.
2.1 ELEMENTS OF NEWS WRITING
Now that you are aware of the definition, significance, and content of news, let us talk about the main components or ingredients involved in producing news. Since news items, or stories as they are also known, are not written in the same style or manner as our letters, articles, or other written works, you have undoubtedly noticed if you have been closely reading your newspaper. These are a handful of the more significant ones: Among other things, these include weather, adventure, conflict, empathy, proximity, prominence, dimension, and consequence. * Timeliness The most crucial component of a news article is the event's timing of occurrence. As soon as feasible, people want to hear about the event. An event that occurred yesterday or the day before yesterday is usually regarded stale and should not be published unless it is exceptionally noteworthy or of an extraordinary kind. Therefore, the timing of an event is very important in determining whether or not it qualifies as news. In today's fight against time, the era of the Internet and cellphones, news may stop being news after 24 or even 12 hours. These days, readers, listeners, and viewers are well aware of the importance of perishability and immediacy in "newsfall" and news reporting. * Proximity For reporters and a newspaper, the proximity of an event or occurrence to the public is critically important. Geographical proximity and audience relevance are two examples of proximity. The more "local" or nearby the location of the incident, the more significant it is to qualify as 26 news.

* Prominence News and Feature It is always going to make headlines if some famous person happens to be involved. For instance, it generates headlines when a celebrity trips and falls in the loo or when the prime minister hurts his ankle walking to the car. The crucial point is that audiences are drawn to the well-known, the notorious, and even the odd. This is also because well-known families value their privacy and frequently make headlines for happy or sad occasions. * Dimension An incident becomes news when a large number of individuals are involved, affected, or lose a significant amount of money. For instance, an earthquake in Manila, the Philippines, that claims 500 lives or more makes headlines even in India because human lives are valuable no matter where they are lost. However, if severe rains in Patna or Mumbai flood low-lying neighborhoods, resulting in the collapse of four high-rise buildings and the deaths of twenty-three individuals, the story immediately makes headlines in India and may even feature photos from the event. * Impact If the U.S. president or British prime minister announces his plans to sanction military aid to Pakistan, it's bound to impact the Indo-US or Indo-British ties, and also Indo-Pak relations. Similarly, if the Union Government increases income tax in its annual budget, or levies a tax on purchase of cars, that make all-India news. * Human Interest Quite often, newspaper reporters come across situations, which induce emotions of mercy or sentiments or sympathy. For example, if a visually- challenged person performs some daring act, such as scaling Mount Everest, or a hearing-challenged boy scores a meritorious position in a competitive examination, these are human interest stories, we call these as human interest stories. You may recall the incident when a four- yearold child by the name of Prince, fell in a way-side 30-foot-deep well some years ago; the rescue work by the army personnel was put out live on many television channels. This was a live human interest story which attracted the interest of viewers all over India for many hours, till the rescue act was completed. * Conflict Conflict of any type - political, social, cultural, communal, among some sections of society, difference of opinion among two or more political parties, conflict among some warring groups, or more of such conflicts always make news. As you would have seen that differences between the Bhartiya Janata Party and the Communist Party (Marxist) and the Indian National Congress on the Indo-US nuclear deal made news in India for several months. You will find that many more such issues figure in newspapers as news very often.

Feature Writing * Adventure As we previously discussed, disabled people who take on challenging undertakings with ease, grace, or daringness consistently make headlines. International headlines was generated when a 70-year-old Japanese woman succeeded in her quest to climb Mount Everest, the world's highest mountain peak. In addition to garnering attention in numerous other nations, this tale of adventure made it to the Japanese first page banner headline. * Novelty News is made of unusual and unique events. For instance, it made headlines throughout the world when an American mother gave birth to eight healthy children, each weighing roughly 200 grammes. Once more, the victory of an eight-year-old Orissan child in a marathon run against adults was considered a first for news coverage. * Empathy We frequently experience a variety of life situations that reflect tragedy, humour, peculiarity, success, and failure from time to time. Many of these incidents draw our attention or compassion: an elderly couple who loses every kid in a fire, flood, or accident; a youngster who falls from its mother's arms and is crushed under the wheels of a speeding bus or train--all of these stories make headlines. Because everyone's heart goes out to the loved ones who are impacted in this way. * Weather / Climate / Environment: Weather - extreme heat, cold, rain, storm, pollution affects all of us; and usually bad weather affects us badly. Remember how the Indian Ocean tsunami made news all over the world in so many countries, including India, which killed hundreds of men, women, children, and wreaked unusual, unimaginable losses of property, animals and marine life. For months together, this was considered as an extra ordinary change in weather, and was forecast to be a prodigious problem of environment for all time to come across the globe. Climatic changes, different aspects of environment degradation, pollution as well as efforts towards environment conservation make news. 2.2.3 Principles of News Writing
As we have already discussed, news articles need to be written in a way that communicates the essential information to the reader in the fewest words and fastest amount of time. As a result, the first paragraph of the news article, also known as the introduction or lead, attempts to convey the main points of the event or occurrence in no more than 24 to 30 words. We will also touch on the subject of creating an introduction or lead and the variety of leads available for news writing. a. 5Ws and 1H The opening paragraph of the news articles uses one H and five Ws. Probably the most fundamental and basic rule of creating a news article is this one. The introduction, also known as the lead or intro, should address the following five Ws and one H: who, what, when, where, why, and how. This is the most important news writing rule that is adhered to globally. The first paragraph of the news item must clearly state as to who is the main actor, character, object, subject or concern of the event, which needs to be told or written about. Is it the President, Prime Minister, any minister, governor, a well-known foreign dignitary, or any other prominent person? Is it a notorious criminal or any other individual of any status, whom people know in some context or the other? The other four Ws and one H are: * What happened? * When did it happen? * Where did happen? * Why did it happen? How did it happen? b. The inverted pyramid Writing the news in the shape of an inverted pyramid is another conventional method. The most significant and primary idea of the news article is presented in the opening paragraph, also known as the lead or the intro. The remainder of the story is further explained, developed, and expanded upon in the news item's body. As a result, the facts in the paragraphs that follow the Lead or the Intro must corroborate the primary ideas expressed in those sections. As a result, the story will appear like an inverted pyramid as seen below if you examine it as a figure or diagram. 29

Feature Writing The most important point in the story should be at the top, followed by less important facts, with the least important ones coming at the bottom, one by one, depending on their importance in the overall structure and length of the news story. Such a technique of writing a story is called Inverted Pyramid. This story (news) starts off with a great lead. Then, short summary of the story, and sometimes a little history for the context of story. Important stuff goes here. Becomes unimportant here. Even more unimportant downright dull, can be cut, often cut, c u t, Cut.
Illustration No. 1: Inverted Pyramid

2.3 FEATURE WRITING
Different from news articles, feature articles are a kind of journalism that informs and entertains. Unlike a news report, it goes into greater depth about a particular facet or feature of a problem, event, topic, or location. Feature stories are becoming more and more important for drawing readers and increasing market presence in print media due to dwindling readership and budgetary difficulties. They are more valuable and have a longer shelf life than news articles since they are written in plain, everyday language. Readers look for features that help them understand difficult subjects in simpler words, learn about unknown topics and locations, or gain insight into well- known people--achievements that news pieces are unable to accomplish.

2.3.1 Important Ingredients of Feature Articles News and Feature
To write a compelling feature article, one needs to possess excellent communication skills and strong command of language. The writer must approach the subject creatively and from multiple angles. Here are key elements that make a feature article stand out:
- Immaculate Language: Use flawless, simple, and grammatically correct
language. Avoid difficult words, jargon, and complex ideas to maintain reader engagement.
- Express Your Views: Readers want to know your perspective. Present
your thoughts logically and engagingly, earning readers' loyalty by offering unique insights.
- Be Personal: Involve the reader by adding personal descriptions and
vivid details. Quoting people or capturing their mood and appearance adds depth and interest.
- Interviews and Dialogue: Quoting on-the-spot conversations enhances
the authenticity of your feature. Always be alert for impactful quotes during interviews.
- Features are Longer than News Stories: Features provide more in-
depth content and are typically longer than news articles--ranging from 1,000-2,000 words.
- Use Pictures: A feature is incomplete without relevant images. Photos
add visual appeal and attract readers to your content.
- Look Ahead: Plan features for upcoming events and holidays. Gather
materials in advance to stay prepared for timely, relevant articles.
2.3.2 Characteristics of Feature
Basically, you want to write a feature that will: (1) be accepted right away by the periodical's features editor; (2) be well-received by readers; and (3) result in requests for additional features. So, how would you go about penning a feature of that kind? Alternatively, to be more specific, what qualities would you want to see in any feature that you worked on, whether it was about ladies, sports, cultural events, or anything else? * Sincerity Firstly, no matter what topic you choose, you must be sincere. By sincere mean that your approach must be free from pretence or deceit. Let us clarify: you must yourself know what you wish to say, and you must be able to assess your own work to see if you have succeeded in putting your message across all dimensions. * Social Objectives Why are you writing, apart from your personal interest in the topic, is a consideration to be kept in in mind all along. Generally, newspapers and other periodicals are expected to be balanced in their approach to social

Feature Writing issues. Some of the issues that could be tackled profitably are women's issues, traditions and change, religion and ritual, education, medicare, social and preventive medicare, diet and sutrition-anything in fact, that pertains to society. * Informative and educative Any feature that is submitted for publication must have some element of information in it. The information must not be pointless either-how many hairs are there on the human head, how many stars can be seen by the naked eye, of how many angels can dance on the tip of a needle. Books like Ripleys Believe it or not or The Guinness Book of World Records are very popular. However, have you ever wondered why? * Clarity What is clarity? If you are clear in your own thinking, you can attain clarity. It goes without saying that you cannot possibly know everything there is to know about a subject, but you still need to be able to define it precisely. Consider the meaning of "civil liberty" as described in the previous two paragraphs. Would you not anticipate learning what to write about if you were to write a piece on civil rights? * The personal touch While education and information are desirable in any feature, anyone can obtain these by visiting a Library. So what would enable the feature to be readable? The personal touch and the human element are what elevate any piece of writing from a mere factual story to a feature. A festival will tell the story of Thanan's hardship instead of the nation's employment situation. It should still be huyen angle even if it is subordinate to the feature's current ita farnaal account of documentation. Examine these excerpts from an article about a well-known actress who is currently experiencing severe anxiety. * Authenticity For any wriner, authenticity should comprise authenticity of facts, authenticity of emotions and authenticity of expression. It cannot be emphasised enough that you and your publisher bear all responsibility for any errors made after a piece is published. 2.4 NEWS AND FEATURE
It is possible that you already know what "news" is and how it is written: A news report must adhere to the textbook discipline of being objective, topical, fresh, and limited to the essential facts--that is, it must fit into a straitjacket frame with five Ws and one H. However, a feature story is not always written in such an exacting way. You are aware that news stories must be written by a certain date in order for them to remain valid. On the other hand, a feature story can be written in a relatively easy, relaxed timeframe. Although it may not always be possible or required, there is plenty of room to include several points of view in a feature. On the other hand, a news report is typically formatted in the pyramid style, which presents the data in an organised fashion from top to bottom. News articles are written in an impersonal style, frequently excluding the reporter's point of view from the main body of the piece. Quotes must be written inside inverted commas ("") and attributed to the primary sources, who are important individuals present whose opinions are significant and added to the story's facts. News articles need to be succinct, precise, snappy, and packed with as much information as possible into the fewest possible words in order to save both the reader's time and scarce newspaper space. However, a feature needs to have a lot more facts, be written in elegant prose with lots of "blossoms and blooms," be visually appealing, and create a lasting effect on the reader in order to be read and hold the reader's attention for longer. Ultimately, because newspapers and magazines serve a variety of purposes and interest groups, the subjects that work well for their respective features will also necessarily need to be diverse. Newspapers, for instance, seldom ever follow the same path as magazines, even though many of them do specialise in topics like human interest stories, contentious national and international concerns, social, cultural, religious, and political issues, and so forth.

2.5 FEATURE AND OTHER JOURNALISTIC
WRITING
Writing features for newspapers and magazines differs greatly, as we have already shown. Features are also different from those of other journalistic writing styles. Although there are not many strict guidelines for classifying or categorising these journalistic pieces, each daily has its own distinct genre. Regardless of the context, a feature story is not classified as hard news, a review, a column, an essay, an editorial, a filler, or an advertorial. In spite of this, there are a lot of global similarities in the editorial contents of newspapers. For instance, editorial and opinion pages are frequently featured in newspapers; these news sections are categorised as district/local, regional/state, national/news from the capital, and international/foreign/ global. Competitive sports, like the World, Asian, African, Twenty-Twenty, Commonwealth, and so on; sports/specific sports: IPL, ICL, hockey, football, cricket, kabbadi, kho-kho, wrestling, athletics, tennis, badminton, table tennis, shooting, swimming championships, etc. Additional editorial content sections cover topics such as business and economy, commodities, bullion rates, real estate, and local, national, and international stock exchanges. These days, entertainment is a major component of any newspaper's content. Review pages for films, CDs, television shows, music, theatre, radio, books, and other media are frequently found. Then there are sections about cars, gardening, public complaints, comic strips, cartoons, restaurants, lodging, food and recipes, wines and drinks, clothing for women and men, and shoes for all ages. Opinion, commentary, views, interviews, news analysis, backgrounders, rejoinders, obituaries, and so forth are typically included in the editorial and 34 op-ed pages. Additionally, some newspapers publish lengthy articles on

certain religions, such as commentary from the Bible, Quran, Mahabharata, News and Feature Bhagwad Gita, and other sacred texts, that are particularly commissioned. It should be noted, nevertheless, that although while none of these literary genres are strictly speaking journalistic, they have all been published regularly and have therefore assimilated into the majority of newspapers' regular editorial material.

2.7 LET US SUM UP
This unit explores the key differences between news and feature writing, starting with defining news as timely, factual, and often surprising information that captivates readers. It highlights essential elements of news writing, such as timeliness, proximity, prominence, and the inverted pyramid structure, which organizes information from most to least important. Feature writing, in contrast, goes deeper into topics, often using storytelling and

Feature Writing personal touches to engage readers emotionally. While news focuses on objectivity and concise reporting, features are more flexible, descriptive, and creative, allowing writers to explore subjects in greater depth, often using interviews, vivid descriptions, and narrative techniques.
2.8 KEYWORDS
* Timeliness: Reporting or writing about something when it is most relevant. * Inverted Pyramid: A writing style where the most important information comes first. * Objectivity: Writing without personal bias or opinions. * Storytelling: Presenting information through a narrative or story format. * Descriptive Writing: Using vivid details to create clear mental images. * Emotional: Writing that connects with the reader's feelings. * Engagement: Keeping the audience interested and involved.

3.2 DIFFERENT TYPES OF FEATURES
There is hardly a subject on which a feature cannot be written. A boy trying to cross a busy street, a cat wanting to catch an elusive rat, a nurse at work ir, a hospital, a vegetable vendor in your street, men and women practising unusual professions, personal accounts of travel, reminiscences of tlie past - in fact, any subject can be turned into a feature. A feature has no specific length. It can be as short as four paragraphs or as long as 40 paragraphs. The list of different types of features are given below:
3.2.1 Historical Feature
A historical feature explores significant events, eras, or figures from the past, offering readers a deeper understanding of history with contemporary relevance or newly uncovered facts. It often includes archival research and expert insights. Example: "Remembering the Revolt of 1857: India's First War of Independence" In 1857, India witnessed a pivotal uprising against British colonial rule, marking a watershed moment in its fight for freedom. The revolt, triggered by political and religious grievances, united soldiers and civilians in a widespread rebellion that would forever shape the subcontinent's destiny. Historians today reflect on its legacy and the ways it continues to influence Indian society.
3.2.2 Human Interest Feature
A human interest feature focuses on individuals and their personal stories, often evoking empathy and emotional connection. It highlights unique or inspiring lives, struggles, or achievements. Example:
"The Street Vendor Who Sent His Daughter to Harvard"
Under the shade of a busy Delhi marketplace, Raj Kumar's fruit cart draws crowds. But few know that, through sheer determination and savings, this humble vendor funded his daughter's dream to study at Harvard. Today, as Priya steps into the prestigious halls of academia, their story of sacrifice and resilience reminds us of the power of education and ambition.

3.2.3 Personal Narrative Feature Types of Feature
A personal narrative feature is written in the first person, where the writer shares a personal experience or reflection. It offers insights into the writer's life while connecting with universal emotions and themes. Example:
"My Journey Through the Pandemic: A Nurse's Story"
When the COVID-19 pandemic hit, I was thrown into chaos, working night shifts in an overwhelmed ICU. Those months blurred into each other, as we fought to save lives and dealt with loss daily. But amid the fear, there were moments of hope--the patient who recovered after 45 days, the colleagues who became family. This is my story of survival, resilience, and the human spirit.
3.2.4 Travel Sketches
Travel sketches feature the writer's experience of visiting different places, capturing the atmosphere, culture, and personal insights gained during the journey. They are often descriptive and engage the reader's senses. Example: "A Serene Morning in Varanasi" As dawn broke over the sacred Ganges, the ghats of Varanasi came alive in hues of orange and gold. Priests chanted as worshippers dipped into the holy waters. I found myself mesmerized by the chaotic serenity--ancient temples stood tall amidst bustling markets, and the air was filled with incense and life. This city, where life and death intertwine, left an indelible mark on my soul.
3.2.5 Science Feature
A science feature explains complex scientific concepts, discoveries, or innovations in an accessible way, often connecting them to real-world implications or human interest angles. Example:
"The Future of AI: Revolutionizing Healthcare"
Artificial intelligence is not just reshaping industries, it's transforming healthcare as we know it. From predictive diagnostics to robot-assisted surgeries, AI is empowering doctors with unprecedented precision and efficiency. In a hospital in Bangalore, doctors are using an AI algorithm that predicts patient complications days in advance, potentially saving thousands of lives. This breakthrough technology could be the key to a healthier future.

3.3 ELEMENTS OF SPECIALISED FEATURES
Writing specialised features is a different kind of art and craft than writing news articles. While some people are gifted with exceptional writing abilities, others gain the requisite abilities and instruction, writing a solid feature requires thorough research and gathering relevant content, whether you are a regular reporter or a freelance writer. Research is needed for a freelance submission in order to create an effective pitch for an editor. To develop a compelling premise, an assigned work needs pertinent background information. Every feature starts with an introduction that has an attention-grabbing, captivating lead. The next three paragraphs, which, for a mid-length piece, consist mostly of information and figures, are the feature's body. The final paragraph summaries and wraps up the earlier paragraphs. Given that the audience of today has a limited attention span, the lead yura is vital. It is often discouraged to include a question or lead in the opening paragraph since you do not want the reader to become distracted by it. It would be ideal if there was a humanising factor that the reader could easily relate to before reading your arguments. A spectacular example or situation would also serve as a hook. An appropriate quotation from a reputable authority would pique the reader's curiosity. Once the reader is engaged, the next four seconds should be spent enticing him or her to continue reading the article. The author ought to try crafting a purely economic element; pertinent data give the middle paragraphs weight and authority. When writing about air pollution, for instance, statistics showing the rise in respiratory disease cases make for interesting reading and strengthen the argument when connected to instances of unusual human suffering.

The concluding paragraph should not introduce any new ideas, but should Types of Feature conclusively prove the writer's point. Cliches like "in conclusion or "finally", are best avoided. The words should he effective enough to linger in the reader's mind. Therefore, whatever you are writing, check for sentence structure, spellings, word choice and veracity of facts. In the subsequent sections, we shall discuss the focus and specifie requirements of different types of specialised features.
3.4 SPECIALISED PROFILE FEATURES
The choice of a subject for a specialised profile piece is of vital importance. For example, the person chosen for the specialised profile feature must have impressive and high credentials, stature and reputation that will excite the reader's attention and interest. Failing which the piece is likely to be ignored. In case, for example, of a specialised sports feature, just being a talented sportsman is not enough; a profile-worthy sportsperson must have won a major championship gold in national or internationals. It is also advisable to find a person wholes not already been profiled by others in the recent times. The best thing for the author would be to look for new and upcoming sports stars A specialised sports profile piece written in third person usually runs between 500 and 1,000 words and is most often on a living person. It is usually based on information gathered in an interview, a face-to-face encounter is preferable, but sometimes e-mail questions can be supplemented with a telephonic conversation. It is also a good idea to interview a few close associates of the profiled person; quotable quotes and facts thus gathered add depth to the article. In-depth research is an essential requisite before the interview happens. Do not frame questions which display your ignorance about the information in public domain available at the click of a mouse. If the subject maintains a blog or has published something, it is best to scroll through them to gain an insight into his/her thought process.
3.5 SPECIALISED ECONOMIC FEATURES
When writing on specialist economic feature of any kind, a writer must give themselves enough time to conduct the analysis needed to understand numerical data in order to write about any topic related to financial trends or economic issues. To produce a concise, convincing conclusion, such data from the samples must be compiled over time. A specialised economic feature follows the format of a traditional feature writing style, i.e., it has a beginning, middle and conclusion. The writer must spend sufficient time to research the premise she is examining or trying to prove. The beginning or intro is usually limited to a paragraph or two. The concluding section of the introduction ends with a preview of the sections to come.

Feature Writing Specialised economic features are not restricted for use in economic journals only. To make such pieces readily acceptable would need an attractive hook to humanise the intro by quoting the example of a particular, but representative individual. For example, Joe, the Plumber, asking President Obama about taxation finally expounded into a theory on redistribution of wealth. Typically, economists and citations to their validated research can also be used to support the thesis statement in the opening paragraph; nonetheless, the article's body should consist of statistical information. These could be line graphs, scatter diagrams, pictograms, etc. that the reader needs to understand. The choice of base-line numbers, which varies depending on the year chosen, is essential for appropriate interpretation.
3.6 SPECIALISED LITERARY FEATURES
Literary features take up a portion of the weekend supplement space in most daily periodicals. Sadly, the amount of information on the books page, which features reviews of both fiction and non-fiction books, has been decreasing. Book reviews now average between 1,000 and 1,200 words, compared to their former 2,000 word limit. Of course, reviews are longer in periodicals that are devoted to the best literary works, like Biblio (the now-defunct Book Review) and The Times Literary Supplement. To gain insight into writing literary reviews, one could peruse past issues of journals, as well as weekend editions of Outlook, Open magazines, and reputable daily newspapers like The Tribune, The Hindu, and The Telegraph. A book reviewer needs to be a voracious reader with the ability to discuss narrative, story, character development, and literary expression in an informed and engaging manner. When writing a review, it is crucial to take into account factors like the comprehension of fiction plots and whether the narrative accurately depicts a certain period and location in human evolution. The author-interview is another genre of literary writing which explores the path of what inspires an author, his/her influences, life interests and experiences, Writing such pieces would require familiarity with author's works. For instance, the spin on popular vs. literary fiction could look at the books of an author whose stories, despite less than literary expression, are very readable and relatable and connect with a section of readers. The themes lend themselves to adaptation on the screen as they follow a very simple story line leading to its popularity.
3.7 NEW TRENDS
3.7.1 Growth in Science Feature
A feature is basically a story written in an interesting manner. Every story, whether straight news or feature, must answer the five Ws-Who? What? Where? When? and How? However, the approach to writing a. news story and a feature is different. For a news story, there is a set format. The writer relies on the inverted pyramid or the logical order, which means that the lead 42 will contain the most important aspect of the story and each subsequent

paragraph will give details in the descending order of the importance. Of Types of Feature course, the writer will have to weave the story with connectives and background material so that the presentation of the news story is not a clumsy string of paragraphs which have little link. Familiarity with news writing is very important for feature writing, because, to a certain degree, the feature writer will have to use this format in complex feature stories. However, unlike the news story, the feature story has no set of rules for leads or for the body or the end of the story. What matters is the presentation in an interesting format. Features may be narrative, descriptive or expository. They may tell stories, paint pictures, explain conditions. A feature is an imaginative piece of writing that tends to touch a reader's curiosity, amaze him, arouse his skepticism, or even make him laugh or cry. It can be dramatic, emotional or sensational, but all the time rooted in fact, not fiction. A scientific feature is a story which informs the reader, in an interesting way, about the advancement of science. It could touch on the plight of patients (AIDS, Kidney) or be on research being done on superconductors or even about a new missile project. Other stories could be on the benefits that have accrued to medical sciences by the use of modem technologies. People could be informed about the lithotripsy which can break the stones in the body by sonic vibrations so that major operations are no longer required to remove stones from the Gall Bladder or the Kidneys or Urinary Bladder. Or they could be informed on the usefulness of taking Aspirin tablets in preventing heart attacks. Many educated people wish to learn more about diseases that might have affected them or their relatives but unfortunately no competent doctor appears to have the time to sit with them to exp!ain how the disease is caused, what is going to be done, what are the chances of cure and any steps that the patients or their relatives can take to prevent further aggravation of the disease process. In today's digital age, the landscape of online journalism is shaping new trends in feature writing, including scientific features. With the vast reach of the internet, there is a growing demand for engaging and accessible science journalism that caters to diverse audiences. Writers are now utilizing multimedia elements, such as videos, infographics, and interactive content, to make complex scientific information easier to digest. The immediacy and share ability of online platforms also mean that science features can reach a global audience quickly, creating a ripple effect of knowledge dissemination. For instance, a recent science feature could delve into the exploration of CRISPR technology and its potential to revolutionize gene editing. The feature might begin by telling the story of a child born with a rare genetic disorder and how research in gene editing offers hope for a future cure. Through interviews with scientists and patients, the article could explore the ethical questions surrounding this technology while explaining its scientific basis in simple terms. This kind of feature would not only inform readers but also engage them emotionally and intellectually.

Feature Writing 3.7.2 Multimedia-Integrated Features
The intensifying rivalry among diverse media platforms has prompted innovation and adjustment to stay current. In particular, e-papers rely significantly on print circulation, and the survival of newspapers is critical to their own. The most recent developments in the digital sphere have been used by e-Papers in order to remain competitive and draw readers. Nowadays, content-sharing websites and cross-media devices are used to view a sizable portion of e-Paper articles. Here are a few instances of how e-Papers are changing to remain relevant in the wider media environment. Customised e-Paper The rivalry for creating and delivering content has increased due to the segmentation of viewers. Readers search for content that are unique to their interests in the fast-paced world of today. As a result, media content that is personalised and catered to individual tastes has increased. The development of e-newsletters, which were eventually supplanted by personalised e-Papers, was a significant advancement in this industry. Readers subscribe according to their areas of interest to receive access to these customised editions, and the e-Paper is sent by email. It has sections with headlines, synopses, images, and connections to in-depth articles about business, sports, entertainment, and academic subjects. Customised e-Papers save time while ensuring readers stay informed on subjects they care about. R.G. Picard, in 'Changing Business Models of Online Content Services' (2000), predicted a future where readers would pay for tailored news and additional information services, a model that is now commonplace.
Smartphone Enabled
At first, e-Papers were meant to be used with desktop or laptop computers, but when more devices became available, media companies had to deal with the issue of platform compatibility. Smartphones are now the primary device used to consume content, including e-Papers. Media businesses are now optimising their digital content for mobile devices as a result of this trend. Despite facing resource constraints, small and medium-sized newspapers have managed to make their e-Papers accessible on mobile devices, albeit with differing levels of user experience.
