Impact on Feature Writing Types of Feature
The shift towards digital platforms, mobile compatibility, and social media integration has also significantly impacted feature writing. Features are now more interactive and accessible, reaching a wider audience through social sharing and customization. Writers can craft stories that not only inform but also engage readers across various devices, adapting to the fast-paced consumption habits of the digital age. As a result, features have become more dynamic, with increased reader interaction and personalization, allowing them to maintain relevance in the evolving media landscape.
3.7.3 Data-Driven Features
Data journalism is the "application of data science to journalism, where data science is defined as the study of the extraction of knowledge from data," according to a report by the Tow Centre for Digital Journalism. To put it briefly, data journalism involves telling stories, examining social and political processes through numbers, and uncovering patterns or tales within numbers. Computerisation, new and developing technologies, digital storage devices, and the ease with which large volumes of data may be shared via the Internet and various public domains have all contributed to the use of massive amounts of data. In recent years, the context and breadth of data journalism have expanded due to the explosion of data generated by different sectors, including government, academia, industry, wider society, individual individuals, social media, and the research community. It is evident that data journalists frequently gather, clean, and publish data for interactive features, mobile apps, and digital maps using open-source software and free, robust web tools. Data journalists have benefited from the easy and flexible access to freely available, open-source data. In contrast to earlier times when poor nations struggled to keep up with global trends, data journalism is now widely acknowledged, even in India. The increasing availability of data has paved the way for a new trend in feature writing: data-driven journalism. In these features, writers leverage large sets of data to uncover trends, provide in-depth analysis, and support their narratives with empirical evidence. Data-driven features go beyond anecdotal reporting, using visualizations like charts, graphs, and infographics to simplify complex information and make it accessible to readers. This method is particularly impactful in stories related to economics, healthcare, or social issues, where numbers and patterns offer deeper insights. With data- backed storytelling, readers gain a more comprehensive understanding of the subject, enhancing the feature's credibility and persuasive power. This approach is not only factually grounded but also appeals to readers who value objective, evidence-based journalism.

Treatment This unit will introduce you to feature writing style and how to execute them At the end of this unit you should be able to: * Identify what are the different parts of the feature. * Select a suitable topic for feature writing. * Find sources for writing your feature. * Understand how to write a feature. * Understand the editing process involved post writing.
4.2 COMPONENTS OF FEATURE
Any feature, irrespective of whether you are writing on a social topic, a cultural topic, a sports topic or even an economic feature has the following parts :
1) Content
2) Structure or method of organisation
3) Language and style
You must pay close attention to all these parts if you are to succeed as a feature writer and make both money and a name for yourself. After all, you may write initially for love but you would certainly be interested in becoming well-known so that you get more chances of writing features and, thus, are able to make it a profitable pursuit.
4.2.1 Content
A feature's contents are all that it displays or says. In contrast to form or style, the subject matter and ideas contained in a piece of writing make up its content. We will discuss here the components of the feature article in relation to its topic. Just starting to write the initial draft of the feature is one method to do it. Consider it as sharing your idea with your closest friend. The benefit of starting with a first draft is that you may focus on content and style without worrying about language usage. Simply jot down anything comes to mind, being sure to include whatever you believe to be important. It is preferable if you have ten times more information than you require. You will be shocked to learn that this raw expression of your opinions, convictions, etc., frequently results in a first draft that is adequate. It will include all of the knowledge you possess and all of your deeply held beliefs. However, not everyone will benefit from this approach. Using reference cards for more enduring records is an additional way to see your feature data. Take notes on various topics on separate pieces of paper. Make a single, major point on every reference card. Then put them in a sensible arrangement, and you will notice that your feature covers more ground.

Feature Writing 4.2.2 Structure Structuring a feature article involves organising your content to ensure clarity and engagement. Begin by focusing on the main message you want to convey. Ensure that the article maintains a consistent theme without unnecessary shifts in focus. Consider whether you've used the right amount of statistics and if rearranging sections could enhance the flow. Experiment with different narrative voices to improve readability. Balance vivid descriptions with factual information, and conclude with a crisp, impactful ending. A strong conclusion should tie back to your introduction, offering new insights while reinforcing the article's central idea.
4.2.3 Language and Style
Even though you could be writing for a lay audience, you should not feel free to use informal language. To produce such an impact, even a piece that appears to be a conversational account of events is meticulously written; this effect is not obtained by the use of slang, informal expressions, or patronising statements such as "Good luck to poor you." Although language and style will be covered later (4.7), we want to emphasise now how crucial it is to select the right language and style for your feature. When writing a feature, consider the seriousness of the subject matter, the type of publication, the target reader's background, and your own purpose--whether it is to reveal, investigate, suggest remedies, evoke emotions, or create sensationalism-- while being clear and honest about your intent. 4.3 HOW TO SELECT A TOPIC
In choosing a topic for a feature that you wish to write, what are the factors 50 you should take into consideration? Three are immediately obvious :

* Area of (your) interest and expertise Subjects and Their Treatment * Principles of Feature Writing policy of publication * Relevance for reader Apart from these three, which we shall discuss in this section, you should actively read the magazines that are currently on the news-stands. By reading actively, we mean that you should take up a paper and pencil and make a list of topics that are covered repeatedly in (i) various issues of the same magazine (2) concurrent issues of different magazines. You would not really be wasting your time if you first wrote, enclosing a stamped, self addressed envelope, (called an "Sae") and asked the editor whether he/she would be interested in a feature on sports, cultural round-up, an unusual personality and so on. You could specify the length, the nature and number of illustrations and approximately when would be the appropriate time of the feature to be published (Diwali, New Year, Holi and so on). This would help you in two ways:
1) You would save effort, time (and stationery) and heartbreak in case the
reply is negative- we do not accept unsolicited articles" for example.
2) You would not need to wait for a reply from one editor before sending
your feature to another. You could simply prepare several such letters and send them to the editors. Once you get a positive reply you can send your article, duly typed. One side only, in double-space, leaving at least 1.5 inch margins on all sides, to the editor of the publication.
4.3.1 Area of Interest and Expertise
It is possible that you have chosen a topic that interests you or that you think the magazine and readers would find interesting. You may have made this solely based on your own subjective and emotional judgement. But it is important to approach this choice practically. Do you possess the requisite knowledge in the field? For example, you may have noticed that environmental and pollution issues are of great interest to individuals. All of the magazines you have looked at regularly feature articles on different facets of pollution and environmental damage. But could you talk about the relevant statistics? In addition to being observed, the consequences of different types of pollution, control measures, and pollution levels all need to be analysed and workable solutions need to be identified. This is not to suggest that you should simply give it up. There are various ways of acquiring the expertise and collecting the materials in order to write such an article. 4.3.2 Policy of Publication
The real thing to keep in mind is the policy of the publication that you would like to get your feature published in. In fact, this should be looked at even before you start working on your Feature. A policy, by definition is "a general set of ideas or plans that has been officially greed upon by people in authority, and which is used as a basis for making decisions, especially in politics, economics or business." A policy could cover areas that must not be discussed (politics in a magazine dealing with travel and tourism for example), what the political leanings of the publishers/editors on leftist, rightist, pro or anti-Government), the kind of print used, the size and number of illustrations (photographs, charts, graphs), the colours to be used, the frequency of appearance, size of rages, ratio of advertisement to reading matter, payment-some pay on acceptance, some on publication, some when they are repeatedly reminded (!) and some do not pay but give you free copies of the issue in which your feature appeared.
4.3.3 Relevance for the Reader
After reading your target publication, you can usually determine who reads it by looking at the subjects that are covered. Readership is influenced by editorial policies, but it also depends on readers' tastes and spending capacity. Editors may choose to include pieces on subjects like astrology or films if people consistently request them. For instance, when targeting housewives, editors need to take into account their financial situation and areas of interest. Activity - 2 Choose any publication you follow and look for a list of features published in it. Then, one by one, list the target audience for each stated feature. This practice will improve your ability to understand and select appropriate themes for writing your own article.

4.4 SOURCES
While making your article readable and entertaining is important, remember that the key to selling a manuscript is authoritative information. This requires a planned, systematic approach and hard work. You might choose your article's theme from an emotive situation, such as an accident or a polluted city, but you will need to report on what you observed and suggest remedies or explore the meaning of the events. To gather the necessary authoritative information, you should systematically collect material and maintain a file as previously suggested. What are the ways in which you can collect facts for the "authoritative information" you need?
4.4.1 Reference and Research Libraries
Visit any good library that is relevant to your needs. Various sources, such as libraries, can provide valuable information in specialised subjects. A British Council Library or American Centre can provide information on printed books, author addresses, journal and magazine material, and up-to-date book collections. Libraries will also advise you about other sources you can tap for more information. You can also consult reference librarian for further information. You will find yourself, then doing three or four different kinds of research. * Primary research-facts that you find out for yourself, not relying on printed statistics. * Scientific research-scientific because you will be making hypotheses and finding validation before you commit yourself to any statistics

Feature Writing * Interdisciplinary research -even if your article deals with sports, you might end with looking at the economics of sports facilities or the cultural reasons for certain states doing well at certain sports. Familiarise yourself with reference books accessible in different fields to avoid searching for material that is already organised in the correct book. You can read Magazine Article Writing by Betsy P. Graham (Holt, Rinehart and Winston, c. 1980) (pg. 42 onwards) for an idea of what we mean.
4.4.2 Collection of Relevant Facts and Material
Depending on the feature you're writing, you'll need to gather relevant facts and materials. This effort is valuable because (1) it ensures your final article is reliable and authoritative, making it more marketable, and (2) unused material can be useful for future articles. The key is relevance. When you start collecting materials, it can become addictive, making it hard to leave out even slightly related information. You may end up gathering more facts and figures than necessary, realising later that you have collected too much material for your feature. What are some of the ways in which relevant facts and materials can be collected? Talking to the people about whom you intend to write, to others who have known them first or second-hand, making phone calls and writing letters, visiting the setting of an incident or trekking to the place you are writing about- all these methods will have to be adopted at one time or the other, depending on your particular area of interest.
4.4.3 Photos
Using illustrations or photographs is beneficial for three reasons: it reinforces your message, allows for interpretation and analysis, and creates reader interest by breaking up the monotony of print. Although it is recommended to provide your own images, editors typically determine the size, placement, and type of illustrations required for your piece. Financial considerations often drive the decision to use or not use drawings. Your feature is your copyright, therefore if you believe certain graphics are essential to your story, explain why. Usually, you can reach an understanding about the topic. Activity - 3 What are the cautions one should keep in mind while using photographs for feature?

4.4.4 Interviews Subjects and Their
Treatment Interviews are a well-established fact-collection method. While library research and reading articles provide general background on a topic, interviews provide more in-depth information. Readers want to hear directly from the achiever, including their likes and dislikes, training methods, and thoughts. Interviewing must be "studied, prepared for and practised". Some people, ofcourse, are more successful at getting interviewees to answer questions but basically, interviewing is a skill that can be acquired, with patience and dedication. To plan an interview effectively, begin by determining its focus, publication details, timing, length, and target reader's interests. Research the interviewee to ask relevant questions, prepare a questionnaire, and schedule an appointment while being punctual. Carry essential tools like a notebook, pens, and a tape recorder for potentially controversial topics. For non-simple profiles, get the interviewee to review your work. If the interviewee insists on manuscript changes, either politely decline or allow them to check for blatant errors without drastic revisions.
4.4.5 Other Sources
Apart from research and reference libraries, and interviews or personal visits, you can find materials for your feature from a number of other sources. You might discover that dictionaries that explain and interpret words often give you a new perspective on an issue. For example, what do society, libel, issues, profile mean? You can often find information not available through primary, first-hand, sources in secondary references. Let us explain: Suppose you are doing a feature on crimes against women. You have looked up recent newspaper reports, talked to social- service organisations and social workers, visited some victims. But still, in order to broad-base your article, to give it a greater depth and make it of more universal appeal what dose could you do? Look up books on "Status of women in South-East Asia" or "Third-world Issues" or similar titles. You should almost immediately find a quotable quote, a final conclusion by an authority on the subject etc. Obviously, it will not be possible or even practical for us to list all the possible sources from which you can obtain information. However, if you are to write more features, you should constantly be on the lookout for related material and keep your clippings-file up-to-date. You will then not need to do too much of last-minute cross- checking or background-information collection. Check Your Progress - 3 Note: 1) Use the space provided below for your Answers.

4.5 WRITING
At last, you will need to write your feature. You should plan to write multiple drafts of your feature. If it makes you feel better, start with an outline. By outline, we mean that you should be able to write out (1) the basic idea of your feature, (2) how you offered to begin, (3) what goes in the major body of text, (4) how you propose to end, and (5) a one-line description of your goals and final conclusion. Let us explain this by taking a concrete example. You have visited a place of great scenic beauty during your holidays. You have made interesting purchases and generally had an enjoyable stay. Now you wish to write a travel feature on it so that others too can benefit from your experience.
4.5.1 Beginning
The beginning of a feature is crucial, as we previously discussed the significance of an engaging title. To continue the discussion, consider: When you begin to write an article, or any piece of prose for that matter, you must make a point-a thesis. The thesis means the point of the feature. Apart from the thesis is the topic the subject which you propose to write about. These two must be very clear in your mind when you structure the beginning of your feature.
Feature Example: Exploring Local Artisans in Varanasi
Thesis Statement: Discover the vibrant world of Varanasi's local artisans, where traditional craftsmanship and contemporary creativity blend to offer unique, handmade treasures. In the bustling streets of Varanasi, the ancient art of weaving and pottery thrives amidst the city's historic temples and lively markets. This feature delves into the lives of the skilled artisans who keep these age-old traditions alive, showcasing their intricate work and the rich cultural heritage of India. You would focus on a subject, a topic and formulate a thesis. These three, while they may not be explicitly referred to in the beginning, must form an integral part of it. The beginning is also caused the lead-a lead is an attention- getting device-because competition for readership is so much, you must immediately catch and hold the reader's attention.

Example: Subjects and Their
Treatment Standing in her small studio in Mumbai, Rhea Kapoor surveys her latest collection - dresses made from recycled ocean plastic, pants crafted from sustainably sourced bamboo, and accessories woven from organic cotton. "I want people to know that fashion can be beautiful without harming the planet," she says with a determined smile. This lead introduces the subject - eco-friendly fashion - and introduces a designer whose work embodies the topic. It hooks the reader with a vivid scene and personalises the abstract concept of sustainable fashion through an individual's story. Activity - 4 Your target is the eighteen year old traveller-assume she has never visited Varanasi. In 30 words, provide an interesting beginning to an article on Varanasi (or any other town that is both a place of pilgrimage and of tourist interest. Remember your target reader) The beginning of your feature must: * capture your reader's attention and tempt her/him to read on * impress upon your reader the importance of your feature so that he wants to read further * set the tone for the rest of the feature (serious, informative, humorous, investigative and so on).
4.5.2 Middle
Proceed with your feature, keeping in mind your opening remarks. Present all of the knowledge you have gained, all of your reasons for why attitudes towards certain things need to change, etc. Show, talk about, and enlighten. Consider the following example: "Eco-friendly fashion has gained significant momentum over the past decade, driven by growing environmental concerns and consumer demand for sustainable products. According to a report by the Ellen MacArthur Foundation, the fashion industry is responsible for 10% of global carbon emissions, more than international flights and maritime shipping combined. However, a new wave of designers like Kapoor is working to change that. From using biodegradable materials to promoting slow fashion - the opposite of fast fashion's high- turnover, low-quality model - these innovators are leading a

Feature Writing movement towards a more sustainable future. But creating eco-friendly fashion isn't without its challenges. "Sourcing sustainable fabrics can be expensive, and educating consumers about the true cost of clothing is a constant battle," says Kapoor. Despite this, the movement continues to grow, with major brands like Patagonia and Stella McCartney paving the way for a greener industry." In the middle section, we delve into the "why" and "how" of eco-friendly fashion, exploring the trends, challenges, and impacts of the movement. It's packed with information, statistics, and expert perspectives, making the story informative and engaging.
4.5.3 End
The end, the conclusion, should give a summary of what you have been discussing. It should give pointers to the possible solution if not provide the solution itself. Often, there is no one possible solution to a problem but there is a point of view that you have been advocating and, within its framework, there would be a solution. Example: As Kapoor prepares for her upcoming show, she remains optimistic about the future of fashion. "Consumers are more conscious now than ever before. The future of fashion isn't just about trends, it's about sustainability, ethics, and responsibility," she says, her hands gently smoothing the fabric of a dress made from upcycled denim. "We all have a role to play in making the world a better place - and that includes the clothes we wear." Here, the story concludes by bringing the focus back to Kapoor, tying the end to the beginning, while leaving readers with a hopeful and thought-provoking message. The conclusion reinforces the importance of sustainability and invites the reader to consider their own role in the movement. Key Points: * Beginning (Hook the reader): Captures attention and sets the stage for the story. It introduces the topic or a central figure to draw the reader in. * Middle (Explore the topic): Delivers the core content, providing background, context, and multiple viewpoints. This is where the story is fully developed with facts, statistics, quotes, and narrative. * End (Wrapping up with impact): Ties everything together, offering resolution or reflection. It should leave the reader with something memorable, be it a strong message or a call to action. Check Your Progress 4 Note: 1) Use the space provided below for your Answers.

4.6 EDITING
Editing is the scrutiny and selection of material and its orderly presentation. The editor selects content for relevance and readability. You must act as your own editor by examining and correcting your text. A professional editor, working for a publisher, selects materials and makes changes according to the publication's policy. As your own editor, review your feature objectively. You may find the need to revise or even rewrite parts of it. Revision is re-seeing the work, often achieved by stepping away and reviewing it with fresh eyes. The process includes several stages:
1) Look at the article as a whole.
2) Review the beginning, middle, and end.
3) Examine the structure, sentences, and words.
During revision, you will edit the material by asking:
1) Did you say what you intended to?
2) Is the article's organisation logical? Does the beginning flow to the end
smoothly?
3) Can you delete any part without affecting the whole?
4) Should you reorganise the article? Maybe introduce a question to engage
the reader.
5) Have you stuck to the point or included unnecessary material?
6) Are you using invented words or words that don't belong?
7) Are you showing rather than telling? Use examples to illustrate points.
Finally, share your feature with someone else for feedback, as a fresh perspective can be invaluable.

4.7 LET US SUM UP
Feature writing involves carefully crafting articles with attention to content, structure, and language. Content refers to the substance of the feature--what it displays or says. Writers should start with a draft to freely express ideas, then refine the content, ensuring it covers all necessary aspects. Structure is about organising the content logically, maintaining a consistent theme, and enhancing readability through appropriate use of statistics and narrative techniques. Language and style must match the seriousness of the subject and target audience, avoiding informal expressions and ensuring clarity and purpose. Selecting a topic involves assessing your area of interest and expertise, understanding the publication's policy, and ensuring the topic's relevance to the readers. Research is crucial for gathering authoritative information, and sources include libraries, interviews, and additional materials. Effective writing requires drafting and revising, focusing on a compelling beginning, informative middle, and impactful ending. Editing involves scrutinising the article for coherence, relevance, and clarity, ensuring the final piece is polished and ready for publication.
4.8 KEYWORDS
* Content: The information or material presented in a feature. * Structure: The way a feature is organized, including the introduction, body, and conclusion. * Language and Style: The tone, vocabulary, and writing techniques used in the feature.

* Topic Selection: Choosing a relevant and engaging subject for a feature. Subjects and Their Treatment * Research: Gathering information and facts to support the feature's content. * Interviews: Conversations with people to gather insights, quotes, or personal stories for the feature. * Editing: Reviewing and improving the draft for clarity, coherence, and correctness. * Revision: Making changes to the feature based on feedback or further reflection.

5.2 POLITICS
Politics is the discourse and struggle over the organization of human possibilities, centering on power and the capacity of agents and institutions to transform or maintain their environment. It involves the resources and forces that shape the exercise of power, cutting across private and public life, and influencing all aspects of human society. Politics shapes the development of collective problems and their resolutions. Politics is difficult to define precisely due to its varied uses and nuances, but it involves collective activity, reconciling differences through discussion and persuasion, and making authoritative decisions for a group. It is an inescapable feature of human life, as groups must make collective decisions. Aristotle viewed politics as essential, marking humans as political animals who express their nature through participation in a political community. Politics, therefore, involves finding common solutions to shared problems through public choice. People generally associate politics with the activities of politicians, often seen in the media, focused on power struggles and leadership. Politics is frequently defined as the rivalry for power among politicians or the relationships between states. Power is a relationship where one person can impose their will on others, leading to leadership, domination, and subordination. Max Weber, in his 1918 lecture "Politics as a Vocation," described politics as any independent leadership in action, highlighting that politics is not just about government but any context where power relations exist, including institutions and structures. Politics extends beyond government to areas like trade unions or "sexual politics," where power struggles and leadership contests occur. However, Weber also narrowed his definition to focus on politics as leadership or influence within a political association, specifically the state. In this view, political questions concern who controls state power, for what purposes, and with what consequences.
5.2.1 Politics and Humans
Hence, despite the fact that the word "politics" is sometimes applied cynically to disparage the pursuit of personal gain masquerading as the common good, politics is an unavoidable aspect of being human. In fact, 66 according to the Greek philosopher Aristotle, "man is by nature a political

animal." He intended to convey that political engagement is what most Politics - The Study
of State and Power
clearly sets humans apart from other animals, not merely that politics cannot be avoided but that it is the fundamental human activity. According to Aristotle, engaging in political society is the only way for individuals to fully express their inherent qualities as moral, thinking beings. Rarely do group members agree on the best course of action, at least not at first. Check Your Progress 1 Note: 1) Use the space provided below for your Answers.

5.3 WHAT IS STATE?
This raises a new question: what is state? There is not a consensus on the appropriate response, nor is the question in any way simple to answer. First, it is vital to recognise that the state exists in multiple forms, each of which is distinct in significant ways. The modern nation-state, which has dominated international politics since the French Revolution, is distinctly different from the Greek city-state. Unlike the fascist states of Hitler or Mussolini, the modern liberal-democratic states found in Britain and Western Europe are distinct from each other. Furthermore, it differs from the states that were present in Eastern Europe and the former USSR. An important part of the study of politics, and certainly an integral element of this book, is the explanation of what is meant by those terms. The purpose is to show how each form distinguishes itself from the other and what the significance of such distinction is

Political Reporting 5.3.1 State: Differences on Account of Political Institutions/
Social Context
States vary not only in the social context in which they are placed and which they strive to preserve, but also in the political institutions that they have. Therefore, the fascist state is ruled by the leader, whereas the liberal- democratic state is distinguished by representative institutions like a parliament and an independent court. In terms of the social context, the key difference between systems of the Soviet and Western types is that the former are integrated into a society that is structured around the ideas of a capitalist economy, while in the latter case the state owns and controls the productive resources of society. In each case, therefore, the state is differently structured, operates in a social framework of a very different kind, and this affects and influences to a large extent the nature of the state and the purposes, which it serves. The state can take on several shapes, but regardless of its exact shape, it does not exist as a single, cohesive entity. To start with, the state is not the same as the government. The government is but one of a complex of interconnected parts. In a liberal-democratic state modelled after the West, the people in power are the government. They assume office with the intention of controlling the levers of state power and speak in the name of the state. However, to adopt a different metaphor, the state owns numerous mansions, and the government resides in one of them.
5.3.2 Ralph Miliband's Views on the State
In 'The State in Capitalist Society', Ralph Miliband outlines key elements that make up the state. The government is the first element, but not the only one. The second is the administrative sector, or civil service, which in liberal democracies is supposed to be neutral but may hold its own power. Third are the military and police, the state's repressive arm, followed by the judiciary, which is intended to be independent to check government power. Local governments, the fifth element, can be politically significant, especially in federal systems with some autonomy from central government. Lastly, Miliband includes representative assemblies and parliaments, where political parties, though not officially part of the state, play a crucial role in enacting the government-opposition dynamic.
5.3.3 Various Forms of State
Modern state is identified as the nation state. The state has come to acquire its present character through a historical process that extends to thousands of years. It is interplay of various factors like religion, kinship, war, property, political consciousness and technological advances. In the process of historical evolution of state, there have been following forms - Tribal State, Oriental Empire, Greek City State, Roman World Empire, Feudal State and the Modern Nation State. The Modern Nation state arose after the Treaty of Westphalia was signed in 1648. It led to the emergence of a territorial state consolidating political authority within a particular territory excluding domestic from external. The separation of territory into distinct states each 68 with their own national spirit paved the way for establishment of Modern

Nation State along with the rise of international law, legal equality of states Politics - The Study
of State and Power
and modern theory of sovereignty. American and French revolutions further contributed to the emergence of nation states. The modern concept of state is dominated by Liberal and Marxist perspectives. The liberal perspective is dynamic as it has changed with time depending on interests and needs of individuals and society. The early liberal view of state was negative as it favored non-interference in individual matters. However, 20th century liberalism is associated with welfare state which tries to reconcile individual liberty with social good. The Marxist notion rejects liberal idea of state, calling the state as an instrument of class and seeks to establish a classless and stateless society through the proletarian revolution. However, that did not happen after the Russian revolution in Russia and instead of a classless and stateless society, we saw power getting concentrated in the hands of a few during Soviet times. Feminist perspectives on state can be mainly seen from two angles - liberal and radical. Liberal feminists say that the state can play a role in bringing equality among men and women by taking steps like increasing seats for women in parliament, extending welfare schemes to women etc. However, the radicals see the state as an instrument of power and blame unequal distribution of labor in a family for women's unequal status in society. Hence, they contest the liberal view that the state is impartial and neutral. Check Your Progress 2 Note: 1) Use the space provided below for your Answers.

5.4 MAX WEBER: POLITICS AS A VOCATION
In his lecture Politics as a Vocation, Max Weber emphasized that the state cannot be defined by its tasks or goals, but rather by its means--specifically, its use of physical force. He defined the state as a community that claims a monopoly on the legitimate use of force within a given territory. This definition includes control over territory, use of force to maintain control, and 69

Political Reporting the crucial legitimacy of that force, acknowledged by most of the population. For Weber, politics is about striving to share or influence the distribution of power, whether among states or within them. Weber also noted that modern states require complex bureaucracies and larger, more sophisticated armed forces and welfare agencies, which is true for both capitalist and socialist systems. This growth is marked by the emergence of skilled, efficient bureaucracies. Even Karl Marx, despite his differing ideology, recognized the growth of state power. However, Marx believed socialism would eventually abolish the state, allowing society to govern itself, whereas Weber argued that socialism would necessitate even more bureaucratic control. Understanding politics as a vocation offers journalists a framework for analysing political power struggles, state functions, and the complexities of governance. Weber's insights into the state's reliance on legitimate force and bureaucracy provide context for reporting on government actions, policies, and political dynamics, making it clear that politics is not just about the actions of politicians but also about the broader machinery that sustains power.
5.5 LEGITIMATE USE OF POWER
Even while the state uses force frequently, coercion is not the only thing that keeps it in power. All those in positions of authority attempt to persuade people under their control of the justice and righteousness of the authority they possess. The process of legitimation is this attempt at explanation to get people's agreement. The rightful use of power, in which individuals under authority acknowledge and accept it, is an essential component. Authority is distinguished from mere power that is used out of fear of punishment by this legitimacy. Individuals submit to lawful authority not only out of fear of punishment but also because they think it is right and just.
5.5.1 Max Weber on Legitimation
Max Weber identified three types of legitimation:
1. Traditional Domination: Power is justified by custom and habit, often
linked to family or historical continuity.
2. Charismatic Legitimation: Authority comes from the extraordinary
personal qualities of a leader, who inspires devotion and obedience.
3. Legal-Rational Authority: Power is exercised according to established
rules, emphasizing procedural legitimacy over personal appeal. This form aligns with modern political structures, where officials govern within defined legal boundaries. Weber's insights reveal that any political system benefits when its power is seen as legitimate, reducing the need for coercion and enhancing stability. The more people voluntarily accept authority, the less force is required to maintain order.

5.5.2 Legitimation: Central Concern of Political Science Politics - The Study
of State and Power
These are the explanations for why "the idea of legitimation is one of the core conceptions of political science," in the words of C. Wright Mills, The strategies used by those in positions of power to justify their authority and the degree to which they are successful are at the heart of the study of politics. Any study of a political system must look into the extent to which the public views the current power structures as legitimate, and consequently, the extent to which consent--as opposed to coercion--is the foundation of that structure. Historical instances, like Poland under Jaruzelski and South Africa during the apartheid era, demonstrate how unstable and prone to overthrow regimes that mostly rely on force are. When those in positions of authority are unable to uphold the consent of the people, a lack of broad legitimacy may result in revolutionary upheaval.
5.5.3 The Process of Delegitimation
This explains why a period of sustained questioning of the prevailing ideals of the system frequently precedes a revolution. This could be referred to as a "delegitimation" process in which the concepts that uphold the current power structure are contested. A contemporary example would be the demise of the Weimar Republic, when significant portions of the German people lost faith in the democratic government and sided with Hitler's National-Socialist party out of fear of a communist takeover. Similar causes had similar effects all over the European Continent. Many western systems of liberal democracy were overthrown and replaced by fascist or semi-fascist authoritarian systems as happened in Italy, Spain, Austria and Hungary. The conclusion, in a general sense, must be that any system loses its stability once it ceases to enjoy legitimacy in the eyes of its subjects. Finally, it must be noted that even in normal times, processes of legitimation and delegitimation are permanent features of any political system. The process of legitimation is carried on in more or less subtle ways through many channels available for the legitimation of the existing order. Legitimising ideas are absorbed from the earliest stages of education, diffused through a variety of forms of social interaction, and spread especially through the influence of the press, television and other mass media. Views, which are accepted or considered to be within the boundaries of the system, are almost forced on readers, listeners and viewers. Action, which goes beyond those limits, is presented as illegitimate. Being made to look very unattractive blocks off a range of political alternatives.
5.6 MANIPULATED CONSENT
Subversive thoughts can still be stopped before they even arise with more potent strategies. They could be intercepted at the point of origin, which is the both the conscious and subconscious minds. The ability to influence and shape people's consciousness to the point where they accept the current situation without ever considering other options is a crucial aspect of power. Thus, consent turns into coerced consent. We are all impacted by the current 71

Political Reporting "climate of opinion" to some degree. From there, an escalating scale leads to a point where the state intentionally manipulates people's thoughts in order to produce a homogenous popular mentality. This was the goal of the Nazi Germany propaganda apparatus led by Goebbels, and this is the goal of all totalitarian governments. According to C. Wright Mills, manipulation is "power wielded unknown to the powerless." "The methods by which awareness is controlled are of growing importance in modern culture," as Peter Worsley notes. Marxist terminology predicted that eventually, this kind of coerced assent would result in a "false consciousness." On the other hand, it could be countered that consciousness manipulation is impossible in environments where people have the freedom to express and make decisions, such as liberal-democratic regimes. Only in one-party systems, where there is no free will, is manipulation possible. Additionally, it is maintained that in cases when individuals possess the freedom of choice but fail to select an alternative to the status quo--for instance, by endorsing political parties advocating for drastic overhauls--it is reasonable to infer that the current social structure represents the general consensus on "what people desire." This would lead to the conclusion that one cannot overstate the significance of having the freedom to freely express one's political preferences. However, a number of things influence "what people want" to varying degrees. Making decisions does not happen in a vacuum. Put simply, the decision itself cannot be wholly isolated from the influence of a legitimation process. Check Your Progress 3 Note: 1) Use the space provided below for your Answers.

5.7 THE ELITE AND STATE Politics - The Study
of State and Power
Several important points arise from the study of political problems, particularly how state power is divided into different sectors, influenced by the political system. These sectors are not simply mechanical but staffed by individuals whose backgrounds shape their perspectives. The composition of the state elite is a critical issue, as illustrated by J.A.C. Griffith, who noted the elite nature of British judges and their consistent political outlook. Elitist theories emphasize the significance of the ruling elite in determining the nature of the political system, stressing that leadership quality is crucial. Max Weber, for example, believed strong political leadership was necessary to prevent control by the bureaucratic class, which he saw as unsuitable for innovative leadership. In contrast, Marxist theories downplay the role of the elite, arguing that the social and economic context in which the state operates is more important. Structural theories also emphasize the constraints imposed by the social framework on the government. Ultimately, the relationship between state and society is key: the state's power is influenced by societal structures, and theorists debate whether the state upholds or challenges social inequalities. The extent of state control over society, particularly in totalitarian regimes, is also a critical concern.
5.8 JOURNALISTIC WRITING AND POLITICAL
CONCEPTS
Journalism students can significantly enhance their education by studying politics and the state, as it equips them with crucial knowledge about power structures. Understanding how political power is structured and distributed enables students to analyze political events more critically. For instance, when covering elections or legislative changes, they can better contextualize the actions of political figures and institutions. This understanding not only enriches their reporting but also fosters balanced narratives. However, the challenge lies in maintaining objectivity while navigating the intricacies of political dynamics, as biases can easily seep into their writing. Another key area of learning is the identification of various political ideologies, such as liberalism, conservatism, and socialism. By grasping these ideologies, journalism students can provide insightful analysis when reporting on political actions and debates. This foundational knowledge allows them to differentiate between political viewpoints clearly, adding depth to their stories. Yet, students must remain vigilant about their own ideological biases, which can inadvertently influence their reporting. Moreover, students develop critical analysis skills through studying political news, allowing them to dissect political speeches, government policies, and electoral strategies. This analytical prowess not only enhances their credibility but also enables them to offer nuanced commentary on political developments. Understanding political communication is another vital lesson for journalism students. By exploring how political leaders and parties engage with the public, they can improve their reporting on campaigns and public statements. 73

Political Reporting This knowledge is particularly important for assessing how narratives are shaped in the media landscape. However, the complexity of political communication poses a risk of oversimplifying issues or misinterpreting messages if not approached thoughtfully. Additionally, studying politics cultivates strong research and investigative skills. Students learn to delve into political systems, laws, and historical contexts, preparing them for investigative journalism focused on uncovering corruption or political scandals. While this enhances their credibility, it also requires significant time and resources, along with the courage to confront potential pushback from powerful entities. In summary, by integrating political understanding into their journalism education, students can provide informed, fact-based reporting that contributes to their credibility in the field. However, they must strive for ethical reporting practices to ensure their narratives remain objective and balanced.

6.2 REPRESENTATIVE DEMOCRACY
6.2.1 Limited and Indirect
Representative democracy is a limited and indirect form of democracy: It is limited in the sense that participation in government is infrequent and brief, being restricted to the act of voting every few years. It is indirect in the sense that the public does not exercise power by itself, but selects those who will rule on its behalf. This form of rule is democratic only as far as representation establishes a reliable and effective link between the government and the governed. Representative democracy is practical for large populations, allows division of labor in decision-making, and maintains stability by encouraging citizens to accept compromises.
6.2.2 Synonymous with Electoral Democracy
The democratic content in representative democracy is the idea of popular consent, expressed through the act of voting. Representative democracy is, thus, a form of electoral democracy, in that popular election is seen as the only legitimate source of political authority. Such elections must respect the principle of political equality based on universal adult franchise, irrespective of caste, colour, creed, sex, religion or economic status. Elections must be regular, open and above all competitive. The core of the democratic process is the capacity of the people to call politicians to account.
6.3 VARIOUS VIEWS ON REPRESENTATIVE
DEMOCRACY
There are different views on representative democracy. One view suggests that in this system, political power is ultimately in the hands of voters during elections. The strength of representative democracy lies in its ability to combine elite rule with meaningful political participation. Politicians are entrusted with governing, but they must respond to public pressure since voters put them in office and can vote them out. In this sense, voters hold similar power in the political market as consumers do in the economic market. Joseph Schumpeter, in Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy (1976), described representative democracy as an institutional arrangement where

Political Reporting individuals gain decision-making power through a competitive struggle for votes.
6.3.1 Pluralist
According to another viewpoint, democracy is pluralist in nature. In its broader sense, pluralism is a commitment to diversity or multiplicity. In its narrower sense, pluralism is a theory of distribution of political power. It holds that power is widely and evenly dispersed in society, instead of being concentrated in a few hands as the elitists claim. An example of pluralism in India is the functioning of various pressure groups and interest groups, such as trade unions, business associations, and ethnic organizations, which influence government policies by representing the interests of their members in the political process, ensuring that power is distributed across diverse sections of society. Wealth or privilege is concentrated justifiably or otherwise. Elitism believes in rule by an elite or minority. Classical elitism, developed by Mosca, Pareto and Michele, saw elite rule as being inevitable, an unchangeable fact of social existence
6.3.2 Elitist
It speaks of a minority that possesses a disproportionate amount of wealth, power, or privilege, whether it is justified or not. Elitism is the belief that a minority or elite should rule. According to Mosca, Pareto, and Michele's classical elitism, elite dominance was unavoidable, a fixed aspect of social life. What does the majority rule entail? Democracy is seen by some as majority rule. The practice of giving the majority's will precedence is known as majority rule. Describe majoritarianism. Majoritarianism suggests indifference to people who are marginalised.
6.3.3 Rival Views
There is a considerable amount of disagreement about the meaning and significance of representative democracy. Some questions raised by scholars are as follows: * Does it ensure a genuine and healthy dispersal of political power? * Do democratic processes genuinely promote long-term benefits, or are they self-defeating? * Can political equality co-exist with economic equality? In summary, different theories have differing interpretations of representative democracy. Marxism, the New Right, Elitism, and Pluralism have advanced the most significant of these perspectives. Representative democracy is simply the best type of political structure, according to many political theorists. Because representative democracy is predicated on the idea that all people are equal and have intrinsic worth, some contend that it is the type of government that best upholds human rights.

6.4 REPRESENTATIVE DEMOCRACY:
FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLE
6.4.1 Popular Sovereignty
It means that the ultimate source of all public authority is the people, and that the government does what the people want to be done. Four observable conditions can be recognised in popular sovereignty: * Government policies reflect what the people want * People participate in the political process * Information is available and debate takes place * Majority rules, i.e., policies are decided on the basis of what a majority of people want.
6.4.2 Political Equality
Regardless of caste, colour, creed, sex, or religion, every individual has equal weight in the management of public affairs, according to this philosophy. However, political theorists held that significant disparities in economic conditions have the potential to develop into political disparities over time. "If citizens are unequal in economic resources... they are likely to be unequal in political resources; therefore political equality will be impossible to accomplish," says Robert Dahl, summarising the issue. The disparity in the power over information and the funding of political campaigns is especially significant in the modern era. Achieving a full democracy is seriously hampered by this uneven influence.

Political Reporting 6.4.3 Political Liberty
This idea states that citizens in democracies are shielded from governmental meddling with their fundamental liberties, including speech, association, mobility, and conscience. Many people believe that liberty and democracy go hand in hand. In addition to the freedom to vote and run for office, the concept of self-governance encompasses the freedoms of speech, petitioning the government, and joining political parties or social organisations. In actuality, democracy can occasionally undermine liberty rather than uphold it. One key criticism is the risk of 'majority tyranny.' This refers to the suppression of minority rights by the majority, leaving little space for minority claims. While this threat is real, Robert Dahl argues that there is no strong evidence to suggest that alternative political systems do a better job of protecting the rights of ethnic and religious minorities. Another criticism is that democracy can lead to bad decisions. Critics argue that representative democracy, being majoritarian, doesn't always guarantee good outcomes. Majorities, like minorities, can be unwise or cruel and may be misled by incompetent or manipulative leaders.

REPRESENTATIVE DEMOCRACY
Having said this, let us now pay attention to the actual working of representative democracy. The chief characteristics of a functioning democracy are: * Free and fair elections * Open and accountable government * Civil and political rights Political parties : In the political process, political parties are very important. They offer a significant political dynamic that is essential to the operation of the system's formal institutions. A political party, in the words of R.G. Gettell, is a group of persons who function as a political unit and are somewhat organised. They want to run the government and impose their broad policies through the exercise of their voting power. Among a political party's fundamental characteristics are: a) People constituting a political party have a certain degree of agreement on fundamental principles. b) They seek to achieve their objectives through constitutional means. c) A political party aims to further national interest rather than sectional interest. d) It seeks to capture political power to enable it to further public interest.

Political Reporting 6.6 ELECTIONS Modern democratic states rely on representative governments due to their large size and population, making direct democracy impractical. In these democracies, elections play a vital role, as representatives are chosen by the people to govern on their behalf. Elections are contests between political parties seeking voter support, though individuals can run independently. Contesting as a party candidate offers several advantages: parties follow clear policies, making it easier for voters to understand the candidate's stance; they provide funds for election campaigns; party volunteers assist with electioneering, and well-known leaders often canvass for candidates, increasing their visibility and support.
6.6.1 Election Process
Elections in a democratic system are founded on the principle of equality, meaning each person has one vote, regardless of caste, color, creed, sex, or religion. The most significant political right is the right to vote, ensuring that everyone has an equal voice in government formation. Secret ballots are used to protect voter choice, allowing individuals to cast their votes privately, free from intimidation or undue influence. To facilitate the election process, constituencies are established, which are territorial areas from where candidates run for office. A single-member constituency elects one representative, while a multi-member constituency elects several. In India, the Election Commission, an independent body, oversees the election process, ensuring it remains free and fair by setting and announcing election dates, as outlined in Article 324. The Election Commission has another very important responsibility. It makes sure that the party in power does not get undue advantage over other parties. The process of election runs through several formal stages. This process comprises of: a) Announcement of dates b) Filing of nomination papers c) Scrutiny of applications d) Withdrawal of applications e) Publication of the final list f) Campaigning g) Casting of votes 131 Representative Democracy and Its Limits h) Announcement of results In fact, the moment the Election Commission announces the dates of elections, political parties start their activities. The first task of political parties becomes the selection of candidates who are going to contest in elections as their party candidates. Modern electioneering is a cumbersome process. It needs a huge organisation to manage it, which is provided by political parties. Moreover, elections require a reasonable amount of fund, which is also provided by political parties

i) Selection of Candidates Representative
Democracy and
Political parties now play an essential and crucial role in the operation of Its Limits representative democracies. In actuality, democratic politics now have an organised form thanks to political parties. Political parties coordinate their campaigns, field candidates, and provide support. Every political party makes announcements about specific policies that it intends to carry out if it wins power. Voters thoroughly understand the platforms and programs of the party they are supporting when they cast their ballots for that candidate. ii) Nomination Once election dates are announced, political parties have to choose their candidates through a process of selection. Then, candidates have to file their nominations to election offices which are appointed by the Election Commission. There is a last date for filing nomination papers. After all nominations have been filed, there is a process of scrutiny. It is done to check whether all information given in nomination papers is correct. If there is a doubt or a candidate is not found eligible, his/her nomination paper is rejected. Once the scrutiny is over, candidates are given a date for withdrawal. The withdrawal process makes sure that a) there is as little wastage of votes as possible and b) that all names printed on ballot paper are those of serious candidates. iii) Symbols The Election Commission assigns symbols to political parties (EC). Each political party is assigned a symbol by the EC, which ensures that the insignia are distinct enough to avoid confusing voters. The following factors make the symbols important in emerging nations like India: They are beneficial to voters who lack literacy and are unable to read candidate names. They assist in separating candidates who share the same name. They represent the political party's ideology in question. iv) Campaigning The process by which a candidate attempts to convince people to cast their ballots for him or her as opposed to others is known as campaigning. Generally speaking, 48 hours prior to voting, campaigning ends. Every political party and candidate seeks to connect with as many people as they can. The electoral process involves several campaign strategies. Among them are: 132 The Rules of Democracy Grammar holding of open forums where candidates and several local and national party leaders speak. postering on walls and erecting both big and tiny hoardings alongside roadways. Handbills that highlight the key points of their manifesto stand out. putting on a parade in favour of many candidates. door-to-door solicitation from prominent members of the community and party.

Political Reporting v) Counting of Votes and Declaration of Results After voting is over, ballot boxes are sealed and taken to counting centres. During counting, the candidate or his representative is present. After counting, a candidate getting a simple majority is declared elected. At times, simple majority leads to problems. The elected candidate represents majority when there are only two candidates, but not so if there are three or more candidates; e.g. if A gets 40 and B, C and D get 20 votes, then A is declared elected. Now, though A has got 40 votes, he does not reflect the majority because 60 votes are actually against him. Elections are a very important part of democracy because the entire fortification of a democratic system depends on how elections are held. 6.7 ALIENATION
To be alienated is to be detached or detached from one's true or fundamental the natural world. In reality, most democratic systems perform badly when it comes to individual liberty and popular sovereignty.The world is generally a small-scale, indirect democracy, which makes each individual person feel alienated. This democracy is essentially what Joseph Schumpeter called a "institutional framework" for making political decisions, where people get the ability to make decisions through a competitive contest for the votes of the people. Radical Democrats have critiqued this institutional structure for restricting public engagement to a nearly meaningless ritual, such as voting for politicians every few years who can only be removed by replacing them with other politicians.

6.8.1 How Media Shapes Public Opinion
Public opinion is formed in many ways and several agencies contribute in shaping public opinion. For a healthy public opinion, citizens should know what is happening around them, in their own country and in the world at large. A country's government makes policies not only about internal problems, but has a foreign policy also. A citizen must hear different opinions in order to make up his/her mind. Thus for democracy to work well, citizens need to apprise themselves of various views. Among the agencies, which help in formulating sound public opinion are the press, the electronic media and cinema. In today's digital age, internet, social networking sites and TV also play an important role in shaping perceptions and opinions. Political parties have their media cells and spokespersons who defend their policies at various platforms. New mediums like Facebook and WhatsApp are being used to strike a direct bond with the voters. At the individual level, democracy allows a person to contribute his/her share of opinion in decision making. For all this, there is a necessity of free discussion and argument. Democratic government gives a lot of freedom to the ordinary citizen. However, citizens have to use freedom with responsibility, restraint and discipline. If people have some grievances, they must show them through channels provided by the democratic system. Acts of indiscipline on the part of citizens might wreck the democratic set up of a system.
6.9 LET US SUM UP
This chapter discusses the fundamental principles and processes of elections in a democratic system. It highlights the core idea of equality, where each citizen, regardless of their background, has the right to vote, ensuring that everyone has an equal say in the formation of government. The right to vote is the most crucial political right, and the use of a secret ballot ensures voters can freely express their choices without fear of intimidation or undue influence. Elections are described as contests between political parties or independent candidates seeking public support, with the election process being organized around constituencies. Constituencies, which are specific territorial areas, allow candidates to contest elections either individually or as part of a multi-member system. This process ensures representation from across regions and sectors. The chapter also explains the role of the Election Commission, particularly in India, which is responsible for overseeing the entire electoral process. The Election Commission ensures that elections are conducted freely and fairly, guaranteeing the democratic principles of participation and representation. It handles key tasks like setting election dates and supervising election protocols. The advantages of contesting elections as a party candidate are

Political Reporting discussed, including party policies, campaign funds, and support from volunteers and leaders. Through this structure, modern democracies maintain political participation and governance, ensuring that citizens play a central role in shaping their governments.
6.10 KEYWORDS
* Right to Vote: The legal ability to choose leaders or decide on laws through elections. * Secret Ballot: A voting method where individuals cast their votes privately, ensuring anonymity. * Constituencies: Areas or districts represented by elected officials in a government. * Representative Democracy: A system where people elect officials to make decisions on their behalf. * Election Commission: An independent body that oversees and manages elections to ensure fairness.

7.0 INTRODUCTION
Political participation and equality are fundamental to democracy, yet unequal participation often undermines political equality. Active engagement beyond voting is crucial for holding governments accountable and fostering informed citizens. Philosophers like J.S. Mill, Aristotle, and Rousseau emphasize that participation helps individuals realize their potential and ensures that laws are more accepted. Despite its importance, modern democracies struggle to ensure broad participation due to societal diversity. Dissent plays a vital role in media and political writing, as it serves as a counterbalance to authority and power structures. By providing a platform for alternative views and challenging dominant narratives, dissent ensures that no single voice or ideology dominates public discourse. It is through dissent that marginalized voices and underrepresented communities can be heard, contributing to a more pluralistic society. In democratic societies, media is not just a tool for reporting facts but also for scrutinizing and critiquing government policies, decisions, and actions. This scrutiny is vital for transparency and accountability, which are key to maintaining a healthy democracy. Moreover, dissent in media writing encourages dialogue and debate, fostering critical thinking among citizens and pushing governments to be more responsive to the needs of all people, not just a select few. By promoting diverse perspectives and questioning the status quo, dissent strengthens democracy and ensures that it remains a system built on collective wisdom and continuous improvement.

This unit aims to provide a basic understanding of political participation and political dissent, their features and some important proponents who have emphasized their importance. After reading this unit, you should be able to: * Comprehend the meaning of political participation; * Understand what dissent is; and * Analyze the relationship between participation and dissent.
7.2 WHAT IS PARTICIPATION?
Sidney Verba and Norman H Nie, in their book Participation in America: Political Democracy and Social Equality, have defined political participation as 'behaviour designed to affect the choice of governmental personnel and/or policies'. It simply means political participation as actions intended to influence government decisions or policies. Voting in elections or joining protests for anti-corruption laws are forms of political participation. Huntington and Nelson in their book, No Easy Choice: Political Participation in Developing Countries define political participation as 'activity by private citizens designed to influence governmental decision making'. In another definition of political participation, H McClosky says it is "the principal means by which consent is granted or withdrawn in a democracy and the rulers are made accountable to the ruled". In general terms, it can be defined as those activities of citizens which affect politics. Political participation is relevant to all forms of governments, but it is central to a democracy. Robert H. Salisbury claims that there are three reasons to be politically engaged intellectually. First of all, it is considered a legitimising act. Citizens approve and legitimise actions made by the government as long as they vote or engage in other forms of civic engagement. This is what a democracy is all about. The second perspective on involvement is instrumental, viewing it as a way to achieve political power that is needed to make up for losses, boost gains, or improve societal or personal advantages. This point of view has served as the foundation for campaigns to increase voter turnout and suffrage. Third, the common understanding of participation is mostly linked to Rousseau and John Stuart Mill, who considered it as a means of resolving social disputes. Through political engagement, citizens, according to Rousseau, would be able to agree on how resources should be distributed and would have a common sense of what the public good is. According to Mill, participating is a process of learning, and individuals who choose not to participate will not be able to pick up the norms needed to form consensus opinions. Huntington has maintained that the political system is being overworked, which is undermining the legitimacy of the government. Government authority declines with too much democracy, therefore there should be a careful balance between government power and restraints. According to Giovanni Sartori, the anti-elitists are more concerned with the horizontal dimension of democracy extension--participation--than the vertical

dimension, or leadership. He backed citizens who were well-informed, Participation and
Dissent in
engaged, and eager to participate in actual decision-making. Formal political Democracy participation through electoral systems and political parties is emphasised in the UN Human Development Report. Check Your Progress 1 Note: 1) Use the space provided below for your Answers.

7.2.1 Types of Participation
Political participation can be classified in two categories - conventional and unconventional. The conventional participation is routine behaviour that uses channels of the government. It can be supportive as it could be a ceremonial act of expressing support for the government or the country. Conversely, it could also try to seek a modification in the government policy. It could involve contacting the party members, politicians and government representatives or activities pertaining to the election process like campaigning and voting. Unconventional participation is relatively uncommon behaviour working against government channels or the dominant culture and hence, it is stressful for both participants and their opponents. Such type of participation may not structurally be embedded in the political system and that is why, it can be illegal. A number of activities like unlawful demonstrations, boycotts, signing the petitions, political violence etc come under its ambit. It has been successful in a number of occasions in influencing government decisions - like the civil rights movement in the US. There are three features shared by people who participate in unconventional ways: * Group consciousness * Sense of political efficacy

Political Reporting * Mistrust of the political system. Michael Rush and Phillip Althoff Nelson in their 1971 book, An Introduction to Political Sociology listed the following activities as political participation: * Holding or seeking political/administrative office. * Active/passive membership in a political organization. * Active/passive membership in a quasi-political organization (like pressure groups). * Participation in public meetings, demonstrations etc. * Participation in informal political discussion. * General interest in politics. * Voting for elections. * Indifference or lack of interest in political activities leading to political apathy.
7.2.2 Levels of Participation
Verba and Nie have given various levels of political participation. Inactives - These are the people who rarely vote and keep a distance from political organizations as well. Voting Specialists - Such people vote but apart from that, they do not participate in political activities. Parochial Participants - They neither vote nor do they participate in election campaigns or civic associations. But, they are not averse to contacting local officials for personal issues. Communalists - Such people mainly stay engaged in local community politics and their education and income is similar to that of the campaigners. Campaigners - They not only vote but also like to campaign. Their education level is higher than that of average voters and they are able to take clear cut political positions due to clear party affiliation. Complete Activists - Such individuals regularly promote a political party and its political ideals.
7.2.3 Factors impacting Political Participation
There are a number of factors that have an impact on political participation. They are listed below. * Psychological factors : The psychology of a person has a significant impact on how involved they are in politics. Politics is appealing to lonesome people since it brings them into numerous social circles. Some people engage in politics in an attempt to fulfil their desire to be powerful. System trust, or a person's faith in the political system, including political parties and leaders, is another crucial component.

* Social factors: A person's degree of education plays a significant role in Participation and
Dissent in
determining whether or not they are inclined to participate in politics. Democracy More intelligent people are more self-assured and possess strong civic virtues. In a similar vein, those that make more money tend to participate more than others. Here, occupation also plays a role. Due to the direct influence of government policies on their jobs, those in the teaching, trading, and government service sectors have higher levels of political participation. Age and sex are other factors that influence involvement. Women's participation in politics tends to be lower than men's because of caste, lack of education, lack of finances, and home responsibilities. India's 2017-18 economic study reveals a low degree of female political participation. * Political factors: When voting procedures are straightforward, political engagement is strong. Political engagement may decline if citizens have too much or too little faith in the government. The many actions that political parties do before, during, and after elections--such as rallies, voter mobilisation efforts, campaigns, etc.--have an impact on participation as well. Sensitisation of citizens to political issues is also aided by grassroots democracy in cities and villages. A nation's level of political engagement can be raised through a variety of mobilising organisations, including associations, the media, and civic groups. * Social Capital: Social capital is the web of connections that exists among members of a society. These connections can be made on an individual basis or through involvement in interest groups, religious institutions, or civil society organisations. In general, a society's high degree of political participation is correlated with its strong social capital. By having an effect on both the volume and quality of political engagement, it aids in the preservation of democracy. The political objectives of civil society groups and other nonprofits are served by encouraging member mobilisation, which raises political engagement. In contrast to political participation, one can also see political apathy in a country which is characterized by a feeling of indifference towards politics. It can be witnessed in the decline in voter turnout in a country. Political apathy could breed corruption and moral decline among leaders as they do not face public scrutiny. Youths and minorities are generally seen as sections that do not have interest in politics. Some people may be content with the political system and hence, do not feel any need to participate. Others may feel that there is no scope for change since every political party behaves in a similar fashion which leads to political apathy. Some may not be sure of their own political leanings while others may not have time and energy for politics.

Some critics believe that online participation does not reflect the reality of offline world and these opinions can be artificially manufactured using technology as a tool. Globalisation is blurring the political boundaries at the global level leading to what some experts call Global Citizenship. This is evident from increasing concerns over human rights violations and efforts to address climate change. These issues generate political participation beyond borders as global survival is at stake. In this context, globalisation seems to have transformed the meaning of citizenship and political participation. Global outcry can put pressure on a government to address concerns of its citizens. However, internet can also play its part in downfall of a government as was the case during the Arab Spring in West Asia. This can prompt the state to crackdown on online participation to ensure its own stability. Check Your Progress 2 Note: 1) Use the space provided below for your Answers.
