7.3 DISSENT
The foundation of a democracy is the people's agreement to allow their elected representatives to rule them. There can be those, though, who disagree with government programs and have other opinions. "An refusal to collaborate with an established source of authority, which can be social, cultural, or governmental," is the definition of dissent. As previously mentioned, dissent is an unusual form of political engagement that may not be ingrained in the political system; hence, the state may view it as unlawful. Acts of dissent include things like marches, protests, boycotts, self- immolations, and civil disobedience. When discontent reaches an extreme point, it might become violent and consider revolution--the overthrow of the current government--as its goal.

Dissent can be collective or individual and organized or spontaneous. A Participation and
Dissent in
certain type of political dissent is found in all democracies in form of moral Democracy criticism of the system and emphasising systemic problems. This is basically public scrutiny of government policies. It does not aim to achieve political power (unlike revolutionaries) and resorts to critical evaluation of political system and culture. By using violence, political dissidents would lose higher moral ground of defending people's interests and would be treated as extremists who want to achieve political power. Dissent is valued and feared in equal measure. Dissent is welcomed if it occurs in a far-off location or in the wonderful, unthreatening past. Galileo,
M. K. Gandhi, Socrates, Martin Luther, and others are well-known dissenters.
Dissidents are valued if they succeed, and if not, they may be singled out. To those whose power it threatens, dissent would appear unappealing. In his book, A theory of Justice, John Rawls has argued that civil disobedience helps in maintaining just institutions. Along with free and regular elections and an independent judiciary, civil disobedience used with restraint and judgement can strengthen just institutions. Marxists believe that communist societies are free of political disobedience as everyone will do as per his capacity and get as per his need. Also, people identify themselves with community well being instead of individual interests in a communist society. Social contract theorist, Thomas Hobbes in his book, Leviathan, has argued that individuals consent to obey the state in return for being protected against violence and threats of violence. If the state cannot provide protection, citizens have the right to disobey its rules. Another social contract theorist, John Locke in his book, Second Treatise, has argued that a state is legitimate because it enjoys consent of its citizens. The purpose of the state is to enforce the law of nature and in case it is unable to do so, the citizens no longer are obliged to obey the government. J S Mill has further said, "If all mankind minus one were of one opinion, mankind would be no more justified in silencing that one person than he, if he had the power, would be justified in silencing mankind". Dissent is associated with critical thinking which seeks to question accepted notions of authority, truth and meaning. Immanuel Kant called it 'leading an examined life'. Michel Foucault, one of the main critics of liberalism and the Frankfurt School regarded dissent as positive and it's near absence in the 19th- and 20th-century democracies created problems in these states. Contemporary democracies are believed to encourage self- censorship, ideals of normality, or intellectually restricted forms of culture. Such a democracy would hinder critical thinking; minimize dissent and public deliberation. Check Your Progress 3 Note: 1) Use the space provided below for your Answers.

7.3.1 Democracy and Dissent
Dissent and the state have a complicated relationship in which the latter attempts to control the former and views the former as a threat. In the past, authoritarian regimes have never allowed opposition to exist inside their political sphere of influence. Every dictator, from Mao to Stalin to Hitler, has eradicated any political opposition that would have posed a threat to their rule. Hitler settled scores with his rivals through the use of civil service purges, concentration camps, and unfair trials, while Mao persecuted intellectuals, dismissed party officials, and curtailed organised opposition. Joseph Stalin likewise implemented similar oppressive measures to maintain his absolute power in the erstwhile Soviet Union. However, in democracies, there is always room for expressing one's views which may be opposed to the government of the day. Some of the rights that deal with expressing dissent in a democracy include: * The Freedom of speech and expression: Voltaire, a French philosopher, had infamously declared, "I will protect your right to say anything you have to say, even if I disagree with what you have to say." In a democratic nation, the freedom to expressing opinions is the foundation of freedom. No outside force should be allowed to impede someone from exercising their right in this way. But it is equally important to remember that this right must be utilised carefully and that other people's sentiments must be considered. * Freedom of Association and Assembly: On the plus side, it would imply that a person has the freedom to belong to the associations or groups of his choosing. On the down side, it implies that an individual can stay away from affiliation with groups with which he does not share interests. The national legislation ought to safeguard both of these facets of this privilege. The freedom to assemble does not include the ability to do so anywhere one pleases because it does not extend to the infringement of another person's property. * Political participation: Engaging in politics can be understood as defending one's freedom to dissent in a democracy. An individual can use this freedom to vote against a government whose policies conflict with their own interests. * Due process of law: - This right protects one's other rights concerning dissent. Due process makes sure that an impartial procedure exists by 94 which any act of dissent can be examined.

However, it could be erroneous to assume that the right to dissent is fully Participation and
Dissent in
protected in democracies. If a government feels insecure and threatened Democracy during internal unrest, it is likely to use force against dissent depending on the medium of protest as well. The level of threat perceived by the government from an act of dissent would also determine its response. Academics believe that a democracy is less likely to see dissent as a threat as 'democracies are generally more legitimate forms of government as well as more tolerant of dissident behaviour'. Democratic systems also provide 'institutionalised and legitimate channels' through which citizens and political opponents can express their dissent. Because opposition organisations are less likely to resort to violence in order to express their dissatisfaction, this is advantageous to both the government and the dissenters. As a result, the government does not view their activities as dangers and is hence less likely to employ repression against dissenters. It implies that using violence as a tactic to voice discontent is unacceptable in democracies. The freedom to dissent defends one's most fundamental civil liberties in a democracy from the government's concentration. Through public institutions that protect free speech and debate, the media, the court, and finally through general elections, it permits a public discussion between liberty and security. A society must value free and critical thought if it is to be genuinely democratic. Galileo and Copernicus were only able to establish that the Sun is at the core of the solar system because of their critical thinking. There are plenty more examples of how opposition has succeeded; in South Africa, it was dissent that brought an end to apartheid. It may contribute to the creation of a society that is less unfair.
7.4 LET US SUM UP
Political engagement and the right to dissent are fundamental pillars of any democratic society. Active participation enables citizens to hold their government accountable, while traditional forms of engagement lend legitimacy to governmental actions. Conversely, unconventional dissent-- such as protests and boycotts--serves to question and confront governmental authority. Modern democracies face the challenge of fostering increased political involvement while simultaneously managing dissent. In democratic frameworks, peaceful dissent is safeguarded through rights including freedom of speech, the right to assemble, and due process. Moreover, political participation itself provides a platform for dissent, as individuals can use their voting power to oppose policies they disapprove of. However, resorting to violence as a form of dissent often leads to state repression, as it is viewed as a direct threat to democratic integrity. To cultivate a truly democratic ethos, fostering critical thinking within society is essential.

* Dissent: Disagreement or protest against policies, leaders, or decisions. * Legitimacy: The acceptance and belief that authority or power is rightful and valid.

Political Reporting * Critical Thinking: Analyzing and evaluating information or arguments before forming a judgment. * Democracy: A system of government where power is vested in the people, who elect representatives to make decisions.

8.2 POLITICAL NEWS GATHERING AND
WRITING
In news organizations - newspapers, radio channels and TV news channels - reporters are assigned beats for the smooth conduct of the reporting job. A beat is the subject area that a reporter is assigned to cover. The assignment of a particular beat helps the reporter to develop expertise in his/her area which includes expanding sources and gaining knowledge and experience for better Performance. In newspapers, the reporting network comprises reporting broadly at three levels; City, State Capital and National Capital. Here, the city reporting or local reporting is referred to reporting from the city from where the newspaper edition is published. It is substituted by metro reporting in the case of reporting from metropolitan cities (if the newspaper is published from a metropolitan area). Every newspaper (from whichever city it is published) has a reporting set up in the state capital and the national capital. This reporting set up is called bureau.
8.2.1 Coverage under Political Beat
There are different beats distributed to reporters in the City Reporting Room, the State Bureau and the National Bureau. However, political beat is common at all the three levels, though the range of coverage differs. A political reporter in the local reporting room covers political activities happening in that particular city; while a reporter in the State Bureau covers political activities having wider reach including affairs related to the State Government. A reporter in the National Bureau covers national and international level politics including affairs related to the Central Government.
8.2.2 Political Newsgathering and Sources
In political newsgathering, reporters prefer to do field reporting or spot coverage. This includes reporting the sessions of legislatures, public meetings, speeches by political leaders, demonstrations and rallies, election campaigning and polling, counting and election results, conventions and

Political Reporting meetings of the parties. On-the-spot interviews of political leaders or bites collected from them is considered an important assignment for political reporters. Thus, a political reporter has to do lot of running around. S/he has to follow a hectic schedule, and his/her job appears quite taxing. Mobility and connectivity are essential attributes of political reporters. Political reporters depend on official sources to a great extent. Press releases issued by political parties and statements issued by their leaders provide significant input for writing news reports. Political reporters never miss the press briefings of political parties and the press conferences organized by ministers and other political leaders. On many occasions, reporters are briefed about the outcome of some party meetings. In the wake of political controversies, political reporters wait for the official version issued by the concerned party.
8.2.3 Political News Writing
In political news writing, the same inverted pyramid news structure is adopted which you would have already gone through. Here, the most important information or fact comes first, followed by the less important information, continued by some extra information and followed by the least important facts. In writing lead of political news reports, the same 5 Ws and I H formula is Applied. Writing Speeches/Press Conferences/Interviews: A political reporter is mostly found writing stories on speeches, press conferences or briefings and interviews. These news stories have a common element; they are one-source stories. Such stories are collection of direct and indirect quotations from the Source. Speeches assume more significance if made by prominent political leaders and government functionaries. A reporter requires considerable skill to report a 5000 - word speech in 300 words, and still give the reader an accurate report of what was said. The task becomes further difficult in the case of really lengthy speeches. All speeches, whether formal addresses on special occasions or impromptu remarks during an unstructured gathering, are handled very much alike. The reporter must consider the following three elements: * The speaker * The audience * The speech A fourth consideration is the possible interpretation that any of the three elements may need. The proportion of the story to be devoted to each element varies with the comparative importance of each, but no story is complete without all Three.

The speaker should be properly identified in the lead. Sometime this can be Political Writing done with a title or a short sentence. The reader needs to know who the speaker is and why his or her statements are worth quoting. Even a description of the speaker's distinctive characteristics and manner of emphasizing certain points is sometimes woven into the story to give it more colour. The audience should also be described. How many people were there? Who were they? Why did they meet? The reporter needs to answer these questions in the news report. The names of persons in the audience need not be given unless it would be of interest to the reader to know the names of a few of the more prominent ones; but the reporter should tell whether they are bankers, teachers, doctors, engineers, farmers or party workers. Audience reaction is also worth noting. In press conferences and interviews, only two elements, the speaker and the speech are considered important. Mostly, a political reporter writes the story in his/her own language and expression while taking care that the meaning of the statements made by the speaker does not change. Wherever required, the reporter decides to keep the statements in quotes. Though direct quotations tend to add emphasis, the reporter should avoid quoting routine, obvious or minor points from the speech or statements made by the speaker. 8.3 REPORT WRITING
Political reporting plays a crucial role in informing the public about the workings of government, elections, political figures, and policies. The aim is to provide an accurate, balanced, and factual account of political events and issues while remaining objective and free from personal bias. A well-written political report allows readers to form their own opinions based on presented facts. A well-structured political report ensures clarity and flow, enabling readers to understand complex political events without difficulty. The key to an effective report is organizing information in a logical sequence and presenting it in a way that maintains the reader's attention.

Political Reporting 8.3.1 Key Elements of a Political Report
* Headline: The headline should be concise, informative, and directly related to the topic. It should capture the essence of the political event or issue being reported and spark the reader's interest. * Lead: The lead or the opening paragraph must grab attention immediately by summarizing the most important aspect of the political event. In most cases, the "what, when, who, and where" should be addressed early on, providing the readers with essential context. * Body: The body of the report should offer a detailed account of the event, explaining the "why" and "how" of the situation. Here, the reporter should present facts supported by credible sources such as official statements, interviews, or documents. It is important to maintain objectivity and balance by including perspectives from different political players or stakeholders. * Conclusion: The conclusion should tie up loose ends, briefly summarizing the event's importance or potential future impact. It can include statements from experts or key political figures, offering insights into what could happen next.
8.3.2 Style and Tone in Political Reports
* Objective and Neutral: Political reports should be written in a neutral tone, free from personal opinions or bias. The goal is to provide readers with facts so they can make informed judgments. Language should be factual, clear, and precise, avoiding inflammatory or emotionally charged words. * Clarity and Conciseness: Politics can often be complex, but it is crucial to break down the information in a way that makes it understandable to the average reader. Reports should avoid jargon or technical terms unless they are explained, and sentences should be concise, getting to the point without unnecessary elaboration. * Fact-checking and Accuracy: Since political reporting can influence public opinion, ensuring that all information is accurate is paramount. Reporters must cross-check facts, dates, and figures, and ensure that sources are reliable. Mistakes in political reporting can not only damage the credibility of the reporter but also mislead the public. By analyzing real-life political reports, journalists can understand the different ways political events are covered. A good example might be a report covering an election result, where the journalist presents a summary of the outcome, reactions from both the winning and losing parties, and an analysis of what the result means for future governance.

( Indian Express, 11 Oct)
8.4 LONG FORM
Long-form journalism is a style of journalism characterised by its depth, creativity, and narrative approach. Unlike traditional, short, fact-driven news articles, long-form pieces explore topics in detail, providing background information, context, and often offering a creative lens to engage the reader. In the digital age, where space is no longer a constraint, long-form journalism has found a new home. The shift from traditional print media to online platforms has allowed for the expansion of detailed reporting, which now includes blogs, journals, discussion forums, and long reads. This transformation has given journalists the freedom to explore topics more comprehensively, delving into the background and history of events without the limitation of column inches or broadcast time. 103

Political Reporting 8.4.1 Characteristics of Long-Form Journalism
Long-form journalism is not a new concept, but its evolution in digital media has introduced several distinct characteristics. These include:
Length and Depth
Unlike short, hard news reports that focus on immediate facts, long-form journalism typically exceeds 1,000 words and aims to offer readers a deeper understanding of a subject. It often addresses broader societal, political, or cultural issues by weaving together historical context, interviews, and expert opinions. With the unlimited space provided by online platforms, journalists can cover complex subjects in exhaustive detail. In earlier times, such detailed articles existed on editorial or opinion pages of newspapers. However, they were limited by word count. Today, long-form journalism allows for storytelling with unlimited scope, which can include not just current events but also their origins, causes, and potential consequences.
Creative Nonfiction and Narrative Style
One of the defining features of long-form journalism is its narrative approach. Also known as literary journalism or narrative journalism, this style combines factual reporting with the storytelling techniques of creative nonfiction. This involves creating engaging, detailed narratives that hold the reader's attention by incorporating vivid descriptions, character development, and emotional depth. The ability to narrate a story over thousands of words while maintaining factual integrity is a core aspect of this genre. Writers often use literary devices such as metaphors and anecdotes to create a more immersive experience for the reader. The result is journalism that reads like a novel or documentary, where facts are presented in an engaging way, making the subject matter not only informative but also compelling.
8.4.2 The Role of Digital Media in Long-Form Journalism
The rise of digital platforms has played a transformative role in the resurgence of long-form journalism. Online media offers an expansive platform where multimedia elements such as videos, infographics, and interactive visuals enhance storytelling. The multimedia elements enrich the reader's experience, offering more than just text to convey the message. Digital platforms have changed the way readers consume journalism. With interactive media, readers can now engage with stories in a multimodal manner--through audio, video, and interactive elements embedded within text. This multimedia aspect allows journalists to present complex stories, such as political or technological analyses, in a more digestible and visually appealing format. For instance, a long-form article on climate change may be accompanied by interactive maps showing rising temperatures, or a profile of a political leader might include interview clips.

While traditional media like newspapers and TV broadcasts have limitations Political Writing in terms of time and space, long-form journalism on digital platforms faces no such constraints. As a result, articles can target specific, niche audiences by delving into specialized topics. For example, an in-depth report on space exploration may appeal to space enthusiasts, scientists, and policy-makers, who appreciate the detailed analysis and expert opinions such content offers. Such pieces can be widely shared across platforms, engaging diverse audiences who are interested in thoughtful, long-form content.
Example of Long-Form Journalism: The New York Times Interactive
Series One of the best examples of long-form journalism in the digital age is The New York Times' interactive series on climate change. The series combines text with infographics, video interviews, and animations, allowing readers to understand the complex issue from various angles. Through engaging narratives, historical context, and expert interviews, the series educates its audience on the multifaceted nature of climate change, its causes, and its global impact.
8.5 OPINION PIECES
Opinion writing is a distinct and impactful form of journalistic expression, where the writer communicates a subjective viewpoint on a current issue or topic of public interest. Unlike news writing, which focuses on objectivity and balance, opinion writing allows for a personal interpretation, supported by carefully chosen evidence. This evidence may be research-based data, expert views, or citations that bolster the writer's stance. While opinion pieces do not necessarily claim to be objective, they are most effective when they are thoughtfully substantiated. Opinion pieces are typically penned by journalists or subject experts and address topics that resonate with a wide readership. These pieces serve as a reflection of ongoing public discourse, addressing developments that capture popular imagination. The key to a successful opinion piece lies in selecting a subject that sparks curiosity and a desire to learn more about the topic. Whether the writer is expressing a strong stance on a political issue or commenting on cultural phenomena, the goal is to engage readers in a conversation that expands their understanding of the subject.
8.5.1 Important Components of Opinion Writing
A well-crafted opinion piece should have several essential components that contribute to its overall effectiveness. First and foremost is a catchy headline. In the crowded media landscape, a good headline is crucial to drawing readers into the piece. It should be intriguing and provocative enough to compel readers to explore the writer's viewpoint. Whether in print, broadcast, or social media, a strong headline can make a significant difference in attracting attention. The topic of the piece must be of current interest, resonating with the public and aligning with ongoing conversations. A timely, relevant subject matter

Political Reporting increases the likelihood of engagement, as it taps into the existing curiosity of readers. Additionally, the piece should have thematic unity, meaning that it should cohesively present the writer's argument without deviating from the central theme. A well-structured and rational presentation of ideas ensures that readers can follow the argument and understand the writer's perspective.
8.5.2 Characteristics of Effective Opinion Pieces
Effective opinion writing in media possesses several key characteristics that enhance its impact:
1. Timeliness: The relevance of the topic is paramount. Opinion pieces
need to address issues that are currently in the spotlight, reflecting what is on the minds of readers. As the pace of news and social media accelerates, readers demand instant analysis and commentary on unfolding events. Legendary editor R. Madhvan Nair emphasized the need for quick reaction, underscoring that a writer's ability to respond promptly to current issues is a vital skill in the media world.
2. Subject Knowledge and Expertise: A successful opinion writer
demonstrates deep knowledge of the subject. This expertise allows the writer to offer unique insights, providing value to readers who are already well-informed. In the age of information overload, readers expect well-researched and thoughtful analysis. Non-journalists who are subject matter experts often contribute opinion pieces, as their specialized knowledge adds credibility and authority to the discussion. A good opinion piece reflects a solid understanding of the topic's background, even if the writer does not delve into a historical overview.
3. Clarity of Viewpoint: Opinion writing thrives on a clear and defined
stance. Unlike news writing, where balance is sought, an opinion piece benefits from a strong, straightforward viewpoint. Readers appreciate forthrightness, as it helps them navigate the complexities of an issue and arrive at their conclusions. A clear, unwavering perspective allows readers to understand the writer's position without ambiguity.
4. Uniqueness of Opinion: Media audiences, especially younger readers,
seek novelty and fresh perspectives. A repetitive or conventional approach may fail to engage readers, who often look for new angles on familiar topics. Writers must strive to offer a distinctive viewpoint that adds something original to the ongoing discourse.
5. Understanding the Audience: While opinion writing is subjective, it is
crucial for the writer to have a strong sense of the audience's intellectual and emotional dynamics. The writer must balance imposing their viewpoint with ensuring that the piece resonates with the reader. While an opinion writer does not follow the "reader is king" rule of marketing, there is still a need to be mindful of how far the audience is willing to go along with the argument. A piece that is overly complex or alienating in tone risks losing readers, whereas simple and accessible language helps maintain engagement.

6. Avoiding Conflicts: Although opinion writing is about advocating for a Political Writing
particular viewpoint, it is advisable to avoid confrontations with opposing perspectives. The aim is to present a well-reasoned, logical argument rather than attacking other viewpoints. A sharp, aggressive tone may alienate readers and reduce the credibility of the writer. Instead, the focus should be on building a rational case for the writer's position, rather than dismissing alternative opinions outright.
8.5.3 Structuring an Opinion Piece
An effective opinion piece requires careful planning and structure. The introductory paragraph is of utmost importance, serving as the first impression of the writer's argument. A sharp, engaging introduction hooks the reader and sets the tone for the rest of the piece. Many editors decide whether to publish a piece based solely on the strength of the first few paragraphs, so getting the intro right is crucial. After the introduction, the body of the piece should delve into the core argument, providing evidence and analysis that supports the writer's viewpoint. The argument should be well-structured, with clear transitions between points. Short paragraphs and concise sentences help maintain the reader's interest. Finally, the conclusion should provide a strong closing statement, reinforcing the writer's main points and leaving a lasting impression on the reader. The conclusion should tie together the argument and offer a final insight that prompts readers to reflect on the issue.
8.5.4 Language, Style, and Editing
The language of an opinion piece should be clear and accessible. Overly complex or aggressive language can alienate readers, whereas straightforward and conversational writing helps to build a connection. As Bryon A. Garner suggests, writers should get to the point quickly, using language that is appropriate for the audience. Each word matters, and the writer must ensure that every sentence contributes meaningfully to the overall argument. After completing the piece, thorough editing and revision are essential. Writers should review their work to ensure that the argument is clear, the language is precise, and the overall message is consistent. A well-edited opinion piece stands out for its clarity and persuasive power, making it a valuable contribution to public discourse.

8.6 EDITORIAL WRITING
Editorials or leaders as they are often called are an essential and most important part of a newspaper or journal. These are written by the head of the editorial team or publisher of a newspaper or periodical journal. Editorials are for thinking people and not for a casual or non-serious readers. Leaders of ruling as well as opposition parties, bureaucrats, senior officers and diplomats read the views expressed in the editorials of good newspapers and news magazine with considerable seriousness.
8.6.1 News Paper Editorial
A journal can cover one or multiple themes, such as politics, economy, sports, science, health, environment, law, media, education, culture, religion, and international relations. Newspapers also range from national, regional to local levels, each with its specific readership. These publications may express differing or even conflicting ideologies. Editors write with their readers in mind, often reflected in editorials, which are considered the heart and soul of a journal. An editorial presents the opinion of the newspaper or journal on a particular issue, usually reflecting the views of the editorial board. Editorials originated from newsletters written by sea-goers, evolving after the development of Gutenberg's printing press in the 15th century. The first editorial appeared in the Courant in 1702. In India, newspapers like Hickey's Bengal Gazette (1780) and Raja Ram Mohan Roy's Sambad Kaumudi (1821) expressed strong views, a trend that continued with major newspapers like The Times of India and The Statesman. Although editorials are key to newspapers, their readership remains limited, attracting mainly serious- minded individuals who influence policy-making. Despite low readership, editorials remain a crucial component of public opinion, shaping the views of governments and society alike.
8.6.2 Content of an Editorial
Editorials differ from journal to journal, reflecting distinct thought streams. No two journals, whether daily, weekly, fortnightly, or monthly, are alike. Editorials are tailored to the overall content of a journal. We now live in an era of niche journals, where publications on topics like science, environment, or health will focus their editorials on these specific subjects. For example, a science journal will not publish an editorial on cricket, no matter how popular the sport may be.

Political Reporting Despite differences, editorials across all journals share common features. They reflect the journal's policy or "editorial line" on significant developments, using a persuasive approach to attract readers. Rational presentation, inviting writing styles, and clear structure--introduction, body, and conclusion--are all essential. A good editorial explains complex issues in simple terms, provides a new perspective, and refrains from personal attacks or name-calling. Constructive criticism, coupled with positive suggestions, leads to a conclusion that enhances readers' understanding. Editorials should also be timely, relevant to the readers, and concise, generally not exceeding 500 words. The language used must be simple, clear, and direct, avoiding slang or outdated expressions. Respectful and non- aggressive language leaves a lasting impression on readers.
8.6.3 Preparing to Write an Editorial
When writing an editorial, it is crucial to follow a clear direction and take specific steps. First, determine your objective before starting. Without a clear aim, you risk confusing readers, leaving them unsure of your message. Therefore, it's essential to establish what you want to convey and how to present it effectively.
Select a Topic
The topic is key when writing an editorial. The best topics are current issues already in the public domain, as they attract immediate attention and readership. Firm up Your Approach You should have a definite policy line on the issue. For instance, when discussing the abrogation of Article 370, you must choose a side and express your stance clearly in the editorial.
Do Basic Work
Craft an attention-grabbing headline and support your argument with facts, figures, and quotes. Develop your case steadily, with the strongest argument presented at the end to convince readers.
Keep Deadline in Mind
Always keep deadlines in mind, as editorial writing involves multiple revisions to ensure accuracy.
How to Write an Editorial
Follow this 10-point guide: choose a subject, present the issue clearly, offer a balanced view, use simple language, encourage critical thinking, keep it concise (500 words), avoid personal pronouns, revise thoroughly, edit carefully, and conclude effectively to leave an impact on readers.

9.0 INTRODUCTION
Development communication is an essential tool in fostering social change and improving the lives of marginalized communities in sustainable ways. Since its emergence, the field has evolved from a method of top-down information dissemination to one that emphasizes participatory approaches, where communication serves as a bridge between policymakers and the people they serve. Initially rooted in strategies to promote economic growth through government interventions and aid, development communication has expanded to encompass more inclusive and democratic processes, focusing on empowering citizens to engage in decision-making at the grassroots level. Today, development communication addresses critical concerns such as poverty, inequality, and social inclusion, especially in developing nations where vast populations experience systemic deprivation. The shift towards participatory communication has introduced a framework where media,

Development technology, and local engagement play significant roles in ensuring that Journalism development initiatives are shaped by the very communities they aim to uplift. In this unit, we will explore various approaches, including the role of media, participatory methods, and new technologies, to understand how development communication contributes to inclusive growth and the empowerment of people. In this unit, we shall discuss various pertinent issues relating to the concept of development communication and its potential as a tool for inclusive growth and empowerment.
9.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After going through the unit, you should be able to: * differentiate between different perspectives of development and the role of development Communication; * explain the concept of Development Communication; * describe the elements and philosophy of Development Communication; * explain the role of Media in Development; * discuss the scope of ICTs as a tool of empowerment; and * describe mechanisms of people's participation and the role of participatory communication in inclusive growth.
9.2 APPROACHES TO DEVELOPMENT
The country's Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth is frequently highlighted in news stories and is often equated with national development. However, many development practitioners and thinkers challenge this notion, arguing that economic indicators such as GDP and Gross National Product (GNP) are inadequate measures of true development. They advocate for the use of social indicators like the Human Development Index (HDI), Physical Quality of Life Index (PQLI), and Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI), which better reflect a nation's overall well-being and progress. The modern understanding of development has expanded to view it as a multidimensional process that improves both the economic and social conditions of a country. This approach also emphasizes enhancing people's freedoms, capabilities, and entitlements to lead better lives. While traditional issues of underdevelopment--such as poverty, health, hunger, food security, illiteracy, and unemployment--continue to afflict less developed countries, including India, the focus has shifted towards social inclusion, equitable growth, and social justice. These principles now shape both the development agenda and the role of development communication. Development communication addresses these challenges by promoting inclusive growth and social justice, with the aim of enabling marginalized communities to live dignified lives with equal opportunities. This approach emphasizes fostering equality and providing opportunities for all to achieve a productive and meaningful life with freedom and dignity. Through its

initiatives, development communication upholds values such as human Development Journalism: rights, equitable resource distribution, equal opportunities, peace, security,
Concept, Evolution,
and the fulfillment of human potential. As a result, development policies Historical must consider both social and economic challenges, addressing the multiple Perspective Debates deprivations faced by poor and marginalized groups.
Mainstreaming Gender and Marginalized Communities
One of the major challenges in development communication is the mainstreaming of gender and marginalized communities. Poverty not only worsen exacerbates existing inequalities but also deepens cycles of deprivation and underdevelopment. Gender inequality and the marginalization of communities are often closely linked. Women in India, for example, continue to face multiple layers of deprivation and constitute one of the most neglected and poorest segments of society. Similarly, marginalized communities such as Dalits, tribals, and other backward groups are trapped in poverty due to limited access to education, healthcare, employment, and communication services. Sustainable economic growth and human development are reliant on the equal participation of women and marginalized sections of society. Development policies, governance issues, and planning must be approached with a focus on inclusion and exclusion. Empowering these communities by giving them a stronger voice and prioritizing their needs is crucial for their integration into mainstream society and for national development.
Environmental Sustainability
Development communication also plays a pivotal role in promoting the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly the principle of environmental sustainability. It supports efforts to empower communities to address the environmental challenges they face. Successful strategies require a blend of traditional and scientific knowledge, robust policy discussions, and collaboration between governments, corporations, and civil society at both national and global levels.
Institution Building
Building the capacity of development professionals and strengthening the institutional infrastructure of organizations involved in development are critical for enhancing the effectiveness of development initiatives and ensuring efficient use of resources. Development communication supports the creation of strong, vibrant institutions that foster freedom of expression, allowing all groups to voice their opinions and engage in development debates. Independent media, which serves the public interest, plays a key role in ensuring transparency and accountability in development programs and involving diverse stakeholders in meaningful discussions.

Development 9.3 CONCEPT OF DEVELOPMENT Journalism
COMMUNICATION
Let us now examine the term 'Development Communication'. Several scholars have provided definitions of Development Communication that vary in their perspectives. These definitions not only help to understand the boundaries that define the field of development communication but also better comprehend how it has expanded in its nature and scope.
9.3.1 Definitions
One of the earliest definitions was provided by Nora Quebral. According to her (1975), "development communication is the art and science of human communication applied to the speedy transformation of a country and the mass of its people from poverty to a dynamic state of economic growth that makes possible greater social equality and the larger fulfilment of the human potential." Quebral highlights the importance of development communication for not just informing and persuading people to adopt new ideas and technologies but also understanding the root cause of people's problems, inequality and marginalisation that they face. These insights need to be combined with the theory and practice of communication for creatively developing appropriate programmes and media strategy for alleviating poverty and improving people's quality of life. According to Everett Rogers (1983) "development communication refers to the uses to which communication is put in order to further development. Such applications are intended to either further development in a general way, such as by increasing the level of the mass media exposure among a nation's citizens, in order to create a favourable 'climate' for development, or to support a specific development programme or project (this type of development communication is often termed as 'development-support communication' DSC"). Rogers, in his Diffusion theory focused upon the application of communication for the purpose of disseminating information and messages to induce change. The flow of information (mostly one-way), help create a suitable environment by providing relevant information and effective messages for persuading people to adopt new ideas or innovations at a fast pace. F. Rosario Braid is of the opinion that development communication is "an element of the management process and the overall planning and implementation of development programmes". And in a broad sense, "the identification and utilisation of appropriate expertise in the development process that will assist in increasing participation of intended beneficiaries at the grassroots level." While Erskine Childers in her definition said "Development support communications is a discipline in development planning and implementation in which more adequate account is taken of human behavioural factors in the design of development projects and their objectives". Thus, development communication plays a key role in engaging people and understanding their varied perspectives and ideas. Incorporating people's viewpoints in the various processes of development projects enables 118 projects to become more people-centric, leading to greater receptivity

towards new ideas, ownership of projects and their consequent success. Development Journalism: In 1997, through Article 9 of General Assembly Resolution 51/172, the Concept, Evolution, Historical United Nations adopted the following definition "Communication for
Perspective Debates
development stresses the need to support two-way communication systems that enable dialogue and that allow communities to speak out, express their aspirations and concerns and participate in the decisions that relate to their development". The Rome Consensus of the First World Congress of Communication for Development (WCCD), held in Rome in October 2009 defined it as: "a social process based on dialogue using a broad range of tools and methods. It is also about seeking change at different levels, including listening, building trust, sharing knowledge and skills, building policies, debating and learning for sustained and meaningful change. It is not public relations or corporate communications". These definitions focus not only upon the participatory nature of development communication but also on its transactional nature and the opportunities that need to be created for people to freely articulate their ideas and dialogue about issues most relevant to them. Focusing upon both the socio-cultural context as well as people's capacities; they draw attention to the diverse factors that can influence integration of multiple voices in development programmes and policies and action towards sustainable change. From above definitions you would have understood that development communication does not merely involve the transmission of information about products, ideas and or facilities for improving peoples' lives, or the exchange of information for problem-solving. It extends to include developing empathy for others, raising aspirations, building new skills and capacities as well as increasing peoples' participation in development activities. Interweaving both mass media and interpersonal communication systems, development communication helps people to understand the linkages between local events and national and global issues; develop new perspectives as well as nurture relationships between different stakeholders' groups, for effective management of development activities and realising the full benefits of development.
9.3.2 Philosophy
Communication for Development differs from other forms of communication, such as corporate and internal communications. Corporate communication helps to build organisational identity and communicate organisational values, mission and activities consistently to the public. Internal communication on the other hand is the flow of information within an organisation and enables timely and effective communications among staff for greater coordination, work efficiency and outputs. Development Communication is a specialised field differing from others because of the role it plays in empowerment processes. It strives towards sustainable change by involving different stakeholders, establishing a conducive environment and use appropriate media and methods for inducing behaviour and social change. Development Communication can be further differentiated from other fields 119

Development by three aspects, i.e. it is Purposive, one looks for specific behavioural Journalism objectives; Positive, affirmative prosocial values are attached to what one communicates about; and Pragmatic, practical and having specific purpose, it is evaluated by the results achieved (Jamias,1975). For example, as a Development communicator, one looks for specific behavioural objectives, such as adoption of high yielding variety of seeds by farmers. This can increase their harvest manifold and hence has a definite positive value attached to it. The development communicator plans interventions knowing well that mere increase in the flow of information does not necessarily result in behavioural changes desired. The intervention efficacy is later revaluated by examining what were the objectives, the intended results, what led to the success/failure of the communication. In this regard, feedback is taken from different stakeholders and not merely by the communication activities performed, such as the number of posters printed or visits made and so on.
9.3.3 Features of Development Communication
From the analysis above, the following key features of Development Communication emerge:
* Communication as a Catalyst for Human Development: Effective
communication is essential for fostering human growth and progress. Using communication strategically for development positively impacts human development.
* Integral to Development Programs: Development Communication
plays a vital role in initiatives and programs aimed at achieving development goals. It also challenges existing hierarchies and power structures to promote equitable and sustainable development outcomes. * Participation as a Core Principle: Meaningful participation is crucial to development communication. It ensures that the voices of the poor and marginalized are heard and integrated into development programs and policy-making processes.
* Dialogic Processes for Empowerment: Development and
empowerment practices are rooted in dialogic, two-way communication. These horizontal processes prioritize communication systems that are sensitive to local contexts, enabling people to openly discuss and deliberate issues affecting their well-being.
* Creating a Collaborative Environment: Development Communication
fosters a constructive environment where stakeholders can collectively identify problems, reach common understanding, explore ideas, negotiate, and find solutions together.
* Contextual Analysis and Empowerment: Development
communication involves analyzing the socio-economic and political contexts of communities, prioritizing their needs, assessing risks and opportunities, empowering people, and strengthening local institutions. * Multimedia Approach: A variety of communication methods are utilized, including interpersonal communication, mass media, and ICTs, to disseminate information, promote behavior change, mobilize 120 communities, and advocate for sustainable social change.

Each society has some traditional values that give people an identity, a sense of belonging and within which their aspirations are intricately embedded. Communication can play a very vital role by making people aware of differing values and beliefs, critically examine new ideas as well re-analyse the relevance and richness of their own values, customs, beliefs and, above all, aspirations in changing contexts. Development 9.4 MEDIA AND DEVELOPMENT Journalism
COMMUNICATIONS
As the concept of development communication has evolved with time, consequently the nature of communications and the role of media have also changed focus. Earlier it was expected to convey all the relevant information regarding a development programme and the benefits that may be reaped by the community. Media was expected to build a favourable climate to implement such programmes by removing doubts, apprehensions or fears about them. Development communications was characterised by the use of mass media that considered people as passive audiences ready to be influenced by the messages they received, and was simple one-way asymmetrical communication (Mefalopulous, 2008). Later the focus of Development Communication moved from a 'communicator' to a more 'receiver-centric' orientation. Advocating 'bottom up' two-way symmetrical approaches it recognises and adopts various participatory methods for inclusion and active participation of the target audience. The emphasis of Development Communication processes has shifted from persuasion to information exchange; from information transmitted to the meaning sought and attributed by audience groups; and disseminating information for which there is a need than creating a need for the information being disseminated.
9.4.1 Mass Media
Mass media as you are aware play a significant role in taking development to the people. Being able to reach large number of heterogeneous audiences scattered over vast geographical area, their ability to provide the same messages simultaneously to a vast and diversified audience remains unparalleled. They have a definite role in spreading information about development, making people aware of their rights and responsibilities, exposing anomalies and corrupt practices, and promoting transparency and accountability through encouraging participation in of development schemes. By not only reporting facts about specialised areas of development, it also strives to provide an interpretation and analysis. Communication interventions for development are made through various media platforms such as the newspapers magazines, radio, TV, Internet or movies and theatres etc. In a country like India, where literacy level is low, the choice of mass media is of vital importance, as they reach out to different groups of audiences. The Satellite Instructional Television Experiment (SITE, 1975-79) was one of the earliest projects primarily undertaken to develop special development programmes through the satellite
communication. Later the Kheda Communication Project, the Indian National
Satellite project (INSAT) (1982); Educational programmes (ETV) Gyan- Darshan Educational Channel (2000); E-Choupal and others have demonstrated the potential of using mass media for Development.
122 The mass media has played a particularly positive role in enlightening

farmers on the use of various technologies to boost agricultural development; Development Journalism: Women programmes cover a range of subjects related to empowerment of
Concept, Evolution,
women as well as programmes on a range of topics like health, sanitation, Historical family planning, education, conduct of democratic exercises like free and fair Perspective Debates elections and monitoring of expenditure or implementation of development plans are some areas media has focused upon.
9.4.2 Alternative Media
Recent years have seen the emergence of a range of alternative, participatory media forms that are separate from and provide an alternative to commercial media as well as state-run public-service media. Also called 'community media,' 'citizen's media,' 'grassroot journalism' it has created local alternatives to mainstream broadcasting like local community newspapers, radio stations, as well as traditional media such as theatre and puppetry. Differing from mainstream media in their aesthetics, independent non-profit orientation, non-dominant discourse and serving the needs and interests of a community it enables peoples participation and their greater access and control of the media and communications in their community. Contesting and challenging mainstream media discourses, community media aids in raising people's awareness, representation and the consequent emergence and democratisation of an alternative public sphere. Some of the most successful alternative media for development are community radio, community video, and community newspapers.
9.4.3 Traditional Media
Traditional cultural forms such as peoples' theatre, puppets, song and dance are also being designed to engage people and communities in positive social change. Sensitive to the needs and context of the communities, folk media are an integral part of the fabric of rural communities. Social ideas, tradition and culture are preserved and disseminated through these highly intimate, flexible and dynamic, traditional media forms. Enjoying immense popularity and appeal they have traditionally been used for entertainment, social communication and persuasive communication. Now, several initiatives have involved folk media for conveying development messages. By presenting messages subtly in local popular artistic forms, they carry the message of development among the masses. Indian People Theatre Association (IPTA), used some of the popular regional theatre forms like "Jaatra" of Bengal, "Bhavai" of Gujrat, "Tamasha" of Maharashtra and "Burkatha" of Andhra Pradesh to increase social awareness and political education. Other initiatives include the Kerala Sastra Sahithya Parishad (KSSP) which organised Science Jathas, a science procession using different folk art forms to spread the message of people's involvement in the development process. The International Planned Parenthood Federation and UNESCO used traditional media for promoting family planning. Folk songs have played a very important in the Chipko and Narmada movements.

Development Organisations like Katkatha for puppetry, Jan Sanskriti, Sahmat and several Journalism theatre groups are using the traditional media innovatively for spreading messages to both urban and rural audiences.
9.5 DEVELOPMENT COMMUNICATION AND
NEW TECHNOLOGIES
The rapid evolution of communication technologies--such as the Internet, Information and Communication Technologies (ICT), mobile phones, and satellites--continues to revolutionize the concept and practice of both development and communication. In current times, these technologies are deeply embedded in our increasingly digital and interconnected societies, where communication networks play a central role in how citizens connect and engage with one another. Access to these technologies is now a key determinant of inclusion and participation in the development process. The ability to exchange information instantly and transcend time and space barriers offers immense potential for addressing various challenges, particularly in sectors like governance, healthcare, and education. Many countries, including India, have developed technology-enabled systems to enhance the efficiency and reach of development programs. Real-time data from these technologies allows for improved monitoring, better decision- making, and more efficient disbursement of benefits, ensuring that goods and services reach underserved populations. E-governance initiatives have expanded, offering citizens faster, more inclusive access to essential services such as clean drinking water, healthcare, electricity, and other civic amenities. These systems also contribute to transparency and accountability by reducing corruption through streamlined grievance redressal mechanisms. New technologies remain affordable, user-friendly, and accessible, creating new opportunities for two-way communication. They enable people to express their ideas, access relevant information, and engage with development initiatives. For example, farmers now receive real-time weather and market information via mobile phones, ASHA workers receive health alerts for monitoring pregnant women, and beneficiaries are notified via SMS when funds or entitlements are transferred into their accounts. Additionally, the availability of government scheme data on websites helps to further minimize corruption. The integration of these technologies is reshaping the field of development communication, giving it new direction and empowering citizens to actively participate in the development process. Through these innovations, the relationship between governments and citizens is evolving, making development more inclusive, transparent, and accountable.
Technology and the Digital Divide
The digital divide continues to highlight the separation between the "digital haves" and "have-nots," with education and wealth enabling certain groups to benefit more from Information and Communication Technologies (ICTs) than others. This divide serves as a major barrier to leveraging technology for 124 poverty alleviation and reducing inequality. Access to digital technology

offers users advantages in terms of skills, knowledge, capabilities, and Development Journalism: increased income, which, in turn, widens the gap between those who have
Concept, Evolution,
access and those who do not. One of the most pressing challenges for Historical development communication today is bridging this digital divide by Perspective Debates empowering those excluded from the digital world to access ICTs and digital services. Differences in the availability, access, and use of these technologies pose significant challenges. In India, a large segment of the population remains digitally illiterate, requiring basic training in computer use as well as digital communication skills. Gender disparities and socio-cultural barriers further restrict access to ICTs for certain communities, particularly women and marginalized groups. Researchers have emphasized that the success of ICTs as tools for social change depends on how they are integrated into specific local contexts and tailored to meet the unique needs of communities. Moreover, there is growing concern that new technologies are increasingly dominated by vested interests and market-driven forces, turning high-tech systems into instruments of exclusion rather than inclusion. The commercialization of these technologies risks deepening inequalities if access and benefits remain limited to more privileged groups. Despite these challenges, ICTs continue to play a pivotal role in development communication. Beyond their use in information dissemination, digital technologies have great potential to support horizontal communication processes, allowing for greater collaboration and engagement. Innovations such as Interactive Voice Response (IVR) systems, mobile apps, low-power technologies used by community radio stations, and participatory video projects are proving to be powerful tools in promoting people's participation and empowerment. By harnessing these technologies effectively, development communication can contribute to more inclusive growth and social change, even amidst the digital divide.
9.6 PARTICIPATION OF PEOPLE AND
DEVELOPMENT COMMUNICATION
As discussed earlier, people's participation is a cornerstone of Development Communication. Inclusive development is impossible without the active involvement of communities in various stages of development initiatives. However, the extent of participation can vary greatly--from mere tokenism to genuine, proactive engagement--and is often influenced by existing power imbalances, issues of empowerment, and inequality within communities. True and meaningful participation requires a deeper understanding and implementation of two-way, participatory communication processes, which enable communities to actively contribute to and shape development projects. Misinterpretations of participation must be avoided, as only authentic involvement can lead to sustainable, inclusive growth.
9.6.1 Participatory Communication
A dynamic, interactional, and transformative process, participatory communication enables people to articulate their ideas, recognise common 125

Development concerns, and seek solutions from within their community. By generating an Journalism open environment, participatory processes enable stakeholders to engage in dialogic processes, build trust and confidence among each other. Consequently, they lead to raising awareness about critical issues, improving access to information, increase utilisation of services, mobilise people around a common issue and encourage them to engage in their own and their communities' development (Singhal, 2003). All participatory communication activities ultimately endeavour to encourage certain changes in attitude or behaviour at the individual, family, and/or community levels. Underpinning participatory communication is the idea of providing communication rights for ordinary citizens. Providing a voice to the voiceless they stress the need to create alternate communication spaces for the poor and the marginalised that strengthen the diversity of cultures and languages in ways not provided by the conventional media. The movement for communication rights was spearheaded by the UNESCO and the MacBride Commission through its report (1980), Many Voices, One World. The Commission highlighted the problems of commercialisation of media, unequal access to information and communication and of a rising communication deficit in the developing and under-developed countries. The commission called for democratisation of communication and this became the basis of many community media projects throughout the world including the community radio movement in India.
9.6.2 Participatory Democracy
Participation is strongly related to the power dynamics in decision making. Letting the poor and marginalised make strategic decisions about programmes and policies influencing their lives involves devolution of power. The 73rd and 74th Amendments of the Indian Constitution provide a participatory framework by giving powers to panchayats and urban local bodies and subsequently for people being in-charge of development of their areas. A significant aspect of these provisions is planning by people through locally constituted District Planning Committees (DPCs) who consolidate and implement plans prepared by the village panchayats and urban municipalities. The success or failure of these plans, and thereby the future of development depends significantly on the citizens' awareness levels and participation through effective communication strategies. Another very important aspect of participatory development is the community monitoring of development schemes. The MG-NREGS has the objective of providing rural employment, and enhancing livelihood security. The scheme also has the provision that the Gram Panchayat hold regular social audits of all development works by making available all relevant documents to the gram sabha.
9.6.3 Policy Formulation and Citizens' Participation
The task of creating awareness and promoting citizen participation in policy formulation is one of the new challenges of development communication. There is a near absence of institutional mechanisms for ordinary citizens to 126 intervene in the processes of legislations or policy making, and policy

making continues to be treated as a matter of expert knowledge, mostly left to Development Journalism: the 'specialist' and not something which can be shared with ordinary citizens.
Concept, Evolution,
Historical The inclusion of ordinary people in policy formulation has become all the
Perspective Debates
more important in the post-liberalisation era when the state has retreated from some key areas in the economy leaving space for the private sector or Public Private Partnerships. It is in this backdrop that the citizens' participation is required to check the possibility of the policy process being dominated by powerful vested interest groups and has direct bearing on inclusive development. 9.7 LET US SUM UP
In this unit, we explored how both the concepts of development and communication are evolving in today's rapidly changing world. It was emphasized that a high GDP growth rate does not necessarily equate to inclusive growth. Traditional top-down, economic growth-driven models are increasingly being replaced by culturally sensitive, participatory approaches that focus on including marginalized and vulnerable communities in the development process. We examined various definitions that broaden the scope of development communication, emphasizing the importance of fostering empathy, raising aspirations, building skills and capacities, and encouraging active participation in development activities. The role of development communication in empowerment, guided by its philosophical foundations of being positive, purposive, and pragmatic, helps us understand its broader impact. Development communication employs a variety of media--mass media, 127

Development community media, and ICTs--to disseminate information, promote behavior Journalism change, mobilize communities, and advocate for sustainable social change. A key focus is on enhancing people's participation and giving them a greater voice through participatory communication. This approach aims to raise citizens' awareness, encourage their engagement with governance, and promote greater transparency and accountability in the development and policymaking process.
9.8 KEYWORDS
Development Communication: The strategic use of communication to foster social change, address inequalities, and empower marginalized communities through participatory and inclusive approaches. Participatory Communication: A two-way interactive process enabling communities to voice their concerns and actively shape development initiatives for sustainable change. Sustainable Development: An approach to development focused on environmental conservation, social equity, and long-term community well-being. Human Development Index (HDI): A composite measure of development assessing life expectancy, education, and per capita income to evaluate overall well-being.

10.0 INTRODUCTION
The mandate of a mass media is to disseminate important and latest information to a wider audience. Such information pertains to an array of subjects, viz. politics, economy, banking, art, culture, music, education etc. In this context, information which particularly concerns development agenda is clubbed under Development Journalism. Development Coverage is reporting on topics related to economic, human and socioeconomic development. It is aimed at actively participating in the social and economic uplift by reporting and analysing government policies and major events that have a bearing on development. For example, press coverage of a conference on the 'Impact of Global Warming' would come under the purview of development journalism. Another example could be writing a series of articles to highlight the impact of vehicular emissions on health and ecology.

10.2 DEVELOPMENT COVERAGE
The era of development journalism began once nations started to focus more on issues of human and sustainable development in addition to the headline- grabbing topics of politics, wars, food, society, entertainment, business etc. It is reckoned that development journalism began in the 1960s with a renewed focus on analysing government projects and their impact on human development. Today, development coverage spans issues of poverty, healthcare, education, clean energy, sustainability, global warming, climate change, waste disposal etc.
10.2.1 Brief Introduction
Journalist and communicator Shelton A Gunarantne described development journalism as an integral part of new journalism that involves analytical interpretation, subtle investigation, constructive criticism and serious association with the grass roots. It is a stream of mass communication to "participate in the social, economic and cultural upliftment of the society by reporting and analysing policies, events and trends that have a bearing on the society's development." The role of a development journalist is to examine critically the existing development programmes and projects, compare the planned project with its actual implementation, and report any observed shortcomings. It seeks to inform readers, listeners or viewers about a gamut of developmental schemes and programmes implemented and executed by the government departments and their agencies.
10.2.2 Development Coverage in India
In India, development journalism broadly aligned with the launch of the flagship Five Year Plans in the early 1950s. The Plans were formulated to bolster the socioeconomic development of India, which had then recently freed itself of the long yoke of British rule. The media outlets of newspapers, magazines and radio enthusiastically followed up on the stories weaved around the successive Five Year Plans, and the hits and misses of its programmes. Today, Right to Information (RTI) Act is a potent tool for the tribe of development journalists in India.

Development The 'Chipko Movement' of 1970s and the anti-Tehri Dam movement (1980s Journalism to early 2000s) were spearheaded by green activist Sunder Lal Bahuguna for the preservation of Himalayan forests. He urged the government to shelve the Tehri Dam Project claiming the proposed site fell under an active seismic zone and building such a large dam could be ecologically catastrophic. Bahuguna's protests were widely tracked and covered by the mass media in India India is a vibrant democracy with a population of nearly 1.4 billion people belonging to different states, religions, ethnic backgrounds and socioeconomic strata. Such a diverse kaleidoscope of humanity has a plethora of issues that concerns economic and human development. Today, with increasing social activities and proliferation of social media outlets, people's dependency on mass media has become more pronounced than ever. Moreover, the number and scope of development programmes have increased. Therefore, the success of any public welfare programmes depends on the strategic use of mass media. In this context, the development coverage in India has witnessed a steady increase in both quantum and quality keeping pace with the growing awareness among the people about such issues. For example, the global conferences on climate change such as the United Nations backed Conference of the Parties (COP) is widely covered by the various newspapers, TV channels, digital platforms, magazines etc. The legacy media outlets including The Times of India, Hindustan Times etc routinely run campaigns to highlight the issues of livelihood, rights, women empowerment, employment opportunities, global warming etc to engage with the readers through in depth reportage and interactive columns.
10.2.3 Elements of Development Coverage
Developmental journalism has the propensity to become an active partner of the government to discover which policies should be pursued for greater benefit of the masses. A development reporter is essentially an independent investigator with a deep knowledge of the subject. S/he could be considered as a critic to point out the lapses and the pitfalls in the existing policies framed by the government. The journalist raises the voices of the people, especially those unheard and the disadvantaged groups such as landless labourers or peasants. A meaningful Development Coverage would tend to force us to re-think our development goals and strategies due to data backed reportage and succinct presentation of facts, while suggesting plausible remedies for the underlying malady. It is advisable that development coverage encompasses the following elements for greater impact: - a) A development reporter should exercise caution in collecting data from a reliable source, and if possible crosscheck for any bias or inaccuracy inadvertently seeping in. It would be in the interest of the report to interact with key officials involved in decision making and/or executing projects that form the basis of the report. Care should be taken to take the 132 version and feedback of the both the sides in the report for credibility.

b) The reporter should shun any bias before writing so that it is given a Development Coverage in India: balanced treatment, and letting the readers decide on the basis of their
Print, Electronics
wisdom. For example, the reporter could be personally in favour of and New Media allowing land acquisition of fertile land for setting up of food processing industries in the rural areas. However, the reporter while writing a report on this development should refrain from expressing his/her opinion or giving weightage to the parties favouring the land acquisition. The best course of action is to give a fair account of the development by giving voices to both the sides. c) Since development coverage is cliched and full of scientific jargons, the reporter should try to maintain a free writing style with simple and short sentences for easy and intelligible reading. The accompanying data, charts, graphics, analysis should be presented in easy understandable format. The jargons or complex terms such as wholesale price index (WPI) should be explained in layman's terms. d) The use of data charts and graphics not only add weight to reports but makes it more appealing for readers, researchers, policymakers, officials, departments etc. The government agencies closely track such reports, and an erudite report is sure to attract the attention of authorities for any course correction, which is fundamentally the purpose of such reportage. It could pertain to garbage disposal, vector- borne diseases, lack of healthcare etc. Write a report in about 500 words to highlight the issue, offering valid suggestions.
