13.3 IDENTIFYING TOPICS IN SOLUTIONS
JOURNALISM
Solutions journalism as an approach to news is evolving both as a concept and in functional areas. Owing to the rapid technological advancements, the landscape of social and economic challenges is fast changing. For example, the contemporary issues of global warming and climate change impacting health, livelihood, social behaviour etc today appear appropriate topics of inquiry than they seemed plausible 10 years back. To this list, we may also add artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) phenomenon, being embedded in every conceivable segment of society, business, professional etc with profound influence on our social, cultural and psychological patterns. In this backdrop, news organisations are striving to discover and redefine how best to tell socially relevant stories. Solutions journalism is filling this gap as a potent tool. Solutions-oriented approach comprises voices, which have the potency to combat social and economic problems, as also those who have been directly impacted. This back-and-forth narrative gives deeper insight into issues than traditional news stories lack. As such, media outlets tend to choose a set of issues that majorly besets the local community. It could pertain to healthcare, education, jobs, farm distress, financial illiteracy, consumerism, discrimination, sanitation, opportunities etc. According to an apt commentary, "Solutions journalism stems from a culmination of several journalistic experiments that reflect a never-ending goal of the profession trying to figure out how to engage audiences with the news."
13.3.1 Planning Solutions Stories/Reports
Solutions journalism is a rigorous, evidence-based reporting on responses to social problems. Therefore, it involves collecting and analysing evidence, and qualitative or quantitative data. Solutions journalism could focus on a past or present problem. However, it is advisable that a solutions journalist does not fall in the trap of such writing that merely waxes eloquent on a person or is perceived just a publicity stunt. A solutions story is not about hero-worship, but focuses on a systemic 177

Public Policy and problem. It should not seek to favour an acquaintance nor should it foster Media activism. According to media practitioners Kyuwon Lee and Rhiannon Davies, a solutions reporter should first identify an issue, then ask what is missing from public conversation, and then start looking for sources for a solutions story. A mine of good solutions story could potentially emerge from sources including think tanks, policy experts, academic experts, datasets, authorities, victims, innovators, Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) professionals, local community ecosystem, fellow solutions journalists etc.
13.3.2 Story Structure
Once a solutions journalist has ascertained, after due diligence, a topic for storytelling, a few questions are worth considering. These include: - * How does the response work? * What parts of the problem are not addressed by the response? * Where did this idea emerge, and is it being replicated elsewhere? * What does the research and critics say? * Effectiveness of the response? Eventually solutions journalism is plainly good journalism, yet such stories are structured differently owing to their welfare objective. The different approaches to solutions journalism are: - stories that explore a positive deviant; one that explains a new idea; one that discusses an ongoing experiment; and one that explores how a community/locality has been transformed. For example, a solutions story could narrate the success of a slum transforming into a tidy civic habitation with the joint efforts of the local municipality, civil society, CSR activities and non-government organisations (NGO). Another story could detail a path breaking experiment in progress to develop a vaccine to protect against vector-borne diseases in the tropical countries like India.
13.3.3 Writing Techniques
Basically, writing technique(s) would depend upon the individual journalist and the topic at hand as to whether the story is in a plain news format or drafted in a long feature format. The following strategies are intended to help a solutions reporter arrive at an informed conclusion in this regard: - * Nearly every issue could be genuinely presented as a solutions news story. * New government programmes are readymade topics for reporting. For example, if the local authorities launch a new programme, the reporter could refer to similar programmes started in other communities elsewhere and the outcome. * Interact openly with sources and officials tasked with implementing the community programme. For example, if the reporter picks up a new

healthcare initiative, then talking to the healthcare officials would add Solutions Journalism heft to the narrative. * Be curious, inquisitive and persistent. Identifying sources and drafting questions that meet the objectives of the solutions is the key. * Never overload the story with evidences to keep the news crisp. * Observing fellow solutions journalists would help in keeping abreast of the evolving reporting template. * Keep the readers hooked through tension in the news report. In a solutions-oriented story, the tension could be portrayed in the headline as "How will they mitigate this problem that has failed others?"
13.3.4 Taking Interviews
For a more impactful story, a reporter must ideally think beyond the basic reporting structures. Only interview people who do not have vested interest in the outcome of the intervention, and consider where your sources get their funding. After preliminary research is the time to interview the stakeholders, comprising concerned authorities, affected persons, critics, donors, experts, activists etc. A few points would come handy before conducting interviews: - * Frame questions to highlight the process rather than individual(s) leading the response. What matters is the knowledge in his/her actions rather than the personality. This approach works as a filter to avoid glorification. * The interviewer must adhere to the basic objective of creating an unbiased news story containing measureable parameters, which are comparable and also commonly understood. * Give equal weightage to the voices of impacted people. Having a personal conversation extracts finer nuances to the response under inquiry. * Keep the tenor of the interview positive rather than skeptical so that the interviewee candidly airs his/her opinions and insights.
13.3.5 Vetting and Fact Checking
The judgment required for a solutions new story is akin to judgment needed to identify a good problem story. A solutions reporter must remember the following points: - * Avoid hyping the response, and claiming that the underlying problem is resolved. Do not claim that the response was the best response to a social issue. As with a normal story, evidence is not just data but it could be surmised from peer reviews, interviews and talking to experts. No solution is perfect; therefore make sure the report includes limitations. * A solutions story must include informed skeptics who do not have vested interest in either the social issue or its resolution. It lends credibility to

Public Policy and the report. Media * Remember there is a possibility of a bias creeping into the report during the process of collating information and data. Therefore, the reporter must not rush to believe what the sources state/claim unless they provide some evidence to support their stance.
13.3.6 Case Study
The Association for Democratic Reforms (ADR) was established in 1999 by a group of professors from the Indian Institute of Management (IIM), Ahmedabad. In 1999, the ADR filed a Public Interest Litigation (PIL) with Delhi High Court for the disclosure of the criminal, financial and educational background of the candidates contesting elections. Based on this, the Supreme Court in 2002, and subsequently in 2003, made it mandatory for candidates to disclose criminal, financial and educational background by filing an affidavit with the Election Commission of India (ECI). In 2002, ADR conducted its first 'Election Watch' for Gujarat assembly elections whereby detailed analysis of the backgrounds of candidates was provided to the electorate in order to help them make an informed choice during polling. Now, ADR conducts Election Watches for nearly all state and parliament elections. It conducts multiple projects aimed at increasing transparency in the political and electoral system of India. Its reports are widely covered in the mass media, and form the basis of an array of reportage on polling, elections, voting, candidates, electoral reforms etc. Check Your Progress 2 Note: 1) Use the space below for your answers

13.4 CRITICISM OF SOLUTIONS JOURNALISM
Solutions journalism is not without criticism, and skeptics claim it delves into 'hero worship' rather than critically examining social issues. Since, there is a renewed awareness towards social and human development, the critics point out that the news organisations at times leverage the format for roping in sponsors and advertisers for solutions articles and campaigns, just milking the approach for increasing revenues. The naysayers also point out to the potential bias in solutions reports since there is possibility of the journalist breaching the fine line between reporting on responses and advocacy. Moreover, some believe that solutions reporters lack adequate knowledge and understanding of the subject matter to write news stories that truly represent the actual state of affairs.
13.5 ADVOCATES OF SOLUTIONS JOURNALISM
On the other hand, solutions approach proponents maintain that a proper evidence-based reporting mitigates potential bias in the news. The US-based Solutions Journalism Network (SJN) is an independent, non-profit organisation that advocates an approach of solutions journalism, an evidence- based mode of reporting on the responses to problems. SJN has collaborated with countless news organisations to foster investigative journalism and solutions-oriented projects. Similar organisations in different countries are working to promote solutions journalism across different media spectrums and focussing on varied socioeconomic domains. These include Boston Globe, Public Radio International (PRI) The World, Center for Investigative Reporting etc.
13.6 NEW MEDIA & SOLUTIONS JOURNALISM
The advent of the new media has changed the practice of journalism. With internet, it has become easier for journalists to make news stories. The new media which rides on digital technology serves as a platform for publication, gathering and disseminating information.

Public Policy and Today, all media houses have online versions, which gives readers prompt Media access to news stories over smartphones, laptops etc. However, in the clamour for speed, there is always the risk of overlooking vital aspects. This could either result in half-baked news or lacking in credibility due to the lack of proper fact checking. Now, anyone with access to communication and electronic gadgets such as smartphones is a potential citizen journalist on social media networks, personal websites, digital platforms etc. Since, this template lacks any formal news filter process, the information thus shared does not meet the journalism parameters, and earns negative sentiments for journalism as well as solutions journalism. While the new media has led to the democratisation of the spectrum, it has also opened the floodgates for potential fake news, propaganda and marketing blitzkrieg. 14.0 INTRODUCTION
Public policy is an essential tool used by governments to address the needs and challenges of society. From ancient monarchies to modern democracies, public policies have been central to governance, helping governments respond to various social, economic, and political issues. Public policies encompass the actions taken by governmental institutions to achieve specific outcomes and are shaped by the political landscape in which they operate. This unit delves into the complex relationship between politics and policy, examining how political decisions influence policy formulation and implementation. It explores the meaning of public policy, its characteristics, and the different types that exist. Understanding public policy is crucial because it affects nearly every aspect of daily life, from healthcare and education to environmental protection and economic stability. The unit also outlines the stages involved in the public policy process, offering insights into how policies are developed, implemented, and evaluated. By the end of this unit, learners will gain a deeper understanding of public policy, its significance, and the factors that shape its creation and evolution in contemporary society.

14.2 RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN POLITICS AND
PUBLIC POLICY
Before discussing the meaning of public policy, it would be better if we are clear about the relationship between public policy and politics. Policy making process is a part of politics and political action. According to Gabriel Almond, political system is a set of interactions having structures, each of which performs its functions in order to keep it like an ongoing concern; it is a set of processes that routinely converts inputs into outputs. Almond classifies inputs of political systems into generic functional categories like political socialisation and recruitment, interest aggregation, interest articulation, and political communication. Output activities are those which are carried on by a political system in response to demands or stresses placed upon the system in the form of inputs. Outputs can take the form of governmental policies, programs, decisions, etc. Another model on the politics-policy relationship is the Feedback or the 'Black Box Model' coined by David Easton. According to this model, the remaining demands which have not been included in the decisions and policies will again be fed back through the same process for the purpose of its conversion into decisions. These two models establish clearly the relationship between politics and policies in a political system.
14.3 MEANING OF PUBLIC POLICY
There are various studies about public policy and many scholars have attempted to define public policy from different angles. Before explaining the meaning of public policy, let us first go through some of its definitions. Robert Eyestone terms public policy as "the relationship of government unit to its environment." Thomas R. Dye says that "public policy is whatever government chooses to do or not to do." Richard Rose says that "public policy is not a decision, it is a course or pattern of activity." In Carl J. Friedrich's opinion, public policy is a proposed course of action of a person, group, or government within a given environment, providing opportunities and obstacles which the policy was proposed to utilize and overcome in an effort to reach a goal or realize an objective or purpose. From these definitions, it is clear that public policies are governmental decisions and are actually the result of activities that the government undertakes in pursuance of certain goals and objectives. It can also be said that public policy formulation and implementation involve a well-planned 189

Public Policy and pattern or course of activity. It requires a thoroughly close-knit relation and Media interaction between the important governmental agencies, viz., the political executive, legislature, bureaucracy, and judiciary. The following points will make the nature of public policy clearer:
1. Public policies are goal-oriented. Public policies are formulated and
implemented in order to attain the objectives which the government has in view for the ultimate benefit of the masses in general. These policies clearly spell out the programs of government.
2. Public policy is the outcome of the government's collective actions. It
means that it is a pattern or course of activity of the governmental officials and actors in a collective sense, rather than being termed as their discrete and segregated decisions.
3. Public policy is what the government actually decides or chooses to
do. It is the relationship of the government units to the specific field of political environment in a given administrative system. It can take a variety of forms like laws, ordinances, court decisions, executive orders, decisions, etc.
4. Public policy is positive in the sense that it depicts the concern of the
government and involves its action on a particular problem on which the policy is made. It has the sanction of law and authority behind it. Negatively, it involves a decision by the governmental officials regarding not taking any action on a particular issue.
Policy and Goals
To better understand the meaning of policy, it is important to distinguish between policy and goals. Goals represent the desired outcomes or conditions that a society or organization strives to achieve. They can be abstract values, like equality or justice, or specific and tangible, such as the removal of poverty. Public policies are primarily concerned with specific, concrete goals and serve as the instruments for achieving them. For instance, if the government announces its goal to provide housing for all members of the deprived sections of society, this statement alone does not constitute a public policy. It is merely a declaration of intent or what the government aspires to accomplish. Often, for political reasons, governments announce goals without a genuine commitment to their realization. For a goal to become a policy, it must be translated into actionable steps. Programs must be created with specific objectives to address the goal. Take, for example, the goal of poverty alleviation. Various programs, such as the
Integrated Rural Development Programme (IRDP) and the National Rural
Employment Programme (NREP), have been implemented with specific targets, funding, and administrative structures to achieve poverty reduction. These programs represent concrete efforts to accomplish the overarching goal. Policy, in this sense, lays out the strategy for achieving a goal. Therefore, a policy is essentially a tool used to meet a goal, while merely stating a goal does not amount to forming a policy.

Policies and Decisions Introduction to
Public Policy: A distinction must be made between a policy and a decision, as they are often Definitions, Types, mistakenly used interchangeably. Individuals, organizations, or governments Significance and
SCOPE
frequently make decisions, but not all decisions can be classified as policies. The core of decision-making is the process of choosing from available alternatives to take action. If there is only one option, no decision is required. Thus, a decision is the act of making a choice when alternatives are available. The study of decision-making aims to understand how to improve this process and expand the decision-maker's range of alternatives. Decisions can be categorized as either programmed or non-programmed. Programmed decisions are routine and repetitive, requiring no fresh deliberation each time they are made. These decisions follow established procedures and rely on habit, skill, and prior knowledge. For example, once a decision is made to open a library from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., no further review is needed to maintain those hours. Non-programmed decisions, on the other hand, are new and unstructured, often arising in unprecedented situations like epidemics or natural disasters. These decisions require innovative thinking and special skills. Public policy provides the broad framework within which decisions are made. While a decision can be a one-time action, a policy consists of multiple interconnected decisions aimed at fulfilling a broader goal. Both decision- making and policy-making involve choosing from alternatives, but policy is a more comprehensive process, encompassing a series of decisions over a longer time frame.
14.4 CHARACTERISTICS OF PUBLIC POLICY
MAKING
The nature and meaning of public policy become clearer by understanding its various characteristics. Some key features of public policy making include:
1. Complex Process: Public policy making is highly complex, involving
numerous interconnected elements linked through communication and feedback loops. Some parts of the process are explicit, while others occur through hidden channels, often unnoticed even by officials themselves. Policies can emerge from a series of decisions without any one decision- maker being fully aware of the overall process.
2. Dynamic Nature: Policy making is an ongoing and evolving process
that requires continuous input of resources and motivation. It adapts over time, with the sequence of sub-processes and phases varying both internally and relative to one another.
3. Involves Multiple Components: The complexity of public policy is
heightened by the involvement of diverse substructures, which may vary in their roles depending on the issue, circumstances, and societal values. Different components of the policy process contribute in unique ways.

Public Policy and 4. Diverse Contributions of Substructures: Various substructures within Media the policy-making process make different contributions, depending on their formal and informal roles, which can vary across societies.
5. Decision-Making Process: Policy making is a form of decision-making,
allowing the use of decision-making models to better understand and analyze the policy-making process.
6. Guideline-Oriented: Public policies typically provide general guidelines
rather than detailed instructions. After these main directives are established, sub-policies are developed to translate them into actionable steps.
7. Action-Oriented: Most public policies aim to result in specific actions,
whether that involves direct implementation, changes to the decision- making process, or other outcomes. Policy-making that focuses on government efficiency, for instance, is oriented toward concrete action.
8. Future-Focused: Public policy making is aimed at shaping future
outcomes, introducing uncertainty and unpredictability. As a result, policies tend to be flexible to accommodate unforeseen circumstances and new developments.
9. Primarily Formulated by Government: While public policy may
sometimes involve private individuals or non-governmental entities, it is primarily formulated by governmental bodies, with secondary effects on other actors.
10. Focus on Public Interest: Public policy is generally oriented toward
serving the public interest, though this concept can be difficult to define concretely. Nonetheless, the idea of public interest often influences the policy-making process.
11. Best Possible Means: Public policy aims to achieve maximum net
benefit, although benefits and costs are often difficult to quantify. Both qualitative and quantitative considerations are necessary when evaluating alternative public policies.
12. Involvement of Multiple Stakeholders: A wide range of bodies and
agencies--including industrial workers, voters, intellectuals, legislators, bureaucrats, political parties, executives, and the judiciary--participate in and influence the public policy-making process. Check Your Progress 1 Note: 1) Use the space given below for your answers.

14.5 TYPES OF PUBLIC POLICY
Public policies can be classified into different types based on their nature and function. Some of the major types of public policy are:
1. Substantive Policies: These policies are concerned with the general
welfare and development of society. Programs like the provision of education, employment opportunities, economic stabilization, law and order enforcement, and anti-pollution legislation are the result of substantive policy formulation. These policies have vast areas of operation, affecting the general welfare and development of society as a whole. They do not relate to any particular or privileged segments of society. Such policies have to be formulated keeping in view the prime character of the constitution, socio-economic problems, and the level of moral claims of society.
2. Regulatory Policies: Regulatory policies are concerned with the
regulation of trade, business, safety measures, public utilities, etc. This type of regulation is done by independent organizations that work on behalf of the government. In India, we have organizations like Life Insurance Corporation (LIC), Reserve Bank of India (RBI), Hindustan
Steel, State Electricity Boards, State Transport Corporations, and State
Financial Corporations, which are engaged in regulatory activities. The policies made by the government, pertaining to these services and organizations rendering these services, are known as regulatory policies.
3. Distributive Policies: Distributive policies are meant for specific
segments of society. They can be in the area of the grant of goods, public welfare, or health services. These mainly include all public assistance and welfare programs. Some more examples of distributive policies are adult education programs, food relief, social insurance, and vaccination camps.
4. Redistributive Policies: Redistributive policies are concerned with the
rearrangement of policies that bring about basic social and economic changes. Certain public goods and welfare services are disproportionately divided among certain segments of society. These goods and services are streamlined through redistributive policies.
5. Capitalization Policies: Under capitalization policies, financial
subsidies are given by the Union government to the state and local governments. Such subsidies are also granted to central and state business undertakings or other important spheres, if necessary. Capitalization policies are different in nature from substantive, regulatory, distributive, and redistributive policies, as no provision for public welfare services is made through these.

Public Policy and 14.6 STAGES IN PUBLIC POLICY PROCESS
Media The stages of public policy in India can be better understood by examining each phase of the process:
1. Policy Formulation: This initial stage involves converting public
demands into concrete policies. It is essential to identify which demands need to be addressed through policy interventions.
2. Policy Interpretation: After formulation, policies are further clarified to
ensure they are easily understandable by all relevant stakeholders, including those responsible for their execution.
3. Policy Education: The government then informs the public about the
new policies through mass media and other communication channels, ensuring awareness and understanding among the masses.
4. Policy Implementation: At this stage, the policies are put into action by
administrative bodies across central, state, and local levels. The proper execution of policies is crucial for their success.
5. Policy Monitoring: Continuous oversight is necessary to track the
progress of policy implementation, ensure that resources are allocated efficiently, and measure the impact on the target population. Monitoring helps prevent overspending and ensures that policies benefit the intended recipients.
6. Policy Evaluation: The final stage involves evaluating the effectiveness
of the policies. This assessment helps determine whether the policy has achieved its goals and provides feedback for improvements. Effective evaluation also requires proper administrative control and adjudicative oversight to ensure accountability in the policy process.

Actually, the scope of public policy is determined by the kind of role that the Significance and
SCOPE
State adopts for itself in a society. In the classical capitalist society, the State was assigned a limited role and it was expected that the State would merely act as a regulator of social and economic activity and not its promoter. With the advent of planned view of development, the State began to be perceived as an active agent in promoting and shaping societies in its various activities. This was considered as a great change in the role of a State. Public policies expanded their scope from merely one of regulation to that of development. Expansion in scope led to several other consequences like many more government agencies and institutions came into being in order to formulate and implement policies. In India, the Planning Commission and its attendant agencies came into being in order to formulate policies and develop perspectives that could define the direction which the country would follow. So, the first major goal of public policies in our country has been in the area of socio-economic development. Wide-ranging policies were formulated in the area of industrial and agricultural development. Many policies were converted into Statutes, like Industrial Development and Regulating Act or Land Tenancy Act. Others were kept as directives in the various plan documents. For all policy directions, the Five Year Plans became the major source. These policies were of two types, one of regulation and the other of promotion. Laws laid down what could be done or not done by the entrepreneurs. This could be in the larger area like what goods can be produced by the public or whether certain goods can be traded only by government agencies. Laws also specified how State agencies themselves were to provide goods and services like electricity, transport etc. The State undertook similar responsibility in the social sphere. Dowry Act, Divorce Act, etc., are examples of this. But socio-economic transformation was not the only problem when India became independent. There were also problems of national integrity, the external environment was a source of threat and the country had to develop suitable policies to defend itself. Apart from this, there have been internal challenges. Regionalism has given rise to fissiparous tendencies that have to be countered in the long-term perspective. These would include not only defence policies but also similar efforts at decentralisation that create greater national cohesiveness. Thus, since independence, public policies in India have been formulated with a view to achieving socio-economic development and maintaining national integrity. These goals have been complex, demanding coherent policies. This has been a difficult task because goals have had to be divided into sectors and sub-sectors. Many a time by its very nature, policies have been contradictory. What may be rational for economic development may not be so for national integration. Thus, the need of a strong Centre to cope with external threats etc. is important but it may go against the principle of decentralisation which provides for greater national cohesion of a heterogeneous society. This is the reason why ascertaining of the actual impact of public policy becomes a necessity.

Public Policy and These days policy analysis is acquiring a lot of importance in the realm of the Media study of public administration. This trend is observable all over the world. The success of policy formulation, execution and monitoring ultimately depends on the success of policy analysis. In India, this trend emerged with the launching of our Five Year Plans. As the years passed by, one Five Year Plan was followed by another and disillusionment started setting in. Goals of socio-economic development could not be achieved. Those who were supposed to benefit from the development effort began to lose. Attention shifted to the management and administration in order to find out why the policies were failing to achieve their objectives. This investigation did not include the questions of policies being right or wrong. It took the crises of the 1960s to raise the issue of correctness of policy. Disenchantment with the development processes followed the two wars in 1962 and 1965. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) enforced a devaluation of the rupee in 1966 and a terrible drought ravaged the land during 1966-68. It became evident that the development policies were in trouble. In the early 1970s another war, drought and the oil crisis gave a jolt to the plan that had been followed until then. The culmination was the imposition of national emergency in 1975 to cope with the rising dissatisfaction. It was the emergence of the turbulent period that led to the questioning of the policies that had been followed. It was no more a question of implementation alone. The argument that began to gain the popular view was that policy itself was faulty and all the blame could not be put on administration. The first to pick up this line of reasoning was the discipline of economics. The economic failures dominated the scene and therefore it was natural that economists were the first ones to raise questions about the appropriateness of policy. Students of public administration began to emphasise that implementation failures could also emanate from inadequacy of public policy and therefore policy analysis should also be included in the area of study of public administration. This argument got support from certain developments in the discipline of public administration. In view of the everyday experience, it was becoming difficult to sustain the classical concept of separation of politics and administration. This distinction categorised policy formulation and implementation as two distinct activities. Policy formulation was regarded as a political activity and policy implementation an administrative one. But this distinction got increasingly blurred and it was not an easy task to determine where policy formulation ended and where policy implementation began. It came to be accepted that both were interactive processes and had to be seen in an integrated way. With this change in view, students of public administration began to devote greater attention to the problems of policy formulation and influence of policy design on implementation. It is in this way that policy analysis has become an important focus of study. Policy makers have also shown great interest in it because it ultimately helps in improving the effectiveness of policy. Many universities and research institutes are involved in policy analysis. The government provides for a lot of funds in this area.

14.8 LET US SUM UP
Public policy plays a crucial role in shaping the functioning of governments and their response to societal challenges. This unit explores the fundamental concepts of public policy, beginning with its definition and characteristics. Public policy refers to the deliberate actions taken by governments to achieve specific objectives, responding to the needs and demands of the public. It is a process influenced by political dynamics, making the relationship between politics and policy central to understanding policy development. The unit distinguishes between policy, decision, and goal, emphasizing how these elements interact in policy formulation. It explains the different types of public policy, including regulatory, distributive, and redistributive policies, each serving distinct purposes within governance. The importance of public policy is underscored, as it affects a wide array of sectors such as healthcare, education, and the economy. By understanding the various aspects of public policy, students can better comprehend the mechanisms through which governments address public issues, navigate political influences, and achieve societal goals.

15.0 INTRODUCTION
In this unit, we will delve into the various models and theoretical frameworks that are employed to understand and navigate the complex world of public policy. We will explore how these models define and dissect policy problems, and how they interact and evolve in the dynamic landscape of policy-making. We will begin by examining the Systems Model, which views policy-making as a process of converting societal demands into policy outputs through a 'black box' mechanism. Next, we will explore the Institutional Approach, which emphasizes the role of governmental structures and institutions in shaping public policy. We will then analyze the Rational Policy-Making Model, which advocates for a logical and efficient approach to decision-making based on clear goals and cost-benefit analysis. Furthermore, we will discuss Lindblom's Incremental Approach, which proposes a more gradual and pragmatic approach to policy- making, acknowledging the limitations of perfect rationality. We will also delve into Dror's Normative-Optimum Model, which seeks to combine elements of rationality with 'extra-rational' factors to improve the policy- making process. Finally, we will explore the Political Public Policy Approach, which views policy-making as a political process influenced by various stakeholders and their interactions.

Public Policy and By examining these diverse perspectives, we will gain a deeper appreciation Media for the multifaceted nature of public policy and the challenges faced by those who seek to shape it. We will understand how different models define and address policy problems, and how they can be applied to analyze real-world policy decisions.

15.2 SYSTEMS MODEL FOR POLICY ANALYSIS
'' The policy-making process has been regarded by David Easton as a 'black box', which converts the demands of the society into policies. While analysing political systems David Easton argues that the political system is that part of the society, which is engaged in the authoritative allocation of Values. The systems approach to political analysis is shown in figure 15.1. Fig. 15.1: The Estonian 'black box' model The intra-societal environment: The extra-societal environment: * ecological system international political systems * biological system international ecological systems * social system international social systems

Models of Public
Policy Above figure gives an idea of what Easton describes as apolitical system. Inputs are seen as the physical, social, economic and political products of the environment. They are received into the political system in the form of both demands and supports. Demands are the claims made on the political system by individuals and groups to alter some\ 'aspect of the environment. Demands occur when individuals or groups, in response to environmental conditions, act to effect public-policy. The environment is any condition or event defined as external to the boundaries of the political system. The supports of a political system consist of the rules, laws and customs that provide a basis for the existence of a political community and the authorities. The support is rendered when individuals or groups accept the decisions or laws. Supports are the symbolic or material inputs of a system (such as, obeying laws, paying taxes, or even respecting the national flag) that constitute the psychological and material resources of the system. At the heart of the political system are the institutions and personnel for policy-making. These include the chief executive, legislators, judges, and bureaucrats. In the system's version, they translate inputs into outputs. Outputs, then, are the authoritative value allocations of the political system, and these allocations constitute public policy or policies. The systems theory portrays public policy as an output of the political system. The concept of feedback indicates that public policies may have a modifying effect on the environment and the demands generated therein, and may also have an effect upon the character of the political system. Policy outputs may generate new demands and new supports, or withdrawal of the old supports for the system. Feedback plays an important role in generating a suitable environment for future policy.
Limits of Systems Approach to Policy Analysis
The systems theory is a useful aid in understanding the policy-making process. Thomas Dye (Understanding Public Policy) says that the value of the systems model to policy analysis lies in the questions that it poses. They are noted below:
- What are the significant dimensions of the environment that generate
demands upon the political system?
- What are the significant characteristics of the political system that enable
it to transform demands into public policy and to preserve itself over time?
- How do environmental inputs affect the character of the political system?
- How do characteristics of the political system affect the content of public
policy?
- How do environmental inputs affect the content of public policy?

Public Policy and - How does public policy affect, through feedback, the environment and Media the character of the political system? The usefulness of the systems model for the study of public policy is, however, limited owing to several factors. It is argued that this input-output model appears to be too simplistic to serve as a useful aid to understanding the policy-making process. This model is accused of employing the value- laden techniques of welfare economics, which are based on the maximization of a clearly defined 'social welfare function'. Another shortcoming of the traditional input-output model is that it ignores the fragmentary nature of the 'black box'. The missing ingredients in the systems approach are the "power, personnel, and institutions" of policy-making. Lineberry observes that in examining these, "we will not forget that political decision-makers are strongly constrained by economic factors in the environment in the political system." The Estonian model also ignores an important element of the policy process, namely, that the policy-makers (including institutions) have also a considerable potential in influencing the environment within which they operate. The traditional input-output model would see the decision-making system as "facilitative" and value-free rather than "causative," i.e., as a completely neutral structure. In other words, structural variations in the systems are found to be having no direct causal effect on public policy. Further, it is argued that both the political and bureaucratic elite shape mass opinion more than the masses shape the leadership's views. The concept of 'within inputs,' as opposed to inputs, has been created to illustrate this point. Thus, policy changes may be attributed more to the political and administrative elite's redefinition of their own views rather than as a product of demands and support from the environment. Quite often, policy initiation does emerge from the bureaucracy. Under certain situations, the bureaucracy becomes a powerful institution in formulating and legitimizing policy.
15.3 INSTITUTIONAL APPROACH TO POLICY
ANALYSIS
In a democratic society, the state is a complex network of governmental structures and institutions aimed at balancing conflicting social and economic interests. The positive state serves as a guardian of all community sections, not favoring any particular class, and seeks to protect economic interests by reconciling them. However, no organization can resolve all policy issues; typically, solutions align with the majority's preferences. In a pluralist society, individuals and groups direct their activities towards governmental institutions such as the legislature, executive, judiciary, and bureaucracy, which are responsible for formulating, implementing, and enforcing public policy. For a policy to be considered a public policy, it must be adopted and enforced by these institutions. Governmental institutions impart three key characteristics to public policy:
1. Legal Authority: Government policies carry legal authority and are
202 characterized by legal sanctions, ensuring obedience from citizens.

2. Universality: Public policies apply equally to all citizens within the Models of Public
Policy state.
3. Coercion: Policies involve coercion through government actions that
support its decisions, with the power to impose penalties and ensure compliance. Given the government's authority to command obedience, formulate national policies, and enforce compliance, individuals and groups strive to have their preferences reflected in policy. Thus, public policy is closely tied to governmental institutions. Social scientists emphasize the study of these structures, making the institutional approach central to understanding public policy. This approach focuses on the interactions between institutions established by the constitution, government, or legislature. In policy-making, power is exercised by various actors, including the
Executive, Cabinet, Prime Minister, Members of Parliament, bureaucrats, and
interest group leaders. Each of these actors influences the policy-making process, which involves a sequence of decisions shaped by these powerful individuals and groups. The institutional approach also explores how social groups and institutions affect decision-makers within the formal system of rules that grant power and authority. Institutionalism, with its focus on the legal and structural aspects of institutions, is applicable in policy analysis. Institutions shape public policy through their structures and interactions. Thomas Dye notes that governmental institutions reflect persistent patterns of behavior among individuals and groups. Historically, the study of these structures often overlooked their impact on policy content. Institutional characteristics significantly affect policy decisions, as rules and arrangements can favor certain interests over others. This highlights how institutional patterns can influence policy outcomes, either benefiting or disadvantaging specific groups. The institutional approach facilitates examining the relationship between institutional arrangements and public policy. It allows for systematic analysis and comparative studies of these relationships. However, changes in institutional structures do not guarantee policy changes unless the intricate relationship between structure and policy is investigated. As Thomas Dye emphasizes, changes in institutional arrangements have limited impact if underlying environmental forces remain unchanged.
15.4 RATIONAL POLICY-MAKING MODEL
Rationality and rationalism are often discussed in social science literature but are frequently more idealized than practiced in policy-making. Rationality is seen as a benchmark of wisdom, emphasizing choosing the best option among policy alternatives based on rational grounds. Robert Haveman defines a rational policy as one designed to maximize "net value achievement." Thomas Dye equates rationality with efficiency, defining a rational policy as the one with the highest positive ratio between the values it 203

Public Policy and achieves and the values it sacrifices. Dye argues that efficiency involves Media considering all social, political, and economic values, not just those measurable in monetary terms. To achieve rationality, policy-makers should: identify and determine goals, rank these goals by importance, identify possible policy alternatives, and conduct a cost-benefit analysis of these alternatives. A rational policy-maker must: understand all societal value preferences and their weights, clarify and rank goals, know all policy alternatives, assess each alternative's consequences, calculate the ratio of achieved to sacrificed values for each option, and select the most efficient alternative aligned with the goals. Herbert Simon suggests that instead of striving for an ideal decision, policy- makers should simplify complex problems into manageable parts, choose the best satisfactory option, and minimize unnecessary uncertainty. Simon also notes that rationality is bounded by individuals' limited cognitive and emotional capacities. Rational policy-making involves several stages: identification of the problem and goal prioritization, identification of policy alternatives, cost-benefit analysis, comparison of alternatives, and selection of the most efficient policy. After implementation, policy-makers must monitor the policy to assess the accuracy of expectations and estimates. The 'feedback stage' allows for policy modifications or abandonment, making the policy system self- correcting or cybernetic if feedback is effectively utilized. However, rational decision-making faces several constraints. Rationality is often more espoused than practiced due to its complexities and idealization. Some key constraints include:
1. Accomplishing Goals: Rational policy-making is challenging. By the
time a rational policy is recommended, the problem may become too complex, leading to decisions based on other goals such as personal rewards. Rationality may thus become more of an exercise than a practical realization of goals.
2. Securing Optimization: The rational model is expected to produce
optimal results, but this often does not occur. Public interest may not align with individual interests, making it difficult to achieve optimal outcomes. For example, policies to reduce air pollution may be costly, and individuals may not be willing to bear the costs, leading to a lack of motivation to maximize net goal achievement.
3. Conflict Between Rational Choice and Need for Action: Policy-
makers often face conflicts between rational behavior and the need for immediate action. Limited time for analysis in emergencies and the sheer number of potential issues can constrain thorough evaluation. Additionally, conflicting societal values make it difficult to weigh and compare values.
4. Dilemma of Political Feasibility: Political feasibility, or the likelihood
that a policy will be adopted and implemented, often conflicts with 204 rationality. Politicians may avoid conflict, stick to previous policies, or

postpone decisions to avoid political costs, thus prioritizing political Models of Public Policy feasibility over rationality.
5. Problem of Cost-Benefit Analysis: Accurately calculating cost-benefit
ratios is difficult when multiple diverse values are at stake. Policy- makers' personal needs and limitations further hinder the assessment of alternatives.
6. Nature and Environment of Bureaucracy: Bureaucratic environments
often obstruct rational policy-making. Fragmented authority, personal goals, conflicting values, limited technology, and uncertainty about alternatives restrict bureaucracies' ability to make rational decisions. Policy analysts caution against relying too heavily on the rational model. Patton and Sawicki argue that the rational model may be compromised due to political feasibility. Rational decisions might not be adopted if they are not politically acceptable. Denhardt notes that technical solutions may displace political and ethical concerns, leading to undemocratic outcomes. Even seemingly minor issues may face political intervention unless decisions are imposed, highlighting the tension between rationality and democratic processes. Overall, while the rational policy-making model sets utopian goals and procedures, it remains crucial for analytic purposes. It helps identify constraints to rationality and underscores the difficulties in achieving fully rational policy decisions. Herbert Simon's view that policy-makers "satisfy" rather than "optimize" reflects the reality that "good" decisions are often made within the limitations of clear goals and sufficient authority, contrasting with the more single-minded profit-maximizing goals of private organizations. Public Policy and 15.5 LINDBLOM'S INCREMENTAL APPROACH
Media Charles Lindblom's 'incremental model' of policy-making, introduced in his 1959 article "The Science of Muddling Through," offers an alternative to the traditional rational decision-making model. He criticizes the rational model, which assumes decision-making involves defining goals, selecting, and comparing alternatives. Lindblom argues that rational decision-making is unworkable for complex policy questions due to constraints of time, intelligence, cost, and politics, which prevent policymakers from identifying societal goals and their consequences comprehensively. Instead, Lindblom advocates the 'successive limited comparisons' or 'branch' method, where decisions are made incrementally. This approach involves building step-by-step from the current situation, relying on past policies rather than starting anew each time. According to Lindblom, "bounded rationality" makes this incremental approach more relevant and realistic. Features of Incremental Decision-Making:
1. Incremental Changes: Policies evolve through small adjustments,
accepting existing policies due to uncertainty about the outcomes of new alternatives.
2. Mutual Adjustment and Negotiation: Decisions are reached through
agreement and negotiation rather than purely through goal achievement. This helps reduce political tension and maintain stability, as agreements are often easier to reach when only minor changes to budgets or programs are involved.
3. Trial and Error Method: The incremental model embraces trial and
error, as policymakers often seek workable solutions rather than the ideal one. This approach focuses on familiar policies, making it theoretically coherent and simple, avoiding unrealistic attempts at comprehensive decision-making.
15.5.1 Strategic Policy-Making
Etzioni criticized both the rational and incremental approaches, proposing the 'mixed-scanning' approach as an alternative. He argued that pluralist decision-making models were biased due to existing inequities in power among participating interests and individuals. In Politics and Markets, Lindblom acknowledges Etzioni's critique, conceding that incremental pluralism is biased. He notes that not all participants in the policy-making process hold equal power, with business and large corporations dominating. In later work, Lindblom suggests improving mutual partisan adjustment through "greatly improved strategic policy-making." In his 1979 article, "Still Muddling Through," Lindblom highlights the core idea of incrementalism as problem-solving skill and suggests improved methods for incremental policy-making. He distinguishes between: 206 1. Incrementalism as a Political Pattern: Refers to step-by-step changes.

2. Incrementalism as Policy Analysis: Advocates 'analytical incrementalism' Models of Public
Policy as a method for balancing power in a pluralist polity dominated by business interests. Lindblom identifies three forms of incremental analysis:
1. Simple Incremental Analysis: Focuses on alternatives marginally
different from existing policies.
2. Strategic Analysis: Given the constraints on complete analysis, an analyst
should adopt a middle position, using methods like trial and error, systems analysis, and program evaluation to make informed choices.
3. Disjointed Incrementalism: This strategy simplifies decision-making by
focusing on a limited number of familiar alternatives, intertwining values with empirical analysis, remedying ills rather than pursuing grand goals, and fragmenting analytical work across partisan participants. In A Strategy of Decision (1963), co-authored with David Braybrooke, Lindblom introduces "disjointed incrementalism" as a method where decisions compare marginally different policies without a grand goal, relying on existing resources and trial and error. This method reflects incrementalism's place on a continuum of decision-making approaches.
15.5.2 Partisan Mutual Adjustment
In The Intelligence of Democracy (1965), Lindblom argues that decision- making is a process of adjustment and compromise that fosters agreement and coordination. He emphasizes partisan mutual adjustment as a democratic alternative to centralized controls, asserting that policy evolves through complex interactions among bureaucrats, elected officials, and interest groups (The Policy-Making Process, 1993). Since his initial advocacy of incremental decision-making in 1959, Lindblom's stance evolved. By the 1970s and 1990s, he critiques pluralism and incrementalism, arguing for radical change in policy areas, though acknowledging that societies often cannot act boldly except in emergencies. He expresses doubts about achieving drastic policy changes due to constraints on decision-making and narrowly defined policy agendas. While Lindblom initially supported incremental decision-making as effective, by the 1970s he became a more radical critic, seeing it as a 'political ideology.' He still believes the policy-making process can improve, albeit slowly. Critics like Y. Dror and A. Etzioni find the incremental model conservative and only suitable for stable situations with sufficient resources. Dror views it as inadequate for addressing major policy shifts or complex problems. The incrementalist approach faces challenges. Critics argue its deductive power is limited by the difficulty in defining an increment, and its applicability is weakened by sudden policy changes that defy incrementalist assumptions of linear growth. Despite its simplicity, the model seems too crude for the complexities of policy-making.

Public Policy and Lindblom's central concern has been the relationship between power, Media knowledge, and politics. He stresses that understanding how power shapes public policy is essential for promoting human well-being and suggests that restructuring power relations is key to creating better policies (The Policy- Making Process, 1993).
15.6 DROR'S NORMATIVE -OPTIMUM MODEL
Yehezekel Dror (1969) critiques Lindblom's Incrementalist Model as conservative and unjust, arguing that it creates a gap between those with power and those without, making change difficult for the latter. Instead of incremental and purely rational models, Dror proposes an alternative approach that emphasizes:
1. The need for rationality (following Herbert Simon's definition).
2. The introduction of management techniques to enhance rationality at
lower levels of decision-making.
3. A policy science approach to handle complex problems at higher levels.
4. The recognition of values and irrational elements in decision-making.
Dror's aim is to increase the rational content of government decision-making while acknowledging 'extra-rational' dimensions such as tacit knowledge and personal experience. He calls this approach "normative optimalism," which combines the rational model's core elements, like cost-benefit measurement, with extra-rational factors. Dror argues that this model better reflects reality while aiming to improve policy-making. He proposes a more complex model than the purely rational approach, comprising 18 stages. These stages are divided into three main phases:
1. Metapolicy-Making Stage: This involves processing values, reality, and
problems; developing resources; designing and evaluating the policy system; and determining the overall strategy.
2. Policy-Making Stage: This includes sub-allocating resources, setting
operational goals, prioritizing values, preparing alternative policies, predicting costs and benefits, comparing alternatives, and selecting the best options.
3. Post-Policy-Making Stage: This focuses on motivating policy
execution, implementing policies, evaluating outcomes, and ensuring feedback for future decision-making. Dror's model operates at two levels--rational and extra-rational. For example, when processing values, the rational sub-phase gathers information on feasibility and costs, while the extra-rational sub-phase involves value judgments, bargaining, and coalition formation. His normative-optimalism approach integrates experts into both the descriptive (real-world) and prescriptive (improvement-focused) aspects of policy-making. Dror's 18-stage model is cyclical, balancing rational and extra-rational components. Its strength lies not just in prescribing steps but in

offering a robust framework for analyzing the policy-making process Models of Public Policy comprehensively.
15.7 POLITICAL PUBLIC POLICY APPROACH
A significant departure from the rationality model is the Political Policy Process Approach espoused in policy-making. Writers such as Laurence Lynn and Peter deLeon have advocated this approach. In this approach, public policy-making is viewed as a 'political process' instead of a 'technical process'. The approach emphasizes the political interaction from which policy derives. Lynn sees public policy as the output of government. According to him, public policy can be characterized as the output of a diffuse process made up of individuals who interact with each other in small groups within a framework dominated by formal organizations. Those organizations function in a system of political institutions, rules, and practices, all subject to societal and cultural influences. According to Lynn, individuals in organizations function under a variety of influences, and "to understand policy-making it is necessary to understand the behavior of and interactions among these structures: individuals holding particular positions, groups, organizations, the political system, and the wider society of which they are all a part." Therefore, instead of involving particular methodologies, policy-making in this approach is a matter of adapting to and learning to influence political and organizational environments. The policy-making process is constrained by factors such as institutions, interest groups, and even societal and cultural influences. The focus in the political process of policy-making approach is on understanding how particular policies were formed, developed, and work in practice. Lynn argues that policy-making "... encompasses not only goal setting, decision-making, and formulation of political strategies, but also supervision of policy planning, resource allocation, operations management, program evaluation, and efforts at communication, argument, and persuasion." Lynn uses 'managers of public policy' who operate under a variety of influences. He observes, "Public executives pursue their goals within three kinds of limits: those imposed by their external political environments; those imposed by their organizations; and those imposed by their own personalities and cognitive styles." Rather than being technical experts, effective managers of public policy, observes Lynn: i) Establish understandable premises for their organization's objectives; ii) Attain an intellectual grasp of strategically important issues; and identify and focus attention on those activities that give meaning to the organization's employees; iii) Remain alert to and exploit all opportunities, whether deliberately created or fortuitous, to further their purposes; iv) Consciously employ the strong features of their personalities as instruments of leadership and influence; and

Public Policy and v) Manage within the framework of an economy of personal resources to Media govern how much they attempt to accomplish and how they go about it. Under this approach, managers use appropriate means to achieve their goals. They work in this way because their own positions are at stake.
15.8 MIXED APPROACH BY HOGWOOD AND
GUNN
In addition to the above approach, there is another approach described by Hogwood and Gunn which is mixed and concerned both with the application of techniques and with the political process. They value the political aspects of the policy process. Hogwood and Gunn set out a nine-step approach to the policy process, which they say is 'mixed', that is, can be used for both description and prescription. The nine steps of their model are: i) Deciding to decide (issue search or agenda-setting); ii) Deciding how to decide; iii) Issue definition; iv) Forecasting; v) Setting objectives and priorities; vi) Options analysis; vii) Policy implementation, monitoring, and control; viii) Evaluation and review; ix) Policy implementation, succession, or termination. James Anderson's model of the policy process reduces these stages into five. They include: i) Problem identification and agenda formation; ii) Formulation; iii) Adoption; iv) Implementation; v) Evaluation. The policy process model by Hogwood and Gunn is a typical one. While its roots may be in the rational model, it does deal with the political aspects of the policy process. They argue for a "process-focused rather than a technique- oriented approach to policy analysis". It is seen as "supplementing the more overtly political aspects of the policy process rather than replacing them". As to the main difference between the two approaches, it may be emphasized that policy analysis looks for one alternative, that is, best or satisfactory from a set of alternatives and is aided by empirical methods in their selection. On the other hand, political public policy sees information in an advocacy role, that is, it realizes that cogent cases will be made from many perspectives, which then feed into the political process.

15.9 KEYWORDS
Systems Model: A framework by David Easton that views policy-making as a "black box" converting societal demands into policy outputs through feedback loops. Institutional Approach: A perspective emphasizing the role of governmental structures and institutions in shaping and enforcing public policy. Rational Policy-Making Model: A decision-making process based on logical analysis, cost-benefit evaluations, and the selection of the most efficient policy alternatives. Incremental Approach: Charles Lindblom's model advocating small, gradual policy adjustments rather than comprehensive changes due to practical constraints. Normative-Optimum Model: Y. Dror's model integrating rational decision- making with extra-rational factors like values and tacit knowledge for optimal policy outcomes. Political Public Policy Approach: A perspective that sees policy-making as a dynamic political process influenced by individuals, groups, and institutions. Mixed-Scanning Model: Amitai Etzioni's hybrid approach combining broad, strategic overviews with detailed incremental decisions for complex problem- solving.

Public Policy and 15.10 LET US SUM UP
Media This unit explored various aspects of public policy, highlighting its importance and the distinct paradigms used to study it. Public policy is examined as a separate approach from public management, with its focus on how government produces policies and their impact on people. There are now two main approaches to public policy, each with its own methods and emphases. The first, 'Policy Analysis,' emphasizes the role of policy research in facilitating the public policy process by providing accurate and useful decision-related information. This approach seeks to apply modern science and technology to societal problems, using good methods and techniques to help policymakers choose the most advantageous actions. It often involves statistical methods and input-output analysis to produce technically sound information. The second approach, 'Political Public Policy,' focuses on the political interactions that shape policy. It is challenging to separate public policy from the political process, which sometimes makes it difficult to determine whether a study is about public policy or politics. Public policy, in this context, is seen as more political than traditional public administration. It applies political analysis methods to various policy areas, including health, education, and the environment, while also considering bureaucratic processes. Political public policy theorists are more concerned with the outcomes of public policy rather than just the methods used. Both approaches are valuable in their own right. Policy analysis helps highlight what governments do and uses empirical methods to aid decision- making, whereas political public policy sheds light on the political dynamics influencing policy formation. The practice of public policy-making often reflects a blend of these perspectives, with managerialism or public management integrating elements from both approaches.

16.0 INTRODUCTION
Public policy is the backbone of governmental action, serving as a strategic tool to address societal needs and guide national development. In a diverse and populous country like India, the formulation and implementation of public policy are complex processes that involve multiple stages and a variety of stakeholders. This unit explores these intricate processes, shedding light on how policies are conceived, developed, and put into action within the Indian context. We begin by dissecting the stages of the policy process, including problem identification, policy formulation, decision-making, implementation, and evaluation. Each stage is crucial, contributing uniquely to the effectiveness of the policy outcomes. Understanding these stages helps in appreciating the

Public Policy and systematic approach required for successful policy-making. Media The unit also delves into the constitutional framework that underpins policy- making in India, highlighting the roles of the legislature, executive, and judiciary. It examines how institutional factors and non-governmental entities like political parties, pressure groups, and the media influence policy decisions. Furthermore, it addresses the challenges of policy implementation, emphasizing the conditions necessary for effective execution and the common obstacles that may hinder the process. By providing a comprehensive overview of the public policy process in India, this unit aims to equip you with the knowledge to understand, analyze, and engage with policy issues critically. It underscores the importance of each phase in the policy cycle and encourages a holistic view of how policies impact governance and society at large.
16.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After reading this Unit, you should be able to: * Understand the policy process as a system; * Describe the policy-making process in India; * Discuss the problems of implementation of public policy; and * Highlight issues related to policy formulation.
16.2 STAGES IN THE POLICY PROCESS
Thomas Dye (2004) sets out the following stages in his analysis of the policy process:
1. Problem Identification: The identification of policy problems through
demands for government action.
2. Agenda Setting: Focusing the attention of the mass media and public
officials on specific public problems as a prelude to decision making.
3. Policy Formulation: The development of policy proposals by interest
groups, officers of the chief executive's office, committees of the legislature, think tanks, etc.
4. Policy Legitimation: The selection and enactment of policies through
political actions by the executive, the legislature, and the courts.
5. Policy Implementation: The implementation of policies through
organised bureaucracies, public expenditures, and the activities of executive agencies.
6. Policy Evaluation: The evaluation of policies by government agencies
themselves, outside consultants, the press, and the public. Hogwood and Gunn (Policy Analysis for the Real World, 1984) have identified nine important stages in the policy process: deciding to decide (agenda setting), deciding how to decide (issue filtration), issue definition,

forecasting, setting objectives and priorities, options analysis, policy Public Policy
Formulation and
implementation, monitoring and control, evaluation and review and policy
Implementation in
maintenance, succession and termination. India The policy cycle of May and Wildavsky (1978) includes agenda-setting, issue analysis, implementation, evaluation and termination. Similarly, James Anderson has also dealt with description of the policy process. His model of the policy process has five stages: (i) problem identification, and agenda formulation (ii) formulation, (iii) adoption, (iv) implementation, and (v) evaluation (Anderson, 1984). There are basic linkages in a policy framework for the systematic analysis of information and its use in a policy-related context. The basis to the framework is information for policy analysis, which is derived from system or programme performance in terms of interaction among: * inputs, which indicate needs and demands * processes concerning the provision of services for long-term care * outputs in terms of the use of services and cost of care * outcomes, which identify the end results of certain courses of action. For example, in the context of the National Health Policy (2017), the inputs (in terms of need and demands) comprise health, illness, and the quality of life, expressed in physical, psychological, social, and environmental terms. Needs are the conditions that call for action. They are among the most important predictors of utilisation, and are mostly described in terms of diagnosis, functional limitation, perceived illness, symptoms, or poor health status. On the other hand, demands are expressed as desires in relation to the services sought, whether they are needed or not. Other inputs include resources, such as manpower (doctors, nurses, and para-medical staff) hospitals, primary health centres, medical equipment and facilities, medicine, and performance standards. On the process linkage, it is concerned with the delivery of services to meet the needs and demands of clients and professionals. Services are described in such terms as their types, delivery, management and controls of cost and quality. Other services include supports such as legal aid, income support, consumer education, and professional development. The outputs of service related programmes are described in terms of the use of those services, the costs and the quality of care. Finally, the outcomes are the responses to the services expressed in terms of the levels of well-being and health, and client and professional satisfaction that are attained as a result. The foregoing analytical framework facilitates programme evaluation, which is expected to lead to rational policies and decisions about health services. In the next section, we will describe the various stages in policy process.
16.2.1 Identifying the Underlying Problem
In an analytical approach, the first step is to determine whether a problem exists and why. Defining the problem involves moving from simple 217

Public Policy and descriptions to a more abstract, conceptual level. Here, an attempt is made to Media diagnose the form of market failure being confronted. For example, an environmentalist investigating alternative pollution control measures for the Ganges might find that the river is being polluted by the dumping of industrial wastes and untreated sewage. Having identified the context of the problem, the next step is to determine the objectives to be achieved in tackling the issue. Too often, we lose sight of the basic objectives. Therefore, paying careful attention to the objectives is important. For instance, providing the services of doctors is merely a means to the end of improving people's health.
16.2.2 Determining Policy Alternatives
The next step is to identify alternative courses of action. Government intervention can take many forms. It is important to determine which kind of intervention is most positive in a given situation. In the case of pollution of the Ganges, consider the following possibilities: i) The government might impose an obligation on abutters in certain catchments or adjoining areas of the river to clean the water. The government would then have the right to sue a polluter. ii) The government may require the concerned industrialists and urban dwellers to stop dumping waste and untreated sewage into the river. It might impose restrictions on the quantity of dumping. The government could permit polluters to purchase rights to discharge a certain amount of pollutants. Polluters might be required to pay effluent charges and install pollution control devices. iii) The state government or local authority could directly undertake the work of cleaning and removing the pollutants that others dump. These are some of the alternatives for pollution control. As difficulties are identified and additional information becomes available, refinement of alternative courses of action will continue throughout the analysis. Determining alternatives for policy choice generally requires expertise or special knowledge in the relevant areas.
16.2.3 Forecasting and Evaluating Alternatives
Having identified the underlying problem and determined the alternatives for policy choice, the policy analyst evaluates the consequences of each alternative. For this, they will turn to a relevant model for forecasting consequences. In the case of the pollution control problem, the models needed would be far more complex. It is necessary here to predict all the effects of the proposed policies, not just the economic effects desired by the decision-maker. If the consequences of an alternative course of action are uncertain, and especially if the possible outcomes differ widely from one another, the analyst may wish to develop a decision tree and evaluate the probability of each outcome. Very often, it is difficult to have a rational policy choice unless the relative merits of alternative options are analysed systematically.

The costs involved in regulation and administration need to be evaluated. Public Policy

Evaluation of the outcomes is of great importance as it reminds us to look
