16.2.4 Policy Selection
The next step in policy analysis involves choosing the preferred course of action. In some cases, the situation may be straightforward enough for the policy-maker to simply review the predicted consequences of each alternative and select the best one. However, when the situation is more complex, the policy analyst may need to prioritize the various possible outcomes, considering how different groups of stakeholders might react to each option and its results. The policy process can be illustrated diagrammatically, as shown in Figure
16.1. It has been observed that numerous policy studies have failed to
produce effective results. Sometimes, this failure is attributed to public decision-makers who neglect to utilize readily available data. Often, however, the analysts themselves must share a significant portion of the blame when outcomes are unsatisfactory. By improving the analyst's ability to forecast the consequences of alternative actions and by providing a framework for evaluating those consequences, the techniques of policy analysis can lead to better decisions and more effective policies.
16.2.5 Policy Implementation (Policy Action)
Ultimately, the success of public administration is measured by how well policies are implemented. Policy implementation is critically important to the success of government initiatives. No matter how excellent the political system, how noble the goals, or how sound the organizational structure, policies cannot succeed if they are poorly implemented. In its broadest sense, implementation is the phase between a policy statement and its operation. It seeks to determine whether an organization can carry out and achieve the stated objectives of its policies. This involves developing and pursuing a strategy of organization and management to ensure that the policy process is completed with minimal delays, cost overruns, and problems. More specifically, the task of implementation is to build a bridge that allows the objectives of public policies to be realized as outcomes of governmental activity. It involves creating a policy delivery system in which specific mechanisms are designed and pursued in the hope of achieving particular ends.
Constraints in Policy Implementation
Implementing policies can become very challenging if implementers are not granted sufficient autonomy and flexibility in carrying out their tasks. Political pressures within a democratic context constitute a major constraint. Another constraint is that the bureaucracy may lack the necessary professional skills required for effective policy implementation. A shortage of resources--such as personnel, financial means, and technical support-- also hinders the implementation of public policy. Additionally, problems may arise due to a lack of response from target groups. Sometimes, people do not 219

Public Policy and show adequate interest in the implementation of a program because they may Media not be aware of its objectives and goals. A lack of public participation often disrupts implementation efforts.
16.2.6 Policy Monitoring
Monitoring is essentially a component of the implementation process. It is an activity that occurs during the course of implementing a policy or programme. It is through monitoring that the implementer begins to observe the results of the policy. The objective of policy monitoring is to ensure, throughout the implementation process, that resource inputs are used as efficiently as possible to achieve the intended results. The standards used for both efficiency of resource utilization and effectiveness of policy implementation are inherent in the policy-making process. The monitor must be able to appraise resource use, technical activities, and policy implementation results with sufficient detail to allow for changes or corrections when necessary. Effective monitoring of public policies aids in cost reduction, time saving, and efficient resource utilization. The key issue in monitoring is to create an information system that enables policymakers and policy implementers to make timely decisions and adjustments. Therefore, it is important that monitoring and control processes are given due importance and are properly designed. One of the serious problems in monitoring relates to the poor design of the implementing system. Secondly, time constraints pose a challenge for policy monitoring. Too often, the implementing staff feels so pressured to achieve results that they take shortcuts and avoid proper monitoring and control. Thirdly, a common constraint for the policy implementation manager is the shortage of corrective actions available when the programme deviates from projected performance. Fourthly, a pervasive obstacle to policy monitoring is ignorance about its role and methods, often due to a lack of requisite skills among key functionaries.
16.2.7 Policy Outcomes
The next stage in the policy cycle is policy outcomes, which are different from outputs. Policy outputs are the actual decisions made by the implementers. The concept of outcomes emphasizes what actually happens to the target groups intended to be affected by the policy. If the intended changes in target groups do not occur, something is wrong. State housing schemes for the poor may illustrate this point. Although targets may be met, including the physical presence of houses, it was observed that in many instances the beneficiaries chose not to occupy them because they were not to their liking in terms of size, ambience, quality of construction, or other deficiencies. The policy outputs were achieved, but not the outcomes.
16.2.8 Policy Evaluation
The final stage of the policy process, in the sequential pattern of activities, is the evaluation of policy. Evaluation concerns what happens once a policy has 220 been put into effect. It is an assessment of the overall effectiveness of a

programme in meeting its objectives, or an assessment of the relative Public Policy
Formulation and
effectiveness of programmes in meeting the expected objectives.
Implementation in
India Evaluation performs several functions in policy analysis. Firstly, it provides reliable information about policy performance. It measures the impact of policies on society and reveals the extent to which particular goals have been achieved (for example, an increase in life expectancy at birth). It also helps us understand the degree to which policy issues have been resolved. Secondly, evaluation helps clarify the values that underlie the selection of goals and objectives. Thirdly, evaluation may result in efforts to restructure policy problems and may contribute to the emergence of new goals and potential solutions. Evaluation during the implementation process of a policy might even suggest its termination altogether. In short, evaluation is primarily an effort to analyze policy outcomes in terms of the set objectives. It is, therefore, helpful in highlighting the utility of the policies under consideration.
16.2.9 Design of Evaluation
Evaluating a public programme involves listing the goals of the programme, measuring the degree to which these goals have been achieved, and finally, suggesting changes that might align the organization's performance more closely with the intended purposes of the programme. Evaluation has a sensitive side; it may sometimes become a point of conflict or reinforce pre- existing conflicts. Negative evaluation of the performance of a public programme may result in its termination. The content of an evaluation, the goals contained within it, and even the organization performing the evaluation--all of these will affect the final assessment. Therefore, there is a need for a carefully designed evaluation conducted by competent persons. This requires adequate information feedback, resources, and political will.
16.3 FORMULATION OF PUBLIC POLICY
16.3.1 Constitutional Framework for Policy-Making
Policy-making in India is shaped within the framework of the constitutional system, of which four features stand out most prominently: democratic and sovereign republic, parliamentary system, the federal character of the Constitution and a broad socio-economic philosophy - reflected especially in the preamble, the chapters on Fundamental Rights and the Directive Principles of the state policy.
16.3.2 Institutional Factors
In addition to these four constitutional factors there are other factors that govern policy-making in India. Legislature Parliament in India is the supreme public policy-making body. It reigns supreme because the council of ministers headed by the Prime Minister is dependent upon the support of a parliamentary majority to remain in force. It enacts laws which will bring the policies into effect. It also legitimises the 221

Public Policy and policy decisions of the government. Media In reality, however, it does not reign supreme. It does not determine policies except in a formal sense. It influences public policies through general discussions and debates. Most of the legislation in India is prepared within the executive and introduced in the legislature by the minister concerned. The executive is assured of a legislative majority for the policy proposals it presents. Executive It is the constitutional task of the executive to decide the policies which are to be submitted to Parliament. The executive at the Union level in India consists of the President of India, the Council of Ministers and the machinery of government. The main bodies engaged in policy formulation in the executive are: i) Cabinet: The real executive is the Council of Ministers consisting of the Prime Minister, cabinet ministers, ministers of state and the deputy ministers. It is well-known that the Council itself hardly meets, and all the policy functions are performed by the Cabinet. ii) The Prime Minister: Within the Council of Ministers in general and the cabinet in particular, the Prime Minister enjoys a special position in the realm of policy-making. The Prime Minister is expected to exercise control over the cabinet decision-making process. iii) Secretariat-Department and Ministry: The secretariat is an administrative organisation to assist the government in the discharge of its executive and legislative responsibilities. It is a complex of departments and ministries whose administrative heads are known as secretaries and whose political heads are the ministers. The secretary acts as the chief adviser to the minister. He assists the minister(s) in the formulation of public policies. As policies can be framed only on the basis of availability and adequacy of data, the secretariat makes relevant information available to the minister, thus helping him to formulate policies. Judiciary The judiciary in India also plays a constructive role in shaping and influencing public policies in two ways: a) by its power of judicial review, and b) judicial decisions. The Constitution empowers the Supreme Court, and High Courts at the state levels to exercise a judicial review of legislation. Judicial review is the power of the courts to determine the constitutionality of actions of the legislature and the executive. They are not only specifying the government's limits with regard to certain actions, but also stating what it must do to promote public interest. Besides, the higher judiciary is also exercising its influence through its decisions in Public Interest Litigation cases.

16.3.3 Non-Governmental Institutions Public Policy
Formulation and
Implementation in
Some non-governmental organisations such as political parties, pressure India groups, media and citizenry are also informal participants in the policy process. Their views and influence are of critical value to the policy-making process.
Political Parties and Pressure Groups
The pressure exerted by pressure groups and political parties is an important factor in the making of policies. The political parties provide impetus to policies through their election manifestoes, and by enlisting support at the time of elections. Pressure groups strive to influence the decisions of the government in manifold ways. Often, these groups are found to have conflicting values on a particular policy issue. Obviously, well-organised and active pressure groups have more influence than groups whose members are poorly organised and inarticulate.
The Individual Citizen and the Media
The people initiate the process of legislation and policy-making by voting for candidates with specific policy preferences. A democratic government is supposed to reflect the wishes of the people. Yet, in reality citizen's participation in policy- making is very negligible. Acting alone, the individual citizen is rarely a significant political force. The media can also influence public opinion in a situation. Media influence, however, depends upon the level of responsiveness from the government.
External Agencies Influencing Policy
External agencies and non-state actors are an important source in the initiation of new public policies or modification of pre-existing policies, especially in Third World countries like India. They include agencies such as the United Nations and its allied agencies (WHO, ILO, UNEP, UNDP, etc.) the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund, the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) and other multilateral agencies is of critical importance in shaping policy outcomes. 16.4 POLICY IMPLEMENTATION
16.4.1 Importance and Meaning
In the final analysis, the success of public administration for development can be measured only in relation to the implementation of policies. Implementation determines the extent to which an organisation is able to carry out and achieve the stated objectives. It involves developing and pursuing a strategy to ensure that the policy process is completed with the minimum of delays, costs and problems. Implementation involves the "creation of a policy delivery system in which specific mechanisms are designed and pursued in the hope of reaching particular ends". Thus, public policies in the form of statement of goals and objectives are put into action- programmes that aim to realise the ends stated in the policy. Putting policy into effect involves not the end of policy-making, but a continuation of policy-making by other means. At the minimum, implementation requires:
1) adequate personnel and the financial resources to implement the policy; 2)
the administrative capability to achieve the desired policy goals; and 3) support from the legislative, executive and judicial wings of the government for the successful implementation of policy.
16.4.2 Implementers
Public policies in India, as in other countries, are implemented by a complex system of administrative organisations and agencies. The main agency which implements government activities and public policies is the bureaucracy. This is an important institution which performs most of the day-to-day work of government. It is the bureaucracy which controls the personnel, money and other resources of the government, and has legal authority for their deployment. Since so much power and control over implementation is held

by the bureaucracy the legislature, the chief executive and judiciary set limits Public Policy
Formulation and
to its discretion and indirectly control its excesses, if any. Though discretion
Implementation in
and delegation are inevitable in a complex policy apparatus specific strategies India exist to exercise control over bureaucracy's operations if things go wrong. In the process the legislature and the judiciary tend to participate in policy implementation.
16.4.3 Conditions for Successful Implementation
Implementation is seen varying along a continuum ranging from most successful to failure. Successful implementation involves many operations and procedures as well as time and resources. Sabatier and Mazmanian (1979) identify five conditions for effective policy implementation. These are:
1. The programme is based on sound assumptions relating changes in target
group behaviour in consonance with the programme objectives.
2. Unambiguous policy directives and structures of the implementation
process to enable target groups to maximise their performance.
3. The leaders of the implementation agencies possess substantial
managerial and political skill and are committed to statutory goals.
4. The programme is actively supported by organised groups and by a few
key legislators (or the chief executive) throughout the implementation process, with the judiciary being neutral or supportive.
5. The relative priority of statutory objectives is not significantly
undermined over time by the emergence of conflicting public policies or by change in relevant socio-economic conditions. Policy-making does not end once a decision is reached. The implementation of a decision is just as important as the policy itself. No policy formulator can assume that decisions will automatically be implemented as envisioned. Policy implementation requires a wide variety of actions, including, a) b) c) d) issuing policy directives that are clear and consistent; creating organisational units and assigning personnel with the information and authority necessary to administer the policies; coordinating personnel resources and expenditures to ensure benefit to target groups; and evaluating implemental actions of the personnel. None of these steps is easy. The implementation of policy thus involves not the end of policy-making, but a continuation of policy-making by other means.
16.5 POLICY-MAKING PROCESS N INDIA
Policy-making is a crucial function at every level of government in India. To facilitate the conduct of government business, specific rules have been formulated under Article 77(3) of the Constitution. These Rules of Business dictate the procedures for decision-making, and within their framework, policy decisions are taken by the Council of Ministers, particularly the cabinet. Notably, the rules do not explicitly distinguish 225

Public Policy and between decisions related to policy and those that are not. Policy and Media administration are intimately connected, forming an integral part of the executive government. Indeed, it can be observed that some significant policy decisions are often made informally. The Prime Minister or a particular colleague, if confident in their ability to implement a certain policy, may announce a decision either in Parliament or publicly. However, such instances are not frequent, especially in a coalition government. The cabinet utilizes a committee system to streamline decision-making in specific areas. Depending on the membership of any cabinet committee, its decision may be final on behalf of the government or may require ratification by the full cabinet committee. A vast number of decisions are, of course, made by individual ministers within the scope of the government's rules of business, and these are considered authoritative decisions of the government. The matters a minister chooses to decide upon, and those he refers to the Prime Minister or the cabinet, often depend on his personality and political stature. Nevertheless, the cabinet as a whole must be convinced of the soundness of such decisions. Therefore, it is observed that cabinet decisions are made by the Prime Minister together with the concerned minister. Technically, most decisions on various matters involving less significant policy issues are taken by the administrative secretaries or committees of secretaries, some of which serve a cabinet committee. The secretary to the government in a particular ministry, senior civil servants of the ministry, heads of government departments, and other officials below the departmental heads are vested with delegated authority in specific matters. For the conduct of government business, there are extensive volumes of departmental rules of procedure and guidance for decision-making in each agency. When a matter is of concern or interest to a ministry or department other than the one considering it, it is incumbent upon the latter to consult the affected ministry or department at the appropriate levels. This provides a somewhat sketchy account of the policy-making process and decision-making procedures. In a complex system like the Union government or that of a State government in India, a multitude of social, political, economic, and administrative factors influence the choice of a policy. The election manifesto of the ruling political party, interest groups, political parties, the administrative and judicial courts, the NITI Aayog, the Goods and Services Tax Council, systems of centre-state consultations, international agencies, and other non-state actors all have functions with a direct or indirect bearing on policy-making. Thus, within the constitutional framework, these institutions or their decisions may exert influence on government policy. The extent of this influence may vary, depending upon a wide range of contextual factors. The policy-making process has, to a large extent, been regarded by David Easton as a "black box" that converts demands into policies but whose structure is unknown and inaccessible to observation. Policy-making is "an extremely complex analytical and political process to which there is no beginning or end and the boundaries of which are most uncertain" (Lindblom, 1968). Somehow, a complex set of forces engage in policy-

making and, taken as a whole, produce effects called policies. Public Policy
Formulation and
The Parliament is empowered by the Indian Constitution to represent the
Implementation in
people in making policy through the passing of laws. The legislative process India is, therefore, a fundamental mechanism for expressing public policy. At the same time, legislation allows for more specific policy-making by the executive branch of the government within the legislative and constitutional framework, alongside the review functions of the judiciary. 16.6 LET US SUM UP
Understanding the public policy process in India is crucial for grasping how governmental decisions shape the nation's social, economic, and political landscape. This unit has dissected the multifaceted stages of policy-making-- from problem identification and agenda-setting to formulation, implementation, and evaluation. Each stage plays a vital role in ensuring that policies are not only well-crafted but also effectively executed to achieve their intended outcomes. The constitutional framework of India establishes a robust foundation for policy-making, delineating the roles of the legislature, executive, and judiciary. Institutional factors, including governmental bodies and non- 227

Public Policy and governmental entities like political parties, pressure groups, and the media, Media significantly influence the policy process. These stakeholders contribute to a dynamic environment where policies are continuously shaped and reshaped in response to societal needs and feedback. Policy implementation emerges as a critical phase, often determining the success or failure of policies. Effective implementation requires adequate resources, skilled personnel, clear directives, and active support from all levels of government and society. Recognizing and addressing the common challenges in this phase can lead to more successful policy outcomes. In conclusion, the public policy process in India is a complex but systematic journey that transforms ideas into actionable programs impacting millions of lives. By comprehensively understanding each stage of this process, policymakers, administrators, and citizens alike can contribute to more effective governance and the betterment of society. This unit has aimed to provide you with the foundational knowledge to critically engage with policy issues, emphasizing the importance of collaborative efforts in shaping India's future.
16.7 KEYWORDS
Policy Process: A sequence of steps involved in the development and implementation of public policies, including problem identification, policy formulation, adoption, implementation, evaluation, and termination. Policy Formulation: The stage where solutions to public problems are developed and debated, often involving multiple stakeholders such as government agencies, experts, and interest groups. Policy Implementation: The phase in which adopted policies are put into action by government agencies and officials to achieve the intended objectives. Policy Evaluation: The systematic assessment of the effectiveness, efficiency, and impact of policies after they have been implemented. Policy Monitoring: Ongoing oversight of policy implementation to ensure that it is proceeding as planned and to identify any issues that need to be addressed. Directive Principles of State Policy: Guidelines in the Indian Constitution that aim to establish social and economic democracy, influencing the formulation of policies. Federalism: A system of government where power is divided between a central authority and constituent political units (states), affecting how policies are made and implemented. Policy Cycle: A conceptual model that outlines the stages of policy development, from initial problem identification to evaluation and revision.

17.0 INTRODUCTION
It is widely recognized that political ideology plays a significant role in shaping public policies. But to what extent does political ideology influence the policies implemented in a country like India, with its vast and diverse population that encompasses various political beliefs? While the ideology of the ruling party does indeed affect the policy-making process, this discussion will not focus on the broader state theories such as Liberalism, Marxism, or Neo-liberalism. Even when a ruling party identifies itself as Neo-liberal or conservative, applying its ideology to policy-making is often far more complex in practice. Governance in India involves multiple stakeholders, with the government being just one among many actors. In a multi-party democracy like India, no single party can impose its ideology on the population. Legislators often encounter both external pressures and internal constraints that limit their ability to pursue policies aligned with their personal ideological preferences. This Unit will, therefore, consider political ideology in a broader context, suggesting that ideology can serve as a useful framework for analyzing the role of legislative elites. It will also investigate the connections between political ideology and its influence on public policy. To begin, it will define the key terms, 'political ideology' and 'impact,' as used in this context.
17.1 OBJECTIVES
After reading this Unit, you should be able to: * Discuss the meaning and nature of political ideology; * Examine the connect between political ideology and public policy; and * Explain the challenges of evaluating the impact of ideology on policy.

17.2 MEANING AND NATURE OF POLITICAL Impact of Political
Ideology on Public
IDEOLOGY Policy
Political ideology is a coherent and consistent set of beliefs or goals, the government (or political party) should pursue. In social studies, a political ideology, as is believed, is a certain set of ethical ideals, principles, doctrines, myths or symbols of a social movement, institution, class or large group that explains how society should work and offer some political and cultural blueprint for a certain social order. It is different from political culture, which is a coherent and consistent set of beliefs and principles. But political culture concerns itself with means that government should use to pursue its ends or goals- e.g., authoritarian vs. Constitutional government. A political ideology thus, is a coherent set of views on politics and the role of the government. Consistency over a wide range of issues is an important aspect of a political ideology. Oxford Dictionary of English defines 'impact' as "the action of one object coming forcibly into contact with another". It means a marked effect or influence. As defined by Rossi and Freeman (1993), "impact assessments are undertaken to estimate whether or not interventions produce their intended effects. Such estimates cannot be made with certainty, but only with varying degrees of plausibility". In a wider context, Thomas Dye (2004) has noted that policy and impact enable us to know the consequences of policy on: * Some specific target situation or group; * 'Spillover effects' on situations or groups other than the target; * Future as well as immediate conditions; * Direct costs, in terms of resources devoted to the programme; and * Indirect costs, including loss of opportunities to do other things. The main objective of an impact assessment is to produce an estimate of the 'net effects' of an intervention. Since evaluation tests whether public policy has worked as intended, the policy impact seeks to measure how the public policy has actually impacted upon the problems to which it was addressed.
17.3 IMPACT OF POLITICAL IDEOLOGY ON
PUBLIC POLICY
Political ideologies have two dimensions: i) goals and ii) methods. How society should be organised is related to goals. Methods are the most appropriate ways to achieve these goals. A few political ideologies are:
Anarchism, Communitarianism, Communism, Conservatism, Democracy,
Fascism, Liberalism, Nationalism, Populism, Socialism, Transhumanist
Politics, and Religio-political ideologies. In addition to the two dimensions mentioned, an ideology is composed of four basic characteristics. Beyond the simple left-right analysis, Liberalism, Conservatism, Libertarianism and Populism are the four most common ideologies in the United States, apart from those who identify themselves as

Public Policy and moderate. Media In India, the most prominent ideologies include Secularism, Liberalism, Socialism, Hindutva, Ambedkarism, and Dravidian ideologies, alongside influences from Marxism and various religious movements. At the international level, many nations adopt such particular ideologies, which are quite vague and unambiguous. But these ideologies carry an appeal to the heart and head and thus help them to secure their desired objectives in international relations. These ambiguous ideologies are referred to as ideologies of anti- imperialism, since most nations in the world seek to denounce actions of their opposing nations as imperialist actions. Three vague and so-called ambiguous ideologies are: * Ideology of national self-determination; * Ideology of the United Nations; and * Ideology of peace and human rights. Giving an example of Pakistan's political ideology, it is believed by some that Pakistan is arguing for national self-determination and freedom struggle for justifying its support for terrorists operating against the people of Jammu & Kashmir (now a Union Territory). It, however, uses anti-Talibanism for justifying its policy of supporting US actions in Afghanistan, which also involves its decision to provide military support to the US operations in Afghanistan. The United States has used the principle of humanitarian intervention to justify its military actions in Libya and other regions, claiming the goal of promoting democracy and stability. China justifies its actions in Hong Kong and Taiwan by framing them as essential for national sovereignty and territorial integrity, portraying its policies as efforts to maintain internal stability. Similarly, Russia has justified its involvement in Ukraine by claiming it is defending Russian- speaking populations and preserving national security. However, China and Russia have both for long projected themselves as anti-imperialist countries that were against the sovereignty of other nations compromised by more powerful nations. From this example, it could be deduced that the policies of the opponents are criticised as policies ignoring the interests of world peace. Even when a nation is engaged in a military action or is intervening in the affairs of another State, it attempts to explain and justify its action as a necessary course for strengthening the cause of durable peace and stability in international relations. This was done by the USA during the Gulf War 1991, and continues to be done. So even now in the 21st Century (Iraq and Afghanistan Wars are on). Hence, ideology is used by Nations for concealing the true nature of the policies they pursue behind the mask of pronounced peaceful intentions and for attracting the goodwill and support of people from every corner of the world. Does political ideology affect public policies? Do governments follow the ideological demands of their electorate and do they respond, if there are

ideological shifts at the individual level? Political ideology seems to be Impact of Political
Ideology on Public
relevant for guiding specific policy decision (Hinich and Munger, 1994), Policy especially, in the State-economy-relationship, the role of the government in regulating the relations among individuals, firms and State. For example, a more leftist ideology implies a favour for State intervention, and policies which are more in line with the preferences of workers, for instance employment protection. On the other hand, liberal/right ideology holds the opposite position. Even if confronted with the same problems, the policy responses derived from different ideologies are different. As a case in point, when faced with the financial crisis of 2008, different ideological leanings offered different solutions to the crisis, and in practice, some governments engaged in stimulus-programmes, others in austerity. The underlying closeness between citizens' ideology and public policy is that individual-level ideology can be aggregated into political ideology, it also expresses itself by voting in elections, by which citizens' ideology is formally translated in the partisan composition of government. Then governments of a certain ideological leaning introduce certain policies, e.g., more government intervention in the market in the case of left governments (Downs, 1957). Different ideologies on the input side will be translated into different policy inputs, maybe even political outcomes. Shifts in the ideology of citizens should precede shifts in public policy of elected governments. Do governments of a different ideological leanings actually differ in their policies? The question is, whether political ideology does indeed affect public policies? Individual political ideology may also affect policy bypassing the electoral process. The median voter theory as mentioned by Anthony Downs (1957) predicts that policies pursued by both left and right wing governments converge towards the median. So, in the end, their policies may not differ that much, regardless of their political ideological label. If the electorate shifts to the left, we will witness a more left-inclined policy regardless of which party is in government. This is not only true for two-party systems, but also systems, where coalition of parties, a left block and a right block, compete and in turn occupy the political offices.
17.4 POPULAR POLITICAL IDEOLOGY AND
PUBLIC POLICY
The question to be examined is: Does popular ideology affect public policies? In other words, is there any impact of popular political ideology, which operates circumventing the loose electoral link from voters to governments and their policies? The following analysis tests for effects of popular and government ideology on three policies: Employment generation and protection, social expenditure in health and education, and government size. While these three policies selected for analysis share the feature that a left- leaning population expresses demand for more of each welfare, they differ regarding the question of whether the government has an interest based on the William Niskanen's argument about the size of the public bureaucracy (Niskanen, as we know gave the Budget-Maximising Model in 1968; wherein 233

Public Policy and he suggested that rational bureaucrats will always increase the budget to Media increase their own power. This would lead to State growth, but social efficiency will be reduced). By setting policies about employment protection, the State sets the rules by which other actors, notably the courts and monitoring institutions have a bigger role to play. So, it is presumed that even if left and right governments differ, the effect of the free floating political-administrative system pursuing its own agenda will express itself in the two other policies without differences between left and right governments. But the political ideology of government is presumed to be relevant for the handling of economic issues (Hibbs, 1977). Similarly, study by Pool and Rosenthal (1997) shows the impact of ideology on policies. However, while ideology was found to be a significant factor in voting behaviour, it is only one among several. At times, there is also a case for the opposite argument, viz that parties formulate their political programmes and their ideology in a relatively vague and broad way, in order to be attractive for voters from a broad range of ideological leanings (Maloney and Pickering, 2008). Citizens are presumed to vote for parties depending on the country's most prominent problems (Swank, 1993). The point is, there is little evidence that the connection between popular ideology and policy hinges on the composition of governments. From the analysis, it is observed that all three policies are correlated, but explained to varying degrees by different factors; they all affect the relationship between the State and the economy, and are related to the factors such as economic development, popular ideology and government composition. Regarding popular ideology, the findings indicate that it affects employment protection, but neither the size of the Welfare State nor the size of government. Regarding the effect of government composition, a government ideological orientation does not matter substantially for any of the three policies under consideration here. A government's ideology does neither matter for the State-economy-relationship, nor for the regulation of the legal relationships between the employees and the employers. There are substantial developments in each of these policies over the last decades. Contrary to employment protection, social expenditure and government size are strongly in vogue. Both are increasing constantly, but not due to the observable ideological shift to the left in the population. Politics involves managing conflicts, and policymakers often prioritize political strategies over rigorous policy analysis. They typically find a political approach more effective than a purely rational one. Conflict resolution is based on compromise, conciliation, and a readiness to accept modest gains. Initial stages of the political approach involve searching for mutually beneficial outcomes through reciprocal support (e.g., "I will back your proposal if you support mine") and bargaining among diverse groups.

In this framework, politics often replaces policy analysis, which, while Impact of Political
Ideology on Public
playing a secondary role, remains significant in the policymaking process. Policy Lindblom and Woodhouse (1993) noted that "strategic analysis and mutual adjustments among political participants are the fundamental processes by which democratic systems achieve effective action. Given the limitations of time, energy, and intellectual resources, strategic analysis must concentrate on those aspects of an issue deemed most critical by participants to persuade one another." Politics significantly impacts policy, but its influence on actual policy outcomes is often debated. The effectiveness of political decisions in addressing or ameliorating problems may be limited. Recent studies on policy outcomes in India reveal that government policies have only a marginal effect on economic and industrial outcomes, such as Gross National Product (GNP), employment, and inflation, compared to larger factors like the international economy. Moreover, the policymaking process is heavily influenced by prior decisions and existing frameworks, which restrict innovation and limit policy options. Even though the ruling party plays a crucial role in shaping policy, its ability to effect substantial change is constrained by several factors. These include historical commitments, public opinion, bureaucratic resistance, and international constraints. This often means that "liberal democratic governments operate at the margin, responding to uncontrollable and unpredictable developments." De Bono (1991) suggests that policymaking is frequently driven by immediate reactions rather than strategic objectives, focusing on addressing 'rear-end' issues rather than forward-looking goals. Charles Lindblom's theory of "muddling through," or incrementalism, supports the notion that policy development is a gradual process of making small adjustments rather than implementing sweeping reforms. Despite the limitations and incremental nature of policymaking, it remains valuable. Public managers play a crucial role in identifying weaknesses within organizations and making necessary adjustments, ensuring that even incremental changes contribute to overall policy effectiveness and organizational improvement. 17.5 EVALUATING THE IMPACT OF
IDEOLOGY ON PUBLIC POLICY
Problems of evaluating the impact of policy programme of the government are innumerable and vary from country to country. Some notable problems are discussed here in brief:
Variations in Analysis of Policy Impact
Both outputs and outcomes are essential to measure, though for different reasons. Determining the actual impact of a policy is challenging. For instance, evaluating the impact of a policy on 'quality of life' raises questions about how 'quality of life' is defined. James Wilson (1973) argued that the analysis of public policy effects depends on one's perspective. If those responsible for implementing the policy conduct the research, the results will likely show the policy in a favorable light. In contrast, independent analysts may highlight the negative impacts of the same policy. This suggests that evaluating the real effects of a policy is more about values and interpretation than objective facts. Additionally, government impact evaluators often lack robust research capabilities. Ambiguity, insufficient comparative data, and the absence of concrete evidence tend to give administrators greater control over evaluations, or at least help mitigate criticism in the event of failure.
Political Influence on Policy Impact
It is often argued that policy outcomes are heavily influenced by political forces. When policymakers initiate inquiries or research into the effects of their policies on areas like health, education, or unemployment, they are actively shaping the context and framing the agenda through which these issues are defined and understood. In this sense, impact evaluation brings us back to the beginning of the policy-making process. The claims about a policy's impact must then undergo scrutiny from other political parties, interest groups, think tanks, researchers, and others, who may challenge its effectiveness in order to advance their own perspectives and proposals. For Lincoln and Guba (1985), who are critics of the quantitative approach to Impact Assessment, the political nature of evaluating the impact of a policy/programme means that more 'qualitative' forms of evaluation are necessary in order to counteract the distorting effects of apparently objective facts.

Complexity in Comparison of Policy Outcomes Impact of Political
Ideology on Public
Different nations produce and use different data, and those data have specific Policy contexts. But comparing the sets of statistics is a very difficult exercise. However, even though there are such clear methodological problems with the idea of comparing policy outcomes, it is the case that in the modern world, outcomes are compared by the use of data produced by international organisations such as the World Bank (WB) and Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). Policy analysts and politicians seek to know why different political systems differ in terms of the actual outcomes: Why do countries spend certain proportions of their Gross Domestic Product (GDP) on health, rural development, education and so on? Why do the performance and effective implementation of policies differ from country to country? Explanations to such questions are, however different and complex. Moreover, the study of impact and evaluation in public administration has been seriously neglected. It suffers not only from the lack of interest and initiative, but also from deficiencies on the methodological front. While doing impact analysis and fixing of standards, policymakers tend to rely on comparison with the past. Dror (1989) has observed that comparison with the past, in many respects, is misleading because it does not provide a 'zero point' for reliable conclusion. The experience of India, in particular, has amply demonstrated that borrowing successful models from countries very different to India have failed to make their impact on social improvement. 17.6 LET US SUM UP
In conclusion, it can be stated that political ideology plays a significant role in shaping public policy and its implementation. Countries often use ideology to justify their own policies while critiquing or rejecting the policies of other nations, particularly adversaries. Governments may employ ideologies as a cover for their real intentions, which often involve maintaining and expanding their power in international relations. Foreign policy typically incorporates various ideologies as tools for both defense and offense in global interactions.

Public Policy and As noted, ideologies in international relations can be both a source of Media cooperation and conflict. Nations with similar ideological orientations tend to cooperate more easily, while ideological differences frequently lead to tensions, especially between countries with opposing views. However, this does not imply that ideology has no influence on international affairs. It remains one of several factors that shape the course and content of global relations. In modern times, ideologies offer nations a set of tools, concepts, and language to communicate their ideas and execute their actions on the international stage. Nations continue to use ideology to explain, justify, and legitimize their policies, providing a foundation for pursuing national interests. However, some argue that with the rise of globalization, the role of ideology in international relations has been diminishing.

BNM-031 COURSE INTRODUCTION : DATA
JOURNALISM
Data is the true currency of our age, especially in the field of journalism. It is the goldmine from which journalists can extract valuable information and use it to tell stories that serve public interest and hold those in power accountable. The course BNM-031 will provide you with the theoretical knowledge and skillset to become adept practitioners of data journalism. You will learn not only about how to handle data, but also incorporate its essence in your stories to make them catalytic and impactful. You will also be introduced to various codes of ethics and editorial guidelines that work to ensure that journalism fosters public trust and societal harmony. As aspiring media professionals, you will feel encouraged to focus on building your analytical skills as a data journalist to remain competitive in the industry.
Block 1: Understanding Data Journalism
This block consists of four units. Unit 1 introduces the fundamental principles of data journalism and its key concepts such as data, storytelling, verification, and data literacy. Unit 2 focuses on the evolution of data journalism, touching upon 20th century developments such as "precision journalism," Computer- assisted reporting (CAR), open data movement, and the Internet. Unit 3 deals with the ethical implications of data journalism to show how public interest and individual rights must always be protected. Unit 4 highlights the concept of measurement and in social science research and its relevance to data journalism.
Block 2: Concepts of Data Journalism
This block consists of five units. Unit 5 traces the coming of online journalism powered by the digital revolution, and its correlation to data journalism as we see it today. Unit 6 discusses the role and processes pertaining to data tabulation, which is central to how data is organised. Unit 7 deals with statistics, a very important process during which data is decoded. Unit 8 introduces the reader to computer applications that a journalist uses to structure their data and tell their story. Unit 9 focuses on data mining, and how journalists can benefit from using this to extract hidden patterns to make meaning of large amounts of data.
Block 3: Data Journalism in Practice
Unit 10 takes us through the process of finding a story within large or small
datasets and how data is preprocessed to clean it and to reduce errors. Unit 11 discusses the importance of reporting data, the guidelines issued by international media agencies and the processes involved in reporting said data. Unit 12 looks Table: at data mashing, Unit 13 focuses on data scraping, Unit 14 explains the concept of Big Data and its impact on journalism and on us as citizens through the use of a case study.
Block 4: Interactive Data Journalism
Unit 15 unpacks the concept of data analysis while also bringing forth the
practicalities of data visualisation. Unit 16 focuses on geographical data and the different ways in which data is mapped in order to make the story grounded.
Unit 17 dwells on the use of AI for the creation of inforgraphics, not just dealing
viii with the technical aspect but also ethical considerations. Unit 18 rounds off with

case studies of exemplary instances of data journalism, in India and overseas, that played a big role in determining public policy and initiated public debate. The course is designed to give a clear, yet concise idea about data journalism, its theoretical underpinnings, the processes involved in its execution, and last but not the least, its very tangible impact on our everyday lives. Upon completion of this course, you will be able to:
- sift through, organise and decipher data pertinent to your story;
- 'find' the story within the data and use it in tandem with ground reports
to elevate your story;
- design infographics and implement visualisations of your data for its
easy comprehension; and
- understand collaborative processes and tools that can allow you to work
across newsrooms to produce hard-hitting, data-backed stories. The knowledge that you gather from this course and the skill set that you develop after a thorough understanding and practice of the course components will make it easier to navigate through the media text that you come across later in this programme and also when you start working in the media industry. ix

BLOCK 1 UNDERSTANDING DATA
JOURANLISM
This block explores the fast-expanding world of data journalism, which has catapulted reporting from a traditional form to a more exciting avatar bolstered by hard data. The goal is to make the reader adept at combining traditional reporting methods with data analysis.
Unit 1: Foundations of Data Journalism, will introduce you to fundamental
principles of data journalism and key concepts such as data, storytelling, verification, and data literacy. You will learn about freely available tools, and national and international open resources for collecting data. In Unit 2: History of Data Journalism, we will trace the evolution of data journalism. You will be introduced to concepts such as "precision journalism," Computer-assisted reporting (CAR), and open data movement, which revolutionised the field. The role of the Internet and allied technologies will be discussed at length.
Unit 3: Ethical Aspects of Data Journalism, deals with the ethical complexities
that undergird the practice of data journalism. The unit will explain how a data journalist should ensure transparency, responsible interpretation, and sensitivity, while staying clear of pitfalls such as data misrepresentation, violation of privacy and biasness. In Unit 4: Levels of Measurement, we will explore the fundamental concept of measurement and its relevance to data journalism. You will be introduced to its types, postulates or principles, and levels before learning about potential sources of errors and ways to minimise them. These four units will offer you an introductory insight into the world of data journalism and its significance in news making today. The block provides you a comprehensive view of how journalists can benefit from it while also being alert to their own roles and responsibilities.

1.0 INTRODUCTION
The evolution of digital media has significantly impacted journalism, giving rise to many new forms and transforming how we consume and interact with the news today. It has redefined the media landscape through interactive visualisations and immersive storytelling. Today, the creation of digital information is exploding in volume. Hundreds of millions of terabytes of data are produced daily and we can access this enormous ocean of data with a click of a button.

Journalists are no longer just storytellers, they are also data detectives equipped with analytical tools and techniques to unpack raw data, uncovering insights that spark conversations and drive change. Data journalism is revolutionising the ways we tell stories; it is not merely about understanding numbers but about revealing hidden patterns to see the larger picture. Data, surveys, and computer- assisted reporting (CAR) have been utilised in journalism for a long time, but it is only recently that journalists have started using new technologies to access these vast volumes of data and draw insights from them. Both the author as well as the reader can now easily explore and understand data, thanks to new and advanced technologies. Since a growing number of decisions are being made based on data, the demand for journalists who can efficiently work with it continues to grow, which makes data journalism an important field of study for aspiring media professionals.
1.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After going through this unit, you will be able to:
- understand the idea of data journalism: concepts, key terms, and their
relevance in modern journalism;
- learn about the basic skills and competencies a data journalist needs to
possess.
- develop a basis for further learning about data journalism;
1.2 DEFINITION AND KEY CONCEPTS
In today's digital media age, data is everywhere. Everything can be calculated and digitally presented in " ones and zeros, " whether it is sports, politics, the environment, tourism, crime, traffic, disease, etc. The future of journalism is data-driven, and the internet has created endless opportunities, especially for media practioners. Journalists need to be data savvy and should be able to see new patterns and developments in raw data. Data journalism is the systematic use of structured data that feeds into traditional forms of storytelling and reporting to investigate, interpret, and communicate stories based on large-scale digital data. It applies computational methods and interactive tools to collect, analyse, and visualise complex information for clarity and engagement. Many media outlets use data to tell stories. Many nations are making different kinds of data available openly, resulting in easier access for journalists. To foster a culture of data sharing and data usefulness for achieving broader socioeconomic goals, the Government of India announced the National Data Sharing and Accessibility Policy (NDSAP) in March 2012. This policy resulted in the creation of the www.data.gov.in portal, which provides access to all data on Indian ministries and departments. Activity 1: Visit https://data.gov.in and find a dataset related to your state or city. Create infographics from that data using free tools like Datawrapper or Tableau Public.
1.2.1 Data
In data journalism, data can be the source as well as a tool to tell the story. It refers to unorganised details, statistics, and knowledge commonly organised in spreadsheets, APIs (Application Programming Interfaces, a set of rules

that allow software to communicate with each other), or databases. The data -numbers, words, images, geolocations, etc. -becomes meaningful only after it is processed. For example, vote counts by district released by the Election Commission of India allow detection of voter turnout patterns or possible irregularities. Similarly, Air Quality Index's (AQI) raw and daily PM2.5 values given by the CPCB (Central Pollution Control Board) help journalists visualise pollution trends over the course of time in Delhi.
1.2.2 Storytelling
Put simply, data journalism helps journalists in breaking down complex datasets and transforming them into stories that are human-centred and engaging narratives so readers can relate and easily understand. If you want to cover a story on the employment gender gap in the industrial sector, instead of simply stating that "female participation is 27%," you can write a story about three or four women from a varied pool, fully backing this with labour force survey data. Similarly, instead of listing numbers, a journalist could show how subsidy allocation changes affect a family's food or LPG expenses.
1.2.3 Verification
The foundation of credibility for data journalism is verification. Careful examination alongside verification of data's relevance, accuracy, and dependability is important before the use of data in a narrative. Information comes from many different sources, which include government organisations, APIs, scraped websites, and leaked documents. A journalist must check if the data is correct, up-to-date and valid in that context. Data that is not properly verified can mislead readers, damage journalists' credibility, and cause real harm, particularly when sensitive subjects like politics, crime, or public health are involved. Data verification is important for ensuring accountability and transparency, and for preventing false narratives. Additionally, it can build trust and avoid legal and ethical issues. A few tips and techniques to verify data
- First, examine the data source and confirm it is from reputable and
official organisations, such as government databases, WHO, and Central Statistics Office, India.
- Cross-verify this information with secondary sources (compare National
Sample Survey Office data with World Bank reports on India).
- Check the most recent update date.
- Confirm the data's accuracy along with its derivation from a representative
sample.
- Speak to professionals within the field, such as data scientists and
statisticians.
- Do the fundamental validity checks; look for missing numbers,
duplicates, and outliers using technical tools such as Microsoft Excel

and R software.
1.2.4 Visualisation
Visualisation is the art and science of turning unprocessed data into visual narratives and is one of the most important tools of data journalism. The human brain processes visuals more rapidly than text. A pie chart, bar graph, or colour- coded map can effectively communicate an idea better than a text explanation. A well-designed visualisation draws attention to the narrative and highlights the story hidden within numbers. Charts, graphs, maps, infographics, and other visual formats are used to help people comprehend complex statistics quickly. During COVID-19, you must have seen newspapers and websites using colour- coded state-wise maps to show the hot spots, number of daily cases, vaccination rates, etc.
1.2.5 Interactivity
Interactivity in data journalism increases engagement and enables users to become investigators. It makes static data dynamic, so instead of simply reading the data, audiences can explore, zoom in, or filter data based on their interest. For example, in an article that shows the growth of OTT platforms' viewership from 2005 to 2025, "Drag the Timeline" feature allowed users to drag a timeline from 2005 to 2025, providing a seamless and real-time visual trip through the shifting media landscape.

1.3 RELEVANCE IN MODERN JOURNALISM
Reporting facts alone is no longer enough for journalism in the age of digital media. To truly flourish, it must expose truth, decode complex information, and engage the audience. Data journalism, by combining traditional storytelling with data analysis skills, helps journalists explore, verify, and visualise digital information. Almost every subject today is deeply data-driven: public health, environmental issues, gender inequality, and economic inequality. But information is embedded in raw numbers; data journalism transforms large and abstract datasets into clear narratives and visuals so that the general public can understand beyond just raw numbers. Indian websites such as Scroll.in and India Spend, for instance, employed interactive dashboards to monitor infections and vaccinations during the COVID-19 pandemic, enabling users to follow the developing situation in real time. Initially, data-driven stories were mostly used for investigative reporting. The most famous cases, the Panama Papers and the Paradise Papers, were based on data-driven analysis of offshore transactions. These cases revealed how politicians, celebrities, and corporations used offshore entities to hide assets and avoid taxes. Data journalism improves public participation and engagement. For example, during elections, by employing live dashboards to visually represent the results in real time by party and region, media outlets offer a more captivating viewing experience. It also increases the accuracy and speed of reporting. For instance, during the 2020 Delhi Riots, independent news outlets and fact checkers used verified user-generated content, maps, and FIR records to counteract misinformation. Most importantly, insights from localised data journalism empower citizens. Informed civic engagement is encouraged via websites like Dataful.in and Citizen Matters, which let users analyse public data on health, education, and sanitation at the city or ward level. Additionally, data journalism raises awareness of issues that marginalised people confront, and encourages inclusivity. In Indian villages, outlets such as Gaon Connection use data from rural surveys to discuss social injustices, healthcare availability, and farmer 17 earnings.

Data journalism gives journalists the ability to clearly, creatively, and credibly present compelling tales that are supported by evidence. Gaining expertise in data journalism is not only beneficial for aspiring journalists but also essential for creating media that empowers, informs, and upholds democracy. Activity 2- Pick any recent case study on data journalism and write a short report (300 words) explaining how data journalism helped uncover or explain it.
1.4 CORE COURSE REQUIREMENTS OF DATA
JOURNALISM
Data journalism requires an organised comprehension of specific domains in the form of building blocks. A data journalism student must develop an understanding of both journalistic principles and data-handling skills, which requires a structured approach to learn technical, analytical, and ethical competencies. If students are comfortable with numeracy and developing basic spreadsheet-based program skills, they will analyse things in more depth using numbers. The course will equip students with skills to gather credible data, clean it, analyse it, and then effectively use it to tell different tales. Some key components of the course will be as follows:
- Data collection and evaluation of source credibility. Students must be
able to understand the nature of data, verify credible public databases, and know how to access information from those large datasets. They should be able to differentiate between official, open-source, manipulated, biased, and peer-reviewed datasets.
- The backbone of data journalism is technical proficiency. To clean,
organise, and perform basic analysis, students must be well-skilled in using digital tools such as Microsoft Excel, Google Sheets, and advanced tools such as Flourish, Tableau Public, Datawrapper, etc.
- The strategic use of data, infographics, maps, and tables to enhance
readers' engagement. This includes the intersection of technical skills and creativity. Data journalists should be proficient in creatively using visuals to enhance stories and avoid overwhelming readers with numbers.
- Students should develop a critical lens to evaluate the role of data in
shaping public discourse. Journalists must be able to question "data-ism, " which is the blind reliance on data, neglecting its limitations. Data can be manipulated, collected with bias, or be incomplete; thus, one must understand that data should balance the rigour of numbers and not overshadow the human element of storytelling.
1.5 SKILLS REQUIRED FOR A DATA
JOURNALIST
A hybrid skillset comprising journalism, programming, design, statistics, and ethics is essential for data journalists today. This section includes a comprehensive review of the essential skills required to be successful in the field of data journalism.

1.5.1 Data Literacy
Data literacy is the heart of data journalism, which goes beyond mathematics, and involves understanding numbers, critical thinking, recognising hidden patterns, questioning the data source, and the methodology used. It helps in identifying manipulative and cherry-picked data. A data journalist must know how to read tables, analyse trends, and detect anomalies and outliers.
1.5.2 Technical Proficiency
Data journalists need not excel in programming, but basic technical skills are essential. They should be proficient in using spreadsheets (Excel or Google) for basic sorting and filtering of data, software such as R for statistical operations, Python for data scraping and analysis, and so on.
1.5.3 Design and Visualisation Skills
This skill involves presenting data in clear and eye-catching visuals. The journalists must know chart types (bar, pie, line, and scatter), colour theory, infographics, and visual hierarchy. They must be able to balance the aesthetic design with accurate representation to make an impactful story. For example, when you want to compare two different categories, like literacy rate in different Indian states, you work with a bar graph, and when you want to show the trend over time, such as GDP growth, you do that by using a line graph.
1.5.4 Basics of Coding
For a data journalist, it is not necessary to be a skilled coder, but knowing the basics of programming can help automate repetitive tasks, perform complex analyses, and scrape websites for data (simply put, importing information from a website into spreadsheets or local files on your computer). Understanding and using programs like HTML, Python, and SQL enables the gathering and analysis of data and enhances storytelling capabilities.
1.5.5 Storytelling Skills
Numbers or data don't speak for themselves. It is the responsibility of data journalists to combine insights from the data with the human element and context. The entire story must not be based on numbers, it must also include human voices and quotes. For example, if you want to write a piece on rising fuel prices over the years based on data, including quotes from daily wage workers will make the story more relatable and impactful.
1.5.6 Fact-checking and Verification
Validation of data for accuracy and transparency, as well as fact-checking, is critical. Cross-checking data sources, speaking to subject-matter experts, and exploring anomalies in the data are all part of it.
1.5.7 Statistics
Statistics can help us better understand the distributions of data, as well as frequency, correlation, and trend patterns. Journalists need to know everything from mean, mode, median, percentage, and ratio to more advanced statistics like standard deviation, margin of error, and correlation.

1.5.8 Ethical Use of Data
In data journalism, responsible data use is essential, especially when dealing with sensitive data such as health care, religion, caste, and so on. Privacy must be respected by keeping the source anonymous, avoiding bias while presenting the data, and refraining from manipulating data with the aim of misleading. 2.0 INTRODUCTION
Journalism dates back to around 59 BC in ancient Rome when 'Acta Diurna, ' a government gazette focused on official record-keeping, was published daily. As a discipline, journalism has been transformed from official record- keeping, yielding new, innovative forms and approaches. While the term 'data journalism' is relatively modern, its foundational ideas have been present for a long time. This form of journalism began as simple statistical reporting but has now developed into dynamic and interactive storytelling. As society grew more complex and the flow of information began to increase, journalists started relying on numbers to reveal underlying trends in issues such as health, politics, population, climate change, and economic changes, etc. In the early 20th century, quantitative reporting expanded due to the influence of social science-inspired ' 'precision journalism, ' which subsequently led to the development of computer-assisted reporting (CAR) in the mid-20th century. By the late 20th century, all the major newspapers were using statistical graphics 24 and database journalism. In the 2000s, as the internet expanded and the amount

of data increased, the rise of the open-data movement led to an explosion of data- driven stories that utilised interactive visualisations. However, data journalism in India experienced significant growth only around 2012, when https://www. data.gov.in/ was launched by NDSAP. This unit on data journalism will cover the history and development of data journalism from the pre-digital era to the current moment of data-rich reporting. The students will have a deeper understanding of the roots of data journalism and how it has transformed with technological advancements over the years.
2.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After going through this unit, students will be able to:
- have a deep understanding of the historical evolution of data journalism.
- recognise how data journalism practices have changed over time, from
the pre-digital era to current digital reporting.
- understand the major technological advancements that have heavily
influenced this field.
- understand the history and growth of data journalism in India.
2.2 ORIGIN OF DATA JOURNALISM (PRE-
DIGITAL AGE)
2.2.1 Data in traditional journalism
Using data for reporting is not a modern journalistic practice. In the Data Journalism Handbook 1, Liliana Bounegru writes that journalists have been using data as a source for stories for centuries. In Europe, during the 18th and 19th centuries, printed broadsheets published statistical tables on mortality rates, weather, and prices to inform their readers. During this era, government and institutions started collecting information about agriculture, economy, population, health, etc., and journalists began using these numbers to support their stories. William Playfair, a Scottish engineer and economist, is known as the inventor of graphical methods of statistics. In 1786, he created various types of diagrams to present data, including area, line, and bar charts. In 1801, he published the first pie and circle charts to show part-whole relationships. Playfair believed that charts communicate better than tables, and his work laid the foundation for later statistical reporting. Another famous example of traditional data reporting is Florence Nightingale, a British nurse and statistician. In the Crimean War (1853-1856), she was serving as the manager and trainer of nurses, and using data collected during her service, she showed how poor sanitation practices were killing more soldiers than battle injuries. She used pie charts to visualise the data, her famous 'coxcomb' diagram. Her work made a strong impact and led to improvements in the military health system.
2.2.2 Use of Government Data in Newspapers
In the early 20th century, data played a significant role in many newspaper stories. Although visualisations were rare, data was used in figure, list, or table formats to report on things like commodities, athletics, crime, trade statistics,

and health. According to Simon Rogers, in 1821, the UK-based newspaper The Guardian began its news coverage with data journalism. It published an investigative story about schools in Manchester. The report had tables showing the number of students who attended these schools and the cost per school. The report revealed that the number of students getting free education was much higher than what official records indicated. Such gaps in data cannot be ignored because it is on their basis that public policy is formed and executed In the world of commerce too, newspapers have historically provided investors with the prices before the electronic stock market system was introduced. Since 1884, Dow Jones and Company has published stock market trends in print via the Wall Street Journal.
2.3 DEVELOPMENT THROUGH THE 20TH
CENTURY
2.3.1 The Advent of Computer-Assisted Reporting
Researchers believe that decades of computer-assisted reporting (CAR) directly evolved into data journalism and the data-rich reporting we see today. The most notable transformation in statistical reporting began in the 1960s-1970s with the development of CAR. When computers became accessible and available in the newsrooms, CAR pioneers like Elliot Jaspin and Philip Meyer started using them to collect and analyse data. Philip Meyer used social science research methods in journalism, and combined these with computers and programming, calling it 'Precision Journalism. ' He used survey data and computer analysis in reporting the 1967 Detroit Riots in the USA and revealed the underlying causes of rioting. His reporting helped the Detroit Free Press win the Pulitzer Prize in 1968. According to Meyer, "Precision journalism is a way to expand the tool kit of the reporter to make topics that were previously inaccessible, or only crudely accessible, subject to journalistic scrutiny. It was especially useful in giving a hearing to minority and dissident groups that were struggling for representation. " This was the era that led to the growth of scientific methods in reporting; newsrooms began hiring statisticians and researchers, and journalists began learning data skills.
2.3.2 Expansion of CAR and Investigative Journalism
In such an environment and with the development of new technical tools and resources for journalists, microcomputers and personal computers revolutionised computer-assisted reporting (CAR). By the early 1990s, CAR techniques were being applied by reporters to several important investigations both in and outside the US. The availability of sophisticated public databases, like finance data, crime statistics, and government budgetary documents, allowed journalists to conduct comprehensive methodological analyses of issues such as corruption, crime, police misconduct, and environmental problems. Prominent news outlets such as The Miami Herald and The Washington Post established specially equipped investigative units with trained data analysts. One of the most standout investigations was 'House of Lies' by The Miami Herald. This Pulitzer-winning investigative report exposed the mismanagement and fraud within the Miami Housing Agency.

2.3.3 NICAR
The Missouri School of Journalism founded the National Institute for Computer- Assisted Reporting (NICAR), a program of Investigative Rerporters and Editors (IRE), in 1989. Indiana University's James Brown conducted the first
Computer Assisted Reporting Conference in Indianapolis, Indiana, in 1990,
and it continued for several years. From the early 1990s to the early 2000s, computer-assisted reporting flourished in the United States, mainly because of the seminars offered by the University of Missouri, and IRE and NICAR, in different parts of the world. IRE held its first Computer Assisted Reporting conference in 1993, after which it became a joint initiative with NICAR.
