2.4 EMERGENCE IN THE DIGITAL AGE
2.4.1 Rise of the Internet and Data Access
Developments in mobile computing, online connectivity, access, and speed, along with an explosion in data creation, fundamentally transformed computer- assisted reporting at the beginning of the 21st century. Multimedia has found its way into every newsroom, with editors and reporters using computers in their day-to-day tasks. The invention of the internet in the late 1990s and early 2000s transformed the availability of data. Websites such as the U.S. Census Bureau and the World Bank, along with open government platforms, started providing free data sets to the public. Journalistic static publishing also started challenging traditional formats of storytelling. Static charts were transformed into interactive dashboards and other sophisticated formats, like searchable maps and personalised calculators. Such a change propelled readers to become more engaged and interact with the data themselves. With the internet providing boundless seas of data, journalists have an array of responsibilities, such as reporting and writing articles, designing interactives and visualisations, crafting storytelling platforms, conducting predictive modelling, developing open-source software, and more. The data journalism field has increased in importance in the last two decades, and learning data journalism is vital because the pace of acquiring new skills has accelerated significantly.

2.4.2 Open Data Movement
In the late 2000s, the Open Data Movement revolutionised the way governments and institutions share information. The US-based website, Data.gov, founded in 2009, was a notable turning point in the history of the open data movement. This site gave the public access to a large number of datasets, promoting transparency. This initiative gave birth to many other similar websites around the globe, such as the Indian government's website Data.gov.in, which was launched in 2012 as part of a policy aimed at enhancing the sharing and accessibility of national data. To assist in the effective and practical use of open data, Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) have been created. APIs provide developers the ability to effortlessly retrieve and add data from different applications. The implementation of the International Open Data Charter in 2015 marked a major shift in the international approach to open data policies. The Charter was first signed by seventeen countries at the Open Government Partnership summit held in Mexico City in October 2015. The charter set several guidelines and suggested approaches that should govern the release of open government data. Today, its principles have been adopted by 172 national and subnational governments around the world.
2.4.3 Web-Based Visualisation and Interactivity
As we have seen so far, modern-day journalism has greatly benefited from the advent of visualisation and interactive storytelling because these can present data stories in a captivating manner. Such methods enable the audience to actively interact with the information at a more indepth level. The digital era has transformed the way of doing things. Back in 2005, Adrian Holovaty's Chicago crime data mashup with Google Maps was a prime example of how journalism could utilise interactive online visualisations. Presently, newsrooms use advanced software such as D3.js and The Upshot by The New York Times to automatically generate interactive narratives loaded with information. In this manner, data visualisation is increasingly incorporated into storytelling to increase audience outreach and comprehension. As listed in Unit 1, numerous free tools enabling data visualisation and interactive storytelling techniques have been provided for students to build captivating data stories using these resources.
2.5 DATA JOURNALISM IN INDIA
2.5.1 History of Data Journalism In India
Before the mainstreaming of digital media, a majority of Indian newspapers used to cover budgets, elections, and education using government data from the 1990s to the early 2000s. This data was often presented in the form of static infographics. With the advent of digital media, there was a growth of data-centric journalism in the 2010s. Data journalism in India has transformed remarkably over the past decade due to better access to publicly available data, the development of new technologies, and an increasing expectation for openness and responsibility in government operations. The launch of IndiaSpend by journalist Govindraj Ethiraj in December 2011 marked a pivotal moment in this evolution. As the first dedicated pan-Indian initiative in data journalism, IndiaSpend used available public data to analyse 28 and inform the public on important social issues, including education, healthcare,

and the environment. The objective was to promote good governance by telling stories with data and making them known to the public. The Indian government started formalising its commitment to open data after approving the National Data Sharing and Accessibility Policy (NDSAP) in 2012, which allowed more government data to be accessed, fostering transparency. Like Ethiraj, Rakesh Dubbudu, an engineer, initiated Factly, a data journalism information portal in 2015. Factly publishes infographics, interactives, and stories using available public data through RTI and other means. Observing the role of data in narratives, The Hindu started a 'Data' section on its website in April 2015. Another newspaper, Hindustan Times (HT), started its data section called 'Interactives' in 2016, with a focus on data-driven news articles filled with visualisations.
2.5.2 Educational Initiatives
Many universities and media training institutes in India have started integrating data journalism courses into their programmes. Indian journalists have been trained on apps such as OpenRefine, DataWrapper, and Google Sheets through workshops organised by the Google News Initiative, DataLEADS, and other global institutions. Under DataLEADS' initiative FactShala, over 58 thousand people have been trained in matters pertaining to media and information literacy across India. This program empowers the community to critically evaluate information available online and fight misinformation. Similarly, under the Google News Initiative, journalists receive rigorous training and mentorship through workshops and online meetings. As part of their Data Journalism Accelerator programme, they provide mentoring and stipends to journalists for publishing data-driven stories. 2.6 LET US SUM UP
The world of data journalism looks very different from the earlier era of manual data collection, which is distinct from present-day's computational, complex digital narratives. In the middle of the 20th century, journalists started working with data in their reporting, with pioneers like Philip Meyer promoting "precision journalism"--the use of social science methods in news stories. Computer- assisted reporting (CAR), which began in the 1960s, allowed journalists to work with large pools of data. Technological advancements introduced new tools and platforms for data visualisations and interactive storytelling. In India, the growth of data journalism started with projects such as IndiaSpend in 2011 and data.gov.in, which focused on data-driven public interest journalism. Special training and workshops are available for aspiring data journalists to brush up their skills. Today, data journalism has expanded to include algorithmic analyses and visualisation tools in practice, allowing journalists to tell stories that serve public interest.
2.7 KEYWORDS
1. CAR: Computer-assisted reporting is a 1960s journalistic practice that
involves computer-assisted research and analysis of data.
2. API: Application Programming Interfaces are tools that allow access
to, and retrieval of, data from servers. APIs allow journalists to pull the most up-to-date or historical data sets from official sources.
3. Precision Journalism: A term coined by Philip Meyer, this is a form
of journalism that employs social science research methods, especially data analysis, to produce more accurate and detailed news reports.
4. Open Data Movement: This is a global movement that promotes free
and open access to data from governments, organisations, and public entities.

3.1 INTRODUCTION
Data journalism combines data collecting with data analysis to shape stories. It is concerned with the collection, cleansing, and analysis of vast amounts of data in order to discover trends. Presenting election results or health statistics following a significant illness outbreak is one example. This technique builds on standard reporting tools such as big data analytics and algorithms. These new tactics update traditional journalistic practices by emphasising data, numbers and their visualisation to increase the efficacy and weightiness of a story. It is critical to use these tools carefully, as they can mislead if misused. The introduction of algorithms and interactive visualisations thus, raises new ethical concerns. Journalists must report data with integrity, explain their methodology clearly, and avoid distortions or sensationalism. In this course, we will look at ethical guidelines for data journalism and, finally, trends in India.
3.2 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After reading this Unit, you will be able to:
- understand journalists' ethical responsibilities when handling data
(accuracy, privacy, and fairness).

- comprehend major ethical codes (e.g., SPJ, GIJN, BBC, and local
institutions) that are applicable to data-driven reporting. learn how these principles play out in practice through real cases (e.g., misleading charts, data privacy breaches).
- ask critical questions about data sources and methods and to insist on
transparency and accountability, andunderstand the consequences of ethical lapses (such as loss of trust or harm to individuals) and benefits of integrity (like informed public and credible journalism).
3.3 ETHICS IN JOURNALISM
'Ethics' implies the norms which a journalist must uphold and cherish in order to keep the integrity and the sanctity of the profession intact. According to Webster's New World Dictionary, "ethics" is a system or code of morals of a particular person, religion, group, profession, etc. Today, when "business" rather than the quality of news is given more importance, it requires quite an effort on the part of a journalist to function in accordance with the ethical norms of the profession. While journalists, like other citizens, are governed by all the laws of the land, there is a sizeable area of activity which remains out of the domain of law. Therefore, a journalist is doubly responsible for upholding a professional code of ethics or principles himself A free press, which is essential for the functioning of democracy, directly results from an environment that is free of fear and violence which a competent government must be capable of providing. Today, it is common for journalists to be threatened, coerced and even killed for doing their job and bringing the truth to light. Yet, even when faced with provocations, greed or dangers, a journalist must function strictly within the framework of ethical norms for media professionals. Given below is a list of basic ethical norms a reporter should follow: a) Accuracy and fairness: A journalist must inform and comment on matters of public interest in a fair, accurate and unbiased manner. Inaccuracy and personal remarks should always be avoided. b) Prepublication verification: Verification and checking of news before publication is all the more necessary where news and the comments based thereon can create complications. c) Caution against defamatory writings: Newspapers should avoid publishing writings that are defamatory or libellous against any individual or organization without doing due diligence and checking. They must have sufficient reason or evidence to believe that the news is true and that its publication will be for public good. d) Privacy: Intrusion or invasion of the privacy of individuals must be absolutely avoided unless outweighed by genuine overriding public interest. In cases such as sex crimes, great caution should be exercised to ensure the names, identity and pictures of victims are not made public. e) Eschew suggestive guilt: Newspapers should eschew suggestive guilt by association. They should not name or identify the family, relatives or associates of a person convicted or accused of a crime if they are not related to the crime or criminal activity, or if a reference to them is not relevant to the matter reported.

f) Corrections: When a factual error or mistake is detected or confirmed, the newspaper should publish a correction promptly, with due prominence and with an apology or expression of regret in the case of a serious lapse. The right to reply and letters to the editor are important places where such grievances can be aired. g) Communal reports: Proper verification must be done before publishing reports regarding communal clashes or disputes. A report should not vitiate the situation. Rather, it should be aimed at soothing ruffled feelings. h) Sensational headings: Sensational headings should be avoided. Headlines should conform to the contents of news stories. They should be clear, unambiguous and authentic. i) Eschew vulgarity and obscenity: Obscene and vulgar items should be prohibited as these offend public sensibilities. Furthermore, violence, in any form, should never be glorified. j) Avoid crass commercialism: In order to make profits, a newspaper should not throw media ethics and journalistic values to the winds. Instead, to the aim should be to create an equilibrium between objectivity and commercialism. k) Avoid caste, religion or community disclosures: In general, a newspaper should refrain from identifying a person based on his caste, religion or community, as these can lead to biases and sometimes, harassment. 3.4 GLOBAL ETHICAL GUIDELINES
Several journalism-based organisations around the world have designed guidelines on ethics pertaining to data work. The following are some prominent organisations and the codes and toolkits they advance:
3.4.1 SPJ Code of Ethics
The Society of Professional Journalists' Code of Ethics (USA) is among the foremost organisations that has laid down principles particularly relevant to data work:

Seek Truth and Report It: SPJ guidelines stress upon accuracy and honesty. They state that journalists should "take responsibility for the accuracy of their work" and verify information thoroughly. In data journalism, this means validating datasets and using original sources whenever possible. Minimise Harm: SPJ's code recommends that reporting must be balanced with respect for individuals. It directs journalists to "balance the public's need for information against potential harm or discomfort." For data stories, this could involve omitting sensitive personal details or anonymising individuals when full disclosure serves little public interest. Act Independently: The code stresses that reporters' first obligation is to the public, not special interests. They should avoid conflicts of interest and be transparent about funding and partnerships. This is especially important when collaborating on data projects. Be Accountable: Accountability means being answerable for one's work and correcting errors based on that assessment. SPJ advises that "sources should be identified clearly" and mistakes corrected promptly. For data journalism, this implies citing datasets and methods, so the public can trust the story. As experts put it, journalists should publish their methodology so others can replicate their work.
3.4.2 Global Investigative Journalism Network (GIJN)
GIJN directions are aimed at fostering best journalistic practices among investigative reporters. Its guidelines on data journalism focus on integrity in the data-gathering process. For example, GIJN's advisory on web-scraping ethics notes that public data published by institutions "should automatically be public", but reporters must respect legal boundaries (if a site restricts access, journalists "should acknowledge these legal barriers...and respect them"). GIJN also encourages data-sharing techniques, and themselves share scripts and tips at their conferences. In their articles, they advocate transparency and cross-checking results with independent sources, important principles for investigative journalists to follow. Thus, the GIJN toolkit approach focuses on verifying accuracy, respecting copyright and considering privacy as being central to ethics of data journalism
3.4.3 European Data Journalism Network (EDJNet)
Many European media companies work together under EDJNet, one of whose primary goal is ethical data sharing: newsrooms working together to create data-driven reports on EU affairs. Each member of the EDJNet charter pledges to "respect journalism's highest ethical and professional standards," thereby upholding strong journalistic standards. Under Creative Commons licences, partners of the network share all gathered data, visualisations, and analysis with one another in line with the principle of openness. Every newly produced dataset, for example, is distributed to all cooperating reporters so they may post concurrently, fostering cross-border verification. By means of cooperation, this open model guarantees responsible use of data (each member retaining editorial freedom but openly checking others work), and hence strengthens public confidence.

3.4.4 Open Data Institute (ODI)
The ODI is a United Kingdom-based organisation that concentrates on data governance and sensible data management. ODI advocates data stewardship, using which one must carefully "determine who has access to it, for what purpose, and to whose benefit" carefully decided upon. Practically, ODI offers tools like the Data Ethics Canvas to enable any data user--including journalists--to identify possible ethical concerns at the outset. Journalists might, for instance, apply ODI ideas to look for privacy concerns or prejudice before releasing statistics. ODI's advices that while data can greatly benefit society (e.g., tracking health trends), without protections it can hurt (e.g., reveal sensitive personal information). Newsrooms that embrace ODI's data stewardship approach will be able to appropriately manage open data, therefore guaranteeing quality, privacy, and public benefit in their reporting.
3.4.5 BBC Editorial Guidelines
The BBC's in-house editorial guidelines are a global standard for news accuracy and fairness. Section 3 of the Guidelines, which deals with accuracy, specifically covers the use of data in journalism.. It states that while utilising statistics, "we should explain the numbers clearly, put them in context, weigh, interpret and present them clearly and attribute them." Stated differently, data points have to be verified and qualified; audiences are entitled to know how numbers were calculated and what they actually mean, particularly in health or crime-related reporting. The guidelines also emphasise risk-contextualising (particularly in terms of numbers, which must be reliable and validated) and clarity. Although the BBC's code lacks a specific data section, its basic policies of impartiality and fairness suggest that charts and data visualisations cannot distort or support any point of view. In essence, the BBC expects data-driven narratives to uphold its current standards of accuracy, balance, and openness.
3.5 INDIAN INSTITUTIONS AND FRAMEWORKS
So far, we have read about charters and guidelines of several international organisations. But it would be impossible in any code of ethics, however comprehensive, to detail all possible situations that may arise for ethical consideration in data journalism. Perhaps you have noted in your earlier reflections that a code of ethics will ultimately rely on the interpretation of its broad principles as they apply in specific contexts--especially in an era of data abundance, algorithmic processing, and AI-driven reporting. Formulating a rigid or exhaustive code of ethics for data journalists is neither feasible nor advisable. Technology and data use evolve rapidly, and so does society. Therefore, cast-iron rules often become obsolete. Yet, some guiding ethical principles are necessary to regulate and improve the quality of data- driven journalism. Justice R.S. Sarkaria, former Chairman of the Press Council of India, had emphasised the need for ethical standards to guide journalists. His views remain relevant in data journalism where algorithmic decisions, data biases, and visualisation choices influence public perception. Ethical codes are not legal instruments but moral compasses that facilitate self-regulation and public accountability.

Different bodies across time have tried to address these evolving concerns. In this context, the principles guiding the All-India Newspaper Editors' Conference (AINEC), the Press Council, and even international forums gain new relevance when viewed through the lens of data journalism.
3.5.1 All-India Newspaper Editors' Conference -Code (1968)
AINEC's foundational principles find new resonance in data journalism:
1. A free press in a free society requires open, verified and responsibly
analysed data. Misrepresentation of datasets or visualisations-- especially around issues like communalism, gender, or caste--can endanger societal harmony.
2. Data journalists must support constitutional goals like democracy,
secularism, unity, and rule of law through responsible sourcing and analysis. They must not allow datasets to be selectively manipulated to incite public unrest or misinformation.
3. Guidelines for ethical data handling during sensitive communal events:
- Editorials or data commentaries should avoid inflammatory language
and data visualisations (e.g., heat maps, bar graphs) that isolate or target communities.
- Generalisations based on community-based data (e.g., crime statistics
by religion) should be treated cautiously, with disclaimers and methodological transparency.
- Deliberate cherry-picking or slanting of datasets on communal issues
should be eschewed.
- Data stories about casualties, crime, or unrest should be contextualised.
Visuals must avoid dramatic emphasis on figures that could provoke fear or anger.
- Emphasis should be placed on datasets and analysis that promote
peace, policy solutions, or harm reduction, rather than sensational impact.
- Names of communities should be anonymised where necessary, with
'majority' or 'minority' terms used with contextual sensitivity.
- Sources of data (government databases, open-source APIs, surveys)
should be clearly cited.
- Data should be verified with triangulation - the process of using
different sources and methods to verify information - before publication. If the data is likely to inflame, it must be carefully reviewed or omitted.
3.5.2 Press Council Guidelines and Data Journalism
The Press Council's broader guidelines remain useful when applied to data journalism:
- Avoid provocative headlines or misleading visualisations.
- Headlines and graphs must reflect the actual meaning of the data they
represent. 37

- Where casualty or crime data varies across sources, report the range
rather than a single figure.
- Allegations (e.g., corruption-based on datasets) must clearly name the
data source and avoid assumptions.
- Avoid inserting subjective judgements into data interpretation.
- Analysis must not be guided by partisan filters or algorithms that
reinforce ideological bias.
- Language used in data stories should be neutral, inclusive, and aim to
build civic literacy.
- Corrections, such as for data mislabelling or misinterpretation, must be
issued prominently.
3.5.3 Press Council Code on Communal Writings in the
Context of Data
The Press Council's code on communalism is particularly relevant for data journalism:
- Exaggerating data on crime, health, or violence vis-a-vis a community
must be avoided.
- Data stories should avoid ethnic profiling through maps or graphs.
- It is unethical to draw inferences from incomplete datasets or to create
causality without adequate support.
- Spurious correlations and flawed AI models that target communities
must be called out.
- Newsrooms must be cautious with social media datasets or visualisations
sourced from unverified crowdsourced platforms.
- Sensationalised charts or dashboards during crises should be avoided.
- Infographics must not imply that a community's identity correlates with
negative traits or behaviours.
3.5.4 Parliament Code and Data Ethics
The Parliament Code adopted in 1976 also provides ethical relevance for data journalism:
- Data journalism must uphold the truth, accuracy, and public interest.
- No dataset should be published without understanding its methodology
and limitations.
- Journalists must resist the temptation to use data for sensationalism or
viral impact.
- Source transparency, respect for confidentiality, and non-partisan
analysis are essential.
- Using data for personal or political gain undermines journalistic integrity.
- Data journalists must not manipulate dashboards or metrics for bribes
or influence.

- Issues of data privacy, especially regarding individuals or marginalised
communities, must be respected.
- Datasets related to caste, religion, or region must be anonymised, unless
the public interest is demonstrable.
3.5.5 International Code (1991) and Data Journalism
The Stockholm International Code offers a modern lens:
- Fair, accurate, and unbiased storytelling with data is the central aim.
- Anonymous data sources must be justified through public good.
- Plagiarism in data scraping or visualisation templates is unethical.
- Data journalists must distinguish clearly between raw data, analysis,
opinion, and inference.
- Do not publish sensitive datasets, such as those involving survivors,
children, or victims, without redaction.
- Do not glorify violence with visual data (e.g., graphic crime maps or
victim photos).
- High standards of data ethics, accessibility, and context must be
maintained.
3.5.6 Ombudsman and Data Accountability
An ombudsman is an officer appointed by the government or an organisation who is responsible for the investigation of complaints, redressal of grievances and resolution of conflicts. Today, most progressive news organisations have ombudsman who work towards mediating conflicts between different parties. Data journalism has ample scope for reader complaints, feedback loops, and external audits. Appointing data ethics officers or ombudsmen in newsrooms helps uphold algorithmic transparency and public trust.
3.6 ETHICAL ISSUES IN INDIAN DATA
JOURNALISM
3.6.1 Data Misrepresentation
Data misrepresentation refers to the distortion of facts through selective use of data, flawed visualisations, or a lack of proper context. In India, the urgency of breaking news, combined with limited data literacy, sometimes leads to unintentional or careless errors. For example, during public reporting on education statistics, some portals have ranked states by absolute enrolment numbers without considering the state's population size or literacy rate. Such comparisons can mislead readers by overlooking proportional factors. Another instance is the use of maps that exaggerate differences between regions by using misleading colour scales or inconsistent baselines. These practices not only weaken public trust but also spread misinformation. Ethical data journalism must prioritise clarity, accuracy, and transparency by including proper labels, sources, and explanations of methods.

3.6.2 Privacy
The rise of digital data has raised concerns about the protection of individual privacy in journalistic reporting. Often, journalists use data from government portals, research studies, or public submissions. However, such data may include sensitive personal details. In India, datasets related to public health, education schemes, or social welfare sometimes contain identifiers such as names, ages, or exact addresses. While this information may be part of public records, publishing it without anonymisation can harm individuals and violate ethical standards. For example, stories based on school exam results or beneficiary databases must avoid sharing identifiable information unless absolutely necessary and justified by public interest. Ethical journalism requires data minimisation--using only the information necessary--and respecting informational consent.
3.6.3 Bias
Bias in data journalism arises when stories reflect partial truths, omit key variables, or reinforce stereotypes. This is especially relevant in a diverse country like India, where data can easily be misread if social and cultural contexts are not properly considered. For instance, comparing urban and rural employment data without accounting for informal labour or seasonal migration can lead to faulty interpretations. Similarly, using English-language search trends to represent national sentiment may overlook regional and linguistic diversity. Bias can also appear in visualisations--such as using selective time frames or emphasising certain groups over others in bar charts or pie diagrams. These subtle choices can shape public perception and reinforce narratives not supported by comprehensive evidence. Journalists must therefore critically evaluate their sources and acknowledge the limitations of datasets. Transparency in methodology and clear disclaimers about data scope can help reduce interpretive bias. Check Your Progress - 2 Note: 1) Use the space provided below for your answers.

3.7 LET US SUM UP
In this unit we have learnt that n the fast-changing landscape of digital reporting, data journalism stands out as a crucial bridge between numerical information and public understanding. While the integration of big data, algorithms, and visualisations improves storytelling, it also introduces ethical complexities.

Upholding journalistic integrity means following established codes of ethics by organisations such as those by SPJ, GIJN, and the Press Council of India, codes that emphasise accuracy, fairness, and accountability. As journalists increasingly rely on data-driven stories, especially in a diverse society like India, their ethical choices directly impact public trust and societal harmony. Thus, data journalists must work towards transparency, responsible interpretation, and sensitivity to to practice trustworthy and socially responsible journalism.
3.8 KEYWORDS

visualisation techniques to report news stories.
- Algorithmic Transparency - The ethical imperative to explain how data
processing or AI tools influence editorial decisions or story outcomes.
- Ethical Codes - Guidelines formulated by professional bodies (like SPJ or
BBC) that set standards for fairness, accuracy, and public responsibility in journalism.
- Prepublication Verification - The process of validating data and sources
before public dissemination to avoid misinformation.
- Data Stewardship - Responsible management of data with attention to
access, purpose, and potential impact, as advocated by institutions like ODI.

4.0 INTRODUCTION
Measurements are particularly important in journalistic techniques, especially when dealing with data and statistics. As a journalist, you must be knowledgeable about the use of these analytical techniques. We use measurements in our everyday lives. For example, while buying groceries, we use currencies. When measuring your weight, you may use units such as kilograms, pounds, and so on. However, in the social sciences and journalism, we lack appropriate measurement methods to address the complexities of human sociology and psychology. You might come across some data about the audience's perception of high-calorie products. What is their perspective on these products? To appropriately report this set of data, we employ analytical methods such as "Levels of Measurement."

While measuring has a long history in science, its use in social science is relatively new. In biological science, the use of measuring dates back to 1850. Darwin's theory of evolution and difference among species greatly influenced the development of measurements in the behavioural sciences. Sir Francis Galton's research on "Human Abilities" laid the groundwork for psychometrics and the measuring of human conduct, drawing on Darwin's ideas. Later, metrics were developed for clinical studies, medicine, psychology, education, and social welfare agencies.
4.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After going through the unit, you will be able to:
- gain clarity on the concept and importance of measurement in social
science research.
- understand the postulates underlying the levels of measurement.
- identify the different levels of measurement, and
- identify appropriate measurements needed in various social science
research contexts.
4.2 MEASUREMENT
4.2.1 What is Measurement?
Measurement is the process of giving numerical values to events, things and the like in accordance with established norms. To clarify, the process of assigning numbers to objects involves representing attribute quantities.
4.2.2 Types of Measurement Situations
The definition above indicates that measurement numbers are assigned based on specific guidelines. There are two types of measurement scenarios: explicit rules for assigning numerical values (e.g., measuring a plant's length in centimetres or inches) and vague rules (e.g., measuring audience views about a new show). Measurement focuses on certain properties or features of the object being measured. Measurement focuses on quantifying the object's properties rather than the object itself. For example, keep in mind that you are measuring the audience's understanding of the new show. The measurement method aims to reveal the degree of a particular quality in the person, thing or entity.
4.2.3 Measurement is Different from Evaluation
Evaluation and measurement are frequently used as synonyms, which causes confusion. However, measuring and evaluation are not the same. Evaluation refers to an appraisal or assessment against a specified standard. For example, if the audience in a survey believes a show is not performing well but the creators believe it is a success, one can conduct an analytical study using this information. This process will be considered an evaluation.

4.3 UNDERSTANDING POSTULATES OF
MEASUREMENT
Before looking at the different levels of measurement, you need to understand the postulates of measurements.
4.3.1 Postulates of Measurement
A postulate can be defined as a type of assumption which stipulates the relationship between groups, objects, or events being measured. According to Guilford (1954), there are nine basic postulates of measurement which can be summarized under three general headings:
- postulates relating to equalities or identities
- postulates relating to rank order
- postulates relating to additively
4.3.2 Postulates of Equalities
There are three variations in postulates relating to equalities or identities. These include: Table: 1. Either a = b or a, b, which means the numbers are either equal (a = b) or they are not equal (a b). Both situations cannot occur simultaneously. This data is of much use in classification.
2. If a = b, then b = a, which denotes that the relation of equality among
members is symmetrical. In such cases, a and b can be interchanged.
3. If a = b and b = c, then a = c. This means that objects that are equal to
the same objects are also equal to one another.
4.3.3 Postulates relating to Order
There are two variations under this postulate relating to the rank order.
1. If a > b, then b < a; this means that the relation between a and b is
asymmetrical. This relationship cannot be reversed by interchanging a and b.

2. If a > b and b > c, then a > c; this is transitively postulate and indicates
a definite order in the ranking.
4.3.4 Postulates relating to additively
There are four postulates of additively:
1. If a = p and b > o, then a + b > p; this postulate indicates a summation
process and
2. shows that when a zero is added, it produces no variability in the result.
3. a + b = b + a, which denotes that in the process of addition, the order of
the
4. numbers are not important, as it will yield the same result, e.g., 2 + 4 =
4 + 2.5. If a = p and b = q, then a + b = p + q, which means that in the process of
addition identical numbers or objects may be substituted for one another without making any change in the result.
6. (a + b) + c = a + (b + c), which shows that in the process of addition the
order of the combinations of objects or numbers make no difference.
4.4 LEVELS OF MEASUREMENT
Stevens (1951) identified four methods for assigning numerical values to object properties. There are four types of measurement scales: nominal, ordinal, interval, and ratio. Let's examine each scale in detail.
4.4.1 Nominal Scale
Nominal measurement is considered to be the lowest level of measurement. In this scale, numbers are used to name, identify, or classify individuals, objects, graphs, etc. Hence, it is also described as a classificatory measurement. Nominal measurement is used for categorising qualitatively different categories to which we attach numbers without their meaning or numerical value. The categories are qualitatively different. For example, in coding, we may use numbers like 1 and 2 as stand ins for "male" or "female," but the numbers 1 or 2 have no arithmetic value in this context, i.e. the number "2" does not mean that items placed in that category have more of the quality than those items placed in the category numbered "1." Another example where nominal measurements are involved includes the: a) Livelihood/occupation of rural families:
1. Farming
2. Business
3. Paid labour
4. Government job
5. Private job
6. Any other

The list of alternative categories should contain those related to the theory and the population investigated, allowing the coder to classify each example. In nominal measurement, members of different groups are never equivalent, but all members of the same group are. The equivalency connection is reflexive, transitive, and symmetric. Only the following statistical operations are acceptable at the nominal measurement level: counting, frequency, percentage, proportion, mode, and coefficient of contingency. Identifying numerals cannot be added, subtracted, multiplied, or divided, as they have no values.
4.4.2 Ordinal Scale
In ordinal measurement, numbers represent the rank order of items or individuals. We sort the numbers in this measurement from highest to lowest or lowest to highest. This scale compares individuals or objects based on their size, weight, brightness, hardness, and other characteristics. Objects may be classified on this scale based on their physical or physiological characteristics, conveying a relationship, such as "greater than" or "lesser than." Hence, it is accurate to say that an ordinal scale contains categories that can be ordered by rank on a continuum with a crude meaning, such as "more" or "less" of the quantity being measured. For example, how farmers may perceive four varieties of crops as highest (4), higher (3), lesser (2) and least (1). This categorisation indicates that "1" means a crop variety in which the yield is less compared to the variety they place in "2." An ordinal scale gives only this information and does not provide any information about the distance between the two values. The distance perceived by the farmer between 1 and 2 may be larger or smaller than the distance between 2 and 3. An ordinal scale does not imply anything about these arithmetic values other than the fact that they are in order. In data journalism, an example of ordinal measurement occurs when people are asked to rate their trust in news organisations using options like "very high," "moderate," "low," and "very low." These responses show a clear order from most to least trust, but the difference between each level is not exactly the same. This type of measurement helps journalists understand and compare public opinion in a ranked way, without using exact numbers. Most social science constructs are measured at the ordinal level. This measurement has its own limitations as it does not represent absolute quantities or equal distances between rank values. Ordinal measuring differs from interval measurement, as it lacks a genuine zero. Using equally spaced rank values in an ordinal scale does not necessarily imply that the underlying trait is equally spaced. Students receiving totals of 90, 85, and 75 can be ranked first, second, or third. Although the rankings are similarly spaced, the interval between each rank's marks varies.
4.4.3 Interval Scale
In an interval scale, all intervals indicate equal amounts of the variable being measured. In other words, for every unit that rises on the scale, the variable increases by one unit. In this scale, numbers indicate that '3' is greater than '2' and '2' is greater than '1', and that the interval between '3' and '2' is equal to the interval between '2' and '1. '

Temperature is measured on the Fahrenheit scale, which is an interval scale. The temperature difference between 33 degrees and 34 degrees is equivalent to the difference between 36 degrees and 37 degrees. The interval scale allows for addition and subtraction of numbers as 20-10 = 40-30. Here, numbers cannot be multiplied or divided, as they lack a true zero and instead have an artificial zero.
4.4.4 Ratio Scale
Ratio scales have a true zero, and as a result, the scale values represent multiple quantities. Examples of ratio scales are measurements of length, breadth and weight (e.g., metre, pound, grams). You may notice that for these physical scales, zero is real and not arbitrary. It is the highest level of measurement and has all the properties of nominal, ordinal and interval scales. Ratio scales include interval scales along with an absolute or true zero point. One important feature of ratio scale is that the ratio of any two numbers is independent of the unit of measurement and therefore, it can meaningfully be equated. For example, the ratio 5:10 is equal to 10:20. At this level, all three groups of postulates of measurement are applicable and statistical operations are admissible. Ratio scales are more common in physical sciences than in the social sciences. The difference between an interval scale and a ratio scale is that the former has only an arbitrary zero point while the latter scale has a true zero point. Fahrenheit is an example of the interval scale, whereas Kelvin is a ratio scale. Check Your Progress - 2 Note: 1) Use the space provided below for your answers.

4.5 SOURCES OF ERROR IN MEASUREMENTS
In an ideal research study, measurement should be precise and unambiguous. However, researchers often fail to achieve this objective fully. As such, the researcher must be aware of the sources of error in measurement. The following are the possible sources of error in measurement: a) Respondent: At times, the respondent may be reluctant to express strong negative feelings, or may have very little knowledge but may not like to admit his ignorance. This reluctance is likely to lead to an interview filled with inaccuracies. Transient factors like fatigue, boredom, anxiety, etc., may also limit the ability of the respondent to respond accurately and fully.

b) Situation: Situational factors may also come in the way of correct measurement. Any condition that places a strain on interviews can have serious effects on the interviewer-respondent rapport. For instance, if somebody else is present during the interview, they can cause a distortion in responses by giving unnecessary inputs or merely by being there. Should the respondent perceive a lack of anonymity, he might hesitate to convey specific emotions. c) Measurer: The interviewer can distort responses by rewording or reordering questions. His behaviour, style, and appearance may encourage or discourage certain replies from respondents. Careless mechanical processing may distort the findings. Errors may also creep in because of incorrect coding, faulty tabulations, and statistical calculations, particularly in the data analysis stage. d) Instrument: Error may arise because of the defective measuring instrument. The use of complex words beyond the comprehension of the respondent, ambiguous meanings, poor printing, inadequate space for replies, response choice omissions, etc., are among a few things that make the measuring instrument defective and may result in measurement errors. Another type of instrument deficiency is the poor sampling of the universe of items of concern.
4.6 CRITERIA FOR JUDGING THE MEASURING
INSTRUMENTS
A measurement, too, must meet specific requirements. The most significant criteria to consider while evaluating a measurement tool are listed below: a) Unidimensionality: This indicates that the scale should measure only one feature at a time; for example, the ruler should measure length rather than temperature. b) Linearity: This means that a scale should adhere to the straight-line paradigm. A scoring system should be developed, particularly one based on interchangeable units. An inch is an inch whether it is at one end of a ruler or the other, but altitude scales do not allow for such interchangeability. In such circumstances, ranking is preferred. c) Validity: This pertains to the ability of a scale to accurately measure its intended parameters. d) Reliability: This is a quality of constancy. A scale should provide consistent findings. e) Accuracy and Precision: A measurement tool should give an accurate and precise count of what we want to measure. f) Simplicity: A scale should be as simple as possible; an elaborate, complicated, and over-refined one may become unduly cumbersome, costly, or even useless. g) Practicability: This is concerned with a wide range of factors, like cost-effectiveness, convenience, and interpretability. Some trade-off is usually needed between an ideal tool and one that the budget can afford. The benefit should be proportional to the expense incurred. 49

The tool should be easily administrable; it should contain proper instructions; it should be readily understandable and conveniently arranged for easy completion. To enable others to interpret the results of a test, one will need aids such as a statement of its function, its construction procedure, and guides for interpreting the result. 4.7 LET US SUM UP
This unit explores the fundamental concept of measurement in social science research, particularly its relevance to journalism and behavioural studies. Measurement is defined as the process of assigning numerical values to attributes of objects or events, based on certain rules. It differs from evaluation, which involves judgement based on standards. Two types of measurement situations are discussed: one with explicit rules (like measuring height or weight) and another with vague rules (like assessing viewer opinions), both aiming to quantify qualities rather than the objects themselves. The unit explains postulates of measurement, which form the philosophical basis for assigning numerical values. These are grouped into three types: postulates of equality (where equal objects are interchangeable), postulates of order (indicating rank but not precise differences), and postulates of additivity (explaining how quantities can be combined meaningfully). These help us understand how different levels of measurement work in practice. The central part of the unit details four levels of measurement as identified by Stevens (1951): nominal, ordinal, interval, and ratio scales. The nominal scale is used for simple classification without any numerical meaning (e.g., gender or occupation). The ordinal scale ranks items in order but does not measure the exact distance between them (e.g., preference rankings). The interval scale has equal intervals between values but lacks a true zero (e.g., temperature in Fahrenheit), while the ratio scale has both equal intervals and an absolute zero, making it the most robust (e.g., height, weight, income). The unit also outlines potential sources of measurement error, including issues arising from respondents' end, instruments, measurement situations, and the measurer themselves. To minimise these errors, the unit presents criteria for judging measurement instruments--such as validity, reliability,

unidimensionality, simplicity, and practicability. These criteria ensure the tools used for measurement are accurate, meaningful, and suitable for practical research contexts.
4.8 KEYWORDS
- Postulate: A fundamental assumption used as a basis for reasoning.
- Unidimensionality: The quality of measuring a single attribute or
concept.
- Additivity: The principle that numerical values can be meaningfully
summed.
- Interval: The equal distance between values on a measurement scale.
- Practicability: The ease and cost-effectiveness with which something
can be implemented.

5.1 INTRODUCTION
Digital media is a technology-driven and evolving medium. New innovations, new ideas and concepts are added to it more frequently than in any other traditional media. The introduction of mobile telephony has made access to news a universal phenomenon. As of early 2025, India has approximately 806 million active internet users, with over 1.12 billion cellular mobile connections (76.6% penetration rate), and around 86.3% of households with internet access. These days, more and more people are using mobile phones to access news and multimedia content. For a better user experience, most media organisations are making their websites dynamic. To sum it up: this is the era of online journalism. Data journalism is among the most significant changes in journalism today, very visible and inevitable. Data has been described as the "new oil," the connotation being that whoever controls this precious resource will control the world in the coming years. Although the use of data, surveys and computer-assisted reporting (CAR) for journalism has been around for decades, journalists have started using new technologies to access very large amounts of data relatively recently. Today, new and emerging technologies are helping both writers and 55

readers understand data, explore it, and act upon the insights derived from it to make sense of the world better than ever before. As we understand it today, data journalism takes journalists and their audiences from mere numeracy to visualising the larger picture through large-scale knowledge mobilisation and an understanding of socio-economic trends and patterns.
5.2 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After reading this unit, you will be able to:
- explain the evolution and characteristics of online journalism,
- understand the influence of the internet on news production and
consumption,
- discuss the emerging trends in online and data journalism,
- recognise the importance of data regulation and surveillance concerns,
- identify key digital platforms and tools for practising data journalism,
and
- explore national and international web resources that aid data-driven
reporting.
5.3 INTERNET AND JOURNALISM
Today, as we are witnessing that all types of work is getting transferred into the online mode, the media industry has also not lagged behind. Rather, it has ventured deeper into it and is exploring new opportunities of online news delivery and related online news businesses. In the prevailing atmosphere of cut-throat competition in the news industry, news organisations which are not adapting to the online medium are expected to lose their competitive edge and may be unable to sustain for long. You must have experienced that while trying to search for any reading material, picture or video on the internet, as you write certain keywords in the search engine, you get results running into several hundreds of web pages. Sometimes these links take you to a blog, many times to a news website and occasionally to government websites. All these links do not belong to online journalism. Only, websites belonging to media houses or blogs created by professional journalists for providing authentic information to their readers can be categorized as online journalism. Actually, in recent times you might have noticed that the line between professional and personal journalistic writings are blurring significantly, mainly due to the proliferation of social media and its popularity. This raises an important question - whether New Media, such as social media, online video platforms, websites, apps and so on, which rely on the internet and foster user-participation and interactivity, can be seen as a threat to conventional media or not? This is a point of debate among scholars. Some believe that online medium will replace conventional media, as it has all the qualities of traditional news media. In the online medium, you can read text, listen to audio and watch videos at your convenient time and pace. Other scholars believe that these different types of media - conventional media and new media - will continue to coexist and the online medium will complement all others. Even at present, different types of media exist together. However, there are growing

examples from the west where print editions are getting significantly reduced in size while correspondingly their digital presence is growing. In India, the current scenario is quite different. We are witnessing a unique situation where, on the one hand, print editions are growing in the regional languages while at the same time online journalism outlets are expanding.
5.3.1 Characteristics of Online Journalism
You have been given a broad overview of online journalism; now let us understand its important characteristics. Online: As the word suggests, it operates on an online platform which can be seen or updated in real time. Here, breaking news and events can be updated as they happen - just like live telecasts on television news channels, live updates in news websites is the norm. While we have had this facility in radio and TV as well, where information is regularly updated, the difference here is that online news can be seen on your computing devices and even handheld gadgets like mobiles with some added features. Shifted time: Online journalism also takes advantage of shifted time. Online publications can archive stories for now or later. Users can read those stories at any time. In other media, this facility is not easily available. In conventional print media, if you want to read a previous day's or month's newspaper, you have to get access to the news organisation's library, or one should collect newspapers on a daily basis and archive it periodically - which can be quite a tedious task. Multimedia: Online journalism can include multimedia elements: text and graphics (newspapers and books), sound, music, motion elements and animation (broadcast medium), 3D, etc. One of the greatest opportunities of multimedia journalism is the ability to combine various media elements for a news story. At present, most media organisations provide derivatives of their 'parent' products. Newspapers are providing digital text, radio organisations are providing audio clips and TV channels are providing streamed video links. But multimedia is providing these news entities an opportunity to adapt other designs also. There are a number of sites where we can see this adaptation. Now, radio channels are not only providing audio files but also complementing them with images and texts - the All India Radio (AIR) and the Voice of America (VoA) websites are testimony to this. Similarly, most print media organisations are not only providing digital text but also video and audio clips. Meanwhile, TV channels are also complementing their video files with text - the opposite of what newspapers are doing. All leading news channels are running their news portals. Seizing this opportunity, online sites are now trying to take full advantage of the array of media formats available. Websites are now complementing a story with flash animation, photo gallery, video and audio clips. Interactivity: Online journalism is interactive and the primary mechanism for this interactivity is hyperlinks. Through hyperlinks, different types of media options are added to a news package to bring more in-depth engagement through the streamlining of lengthy and complex elements and components. An important aspect of a the work of an online journalist is hyperlinking their own

web pages to other websites that may be relevant to their stories. Interactivity also provides users the option to comment and add information to the existing content. Online sites also conduct online polls that enable more interactivity. This feature of online journalism is helpful in several ways:
- It makes the users' experience more enjoyable.
- It helps users gain more information.
- Users perceive the site's navigation easily.
- It makes users spend more time on the web page.
Immediacy: As per the Encyclopedia of Journalism by Christopher Sterling, "News is like bread - it is best served fresh, as it goes stale quickly." Immediacy is a key component of journalism and what better way for a journalist to dispatch information speedily than through the internet. It is the fastest medium, and through this information can be disseminated from personal computers to mobile phones at the click of a button. With the ability to upload content anytime through a basic internet connection, online media is as quick as we can get. But then the question arises - whether immediacy wins over accuracy. What should be the priority? As we know, on the internet, information can be uploaded by any individual on any social networking site or a blog. Individuals cannot be expected to be guided by professional ethics and codes of conduct applicable to organisations. In this scenario, any wrong information uploaded can create a chaotic situation. Hence, it is important for online users to know how to find reliable information. Hyper-textuality: Hyper-textuality is a prime 'tool' used to introduce interactivity in a web page. Hypertext is a web link which can be used to provide a variety of information on one page. These links provide a variety of media content (audio, video, graphics, animation, etc.) in a story. Through hypertext, journalists enrich their content, making it a distinctive and unique characteristic of online journalism. It helps differentiate online media from other forms of media. Traditional journalism provides for linear presentation of a story, while online media brings multi-linearity to the story. It also enables users to be participants when they click their way through a hyperlinked set of pages.
5.3.2 Data Surveillance: The Dark Side of the Internet
The internet is often called a democratic space or a real level playing field because it does not differentiate between rich and poor users. True, the digital divide puts the poorest of poor people in the global South at a huge disadvantage, but that does not take away the fact that the Internet does not differentiate (or discriminate) between individual users. However, it is increasingly being argued that the democratic nature of the Internet could well be, at best, a myth and, at worst, a ruse for promoting predatory market forces. Yasha Levine (2018) argues in "Surveillance Valley: The Secret Military History of the Internet" that the Internet was built by the US government to spy on its citizens. The author believes that manipulating the personal data of unsuspecting users is quite central to the political economy of powerful Western countries like the US. Looking at data from the perspective of new and emerging tech-industry giants like Facebook, Google and Twitter, and marketing 58 companies like Amazon, he argues that these companies' business is to spy on

their users by collecting a variety of data to maximise their profits. Focusing on the emergence of a new military-digital-complex, the author asserts that the military and the industry often complement one another. Nick Couldry and Ulises A. Mejias (2019) argue that the capture and processing of data (social or personal) unfolds through new "data relations" which may be understood through new forms of data colonialism. That is why most governments the world over are getting incrementally more cautious about protecting their citizens' data from predatory digital invaders. 5.4 DATA REGULATION
We have learned from the above discussion that it is common for tech companies to do regular and real-time data snooping and tailor algorithms to customise information for individual users. It is precisely for this reason that data protection laws are necessary. Data protection in India is poor mainly because it is a relatively new area for citizens and governments. However, data journalists need to understand the need for, and the ramifications of, data protection. It has also become important in the light of widespread complaints of cybercrime and data (and identity) theft. Personal data of the citizens is frequently stolen from banks and insurance companies. It is often seen that even government- controlled data is sometimes leaked or stolen. One of the biggest problems then is the absence of an effective framework of data protection. To this end, in August 2017, the Supreme Court of India declared privacy a fundamental right through a landmark judgment in the Justice K.S. Puttaswamy case. The Apex Court warned against threats to privacy from both state and non-state actors, urging the government to establish "a robust regime for data protection." The existing data protection laws (i.e., the Information Technology Act, 2000, and its rules framed in 2011) cover only corporates, not government entities, and only sensitive personal data, such as medical history and biometric information. Ultimately, there is a lack of recourse for citizens--breach of personal information is not sufficient grounds for seeking redress, except in cases of financial loss. The absence of a dedicated regulator continues to be a key weakness of the system. The Justice B.N. Srikrishna committee, set up in 2017 to suggest an effective data protection regime, proposed the Personal Data Protection Bill in 2018. This evolved into the Digital Personal Data Protection Act (DPDPA), 2023, which received presidential assent on August 11, 2023, but its substantive provisions are yet to be fully notified and enforced. Draft rules under the DPDPA were released in January 2025 for public consultation.

5.5 TRENDS IN ONLINE JOURNALISM
With new technologies in the digital world cropping up every day, along with the changing desires of users, are creating new trends in online journalism. These trends are not only helpful in tapping more users but also in providing new experiences to users.
5.5.1 Time-Shift Journalism
The days of waiting for re-telecast of a programme on television are over. Similarly, we do not have to make arrangements for individually recording our favourite shows. Because now, in the age of internet, all we need to do is to search for the content online and watch it at our convenience. The reason is simple: now is the time of time-shift journalism or time-shift content. This simply means that the time we first encounter an information and the time we consume it can be different. That is why tab options like 'read later' or 'watch later' have become quite commonly used.
5.5.2 Emergence of New Digital Platforms
In order to meet these consumers' demand, new technologies are emerging and giving opportunities for new experiences of news. But the emergence of several new devices like tablets and smart phones has become very challenging for online journalism. Compounded with this challenge is the increasing number of operating systems. For example, there are two major types of operating systems, iOS, and Android in the mobile market. These new devices are changing the way we consume news. Online media houses have to be compatible with these changing technologies. Many media houses are coming up with new applications to meet these challenges. But as the product life cycles are getting shorter and shorter in this digital age, it is finally up to different news organisations and other online entities to try and figure out how they can produce the kind of product that will fit into these sorts of niches.
5.5.3 Taking the Lead
Web 2.0 is the new talking point in online media. It enables users to play an active role in content creation. In the world of Web 2.0, content power is not with media but with the masses. Web 2.0 provides the basic structure of participation, such as: Architecture of participation: These are online facilities for user-generated content such as blogs and wikis. The most popular website based on Web 2.0 is Wikipedia, where every registered user can contribute/edit/delete content as per the existing Wiki community norms. Crowdsourcing: This is a collaborative form of reporting where, with the help of Web 2.0, a group of people work together to gather information. Each contributor researches a part of the overall project and piece it together. By using such facilities, these websites enabled by Web 2.0 are trying to elicit more participation from its readers. These websites focus on submission of users, rather than staff reporters or editors. Such content is gathered from a variety of online options: blogs, photos, podcasts, video sharing, reviews, forums, etc. The premise is that the group knows more than an individual at any point in time, and new technologies are enabling such an effective form of collective and collaborative action. This is encouraging citizens to take active part in this

new form of journalism. Besides, as Beth Simone Noveck has argued, this will strengthen the democratic process in a way that will bring people together, not just to create content, but also to create power.
5.5.4 Online Publishing
Publishing online has become easy with the advent of many online platforms and new technologies. Publishing content on blogs and social networking sites has become very common and popular among youth. On social networking sites too, the youth are dominating. Another new popular development among the youth is 'mobile phone blogging.' This is location-based instant blogging, in which they use their cameras to shoot or click a photograph and post it instantly. It has made online journalism more competitive. Now the success of a website does not depend only on the quality of its own content but also on gathering content from different platforms like blogs, microblogging websites and social networking websites.
5.6 DATA JOURNALISM AND INTERNET
According to a report from Tow Center for Digital Journalism, data journalism is the "application of data science to journalism," where data science is defined as "the study of the extraction of knowledge from data." In short, data journalism is about narrating stories or analysing social and political processes around us using numbers or finding stories/patterns in numbers. The use of humongous amounts of data has been made possible by computerisation, new and emerging technologies, digital storage devices, and the opportunities of easy sharing through the Internet and multiple public domains. Due to the explosion of data generated by various sectors, including government, wider society, industry, academia, individual citizens, social media and the research community, both the context and scope of data journalism has expanded in recent years. One can observe that data journalists often use free, powerful online tools and open-source software to collect, clean, and publish data through interactive features, mobile apps, and digital maps. The availability of free and open-source data in a convenient and the modifiable form has lent a helping hand to data journalists. Unlike in the past, when the global trends took a long time to spread in developing countries, data journalism is already an accepted phenomenon worldwide, including in India. 5.7 SIMPLIFYING THE CHALLENGES OF DATA
JOURNALISM
Data journalism is skill-oriented work that can be learnt by following a method; however, it is never easy to deal with numbers when they come in huge quantities or in the form of time series. Even the most accomplished researchers and data scientists ensure data integrity and check and recheck data before coming to conclusions. But, data journalism is no rocket science - what must always be kept in mind is that data is not something unusual but part of everyday life. It is impossible to understand government policies without an understanding of data. It is also difficult to comprehend environmental issues like polluting factories or climate change or medical data like cancer research and the spread of diseases without deploying long-term data. Fortunately, there are enough web-based resources available to journalism students today to hone their skills. It is a huge relief that once basic proficiency is acquired in making sense of data, the process can be very enlightening and empowering. No politician or bureaucrat can deceive or delude a data journalist by providing half-truth or even excessive data.

6.0 INTRODUCTION
The essence of data journalism lies in the ability to manage and interpret data accurately; the process by which this is achieved is known as data tabulation. It is one of the most essential skills that a data journalist must excel in, as it supports fact-based journalism. The collected data is processed, which involves steps such as editing, coding, classification and tabulation of data. The processed data is presented in the form of tables or graphs. Data tabulation enables data journalists to discover hidden patterns and trends, communicate findings with accuracy and clarity, and ask critical questions. When data is presented in tabular formats, it enhances clarity and transparency, facilitates easy comparison, and most importantly, simplifies complex data so that a general audience can understand it. Tabulated data reveals trends and disparities that would not be easily detected in narrative formats or dense reports; thus, tables are not just tools for presenting data, they also serve as analytical devices.

6.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
This unit covers the foundational concepts of data tabulation. After going through this unit, you will be able to:
- understand the importance of data tabulation in data journalism, why it
matters, and how to use it effectively.
- understand the structure and components of different types of tables.
- understand how to create tabulated datasets.
- understand various digital tools used for data tabulation.
6.2 DATA TABULATION
6.2.1 What is Data Tabulation?
Data tabulation refers to the systematic arrangement of raw data into rows and columns to make it easier to read, interpret, and analyse. It is useful in bridging the gap between raw data and meaningful information. The processed data is presented in tabular form with reference to time and other variables. Tabulation simplifies the summarisation and condensation of data. With tables, it is easier to communicate findings clearly and understand the trends, relationships, and outliers in a dataset. For example, if you want to gather the data on literacy rates among several states of India, presenting the obtained numbers in a table format would make the comparison easier and simpler. Tabulation of data can be classified into various types: simple, double, and complex tabulation, based on how many characteristics of data are interrelated at a given point.
6.2.2 Uses of Data Tabulation in Journalism
Now that we are familiar with the definitiom of data tabulation, let us see how it becomes applicable in data journalism. Tabulation serves multiple essential purposes in transforming raw datasets into meaningful insights that inform news reporting and storytelling.
1. Simplifying Complex Information
In journalism, stories are built on complex datasets such as government budgets, survey responses, etc. With tabulation, this data is simplified into manageable and understandable units. For example, a table showing the voter turnout in different districts would be far better than listing it in hundreds of rows of written text.
2. Promote Data-Driven storytelling
Tabulation forms the narratives of data-based stories. It becomes a visual and factual element that makes the story more appealing, concise and clearer than a plain paragraph.
3. Facilitates easy comparisons
Data stories in journalism are usually based on two or more variables/ characteristics, such as comparing demographic data (literacy rate, 66 unemployment rate, mortality rate) or tracking changes over time; thus,

tabulation facilitates the easy comparison across categories, making it easier to spot the pattern and anomalies at a glance.
4. Enhance Accuracy
By eliminating ambiguity in the data, a tabulated dataset clearly lays out the facts in tables, reducing the risk of misinterpretation and cherry- picking. It enhances the transparency and enables readers to verify the claims.
5. Build Reader-Friendly Stories
Stories using tables to present data and facts convey critical information simply and quickly. The audience today scans the information rather than reading in detail, and a data table communicates more than several text paragraphs in print or online mode.
6.2.3 Key Characteristics of a Table
a. Title Each table should have a suitable title placed above the body of the table, which should be self-explanatory; the title should convey the subject the table contains and should be clear and brief. b. Table Number Each table should be assigned a unique number (e.g., 1.1, 1.2, 1.3), which makes the navigation and cross-referencing easy, avoiding ambiguity. c. Caption A caption is the column heading that explains what the column represents. One table may contain one or more column headings under which there may be subheads. d. Stub A stub is a row heading. They perform the same function for the horizontal rows as the column headings do for the vertical columns. e. Body of the table This is the main part of a table; it contains the numerical information. The data present in the main body is arranged according to the classification of stubs and captions. f. Headnote The headnote is present below the title and table number. A headnote is a brief explanatory statement applying to all the values present in the table. g. Unit of measurement Each table should indicate the unit of measurement (such as kilometres, rupees, percentage, or millions) either in the captions (column heading) and stubs (row heading) or as a note below the table, avoiding misinterpretation of the data. h. Footnote A footnote is placed below the body of the table. It should explain the unusual terms and calculation methods used, which maintains clarity while providing supplementary information.

i. Source At the bottom of the table, always mention the source/sources from which the data is obtained. This builds credibility and allows verification. j. Abbreviations Use minimum abbreviations, as their excessive use confuses readers. They should be standard and clearly explained within the table or as a footnote. k. Numbering When working with complex tabulation and dealing with multiple columns, numbering each column facilitates easy referencing. l. Simplicity A table should be well-designed and simple, without any complex formatting. Avoid overloading it with excessive information, instead keeping it logical and clear. m. Organising Data in the table should be organised strategically, such as in chronological order, alphabetical order, or ascending/descending order. Choose the arrangements that best align with the purpose of the analysis. Activity 1: Choose any recent news report that contains a chart and recreate its data in a tabular form.

Choosing the right type of tabulation is important for clear communication. a. Simple Tabulation Simple tabulation presents a quick overview. It is one-way tabulation; the data presented concerns one characteristic or variable of data. It presents the number of observations falling into each category of one variable. Example: The table below shows the number of students enrolled across different departments in a college. It shows only one variable.
