6.4 UNDERSTANDING TABULAR DATA
6.4.1 Structure of a dataset
Let us understand the two elements that help in structuring a dataset. a. Rows A row in a table represents the horizontal arrangement of a dataset corresponding to a single record or entry. These are often referred to as 'entries, ' 'records, ' or 'observations.' Each row is assigned appropriate stubs (headings) that explain the nature of the information given in the table. b. Columns A column shows the vertical arrangement of data in a table. Each column in a dataset represents a different variable that applies to all records. This is often referred to as 'variables' or 'fields' in dataset terminology. Variables define the kind of information being stored. Like rows, each column is assigned appropriate captions (subheadings).
6.4.2 Metadata and Headers
The 'data about data' is called metadata. Metadata helps in the accurate presentation of a dataset. It includes column and row names, units of measurement, time frame, sources, updated frequency, footnotes, etc. The top row of a table includes headers and labels of each column. It helps the reader understand what each column represents. For example, a header like 'Unemployment (2025)' clearly establishes the variable and the time frame.
6.4.3 Common Data Types
Based on the nature of the variables, we find there are different types of data; understanding these data types can help us in selecting suitable analysis and visualisation tools. a. Numerical Data Numerical data consists of quantitative measurements and is of two types: discrete and continuous. Discrete data represent information that can only take specific and distinct values, such as the number of students or the number of hospitals, while continuous data can take on any value within a range, such as weight, GDP, temperature, etc. This type of data is visualized using graphical tools such as bar charts, histograms, scatter plots, and the like, which will be discussed subsequently. b. Categorical Data This kind of data is represented in groups or categories and is usually represented as textual labels. For example, state names (Assam, Punjab, Delhi) and gender (male, female, or other). c. Temporal Data As the name conveys, this data type refers to date and time and is useful for time series analysis. Its use aids in understanding the trends in variables such as unemployment rate, fuel prices, and global temperature 70 increase over a particular time frame.

d. Geospatial Data This type of data includes location-based information and is most commonly used in mapping. It is central to reporting on environmental issues, pollution, population, disaster coverage, and the like.
6.5 TECHNIQUES FOR DATA TABULATION
In data journalism, data tabulation is not merely the presentation of data in the form of a table; it involves organisation, filtration, and summarisation of information to uncover the insights it has to offer. There are tools like Microsoft Excel and Google Sheets that are used for tabulation; these are powerful tools that are easily accessible for data journalists. Let's explore some methods commonly used for data tabulation.
6.5.1 Manual Tabulation
This involves manually entering the collected data into a spreadsheet and arranging it in rows and columns using the spreadsheet software. The most commonly used softwares for this purpose are Microsoft Excel and Google Sheets because they are very user-friendly and offer many extensive features. Manual tabulation aligns data properly, removes duplicates and irrelevant entries, and provides features like cell formatting, colour coding, and formulas, which enable the user to make the data more readable and visually appealing. However, this can be time-consuming, especially when working with large datasets, but this technique is usually beneficial for beginners to learn how data is structured and cleaned.
6.5.2 Sorting and Filtering
Sorting and filtering tabulated data is essential in order to organise and analyse it clearly. Sorting is the process of systematically organising tabulated data, whether alphabetically, numerically, or by date. It helps in revealing patterns within the dataset. For example, one can sort a table to rank states from higher to lower levels based on literacy rates. On the other hand, filtering allows users to display certain specific subsets based on set conditions. For example, a filter can be set to show only states with literacy rates above 70%; this feature allows users to identify relevant areas easily without scrolling through the entire dataset. Both these features are particularly helpful for big datasets, and available in Microsoft Excel and Google Sheets.
6.5.3 Pivot Table
Pivot table is another essential feature available in Excel and Google Sheets, which allows the quick summarisation and analysis of complex datasets without needing programming or statistical software. It helps in arranging data dynamically and can perform calculations like sum, average, and percentage, answering different questions simultaneously. For example, a table analysing the voter turnout across states and age groups can simultaneously compare state-wise turnout, calculate the average turnout per age group, and identify related anomalies. Activity 2: Build a table on media consumption, collecting data from your classmates on platform usage and frequency.

Column (Variable): Every vertical line in a dataset is a column, holding a specific type of data for all observations. e. Temporal data: It is related to time and date and is helpful in understanding trends and the chronology of events. g. 7.0 INTRODUCTION
The modern era of journalism is no longer about words; it is about numbers and data. From pollution to population, from pandemic to budget analysis, the data tell the story. Data journalism involves finding relevant stories within complex datasets, and to achieve this, journalists need an understanding of statistics. Statistical analysis gives meaning to raw data. However, while statistics can 76 seem intimidating, they are simple. Knowingly or unknowingly, most of our daily life decisions are based on statistics. For instance, before making a

purchase online, you examine the average rating of a product and look at the customer satisfaction rate. While choosing a restaurant, you first look at its rating; before heading out, you examine the weather forecast or traffic details. Such simple choices are based on statistical thinking. Evidence suggests that we are highly dependent on data for decision-making; our decisions today are data-driven. However, when we work with large and complex datasets, we need some scientific tools to organise and analyse the data and make sense out of it; this is where statistics comes in. Statistics is a powerful tool for storytelling in the modern information age.
7.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
This unit introduces students to the basics of statistical concepts. After reading this unit, you will be able to:
- understand the importance of statistics in data journalism,
- learn about types of data,
- understand the measurements of central tendency and dispersion,
- comprehend frequency distribution,
- use basic statistical tools to organise and analyse your data, and
- accurately interpret statistical results and communicate findings
effectively.
7.2 WHAT IS STATISTICS?
Statistics is a branch of mathematics and a scientific tool that deals with data. It is defined as a scientific tool that applies mathematical procedures to collect, organise, summarise, and analyse the available data. By providing tools and methods, statistics enables us to understand and analyse complex data, uncover hidden patterns, support decision-making, and make predictions about a large population based on a sample. Broadly, statistics are of two types: a. Descriptive Statistics Descriptive statistics provide a quick overview of trends and distributions in data by summarising the main features of a dataset. It is done using numerical measures such as measures of central tendency (mean, mode, and median) and measures of dispersion (range, variance, and standard deviation). It only describes the main features of a dataset and does not go further than that. b. Inferential Statistics Inferential statistics go beyond summarising the main features of a dataset. It employs probability theory and allows predictions for larger populations based on data collected from a suitable sample. For example, in a village election, collecting data from 500 to 700 people out of a total population of around 4000 provides a probable indication of which candidate is likely to win. Inferential statistics include hypothesis testing, regression analysis, correlation, confidence intervals, t-test, Chi-Square test, ANOVA, etc. 77

7.3 ROLE OF STATISTICS IN JOURNALISM
Today, statistics are one of the most essential tools in journalism. Data journalism uses statistical tools and techniques to uncover hidden truths. Traditional journalism practices rely on interviews and anecdotal evidence, whereas data journalism emphasises objectivity, transparency, and accuracy based on quantitative analysis. a. Simplifies Complex Information Statistics assist journalists in transforming large datasets into information that is both understandable and meaningful. Using statistical tools like averages, percentages, and charts to present data enables the audience to quickly grasp the key points from complex datasets. b. Discovering Trends and Patterns Descriptive statistics enable journalists to summarise the main findings of a dataset and identify meaningful trends and patterns that are not visible otherwise. c. Supports Evidence and Credibility When a report uses statistical analysis, it enhances the credibility of the journalistic claims. For example, a report that includes statistics from NCRB data shows a 20% rise in cybercrime cases compared to the previous year. This year-on-year comparison, backed by the official statistics, enhances the credibility of the report and provides evidence for the seriousness of the issue. d. Fact Checking To verify any claims made by the government, institutions, politicians, organisations, and journalists, use official data to prove or debunk the truth. This helps maintain transparency and accountability. e. Improve Visual Communication Statistical data is visualised using tabulations and graphical tools like infographics, charts, maps, etc., which makes complex data more engaging and interactive. f. Audience Analysis Statistics are also beneficial for media outlets. Tools like Google Analytics help us better understand audience preferences and engagement and guide our content creation strategies.
7.4 TYPES OF DATA
We collect data in the form of numbers, facts, and figures for analysis and interpretation. Before investigating the data analysis process, it is important to understand what kind of data you are dealing with. Different kinds of data require different analysis methods and tools. Broadly, data is divided into two types--quantitative and qualitative.

7.4.1 Quantitative Data
Quantitative data consists of numbers and is referred to as numerical data. It represents quantities that can be counted and measured. The quantitative data analysis method includes descriptive and inferential statistics. It is of two types-- a. Discrete Data Discrete data is countable and consists of whole numbers. It cannot be broken into decimals or fractions. Consider a company's employee count or the number of news channels in a specific area. b. Continuous Data Continuous data is measurable and takes any value within a range. It often includes values in decimals. The values of height (165.5 cm), distance (20.8 km), and weight (50.5 kg) are examples of continuous data.
7.4.2 Qualitative Data
Qualitative data is referred to as categorical data. This is non-numerical data and is used to classify or label things. It describes the qualities and categories of a dataset and cannot be measured numerically. Qualitative data analysis methods include thematic analysis, discourse evaluation, narrative analysis, and grounded theory. It is of two types: a. Nominal Data Nominal data includes names or labels used to identify different categories. This data cannot be ranked or ordered and lacks logical order. It can only be categorised, and the categories are mutually exclusive, which means that each data point fits in only one category. For instance, the categories include yes/no, male/female, and news genres such as entertainment, sports, and politics. b. Ordinal Data Ordinal data includes categories that can be logically ranked or ordered; however, the difference between them is not measurable, as it shows relative positioning. For example, satisfaction level, viewer rating, trust levels, etc. Check Your Progress - 1 Note: 1) Use the space provided below for your answers.

7.5 FUNDAMENTAL CONCEPTS OF STATISTICS
7.5.1 Population
Population refers to the entire group of individuals or items that a researcher wants to study. Studying the entire population is a difficult task because of time, cost, and accessibility. Therefore, researchers draw a sample from the population.
7.5.2 Sample
A sample is defined as a subset of a population that is selected for analysis. The sample is a representative of the entire population so that the findings can be generalised to the whole population. The size and selection method of the sample and sample size will directly affect the accuracy and validity of the results.
7.5.3 Variables
A variable is the characteristic or attribute that is measured, analysed, and manipulated. It can vary across individuals, items, groups, or over time. The variable that is manipulated and controlled is called the independent variable; it depicts the cause-and-effect relationship. The variable on which the effect of manipulation is measured or observed is called the dependent variable. For example, if you want to find out whether the length of a commercial affects viewer attention, here, the length of the commercial is the independent variable and the viewer attention span is the dependent variable.
7.5.4 Scales of Measurement
There are four scales of measurement used in statistics, introduced by Stanley Smith Stevens in 1946.
- Nominal Scale
- Ordinal Scale
- Interval Scale
- Ratio Scale
These scales differ in the type of data they represent and the mathematical operations that are applied. Unit 4 (Block 1) is devoted to levels of measurement. You can revisit the unit to refresh your knowledge on scales of measurement.
7.6 FREQUENCY AND PROBABILITY
1. Frequency
Frequency is a basic concept in descriptive statistics. It is measured as the number of times a particular value appears in a dataset. It is used to summarise the data and provide a clear and simple picture of the pattern in the data, making the interpretation easier.

Types of Frequency:
a Absolute Frequency
Absolute frequency represents the actual counts of how many times a particular value occurs in a dataset. b Relative Frequency Relative frequency is calculated by comparing the proportion of time a value occurs to the number of total observations. c Cumulative Frequency Cumulative frequency is the running total of frequencies up to a certain point and is very useful when we want to know how many observations fall below or equal to a set level. The last cumulative frequency is always equal to the total number of observations. Example: Let us suppose there's a survey of 10 students on the number of news articles they read per day.
News Articles Read Frequency
0 1 1 3 2 2 3 3 4 1 Here, if you want to calculate the absolute frequency for 2 news articles, it is 2; the relative frequency for 2 news articles is 2/10 = 0.2 or 20%. The cumulative frequency up to 2 news articles is 1 (for 0) + 3 (for 1) + 2 (for 2) = 6.2. Probability
Probability is fundamental in inferential statistics. Probability measures the likelihood of an event happening. It helps in understanding the randomness and uncertainty, and makes predictions based on data. Formula for Probability = Number of favourable outcomes / Total number of possible outcomes. Types of Probability: a. Theoretical Probability It is based on reasoning or mathematical models. For example, when you roll a 6-sided dice, the chances of getting a 2 are 1/6. b. Experimental Probability It is based on repeated experiments and observations. Let's say that 100 people are asked to identify fake news. 70 people correctly identify the fake news, so the probability in this scenario is 70/100 = 0.7, or 70%.

c. Subjective Probability This is not based on data but on personal opinions and intuition, and is mostly used when precise data is not available. For instance, based on experience, a doctor suggests that there is a 60% chance that the patient will recover, or based on experience, a social media manager predicts the virality of a story.
7.7 MEASURES OF CENTRAL TENDENCY
These are the statistical tools used to describe the central point of a dataset. Central tendency is defined as "a single value that represents the large and widely scattered data, either in the form of a mathematical average or positional average, or concentration of the highest frequency, mean, median, and mode." The three most common measures of central tendency are mean, mode, and median.
7.7.1 Mean
The mean average, or arithmetic average, is the most commonly used measure of central tendency. It is the average of a given dataset. It is calculated by adding all the values in a dataset and dividing this by the total number of values. The mean is used when the data is evenly distributed. The mean is the most reliable measure of central tendency and is strongly influenced by outliers (data points that are vastly different from other observations in a dataset). Mean = Sum of all values / Total number of values Example: The dataset represents the number of news articles on environmental issues published daily over a week: 4, 5, 6, 5, 7, 6, 7. Mean = 4 + 5 + 6 + 5 + 7 + 6 + 7 / 7 = 40 / 7 = 5.71 The mean is 5.71, which suggests that, on average, around 5 news articles are published daily in the newspaper on environmental issues.
7.7.2 Median
When the data is arranged in a sequential order, the middle value of the data is called the median. For example, when arranging the above data in descending order - 7, 7, 6, 6, 5, 5, 4 - the median is 6. But when you have even values in the data, to arrive at the median, add the two values in the centre and divide by 2. Let's say the data is 7, 7, 6, 6, 5, 5, 4, 4, the median here is 6 + 5 = 11/2 = 5.5. The median is not affected by the outliers as much as it affects the mean.
7.7.3 Mode
The mode in a dataset is the most frequently occurring value. A dataset can be unimodal (one mode), bimodal (two modes), or multimodal (more than two modes). The mode is not affected by the outliers. Mode is commonly used for qualitative data to find the most common category or value. Example 1 - Examine the following score: 1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 5, 5, 5, 6, 6, 7; the most occurring value is 5, so 5 is the mode here. Example 2 - 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 5, 5, 6, 6. The mode here is 2 and 5.

Example 3 - 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12: In this data, there are no values that occur twice, so there is no mode in this set of data.
7.8 MEASURES OF DISPERSION
These are the statistical tools that describe the variability of a dataset. It is defined as the degree of variability in a set of scores. Central tendency describes the central point of the data, while dispersion describes how the data is spread around the centre. The most commonly used measures of dispersion are range, variance, and standard deviation
7.8.1 Range
It is the simplest measure of dispersion and is highly affected by the outliers. It is calculated by subtracting the lowest value from the highest value in a dataset. But range is not the most reliable measure of dispersion, as it only takes extreme values into account. Range = Maximum value - Minimum value Example: the data represent the number of shares on 5 social media posts: 150, 180, 220, 250, and 300. Range = 300 - 150 = 150, which suggests that the data varies by 150 shares.
7.8.2 Variance
Variance indicates how far each value is from the mean. A low variance means that the values are less spread out and are closer to the mean, while a high variance indicates that the values are more dispersed from the mean. Variance measures the distance, but it is squared to eliminate negatives and highlight larger differences. Steps for variance: Step 1. Find the mean of the dataset. Let's take a small dataset: 4, 5, 6, 3, 2 Mean = 4 + 5 + 6 + 3 + 2 = 20 / 5 = 4. Step 2. Find the deviation of each value from the mean. Step 3. Square each deviation
Value Deviation Squared Deviation
4 4-4 = 0 0 5 5-4 = 1 1 6 6-4 = 2 4 3 3-4 = -1 1 2 2-4 = -2 4 Step 4. Find the average of the squared deviation Variance = 0 + 1 + 4 + 1 + 4 = 10 / 5 = 2.7. 8.3 Standard Deviation
The standard deviation is also known as the root mean square deviation. It is the most reliable measure of dispersion. Standard deviation is always calculated

from the arithmetic mean. It shows the average distance of each value from the mean and is sensitive to outliers. Steps for standard deviation: Step 1. Find the mean of the dataset. Let's take a small dataset - 4, 8, 5, 6, 3 Mean = 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 + 8 = 26 / 5 = 5.2 Step 2. Find the deviation of each value from the data This means to subtract the mean from each value. Step 3. Square each deviation.
Value Deviation Squared Deviation

Variance = 1.44 + 7.84 + 0.04 + 0.64 + 4.84 = 14.8 / 5 = 2.96 Step 5. The unit explores the basic statistics essential in the field of journalism to understand, interpret, analyse, and communicate data effectively. We first covered the statistics and their importance in modern-day journalism. After that, we discussed the two major types of statistics, descriptive and inferential statistics. We also learnt about the types of data, quantitative and qualitative, and the different methods of analysis based on the nature of the data. Some fundamental concepts of statistics, like population, sample, variables, and scales of measurement were also covered in this unit, alongside frequency and probability and their types. Finally, we delved into the measures of central tendency (mean, median, and mode) and measures of dispersion (range, variance, and standard deviation). This unit can help aspiring journalists master the basics of statistics and prepare themselves to critically engage with statistical information.
7.10 KEYWORDS
- Statistics: A scientific tool that applies mathematical procedures to
collect, organise, summarise, and analyse the available data
- Population: A complete set of individuals, items, or groups that a
researcher wants to study.
- Sample: Subset of population.
- Variable: An attribute that can take on any value.
- Independent Variable: Can be manipulated to observe its effects.
- Dependent variable: The variable on which the effects are being
measured.
- Descriptive statistics: Provides a summary and the main features of the
data.
- Inferential Statistics: Allows us to make predictions about a population
based on a sample.
- Dispersion: The extent to which all the values in the data vary from the
mean.
- Range: The difference between the highest and lowest value in a dataset.

1. Statistics is a scientific tool that applies mathematical procedures to
collect, organise, summarise, and analyse data. In data journalism, statistics help in sorting complex datasets and make it easier to find the hidden trends and patterns, providing new insights and supporting fact- based reporting.
2. Descriptive statistics describes the main features of a dataset, providing
an overview of trends and distributions in data, while inferential statistics allows predictions and generalisations about a population based on sample data.
3. Broadly, there are two types of data:
a. Quantitative Data, also called numerical data, represents quantities that can be counted and measured. It is of two types: discrete data and continuous data. b. Qualitative Data, also called categorial data, describes the qualities and categories of a dataset and cannot be measured numerically. It is of two types: numerical and ordinal data. Check Your Progress - 2
1. Population refers to the entire group of individuals or items that a
researcher wants to study, while the sample is a subset of a population that is selected for analysis. The population is very large and hard to manage, but the sample is a small representative unit and is manageable. A population gives you the exact parameters, while a sample only provides an estimate of the population.
2. A variable is the characteristic or attribute that is measured, analysed,
manipulated, and varies across the observations in a dataset. There are two types of variables: independent variables, which can be manipulated and controlled, and dependent variable, on which the effect of manipulation is being observed.
3. Probability measures the likelihood that an event will occur. Types of
probability are: a. Theoretical probability is based on logical and mathematical reasoning. b. Experimental probability based on experiments and observations. c. Subjective probability is based on personal opinions and experiences.

4. The three measures of central tendency are mean, mode, and median.
Mean is the average of a given dataset. Median is the middle value of the dataset, while Mode is the value that occurs most often in the dataset.
5. Variance measures the squared distance of each value from the mean,
while standard deviation shows the average distance of each value from the mean.

8.2 OPEN-SOURCE SOFTWARE
Open-source software includes source code with a licence that allows for modification and improvement. It is frequently produced in public and collaborative in nature. Richard M. Stallman's free software concept, developed in 1983, laid the groundwork for the open source movement in terms of technology, law, and ideology. Other prominent philosophers in the free software movement include Eric Raymond, Bruce Perens, and Eben Moglen, in addition to Richard Stallman himself. Open-source development follows the bazaar concept. Open-source development models lack clear roles. As in the marketplace of ideas, the best features and functionalities become widely used. Development is a collective process that does not rely on limited resources or a single organisation. Users are treated as co-developers and should have access to the software's source code. In 1998, the Open Source Initiative (OSI) aimed to align free and commercial software development processes. The OSI aimed to foster collaboration across various open-source communities. The Open Source Initiative certifies software licences as open source. The website (www.opensource.org) provides a comprehensive list of certified licences. OSI has already certified practically any licence agreement that meets the open-source definition. Recently, the policy changed to require newly certified licence agreements to not only meet the open-source definition but also differ significantly from existing licences. This is part of the non-proliferation movement in open source.

8.2.1 Free Software Definition
The definition of free software is based on the four freedoms listed below:
1. The freedom to use the application for any purpose.
2. The ability to examine how the application works and customise it to
your specifications
3. The ability to redistribute copies to benefit a neighbour.
4. Freedom to improve the programme and share it with the community for
everyone's benefit.
8.2.2 Open-Source Definition
The alternative definition is OSI's Open Source definition. This wide term encompasses permissive software licensing. The elements are:
- Free redistribution.
- Source code is available.
- Derivative works are permitted.
- Integrity of the author's source
- No discrimination against individuals or groups.
- There is no discrimination against spheres of endeavour.
- Distribution of licenses with derivative works
- Licences must not be product-specific.
- Licences must not prohibit the use of other software.
- Licenses must be technological-natural.
8.2.3 Open-Source Development Model
The open-source development model is a collaborative one. This approach assumes multiple developers working together to create a single product or module. Open-source projects can have a large number of contributors, although in reality, this is rarely the case. Most open-source projects are small, with only one or a few contributors. Some open-source projects, like Linux or Apache, are massive development efforts. Despite having numerous contributors, these projects rely on a small group of gatekeepers known as "committers", to choose which additions are accepted into the official source tree. In this respect, the model does not represent a pure bazaar. It is similar to a free market with a specialist's desk. Some of the world's most respected computer scientists serve as gatekeepers in popular open-source initiatives. The gatekeeper determines which updates to include in the source tree based on technical concerns such as code security, stability and compatibility with other technologies, and community preferences for features and functionality. The Concurrent Versioning System (CVS), licensed under GNU General Public Licence, is the most widely used open-source utility among gatekeepers. A revision control system restricts code check-ins to specific individuals. Computer Applications keeps track of published versions, including additions, modifications, and deletions, as well as who made the changes. This helps resolve contradictory changes.

The primary features of the open-source development paradigm are: Users should be regarded like co-developers Users are treated as co-developers and should have access to the software's source code. Early releases Early publication of the product increases the likelihood of recruiting co- developers. Frequent integration To avoid costly bug fixes at the end of a project, incorporate code changes as frequently as feasible into a shared code base. Some open-source projects automate integration on a daily basis. There are several variants There should be at least two software versions: one with more features and one with fewer bugs. The flawed version, often known as the development version, is intended for customers who want to use the latest features right away but are willing to take the risk of using untested code. Users can contribute to the development process by reporting bugs and giving patches. High modularity Software should be modular, allowing for parallel development of individual components. Dynamic decision-making structure A formal or informal decision-making structure is necessary to make strategic decisions based on evolving user needs and other considerations. Eric Raymond proposed the bazaar model, which is commonly used in open-source software. These projects include the Linux kernel, Firefox, Apache, the GNU Compiler Collection, and Perl.
8.2.4 Open-Source License
The licence describes the rights and obligations that a licensor grants to a licensee Open-source licences allow licensees to copy, alter, and redistribute source code or content. These may contain obligations, such as distributing modified code in source code form and providing author attribution in programmes and documentation. Open-source licences grant licensees full copyright rights over the licensed software. Open-source software licences may include both explicit and implicit licence grants. The licences typically include substantial warranty disclaimers and liability limits. Most also include disclaimers about any license grant under any trademark of the licensor--not that any such grant would necessarily be implied in the first place. When an author contributes code to an open-source project (e.g., Apache. org), he/she does so under an explicit license (e.g., the Apache Contributor License Agreement) or an implicit license (e.g., the Open Source license under which the project is already licensing). Some open-source projects do not take contributed code under a license, but actually require (joint) assignment of the

author's copyright in order to accept code contributions to the project (e.g., OpenOffice.org and its Joint Copyright Assignment agreement). Placing code (or content) in the public domain is a way of waiving an author's (or owner's) copyrights in that work. No license is granted, and none is needed, to copy, modify or redistribute a work in the public domain. Examples of free software licences/open-source licences include the Apache License, the BSD License, the GNU General Public License, the GNU Lesser General Public License, the MIT License, the Eclipse Public License and the Mozilla Public License.
8.3 PROJECT MANAGEMENT SOFTWARE
So far, we have read about open-source software and various facets of its wokrings. Now, we shall study project management, which involves planning, organising, and managing resources to successfully complete specific project goals and objectives.
8.3.1 Introduction
A project is a temporary endeavour with a clear start and end, undertaken to meet particular goals, usually to bring about beneficial change or added value. The temporary nature of projects contrasts with repetitive or permanent business functions. The main challenge of project management is to achieve all goals within scope, time, and resources. A secondary challenge is to optimise inputs to meet objectives. Typical project phases are:
1. Initiation
2. Planning or design
3. Implementation
4. Monitoring and controlling
5. Completion
8.3.2 Project Manager - Role and Responsibility
A project manager is a professional responsible for the planning, execution, and closing of projects. They are accountable for completing the project within a set timeframe. Key responsibilities include setting objectives, defining requirements, and managing cost, time, and scope.
8.3.3 Software Project Management
Software project management includes planning and leading software projects. It involves defining the project scope, estimating the amount of work, and creating schedules. Project planning begins with requirements and leads to a project plan describing the tasks to complete. Monitoring keeps everyone updated on progress; if deviations occur, the manager can take corrective action. Monitoring involves status meetings, and changing approach to keep products current. Following the project cycle helps achieve objectives on time.
8.3.4 Project Management Software
Project management software includes tools for scheduling, cost and budget management, resource allocation, timesheet management, collaboration, 92 communication, quality, and documentation. These tools help one to handle large project complexity.

- Scheduling: This is used to schedule tasks and events, handle task
dependencies, resource scheduling, and uncertainties in task duration.
- Critical Path: Highlights tasks that affect project length, helping
optimise effort.
- Providing Information: Project software gives task lists, resource
allocation, timeline info, risk warnings, workload planning, historical data on past projects, and optimal resource use.
- Timesheet Management: Tracks hours on tasks, task details, and
operations. Helps managers track productivity and employees assess their performance. Timesheet tools like Timesheet Reporter, Ace Project, Time Reporting, Qtime, and Time Control are easily available.
8.3.5 Tools for Project Management
Project management software tools include:
- Desktop applications: Installed on a PC (e.g., MS Project, Gantt Project).
- Web-based Services: Online applications accessed via the internet (e.g.,
iTeam Work).
- Web-based Systems: Installed on a local network (e.g., dot Project).
8.3.5.1 Microsoft Office Project
MS Project is widely used for planning and managing resources. It uses a scheduling engine to align tasks with resources. It needs task durations, dependencies, and constraints to calculate start and finish dates. It helps manage resources and adjust schedules as needed. 8.4 OFFICE AND SPREADSHEET APPLICATIONS
This section will introduce the world of office applications that are used widely by all of us to carry out day-to-day tasks like writing a project document, preparing our monthly budget, corresponding with each other on email, or scheduling our daily calendar.

Word Processing
A word processor (more formally known as a document preparation system) is a computer application used for the composition, editing, formatting and printing of any sort of printable material. Word processing was one of the earliest applications for the personal computer in office productivity. Most modern word processors take advantage of a graphical user interface, providing some form of "What You See Is What You Get" editing. Most are powerful systems consisting of one or more programmes that can produce any arbitrary combination of images, graphics and text, the latter handled with typesetting capability. Microsoft Word is the most widely used computer word processing system; Microsoft estimates over five hundred million people use the Office suite, which includes Word. There are also many other commercial word processing applications, such as WordStar and WordPerfect, which dominated the market from the mid-1980s to the early 1990s, particularly for machines running Microsoft's MS-DOS operating system. Open-source applications such as AbiWord, KWord, LyX and OpenOffice.org Writer are rapidly gaining in popularity. Online word processors such as Google Docs are a relatively new category. Word processing typically implies text manipulation functions that extend beyond a basic ability to enter and change text, such as automatic generation of batch mailings using a form letter template and an address database (also called mail merging); indices of keywords and their page numbers; tables of contents with section titles and their page numbers; tables of figures with caption titles and their page numbers; cross-referencing with section or page numbers; footnote numbering; and version control of a document using variables (e.g., model numbers, product names, etc.). Other word processing functions include "spell checking", "grammar checking", and a "thesaurus" function. Other common features include collaborative editing, comments and annotations, support for images and diagrams and internal cross-referencing. Almost all word processors enable users to employ styles, which are used to automate consistent formatting of text body, titles, subtitles, highlighted text, and so on. A few features of Microsoft Word 2007 are described here.
Adding Header, Footer or Page Number to a Document
To add a graphic or text on the top or bottom of a document, a header or footer has to be added. Click on the Insert tab, and select the Header or Footer or Page Number from the Header and Footer group. You can select from the available gallery and choose the design required. After selection, the same design chosen will appear in the document. To add a design for the header or footer, double- click on the header or footer area in the document. After making the required changes to the design, close the header/footer area.
Creating a Table in Word
In Word, a table can be inserted either by choosing from a gallery of preformatted table templates or by using the table menu to choose the number of rows and columns that are required.
Creating a Table of Contents
The Table of Contents (TOC) is created by applying heading styles to the text 94 that is to be included in the TOC. Word will search for those headings and

create the TOC in the document. The Table of Contents can be selected from the design gallery provided in Word.
Mail Merge
Mail merge is a software function describing the production of multiple documents from a single template form and a structured data source. This helps to create personalised letters and pre-addressed envelopes or mailing labels for mass mailings from a word processing document which contains fixed text and variables, which act as placeholders that are replaced by text from the data source. The data source is typically a spreadsheet or a database. When the mail merge is run, the word processing system creates an output document for each row in the database, using the fixed text exactly as it appears in the template, but substituting the data variables with the values from the matching columns. Spreadsheet A spreadsheet is a grid made of columns and rows known as cells and is used for making tables and charts used for mathematical and statistical analysis as well as business calculations. One of the widely used spreadsheet software is MS- Excel. Each cell on a spreadsheet can have any of the following data: Text or labels, numbers or constants, and formulae, which are mathematical equations to do all calculations. Each cell is designated with a name which is actually the COLUMN NAME and ROW NUMBER. The following are the three basic types of data that a cell may have: labels, values, and formulas, which always begin with an EQUAL SIGN (=). The spreadsheet consists of various sheets, like sheet1, sheet2, sheet3, etc., within the workbook. These sheets can be also be given specific names. The format of the cells on the sheets can be modified using the Home->Cells- >Format->Format Cells option on the menu. The contents of the cells can be cut, copied and pasted using the Home->Clipboard options. There is an option of "Paste Special", which allows only certain aspects of the cells copied to the clipboard to be pasted. It is possible to protect the cells so that the data cannot be changed or modified. Protecting a Worksheet: Click Tools, click Protection, and click Protect Sheet. Enter a password (only if desired). Confirm password (only if entered). Click OK. Protecting a Workbook: Click Tools, click Protection, and click Protect Workbook. Enter a password (optional). Choose to protect the structure, windows, or both. Click OK. There are different categories of functions that can be incorporated in the sheets, like Date & Time, Mathematical, Statistical, Logical, text functions, etc. Charting Charts and graphs can be created based on data in the sheets. To create a chart to represent data graphically: Select the data, go to Insert, select the chart type from the options available like Bar, Line, Pie, Scatter etc. Macros A macro is a short program written using Visual Basic Application that can be used to carry out a specific task. VBA is a programming language that is included with all of the Microsoft Office applications, for example, Word, Access, PowerPoint, and Excel. To record a macro: Go to the Tools menu, 95

go to "macro" and then "Record New Macro", assign a name and description, and then perform the actions. Once you're done recording your macro, press the Stop button. Macros can be executed in the following ways: by using the menu command, by pressing a CTRL combination shortcut key, or by clicking a toolbar button.

8.5.1 What is email?
Email Accounts can be provided by an the Internet Service provider, employer, or webmail services like Yahoo, Gmail, etc. Outlook doesn't have its own accounts but uses these POP configuration to access web-based servers for emails. Post Office Protocol (POP) is an application-layer Internet standard protocol used by local e-mail clients to retrieve e-mail from a remote server over a TCP/IP connection. POP supports simple download-and-delete requirements for access to remote mailboxes. Although most POP clients have an option to leave mail on server after download, e-mail clients using POP generally connect, retrieve all messages, store them on the user's PC as new messages, delete them from the server, and then disconnect. To send or receive email messages with Microsoft Outlook, these email accounts Information has to be added. Email accounts are contained in profiles. An email profile consists of email accounts, data files and settings as to where the emails are to be stored. There can be one profile or more than one profile depending on the requirement of the user. There can be one or more email accounts within a single Outlook profile.

9.0 INTRODUCTION
Our current era, known as the information age, has seen massive data collection. Advancements in technology, like computers and satellites, have made communication easier. Computers and digital storage made it possible to collect and store a wide range of data. Unfortunately, the large amount of data saved on various storage devices became overwhelming over time. Database management systems (DBMS) were thus developed to address the chaotic nature of data storage. Improved database management systems facilitate large-scale data collection. We now have an overwhelming amount of information to manage, including satellite images, text reports, economic transactions, scientific data, military intelligence, medical and personal data, games, and digital media. Effective decision-making requires more than just retrieving information. To make better managerial judgements, we have developed new requirements in response to large data gathering. Requirements may include automatic data summarisation, information extraction, and pattern recognition in raw data. Data mining is a technical process that identifies consistent patterns through exploration, sorting, and organisation. It is used to provide two primary advantages: (i) to give businesses the predictive power to estimate the unknown or future values and (ii) to provide businesses the descriptive power by finding interesting patterns in the data.

9.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After going through this unit, you should be able to:
- understand the definition of data mining;
- identify the purpose of text mining;
- describe the process of data mining;
- narrate the key differences between the data mining and data warehousing;
- list and discuss various data mining tools, and
- discuss various data mining applications.
9.2 DATA MINING AND ITS BENEFITS
Data mining, also known as knowledge discovery in data (KDD), is the process of extracting patterns and valuable information from huge datasets. Data mining techniques have become increasingly popular recently due to advancements in data warehousing and big data. They help firms translate raw data into valuable knowledge. Although technology has evolved to handle massive amounts of data, leaders still confront issues with scalability and automation. Data mining enhances corporate decision-making through meaningful data analysis. Data mining approaches serve two purposes: describing the dataset and predicting results using machine learning algorithms. These methods arrange and filter data to highlight relevant information, including fraud detection, user behaviour, bottlenecks, and security breaches. Data mining serves multiple purposes, including predicting outcomes, modelling target audiences, and collecting product information. This technique involves analysing and converting data into relevant information. This improves commercial decision-making accuracy and effectiveness. It enables wise market decisions, accurate marketing, and predictions. Data mining allows us to examine client behaviours and insights. This leads to tremendous success and data-driven business. Data mining extracts patterns from databases to provide insight into client behaviour. Acquiring knowledge enables companies to provide high-quality services.
9.2.1 Benefits of Data Mining
Data mining helps us solve difficulties in today's tough information age. Data mining provides companies with trustworthy information.
- It is a more efficient and cost-effective solution than other data
applications.
- It enables organisations to make profitable production and operational
improvements.
- Data mining employs both new and legacy systems.
- It enables firms to make educated judgements.

- It aids in detecting credit concerns and fraud.
- It enables data scientists to effortlessly evaluate massive amounts of data
quickly.
- Data scientists may utilise this information to prevent fraud, create risk
models, and enhance product safety.
- It enables data scientists to quickly predict behaviours and trends,
uncovering hidden patterns.
9.2.2 Types of Data that can be Mined
In principle, data mining is not limited to a single sort of media or data. Data mining can be applied to any type of information store. Algorithms and techniques may vary depending on the type of data. Various sorts of data provide unique issues. Data mining is applied to various databases, including relational, object- relational, and object-orientated databases, as well as data warehouses, transactional databases, and unstructured repositories like the World Wide Web, social media data, spatial databases, multimedia databases, time-series databases, textual databases, and flat files.
9.3 How Does Data Mining Work?
The Cross-Industry Standard Process for Data Mining (CRISP-DM) is an established method for guiding data mining activities. The technique outlines project phases, associated tasks, and their relationships. The process model offers an overview of the data mining life cycle. The CRISP-DM model is adaptable and may be easily adapted. The life cycle model contains six phases, with arrows illustrating key dependencies between them. Before getting started, however, one must ask themselves the following questions:
- What is our goal?
- What problem are we trying to solve?
- What data is required to solve the problem?
Do remember, improper data mining can lead to inaccuracies, erroneous results, and unanswered questions. The order of the following six phases of CRISP-DM is not exact. Most projects frequently transition between them. Data Understanding: Once the overarching goal has been decided, appropriate data must be collected. Relevant data can be gathered from various sources, including sales records, consumer surveys, and geolocation data. This step aims to guarantee that all relevant data sets are included to achieve the objective. Data Preparation: The preparation phase is the most time-consuming and involves three steps:

extraction, transformation, and loading (ETL). Data is extracted from several sources and stored in a staging area. During the transformation process, data is cleaned, null sets are populated, duplicate data is deleted, errors are handled, and all data is assigned to tables. Finally, prepared data is imported into the database for use. Modeling: Data modelling involves analysing relevant data and determining the optimal statistical and mathematical approach to answer the objective question(s). There are various modelling techniques, including classification, grouping, and regression analysis. Using multiple models on the same data to achieve specific goals is typical practice. Evaluation: After building and testing the models, it's time to assess their effectiveness in addressing the highlighted business questions. This is a human-driven phase where the project manager assesses if the model output fits their objectives. If necessary, construct a new model or prepare new data. Deployment: Once the data mining model is accurate and successful in answering the objective question, it is time to apply it. Deployment can take the shape of a visual presentation or report, offering insights. It can also prompt action, such as developing a new sales strategy or applying risk-reduction measures.
9.4 CLASSIFICATION OF DATA MINING
SYSTEMS
There are several criteria for categorising data mining systems, including:
- Data mining systems are classified based on their data source type,
including geographic, multimedia, time-series, text, and World Wide Web.
- Data mining systems are classified depending on their data models,
including relational, object-orientated, data warehousing, and transactional.
- Data mining systems are classified by the type of knowledge discovered,
including characterisation, discrimination, association, classification, and clustering. Some systems combine multiple data mining functionalities.
- Data mining systems use a variety of approaches to classify data.
This categorisation classify data mining systems based on their data analysis strategy, including machine learning, neural networks, genetic algorithms, statistics, visualisation, database-orientated, and data warehouse-orientated. The classification might consider the level of user participation in data mining, including query-driven, interactive, and autonomous systems. A comprehensive system offers a range of data mining approaches to suit various situations and user participation levels.

9.5 DATA MINING TECHNIQUES
Data mining is most useful in identifying data patterns and deriving useful business insights from those patterns. To accomplish these tasks, data miners use a variety of techniques to generate different results. Here are five common data mining techniques:
9.5.1 Classification Analysis
With this technique, data points are assigned to groups, or classes, based on a specific question or problem to address. For instance, if a consumer packaged goods company wants to optimise its coupon discount strategy for a specific product, it might review inventory levels, sales data, coupon redemption rates, and consumer behavioural data in order to make the best decision possible.
9.5.2 Association Rule Learning
This function seeks to uncover the relationships between data points; it is used to determine whether a specific action or variable has any traits that can be linked to other actions (e.g., business travelers' room choices and dining habits). A hotelier might use association rule insights to offer room upgrades or food and beverage promotions to attract additional business travellers.
9.5.3 Anomaly or Outlier Detection
In addition to searching for patterns, data mining seeks to uncover unusual data within a set. Anomaly detection is the process of finding data that doesn't conform to the pattern. This process can help find instances of fraud and help retailers learn more about spikes, or declines, in the sales of certain products.
9.5.4 Clustering Analysis
Clustering looks for similarities within a data set, separating data points that share common traits into subsets. This is similar to the classification type of analysis in that it groups data points, but, in clustering analysis, the data is not assigned to previously defined groups. Clustering is useful for defining traits within a data set, such as the segmentation of customers based on purchase behavior, need state, life stage, or likely preferences in marketing communication.
9.5.5 Regression Analysis
Regression analysis is about understanding which factors within a data set are most important, which can be ignored, and how these factors interact. With this technique, data miners are able to validate theories such as "when a lot of snow is predicted, more bread and milk will be sold before the storm." While this seems obvious enough, there are a number of variables that need to be verified and quantified for the store manager to make sure enough stock is available. For example, how much is "a lot" of snow? How much is "more milk and bread?" Which types of weather forecasts tend to cause consumer action, and how many days before the storm will consumers start buying? What is the relationship between inches of snow, units of bread, and units of milk? Through regression analysis, specific inventory levels of milk and bread (in units/cases) can be recommended for specific levels of snow forecasted (inches) at specific points in time (days before the storm). In this way, the use of regression analysis maximises sales, minimises out-of-stock instances, and helps avoid overstocking, which results in product spoilage after the storm.

9.6 DATA MINING VS. DATA WAREHOUSING
Data warehouing is a technique for collecting and managing data from varied sources to provide meaningful business insights. It is a blend of technologies and components, which allows the strategic use of data. A data warehouse is repository of a large amount of data, which is designed for query and analysis instead of transaction processing. It is a process of transforming data into information and making it available to users for analysis. On the other hand, data mining is looking for hidden, valid, and potentially useful patterns in huge data sets. Data mining is all about discovering unsuspected/ previously unknown relationships amongst the data. It is a multi-disciplinary skill that uses machine learning, statistics, AI, and database technology. The insights extracted via Data mining can be used for marketing, fraud detection, and scientific discovery, etc. Check Your Progress - 1 Note: 1) Use the space provided below for your answers.

9.7 DATA MINING TOOLS
Data mining techniques utilise the domain knowledge from statistical analysis, artificial intelligence, and database systems in order to analyse data in a proper manner in view of different dimensions and perspectives. Data mining tools discover patterns or trends from the collection of large sets of data and transforming data into useful information for making decisions. The most popular data mining tools are: Orange, SaS, Rattle Data Mining, RapidMiner, DataMelt Data Mining, Oracle BI, and the like.
9.7.1 Orange Data Mining
Developed at the bioinformatics laboratory at the faculty of computer and information science, Ljubljana University, Slovenia, Orange is a machine learning and data mining software suite. It supports data visualisation and is software-based on components written in Python. The components of Orange are called "widgets." These widgets range from data visualisation and preprocessing to assessing the algorithms and are used for predictive modelling. Widgets deliver many important functionalities, such as:
- Displaying data table and allowing to select features
- Reading of data.
- Training predictors and comparison of learning algorithms
- Data element visualisation, etc.
Data coming to Orange is formatted quickly to the desired pattern, and the widgets can be easily transferred wherever and whenever needed. Orange is quite interesting to users as it allows them to make smarter decisions in a short

time by rapidly comparing and analysing the data. Data mining can be performed via visual programming or Python scripting. Many analysis are feasible through its visual programming interface (the drag and drop connected with widgets) and many visual tools tend to be supported, such as bar charts, scatter-plots, trees, dendrograms, and heat maps. A substantial amount of widgets (more than
100) tend to be supported.
The instrument has machine learning components, add-ons for bioinformatics and text mining, and it is packed with features for data analytics. This is also used as a Python library. Orange comprises a canvas interface onto which the user places widgets and creates a data analysis workflow. The widget proposes fundamental operations. For example, reading the data, showing a data table, selecting features, training predictors, comparing learning algorithms, visualising data elements, etc. Orange comes with multiple regression and classification algorithms. Orange can read documents in native and other data formats. It is dedicated to machine learning techniques for classification or supervised data mining. There are two types of objects used in classification: learners and classifiers. Learners consider class-levelled data and return a classifier. Regression methods are very similar to classification in Orange, and both are designed for supervised data mining and require class-level data. The learning of ensembles combines the predictions of individual models for precision gain. The model can either come from different training data or use different learners on the same sets of data.
9.7.2 SAS Data Mining
SAS stands for Statistical Analysis System. It is a product of the SAS Institute created for analytics and data management. SAS can mine data, change it, manage information from various sources, and analyse statistics. It offers a graphical UI for non-technical users. SAS data miner allows users to analyse big data and provide accurate insights for timely decision-making purposes. SAS has distributed memory processing architecture that is highly scalable. It is suitable for data mining, optimisation, and text mining purposes.
9.7.3 Rattle Data Mining
Rattle is a popular GUI for data mining using R, the programming language. It presents statistical and visual summaries of data, transforms data so that it can be readily modelled, builds both unsupervised and supervised machine learning models from the data, presents the performance of models graphically, and scores new datasets for deployment into production. Rattle is free open-source software. A key feature is that all of your interactions through the graphical user interface are captured as an R script that can be readily executed in R independently of the Rattle interface. Use it as a tool to learn and develop your skills in R and then build your initial models in Rattle to then be tuned in R, which provides considerably more powerful options.
9.7.4 RapidMiner
RapidMiner is one of the most popular tools for performing predictions. It is written in the Java programming language. It offers an integrated environment for text mining, deep learning, machine learning, and predictive analysis. The instrument can be used for a wide range of applications, including company 106 applications, commercial applications, research, education, training, application development, machine learning.

RapidMiner provides the server on-site as well as in public or private cloud infrastructure. It has a client/server model as its base. This data mining tool comes with template-based frameworks that enable fast delivery with few errors (which are commonly expected in the manual coding writing process).
9.7.5 DataMelt
DataMelt is a free-to-use tool for numeric computation, mathematics, data analysis, and data visualisation. This program offers you the simplicity of scripting languages, like Python, Ruby, and Groovy, with the power of hundreds of Java packages.
9.8 APPLICATIONS OF DATA MINING
Data Mining is primarily used today by companies with a strong consumer focus, in areas like retail, financial, communication, and marketing organisations, to "drill down" into their transactional data and determine pricing, customer preferences and product positioning, impact on sales, customer satisfaction, and corporate profits. With data mining, a retailer can use point-of-sale records of customer purchases to develop products and promotions to appeal to specific customer segments. Following are some of the applications of data mining:
Basket Analysis
In its most basic application, retailers use basket analysis to analyse what consumers buy (or put in their "baskets"). This is a form of the association technique, giving retailers insight into buying habits, allowing them to recommend other purchases. A less familiar application is one used by law enforcement, where vast amounts of anonymous consumer data is analysed, looking for combinations of products one would use to make bombs or in the production of methamphetamine.
Sales Forecasting
Sales forecasting is a form of predictive analysis to which businesses are devoting more of their budgets. Data mining can help businesses project sales and set targets by examining historical data such as sales records, financial indicators (e.g., consumer price index, inflation markers, etc.), consumer spending habits, sales attributed to a specific time of year, and trends which may impact standard assumptions about the business. Bioinformatics Data mining approaches seem ideally suited for bioinformatics, since it is data- rich. Mining biological data helps to extract useful knowledge from massive datasets gathered in biology and in other related life sciences areas such as medicine and neuroscience. Applications of data mining to bioinformatics include gene finding, protein function inference, disease diagnosis, disease prognosis, disease treatment optimisation, protein and gene interaction network reconstruction, data cleansing, and protein subcellular location prediction.
Inventory Planning
Data mining can provide businesses with up-to-date information regarding product inventory, delivery schedules, and production requirements. Data mining can also help remove some of the uncertainty that comes with simple

supply-and-demand issues within the supply chain. The speed with which data mining can discern patterns and devise projections helps companies better manage their product stock and operate more efficiently.
Customer Segmentation
Traditional market research may help us segment customers but data mining goes in deep and increases market effectiveness. Data mining aids in aligning customers into a distinct segment and can tailor the product according to the needs of the customers. Marketing, after all, is always about retaining customers. Data mining allows companies to find a segment of customers based on vulnerability and the business could offer them with special offers and enhance customer satisfaction.
Customer Relationship Management
Customer Relationship Management is all about acquiring and retaining customers, and about improving customers' loyalty and implementing customer-focused strategies. To maintain a proper relationship with a customer, a business needs to collect and analyse data pertaining to customer behavior, and this is where data mining plays its part. Instead of being confused about what can be done for customer retention, businesses get filtered and clear cut results. Healthcare Mining can be used to predict the volume of patients in every category. Processes have been developed to ensure that patients receive appropriate care at the right place and at the right time. Data mining can also help healthcare insurers to detect fraud and abuse. Education There is a new emerging field, called Educational Data Mining (EDM), concerned with developing methods to discover knowledge from data originating in educational environments. The goals of EDM are identified as predicting students' future learning behavior, studying the effects of educational support, and advancing scientific knowledge about learning. Data mining can be used by an institution to take accurate decisions and also to predict the results of the student. With the results, the institution can focus on what to teach and how to teach. The learning pattern of the students can be captured and used to develop techniques to teach them.
Intrusion Detection
Any action that will compromise the integrity and confidentiality of a resource is an intrusion. The defensive measures to avoid an intrusion includes user authentication, avoid programming errors and information protection. Data mining can help improve intrusion detection by adding a level of focus to anomaly detection. It helps an analyst to distinguish an activity from common everyday network activity. Data mining also helps extract data that is more relevant to the problem.
Criminal Investigation
Criminology is a process that aims to identify crime characteristics. Actually 108 crime analysis includes exploring and detecting crimes and their relationships

with criminals. The high volume of crime datasets and also the complexity of relationships between these kinds of data have made criminology an appropriate field for applying data mining techniques. Text-based crime reports can be converted into word processing files. This information can be used to perform crime matching Process.
Fraud Detection
While frequently occurring patterns in data can provide teams with valuable insight, observing data anomalies is also beneficial, assisting companies in detecting fraud. While this is a well-known use within banking and other financial institutions, SaaS-based (Software as a Service-based) companies have also started to adopt these practices to eliminate fake user accounts from their datasets.
Operational Optimisation
Process mining leverages data mining techniques to reduce costs across operational functions, enabling organisations to run more efficiently. This practice has helped to identify costly bottlenecks and improve decision-making among business leaders. Check Your Progress - 2 Note: 1) Use the space provided below for your answers.

9.10 KEYWORDS
Data Mining: The process of extracting meaningful patterns and insights from large datasets using statistical and computational techniques. Classification: A data mining technique that assigns items in a dataset to predefined categories or classes. Clustering: A technique used to group similar data points together based on their characteristics, without predefined labels. Data Warehousing: A system used to store, manage, and retrieve structured data from multiple sources for analysis and reporting. Association Rule Learning: A method used to find interesting relationships (associations) between variables in large datasets.

10.0 INTRODUCTION
From what we have learnt so far, we have recognised the importance of data and numbers in modern-day journalism. Data serves as the foundation for stories, and the distinction between journalism and data science is becoming increasingly hazy due to the need for journalists to possess proficiency in data analysis. By collecting, analysing, and interpreting complex data, journalists find hidden stories and present them in a narrative format. Story finding and data cleaning are two interconnected concepts in data journalism; together, they enable journalists to uncover meaningful narratives from raw data and report them in the public interest.

As argued by Gray, Chambers, and Bounegru (2012), "Data journalism is bridging the gap between stat technicians and wordsmiths." Story finding is a creative and analytical skill, while data cleansing is more of a technical skill. Data cleaning is part of the data analysis process; it helps to identify hidden patterns and gaps in a dataset, which are important to determine the relevant and impactful stories. Unclean data can distort a good story and narrative, and if a journalist cannot find a good story with clean data, then that data may go unused. Data cleaning and story finding together form a cyclic process. By cleaning messy data, finding stories with a valid narrative becomes easy, and in return, the stories further guide the refinement of data. In this unit, we will understand this cyclic process better because both these concepts together form the foundation of effective data journalism.
10.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
This unit covers two important and interconnected concepts in data journalism: story finding and data cleaning. After going through this unit, students will be able to:
- understand the process of data cleaning in data analysis and the process
for finding the most potential stories from the datasets.
- understand the relationship between data cleaning and story finding and
how both concepts are interdependent.
- understand the basic methods for data cleaning, such as filtering and
sorting, using both manual and digital tools.
10.2 THE ROLE OF STORY IN JOURNALISM
Journalism is about telling and writing stories that matter to the public. The story is the soul of journalism, and every compelling piece begins with a story. A well- crafted story turns raw information into something meaningful and adds context to facts and events that the audience can relate to. Without a clear, structured narrative, the information about the daily facts and events is just updates with no proper connection or impact for the audience. In data journalism, stories are not as easily found as they are with traditional forms of journalistic practices, such as interviews, investigative reporting, or field reporting. Finding stories in large, messy datasets is like solving a complex puzzle. In data journalism, journalists must actively look for the patterns, trends, leads, and correlations present in the data and then communicate those findings in a narrative form.
10.3 STORY FINDING AND STORYTELLING
In journalism, story finding and storytelling are complementary yet distinct processes. Story finding is the initial stage; it is the discovery process, and storytelling is a creative and communicative process. Story finding involves exploring and finding trends, patterns, hidden issues, and narratives within data and events. While discovering a story, journalists often ask questions such as, Is there any pattern here? Is there something unusual about the data? Are there any anomalies in the data? Are there any linked issues worth exploring? Once we identify the story, we move on to the second stage: storytelling. It involves providing engaging and interesting answers to the questions derived from the data and events. It is the process of communicating the story in narrative

form, adding a human angle. It aims to present the story in a clear, accurate, and engaging manner. The main task in storytelling is choosing appropriate formats: text, language, and visuals based on the targeted audience. In data journalism, visualisation is the key tool used for telling stories. The NCRB data, for instance, demonstrates a steady rise in violence against women over a six- year period. The story-finding process includes noticing this trend and asking relevant questions, while storytelling involves narrating it, adding a human angle by interviewing women, experts, and responsible authorities, and presenting the information through maps, charts, and infographics, while quoting the victims.
10.4 FINDING STORY WITHIN DATA
In traditional reporting, finding a story is easier; the lead for the story can be a press release, a public event, or a tip from a source. Journalists then need to explore more of the issue and craft a narrative. In data journalism, a story is not always visible upfront; journalists need to closely inspect and question the datasets. The story emerges from numbers, and a journalist needs a solid understanding of data analysis as well as the social and political context. A data-driven story emerges from the trends, gaps, patterns, anomalies, and relationships found within datasets. The journalists must explore the data by filtering and sorting it into rows and columns, comparing variables, and visualising the information.
10.4.1 DATA
Data is at the core of the story in data journalism. It can be the whole story and also be used as a tool to support a specific narrative. When data is used as a tool to support a narrative, it is usually followed by a long article or feature, and the data is visualised in a format that supports the structure of the story. Data transforms journalism from anecdotal storytelling to evidence-based reporting. When journalists work with data, they are the first to report the news and explain how it affects people. Data enables journalists to move from individual cases to broader social implications.
10.4.2 Visual Design for A Story
The main difference between traditional text-based stories and modern data- driven stories is that the latter are more interactive and encourage higher engagement, where the audience becomes an active participant and explores data by clicking, zooming, and filtering through it, finding their own patterns or stories relating to their interests. Data-driven stories are presented using visualisation tools such as charts, graphs, maps, infographics, etc. However, in data journalism, visualisation serves as a tool to discover the story as well as a medium for storytelling. Journalists frequently utilise charts, histograms, and scatter plots to first examine datasets in order to identify anomalies or outliers that could lead to a more in-depth story. Furthermore, journalists use visual tools to convey the story with greater ease and clarity compared to text. It is important to understand how different design elements (fonts, text sizes, colours, shapes, textures, lines, alignment, etc.) are used to present a story because they are not just for aesthetics; they play an important role in helping the audience understand and follow the story. They organise the information, showing connections between different parts and making navigation easy.
