10.5 DATA PREPROCESSING
Data preprocessing is the process of cleaning and organising data. It ensures consistency of the data and presents it in a usable format. If the data is inconsistent or unclear, the developed story and narrative will be misleading. Moreover, the real-life data is raw, messy, and noisy and cannot be used for analysis; thus, data preprocessing is important to remove the mistakes, duplicate entries, and missing values to make the data error-free. It transforms the data into easy formats that computers can work with and enables meaningful insights later during data analysis and visualisation. Well-pre-processed data is clean, consistent, complete, accurate, and valid for understanding the relationship among different variables and building a narrative. The following are the four important steps in data preprocessing:
10.5.1 Data Integration
After collecting the data from reliable sources, the first step is data integration. When you are gathering data from multiple sources, integration ensures that all the data merges perfectly. It helps in improving the consistency of the data by resolving all the format and code conflicts.
10.5.2 Data Cleaning
Data cleaning is one of the most crucial steps in data preprocessing. Unclean data can lead to misleading stories and wrong conclusions. Data cleaning requires removing duplicate values, filling missing values, removing irrelevant data, and correcting inconsistencies. We will learn more about this step later in this unit.
10.5.3 Data Transformation
The process of converting data from one format to another suitable format is known as data transformation. This step helps in standardising values by merging 116 or splitting fields, and it enables the proper logical and mathematical alignment

of data. The quality of the data is improved by the data cleaning process, and then its transformation converts it into a usable format. For example, time can be in seconds, minutes, or hours, or responses like YES/NO can be coded as 0 and 1.10.5.4 Data Reduction
Data reduction is used to simplify the data by reducing its quantity. It involves removing irrelevant data by dropping unnecessary columns and rows and aggregating data, but while maintaining the integrity of the original and not losing any important information. This step is important, especially when working with large datasets, because smaller, focused datasets are easier and faster to analyse and visualise.
10.6 DATA CLEANING
So far, we have understood that cleaning data is the most essential step in data journalism. The accuracy of every other step depends on how clear our data is. In data journalism, the credibility of any story depends on the reliability of the data. Real-world data is large, raw, and messy, with many inconsistencies, which makes it unfit for analysis. Such data, if not handled properly, distorts insights and can mislead the audience. Data cleaning, also known as data scrubbing, is a systematic process of identifying, removing, or correcting errors, duplicates, and irrelevant data to ensure its validity, reliability, and usability. It enhances data quality and enables smoother data analysis and visualisation, as well as better machine learning results.
10.7 DATA CLEANING TECHNIQUES
a. Removing Duplicate Entries Most of the time, the same data appears more than once in a dataset. Usually, it happens when data is manually collected or inserted into sheets. Removing these double numbers is important because they mislead the results by distorting the total and average. b. Missing Values This term refers to the blank entries in datasets where data is expected to be present. Handling missing values is important because it can distort outcomes, especially when many values are missing in the essential fields. There are various methods to fill the missing values, like mean, median, and imputation.
- Imputation: This method is suitable for numerical data. The missing
values are filled with the mean, median, or mode. For example, these are the scores obtained by a student in four different subjects, but one value is missing. Maths - 75 Physics - 80 Biology - ? Chemistry - 85

Here, to fill the missing value, we can use the mean score: 75 + 80 + 85 / 3 = 80
- Delete: One can delete a row where only a few values are missing,
and also the irrelevant data.
- Backward/Forward filling: The previous and next values can be
used to fill the missing data, especially when you are working with time series data.
- Replace with Unknown: When dealing with categorical data,
rather than leaving missing values blank, it is better to mark them as unknown. c. Standardisation If the same data is recorded in different formats, it leads to inconsistencies in datasets. For example, if male is recorded as male, men, and M. Therefore, standardising formats such as date, time, and address is important for maintaining uniformity in the data. d. Dealing with Outliers Outliers are extreme values that significantly differ from other observations in a dataset. Removing or adjusting these values based on specific context is important because they affect the average of the category. After determining if the outliers are errors or relevant to the story, they must be addressed based on their importance. e. Remove Irrelevant Data It is better to work with variables that are essential to your story and drop unwanted categories and rows and columns that are not useful for analysis. For example, if you want to understand the relationship between gender and salary in a particular institution, then data fields such as emails and phone numbers are not necessary. f. Data Validation Before using the data for analysis or storytelling purposes, it is essential to check and validate the clean data against a set of rules. One must also check if it is accurate, logical, and consistent, and ensure that it meets the set criteria. The above procedure is the final step in data cleaning and is essential for a quality check.
10.8 NOISY DATA
Data with random variations, irrelevant or incorrect values, outliers, and errors is known as noisy data. Such data needs to be cleaned before using it for storytelling. There are many methods to clean noisy data; some common ones are listed below:
10.8.1 Smoothing by Binning
The binning technique is used to reduce the variation in a dataset. This technique involves grouping data into 'bins' and 'intervals' and then smoothing to reduce variation. Binning is of three types:

a. Smoothing by bin mean In this method, all the values in a bin are replaced with the mean (average) value of the bin. b. Smoothing by median In this method, all the values in a bin are replaced with the median (middle value) of the bin. c. Smoothing by bin boundaries In this method, all the values in the bin are replaced by the closest boundary value. The minimum and maximum values in a bin are its boundary values. The approach is useful when the extreme values in the datasets need to be maintained. Let's clear the noise from the data using smoothing techniques from the following details: The test scores of a student are as follows: 35, 38, 74, 36, 72, 42, 70, 39, 71, and 75. Please group these values into two bins. Bin 1: 35, 36, 38, 39, 42 Bin 2: 70, 71, 72, 74, 75
- Smoothing by bin mean
Mean of bin 1 = 38 Mean of bin 2 = 72.4 Result: 38, 38, 38, 38, 38, 72.4, 72.4, 72.4, 72.4, 72.4 * Smoothing by bin median Median of bin 1 = 38 Median of bin 2 = 72 Result: 38, 38, 38, 38, 38, 72, 72, 72, 72, 72
- Smoothing by bin boundaries
For bin 1: replace the values with 35 (minimum) or 42 (maximum) (35, 35, 35, 42, 42) For bin 2: replace the values with 70 (minimum) or 75 (maximum) (70, 70, 70, 75, 75) Result: 35, 35, 35, 42, 42, 70, 70, 70, 75, 75.10.8.2 Regression
A statistical tool known as regression fits a line or curve to data. By predicting the trend, it aids in identifying patterns and trends, thereby eliminating noisy values. For instance, the following dataset illustrates the evolution of a school's admission percentage over time:

Year Growth (in percentage) 2020 5.6 2021 5.8 2022 5.9 2023 8.2 (noise value) 2024 5.8 In 2023, 8.2 is an outlier; however, the noise value can be replaced and corrected by predicting the trend, and using the line, the predicted value is 5.8.10.8.3 Clustering
In this method, similar data is grouped into clusters, and outliers are detected. When similar data values are clustered, the outliers are visible. Values that will not fit in any clusters are noisy and outliers.

10.10 LET US SUM UP
In this unit, we explored the two important and interconnected concepts of data journalism: story finding and data cleaning. We understood the interconnection and cyclical nature of these two concepts. Story finding guides the further refinement of the data, while finding a compelling narrative is only possible when the data has been cleaned. We also learned how story finding and storytelling are related yet distinct terms and require different sets of skills. Furthermore, journalists use visual tools to convey the story with greater ease and clarity compared to text. In data journalism, visualisation serves as a tool to discover the story hence the frequent use of charts, histograms, and scatter plots to examine datasets in order to identify anomalies or outliers that could lead to a more in-depth story. This unit also covered processes such as data preprocessing which through a cleaning and organising of data presents it in a usable format. We were also introduced to the concept of noisy data or data with random variations, irrelevant or incorrect values, outliers, and errors. Such data needs to be cleaned before using it for storytelling. For this, there are many methods and various techniques, including methods such as binning (grouping data into 'bins' and 'intervals' and then smoothing to reduce variation), regression (fitting the data in a line or curve and thereby aiding in identifying patterns and trends), and clustering (similar data is grouped into clusters, and outliers are detected, which help to make outliers visible), which are used to remove or correct noisy values in a dataset.
10.11 KEYWORDS
Story Finding: The process of discovering a meaningful narrative from data. Data Cleaning: The process of removing and correcting duplicate values, missing values, and inconsistencies from data to improve the quality. Noisy Data: Datasets that contain errors, outliers, and irrelevant values. Storytelling: The process of visualising and communicating findings interactively. Outliers: Extreme values in a dataset that are far from other observations. Data Preprocessing: Methods used to prepare raw data for analysis and visualisation by cleaning, integrating, transforming, and reducing data.

11.1 INTRODUCTION
In the time and age, we all are constantly working with numbers and data. Finding and exploring that data is a laborious process. Data can be obtained in a variety of ways and through a wide range of media. How we convey that larger picture behind that data is the crucial task for a journalist. Everything that comes after the data collection procedure is included in data reporting. The aim is to handle and process that information to present it in a cohesive way. This unit will examine every possible approach to doing that correctly. We will

discover the methods by which we can give our data insight and significance. It becomes essential for data journalists that the information they gather is simple and comprehensible.
11.2 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After completing this unit, you should be able to:
- understand the meaning and scope of reporting data in journalism,
- explain the processes of collecting, verifying, and sourcing data,
- apply methods of data cleaning, reduction, and transformation,
- use measures of central tendency, dispersion, and relative position in
data analysis,
- interpret and present data through visualisation tools and techniques, and
- examine international and Indian perspectives and principles of reporting
data.
11.3 REPORTING DATA
Data reporting is a crucial journalistic technique that makes it possible to present stories and evaluations that are supported by evidence. Knowing how to gather, validate, source, and categorise data efficiently is essential for credible reporting in a world where digital tools are influencing society increasingly.
11.3.1 Collecting Data
Data collection is the foundation of credible journalism. Data can be collected in a variety of ways, including interviews, surveys, focus groups, observations, documents and online data. Data collection begins with identifying the news value in something, developing a question, and putting together a systematic, replicable plan that fits the type of story the journalist is trying to create (e.g. investigative reporting, civic journalism or beat reporting). Data collection should be done with objectivity, awareness of detail, and a sense of ethics, especially when it involves collecting sensitive data, or when reporting on vulnerable individuals. Primary data is generated when individuals collect new data from the source; traditional examples of primary data, for journalists, would be an eyewitness report or one-on-one interviews. Secondary data is used or created from published data or interviews that had already been interpreted and processed; sources may include published reports, press releases from government entities, institutional documents or reports, and statistical bulletins. In a digital age, primary data collection also includes collecting data via online surveys, tracking social media, web scraping, or collecting publicly available data from websites created by open government agencies.
11.3.2 Verifying Data
The trustworthiness of journalism depends on confirming data that has been collected. To confirm information means that a journalist must cross-check facts with multiple credible sources, verify the information against the official documents, and establish independent confirmation when appropriate.
124 Journalists should create a habit of checking every aspect of the data -name,

figure, date, location and so on - before it is published. Means of verification include making phone calls to credible sources, sending emails, comparing similar published reports, and fact-checking services for content found on the web. Verification is not limited to just finding out if information is factually correct. There is also extenuating verification that includes verification of the timeliness, verification of the relevance and elimination of bias (and potentially other) issues with a given set of data. With the increase in misinformation and "fake news" on digital platforms, journalists need to be aware of manipulated images, inaccurate data visualisations, and false statistics.
11.3.3. Data Sourcing
Effective data reporting goes beyond collecting and verifying data, it also includes getting your data sources correct. There are different types of data: primary (collected by the journalist) and secondary/tertiary (data that has been obtained from other sources). Such reports might include government databases, police reports, election results, health records, financial records, etc. Other institutional sources - such as NGOs, research think tanks and international agencies (e.g, UNICEF, WHO, UNDP) - provide useful data, and are regarded as more reliable than secondary data. They provide context to what the journalist is doing, which adds authority to their report. When it comes to learning about sourcing data, students of journalism must be mindful not just about the credibility of the source and reliability of the data, they must also take into account ethical considerations about the data, such as, privacy, consent, protection of data. For example, the use of public domain datasets will require less scrutiny; use of private or sensitive data will require permissions and anonymisation measures before releasing the data or using it in their stories. Students should also be aware of the range of online open data portals (e.g, data.gov.in, portals of various ministries, WHO databases, and so on), but also reflect carefully on the authenticity of their datasets.
11.3.4 Types of Data
One can classify data for reporting purposes into several key types:
- Quantitative Data: Numerical information like statistics, percentages,
survey metrics, and demographic indicators. Journalists use quantitative data to identify patterns, trends, and correlations in society, politics, health, education, and economics.
- Qualitative Data: Non-numeric insights derived from observations,
interviews, descriptive narratives, photographs, and documentaries. This type of data adds context, colour, and depth to reports and is critical for interpretative, feature, and human-interest journalism.
- Time-Series Data: Data collected over regular intervals (such as
economic growth rates, development budgets, election results across years), allowing analysis of changes and prediction of trends.
- Metadata: Data describing the structure, source, collection method, and
context of the main data. Metadata strengthens transparency and enables reproducibility for journalistic investigations.

Students should not only learn how to distinguish between these data types, but also how to use appropriate methods for collecting, verifying, and integrating them into comprehensive journalistic narratives.
11.4 DATA CLEANING
Data cleaning is an essential step in data pre-processing and is also referred to as scrubbing. It is crucial for the construction of a good model but is frequently overlooked by people working with data. Real-world data typically exhibit incompleteness, noise, and inconsistency. In addition to addressing discrepancies, data cleaning entails filling in missing numbers, smoothing out noisy data, and eliminating outliers, which are discussed in the previous unit. Errors are decreased, and data quality is enhanced via data cleaning. Although it might be a time-consuming and laborious operation, it is necessary to fix data inaccuracies and delete bad entries.
11.4.1 Data Reduction
As explained in unit 10, in this phase, data is trimmed. The number of records, attributes, or dimensions can be reduced. When reducing data, one should keep in mind that the outcomes from the reduced data should be identical to those from the original data. The following are methods of data compression: dimensionality reduction, and numerosity reduction. Dimensionality reduction refers to the process of lowering the number of random variables or qualities. Numerosity reduction strategies substitute different, more compact forms of data representation for the original data volume.
11.4.2 Data Transformation
Data transformation involves transforming or consolidating data into analysis- ready formats. This involves several processes. Smoothing attempts to reduce data noise. Attribute construction (or feature construction) is where additional attributes are constructed. Aggregation subjects data to summary procedures to calculate monthly and yearly totals; for instance, the daily sales data of a company may be combined to produce monthly or yearly sales. Normalisation resizes the attribute data to fit a narrower range, such as -1.0 to 1.0; or 0.0 to 1.0. Discretisation uses interval or conceptual labels to replace raw numeric values. A concept hierarchy for the number attribute can then be created by recursively organising the labels into higher-level concepts like a city or country.
11.5 DATA ANALYSIS
So far, we have learnt about processes such as data collection, verification and cleaning. We shall now turn our attention to data analysis. Statistical methods are extensively used in analysing quantitative data. Generally, these methods are classified as 'descriptive statistics' and 'inferential statistics'. Descriptive statistics are computed to describe the characteristics (attributes) of a sample or population in totality and thus limit generalisation to the particular group (sample). No conclusions are extended beyond this group whereas inferential statistical methods are used to draw generalisations beyond the sample with a known degree of accuracy.

In this unit, we shall confine our discussion to the understanding of four measures of descriptive statistics used commonly. These include measures of (i) central tendency or averages; (ii) variability or dispersion; (iii) relative position; and (iv) relationship.
11.5.1 Measures of Central Tendency or Averages
We use averages to describe the characteristics of samples (groups) in a general way. Economic status of groups is indicated by 'average income', performance of students in a class is judged by 'grade point averages', or the climate of a city is reported by 'average temperature'. In data journalism, averages may describe 'average readership of news articles' or 'average time spent per story'. Of the many averages, three are mostly used: Mean, Median and Mode. The Mean is the arithmetic average. It is perhaps the most familiar, most frequently used and well-understood average. Instead of showing mathematical formulas, we can say: if five news stories had readership of 100, 120, 80, 110 and 90, the mean readership is the total divided by five, i.e., 100. Mean is useful when observations are distributed symmetrically, and when stable measures are needed. The Median is a point in an ordered arrangement of observations, above and below which one-half of the observations fall. In journalism, if we rank 11 news articles by their readership, the readership of the sixth article is the median. Median is used when data are skewed or incomplete. The Mode is the most frequently occurring observation. If out of 20 news stories, five stories received exactly 500 views each, more than any other number, then 500 is the mode. Mode is useful when we want the most typical case.
11.5.2 Measures of Variability or Dispersion
Measures of central tendency describe location along a scale but they do not show how data are spread. For this, measures of variability are used. These include range, average deviation and standard deviation. The Range is the difference between the highest and lowest score. For example, if the highest readership of an article is 10,000 and the lowest is 1,000, then the range is 9,000. Average Deviation (AD) is the average of how far each value differs from the mean, ignoring signs. For instance, if most news stories cluster near the mean readership, AD will be small. Standard Deviation (SD) is the most general and stable measure of variability. It shows how tightly or widely data are clustered around the mean. In news readership, a low SD means most articles get similar views, while a high SD means some articles go viral while others perform poorly.
11.5.3 Normal Probability Curve
A normal probability curve is based upon the law of probability. It is bell- shaped and symmetrical. In such a curve, the values of mean, median and mode coincide. Most observations cluster around the mean. In data journalism, article readership may often follow this shape, with most articles receiving moderate views and a few stories receiving either very high or very low readership. Normal curve applications include finding the percentage of cases between ranges and comparing scores across groups.

11.5.4 Measures of Relative Positions
A raw score, taken by itself, has no meaning. It gets meaning only by comparison with some reference group. For this, measures like sigma scores (Z-scores), T scores and percentile ranks are used.
- Z-scores tell us how far a value is from the mean in units of standard
deviation. For instance, if an article's readership is far above the average by two standard deviations, it has a high Z-score.
- T scores convert Z-scores into a more convenient scale, avoiding
decimals and negatives.
- Percentile rank shows the percentage of scores that fall below a given
score. If a news story is at the 80th percentile, it performed better than 80% of other stories. Check Your Progress - 1 Note: 1) Use the space provided below for your answers.
2) Compare your answers with those given at the end of the unit.

considered essential before reporting?

11.6 DATA VISUALISATION
Data visualisation is crucial and serves as a powerful tool for news organisations. The use of graphs and charts in news stories helps elevate the story and get the message across with ease for the reader. Visualisation is not only about showing numbers but also about telling a story. In data journalism, visualisation is important because it helps transform raw data into meaningful narratives, and in other units we have studied how it complements data gathering, cleaning and analysis. Data visualisation can be done in numerous ways and using many tools, which be discussed at length in unit 15. For now, let us briefly touch upon these to give you a sense of how one can go about visualising data when reporting data.
1. Scatter plots are the most commonly used chart when observing the
relationship between two quantitative variables. They work particularly well for quickly identifying possible correlations between different data points.
2. Heat maps are two-dimensional graphics that show data trends
through colour shading and are more frequently used to present a more comprehensive view of massive amounts of data.

3. Bar charts are one of the most common ways to represent numerical data
using rectangles with equal widths and varied heights. Following are some tools which can help you in data visualisation:
- Microsoft Excel: Widely used for creating basic charts.
- Tableau: Powerful tool for making interactive dashboards.
- Power BI: Integrates analysis and reporting.
- Google Data Studio: Builds interactive visualisations that update in
real time.
- Python/R: Offers advanced libraries for customised visuals.
Some other latest tools and websites like Canva can help you to make catchy presentations. Visualisation is not only about displaying numbers but about telling a story. By linking graphs and charts into a coherent flow, journalists create a visual narrative that helps audiences grasp insights quickly and meaningfully.
11.7 REPORTING DATA: INTERNATIONAL
PERSPECTIVE
We have seen how data journalism has become the corner stone of modern-day journalism. Now, let us focus on organisations that recognise the need for, and encourage excellence in, reporting data.
11.7.1 UNESCO
UNESCO has reiterated the importance of data reporting to bolster support for freedom of expression, access to information, and protection of human rights in the digital age. Their Toolkit on Data Journalism states that data journalism engages extensive amounts of digital data whether it is statistical, or dealing with trends in health, migration or scientific activity to tell clearer stories that benefit societies. UNESCO suggests that journalists utilise open data, and engage in visualising complex pieces of information while understanding that ethical standards should always be followed. These include protecting the privacy of individuals and vulnerable groups, and also defending the rights and security of marginalised groups. They are also committed to the safety of journalists, especially in conflict zones, providing guidelines to journalists who work in fraught or violence-prone environments and situations.
11.7.2 Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism
The Reuters Institute conducts global research about news and media, and stresses the importance of journalistic principles such as accuracy, transparency, and trust as part of reporting data. Their Digital News Reports outline different data journalism practices and recommends that journalists examine their sources of data closely, pay attention to trends across regions, and employ storytelling techniques that allow information to be accessible to broad audiences. It emphasises reader's comprehension of key issues, the building of public trust in the news, and the role of the media in reinforcing fact-checking.
11.7.3 World Health Organization (WHO)
The World Health Organization advocates that public health reporting, as well as their own guidance for use in public health, should be based on accurate data.

WHO wants journalists to use accurate official data in their health reporting, and generally show numbers in uncomplicated, non-sensational ways. WHO has also made a case for the need to report data in a way that links it to previous reports and public policy that is being implemented. Moreover, it advocates that data remain part of the 'ongoing' public health communication and/or advocacy campaigns. This would help better understand and clarify their data, making it useful and understandable for target communities worldwide.
11.7.4 International Principles
Media organisations have largely come to agree that reporting data in itself is part of fulfilling their social responsiblities. Data reporting is a responsibility in that it requires transparency and accountablity when reporting credible information, its presentation of complicated material in an understandable way, and making those who hold power accountable. They encourage journalists to use their digital reporting tools judiciously pay attention to their factual accuracy, and remain aware of the needs and rights of their public, at every stage of preparing to search, verify, then tell the story using formats that are accessible (to diverse communities).
11.8 INDIAN CONTEXT
In India, several organisations are developing codes and principles that influence the reporting of data. The Press Council of India (PCI)'s journalism guidelines uphold a commitment to accuracy, fairness or balance, and accountability, which are equally relevant to data journalism. The National Data Sharing and Accessibility Policy (NDSAP) enacted by the government commits public data to be open-access data, yet there is no systematic approach to build the literacy or capacity of journalists with regards to data. However, there have been various initiatives vis-a-vis data journalism emerging primarily in NGOs and start-up sectors like IndiaSpend, which contributes to the development of data-driven reporting for increasing transparency and public awareness about economic and social issues. Following the open-access data movement, some organisations in India have established data desks, where they have begun to explore digital tools to facilitate visualisations and analysis of data. However, the application of these data tools still appears to be limited in terms of resources and skills. Although interest in data journalism has increased, there are multiple difficulties facing data journalism in India. Journalists often have poor access to new and well-established data. This is often a result of government or official datasets being poor or outdated, while other datasets are simply more difficult to consider as they are in a scanned PDF type of file. There is a lack of training on data extraction, analysis, and visualisation technology. While some reporters have had training, it is not uncommon for reporters to rely on second hand data. Very few newsrooms have teams dedicated to data journalism, and as such newsrooms rely on freelancers or on using an external platform to create a data story or use data in their story. The absence of strong data protection legislation in India, combined with inconsistent regulation about the mode - online or offline - by which digital data can be used, further restricts responsible data journalism. Overall, while some companies lead and support solid data journalism, industry support through

improved infrastructure and management of potential newsworthy data stories is needed before data journalism can be mainstreamed in India's news landscape. Check Your Progress - 2 Note: 1) Use the space provided below for your answers.

11.10 KEYWORDS

Data Cleaning - The practice of correcting or removing incomplete, noisy, or inconsistent data. Central Tendency - Statistical measures (mean, median, mode) that describe the typical value in a dataset. Visualisation - The graphical representation of data that helps transform raw numbers into meaningful stories. Metadata - Data about data that describes its source, structure, and collection method for transparency.

14.0 INTRODUCTION
Our lives are today enmeshed within large and complex datasets that are filtered by experts to make sense of our world. These datasets are what Big Data is all about. This unit is centred on Big Data and the key methodologies and technologies used in Big Data analytics. This process of analytics is meant to collect, integrate, and prepare time-and-space-dependent data from sensors, complex systems, and physical assets to collate them into meaningful results. This compilation highlights cutting-edge developments in this area and understanding these methodologies will enable you to actively contribute to Big Data analytics efforts. This chapter introduces fundamental topics such as big data properties, applications, and statistical tools.

14.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After completing this unit, learners will be able to:
- define and explain the concept of Data Science and its relationship with
Big Data,
- understand the definition, nature, and importance of Big Data in today's
digital environment,
- describe Big Data Analytics and explore its tools, techniques, and real-
world applications,
- identify and elaborate on the five V's of Big Data -- Volume, Velocity,
Variety, Veracity, and Value,
- analyse a case study demonstrating the practical use and impact of Big
Data in a specific domain, and
- evaluate the challenges and opportunities that Big Data brings to
industries and society.
14.2 DATA SCIENCE
One of the more recent fields of study to emerge in recent years has been data science, which has supplanted earlier names like data mining and knowledge discovery in databases. The phrase first surfaced near the close of the 20th century and began to gain traction. By definition, data science focuses on assessing the present and facilitating well-informed judgments about the future by employing disaggregated data in a more exploratory manner. Finding or identifying patterns and assessing them are among the most crucial components of data science. We refer to these patterns as models.
14.3 BIG DATA
The term "Big Data" describes data collections that are much too large to manage with conventional systems. Regular software like statistical tools, database systems, and others are often unable to compute this kind of data. Data-gathering capabilities have grown rapidly in recent years, making it increasingly difficult to store and analyse the generated data. Software like statistical tools, database systems, and others too are not ideal in order to work with big data. One unit of storage in a computer's memory is called a byte. A single number, letter, or symbol is represented by a byte. Eight bits make up a byte, and each bit can be either a 0 or a 1. A petabyte of data is made up of 1 x 10^15 bytes, which comes to about 1,000 trillion bytes. These are the kinds of datasets we are dealing with when we think of Big Data. In the early days of data, its structured format meant that it could be organised in rows and columns and that data warehouses could be utilise handle enormous information repositories. But in the 2000s, things changed, and a wide variety of data sources exploded. Additionally, a variety of tools for handling this type of data emerged, and data started to grow in size and be measured in petabytes. There has been a paradigm shift in the ensuing ten years, starting in 2010. These days, everything and everyone has a digital footprint. These applications offer

chances for new analytics and create new value for enterprises by producing data quantities that can be measured in exabytes, which translates to 1,000 petabytes. A study (https://www.domo.com/blog/2015/08/data-never-sleeps-3-0/) on big data calculates how much data is produced on well-known internet sites every minute. Nearly 4.16 million pieces of material are shared on Facebook, nearly 300,000 tweets are sent on Twitter, nearly 1.73 million photographs are liked on Instagram, 300 hours of new video content are uploaded on YouTube, and nearly 51,000 apps are downloaded by Apple users - every minute. Approximately 110,000 new calls are made by Skype users, 4300 new people browse Amazon, 694 Uber users take trips, and Netflix customers watch about 77,000 hours of video - every minute. The sheer volume of these transactions boggles the mind and is beyond the computing abilities of regular infrastructures. Hence, the need for systems like the ones we will be discussing now.
14.4 BIG DATA ANALYTICS
Applications of big data span a wide range of domains such as web, retail and marketing, banking and financial, industrial, healthcare, environmental, Internet of Things and cyber-physical systems. Analytics is a process of extracting and creating information from raw data by filtering, processing, categorising, condensing and contextualising data. Raw data in itself does not have a meaning until it is processed into useful information. The objectives of the analytics are (1) to predict the future event, (2) to explore the trends and patterns, (3) to find and establish the relationships in the data. There are four types of big data analytics:
14.4.1 Descriptive Analytics
Analysing historical data and presenting it in an understandable summary is known as descriptive analytics. The goal of descriptive analytics is to determine what has transpired. Descriptive analytics using statistical functions like counts, maximum, minimum, mean, percentage, etc., make up a significant amount of analytics performed nowadays. These statistics provide a summary of the data and aid in describing patterns within it. Descriptive analytics can be used, for instance, to determine the average monthly rainfall, the average number of likes on a specific post, or the average monthly number of visitors to a website. The data can be summarised with the help of descriptive analytics.
14.4.2 Diagnostic Analytics
Diagnostic analytics can offer additional insights into the reasons behind specific problems based on trends in sensor data for prior faults. While descriptive analytics can be helpful for summarising the data by computing various statistics (such as mean, minimum, maximum, variance, or top-N), the goal of diagnostic analytics is to determine why it occurred. Analysing historical data to determine the causes of specific events is known as diagnostic analytics.
14.4.3 Predictive Analytics
What is likely to happen is the question that predictive analytics seeks to answer. For instance, they can be used to forecast pollution levels or anticipate 135

the onset of natural disasters like river floods or forest fires. Predictive models are used in predictive analytics. The accuracy of prediction models depends on the quality and volume of the existing data available for training the models, so that all the patterns and trends in the existing data can be learned accurately. These models use the data to learn patterns and trends and forecast numbers (regression models) or the likelihood of an event occurring or its likely outcome (classification models).
14.4.4 Prescriptive Analytics
What can we do to make something happen is the question that prescriptive analytics seeks to address. Based on the present course of action, prescriptive analytics can forecast potential outcomes. It makes use of various prediction models for various inputs and then suggests courses of action or the optimal course of action among the possibilities available. Prescriptive analytics is different from predictive analytics because the latter uses prediction models to forecast the likely outcome of an event, whereas the former also offers optimal course of action. 14.5 CHARACTERISTICS OF BIG DATA
The five factors (5 Vs) that distinguish big data from other types of data are: Volume, Velocity, Variety, Veracity and Value.
14.5.1 Volume
As you might expect, volume refers to the quantity of data being generated. A propagation of new sources generates massive amounts of data on a continuous basis. The sources include, but are certainly not limited to, the following:
- Internet forums
- YouTube
- Facebook
- Twitter
- Cellphones (videos, photos, texts)
- Internet search engines
- Political polling

The volume of data being created is accelerating rapidly, requiring new terminology to describe these massive quantities. This terminology includes names that describe progressively larger amounts of storage. These names can sound quite strange in a world where people are familiar with only megabytes (MB) and gigabytes (GB), and maybe terabytes (TB). Some examples are the petabyte (PB), the zettabyte (ZB), and the yottabyte (YB), which are exceptionally large amounts of digital information. An interesting name for a very large number, 1 x 10^100 is called a googol. The name of the search engine Google is derived from this word. Speaking of Google, the company is currently processing over 20 petabytes of information each day, which is more than the estimated amount of information currently stored at the US Library of Congress. The volumes of data generated by modern IT, industrial, healthcare, Internet of Things, and other systems is growing exponentially, driven by the lowering costs of data storage and processing architectures and the need to extract valuable insights from the data to improve business processes, efficiency and service to consumers. Though there is no fixed threshold for the volume of data to be considered as big data, however, typically, the term big data is used for massive scale data that is difficult to store, manage and process using traditional databases and data processing architectures.
14.5.2 Velocity
Velocity refers to the speed at which data is gathered. Big datasets consist of data that is continuously gathered at very high speeds. Velocity is another important characteristic of big data and the primary reason for the exponential growth of data. High velocity of data results in the volume of data accumulated to become very large, in short span of time. Some applications can have strict deadlines for data analysis (such as trading or online fraud detection) and the data needs to be analysed in real-time. Specialised tools are required to ingest such high velocity data into the big data infrastructure and analyse the data in real-time. Data generated by certain sources can arrive at very high velocities, for example, social media data or sensor data. For example, it has been estimated that Twitter users generate more than a quarter of a million tweets every minute. This requires a massive amount of storage space as well as real-time processing of the data.
14.5.3 Variety
Variety refers to the forms of data. Big data comes in different forms such as structured, unstructured or semi-structured, including text data, image, audio, video and sensor data. Big data systems need to be flexible enough to handle such a variety of data and different formats such as spreadsheets, videos, music clips, email messages, and so on. Storing a huge quantity of these incompatible types is one of the major challenges of big data.
14.5.4 Veracity
Veracity refers to how accurate the data is. To extract value from the data, it needs to be cleaned to remove noise. Data-driven applications can reap the benefits of big data only when the data is meaningful and accurate. Therefore, cleaning of data is important so that incorrect and faulty data can be filtered out. 137

14.5.5 Value
Value of data refers to the usefulness of data for the intended purpose. The end goal of any big data analytics system is to extract value from the data. The value of the data is also related to the veracity or accuracy of the data. For some applications, value also depends on how fast we are able to process the data. 14.6 CASE STUDY
Now, let us look at a case study from India wherein Big Data and Analytics have enabled the improvement of existing systems and services.
14.6.1 Smart Meters and Big Data
Energy distribution and consumption has always been a sector that has been riddled with problems such as production, distribution, financial, infrastructural, and so on. The coming of smart meters has helped in providing high-resolution and real-time energy consumption data which can help in promoting energy efficiency from the end of the production as well as consumption. However, the coming of this system was a long-drawn process, which we shall now discuss. In 2010, the India Smart Grid Task Force (ISGTF) and the India Smart Grid Forum (ISGF) were set up to advise the Ministry of Power on policies, programmes and developments with respect to developing smart grids in India. Following this, in August 2013, the Government of India notified its "Smart Grid Vision and Roadmap for India" which sought to "enable the development and deployment of an Indian Smart Grid model." Numerous initiatives were undertaken beginning with 14 Smart Grid pilot projects commissioned by the Ministry of Power in 2013, wherein the government covered 50% of project cost. The first trial was conducted in Puducherry where the state government signed a Rs. 46 crore deal with Chinese firm DongFan electronics for a smart meter project. A similar project was undertaken in Assam in 2016 in collaboration with Ericsson, the Swedish telecom firm, which signed a deal to install 15,000 smart meters over the next three years. In 2016, the Government of India also launched the Ujwal Discom Assurance Yojana (UDAY) to increase efficiency of electricity distribution, where one of the commitments was to make installation of smart meters compulsory for consumers using more than 200 units of electricity a month.

Smart meters in India present an opportunity to harness the potential of big data in providing electricity, and in services like transportation. By providing insight into energy consumption on the end of the user, these meters have the potential to increase energy saving and decrease energy spending. They increase efficiency at all levels of the energy supply chain through the power of big data and analysis. However, the data that drives this efficiency also poses a number of big data risks and concerns, which shall be discussed subsequently.
14.6.2 Benefits
Efficient Demand Side Management (DSM): Data collected can help in using and providing electricity more efficiently. The aggregate technical and commercial losses are around 27-28% in India's power distribution segment, and smart meters have the potential to reduce these network losses. Accurate shaping of the market and industry Smart meters provide data on how much excess energy will be available, whether the grid can transmit it and in turn, whether to sell it. Smart meter data can also help determine when and where equipment downtime and power failures are most likely to occur, helping in better load management and allocation of resources. Security of supply Smart meters enable usage of predictive models capable of applying knowledge acquired through the grid to improve daily performance. This means a steadier supply of electricity or more specifically, security of supply.
14.6.3 Harms
Unintended Behavioral Analysis Tool
Smart meters will be able to recognise appliance load signatures to make a detailed map of an individual's energy usage. Based on the data that can be collected by these meters, it is possible to determine a person's health (how many microwaved meals are consumed?), work ethic (what time does she leave home? how much time is spent in front of the TV?), social life (how often is the person home on the weekend?), and so on. Hackers, too, have been able to identify the number of devices in a home, and what was being watched. This information makes owners of smart meters vulnerable to theft, and pressures from law enforcement, creditors, insurance companies, etc.
Social Polarisation
Affording initial investment in smart meters is a luxury that all households do not have. This discrimination harm can lead to an invisible, gradual polarization of those households that are not yet consumers. Low income and poor households consume small amounts of energy and are often associated with non-payment of bills, debt and disconnection, all of which raise significant costs for utilities. Their gradual marginalisation also ends up making access to energy services an invisible issue.
14.7 LET US SUM UP
In this unit, we learned how data science supplanted earlier concepts like data mining and knowledge discovery in databases. It is driven by Big Data, which

has transformed the way organisations, governments, and individuals interact with information. As this unit illustrates, data science serves as the foundation for understanding and leveraging Big Data, while analytics provides the tools to extract insights and make informed decisions. With its defining characteristics, the five Vs -- volume, velocity, variety, veracity, and value, -- Big Data is not merely about the size of data but also about its complexity, speed, and potential value. We learned that analytics is a process of extracting and creating information from raw data by filtering, processing, categorising, condensing and contextualising the data. We then discussed the four types of big data analytics: descriptive analytics (analysing historical data and presenting it in an understandable summary), diagnostic (analysing historical data to determine the causes of specific events), predictive analytics (uses prediction models to forecast the likely outcome of an event), and prescriptive analytics (forecasts different outcomes and suggests optimal course of action for each). Through a case study, learners gain insight into the practical application of Big Data Analytics and challenges in the case of installation of Smart Meters initiative of the government of India. A thorough understanding of Big Data enables students to appreciate its vast influence on modern technology, business intelligence, and societal developments.
14.8 KEYWORDS
Big Data - Extremely large data sets that require advanced tools to capture, store, process, and analyse. Data Science - An interdisciplinary field focused on extracting knowledge from data using techniques from statistics, computer science, and machine learning. Big Data Analytics - The process of examining large and varied data sets to uncover hidden patterns, correlations, and insights. Five Vs of Big Data - Characteristics defining Big Data: Volume, Velocity, Variety, Veracity, and Value. Predictive Analytics - A branch of analytics that uses historical data to make predictions about future events.

15.0 INTRODUCTION
In data journalism, data or numbers are of no use if they are not critically examined and presented in an effective way. Once the data is collected and cleaned, the next step is to generate insights and meaningful stories from the data; this process is called data analysis. When the data is explored and trends or patterns are identified, then the obtained information needs to be presented in an effective way using graphical tools such as maps, charts, or infographics to enhance engagement, which is achieved through data visualisation. Data analysis and visualisation are central to making sense of the data, discovering stories, and communicating them. In this unit, we will explore the dual aspects of analysing and visualising data.
15.1 LEARNING OUTCOME
The unit will introduce students to the basic concepts and principles of data analysis and visualisation. After reading this unit, students will be able to:
- Understand the importance of analysing and visualising data in data
journalism.

- Understand how to identify trends, patterns, and correlations from data.
- Understand the importance of visual designs for maintaining clarity and
interactivity in storytelling.
- Understand the different types of visualisation tools, like histograms,
scatter plots, bar charts, and heat maps, and their usage according to the type of data.
15.2 DATA ANALYSIS
Data analysis is one of the most essential skills in data journalism. It provides the context and helps to answer what and why questions. It is a systematic process of critically exploring and examining data to obtain meaningful information and support decision-making. It helps identify the trends, patterns, and correlations among variables hidden within a dataset. After the data is collected and preprocessed, it is analysed to understand the relationships among variables and uncover deeper insights. Analysis supports tentative hypotheses and provides evidence to support these from the data, adding depth to the reporting. Many a time, data analysis reveals a different narrative for a story, or an entirely different story may be discovered. Statistical analysis is used to understand the features of the dataset. Descriptive statistics such as mean, median, mode, range, variance, and standard deviation are used to summarise basic features of the data. Inferential statistics, including hypothesis testing, regression analysis, and correlation, go beyond summarising the general features of data and allow prediction for larger populations utilising probability theory.
Unit 7 (Basic Statistics for Data Journalism) is dedicated to statistical analysis.
Go back to the unit and revise to refresh your memory.
15.3 TYPES OF DATA ANALYSIS
There are four types of data analysis. These are: a. Descriptive Analysis Looking at the past data, this describes and summarises the general features of a dataset. Descriptive analysis helps in answering what questions. Using methods such as mean, median, mode, etc., it presents data in a simplified form. For example, a news article on road accidents shows the number of total cases and deaths, using visualisation tools. b. Diagnostic Analysis Descriptive analysis reveals trends and patterns while diagnostic analysis reveals the cause behind them. It helps in answering the why question. It reveals the reason and frequency behind a specific outcome. c. Predictive Analysis This type of analysis provides answers to the question: What is likely to happen? It helps in predicting a future outcome based on past trends and patterns, like predicting weather, rainfall, etc. It uses statistical methods and machine learning to make informed predictions.

d. Prescriptive Analysis It prescribes the possible and suitable actions to be taken to solve or improve a certain issue. This provides an answer to the question, What should be done? Recommendations for course-correction are based on predictive analysis. To learn more about the types of analysis, refer to Unit 14 (Understanding Big Data).

15.5 DATA VISUALISATION
Visualisation is defined as the art and science of turning data into visual narratives. In data journalism, presenting data using visual design is an essential creative skill. This skill involves presenting data in clear and eye-catching visuals because the human brain processes visuals more rapidly than text. Tools such as charts, plots, maps, and infographics can effectively and interactively communicate a story better than a text article. Visualisation helps transform complex data into understandable and engaging formats. It facilitates the comparison between two categories and highlights the trends and patterns. One must have knowledge about chart types (bar, pie, line), plots, colour theory, infographics, and visual hierarchy and how to properly use these tools to balance the aesthetic design with accurate representation of data to communicate the story effectively.
Role of Visualisation in Data Journalism
- When you look at numbers, they can appear confusing, and often you
cannot figure out the meaningful information from them. On the other hand, if we present data systematically and creatively, then it becomes easily understandable as well as engaging.
- A journalist's job is not only to analyse data and discover impactful
narratives but also to communicate these narratives/stories so simply that even the people who are unfamiliar with technical terms can make sense out of the visuals they look at.
- The main goal of visualisation is to break complex data into understandable
and clear visuals, and by doing so, the patterns, trends, anomalies, and correlations among variables can become easily noticeable.

- Visualisation aids effective communication, captures the interest of the
audience, and makes data-driven stories more interactive.
- For example, during COVID-19, you may have noticed that nearly every
news website displayed data visually and made it more interactive by allowing the audience to navigate through, and even customise, the visuals according to their preferences. They could use filters and havoc effects to explore and personalise the visuals.
- Data visualisation not only makes it easy to access accurate information
but also saves a lot of time by enabling easy side-by-side comparisons. Check Your Progress - 1 Note: 1) Use the space provided below for your answers.

15.6 TYPES OF DATA VISUALISATION
So far, we have learnt what data visualisation means and its role in journalism. Now let us read about the different types of data visualisations. Here, we will discuss some of the most commonly used tools for communicating data-driven stories effectively:
15.6.1 Bar Chart
Bar charts are the most commonly used visual tools because they are simple and easy to interpret. A bar chart is used when you deal with categorical data. It allows an easy comparison among categories and is also used to study trends over time. It uses bars in a rectangular shape with equal width but different heights. Bar charts are of two types: horizontal and vertical. In a horizontal bar chart, the categories of data are indicated on the y-axis. In a vertical bar chart, the categories of data are indicated on the x-axis. Example: The bar graph below compares the literacy rates among different Indian states.

States Literacy rate (in percentage) Tamil Nadu 84 Kerala 94 Maharashtra 82 Uttar Pradesh 75 Bihar 70 Gujarat 80.5
Figure 1. Vertical Bar Chart
Figure 2. Horizontal Bar Chart
15.6.2 Pie Chart
A pie chart, also known as a circle chart, is a graphical representation used when you want to show percentage and proportion. It shows the parts into which a particular dataset is divided. A pie chart is used when the number of categories is less than 10. It is circular and divided into slices, each slice representing a specific category. The total value of the pie chart is always 100%. The formula for a pie chart is: Given Value divided by the Total Value of the Data, multiplied by 360deg. You may have noticed that when the union budget is announced, the allocation among sectors is represented using a pie chart. Example: The pie chart below shows the allocation of budget by the state government in different sectors.

Sector Budget share (in percentage) Education 25 Health 20 Agriculture 15 Sports 18 Infrastructure 10 Others 12 Figure 3.15.6.3 Line Graph
The line graph is used to understand the trend and changes in a dataset over a short and extended period of time. It is mostly used when the data includes time series like week, month, and year. In this graph, data points are plotted according to values, and a line connects these points, showing a trend. A line graph is useful in showing the continuous decline or growth in data. Example: The line graph below shows the average temperature in Delhi over a year. The line graph or curve here will show the seasonal variation. Months Average Temperature (in degC) January 15 February 18 March 24 April 27 May 32 June 38 July 35 August 32 September 30 October 26 November 18 December 14

Figure 4.15.6.4 Histogram
A histogram is used to show the representation of numerical data (continuous data). It is used to show the frequency distribution in a dataset. A histogram is like a bar chart; it also consists of rectangular bars. However, unlike in a bar chart, where bars are not attached, in a histogram, there are no spaces between the bars; they are adjacent because the data is continuous. Here, the data is grouped into bins and intervals. It helps in identifying patterns in a dataset, like skewness, outliers, and normal distribution. Example: we have a final score range and the number of students.
Score Range No. of Students
0-10 2 10-20 5 20-30 10 30-40 20 40-50 35 50-60 45 60-70 40 70-80 25 80-90 10 90-100 3 Figure 5.15.6.5 Scatter Plot
A scatter plot is utilised to show the relationship or correlation between two variables. It is also known as a scatter diagram or scatter graph. It is the type of data visualisation in which dots (points) display the values for two continuous variables on a Cartesian plane. Every mark indicates one observed datum, located through its amounts for the two factors. One is on the X-axis (independent variable), along with the other on the Y-axis (dependent variable). Scatter plots are very useful when you want to display both the distribution and the relationship between two variables Example: The data below shows two variables, average monthly income and education level. Let us see the correlation between these two variables using a scatter plot. Education level Average monthly income No Schooling 8000 10th 12000 12th 16000 Diploma 19000 Graduation 25000 Post-graduation 35000 PhD 45000 Figure 6.15.6.6 Heat Map
Heat maps are two-dimensional graphics that use colours to show data trends and represent values. A simple heat map offers the data a fast visual while a more detailed heat map will help a user to comprehend complex data sets. Heat maps do come in a variety of presentations; however, they all use colour in order to show correlations between data values. Colours are especially helpful because they are simpler to identify as well as understand as compared to plain numbers. Heat maps exist with high flexibility. Trends are highlighted by them as well. Enormous amounts of data within a dataset are better shown using heat maps, which can help guide users to the most important parts of data visualisations. 15.8 LET US SUM UP
In this unit, we have explored two key aspects of data journalism: data analysis and visualisation. Data analysis helps make sense of the data and provides context to the story by identifying trends, patterns, and relationships among variables. We discussed various types of analysis, like descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, and prescriptive. With data analysis, crafting a narrative for the story becomes easier, and data visualisation is needed to communicate this narrative effectively so that the general public can understand and relate to it. There are many visualisation tools, but the knowledge of when to use which tool according to the type of data is important. A bar chart is beneficial when there is categorical data, a line graph is useful when the data is based on a time series, and a histogram is used for frequency distribution. The unit has further explored visualisation tools like histograms, pie charts, heat maps, etc. An effective visualisation not only depends on selecting the right graphical representation but also on choosing design elements like text, colour, font, scale, and layout. Therefore, data analysis and visualisation are the two fundamental pillars of data journalism. Without analysis, the data are just numbers with no clear meaning and impact, and without visualisation, the data can be difficult to interpret and communicate.
15.9 KEYWORDS
1. Data analysis: The process of critically exploring and examining datasets
to understand the trends and patterns.
2. Data visualisation: The process of communicating the information using
graphical representations like charts, maps, plots, and infographics.
3. Diagnostic analysis: Based on past trends and patterns in a dataset, it
diagnoses the cause behind an outcome.
4. Descriptive analysis: It describes and summarises the general features of
a dataset using methods like mean, mode, and median.
5. Predictive analysis: By understanding the past trends and patterns, it
makes informed predictions about the population.
6. Prescriptive analysis: Based on data predictions, it suggests suitable
actions.
7. Histogram: A type of visualisation tool used for frequency distribution.
8. Heat map: A data visualisation tool that uses colour-coded values to
represent the magnitude of the values in a dataset.

16.0 INTRODUCTION
One of the most important questions a journalist can ask is, "Where?" The answer isn't just about a dot on a map. It is about providing context and finding hidden threads that connect people and events. When you are working with data, the map is your best tool for answering that question. These aren't just static pictures; modern data maps are living, breathing tools for investigation that can form the centrepiece of an investigation. Think about it: you can track a disease spreading from one district to the next, show the gaps in infrastructure between states, or pinpoint air pollution hotspots in real time. Data mapping takes numbers and turns them into stories that people can see and relate to. It helps your readers understand how a big national story actually affects them in their own neighbourhood, making your work more personal and much more powerful. This unit provides a comprehensive introduction to the world of geographical data and data mapping for journalists. We will start by breaking down what geospatial data actually is, where to find it, and what to do with it. Then, we will jump into the most common types of maps you will see in newsrooms, from the classic choropleth to more specialised visuals like flow and heat maps. Crucially, this unit will equip you with a step-by-step workflow for creating a data map, from finding the right data to joining it with a map file and making critical design decisions. We will also navigate the significant ethical considerations inherent in mapping.
16.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After completing this unit, you will be able to:
- explain what geospatial data is and tell the difference between its types
and formats.
- find and evaluate the quality of geographic and statistical data for a
mapping project.
- understand why maps are so important for telling stories with data.
- know the difference between map types like choropleths, symbol maps,
and point maps, and when to use each one.
- follow a clear workflow to make a basic data map by joining a spreadsheet
to a map file.
- pick the right mapping tool based on different levels of complexity and
technical skill.
16.2 UNDERSTANDING GEOGRAPHICAL DATA
Before you can make a map, you need to get to grips with the special kind of data that makes it work. This is the world of geographical data, also called geospatial data.
16.2.1 What is Geospatial Data?
Simply put, geospatial data is any piece of information that can be tied to a 158 specific place on Earth. It describes things, events, or features by their location.

Sometimes that location is explicit, like a latitude and longitude coordinate (e.g., 28.7041deg N, 77.1025deg E for Delhi). Other times, it can be implicit, like an address ("10 Downing Street, London") or just a name ("Mumbai"). For a computer to turn this into a map, that location info needs to be in a structured format it can read.
16.2.2 Types of Geographic Data
Geospatial data generally comes in two main varieties:
- Vector Data: This is the most common type used in data journalism.
Vector data represents the world using basic geometric shapes: points, lines, and polygons.
- Points: A single spot, marked by a latitude and longitude. Perfect for
things like cities, hospitals, the centre of an earthquake, or a specific address.
- Lines: A series of connected points. Used to show things like rivers,
roads, railway tracks, or an aeroplane's flight path.
- Polygons: A closed shape made of connected points. These represent
areas with boundaries, like countries, states, districts, or parks.
- Raster Data: Raster Data uses a grid of tiny squares called cells (or
pixels), and each pixel has a specific colour or value. This grid-based approach makes raster data perfect for showing things that don't have clear boundaries but instead blend into each other, like temperature, air quality, or elevation across a landscape.
- Examples: Common examples are satellite photos, aerial imagery,
and maps that show continuous information like temperature or rainfall.
- While less common for direct use in typical news maps, raster data is
often the source from which vector data (like the boundary of a flood zone) is derived.
16.2.3 Common Geographic Data Formats
When you go looking for map files, you will encounter a few common types:
- Shapefile (.shp): A very common vector format from a company called
Esri. It is actually a collection of several files (.shp, .shx, .dbf, .prj, etc.) which have to be kept in the same folder since they contain information about different geographic featureswhich is then put togetherand interpreted. It is a standard format supported by almost all Geographic Information System (GIS) software.
- GeoJSON(.json or .geojson): A modern, open-standard format for
vector data. It is web-friendly, human-readable, and the preferred format for most interactive web mapping libraries. All the data is stored in a single text file.
- KML (Keyhole Markup Language, .kml): This was originally made
for Google Earth. It is useful for sharing geographic data and can be dropped right into tools like Google My Maps.

- TopoJSON: This is an extension of GeoJSONbut is much smaller in file
size. It works by defining shared borders only once instead of repeating them, which makes it efficient for fast-loading web maps.
16.2.4 Sources of Geographical Data for Journalists
There are two kinds of geographical data that can be sourced by a journalist: geographic data which gives spatial information about geographical features (e.g. map shapes or road networks), and statistical data which gives numerical information or the numbers you want to visualise (e.g. population counts). These are most commonly found in the following sources:
- Official Government Portals: In India, places like the Survey of India
and ISRO's Bhuvan portal are good sources for official administrative boundaries. Many government departments and data portals (like data. gov.in) also publish data that has location information.
- OpenStreetMap (OSM): This is like the Wikipedia of maps, a
collaborative, open-source map of the entire world. It is an excellent source to find detailed information on roads, buildings, and points of interest. You can pull data from it using tools like the Overpass Turbo API.
- Natural Earth: This is a public domain map dataset that provides free,
high-quality global vector and raster data at various scales, perfect for country-level or world maps.
- Humanitarian Data Exchange (HDX): A great resource for
finding geographic and statistical data related to humanitarian crises, development, and disasters.
- Academic Institutions and NGOs: These organisations often publish
their research along with the datasets they use, which can include valuable geographic info. Check Your Progress - 1 Note: 1) Use the space provided below for your answers.

16.3 THE POWER OF MAPS IN DATA
STORYTELLING
So far, we have explored what geographical data means. Now, we shall turn our attention to maps. Maps are not just navigational aids. They are powerful tools for analysis that can tell significant stories. Knowing why you are making a map is just as important as knowing how to make it.
16.3.1 Why Map Data? Four Key Functions
In journalism, a map usually does one or more of these four things:
1. Show Location and Give Context: The most basic job of a map is to
show where something happened. A simple locator map for a news story gives the reader immediate context.
2. Reveal Patterns and Distribution: Maps excel at showing how things
are spread out across an area. Is poverty clustered in one particular region? Are polling booths spread fairly across a constituency? A map can tell you all this.
3. Compare Different Places: A map is a very intuitive way to compare
the same variable in multiple locations. For example, a map of literacy rates by state instantly shows you which state is ahead and which is falling behind.
4. Show Relationships and Connections: You can use maps to illustrate
how places are connected, whether you are showing migration routes, trade flows, or the path a storm is taking.
16.3.2 Foundational Principles of Cartography
Put simply, cartography is the art and science of making maps. You don't need to be a professional cartographer to make a map, but you do need to know a few basic principles that will make your maps accurate and honest.
- Projection: A map projection is how you take the curved surface of the
Earth and flatten it onto a screen or on a piece of paper. All projections distort reality in some way, whether in shape, area, distance, or direction. When you are making a map of the whole world, your choice of projection can make some continents look way bigger than they really are. This is less of a problem for local maps, but it is good to remember that no flat map is ever a perfect picture of the globe.
- Scale: Scale is the ratio between a distance on your map and the actual
distance on the ground. A map of a single city is called "large-scale" because it shows a lot of detail. A map of the world is "small-scale" because it shows less detail. The scale you choose determines how much detail you can show.
- Symbolisation and Generalisation: A map is always a simplified
version of reality. Cartographers use symbols (like points, lines, and colours) to stand in for real-world things. They also have to generalise, which means simplifying complex features to keep the map from getting cluttered. For example, a river with thousands of tiny bends might be shown as a single smooth line. The choices you make here have a huge impact on the story your map tells. 161

16.4 COMMON TYPES OF DATA MAPS IN
JOURNALISM
Maps have a specific role in data storytelling, and so, picking the right kind of map is key to telling your story clearly and accurately. Here are the main types of maps you can use.
16.4.1 Choropleth Maps
This is the most widely used type of data map. A choropleth (from Greek words meaning "area" and "value") is a map where areas like states or districts are coloured in to represent the value of something. This is used to show rates or ratios, such as population density (people per square km), literacy rate, or per capita income. However, you must never use a choropleth map to show raw numbers (like the total population or the total number of crimes). Why? Because bigger areas will almost always have bigger numbers, so they will look darker on the map. Your map will end up being a map of area size, which will be misleading. You always have to normalise your data first by turning it into a rate or percentage (e.g., by dividing by the population or the area).
16.4.2 Proportional and Graduated Symbol Maps
These maps use symbols, usually circles, on top of different areas. The size of the symbol will change based on the value of your data. This is used to show raw counts or totals. For example, a map showing the total number of COVID-19 cases in major cities could use circles of different sizes for each city. This avoids the problem that choropleths have. In a true proportional symbol map, the area of the circle is directly proportional to the value. In a graduated symbol map, the data is grouped into classes (like 1-100, 101-500), and everything in the same class gets the same size symbol.
16.4.3 Point (or Locator) Maps
This is the simplest kind of map. It just uses dots to show the location of individual things. This is used to show the exact location of specific events (like the sites of recent protests), buildings (like all the public hospitals in a city), or just to give context for a news story (a "you are here" kind of map).
16.4.4 Heat Maps (Density Maps)
A heat map shows you the geographic density of your points. It uses colour to show where your points are most clustered together. This is used when you have so many points that plotting them all individually would just be a mess. A heat map can reveal the "hotspots" in your data. For example, you could map thousands of traffic accidents to see which intersections are the most dangerous.
16.4.5 Flow Maps
These maps use lines of different thicknesses or colours to show how people, things, or information move between places. This is used to show things like migration patterns, trade routes, air traffic, or how an idea spread on social media.
