16.5 A SURVEY OF POPULAR DATA MAPPING
TOOLS
From maps, let us now move to learning about tools that can be used to make maps. The tool you choose will depend on your technical skill, the complexity of your map, and your budget.
16.5.1 No-Code Tools for Beginners
These tools run in your web browser, are usually free or have good free options, and don't require any programming.
- Datawrapper: It is a favourite in many newsrooms. It is incredibly easy
to use and makes clean, interactive maps (choropleth and symbol). It guides you through the process of making a good map. You just copy and paste your data, and it does the hard work.
- Google My Maps:This tool is great for making simple point maps. You
can easily add points, lines, and shapes, change how they look, and share your map. It is perfect for showing the locations of a series of events.
16.5.2 Low-Code Tools for Intermediate Users
These platforms give you more options for customisation and analysis.
- Tableau Public: This is a very powerful data visualisation tool that
is also great at mapping. It lets you do more complex analysis, layer different datasets, and build interactive dashboards that include maps. The learning curve is steeper, but it is much more flexible.
- Flourish: It is known for making beautiful, animated data visualisations,
including cool map types like 3D maps and flow maps. It is built around a story-driven approach to making presentations with maps.
16.5.3 GIS Software and Code Libraries for Advanced Users
If you want total control, need to do custom analysis, or want to create a truly unique map, you will need to use these tools.
- QGIS: This is free, open-source, and professional-level Geographic
Information System (GIS). It is the top choice for any serious map analysis because it lets you edit map files, run complex spatial queries,

and get your data ready for other tools. It is a desktop program with a very steep learning curve.
- Mapbox / Leaflet.js: These are JavaScript libraries for building your
own custom interactive maps for the web. You need to know how to code, but they give you complete control over the design, interactivity, and data. This is how places like the New York Times build their well- grounded, award-winning map stories.
16.6 CRITICAL CONSIDERATIONS IN MAPPING
A map may seem like a piece of scientific evidence, but it is made by a person making choices, and every choice can introduce bias. A good journalist has to be aware of these traps, which can be as follows
16.6.1 The Modifiable Areal Unit Problem (MAUP)
The story your data tells can change depending on how you draw your boundaries. For example, a map of wealth might look one way if you group the data by state but completely different if you group it by district. State-level averages can hide small pockets of extreme wealth or poverty. Always be aware that the geographic units you choose might be hiding part of the story.
16.6.2 The Ecological Fallacy
This is a logical error that occurs when you make inferences about an individual based on aggregate data for their group. For example, if a district has a high literacy rate, you can't assume that any random person you pick from that district is literate. Your map shows trends for areas, not for the people in them. Your language must reflect this. Rather than saying "People in this area are poor," say, "This area has a high poverty rate."
16.6.3 How Classification and Color Choices Create Bias
The way you group your data (classification) and the colours you use can completely change the message. You can make a map look scary or harmless just by changing the class breaks in the legend. The right thing to do here is to be transparent. Always explain in your methodology why you chose a certain classification method. Use tools that let you try different methods so you can pick the one that tells the most honest story about the data.
16.6.4 Privacy and Anonymity in Point Maps
When you are mapping very specific data, like the location of individual disease cases or crime victims, you run a serious risk of violating someone's privacy. Plotting an exact point on a map could make it possible to identify a person's home. A journalist needs to protect the identities of individuals. Either group the data into a larger area (like a neighbourhood or a census block) or "jitter" the points by adding a tiny bit of random error to their location so they don't land on the exact address.

16.7 CASE STUDY: MAPPING ELECTION
TURNOUT IN INDIA
Having learnt the basics of geographic data and map-making vis-a-vis data journalism, let us now do a case study on mapping participation in a national- levelelection in India. Scenario: A data journalist wants to show the voter turnout from the recent Lok Sabha election for all states and Union Territories to see where participation was highest and lowest. Workflow in Action:
1. Story & Question: The question is, "How did voter turnout vary across
India in the 2024 Lok Sabha election?" The goal is to make a choropleth map for a news article.
2. Data Acquisition:
- Statistical Data: The journalist gets the official turnout data from the
Election Commission of India (ECI) website. It is a spreadsheet with state names and their voter turnout percentages.
- Geographic Data: The journalist downloads a GeoJSON file of Indian
states from a reliable source like Natural Earth.
3. Joining Data: The journalist uses Datawrapper. They upload the
GeoJSON file, then copy and paste the data from the ECI spreadsheet. Datawrapper automatically tries to match the "State Name" column from the spreadsheet to the state name property in the map file. The journalist double-checks that every state was matched correctly.
4. Choosing Map Type: The data is a rate (a percentage), so a choropleth
map is the right choice.
5. Designing the Map:
- Classification: The journalist uses Datawrapper's default "Natural
Breaks (Jenks)" setting, which is good at finding logical clusters in the data. They pick 5 classes to make the visual differences clear.
- Colour: They pick a single-colour sequential palette (from light blue
to dark blue), where darker colours mean higher turnout. This is an intuitive choice.
- Context: They give the map a clear title: "Voter Turnout in the
2024 Lok Sabha Election." They add a legend that clearly shows the
percentage range for each colour. They add the source: "Source: Election
Commission of India."
6. Review & Annotation: The journalist looks over the map. They see
that states like Nagaland and Manipur had very low turnout. They use Datawrapper's annotation tool to add a small note right on the map, pointing to these states and saying, "Turnout in some northeastern states was significantly lower than the national average." This gives the reader extra guidance. They also turn on tooltips, so when a user hovers over a state, they'll see the exact turnout percentage.

The final product is an accurate, ethical, and informative map that clearly tells the story of how voter participation differed across the country.
16.8 LET US SUM UP
Knowing how to map geographical data is a crucial skill for any data journalist today. This unit gives you an insight into how to put information in context, reveal spatial inequality, and tell stories that are grounded in a real sense of place. In this unit, we have walked through the whole process, from the basics of geospatial data to the final product. We have looked at what maps can do in journalism and surveyed the most common types, stressing how important it is to pick the right visual for your data and your story. We also waded into the ethical minefield that every journalist has to navigate when making a map. Understanding how your choices about classification, colour, and scale can create bias is the key to producing work that is not just eye-catching but also honest and responsible. By mastering these concepts and tools, you can unlock the stories hidden in the data and present them to your audience with clarity, accuracy, and impact.
16.9 KEYWORDS
- Geospatial Data: Information that has a geographic component, linking
it to a specific location on Earth.
- Vector Data: A type of geospatial data that represents features using
points, lines, and polygons.
- Choropleth Map: A map that uses differences in shading or colouring
within predefined areas to indicate the average value of a property or quantity in those areas.
- Normalise Data: The process of adjusting raw counts to account for
differences in population or area, typically by calculating a rate or percentage. This is essential for creating accurate choropleth maps.
- GeoJSON: A standard, web-friendly file format for encoding vector
geographic data.
- Shapefile: A common, multi-file format for storing vector geographic
data.
- Join (or Merge): The process of combining statistical data from a table
with a geographic data file based on a common matching column (key).
- Data Classification: The process of grouping data into classes or bins for
visualisation on a map, for example, using methods like equal interval, quantiles, or natural breaks.
- Ecological Fallacy: A logical error in the interpretation of statistical
data where inferences about the nature of individuals are deduced from inferences about the group to which those individuals belong.

1. Maps serve several important purposes in journalism. Most significantly
they give information about the location of the story and how information pertaining to that story occurs on ground through that geographical area. They help us do a comparative analysis of relevant data from multiple locations and show relationships and connections between them.
2. It will be incorrect to use a choropleth map in this case because a
choropleth map is used for rates or densities, not raw counts. Using it for the total number of schools would be misleading, as larger states would appear darker simply because they are bigger and have more schools, not necessarily because they have better school coverage.

17.0 INTRODUCTION
In the realm of data journalism, infographics emerge as a powerful medium for presenting the data to the readers. They matter because data can be hard to read and understand for an audience that doesn't want to dig deeper. This is where infographics come in. They are the translators, turning concrete data into

visual stories that people actually want to look at. Until recent times, making infographics was a very difficult task that required the triad of talent: a designer's eye, a statistician's brain, and a journalist's storytelling instincts. But now, with the emergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Large Language Models (LLMs), there has been a paradigm shift that allows us to create infographics in an easy, quick, and cheaper way. AI is no longer a futuristic concept; it is a practical toolkit that is reshaping content creation across all media, including infographics using simple prompts (in some cases, without even using prompts). AI is a practical partner that can elevate a journalist who has a story to tell into a competent visual communicator. In this unit, we will focus on learning how AI tools can be used to create infographics. We will examine different types of AI tools available, which include models that assist with a specific task and also models that claim to generate entire infographics with a single click. However, we must exercise caution. The shift towards AI is not without challenges and ethical issues. There are serious concerns regarding issues of accuracy, algorithmic bias, data privacy, and transparency. This newfound power comes with critical responsibilities. Therefore, this unit will also let you draw the fine line between making the journalistic work easier and giving an algorithm the power to shape your story.
17.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
Once you've worked through this unit, you should be able to:
- understand the role of infographics in data journalism and the emerging
role of AI in creating them.
- tell the difference between the various AI tools available for analysis
and design.
- learn how to create infographics using AI tools.
- critically examine the ethical issues that come with AI in journalism,
from bias to copyright.
17.2 THE CONVERGENCE OF AI AND VISUAL
STORYTELLING
To appreciate the impact of AI on infographics, we must first understand the foundation upon which this new technology is being built. People have been telling stories with pictures forever, but infographics as we know it is a product of some key moments in human history.
17.2.1 A Brief History of Infographics
Visualising data is nothing new. Back in 1854, Dr. John Snow, a physician, mapped a cholera outbreak in London, and in doing so, created a visual argument that saved lives by showing where the disease was coming from. Florence Nightingale's "coxcomb" charts did something similar, convincing the British government that unsanitary conditions were responsible for more soldier deaths than battles. These early examples established a core principle: that visual representation can reveal patterns and insights that raw numbers

cannot. The 20th century saw the formalisation of graphic design and the rise of mass media, which brought charts and raphs to newspapers and magazines. However, creating these images was a manual and highly specialised craft. The digital revolution of the late 20th century, with softwares like Adobe Illustrator, democratised tools for image-creation, but still one required significant technical skill to make good quality images. This situation changed in the 2010s, when web-based, template-driven tools like Canva and Piktochart appeared; suddenly almost anyone could make something that looked polished and professional.
17.2.2 The Power of Infographics in the Digital Age
Information overwhelms us today. Attention has become an incredibly scarce resource. This is an environment where infographics thrive. Scientific studies have shown the human brain processes images at a speed that text simply cannot match. For a data journalist, that is a huge advantage. Infographics do several things incredibly well:
1. Simplification: They slice through complexity to deliver the main point.
2. Engagement: They catch the eye and are perfect for sharing on social
media, giving a story legs.
3. Accessibility: They make information accessible to people who might
otherwise be intimidated by it.
17.2.3 The AI Revolution in Content Creation
The current wave of AI, particularly generative AI, represents the next major leap in content creation. Unlike previous technologies that were primarily tools for execution (e.g., a digital paintbrush), generative AI is a partner in creation. Large Language Models (LLMs) like GPT-4 can understand and generate human-like text, while diffusion models like Midjourney and DALL-E 3 can create novel images from text descriptions. This technology is not just an incremental improvement; it changes the fundamental workflow. Instead of manually designing an icon, a user can describe it. This shift from direct manipulation to instruction-based creation is the core of the AI revolution and has profound implications for how infographics are conceived, designed, and produced. 17.3 UNDERSTANDING THE AI TOOLKIT FOR
INFOGRAPHICS
Now that we have a sense of how AI is affecting the creation of content, we will learn about the tools that accomplish this and how. Using AI for infographics isn't about a single, magical "create infographic" button (though some tools are moving in that direction). Think of it more like unlocking a new suite of capabilities that you can deploy at various stages of your project. These tools can be broadly categorised as follows.
17.3.1 AI for Visual Asset and Layout Generation
This is perhaps the most visually striking application of AI.
- Icon and Illustration Generation: Instead of searching stock photo
libraries, you can generate custom icons and illustrations with a text prompt (e.g., "a simple flat icon of a wind turbine, green and white"). This allows for a perfectly consistent visual style.
- Colour Palette and Font Suggestions: Many AI tools can analyse
the topic or mood of your infographic and suggest appropriate and harmonious colour palettes and font pairings.
- Data Visualisation Suggestions: Based on the data you provide, AI
can recommend the most effective type of chart (bar, line, pie, etc.) to represent it accurately.
- Automated Layout: Some tools can take your content (text and visuals)
and automatically arrange it into a balanced and aesthetically pleasing layout, saving significant design time.
17.3.2 All-in-One AI Infographic Platforms
A new crop of tools from companies like Canva Magic Design, Flourish, Piktochart AI, Visme, and Napkin.ai are trying to put everything under one roof. The idea is for the user to type in a single command, and the AI will try to do it all: outline the story, write the words, make the pictures, and hand you a finished, editable draft. (e.g., "Create an infographic about the benefits of remote work for employee well-being.") They are very suitable for getting a project off the ground in a hurry. But you should never forget that what they produce is a starting point. Your brain and your critical eye are still the most valuable tools in the box.
17.4 A MODERN WORKFLOW: CREATING AN
INFOGRAPHIC WITH AI
Adopting AI doesn't mean you forget everything you know about journalism. It means you have a new, powerful assistant. You are still the project lead, the strategist, and the ultimate fact-checker. Here is a simple workflow that might be useful for you to tell a story using AI-generated infographics: 171

Step 1: Defining the Core Message and Audience (Human-led) This is the bedrock. Before you open a single app, you need to be clear on your purpose. You must answer the following questions:
- Who are the audiences?
- What is the one key takeaway you want to leave with your audience?
- What do you hope they will do or understand after seeing your work?
Remember, answers to these strategic questions will shape every prompt you write. Step 2: Data Acquisition and Preparation (Human-led) A journalist is only as good as their sources. That means doing the legwork to find trustworthy data from official reports, government databases, or academic research. The data must be cleaned and structured, a process detailed in Unit
10. AI can offer a hand here, but the final responsibility for the data's integrity
is yours and yours alone. Step 3: Leveraging AI for Data Exploration (AI-assisted) Once your data is in good shape, you can use AI to start looking at it to find stories.
- Action: Upload the dataset or report to an AI analysis tool or LLM.
- Prompt Example: "Analyse this air quality data. Which three cities are
the most polluted? Is there a clear trend over the last five years?"
- Outcome: The AI will give you statistical starting points. Your job is to
treat these like tips from a source, which you must then independently verify against the original data. This is a process of discovery, not blind acceptance. Step 4: Generating Visuals and Layouts with AI (AI-assisted) This is where the concept starts to become reality. With the data points finalised, you move to a visual AI tool or an integrated infographic platform.
- Action: Use a tool like Canva's Magic Design or Piktochart AI.
- Prompt Example: "Create an infographic titled 'India's Unbreathable
Air: A 5-Year Analysis.' Use a colour palette of dark blue, orange, and grey. The tone should be serious and data-driven. Include sections on 'Top 3 Most Polluted Cities,' 'Health Impacts of PM2.5,' and 'Proposed Solutions.' Use clean, modern icons."
- Outcome: The AI will give you a starting layout. It might be good, but
it will almost certainly need your personal touch to become great. You might decide to use a separate AI image generator to create a truly unique and powerful header image that the all-in-one tool couldn't produce. Step 5: The Human-in-the-Loop: Review, Refine, and Fact-Check (Human- led) This is the most crucial part of the process. The AI's output is a draft, not a finished piece. You must:

- Fact-Check Every Number: Did the AI pull the correct data? Did it
perform calculations correctly? AI can "hallucinate" or misrepresent data.
- Review for Nuance and Context: Does the infographic tell the whole
story? Is there any missing context that could make the data misleading?
- Check for Bias: Are the icons and images representative and free from
stereotypes?
- Refine the Design: Adjust the layout, improve readability, and ensure
the visual hierarchy guides the viewer's eye to the most important information.
- Verify Sources: Add a footer citing all data sources, a cornerstone of
journalistic ethics. This human-centric final stage is what elevates a graphic from being merely AI-generated to being a piece of real journalism
17.5 POPULAR AI INFOGRAPHIC TOOLS
As we are now familiar with the workflow for creating infographics using generative AI, let us move on to the tools to do the same. The marketplace for these tools is changing fast, but here are some of the key tools a journalist should be aware of today.
17.5.1 Napkin.ai
Napkin.ai is built for speed and simplicity, bridging the gap between your notes and a visual representation. Its magic lies in turning text directly into clean diagrams, flowcharts, and visual notes without needing you to write complicated prompts. You can just paste your text, and it will generate a visual that illustrates your point. It is less about creating a full, data-heavy infographic and more about the quick, on-the-fly process of making your ideas visible, making it ideal for brainstorming, explaining a process, or adding a simple visual to a presentation or post.
17.5.2 Canva Magic Design
Canva, already a dominant force in template-based design, has integrated a suite of AI tools called "Magic Design." Think of Magic Design as your creative shortcut. You can just tell it what you want, maybe "an infographic about the benefits of coffee," and it will instantly whip up several different, fully editable templates. It pulls from Canva's gigantic library of photos, icons, and fonts, so you get a polished starting point in seconds. Its main advantage is pure, simple speed and having all those creative assets right at your fingertips.
17.5.3 Piktochart AI
Piktochart has been making infographics for a long time, and their AI reflects that deep experience. It is specifically trained to think like an infographic designer. You can feed it a simple topic or even upload a whole document, and it will intelligently structure the information, suggest relevant sections, and lay everything out in a classic infographic format. It is especially good at taking dense, text-heavy content and figuring out how to break it down into a visual narrative, making it a go-to for anyone who needs to create a structured, data- rich visual story from scratch.

17.5.4 Flourish
Flourish is less about general design and much more focused on creating stunning, interactive data visualisations. It has kept its identity as a powerhouse for serious data storytellers who need to turn complex spreadsheets into something clear and compelling. It has features that are specially designed for journalists, and is being used in newsrooms.
17.5.5 Standalone Generative Tools
For more granular control, journalists can use a combination of specialised tools:
- Image Generation (e.g., Midjourney, Gemini, ChatGPT): These tools can
offer more artistic control for creating unique header images, illustrations, and backgrounds. They require more skill in prompt engineering but provide results that are far less generic than library assets.
- The trade-off is a less streamlined workflow, requiring the journalist to
copy and paste content between different applications.
- Infographics Generation (e.g., Gemini, NotebookLM, Claude): These
can create infographics based on data provided by you. These are not single-click generation infographics, but they can be useful for more customisation and experimentation. Check Your Progress - 2 Note: 1) Use the space provided below for your answers.
2) Compare your answers with those given at the end of the unit.

17.6 THE ETHICAL CHALLENGES OF USING AI
We have thus far read about the benefits of AI, but like every other technology, it too must be used with discretion. When we bring AI into the newsroom, we are also bringing in a host of ethical challenges. The speed and convenience are tempting, but they force us to be more vigilant than ever about the potential for error, bias, and misuse.
17.6.1 Accuracy and the Danger of "Hallucinations"
Generative AI models, particularly LLMs, do not "know" facts. They are probabilistic models that predict the next most likely word in a sequence. Sometimes this process goes off the rails, and AI mdoel confidently states something that is completely false. We call this a "hallucination," and in journalism, this is a disaster. A made-up number in an infographic vaporises

your credibility. The only defense is a hard and fast rule: a journalist must personally verify every single fact the AI model provides. AI can be used for a first draft, but the final numbers must be checked against the original, trusted source.
17.6.2 Algorithmic Bias in Data and Visuals
Where does an AI learn about the world? From us, by reading the internet. That means it learns all of our societal biases, too. This bias can manifest in several ways in an infographic:
- Textual Bias: An AI might use language that reinforces stereotypes
when describing demographic groups.
- Visual Bias: An image generator prompted with "a picture of a doctor"
might overwhelmingly produce images of white men. A prompt for "a person living in a poor neighbourhood" might generate stereotypical and demeaning imagery.
- Data Interpretation Bias: An AI analysing data might draw
correlations that are spurious and reflect societal biases rather than causal relationships. The journalist must be the firewall here. It is our job to spot slippages, correct them, and be deeply skeptical of any conclusions the AI seems to draw from the data it analyses.
17.6.3 Copyright, Ownership, and Intellectual Property
The legal system is playing catch-up with AI, grappling with questions like: Who owns an image that an AI model creates? In many countries, the answer right now is "nobody," since a human did not make it. And what about the billions of images the AI was trained on? Many were scraped from the web without permission, creating a legal and ethical mess. For now, newsrooms need to have clear rules. The safest approach is to use AI to make something new, not to copy a specific artist's style, and to know that you might not own the copyright to what you create.
17.6.4 The Need to Be Transparent
Public trust hinges on transparency. Audiences have a right to know how the information they consume is created. Hiding the use of AI can be seen as deceptive. The best policy is to be upfront. A simple, clear disclaimer in the footer of an infographic usually does the trick: "Artificial Intelligence helped us generate text and images for this graphic. Our editorial team verified all the data."
11.6.5 Deskilling and the Evolving Role of the Designer
It is a reasonable question to ask: When anyone can type a sentence and get a pretty good design, where does that leave the professionals? The balanced way to see it is that AI is not a replacement, but a tool. It is something that can automate the boring stuff, freeing up human designers and journalists to focus on the parts of the job that require real creativity, strategy, and judgment. Your role shifts from being a maker of things to a director of tools, guiding them to produce work that isn't just passable, but exceptional.

17.7 CASE STUDY: VISUALISING URBAN AIR
QUALITY DATA WITH AI ASSISTANCE
Scenario: Let's get practical. Imagine you are a data journalist and a new government report on air quality lands on your desk. It is a 150-page PDF from the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) detailing PM2.5 levels in major Indian cities over the last five years. Your mission is to turn this mountain of data into a single, shareable infographic for social media that makes people sit up and pay attention. Workflow in Action: Strategy (Human-led): First you need a story. You decide the core message isn't just that pollution is bad, but that it is getting alarmingly worse in specific cities and that it has real health consequences. Your target is the average person living in those cities. Data Prep (Human-led): This part is non-negotiable. You manually pull the key data tables from that massive PDF. You put them into a clean CSV file, double-checking every number to make sure it is transcribed perfectly. Garbage in, garbage out. Story Finding (AI-assisted): You upload your clean data to an analysis tool or just paste it into an LLM. You ask it: "Look at this data on PM2.5 levels. Which 3 cities have the biggest percentage increase between 2020 and 2024?" The AI comes back in seconds. It flags Delhi, Lucknow, and Patna. Visual Generation (AI-assisted): Time to make it visual. You open Piktochart AI and give it a prompt: "Create an infographic called 'Choking Cities: India's Air Quality Crisis.' I want a stark color scheme: red, dark grey, and white to show this is urgent. It needs a bar chart for the 'Top 3 Cities with Rising Pollution,' a big, bold number showing the '12x Over the Limit' fact, and a section on 'Health Risks' with some simple icons." Piktochart generates a draft. The chart looks good, but the health icons are a bit bland and generic. Review & Refine (Human-led):
- Fact-Checking: You run the numbers yourself in your spreadsheet to
confirm the percentage increases and the average. It checks out.
- Icon Refinement: You use an icon generator with specific prompts like
"simple line icon of human lungs" and "minimalist icon of a human brain" to create visuals that are much clearer.
- Transparency: You add a footer to the final design: "Source: CPCB
Annual Report (2020-2024). AI was used to assist in data analysis and visual generation under editorial supervision." What you have now is an infographic that is accurate, ethically sound, and visually powerful. It was created in a tiny fraction of the time it would have taken the old-fashioned way, but every critical decision was made by a human.
17.8 LET US SUM UP
This unit looks at the integration of Artificial Intelligence into the creation of infographics. AI tools offer unprecedented speed and new creative possibilities, 176 capable of assisting in every stage of the workflow, from analysing data and

finding stories to drafting text and designing visual layouts. Platforms like Canva and Piktochart, along with specialised generative tools, have placed powerful capabilities at the fingertips of journalists. However, this technological advancement is not a substitute for journalistic integrity. The core of this unit emphasises that AI is a co-pilot, not an autopilot. The most critical skills for the modern journalist are no longer just about creation but about direction, critical evaluation, and ethical oversight. Navigating the challenges of AI-induced inaccuracies (hallucinations), algorithmic bias, and complex questions of copyright and transparency is non-negotiable. This unit concludes that the responsible use of AI can empower journalists to tell more compelling, data-driven stories to a wider audience, more efficiently than ever before. The future of visual storytelling lies in this synergy between human intellect and artificial intelligence, where technology serves the enduring mission of journalism: to inform the public accurately and ethically.
17.9 KEYWORDS
- Generative AI: A class of artificial intelligence models capable of
generating novel content, including text, images, and sounds, based on the data they were trained on.
- Infographic: A visual representation of information, data, or knowledge
intended to present complex information quickly and clearly.
- Prompt Engineering: The process of structuring text instructions
(prompts) to be interpreted and understood by a generative AI model to produce the desired output.
- AI Hallucination: A phenomenon where an AI model generates outputs
that are nonsensical or factually incorrect but are presented as if they are factual.
- Algorithmic Bias: Systematic and repeatable errors in an AI system
that result in unfair outcomes, such as privileging one arbitrary group of users over others.
- Large Language Model (LLM): A type of AI model designed to
understand, generate, and process human language, such as GPT-4 or Gemini.

18.0 INTRODUCTION
Throughout this course, we have explored the foundational theories, tools, and techniques of data journalism. We have learned how to find, clean, analyse, and visualize data to create compelling and evidence-based stories. Now, we transition from theory to practice by examining real-world examples of data journalism. This unit takes a case study approach. We look at three examples from India and three international ones. For each, we ask four simple questions: What was the context? What data did the journalists use and how did they clean and analyse it? How did they tell the story so that a busy reader could understand the key points? What happened after publication in terms of public debate, policy response or follow-up reporting? Along the way, we also pay attention to ethics, such as privacy, fairness, and harm minimisation. These cases will show that data journalism is never about numbers alone. It's about digging out the human story hidden inside the rows and columns, giving context, and arming the public with clear, evidence-based insight. Whether it is global exposes based on leaked financial troves or local reporting on civic services, the examples will prove just how versatile and vital data journalism has become in today's media landscape.

18.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After going through this unit, you will be able to:
- understand how data journalism is applied in real-world scenarios to
create impactful stories.
- identify the different types of data sources, analytical techniques, and
visualisation methods used in professional data journalism projects.
- analyse the processes behind major data-driven investigations, from
data acquisition to storytelling.
- recognise the ethical considerations and challenges involved in data
journalism projects.
- draw inspiration and practical lessons for developing your own data-
driven stories.
18.2 WHY CASE SUDIES?
Case studies bring the craft to life. In a classroom, we can discuss sampling or chart design, but it is only when we study a real investigation that we see how choices are made under deadline pressure, with incomplete data and competing interpretations. The case method is widely used in professional programmes because it builds judgment through examples, counter-examples and reflection. For data journalism, it teaches three habits. First, process thinking, where we track how an idea becomes a dataset and then a story. Second, impact thinking, where we ask what changed because of the work. Third, method thinking, where we look at what was done well and what could be improved next time. In India, organisations such as DataLEADS and institutes such as IIMC have carried out hands-on training that is case-based and tool-based. Globally, schools such as Columbia Journalism School and newsrooms such as the BBC Academy use completed projects to teach both technique and ethics. A mix of Indian and international examples will help the learners because data access, media economics and audience expectations differ across contexts. Learning to adapt is part of the craft.
18.3 INDIAN CASE STUDIES
Data journalism in India has matured significantly, with news organisations increasingly using data to report on complex issues with depth and precision. Here are a few notable examples.
18.3.1 The Panama and Paradise Papers: Uncovering
Offshore Secrets
Context matters here. After the 2014 general election, public interest in corruption and black money was high. When the Panama Papers leaked in 2016, and the Paradise Papers in 2017, Indian readers wanted to know who used offshore financial structures and why. The Indian Express worked with the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists to go through millions of files from law firms such as Mossack Fonseca and Appleby. These files included incorporation documents, emails, and spreadsheets that linked people to shell companies in tax havens.

The data was huge and messy. Reporters used forensic search tools such as Nuix to index and query documents, and network-mapping tools such as Linkurious to find patterns of ownership. They matched names against the Ministry of Corporate Affairs database, stock exchange filings, court records and even old magazine profiles. Verification was slow work. The team had to separate legal tax planning from illegal tax evasion. They had to confirm identities where names were common. They also had to decide what served the public interest. Publishing every name would be unfair. Publishing nothing would be a disservice. The editorial line was to publish only where the connections were clear and public interest was strong. The storytelling balanced depth and simplicity. The Indian Express ran long explanatory pieces that defined terms such as beneficial owner and shell company. It used simple diagrams to show how one person controlled many entities through layers of ownership. It also wrote short Q & A pieces so that a first-time reader could follow. The impact of this journalistic investigation was resounding, leading to income tax probes, questions in Parliament, and debate about transparency and beneficial ownership norms. At a global level, the leaks added fuel to reforms around company registries and information sharing. From a learning point of view, the case shows three things. First, collaboration across borders and within a newsroom is essential when the dataset is too large for a single reporter. Second, method and ethics travel together. Without a clear method and a clear sense of fairness, such reporting can slip into trial by media. Third, visuals are powerful when they clarify the control relationships that are otherwise hidden in text. Activity - 1 Explore the Investigations yourself: The Indian Express: Panama Papers - https://indianexpress.com/about/ panama-papers/ The Indian Express: Paradise Papers - https://indianexpress.com/about/ paradise-papers/
18.3.2 IndiaSpend: Reporting on Social and Environmental
Issues While The Panama and Paradise Papers investigations were backed by an established media house, i.e. The Indian Express, we will now focus on a smaller organisation that was just as effective in highlighting issues at a more regional level. IndiaSpend is a not-for-profit newsroom that focuses on social sector issues. Two strands of their work illustrate how a small team can punch above its weight with careful method and patient reporting. The first case pertains to their coverage of air pollution. IndiaSpend combined Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) sensor data with satellite readings and its own low-cost sensors installed at key points in cities. Raw air data can be full of gaps, time stamps can be misaligned, and individual sensors can drift. The team standardised time zones, removed obvious outliers, and ran checks by comparing nearby stations. They then produced city-wise and seasonal trend charts that ordinary readers could follow. Alongside the charts, the stories explained which pollutants matter and what long-term exposure does to lungs and hearts. IndiaSpend also used maps to highlight hotspots near traffic corridors

and industrial clusters. The larger impact was to initiate citizen conversations, legal action, and the policy push that led to the National Clean Air Programme. None of this happened overnight. It took months and years of steady, credible work. IndiaSpend's second investigation pertained to reporting on women's work. Using the Periodic Labour Force Survey and earlier National Sample Survey Office (NSSO) rounds, IndiaSpend looked beyond the headline employment rate and asked which women were dropping out, when and why. Disaggregation by state, education and rural-urban location revealed clear patterns. The stories combined numbers with voices. Women spoke about childcare, safety, long commutes and social norms. The analysis avoided simple blame. It focused on constraints and solutions, such as better transport, safe workplaces, and flexible hours. The reporting was cited by think tanks and used in policy debates. The method lesson here is that a national average can hide more than it reveals. Breaking the data and bringing in lived experience makes the story real and useful. Activity - 2 Explore the Projects:

18.3.3 Hindustan Times: Data-Driven Economic and Political
Analysis Another very good example of data journalism includes Hindustan Times' series on nutrition and on elections. The newspaper has invested in a data and political economy team that writes the Plain Facts column. These two stories emerged as part of this initiative. In the story on nutrition, instead of just quoting India's headline malnutrition rate, the team starts by crunching household-level spending data from the NSSO to calculate the minimum cost of a nutritionally adequate diet. They then compare that cost with what rural families actually spend on food and break the gap down by income decile, a statistical tool that helps in analysing income distribution and inequality. To cross-check, the team lines up the results against related indicators such as child stunting rates and cereal-price inflation. When the official calorie or protein norms are revised, the explainer spells out how that affects the affordability threshold, the point where costs become excessively high for a household, so readers can still compare trends over time. The other area they team works on is elections. After major polls, the team digs into the Election Commission dataset to analyse vote share shifts, strike rates and regional swings. It often reads these numbers with independent surveys such as those by CSDS-Lokniti to understand voter blocs. The pieces do not

stop at who won and who lost. They ask where the swing happened and why. Maps and tables are used, but sparingly. The impact of this kind of work is better public debate. Politicians and analysts may disagree with the interpretation, but the base evidence is laid out for all to see. Together, these Indian cases show that even with imperfect data systems, solid method, clear writing and basic visuals can carry a story far. They also show the value of steady beats. Air quality, women's work, and economic health are not one-off topics. They need follow-up and continuity. 18.4 INTERNATIONAL CASE STUDIES
So far, we have seen some examples of exceptional data journalism in India. Internationally, data journalism has been a prominent feature of major newsrooms for over a decade, producing a wide range of innovative and impactful projects.
18.4.1 The Guardian's The Counted: Holding Power to
Account In 2015, there was no single official record of people killed by the police in the United States. The Guardian US launched The Counted to fill this gap. Reporters and researchers tracked local news, official statements, and tips from the public. Every entry was verified with more than one source before it went into the database. The team recorded details such as age, gender, ethnicity, location and whether the person was armed. The database was updated continuously. Alongside the numbers, The Guardian ran features that told the stories of individuals and their families.

The project mattered because it converted a debate into a dataset that could be tested and improved. Researchers and activists used the numbers to check patterns and argue for change. The attention helped push authorities to improve official data collection. The method lesson is simple and powerful. If the data you need does not exist, build it carefully and openly, and invite the public to help improve it. The ethical lesson is equally clear. When people have lost their lives, reporting must be accurate and sensitive. Activity - 4 Explore the Project: The Guardian: The Counted - https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/series/counted-us-police-killings
18.4.2 ProPublica's Surgeon Scorecard: Data for
Transparency ProPublica, a non-profit newsroom, published the Surgeon Scorecard in 2015. The idea was to give patients a sense of how often complications occurred after common elective surgeries. The team used Medicare billing records, which are large and complex administrative datasets. They worked with academic statisticians to adjust for factors such as patient age and health so that surgeons were compared more fairly. The findings were presented through a searchable tool that let people look up hospitals and surgeons. The project sparked intense public debate. Some doctors felt that administrative data could not capture the complexity of cases. ProPublica responded by publishing a detailed method note, spelling out limits and caveats. This transparency was crucial. It showed respect for the medical community and for the readers. The larger point was not to shame but to inform. Patients rarely get to see comparative risk in a simple format. The Scorecard gave them a starting point for questions and second opinions. Activity - 5 Explore the Project: ProPublica: Surgeon Scorecard - https://projects.propublica.org/surgeons/
18.4.3 BuzzFeed News' Xinjiang investigation: Mapping
hidden detention sites BuzzFeed News reported one of the most important open source investigations of the last decade on mass detention of millions of Uighur Muslims in Xinjiang, China. Working under severe constraints, the team led by Megha Rajagopalan, with architect Alison Killing and programmer Christo Buschek, set out to answer a simple question that official data would not: where are the detention facilities and what do they look like. Since on-ground access and official records were limited, the team built its own evidence base from satellite imagery, procurement traces and human testimony. The method was a careful mix of open data and verification. The team scraped and read thousands of construction tenders, company brochures and local government notices for keywords that hinted at high walls, watchtowers, security fencing and dormitory blocks. Using large archives of commercial and public satellite imagery, they scanned vast areas of Xinjiang, looked for site

footprints that matched prison-like layouts, and tracked construction phases over time. Building geometry, perimeter walls, internal courtyards and lighting patterns helped distinguish ordinary factories or schools from high-security compounds. Code was used to sift imagery at scale, but every candidate site was checked by humans and cross-referenced with documentary traces. Where possible, the team interviewed former detainees and families to connect maps to lived experience, while protecting sources and withholding precise coordinates in sensitive cases to avoid harm. The storytelling combined interactive before-and-after satellite views, annotated site diagrams and plain language explanations so that a general reader could follow how each conclusion was reached. The impact was significant. The series mapped hundreds of facilities, brought international attention to the scale of detention and re-education sites, and won the 2021 Pulitzer Prize for International Reporting. It also showed newsrooms a repeatable path for reporting when official statistics are missing or access is blocked: use open imagery, procurement breadcrumbs and careful interviews, publish methods clearly, and centre the people affected. The ethical lesson is equally important. When reporting on vulnerable communities, protect identities, minimise risk and be transparent about the limits of what remote sensing can and cannot prove. 18.5 KEY TAKEAWAYS FROM THE CASE STUDIES
Having read these exemplar case studies of data journalism, let us now rethink their significance as aspiring data journalists. Analysing these diverse case studies reveals several common themes and important lessons:
- Data Is a Source and a Tool: Data can be the starting point for an
investigation (as with the Panama Papers) or a tool to explain an ongoing issue (like IndiaSpend's work). Sometimes, the story is the lack of data, prompting journalists to create their own datasets (as with The Counted).
- Collaboration is Key: Many of the most impactful projects, especially
those involving massive datasets, are the result of collaboration between

journalists, data scientists, designers, and even other news organisations.
- Methodology Matters: The credibility of a data story rests on the
soundness of its methodology. This includes being transparent about data sources, cleaning and verification processes, and any statistical methods used.
- Story Is Paramount: Data analysis alone is not journalism. The insights
from the data must be woven into a compelling narrative that provides context and explains the significance of the findings to the audience. Adding a human element is crucial to making a story relatable.
- Visualisation Serves the Story: The choice of visualisation should
be driven by the story you are trying to tell. The goal is clarity and understanding, not just decoration. A simple, well-chosen chart can be more effective than a dazzling but confusing interactive graphic.
- Impact Can Be Measured in Many Ways: The success of a data
journalism project can be seen in policy changes, official investigations, public awareness, or simply by empowering individuals with the information they need to make better decisions.
18.6 LET US SUM UP
Data journalism in India and elsewhere shows that good public interest reporting does not depend on perfect conditions. It depends on method, patience and clear writing. The Panama and Paradise Papers showed how to handle very large leaks with care and fairness. IndiaSpend demonstrated how to mix official and independent data to track air quality and women's employment in a useful way. Hindustan Times showed how a steady beat can improve public debate on growth and elections. The international cases covered in this unit revealed other strengths of data journalism. The Guardian taught us how to build a missing dataset and keep it credible. ProPublica showed how to open up a complex area like surgical risk and still be fair to professionals. Ultimately, these case studies reinforce that data journalism is a multidisciplinary field that combines the core principles of reporting - curiosity, skepticism, and a commitment to public service - with the technical skills of data analysis and the creative art of storytelling. By learning from these examples, we can better equip ourselves to produce journalism that is not only informative but also impactful and essential in a data-driven world.
18.7 KEYWORDS
- Case Study: An in-depth, detailed examination of a particular instance
or event, used as a basis for analysis and learning.
- Investigative Journalism: A form of journalism in which reporters deeply
investigate a single topic of interest, such as serious crimes, political corruption, or corporate wrongdoing.
- Accountability Journalism: A form of journalism that aims to hold
powerful individuals and institutions, including the government, to account for their actions.

- Leaked Data: Confidential information that is released to the public or
journalists without authorisation.
- Open Data: Data that is freely available for everyone to use and republish
as they wish, without restrictions from copyright, patents, or other mechanisms of control.
- Crowdsourcing: The practice of obtaining information or input into a
task or project by enlisting the services of a large number of people, either paid or unpaid, typically via the Internet.
- Interactive Visualisation: A graphical representation of data that allows
the user to explore, filter, and manipulate the data to discover insights.

1.0 INTRODUCTION
What exactly is communication? The word is derived from the Latin word 'communis', which means 'to make common'. At the simplest level, communication involves understanding what someone conveys and means and, in turn, making someone else understand what you mean. However, for communication to occur, it is important for some basic understanding to exist, which is possible only when the two people feel and think about that subject on common lines. The more common between two people, the better their communication gets. The person who sends a message or communicates is called the Sender/ Source, and the one who receives it is called the receiver. A well-known media expert, Denis McQuail, in his book "Mass Communication Theory", defined communication as: "The process that increases commonality but also requires elements of commonality to occur at all." Many social scientists have attempted to define communication from different perspectives. One of the oldest and most widely quoted ones is from a Western political scientist, Harold Lasswell (1948), who posed some questions with the answers to which would have communication defined. He described it as: "Who says what in which channel to whom with what effect?" Channel here stands for the medium of communication, which may be language, book or even a mass medium like radio, television or newspaper. The effect is the common understanding that communication aims at the building. According to John C. Merrill and Ralph L. Lowenstein, communication is:

"A meeting of minds, a bringing about of a common set of symbols in the
and Communication
minds of participants - in short, an understanding."
1.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After reading this unit, you will be able to: * analyse communication, its process and need; * describe forms of communication and effective communication; * development of communications media; * differentiate between conventional and new media, and * interpret how the media plays a role in the social construction of reality.
1.2 NEED FOR COMMUNICATION
Communication is as important a need for all living beings as food and shelter. All living beings invariably communicate within their community, be it the birds' evening call to return to their homes, barking dogs in protest when a non-member enters their territory or the dance of the honeybees to convey to other members where nectar can be found. For human beings, too, this is a natural individual and social need, as man is a social animal. No normal human being can exist in isolation, irrespective of age, gender and interests.
1.2.1 Communication Process
Communication creates meaning shared between the participants as a continuous, cyclic process. The sender shares knowledge or information based on his experiences with the receiver. What the sender understands as an outcome of those experiences is what he further conveys to the receiver. So, one common functional definition for communication can be: "A cyclic process of sharing of experiences between two or more participants" This brings us to the process of communication. The process of communication involves four basic elements - the sender (S), the message (M), the channel (C) and the receiver (R) - what is also called the SMCR model of communication. The representation below (Fig.1.1) indicates how communication takes place in a cyclic process: Encoding Interpretation Decoding (SENDER) Channel (language/mass media/gestures) COMMUNICATION PROCESS (feedback) (feedback) Decoding Interpretation Encoding (RECEIVER The sender initiates communication by sending a message, and the receiver or the audience is/are the one(s) who receives it; the message is the actual content that the sender desires to convey, and the channel is the medium of conveying that message. Channel, the medium of conveying the message, can be mass media, language, gestures, body language, signs and symbols. When the sender sends a message through some channel to the receiver, the receiver decodes that message in his brain, makes meaning out of it (interpreting) and then encodes the response of that message in his mind and conveys it back to the

o Media sender. This process of conveying back is called feedback, an important Communication Process component in communication. Feedback indicates whether what has been understood is what the source/sender meant or is different from the source's understanding. While receiving the feedback, the sender becomes the receiver, and the receiver becomes the sender.
1.2.2 Effective Communication
Communication is considered effective if it produces the desired results. For example, if a political leader, through his speech, can motivate the electorate to cast their votes for him, his communication may be termed effective. A child tends to take his parents' or teachers' warnings or instructions seriously but will not listen to a stranger. His parents' communication with him is effective, but the latter is not. Both examples clearly show that the relationship between the source and the receiver communicates; this factor decides how the meaning would be interpreted at the receiver's end. The perception of the source by the receiver or the trust factor in their relationship decides how positively the receiver would respond to the source's message. Any communication is called effective if the meaning of the message interpreted by the receiver is the same as that desired by the sender. The effectiveness of the message would be clear from whether or to what extent any desired behavioural change is brought about in the receiver. This is also termed feedback, which can be in words and/or actions. The response that a communication message emanates from the receiver is termed feedback. Feedback may be positive, negative or neutral. When an employee continues to come late to the office despite repeated reminders, it is negative feedback as the communication is not getting the desired response from the employee. When a student makes all efforts to meet the assignment deadlines of a teacher, it is positive feedback as it results from the high regard the student may have towards the teacher. Hence, the teacher's communication is termed effective. When a voter does not exercise his right to vote, let alone vote in favour of or against a political leader, it is called neutral feedback, as the communication did not affect him.
1.2.3 Barriers to Communication
There are certain communication barriers which may hinder its effectiveness. These may be of varied types: * Communicating to the receiver at a wrong/inconvenient time. * For some reason, the message communicated is distorted (i.e., a change in the message's meaning due to noise). Noise is termed as the change introduced in the message so that its meaning does not remain what was intended by the source. * Information overload is yet another barrier as every individual has a limited attention span during which he/she is receptive to communication messages. * Besides technical barriers, there are also language and psychological barriers to communication. Language barriers may be of two kinds: * Vocabulary (use of difficult words that the receiver may not understand) * Semantics (when the message's meaning is unclear to the audience or 9

what the audience understands is different from what the source meant).
and Communication
* Psychological barriers may include these factors: * Noise: Sometimes, when the student in the class thinks of an India- Pakistan cricket match that will take place that evening, what the teacher says may be noisy. Alternatively, any disturbance in the frequency of a radio channel can create a disturbance, and the audience may be unable to hear what is being broadcast. * Perception set differences: Over a period of time, individuals build a certain tendency to perceive a message in a certain way. For example, some people believe what advertisements claim about a certain product as their experiences with it may be positive. Alternatively, others may not believe such messages, as their experiences with the same product/ service may not be satisfactory. This tendency is called the perception set. Due to differences in experiences, value systems, beliefs and social realities of individuals, differences in perception set will always exist, so a message may not have the same effect on all individuals. * Lack of trust and jealousy may also be why a message may not have the desired effect on the audience. * Information filtering: The receivers tend to accept only those messages that they find interesting or reinforce the notions and beliefs they already have. They filter such information and leave out the rest, becoming another psychological barrier. Check Your Progress 1 Note: 1) Use the space provided below for your answers.

1.3 TYPES OF COMMUNICATION
Knowing what communication is, what makes it effective and what reduces its effective capacity, it is also important to know the different forms in which this process is carried out. Though we are exposed to each of these forms daily, we may have never paid any attention to them. Communication 10 scholars agree that there are four basic forms of communication:

o Media Interpersonal communication: This is the kind of communication in which Communication Process there is only one participant, the sender and the receiver. This is also known as auto communication or introspection. Talking to oneself is a good example of this. Interpersonal communication: This communication occurs between two participants, and the exchange may be formal or informal. It is the ideal kind of communication, as the sender can get feedback instantly. As it is one-to- one communication, the sender can also study the receiver's body language (gestures, postures, facial expressions, etc.), which gives an ample idea of what the receiver means and whether what is said is also what is meant. Influencing and persuading the other person is also easy, and there is a greater scope of appealing to the receiver emotionally by means of motivating, encouraging and coordinating. It is also known as dyadic communication. Group communication: This is an extension of interpersonal communication, and the exchange involves more than two people, where the participants get a chance to express themselves on subjects of common interests. This communication serves many goals like collective decision- making, self-expression, and relaxation and is effective as it allows interaction directly with the receivers. One common aspect of such communication is the emergence of a leader coordinating the communication within the group. Mass communication: This is communication that takes place with the help of a mechanical device that simultaneously multiplies messages and takes them to a large faceless audience. Mass media like newspapers, radio, television and the Internet are needed for this communication. The source and the receiver are physically separated in time and space. The audience is anonymous and heterogeneous. The feedback in mass communication is slow, weak and delayed. Different forms of communication mentioned above are effective in different communication contexts. The widest reach is of mass communication, but the most effective is interpersonal communication. For example, to make the general public aware of a new product, advertisements and publicity are the best ways for which the use of mass media is mandatory. On the other hand, for a desired change in an individual's behaviour, like quitting smoking, it is more fruitful to counsel him personally, i.e. interpersonal communication would be more effective.
1.4 GROWTH OF COMMUNICATION AND
MEDIA
When there was less communication and communication channels in society, people lived based on equality as there was no hierarchy among people. Later, those who controlled the communication channels emerged stronger while the others were weak. With changing times and technology, the communications media developed as people realised the subtle but strong effect media could have in influencing public opinion. In earlier societies, the

number of women a man had determined his status in society. Later, the
and Communication
number of cattle one owned indicated one's status. Even later, it was how much land one had that determined it, and then it was the riches that counted most. These stages of societal development based on economic development are identified as: * Pre-agricultural societies: Small communities existed with mostly spoken words as their means of communication and consisted of hunters and food gatherers. * Agricultural societies: People practised agriculture to earn their living, writing came into being, and these were more developed societies with a complex social structure. But a huge chunk of the population remained illiterate. * Industrial societies: This was the machine age and was marked by the publication of Gutenberg's Bible as early as 1455. This drastically improved the speed of book printing that was earlier copied by hand using movable metal type. Mass production became the mantra, and industrial production was centred in cities, which led to a huge migration of people from rural to urban areas. Jobs in these industries became more important than farming. Information society: The second half of the 1900s saw the emergence of information societies, primarily in the United States. But from the second half of the century till its end, most economies of the world had drifted towards it, because of which media became much more important than before. One important invention of the time was the computer, which became the main tool for handling information, its creation, processing and distribution. Today, information is power. Those with better information sources are more resourceful and stronger in society; they are opinion leaders and are listened to, while others do not wield such control. The information society has also seen different conventional media forms merging into one, thus becoming cheaper, more accessible and faster. The conventional media forms comprising different communication technologies merged into a computer- readable digital form. The earlier technologies were analogous or linear in nature, while digital technologies could be stored and used in any format and were easy to use. This process of merging technologies to give a better output of more than one conventional media technology is called 'convergence'. For example, a mobile phone serves the purpose of a phone and a computer as emails can be accessed on it, and the Internet can be browsed. Also, a computer acts as a television as channels can be accessed on it. Television and computers, on the other hand, have made DVD players outdated. All these examples show how the output of more than one technology can be had from a more compact and cheaper technology. Also, these technologies are interactive, making feedback an inclusive communication process. It enables the improvement of messages. This fast exchange of information through cyber networks has led to the coining of the term information superhighway irrespective of the communication objective, which may be social networking, e-commerce, e-governance or professional communication.

o Media Before we delve further into this discussion of twenty-first-century Communication Process technology, let us view the characteristic features of conventional media that have dominated the communication media scene for a long time and the new media that has lately emerged. Newspapers: The ancestors of newspapers were called Corantos, which were news sheets published as long back as the 1620s in England and Holland with irregular periodicity. Later, around the 1640s, Diurnals appeared in England that were dailies publishing reports on domestic events. They were the actual ancestors of the newspapers we see today. We have two formats in which newspapers appear: broadsheets (for example, The Indian Express, The Times of India) and tabloids (for example, Mail Today and Mint). Broadsheets are the morningers that carry hard news and opinions based on them, while most tabloids are eveningers or evening papers that are more of news magazines or feature newspapers. While broadsheets come up with fresh news, tabloids carry features and detailed stories based on them. While the advantage of newspapers is that they sell cheap, they can reach out only to the literate section of the population. Over the last six to seven years, a lot of experimentation has been done in Indian newspapers, from reducing their sizes to make them portable to dividing them into as many sections as can be covered to cater to the maximum number of readers. Innovations are also brought out to market them as a product and as a viewpoint. While their circulation is dying out in the West, they are soaring high in India. Magazines: The earliest magazine was published in England in the 1730s. Though they primarily focused on politics, they were then called miscellanies as they carried various contents. In the later part of the 1800s, magazines made efforts to popularise magazine reading. There was widespread growth due to increased literacy and reduced costs to ensure greater sales, and because, in that era of industrialisation, more and more businesses wanted a platform to put forth their advertisements and publicity messages. Today, magazines are generally classified into general interest and special interest magazines. The first category is those magazines that cover several subjects to cater to wider masses (for example, India Today, Outlook), and the second category is the one that caters to a niche audience (for example, Better
Photography, National Geographic and Business World). Most newspaper
groups own the magazines that one generally sees on the newsstands. The reason is that the newspaper's publishing capacity increases with ad flow. Newspaper groups come up with sister concerns in the form of magazines that have a longer shelf life and hence make advertisement publication a costlier affair. Radio: Radio was first invented by an Italian named Marconi in the 1890s. He is called the 'Father of Radio'. Broadcasting, or transmitting voices and music to a geographically separated large audience, had begun through the telephone, invented by Alexander Graham Bell before the advent of radio. That is when radio became a mass medium. The first licence for transmitting a broadcast in India was given in February 1922, while the AIR was formed in June 1936. The most important time in the history of radio was during the Second World War when this medium of addressing the masses became immensely significant. This was because the Nazis in Germany used it for

propaganda, and by playing German music which would give an impression
and Communication
that they had conquered the areas where the music was played, they could damage the morale of their rival forces. FM broadcasts started in Chennai (then Madras) in 1977 and Jalandhar (Punjab) in 1992. Private players came into the picture only in 1993. Radio later developed into a youth medium. Today, radio's approach is more local, from updating traffic to playing popular music. The advantage of this medium is that it is mobile, does not require reading ability and can be enjoyed without demanding sole attention on the medium itself (unlike television). These days, the emergence of community radio is seen in large numbers, which makes more specialised programmes for a niche audience. Television: Television first started developing in the 1920s and 1930s. After the printing press, television is considered to be the most important communication invention. By the late 1940s and early 1950s, television had become a part of life in most of the developed countries. In India, television was introduced to bring about development in the year 1959. By 1970, the content on TV included news, information and entertainment programmes, including 'Krishi Darshan', which began in January 1967 for farmers in 80 villages. Commercials were first telecast in January 1976. Today, the number of television channels in India outnumbers the time one can afford to watch them, even once a week. The race for TRPs (Television Rating Points), which decide the popularity of a TV show or a channel, is of prime importance as it directly affects the channel's ad revenue. In fact, for that very reason, channels do not mind compromising on work ethics or building an agenda for public discussion for their vested interests. 24-hour news channels have become a reality with no sanctity of what should be called news. Television creates a reality that may sometimes not be real. For example, the portrayal of superwomen in Indian media- one who can single-handedly carry out all personal, professional and social tasks without faltering at any time- is the ideal modern Indian woman. Cinema: The earliest cinema portrayed real event shots in motion without any sound, storyline or plot. They were just black and white, larger-than-life- size silent scenes that first appeared as early as 1896. The first Indian movie is said to be 'Raja Harishchandra', a silent movie made in 1913 by one of the pioneers of Indian cinema, Dadasaheb Phalke. The first talkie (a film that could talk) in India was Alam Ara, made in 1931. In the years to come, regional cinema also flourished. Contemporary films have not just remained a form of art for its lovers to delight in; they have also started taking up contemporary issues, making for entertainment and food for thought. The relationship of cinema with society is very complex. It has been found to have an effect on the psychology of the audience. In contrast, the degree of audience acceptability has varied from one film to another, looking at their experimental nature and low investments over the past four to five years. While romance, comedy and depiction of real-life situations click with the audience, most of the time, horror films are much less accepted. The Central Board of Film Certification in India looks into what can go to the larger masses and what may disturb their sensibilities. Following a certain 'Code of Ethics,' they either allow or censor objectionable

o Media scenes in a film. Also, based on whether they can affect the minds of the Communication Process more impressionable section of society, the films are certified as 'U' or universal (meant for all age groups) and 'A' or adult (meant for people only above 18). Folk media: This medium has been alive in our society since ancient times and has been used for conveying political, social and moral messages. The advantage of such a medium is that it is personalised (members of the same community perform it) and is used where the audience fully accepts it, which makes the communication effective. It relates to all age groups of people and is inexpensive. Mainly confined to rural India, this is special in every part of the country. For example, Tamasha and Pawala in Maharashtra, Yakshagana in Karnataka, Jatra in Bengal, Bhavai in Gujarat and Nautanki, Ramlila and Raslila in the northern states of India. Sometimes, their messages may be satirical or sharp, but they are efficient communication tools. Many NGOs also use these forms, considering how powerful a medium it is. Government bodies in rural areas also use folk media to pass on health agriculture or any other development issue-related messages that are smartly imbibed in traditional folk songs, dances and mythological stories. That is what makes it a powerful tool for development communication. So far, we discussed conventional media; the new media is the Internet. Let's see how it has revolutionised the world. Internet: The first calculator, the 'abacus', was the predecessor of the computer, which was first used by Egyptians in 460 BC. Some scholars also mention the Chinese abacus. Charles Babbage, an Englishman, is called the father of computers who first produced designs for a computer that could make calculations based on stored memory. The Internet as we know it today has fast developed to replace and merge most communication devices and technologies. Today, they are used in educational institutions, commercial and business organisations, government departments, international organisations and the defence sector. But these are the major sectors; it has made its inroads even into most individuals' lives and given them an internet identity. Virtual reality has almost become literal with the kind of involvement it has in our day-to-day lives. It has the most evident advantages but also perils that stand out. While social networking has helped build interpersonal connections in far and distant lands for personal and professional reasons without spending as much as a penny, it has also led to anti-social and aggressive behaviour on the net. For example, writing hate mail about personalities, organisations and religions, defaming and harassing people by posting morphed photographs or posting nasty things by hacking their accounts and different kinds of cyber crimes like hacking bank accounts and even child molesters contacting children through chat rooms. Whatever its dangers, the Internet has taken the world by storm, and there is no stopping it.
