6.5.3 New Media
Of late, a new technological advancement has emerged on the scene. As mobile internet and smartphone technology surfaced on the world's horizon, New Media, also referred to as multimedia or digital media, came to the fore. A combination of text, images, videos, audio and graphics, New Media presents unique and distinctive characteristics like being direct, instantaneous, engaging and interactive. The three R's define it (New Media) all - Instant, Interactive and Immediate. While Mitra (2011) defines New Media as a broad term that emerged in the later part of the 20th century to encompass the amalgamation of traditional media such as films, images, music, spoken and written words, with the interactive power of computers also called convergence, computer-enabled consumer devices and most importantly the internet, it holds out a possibility of on-demand access to content anytime, anywhere on any digital device, as well as interactive user feedback, creative participation and community formation around the media content. Cote (September 2022) observed that New Media is any media - from newspaper articles and blogs to music and podcasts - that are delivered digitally. Any internet-related form of communication can be considered new media, from a website or email to mobile phones and streaming apps. Social media networks, virtual and augmented reality, websites, blogs, music, and television streaming services are a few examples of New Media. The New Media Institute defines New Media as a catchall term used to define all that is related to the internet and the interplay between technology, images and sound. As new technology evolves, develops and is adopted, it continues to modify or transform the society in an apparent or subtle manner. This human-created technology comes to their rescue in case of any contingency or disaster. Say, for example, that humans recently encountered highly contagious COVID-19 that consumed millions of lives and where maintaining physical distance at one point in time became mandatory. Technology helped them to stay virtually connected. Streaming services like Netflix and Spotify and e- shopping showed an upward trend. Physical classrooms paved the way to virtual classrooms; work-for-home became a new norm, and takeaways from restaurants became a common feature. These are the perfect examples to explain how technology came to the rescue of people in times of crises that humans might not have imagined in their wildest dreams. So, technology tries to connect with human necessities. All these technological advancements are the creation of the human mind.

7.0 INTRODUCTION
Democracy is fundamentally structured primarily on the freedom provided to the functioning of its Legislature, Executive, and Judiciary, and the autonomous status provided to the Media. Each of these four pillars must be strong for democracy to be strong, and they work in unison to support one another. A democratic system should act within its domain without losing sight of the larger picture. Media being the fourth estate, in this chapter, we will learn more about the functioning of the fourth estate in a democratic setup, particularly from an Indian perspective. This Unit covers various aspects related to democracy and media. It begins by defining democracy and introducing the Four Pillars of Democracy. It then delves into the significance of the Fourth Estate and explores the concept of Freedom of the Press. The chapter also examines the relationship between the Constitution and the media, shedding light on the roles and responsibilities of the press. Furthermore, it discusses the media's challenges, including attacks to restrict media freedom. Finally, the chapter concludes with a summary of the key points discussed.

7.2 CONCEPT OF DEMOCRACY
India's democracy is regarded as the world's largest democracy. Democracy is described as the government by the people, for the people, and of the people. The primary merit of the democratic system is that it gives freedom of expression to its citizens, among the other Fundamental Rights guaranteed to them. The rule of the country is through its elected representatives. The word "democracy" has its roots in the ancient Greek word "Kratos," which denotes "power" or "rule," and "Demos," which stands for "the people" or "the many." As a result, democracy is defined as "rule by the people" or "rule by the many." Alternatively, we might state that democracy is fundamentally a form of government in which the populace will have direct or indirect control over the political process through regularly elected representatives. Therefore, in this sense, it can be claimed that in a democratic republic like India, the people hold authority. The preface of the Indian constitution is based on the concept of sovereignty. India offers a representative parliament where the government is always accountable to the legislature for its decisions and policies. Indian citizens enjoy Political Democracy, Social Democracy, and Economic Democracy. Thus promising social, economic & political justice to all its citizens by promising fundamental rights.
7.2.1 Freedom of Expression
From time immemorial, man has communicated his ideas through various means, such as symbols and signals. Expressions, either in the form of speech or printed, are also now adapted to suit innovative communication technology. The flow of information and ideas is crucial for developing and surviving the democratic society we live in. The Indian government, the Preamble of the Constitution of India, resolves to secure liberty of thought and expression in Part III of the Indian Constitution for the citizens of India. The Right to Freedom of Speech and Expression can be traced in Article 19 (1)(a). Check Your Progress 1 Note: 1) Use the space provided below for your answers.

7.3 BRIEF INTRODUCTION TO THE FOUR
PILLARS OF DEMOCRACY
The balance of democracy is maintained by the three strong pillars of democracy: the Legislature, Executive, Judicial, and Fourth Estate. The Executive: The Prime Minister's Office and several ministries comprise the Executive, which oversees numerous procedures. The Executive Body
comprises the President, Vice-President, Prime Minister, Cabinet Ministers,
Secretaries, and Civil Services. The Legislative: The Legislature is the assembly making laws for political entities like a country or a city. The legislature enacts laws that are called primary legislation. The Judiciary: A crucial aspect of democracy is the judiciary. The judiciary is responsible for enforcing laws. When a constitution has significant authority, a mediator who can protect citizens' rights should be present. The judiciary protects the rights of citizens guaranteed by the Constitution. The Fourth Estate: In a democracy, the media is the fourth pillar. The media must play a significant role in maintaining democracy. It serves as a conduit between the government and the populace, educating the latter on the acts, regulations, and inefficiencies of the former. For a democratic country to operate its system to its best, public participation is imperative. It is essential to have a well-informed public, and disseminating information to the right- minded people effectively is the responsibility of the mass media.
7.4 THE FOURTH ESTATE
Media is known as the fourth pillar of democracy. Press and news outlets are called the fourth estate or fourth power because of their stated advocacy roles and their subliminal propensity to define political issues. Media is expected to function like a mirror that reflects the true and harsh realities of the world. However, a closer look at the functioning and content published details us that media functions like a double-edged sword today. India is recognized as the place for the largest Media market, with over 82,237 newspapers published in English and other regional languages and more than 900 television channels dedicated to broadcasting news 24/7. However, though television channels owned by private agencies have been permitted to telecast news in India, private radio stations have not been permitted to broadcast news. In addition to all the formal sources of providing public news, there are uncontrolled, unrestricted new media

nd Media platforms like WhatsApp, Facebook, Twitter, and many more, which pour Democracy and the
Fourth Estate
news from the political, entertainment, and corporate world without any restrictions. However, it is essential to note that the media's main function is to provide accurate news to its consumers. Among the many challenges, today's media faces the threat of fake news, paid news, or toned news on all platforms, and it goes uncontrolled in New Media platforms. 7.5 INDIAN CONSTITUTION AND FREEDOM
OF THE PRESS
Speech and expression are essential components of democracy, and both the
Indian Constitution and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights
guarantee these rights. Media plays an important role as it influences people in forming opinions and making decisions. Communication Theorists have proved that media content influences its consumers as it not only influences but also sets an agenda. Considering the influence and the reach, the Constitution of India has made certain provisions for laws and regulations that can govern the functions of the media. Some of the laws and regulations are discussed below:
7.5.1 Freedom of the Press - Article 19(1)(a)
The absence of legal and administrative restrictions on disseminating information, viewpoints, knowledge, and ideas is press freedom. From the world's perspective, the origin of the concept of freedom of the Press took place in England. The invention of printing in the later part of the 15th century and the appearance of the newspaper as a powerful medium of expression made persecution for the expression of opinion, even in matters relating to science or philosophy, restored by both the Church and the State. Newspapers played the role of opposition against monarchical absolutism and fought for Freedom of Expression. The enlightened public supported the cause. In his Areopagitica (1644), Milton argues "that free men must have the 'liberty to know, to utter, and to argue freely according to conscience, above all liberties". The newspapers won their Right to expression. The history of

press freedom in England thus represents a victory of the public over the
in the Digital Age
authority of the licensor. In England, the term "freedom of the press" refers to the freedom to print and publish anything that is not illegal or otherwise unlawful, such as sedition, contempt of Court, obscenity, slander, or blasphemy. The freedom of the Press was first guaranteed by the Constitution of the USA in the year 1776. It is worth recalling the declaration made by Jefferson during his First Amendment towards Freedom of the Press. He said, "Were it left me to decide whether we should have a government without newspapers or newspapers without a government, I should not hesitate to prefer the latter." Pt. Jawahar Lal Nehru, the first Prime Minister of India, echoed similar views: "I would rather have a completely free press, with all the dangers involved in the wrong use of that freedom, than a suppressed or regulated press." Voltaire once said, "I do not agree with a word you say, but I defend to the death your right to say". Interestingly, contradicting the opinion expressed by Pt. Nehru, Mrs. Indira Gandhi, daughter of Pt. Nehru also adorned India's Prime Minister's position and never strongly believed in absolute freedom of expression. She first expressed her worries about the media in her speech to the International Press Institute Assembly in New Delhi on November 15, 1966. Where she accused it of giving the nation's student turmoil widespread coverage, she said, "How much liberty should the press have in a country like India, which is engaged in fighting a war against poverty, backwardness, superstition, and ignorance." Mrs. Gandhi remarked that the country's main publications and journalists should decide whether to impose any limits on the Press. Nine years later, Mrs. Gandhi declared an emergency, prompting immediate action against the Press and the imposition of complete censorship. The constitution of India has provided Freedom of Speech and Expression for its citizens under Article 19(1)(a) of the constitution, which deals with fundamental rights. The Freedom of the Press or media, which is an influential medium of mass communication, is not specifically mentioned in this article; however, it is implied. In the debates of the constituent assembly, Dr. B R Ambedkar, Chairman of the Drafting Committee, made special reference to the concept of "Freedom of Press" and said, "that no special mention of the freedom of the press was necessary at all as the press and an individual as a citizen are same as far as their right of expression is concerned". Supreme Court upheld this in the Romesh Thaper vs. State of Madras and Brij Bhushan vs. State of Delhi cases. The Right to freedom of the Press includes the freedom to print, publish, and disseminate one's thoughts, opinions, and viewpoints through all media without restriction. Three key components make up press freedom. They are:
1. Freedom of access to all sources of information.
2. Freedom of publication, and
3. Freedom of circulation.
However, press freedom is not unrestricted. Particularly the freedom of expression of Mass Media, which can influence a large section of society, which comprises not only heterogeneous social, cultural, and educational

nd Media backgrounds but is also super sensitive to religious and political needs. The Democracy and the
Fourth Estate
technological revolution has gifted mankind with not only multiple access to media. Still, it has also made provisions for morphing, slanting, tainting, and faking the content, which needs to be monitored in this era of technological revolution, where a tremendous amount of information is available at the fingertips and can be accessed. The unauthenticated information being published by multiple media platforms needs to be monitored. Pre- independence, there were several regulations to curb the freedom of the Press or media. However, after its independence, India removed many of the regulations in force. Some examples are the Vernacular Press Act of 1878, The Censorship of Press Act of 1799, The Press Act of 1835, and the Metcalfe Act. The Constitution of India has made provisions to safeguard the benefits of the fundamental Right provided under Art 19(1)(a) by Art 19(1)(2), which lays reasonable restrictions on the freedom of expression in the affairs influencing the Sovereignty and integrity of the State. The Indian Constitution's Article 19(2) lists the following legitimate limitations on the Right to free speech and expression: Sovereignty and integrity of the State: The argument was included by way of an amendment to calm down the agitated response of the people, which was calling for separate entities for the various regions of India. Security of the State: It is forbidden to exercise freedom of expression in a way that compromises the state's security in any way. Ex: State of Bihar v.
Shailabala Devi
Public Order: The Constitutional (First Amendment) Act of 1951 inserted the word public order. Ex: Romesh Thappar v. State of Madras, where the Court had ruled that the freedom of speech and expression includes the freedom of circulation. Decency or morality: Sections 292 to 294 of the Indian Penal Code provide more detail on this defence. Ex: Ranjit Udeshi v. State of Maharashtra. Contempt of Court: An act of disdain, disobedience, or interference with a court's orderly procedure is known as contempt of Court. Examples are disrupting court proceedings, interfering with attempts to obtain evidence, destroying evidence, disobeying a court order, and intimidating witnesses. Defamation: Writing, publishing, and speaking a false statement that harms someone's reputation and good name for personal gain is defamation, which is both a criminal and a civil offence. The Law of Torts governs civil defamation remedies. The ability to speak and express oneself freely does not involve doing anything that can compromise someone's status. Defamation seriously constrains the Right to freedom of speech and expression since it injures someone's reputation. The Indian Penal Code, 1860's Sections 499 and 500 allow the victim to bring legal action for defamation against the offender.

7.6 ATTEMPTS TO CURB FREEDOM OF MEDIA
A senior journalist, Kuldip Nayar, wrote to Mrs. Gandhi shortly after she declared the emergency, "If newspapers have criticized the government, it is largely because of its sluggish administration, slow progress in the economy field and the gap between promise and performance. My concept of a free press is to ferret out the truth and let the public know." People's freedom of expression is crucial for maintaining a democratic way of life and for communicating their opinions to the general public. As an effective tool for mass communication, the media should be allowed to contribute freely to creating a robust, sustainable society. Denying media freedom directly relates to denying citizens the ability to shape public opinion. There are numerous occasions where the government violated press freedom. For example, in Sakal Papers v/s Union of India, the Daily Newspapers (Price and Page) Order, 1960, which set the number of pages and size that a daily might publish at a price, was found to violate the freedom of the Press and to not be a reasonable constraint under Article 19(2). Similar to this, in Bennett Coleman and Co. v. Union of India, the Court ruled that the Newsprint Control Order, which set the maximum number of pages, was invalid because it violated Article 19(1)(a) and did not constitute a reasonable restriction under Article 19(2). The Government's argument that it would aid in the expansion of small newspapers was rejected by the Court. Among many such attempts to curb the freedom of media, the imposition of emergency can be considered a major blow to the democratic situation in India and the media in particular. Considering Indian Express Newspapers Vs. Union of India was related to interference from the authority in the circulation of newspapers. Speaking about the effectiveness of freedom of the Press regarding the content of circulation, the Court observed that expression means freedom from interference from authority. The Court's primary responsibility is to defend journalistic freedom. In the case of Brij Bhushan v. the State of Delhi, the validity of censorship was a point of discussion. An order was made in this case against the printer, publisher, and editor of the weekly Organiser. While many such cases are fought individually by respective newspapers or other

nd Media forms of media, a major threat to freedom of expression was experienced in Democracy and the
Fourth Estate
India when the executive pillar of the country unanimously decided to curb the freedom of expression of the other three pillars of democracy.
7.6.1 Emergency and the Media
One of the most important instances of when freedom of the media was severely curbed was the declaration of an Internal Emergency in India in
1975. Mrs. Indira Gandhi, the then Prime Minister, following the Allahabad
High Court judgment against her, decided to impose an emergency. The "darkest period" of independent India is often called the emergency period, which went on from June 25, 1975, to March 21, 1977. The rule limited the freedom of speech and expression and suspended all civil rights. The initial response to the emergency from mainstream media was shock. It was hard to believe that the Press and other pillars of democracy were under threat. Interestingly, after the initial disbelief and protest, everyone bowed down to the pressure. In an interview, a senior political leaders L.K. Advani, a major opposition figure at the time who later served as a minister in the Morarji Desai and Atal Behari Vajpayee administrations, emphasized, "When Mrs. Gandhi asked the media to bend, they crawled". This quote effectively sums up a large portion of the media response. Apart from Newspapers, Radio and Cinema were the other popular mass media formats available. The government controlled the cinema content using the censor board. The government did not encounter resistance from All India Radio's staff because it was under the Ministry of Information and Broadcast's supervision. 7.7 ROLES AND RESPONSIBILITY OF THE
MEDIA IN A DEMOCRATIC
ESTABLISHMENT
The constitutional makers of India did not offer any separate provision for the Right to speech and expression. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, the Chairman of the

Drafting Committee, powerfully argued that "The Press is simply another
in the Digital Age
way of describing a citizen or an individual. The media has no superior privileges which are not to be given or which are not to be exercised by the voter in his separate capacity. The executive of the Press or the editor are all citizens. Therefore when they select to write in a newspaper, they are just exercising their Right to freedom of speech and expression, and in my decision then, no special mention is necessary of the freedom of the Press at all". Despite the Indian constitution not providing any special privilege to the media, the judicial procedures have promoted and safeguarded the freedom of the Press. Media being an influential tool of Mass Communication in a country like India, it must be an autonomous institution to effectively perform its function as the fourth pillar of a democratic setup.
7.7.1 Responsibility of Median in Democratic Country
Media need to play a pivotal role in building a society for a better tomorrow. Some of the responsibilities of media are:
1. Media should provide the public with fair and factual information.
2. Dissemination of knowledge that suits the structure of Indian society,
which is multicultural and multilanguage. With a major part of its population still being illiterate and poor, it is essential to control information that lacks credibility and flows through various forms of mass media, including internet-based applications. Enabling people to form the right kind of opinion is the primary responsibility of the media.
3. The responsibility of the media is not just information and entertainment
but also education. Content of Media should necessarily highlight the way against the people who are accused of any antisocial actions, irrespective of any political connection.
4. The content published should build the faith of people toward democracy
and justice. Sensationalizing an event should be avoided.
7.7.2 Media's Role in Indian Democracy
Media, the backbone of a democratic setup, plays a significant role among the general public.
1. Watchdog Function: The media works as a watchdog about the various
activities of the government and carry fair report.
2. Information: Provided information should educate the media consumer
about various activities that occur in society, e.g., politics, sports, science, development, etc.
3. Educate: The media should highlight the loopholes in a democratic
society. Awareness, thus created, will ultimately help the government be accountable and responsive, which is the true essence of a democratic setup.
4. Opinion formation: Media is an effective tool for disseminating
information; the role of media is to create the right opinion based on

nd Media factual news. Democracy and the
Fourth Estate
5. The function of media is to provide the right kind of information related
to critical subjects like childbirth, child care, domestic violence, sexual harassment, and many other similar sensitive areas that demand a break from stereotypical thoughts.
6. Media should emphasize providing information in an objective sense.
7. Revolutions in Information technology have brought a mammoth change
in content and introduced various mass media formats. The content published on digital media like Facebook and Twitter and traditional media like print and audio-visual media play an important role in bringing in the desired social change. Ex: #metoo, stopping domestic violence, the importance of voting, and the plastic ban are some examples worth mentioning. The success of such campaigns highlights the content creation and positive use of the media for social change. When creating information appropriate for the social fabric, the wide reach and free dissemination of the internet and social media platforms are crucial components. It is interesting to observe the extensive use of new media platforms by political parties and government departments to promote the schemes. Such attempts can offer transparency in politics. 8.0 INTRODUCTION
As a journalism and mass communication student, you would have observed that journalists worldwide have adapted themselves to diverse technologies to excel in their profession. New technologies have immensely helped them to upgrade their professional skills and perform better in their vocation. Mobile technology, in general, and smartphones, in particular, have helped them to make their jobs faster and more effective. Online editions and mobile applications of newspapers, magazines, radio and television, the newest newsgathering devices, have evolved and facilitated their performance over the years. Journalists have also progressed with the efficient support of the 30 and 40-enabled Smartphones. Thus, smartphones have proved to be the real game changer in modem journalism. Mobile journalism is fast emerging as a new creative trend in the media industry, revolutionising how news is gathered and disseminated to diverse audiences. Reporters and correspondents are trained to handle their mobile devices to broadcast news content using smartphones, tablets, digital cameras and laptops. Since the emergence of smartphones, news media personnel have become more mobile and independent. 'Pop- up' newsgathering has

nd Media become the order of the day in the media industry, where a single reporter Mobile Journalism can report from his/her beat. In this Unit, we shall discuss the concept and opportunities of Mobile Journalism, also known as 'MoJo', and how it's different from Citizen Journalism. We shall also study the tools and accessories required for MoJo and its potential professional challenges. We will critically examine how reporters and news organisations use fast-emerging mobile devices to gather and disseminate news through diverse media forms.
8.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After going through this Unit, you should be able to: * define mobile journalism; * identify the tools needed for shooting, editing and distribution of the content for mobile journalism; * describe the process of using smartphones for Mojo; * outline opportunities and challenges of MoJo; and * Critically assess the ethical issues in MoJo.
8.2 WHAT IS MOBILE JOURNALISM?
Mobile Journalism (MoJo) is a form of digital reporting where trained journalists use mobile devices to gather news. A mobile device refers to a Smartphone or a Tablet with iOS or Android operating systems. Reporters use mobile devices as tools to shoot, edit and broadcast news content. Media persons have become more mobile and independent in executing their assignments using Smartphones. It is gradually gaining popularity among reporters and news organisations as it helps organisations spend less on hiring crew and expensive equipment. MoJo is cost-effective as smartphones are more convenient than traditional cameras, are heavy, and require additional human resources. Sometimes, sending Outside Broadcast Vans (OBV) to cover news breaks simultaneously at several spots is impossible. It is during such situations that smartphones come in handy for timely coverage of news occurrences. As smartphones are thoroughly equipped with in-built audio- video settings with different MoJo apps, reporters can quickly shoot, edit and upload their news content on the web or to their organisation.
8.2.1 Mobile Journalism and Citizen Journalists
The term 'Citizen Journalist' has become exceedingly popular in recent times. Newsrooms all over India, in fact, the world, have opened their doors for citizens to report civic, social, political and other reader-interest issues. Citizen Journalism has also helped establish vital links between the government and common people, as they offer suggestions to the government through various media platforms. Since it is not humanly possible for reporters to be present at every news location whenever a news event occurs, the citizens send reports of the event using their mobile phones. Television

news channels have often acknowledged the use of footage sent by citizen
in the Digital Age
journalists, attributing the source. From company executives to rickshaw pullers, vegetable vendors, and daily wage labourers, everybody can own a smartphone these days. Nowadays, Owning a smartphone has empowered the common people to express themselves more openly than ever before. This increased access to mobile phones has facilitated citizen journalists enormously to perform their jobs promptly. They can instantly record and upload the news event to web outfits or news media establishments. However, being responsible before uploading videos and audio is important, as truth and credibility are essential features of objective and ethical journalism. The same is expected from Mobile journalists, too. Verifying, checking and rechecking the facts under coverage is necessary before uploading.
8.2.2 Strengths of Mobile Journalism
It is often said that owning a smartphone is like carrying a portable newsroom. There are several occasions where breaking news has been flashed using mobile phones and exclusive news stories uploaded on the web worldwide. MoJo is gradually becoming popular with journalists, media, and news broadcast organisations because of its various benefits. The work of a journalist has, of late, become much easier and faster, thanks to smartphones. The benefits of mobile journalism are that it is prompt, helps reporters beat deadlines, and is affordable. Also, smartphones are easier to carry, and trained reporters can broadcast breaking news or events from unlikely locations where broadcast crews find it hard to reach on time. MoJos have captured shocking incidents and sights while happening and have drawn international attention. Accidents and disasters occur without warning; in such cases, smartphones capture the authentic moments of the story. There are numerous opportunities for mobile journalism where videos can capture historical moments instantly transmitted to the web. You may recall videos of people or cattle marooned in floods in different parts of the country or landslides in the hills of Uttarakhand captured on smartphones making their way into news bulletins. Smartphones have made the lives of reporters easier as they have become 'mobile' in their work and can work independently without being assisted by a large production crew. It is also cost-effective for media organisations as they do not have to hire additional professionals and instead spend funds on modem equipment for improved production techniques. Mobile journalists can also go to those places where it's challenging to place camera equipment and hold interviews with people who are uncomfortable to face the production crews. It has been observed that most people are willing to speak in front of smartphone cameras, while they get conscious or nervous in front of professional cameras with large crews. Even remotely, reporters can use their smartphones to cover news events without depending on computers or heavy broadcast equipment. The LIVE news broadcast with the

nd Media help of a smartphone is generally viewed as authentic coverage because Mobile Journalism people trust live reports of news events. Mobile journalists must be first trained on using a smartphone for newsgathering, editing and broadcasting before being sent for field reporting. Once a reporter is trained in MoJo, it becomes convenient to telecast exclusive news from any corner of the world. Activity-1 Identify some news items in a television news bulletin using smartphones. 8.3.1 Equipment Required
Smartphones: Any smartphones with iOS and Android with good Internet connectivity can be used for MoJo. These days, smartphones are available with high-quality video and audio features. Tablets: Tablets are also equipped with high-quality audio and video facilities to record so the news can be live-streamed easily. Digital Cameras: Digital cameras, like smartphones, are light, convenient, and easy to carry. High-quality images and videos can be recorded using digital cameras and later conveniently transferred to computers and/or laptops for streaming online. Tripod: For stability, a light tripod is required. A tripod mount is also needed

to support the smartphone.
in the Digital Age
Grips: It is attached to the tripod to move the camera around as you film. Microphones: A clip-on microphone helps capture audio in a noisy and windy environment. Video Light: All smartphones have built-in camera lights, but external light is also crucial for better results. However, natural light gives good results while shooting outdoors, compared to artificial light. Power-Bank and Extra Batteries: Smartphone batteries do not last long when shooting videos. Therefore, carrying a power bank and extra batteries for shooting is always advisable. Backpack: A light, sturdy backpack is needed to carry all the equipment.
8.3.2 Mobile Applications
Mobile Applications for MoJo are more valuable than other audio-video editing applications, which are convenient to learn and use by mobile journalists. To master the software, users have to be adequately trained. These apps help in recording, editing and distribution of news content.
8.3.3 Webcasting
Webcasting is the same as the LIVE broadcast of an event with the help of cameras. In webcasting, a mobile phone is used to do LIVE coverage of an event with the help of Social media platforms. Facebook, Twitter and YouTube are the popular social platforms where live streaming of videos can be done for news channels and independent reporters. Even mainstream mass media often rely on social media to reach their target audiences.
8.4 PRODUCTION ASPECTS OF MOBILE
JOURNALISM
Shooting videos for journalism has to be taken seriously and done professionally. Reporters must follow specific rules while shooting and preparing storyboards, with proper sequencing. There are certain production aspects that every trained journalist needs to follow to produce quality news content.
8.4.1 Shots
While shooting for news content, knowing and presenting the shots professionally is essential. An image is a single photographed scene taken from continuous filming. It is a single piece of action taken by the camera. There are several types of shots. Extreme Wide: It is also known as the 'establishing shot' - to show the viewer the surroundings of the scene being recorded. Wide: Popularly known as a long shot, it includes a full view of the scene or shows a person's whole body from head to toe.

nd Media Mid-shot: A shot framing the person from their head to their knees. Mobile Journalism Medium: Medium shots are usually taken during interviews or dialogue sequences. This shot is essential to capture the emotions and body language of the participants. This particular shot is aimed at showing the object from the head to the waistline. Medium Close-up: The shot focuses on the face of the subject. It is taken from the head and cuts off around the chest. This shot, also commonly used during interviews, concentrates on the subject, not the surroundings. Close- up: This shot shows the subject from the head to the neck. The frame is filled with the subjects' faces, while it captures the emotions and expressions. Extreme Close-up: This shot focuses on a particular part of the subject - such as the eyes. It frames only a part of the face to highlight the emotions during the interview. Two-shot: This shot is often used in interviews to bring the interviewer and interviewee into the frame. Over the Shoulder: The shot is taken from behind a person taking the interview on the subject and may also show the interviewer. The shot is commonly cut in between the conversations, alternating the two speakers' views. Reverse over the Shoulder: The interviewer's frame is taken from over the shoulder of the interviewee. Cutaways: During interviews, extra shots are taken of the hands and eyes engaged in an activity to create variety and give context to specific points in an interview. Cutaways can be taken for a maximum of 10 seconds because, during editing, only 3 or 4 seconds will be used for the content. Overlay: The shot is taken of different scenes from internal and external locations that support the story. Overlay shots are important during edits.
8.4.2 Sequencing and Storyboards
Sequences are essential to support the visual narrative of the content. It is a well-established form of narrating the story with a video. Sequences are formed using different types of shots that we have discussed above. Storyboards or Filming for Editing Shots: Storyboards are graphic illustrations of stories created before any film shot and are used in filmmaking, documentary making and dramatic films. The drawings are the sequence of shots to make the edit much more accessible. The series of graphic drawings is also known as filming for edit. Creating a storyboard for live events is impossible, but it's helpful when the story is offline and based on news content. A storyboard will have some of the following information: Title of the story: Date:
Sr. No. Voiceover Type of shots Bytes

8.5 CHALLENGES OF MOBILE JOURNALISM
With the advent of 2 G, 3G, and 4G technologies in India, mobile companies are producing high-end smartphones at affordable costs. The prices of smartphones are quite competitive, and consumers have wide choices to pick and choose the brand of their preference. Let's discuss some of the challenges faced by MoJos. Several technological, financial and logistical issues may arise while shooting with mobile phones. Some of these are listed below: Battery Related: The average life of a smartphone battery is low, especially while shooting. To avoid abrupt disconnection during important shoots of an event, it is advisable to carry extra batteries and chargers. Solar batteries can be used to prevent such challenges. A power bank can also be helpful in such situations. Quality of Shots (4K or HD): Mobile Journalists should be familiar with the quality and standard of shots. Whatever the medium of output is, it is highly important to shoot with 4K or high-definition cameras. 4K is also known as Ultra HD; its dimensions are 3840 x 2160 pixels. It is called 4K because its pixel size is four times the resolution of HD, which has a pixel size of 1920 x 1080 pixels. While shooting with mobile phones, the format should be set before the shoot commences. When buying mobile phones, checking for high-resolution cameras is essential. Internet-Related Issues: Despite the fourth-generation 4G-network connectivity, sometimes, due to poor networks, journalists have to face problems in broadcasting live news content. Uninterrupted Internet connectivity is essential while covering a live event or managing live chats. Without Internet connectivity, it becomes challenging to execute the job. Reporting Challenging Situations: MoJos may face uncertain situations. For example, while covering protest demonstrations or riots where police or agitators indulge in violent clashes, police may use water canons to thwart the agitators. The reporters could become victims of such circumstances in which expensive reporting equipment and smartphones could be damaged or destroyed. Covering the smartphone with a waterproof casing is advisable to safeguard one's equipment and gadgets during such situations. Selfie sticks and mobile tripods should also be taken adequate care of. Additionally, reporters may be unable to send live feeds to their stations. If there is no connectivity, reporters can look for a place where there is a

nd Media Broadband connection or a Wi-Fi facility. If reporters cannot send live feeds, Mobile Journalism they can record the events and send the tapes or the clips later when internet connectivity is restored. Theft of mobile phones: In the event of theft, valuable inputs and news recordings already collected may get lost; therefore, it is always advisable to keep mobile phones safe to avoid theft or loss. 8.6 ETHICAL ISSUES MOBILE JOURNALISM
As discussed in the previous sections. Mobile Journalism has emerged as an integral part of journalism today. Hence, specific professional standards of journalism must be adhered to during gathering and broadcasting new or option pieces.
8.6.1 Credibility
Though reporters have the freedom to shoot and film, edit and broadcast news coverage through smartphones, the standards of professional journalism

must be maintained at all times. Multifarious skills and deep knowledge of
in the Digital Age
regional and national issues for journalists are essential to approaching the right source of information, reporting it accurately and following the basic rules of news reporting. Reporters should consider smartphones a newsgathering tool and must not forget the basic tenets of news writing. If a mobile journalist does not follow professional regulations, s/he could be accused of defying fundamental norms of professional journalism. The Information Technology Act, the Official Secrets Act, and laws relating to defamation, contempt of legislature, and contempt of court are some of the most stringent laws that must be abided by at any cost. Any infringement of any of these could cause serious damage to the credibility of the news organisation and the MoJo reporting stories containing any such elements.
8.6.2 Fake News
Fake news is one of the biggest threats to the news industry today. The Internet is flooded with information on social media platforms, so it is essential to separate genuine videos from fake ones. Many fake videos go viral and may lead to heinous crimes such as lynching, abduction, and rape, followed by murders or suicides. Therefore, the role of a trained MoJo reporter would be to comprehend the credibility of the news content and check and recheck the accuracy of the subject being covered. MoJo reporters should endeavour to be impartial and fair in their narrative. While covering news stories, they should contact as many sources and parties involved as possible. Unauthorised and non-licensed versions of mobile applications should not be used. The credibility of the content is significant. Therefore, it becomes imperative for trained reporters to use apps with great caution and take due care while shooting and editing journalistic content.
8.6.3 Sensitivity
MoJos are often compelled to work under tremendous pressure. However, they should not be overwhelmed by the situation around them and unduly dramatise the events, which might deviate from the actual situation. While covering serious events, such as rapes, murders, road accidents or other heinous crimes, proper precautions should be taken. Reporters should not reveal the identities of victims of sexual harassment or their relatives. It is always safe to avoid live coverage, and footage not allowed by law should not be shared or uploaded on the web. Reporters must know how, where and where they should capture videos. Though pushing the red button on the mobile phone to capture critical moments and sensitive times is very tempting, it is better to restrict oneself from transmitting any such information which might pose serious threats to the public and national security. They should strictly follow the Press Council of India and other regulatory bodies' guidelines.

Although the industry has underplayed its dependence on technology, it is quite evident that advances in technology from the first day of its invention have facilitated the growth of the media as an industry and provided a competitive edge to the working method. The chapter explores the industry's symbolic relationship with technology by tracing the developments that have shaped and given birth to newer media formats. 9.5 THE MUZZLED PRESS
The muzzled press refers to a situation where the press or media is restricted in reporting or sharing information freely. This can happen for various reasons, including censorship, government control, corporate influence, and legal threats. In such situations, the press may not be able to fulfil its role as a watchdog of society and provide accurate and unbiased news to the people. A free press should function in its true sense, as such an action will ensure transparency, accountability, and credibility in a democratic system.
9.6 INFLUENCE OF TECHNOLOGY ON
FREEDOM OF THE PRESS
From time immemorial, we have observed technology plays an important role in news distribution. However, it is important to understand that the two cannot be treated synonymously as news distribution is a sociotechnical enterprise wherein political economy and strategic organisational practices shape technology's influence on news distribution patterns. For example, television's advent brought predictions of cinema halls' death. The cinema and the present-day OTT platforms gradually provided new methods of releasing and viewing cinema.

Moreover, there has been a cultural shift over the past decade among journalistic actors from suspicion of interest in audience participation. Despite the arrival and advantages of technology, unfortunately, for various reasons, press freedom continues to be threatened and eroded. Michael Vatikiotis, a writer, journalist and private diplomat working in Southeast Asia since 1987, observes journalists working for various media formats continue to face threats. In addition to the laws governing the freedom of the media, the journalists continue to face attempts of bribery in the form of cash, gifts and awards. The media persons also receive threatening phone calls. Supporting Michael Vatikiotis's observations, the reports released by the Reporters Without Borders (RSF) Press Freedom Index measures the degree of freedom available to journalists in 180 countries. Until 2021, the mean average score for all countries worsened, rising from 36.3 to 38. The latest RSF index for 2022 shows that only 8 out of 180 countries provide a good environment for journalism. Interestingly, the status of press freedom, even in countries like the UK, France, the USA and Canada, remains satisfactory. While Russia's situation is serious, North Korea is ranked lowest. 9.7 LET US SUM UP
Technology has played an important role in the historical development of journalism. For example, the telegraph helped foster the development of newswire services and the proliferation of computers replaced typewriters. Today, the linkage between technology and journalism is as deep and complex as ever. Technologies have transformed key aspects of contemporary news production, distribution, and consumption apart from challenging the foundational theories of mass communication. The technological revolution has led to the development of new forms of media which demand specific methods while creating content apart from technology. Limitations of words and a combination of AV media provide a transmedia look to every social media platform. Technology has been key in developing new logic and forms for news production or taking something perceived as newsworthy. It has provided

shape and direction to the concept of News and to the actors, actants, and
in the Digital Age
activities related to the news. Lewis and Westlund (2016) identify four dimensions of newsgathering. They are: Human-centric journalism: Here, technology has a limited impact on journalistic activities. Technology-supported journalism: Human actors are largely autonomous relative to technological actants. A majority of today's mainstream media functions on this dimension. Technology-infused journalism: Highlights the institutionalisation of technology for news production and distribution. This form has become more prominent in recent years. An example of that is ambient journalism. In ambient journalism, stress is gathering and communicating news information drawn from streams of collective intelligence made available through social media platforms. Technology-oriented journalism: Human actors and technological actants become interdependent in this form. An example is automated journalism, a form of journalism governed by human-created algorithms that automate some stages of news production to fasten journalistic products. A working journalist enjoys the right to protect the identities of their confidential sources. While technology's influence, including the use of artificial intelligence, in journalism is meant to aid journalists and provide readers with quality news, it can create more significant difficulties for journalists and change how people consume their news. Whether they know it or not. Journalists and news sources should move forward cautiously when using artificial intelligence to produce news articles. Relies on an inconsistent set of court decisions based on constitutional and common law interpretations and state statutes. Efforts to bring consistency to federal law through the passage of a shield law have stalled. At the same time, journalists face new threats because of the vulnerability of their communications to discovery and monitoring by third parties. Also, the entry of non-professional communicators into the news ecosystem is causing courts to re-evaluate and redefine long-standing protections. This article proposes four ways that sources could be better protected from unmasking without the passage of a shield law: improving whistle-blower laws to protect better people who report illegal or unethical actions to the media; vastly reducing the number of government secrets to making "leaking" less attractive or necessary; changing legal strategy to focus on protecting the anonymity of sources instead of the rights of journalists to keep secrets, and more widespread and intelligent use of encrypted applications and software could all improve the security of journalistic sources. Because of the complexity of amending multiple whistle-blower protection laws and changing the government's document classification system, the best solution is to persuade news organisations to change legal tactics and use better encryption technology.

14.0 INTRODUCTION
In today's digital-first world, every click, search, and scroll you make contributes to something much larger than you can see, a vast pool of digital information called Big Data. From online shopping and food delivery to watching reels and sharing memes, everything you do online leaves behind data trails. Now imagine billions of such trails being collected and analysed every second, that's Big Data at work!

But what does this mean for brands? For any brand to succeed today, knowing its audience deeply is crucial. Gone are the days when companies relied only on intuition or simple surveys. Today's brands listen to their customers through data, understanding what they buy, when they buy, how they feel, and what they expect next. This deep understanding, powered by Big Data, helps brands make smarter decisions, build stronger identities, and maintain meaningful relationships with their customers. This unit takes you behind the screens of modern branding to explore how insights drawn from Big Data are quietly shaping everything you see online: the ads you notice, the recommendations you get, and even the conversations brands start. You will learn how data fuels creativity, strategy, and reputation management in the digital ecosystem. And, we'll also look at the fine line between smart data use and misuse, privacy, ethics, and the evolving laws that protect you as a digital citizen. By the end, you'll appreciate data not just as a tool, but as a powerful storyteller in brand communication.
14.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After completing this Unit, you will be able to: * Define and explain the concept, characteristics, and scope of Big Data in the context of digital branding and communication. * Analyse how Big Data helps in understanding consumer behaviour and shaping brand strategies through data-driven insights. * Evaluate the ethical, legal, and professional implications of using Big Data for branding and digital public relations.
14.2 UNDERSTANDING BIG DATA
If you've ever wondered how Netflix seems to know exactly what you'd like to watch next or how Amazon recommends products you didn't even realise you needed, the answer lies in Big Data. Every online action you take: a "like," a "share," a "view," or even the time you spend on a post, contributes to a growing pool of data that tells stories about your habits, choices, and preferences. Big Data is more than just "a lot of data." It's a powerful collection of large, complex, and dynamic data sets that cannot be managed using traditional tools or manual analysis. For brands and communication professionals, Big Data acts like a treasure chest filled with clues about audiences, what they think, what they do, and what influences them.
14.2.1 Definition and Characteristics of Big Data
There are many definitions of Big Data, but one of the most widely accepted is given by Gartner: "Big Data is high-volume, high-velocity, and high-variety information assets that demand cost- effective, innovative forms of information processing for enhanced insight and decision-making." Simply put, Big Data refers to huge amounts of structured and unstructured data generated from digital activities: social media interactions, search queries, online purchases, GPS tracking, app usage, and more. In media and communication, this data helps us understand audience behaviour and predict what kind of messages or campaigns will work best. For instance:

* When you scroll through Instagram, the app tracks what you pause to see, giving marketers clues about your interests. * News websites analyse which stories get the most clicks to decide what topics readers prefer. * Streaming platforms use your watch history to personalise recommendations. What makes Big Data unique is not just its size but its speed, diversity, and usefulness. That's where the concept of the 5 Vs of Big Data comes in.
14.2.2 The 5 Vs of Big Data
To understand how Big Data operates, let's break it down into five defining dimensions often called the 5 Vs:
1. Volume: This refers to the enormous quantity of data being generated every second. Think of
millions of YouTube views, tweets, or Google searches happening simultaneously. For instance, every minute, Indians upload thousands of Instagram reels generating a massive volume of user- generated content.
2. Velocity: This is the speed at which new data is created and shared. In the digital world,
information travels instantly. For brands, this means that trends, customer feedback, and public opinion can shift within hours.
3. Variety: Data comes in many forms: texts, videos, photos, emojis, tweets, comments, and even
voice notes. The diversity of data allows brands to understand emotions, tone, and intent; not just facts and numbers.
4. Veracity: Not all data is accurate or reliable. Veracity deals with data quality, ensuring that
what you analyse reflects real consumer behaviour, not fake or misleading inputs. For example, bots or fake accounts can distort analytics on social media.
5. Value: Ultimately, all the data in the world is meaningless unless it provides value. The real
strength of Big Data lies in turning raw information into actionable insights. Brands use analytics to extract meaningful patterns that guide their marketing strategies. These 5 Vs help us see Big Data not as a messy flood of information but as an organised system that can reveal patterns, relationships, and predictions if we know how to interpret it.
14.2.3 Importance of Big Data in Media and Communication
The media and communication industry thrives on understanding people, what they watch, read, share, and talk about. Big Data gives professionals a magnifying glass into these audience behaviours. It helps them: * Identify trends in real time (like viral hashtags or breaking stories). * Measure audience engagement with precision (likes, shares, dwell time). * Design targeted messages for specific groups of people rather than "one-size-fits-all" campaigns. * Evaluate campaign performance instantly, seeing what's working and what needs improvement. Let's understand with an example. During the 2023 ICC Cricket World Cup, brands like Dunzo and CRED used Big Data analytics to track conversations on X (formerly Twitter) and Instagram. They could spot trending memes, fan emotions, and match reactions to release quick, witty social media

responses that went viral within minutes. That's Big Data in action, fast, responsive, and insight- driven communication. For public relations professionals, Big Data allows listening at scale, tracking what people say about a brand across thousands of online spaces. Whether it's a new product launch or a controversy, PR teams use data to manage reputation and craft the right messaging. Thus, Big Data is the new currency of communication. It helps brands move from guesswork to evidence-based storytelling, building stronger and more personal connections with audiences. Activity 1 Find and Reflect: Think of a brand you follow on social media (like Nykaa, Zomato, or Swiggy). Observe its posts for a week. Now ask yourself: * What kind of content gets the most engagement (likes, shares, comments)? * What might this data tell the brand about its audience? Write your reflections in 100-150 words.
14.3 BIG DATA AND CONSUMER INSIGHTS
Imagine standing in a crowded shopping mall, thousands of people around you, each with their own choices, habits, and moods. Now imagine you could "see" what each person wants to buy, how they decide, and what makes them pick one brand over another. That's exactly what Big Data enables brands to do: digitally. In today's world, where most interactions happen online, understanding consumer behaviour is no longer guesswork. Every like, click, search, and purchase creates a data point that tells a story. By collecting and analysing this information, brands can draw consumer insights, deep understandings about what people value, how they think, and how they make decisions. These insights are what turn marketing into meaningful communication.
14.3.1 How Data Reflects Consumer Behaviour
Consumer behaviour is shaped by a mix of emotions, habits, social influences, and personal needs. Big Data helps marketers decode these patterns by turning online activities into meaningful signals. For example: * When a user searches for "eco-friendly detergents," it reflects their environmental concern. * When someone repeatedly watches travel vlogs, it indicates an aspiration for exploration. * When thousands of users order biryani on Sunday nights through food apps, it signals a cultural pattern. Brands collect such data through multiple sources: social media interactions, e-commerce platforms, customer feedback forms, web cookies, and app analytics. These datasets, when analysed together, help companies understand the "why" behind the "what." Sugar Cosmetic, the beauty and wellness brand, uses consumer browsing and buying data to recommend personalised product bundles. If a customer frequently checks skincare content and reviews, Sugar highlights new serums or organic products in that category. This data-backed

recommendation not only boosts sales but also enhances customer satisfaction by giving users exactly what they want. So now you get it, Big Data makes it possible for brands to move from mass communication to micro communication, talking to individuals, not just audiences.
14.3.2 Data Analytics and Market Segmentation
Once data is collected, the next step is to make sense of it and that's where data analytics comes in. Data analytics is like a microscope that helps brands observe patterns within large numbers. Through analytics, marketers can segment their audience, that is, divide them into smaller, meaningful groups based on shared traits such as age, interests, location, or behaviour. For instance: * Netflix divides its audience based on genres they watch most: thriller lovers, comedy fans, or documentary viewers. * E-commerce platforms like Ajio or Myntra use purchase history and browsing behaviour to create categories like "bargain seekers," "fashion trend followers," or "festival shoppers." By identifying such segments, brands can design customised messages and personalised offers that appeal to each group differently. Traditional marketing segmentation relied on surveys or focus groups, which gave limited insights. Big Data analytics, however, analyses millions of digital footprints in real time. This enables dynamic segmentation, where consumer groups can change or evolve as new data comes in. For PR professionals, this means that media outreach and influencer collaborations can be tailored to each audience type, ensuring that the right message reaches the right people at the right moment.
14.3.3 Predictive Analytics and Trend Forecasting
Wouldn't it be amazing if brands could predict what consumers are going to want next month or next season? That's exactly what predictive analytics does. Predictive analytics uses algorithms and historical data to forecast future trends. It looks at past behaviour patterns to anticipate what might happen next. For example: * During festive seasons like Diwali, e-commerce giants such as Amazon India and Flipkart use predictive analytics to forecast product demand stocking up on categories likely to see higher sales. * Streaming platforms like Spotify and Gaana predict what kind of music will trend based on current listening patterns and regional preferences. * PR professionals use predictive analytics to monitor social media chatter and foresee possible reputation risks or crises before they escalate. These insights allow brands to prepare marketing strategies in advance and stay ahead of competitors. In a fast-moving digital world, being predictive rather than reactive gives brands a huge advantage. At the same time, predictive analytics helps brands build emotional connections. If data suggests that consumers are becoming more health-conscious or sustainability-focused, a brand can craft communication around those evolving values showing empathy and relevance.

In this way, Big Data not only supports business goals but also helps brands stay in tune with social change. Check Your Progress: 1 Note: a) Use the spaces given below for your answers. b) Check your answer with those given at the end of the unit.

14.4 BIG DATA IN BRAND MANAGEMENT
In today's digital marketplace, brand management is no longer just about creativity or intuition. It is about decisions guided by data. Big Data has transformed the way brands plan, communicate, and grow. It tells brands who their audiences are, what they want, and how to reach them most effectively. From small start-ups to large corporations, every successful brand today uses data as a compass to guide its direction, measure performance, and adjust its strategy in real time. In this section, we will explore how data helps in shaping brand strategy, enhancing customer experiences, and building loyalty through personalised communication.
14.4.1 Data-Driven Brand Strategies
A brand strategy defines what a brand stands for and how it wants to be perceived by its audience. Traditionally, brand managers relied on intuition, market surveys, and advertising feedback. But with Big Data, they can make decisions based on real-time insights rather than assumptions. Data-driven brand strategies are built on three key pillars:
1. Understanding the audience deeply: using analytics to know who your customers are, what
they value, and how they behave online.
2. Measuring brand performance: tracking engagement metrics, sentiment scores, and
conversion rates to understand how people feel about your brand.
3. Optimising campaigns continuously: testing, analysing, and improving based on data feedback
rather than waiting for post-campaign reports.

For example, when a brand launches a new product, Big Data allows it to track reactions instantly across multiple platforms: social media mentions, website traffic, reviews, and even chat queries. If negative comments appear, the brand can act immediately, addressing issues before they escalate. A good case is Swiggy's data-driven marketing. Swiggy analyses user data to determine eating habits, time preferences, and even regional food choices. This data guides their promotional strategy, showing breakfast offers in the morning, snack deals in the evening, and biryani combos on weekends. Each communication is timely and relevant, reinforcing the brand's promise of convenience and satisfaction. Through such strategies, Big Data enables brands to stay agile, responsive, and deeply connected with consumer expectations.
14.4.2 Personalisation and Customer Experience
If you think about the brands you love most, chances are they make you feel seen and understood. That's what personalisation does. It transforms customer experience from generic to meaningful. Big Data is at the heart of this shift. By analysing browsing patterns, purchase history, location, and even sentiment, brands can tailor messages that feel personal. For instance: * Blinkit shows "Recommended for You" products based on past browsing and purchase behaviour. * Zomato sends push notifications around lunchtime or dinner hours, using your order history to suggest dishes you love. * YouTube creates personalised thumbnails and recommendations, ensuring no two users see the same homepage. This level of personalisation is only possible because of Big Data. Behind every "You might also like..." suggestion is an algorithm trained on thousands of data points. But personalisation isn't just about sales. It's also about emotional connection. When customers feel that a brand "gets" them, loyalty grows naturally. A user who receives relevant suggestions, timely reminders, and helpful responses is more likely to trust the brand. However, with personalisation comes responsibility. Brands must respect privacy and use data ethically. Many companies now highlight their data protection policies and offer users control over what data is collected. This transparency enhances trust, which is an essential element of long-term brand success.
14.4.3 Case Studies: Indian Brands Using Data
Let's now look at some brands that prudently use Big Data in their brand management practices.
1. BigBasket
BigBasket leverages Big Data to forecast demand, manage inventory, and personalise user recommendations. By studying customer purchase cycles--such as when households restock essentials--it predicts future orders and suggests relevant add-ons. During festive seasons, data analytics helps the brand anticipate surges in specific product categories, ensuring smoother supply- chain management.
2. Ola Cabs
Ola uses real-time data analytics to optimise ride allocation, pricing, and driver incentives. The app analyses traffic conditions, location demand, and customer feedback to minimise waiting time and

improve service reliability. Its surge-pricing algorithm, based on predictive data modeling, helps balance demand and supply efficiently--especially during events, festivals, or bad weather.
3. Amazon India
Amazon's recommendation engine is a textbook example of Big Data in action. The brand analyses every customer's past behaviour--searches, purchases, ratings, and even browsing duration--to suggest what they're most likely to buy next. This creates a seamless, personalised shopping experience that feels intuitive.
4. Plum Goodness
Plum Goodness, a vegan beauty and skincare brand, uses data insights from its e-commerce platforms and social media engagement to track emerging beauty trends. It analyses product reviews, search queries, and influencer content performance to fine-tune marketing messages and product development. Data-driven insights also guide its decisions on new product launches and inventory management. These examples show that Big Data is not limited to large corporations; even home-grown Indian brands are using it creatively to connect, engage, and grow. By now, you can see how Big Data is not just about technology or analytics; it's about creating experiences that matter. When used thoughtfully, data gives brands the power to be more human, understanding emotions, anticipating needs, and building trust that lasts.
14.5 BIG DATA AND DIGITAL PUBLIC RELATIONS
In the age of digital media, public relations (PR) has moved far beyond press releases and newspaper clippings. Today, conversations about brands unfold across millions of online spaces from tweets and blogs to YouTube comments and review sites. Managing a brand's reputation in this complex digital environment requires more than human intuition, it demands data intelligence. Big Data helps PR professionals listen, analyse, and act with speed and precision. Let's explore how Big Data is shaping two major PR functions -- sentiment analysis and crisis communication.
14.5.1 Sentiment Analysis and Online Reputation Management
Every post, tweet, comment, or review about a brand contributes to its digital reputation. With Big Data tools, PR professionals can now track these conversations in real time and decode how people feel about the brand -- whether positive, negative, or neutral. This process is called sentiment analysis. Sentiment analysis uses natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning to scan vast volumes of text and categorise opinions. For example: * If many users say "Love the new packaging by MamaEarth!", the algorithm marks it as positive sentiment. * If others post "Delivery delays ruined my Zepto experience," it flags negative sentiment. * Mixed or uncertain comments get labelled as neutral. This continuous analysis forms the foundation of Online Reputation Management (ORM). It helps PR professionals:
1. Measure public mood - knowing whether the sentiment is improving or declining.

2. Identify influencers and critics - recognising who shapes public opinion most.
3. Respond strategically - thanking satisfied customers or addressing complaints before they
escalate. For instance, Uber and Cred actively monitor Twitter, Reddit, and Instagram for customer feedback. When a negative experience trends, their PR teams respond within minutes, often with humour or empathy -- turning potential backlash into brand goodwill. Big Data tools like Brandwatch, Talkwalker, Sprinklr, and Hootsuite Insights make this possible. They visualise data on dashboards showing spikes in mentions, trending keywords, and sentiment ratios -- giving PR managers a "pulse" of public perception at any moment.
14.5.2 Real-Time Feedback and Crisis Communication
Crises can strike suddenly -- a product recall, data breach, insensitive ad, or viral complaint. In such moments, speed and accuracy of response determine whether a brand's image survives or collapses. Big Data analytics provides real-time feedback, enabling PR teams to act fast and with context. For example, if a negative hashtag starts trending, PR teams can: * Track its origin -- where and when it began. * Identify key amplifiers -- who is making it viral. * Analyse engagement velocity -- how fast it's spreading. * Prepare data-backed statements and FAQs to control misinformation. A well-known case is when Maggi noodles faced a major safety controversy in India in 2015. Although the brand was temporarily banned, Nestle used continuous monitoring of social media data to understand consumer emotions, rebuild trust, and plan a comeback campaign once the product returned. Similarly, during the COVID-19 pandemic, several companies, from airlines to e-commerce platforms, used data analytics to track customer sentiment about safety measures, refund policies, and delivery reliability. The insights helped them adjust their messaging and reassure anxious customers. Today, many PR teams rely on AI-based dashboards that alert them instantly when brand mentions spike unusually = often the first sign of a brewing issue. This predictive function allows brands to move from reactive to proactive crisis management. Beyond crisis control, Big Data also helps in strategic storytelling. By understanding what people are already talking about, PR professionals can craft campaigns that resonate emotionally and socially. For instance, Sirona's campaigns during Women's Day or Dream 11's IPL-based humour posts are rooted in social media trend data, showing how insights can drive positive engagement as well. Big Data has revolutionised PR by turning the internet's chaos into meaningful intelligence. It enables professionals to listen better, understand faster, and respond smarter. Whether it's managing a crisis, protecting reputation, or simply knowing what customers feel -- data ensures that PR strategies are grounded in truth, not guesswork. As media options grow more complex, tomorrow's PR professionals must become fluent in data interpretation -- blending the heart of communication with the precision of analytics.
