10.5.2 Youth Empowerment and Participatory Politics
Young people who mainly hail from marginalised communities tend to utilise the online platform for their improvements, voice the concerns of their respective community issues and explore diverse sets of knowledge. These explorations for their individual as well as community welfare over a period of time leads to more attachment with the public causes and strengthens the interest of young people towards the upliftments of disadvantaged sections of the society. The digital platform provides horizontal level of communication among its members and all these interactions are in the non-hierarchical category. It helps the young people to access, discuss, share and mobilise resources and people for a change in their community or they are motivated to expect an action and reaction within the broader social context. These motivated engagements with the digital media platform tends to provide a positive change within individuals as well as results better expected outcomes for their community as a whole. Based on a study on online racial discrimination in academic motivation published in 2015 by Tynes BM et al. it was discovered that when young people seek political information or express political voice online, they may expose themselves to stereotypes and hate speech, which can have a negative impact on well-being particularly for the minority youth. However, overall studies of media used by politically active youth reveal that many are aware of the potential consequences of online political expression and navigate those risks in varied ways. The Occupy movement stopping the Stop Online Piracy Act (SOPA) and the power of six million users of change.org are only two among many examples of how new media has impacted politics in the USA, especially as politics that is practised among young people. The use of social media by the Obama campaign in 2008 helped to produce record turnout, especially among young Blacks and Latinos. In the 2012 elections, all those involved in campaigns were relying more heavily on social media than ever before. The intersection of youth, new media, and politics is not exclusively a story from the United States. The recent movements from Tunisia to Egypt to Russia indicate that the significance of new media's impact on political expression is international in its scope. To consider the impact of new media on the political and civic behaviour of young people, The MacArthur Research Network on Youth and Participatory Politics (YPP) developed and fielded one of the first large-scale, nationally representative studies of new media and politics among young people. The two principal researchers for the survey component of the YPP, Cathy J. Cohen of the University of Chicago and Joseph Kahne of Mills College,

oversaw a research team that surveyed nearly 3,000 respondents between Participatory Online Media the ages of 15 and 25 years of age. Unlike any prior study of youth and new media, this study included large numbers of Black, Latino, and Asian American respondents, which allowed for unique and powerful statistical comparisons across race with a focus on young people. The YPP study findings suggest that fundamental changes in political expectations and practices may be occurring-- especially among the youth. The analysis of the data collected reveals that youth are taking advantage of an expanded set of participatory practices in the political realm in ways that amplify their voice and sometimes their influence, thus increasing the ways in which young people participate in political life. The YPP researchers label this expanded set of opportunities and actions as participatory politics. While the topic of new media and youth politics has garnered lots of attention from pundits, politicians, and journalists, these reports often focus on anecdotal or single-case examples of a protest mobilisation where new media played an important role. To date, there has been limited opportunity and data available to explore the relationship between new media and the political action of young people in a more comprehensive manner. This new survey data provides a strong basis for five major findings, summarised as follows:
1. Large proportions of young people across racial and ethnic groups
have access to the Internet and use online social media regularly to stay connected with their family and friends and pursue interests and hobbies.
2. Participatory politics is an essential dimension of politics.
3. Participatory politics is an addition to an individual's engagement
rather than an alternative to other political activities.
4. Participatory politics are equitably distributed across different racial
and ethnic groups.
5. Youth get news through participatory channels but believe they would
benefit from learning how to judge the credibility of what they find online. Participatory politics is a significant dimension of the political life of young people giving them greater control, voice, and potential influence over the issues that matter most in their lives. New media has the potential to facilitate equitable distribution of political participation among young people from different racial and ethnic groups. Participatory politics is generally equitably distributed across different racial and ethnic groups. Youth now consume a great deal of news through participatory channels. 10.6 ROLE OF SOCIAL MEDIA IN ONLINE
PARTICIPATORY COMMUNICATION
Social media applications, including social networking sites, blogs, podcasts and content shares, have been used to facilitate a participatory cultural experience by several institutions. Participatory culture is a term that is often used for designating the involvement of users, audiences, consumers and fans in the creation of culture and content. Many scholars actively believe that culture and society have become more democratic with the users and the audiences creating and producing their own content rather than being mere passive receivers. Examples are the collaborative editing of an article on Wikipedia, the uploading of images onto Facebook, the uploading of videos onto YouTube and the creation of short messages on Twitter. It enables more and more people to become media producers and distributors as well as consumers. Traditional media institutions have failed in providing online spaces to foster public speach and interactions among citizens. Citizens, in their daily use of social media, encounter different identities and political positions, which challenge their own perceptions and attitudes towards 'the political'. Secondly, it will present how social media become spaces where debate spreads more quickly than in online spaces. By doing so, social networks are contributing to challenging one of the former hegemonies of traditional media institutions viz. the conception of news media as the main actors that enhance debate among citizens, selecting the issues of the day and facilitating current affairs content through which citizens can comment and debate. However, euphoria about the potential for social networks to reshape the media sphere should be limited. According to Jenkins, an American media scholar, the main characteristic of "social media"/"web 2.0" is that they are spreadable media (Jenkins, Li, Krauskopf and Green 2009): "Consumers play an active role in 'spreading' content [. . .] Consumers in this model are [. . .] grassroots advocates for materials which are personally and socially meaningful to them" (Jenkins et al. 2009). Spreadable media are based on the logic "if it doesn't spread, it's dead" (Jenkins, Ford and Green 2013) and involve audiences that "actively" shape "media flows" so that culture becomes "far more participatory." According to Jenkins, social media is also an expression of participatory culture. Jenkins defines participatory culture as culture "in which fans and other consumers are invited to actively participate in the creation and circulation of new content" (Jenkins 2008). It also involves "participants who interact with each other" (Jenkins 2008). Participation involves, for Jenkins, "new forms of participation and collaboration" (Jenkins 2008). Jenkins points out, based on Pierre Levy (1997), that those who engage in "participatory culture" pool resources and combine skills so that collective

intelligence emerges as "an alternative source of media power" (Jenkins Participatory Online Media
2008) .
The online space is both a space of participation on the one hand and also a space for commodification. Convergence is both a top-down corporate- driven process and a bottom-up consumer-driven process. There is no doubt that Web 2.0 users are creative when they generate and diffuse user- generated content. However, the question is also how many Web 2.0 users are active and what degree of activity and creativity do their practices have. Creativity is a force that enables Internet prosumer commodification, the commodification and exploitation of the users' activities and the data they generate. Creativity is not outside or alongside exploitation on web 2.0; it is at its very foundation. Jenkins (2008) argues that YouTube is a site "for the production and distribution of grassroots media" and that on YouTube "participation occurs at three distinct levels [. . .] - those of production, selection, and distribution" (Jenkins 2008). Because Google owns YouTube hence, that the revenues that are accumulated with online advertising on YouTube do not belong to the immediate content producers, but the shareholders of Google. Jenkins here neglects ownership as a central aspect of participation. The most popular YouTube videos stem from global multimedia corporations like Universal, Sony and Walt Disney. Google and Facebook are based on targeted advertising models and a commercial culture, which results in enormous profits for these companies. In the corporate social media sphere, attention is unequally distributed: big companies, celebrities and well-known political actors enjoy attention advantages and the most active prosumers come from the young, educated middle class. Jenkins (2008) celebrates blogs as a "means for their participants to express their distrust of the news media and their discontent with politics as usual," "potentially increasing cultural diversity and lowering barriers in cultural participation," "expanding the range of perspectives," as "grassroots intermediaries" that ensure "that everyone has a chance to be heard" (Jenkins 2006). He forgets the lack of visibility in the public sphere of most political blogs. Political blogs have hardly been able to reach the large numbers of readers of the websites of big corporates like CNN and The New York Times. 10.7 EXPERIMENTS/STORIES FROM INDIA
When CNN introduced the 24x7 news TV in 1981, the power of 'live' reporting from the battlefield rendered audiences speechless, mesmerised, glued in front of their TV screens. Today web video is everywhere. Breaking news is catapulted into cyberspace through Twitter or Facebook by the random witness-turned-reporter who uses his/her smartphone and captures the 'exclusive' story. People love being part of the innovation game. Young audiences have become more important and influential than ever before. It is as if they are born with an innate ability for text messaging, 'iPodding', gaming and multi-tasking on multiple platforms. They are tech-savvy, and they are active players, influencers, and decision-makers. The option to share content freely on sites like YouTube and peer-to-peer networks like BitTorrent means that consumers can bypass official media distribution channels, eroding media companies' traditional revenue streams of ad impressions and purchasing or subscription fee. It is essential to begin by understanding various social media sites and the ways they can enhance the work journalists do. A regular perusal of sites like 10000words.net and savethemedia.com is a great way to do this. However, it is also essential that we move beyond acquainting ourselves with this world and figure out how to "use" it for journalism, which requires understanding its nature and impact on participants and public life? What needs our attention is how we are going to play roles that bring journalistic values into this vast social media territory. According to the Internet and Mobile Association of India (IAMAI) report, the number of social media users in urban India had reached 400 million by December 2019. Nearly three out of four of all active internet users in urban India use social media.

Hence, in order to capitalise on the use of mobile phone and Internet for Participatory Online Media mobilising communities in a participatory manner, there are organisations in India who are working with the communities, youth and children. * CGNet Swara is a platform to discuss issues related to the Central Gondwana region in India. (http://cgnetswara.org/) * Gaon connection is Indian rural media platform where the attempt is to sustain the rural journalism through online spaces (https://www. gaonconnection.com/) * Radio Brahmaputra is the only grassroots community radio of the Northeastern region located in Dibrugarh, Assam. * Project CHIME (Children in Media Experiments) is the first participatory video initiative from Northeast India from Shillong, Meghalaya. Social networks are contributing to challenging one of the former hegemonies of traditional media institutions viz. the conception of news media as the main actor that enhance debate among citizens, selecting the issues of the day and facilitating current affairs content through which citizens can comment and debate.

11.0 INTRODUCTION
There are billions of Internet users, and for any given topics/issues we may find millions of users who are interested in it. A good number of interested users might want to go beyond accessing the information on their interested topics/issues, mainly they are interested in associating themselves with a cause. Some of them may be motivated enough to go for offline demonstrations to impress upon the concerned authorities or groups or individuals to change the situation or implementation of the new policy. Many of the like-minded Internet users simply give their support by changing their 'status' in social media accounts in solidarity with the groups in which they are associated. These online/offline actions for a cause/change using any tools of digital platforms are the focus of this Unit - Online Activism. At the very outset, let us understand this Unit with the definition of online activism and in particular the different associated terms - like cyberactivism, Internet activism or broadly speaking media activism. The Unit would further discuss the historiography and the development of online activism. It would introduce you to different cases from across the world, which became the guiding force for online activism. In doing so, the reference to the Indian perspective would also be discussed. A distinction needs to be made

India's Experience with the between offline and online activism. Later on, we would like to conclude Internet by discussing how this activism is taking shape in the present century with the development of information technology and changing socio-politico- economic scenario. Through the Unit, you would get a broader outlook on the concept of online activism and its different aspects.
11.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After reading this Unit, the you will be able to: * understand the concept of online activism; * explore the historiography of activism worked at different times and particularly after the advent of the Internet and new media; * identify the characteristics, tools, and significance of online activism; * distinguish between offline and online activism and different types of online activism; and * describe some of the cases related to online activism in the global as well as Indian context.
11.2 UNDERSTANDING ONLINE ACTIVISM
Let us first discuss the definition of online activism, and then we would understand the views given by different scholars on this phenomenon.
11.2.1 Definition
The term online activism is the offshoot of media activism which has always been part of mainstream media and citizen journalism. Digital activism, also known as cyberactivism, is a form of activism that uses the Internet and digital media as crucial platforms for mass mobilisation and political action. Apart from the news and stories put forth for public discussion and decision making, there are times when the media plays an active role in deliberately bringing some stories which are socially relevant which is defined as media activism. The public comes out and supports that issue, but otherwise, it usually is not given adequate importance by the other social institutions. Thus, media apart from working as a watchdog also turns into the role of an activist raising voice for specific issues. Another term, as mentioned earlier, citizen journalism is the concept where the ordinary public acts as the eyes and the ears of the media organisations. Moreover, this common public, the citizens, address specific issues of their locality and make media contents which they may send to the media organisations for telecast or be uploaded onto new media platforms. Based on the news values of relevance, timeliness, and other factors, media organisations may choose to show that content to the public. These citizen journalists might also independently start their online channels on social media platforms. Earlier in the case of print media, there were sections, which still exist, as 'letters to the editor' where the readers would bring to the notice of the newspaper, specific issues of their locality which were deemed as an essential issue.

Now with the advent of new media and the Internet, the citizens/users have Online Activism got the opportunity to speak on the issues relevant to them. Furthermore, everyone is connected through the networked world. This not only gives amplification to the voice but also makes it prominent to be heard by the policymakers, government, judiciary, other law enforcement agencies, and the world watchdogs and official bodies. In this networked world, especially, with the advent of Web 2.0 and the emergence of different social networking sites, the impact of online activism has gained prominence. Nevertheless, online activism has its own pros and cons, which we will discuss later. However, mostly the voices are put on the platforms which are further amplified to be heard by the world connected by the network.
11.2.2 Perspectives on Online Activism
Guobin Yang (2009) explains that "In online activism, most common forms include online petitions, the hosting of campaign websites, and large-scale verbal protests." He further elaborates that "The most radical form is the hacking of websites. These forms of contention may be found in blogs, Internet bulletin boards, online communities, and podcasts and YouTube- type websites." Graham Meikle (2014) has defined Internet Activism as "Political uses of networked computers that attempt to effect social or cultural change in the offline world: a politics which can use the graphical and multimedia capabilities of the web as well as text-based applications such as email." Further, Allen Rusbridger, the former editor of The Guardian has defined the characteristics of new media by stating that this technology has brought a new model of transmission of information, messages, and news compared to the traditional gatekeeping model/top-to-bottom approach of news flow. Rusbridger explains that with this new technology, now the bottom-to-top approach would come where news and its content would be directed by the audience what they want to see and the issues they want to address. He gave the example of The Guardian, where first the news provider floats an issue for the netizens to react and give their responses. Accordingly, then the newspaper takes up that issue for transmission. So, there comes an almost opposite model from top-to-bottom to a bottom-up approach. Manuel Castells (2015) has defined networked communication as mass- self communication. It is mass communication because it processes messages from many-to-many, with the potential of reaching a multiplicity of receivers, and of connecting to endless networks that transmit digitised information around the neighbourhood or around the world. It is self- communication because the production of the message is autonomously decided by the sender, the designation of the receiver is self-directed, and the retrieval of messages from the networks of communication is self-selected. Mass self-communication is based on horizontal networks of interactive communication that, by and large, are difficult to control by governments or corporations.

11.3 ACTIVISM AND SOCIAL MOVEMENTS
As you are aware that activism as a concept is not a new phenomenon. It had existed ever since the world started when somebody stood up to encounter the ruling and authoritative force trying to set rules or making decisions that do not go well with the common people. In the modern sense, we can find a lot many examples where people stood for what they believed and challenged those in power to bring about change. We can see the civil rights movement in the USA, the French revolution, the Russian revolution, the Hippie movement throughout the world, the feminist movement, and many others. In the context of India, in modern history, we can find the Santhal rebellion, the first struggle for India's independence, and Mahatma Gandhi's non- violence movement. Ambedkar's movement leading the Dalits was a social-political movement, and the JP Movement was a youth movement for bringing societal and political change. The Chipko movement was started by a group of women and Chandi Prasad Bhatt to protect trees and the environment. After the 1960s (post-industrial economy), the new social movements came into existence. These mostly catered to issues not related to economic well-being but human rights. There are instances of local people and tribes who also stood against the corporate and government projects. One can find a lot many socio-economic- politico and environmental issues where people protested by coming on the streets and showed solidarity for the movement by different measures either by funding or physical support.
11.3.1 Impact of Internet Activism
With the advent of new media and particularly social media and mobile revolution in India, the protests and their expression have changed. People shifted from grass-roots activism to virtual activism, and in most cases, it was the combination of two. Whether such activism has helped or not, however, this needs to be understood and discussed. Also in the clutter of social media content with no authority or gatekeeper, it is not clear who is ultimately going to set the tone to the communication around any given area/topic; whether the issues discussed are the real issues; whether any positive change has resulted or not. These perspectives need to be pointed out. In this context, the Internet has become an essential tool

for raising the voice, while at the same time, it causes discord, chaos, and Online Activism hostility among the public. Manuel Castells (2015) has described the whole phenomenon as individuals expressing their views which are against the government and corporations leading to mass communication in the face of fear and despair leading towards hope. This networked society is governed by the programmers and switchers. 11.4 TECHNOLOGY AND ACTIVISM/SOCIAL
MOVEMENTS
Increasing accessibility and the ability to communicate with thousands of citizens instantaneously has made the Internet, a tool of choice for individuals or organisations looking to spread a social message far and wide. Independent activists, the world over, are using the Internet and digital tools to build their community, connect with other like-minded people outside their physical surroundings as well as the lobby, raise funds, and organise events. Simply put, digital activism is where digital tools (the Internet, mobile phones, social media, etc.) are used towards bringing about social and/or political change. Digitalisation started to change with the advent of web 2.0 and the dot com boom. The introduction and rapid growth of social media platforms such as Facebook and Twitter post-2004 have helped digital activism to the point where entire campaigns can now be run online with a broad reach. Many scholars argue that digital tools alone do not suffice when it comes to galvanising people towards creating change. According to the online activism think tank Meta-Activism Project, digital activism should serve six key functions: shaping public opinion; planning an action; protecting activists; sharing a call to action; taking action digitally, and transfer of resources. Let us explore these six key functions of online activism in brief details.
1. Shaping Public Opinion: Usually, the mainstream media sets the
agenda for society. By this method, they tend to deliberately ignore various issues due to their professional and business-centric nature of their operations. In this context, people who are aggrieved and oppressed mobilise constant and continuous discussion over the various online platforms, mainly through social media. According to the Meta-Activism project, "Social media is different because the means of information transmission also creates collective identity and collective grievance creates optimism."

India's Experience with the 2. Planning an Action: Changing public opinion and creating new Internet perspectives on any given issues or circumstances is quite possible through social media, the reason is that in the social media platform every individual is in touch with almost everyone participating in it. Hence many-to-many communication facilitates a collective identity, and that facilitates a changing public perception and opinion. Once public opinion gains momentum, it needs to be translated into action in the ground - in the offline environment. An effective planning process is required to carry out an action to take it forward to the collective identity and public opinion. For effective planning of a social movement, a small group of strategists is sufficient, unlike the mass members required for public opinion formation.
3. Protecting Activists: Mobilising public opinion against powerful
groups is not an easy way, it brings its own consequences. Incidentally, the Internet provides ample scope for many activists to work/operate anonymously - pseudonyms or anonymous names are popular deceptive methods adopted by many activists in order to escape the wrath of powerful groups. However, the deceptive strategies, are hardly escape the digital footprints.
4. Sharing a Call to Action: Updating "status" or changing "profile"
pictures or similar personal updates in social media, conveys a strong message to intended audiences - it is a low-cost broadcast to mass audiences. Similar to chain reactions, individuals are provoked to continue the stated actions which further spread the messages to various audiences.
5. Taking actions Digitally: Culmination of the first stages of digital
activism lands in taking some concrete steps to make the "voices" are heard. As mentioned earlier about various forms of activism, according to Guobin Yang, signing e-petitions, writing emails, hosting online banners, and similar digital-only tactics to convey the message to the intended audience - here the policymakers or government officials or corporate groups or powerful elites.
6. Transfer of Resources: In order to sustain the first five stages of
digital activism, constant financial support is required. Since some of the social movements engage in innovative ways of crowd funding to seek financial support from like-minded individuals. These six stages of digital activism is a generalised pattern after observing many social movements that are carried out with the significant support of social media. You will find differences and similarities between these six stages if you closely scrutinise any specific digital activism based social movements. Owing to the technological development and availability of smartphones and in-built applications, millions of users can be connected in one platform. Also, there is a limited level of screening/censorship/gatekeeping on this medium until somebody reports to the administration of the service provider of the application. This helps to repress the user's voices uncensored/unedited for the friends and public to respond. This medium also becomes the extension of the public sphere where people can participate in the rational debates expressing their views on topics of public interest. However, sometimes

people burst into an expression of emotion and passion on this platform Online Activism which leads to contention and hate views being propagated. There is a self/social gratification among the audience/users. The users have become now the creators of the content. This content generated by the user generally gratifies their need which not necessarily be based on any rationale. This process comes under the framework of uses and gratification theory.

11.5 CHARACTERISTICS OF ONLINE ACTIVISM
The characteristics of online activism lie in its potential for bringing people together who are separated by time and space to discuss issues of socio- political relevance. Let us discuss all these aspects one by one. i. Formation of public sphere (concept given by Jurgen Habermas): The new media provides a platform where people separated by time and space get a chance to interact on issues of social relevance to form a consensus through rational and critical debates. ii. A large number of people available on one platform. So platform of solidarity and dissent. iii. Can guide public opinion formation. Influential people can air their thoughts, opinions, reactions which may be followed by the followers. iv. Act as a pressure group on government, policymakers, and law- abiding agencies. v. As a social watchdog, people can go 'live' on cases of corruption and ill-treatment. That voice can be amplified by the people.
11.5.1 Types of Online Activism
i Active Online Activism/Ground Change Activism
This form of online activism brings about change at the grass-root level. People's voices take prominence, and public opinion leads to social change. ii. Hacktivism Many attribute it as online extremism where individuals without authorised permission breach the security of a nation, company, banks, or security agencies. This breaching leads to getting unauthorised access to classified documents and sometimes money/bonds. When the same act is done against one's own country, then it is termed as online extremism but if done in favour then called ethical hacking. Online users resort to hacking for different purposes. They are also known as hacktivists (hack + activist) or cyber terrorists. There are instances of the army of one country/terrorist organisation hacking the sites and security sites of other countries. Some enthusiastic hackers went into the government database to show that personal details which are private data of a person uploaded by the government are not secure. Many times people from neighbouring countries hack the sites of each other and put the flag of his/her country to humiliate the other. Online hacking mainly threatens the stability of a country, institutions, etc. and the cordial relations among the two countries.

iii. Passive Activism/ Slacktivism/ Clicktivism Online Activism
Passive activism means when people talk and discuss some issues on different social media platforms, but no real change is visible on the ground level. It is a passive form of resistance where people criticise government decisions, policies, or systems by being at home without facing the real situation and going through its direct effects. There is much criticism for this type of activism. Many attributes that at least communication is going on but many questions its motive; yet there are some instances of it leading to political changes. The main criticism comes about the youth and urban middle class who are using these social media platforms and are tech-savvy. It is said that the middle class is revolution averse. Although they talk about change in the capitalist world, post-LPG (Liberalisation, Privatisation, and Globalisation) of the 1990s but they are not interested in changing the ground reality. iv. Mind Influencers/Alters (Viral Content Production) Many times videos, memes, posts in support of some views are generated to reach larger masses in order to influence their mind/ attitude/behaviour. In such cases, those contents become viral and are consumed by a massive number of people. Here the propagandist views with hidden facts/fake news are shared to serve one's interest/ influence action in a particular context. It is used mainly for malafide intentions and results in negative consequences. v. Cyberbullying/Trolling We all are aware of cyberbullying and trolling in the present world of viral/hashtag culture. Social media not only provides a platform for activism but also allows bullies to target those whom they dislike or they find something which does not go with their taste, culture, ideals, ideology, and beliefs. Troll, in essence, means someone who leaves an intentionally annoying message on the Internet, in order to get attention or cause trouble. Through social media, not only voices can be amplified, but the same voices can be targeted by the people who think contrary to you. On many occasions, this bullying becomes abusive and to such an extent that a person is intentionally trolled for everything they do.
vi. Social-media Campaigning, Virtual Sit-ins
Marcela A. Fuentes talks about virtual sit-ins which are a form of online demonstration in which a networked community gathers on one or several sites to carry out an act of digital dissent. The action is undertaken through a web-based program that sends repetitive requests to the targeted web pages. The protesters' automated 'clickings,' simultaneously enacted from multiple computers around the world, provoke such an excess of traffic that the targeted site's server is unable to handle it. By clogging the bandwidth, the action slows down the site and eventually causes it to shut down.
11.5.2 Tools of Online Activism
With the rapid growth and evolution of technology, the list of tools keep on changing. Some of the existing tools are mentioned below: Websites/Online Petitions: Some websites act as a hub of online activism.

India's Experience with the Here people can communicate about their cause which by default reaches Internet world audience.
Social Networks and Microblogging Sites: Facebook, YouTube, Twitter
and many more have proven beneficial in spreading messages and garnering support. These sites bring the public's attention on a subject that mainstream media might not focus on. Some of the ways adopted for online activism using this tool are Page Likes, Sharing, and Subscription; different ways of showing solidarity and dissent (like changing profile picture or cover photo); cartoons/screenshots/sarcastic comments/status; and live streaming. There are Groups/Forums/Event Pages, here people of the same interest come together and discuss the issues in detail. Also, Twitter's hashtag function (#) allows people to make their tweets available for multi-user conversation. It is facilitated by a keyword or phrase preceded by a hashtag. Blogs: Blogs are an online diary. It is a form of citizen journalism providing an effective means of communication to the masses pertaining to any topic. It has been used in many online campaigns. Mobile Phones and Apps: A UK Uncut activist created a tool, Sukey. Sukey's combination of Google maps and Swiftriver (real-time data verifying service from Ushahidi Inc.) provided an avenue for the protesters to follow the action in the UK. Users could use Sukey on a browser-based tool called 'Roar,' or through SMS service 'Growl.' The Ushahidi software was used to plot activity in disaster zones like earthquakes in Haiti and New Zealand and floods in Australia and the USA. Some other examples are Off-the-Record Messaging (OTR) software and Crabgrass. Web Proxy Servers. Online protesters use proxy servers for avoiding government interventions on online activism. These servers are the intermediaries between a user and a site that protects the user from being identified. Check Your Progress: 2 Note: 1) Use the space below for your answers.

11.6.2 Indian Trends
Some cases from India related to online activism are discussed briefly here. Few prominent cases India Against Corruption, the Nirbhaya case, and the MeToo case, are mentioned below:
India Against Corruption
Due to the support of people from all over India and netizens sharing posts to arrange mass agitation on streets, it forced the government to pass the Lokpal Bill within the stipulated time. This movement was influenced by the Arab Spring.
Nirbhaya Case and Women Issues
In New Delhi in 2012, a heinous crime was committed where a young woman was raped in a moving bus, later she succumbed to death, which led to a burst of public outrage, and people came on the streets against the crime. Social media mainly Facebook and Twitter, built solidarity for the issue. There were protest marches on the streets of New Delhi and around the country. Moreover, a hashtag campaign in the name of #Nirbhaya, #Damini & other names were promoted. People even changed their profile picture into black as a mark of protest. This protest forced the government to frame a new law for the protection of women, and stringent punishment was put in for the heinous crime of rape committed against women. Since this incident, many women related issues have been raised on the online medium following the trend of giving voices to women who do not normally gets adequate space in the mainstream media.
MeToo Campaign
The MeToo campaign is the social media movement where women came out and narrated their stories of sexual harassment and exploitation by the men in power. They challenged the patriarchal structure of the society and publicly humiliated and shamed people who dishonoured them in the past. The 'MeToo Movement' was started by the social activist Tarana Burke in the year 2006. It took centre stage of world glare when the Harvey Weinstein Scandal happened in the USA. In India, this movement picked up when Bollywood actress Tanushree Dutta accused her male co-star. She went on to say that the MeToo campaign would not take shape in India as we do not have a structure supporting women. Also, this incident prompted other women to come out narrating their own #MeToo stories.

11.8 KEYWORDS
Activism: Field-based actionable efforts on specific issues are called activism - environmental activism, climate change activism, political activism, etc. are some of the popular examples. Campaign: It is a series of planned activities to achieve intended objectives. The campaign is actively pursued by a group of people or a group of organisations for more extended periods of time to meet their desired goals. Political parties, non-governmental organisations and civil society members, and groups in specific areas usually undertake campaigns in their respective fields. Social Movements: Large numbers of people take part in a protest for the change or implementation of social change or political issues. Usually, the individuals involved in this kind movements are loosely connected, however recently in the advent of social media, the collaboration made more beneficial to the collective efforts as well as many organisations have got the opportunity to mobilise the public opinion in favour or against the change or implementation of social or political matters. Trending Culture: Any person/issue/event which is popular among the people, mainly social media users. One which everyone talks about.

12.0 INTRODUCTION
Democracy is centred around the ideas of power to the people whereby they decide what the policies which are right and appropriate for them so that their rights can be safeguarded. Digital media has a role to play in ascertaining such democratic freedom to the people and securing their rights. It then becomes essential to understand how digital media can enable a greater democracy by encouraging greater participation of people in it. This Unit covers the aspects of how the Internet is changing and how people are participating in movements for democratic rights, reforms, and freedom. This Unit also includes certain case studies about social media movements that gave rise to greater participation by people in democracies around the

India's Experience with the world that have altered the systems of governance in countries. Social media Internet has brought several people together under a single leadership in ways that could not have been envisaged by mainstream media or political parties. In this Unit, we shall discuss a few global and Indian experiences of digital media and democracy and how these can affect us in making our society more responsible.
12.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After reading this Unit, you will be able to: * discuss the fundamental relationship between democracy and digital media; * elaborate on the different avenues of digital platforms for democratic participation; * explain the users' participation in democracy; * understand various definitions around democracy and digital media; and * draw linkages between elections and digital media.
12.2 UNDERSTANDING CONCEPTS OF DEMOCRACY
According to Susan D. Moeller (2010), 'democracy is a system in which everyone has a voice and all voices are heard.' Further to that Moeller states that democracy is not just a political term that stands for 'power to the many' or 'greater participation' of people as that would merely be a hollow description of the word. The true meaning lies in how and in what ways are the various voices being heard. Thus there is a need for an aggressive and independent 'fourth estate' as that can be a vital and significant tool in making 'democracy' a truly vibrant one with diverse opinions, voices, views, and concerns. However, the fact of whether those concerns will find a proper hearing and will have an impact and effect on policymakers is a subject of debate.
12.2.1 Basics of Democracy
You might have heard about the term democracy is derived from two Latin words- 'Demos' and 'Kratos' where 'demos' means common people of an ancient Greek State and 'Kratos' meanings power. Thus, the 'power of the people' is what democracy truly means. Dahl (1971) identifies seven main criteria that should exist in a country to be called a 'democracy' or a 'polyarchy' (power vested in many). These criteria are: * control over government decisions; * frequent and fair elections; * universal adult suffrage [right to vote]; * right to run for public office; * freedom of expression; * access to alternative sources of information that have not been monopolised by a few; and * freedom of association.

Hence we see that a democracy needs to be vibrant and dynamic with Democracy and Digital Media voices of people being heard. This is possible only when diverse voices are raised through various media platforms, different channels, and sources of information. The Internet seems to be bridging the gap, which seems to have existed for a long time in the field of media. This brings us to the section on what exactly is the interplay between democracy and digital media and what all does it include.
12.2.2 Democracy and Media
Digital media includes all such content and form that uses technology and is coded, modified, and distributed on digital electronic devices and platforms. It includes not just websites of mainstream media organisations but also blogs, Wikis, YouTube and Instagram, etc. These days the microblogging websites are doing valuable work on keeping mainstream media on its toes. However, there are different challenges and numerous goals related to the state of media within a digital landscape. One of the most significant challenges is to keep up with the changing face of modes of production, use, and practices related to online technology. There is a need to strike a balance between theory and practice. The practices mainly include reform or changing policy and legislation around ownership and concentration, or the establishment of grassroots and independent news channels. Another aspect of digital platforms is that it helps you to understand how independent channels are revolutionising and engaging the Internet and masses. 12.3 LINKAGES BETWEEN DEMOCRACY AND
Internet
DIGITAL MEDIA
The media needs to become more accountable in a democracy by holding those in power accountable to the public. They freely question or are at least supposed to ask questions to authorities based on their framing of events. In order to assist in the functioning of a healthy democracy, it becomes imperative that the media itself is free, independent, and accountable. With the proliferation of new voices, the responsibility is on the media of putting information across with accuracy. In this regard, 'digital media' has made sure that such voices have emerged but with what consequence is the larger question. Here we will assess how those diverse voices that find a platform online can be heard with effective outcomes and meanings for elections, political participation, and democracy in general.
12.3.1 Elections and Digital Media
Williams and Delli Carpini (2011) argue that among other things, what is considered "political" has widened with digital media beyond what was set out by traditional media. Another theory that is prominent and that focuses on individual media is agenda-setting theory (McCombs et al., 2013) which tells us those specific political topics are foregrounded in the media and force us to think about them instead of others. It is said that India and China account for one-third of the world's online population. In India, however, Internet penetration is still low, and the use of digital media is heavily skewed towards the elite. The debates around new media and politics have, however, focussed on two broad themes-democracy and the public sphere (Habermas, 1982) and how capitalism skewed politics towards powerful economic elites (Castells, 2011).
12.3.2 Political Parties and New Media
When we study the scenario vis-a-vis political parties, it raises concerns about whether the media contribute to more responsiveness by the government, or the opposite-more elite control? Here one notices that there has been strong collusion between political and economic elites which also indicates that in the Indian media system autonomy is weak. However, the Internet has been a strong force among a small, mostly young and urban population. Although smartphones are yet to reach the majority of the population, online politics is shaped by how smartphone adoption fits into the broader-skewed-media landscape. Most political parties now have thousands of WhatsApp groups and social media accounts to reach a wider group of citizens. However, the reach is limited to the urban elite. Among various political parties, political ideologies arise from the public, and they are articulated within parties and in the media and the contest for legitimacy and power. Even without widespread Internet penetration, new technologies can be vital for politics, and this is illustrated via the use of mobile phones in an Indian election. Online activism increasingly influences politics in recent times, more so because it provides an alternative to entrenched political power and its nexus with the traditional media.

12.3.3 Social Media and Politics Democracy and Digital Media
There has been a meteoric rise in social media platforms and citizen journalism with examples ranging from leaked photos of Abu Ghraib to a cellphone video of Saddam's hanging, the Indian Ocean tsunami of 2004, and London bombings of July 7, 2005. There are pictures clicked by ordinary citizens that are being used by mainstream media to depict a variety of voices which is seen as a measure of 'publicness' (Heikkila & Kunelius, 2002). There are many instances where it can be shown that social media has affected social change in unprecedented ways. These changes are visible in the way politics is done by political parties and how governments are run-both in developed and developing countries. In the recent parliamentary elections in India, it is pointed out that parties were strategically engaging in new and old media to maximise their reach and information was being shared digitally in large numbers which have now become a potent way of political involvement. In a study in Norway it was found that as individual candidates took part in Twitter campaigning individually for themselves and their parties, they were likely to exercise more influence than those who did not take up such online campaigning on the microblogging site (Karlsen & Enjolras, 2016). Valeriani & Vaccari (2016) suggest through a survey study in Germany, Italy, and the United Kingdom that social media serve as a virtual platform to bridge the gap between the political parties and the public and those who are not party- members but are party loyalists engage in online activity to reach out to people. Thus, Chadwick & Stromer-Galley (2016) argue that digital culture is changing how parties reach out to the people telling them about their ideology, social work and election campaign. 12.4 AVENUES OF LINKAGES
This brings us to the section where we will draw linkages between mainstream and alternative media on the online spheres - are these complementary to each other or are they contesting each other for media space vying for audience attention?
12.4.1 Mainstream Media
A lot has been talked about media reform, activism, and resistance on the Internet where such political movements have been presented as networked

India's Experience with the forms of communication at the transnational level (Castells, 2004). However, Internet at another level, these are just tools and technology not more than a plane of interaction. In recent times there is a clamour among mainstream media organisations to vie for online space for their news content. Simultaneously, there is also a trend towards using social media as 'vox pops' within the media dialogues that take place on-screen or in newspapers even as online media are converting into 'multimedia newsrooms'. Social media has created such a competition for the mainstream media that specific progressive mainstream media organisations are struggling to come to terms with blogs, wikis, and other content management systems making it more participatory within the journalism conversations (Gillmor, 2003) and making such audiences as equal partners and collaborators in the news process. Despite such voices one being heard within mainstream media, it is the alternative media which is more participatory and redefines a publicness by altering the nature of journalism so that the facts are determined not by a handful of journalists or reporters or editors in an organisation but by highlighting the discursive, dialogic and deliberative nature of public engagement with the news.
12.4.2 Alternative Media
As we continue to debate whether participatory journalism and traditional journalism collide head-on or complement each other (Lasica, 2003), let us discuss here a few of instances that go on to indicate how the meaning of empowerment and information are being redefined through independent media. Alternative media, on the one hand, makes significant contributions to the social and political life of amateur media producers, on the other hand, these also challenge the structures of mass media. In more ways than one, they have played a role in empowering the people who have used them, at the same time making efforts to bridge the 'digital inequality'. The Sao Paulo Project, in Brazil, for one has brought together grassroots undertakings towards bridging the digital gap by working with computer recycling and using Linux so that activists/artists collective, independent media, and the institutional segment who work with the marginalised and poor people access to the digital age and can come to the fore (Rosas, 2004b). It has created a network of Brazilians who had not previously met, and it has laid the conditions both for the organisation of the event and for future collaborations. There are also examples of the American Indymedia and South Korean Ohmy News which point to the early successes of alternative media. Instead of becoming simply PR tools for opposition groups, such media promote activism and reform. This brings us to the question of what are the different forms of alternative media. Let us discuss that in the next section.
12.4.3 Genres of Alternative Media
Alternative media as we know by now (as we have discussed it in detail in the course MJM024) question the dominant cultures and themes and are viewed as 'counter-hegemonic' if viewed from the lens of Antonio Gramsci.

These forms of media may include anything from print, radio, video, film, Democracy and Digital Media Internet to street art, performance, and music. As far as the genres of new media and their role in alternative media projects are concerned, there are few main types, e.g. culture jamming, participatory journalism, alternative computing, mediated mobilisation, and shared knowledge. Culture jamming comes in the form of Internet memes and marketing and is a commentary on popular culture, advertising, and such art forms dealing with issues of consumerism and capitalism. Participatory journalism refers to radical news on web-based sources which are mainly critiques on online news services and blogs. While alternative computing deals with the material infrastructure of information and communication technologies (hacking, open-source software and file sharing are few examples), mediated mobilisation refers to communication practices that ignite social movements or cultural projects. Common knowledge provides alternatives to top-down creation and dissemination of knowledge (Wikipedia being one such example). Alternative media has also recently come to be an umbrella term that includes such media as tactical media, second-tier media, DIY (Do-It- Yourself) media, and independent media. Tactical media talks about a form of media activism that promotes temporary media alternatives to permanent alternative media outlets. First-tier sites such as Facebook, LinkedIn, and Twitter are quite popular but recently second-tier social media sites (Meebo, Tumblr, Pinterest) have been gaining popularity as they house information that can connect back to the first-tier sites. DIY media may be defined as the use of Web 2.0 applications, specifically in terms of allowing users to become producers and not merely consumers of media. 12.5 CITIZEN JOURNALISM AND SOCIAL CHANGE
Internet Citizen journalism and social media management to bring about social change, but what about its access, equality, and outreach in a world dominated by capitalism. Ideals of access, inclusion, discussion, and participation come to take place within technological networks which make us question its efficacy for most of the world's people (Dean, 2005). Communicative capitalism mentions that capitalism can be viewed in the broader context of network and communication technologies where the citizen is missing. McChesney (2013), in this regard, says that capitalism and democracy vie for opposite outcomes-the former creates massive inequality, and the latter is premised upon political equality. On similar lines, Khiabany (2016) notes that the Green Revolution did not bring much change in Iran, but it was perfect for Twitter's business. This also brings us to the debates around democracy and democratic freedoms. Let us now talk about what are the central tenets of citizen journalism and its forms, how it affects the Internet, and how such forms of journalism promote democratic participation.
12.5.1 Tenets of Citizen Journalism
There are many essential principles or tenets that open journalism should follow, and these are transparency, responsiveness, substantive participation, collaboration, and networked presence. Transparency is coming up as an essential hallmark of citizen journalism where there is freedom of expression and space where diverse views are shared more openly and without any inhibitions and pressures. News gathering and disseminating of information become more responsive to various needs. There is a lot of debate and discussion around it on multiple platforms. Many reporters and editors are using such platforms to diversify opinions and participation. The information-sharing level is high on this platform, from fan communities to blogs and digital community-building that takes place. Citizen journalism, however, can take up many forms.
12.5.2 Forms of Citizen Journalism
It can be opportunistic when there is a bystander, and a citizen just happens to be present at the place, and the incident occurs. They are there as witnesses and click photographs, or create an account of what happened at that point. What the person does with the information is his/her own choice-they may post it on their social media accounts or work with the media to get the message across. The other form is where the journalist has placed himself purposely in that sort of situation in order to capture an event as it unfolds to communicate it to the rest of the world. The individuals would not have any journalistic training or background and therefore get classified as citizen journalists, an ordinary person reporting like 'professionals'.

12.5.3 Digital Media and News Values Democracy and Digital Media
Regarding some fundamental news values on digital platforms, Mark Lipton says that "One can argue that the sociability of new web processes is producing new pathways for 'truth'. Truth is the main guarded principle around which journalism functions." Boler (2010) says that if we go by this definition of truth, then there are two ways of viewing it-that truth is being constructed by mainstream media and truth as being constructed by other forms of media and sources available on the Internet, on blogs, wikis, Instagram posts, Facebook, to name a few. Whenever you begin to doubt the dominant discourses within the mainstream media and the 'social construction of reality' by the dominant media with the help of public relations and 'spin,' we are often accused of being paranoid conspiracy theorists. However, the Internet offers several 'facts' in addition to those being presented in mainstream media. Thus, while the credibility of mainstream media organisations is at stake here, on the one hand, on the other, the bigger question is how far can the online news be trusted? It thus becomes essential to understand how alternative media, independent media, citizen journalism, etc. create agendas, and how are they performing the function of agenda-setting online? Boler (2010) says that there are three main issues to think about around such media spaces-the idea of space as socially constructed, the concept of the flow of ideas, and the role of imagination in the construction of 'subjectivities'. Pierre Bourdieu (1991) argues that symbolic power is the power to construct reality. Alternative media, thus, constructs a reality that opposes the conventions and representations of mass media. The challenge, in no small extent, what is out there on channels, on your radio set, and in your newspaper. However, the credibility question of these online news sources also looms large. While the journalists and publicists can manipulate both the element of change and relevance to a story to maximise its strength for the audience, there is little scope for such manipulation in the blogs and independent media. There is also a lesser chance of bias creeping in media platforms online. Even if there is subjectivity around a blog, the audience is free to reject it and move on to some other more credible source of news. However, there is still greater participation by citizens in countries around the world in online platforms and its usage for meaningful change and for promoting 'deliberative democracy'. Let us now expand on what is user-generated content, yet another term used in the context of digital media.
12.5.4 User Generated Content
User-generated content is a term applied to mean that consumers or customers are no longer passive receivers of information, whether it is on sites like YouTube or blogs, products featured on e-commerce sites, etc. These interactions take the form of product reviews and other consumer- initiated contributions. This form of content points to the increasing form of media pluralism and indicates that the content we have access to is more diverse than we have

India's Experience with the ever had in the past. There has, however, been recent concern regarding the Internet dominance of a few platforms in many democracies (Twitter in Japan, Naver in the Republic of Korea, Instagram and LinkedIn in Africa, Vkontakte and Odnoklassniki in Russia and Central and Eastern Europe, and WeChat and QQ in China). Such content has been incorporated in mainstream journalism and in marketing where it is said to build more trust for the brand and organisation, encourages more participation, encourages more traffic to the brand websites, increases follower count, and ensures that the purchase decisions are maximised. Thus, we see there are many benefits of such content, including personalisation which is a welcome trend. Activity - 3 You should create an account on any of the platforms of citizen journalism. 12.6 EXPERIENCES OF INTERPLAY
There have been instances in India and abroad that indicate the growing use of digital media, social media in particular, for political and social activism. Many cases are reported from Africa, Asia, and the West that have shown the growing importance of online activism and politics, especially during elections. Some cases from India, China, Sweden, and the United States of America have been discussed below.
12.6.1 Global Trends
For example, in February 2003, millions of people worldwide were mobilised to protest against the Bush administration's push for war against Iraq. The Arab Spring of 2010 can be cited too. Another example is the Egyptian revolution of January-February 2011 where thousands of protestors, demonstrators, and youth decided through online methods to meet at Cairo's Tahrir Square and protest against the high-handedness of President Hosni Mubarak of Egypt and his regime which was fraught with corruption, electoral fraud, unemployment, state-of-emergency laws among other such practices. This resulted in the overthrow of the Mubarak government. So digital media cannot be undermined.

Larrson & Kalsnes (2014) found that Twitter and Facebook are used Democracy and Digital Media extensively by politicians in Sweden and are used more by politicians who are 'underdogs', tend to be younger and non-incumbents and outsiders rather than prominent insiders. Regarding the scene in the United States, the debate is that digital media leads to political polarisation. However, Messing & Westwood (2014) show that endorsements of news items via social network sites (Facebook likes, for example) prompt more people to read these news items. Some Congressmen, however, use Twitter more for self-promotion rather than engaging with the public. In the case of China, Pan (2016) argues that Baidu (Google equivalent), WeChat (Facebook or Twitter equivalent) and Alibaba's Taobao (Amazon or eBay equivalent) better meet the needs of the Chinese markets but face problems finding inroads into foreign markets due to policies or legal loopholes. Regarding online protests in China, Yang (2014) says "Although hundreds of Internet protests occur every year, the main issues focus on corruption, social injustices against vulnerable persons, abuse of power by government officials."
12.6.2 Indian Experiences
Similarly, India Against Corruption movement in April 2011 was seen as a 'social media revolution' when Anna Hazare decided to go on fast unto death at Ramlila Maidan in New Delhi demanding enactment of the long- pending Jan Lokpal Bill. In India, Doron and Jeffrey (2013) point out that the use of mobile phones was a crucial factor in the victory of Mayawati in Uttar Pradesh state legislative assembly elections in 2007 although influential newspapers and television channels were disdainful of her party, the BSP (Bahujan Samaj Party) and hostile to Dalit politics. The other parties, they argue, lacked such mobile-phone-based mobilisation through which irregularities were reported to the Election Commission and mainstream media was bypassed. In India, there is significant concern around internet penetration and digital exclusion which presses us to discuss the topic of 'digital inequality'. Digital inequality is a term that refers to how technology and its usage and non-usage can create divisions in society as 'haves' and 'have-nots'. There is still a section of the society who are left out of the benefits of technology. This itself leaves those marginalised communities outside the gambit of 'democracy' where the real action is taking place in terms of politics, social change, protests, and movements. If the infrastructure is not provided to the poor for their fullest development through technology and ICT (information and communication technology), then how can social and economic growth take place, this is a pertinent question before scholars.
12.7 LET US SUM UP
It may thus be concluded that digital media takes up many forms where there are mainstream media with their web portals vying for media space and audience engagement; at the same time, there are various alternative media with opposing voices and voices that redefine meanings of various issues.

India's Experience with the In the form of digital media, social media is becoming a more prominent Internet player who is redefining even news and journalism. There are ways in which social media is allowing democracy to reshape the future and assist citizens in being a more active part of it. The recent case of mob lynching incidents on social media in Indian cities is an example to show how there is a close relationship between social media and democracy. Such media becomes a mediated platform for struggles, crimes, movements, protests, and dialogue by various groups, organisations, communities, and people that are marginalised. It is believed by some that despite such activity out there on the Internet, these struggles have less meaning for the ones who do not have access. Hence, digital media platforms generate debates around inclusion, access, privacy, openness, and diversity.
12.8 KEYWORDS
Alternative Media: Such forms of media that are not in the mainstream and are more participative and accommodative of audience voices and perceptions. It provides a sense of 'empowerment' and 'identity'. Mainstream Media: It is also used interchangeably with the word corporate media, which means news that is being produced with a profit motive. Media Reform: This essentially means the change in policies and agendas of media in a way that it is more catered to public needs and away from corporate or other bias. Net neutrality: It means internet service should be provided equally to all for use instead of differentiating or discriminating between users. Open Source Software: It is a type of computer software in which the copyright holder grants it for use and distributes the software to anyone for any purpose. Tactical Media: It is a peculiar term that implies expressions of dissent through artistic and do-it-yourself approaches which are readily available, including cheap technology. Web 2.0: This term usually means user-generated content, participatory culture and interoperability of media (mainly blogging, wikis and syndication).

13.0 INTRODUCTION
Information and communication technology (ICT) is playing a significant role in every field of life, including education. Modern ICT tools have brought about significant changes in the education sector at all levels, from school education to higher education. You can easily experience the impact of ICT on education. Traditional classrooms are being converted into smart classrooms; time and space-related barriers are being removed, and the concept of learning anytime and anywhere is getting more and more popular. Now an ocean of knowledge is available for you on the internet. You can get and submit your home assignments online. A number of online courses developed by the institutions and experts of different countries are available for you. You can watch many interesting audiovisual programmes related to your subject topics on the internet. You can do many practical activities through virtual labs. You can watch the lectures of the world's best faculties and interact with them sitting in your room or workplace situated in a small town. You can get access to a massive stock of knowledge completely free of cost available as open educational resources (OER), and a lot more. Education is an essential indicator of development and 'education for all' is quite crucial for inclusive development of our society. Do you think ICT can help to make the quality education available to all? In this Unit, we will discuss the different aspects of ICT for education.

13.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After reading this Unit, you will be able to: * describe the scope of ICT in education at different levels; * explain the primary requirements for successful integration of ICT in our educational system; * describe the current Indian scenario of ICT integration in education; and * critically discuss the issues and challenges in the successful integration of ICT in the Indian education system.
13.2 SCOPE OF ICT IN EDUCATION
We can divide the whole educational transactions into two major parts : (i) teaching-learning activities and (ii) administrative activities or management of educational institutions. ICT plays a crucial role on both fronts. We shall discuss the scope of ICT in both types of educational transactions in coming sub-sections.
13.2.1 ICT For Teaching-Learning Process
In this subsection, we shall discuss the scope of ICT in the teaching-learning process. ICT can play a very influential role in the following crucial areas of teaching-learning: i. Communication (between teacher & learner and learner & learner): Communication or interaction is an essential part of any teaching- learning process. Interaction between teacher and learner is the base of our learning process, but peer interaction is also significant for effective learning. While highlighting the role of modern information and communication technology in education, Wedemeyer (1978) stated that there are four essential elements in a teaching-learning situation. They are the teacher, the learner, the communication system or mode, and the content/curriculum (something to be taught/learnt). Wedemeyer argued that in earlier days, the speech was the only communication mode between a teacher and a learner, so it was obviously required for teachers and learners to be at the same place and same time for the teaching-learning activities. The time and distance between teacher and learner are dependent upon the communication mode. Nowadays, advanced communication technologies are available, and the speech can easily be replaced with them. The integration of communication technology liberates the education system from the 'space' barrier. Teaching-learning can happen even after the class timings or during vacations or through distance mode. ICTs can provide virtual platforms for the teacher- learner interactions and peer interactions as well. ii. Content generation: ICTs have vast potential to create effective educational content for all levels of education from primary classes to higher education. With the capacity to converge various media, it can produce excellent learning materials equipped with text, graphics,

animations, photographs, audio, video etc. Complex concepts can be ICT for Education demonstrated with the help of videos and animations more easily and interestingly. Hypertextuality gives an opportunity to provide more and more in-depth information. With the help of modern ICT tools, we can create various simulations which can make our learning more useful and interesting. Simulations can provide experiences very near to reality in a cost-effective manner. You can take the example of virtual labs. Virtual labs can provide practical facilities to the students of educational institutions situated in backward areas and struggling for proper infrastructure. iii. Storage and Access to the Content: When we discuss the scope of ICT in the teaching-learning process, storage of vast amounts of e-content and providing smooth access to these content are the primary concern. ICT has made these things possible at a very minimal cost. E-repositories can be created, and learners can get access from any part of the world. ICT has completely changed the scenario of knowledge creation and dissemination. A considerable amount of information is available on the Internet on both categories, free of cost and paid. You can access this ocean of knowledge from any corner of the world. Open Educational Resources (OER) are also by product of ICT. These free educational resources are beneficial for learners as well as teachers. It provides the environment of collaborative knowledge creation and consumption across the globe at almost zero cost. Now we shall discuss the scope of ICT in the management of educational institutions which is also an important area.
13.2.2 ICT for Management of Educational Institutions
Apart from core teaching-learning activities, educational institutions are also involved in other management related works. Management of educational institutions encompasses several activities like- admission, examination, record-keeping, communication with parents, result declaration, attendance, scholarships, transportation, leaves, finances, etc. ICT is playing a very crucial role in these management related activities. Various ICT based solutions or systems are available with different modules which can take care of teaching-learning as well as administrative activities of educational institutions from school to university levels. Government educational institutions, from primary schools to universities, are the only destinations for a significant segment of our population, mostly belonging to the weaker sections. Effective and transparent management of government educational institutions can enhance the quality of education in these public-funded institutions, which finally help to achieve the goal of quality education for all. Here, ICT can play a significant role. For example, an ICT based attendance system for teachers and students can ensure the conduct of proper classes. The central government and many state governments are taking steps to integrate the information and communication technology in the management system of their institutions, but it is not a smooth path. There are various challenges and hurdles too. We shall discuss these issues and challenges in section 13.6.

Activity- 1 There are many online courses available on the Internet. Many are also free. SWAYAM is one such platform that offers free online courses. Enrol in any short course and try to analyse whether that course has used all the benefits of ICT to enhance the learning experience of students or not.
13.3 ICT IN EDUCATION: MAJOR REQUIREMENTS
No doubt, effective integration of modern ICT in education has many advantages, but it needs congenial frameworks and environments. Proactive leadership, favourable policies and financial support may create such an enabling environment where successful integration can happen. Here, we shall discuss some critical requirements for effective integration of modern ICT in education. These are as follows: i. Proactive Leadership: Proactive leadership is the key to successful incorporation of any change or any innovation in any field of our life. The same is applicable here also. ii. Favourable Policies: Enabling policies to prepare the right path for any transformation. Supporting policies may steer all the stakeholders towards adopting ICT enabled education systems. We shall discuss the various policies of the government that support technology integration in the later part of this Unit. iii. Financial Support: Nothing can be done without financial resources. Adequate financial support is a must for the successful integration of ICT in the Indian education system. iv. ICT Infrastructure: Reliable ICT infrastructure is a prerequisite for ICT enabled education. It encompasses a variety of things such as
- devices (computers, laptops, smartphones, tablets, etc.), software,
high speed and affordable Internet services, etc. If we want to enjoy the fruits of ICT enabled education, we need adequate and dependable ICT infrastructure across the country. v. Development of Digital Content: After having good ICT infrastructure, now we shall use this infrastructure for two essential purposes - development of digital content and dissemination of these content. Development of quality digital content is one of the major requirements for the successful use of ICT in the field of education. With the help of modern ICT tools, excellent digital content equipped with all the advantages of modern technology can be produced. We all know that digital content provides an opportunity to converge all the media elements. Texts, photographs, graphics, animations, audios and videos and all types of content can be integrated with each other along with the interactivity. This type of multimedia oriented and authored content improves the learning experience of the students. vi. Dissemination and Sharing of Digital Content: Proper dissemination of the digital content is equally important. In order to distribute digital content among the target population requires a fair amount of financial and human resources. Many times, due to lack of proper dissemination, learners are deprived of quality study materials.

vii. Capacity Building of Teachers: Teachers are one of the main ICT for Education stakeholders of the education system, and without their active participation, any attempt to integrate modern technologies in education will undoubtedly fail. In this context, the capacity building of teachers includes three significant aspects: a. teachers should be aware of the advantages of ICT enabled education; b. they should be skilled enough to integrate modern ICT tools in their teaching practices effectively, and c. they should be trained to create and disseminate the quality digital study material. viii. ICT Literacy among Learners: Learners are the centre of focus in any educational transaction. They are the end-users. If they do not know how to utilise the ICT enabled learning facilities, the whole process of ICT integration will go in vain. So, ICT literacy of learners across the country is one of the main requirements for successful integration of information and communication technology in the Indian education system.
