13.4 ICT IN EDUCATION: INDIAN SCENARIO
What is your observation about the utilisation level of ICT in education in India? Answers may vary from person to person, but nobody can deny that we are progressing. We can quickly notice that a large section of students, teachers and non-formal learners are using digital technologies for their learning purposes. In this section, we shall discuss the use of ICT in education in the Indian context.
13.4.1 Use of ICT in Education
Being the second most populated country in the world, India has an extensive education system in terms of a number of institutions. The whole education system may broadly be divided into two parts, i.e. school education and higher education. There are 15,22,346 schools (primary, upper primary, secondary and senior secondary) and 51,793 all types of higher education institutions running in this country (MHRD, 2018).

ICT for Development In India, both the public (Government) and private sectors are actively involved in the field of education, and both are trying to integrate more and more ICT in education. Private sector looks more active on this front, but government institutions are also trying very hard to provide the benefits of modern digital technologies to their students and teachers. The Indian education world is integrating ICT in both the fields, teaching-learning activities as well as management of the institutions. University Grant Commission (UGC) has instructed all the higher education institutions to adopt the online admission system ultimately. Online examinations activities are quite common. The National Testing Agency (NTA) was established in 2017, and it is conducting massive (in terms of a number of students) examinations through online across the country. Institutions are adopting various educational technologies like smart classrooms, digital learning materials, Learning Management System (LMS), etc. Social media is also being used for educational activities. You may find thousands of YouTube channels providing lectures on different subjects in different languages. Both government and private sectors are taking steps to enhance the level of ICT integration in educational transactions. We shall discuss these steps in the coming sub-sections of this Unit.
13.4.2 ICT in Open and Distance Education
Distance education allows the learner and teacher to be physically apart during the teaching-learning process and maintain communication in a variety of ways (Keegan, 1986). The need for maintaining communication in a variety of ways demands various communication technologies in open and distance education. According to Moore (1989), interactivity is a necessary ingredient of the education process and effectiveness of distance education depends upon the level of interactivity provided to the learners and instructors. For enhancing the level of interactivity, various contemporary technologies may be used. You can observe that both scholars emphasised the use of modern and advanced communication technology to make distance education more effective. Thus, ICT has a more significant role in open and distance education in both segments: administrative activities and academic transactions. On the basis of the level and type of technological interventions, UNESCO (2002) classified open and distance learning (ODL) into the following three generations: i) The First generation: The first generation ODL programmes were popularly known as correspondence courses. The print was the only form of teaching-learning content, and postal services were used for delivery of the content and communication between teacher and learner. ii) The Second generation: This generation came after the establishment of open universities. Print remained a significant component, but other media were also introduced. Audio, video and multimedia programmes were produced and sent to the learners along with the print materials. Besides postal services, radio, television, telephone and face-to-face contact sessions were used to communicate with learners. iii) The Third generation: It has the components of earlier generations, but the two-way communication between teacher and learner has become

relatively fast and effective. Internet-based e-learning platforms have ICT for Education converged all the media elements and providing communication tools like audio and video chat. This is the generation of e-learning and mobile learning. We can easily witness that the majority of the ODL programmes belong to the second generation, but we are trying to move towards the third generation of ODL. Now, you can understand the significant role of ICT in distance education because more ICT integration will improve the generation of our distance programmes.
13.4.3 Government Interventions
In a democratic country like India, where we believe in the concept of the welfare state, the government plays a vital role in the field of education as it is considered an essential factor for inclusive development. As far as the integration of ICT in education is concerned, the government can intervene mainly in two ways. First, by formulating policies which can validate, regulate and boost the use of ICT in education at various levels. If the government formulates favourable policies, they can instruct all the stakeholders, including private educational institutions, to adopt more ICT enabled education. Moreover, second, the government can run their own projects. Through these government-funded projects, the government can promote more ICT enabled education in the country. Here, we shall discuss both types of government interventions.
i. Government Policies on ICT for Education
In India, the government has been emphasising the use of technology in education at all levels for a long time. The National Policy on Education (NPE), 1986 (modified in 1992) has also highlighted the potential of educational technology and the need for technological integration in educational transactions. NPE (1986) says, "Modern communication technologies have the potential to bypass several stages and sequences in the process of development encountered in earlier decades. Both the constraints of time and distance at once become manageable." After 1986, the government of India came up with several policies for promoting the use of ICT in education at both the levels - school education and higher education. The National Curriculum Framework (NCF) 2005 has also highlighted the significant role of ICT in school education. The
revised National Policy on Information and Communication Technology
in School Education came in 2012 as a comprehensive policy, including all aspects of ICT integration in school education in the context of our country. This policy talks about ICT literacy among teachers and students, ICT for the students with special needs, ICT infrastructure, use of ICT in school management, development of digital learning content, dissemination and sharing of digital learning material, ICT for open and distance learning, capacity building of teachers and educational administrators, financial sustainability and monitoring. The Government feels the need for technology integration in higher education too. They are keen to use various technological resources to fulfil their mission to provide quality higher education to all students (MHRD, 2016). Recent regulations show the government's emphasis on ICT integration in

ICT for Development higher education. We can discuss the few following significant regulations which will promote the use of ICT in higher education: UGC (Credit Framework for Online Learning Courses through SWAYAM) Regulation, 2016: The Government of India announced its policy on blended learning in higher education, the mixture of conventional classroom teaching and e-learning. The University Grant Commission (UGC) notified the rules and regulation for blended learning. Students of conventional face- to-face mode can earn a part of their programme credits through MOOCs (Massive Open Online Courses) available on SWAYAM (Study Webs of Active Learning for Young Aspiring Minds) platform. This step may be considered as an essential milestone for technology-enabled learning in India.
University Grants Commission (Open and Distance Learning) Regulations,
2017: This regulation also encourages the active integration of ICT in distance learning programmes. It allows the integration of ICT based learning components in every element of a distance programme such as study material, contact classes, assignments and practicals. According to this regulation, institutions offering distance programmes can utilise virtual labs for practical sessions (up to 20%).
University Grants Commission (Online Courses or Programmes)
Regulations, 2018: It can be considered a revolutionary regulation which allows complete online courses or programmes. In these programmes, the highest level of ICT integration can be seen. National Eduction Policy 2020: In a major shift, NEP gives a higher importance to technology enabled inclusive learning. These regulations give clear indications that the government is quite keen to promote ICT in educational transactions at all levels. ii. Government Projects The Government of India is of the view that the three fundamental principles of its Education Policy viz., Access, Equity and Quality can be achieved through the use of ICT in education. The National Mission on Education through Information and Communication Technology (NMEICT) is the result of it (MHRD, 2016). NMEICT is an umbrella project for all the initiatives in the field of technology integration in Indian higher education. The government is working on two significant fronts. First, the creation of quality digital learning material in all disciplines and second, creation of networks and platforms to share the knowledge among all higher education institutions across the country. SAKSHAT has been developed as a free one-stop online delivery platform for all the generated digital content under NMEICT. Programmes such as the National Program on Technology Enabled Learning (NPTEL), Virtual labs, Talk to a Teacher, National
Digital Library, Vidwan (Expert Database and National Researcher's
Network), E-Yantra, E-Kalpa, Study Webs of Active Learning for Young Aspiring Minds (SWAYAM) and SWAYAM PRABHA are running under the umbrella of NMEICT. SWAYAM has been developed to offer online courses, whereas SWAYAM PRABHA is a group of 32 DTH educational channels for different academic disciplines.

Though the primary focus of SWAYAM is on higher education, school level ICT for Education online courses are also available on this platform. SWAYAM PRABHA is also with similar options. While a majority of the channels are dedicated to higher education, yet a few channels are devoted to school-level education too. ePathshala, eBasta, ICT @ Schools Scheme, etc. are a few other essential government projects at the school level.
13.4.4 ICT Enabled Education and Private Sector
The private sector too has a strong presence in Indian education. They are involved in all types of education, for example - formal education, tutoring, preparation of competitive examinations, etc. At the same time, they are also the big promoters of ICT enabled education in India due to various reasons. If we talk about formal education, the private sector is increasing technological integration at both the levels, school education as well as higher education. Private schools, colleges and universities are adopting various educational technologies like smart classrooms, digital learning materials, virtual labs, (LMS), etc. You can quickly notice that ICT is being used in tutoring and preparation for competitive examinations in a big way. A number of advertisements of various learning apps and online coaching can be seen on all media platforms. The private sector is utilising the capabilities of modern ICT tools to provide quality study materials in a more interesting and easy to understand the way to their target population. Market competition compels them to be more innovative and creative. They are using various components such as-video lessons, tests, quizzes, games, interactive lessons, live streaming, etc. They are also merging educational components with virtual reality which gives a unique experience to the students and also help them to get clarity on various concepts that need more practical explanations. Apart from these, they are providing very detailed performance analysis to the students. You must have used or noticed many educational apps for tutoring and preparation of various competitive examinations. Gradeup, Unacademy, Toppr, Adda247, Vedantu, STEPapp, BYJU's, etc. are a few examples. Apart from formal education and coaching, the private sector is actively involved in creating platforms for online courses. Nowadays, the needs of various job providing sectors are changing very fast. Employees need to be updated with fast-changing technologies and knowledge. Micro degrees that are highly focused on specific skills are in huge demand, and many private players have developed different platforms to offer various online courses relevant to the employees and job seekers. Coursera, edX, Udacity, FutureLearn, Udemy, etc. are a few examples of online course platforms run by the private sector. As per their experience, compare the online learning environment with the conventional classroom learning method.

13.5 INTEGRATION OF ICT IN EDUCATION: ISSUES
AND CHALLENGES
We all agree that ICT has tremendous potential to bring about positive transformation in all dimensions of Indian education. It can help us to achieve the goal of providing quality education to all. As a country, we are working hard to utilise the advantages of modern ICT tools for our education system, and we have achieved many successes too. However, we have still to cover a long distance. India is full of diversities, and the picture of rural and remote tribal areas may be completely different from the cities in this context. Even in the cities, there may be different levels of ICT integration in government educational institutions and private ones. You may observe that in the same city, there are few private schools having world-class ICT integration in their educational transactions and on the other hand, many government schools are still struggling for the basic ones. So, the successful integration of ICT in education is not an easy task in a developing country like India. There are some hurdles also. Few hurdles are universal and common in all cases, but few are country-specific due to the social and economic status of that particular country. Now, we shall discuss the issues and challenges in the effective integration of ICT in the Indian education system. These are as follows: i. The Attitude of Teachers and Students: Users' attitude is one of the universal challenges for the effective integration of ICT in

educational transactions. Emphasising the importance of teachers' ICT for Education attitude, Johnson (2012) states that the attitude of teachers towards educational technology is one of the crucial factors influencing the process and success of technology integration in higher education. Teachers should have complete clarity on why technology is important for education and why they should change their role from 'sage on the stage' to 'guide on the side'. Apart from teachers, students should also have a positive attitude towards ICT enabled learning. In brief, perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use for ICT enabled teaching-learning should be on a higher side among students and teachers. ii. Digital Inequality: You must have learnt the term 'Digital Inequality in Unit 3 in this course. Digital inequality refers to the differences in access and use of digital technology between two or more groups of people. There will be a digital inequality if one group of people has higher access to ICT in comparison to another group. In the case of digital inequality, the digitally marginalised section is deprived of the benefits of modern information and communication technologies. It is one of the significant challenges for the successful integration of ICT in the Indian education system because India is suffering from an extensive digital inequality scenario. Digital inequality may be existing due to several reasons like - education, ICT literacy, socio-economic condition, language, area of residence (rural, urban, remote tribal), age, etc. We all know that India is a country full of diversity. We have a diverse population on the basis of language, residential area, income, education and socio- economic conditions. We still have a large section of the population illiterate. Take the example of a student from a small town of Uttar Pradesh. She has proper access to ICT, and she is skilled too, but her medium of education is Hindi. She wants to use ICT to get better subject contents, but most of the content available on the Internet is in English. Thus, despite having access and skill, she suffers due to digital inequality. Here, language is the cause of digital inequality. Similarly, many Indian languages are facing this crisis. iii. Availability of Digital Content in Indian Languages: India is a multi-linguistic country having 22 official languages listed in the 8th schedule of its constitution. We all know that an extensive section of our population is getting an education in their own mother tongues, for example - Hindi, Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, Marathi, Gujrati, Malayalam, etc. Thousands of schools, colleges and universities are providing education at various levels in Indian languages. We have already discussed an example where language caused a digital inequality. Therefore, if we want to extend the benefits of modern ICT to all the students without any discrimination, creation of digital study materials in Indian languages is a must, and at the same time, it is a big challenge too. iv. Infrastructure: For effective integration of ICT in Indian education, we need reliable information and communication infrastructure across the country, and it is a big challenge. We all know that the availability

ICT for Development of adequate ICT infrastructure creates a digital inequality between urban and rural areas (we have covered the access and penetration of ICT in Indian in Unit 3 of this course). We need to equip our rural and remote tribal areas with high-speed, dependable Internet services only then can we achieve our dream goal of transforming India into a digitally empowered society and knowledge economy. This is also the vision of "Digital India' programme. Reducing the digital inequality between urban and rural areas has been on the government's priority list. In 2011, the government of India had approved the setting up of National Optical Fibre Network (NOFN). Project Bharatnet has been started to connect 2,50,000 Gram
Panchayats with broadband. Bharat Broadband Network Limited
(BBNL), a government of India undertaking, is continuously working on it. As on 27th December 2019, optical fibre cable of 3,99,375 Kms of length has been laid down in 1,44,670 Gram Panchayats (BBNL,
2019) . The efforts show that providing ICT infrastructure to all in a
non-discriminatory manner is a priority, and we shall overcome the challenge of infrastructure one day.
v. Capacity Enhancement of Related Human Resources: Effective
integration of technology in education needs skilled stakeholders. Capacity enhancement of students, teachers and other support staff is a need and at the same time a challenge also. The gap between ICT skills of different groups of teachers and students also cause digital inequality and put a hurdle in the way of smooth and inclusive integration of ICT in education without any discrimination. If you compare, you will find a massive gap between the ICT capabilities of teachers coming from metros and remote rural areas. It is a big challenge, and we have to enhance the ICT related capacity of our teachers, students and support staff coming especially from rural areas. iv. 14.0 INTRODUCTION
In this Unit, we shall discuss the role of ICT in communicating health messages, how to seek health information from the Internet, strategies and skill development for acquiring health information and significant barriers and problems in acquiring health information. Health communication focuses on the development of effective messages through different media. It serves as a critical platform for health literacy messaging. Even though the term health communication is used in a broader sense, this has a long history.

ICT for Development Ensuring healthy lives and promoting well-being at all ages is essential for social development, particularly as part of the Sustainable Development Goal (SDG 3). Significant progress has been made in improving the health of millions of people. However, at least half of the world's population is still without access to essential health services and information. For promoting and protecting health, of yourself and others, you can raise awareness in your community about the importance of good health, healthy lifestyles as well as people's right to quality health care services, especially for the most vulnerable such as women and children. You can also hold your government, local leaders and other decision-makers accountable to their commitments to improve people's access to health and health care. However, for all these to work out, you should have some knowledge about what it is, what to communicate through which medium, how to collect information and so on. In this information age, technology has a significant role in communicating information. Through better usage and improvement can ensure health lives. In this Unit, we shall discuss the growing significance of Information and Communication Technology (ICT) in the fields of public health and community welfare.

14.2 HEALTH SECTOR AND ICT
Health Communication is the study and use of communication strategies to inform and influence decisions and actions to improve health. It has clear- cut objectives to promote changes, create awareness, knowledge, and if needed, appropriate changes in attitudes and beliefs. Strategic approaches for communicating health messages and information have been practised informally for years. The term health communication was first used in 1961 when the National Health Council organised a National Health Forum to discuss challenges faced in the communication of health information (Helen, 1962). The term was used again in 1962 when Surgeon General Luther Terry organised a conference on health communication to discuss how various techniques of communication can be used to make health information available to the public (US Department of Health Education and Welfare, 1963). The term was adopted officially by members of an interest group at the International Communication Association ICA in 1975. And, in 1997, the American Public Health Association recognised health communication as a discipline within the broader fields of Public Health Education with health promotion and health communication as subjects to undergo comprehensive growth and change.

14.2.1 Need for Health Communication Health and ICT
Before understanding the need for health communication, we should know the six principles given by the World Health Organisation which describes the role of communication system in the health sector.
1) Accessible to decisions-makers: Communicators should identify
all channels that are available and map their comparative capacities to reach priority audiences. Using the right mix of channels helps empower audiences with the information they need in order to make informed decisions.
2) Actionable by decisions-makers: Communicators must understand
the knowledge, attitudes and behaviours of the target audience in order to create messages that address barriers and encourage decision- makers to take the recommended steps.
3) Credible and trusted as perceived by decision-makers: The reputation
of WHO is a crucial factor in deciding whether individuals will take action on its advice and guidance. The more decision-makers trust WHO, the more likely they will believe, and act on the information communicated by the Organisation.
4) Relevant to decisions-makers: In order to be relevant, communications
must help decision-makers understand that there is a health risk for themselves or for those they care about, that the risk could be severe and that they can reduce that risk by undertaking recommended actions.
5) Timely to enable decision-making: Across all health issues, WHO
must make information, advice and guidance available in a timely way, so audiences have the information they need when they need it in order to make appropriate health decisions.
6) Understandable to decision-makers: The WHO communicates
with a wide variety of decision-makers. Some have backgrounds in medicine and public health and rely on WHO for technical information. However, many key audiences are not technical experts. They need information that is easy to understand in order to understand health risks and take appropriate actions. From the above perspective there arises the need for health communication which can reduce the level of awareness by : * Increasing risk perception; * Reinforcing positive behaviours; * Influencing social norms; * Increasing the availability of support and needed services; * Empowering individuals to change or improve their health conditions. A range of organisational and institutional developments associated with the technological changes have altered not only patterns of production and distribution of goods, but also, even more significantly, patterns of services especially the nature of the delivery of many essential services such as health.

ICT for Development 14.2.2 ICT in Health Communication
ICT can play a critical role in improving health care for individuals and communities by providing new and more efficient ways of accessing, communicating, and storing information. ICTs can help bridge the information divide that has emerged in the health sector in developing countries--between health professionals and the communities they serve and between those involved in health research and the practitioners who need it through the development of databases and other applications. ICTs can also provide the capacity to improve health system efficiencies and prevent medical errors. ICT can affect health conditions in developing countries both directly and indirectly. It can work directly by improving health care provision and disease prevention. It also works indirectly on the health status of the population through its effects on the broader determinants of health, such as growth, the economic position of households, and the social infrastructure. The first is its role as an instrument for continuing education and lifelong learning that will enable doctors in developing countries to be informed about and trained in the use of advances in knowledge. The second is its use as a delivery mechanism to poor and remote locations of a wide variety of services varying from improved public health education to emergency advice, including advice on dealing with and mitigating the consequences of natural disasters. The third is its potential use as a mechanism to increase the transparency and efficiency of governance, which would, in turn, improve the availability and delivery of publicly provided health services.
14.2.3 Health IT
The term "Health Information Technology" (Health IT) refers to the electronic systems health care professionals, and increasingly, patients use to store, share, and analyse health information. Technological innovations have greatly improved the ability to access information, facilitate communication and improve efficiency in nearly all aspects of life. Similarly, the use of technology to directly impact the health of populations, as well as to provide access to crucial public health information, holds great promise that is emerging at the forefront of medical care and public health industries. Technology can also cut across the barriers to reaching out to diverse populations to meet their needs, and using health information technology interventions for vaccinations. 14.3 HEALTH INFORMATION ONLINE
You may be turning to the Internet to obtain information about health and health care. Internet use has grown dramatically over the last decade, and searching for health information is an essential application for many users. What makes you search the Internet for health information? Have you ever been confused by seeing lots of information? You may be confused the complexity, which is the right one to choose? With the emergence of internet health information, its broader aspect has been growing, and new branches have emerged in the health sector.
14.3.1 E-health:
There are many terms used to describe the use of ICT in supporting healthcare. These terms are often used interchangeably, and thus can contribute to misunderstanding or misconceptions. Terms include eHealth, mHealth, tele-health, tele-rehabilitation and telemedicine. For instance, the World Health Organization (WHO) uses the term e-Health to describe the use of ICT to support public health and healthcare areas. E-health is an emerging field in the intersection of medical informatics, public health and business, particularly its application in health services and information delivered or enhanced through the Internet and related technologies. In a broader sense, the term e-health characterises not only a technical development, but also a state-of-mind, a way of thinking, an attitude, and a commitment for networked global thinking to improve health care locally, regionally, and worldwide by using ICT. This definition hopefully is broad enough to apply to a dynamic environment such as the Internet and at the same time, acknowledges that e-health encompasses more than just "Internet and Medicine." As such, the "e" in e-health does not only stand for "electronic," but implies several other "e's," which together best characterises what e-health is all about (or what it should be). Efficiency - one of the promises of e-health is to increase efficiency in healthcare, thereby decreasing costs.
1. Enhancing quality of care - increasing efficiency involves not only
reducing costs but at the same time improving quality. E-health may enhance the quality of healthcare, for example, by allowing comparisons between different providers, involving consumers as additional power for quality assurance, and directing patient streams to the best quality providers.
2. Evidence-based - e-health interventions should be evidence-based in
the sense that their effectiveness and efficiency should not be assumed but proven by rigorous scientific evaluation. Much work still has to be done in this area.

ICT for Development 3. Empowerment of consumers and patients. By making the knowledge bases of medicine and personal electronic records accessible to consumers over the Internet, e-health opens new avenues for patient- centred medicine and enables evidence-based patient choice.
4. Encouragement of a new relationship between the patient and health
professional, towards a true partnership, where decisions are made in a shared manner.
5. Education of physicians through online sources (continuing medical
education) and consumers (health education, tailored preventive information for consumers).
6. Enabling information exchange and communication in a standardised
way between healthcare establishments.
7. Extending the scope of health care beyond its conventional
boundaries. This is meant in both a geographical sense as well as in a conceptual sense. E-health enables consumers to obtain health services online from global providers quickly. These services can range from simple advice to more complex interventions or products such as pharmaceuticals.
8. Ethics - e-health involves new forms of patient-physician interaction
and poses new challenges and threats to ethical issues such as online professional practice, informed consent, privacy and equity issues.
9. Equity - to make healthcare more equitable is one of the promises
of e-health, but at the same time there is a considerable threat that e-health may deepen the gap between the "haves" and "have-nots." People who do not have the money, skills, and access to computers and networks cannot use computers effectively. As a result, these patient populations (which would benefit the most from health information) are those who are the least likely to benefit from advances in information technology, unless political measures ensure equitable access for all. The digital divide currently runs between rural vs urban populations, rich vs poor, young vs old, male vs female and between neglected/rare vs common diseases. In addition to these essential e's, e-health should also be * easy-to-use, * entertaining (no-one will use something boring!) and * exciting- and it should exist. ICT for health (or e-health) programs are often considered to be expensive, time-consuming, risky, and otherwise distracting from the primary focus and intent of health sector programs. In some cases, these criticisms may be valid. There are, however, a wide range of low-cost and sustainable ICT for health program components that can augment capacity and improve the overall effectiveness of health development programs. e-Health literacy is a concept that combines health literacy and also information literacy, along with an addition of traditional literacy, media literacy, computer literacy and scientific literacy

E-learning can also be termed as a network-enabled transfer of skills and

knowledge, and the delivery of education is made to a large number of Health and ICT recipients at the same or different times. With rapid progress in technology and the advancement in learning systems, it is now embraced by the masses. The introduction of computers was the basis of this revolution and with time, as we have got hooked to smartphones, tablets, etc. Learning has a broad scope in the health sector. It aims to improve the coverage and quality of health services for rural and remote areas. Through e-learning usage of website portals, audio, video and digital presentations, communications are given to healthcare professionals and workers. In the health sector, where knowledge and skills require frequent updates alongside growing complex non-communicable diseases and frequent changes in medical techniques and technologies, e-learning platforms support the health workers to effectively implement prevention, management of treatment for various health issues. The e-learning platform which transcends the physical border and locations is also expected to provide a useful forum and venue to frequently facilitate and host a continued technical discussion and peer learning with skilful medical practitioners globally.
14.3.3 Case studies
To take up Digital India initiative ahead, the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has started various e-Gov initiatives in healthcare sectors in India, and the division is named as eHealth division. e-Health is broadly defined as the use of Information and Communication Technology (ICT) in health. It will make a world of difference in India, where mobile technologies have been penetrating at a rapid rate. As India has a strong presence in IT, the integrated health information system seems to have the potential to serve the needs of all stakeholders, by contributing approximately eight per cent to the GDP. The eHealth initiatives have the vision to deliver better health outcomes in terms of * access; * quality; * affordability; * lowering of disease burden and * efficient monitoring of health entitlements to citizens. The scope of these initiatives is to make all medical facilities available every time from any part of the world through web services, mobile services, SMS, or Call centre services. 14.4 STRATEGIES FOR HEALTH COMMUNICATION
The materials reflect the situations that 'old' and increasingly 'new' technologies are often included in an analysis of media and health communications, as they constitute a large portion of media (only print is not an 'ICT', but this definition is also not always apparent, as the literature show

ICT for Development that increasingly the Internet is also delivering content that was traditional 'print', and there is a convergence between newsprint and internet versions of newspapers and other publications). The gathered literature point to the pre- eminence of communication in much of the ICT for development discourse, and the importance of the processes of communication in speaking about the effectiveness of ICT usage.
14.4.1 Health Literacy
The concept of health literacy, typically used within health sciences and health communication, is often defined as 'the degree to which individuals have the capacity to obtain, process, and understand basic health information and services needed to make appropriate health decisions', the focus is on the individual's abilities to make decisions. However, there is also a definition where the cognitive and social abilities, and the aim to promote and maintain an individual's health, are emphasised. The Health Promotion Glossary of the World Health Organisation defines the concept in the following way: "Health literacy represents the cognitive and social skills which determine the motivation and ability of individuals to gain access, to understand and use information in ways which promote and maintain good health."
14.4.2 Health Information Literacy
As a concept, information literacy was introduced in the early 1970s and has since spread from being used within information management in organisational contexts and also to be shared in other information environments. The approach is increasingly moving away from being focused on individual skills towards attaining individuality. A related concept that describes health-related information behaviour, includes seeking and using of information related to health or medicine is Health Information Literacy (HIL). The Medical Library Association defines HIL as the ability to recognise a need for health information, to know how and where to find health information, and how to evaluate and use this information in everyday life to make right health decisions. The concept is a combination of health literacy and information literacy. An information-literate person has, according to a widely used definition, the ability to determine the extent of information needed; access the needed information effectively and efficiently; evaluate information and its sources critically; incorporate selected information into one's knowledge base; use information effectively to accomplish a specific purpose; and, to understand the economic, legal and social issues surrounding the use of information, and to access and use information ethically and legally.
14.4.3 Information Dissemination
The study and use of communication strategies to inform and influence individual and community decisions that affect health links the fields of communication and health and is increasingly recognised as a necessary element of efforts to improve personal and public health. Dissemination is the targeted distribution of information and intervention materials to specific public health or clinical practise audience. The intent is to spread

knowledge and associated evidence-based interventions. Dissemination Health and ICT occurs through a variety of channels, social contexts, and settings.
14.4.4 Perspective of Health Information
Government organisations, media, civil society, community and political leaders and even the academic and research organisations can impart health literacy. The government can play a decisive leadership role in developing and implementing health-related strategies. Additional stakeholders include the insurance industry, policymakers, and educational training institutions". The long-term solution lies in "improving the literacy of the population" at large through schools and other communities. Governments can take up a vital leadership role in developing and implementing health literacy promotion policies by providing sustained funding, setting up special projects, coordinating action across sectors, and conducting health literacy surveillance regularly. Improving and measuring health literacy (both strengths and needs) is particularly important in poorer areas, so that vulnerable populations are empowered to engage in early and sustained health-promoting actions, whether to prevent acute and chronic conditions or to promote active and curative treatments. Government agencies and institutions, advocacy groups, media organisations, researchers, and other interested stakeholders can all carry out communication activities. They may use various techniques to communicate evidence so that target audiences can understand it better. Individuals: The individual is the most fundamental target for health- related change since it is individual behaviour that affects health status. Communication can affect an individual's awareness, knowledge, attitudes, self-efficacy, and skills for behaviour change. For example, counselling on sexual risk reduction as well as HIV testing is an effective way to change behaviour and protect health.
Print, Television, Radio, New Media Campaigns
Inquiry into health communication also involves the examination of many communication channels face-to-face communication between providers and consumers, members of healthcare teams, and support group members etc. You should have seen and listened to Public Service Advertisement (PSA) in newspapers, magazines, radio and television channels on vaccination, child and maternity care and various other health-related issues. Moreover, in rural areas still, public announcements and awareness programs are being carried out. A broad range of both personal communication media (e.g., telephone, mail, fax, e-mail) and mass communication media (e.g., radio, television, film, billboards) have also been the focus of much research. On 7th April 2012, the world's most extensive communication programme was launched in India. The "Swasth Bharat" programme is being telecast and broadcast through 30 Regional Kendras of Doordarshan and 29 Stations of All India Radio covering 27 States. The half an hour programme was telecast for five days a week in Regional languages at prime time. The objective of the programme was to empower citizens with Information,

ICT for Development Education and Communication on health-related issues. The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare is the first Ministry in Government of India to have signed a Memorandum of Understanding with Prasar Bharti to start such an outreach programme to be able to reach out to a broad spectrum of the population through mass media. Even as more new communication technologies are being developed, and they have been examined as important media for health communication. These new media, especially the interactive computer technologies and the Internet, have become increasingly important sources for relevant health information and support for many consumers and healthcare providers.
Intermediates-Health Workers-ASHA, ANM, Anganwadi Workers
Community Health Workers (CHW) are the link between the government and the common people. CHW educates the population to attain health literacy. The World Health Organisation (WHO) defines Community Health Workers as "members of communities where they work, selected by and answerable to the communities for their activities, supported by the health system but not necessarily a part of the organisation, and have shorter training than professional workers." Effective use of communication and technology by healthcare professionals can bring about change in public centred health information and service. There is evidence through experience that their approach to health is comprehensive. Their tasks vary from health service navigation, primary health care and social services provision to community development and advocacy concerning the social determinants of health.
Community Health Workers in India
CHW's programme has been implemented in India from 1950 onwards. However, it was widely accepted and marked in its implementation as the Integrated Child Development Scheme (ICDS) programme of 1975, which was initiated with the support of UNICEF and World Bank. Two local women each were selected and trained to meet the antenatal and postnatal care needs in villages. They were named as Anganwadi Worker and Helper who worked solely in their village and focused on providing food supplements to young children, adolescent girls and lactating women. The Auxiliary Nurse-Midwife (ANM), was based at a Sub-Centre and visited villages in addition to providing care at the sub-centre. In 1977, the Swasthya Rakshak Scheme was initiated for villages with male Community Health workers. However, the scheme existed only in some parts, and later the government began to give more importance to maternal and ante-natal care, and more females CHW's were recruited. In the year 2006, India implemented ASHA (Accredited Social Health Activist) as one of the critical components of the National Rural Health Mission. The main agenda was to provide every village in the country with a trained female community health activist. Selected from the village itself and accountable to it, the ASHA woekers is trained to work as an interface between the community and the public health system. ASHA workers stimulated or motivated change in the individual's perception of behaviour or beliefs. ASHA workers focused on the promotion of MCH, including

immunisations and institution-based deliveries, for which they received a Health and ICT performance-related fee. The Ministry of Women and Child Development (WCD) is undertaking a complete revamp of the Integrated Child Development Services, including digitisation of 13 lakh Anganwadis for real-time monitoring of every child and lactating mother. As part of the digitisation drive, 13 lakh Anganwadi workers were to be given smartphones, and their supervisors were to be given tablets. Both the hardware and software for the project was to be provided by the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation. A memorandum of cooperation between the ministry and the foundation in this regard was signed in May 2019. The respective state governments were to provide training to Anganwadi workers to help them switch to the new IT-based system. Though not wholly, ASHA workes were also digitally empowered to some extent. Mobile phones as media are now comparable to popular media like radio and television, which have been used for spreading healthcare awareness messages. It has the capability to provide individually tailored and customised services to underserved people. M-Health could be used by ASHA workers, especially for point-of-care services, provision of health information, counselling, drug adherence, data collection and monitoring. Mobile apps and digital video production training are given to them. Moreover, in the coming years, India may become the largest public sector with digitised community health workers in the world. 14.5 SKILL ACQUISITION IN HEALTH - THEORY
AND MODELS
Skill acquisition refers to how individuals gather and use health information for their health. Whether print or Internet, it provides access to a vast number of documents on health-related topics, but the nature of choosing completely depends upon the skill of users. These skills depend upon an individual's behaviour which contributes to the development of health theories and models.
14.5.1 Health Belief Model
The Health Belief Model (HBM) is one of the models which identifies behavioural health change. The Health Belief Model focuses on individual

ICT for Development beliefs about health conditions, which in turn can predict the individual health- related behaviour. It is the most widely accepted model for understanding health behaviour. HBM explains the impact of an individual's perception and attitude toward disease and how those perceptions and attitudes impact their health-related decision-making. The model has been evolved as a concern in public health. The Health Belief Model can be used to design short- and long-term interventions. Health belief models can be used to identify key determinants that influence health behaviour. The essential components of the HBM depend primarily on two variables (1) the value of a goal to an individual, and (2) the individual's appraisal of the likelihood of action in achieving that goal. It emphasises the role of moderating factors (demographic, social, and structural factors) and individual perceptions (perceived sensitivity, perceived severity, perceived benefits, perceived barriers, cues to action, and self-efficacy) in determining the likelihood of performing a behaviour. HBM is used as a framework to identify social determinants.
Theoretical Constructs
Perceived behaviour and barrier are the reason for individual behaviour. Since HBM is a social behaviour theory, it is used as a conceptual framework for the identification of social determinants of health.
Perceived Susceptibility
In HBM, perceived seriousness and perceived threat are the two factors which can be studied to know how much the individuals are literate. Even though health information and communication is increasing, social determinants act as a barrier to attaining health literacy.
Perceived Severity
The level of health information literacy of an individual can be measured by assessing their knowledge on sharing particular conditions. Cues of Action-Perceived barriers and perceived susceptibility leads to action, and this action is measured to know about the determinants of health literacy. Self-Efficacy-In order to meet the communication needs, the best approach to health information should be to transform efficiently, identifying the worth of health information. Individuals with low perceived susceptibility may deny that they are at risk of contracting a particular illness. The model does not take into account how emotions such as anxiety or fear affect rational thought and decision-making. Even though HBM is the most accepted model for health communication research, the model lacks the measure of the effectiveness of future consequences, self-identity, concern for appearance and perceived importance.
14.5.2 Anderson's ACT theory
Adaptive Concept of Thought is a cognitive theory developed by John R Anderson, an American psychologist. Cognition is the process of understanding or acquiring knowledge and information through thought, experiences and other senses. The architecture is made with the framework or model which shows the process of understanding and acquiring knowledge and information.

This theory tells us several steps and processes to consider every task Health and ICT performed by human beings. It provides a model or framework for the processes that happen in our mind. The framework or model may look like a programming language. The theory works on psychological assumptions of human nature which were derived from numerous scientific experiences and experiments. The main components of ACT are Modules, Buffers and Pattern Matcher. Every human task can be made into a model by this theory. The models of every person will be different from one another. It incorporates research on automaticity and explains the development of cognitive skills necessary for processing health information from a variety of electronic sources.
14.5.3 Transtheoretical Model
The Transtheoretical Model (TTM) (or Stages of Change Model) is a cyclic model developed by Prochaska and Diclemente (1983). The model suggests that people change their behaviour at certain stages in life, rather than making one significant change. During these incremental stages, they consider whether or not to make changes to their behaviour. This cyclic model is based on the premise that people at different levels of readiness change, and during the change process, they move through a series of stages. People move from pre-contemplation (not ready to change) to contemplation (thinking of change), to preparation (getting ready to change), to action (performing the change), to maintenance (continuing the change), to relapse (abandoning changes and reverting to former behaviours). A person may start at any of these stages and may move between stages. This theory finds application in acquiring health information of individuals as they are changing behaviour at specific points of life and can add their information gathering habits. These are only some of the theories and models which find application in health information and the Internet, as online health care is enabling the growth of the practitioner-patient relationship and as the new roles of health workers and caretakers are refining, all these models and theories are also changing.
14.6 BARRIERS TO HEALTH INFORMATION
LITERACY
Socio-cultural disparity and superstitious beliefs exist in most sections of society. Access to healthcare is still in a deprived condition due to the cultural backwardness and the belief system prevailing within them. They are linked with culture, language and facets of life that vary widely among socio-economic conditions. People with low levels of education and occupation is also a factor. Those who are using and depending on technology for their information seem to be more interested in HIL. Language and communication issues also form barriers. Media literacy forms the basis for this. Vulnerable people face problems in communicating with health professionals and depend more on traditional healthcare providers prevalent in their area. In the global world, migration and immigration are increasing, and hence, the language may form a major barrier.

14.6.2 Problems of Usage
The competence and skill of the people can only assure better health in society. More motivated people, i.e. interested in health information and more active at obtaining it, are also more confident in their ability to do so. Lack of knowledge or confidence to seek health information is a barrier to obtaining such information. Information and reports are increasing day-by- day, but the authenticity of the information and quality of information is still in debate. Evidence-based practices and public awareness are the best way to ascertain it. Government initiatives towards training and training to access the information to health workers and caretakers are essential in the information loaded world.
14.6.3 Social Determinants
According to the World Health Organisation (2008), health disparities are associated with gradients in social determinants such as income, age, education, and marginalisation or disadvantages due to race and gender. Educational level, age, gender, cultural beliefs, low socio-economic condition, language and communication strategy all form the social determinants. Family culture, ability and interest to learn all form the determinants of health literacy. Safe housing, transportation, and neighbourhoods, racism, discrimination, and violence, education, job opportunities, and income, access to nutritious foods and physical activity opportunities, polluted air and water, language and literacy skills all determine the individual's health.
14.6.4 Issues in India
India is one of the leading countries which is trying to provide quality healthcare services as it spends 5.2% of the GDP every year. The primary healthcare centres are the main source of healthcare service in rural areas other than secondary care and tertiary care services provided in urban areas where information technology is used, especially in urban hospitals. Specific characteristics such as cost and complexity tend to cause barriers for information technology adoption in the healthcare industry. However, the significant aspects of quality and efficiency gains remain through the use of information communication and technology. Yet, access to these technologies is still deprived for many. Most Indian metro hospitals, as well as small private clinics, are using the information technology for administrative purposes. Instead of accessing the medical records (birth to death) at any point of care by both patients and physicians is said to be a critical aspect of healthcare in these setups.

14.8 KEYWORDS
Adaptive Control of Thought is a learning theory created by Canadian Psychologist John Anderson, that explains the process of acquiring knowledge and information through cognition. The main components of ACT are Modules, Buffers and Pattern Matcher. Health Belief Model is the most widely accepted theoretical model to explain and predict changes in health behaviours. The model defines the key factors that influence health behaviours as an individual's perceived threat to sickness or disease (perceived susceptibility), the belief of consequence (perceived severity), potential positive benefits of action (perceived benefits), perceived barriers to action, exposure to factors that prompt action (cues to action), and confidence in the ability to succeed (self-efficacy). Health Information Literacy: Health information Literacy (HIL) the set of abilities needed to recognise a health information need, identify likely information sources and use them to retrieve relevant information, assess the quality of the information and its applicability to a specific situation, and analyse, understand, and use the information to make right health decisions." Health IT: The term "health information technology" (health IT) refers to the electronic systems being used by health care professionals - increasingly for patients which they use to store, share, and analyse health information. Health Literacy: Health literacy(HL) is defined as the skills and competencies to which individuals have the capacity to obtain, process, and understand necessary health information and services needed to make appropriate health decisions. Transtheoretical Model (TTM) (or Stages of Change Model) is a cyclic model developed by Prochaska and Diclemente (1983). TTM conceptualises behaviour change as a process involving a series of six distinct stages: pre-contemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, maintenance and termination. Each stage undergoes motivation to change, individuals apply cognitive, affective, and evaluation processes to progress forward. Each stage brings an individual closer to making or sustaining behavioural changes which are, in turn, explained as healthy behaviour change.

15.0 INTRODUCTION
Reinventing government has been a dominant theme since the 1990s, wherein governments world over are attempting to improve the systems of public service delivery. Rapid strides made in the field of Information and Communication Technology (ICT) have facilitated the reinvention of governments and prepared them to serve the needs of a diverse society. In other words, the information age has redefined the fundamentals and transformed the institutions and mechanisms of service delivery forever. The vision is the articulation of a desire to transform the way government functions and the way it relates to its constituents. The concept of electronic governance, popularly called e-governance, is derived from this concern. Democracies in the world share a vision of the day when e-governance will become a way of life India has been at the forefront of the IT revolution and has had its effect on the public administration systems, as we would see later in this Unit. If the potential of ICTs is harnessed properly, it has many opportunities, especially in the social and economic growth of the developing world.
15.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After reading this Unit, you will be able to: * discuss the concept and significance of e-governance; * explain the various stages of e-governance; * examine the various models of e-governance; and * analyse the issues and challenges

15.2 CONCEPT OF E-GOVERNANCE
E-governance is the application of ICT to the processes of government functioning for good governance. In other words, e-governance is the public sector's use of ICTs to improve information and service delivery, encourage citizen participation in decision-making and make government more accountable, transparent and efficient. The Ministry of Information and Technology states that e-governance goes far beyond mere computerisation of stand-alone back-office operations. It implies fundamental changes in government operations; and a new set of responsibilities for the legislature, executive, judiciary and citizens.
According to the Comptroller and Auditor General, UK, e-governance
means providing public access to information via the Internet by government departments and their agencies. So in essence, e-governance is the application of ICT in government functioning to bring in SMART governance, implying: simple, moral, accountable, responsive and transparent governance. Simple- meaning simplification of rules, regulations and processes of government through the use of ICTs and thereby providing for a user- friendly government. Moral- connoting emergence of an entirely new system of ethical values in the political and administrative machinery. Technology interventions improve the efficiency of anti-corruption agencies, police, judiciary, etc. Accountable-facilitating design, development and implementation of effective Management Information System and performance measurement mechanisms and thereby ensuring accountability of public service functionaries. Responsive- streamlining the processes to speed up service delivery and make the system more responsive. SMART governance, thus, helps in: * improving the internal organisational processes of governments; * providing better information and service delivery; * increasing government transparency in order to reduce corruption; * reinforcing political credibility and accountability; and * promoting democratic practices through public participation and consultation.
E-governance and E-government
E-governance and e-government are often used interchangeably, so distinguishing between them at this stage is imperative. According to Thomas B. Riley government and governance are both about getting the consent and cooperation of the governed. However, whereas the government is the formal apparatus for this objective, governance is the outcome as experienced by those on the receiving end. E-government can be a more productive version of government in general if it is well implemented and managed. E-governance can evolve into participatory governance if

it is well supported with relevant principles, objectives, programmes and E-Governance architectures. E-government is, thus, the modernisation of processes and functions of the government using the tools of ICT to transform the way it serves its constituents. As per the World Bank, e-government refers to the use by government agencies of information technologies (such as wide area networks, Internet and mobile computing) that have the ability to transform relations with citizens, businesses and other arms of government. It is the use of technology to enhance the access to and delivery of government services to benefit citizens, business partners and employees. E-governance, on the other hand, goes beyond the service delivery aspects and is seen as a decisional process. It is about the use of ICTs in the systems of governance that is, using ICT to involve multi-stakeholders in decision-making and in making governments open and accountable.
15.3 STAGES OF E-GOVERNANCE
Different stages of e-governance are identified on a specific set of criteria. These stages are: * Simple information dissemination (one-way communication)- is considered as the most basic form, as it is used for merely disseminating information; * Two-way communication (request and response)- is characterised with email system and information and data-transfer technologies in the form of the website; * Service and financial transactions- is online services and financial transactions leading to web-based self-services; * Integration (both vertical and horizontal)- in this stage the government would attempt inter and intra-governmental integration; and * Political participation- this stage means online voting, online public forums and opinion surveys for more direct and broader interaction with the government. Another classification of e-governance has six stages, of which the first two are similar to that of the above classification. The remaining four are: * The third stage- refers to multi-purpose portals, which allow customers to use a single point of entry to send and receive information and to process transactions across multiple departments; * The fourth stage- consists of portal personalisation, wherein customers are allowed to customise portals with their desired features; * The fifth stage- is when government departments cluster services along standard lines to accelerate the delivery of shared services and clustering of standard services; and * Sixth and final stage- technology is integrated further to bridge the gap between the front and back office. After our discussion of the concept and stages of e-governance, we will now deal with significant models of e-governance that can be used in designing e-government initiatives.
