15.4 MODELS OF E-GOVERNANCE
Prof. Dr. Arie Halachmi in his paper, namely, ' E-Government Theory and Practice: The Evidence from Tennessee (USA),' has given five essential models of e-governance, which can be used as a guide in designing e-government initiatives depending on the local situation and governance activities that are expected to be performed. These models are: * The Broadcasting Model * The Critical Flow Model * The Comparative Analysis Model * The E-Advocacy/Mobilisation and Lobbying Model * The Interactive-Service Model We will now discuss these models individually.
The Broadcasting Model
The model is based on dissemination/broadcasting of useful governance information, which is in the public domain into the wider public domain with ICT and convergent media. The strength of the model rests upon the fact that a more informed citizenry is better able to judge the functioning of existing governance mechanisms and make an informed opinion about them. Consequently, they become more empowered to exercise their rights and responsibilities. Widespread application of this model corrects 'information failure situations' by providing people with the relevant information relating to the governance sphere to make an informed opinion and impact governance processes. Further, the use of ICT opens an alternative channel for people to access information as well as validate existing information from different sources.
The Critical Flow Model
The model is based on disseminating/channelling information of critical value to the targeted audience or into the wider public domain with ICT and convergent media. The strength of this model is that ICT makes the concept of 'distance' and

'time' redundant when information is hosted on a digital network, and E-Governance this could be used advantageously by instantly transferring the critical information to its strategic user group located anywhere or by making it freely available in the wider public domain.
The Comparative Analysis Model
This model is a highly significant model for developing countries and can be used for empowering people. Essentially, the model continuously assimilates best practices in the areas of governance and then uses them as benchmarks to evaluate other governance practices. It then uses the result to advocate positive changes or to influence 'public' opinion on these governance practices. The comparison could be made over a time scale to get a snapshot of the past and present situation or could be used to compare the effectiveness of an intervention by comparing two similar situations. The strength of this model lies in the infinite capacity of digital networks to store varied information and retrieve and transmit it instantly across all geographical and hierarchical barriers.
The E-Advocacy/Mobilisation and Lobbying Model
This model builds the momentum of real-world processes by adding the opinions and concerns expressed by virtual communities. This model helps the global civil society to impact on global decision-making processes. It is based on setting up a planned, directed flow of information to build strong virtual allies to complement actions in the real world. Virtual communities are formed which share similar values and concerns, and these communities, in turn, link up with or support real-life groups/activities for concerted action. Hence, it creates a diversity of the virtual community, and the ideas, expertise and resources are accumulated through this virtual form of networking. Besides, it can mobilise and leverage human resources and information beyond geographical, institutional and bureaucratic barriers and use it for concerted action.
The Interactive-Service Model
It opens avenues for direct participation of individuals in governance processes and brings in greater objectivity and transparency in decision- making processes through ICT. Fundamentally, ICT has the potential to bring in every individual in a digital network and enable interactively (two-way) flows of information among them. Under this model, the various services offered by the government become directly available to its citizens in an interactive manner. It does so by opening up an interactive Government to Consumer to Government (G2C2G) channel in various aspects of governance, such as the election of government officials (e-ballots); redressing online of specific grievances; sharing of concerns and providing expertise; opinion polls on various issues; etc. (adapted from Prof. Dr.Arie Halachmi 'E-Government Theory and Practice: The Evidence from Tennessee, USA'). After our discussion about the models of e-governance, we will now focus on the legal and policy framework for the implementation of ICT and e-governance in the country.

15.5 LEGAL AND POLICY FRAMEWORK
The following provisions have laid down the legal and policy framework for ICT and e-governance. Information Technology Act of 2000: The Action Plan endorsed by the Conference of Chief Ministers in 1987 had already addressed the pertinent issues of accountable and citizen-friendly administration; and transparency and right to information. In pursuance of these issues, the Information Technology Act was promulgated in 2000. The objective of the Act is "to provide legal recognition for transactions carried out by means of electronic data interchange and other means of electronic communication, commonly referred to as 'electronic methods of communication and storage of information'; to facilitate electronic filing of documents with the Government agencies; and further to amend the Indian Penal Code, the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, the Banker's Book Evidence Act, 1891 and the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto." Both e-commerce and e-governance transactions are covered under the ambit of this Act, which facilitates acceptance of electronic records and digital signatures. The Act, thus, stipulates numerous provisions. It aims to provide for the legal framework so that legal sanctity is accorded to all electronic records and other activities carried out by electronic means. The said Act further states that unless otherwise agreed, an acceptance of the contract may be expressed by electronic means of communication and the same shall have legal validity and enforceability. CHAPTER III of the Act details about 'Electronic Governance' and provides amongst others that where any law provides that information or any other matter shall be in writing or the typewritten or printed form, then, notwithstanding anything contained in such law, such requirement shall be deemed to have been satisfied if such information or matter is: * rendered or made available in an electronic form; and * accessible to be usable for a subsequent reference. Report of the Working Group on Convergence and E-governance 2002-07 Report of the Working Group on Convergence and E-governance proposed the need for the administration to transform itself from a passive information and service provider to a platform/ forum for the active involvement of citizens. This report primarily concerned itself with public investments. It could not visualise the extent of private initiative that could be expected to come forth in the convergence area or e-commerce or allied segments. It felt the need to set up a central body for taking stock of the total IT picture in the country. This central body could be a 'Council for E-governance' or an ad hoc 'Commission on Re-engineering Administrative Procedures for E-governance.' Another alternative it suggested was to set up a National Institute of Smart Governance. Common Minimum Programme: The importance of e-governance has been recognised in the Common

Minimum Programme of the UPA Government, which inter-alia states that E-Governance e-governance will be promoted on a massive scale. It made a solemn pledge to the people of the country with a government that would be corruption free, transparent and accountable; and an administration that would be responsible and responsive at all times. National E-Governance Plan: Three important elements of the National E-Governance Plan, which form the core infrastructure for effective service delivery are- Data Centres, State Wide Area Networks and Common Service Centres. The 10-point agenda of the Department of Information Technology announced for growth of ICT in the country includes expeditious implementation of a 'National E-Governance Plan' to bring about transparency and citizen-centric approach in administration. Expert Committee: An expert committee had also been constituted for the amendments in the IT Act 2000 to include the technological developments post IT Act 2000. The Expert Committee completed its deliberations and submitted its report in August 2005. Now the Expert Committee's recommendations have been put on the website of the Department of Information Technology for inviting public views and suggestions. The Committee, during its deliberations, analysed some of the relevant experiences and international best practices. The Committee, while formulating its recommendations, kept in view the twin objectives of (i) using IT as a tool for socio-economic development and employment generation; and (ii) further consolidation of India's position as a significant global player in the IT sector. Right to Information Act 2005 The Right to Information Act 2005 confers on the citizens the right to: i. inspect works, documents and records of the government and its agencies; ii. take notes, extracts or certified copies of documents or records; iii. take certified samples of material; and iv. obtain information in the form of printouts, diskettes, floppies, tapes, video cassettes or in any other electronic mode. This has ensured a transparent and accountable government to the people. It has also established a two-way dialogue between the citizens and the government. It has enabled citizens to make well-informed decisions. Further, it is an essential step towards tackling corruption and has ensured better monitoring of services provided by the government.
15.6 SIGNIFICANCE OF E-GOVERNANCE
ICT applications impact the structures of public administration systems. Technological advancements facilitate administrative systems by enabling: * Administrative Development; and * Effective Service Delivery We will now discuss them individually.

ICT for Development Administrative Development
Administrative reforms, often, have focused on procedural details and restructuring of systems and processes of government organisations. The primary objective of these reforms is to enhance the capacities of the systems. ICTs can be used and are being used now to give further impetus to the process. They help in the following manners:
Automation of Administrative Processes
A truly e-governed system would require minimal human intervention and would rather be system driven. While initially, the solutions that were offered were relatively primitive with poor information layout, inadequate navigation provisions, occasional disruption in services, periodic outdated content and little or no 'back office' support. However, technological advancements and increased pressure from citizenry have prompted improvements in these areas. Now administrative departments are computerised and connected through networks. The software has been built and designed around government departments ensuring efficiency in operations. The departments have launched individual websites carrying information of their respective departments. This has enabled online carrying of operations and file movements. Budgeting accounting, data flow, etc. has become easy. This has increased the efficiency of office operations and processes and has reduced unnecessary delays.
Paperwork Reduction
An immediate impact of automation would be on the paperwork. Paperwork is reduced to a greater extent with communication being enabled via electronic route and storage and retrieval of information in the electronic form. All this has led to the emergence of 'less paper office'. This concept is defined as an office situation where all the information (file and mail) amongst various functionaries is distributed online. In the words of Dubey, less paper office is the implementation of effective electronic communication processes that enable elimination of reproductive works and unnecessary papers. The concept is where files and emails (information) are transmitted over wires to small computers at each employee's desk. Office work, such as file movements, notings, etc. is computerised, and documentation, report preparation, databases are now maintained in computers. Due to interconnectivity through LAN, transfer of information and files take place online, thus reducing the physical movements and consumption and storage of vast piles of paper.
Quality of Services
ICT helps governments to deliver services to the citizens with greater accountability, responsiveness and sensitivity. Quality of services improves, as now the people can get services efficiently and instantaneously. As volumes of transactions and information can be electronically handled and delivered over a wider area through the net and web, qualitative services become possible in the least time, in the least cost, in the least difficulty and greater convenience. By ensuring online redressal of grievances, the accountability of officials is ensured. They have become sensitive to the issues affecting people. Monitoring by way of video teleconferencing has further facilitated central monitoring, reporting and face to face communication that has assured effective service delivery by the officials.

Elimination of Hierarchy E-Governance
ICT has reduced procedural delays caused by hierarchical processes in the organisation. Through Intranet and LAN, it has become possible to send information and data across various levels in the organisation at the same time. Computerisation and communication patterns facilitated by ICT have increased efficiency and have led to the involvement of all levels in decision-making.
Change in Administrative Culture
Bureaucratic structures have been plagued by characteristics aptly described by Victor Thompson as 'bureau-pathology'. From the days of New Public Administration, efforts have been made to find ways to deal with the pathological or dysfunctional aspects of bureaucratic behaviour and to make delivery of public services effective and efficient. With e-governance, public actions coming under public glare would certainly induce norms and values of accountability, openness, integrity, fairness, equity, responsibility and justice in the organisational culture. Instead, the administration would become efficient and responsive.
Effective Service Delivery
ICTs play an essential role in effectively delivering services to people. ICTs ensure: * Transparency by dissemination and publication of information on the web. This provides easy access to information and subsequently makes the system publicly accountable. Also, as the web enables the free flow of information, it can be easily accessed by all without any discrimination.
Economic Development
The deployment of ICTs reduces transaction costs, which makes services cheaper. For example, rural areas suffer on account of lack of information regarding markets, products, agriculture, health, education, weather, etc. and if all this could be accessed online would lead to better and more opportunities and thereby prosperity in these areas.
Social Development
The access to information empowers the citizens. Informed citizens can participate and voice their concerns, which can be accommodated in the programme/ project formulation, implementation, monitoring and service delivery. Web-enabled participation will counter the discriminatory factors affecting our societal behaviour.
Strategic Information System
Changing the organisational environment and increasing competitiveness have put pressures on the performance of the functionaries. Information regarding all aspects needs to be made available to the management at every point to make the routine as well as strategic decisions. ICTs effectively enable putting such strategic information systems in place. After the discussion, as mentioned above, on the significance of ICTs in governance, we will now highlight specific measures that will enable its effective implementation.

15.7 CHALLENGES AND OPPORTUNITIES
The above discussion highlighted the critical role of ICTs in governance. In order to harness the benefits of ICTs maximally, we need to develop sufficient and adequate infrastructure, provide sufficient capital and investment, enable easy and more comprehensive accessibility and generate ample and skilful human resources. These are some of the immediate and pertinent challenges to effective implementation of ICT and e-governance. We will now discuss these issues individually. Infrastructure: The foundation of e-governance is based on telecommunication services. To develop telecommunication, infrastructures are to be created so that the end-user can access the services promptly and effectively. To strengthen the infrastructure, 'The National Task Force on Information Technology and Software Development' in 1998 recommended broadband connection (also known as 'the last mile') linkage for IT Applications Service Providers (ASPs), Internet Service Providers (ISPs) and IT promotional organisations, either by fibre optics or by radio communication, intending to 'boost efficiency and enhance market integration' through Internet/Intranet for sustainable regional development. Capital: A high rate of investment in IT capital and a supportive environment is necessary to achieve a digital economy. Given the resource crunch with the government, there is a need to generate resources from the market and private sector. The public-private partnership may be beneficial in this regard, as the private sector can participate and contribute to capital and expertise support. Access: At present, there are more than 10 million users of the Internet in the country. However, the irony is that more than 75 per cent of these users are in urban India. The Internet has still to reach the rural and disadvantaged sections. However, efforts are being made to expand ICT connectivity into rural areas through the involvement of Gram Panchayats. NIC has developed a comprehensive web-based software for Panchayati raj and rural applications, which is being implemented in states like Andhra Pradesh. With most of the panchayats getting computerised, accessibility to various services has become easy. The utility of information: There is a need to provide information, which is useful. The content of the information should be such that it should be attractive, beneficial and appealing to the people. In this regard, the Government of India and some of the state governments have prepared a vision document for e-governance keeping in mind the needs of the citizens. Though Citizens' Charters of many departments are available on the net, further publicity of such facilities is required to enable the public to access the necessary information. Human Resource Development: Despite the ascending growth rate observed in employment in the IT sector, there is a dearth of quality human resources. There exist a demand and

supply gap in the IT human resources market. India needs to have more E-Governance technical institutes to impart education and training to build a pool of human resources in the field. Capacity Building: Service delivery will be useful if there are trained human resources. Though computer training is being imparted to all the necessary public functionaries, except in a few cases, effective use of ICT is yet to be seen. Moreover, there is an immediate need to launch a nationwide 'Train the Teachers Programme' (3T Programme). This should be done at all levels, including schools and colleges. A combination of physical and virtual training also needs to be imparted. Changing the Mindset of Government Functionaries: To accept the change, there is a need to change the mindset of service providers and receivers. The government functionaries need to be made aware that they are there to serve the clients as per the policies and programmes and that technological advancement is only a facilitator to solutions of problems faced by people and not a solution in itself. To change the mindset of the service providers there is a need to impart orientation and training programmes to them. Language: The success of e-government also depends on communication with the people in their local languages. Currently, the most widely used language is English for e-government. Nevertheless, given the Indian social conditions, unless we develop interfaces in vernacular languages, it would remain out of reach of many people who are not capable of accessing these services in English. In this context, it is essential that a clear strategy is formulated to provide access to local level databases maintained in regional and local languages as well as to use appropriate interfaces to aggregate such data. However, it may be mentioned here that organisations like the Centre for Development of Advanced Computing (CDAC) have developed multilingual software for the purpose. Standardisation in Data Encoding: Once multiple access points maintained in various languages at various levels are established, there is a need to update them in conformity with similar standards for data encoding-an application logic for a common horizontal application and data dictionary. This is also important for finding aggregates in the national context. Grievance Redressal Mechanism: The mechanism planned for various functions needs to make provision for grievance redressal as well. Interactive platforms on the Internet may speed up the process and may be useful in this regard. The BMC-Praja Foundation's joint initiative of the Online Complaint Management System (OCMS) is perhaps the world's first in citizen-government partnership for solving public grievances in municipal services. Inaugurated in April 2003, the OCMS has been receiving grievances on behalf of citizens availing services of municipalities in Mumbai. It uses IT as a tool to bring in efficiency and effectiveness into the system. One can register his/her complaint online regarding various municipal services, and the Municipal Corporation will

ICT for Development redress this complaint in the time stipulated in the Citizens' Charter adopted by the Corporation. The Central Vigilance Commission has also provided such a platform for people to register their complaints against corrupt officials. Such sporadic instances need to be made broad-based and effective, though it may be conceded that more and more public service agencies are now providing or contemplating such facilities. Cyber Laws: The government needs to enact appropriate laws, especially those, which are necessary to enable transactions over the Internet. Safety concerns regarding the use of credit cards or other modes of payment stop the consumers from using such facilities. The Mahanagar Telephone Nagar Limited, Delhi, for example, has provided the online facility for payment of telephone bills. However, not even one per cent of its consumers are making use of this provision. Hence, security has to be ensured for generating confidence in the system. 15.8 LET US SUM UP
According to Traunmuller and Lenk, e-governance is a global phenomenon today, and it is the most recent paradigm in public administration. The speed and transparency associated with e-governance have the potential to make public administration responsive and effective. As the development of e-governance gets past the phase of pilot projects, it becomes apparent that sustainable development of e-governance will depend on an adequate institutional framework that will enable public administration to manage and harmonise the emerging multitude of technical and organisational changes at all levels of government The time has come to focus on the challenges in implementation, especially those related to cross-level applications and institutional framework, which would enable to bring in broader changes in governance.

16.0 INTRODUCTION
The rise in Internet penetration and the growing number of digital device users have spurred a new wave of digital media entrepreneurship in India. The change is most visible in the news media space. These news ventures are not only expanding the media market but are also willing to experiment with new business models. Some of the digital news media ventures are offering news as a public service under a not-for-profit organisational structure in a media landscape dominated by corporate-controlled mainstream news media, which are susceptible to commercial and political pressures. There are other digital news media ventures that are catering to a niche audience in a subscription-based business model. The possibility of the reduction in entry barriers for such ventures is offered by technology as it can bring down the cost of news production and distribution significantly. Digital news media ventures have also opened up new opportunities for media students. Despite the challenges that remain due to the ownership and control of technological resources by big corporates, the growth in digital news media entrepreneurship stimulates hope for a democratised, alternative media space in the country.

ICT for Development In this Unit, we will closely examine the process of entrepreneurship and the growth of digital news media ventures in India.
16.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After reading this Unit , you will be able to : * understand the process of entrepreneurship; * analyse different types of entrepreneurial ventures; * examine the growth and development of digital media entrepreneurship
in India; and
* understand the opportunities and challenges in building a digital news media career.
16.2 ENTREPRENEURSHIP
It is not easy to find a satisfactory definition of entrepreneurship. This is because definitions are context-related and different people look at entrepreneurship from different perspectives. However, one common thread among the different definitions is that they all consider entrepreneurship as a process. A person who initiates this process is called an entrepreneur. So, let us understand the starting point of this process and how to define it.
16.2.1 Idea, Innovation and Definition
Every process of entrepreneurship starts with an idea. An idea can be about anything. Some people think and come up with a new invention - a new product. However, in today's world, one hardly comes across an invention like the light bulb by Thomas Alva Edison. Human society has made so much technological progress that today even the most remarkable invention would feel like an incremental addition. Little wonder then that these days the process of entrepreneurship mostly starts with a simple idea to improve an existing product or service. Did you know that in 1997 Reed Hastings started Netflix as a DVD rental service? What made the company different from other DVD rental stores was its monthly subscription model. Unlike other stores, Hastings offered his customers unlimited rentals at a flat rate without any due dates. It was this idea to manage an existing service in a better customer-friendly manner that blossomed into a highly successful media company. Similarly, Apple, in 2007, made touchscreen technology available to a broader audience with the launch of the iPhone. You have to remember that Apple neither invented mobile phones nor touchscreen technology. The company just improved an existing product (in this case, a mobile phone) with better technology (touchscreen). What do Netflix and iPhone case studies tell us about entrepreneurship? Both the models became successful because these companies found a gap or room for improvement in an existing service or product. In other words, these companies identified an opportunity. From these two cases, it can be considered that entrepreneurship is a process of developing an opportunity to launch a better service or a product. Developing an opportunity is not an easy process. It requires fresh thinking and a different approach. This is called innovation. In fact, innovation is

the backbone of entrepreneurship. It is an innovation that helps develop an Entrepreneurship and Digital opportunity to create value. This value creation can take different forms, such Media as an improved product, a better service or a more convenient distribution network like an online delivery system. In this sense, entrepreneurship can be considered as the process of creating value for society and the company using innovation. Entrepreneurship, therefore, also leads to overall economic development in the society.
16.2.2 Launching a Venture
Ideas and innovation do not automatically translate into successful entrepreneurship. Execution of an idea requires resources and people. Besides, great ideas and technological innovations can fail if customers do not accept them. As a result, entrepreneurship involves substantial risk analysis and assessment. Remember what happened to Nokia, Yahoo and Orkut. All of them failed to sustain their initial momentum; eventually faced heavy losses and shut down their services partially or wholly. It is not easy to mobilise resources for entrepreneurship, especially in India, due to the risks involved. In the initial stage, the money mostly comes from friends, family and one's own savings. The Wire (www.thewire.in), a news website which was started in 2015 with Rs 10 lakh pooled in by its founders from their own savings. If you are an entrepreneur, in order to take your idea forward and execute it, you need to set up a venture. It basically functions as a launchpad, where people come together and work towards designing and introducing a new product or service through an innovative approach. The workforce needed can be in the form of employees, contract workers, volunteers or anybody who can contribute to the development of a venture. At the starting point, we will not call it a company or an office as an entrepreneur can set up different types of ventures. All of them need not have the structure of a company. Besides, with the popularity of online technologies, many new ventures do not have a brick and mortar office. They exist only in the online sphere. We will learn more about this in the next section. Setting up a venture and launching a product or service is not an easy task in a developing country like India due to various reasons. More than funding, the most challenging aspect of entrepreneurship in India is securing government approvals. Although online ventures have it easy as compared to others, it is difficult to register a venture here. As an easier option, many Indian entrepreneurs register their companies in countries like Singapore, although they operate in the Indian market. Another challenge is dispute resolution through the legal process, which can be time-consuming. These are unique challenges specific to India. So, you should understand that it is not fair to compare the success stories of entrepreneurial ventures in developed countries like the US and European nations with that of India.
16.2.3 Business Model and Types of Ventures
As discussed earlier, entrepreneurship requires resources. Ventures need money to pay salaries to their employees, to buy raw materials, for developing technological know-how and to design a product or service. If it is an offline venture, additional funding will be required to set up an office, pay rentals or to acquire land. Depending on the type of venture, resources are spent

ICT for Development on marketing and distribution as well. All these requirements come under the cost of operations. In other words, a venture needs to spend money to introduce a new product or service. Although the amount of money required varies depending on the type of product, service and the market, no venture can survive without incurring a certain amount of expenditure. Most of these costs (barring machinery and land) are recurring expenditure, i.e., these are ongoing expenses that are needed to operate a venture. If the entrepreneurship is successful, revenues from the new product or service will help the venture to cover these costs. Surplus revenues lead to profits. Profit is what a venture earns after deducting all expenses, including taxes. Entrepreneurship, therefore, requires careful planning on how to earn money. The plan that explains how the venture will generate revenue and gain profits is called a business model. A business model, therefore, involves identifying various sources of revenue, intended customer base and how to reach them through marketing and a detailed plan on how to manufacture or design a product or launch a service. Overall, a business model offers a rational description of how a venture plans to create and deliver economic, social and cultural values, depending on the type of organisation and at what cost. It is a business plan that defines the character of a venture. Based on the business plan, ventures are mainly classified into two - business venture and social venture. Accordingly, entrepreneurship can also be divided into two - business entrepreneurship (associated with business venture) and social entrepreneurship (associated with social venture). A business venture is a company or an organisation whose main objective is to create shareholder wealth. The nature of such an organisation is minting profit. A shareholder is a person or an entity that invests in a venture expecting returns in future. While the main objective of a for-profit venture is to create and deliver value for itself and its shareholders, this value creation can lead to overall wealth creation and economic progress in society. Facebook, Amazon, Google and Indian news media sites, such as The Ken (the-ken. com) are for-profit business ventures. Ventures set up by social entrepreneurs focus on improving the lives of people and society. They look beyond profit and success for them is about supporting a cause and contributing towards it. Social ventures can be for- profit or not-for-profit in nature. Whatever be the nature of these ventures, they need to earn money to sustain their operations. Similar to a business venture, a not-for-profit social venture sells products and services. However, their customers know that they are paying to support a specific cause and that the earnings from their purchase will help improve the society as the venture's explicit objective is to create social and cultural values rather than earning money. If the venture is not-for-profit in nature, the surplus revenues earned by it get reinvested within the company. An investor in a not-for-profit venture does not get any direct returns. In the broadest sense of the term, we can even consider organisations that accept government grants to solve a social problem as social ventures. SHEF (Study Hall Education Foundation), an organisation dedicated to offering education to the most disadvantaged girls in India falls under the category

of a not-for-profit social venture. People's Archive of Rural India (PARI), Entrepreneurship and Digital an online journal and archive of rural news, data and stories is another Media example. For-profit social ventures, on the other hand, work more or less like a company, except that they make their money by improving the lives of people and society. In this case, investors can expect a share from the surplus revenues or the profit earned by the venture. Frontier Markets, a rural marketing and distribution company that provides affordable durables to low-income households, is an example of for-profit social ventures. Desi Crew, a rural business process outsourcing (BPO) firm, focusing on creating jobs in rural areas, is another example. Check Your Progress: 1 Note: 1) Use the space below for your answers.

16.3 DIGITAL MEDIA
Media and communication sectors worldwide are experiencing a period of rapid change. The rise of digital connectivity, the popularity of Internet- related applications and the convergence of technologies have opened up new opportunities for media and technology companies. As a result, new media organisations are coming up across the world that is utilising the Internet's potential to attain audience reach and scale in order to offer information and entertainment-related products and services. Digital media makes use of digital technologies such as computers, mobile phones and the Internet to produce, store, distribute and retrieve information and entertainment-related products and services. The digital media sector in India has quite the potential to grow. India is the second-biggest smartphone market in the world after China. Our country also has the second largest number of Internet users with Internet penetration at 604 million users (5 years and above) until December 2019 in India (TRAI, 2020). As digitisation is set to make exponential growth in India, it is crucial to understand how the digital technologies have

ICT for Development helped create a new wave of digital entrepreneurship in India and also to comprehend the scope of growth in the Indian digital market. In order to do so, we need to analyse the media market in India. In the following sections, we shall offer a brief history of digital media in the world as Indian digital media entrepreneurship is intrinsically linked to the growth of international digital firms. The following sections will also offer an overview of the characteristics of digital media, types of digital media, products, revenue model, market opportunity and their use of technology. We will also analyse the issues and challenges faced by the media from a critical perspective.
16.3.1 Evolution of Digital Media
Universal accessibility of products and services is a major distinguishing characteristic of digital media. Unlike traditional media (print/broadcast), digital media makes use of the Internet to reach out to a larger mass of customers across the globe. Another distinct characteristic of digital media is that they are not constrained by space or time like print and broadcast media. These advantages have triggered the traditional media to digitise their products and services so that they can expand their reach and customer base. It was the popularity of personal computers in the 1990s that helped usher in a digitally connected world. Personal computers and world wide web (www) changed the way people do shopping, research, reading, banking and consuming news in the US which led the entrepreneurs to find a great opportunity in the interconnected world and to set up web portals or dotcom companies. During this time, India was witnessing its own revolution in the form of information technology outsourcing. The Internet and the government's liberalised economic policies in 1991 made it easy for business organisations in the US and Europe to outsource their technology requirements to India. While the world wide web completely changed the news cycle in the US, India saw the entry of private cable TV networks and 24-hour news channels during the period 1991-1999. However, during 2000
- 02, the US experienced a downward spiral in the technological sector.
Many of the dotcom companies closed down as their business model failed to bring in any revenues. The US market started to recover in 2003, and interactive web 2.0 technologies became extensively popular. Web 2.0, in the present scenario, helps an average user to collaborate with others and to become a content producer on the Internet. As the US technology market began to grow, it witnessed the emergence of a slew of new social networking sites. MySpace was born in 2003. Twitter and Facebook came about in 2004. Now defunct Orkut was set up in 2004. Video blogging started in 2004, followed by the launch of the video-sharing site, YouTube in 2005. From the perspective of Indian media, the English print media initiated the digitisation process of media in 1995. Nevertheless, the momentous change came about in late 2000 when people started using social networking sites that maximise the potential of the interactive nature of web technologies. What accelerated this adoption in our country was the growth in Internet connectivity and mobile phones coupled with the rising number of private telecom operators, who offered affordable services.

16.3.2 Indian Scenario Entrepreneurship and Digital
Media Digital media can be created in two ways. The first route is to digitise the existing media content, like print. All the newspapers in India have a dynamic online portal that offers instant content updates to customers. The second route is to author content digitally. Digitisation of the existing content by newspapers or TV channels does not come under the entrepreneurship category. Several print companies have already invested heavily in digital media, making services such as news delivery possible via mobile applications and web portals. Legacy news media titles like Times of India, NDTV, and Dainik Bhaskar are investing in their digital operations. With China mostly being closed off as a market due to tight government control and censorship, major Western Internet players are looking towards India for growth. Google, Facebook, Amazon, Netflix and other technology companies have all made major investments in India. International publishers like The Huffington Post, BuzzFeed Quartz, and others have been slowly expanding since they arrived in the last couple of years. Digital Entertainment segment in India is dominated by existing big companies like Sun Nxt from SUN TV Network, Alt Balaji by Balaji Telefilms and Voot by Viacom 18. Independent content creators like TVF and AIB are dependent on these streaming sites or Netflix, Amazon Prime or Disney+Hotstar for content distribution. Unlike the entertainment content, the journalism sector in India has witnessed the entry of a vibrant group of digital media entrepreneurs. These entrepreneurial ventures are not only experimenting with content but also revenues models. The Ken, Scroll, The Wire, The Print, Caravan
Magazine, IndiaSpend, PARI, Newslaundry, YourStory, Deal Street Asia
and ScoopWhoop are challenging the news production and distribution strategies of the traditional media. The growth of digital news media entrepreneurship that started in the late 2000s can be considered as the third major turning point in the history of Indian journalism. The first transformative phase was the post-colonial press that played a significant role in nation-building. The second critical moment was after 1991, when the country opened up its markets. The second phase witnessed the complete corporatisation of the news media. It also changed the nature of labour. Newspapers abandoned the wage board system, and with the advent of private news channels, journalism became a contractual job.
16.3.3 Benefits of Technology
As mentioned earlier, one of the characteristics of digital media is its reach and the universal accessibility of its products and services. Its reach and accessibility offer significant advantages to digital media entrepreneurship. It is easy to produce, store and distribute content on the web. The Internet helps digital media products and services to reach a large number of customers cost-effectively. It is possible for an Indian digital media venture to launch a news portal and reach its target audience in the US and Europe with no additional distribution cost. A web portal does not require much money to set up compared to a newspaper or TV channel. Distribution is

ICT for Development almost free except the charges to be paid to the telecom operator for Internet access. Hence, social media sites have become effective marketing channels to reach out to the intended audience. A digital media entrepreneur does not need to hire an office or employees to produce content. The Internet makes it possible to connect with people sitting across different parts of the world almost instantly. As a result, a digital media venture can get an army of freelancers who can contribute content from various places. In this case, most of the coordination, content discussion and editing takes place online, thereby further reducing the operational cost of a venture. The Ladies Finger (theladiesfinger.com), an online women's magazine was started in 2013 as a volunteer-run organisation, where the founders and writers were all working in different firms and also running the site. Besides, very few approvals and clearances are required in India to launch a digital media venture as compared to print or broadcast media. Print, TV and Radio need to register with the Registrar of Newspapers for India. They also have to seek approval for raising funding. However, digital media is not governed by these rules. Another advantage of digital media is its interactive nature. Viewer or reader of a web series or news portal is an active customer, who can instantly send feedback to the service or product provider. The digital media readers/ viewers, therefore, are considered as prosumers, who consume as well produce content. Such interactive nature of the technology helps digital media entrepreneurs to understand their customers better. They can modify an existing product or service or launch a new product or service as the feedback is instant, and the cost of production is cheaper. Expanding the customer base, therefore, becomes comparatively easy for a digital media entrepreneur. It is believed that the interactive nature of the web is the reason why the Internet can democratise the production process of media. In the case of print or traditional broadcast (before the introduction of SMS and phone-in programmes), the content was controlled entirely by professional producers, such as journalists, series directors, scriptwriters etc. Viewers or readers were just passive consumers who did not have a say in the production of content. With the user-generated content in the form of comments, digital media customers have become an active part of the production process.
16.3.4 Digital Media Business Model
The media industry is different from other industries due to its dual product character. The two products of media are - content and audience (reader/ viewer). Unlike other industries, media cannot separate these products because without audience content has no value. Media, especially print and broadcast business models, are centred around the audience as advertising is a major revenue generator for the media. Advertisers make payments to media firms in return for audience attention. Media monitors its readership/ viewership and categorises the audience into various socio-economic groups. Advertising rates depend on the type of audience (socio-economic category) and the total number of audiences a media firm has. At times, the media firms can command very high advertising rates, even with a smaller

number of readers/viewers. This is because their readers belong to the top Entrepreneurship and Digital socio-economic category, and advertisers are willing to pay higher rates for Media their attention because of their high purchasing power. For-profit traditional media (both print and TV) belongs to this category. The process of categorisation of the audience by media and selling them to advertisers for revenue generation is called audience commodification. You get a 20-page newspaper for just Rs 5 because the advertisers subsidise the content. In fact, under this business model, the media uses content to attract the audience, but their main product is the audience. Some media, however, do not follow this model. Films are an example of such media, where viewers have to pay for the content. Movie channel HBO also follows a premium subscription model in the US, where viewers have to pay for watching its content as its shows are ad-free. While most digital news media follow an advertising-based revenue model, some use the subscription-based model. A few offer a mix of both -- free content and subscription-based premium content. Several not-for-profit digital news sites offer free content without any advertisements. They depend on donations from foundations and readers in order to sustain their operations. The Ken is one of the very few news portals that offer subscription-only content. Newslaundry and The Caravan Magazine has adopted a mix of free and subscription-based content. The business model of Scroll (www. scroll.in) is slightly different. The site has two versions. To access the ad- free version, readers have to pay. Its subscribers also get certain benefits like full access to its four-year archives. However, readers can access its basic version with advertisements for free. The Wire, IndiaSpend and PARI are not-for-profit news portals that depend on donations and contributions from readers and corporate foundations. Digital media ventures that are not purely subscription-based make use of social networking sites and YouTube extensively to market their content and reach out to the audience. One of the major advantages of news is that as a product, it does not get used up or destroyed in the act of consumption. Replication cost of digital media news is almost zero because of this inexhaustible characteristic. Thereby, it is easy for a digital media entrepreneur to achieve economies of scale. The media industry is also characterised by economies of scope, i.e., the nature of media output is such that it is possible for a product created for one market to be reformatted and sold through another. However, it is not easy to monetise news-based products and earn revenues. India is still a developing country, and the vast majority of the people are illiterate. The news comes relatively low in their hierarchy of needs. A few discernible readers or viewers who crave for news have a vast array of choices before them - starting from free news websites to newspapers to a plethora of television channels. The biggest challenge for digital news media ventures is how to create a unique news product or to differentiate its products from others in such a way that a value-conscious customer is willing to pay for it. Although it is difficult to create product differentiation in the general news category, it becomes more comfortable in specialised sections like business news, technology, trade etc.

ICT for Development Not-for-profit digital news media ventures, however, face another issue. News is a public good and not a commodity. News is supposed to benefit society. If you try to monetise news and push it behind a paywall, it ceases to become a public good. The question before the not-for-profit digital media now is how to sustain themselves without selling news as a commodity. This is precisely the reason why many of them are accepting advertisements for revenues as donations or foundation funding are hard to come by. 16.4 OPPORTUNITIES AND CHALLENGES FOR A
MEDIA STUDENT
Gone are the days when media students had to wait for that big break in the media. Gaining work experience or obtaining placements or internships have become easy, with an increase in the number of digital media organisations. Due to budget constraints, most of the digital media firms are looking for freelancers who can contribute. These days, you can even start your website without any upfront investment if you know how to use free online tools. Social media sites also offer youngsters opportunities to create their own media, distribute it and gain readership/viewership at no cost. Sometimes a popular social media profile is all you need to land a staff job at a digital new media venture as most editors want employees with a robust online presence. Once on the job, maintaining regular social media posts and updates becomes part of your job profile. Besides, there are a large number of organisations that creates specialised content like YourStory that focuses on start-ups and entrepreneurs, e.g. The Ladies Finger and PARI. These specialised content creating sites are the best places to hone your skills and improve your knowledge if you have a passion for a particular subject or you want to become an expert in a specialised topic.

16.4.1 Accuracy Vs Speed Entrepreneurship and Digital
Media The skillset and technological know-how needed to work as a digital media journalist are slightly different from that of traditional media. The web is an integrated media. You need to have a broader understanding of how each of this medium (audio, video or text) operate and how to tune yourself according to the demands of a podcast (audio), video (visual) and writing (text). In other words, you should be prepared to function as a print/radio/ video journalist -- all rolled into one. While the flexibility in employment aided by the interactive technologies has offered hitherto unseen opportunities to media students, it has also thrown up a few challenges. The Internet and digital media have changed the news cycle. We are constantly checking our social media feeds in search of the next big news. As a result, the Internet economy is pushing news media organisations to publish stories with more incredible speed and at an increased frequency.
16.4.2 Adapting to Digital Media
The false sense of immediacy to fill in infinite space has led to a scenario, wherein journalists are producing more words, and the readers are spending far more time to read. However, news media organisations are unable to help readers understand their world. As most of the digital news media's business model is based on their ability to get the reader hooked and to keep them clicked, news stories often tend to miss clarity, context and understanding. Most national events have international repercussions. Similarly, many international events directly affect our political and economic environment. You need to deal with the challenges of working round the clock in a global news environment. The US presidential decisions on immigration laws and visa restrictions, for instance, can have a major impact on our services, exports, forex reserves and employment opportunities. With networks across the world being accessible to people in India, a digital media journalist cannot wait for a day or two to analyse the US policy decisions. Your success lies in how you balance accuracy and speed without losing focus on the context of the story. One way to do this is to prepare yourself to analyse an event. Most governments generally announce dates on which they make major policy decisions. This will help you anticipate and prepare a basic framework on how to write the news. Increase in the number of media organisations has led to heightened competition. This, in turn, is putting tremendous pressure on journalists to work extended hours for the same pay. Besides, a digital media professional has to maintain a very active social media profile as social media sites, especially Facebook and Twitter can route traffic to the news sites. So, a journalist also becomes a marketing professional on social media. These days, many media organisations link their performance-based incentives to journalists' post on social media and its impact. As a result, a career in digital journalism is not only about providing information, but it involves innovative marketing too. Digital media segment is growing fast even while the traditional media is ramping up its digital content in India. However, the career opportunities

ICT for Development are not on an upswing. As balancing costs and benefits is an important strategy in business, most traditional media houses expect its existing employees to work across multiple formats, including social media. Digital media organisations also operate under similar constraints of money. Unlike traditional media owned by companies with deep pockets, most of the digital news media ventures are owned and operated by journalist turned entrepreneurs. With the growth in the number of new media firms, it is becoming increasingly difficult to find funding to maintain and expand operations. Besides, they compete with the digital arm of the traditional media for advertising, making it difficult to gain revenues. Going is all the tougher for those digital ventures that are dependent on donations, subscriptions or foundation funding. The consequence of such a situation is that journalists are increasingly becoming contributors, and at times it is difficult to find formal employment. Most journalists write for different websites and get paid for each piece. If you look at the websites of digital media ventures, you will find that they just have one office and maximum 20-25 employees. With employees accounting for more than 80% of the operational cost of a media, it is not surprising that digital news media ventures source writings from contributors. As a result, journalism is slowly becoming an informal career option.
16.5 CRITIQUE OF TECHNOLOGY AIDED
BUSINESS MODEL
The popularity and growth of digital news media entrepreneurship are celebrated in India because of its perceived ability to usher in a change in the way media function in the country. With the mainstream media constantly coming under fire for its corporate ownership, profit maximisation strategies and protecting the interest of the ruling elites, people expect digital media ventures and interactive technologies to democratise the news space and challenge the monopoly of the traditional media corporations. The Internet and related technologies are generally considered as difficult to be controlled by the government. Due to its global nature, censoring content on the Internet is expected to be almost impossible. However, contrary to these generally held notions, technology can be controlled by the government and powerful interests. The Indian government has always tried to control dissenting voices through draconian laws such as the Information Technology Act of 2000. Governments in India - both the Centre and States
- have shut down the Internet for political reasons. Indeed, this is almost a
regular activity in conflict-ridden Kashmir. Technology and telecom infrastructure are also controlled by corporates. Although the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) has offered its support to keep the Internet open, its recommendations are likely to benefit large companies. These large telecom companies are integrated operators who own both telecom infrastructure and content, and TRAI has decided to exempt these content delivery networks from the regulation. Reliance is India's largest company, and it is also one of the largest media owners in the country. With significant telecom infrastructure under its control, it is not easy for digital news media ventures to challenge corporate domination of companies like Reliance in the news business.

The web is also a literate medium. Besides, most of the digital media Entrepreneurship and Digital entrepreneurship is focussed on delivering content in English. It is difficult Media to find funding for regional language digital news firms due to the socio- economic profile of their readers. This, in a way, is widening the already existing digital information divide in the country.
16.5.1 Democratic Potential of Technology
Everything associated with the technology is not always emancipatory and democratic. Irrespective of a media organisation's economic character - whether for-profit or not-for-profit - digital news media's distribution and audience reach are mediated by the multinational social media corporations. Digital news media have to commercialise their content by using social media for marketing. In return for the free space provided for advertising its content, social media collect information on digital media users and employees, and then sell this information as a commodified product to advertisers, thereby compromising on the privacy of users. Indirectly, digital news media becomes an ally in social media's business, where it helps bring human activities to the marketplace and facilitates social media corporations to accumulate profit. Unfortunately, even the educated and upwardly mobile customers are unaware of these pitfalls of technology. They consider digital news ventures as content providers, producing and interactively distributing news. They consider themselves as an active reader, who has a role to play in the news production process. With the expose of the Cambridge Analytica case
- where the illegal data mining of about 87 million Facebook users by
the company became public, concerns have been raised in India as well. However, unless the social media business model that is based on selling user information to potential advertisers - changes, privacy concerns are here to stay. This is the flip side of the interactive nature of Internet technology, where even the feedback of a reader becomes a saleable commodity to the advertiser. Besides, technology alone cannot ensure the success of a digital news media venture. Although technology can help bring down the initial cost of setting up a firm, eventually a digital news media venture will have to invest vast amounts of resources for marketing, discovery and accessing readers to expand its market share. If the venture failed to do so, it would be wiped out by competition. Check Your Progress: 3 Note:1) Use the space below for your answers.

16.6 LET US SUM UP
In this Unit, we discussed the process of entrepreneurship. We looked at the process of entrepreneurship and its definitions. We analysed the execution of an idea and the resources required for it. Briefly, we touched upon specific challenges of the Indian market. Then we discussed in detail the different types of entrepreneurial ventures and various business models adopted by them. In the digital media section, we traced back the evolution of digital media in the world. After that, we have moved to the Indian market and looked at the growth and development of digital media in the country. We found that the new wave of digital news media could be considered as the third major turning point in the history of Indian journalism. Besides, we examined the advantages of technology and how it is benefiting and facilitating digital media entrepreneurship. We discussed in detail the business model of digital media ventures. We found that media operates in a dual product market. The most widely adopted business model of media is based on advertising revenues, in which media sells audience attention to advertisers. Our analysis showed that while digital media enjoys certain advantages due to the inexhaustible nature of news, it is difficult to gain revenues from news content. We examined the opportunities provided by the rapid growth of digital media entrepreneurship and how students can take advantage of it. We also analysed the difficulties involved in building a career in the field of digital journalism. Finally, we looked at technology from a critical perspective. Our analysis found that everything associated with the technology is not emancipatory. Due to the disparities in ownership and control of technological resources, it is difficult for digital media ventures to challenge the monopoly corporations that own large media houses. We can conclude that digital media entrepreneurship is set to grow in India. People are experimenting with different business models, and some are offering news under a public service model without any profit motives. While it may not be easy for digital media ventures to sustain themselves in a highly competitive market, they are expanding the market. They are trying to challenge the commercialisation of news by large media corporations.

COURSE INTRODUCTION: MEDIA,
INFORMATION AND EMPOWERMENT
Media draws its sustenance from the society and does not exist in isolation.
Course MNM-013 Media, Information and Empowerment takes an
encompassing view of the role of media on a wide range of issues including media and development, media and contemporary issues - both at the national as well as global levels. Block 1: Mass Media and Society covers the broad areas of media audiences, media literacy and policies. Unit 1: Understanding Media and Society outlines various aspects that are relevant to the understanding of the concepts, context and relevance of media in society. Unit 2: Media Audiences examines the characteristics, types and theories of audiences, and audience research approaches. Unit 3: Media and Information Literacy empowers you to understand the rationale of media messages, implications of visual images and economics of the media industry. Unit 4: Mass Media Policies deals with the significance of media and communication policies in the life of the people of a country. Block 2: Media and Development looks at the concept and theories of development, development communication, social and behaviour change communication and some case studies related to SBCC. Unit 5: Development: Concept and Theories takes an overview of the concept of development and discusses various theories of development as well as some recent debates in communication for development. Unit 6: Development Communication discusses its potential as a tool for inclusive growth and empowerment. Block 3: Media and Contemporary Issues examines the role of media in the crucial areas of health, education, gender, environment and human rights.
Unit 7: Media and Health Issues argues that health communicators can
provide a consistent and tangible approach to sustaining health and making policies and programmes more people-friendly and transparent. Unit 8: Education and Media looks at how media and ICT can be harnessed to expand access, promote efficiency, improve quality of learning, enhance quality of teaching, and improve management systems at various levels of education.
Unit 9: Gender and Media observes that skewed media portrayal of gender
promotes stereotypes and misrepresantation. Unit 10: Media and Environment focuses on how media can investigate various processes and popularise innovative ideas to help conserve our natural resources. Unit 11: Media and Human Rights examines the individual natural rights as well as collective rights of people. Unit 12: Alternative Media stresses the need for alternate media to give impetus to grassroots journalism and highlight the issues of the marginalised sections of society. Thus, this Course provides you with necessary theoretical perspectives on communication for social change and enables you to apply the available

information structures to bring changes for improvement in people's lives. We hope that after completing this course, you would be able to: describe the complex interplay between media and society; discuss the concept, need and importance of media literacy and policy; critically analyse the role of media in various contemporary issues such as health, education, gender, environment and human rights; examine the emergent issues of intercultural communication, technology, globalisation and the role of alternative media in society; and apply the knowledge and skills gained in your own work.

BLOCK 1 INTRODUCTION: MASS MEDIA AND
SOCIETY
Media is integral to society and communication is essential for both continuity and change in any society. In this first Block of the Course MNM- 013: Media, Information and Empowerment you will learn about the complex relationship between media and society at different levels.
Unit 1: Understanding Media and Society outlines the conceptual
framework to understand the relationship between media and society. The role of media in opinion formation has been discussed in a historical context from press to digital media. It will help you in understanding the political, social, economic and cultural developments in today's world.
Unit 2: Media Audiences examines the concept of media audiences and its
development historically. It explains 'group', 'crowd' and different 'media audiences' and their characteristics. How different audiences are influenced by communication has been a subject of research and debate, more so, with the rapid expansion and penetration of media. Different theoretical perspectives have been discussed in the unit to understand media impact on audiences.
Unit 3: Media and Information Literacy stresses the need for media
education in the present globalised media environment. The unlimited avenues for information generation and dissemination have led to blinding glare and often less clarity about the true meaning and role of media in society. Media literacy helps in differentiating between 'reel' and the 'real' and as such make better use of communication and media resources.
