10.3 DATA: EXPLORING THE ETHICAL
CONSIDERATIONS
Ethics are moral compasses that guide one's decisions in both general and particular situations. They could help us classify situations as good/bad or right/wrong. Ethics can be understood as the rules of conduct for doing the right thing. In social media, ethics involve maintaining trust, protecting users' privacy, and avoiding misleading practices. As we have seen earlier in this unit, social networking sites have digital records of users' data. This data could be traded to third parties for various purposes, including marketing and analysis. Legally and ethically, the platforms must obtain informed consent to collect, store, process and resell the data. Often, the users may consent without reading the terms and conditions as the documents are lengthy or without comprehending their consequences. Facebook and Twitter have been legally charged for trading users' personal data. Addressing these issues is of tantamount importance and needs concerted effort, as technologies and affordances keep changing. Data is one of the most valuable assets of our time, and the biggest challenge is ensuring the appropriate use of data. Data ethics is emerging as a new field that addresses responsible data use. Data ethics refers to ethical principles and practices that govern the gathering, processing, and using of data fairly and responsibly. These moral obligations and guidelines aim to use data with accountability and are key to building trust and integrity. Most importantly, ethical practices respect privacy, consent, and other boundaries.
10.3.1 Principles of Data Ethics
Data ethics has five guiding principles, known as the 5Cs: Consent, Clarity, Consistency, Control, and Consequence. Consent: Privacy is the expectation that personal data will be protected from unauthorised exposure. Therefore, organisations must honour user agreements regarding consent, implement robust security measures against privacy violations, and meet the privacy protocol. They are responsible for ensuring that data encryption and access control mechanisms are in place to protect sensitive user information.

Clarity: Organisations should be open and transparent about the intended Privacy and Ethics purpose of data collection, storage and sharing. They should follow ethical frameworks in data practices, including providing clear and accessible privacy policies, informing individuals about their data rights, and allowing them to control their data. Even algorithms and models used in data processing should adhere to transparency. Consistency: Uniform ethical standards or fairness are an important principle. Organisations must avoid bias and ensure data practices do not unfairly disadvantage any group. Fairness in data ethics focuses on preventing bias in data collection, processing, and interpretation, as it could lead to discriminatory practices that disproportionately affect certain groups - the marginalised, the minority, etc. Fairness requires diverse and representative data sets, bias detection mechanisms, and regular audits to identify and mitigate biases. It is essential that data scientists and engineers are aware of and actively work towards eliminating biases in their models and algorithms. Control: Individuals should have control over their personal data, including the ability to access, rectify, or delete their information. Consequence: Organisations must be accountable for the data they collect, including protecting it from breaches of confidentiality and misuse. They must also be held accountable for their data practices and the impacts these practices have on individuals and society. This involves establishing clear policies and procedures for data governance, regular audits, and independent oversight. When data breaches or ethical violations occur, organisations must take responsibility, rectify the issues, and provide restitution to affected individuals.
10.4 IMPLICATIONS OF SURVEILLANCE
PRACTICES
Social media surveillance refers to aggregating, curating and processing extensive personal data from social networking sites, often through automated technology. The entire social media business model thrives on the capital of data warehousing as big data is of big value for politicians, governments, corporations, intelligence and law enforcement agencies. This mass surveillance could have frightening potential for abuse. These highly sophisticated surveillance mechanisms and control strategies could raise significant ethical, legal, and privacy concerns, as discussed
- privacy violations, lack of transparency, lack of informed consent and
control, discrimination and bias. The surveillance mechanism collects data from personal information, purchase history, browsing habits, location data, and online interactions using user profiles, cookies, tracking activity and third-party integrations like apps. The gathered data is analysed to understand user behaviour, preferences and interests. Accordingly, advanced algorithms and machine learning models predict future actions, segment audiences, tailor content, optimise advertisements, and enhance real-time bidding. This is known as surveillance advertising or behavioural advertising. As a Former Federal

Social Media and Society Trade Commission Commissioner noted, "Behavioral advertising generates profits by turning users into products, their activity into assets, their communities into targets, and social media platforms into weapons of mass manipulation". Surveillance advertising is one kind of misuse. Facebook was involved in one of the most significant data breaches, allowing Cambridge Analytica, a political data-mining firm associated with the Trump election campaign in the US, to access the personal information of 87 million Facebook users in 2018. In another instance, the European Union fined a record $1.3 billion in 2023 on Meta, the parent company of Facebook, for violating privacy laws by transferring EU user data to US security agencies. Meta itself has acquired Facebook, WhatsApp, Instagram and Messenger, and such acquisitions by mega corporations are raising further concerns as tremendous big data will be under the control of such big corporate players. Many governments, particularly authoritarian governments, monitor user activity by recruiting a vast workforce, citing national security concerns, limiting fake news and maintaining public law and order. Dissenters have been tracked and arrested, particularly those expressing political, social and religious views, and minorities and migrants have been persecuted, corroding the space for freedom of speech. Many governments have invested heavily in social media surveillance programs and even specific social media surveillance tools specially designed by companies. Such companies claim features like a national firewall and 'monitor the target', 'monitor public opinion for election', 'monitor certain ethnicities' and so on. Some tools can bypass encryptions and passwords, too. Therefore, mass surveillance could undermine democracy, civil rights and privacy. These issues call for drafting and implementing robust data protection laws and regulations, demanding that platforms disclose data practices enabling users to understand and control their digital experiences and demonstrate accountability, empowering users to customise their feeds, and demonstrating ethical design in developing technologies that consider user rights. 10.5 ROLE AND CHALLENGES OF OBTAINING
USER CONSENT IN SOCIAL MEDIA
All social media platforms display terms and conditions, which users need to read and agree to before signing up. However, users may agree to consent without reading the terms of conditions because they are too lengthy and complex, or they may not comprehend the consequences of that consent. While the age of digital consent varies from 13 to 16 across countries, users of this age group may not have the capacity and competence to understand and make decisions. Therefore, a huge population in this category, which uses social media, authorises agreement without informed consent. They are ignorant and lack any intention to provide data for political or other purposes for which the data may be used. The default setting itself is public. Unless the privacy setting changes, the companies can claim that they have followed privacy policies in capturing data. Therefore, the terms and conditions should be brief and concise and indicate if any monetisation of data is intended. The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), 2016, the European Union regulation, states that consent should be freely given, specific, informed, explicit and unambiguous, and consent can be withdrawn by the data subject/user at any time.
10.5.1 Role of Obtaining User Consent
Obtaining user consent can ensure the platforms comply with data protection regulations like GDPR. Legal compliance can help platforms avoid legal penalties and maintain operational legitimacy. Transparent and ethical data practices, including seeking user consent, build trust between platforms and their users. Secondly, consent mechanisms empower users by giving them control over their data.
10.5.2 Challenges of Obtaining Consent
Consent forms and privacy policies are often complex and lengthy, making it difficult for users to understand. The challenge is to simplify and shorten the documents without losing essential details. Then, ensuring that consent is truly informed requires users to fully understand the implications of data sharing. Achieving this level of understanding can be challenging due to the varying age categories of users and levels of digital literacy. Secondly, gaining user engagement with consent forms is difficult. Many users quickly skim through or ignore consent requests due to time or other constraints, leading to uninformed or passive consent.

Social Media and Society Thirdly, robust mechanisms that enable users to withdraw their consent and ensure that their data is deleted or anonymised need to be developed to manage the data lifecycle and user preferences. This poses significant technological challenges, including designing user-friendly interfaces and ensuring data security.
10.6 ETHICAL DESIGN OF SOCIAL MEDIA
PLATFORMS
Having discussed the issues related to ethics in media, the question before us is how to incorporate ethical values within social media platforms to create a responsible and trustworthy digital environment. Ethical design is designing social media services in a way that respects users' privacy, is accessible, and is free of bias. Authors Zuboff and Kilofour et al define ethical design as creating products and services that pursue positive morality over profits. Aral Balkan and Laura Kalbag, who drafted an Ethical Design Manifesto from the Ind.ie company, conceive an ethical hierarchy of needs as technology that respects human rights, effort, and experience (Refer Diagram 1). Even if one of the layers of the pyramid is unfulfilled, it will collapse. The manifesto states, "technology that respects human rights is decentralised, peer-to-peer, zero knowledge, end-end encrypted, free and open source, inoperable, accessible, and sustainable."
Diagram 1: Pyramid of Ethical Hierarchy of Needs
There are discussions about privacy-enhancing technologies (PETs) where scientists and innovators could consider and incorporate ethical considerations into new technologies and innovations. Tools like Open AI's Moderation API enable real-time detection of harmful content. Apple has introduced App Tracking Transparency (ATT), a simple way for users to opt out of data collection. Platforms should provide opt-in and opt-out default settings for selling access to private data.
10.7 GLOBAL PRIVACY REGULATIONS ON
SOCIAL MEDIA COMPANIES
Many countries have formulated privacy regulations to address the challenges to the security of personal data. With the unprecedented growth of technologies like AI, the Internet of Things (IoT) and the development of Big Data analytics, the challenges are expanding multifold. The privacy

regulations and compliance requirements vary from country to country. Still, Privacy and Ethics cross-border cooperation among privacy enforcement authorities is seen as a necessity with unrestricted flows of information across borders. The key components of most of the regulations are consent, data minimisation, user control and data security. The European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) is the benchmark for regulatory standards.
The General Data Protection Regulation
The GDPR is a regulation in European Union law for data privacy and protection. All citizens of EU countries are brought under the purview of GDPR, and it applies to all businesses dealing with data of the EU, irrespective of whether companies are situated in or outside the EU. The GDPR includes the users' right to access, rectify and revoke data within the regulation. It has followed seven key principles :
1. Lawfulness, fairness, and transparency
2. Purpose limitation
3. Data minimisation
4. Accuracy
5. Storage limitation
6. Integrity and confidentiality
7. Accountability
The broad principles of GDPR are reflected in the Digital Personal Data Protection Act of 2023 of India. However, some differences exist, like data localisation, which authorises local data storage. Further, the law entrusts the government with the power to exempt any agencies from compliance. Check Your Progress: 3 Note: 1) Use the space provided below for your answers.

10.8 LET US SUM UP
Privacy is one of the major concerns in the current digital environment. Two types of privacy issues need to be addressed - one, from within the networked communities and two, from third parties. Privacy problems within networked communities can harm an individual's dignity and reputation and harm financial, psychological and social well-being. Data privacy issues related to third parties can undermine democracy and give rise to surveillance capitalism. Therefore, social media platforms need to develop robust data ethics frameworks, ensure transparency, establish accountability mechanisms and comply with laws and regulations on data protection. Scientists and innovators have to adopt ethical design to ensure user rights.
10.9 KEYWORDS
Content Moderation: Policies that regulate harmful or inappropriate content on platforms, including mechanisms like content removal, account suspension, and rule enforcement to maintain digital safety. Cyberbullying: Acts like stalking, harassment, trolling, and blackmailing performed using digital platforms, often targeting individuals through persistent or aggressive online behaviour. Digital Footprint: The data trail left behind by users during online activity, including search history, posts, clicks, and interactions, which can be tracked and analysed. Ethical Design: Developing digital platforms that respect user privacy, ensure accessibility, eliminate bias, and prioritise human rights in technological architecture and user interface. Informational Privacy: The individual's right to control how their personal data is collected, processed, stored, and shared by online platforms and third-party entities. Mass Surveillance: Systematic, large-scale data collection by states, intelligence agencies, or corporations for monitoring populations, often raising ethical and human rights concerns. Personal Publics: Social media users whose communication blurs traditional boundaries between private and public spaces, creating semi- public digital personas and shared personal content. Privacy: The fundamental right to be free from unauthorised interference or intrusion into one's personal life, behaviour, communications, or information.

Privacy Paradox: Users express concern about privacy yet fail to Privacy and Ethics implement protective behaviours, often willingly sharing data despite known surveillance and data mining risks. Targeted Advertising: Marketing technique using user data, such as browsing habits and interests, to deliver personalised advertisements intended to influence consumer decisions.

11.0 INTRODUCTION
In the digital space, especially in India, social capital is growing through platforms like WhatsApp, Facebook, and Twitter. For example, during the COVID-19 pandemic, many people in India used WhatsApp groups to share important information, help each other find medical supplies, or arrange

transport for those in need. This shows how social connections online can Social Capital and create a support system, build trust, and help communities solve problems Audience together, even when they are physically apart. Digital platforms, therefore, enhance social capital by connecting people across distances and enabling collaboration.

11.2 SOCIAL CAPITAL IN DIGITAL SPACES
In this session, learners can understand what Social Capital and digital Space are and how Social Capital is built and maintained in the Digital World. Social capital is like the value of your relationships, and here we discussed the trust, support, and connections you have with others in the digital world. For example, having many friends, family members, and people in the neighbourhood who trust and respect you is a sign of substantial social capital. Digital space is where people can interact, such as social media platforms, online forums, or gaming communities. You increase your social capital by using these spaces to build relationships and trust with others.
11.2.1 Social Capital
Social capital refers to the value of your relationships. It is about your trust, support, and cooperation with others in social relationships, networks, and institutions. When you have substantial social capital, you can achieve more together than alone. We can divide Social Capital as follows.
- Bonding capital (within groups)
- Bridging capital (between groups)
- Linking capital (across social strata)
Bonding Capital is the trust and support you have within your groups or communities, like family, friends, or neighbours. Bridging capital refers to connections with people outside your immediate circle, such as people from different backgrounds or communities. Linking capital is about connections with people in power or influence who can help you access resources or opportunities.
Village Panchayats, Religious Communities, and Self-Help Groups are
examples where we can build and see social capital. The local governing bodies often rely on social capital to mobilise community members for development projects or disaster relief efforts. SHG groups of women, especially in rural areas, use social capital to access loans, save money, and improve their livelihoods. Many religious communities have substantial social capital that helps members support each other and provide assistance in times of need.

Social Media and Society One can build social capital by participating in community activities, local events, festivals, or volunteering. Joining social organisations is another way of building social capital, such as joining clubs, societies, or associations that align with your interests. Building trust, helping others, and enhancing the reliability, honesty, and support of others are the keys to your Social Capital building. Social capital is a valuable asset that can help you build strong relationships and participate in your community.
11.2.2 Digital Spaces
Definition: Digital space refers to the virtual environment created by the Internet and digital technologies, which enables communication, interaction, and the exchange of information across vast distances. In Western academic discourse, the digital space is understood as an interconnected virtual environment enabled by digital technologies, where information is exchanged, communities are formed, and social interactions occur. In works like "India Connected: How the Smartphone is Transforming the World's Largest Democracy" by Ravi Agrawal, the digital space is presented as a catalyst for economic and social change. The rapid penetration of smartphones and internet connectivity has redefined how Indians communicate, access government services, and consume media. The digital space, especially in India, is not just a tool for the elite but is empowering millions of people by providing them access to education, employment, and financial inclusion, reshaping the socio-economic landscape of the nation.
11.2.3 Online Communities and Social Capital
The relationship between social capital and audiences is vital in today's digitally interconnected world. As we have discussed, social capital is the value of your relationships. So, the content in digital space must have the value that connects audiences, which are the people who consume content or engage with your message. Social media platforms like Facebook, X, and Instagram can help people connect with others who share their interests and build social capital. Online Communities and forums allow people to discuss shared topics and form strong bonds. WhatsApp Groups are widely used in India for community communication and enlistment, fostering substantial social capital among members. By understanding the connections between social capital and audiences, we can better navigate the complexities of our interconnected world and harness the power of social relationships to achieve our goals. Identify characteristics of online communities and examine how online communities facilitate information sharing and foster social capital. The Size, Density and Centralisation are the main characteristics. Size can impact the diversity of viewpoints and the comfort of communication. Smaller communities may foster stronger ties due to increased familiarity, while larger communities may offer a broader range of opportunities for collaboration. Density refers to the concentration of people and resources within a given area. Centralisation refers to the concentration of power and resources within a community. A highly centralised community may

limit opportunities for participation and decision-making, while a more Social Capital and decentralised community can empower individuals and groups to take Audience initiative.
11.2.4 Online Community Engagement
Community engagement is the active involvement of individuals and groups in the development and well-being of their communities. It's a process that fosters collaboration and participation among community members. Community Engagement has A Three-Tiered Approach:
- Transactional (information sharing)
- Transitional (relationship building)
- Transformational (social change)
Transactional Engagement is the most basic level of engagement. It focuses on sharing information and collecting feedback. For example, a local government might organise a public meeting or hearing to discuss changes, where residents can share their opinions. This type of engagement helps people stay informed, building awareness and understanding, but it doesn't usually lead to significant changes in decision-making. Transitional Engagement moves beyond information sharing and focuses on building relationships and trust within the community. This involves creating opportunities for people to connect, collaborate, and develop. Community-based organisations might organise volunteer events, social gatherings, or cultural festivals to create a sense of belonging. For instance, a neighbourhood or residents' association organises a party to unite residents and strengthen community bonds. Transformational Engagement is the deepest level of involvement and aims to create real social change. It empowers people to take control of decisions that affect their lives. For example, a community might organise a campaign to get government attention to improve public transportation. This type of engagement challenges existing systems and requires a long-term effort to make lasting improvements.
11.2.5 Challenges and Opportunities in Online Community
Engagement Online Community Engagement creates deep-rooted and rapid changes. Due to its characteristics, it presents several challenges and opportunities. Online Harassment, Information Overload, and decreased attention Span are some major challenges. Reach, diversity, tools of social change, and activism are notable opportunities. Let us discuss the points.
11.3 DIGITAL INFLUENCE
Digital Influence- In this topic, we discuss how individuals and groups influence digital communities. In places like India, most people use the Internet and have social media, so digital space is one of the powerful tools for influencing them. Also, as we are in this web-like connected world, digital influence plays a significant role in shaping opinions, behaviours, and decisions across online platforms. Individuals and groups can influence

Social Media and Society public opinion, lead movements, or build brand value through digital platforms. Let us discuss the types of Digital Influence.
11.3.1 Types of Digital Influence
We can divide digital influence into four types: Social influence, digital opinion leadership, network effects, and algorithmic influence. Social Influence- The tendency to change one's behaviour or beliefs to align with the norms of a group. In digital spaces, conformity can be seen in how individuals adopt popular trends or opinions to fit in with online communities, and the willingness to follow orders or instructions from an authority figure. Online authority figures can include influencers, experts, or organisations--the process of influencing someone's attitudes, beliefs, or behaviours. Persuasion techniques are widely used in digital marketing and advertising. In the Indian context, social influence can be seen in how people conform to trends on platforms like Instagram or YouTube. Whether supporting a political cause or following a social trend like #VocalForLocal, users often obey social norms created by their peers or prominent personalities. A recent example is the widespread adoption of eco-friendly practices due to increased awareness shared by influencers and activists online, persuading people to take environmental action. Digital Opinion Leadership- Individuals recognised as experts in a particular field can shape public opinion. Influencers in India, such as YouTubers like Bhuvan Bam or tech reviewers like Geeky Ranjit, play a huge role in guiding public opinion. These thought leaders have built credibility and expertise in specific domains. For instance, when they review gadgets or support causes, their opinions reach millions and shape perceptions. Thought leaders also help push important agendas such as women's rights, mental health, and environmental sustainability, influencing their audience. Network Effects: The rapid spread of information or content through a network. Viral content often goes viral due to its shareability and appeal to a wide audience, spreading ideas, behaviours, or emotions from one person to another. In digital spaces, contagion can occur through social media, messaging apps, and other online platforms, spreading innovations or new ideas through a population. Diffusion can be influenced by factors such as social networks, media, and government policies. This network-driven diffusion of ideas can have positive effects, like spreading important health information during the COVID-19 pandemic, and negative consequences, such as spreading misinformation or fake news. Algorithmic influence: This is an unnoticed influence, but it plays a critical role in keeping people engaged with content that aligns with their interests. It personalises recommendations by providing preference and their online space behaviour. It also provides recommendations based on their past interactions. For example, platforms like Amazon, Flipkart, Netflix, and YouTube recommend content based on user preferences.
11.3.2 Digital Influencers and Their Role
Digital influencers are individuals or personalities who influence their audience through online platforms such as Instagram, YouTube, and X. They are categorised into different types based on their follower count.

Nano-influencers have fewer than 1,000 followers and tend to have close- Social Capital and knit, highly engaged audiences. Micro-influencers, with 1,000 to 10,000 Audience followers, often focus on niche areas like food blogging or fitness coaching, building personal connections and trust with their followers. Macro- influencers with 10,000 and 100,000 followers include more prominent figures, such as regional celebrities or well-known YouTubers. In contrast, mega-influencers, with over 100,000 followers, have massive reach and are often national icons or celebrities, such as Bollywood actors or top athletes. In India's influencer ecosystem, each category plays a unique role, with micro-influencers providing genuineness and relatability, while macro and mega-influencers, such as Virat Kohli and Sachin Tendulkar, influence trends and public opinion on a larger scale. The effectiveness of digital influencers is often determined by their authority, credibility, and reach. In India, influencers like Shah Rukh Khan or Virat Kohli command high trust and authority built over years of engagement with their followers. Credibility is especially vital, as fake endorsements or misleading promotions can lead to public backlash. Digital influencers often engage with their communities through participatory platforms, creating dynamic digital spaces that thrive on interaction and build social capital in the digital space.
11.3.3 Ethics and Responsibility in Digital Influence
Brands in India have adopted influencer marketing to great effect. As digital influence grows, so does the responsibility of influencers and brands to act ethically. There is a fine line between influence and manipulation in India, where social media influencers have large audiences. For instance, Indian YouTubers or Instagram influencers often face criticism if they fail to disclose paid promotions. For example, many beauty brands collaborate with Instagram beauty influencers to reach younger audiences; ethics play a major role here. If an influencer only goes for money to attract a cheap brand, it affects their audience and breaks the influencer's social capital. Consumers expect transparency, so brands and influencers need to disclose paid partnerships, ensuring that the trust between influencers and their followers remains intact. Ethics, morality, responsibility, transparency and disclosure, digital wellness, mental health, addiction, and digital detox are the same ethical standards that influencers must follow. 11.4 AUDIENCE BEHAVIOUR ANALYSIS
This unit will discuss how audiences consume, interact with, and share content. Audiences are those reading, listening, watching, or reading the content. In Digital Space, audiences connect people from all corners of the world and create a diverse and global audience. The main characteristics of the digital audience are active participation in discussions and sharing content; they are more engaged and interactive than traditional audiences, and digital audiences are split into different platforms due to the innumerable online channels. Understanding and analysing digital audiences is crucial for creating social capital in the digital space, as their preferences and behaviours constantly evolve due to technological advancements and emerging trends.
11.4.1 Types of Audience
Before we learn to analyse the Digital Audience, it is important to understand the types of Digital audiences. Based on the Audience Content Participation, they can be categorised into three types: Lurkers, Participants and Creators. Participants and Creators. Lurkers are passive consumers who use content without actively participating in discussions or creating their own content. They may read articles, watch videos, or scroll through social media feeds, but hardly react or interact by liking, commenting or sharing. Participants actively engage with content. They read the article, watch the videos, scroll through the comments, and comment, share, and like posts, often feeling connected to the content or community. Creators produce and share their own content, often creating blogs, videos, podcasts, or other forms of content. However, this categorisation is not exclusive. It changes based on individuals' preferences regarding the context and content. Based on demographic segmentation, the audience's behaviour pattern changes based on age, gender, income, and education. Understanding this demographic segmentation is important for producers to focus on the target audience. For example, young adults in urban areas may be targeted with content related to career growth or fashion, while rural users might

be more motivated towards content in local languages. Women in India Social Capital and are an increasingly active audience with higher purchasing power. They Audience are often interested in beauty, fashion, health, and family. Men in India are often interested in sports, technology, and current affairs. Income is another important factor. High-income individuals may be more interested in luxury goods and premium brands, while middle-income and low-income individuals may be more price-sensitive. Individuals with higher education may be more interested in intellectual pursuits and knowledge, while those with lower education may have different priorities. Based on the psychographic segmentation, audiences are divided according to their psychological features, including personality, values, interests, lifestyles, and attitudes. This will help us understand how different digital audiences build and leverage social capital. For example, some individuals who desire social status and recognition may be interested in luxury brands and premium products. They are 'status seekers'. These individuals accrue social capital by showcasing their achievements or possessions on platforms like Instagram, where they gain likes, followers, and social influence. Other categories are 'community builders' and 'Knowledge seekers'. They focus more on connection and information sharing. Community builders create and manage digital spaces, such as online groups or forums, where members can interact, share advice, and collaborate. Based on Content Consumption Patterns. Audiences consume content in different ways. Some prefer binge-watching on platforms like Netflix and Amazon Prime and gaming, where they watch multiple episodes or movies in a single sitting. Others prefer 'snacking', consuming short-form content on platforms like YouTube Shorts or Instagram Reels, which offer quick entertainment in small doses. Scanning, where users browse headlines or summaries, is common on news apps like Inshorts, which provide bite-sized news for on-the-go consumption. Several factors influence an individual's decision to participate in an online community:
11.4.2 Factors Influencing Participation
Motivations: Individuals may participate for various reasons, including social connection, information seeking, self-expression, or a sense of belonging. Barriers: Several barriers can hinder online participation, such as a lack of access to technology, digital literacy, or fear of online harassment. Incentives: Organisations and individuals can provide incentives to encourage participation, such as recognition, rewards, or opportunities for collaboration. 11.5 TRUST AND CREDIBILITY
In this session, you must understand the role of trust and credibility in online communities. In the digital world, trust and credibility are essential for building and maintaining strong online communities and Social Capital in Digital Space. Understanding these concepts is crucial in India, where internet penetration and social media usage are rapidly growing. Trust refers to the expectation of reliability, honesty, and goodwill in interactions, while credibility is about the believability and expertise of individuals or organisations. In an online context, trust and credibility become more complex due to anonymity and pseudonymity, especially in platforms like Twitter, Facebook, and Instagram, where users often hide their real identities but still form reputations based on their behaviour.
11.5.1 Defining Trust and Credibility
Trust is the firm belief in the truth or ability of someone or something. It is built on reliability and honesty. Similarly, credibility is the quality of being convincing or believable. If we analyse trust and credibility in Digital Space, users on platforms like Flipkart or Amazon develop trust in sellers based on product reviews and ratings. Another example is that online educational apps are credible because of the consistent quality of their content and the expertise they demonstrate in their field. In online spaces, users' reputations are often shaped by their contributions, feedback from others, and the trustworthiness they establish over time. This builds social capital. Digital Space offers a unique space where individuals can interact and communicate anonymously or pseudonymously. This facility to conceal one's true identity has both positive and negative consequences for online communities and the building of Social Capital.

Social Media and Society Anonymity refers to being unknown or nameless. In this context, individuals interact anonymously and freely express themselves without fear of social consequences. This can encourage open dialogue and the sharing of sensitive information. However, this anonymity can also lead to harmful behaviours like cyberbullying and hate speech. Pseudonymity is the use of a false name. It does not provide the same level of anonymity as an unidentified identity. However, pseudonyms can be used to protect one's personal information from negative consequences. Reputation is the perception of an individual's character or face in a community. In the Digital Space, reputation is often based on interactions with others and the content one creates or shares. Building a positive online reputation can benefit individuals and organisations, as it can enhance credibility, trust, and Social Capital. However, a negative reputation online can seriously damage one's personal and professional life.
11.5.2 Building Trust in Online Communities
Building Trust in Online Communities is critical to developing sustainable digital spaces. In this world scenario, online communities play a vital role in easing communication, collaboration, and information sharing. However, the anonymity and multiplicity of the online atmosphere can make it more challenging to establish a trusting community. Building trust in an online community can be segmented into three stages.
- Initial trust development
- Continuous trust expansion
- Trust repair
Initial trust development and building trust in online communities start with preliminary impressions. The design of a platform and its user-friendly interface play a significant role in trust formation. Food delivery sites like Zomato and Swiggy, shopping sites like Flipkart and Amazon, and taxi services like Uber are in their initial stage, creating a sense of professionalism and reliability and encouraging users to trust the service. Continuous trust development happens through steady and regular interactions, positive reviews, and helpful customer service. For example, Indian e-commerce platforms maintain trust by promptly responding to customer queries, ensuring product quality, and offering hassle-free returns. Another example is TATA and Amul. Even though they have trust among consumers, they understand the benefits of Online Platforms and have developed well-established Social Capital in the Digital Space. Repairing Trust in Online Communities is essential. There is a chance of breaking trust in online communities due to errors or negative experiences among users. They can observe money transfer sites like Gpay, Paytm, and banking systems. Whenever they face service outages or transaction failures, they often apologise publicly through social media and provide explanations and refunds to restore trust. Similarly, major brands or influencers who lose credibility due to missteps repair trust through live sessions with their followers and, if needed, they apologise and offer compensation or explanations to their consumers or audience.

11.5.3 Measuring Trust and Credibility Social Capital and
Audience Understanding trust and credibility in online communities is essential in today's Digital Era. Proper research and measurement help us understand the factors contributing to trust and credibility and gain valuable insights into the dynamics of online interactions. Surveys and questionnaires, Behavioural Metrics, and Network Analysis are methods for measuring trust and credibility. Surveys and questionnaires: Self-reported trust and credibility are the most common methods for measuring trust and credibility. The self- reported method allows the researcher to ask the users questions directly. By analysing the survey responses, researchers can identify key factors influencing trust and credibility in the Indian context. Brands like Flipkart and BigBasket regularly conduct customer satisfaction surveys to gauge the level of trust and satisfaction among their users. Behavioural metrics: Engagement, retention, and recommendation. Engagement metrics such as likes, comments, and shares indicate users' interest and interaction with content. Retention rates, the percentage of users who continue to use a platform over time, can indicate trust and satisfaction. Furthermore, recommendation rates, such as the number of products or services users recommend to others, can be a sign of trust and credibility. Network analysis: Centrality, betweenness, clustering -Network analysis is another powerful tool for measuring trust and credibility in online communities. By examining the structure of social networks, researchers can identify the most influential and trusted users. Metrics such as centrality and clustering help to identify individuals who are well-connected and have a strong influence on others. These individuals are often seen as trusted sources of information and can play a crucial role in shaping the dynamics of online communities.
11.6 AUDIENCE AS PRODUCERS
We learned as we checked the trust and credibility concerns in online platforms. We are about to discuss the audience as producers in Online Media, exploring how audiences contribute to content creation and blurring producer-consumer boundaries. Online media provides a good space for consumers to create content, which narrows the gap between content creators and users.
11.6.1 User-Generated Content (UGC)
Any kind of content the audience creates is User-Generated Content (UGC). Technically defined as any content created by users of a platform rather than by the platform itself. This can include comments, reviews, videos, podcasts, and more. Users create this content for self-expression, social interactions, and reputation by sharing thoughts, opinions, and creative work and establishing themselves as experts in a particular field. Also, it is a platform where social connection and community building are recognised. Through this process, Social capital will be established, and the trust and support already gained by the content creators and influencers will also be achieved by the users.

Social Media and Society 11.6.2 Co-Creation and Collaborative Content
There are two kinds of user-generated content: co-creation and collaborative content. Both are closely related concepts involving multiple persons working together to create content, but they differ. Co-creative content involves working with customers or external people to develop a new idea, content, or product. Here, the stakeholders actively contribute to the content and look for a good outcome. A brand working with customers to design a new logo, packet, or tag on Wikipedia, where users edit content, is an example of co-creative content. Collaborative content refers to content created by multiple individuals, such as a group working to produce an article, video, or social media post or influencers working to create cross-promotional content, etc. Another example is when several authors contribute to a research paper, book, or digital marketing team, and different departments, such as designers, copywriters, and marketers, work together for a campaign.
Benefits of Co-Creation and Collaborative Content
Innovation--When a group generates an idea, it tends to be more original and unique. It enhances the quality of content. Personalisation - This content is close to the audience's view and fulfils their needs. Engagement--When users generate content, engagement from those involved increases, whether they are customers or team members. All these lead to trust, support, and cooperation with others in social relationships, networks, and institutions. This is the most important element for building social capital. You can accomplish more together than alone if you have strong social capital.
11.6.3 Prosumer Culture
When we learn about the audience as producers, we must know the term "prosumer Culture." Alvin Toffler coined the term, 'Prosumer,' in his book The Third Wave in 1980. It describes the individual who blurs the lines between producer and consumer. As this is the blend of producer and consumer, one of the most reflective effects of prosumer culture is the shift in power dynamics. It breaks down the traditional format where the dominant position is for content producers. With the rise of prosumers, consumers are increasingly becoming co- creators. For example, many people work together to create open-source software. Where individuals can contribute to the development of code and hold ownership rights over their contributions, even though they don't own the whole thing, an example of this is initiatives like the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Madras' open-source software development lab, fostering a community of prosumers. The main characteristics of Consumer Culture are Active Participation and Creative Contribution. Prosumers are actively involved in creating or altering products and services and contribute their own ideas and skills to the development of content and products.

11.6.4 Fan Communities and Content Creation Social Capital and
Audience Fandoms are another essential term to understand in User-Generated Content. A 'Fandom' is a group of people who share a common interest in a particular thing, such as books, movies, TV shows, music, sports, or video games. Fans often create their own content related to their interests, such as fan art, fan fiction, and cosplay. This can be a form of self-expression, community building, and engagement with the original content. India has a rich fandom history, including the ancient epics Mahabharata and Ramayana; countless fans have been there over the years, and the adapted works in media have fostered a new generation of fans. Bollywood and South Indian movies have produced numerous iconic films garnered massive fan followings. Fans often engage in discussions, create fan pages, and attend film premieres to express their love for their favourite movies and actors. The growth of online media has further amplified the impact of fandoms in India. Platforms like Twitter, Instagram, and Facebook have provided a space for fans to connect, share content, and participate in online discussions. This has led to large and active online communities centred on various fandoms. They become the creators of the content.
11.6.5 Intellectual Property
The main challenge for user-generated content is intellectual property and ownership. The WTO defines intellectual property rights as the rights given to persons over the creation of their minds. These rights usually give the creator an exclusive right to use his/her creation for a certain period of time. Creating and distributing Generated Content can raise questions about intellectual property and ownership rights. When people create content online, such as videos, photos, or articles, and share it on a website or app, they often give the website or app permission to use it. This can cause problems because sometimes people argue about who owns the content. Another problem is that people sometimes use other people's work without permission. This is called copyright infringement. To avoid these problems, it's essential to have clear rules about who owns content online and to provide proper education about copyright laws so people know what they can and cannot do with other people's work. 11.7 LET US SUM UP
Social capital is a valuable asset that enables communities to achieve collective goals. Bridging social capital involves connections across social networks, such as relationships with people from different backgrounds or social groups. These connections can facilitate information exchange, resource mobilisation, and access to opportunities. Linking social capital in digital space refers to connections between individuals and organisations at different levels of society. Social capital influences audience reception and interpretation through trust, shared values, social proof, and community building. Trust is when you have substantial social capital, and people are more likely to trust your opinions or recommendations. The audience shares the values of those who have significant social capital. If your friends and peer group are actively involved with your activities and follow the same, it is strong social proof that you have social capital. Social Media tools connect different levels of society, such as government officials, business leaders, and community activists. These connections can provide access to resources and influence.

12.0 INTRODUCTION
Social media has entirely changed the way we communicate, the networks we build, and the communities we create. It is the most effective means of connecting and building communities across borders with common interests. Apart from networking and information sharing, it has profoundly changed how activism is conducted. The participatory nature of the social media environment strengthened two important aspects of human communication in cyberspace: the expansion of online communities and the use of common interests for collective change. These two dimensions have contributed to a massive expansion of activities related to online activism, particularly using social media platforms for personal and social changes. This Unit captures the dynamics of social media-based activism. You are encouraged to recall similar units we covered in earlier courses on activism over digital media. This Unit expands on that discussion.

12.2 SOCIAL MEDIA MOBILISATION AND
ACTIVISM
According to the Oxford Dictionary, 'Mobilisation' refers to bringing together the things needed for a particular purpose. <Activism, on the other hand, refers to working to achieve social or political changes, especially as a member of an organisation with particular aims. Sociala facilitates the process of mobilisation by bringing together people who believe in a common cause or have similar interests. According to a study by Kristen Lovejoy and Gregory D. in 2012, to qualify for social media activism, the first role is to share information about a particular issue. This is followed by building the community around issues of common interests, and the last but most significant activity of activism is enabling an action that could or may not be related to mobilisation.
12.2.1 Social Movements or Activism
A social movement or social activism is motivated by a social process in which collective actors are given space to voice their thoughts, express their grievances, and views. In most cases, social movements have few core issues in common. Primary among them are Identifying an area of interest: Usually, the area of interest that determines my common interest. These issues could be long-term and as major as opposing a war or something as trivial as opposing a certain order. Formal and informal networks: Giving the movement shape through formal and informal networking is a core area of social activism. In the case of social media activism, the different social media facilitate connectivity and create room for dialogue. Sustainable and effective momentum: It is crucial to create a momentum that is both effective and sustainable. Social media itself creates room for action-oriented work. The action could be signing a petition, advocating for the cause, carrying out rallies, or putting pressure on authorities.

Activism in contemporary times is digitally-centric. World War I laid the foundation for global communication, a key tool for disseminating propaganda through connectivity. Social media and the digital sector are key in mobilising people, constituting social movements and global organisations. 12.3 GRASSROOTS CAMPAIGNS
Campaigns are both vertical and horizontal. Vertical campaigns like vertical marketing are specific and have target audiences, whereas Horizontal campaigns aim to reach a wide range of people spread across different parts of the world. Grassroots campaigns are mostly vertical since they focus on specific issues relevant to specific groups. Some of the components of grassroots campaigns are: a. The campaigns are conducted in districts, communities, or villages. They are directed towards a common issue or dealing with a specific brand, where people are mobilised collectively to come to a common stand. b. As opposed to the time with limited multimedia resources or that of traditional media, the popularity of social media has changed the way communication takes place. Grassroots activism emanated from different sources and expressed itself through different media. One of the finest examples of grassroots activism is the formation of Khabar Lahariya. A women>s newspaper published in various rural dialects of Hindi, including Bundeli, Avadhi, and Bajjika dialects. Starting with Nirantar, a Delhi-based non-governmental organisation, the newspaper focused on gender and education. Khabar Lahariya went completely digital in 2015, housed by Chambal Media, a digital media social enterprise founded by Disha Mullick and Shalini Joshi. It slowly expanded its horizons to other areas, such as local political news, crime reports, social issues, and entertainment. The main crux is that it reported everything from a feminist perspective. What started as a grassroots movement directed towards India>s only women-run brand of ethical and independent rural news. Thiss grassroots movement amplified its reach to 5 million people when aided by digital intervention. The newspaper now has a network of 30 women reporters and stringers spread across 13 districts of Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh. This is considered a powerful watchdog which is instrumental in enforcing accountability by the government and policymakers in the area. It has more than 150 million views and 540,000 YouTube subscribers. While Khabar Lahariya is a fine example of grassroots activism, Mats activists have used digital media to a large extent. Of course, this has also initiated malpractices of bribery and incitement. Application in the hands of all: Grassroots activism ensures that activism is initiated and progressed through the hands of all. Narratology is one of the fundamental outcomes of media implosion, where there are multiple narrations of a single story, and each narrative takes the entire story in a different turn of events. Almost all the issues currently dominating national and international media have many aspects that are not the sole determinants of how the story is narrated. However, the media manipulates and twists a story to favour its interests. Media narratives aid the readers in constructing their imagination, sometimes remaining loyal to their ideology and often following a particular style based on earlier narrative experiences.

Social media is essentially considered an echo chamber that reflects the Social Media and profound ways political or social issues are discussed or analysed. The Contemporary Activism discussions take place entirely from an individualistic perspective, and sometimes, this content becomes a source of common topics. This has a subsequent impact on individual attitudes and amplifies polarisation. Socio- political theorists have given this shared exposure the prominence of being able to disseminate a healthy political deliberation that takes place in thriving democratic societies. Hate speech: Apart from activism, there is visible online hate speech and overhyped ethnic violence. From the narrative that emanated from the Russia-Ukraine war, as well as the anti-Semitic attacks on Jewish journalists, to reports of social media>s role in mobilising ethnic violence in Myanmar and Sri Lanka, the offline consequences of online hate speech appear increasingly dire. Fearing that this harmful rhetoric is inciting violence and driving extremism, governments worldwide are passing regulations and pressuring social media companies to implement policies to stop the spread of online hate speech. Similarly, Twitter's terms of service state that the company prohibits "hateful conduct", including "promoting violence against or directly attacking or threatening other people on the basis of race, ethnicity, national origin, sexual orientation, gender, gender identity, religious affiliation, age, disability or disease.>> The company also emphasises that it does not allow accounts whose <<primary purpose is inciting harm towards others on the basis of these categories>> (Twitter, 2018). Facebook>s definition of hate speech does not contain the incitement to violence language employed by Twitter and YouTube, instead identifying hate speech as <<content that directly attacks people based on their race; ethnicity; national origin; religious affiliation; sexual orientation; sex, gender, or gender identity; or serious disabilities or diseases" Crosscutting interactions: Narrative allows for more diverse viewpoints and accommodates more rationales and opposing viewpoints. Digital technology, the conjunction of form and content, allows a particular style to emerge that can prompt us to reflect on our own moral situations significantly differently than we can with philosophical, ethical treatises. Objectivity and credibility: This leads to a dilemma of ethics since narrative construction is inseparable from a reader>s search for truth, objectivity, and credibility in the form and content of a journalistic narrative. 12.4 HASHTAG ACTIVISM
The idealism associated with activism is often contested as unreal. According to many critics, this activism has many demerits. Sitting with a digital device, pretending to be a part of something, makes one believe that one>s role is much more whole. These virtual participants are called keypad warriors' or <hashtag activists>. This phenomenon is eventually called 'hashtag activism'. Hashtag activism has become a global trend. Of course, the role of the internet in mobilising people cannot be undermined, but there are distinct challenges in the garb of hashtag journalism. Notable among them are: Superficial: Most people who participate in favour of a particular cause often find themselves unaware of the issue from all angles. Many are aware of the issue as a trending problem, but lack an in-depth study of it. Large networks: Hashtag activism tends to attain an extensive network of people scattered across the globe. This is both advantageous and disadvantageous. The positives are that it attracts global attention and creates subsequent pressure. Digital dependency: Hashtag activism thrives on digital presence. If people do not access digital media, activism will not survive, subsequently limiting people>s involvement in a movement. Most countries have a large- scale digital divide, where the digital gap fails to meet the normative goals and creates hurdles for social and economic justice. Civil society's failure to update normative goals accentuates the feudalistic attitude towards information. Relatively lesser self-life: If an issue is trending on social media, it prolongs the movement>s life. In the wake of another issue, the uproar over the previous issue dies down and distracts digital activists> attention.
12.4.1 Understanding Slacktivism
When activists and advocacy groups receive support through <<clicks,>> <<tweets,>> <<likes,>> or <<shares>> of their messages on social media platforms, that trend is usually referred to as slacktivism. The intrusion of Facebook, Instagram, X, and YouTube, among others, is a good option to garner popular

support for any social issue debates. Uphold the idea that if slacktivism is Social Media and measured only by gaining awareness of a cause, the other elements closely Contemporary Activism related to activism would surely fall short. Online activism, in itself, is not enough. We need to be realistic about what will create advocacy and long-term support. Awareness is only one part of a multi-tiered set of tools we employ. To be successful, causes need to be activated, such as social change, fundraising, participation, and the like. If I look at the causes and events that have been the most successful, participants become activated right from the start. They feel more involved as they have skin in the game. Social media>s role is stated to be overrated, and the role of other aspects, like the cab drivers and the conversations at the coffee house, determines its overrated potential. The Occupy movement has had great success in focusing the conversation on inequality, but has been less effective in changing the policies that sustain it. Despite its loud presence on social media, the movement could not gain the momentum anticipated in real life. Austerity policies in Europe continue despite large numbers of protesters carrying out sustained occupations in multiple countries, including Spain and Greece. Of course, the power of the media here is apparent. The advent of blogging and the rise of cheap cell phones with video cameras also created major changes as activists started acquiring, publishing, and circulating video evidence of the many grievances that made everyday life difficult for citizens. One well-known blogger, Wael Abbas, became an investigative journalist--a profession that had been somewhat rare in Egypt before the revolution--and published videos of police corruption, torture, women being harassed on the street, traffic, bribery, and many other issues that were of great concern to the public. In India, vloggers like Dhruv Rathee, CarryMinati, and Flying Beast, among others, have a huge fan following and cover the most significant issues impacting the election mood.
12.4.2 Resilience and Sustainability
As discussed previously, mobilising people using social media is simpler. Getting them to do something requires patience and sustenance. However, sustaining the movement or the process considerably longer is challenging. Several theories have been associated with the sustenance of social media movements. One such theory has been Anthony Downs' Issue-Attention Cycle. Down>s Issue AttenCycle divides the stages of activism into five stages. They are
ThPre-Problemem Stage
In every activism or advocacy, there lies the pre-problem stage. This stage is when people realise that whenever an issue exists, the social condition that persists is unacceptable and has not been able to garner mass support. This is especially concerning since some experts or interest groups could have already been troubled by it, but could not get support.

Social Media and Society Alarmed Discovery and Euphoric Enthusiasm
The transformation into the second stage is sudden but natural. In this stage, people are triggered by dramatic events, and now they understand the potential threat the issue carries in its subsequent outcomes.
Realisation of the Costs
The third stage in Downs> model is the gradual awareness of the movements> limits. This involves the impracticalities and high costs, a gradual realisation of the high level of commitment to significant progress, and the realisation that the problems have benefited many.
Decline in Intensity of Interest
A key part of the third stage is the increasing recognition that a relationship between the problem and its solution is required. In this part, the activists understand the inordinate sacrifice that leads to the fourth stage and, hence, the gradual decline in intense public interest.
Post-Problem Stage
The fifth and final stage, the post-problem stage, is called a twilight realm of lesser attention. However, it is distinct from the pre-problem stage in that new institutions and bureaucracies continue to impact policy and allow for more attention than issues in the pre-problem stage. Here, the activism appears at a sporadic level. The passionate activists keep generating awareness on the issues from time to time. 12.6 KEYWORDS
Activism: Intentional action taken to bring about social or political change, often involving protest, advocacy, or campaigning, both online and offline, for justice-oriented goals. Automated Surveillance: Using algorithmic systems and digital technologies to monitor, collect, and analyse individual behaviour data, often without explicit consent or visibility. Digital Operations: Planned online activities and strategies implemented by organisations or groups to manage information flow, influence audiences, or execute campaigns using digital platforms and tools. Grassroots Campaigns: Community-based movements driven by ordinary citizens rather than elite leaders, aiming for social or political change through local organising, advocacy, and public engagement. Hashtag Activism: A form of digital activism using hashtags to amplify causes, build awareness, and foster virtual communities around social justice, often leading to real-world engagement. Narratology: An academic discipline studying the structures, elements, and functions of narratives across media, examining how stories are constructed and interpreted by audiences. Slacktivism: Minimal-effort digital support for causes, such as likes or shares, is often criticised for replacing deeper political engagement with symbolic, feel-good online gestures. Social Media Mobilisation: The strategic use of social media platforms to organise people, disseminate information, and coordinate collective actions for social, political, or cultural causes. Social Movement: A collective, organised effort by a group aiming to promote or resist change in society's norms, policies, or institutions, often sustained over time. Visual Narratives: Stories conveyed primarily through images, videos, or multimedia elements, shaping audience perception and understanding by combining aesthetics with emotional and informational content. Vloggers: Individuals who produce and share personal video content regularly on platforms like YouTube, blending storytelling, entertainment, and commentary to engage online audiences.

13.0 INTRODUCTION
Influencer marketing involves partnering with influential people, such as bloggers, vloggers, and social media personalities, to promote your brand, product, or service. It is a powerful tool to help you reach a wider audience, build trust and credibility, and drive sales. Blogging, on the other hand, is a content marketing strategy that involves creating and sharing valuable, relevant, and consistent content to attract and engage a clearly defined audience. It is a cost-effective way to establish your brand as a thought leader, generate leads, and build customer relationships. By partnering with influencers who resonate with their target audience, brands can leverage the influencers' credibility and reach to enhance brand visibility and awareness. Influencers act as trusted voices, providing recommendations and reviews that can influence consumer perceptions and behaviours. Similarly, blogging allows brands to establish thought leadership, share valuable insights, and engage with their audience more deeply. Through informative and engaging blog content, brands can showcase their expertise, address consumer needs, and foster a sense of community. Blogging also plays a crucial role in search engine optimisation (SEO), driving organic traffic to the brand's website and improving its online visibility. Influencer marketing and blogging are significant because they can humanise brands, create authentic connections with consumers, and influence purchasing decisions. In this unit, we will focus on the Indian market and advertising world, providing examples and case studies of successful influencer marketing and blogging campaigns. We will also discuss the challenges and opportunities of influencer marketing and blogging, and how to overcome them. So, let's get started!
