15.5 IMPACT OF SOCIAL MEDIA ON
DEMOCRATIC PROCESSES AND
PARTICIPATION
Digital democracy is seen as an emergence of a new paradigm characterised by the rise of 'governance by networks' and 'rule by data' from the standpoint of inclusive citizenship (IT for Change, 2017). Citizens use internet tools to obtain information, engage in governance-related activities, and communicate with stakeholders, much of which is transacted through social media platforms. Reliable information is at the heart of communicative practices, constituting a healthy democracy. India is witnessing this transition of democratic deliberations in online spaces, something that traditional media gatekeepers did not allow earlier. So we see many citizens, activists, journalists, policy makers and civil society representatives taking to Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, BlueSky, Mastodon and other social media platforms as they can voice their ideas and contribute to shaping democratic processes by enhancing citizen participation. In many ways, they contribute to the idea of the public sphere (Habermas, 1989) as they bring together diverse opinions and provide open discourse, which is vital for any democracy. In the last few years, facilitated by smartphones and cheap internet access, the public of India has actively engaged online for political discourse, policy debates and electoral practices. E-Democracy and E-Governance allow citizens to engage directly with leaders and policymakers and also enable them to raise questions. For instance, during the #anti-CAA movement in Delhi and many other parts of India, people from diverse backgrounds took to social media, created a ripple effect across political, social and cultural arenas, holding the policy makers accountable and sparing broader debates on the Citizenship Amendment Act. In many cases, the marginalised communities are finding their voice on these platforms. Fostering inclusivity was seen in the Rohith Vemula Case. The supporters took to social media to mobilise public opinion and counter misinformation about his death, thus facilitating grassroots activism through collective networked participation - the online activism feeding into the offline protests and other activities. Sen and Narayanan (2016) wrote that the Indian government is proactively encouraging government departments and ministers to be present on new media, with the President and the Prime Minister leading by example. Along with the e-governance policy and its initiatives, guidelines on engaging with the public on social media platforms have also been issued. The launch of the Digital India programme to transform the "entire ecosystem of public services through the use of information technology" in July 2015 reveals the government's emphasis on e-governance (DeitY, 2015). M-governance is the latest buzzword in the Indian government. In May 2014, its Mobile Seva platform garnered the United Nations Public Service Award 2014 in
the "Promoting Whole-of-Government Approaches in the Information Age"
(DeitY, 2014). More and more people are participating in policy discussions owing to the increased implementation of e-governance programs like MyGov.in. #Digital

India and campaigns like #swachhbharat and #viksitbhara by governments, Political Power of both at the centre and in states. In the last few years, the Ministry of External Social Media Affairs has successfully used Twitter for real-time crisis management, such as evacuations during international conflicts and COVID-19. During the pandemic, for instance, the state-citizen interactions enhanced as online communication assumed a central role in crisis management. The flip side of social media is that it also challenges democracy by spreading fake news, misinformation, and disinformation, making it difficult for users to discern truthful information and hampering their decision-making processes, especially during elections. The WhatsApp ecosystem has often been misused for motivated campaigns and the polarisation of voters. It is argued that social media actively contributes to societal polarisation as platforms such as X and Meta face backlash over misinformation, fact- checking, conspiracy theories and toxic discourse (Ittefaq, 2025). For instance, a video released by a party shows the bad roads of Delhi to influence voters. On fact-checking, AltNews and Google Maps showed that the street was not in Delhi but another state. Allport and Postman (1947) warn of rumour propagation and emphasise the dangers of unchecked information dissemination. Democracies are under threat across the world due to partisan media, and that short-circuits thoughtful deliberations to the extent that Vaidhyanathan (2018) argues that social media and Facebook in particular have become ubiquitous and deeply embedded in surveillance, manipulation, disinformation and digital imperialism. The Pegasus spyware episodes in India are reminders about state surveillance of dissenting voices coming from journalists, human rights activists and lawyers, demonstrating how spyware can be used as a weapon to collect vital online and offline information of individuals. Similarly, Cambridge Analytica's role in manipulating voter behaviour underscores the risks of data misuse. In the much-talked-about documentary film 'The Social Dilemma' on Netflix, it is seen that algorithms reinforce biases that are instrumental in amplifying divisive narratives. This results in limited different groups consuming entirely separate narratives. For example, during the Shaheen Bagh protests (2019-2020), social media enabled rapid information sharing and international visibility, but it also became a battleground for competing narratives and combating misinformation. The fragmented narratives ensured those supporting the protests saw it as an important democratic intervention. In contrast, those opposing it saw the protests as an unwanted disruption, hindering the smooth passage of the CAA bill. These divergent realities that emerge from micro-targeting of voters, also furthered through WhatsApp, demonstrate how powerful these tailored messages shape public discourse on an issue. The ability of social media to reach specific demographics, such as first-time voters or regional communities in different languages, has redefined campaigning in India. Thus, social media is both an enabler and a disruptor. It democratises access to political discourse, enhances participation, and amplifies marginalised voices. However, misinformation, polarisation, and surveillance must be addressed to ensure their positive contribution to democratic processes.

Social Media and Society As we go along, it is important to understand its transformative powers in reshaping the contours of democracy in India. Scholars of democracy posit that open access to information is vital for an informed citizenry (Habermas, 1989; Neyazi et.al, 2016). To some extent, web platforms create a modern public sphere where diverse voices converge, promoting transparency and accountability in disseminating political content, such as live streams of parliamentary debates or citizen- driven fact-checking efforts during elections. The online tools allow citizens to engage directly in political processes, such as voting campaigns, public consultations, or online petitions. Citizens often channel spare time into collective action, fostering participatory democracy by lowering barriers to entry. In India, platforms like Change.org and MyGov have empowered citizens to participate in policy-making and issue-based campaigns. Networked mobilisation helps organise collective action rapidly beyond geographical constraints, creating a ripple effect. Politicians, influencers, and media outlets compete to frame narratives, telling people 'what to think about'. Though social media enables diverse perspectives, the algorithms running in the background tend to create structures resembling echo chambers where a person only encounters information or opinions that reflect and reinforce their limited exposure to alternate perspectives. This often throws a distorted world view, leading to misguided citizens influenced by false premises. There have been several cases where governments and corporations have used these platforms for spying and stifling dissent, in that sense, threatening individuals, groups and democratic structures. As Foucault's Panopticism (1975) describes, surveillance leads to self- censorship, limiting freedom of expression. Digital democracy hinges on fair access to online resources. Socioeconomic inequalities, however, tend to leave behind marginalised groups, and the digital divide brings to the fore existing differences in access to technologies. This dilutes the democratic promise of networked environments. Highlights inequalities in access to technology, which undermine the democratic potential of these networked spaces. In India, rural populations often face access to information and communication technology barriers, limiting their participation in online political discourse. Big technology platforms and often local and global forces interact to shape socio-political structures. The web platforms embody this interaction, impacting domestic politics. Facebook's controversial moderation policies in India during the 2020 Delhi riots highlight how global corporations impact local democracy. The Supreme Court of India intervened and observed that the episode highlights the "necessity of greater accountability by... (social media) intermediaries which have become big business corporations with influence across borders and millions of people". On the one hand, networked participation is about information accessibility, political participation, mobilisation, etc., and challenges of misinformation, polarisation, and surveillance. It empowers citizens and enhances democratic engagement, and introduces risks that must be mitigated through regulation and media literacy.

15.6 SOCIAL MEDIA AND POLITICAL
Social Media
POLARISATION
Social media facilitates instantaneous, worldwide engagement, but it also increases political polarisation by fuelling ideological divisions, intensifying extremist viewpoints and limiting the room for reasonable conversations. Algorithms favour anything by the users' choice, creating echo chambers where users encounter beliefs and views that coincide with their own, reinforcing limited perspectives and alternate ideas are not considered. This selective exposure to information reinforces ideological rigidity. Supporters and opponents of government initiatives typically consumed completely different narratives on various topics, frequently with little overlap or interaction. Additionally, the attention-grabbing characteristics of the platforms often supported by engagement-driven algorithms prioritise reward sensationalism and controversy, aligning with extreme political ideologies. It is a common experience that rational discourse gets overshadowed by content pushed strategically on social media, causing ideological polarisation between differing factions. Group polarisation occurs when discussions with homogeneous groups exacerbate ideological rigidities. Social media platforms have failed to take action when needed to stop the spread of misleading narratives about caste, religion and more. Hate speech is a reality of the times. Structures of social media networks encourage misinformation and deepen ideological divisions by twisting facts that are antagonistic. Fake news spreads faster than credible information, particularly in a polarised environment. Social media hastens the spread of misinformation with minimal oversight in most cases. Furthermore, it has created an era of personalised politics where identities are politicised through community-related complaints and claims. People are likely to obtain a sense of pride and self-esteem through groups created on social media. It also helps build identity-specific factions as these memberships build identity assertions and contentions. The growth of caste and religion-related content has, on the one hand, led to increased visibility of issues otherwise overlooked by mainstream media; it has also caused fragmentation of political discourse that adversely impacts the public sphere, which is essential in a democracy. It has been emphasised that inclusive dialogue is important for democracy. However, social media creates fragmented, insular spaces for political debate. The television debates on platforms like Twitter often devolve into partisan attacks, with little room for constructive dialogue. Political influencers, including activists and celebrities, often use it to mobilise support for specific ideologies, inadvertently fostering polarisation. As observed in the Two-step flow theory (Lazarsfeld, Berelson & Gaudet, 1944), which suggests that opinion leaders play a significant role in shaping public opinion, it also allows influencers to frame issues in ways that resonate with their audience's ideological leanings, further deepening divisions. Social media-induced polarisation is not unique to India. Global examples

Social Media and Society highlight similar dynamics. In Brazil, for instance, WhatsApp was central in spreading polarised narratives during the 2018 elections, aligning with Jair Bolsonaro's rise to power (Klein & Robinson, 2020). Addressing polarisation requires a multi-pronged approach that includes strengthening media literacy to identify misinformation, reforming algorithms to promote diverse viewpoints, encouraging dialogue across ideological lines to rebuild trust and making platforms accountable for gaps in their policies. Intergroup contact under appropriate conditions can reduce prejudice. Social media can be a virtual meeting ground for individuals from diverse ideological, ethnic, or cultural backgrounds. Initiatives like Facebook's "Common Ground" project aimed to reduce polarisation by promoting stories that bridged political divides. In India, online forums discussing communal harmony during the COVID-19 pandemic brought diverse voices together to address shared challenges. It enables real-time, cross-partisan conversations that foster mutual understanding and diminish polarisation. Deliberative Democracy Theory (Habermas, 1989) emphasises the importance of open, inclusive dialogue in democratic societies. Social media provides a platform for such discussions, especially when designed to prioritise constructive engagements. Online discussions often host debates on contentious issues like the economy or education, involving participants from across the political spectrum. Personal stories on these platforms can humanise political opponents, fostering empathy and reducing polarisation. Stories can influence attitudes by allowing individuals to see the world through others' perspectives. Campaigns like the #ShareYourStory initiative in India encouraged citizens to share their experiences with caste or religious discrimination, helping others understand complex social issues. Social media platforms often collaborate with fact-checking organisations like Alt News, BoomLive, and others to counter misinformation. This is the need of the hour since these organisations help counter fake narratives through facts and help reduce ideological rigidity, particularly during elections. By debunking fake news and myths, they also focus on shared societal goals and interests that are important for building common identities. Election campaigns focusing on national development and economic growth, such as 'My first vote for the country', exemplify how the same platforms can unite supporters from various political affiliations. As discussed earlier, social media has the potential to achieve collective action for non-partisan purposes, bringing people together across ideology. Online campaigns during natural disasters, as seen when floods hit Kerala in 2018, rallied support from various political ideologies, building a sense of a larger collective purpose. Educational campaigns can increase online literacy, allowing users to assess information and fight against polarising content critically. Media Literacy Theory (Livingstone, 2004) highlights the importance of education in enabling informed media consumption. Google has initiated programmes like Internet Saathi in India to train rural women in the responsible use of the internet, so that they do not fall for the divisive posts. Technology may shape the user's behaviour, but design elements may direct it towards desired positive changes.

An example is Twitter's innovative testing of prompts that expected users Political Power of to read the message before resending it, thus reducing mindless sharing of Social Media questionable content. Such initiatives are much needed today to counter hate speech with all its promises. Social media's potential in resolving problems emanating from polarisation is limited due to its revenue model based on profit-driven algorithms prioritising engagement, not moderation. Thus, dismantling echo chambers and filter bubbles appears difficult in the existing social media model. The larger issue of the digital divide persists, which excludes marginalised communities from participating in the efforts to resolve these challenges.
15.7 ROLE OF GOVERNMENT SURVEILLANCE
AND CENSORSHIP ON SOCIAL MEDIA
PLATFORMS
While social media aid in freedom of expression, enabling citizens to express their opinions, form collectives for specific actions, and hold governments and those in power accountable, it also serves as an agent of repression. Surveillance and censorship enable authoritarian regimes to crush dissent, often in the name of ensuring national security, public safety and order and fighting fake narratives. In India, just as in other parts of the world, some government regulatory policies and their implications for surveillance and censorship have fuelled debates on their intent and implementation. Government surveillance means tracking one's activities, often in the garb of a measure to combat extremism, misinformation, or cybercrime. The enactment of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, gave the government enhanced power over platforms. According to the rules, intermediaries, such as Facebook, WhatsApp, and Twitter, are instructed to appoint grievance officers, delete illegal content within 36 hours of a complaint, and find the originator of particular information. Experts and critics add that locating the messages' source per the rules may compromise end-to-end encryption, as seen on say WhatsApp, jeopardising user privacy. The Puttaswamy Judgment in 2017 acknowledged privacy as a constitutional right as per Article 21. However, surveillance measures are at variance with this landmark judgement. The role of surveillance as an instrument for controlling and exerting power has long been debated, especially with regard to perpetual policing that undermines free expression and instills fear in citizens. Censorship means restraining content considered adverse, unsuitable, or threatening to national interests by the government. In the last few years, India has stepped up attempts to control social media sites by blocking accounts, deleting posts, or flagging hashtags criticising government policies. For instance, in the 2020-2021 farmers' protests, the Indian government directed Twitter to block several accounts, including those of journalists and activists, on the grounds of maintenance of public order (Al Jazeera, 2021). Likewise, material critical of the government's response to the COVID-19 pandemic was deleted under official instructions (Singh, 2021).

Social Media and Society The IT Rules 2021 also mandate platforms to follow a Code of Ethics that aligns with Indian laws. While supporters say that these steps can check damages from hate speech or misinformation, critics argue that they may be used to suppress dissent and silence differing voices. Critics contend that such policies undermine the distinction between regulation and censorship, impacting freedom of speech and expression guaranteed under Article 19 (1) (a) of the Constitution. Reports by groups such as Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch have questioned them for heightened internet shutdowns and arbitrary censorship (Amnesty International, 2023; Human Rights Watch, 2022). Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) adds that such measures impact marginalised communities and dissenting voices disproportionately (Internet Freedom Foundation, 2021) Noam Chomsky's Propaganda Model demonstrates state manipulation of media accounts to manufacture consent and constrict counter-hegemonic ideas. This also applies to the social media environment, as everywhere in the world, there are debates over maintaining the fine line between control and liberty. For example, the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) of the European Union concentrates on safeguarding user privacy (European Commission, n.d.). In India, however, the response is usually singled out as excessively control-oriented. The U.S. has opposed strict regulation, relying on technology platforms to regulate themselves. Surveillance and censorship by the government have far-reaching implications for democracy. While protecting national security and public order is necessary, over-control can whittle away at democratic ideals, stifle opposition, and restrict civic participation. The fine line between regulation and liberty is maintaining openness, accountability, and strict compliance within constitutional norms. As social media further influences public opinion, it becomes the task of the judiciary, civil society, and independent monitors to check abuse. 15.8 LET US SUM UP
Social Media
Social media has become influential in politics, impacting campaigns, public opinion, and democratic engagement. In India, platforms such as WhatsApp, Twitter, and Facebook have transformed political communication, providing avenues for interaction but also generating fears about polarisation, disinformation, and surveillance. From the Anna Hazare campaign to election campaigns to the recent elections of 2024, Indian politics has seen online strategies determining actions on the ground. Political agents use it for outreach, mobilisation, and narrative control. Internationally, its contribution to mobilising activism and empowering movements from below, as witnessed during the Arab Spring, shows its influence in calling for collective action. Social media has also been exploited to magnify societal cleavages by encouraging echo chambers. State intervention in social media governance in India has triggered serious concerns regarding freedom of speech, expression and privacy. Regulations such as the IT Rules 2021 outline the state's effort to balance security and accountability in the face of criticism for overreach and censorship. Theoretical works such as Foucault's Panopticism and Chomsky's Propaganda Model provide lenses for analysing the effects of surveillance and content moderation, highlighting the danger of subverting democratic processes. While India struggles to balance these issues, international comparisons--such as the EU's GDPR and U.S. models--emphasise other avenues for governing online communities without suppressing civic participation. Maintaining democratic principles, promoting transparency, judicial oversight, and safeguarding user rights are still crucial.

16.2 DATA, INFORMATION, AND
INTELLIGENCE
In most IT settings, the phrases intelligence, information, and data are bandied around very freely, inevitably leading to people mistakenly mixing them. Data, information, and intelligence all refer to the same thing. Yes, they differ in definition and purpose, but they are equally crucial for making appropriate decisions. All three factors must be considered when developing a plan to solve a business challenge. If you miss one, you will make strategic judgments based on insufficient data or information, which might be disastrous for your bottom line. The following is a straightforward explanation of how the linked phrases differ from one another and how they interact.
16.2.1 Data
Data is made up of raw, individual, and indisputable facts. Data is a recorded fact in its most basic form from a certain time. It's a snapshot of a moment in time. Such an event includes a chat, a sale, or an encounter with your company's website. Data is gathering outcomes from those occurrences that are quantifiably documented so that organisations can evaluate them readily. They're factual claims that can't be refuted.
16.2.2 Information
The term 'information' refers to a simple method of combining facts. When you put data from an event into a story, you will have information rather than data. The data context allows you to answer queries like how many students are enrolled in an IGNOU Cybersecurity course or how long the sales cycle takes. The replies create information for those questions. It's all about converting data points into information about your company. Information is the collection of material that may be used to answer a common query. For example, whether a country's GDP is more significant than average or whether a specific plant is native to California.
16.2.3 Intelligence
Intelligence combines the information into a form that tells a story and informs decisions. Intelligence takes it a step further and uses the information to drive decisions. Instead of telling a story (like information

does), intelligence paints a picture. For example, if you sell to more people Information Gathering in India, intelligence answers why that might happen. Intelligence will look Through Social Media at the number of events, ad spend, or marketing campaigns Indian clients receive and compare them to other clients in other regions and markets. Through this analysis, you might see more significant client interactions (events, emails, or meetings) in the India region, and you can deduce that you need to do the same in North America or Europe to increase sales. Intelligence is decision-making assistance. It's a tool for generating intelligent predictions based on a thorough understanding of the present to take action that improves outcomes. If intelligence is your ultimate aim (which it should be), you must first and foremost have clean, accurate data. As a result, you must collect data from your internal and external operating environments throughout your organisation. You never know what discoveries will emerge; the continuity will come apart without data. For example, Tesco, a well-known retailer in the United Kingdom, introduced a loyalty card in 1995 to gather more information on its customers through their transactions. Information and intelligence began to take shape as a possible output only after the data was collected. Data is worthless without the context that the report gives. As a result, you must ask key questions about the information you've obtained to decide on your company's sales increase. Tesco, for example, used Clubcard data to evaluate how often their consumers bought at their shops vs their competitors, what sorts of purchases they made when they liked to shop, and more. To complete the knowledge continuum, you must analyse your data and information to determine why specific outcomes occur to make better business decisions. Customers in densely populated areas liked "express" stores that held basic items because they offered a faster and more convenient shopping experience. Tesco redesigned several of its stores to the "express" model to appeal to the communities they served using this information. The Tescos of the world are not the only ones who use business analytics. Businesses typically fear big data, how it works, and its expenses. However, because no personnel or server expenses are connected with SaaS technology, collecting data, creating information, and extracting intelligence have become significantly more affordable and accessible.

Every social media network relies on inputs. Metrics such as the number of likes, growth in followers, number of shares, interaction time, and more are included in the data. Any information acquired from social media platforms that gives insights into the actions of users on the platform is referred to as social media data. Personal data collection is a touchy matter in online forums and the legislative community. This is because collecting data about users' activity on various social networks is acceptable and regarded as ethical, while collecting personal data is not. Companies may use personal data to influence more than simply their consumers' purchasing behaviour. They have sway over something as significant as their electoral decisions. The Cambridge Analytica affair is an excellent illustration.

16.5 INFORMATION GATHERING
There are a couple of approaches to leveraging the Internet for intelligence- gathering. Delivering on the propositions has been far more problematic, especially in public spaces, especially in a country such as India, where public space infrastructure is either developing or dilapidated. The issues can be categorised as functional and non-functional, as discussed in the following discussion.
16.5.1 Social Network Analysis
Social networking has been used to track and locate suspects since the days of scientific police detective work, except that it has been a manual and detailed activity. The first change was with the manual social network charts going digital, using a software tool called Social Network Analysis (SNA). SNA is a method of analysing social networks (the connections between a suspect and individuals in their relationship network) quantitatively and qualitatively through numerical or visual representation. The networks can consist of the family (immediate and extended), professional links (office colleagues or the suspect's business-card folder), membership on networking sites such as Facebook, LinkedIn, Twitter, social circle, mobile phone records, and others. SNA software is used in applications as diverse as market research, competition analysis, medical research, and social research, apart from law enforcement and intelligence-gathering. There are open-source packages available (Gephi, igraph, NetworkX, SNAP), which require a fair amount of software development and data analysis. Similarly, commercial packages (i2 Analyst, Sentinel Visualiser, SilentRunner Sentinel) are also available, and all the users have to do is start entering data.
16.5.2 Complementary Intelligence-Gathering
The complementary intelligence approach to leveraging the Internet for intelligence-gathering uses complex data from Human Intelligence (HUMINT) and Data Intelligence (SIGINT, IMINT, MASINT) operations to search for online links to the various references in the acquired data. The data will be entered into the SNA software, and the resulting visual and numeric representations will be used as references for online searches. Typically, these searches will involve surfing the Internet and social networking sites for new connections and leads that will feed further information into the HUMINT/DataINT networks. This cycle of refinement of information leads finally to the achievement of the intelligence objective, as happened recently in the case of the tracking down of al-Qaeda leader Osama Bin Laden.
16.5.3 Normative Social-Networking Sites Research
While using social networking sites (and SNA software) as complementary sources of information helps track a known suspect (individual or

Social Media and Society organisation), it is of limited use in unearthing fresh or new sources of concern. Given the silo-style operational style of many insurgents or insurgent groups, it is imperative to identify potential sources of trouble before they erupt. It is here that social networking sites provide the most valuable information: as long as the potential source of concern is not a loner who, since s/he does not have to communicate plans with anyone, is, therefore, less likely to need to use the Internet. Joining online discussion groups and forums dedicated to specific causes or ideologies and befriending potential trouble-makers are ways to identify incipient plots and terror threats. Several sting operations (targeting potential terror threats) in the USA have come about due to law enforcement agencies being incognito at such sites.
16.5.4 Limitations of Social Sites Intelligence-Gathering
Leveraging social networking sites and tools can be a valuable boon to intelligence-gathering agencies. It should be noted that there are limitations to the information the sites can provide, apart from the fact that if the individual/organisation needs to have some online presence:
- Level of Communication: The quantity and quality of information
available online on a suspect individual/group is as much as that made available by the most communicative (either unnecessarily talkative or forced to use communications media) group member. In a highly disciplined and carefully communicative group, the possibility of gleaning valuable information from the Internet is likely low to very low.
- Internet Penetration: Digital trails are much more difficult to unearth
in countries with low computer usage and Internet penetration. Unlike in the West, the overwhelming majority of Indians are not represented on the Internet, which reduces the efficacy of using social networking sites as repositories of secondary intelligence.
- Encryption/Steganography: Even if an individual or group is present
and active on the Internet, techniques such as encryption and steganography (which are even more difficult to detect) can mask the contents of communications between group members.
16.6 SOCMINT
Social media sites open up numerous opportunities for online investigations because of the vast amount of helpful information in one place. For example, you can get personal information about anyone worldwide by checking their Facebook page. This type of information often includes the interests of the concerned person and their connections on Facebook.
16.6.1 Social Media Intelligence (SOCMINT)
It is a sub-branch of Open Source Intelligence (OSINT), which refers to the information collected from social media websites. The data available on social media sites can be open to the public (e.g., Public posts on Facebook or LinkedIn) or private. Private information - such as content shared with a friend's circle- cannot be accessed without proper permission from the creator. Data available on social media sites can be classified into two categories:

- The user posts original content, such as a Facebook text or an uploaded Information Gathering
image/video. Through Social Media
- The metadata associated with original content--multimedia file
metadata, the date/time, and geo-location info associated with the posted content. There is a debate between privacy advocates and OSINT researchers about whether the information on social media sites is OSINT. Although most social media sites require users to register before accessing the content, many surveys show that users expect some form of privacy for their online activities (even when posting content with public access). However, OSINT experts generally consider the information shared on social media sites to belong to the OSINT domain because it is general information shared on public online platforms. Thus, it can be exploited for intelligence purposes. Using the information gathered from social media sites in a legal case is generally allowed under these two conditions:
- When a court grants permission to gather information about a specific
user, a court order is sent to the intended social media site to hand over the information to authorities officially.
- If the information is publicly available (e.g., public posts, images, or
videos), law enforcement can acquire it without a permit, which is the essence of the OSINT gathering concept. Private OSINT gatherers should have a legal basis when collecting personal information about targets; data protection laws (especially the GDPR in Europe) restrict how online investigators collect, process, and retain citizens' personal information. Discussing the legal issues surrounding OSINT is beyond the scope of this article; however, as a rule of thumb, make sure to have legal intent when collecting personal information from public sources and destroy this information as soon as you finish your investigation without any delay.
16.6.2 Social Media Content Types
People interact with social media sites for different purposes. The following are the general interactions used across other social media sites:
- Post/comment: People access social sites to post or write paragraphs
of text that other users can see. Such posts can also include the user's geographical info (On Facebook, they call this feature a "Check in").
- Reply: This is a text message (it can also be an image, video, or URL)
that replies to another user's post, update status, or comment.
- Multimedia content (images and videos): Multimedia is famous;
users can upload a video or double it as a part of their post. Many social platforms allow users to upload multiple images/videos to form an album. Live streams are available on social media sites like Facebook, Twitter, and YouTube. This feature allows users to broadcast live videos and display the recording on their profiles for later viewing.
- Social interactions are the essence of social media sites, where people
connect online by sending and responding to other users' requests.

Social Media and Society y Metadata: The results from user interactions with the social platform. Examples include the date and time when a video/image was uploaded, the date and time when a friend request was accepted, geo-location data--if enabled--of the uploaded multimedia file or post, and the type of device used to upload the contents (mobile or a standard computer). SOCMINT is interested in gathering all these content types. However, the ability to do this depends on the privacy control level set by each user when publishing posts/updates online. For example, it is not possible to see other people's updates on Facebook if they restrict a post's visibility to some friend circles or set it to "Only me." Many people use social media and social networking interchangeably to refer to Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, and related social platforms. It is not wrong, but it is inaccurate because social media is the central umbrella that contains other categories, such as "social networking," which holds sites like Facebook. The following are the leading social media types classified according to function:
- Social networking allows people to connect with others and businesses
(brands) online to share information and ideas. Examples include Facebook and LinkedIn.
- Photo sharing: Such websites are dedicated to sharing photos
between users online. Examples include Instagram and Flickr.
- Video sharing: Such websites are dedicated to sharing videos,
including live broadcasts. The most popular one is YouTube. Please note that Facebook and Twitter also offer live video broadcast services.
- Blogs: This informational website contains posts on one topic or
subject, organised in descending order according to the publication date. The most popular blogging platforms are WordPress and Blogger, which Google powers.
- Microblog: This allows users to publish a short text paragraph (which
can be associated with an image or video) or a link (URL) to be shared with other audiences online. Twitter is the most famous example.
- Forums (message boards): This is one of the oldest types of social
media. Users exchange ideas and discuss in the form of posted messages and replies. Reddit is an example.
- Social gaming refers to playing games online with other players
in different locations. It has gained more popularity recently. KAMAGAMES and Zynga are examples of this type.
- Social bookmarking: These websites offer a similar function to your
web browser's typical bookmark. However, they allow you to do this online and share your Internet bookmarks with friends, adding annotations and tags to your saved bookmarks. Examples include Atavi and Pinterest.
- Product/service review: These websites allow users to review and
give feedback about any product or service they have used. help and Angie's List (www.angieslistbusinesscenter.com) are examples of this type.

Now that we understand the different types of social media sites, it's time to Information Gathering discuss how to use other tools and techniques to acquire intelligence from Through Social Media these platforms. We will limit our discussion to the two most popular social media sites: Facebook and Twitter.
16.6.3 Facebook Information Gathering
Facebook is the most popular social media platform; it falls under the social networking type and has the most extensive user base. Facebook offered an advanced semantic search engine to search within its database using natural English language phrases and keywords. This semantic search engine, called Graph Search, was first introduced in early 2013; it allows Facebook users to type in their queries in the Facebook search box to return accurate results based on their questions/phrases or combined keywords. For example, you can type: Pages liked by *********, replacing the asterisks with the target's Facebook username to return a list of pages selected by the specified user. In 2019, Facebook removed the Graph search functionality; although users can still utilise it, they must manually build their Graph search queries. After releasing its direct support to Graph Search, Facebook has improved its search functionality, making it more accurate; it also adds many filters to refine your search as necessary. 16.6.4 Twitter Information Gathering
After logging into your Twitter account, Twitter has a built-in search functionality on the screen's upper-right side when using the Twitter web interface. A simple Twitter search allows you to perform a basic search within the Twitter database. However, do not underestimate this little box. You can add advanced search operators, similar to Google advanced search operators known as Google Dorks, to your search query to force it to dive deep and return accurate results, as you will see next. To begin your search against the Twitter database, it is advisable to go to the Twitter Advanced search at https://twitter.com/search-advanced; from this page, you can customise search filters to specific date ranges, people, and more. Like Google, Twitter allows you to use specialised operators to find related tweets more precisely. Twitter search operators are already available on the Twitter developer site; go to https://developer.twitter.com/en/docs/tweets/rules-and-filtering/ overview/standard-operators to view them. Twitter search operators can be incorporated with other criteria to create more advanced search queries to find related tweets more precisely; the following are some advanced Twitter search queries to start your search,

- The negation operator (-) excludes specific keywords or phrases from Information Gathering
search results. Example: virus -computer Through Social Media
- Use the (#) operator followed by the search keyword for hashtags. For
example, #OSINT
- Use the (until) operator to search for tweets sent up to a specific date.
Here's an example: OSINT until 2019-11-30(this will return all tweets containing OSINT and sent until November 30, 2019).
- To search for tweets sent since a specific date, use the (since) operator
followed by the date. An example is OSINT since 2019-11-30 (this will return all tweets containing OSINT sent since November 11,
2019) .
- Use the (images) keyword to return tweets containing a photograph.
Here's an example: OSINT Filter: images (this will return all tweets that contain the keyword OSINT and have an image embedded within them).
- To return tweets embedded with video, use the (videos) keyword
(similar to the images filter). Here's an example: OSINT Filter: videos
- Use the (Periscope) filter to search for a video uploaded using the
Twitter Periscope service. An example is the OSINT filter Periscope (this will search for all tweets containing the OSINT keyword with a Periscope video URL).
- To return tweets with either image or video, use the (media) operator.
Here's an example: OSINT Filter: media
- To return tweets that contain a link (URL) within them, use the (links)
keyword. Here's an example: OSINT Filter: links
- Use the URL keyword to return tweets containing a link (URL) and
hold a specific word within that URL. Here is an example: OSINT URL: amazon. This will return all tweets that contain OSINT and a URL with the word "Amazon" anywhere within it.
- To return tweets from verified users only (verified accounts have a
blue check mark near their names), use the (Verified) operator. Here's an example: OSINT Filter: verified
- Use the (min_retweets) operator followed by a number. Here is
an example: OSINT min_retweets:50 (this will return all tweets containing the OSINT search keyword that have been retweeted at least 50 times)
- Use (min_faves) followed by a number to return all tweets with
NUMBER or more likes. Here's an example: OSINT min_faves:11 (this will return all tweets that have at least 11 or more preferences and that contain the OSINT search keyword)
- To limit Twitter returned results to a specific language, use the (lang)
operator. An example is OSINT lang: en (this will return all tweets containing OSINT in English). To see a list of Twitter-supported language codes, visit https://developer.twitter.com/en/docs/twitter- for- websites/twitter-for-websites-supported-languages/overview.
- To search for tweets with a negative attitude, use the following
symbol :( For example, OSINT :( I will return all tweets containing the keyword OSINT written negatively.

Social Media and Society We can combine multiple Twitter search operators to perform a more precise search. For example, type "OSINT" from darkness-gate -Filter: replies lang: en to get only the tweets containing the exact phrase OSINT from the user darkness gave that are not replies to other users and in English only.

16.7 TRACK USERS ACROSS SOCIAL MEDIA
PLATFORMS
Most internet users have more than one social media account; according to Statista, the average number of social media accounts per internet user was 8.5 in 2018. This information is valuable and should be present when searching social media sites; for instance, many people prefer to use the same username on multiple social media platforms. If we know the username of one social media account of the target, we can search to see where this username is used on other social media platforms. You can check specific usernames to see where they are being used (e.g., social media Sites) or to know whether a particular username exists using any of the following free online services.
- Check User Name (http://checkusernames.com): Check for using a
specific username on 160 social networks. This can help you discover target social media accounts and see if they use the same username on multiple platforms.
- Namechk (https://namechk.com): Check to see whether a specified
username is used for important domain names and social media sites.

- Namecheckr (https://www.namecheckr.com): Check a domain and Information Gathering
social username availability across multiple networks. Through Social Media
- User Search (https://www.usersearch.org): Scan 45 popular social
media websites.
- UserRecon (https://github.com/thelinuxchoice/userrecon): A Linux
tool to find usernames across over 75 social networks.
- Sherlock (https://sherlock-project.github.io): The Sherlock Project
can find usernames across many social networks. It requires Python
3.6 or higher and works on macOS, Linux, and Windows.
The psychological status of the person posting the content on their profile can also give important information, even more than the content itself (in some cases). For instance, the true identity of an anonymous Twitter account can be revealed by performing a linguistic analysis of the target account. In addition, people can be tracked online by examining how they use language when they chat or broadcast their thoughts online (for example, how a target uses capitalisation, omits or includes words, and pronounces some words). The advances in artificial intelligence systems will make analysing social media accounts more effective and help examiners uncover the true identity of anonymous social media accounts. This online service (https:// tone-analyzer-demo.mybluemix.net) offers free linguistic analysis to detect human feelings found in text such as tweets, emails, and Facebook messages. In today's digital age, it is rare to see an Internet user who does not have at least one account on one or more social media sites. People use social media services to post all types of content online, such as photos, videos, text messages, and geo-location data. They also mention their education, employment history, and the addresses where they live. Personal information such as social connections, places visited, habits, likes and dislikes, family members, spouses, and more can all be found easily. Although social networking sites allow users to tighten their privacy controls to prevent others from seeing posted content, few people care about such issues and post many of their activities, including text posts and check-ins, in public status. It makes a large volume of accessible data about citizens' lives readily available to different kinds of online investigations, and this is the essence of "social intelligence" (SOCINT).
16.8 LET US SUM UP
In the final analysis, leveraging social networking sites and intelligence- gathering tools supports the traditional HUMINT/DataINT intelligence sources. Some governments are farther down the road to using the Internet for intelligence gathering. This unit discussed how the Internet and social media platforms could be used to expand intelligence, explain social media analytics, and describe social media intelligence (SOCMINT).

1.0 INTRODUCTION
Till now you have learned about the various tools of marketing including advertising, public relations and event management etc. In this you will be exposed to the new umbrella term- Marketing Communication Mix, commonly known as Integrated Marketing Communications (IMC) which makes use of various online and offline tools to achieve the marketing objectives. This unit will help you develop an understanding into the strategic use of these tools. Also, you will get a glimpse of how to establish strong business relationships with the audiences through marketing and communication mix.
1.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After working through this unit, you will be able to: * understand Marketing Communication Mix, its need and tools. * recognize and appreciate the benefits of integrated marketing efforts. * identify the important elements for making an integrated marketing plan
1.2 WHAT IS MARKETING COMMUNICATION MIX
Remember the last time when you planned to buy a smartphone or smart watch? You saw a friend wearing a branded smartwatch or a relative using the phone which you thought of buying. Then one day you saw a newspaper advertisement of these two commodities, followed by a small survey that you did for yourself by visiting the brand's store or asking from Google. This means that as a customer when you want to consider a product for purchase, you start seeking the information about it.In case of digital media, the purpose of a website is to help the customer. A website makes use of all the media components optimally to convey the message to the visitor in the best possible manner. So, we find the

use of text, visuals, audio as well as audio visual whenever needed while focusing on what needs to be conveyed in our communication through the site. The selection of media (text, audio, visuals and audio visuals) are done keeping in mind which medium can best make the point; we, as marketers, want to stress upon. Therefore, marketing communication mix is basically the use of different marketing tools optimally keeping in mind the target to achieve. Before proceeding further, let us quickly understand some of the basic concepts of marketing communication mix. Marketing: According to the American Marketing Association, marketing is defined as the process of planning and executing the conception, pricing, promotion, and distribution of ideas, goods and services to create exchanges that satisfy individual and organizational objectives. Marketing is a customer focused activity which involves the study and management of exchange relationships. Communication: According to Merriam Webster Dictionary, communication is a process by which information is exchanged between individuals through a common system of symbols, signs, or behavior. It is the sharing of experiences between two or more participants. Marketing mix: The strategy formulated by an organisation on the basis of product, price, place and promotion to formulate its product or service for its customers is called marketing mix. In case of services, there are three additional factors to be considered while designing the offering - people, process and physical evidence. Communications mix: This is a tactical combination of communication tools, used by the organisation, keeping in mind the strategy devised to achieve the desired objectives. This includes the use of both online and offline tools like advertising, public relations, sales promotion, sponsorship and others. Now let us look at the definition of integrated marketing communications (IMC). Simply put, integrated marketing communications involves the best use of resources to achieve best results by incurring minimum costs. It is a strategic management process, which is economic, efficient and effective and makes use of marketing communications, and is suited to any type of organisation. For instance, a cola or a soft drink brand uses television, print, cinema and digital media as key media channels to reach their target audiences and build brand awareness. However, to sustain in the competitive market doing so is not enough. So they use other activities to build a brand experience for users. To achieve this, the cola/soft drink brands associate themselves with sports, cultural and musical events. They integrate with various marketing communication tools to maximise the output. We will discuss these tools later in this unit. Activity 1 Select any commodity of your choice. Observe and describe the various marketing communication tools used to promote the product.
1.3 IMPORTANCE OF MARKETING COMMUNICATIONS MIX
It is important to integrate customer data, employees and marketing communications tools in order to maintain consistency of communication and ensure resource optimisation. As communication tools are multifarious, both online and offline, there may be multiple ways of more than one communication about the same product/service reaching the audience. Too much communication or communication from multiple sources may lead to confusion in the mind of the customer. Hence customer profile, particularly about demography, psychology, media habits and point of purchase, need to be built and the communication with the customer needs to be monitored. When various communication tools are used simultaneously to reach out target audience the compound effect is created. The messages complement and resonate with overall goals of marketing campaign. Effective marketing touches on a broad range of areas as opposed to fixating on one message. This helps to reach a wider audience and by integrating the various tools of marketing can help organizations make strategic decisions, thereby getting desired results.

1.4 TOOLS OF MARKETING COMMUNICATION MIX
1.4.1 Advertising
The word 'advertising' is derived from its Latin root 'adverter', which means 'to turn towards' or 'to attract attention to'. In this broad sense, it comprises all acts that are directed towards drawing attention. Advertising is defined as "any paid form of non-personal presentation and promotion of products, services or ideas by an identified sponsor which results in influencing the behaviour of the target buyer. Advertising can be defined by various features:
1) It is paid communication. Whether the money is spent on creating the message or buying media
space, advertising involves huge budgets.
2) It is non personal. As the process involves mass media, there is no face to face interaction
between the buyer and the seller.
3) Promotion of ideas. It not only tries to sell a product/service, it also tries to sell an idea.
4) Identified sponsor: The person or the company behind the ads is always known, even if not stated
in the ad.
5) Influencing buyer's behaviour: from affecting the attitude by the taglines used, advertising tries
to create a recall value.
1.4.2 Public Relations
Public Relations is a planned effort to positively influence public opinion through responsible behaviour and build goodwill for the organization and its products. Public relations is management of many strategic relationships forged by the company. The publics of public relations include media, neighbouring community, customers, shareholders, employees, government, investors and bankers etc. The types of public relations activities that build a positive image or publicity for products are called marketing public relations, an area that marketing communication managers have to deal with the most. The process includes effective communication, mutual adjustment by all the parties and sharing values over commitments.. The Public Relations process cohesively manages the perceptions of the public about the brand, product or service. For creating a favourable image of the company, the complete communication process, including feedback at several stages, needs to be completed. The process, of maintaining public relations includes: * Assessing and estimating the expectations from the company by the public and stakeholders * Involving this view of the company to reflect in all the managerial as well as market decisions * Researching about the courses of actions, their outcomes and effects on the company's image * Planning and implementing the objectives in a manner to create a favorable image for the company. * Troubleshooting and control in the times of crisis Public relations professionals organize press conferences to disseminate the information in the society via media. They create press releases- which is a text/graphical or audio-visual document, containing the related news. The press release is handed over to the journalism/media professional along with a media kit.
1.4.3 Sponsorship
An emerging part of the marketing communication mix is sponsorship. It is the financial association of companies with other companies or events. Sponsorship not only helps in forging cross platform and cross media ties; it also helps in creating and reaffirming the brand image and values. Sponsorship entails fully or partially taking care of the economics of an event, cause or organisation. It can also include donations in cash or kind. For example, a shoe brand sponsoring a sports event.

Figure1: Showing different tools of marketing communication mix Activity 2 Which communication tools and how many types of media can you identify in a movie launch? Make a list of them and analyse.
1.4.4 Sales Promotion and Gamification
Sales Promotion is a collection of tools that catalyse the sale in terms of quick and bulk purchase by consumers or trade for a limited period of time. Sales promotion changes the price-value relationship of a product by lowering the price, increasing the value or both. . The discounts offered by retailers during festivals is one such example. It is done to lure customers. Consumers get attracted towards such offers and make quick purchases of the products which they may not need immediately. Some of the techniques employed during sales promotion are publicity through media; incentivise; loyalty schemes etc. Let us quickly understand the techniques employed during sales promotion.
1) Publicity through media: News stories or advertisements in media inform, orient and persuade
the buyer in order to make a sale. At times the customer buys the product or service due to the personalised attention and at times the new information provided in media makes the purchase inevitable.
2) Incentivise: The manufacturer or retailer offers incentives or throws in freebies for the customer
to lock in the purchase. At times few discount coupons are also handed out to motivate further purchase in future.
3) Loyalty schemes: You must have seen such advertisements in media or display boards in malls
which offer cash back for next purchase. Memberships with a promise of incentives in the near future are also offered in order to garner loyalty from the customers. Other tools and techniques utilized by the sales promotion team include: Letters and mails, point of purchase displays, demonstration of the product, offers and discounts; giving coupons and gifts etc.

Gamification: While talking about gamification, it is important to understand that it is an approach that keeps the consumers engaged and motivated by integrating game mechanics into a sales process. It could be something as simple as collecting wrappers of a chewing gum to exchange later for another pack or getting reward points in a membership card after each purchase from a store, which can be redeemed later on.
1.4.5 Direct Marketing: Mail ,E-mail and Online Messaging
Mailers are an extremely cost effective yet personal way of reaching out to a target group. It can be utilised for sending reminders or coupons for existing customers and easy samples and demonstration options to acquire a new customer base. One can also use it to inform the customers about new products or additions and thus build brand loyalty. Mailing lists with various target profiles are provided by many service providers. Bulk emails and mails are any day much cheaper than any other form of reaching out to the base. Mailers can be designed in a manner that suits the target group thus making the communication more effective. While a generic ad has to reach out to a larger mass of people, mail is more personal and niche. With the help of coupons sent out, one can easily assess the profitability and the response ratio of the mailers.
1.4.6 Events and Experiences
Cultural and corporate events along with exhibitions and conferences are a great way to congregate and socialize. These events communicate a lot about the brand in any society. Be it some promotional event, press conference or display of products, events prove to be great tool to inform and persuade the target group. These events are of different types ranging from charity and cultural to sports and corporate. Each event serves a different purpose and different audience. Before planning an event it is extremely important to analyse the purpose of organising it and the understanding of your audience. This is followed by the plan of action, which means welcoming and engaging the audience and arranging for their takeaways. The last step of organising an event includes deciding the venue. The venue also plays a very important role in the scheme of things. Adequate parking space, accessibility and enough space for moving about are important considerations to make. With the advent of technology, event management industry has also found ways to incorporate it. From barcode scanners to virtual meet-ups, apps to register and social media to send reminders and registration details; there are a multiple number of ways how technology is aiding real world socialisation as well. Some other tools of marketing Communication mix include Merchandising and Point of Sale; and Packaging. These are discussed below.
1.4.7 Merchandising and Point of Sale
Merchandising involves all the activities that boost and promote the sale of goods or services at retail. It includes a variety of activities including determination of packaging and display, creating display designs, developing communication strategies and promoting discounts and coupons. Retailers may or may not be the producers of the product. In this case, the merchandisers ensure that the product finds a favorable representation at the outlet in order to create sales. It is worth noticing here that merchandising is never uniform. It may differ on the basis of place, time, occasion and competition. With the advent of social media, merchandising has grown its wings. With the help of social media and ecommerce, various merchandise promoting shows, films and characters can also be seen being sold. Point of sale is the marketing material which enables the customer in making the buying decision promptly. Ranging from shelf decorations to streamers, banners and other paraphernalia in the store, POS solidifies the brand image in a consumer's head. Working as a silent salesperson, these displays are non-intrusive and decorative.
1.4.8 Packaging
Packaging is the first impression of anything/any person on the other person. In our everyday life we often observe that any commodity in a nice packaging attracts the audience to a large number. It is often said that a person is a complete package, which means that he/she comes as a complete solution

to a problem. In terms of a product, packaging primarily means the process of designing and producing the wrapping for a product. It can also mean adding related freebies along with the product that will aid its usage or a freebie just to attract its audience. For e.g. A small toy or puzzle with a packet of chocolate. This is to lure children to buy the product. Packages are usually made after identifying the brand image and the needs of the consumer, in order to come up with feasible solutions. At the airports, food packets available by different food outlets are in leakproof and pressure-proof packaging in order to make them survive the flights that their buyers would board, after purchasing them. The product's MRP may vary depending upon the type of packaging. You must have seen on e-commerce sites that products have different MRP when compared to the same product being sold offline. Overall, a package needs to be Compact, Lightweight, Easy to carry, Attractive, Designed in adherence to the brand image and designed depending upon the use of the product. Packaging gives the first impression of the product and at times helps in making or breaking the decision at the time of purchase. Studies have shown that in the case of two products of different brands, in the same price range, available to the customer, the packaging plays an important role in making him/her decide what to buy. 1.5 BENEFITS OF MIXING THE MARKETING COMMUNICATION TOOLS
The concept of integrated marketing communication came into existence in 1980 when there was a need for a strategic integration of promotional tools, instead of using all the communication tools separately. Mixing of tools realigned various communication departments to emerge from their wells and look at the common organizational goal, to cooperate rather than compete with each other to deal with external challenges. There are several benefits of IMC. Some of them are as follows:
1. It brings consistency to the communication made with the audience, bringing clarity to them..
2. Clear, consistent range of messages brings credibility to communication.
3. Integrating marketing communication efforts optimizes the use of resources and avoids wastage
and duplication.
4. As customers become more aware through clear, consistent communication, there is a greater
chance of making a positive purchase decision.
5. It helps in consolidating the image of an organisation.
6. It helps in building a dialogue with the customer which leads to building a relationship, which In
the longer run, can ensure brand loyalty.
7. Since marketing communication mix is more effective, it increases profit for the organisation and
creates a competitive advantage for the organisation. Keeping the benefits of Marketing Communication Mix in mind, let us now learn how to plan an integrated marketing communications campaign.

1.6 PLANNING A MARKETING COMMUNICATION MIX
Till now we have understood that marketing communication mix refers to a set of tools used to promote services or products to a set of consumers, known as target audience. The key is in the name of communication, meaning a list of important principles and factors that are used to promote these products or services. There is no fixed approach for making a marketing and/or a communications plan. But there are always some essential elements which must be a part of the plan to ensure its success. One widely used approach is SOSTAC, elements of which are discussed below. S-Situation: Meaning - 'where are we now?' A study of the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats (SWOT) helps in ascertaining the need and pace of performance in order to achieve the objectives. O- Objectives: It answers the question - 'where are we going?' These are the long-term and short- term objectives that marketing communications would focus on. These are the measurable objectives that an organisation is set to achieve in a given time like building sales volume, increase in share prices, increasing awareness among the customers and positioning a product. S-Strategy: It answers the question - 'how do we get there?' In order to achieve the set objectives, strategy is planned keeping in mind the target to be achieved, the budget and the time available. T-Tactics: The tactics answers the question - 'what is the detail of the strategy?' It spells the details of the strategy to be used, the marketing communications mix. Tactics entails the decision on the tools of communication to be used and in what sequence and how much would be spent on the activity. A-Action: The action answers the question - 'what steps are required to put each tool in action?'This decides the actual plan of action required so that all the activities fall in line as per the plan. It includes the background work to be done and internal activities to take place for creating the tools to deliver the strategy. C-Control: It answers the question - 'are we getting there or not?' It is important to introduce some checks and balances in a marketing communications activity to ensure that the activity is on the right track. Control helps one to know whether the targets are being met and how the outcome can be maximised.
1.7 ROLE OF SOCIAL MEDIA IN COMMUNICATION MIX
The increased usage of the internet has forced the brands to integrate social media in their marketing communication channels. The marketing world has never been more intertwined than now. While the marketers have a new set of tools to reach out to the audience, it has also made it important to know and understand the audiences' habits, perceptions and tastes in order to create a positive influence on them. Over the last decade, a number of innovative techniques have made their way into marketing communications which has taken marketing to the next level. The internet and digital technologies have enabled new interactive forms of communication, where the receiver has an important role to play in the process of communication. A popular trend is that of content marketing. It is the process of generating content in order to sell the products. Be it a travel blog on a travel agent's site or photos uploaded by amateur stylists on a clothing ecommerce app with the help of digital media, creation of content has become much easier and with the help of social media, reaching out to a large number of people has become much faster for the brands. It is the content marketing, which has made teenagers using Instagram, the new age influencers. Also, with time social media has significantly transformed the marketing communication mix. Few ways by which it has impacted the business include: Two-way Communication- Through social media direct interaction between the brand and the audience can be established. This increases brand visibility and fosters trust among the audiences. For example using ratings and feedback from the customers brings transparency. Targeted Advertising- social media gives precise control over the audiences. By creating relatable ad content, it helps to reach the potential audience. Like you must have experienced seeing ads related to your brand preferences and choices on your social media handles.

Shift in Promotional Activities- Social media allows businesses to promote products and services more effectively. Examples can be the influencers that you often come across on social networking sites. This has changed the scenario when compared with the traditional promotional methods.
