1.0 INTRODUCTION
In essence, journalism is about presenting facts, evidence and the truth, so naturally, it is deeply connected to research. Research is a systematic process for investigation and producing knowledge. A journalist uses research-based methods to understand and explain the contexts, claims and patterns related to any event. You must have seen reports during elections, which are based on surveys and polls. These are classic examples of social science research methods. Today, journalism and mass communication research is a full-fledged, multi-faceted academic field drawing on interdisciplinary methods from the social sciences like political science, psychology and sociology, and the like. For the field of journalism and mass communication, social science research is more valuable because it helps in understanding the dynamics of society. Journalists used these methods to produce accurate, balanced and insightful news stories.

This unit will provide learners with the broad concepts and methods of social science research applied within journalism and mass communication. After this unit, learners will develop a clear understanding of the importance of research in maintaining reliability, objectivity, and credibility in news stories and how it strengthens journalism.
1.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
This unit will cover the broad concepts and methods of social research applied within journalism. After going through this unit, students will be able to: understand the role and importance of research in journalism, understand the difference between various types of social science research methods, and understand major social science research techniques such as surveys, interviews, ethnography, etc.
1.2 UNDERSTANDING RESEARCH
1.2.1 Definition
According to W.S. Monroe, "Research may be defined as a method of studying problems whose solutions are to be derived partly or wholly from facts." The word 'research' comes from the French word, 'recherche', which means to go about seeking or to search again. It is a systematic process for gathering information, analysing it and drawing conclusions based on it to produce new knowledge or solve specific problems. For journalists, research works as a tool for crafting good stories as well as a method for understanding society. A journalist relies on research to collect information, analyse data, verify claims, and present insights in a way that informs the public. For example, a news report on literacy rates in India would include records of government data and interviews with officials, as well as anecdotal elements, which would make the story more credible, reliable, and also provide it a human angle. This way of research allows journalists to dive deep into any issue and move from surface-level reporting to investigative journalism.
1.2.2 Characteristics of Research
There are many characteristics of research that make it different from casual information- gathering. Some of these are: Research is a systematic process. It follows a step-by-step approach to find the answers to any problem. Generally, it involves eight steps: a) Select a problem. b) Review existing literature c) Develop hypotheses or research questions d) Develop methodology/research design e) Data Collection f) Analyse and interpret the results g) Present the results in an appropriate form h) Replicate the study (when necessary). Research is empirical. The term empirical comes from the Greek word 'empeirikos', which means experienced. This means research is based on observable and verifiable evidence. Research is objective and based on facts. There is no space for personal biases.

Research is logical. It is based on clear, coherent and rational reasoning. All the steps involved in research follow a clear logic, so others can easily understand how the results are obtained. Research is replicable (can be reproduced). Replicability in research enhances its reliability and validity of the findings. If any other researcher follows the same research design, they should get the same results. Research is predictive. It helps in developing theories that are useful in understanding the past and present, and also in predicting future behaviour in different situations. Research is public. Research should not be hidden or private; instead, it should be shared publicly. The openness in research allows others to evaluate it and further build on the work. Research should be ethical. It is the responsibility of the researchers to minimise any harm, deception or exploitation, and ensure the safety and privacy of the participants.
1.3 TYPES OF SOCIAL SCIENCE RESEARCH
1.3.1 Basic Vsersus Applied Research
Basic research, also known as pure research, aims to expand knowledge. It is primarily based on intellectual curiosity without any practical application. The goal here is not to solve any problem, but to discover, develop and test theories. For example, basic research can be conducted to understand how young users interpret social media news. Applied research has practical application and is designed to solve practical, real-world problems. It aims to improve existing practices, products or services. It is highly context- specific and uses the existing knowledge to find the solution. For example, analysing audience ratings to understand the popularity of a programme. Journalists use applied research more because reporting covers pressing societal issues.
1.3.2 Descriptive Research
Descriptive research provides a detailed description of the topic under study. It aims to answer 'what' rather than 'why' questions. It provides a detailed description of any event, phenomenon, population or situation. For example, a report on the current social media usage habits of users containing information such as different age groups, the platforms that are widely used, the duration of use, and the kind of content people prefer, mapped through graphs and figures, is descriptive in nature.
1.3.3 Analytical Research
Unlike descriptive research, analytical research goes beyond description; it involves a critical evaluation of the data/information. It focuses more on 'why' questions. The aim is to understand and interpret the relationship, causes and effects. Analytical research looks at an issue from different perspectives and compares them to explain the relationship. Analytical research is important in journalism. For example, if a feature writer wants to understand the surprising uptick in book readership over the last five years, descriptive research would provide her with the numbers or data in a detailed manner, but analytical research would better explain the reasons and causal relationship among the factors involved.
1.3.4 Exploratory Research
Exploratory research is used to explore more about a certain situation, event or topic when little is known about it. This kind of research is more flexible, open-ended and unstructured. The aim here is to gather initial insights and be familiar with the topic. For example, if a new social media app is introduced, so little is known about how users perceive it; thus, a journalist can conduct exploratory interviews to understand the possible trend.
1.3.5 Explanatory Research

The main goal of explanatory research is to establish the cause-and-effect relationship between two or more variables. This kind of research is the deepest level of inquiry and provides a deeper understanding of a phenomenon by focusing on 'why' and 'how' questions. By establishing the cause-and-effect relationship between variables, it also helps in predicting the future occurrences of a phenomenon. For example, explanatory research can help in understanding the relationship between exposure to violent video games and aggressive behaviour in young adults. 1.4 KEY SOCIAL SCIENCE RESEARCH TECHNIQUES
Very broadly speaking, research can be divided into two broad categories: quantitative research ssand qualitative research. While these will be dealt with at length in upcoming units, let us look at some key social science research techniques from both categories:
1.4.1 Quantitative Research Techniques
Quantitative research deals with numbers, measurements and statistical tests to analyse data, and interpret themes and patterns. It involves systematic collection of data and uses structured tools like surveys, questionnaires, experiments, etc., to produce measurable and objective results. Here are the key techniques used in quantitative research:
1.4.1.1 Surveys and Questionnaires
Survey is one of the most commonly used research methods. It consists of a set of standardised questions to ask of a population. A questionnaire is the instrument or tool that is used to carry out surveys. Questionnaires can be a physical or digital document, consisting set of questions that respondents need to fill in order to collect the data. A survey always uses a questionnaire to collect data, but a questionnaire in itself is not a survey. The questionnaire consists of open-ended (for qualitative data) or closed-ended questions (for quantitative data). In journalism, the most widely used method for data collection is a survey, as it helps in understanding the attitudes, behaviours and opinions of a population. Opinion polls conducted during elections are based on surveys of the voters.
1.4.1.2 Experiments and Quasi-Experiments
Experiments or true experiments are a core quantitative research technique. In this method, the researcher tries to understand a cause-and-effect relationship by manipulating the variables. Key characteristics of experimental technique are as follows: It includes two groups, the experimental group and the control group. In a medical experiment, for instance, the experimental group receives the treatment, while the control group does not receive any treatment. The control group is simply used for comparison. The researcher manipulates the independent variable (IV) to see if it has any changes over the dependent variable, under controlled conditions. For both the experimental and control groups, participants are assigned randomly. Because of randomisation and control, this method has high internal validity, which means that the effect or change (if any) on the dependent variable is caused by the independent variable.

For example, students are randomly divided into two groups. One group is shown positive political news, while the other group is shown negative news. The researcher then measures the difference in their perspective towards the political scenario in the country. Quasi-experiments also try to establish the cause-and-effect relationship, but the component of randomly assigning participants is lacking here. However, it does involve some manipulation of the independent variable to see its effect on the dependent variable, but the researcher studies the pre-existing groups or conditions wherein randomly assigning participants is not possible or ethical. Due to the lack of randomisation and less control, it has lower internal validity.
1.4.1.3 Correlational Research
Correlational research is also called non-experimental research method. This method also aims to measure the relationship between variables; however, it does not manipulate the variable. The variables are measured or observed in their natural setting and aim to understand the degree or direction of the relationship. This relationship between variables is expressed as a correlation coefficient (r). The value of r ranges from -1 to +1. The (-) sign suggests a negative relationship, which means that both variables move in opposite directions. If one variable increases, the other decreases. The (+) sign stands for a positive relationship, suggesting that both variables move in the same direction. If one variable increases, the other also increases. In case the value of r = 0, this means that there is no relationship between the variables. For example, a researcher is investigating the relationship between learners' usage time of digital education tools and their academic performance. If we get a result of +0.8, it means that higher use of digital education tools is associated with good academic performance. In case the result is -0.8, it suggests that higher use of digital education tools is associated with lower academic performance.
1.4.2 Qualitative Research Techniques
Qualitative research focuses on exploring people's experiences, perspectives, emotions, and social context. It collects non-numerical data using unstructured or semi-structured techniques like Interviews, FDGs, observation, case study, etc which allows flexibility to gain deep insights into human behaviour. Let us look at some key techniques used in qualitative research:
1.4.2.1 Interviews and Focus Group Discussion
An interview is one of the most widely used research methods for collecting in-depth information on a topic. It is a one-on-one conversation between an interviewer and an interviewee, and is the most commonly used research method in journalism. It is useful in understanding the personal and real-world experiences of individuals. Based on the structuring, interviews are of the following types: Structured Interviews: Such interviews are highly rigid and follow a predetermined, fixed set of questions. It dominantly consists of closed-ended questions, and there is no scope for flexibility. Semi-Structured Interviews: Such interviews offer some scope for moderate flexibility. It consists of a predetermined set of questions, but allows the interviewee to dive deeper. Along with closed-ended questions, it consists of some open-ended questions as well. Unstructured Interviews: These are the most flexible kind of interviews, which consist of open-ended questions and allow free-flowing conversation. There is no predetermined set of questions; the goal is to get information in the most detailed manner. For example, the interview with a government official will follow a structured approach, while an interview with any individual from the entertainment industry would be mostly unstructured.

Another method here is a focus group discussion, which is the process of gathering a group of individuals or experts (often 6-10 people), and engaging them in a conversation on a specific topic. The conversation is guided and moderated by a moderator. The discussion among the participants provides richer and more interactive data than interviews.
1.4.2.2 Case Studies
The case study research method involves an in-depth and detailed investigation of a single case or event within real real-life context. The case can be any individual, institution, group or community, etc. It includes multiple sources of evidence to understand how various factors are related in a specific setting. This type of research method lacks generalisability. Generalisability means how much the results of a study can be applied to people or situations other than the ones studied. This research method is mostly useful for feature and narrative journalism.
1.4.2.3 Ethnography and Participant Observation
Ethnography is a qualitative research method that involves observing people in their natural environment. Ethnography is important because it allows researchers to explore and understand contexts, different cultures, rituals and lived experiences of individuals or communities. The key characteristic of ethnography is that it requires long periods of direct observation and fieldwork. It allows the researcher to see a topic from the subject's frame of reference. The key data collection tool for ethnography is participant observation. The researcher actively engages with the group or community they are studying and records their behaviours. The researcher may be a detached observer or a participant in the process under study.
1.5 CHALLENGES IN SOCIAL SCIENCE RESEARCH FOR
JOURNALISTS
1.5.1 Reliability and Validity Issues
Reliability and validity are the two most important elements in research. Reliability refers to 'consistency', and validity refers to 'accuracy'. When research measures produce the same results under the same conditions several times over, the results are considered to be reliable. Validity suggests how accurately a tool measures what it is supposed to measure. In journalism, maintaining reliability and validity is often very challenging. This is mostly because, first, there is scope for subjectivity in all the widely used research methods for data collection by journalists. Second, the dynamic nature of the media content may often lead to a flux in the results. For example, a news story on a viral video may face reliability and validity issues because it may not be reproducible due to the constantly changing nature of the media content.
1.5.2 Bias and Objectivity
One of the major concerns in journalism is maintaining objectivity and avoiding bias. Most of the time, the perspectives and beliefs of journalists may influence their work, and it can reflect while framing the questions, structuring the interviews, analysing and interpreting the data. Journalists can do this to influence the responses. This is ethically unacceptable. One must be aware of their biases and should adhere to the systematic process of research to ensure objectivity. Journalists should also be critical of the fact that biases can occur from sources as well, as their responses are based on their own perspectives, experiences, interests and loyalties, etc. It is their responsibility to cross-check the information and clearly separate facts and opinions. 1.6 LET US SUM UP
This unit is the foundation for understanding social science research methods, particularly in the context of journalism. We have learned that research is a systematic and objective process for producing knowledge or finding a solution to a problem. Along with the key characteristics of research, we also discussed the various types of social science research methods, such as basic, applied, exploratory, descriptive, etc. Research is essential in the field of journalism and communication as it allows journalists to dive deep into any issue and move from surface-level reporting to investigative journalism. The unit further explored the major techniques that are used for data collection in social science research, also delving into the issues of reliability, validity, bias and objectivity in journalism research.
1.7 KEYWORDS
Descriptive Research: It focuses on 'what' and explains a topic in a detailed manner. Analytical Research: This critically evaluates and analyses the relationships and patterns. Exploratory Research: Aims to explore an idea or topic when little is known about it. Explanatory Research: It focuses on 'why' and 'how' and explains the cause and effect relationship between two or more variables. Ethnography: A type of qualitative research method where the researcher observes a group or community in their natural setting. Reliability: It refers to the consistency of a research result. Validity: It is the accuracy of a measurement tool, how accurately it measures what it is supposed to measure. Objectivity: The practice of being neutral and impartial in research. Uses and Gratification: A communication theory that explains why and how people actively choose any media to fulfil their personal and psychological needs.

10.1 INTRODUCTION
In order to make sense of the voluminous amounts of data available to us today, organisations need to follow due processes that have been put in place through years of R&D. One cannot simply pick up a large dataset and start working with it haphazardly to arrive at their desired goal of understanding this data. They must follow step-by-step procedures to maximise their chances of deciphering and using this information. A key step in this process is data mining, also known as knowledge discovery process, as it involves the 'mining' of knowledge from the data available with us. This process is used extensively in different fields of public life today, whether it is businesses and finance, healthcare, research, and telecommunications, and so on. In the unit, we will be approaching data mining from the point of

view of digital journalism, trying to understand its applications in this field and how it has brought many new developments in its wake.
10.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After going through this unit, you will be able to: * understand the process of data mining, and how it differs from other data-centric processes used today; * learn concepts and techniques related to data mining and their application in digital journalism; and * understand the issues, practical as well as ethical, pertaining to it, especially in its use in the media sector.
10.2 DATA EXTRACTION, DATA WAREHOUSING, AND DATA
MINING
We will begin by discussing three interconnected processes that lie at the heart of managing and analysing data - data extraction, data warehousing, and data mining. These terms can be a little confusing for a beginner. Therefore, before we get into the technological nitty-gritty of these processes, let us use a simple analogy to understand these processes. Imagine that you are tasked with building a library. The first step would be to collect books from different sources, including publishing houses, authors, educational institutions, and private collections. This process of building a collection would be data extraction. Once these books are collected, you will need to organise these books. During this process, you will need to ensure that the books are clean, labeled, catalogued and placed on the correct shelves to provide the users easy access. This would be comparable to data warehousing. Finally, once this is done and the library is open for use, users will search and analyse the books they need for specific information, and make connections between different books, drawing their conclusions and insights from them. This final process would be akin to data mining. Now, let us go through the three stages of data integration step by step.
10.2.1 Data Extraction
The first in this sequence is data extraction. This is where raw data is collected or retrieved from various original sources, such as databases, files, and external applications. The data at this stage is often disorganised and may not be ready for analysis. First, the sources of this data are identified, and then a connection is established with the data source to access this information. This data is then retrieved using queries and bots from database management systems and underlying HTML codes respectively.
10.2.2 Data Warehousing
The second process in this is data warehousing, a method of centralising data from different sources into one common repository. It is a blend of technologies that consolidate, store and manage data in the form of information, making it available to users for analysis at a later stage. The key processes involved in data warehousing are ETL, a three-phase computing process involving extraction (collection of data), transforming (cleaning and standardising of data into a common format) and loading (storing of data into output data containers called data warehouses). Data warehousing occurs before data mining.
10.2.3 Data Mining
Data mining is the process of analysing large amounts of data to find unknown patterns in them. It is used by organisations when they need to make sense of information made available to them; for instance, a company wants to know customers' response to a particular product. Data mining can help

them predict patterns and take future course of action based on that information. The goal of data mining is to find valuable information hidden within huge datasets, information that may otherwise not be immediately obvious. Its three key processes include: * Data preparation, or the cleaning and pre-processing of data. * Pattern discovery, or finding recurring tendencies within that data. * Model building, or designing statistical techniques that train algorithms to use smaller portions of a large dataset to find these patterns and tendencies.
10.3 DATA MINING: WORKFLOW IN JOUNRNALISM
Before we get into the different applications of data mining in journalism, let us understand the process and how it plays out in the newsroom.
10.3.1 Formulating the Question
Before embarking in pursuit of a story, a journalist must ask themselves what is the objective of their story, what is the central question they are posing. The ensuing processes, from seeking data to finally presenting it to their readers, are hinged upon this question. It is this question that determines the nature of the data that will be collected and analysed. For example, a reporter wants to study if there is a correlation between the deployment of face recognition technology and crime rates in a city. The question could be: Does the deployment of facial technology in a city's 'hotspots' help reduce crime rates? This central question will determine the subsequent processes, from choosing data sources and their analysis to narrativising the story and its visualisation.
10.3.2 Data Collection and Cleaning
Once the central question of the story has been formulated, a journalist will start gathering data from different sources. These could include structured and unstructured data from government databases, databases of international organisations, caches of private documents, and the like. Data can also be scraped from websites and saved in the form of spreadsheets and databases that are easily understandable. It is important to remember that at this stage, ethical considerations pertaining to obtaining data legally and avoiding harmful data are paramount. When relevant data has been collected, it is collated into a single, cohesive dataset. Now, it is time to clean the data, and prepare a smaller dataset for analysis. Raw data is often messy and unusable. This phase ensures that data is accurate and reliable. Problems such as missing values, duplication and irrelevant information are addressed at this stage. After this, data is set in standardised formats for further processing. For journalists, this step is also a form of due diligence to verify the information's integrity through verification and cross-referencing with other sources.
10.3.3 Analysis and Pattern Evaluation
This is the most important step in data mining, whether in the context of business or finance, healthcare, telecommunication, and so on, because it is at this stage that the collected data is analysed. In the case of journalism, it is here that recurring patterns are spotted, providing evidence for stories that might otherwise be missed. One first needs to select the appropriate tools and algorithms based on one's objectives and dataset. A mix of statistical, computational and journalistic methods is then used to find tendencies, oddities, and connections that can form the basis of a story. Some techniques of data mining will be discussed later in this unit. For now, returning once again to the example of the story about face recognition technology and crime rates, a reporter will most likely access data from National Crime Records Bureau, police departments, and the ministry of electronics and information technology. Data can also be sourced from human rights organisations, think tanks, and legal aid institutions that provide an alternative to the government's claims about falling crime rates. The correlations between these datasets will then

be analysed and their patterns evaluated to decode if the deployment of this technology has indeed led to a drop in crime rates. Data mining can provide that kind of data-driven evidence to the reporter.
10.3.4 Creating Narratives
Now it is time to present one's story. Armed with relevant data and insights that their analysis offers, the reporter translates these numbers into a coherent and accessible story. Data results and estimations are overlaid with storytelling from the ground; for instance, in our facial recognition technology- crime rate story, a reporter might speak to police officers, IT experts, lawyers and human rights activists, and also the family members of those arrested through the use of this technology, in order to craft a powerful narrative about how, while this new technology does increase public safety, it sometimes violates the rights of people in cases of mistaken identity. One can always provide links to sources and websites that contain raw data in order to foster transparency. Either way, the goal is always to "humanise the data."
10.3.5 Data Visualisation
A crucial part of this process of knowledge presentation is data visualisation. It is important to keep in mind that visualisation plays a role not only in the presentation of data in the final published news story, it is also a crucial step during the process of reporting itself. For instance, when used during reporting, visualisation helps identify themes and questions, outliers and even errors in data, sometimes showing glaring gaps in the process of reporting itself. Whereas when used to accompany the text, they illustrate important points in a more understandable way. This way, it allows the removal of dense technical information from the text, and offers the user a chance to interact with the data.
10.3.6 Distribution through Machine Learning
So far we have seen how data mining is central to the process of news making. Now we shall see shall how data mining plays a significant role in news and content distribution. In the digital era, news is personalised, real-time and prioritises user-engagement. In order to make this possible, the media industry uses machine learning algorithms that mine user data to recommend articles that might interest them. This data-driven approach personalises news content, and in this way, creates new distribution patterns for digital journalism. This also allows the audience to engage with the content and give feedback that can help to refine the original report. Check Your Progress: 1 Note: 1) Use the space provided below for your answers.

10.4 TECHNIQUES OF DATA MINING
So far, we have discussed data mining in relation to the data integration process, and its workflow in digital journalism. Now, we shall discuss its different techniques. These techniques are distinct

methods that help to find useful patterns from large amount of data. We will use each of these techniques to illuminate how they can be used by journalists for crafting their stories.
10.4.1 Classification Analysis
In this technique, data from large datasets is assigned to categories (or classes) by models. Models are simply mathematical functions that are trained to classify new data on already learned data patterns and rules. For example, our mobile phones have the feature to detect spam through the use of spam filters. Training models teach these filters to separate spam from regular calls and messages. In journalism, classification techniques of data mining can be applied in numerous ways, such as to categorise news content, analyse public sentiment on social media, identify trends, and even for source attribution. Let us look at a common use of classification technique in journalism today. * Election analysis is an important area where classification techniques are used to analyse voting data and predict election results. For this, models are trained using data on voter characteristics (such as demographics) and their voting patterns. The algorithm then assigns this data into predefined 'classes' such as a specific political party or the inclination voters based on voter characteristics. Based on this, the most likely voting patterns emerge, giving the reporter an insight into what happened in the election. Techniques like predictive modeling, data visualisation and even sentiment analysis can help to identify possible voting behaviours based on demographics and geographic information.
10.4.2 Cluster Analysis
Clustering is the division of data into groups of similar objects in order to reveal their patterns and structures. It is different from classification as classification uses predefined labels and is supervised, while clustering does the grouping based on similarities (not labels), and is unsupervised. This means, since clustering works on data that does not have pre-assigned labels, it allows the algorithm to find patterns on its own. Clustering aims for data simplification, providing concise summaries of the data. This is why it is a preferred technique in the newsroom. An example of this is as follows. * Analysis of public datasets such as legal records and crime statistics is often done using clustering to identify patterns and find hidden connections. For example, clustering analysis can be used to decipher a large dataset of unstructured police reports. With vital information such as time, location and nature of crime given, a reporter can use algorithms to make groups with similar incidents, such as carjacking at night in a certain area. This can in turn lead to an in- depth story on a car-theft gang operating in the city. The best technique for this would be K- means clustering, a simple method that partitions data into a pre-defined number of clusters, which could include time and day, nature of crime, description of suspects, and the like.
10.4.3 Association Rule Mining
This type of data mining seeks to uncover the relationships between data points. It is based on the principle that 'if Event A happens, then Event B will also likely occur.' As the name suggests, associate rule mining is used to determine whether a specific action or variable can be linked to other actions; for instance, when an e-commerce site recommends that customers bought these extra items along with the main one. Simply put, association rules mining identifies items that frequently appear together. Techniques such as K-means clustering, decision trees and Naive Bayes are often used here as well. Let us look at an example. * A data journalist can use association rule mining to find patterns between economic indicators. Working on a government dataset and market reports, they might discover that when fuel prices rise, food inflation also goes up, and so consumption decreases. Such a story can help predict changes in consumption behaviour in the future.
10.4.4 Anomaly Detection
In addition to searching for patterns, data mining seeks to uncover unusual data within a set. Anomaly detection helps in that by finding data that doesn't conform to the pattern. It identifies instances or

outliers that can help detect fraud, security breaches, and other such occurrences. The process begins by analysing a dataset to understand typical patterns. Once this 'norm' has been established, anomaly detection algorithms can pinpoint data that falls outside the normal range, which can help in determining risks or to correct the flawed data. Let us now discuss an example from contemporary journalism where anomaly detection played a crucial role in investigation. * In July 2020, journalist Ian Urbina did an expose in the American news network NBC News on Chinese industrial fishing vessels operating illegally in North Korean waters. By doing so, these vessels were violating UN sanctions, and also causing destruction of an ecologically sensitive marine environment. In his report, Urbina used data gathered by Global Fishing Watch (GFW), an NGO that enables lay users to monitor commercial fishing activity to reduce "global overfishing, illegal fishing and habitat destruction." For this report on the Chinese "invisible armada," anomaly detection technique was applied to GFW's data to flag suspicious vessels. They used satellite data and vessel tracking to detect "dark vessels," ships that intentionally turn off their transponders to hide their location and activities. The team also tried to identify suspicious patterns of vessel movement; for instance, they paid close attention to 'anomalies' such as ships loitering in protected areas, ship-to-ship cargo transfer rather than transfers at ports so that one can evade law enforcement, and sudden and unexpected change in a vessel's route. Advanced techniques using machine learning were trained to recognise ships in satellite images and analyse their activity to find these 'anomalies,' achieving a high degree of accuracy. Using these techniques, Urbina's report was able to highlight widespread illicit fishing activity. This news story is emblematic of how data mining, especially anomaly detection, can propel investigative reporting.
10.4.5 Regression Analysis
Regression analysis is a statistical way to estimate the interaction of variables, or to put it simply, how one factor interacts with the other. It is about understanding which factors within a dataset are most important, which can be ignored, and how these factors interact. The goal is to find the relationship between these variables to order to make predictions for the future. In journalism, a reliable and widely used technique for finding such connections and making predictions based on past data is linear regression. Let us discuss it using an example. * Let us say a sports reporter wants to do a story on key factors that influence a country's Olympic Games medal count. The reporter can use data from the past ten years and look at factors such as the country's population, economic strength, sports investment, athlete attributes and training. By comparing the interaction of these factors, the report can show that countries investing in sports training and athlete development tend to win more medals. These are some techniques that can help a journalist to use data mining techniques to analyse data in order to identify patterns, and sometimes even make predictions about the future. What one needs to do is to ask the right questions and find the right techniques.
10.5 ISSUES AND CONCERNS
As with every new technology, there are various aspects of data mining that raise concerns relating to its practical use, security issues, the use of data and the management of volume. Let us discuss some of these issues and concerns.
10.5.1 Misinterpretation of Data
Data misinterpretation can result from intentional or unintentional deciphering of data. Various factors can contribute to this, such as poor data quality, which will undoubtedly lead to incorrect conclusions; inadequate data literacy, which might result in poor analysis; data bias, which can result in prejudiced and/or skewed results; and visual misrepresentation, which too can easily mislead the viewer.
10.5.2 Scalability

A key challenge in data mining is the problem of scalability, which refers to the ability to increase performance even as the technology as well as the accuracy remains the same. Scalability issues tend to crop up whenever new data from multiple resources is integrated with data from older systems. The increased flow data requires numerous modifications and updates in technological systems to enable easy integration.
10.5.3 Safeguarding Data
Data security is a major issue in digital technologies and systems. In the context of data mining, organisations and individuals involved in this process must put in place a host of measures to guarantee the protection of sensitive information. They must ensure thorough network security to prevent breaches in these security systems. This is done through systems such as end-to-end encryption, firewalls, securing connections through VPNs, and continuous monitoring. Remember, these measures are intrinsically related to ethical considerations pertaining to data mining, especially those concerning accuracy and fairness, privacy and consent, and finally, security and accountability. 10.6 LET US SUM UP
In this unit, we discussed data mining, which is the process of analysing large amounts of data to find unknown patterns in them. We explained how it different from two other related processes, data extraction and data warehousing, which are, respectively, the processes of acquiring data, and then storing that data. Together, these processes are important in gathering, storing and categorising large amounts of data from digital sources, and then identifying patterns and analysing them to make sense of this data. The focus of this unit is the application of data mining in journalism, and so, we elaborate upon the workflow of data mining in journalism, which begins with the formulation of the right question. Subsequently come processes like data collection, data cleaning, analysis of data and identification of patterns, creative narratives for news stories, data visualisation, and the distribution of these stories through machine learning. In the next section, we elaborated upon some techniques of data mining such as classification analysis, cluster analysis, association rule mining, anomaly detection analysis and finally regression analysis. All these are explained using examples of how they can be applied to journalism. We wind up the unit with some key issues and concerns pertaining to data mining today, including misinterpretation of data, problems pertaining to scalability, and data security.
10.7 KEYWORDS
Data Mining: The process of analysing large amounts of data to find unknown patterns in them.

Data Extraction: The process wherein raw data is collected or retrieved from various original sources, such as databases, files, and external applications. Data Warehousing: It is the process of centralising data from different sources into one common repository, making it available to users for analysis at a later stage. Machine Learning: A branch of artificial intelligence (AI) where systems learn from data, rather than from programmes. Classification Analysis: This is a process of data analysis where data is categorised into 'classes' by learning from already labelled datasets. Clustering Analysis: This involves the division of data into groups of similar objects in order to reveal patterns and structures. Association Rule Analysis: This is used for discovering hidden relationships between different items or data points within a dataset. Regression Analysis: It is statistical technique used to estimate the interaction of dependent variables with one or more separate variables.

10.0 INTRODUCTION
In recent years, climate change as a science has received unprecedented attention from both scientific institutions and academia. Climate change as an environmental problem is impacting every aspect of life including international economy, public health, migration, livelihood, international peace and security. Millions of the world's poorest people are already being forced to cope with impacts of climate change. But increased exposure to drought, to more intense storms, to floods and environmental stress is holding back the efforts of the vulnerable population particularly the poor to build a better life for. The present unit will focus on the historical origin of the climate change debates; Rio declaration on Environment and Development; significance of UNFCCC and IPCC; Kyoto Protocol and Paris Agreement on Climate Change.
10.1 OBJECTIVES
* After studying this unit, you should be able to: * discuss the history of climate change debate; * discuss the Rio declaration on Environment and Development; * explain the significance of UNFCCC and IPCC; and * discuss the Kyoto Protocol and Paris Agreement on Climate Change.
10.2 HISTORY OF CLIMATE CHANGE DEBATE
The development of the climate regime can be traced from the environmental activities of the 1980s and 1990s. Climate change as an environmental fact began in 1987 with the release of the Brundtland Commission report, Our Common Future. The report comprehensively focused on the issues of environmental pollution with regard to depletion of ozone layer, loss of biological diversity and the rising greenhouse gas concentration and argued for achieving sustainability by formulating effective

socio-economic policies. Bodansky has divided the development of the global climate change regime into five phases prior to the Kyoto protocol. The five periods are as follows; * The foundational period expresses scientific concern about global warming. * The agenda-setting phase (1985-88) intended to transform the scientific concern into policy matter. * Pre-negotiation period (1988-1990) involved government in the process of climate change regime * The formal intergovernmental negotiation (1992) impressed upon the adoption of FCCC by May, 1992 * The post-agreement phase focused on the elaboration and implementation of FCCC and the adoption of Kyoto commitments.
10.3 UNFCCC
The UN Framework Convention on Climate Change was adopted at the Earth summit at Rio de Janeiro in 1992. It is a treaty signed by 192 countries. It does not set any binding targets on countries for cutting emissions. It only calls for stabilizing carbon emissions. But it set in motion international negotiations for settling the issue of who will cut and how much. The parties to the convention have met annually from 1995 onwards in conference of parties (COP). The Conference of the Parties is the governing body of the Convention, and advances implementation of the Convention through the decisions it takes at its periodic meetings. Table 10.1 COP Meetings

COP 2 Geneva, Switzerland Geneva Climate Change Conference-1996
COP 3 Kyoto, Japan Kyoto Climate Change Conference - December 1997 COP 4 Buenos Aires, Argentina Buenos Aires Climate Change Conference - November 1998 COP 5 Bonn, Germany Bonn Climate Change Conference - October 1999 COP 6 The Hague, Netherlands The Hague Climate Change Conference - November 2000 COP 6 2 Bonn, Germany Bonn Climate Change Conference - July 2001 COP 7 Marrakech, Morocco Marrakech Climate Change Conference - October 2001 COP 8 New Delhi, India New Delhi Climate Change Conference - October 2002 COP 9 Milan, Italy Milan Climate Change Conference - December 2003 COP 10 Buenos Aires, Argentina Buenos Aires Climate Change Conference - December 2004 COP 11 Montreal, Canada Montreal Climate Change Conference - December 2005 COP 12 Nairobi, Kenya Nairobi Climate Change Conference - November 2006 COP 13 Bali, Indonesia Bali Climate Change Conference - December 2007 COP 14 Poznan, Poland Poznan Climate Change Conference - December 2008 COP 15 Copenhagen, Denmark Copenhagen Climate Change Conference - December 2009 COP 16 Cancun, Mexico Cancun Climate Change Conference - November 2010

10.4 IPCC
The IPCC was set up jointly by the United Nations' and the World Meteorological organizations and convened its first meeting in the year 1998 to discuss the scientific uncertainties over climate change. The IPCC has described the climate uncertainties in relation to magnitude, timing, and regional political interest among countries over the world to participate in the development of models to address the challenges of global climate change. The IPCC has produced comprehensive assessment reports in 1990, 1995, 2001, 2007, 2014, and a 1.5oC special report in 2018. In the preparation of these reports, much debated and contested fact was the climate change of the twenty-first century. In particular, many of the scientists felt that the climate uncertainties are such that it is refraining scientists from making any prediction and estimate for future climate variability (Ibid.). IPCC being an inter-governmental body assured the involvement of government representatives, scientists and policy makers in the process. The acceptance and realization of the problem of global warming at the global platform has led to the formulation of the international Framework Convention on Climate Change (FCCC), which was signed by over 160 countries. After the Earth Summit in 1992, the arguments concerning the scientific importance of IPCC were intensified in the world's press. The Climate Convention signed at the Rio conference acknowledged the importance of the balanced relationship between humans with their environment. The Convention emphasized to maintain the harmonious relationship between human society and their environment towards stabilizing the greenhouse gas concentration in the environment. Further, it set the objective for concrete action to reduce and stabilize climate change. The signatories to the Convention consensually agreed upon the initiation of mitigation actions to combat the impacts of climate change. Box 10.1: The Climate Convention The convention concerned that human activities have substantially increased the concentration of greenhouse gasses in the atmosphere. * Convention noted that the largest share of global greenhouse gasses emission originates in developed countries as compared to developing countries. * The convention recognizes that various mitigation actions can be justified economically and can further help in solving other environmental problems. * The convention specified areas/countries such as low-lying countries, countries with low-lying coastal areas, and semiarid areas or areas liable to flood are vulnerable to climate variability. * Convention affirmed that action responding to climate change needs to be coordinated with socio- economic development in an integrated pattern. * The Convention is determined to protect the climate system for both present and future generations.

The primary objectives of the Climate Convention those were contained in the Article 2 are as follows: * To prevent any anthropogenic interference with the climate system, there is a need to stabilize the concentration of greenhouse gasses in the atmosphere. * The stabilization of the concentration of greenhouse gasses needs to be achieved within a specific timeframe while ensuring effective food production and economic development in a sustainable way.
10.5 KYOTO PROTOCOL
In the UNFCCC process a treaty was adopted on December 11, 1997 at the Kyoto (Japan COP). The Kyoto protocol as it is known, came into force in February 2005. The most notable exception is the US. Under the protocol, 39 industrialized countries, Annexure I countries, committed themselves to reducing the emissions by 5.2 per Cent of the 1990 levels by 2012. The protocol set up mechanisms for carbon trading. Under this, a country can finance carbon dioxide saving measures in another country and thus offset its own emissions. Similarly a country can buy carbon credits from another that has accumulated them by reducing emissions or through other measures (like forestation). The protocol also set up a fund for helping developing countries adapt to the changing climate. The UN climate change secretariat based in Bonn, Germany is an international transaction log to verify that the transactions are consistent with the rules of protocol. Reporting is done by parties by way of submitting annual emissions inventory and national reports under protocol at regular intervals. A complaint system ensures that parties are meeting their commitments and it helps them to meet their commitments if they need help or if they are in trouble. The Kyoto protocol also assists countries in adapting to the adverse effects of climate change. It facilitates the development and deployment of techniques that can help increase resilience to the impacts of climate change. The adaptation fund was established to finance adaptation projects and programmes in developing countries that are parties to the Kyoto protocol. The fund is financed mainly with the share of proceeds from Clean Development Mechanism project activities. The Kyoto protocol applies to industrial nations only. Developing countries like India and China were not required to commit to reductions because their per capita GHG emissions are much lower than those of developed nations. Poorer economies of developing countries are unable to absorb the cost of switching from the fossil fuel based system to cleaner fuel system. Once the cleaner technologies are developed, the poorer countries will be actively involved in reduction in carbon emission and climate change agreement. The Kyoto Protocol was formulated on the basic principle of CBDR and specified that industrialized countries will have to take lead in the process of reduction of greenhouse gas emission. The basic structure of the Protocol and Commitments were agreed at a meeting of the Conference of the Parties in Kyoto in the year 1997 (Ibid). The Protocol embodies substantive obligations in relation to climate change for both developing and developed countries. For instance, in the first commitment period from 2008-12, the industrialized countries committed to specific quantitative reductions in emissions. The Protocol involved inbuilt mechanisms to facilitate concrete action plan for combating climate change and the action plan aimed towards including the developing countries under the general obligations of the Climate Convention. The Kyoto Protocol involves specific principles and mechanisms to reduce the greenhouse gas emission; however, it does contain any obligations for developing countries with regard to reduction of emission. Therefore, the protocol had led to intense controversy on the issue of equity over climate change. In this context, most of the debates had happened with regard to the principle of general obligations of all the states to cooperate and protect the environment. As Atapattu writes, it is important to recall the wordings of the Rio Declaration, i.e., the common obligation of the states to protect the environment. This emphasizes on the two dimensions of the climate change debate such as: global partnership in preserving the environment; and the obligation is common to both developing and developed states with regard to protecting the environment. The Kyoto Protocol becomes problematic as it does not contain any differentiated responsibilities for developing

countries - on the contrary, it contains no obligations for developing countries for the commitment period (ibid: 8). On the contrary, it was argued that since the Kyoto protocol applies for the commitment period; therefore, no specific obligations were formulated for the developing countries on the basis of their minimal contributions to greenhouse emission. The exclusion of developing countries from the global climate change regime has reflected the notion of differential principles for developing vis-a-vis developed countries. Further, it was argued that there may be a need to impose differential policies within the developing countries with regard to climate change policies. In this reference, alternative apprehensions emerged-- many climate change protagonists assumed that in the second commitment period, developing countries may be imposed with emission reduction obligations similar to developed countries. Though, both the climate change regime and ozone regime applied the CBDR principles, the two regimes treated the principle of differential responsibility in different ways. Similarly, developing nations have shown their commitments towards the global climate change regime differently. The Kyoto protocol is generally seen as an important first step towards the truly global emission reduction regime that will stabilize greenhouse gasses (GHG) emissions and provide essential architecture for any future international agreement on climate change. By the end of the first commitment period of the Kyoto protocol in 2012 a new international framework has to be negotiated and ratified that can deliver the stringent emission reductions as indicated by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC). Based on this commitment the protocol has evolved five key principles as follows:
1. Commitments
2. Implementation
3. Minimizing impacts
4. Accounting, reporting
5. Compliance

10.6 PARIS AGREEMENT ON CLIMATE CHANGE
At the Durban Conference (COP 17) an "Ad-Hoc Working Group on the Durban Platform for Enhanced Action" was established "to develop a protocol, another legal instrument or an agreed outcome with legal force under the Convention applicable to all Parties", by COP 21 so that it can be adopted no later than 2015. Indeed the Paris Agreement is the outcome of a four-year negotiating process and multilateral diplomacy. Article 2 of the Paris Agreement, states that "in enhancing the implementation of the Convention, including its objective, the agreement aims to strengthen the global response to the threat of climate change, in the context of sustainable development and efforts

to eradicate poverty, including by: (a) Holding the increase in the global average temperature to well below 2degC above pre- industrial levels and pursuing efforts to limit the temperature increase to 1.5degC above pre-industrial levels, recognizing that this would significantly reduce the risks and impacts of climate change; (b) Increasing the ability to adapt to the adverse impacts of climate change and foster climate resilience and low greenhouse gas emissions development, in a manner that does not threaten food production; and (c) Making finance flows consistent with a pathway towards low greenhouse gas emissions and climate-resilient development". Paris Agreement entered into force on 4th November, 2016. The main features of the agreement are universal application; the principle of equity and principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities; and "legally binding agreement that will apply to those states that have expressed their consent to be bound by means of ratification, acceptance, approval, or accession". With respect to our country, the agreement demands India to submit "national contributions" every five years; and to embark on a low carbon development pathway.
10.7 INDIA'S RESPONSE FRAMEWORK
Within the developing nations, India's around 700 million rural population is dependent on the climate sensitive sectors such as agriculture, forest, fisheries, water, biodiversity and coastal zones. Further, the rural population is more vulnerable to climate variability as they have low adaptive capacity in relation to extreme and fluctuating weather conditions. The National Commission Report found out that the impact of climate change can be felt in sectors of the natural ecosystem and the socio-economic system. The IPCC assessment report reveals the following: * Increase in rainfall over the Indian sub-continent by 6-8 per cent. * Extreme rise of maximum and minimum temperature is expected in the West Coast of India and West Central India. * Heat spells have become common in Northern India. * There were around 15 major droughts in the past 50 years, which affected the productivity of rain fed crops in drought years. * Food security is under threat due to occurrence of drought and flood, and variability in the climate. The adverse impact of climate change has already threatened the existing livelihood in India, for which India has undertaken various sectoral mitigation measures to contribute towards the objectives of United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). India's development plan is based on the primary principle of sustainability along with inclusive economic growth. There have been initiatives taken in sectors like coal and oil, renewable energy, hydropower, social energy, energy efficiency and conservation, transport, agriculture, power sector, and so on. The current government expenditure on adaptation has exceeded two percent of GDP. The broad areas where the adaptation measures have been carried out include: * Crop Improvement * Drought Proofing * Health * Risk financing * Disaster management * Livelihood Preservation
10.7.1 National Action Plan on Climate Change
India's first Action Plan on Climate Change was prepared in the year 2008 by focusing on the adaptation and mitigation policies and programmes. The plan identifies eight core national missions

to be implemented as part of adaptive strategies of climate change in areas of sustainable agriculture, water, Himalayan Ecosystem, enhanced energy efficiency, and accumulation of strategic knowledge on climate change. The plan identifies measures for economic growth, increasing living standards while yielding co-benefits for addressing climate change effectively. Under the economic liberalization policy, the private sectors both domestic and foreign investors, are playing a key role in developing alternative efficient technologies to deal with climate change. For example, due to import liberalization, joint ventures are possible in providing a wide range of consumer goods like energy efficient cars and refrigerators in the market. Consumers are showing preference in the buyers' market and exercising their choice for energy efficiency products. The energy sectors are switching in the direction of using alternative fuel. For example, the power sector is permitted to use natural gas and the coal-based energy plants have become dysfunctional. In the present scenario, India is actively and decisively participating in the climate change negotiation debates. India's position is not difficult to comprehend, however certain questions have emerged in the discourse of climate change negotiation. Questions include what concentration level is accepted by the developing countries, how the commitments towards emission reduction will be available to developing countries, how do you ensure that India will have fair share in the global environmental places. 10.8 LET US SUM UP
Climate change is the biggest threat in the 21st century. The international scientific community urged the world to stabilize the level of emissions in the atmosphere in order to avoid future potential impact. In doing so, the world countries have proposed several international summits to discuss climate change and to find solutions to the problems of climate change.Through this unit, we discussed climate change as a global - political issue in the context of human's contribution to climate change and the possibility of framing the action plan for combating the climate change events. 10.9 KEYWORDS
Clean Development Mechanism : The CDM allows emission reduction(or emission removal) projects in developing countries to earn Certified Emission Reduction (CER) credits, each equivalent to one tonne of carbon dioxide. CERs can be traded and sold, and used by industrial countries to meet a path of their emission reduction targets under Kyoto protocol. (Source: http://cdm.unfccc.int)

South-South Cooperation : South-south cooperation is a new UNEP initiative that is being promoted as an essential cross cutting mechanism designed to enhance UNEPs ability to deliver capacity building and technology support activities in the field of environment in developing countries and regions of the south. The implementation of the south-south cooperation initiatives is being carried out in the context of the Bali Strategic Plan (BSP) for technology support and capacity building. The BSP serves as an umbrella framework for coherent, coordinated and effective delivery of environmental capacity building and technical support activities in response to well defined countries priorities and need source:www.unep.org/souths outhcoperation). Bonn Agreement : It is an informal term of political deal reached at COP-6 in Bonn, Germany in 2001 by which governments agreed on the most politically controversial issues under the Buenos Aires Plan of Action. Human Security : Human security is an emerging paradigm for understanding global vulnerabilities whose proponents challenge the traditional notion of national security by arguing that the proper referent for security should be the individual rather than the state. Human security holds that a people- centered view of security is necessary for national, regional and global stability.

11.0 INTRODUCTION
This unit focuses on the history and evolution of Public Relations, highlighting the importance of corporate houses and governments communicating with their target publics through formal or informal means. Communication can include products, services, ideas, policies, and social welfare programs. Different channels of communication are used for different publics, considering their reach and accessibility. Digital media, particularly social media platforms, has become popular among governments and corporations. The unit covers tools and techniques for reaching different publics.
11.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After this unit, you will be able to: * Understand Public Relations tools. * Identify appropriate tools for different audiences * Analyse internal and external communications * Recognize the importance of PR tools
11.2 TARGET AUDIENCE
You already know how important public relations is in today's social, political, business, and economic arenas., with objectives like gaining attention, fostering mutual understanding, creating goodwill, and winning over publics. PR practitioners communicate tailored messages to different audiences. For example, a politician may organize rallies or use the media to reach voters, while an NGO might use publicity or events to raise funds. Target publics are directly or indirectly influencing a corporate entity, celebrity, or political party. Effective communication with these publics is crucial. PR tools, such as news stories or films, are used to reach both internal and external publics.
11.3 INTERNAL PUBLICS
For any organisation, internal publics are the people working within the organisation, such as employees, suppliers, and shareholders, who are crucial to its growth. In an educational institute, students and teachers are considered internal publics. Success depends on maintaining good relationships with these groups, and effective communication is key. To engage internal publics, the following tools are used:
11.3.1 House Journal
It's possible that you contributed to the school magazine during your time there, which featured articles on news, artistic creations, and the accomplishments of both teachers and students. Teachers and students were the internal publics that these journals were intended for.. Similarly, corporate houses use house journals to communicate with their internal publics, and sometimes these journals are also shared with external audiences. The primary goal of a house journal is to provide a platform for sharing thoughts and experiences, acting as a bridge between the internal publics and management. As companies expand globally, house journals help connect employees across different countries. The content, format, and design of these journals are based on the organisation's philosophy, needs, and budget. Typically, the PR department or Public Relations manager serves as the editor, but the editorial policy is set by corporate management. Conservative organisations might use the journal for one- way communication, while more liberal ones promote two-way communication. Distribution has also evolved. Whereas school magazines were handed out by teachers, house journals were traditionally printed and distributed by hand or post. However, due to the expense and time involved, many organisations now prefer e-house journals, which can be distributed instantly and cost-effectively to a large audience.

11.3.2 Bulletin Boards
Bulletin boards are increasingly used as a communication tool in organisations, especially in common areas like food courts, cafeterias, and receptions. These boards can be rectangular, square, simple, or fancy in design. They can convey important messages from management, such as changes in policies, celebrations, events, or human resource schemes. Bulletin boards also serve as a platform for employees to share their viewpoints and information, potentially leading to better relations between employee-employee and employer-employee. The number of bulletin boards can vary, with some organisations having separate boards for human resources, corporate communication, finance, and sales departments. They can also be theme-based to give them a fresh look and be decorated with corporate colours. E-bulletin boards are also becoming more popular, as they can be kept in 'read it later' settings for busy work schedules.
11.3.3 Newsletter
A newsletter is a communication tool used by organisations to convey news, activities, and messages to employees. It can be printed or e-mailed, and the content is tailored to the organisation's policies. It can also be sent to external publics if the content aligns with their interests. The design of the newsletter is influenced by the organisation's corporate identity and can be arranged in various ways.
11.3.4 Email
Postmen are being replaced by electronic mail due to the internet and inexpensive technology. Email is an instant communication tool, allowing messages to be sent to multiple people with a single click and immediate feedback. Its main advantage is the permanence of the record, allowing for reference and tracking. The easy accessibility of the internet and reduced costs have made email user-friendly, making it popular for communication with both external and internal publics.
11.3.5 Face-to-Face Communication
Interpersonal and group communication are effective for instant feedback, and Public Relations practitioners should ensure face-to-face management communication with employees, such as meetings and discussions, to boost employee morale.
11.3.6 Shop Floor Discussions
Management can use shop floor discussions with employees to provide fair feedback on important issues. These discussions are an effective tool for interpersonal communication and can be held frequently or infrequently. They allow staff to express opinions on daily issues, gain insights from those with whom regular meetings aren't possible, and boost employee morale through face-to-face communication.
11.3.7 Minutes of Meetings
Corporate and government departments hold meetings to make changes, formulate policies, launch products/services, and organise events. The decisions made are recorded in Minutes of Meetings (MOM), which are crucial for the smooth functioning of the organisation. Previous minutes are used to track decision-making progress.
11.3.8 Closed circuit TV
Digital technologies are crucial for modern organisations, especially as companies expand globally. Management struggles to maintain communication without wasting time in one location. Closed- circuit TVs are effective and inexpensive for virtual meetings and publicising organisational philosophy through corporate films. They can also be installed in reception lounges to promote the organisation's philosophy.
11.3.9 Celebrating Festivals
In India, diversity is a significant part of culture, and metropolitan cities are becoming symbols of modern mini-India. Companies are now recognizing the benefits of celebrating festivals together

with their employees, including religious and national festivals, as a goodwill gesture. This cosmopolitan scenario fosters a sense of belonging among employees.
11.3.10 Speech
The CEO or Managing Director can establish themselves as an industry leader by delivering a well- written speech, which can be published in newspapers, magazines, or radio. Prominent figures with impressive oratory skills, such as Pt. Jawahar Lal Nehru, Indira Gandhi, Narender Modi, and Mahatma Gandhi, are often sought after by staff members. Activity - 1 Take a listen to any well-known leader's speech. Jot down the salient features and the reasons that appeal to you.
11.3.11 Visit by Management
Informal visits by management to employees' workstations are crucial for interpersonal communication and employee morale. These interactions allow top officials to understand employees better, share problems, ideas, and suggestions without filtering, and promote bottom-up communication within the organisation.
11.3.12 Fun Days
Dale Carnegie's quote, "People rarely succeed unless they have fun in what they're doing," is relevant in today's stressful life. Corporate houses plan annual fun days for employees, enhancing work performance and making life light and strong. Check Your Progress: 1 Note: Use the space below for your answers.
1. List the resources available to the internal public and provide arguments in support of your
response.

2. What makes annual reports a valuable instrument for influencing the financial public?

11.4 EXTERNAL PUBLICS
Government policies like demonetization, GST, and mutual fund taxes have impacted businesses in India. Pesticides in soft drinks and chemicals in noodles have affected sales and availability. External public, including customers, government, mass media, pressure groups, financial institutions, and regulatory bodies, are crucial for organisations. Corporate houses use tools and techniques to effectively communicate with these publics.
11.4.1 Press Release
A press release is a concise written communication with a headline for media houses, including audio, video, or media releases. IIt addresses 5Ws and 1H with detailed information on the organisation and is written in the style of an inverted pyramid. Writing a Press Release: Press releases are a crucial tool in media relations, but their misuse can lead to the loss of important information. Therefore, a PR practitioner must be proficient in writing a press release to secure a favourable media space.

Elements of a Press Release
News organisations need to adhere to a particular structure in order to receive coverage from press releases. Knowing the format makes it easier for journalists to publish it in the manner you would like. A press release typically has four to five paragraphs and a word count of between 500 and 800. The components of a strong press release structure are as follows: * Headline: The attention of journalists should be drawn in with a compelling headline. Journalists will not read a headline if it is uninteresting. * Dateline: The information you wish to communicate with the media should include the date of release and, most of the time, the city of origin. If you would like your news not to be published right away, you can indicate the date you would like it to be published. That would convey to the media that the sender is asking for a press embargo. * Introduction: Similar to a news article, the press release's first paragraph should address the who, what, when, where, why, and how of the information. * Body: The next paragraphs should include further information on the incident, an explanation of the problem, pertinent data, and background information on the subject. * Boiler-plate: It is a crucial component of the release, which usually consists of a brief "about" section with impartial background information about the issuing business, entity, or person. * Closing: To let the media know that the release has concluded, news agencies have typically used the sign "-30-" to appear after the body or boilerplate and before the media contact information. However, the "###" mark now denotes the release's end. You can use any of these. * Contact Information: Following the release, the PRO's name and contact information (phone, email, postal address, etc.) should be included. News organisations may be able to get in touch with the appropriate individual if they need further information on any particular fact. * Sample - Press Release

National Green Energy Initiative Launches New Solar Energy Program to Empower
Rural Communities
BANGALORE, 15 March 2024 - In a significant step towards promoting sustainable energy solutions, the National Green Energy Initiative (NGEI) in collaboration with the Renewable Energy Development Agency (REDA) has announced the launch of a new solar energy program aimed at empowering rural communities across India. The program, which will kick off on 20 March 2024, is designed to provide solar power solutions to underserved areas, fostering energy independence and environmental sustainability. Under the new program, rural regions across India will receive solar panels and related infrastructure to support clean and renewable energy generation. The initiative seeks to address energy access challenges and contribute to the reduction of carbon emissions, aligning with the Government of India's commitment to combating climate change and promoting green energy solutions. The launch event, to be held at the Bangalore International Convention Centre, will feature a series of discussions and presentations by leading experts in renewable energy and sustainable development. The event will also include hands-on demonstrations of solar technology and presentations by beneficiaries who have successfully implemented solar solutions in their communities. The program will involve the distribution of solar kits to over 150 villages, providing a substantial boost to local energy resources and promoting sustainable living practices. Dr. Aarti Sharma, Director of the National Green Energy Initiative, emphasised the program's impact: "This initiative is a major milestone in our effort to enhance energy access and support rural development. By integrating solar technology into these communities, we aim to create a sustainable model that not only addresses energy needs but also encourages environmental stewardship." Following the launch event, selected rural areas will begin receiving solar kits and training on installation and maintenance. The initiative includes a comprehensive support system with technical assistance and regular follow-up to ensure the effective implementation of solar projects. The National Green Energy Initiative, supported by the Renewable Energy Development Agency and various philanthropic partners, is committed to advancing India's green energy goals and fostering equitable development through sustainable solutions.
