12.0 INTRODUCTION
Let's be honest: for many of us journalists, who live and breathe words, a spreadsheet full of numbers can feel like a foreign language. We are drawn to the human story, the powerful quote, the narrative that makes people feel something. But in the 21st century, claiming to be a journalist who "doesn't do numbers" is a dangerous blind spot. Our world runs on data. Budgets, public health, the economy, and elections are all stories told primarily through numbers. If you ignore them, you are missing the story. A report that skips over data is incomplete at best and misleading at worst. The goal here is not to turn you into a statistician overnight. It is to make you a confident, critical interpreter of the numbers that shape our reality. When a politician announces a multi-crore project, they are using data to frame a narrative. A journalist who can't question that data, ask where it came from, or place it in context, risks becoming little more than a stenographer, a passive mouthpiece for those in power. Our job is to ensure accountability, and we cannot hold power accountable if we do not speak its language. This unit will give you the toolkit to ask the right questions, and spot when the numbers don't add up. In an age of

"alternative facts," this isn't just a skill; it is a defense of truth itself.
12.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After working through this unit, you should be able to: make a compelling case for why journalists cannot afford to be "bad at maths"; spot common statistical traps, like confusing correlation with causation, before they end up in your story; give context to any number you see by using rates, percentages, and historical data for comparison; and follow a clear, systematic process for finding, checking, and reporting on numbers accurately and responsibly.
12.2 WHY NUMBERS MATTER IN JOURNALISM
In a media world saturated with opinions, data-driven reporting offers a powerful anchor to reality. But before we get into the "how" of understanding numbers, let us look at some of the reasons "why" they are important.
12.2.1 The Credibility of Concrete Data
Numbers give your reporting a backbone of authority. Read the two statements given below and think about which one carries more weight:
1. "The government plans to spend more on education."
2. "The government increased the education budget by 12% this fiscal year, allocating an additional
Rs50,000 crore specifically for primary school infrastructure." The first statement is forgettable. The second is concrete, verifiable, and packed with information. It tells the reader you have done your homework as a journalist. That precision builds trust, grounding your story in objective facts that are hard to dispute.
12.2.2 Moving Beyond Anecdotes
Anecdotes are the heart of storytelling. For example, the account of a single farmer drowning in debt is powerful and necessary. But it also begs the question: Is this farmer's experience an isolated tragedy or part of a widespread crisis? Data answers that question. The Anecdote: A farmer in Vidarbha took his own life after his crops failed and he could not repay his loans. The Data: Government data reveals that farmer suicides in the Vidarbha region have climbed by 40% over the last two years, with official records attributing 60% of those cases to bankruptcy and debt. The data provides scale and context, proving that the individual story is not an outlier but an example of a larger trend. The best journalism fuses the two: it finds the human story to illustrate the trend that the data has revealed. Data acts as a check against our own bias. As journalists, we might find one or two anecdotes that seem to point to a new trend. But if the data for the entire population does not support it, our "trend" might just be a coincidence. Data keeps us honest.
12.2.3 The Dangers of Innumeracy
Innumeracy, i.e., not being able to understand and work with numbers, is the journalistic equivalent of illiteracy. It makes you vulnerable. A reporter who is uncomfortable with numbers can be easily "played"

by sources who know how to spin statistics to their advantage. A simple mistake, like a misplaced decimal point, can change a story's entire meaning and destroy your credibility. Imagine reporting on a medical study where a new drug reduces risk of a disease from 0.02% to 0.01%. A source might tell you it "cuts the risk in half," which is technically true (a 50% relative drop). However, the absolute change is very little (one-hundredth of one percent). An innumerate reporter might not understand this and run a sensational headline like "New Drug Slashes Disease Risk by 50%," misinforming the public. Even a simpler error or typo, like reporting a 0.5% increase as a 5% increase, can wrongly suggest a massive shift and cause unnecessary panic or flawed policy debates. These are not just typos; they are fundamental errors of fact.
12.2.4 The Quality of Data Matters
Never assume data is objective truth. The old saying "garbage in, garbage out" is the first rule of data journalism. Before you use any dataset, you have to interrogate it like you would any human source. Always ask yourself these questions: Who is behind the data? A neutral government agency (like the National Statistical Office), a university, or a corporate-funded think tank? What is their agenda or bias? How did they get these numbers? What was the methodology? If it is a survey, was the sample size big enough? Was it representative or did they only poll one demographic (like urban residents, or people with internet access)? What questions were asked? For a survey, the wording of a question can dramatically change the answer. "Do you support a plan to improve public safety?" will get more "yes" votes than "Do you support a tax increase to hire more police?" How old is this data? Using a five-year-old report to describe the "current" economy is journalistic malpractice. What is not included? If you are looking at crime data, does it include crimes that are often unreported? If you are looking at employment data, does it count informal workers? What is missing from the dataset can be a bigger story than what is included in it. Is there better data out there? Don't just settle for the summary in a press release. Hunt down the complete original report.
12.3 PUTTING NUMBERS IN CONTEXT: A JOURNALIST'S
GUIDE
A number floating in a void is meaningless. As a journalist, your job is to give that number context. Here are five fundamental ways to do that for every statistic you encounter.
12.3.1 Questioning the Frame: Absolute versus Relative Change
This is one of the most common ways numbers are used to mislead. A press release will almost always favour the more dramatic-sounding figure. Consider the example below, in the light of the following terms: Absolute Change: The straightforward, raw difference between two numbers. Relative Change (Percentage): The size of that change in relation to the starting point. Example: A company might boast a "100% increase in profit," which sounds amazing. But if their profit went from Rs1 lakh to Rs2 lakh, the absolute change is quite small. On the flip side, a "Rs10 crore" budget cut sounds huge, but if the original budget was Rs1,000 crore, it is only a 1% relative decrease.

A journalist should always ask for both. Reporting both is the only way to give your audience a complete and unbiased picture of what is really going on.
12.3.2 Finding the 'Typical': Questioning Averages
When a source gives you an "average," your first question should be, "Which one?" You must be familiar with following three measures for finding averages or a middle: Mean: This is the one we usually think of, adding everything up and dividing. This method is simple but the mean is easily distorted by extreme outliers. Median: It is the true middle value if you line up all the numbers in order. The median is not so affected by outliers. Mode: This is simply the value that shows up most often. Imagine reporting on the "average" income in a village, with nine people earning Rs. 50,000 a year, and one billionaire. The mean income would be in crores, but it would be a useless, misleading number, since barring the billionaire, everyone's income is modest. However, in this case, the median income, or even the mode income, would be Rs. 50,000, a far more honest reflection of a typical person's earnings. For data on income, housing prices, or anything with a wide range, the median is almost always a more reliable measure of the "typical" experience than the mean.
12.3.3 Making Fair Comparisons: The Power of Rates
Comparing raw numbers between groups of different sizes is a classic mistake. Announcing that "City A had 500 murders last year, while City B only had 200" makes City A sound far more dangerous. But what if City A has 5 million residents and City B has only 500,000? You need a rate to make a fair comparison. Rate Calculation: (Number of Events / Total Population) x a standard unit (like 100,000). * Example: City A's murder rate is (500 / 5,000,000) x 100,000 = 10 per 100,000 people. City B's murder rate is (200 / 500,000) x 100,000 = 40 per 100,000 people. Here, the real story is that City B is, per capita, four times more dangerous. This applies everywhere. "School A has 50 students who passed the exam" vs. "School B has 100." It is meaningless without knowing if School A has 60 students and School B has 200. We need the pass rate (83% versus 50%) to see that School A is performing better. You should never compare raw counts across different locations or populations. Always calculate a rate (per 1,000, per 100,000, etc.) to create a true apples-to-apples comparison.
12.3.4 Probing the Relationship: Correlation is Not Causation
Memorise this rule; it is the most important one in data interpretation. Just because two things trend together (correlation), does not mean one caused the other (causation). The classic example: ice cream sales are strongly correlated with drowning deaths. Does ice cream cause drowning? No. A hidden factor, or lurking variable, is hot weather that causes both. More people buy ice cream and more people go swimming when it is hot. Here is another example: Studies might find that people who drink one glass of red wine a day live longer. Does the wine cause longevity? Or is it that people who drink moderately tend to be wealthier, have better diets, less stressful jobs, and better access to healthcare? The wine is not the cause; it is a marker for a different lifestyle. You should be deeply skeptical of any claim that X caused Y. Use cautious, precise language. "The data shows a link between X and Y" or "X is associated with Y." Proving causation is extremely difficult and

rare.
12.3.5 Understanding Uncertainty: What Margin of Error Really Means
No poll that samples a small group can be perfectly accurate for the whole population. The margin of error (MoE) is a poll's built-in acknowledgement of that uncertainty. It is a plus-or-minus range that the real number is likely to fall into. This uncertainty is due to sampling, which is only indicative of the larger population. By interviewing 1,000 people, we are making an educated guess about what 100 million people think. If a poll says Candidate A has 48% support and Candidate B has 45%, with a margin of error of +-3 points, you cannot say Candidate A is winning. It is a statistical tie. Candidate A's true support could be as low as 45% (48 - 3) and Candidate B's could be as high as 48% (45 + 3). Their support ranges overlap. A difference is only "statistically significant" if the gap between the two numbers is larger than the combined margin of error. If the gap between two numbers in a poll is smaller than the margin of error, you must report it as too close to call. Always include the MoE in your story. 12.4 WHY NUMBERS CAN MISLEAD: HOW TO SPOT AND
AVOID TRAPS
Some people use numbers not to inform, but to deceive. Here are the most common tricks to watch out for.
12.4.1 Cherry-Picking Data
This is the classic trick of showing only the data that supports one's argument while hiding the rest. A pharmaceutical company might publicise the one small trial where their drug worked, while burying the three larger trials where it failed. Or a politician might boast about job growth since they took office, but intentionally start their timeline after a major recession, ignoring the jobs lost before. How to spot it: Always ask, "What aren't you showing me?" Demand the full dataset, not just the summary. Check the timeframe. A graph showing a stock's impressive rise in the last six months might be intentionally hiding a catastrophic crash the year before.

12.4.2 The Big Number Trap
This tactic uses a large, scary-sounding number without any context to trigger an emotional reaction. A headline about a "Rs. 10,000 crore government plan" sounds huge, but is it really? Your job is to bring that big number down to a human scale. Divide it by the population. Compare it to last year's budget. What percentage of the total is it? A Rs. 10,000 crore plan for a country of 1.4 billion people is only about Rs. 71 per person. This context makes the number understandable. How to spot it: When you see a big, abstract number, immediately anchor it to something relatable. Context is everything.
12.4.3 Misleading Visuals
Charts can clarify data, but they can also be used as potent tools for distortion. Truncated Y-Axis: This simply means a short Y-axis. A bar chart's vertical axis (the Y-axis) should start at zero, but a truncated Y-axis does not. Starting it higher (say, at 40% to compare 45% and 50%) makes tiny differences look like a massive chasm. It visually exaggerates the change. This is the most common sin in data visualisation. 3D Charts: The 3D perspective distorts the size of the slices or bars, making those in the foreground appear larger than they are. Avoid them. Improper Scaling: Using the wrong scale on a line graph can flatten a sharp increase or make slow growth look exponential. Dual Y-Axes: Plotting two different things (like "number of pirates" and "global temperature") on two different y-axes can create a completely meaningless and spurious correlation by manipulating the scales. Cumulative Data: A graph of "total COVID-19 cases" will only ever go up, which can look alarming even when the crisis is fading. The more honest chart would be "new daily cases," which shows whether the situation is getting better or worse. How to spot it: Scrutinise the axes of every chart. Ask yourself: "Does the Y-axis start at 0?" "Is this showing a cumulative total or new data?" Be wary of overly flashy graphics that seem to prioritise style over substance.
12.5 A JOURNALIST'S WORKFLOW FOR HANDLING DATA
Working with data is a process, not a magic trick. A repeatable workflow prevents errors and saves you from headaches. Let us go through the process one step at a time.
1. Acquire: Get the data. This is the first hurdle. Look for it on government portals like the National
Data and Analytics Platform (NDAP), RBI's Database on Indian Economy, or the National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB). If it is not public, file a Right to Information (RTI) request. Always push for the raw, machine-readable data (like a CSV or spreadsheet file), not a PDF.
2. Clean: This is the unglamorous but absolutely essential grunt work. Raw data is almost always
messy. You will find typos ("Mumbai," "Bombay," "Mumbai (City)" all in one column), inconsistent formatting, and missing values. You have to fix these (e.g., standardise all spellings to "Mumbai") before you can trust your analysis.
3. Explore and Analyse: Now the fun begins. Open the data in a spreadsheet programme like Excel
or Google Sheets. Start looking for the story. Sort, filter, and pivot the data. Look for patterns, outliers (shockingly high or low numbers), and trends. Apply the questions we discussed earlier in Section 12.3: What are the rates? What is the median?

4. Visualise: Create simple, clean charts for your own analysis, not just for the final story. A basic bar
chart can instantly reveal a pattern that was invisible in a thousand rows of a spreadsheet. This is a tool for discovery.
5. Verify and Contextualise: This is the most important step for a journalist. Your data analysis is a
source, and it needs to be verified. Take your findings to real people. Call experts, academics, and people on the ground. Ask them if your conclusions make sense. They can provide the crucial "why" behind the "what" that your data shows. This is what turns numbers into journalism.
12.6 CASE STUDY: DECONSTRUCTING A HEALTH SURVEY
PRESS RELEASE
Imagine this press release lands in your inbox:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE: "SUPERFOOD X" BOOSTS HAPPINESS BY 30%
A groundbreaking new study from the Health Research Institute proves that a daily dose of our supplement, SuperFood X, leads to a significant increase in happiness. The study of 500 adults found that participants who took SuperFood X for one month reported their happiness levels increased by an average of 30%, compared to just 5% in a placebo group. A numerically-literate journalist's internal monologue would be something along the following lines:
1. Check the Source: "Health Research Institute"? Never heard of them. A quick search shows they
are funded entirely by the company that makes SuperFood X. That is a massive conflict of interest. The study is not independent.
2. Attack the Numbers:
"30% increase" is a relative change. But 30% of what? How did they measure "happiness"? On a 1-to-5 scale? If the average score went from 2.0 to 2.6, that is a 30% jump, but it is hardly a life- changing leap. The press release conveniently leaves that out. "Average of 30%" - is that the mean or the median? If a couple of people felt ecstatic and most felt nothing, the mean would be high but misleading.
3. Question the Method:
500 people sounds okay, but who were they? Healthy, young college students? That is not representative of the general population. They used a control group, which is good. But placebo effect, in which a group of trial subjects are given neutral product, making them 'feel better,' is powerful. Did they control for other lifestyle changes?
4. Find what is Missing:
Where is the Margin of Error? Without it, we don't know if the gap between 30% and 5% is even statistically significant. It is "safe," they say. But were there any side effects? Did 20% of the participants get sick? Has this been peer-reviewed and published in a reputable scientific journal? If not, it is just marketing, not science. This is the gold standard for any scientific claim. The Real Story: Having diligently applied the workflow discussed above, you would not write a headline like "New Supplement Boosts Happiness." Rather, you would weigh and measure words and numbers, and write something like this, "Company-Funded Study Claims Supplement Boosts Happiness, but Experts Urge Caution, Citing Methodological Flaws." Essentially, you turn a piece of advertising into

a story about scientific standards and transparency. Check Your Progress 2 Note: 1) Use the space provided below for your answers.
2) Compare your answers with those given at the end of the unit.
1. What is a "truncated Y-axis," and why is it a misleading visual technique?

2. A study finds a strong correlation between the number of firefighters at a fire incident and the
amount of damage caused. Does this mean firefighters cause more damage? Explain your reasoning using a concept from this unit.

12.7 LET US SUM UP
In this unit, we have made the case that number-savviness is a non-negotiable, core competency for any modern journalist. Data provides the credibility and scale that lifts a story beyond a simple anecdote. We have equipped you with a critical toolkit: to question averages, to demand rates for fair comparisons, and to never, ever confuse correlation with causation. We have also highlighted the common traps, from cherry-picked data to misleading charts that are designed to manipulate public opinion. By learning to embrace numbers not as an obstacle, but as a powerful tool for finding stories and holding power to account, you become a more effective, more credible, and more valuable journalist.
12.8 KEYWORDS
Absolute Change: The raw numerical difference between two values. Correlation: A statistical relationship between two variables. Causation: A relationship where one variable directly causes a change in another. Innumeracy: The inability to understand and work with numbers. Lurking Variable: A hidden factor that can be the true cause of an observed correlation. Margin of Error (MoE): A statistic expressing the amount of random sampling error. Mean: The average calculated by adding all values and dividing by the count. Median: The middle value in a sorted list of numbers. Rate: A measure for fair comparisons (e.g., crimes per 100,000 people). Relative Change: The change in a value expressed as a percentage of the initial value. Statistical Significance: A measure of whether a result is likely due to a real effect rather than random chance.

12.10 CHECK YOUR PROGRESS: POSSIBLE ANSWERS
Check Your Progress: 1
1. Relying solely on anecdotes is misleading because a single story, no matter how powerful, is not
necessarily representative of a broader reality. It might be an exception rather than the rule. Data provides the necessary context to determine if an anecdote illustrates a widespread trend or an isolated incident.
2. To make a fair comparison, you need the population of each town. With the population, you can
calculate the rate of the disease (e.g., cases per 1,000 people). This allows you to determine if the disease is truly more prevalent in Town A, or if it just has a larger population. Check Your Progress: 2
1. A "truncated Y-axis" is a technique used in bar or line charts where the vertical axis (Y-axis) does
not start at zero (e.g., it starts at 40% instead). It is misleading because it visually exaggerates small differences, making them look like a massive chasm or a dramatic change when they are actually very modest.
2. No, this does not mean firefighters cause more damage. This is a classic example of correlation not
being causation. The lurking variable is the size of the fire. Larger, more serious fires cause both more firefighters to be sent to the scene and more damage to occur. The firefighters and the damage are correlated, but they are both caused by the third variable (the fire's size).

13.0 INTRODUCTION
Crisis Communication is an integral part of public relations. As effective communication becomes vital during a disaster, crisis handling becomes the backbone of any government, organisation, institution etc in order to reach out to its citizens through PR practices. Public relations department in any organisation plays a vital role not only in the pre-crisis phase but also during the crisis and in the post crisis phase. In this Unit, we shall discuss the various kinds of crisis and the importance of communication during a crisis and the role of PR practitioners in the times of crisis.
13.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After working through this unit, you should be able to: * Understand various classifications of crisis * Learn from the case studies in crisis communication * Gain insights from the real examples
13.2 DEFINING CRISIS COMMUNICATION
13.2.1 What is Crisis
A crisis can be defined as an adverse event, a great and sudden calamity that needs immediate addressing. Crisis can be man-made or may occur due to natural reasons. Famines, droughts,

cyclones, earthquakes, tidal waves, insurgency, terrorism, wars, epidemics, corporate warfare, employee agitations, project closures, product recalls, and scams et al, all qualify to be called a crisis. Let's look at the various phases of a crisis.
13.2.2 Phases of Crisis Management
Pre-crisis phases * Preparedness * Mitigation * Prevention
Crisis Phase
* Response * Recovery * Development
Post-crisis Phase
* Relief * Recovery * Rehabilitation
13.3 IMPORTANCE OF COMMUNICATION IN CRISIS MANAGEMENT
* Identifying stakeholders * Identifying means of communication for reaching out to various stakeholders * Smoothing the flow of information The success of each phase of crisis management impinges on effective communication.
13.3.1 Types of Crisis
Hill and Knowlton, a leading PR consultancy in the U.S.A., has classified crises in the following four segments: a. Actual disasters such as fires, explosions, accidents, earthquakes, floods, famines etc. These can be termed as exploding crises. b. Controversial or scandalous incidents, involving companies, individuals, governments et al. these are referred to as immediate crises. c. Anticipated crisis due to premeditated decisions like closure of a plant, discontinuance of a service, retrenchment etc. Crises falling in this category are classified as building crises. d. Continuing crisis: when an organisation, a product or a service is under long-term attack from some stakeholders like special interest groups, media, judiciary, consumer group et al. The National Disaster Management Authority in India defines disasters/crises as under: * Natural sudden disasters (earthquakes, cyclones, tidal waves, tropical storms, volcanic eruptions, landslides, floods) * Slow impact disasters: (droughts, famine, environmental degradation, deforestation, pest infestation) * Manmade, complex emergencies: (industrial, displacement, terrorism, food scarcity, food insecurity et al).
13.3.2 Knowing the crisis
How would one know that there is a crisis? All crises are not sudden like an earthquake, an accident or a Tsunami; there are crises that simmer for some time before they explode, like employee attitude, absenteeism, drug abuse at workplace, lifestyle behavior, or a long-drawn case with an inquiry committee that is being waited upon. A management, corporate or political

party, which does not have the "sixth sense" about dormant critical issues, is doomed to face larger crises anytime soon. Early corrective action often helps in solving the problem when at the ascent stage. It saves time, effort, resources, both manpower and financial, besides reputation. You would be better able to appreciate the crisis situation emergence and need of its management with the help of some real-life examples. You would have noticed these situations too. Now let us dissect them with respect to the Identification of the Crisis and the need to address it well in time, with appropriate communication strategies. These instances will make it clear to you, how some situations could have saved adversity only if these were addressed in time and with proper communication. How, some issues that were ignored earlier, became hugely harmful for the image later. Be it a political party, an industry or a celebrity, a crisis must be addressed while it can be controlled. Let us go through some situations, where it was not done so and hence the harms had to be reaped. Example 1: Political Crisis: Let us see an example of a crisis faced by a political party. This example will help you understand that a crisis is not always real, it can be due to perceptions as well. Sometimes, it does not matter whether you are right in a situation or actually the wrongdoer, all that matters is the public perception of your actions and the lingering effect that the perception has. Individuals can fall prey to such misperceived or lingering effects. But, even strong entities like political parties are not spared of the 'crisis of perception'. It is noteworthy that despite having a strong PR machinery, a political party cannot wipe out its perceived perceptions leading to crisis situations off and on. For example, the demolition of the Babri Masjid was a major political crisis that shook the secular fabric of the nation. It not only brought about huge amounts of violence, but also showcased a sense of insensitivity towards a religious minority of the country. Example 2: Industrial Crisis: InJuly 2012, industrial unrest was simmering in the Manesar plant of Maruti-Suzuki, but the management did not seem to appreciate the extent of trouble, till a mob led by some trade union leaders went on rampage that resulted in over 100 persons getting injured and head of the human resource department losing his life. The management gave a feeling that the trigger was provided by the suspension of a person by the name Gia Lal, who had punched a supervisor at the plant and hence was suspended. His suspension had sparked the workers' protest, which snowballed into a large-scale violence as a laborer's mob attacked company officials. If one analyses the situation there was more to the story than this. The organisation, as per media reports, had fewer permanent employees and a lot more employees on contractual terms. The difference in the carry home salary of both the categories was manifold. Interestingly, both kinds of employees, the regular and casual ones, were engaged in the same kind of work. The employees on contractual basis did not enjoy any fringe benefits. For instance, if the regular employees received a packet of sweets on a festive occasion, the contractual employees would not be given that gift. Activity 1 Do you remember any crisis that a popular brand went through in the last one year? Try to find out more about this situation and what strategies did that brand use to get out of this crisis situation.
13.3.3 Crisis Management Schedule
A crisis management schedule is always patterned to fit the organisation's own potential exposure to calamity. To illustrate, the crisis management plan of a nuclear plant would be very different from that of a steel plant because the potential risk areas are quite different in the two cases. In times of a terrorist strike in a particular city, the police are generally put on "red alert" in other cities, which amounts to gearing up to the immediate possibility of similar strikes in other cities.

13.4 THE SIGNIFICANCE OF COMMUNICATION
Whenever an organisation is faced with a crisis, it has to communicate with a number of stakeholders from its perspective and also to respond to the information needs of these stakeholders. Media, which represents the public voice, is the most critical stakeholder to handle in times of a crisis. The strength of character of a person, as goes the age-old adage, is judged in adversity, so can be said of an organisation. Every crisis poses a test about how an organisation would respond to an emergency, how it takes care of the people who are affected and how it is going to rebound after a crisis. When an organisation is undergoing a crisis, its leadership is constantly in public gaze and on media radar, so the resilience of the top management and its action plan to avoid a similar kind of disaster is important both from the perspective of the organisation and its stakeholders. To quote an instance, Ratan Tata, Chairman of the Tata Group displayed enormous grit and resilience, at the same time firmness in analysing the situation and taking charge, after Hotel Taj, a Tata property became the target of terrorist siege in November 2008. He did not mince words, when he said that the emergency response from authorities was less than adequate and announced that for the safety of the guests and employees, the Tata Group would put its own security in place "to serve as an impediment" to such happenings and "not to create heroes" after the event had occurred. Ratan Tata's whole demeanor reflected that there was a person who was in command. On the other hand, as will be reflected in the case study given later in the chapter, it cost both the Chief Minister and the State Home Minister their jobs for appearing indifferent and insensitive. Each category of crisis whether it is man-made or natural, requires careful handling, especially when life is involved. When a crisis has occurred, one cannot turn back the clock. The damage to reputation may be a reality, but honest intentions coupled with effective communication, would help an organisation to tidy up their image sooner or later. Communication takes the center stage from the perspective of various stakeholders. Everyone wishes to be told the truth -the employees, the shareholders, the suppliers, the policy makers, the financial institutions, and above all the media. While it may take some time to know the reasons behind that crisis, communication cannot wait. In almost every crisis, confidence of the alleged victims and those who empathise with them need to be restored. Following points are critical in a crisis situation. * Enormity of the disaster/loss of human life. * Perceived abettors and victims. * Perceptions about the crisis. * Media coverage/media stand. * Action plan to deal with the crisis on hand. Two aspects from disaster management's perspective become crucial. In fact, the success of a crisis management impinges on:

* How the organisation responds to the victims. * Is it communicating what it is doing, and how it rebound. Exactly after a month, both the hotels The Taj and the Trident, victims of terrorists strike in Mumbai in November 2008 were back serving their clients, notwithstanding the fact that a lot of repairing work was still going on in many areas. The whole idea behind this was to convey that despite what they underwent, their spirit could not be killed. Media wholeheartedly covered the incident talking about stories of human courage, determination and resilience.
13.4.1 The Role of Sharing Information
It is generally said of the media that they feast on crises. Bigger the crises, the better they feel, because it gives them the opportunity to showcase their alertness in bringing issues to the public domain; pull up authorities and get closer to their viewers/readers and of course the TRPs rise as more and more people sit glued to their television sets. In the aftermath of a crisis, or even while a crisis has not subsided, getting hold of information as fast as possible is very important for the media. Due to fierce competition among various channels and in print media, every channel / newspaper wishes to give the "breaking news". Therefore, it is important for Public Relations practitioners to understand that the media will get information somehow, so it is in the interest of the organisation to share official versions and be heard constantly. Ducking or not sharing information can be suicidal. The 24-hour channels can be seen as a problem or an opportunity. Public Relations practitioners are often criticised for "engineering consent" and "manipulating" the minds of the stakeholders in critical times to salvage damage done to their organisations, even when they may know that their organisations were guilty of unethical practices or poor corporate governance. This may not always be true, but exceptions are always there. Activity 2 Follow any two celebrities on Instagram. Find out the kind of information they share on their social media platform.
13.4.2 The Advisory Role of Public Relations
Public Relations is a "staff function" that advises the top management on information management both in routine and critical times. Many case studies, be it the Watergate scandal, the taking of embedded journalists for coverage to Iraq, the Enron or Satyam frauds, all amply reinforce that communication of just any kind cannot help individuals or organisations to come out clean, if they indulge in unethical practices. Critics often call the public relations department the "white wash cell". Can any amount of whitewashing save a crumbling wall? Bill Clinton's initial lies about his affair with an intern did not help him in the long run. Led by the events, Satyam CEO. R Raju had to send a confessional letter that helped unearth the scam. If public relations strategies are used to get fair comments in the media through unfair means (of which the media would be equally guilty), it may only end up doing many times more damage to the organisation once the truth surfaces. Shooting the messenger is a bad strategy and does not help.
13.4.3 What Should One Communicate in Crisis?
In the pre- crisis phase relating to natural disasters, alerting the people on preparedness is important. Local governments, as soon as they get data from the meteorological department, announce to people about impending cyclones, rainfall, and possible tidal waves. They make

arrangements to evacuate them. After the disaster has occurred, informing people about succor, rehabilitation, medical facilities, compensation etc. is important. Involving people in rescue operations and communication will result in ownership of operations. One has been watching some very impactful disaster preparedness campaigns, especially on earthquakes, mounted by The Disaster Management Authority in various media. As a precautionary measure, the people are being asked to get their houses checked for earthquake resistance, and how to go about correcting them, if there is a problem. On the other hand in case of man-made crises, the strategy cannot always be preempted, especially in cases of frauds and scams. When Satyam fraud was unearthed after a confessional letter from the CEO of the company, the company obviously remained silent for a while till a new Board was in place. However, thousands of blogs surfaced in no time. Communication was coming from various sources that included the regulatory bodies, the industry, the media and of course the political class.
13.4.4 Message Content
From the perspective of public relations, the message content in a crisis, according to Lawrence Warner should include the following, "public's message elements, communication techniques, responsibilities, time and schedule commitments, and accountability factors". The stakeholders need to be listed in order of importance. The critical ones must be reached on priority. The concepts need to be communicated to the target audience, keeping in view the core message. The techniques of communication will include the decision about various channels, both paid and unpaid. Provision must also be made for budgeting and evaluation and feedback. In a crisis situation, free media may not suffice. The crisis team may think it prudent to buy space and put across its viewpoint, without the fear of its curtailment, if sent as a press release. Ratan Tata, for instance, after pulling out from West Bengal issued a large advertisement expressing his angst against those he thought were responsible for the mess. 13.5 CASE STUDY
The TATA 'Nano' Story -A Crisis Aggravated by Political Forces Nano, the smallest and most economical car from one of the globally respected conglomerates, the Tata group faced major hassles; before the little car was seen test-driving in media programs as a build up, before the bookings for the car began in April 2009. The company got embroiled in State politics as soon as Ratan Tata, the Group Chairman announced a small car project that he wished to set up in the Left- run West Bengal. The project incidentally was announced on the day, Buddhadeb Bhattacharya was sworn in as the Chief Minister of West Bengal in May 2006. What was the issue? The Tata Group was allotted 404 hectares of land to build its factory in a place called Singur, which became the bone of contention. Some farmers led by Trinmool Congress Chief Mamta Banerjee questioned the decision of the State Government in taking away "forcibly", a multi- crop fertile land by revoking the archaic Land Acquisition Act of 1894. The construction work for developing the infrastructure was in full swing and Tata's had put its first batch of engineers in place from January 2007.

All the while, the Tata Group kept itself out of direct dialogue with the agitators, who held demonstrations many times. Once they were joined by Medha Patekar of Save Narmada fame, who was booked on charges of rioting and disturbing the peace of the place. Things took a turn and the agitation gained momentum when the Trinamool Congress was able to garner majority seats in the local self-governing bodies in May 2007. This gave momentum to agitation. Ratan Tata however, categorically said there was no pulling out from Singur. The chief protagonist went on a 25 day-long hunger strike in December 2007. The Governor of West Bengal played the informal arbitrator, but nothing came out of it. The various agitations that also included torching of the fence of the factory had the Tata employees worried about their life and security, when a disheartened Ratan Tata took a call and decided to pull out of West Bengal, amidst promises from the State government that things would be sorted out. The entire industry rallied around Ratan Tata. FICCI publicly said that such events might lead other industrialists to pull out from West Bengal. Many Chief Ministers offered Ratan Tata to shift to their States, and he settled for Gujarat in October 2008. This meant a loss of Rs. 500 Crores to the company and settling of claims of vendors who put up cumulative claims of over Rs 250 Crores on the company for their investment and borrowings from the banks as reported by the media. The Central Government by and large kept out of the controversy. Although the Tata's left the place, it would take long before issues are settled with local people as the infrastructure is still there and claims pending. All the while, Ratan Tata, resisted from making any comment on the agitators, led by Mamta Bannerjee. All he would say was that since the lives of the employees were at stake, Tata Motors had no alternative, but to withdraw from the State. However, three weeks later, in an 'Open Letter to the Citizens of West Bengal' that appeared in a number of newspapers in West Bengal, Ratan Tata minced no words when he openly criticized the Trinamool Congress led by Mamta Banerjee and supported by "vested interests and certain political parties" that caused serious disruption to the progress of the Nano plant. Some key insights from Ratan Tata Case Study are : * In a crisis situation many stakeholders get embroiled, who may or may not be the concerned "parties" in the crisis per se, but can wield influence. The political environment is an important constant factor, which needs to be taken into account by the industry. In other words, the importance of "pre-thinking" should not be underestimated. * The goodwill of the Tata group was amply visible, when the entire industry rallied around Tata Group in its struggle in Singur. * Taking land through the State Government, meant the company did not invest much effort, if at all, in interfacing with the community, who rightly or not, could be indoctrinated by vested interests. The compensation received by the farmers for their land, presumably was much lower, despite that the land being fertile vis-a-vis other States, where the farmers are said to have received many times the amount even for non-fertile land. * Companies often conduct baseline surveys and social audits, before deciding on a place. To quote a contemporary example, the Reliance Industries limited (RIL), which has been acquiring thousands of acres of land in the State of Haryana SEZ, has put in place an extensive corporate social responsibility (CSR) initiative to win the trust of the local communities, before land deals could materialise. * Some felt that it did not really suit the stature of an industrialist like Ratan Tata, to openly criticise a political party and its leader, reflecting his political prejudice. While others felt that after losing so much time, effort and money, he had nothing more to lose. Calling a spade, a spade therefore, was a good strategy.

* Tata' by and large had a very supportive press, especially, the national media. * When the car was demonstrated at the India International Fair in 2007, it created a frenzy among Delhi citizens. The media played on the sentiment. It covered front-page stories on how Ratan Tata had once seen a family of four riding a scooter, when he pledged that he would soon produce a car that will be affordable to the common man. The design and the designers of the car were kept in a closet until the day the car was demonstrated to people at last. With a highly cluttered car market especially in the low category, the company was not able to generate as many bookings as it probably expected. As per media reports, the company could attract 2.5 lakhs bookings, the highest at 50% in the top category, costing Rs. 1.84 Lakhs. It would have been a good idea, if Tatas' could compile a demographic profile of the people to see whether it were the two-wheeler owners (who were the primary TA) who have booked, or others. * Racing against time, the Tata's began booking Nano within six months of shifting from West Bengal. Interestingly, against the application fee of Rs. 300/- the company gave a credit voucher of equal amount to be redeemed at its West Side departmental stores against a purchase of Rs. 3000 in a single shot. It has also been announced that if the delivery of the car were delayed beyond six months, then it would attract payment of interest to the applicant. * Media carried various interesting stories as soon as the booking began. One of them had that after all Singur would get to see Nano playing on its roads as one form was collected from there! Another story had how a beggar was interested to buy the Nano from his lifetime savings! Times of India for days called its column "News in Brief" on the front page to "Nano News". The Tata Group hopefully would analyse the Singur Saga ardently and draw some useful insights on crisis management.
13.6 LET US SUM UP
In this Unit, the concepts, role and scope of crisis communication has been discussed. The role of public relations in crises and the misperceptions surrounding it were deliberated upon. Poor corporate governance and non-perusal of ethical principles often puts organisations on public opinion radar. Communication not based on honest intentions often boomerangs. We learnt all this with examples and case studies from our country. Crisis Management is a Public Relations function. No organization can escape crises. The lesson to be learnt is that a crisis cannot be reversed, it can only be managed. Public Relations department which has expertise in communication and who are apt in their understanding of how media functions is best suited to handle crises on behalf of organizations and celebrities.

13.8 GLOSSARY
Crisis of Perception: A situation which is perceived by citizens or audience as one full of acute problems and struggles Development: Those tasks that are done by governments or non-government bodies to build a place or organization, its infrastructure or the entire workforce

Rehabilitation: After the occurrence of a disaster or crisis, work done by governments to settle a population Stakeholders: People, organizations, structures that invest their time, money and resources in a particular task, feeling accountable for its development and growth

13.0 INTRODUCTION
Data journalism helps journalists leverage large datasets to narrate data-heavy stories engagingly. An essential component in this data-to-news-story journey is spreadsheets, which have become an indispensable tool in modern-day data journalism. As per the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ), "improving spreadsheet literacy is a big step towards being more comfortable with data." This shift from manual calculation to computational analysis has fundamentally changed how journalists can quickly investigate and find stories hidden in datasets. In this unit, we will learn about the basics of spreadsheets, and how journalists can use it to gather, interrogate and present data effectively.
13.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After going through this unit, you will be able to: understand spreadsheets and their role in data journalism;

learn basic functions of a spreadsheet; understand basic concepts of data handling and visualisation; use basic formulas for smarter use of spreadsheets; and learn how to use spreadsheets in reporting.
13.2 UNDERSTANDING SPREADSHEETS
Simply put, a spreadsheet is a digital document with search-enabled multiple rows and columns, which can be used to store, manipulate and analyse data. Spreadsheets can help journalists gather and manage large amounts of data, do complex calculations and analysis, and visualise information hidden in a dataset.
13.2.1 Why Spreadsheets are Important for Journalists?
Spreadsheets are important for journalists because they serve many critical functions, such as acquiring data from external sources, cleaning and analysing data in structured formats, performing automatic calculations, and then identifying patterns that lead to a meaningful story. In fact, spreadsheet literacy is becoming a core competency across all major news organisations. Many international and national news organisations, such as The New York Times, The Guardian, BBC News, The Hindu, India Today, NDTV and many others have dedicated data journalism teams that regularly produce news stories with the help of data analysis and data visualisation.
13.2.2 Spreadsheets in Journalistic Workflow
The fundamental principle of spreadsheet use in journalism is simple: just let the software do the "counting and calculating," while journalists can focus on the story emerging from that dataset. While there is some time investment required to learn spreadsheets, such skills once acquired can actually help journalists in their day-to-day work such as: gather data easily in a structured format automate a wide range of calculations analyse data to find stories hidden inside the data cross-check and verify data visualise data for reporting and presentation Some of the most commonly used spreadsheet software today include Microsoft Excel, Google Sheets, Apple Numbers and Zoho Sheets, which will be discussed later in the unit.
13.3 CORE COMPONENTS OF A SPREADSHEET
Think of your spreadsheet like a filing cabinet. Rows are individual files, columns are the categories in each file, and cells are individual pieces of information. Once you understand this structure, everything else makes sense. Now, let's understand how a spreadsheet works, by looking at its building blocks.
Worksheets and Workbooks
A worksheet is the basic unit in Excel or Google Sheets, while a workbook is a collection of worksheets. A worksheet (or just "Sheet") is a single Excel sheet/document with datasets laid out in columns and rows. A workbook, on the other hand, is a document containing one or more worksheets, usually on a related subject matter. In fact, as soon as you launch Excel on your computer, it will offer you to start a "blank workbook". As you click on it, it will begin with "Sheet1", with an option to add more sheets at the bottom left (see sign "+"). You can have multiple sheets in a workbook, and rename each sheet as required. A workbook can hold all of your work, reports, charts, etc., together in one place, in a single or multiple sheets.

Figure 1 & 2: An example of a workbook containing many worksheets. These can help journalists keep their investigation organised. For example: Sheet 1 can contain raw data (exactly as you received it), Sheet 2 can contain cleaned data (after fixing errors), and Sheet 3 can contain analysis (your calculations and findings) Remember: Never work directly on your raw data. Always keep the original untouched. Rows Rows run horizontally across your spreadsheet. They're numbered 1, 2, 3, going down. Each row usually represents one record. For example, if you're tracking national expenditure budgets, each row would be one ministry and its department's budget. In the figure given below, you will see donors' names in the rows. You can see the amount and date of their donation in their respective rows. Columns Columns run vertically. They're labelled with letters A, B, C, going across. Each column represents one type of information. In a simple donations dataset, you will have: Column A: Donor name Column B: Amount donated Column C: Date of donation

Figure 3: A simple donation data, to explain columns and rows. Cells A cell is one box in your spreadsheet. It holds a single piece of information--one number, one name, one date. How to find a cell? Each cell has an address made from its column letter and row number; i.e. Cell A1 means column 'A', row '1'--the very first box in the top-left corner. Similarly, Cell B2 means column 'B', and row '2'. A single spreadsheet/worksheet in MS Excel can hold 1,048,576 rows and 16,384 columns.
Cell References
Each cell has an address, and you use these addresses in formulas. For example, the formula =SUM(A2:A10) means "add up all the numbers from cell A2 to cell A10." The colon (:) means "through" -- so A2:A10 means "A2 through A10" or "all cells from A2 to A10." In Figure 3, the darkly outlined box is Cell 'B5'. Headers The first row should always contain headers--clear labels that explain what's in each column. Always label the headers clearly, for example "Donation Amount" rather than just "Amount", or "Donor Full Name" rather than just "Name". Clear headers make your work easier and your formulas more readable. In Figure 3, see the header titled as "List of Donors".
Pivot Tables
Pivot Tables are powerful tools for organising and analysing large datasets. They let you group, summarise and aggregate data to find trends and patterns that may not be clear at first. Highly customisable, pivot tables allow you to reshape your data in different formats. Their key function is to provide advanced summaries - you can summarise totals by category or show counts by region, making complex data easier to understand and report.
13.4 POPULAR SPREADSHEET SOFTWARES
There is a wide array of spreadsheet software available for use today. Most of these offer collaboration in online mode and have AI features built into them. Let's discuss a few of them here.
Microsoft Excel
It is the industry standard for data journalism, particularly in large newsrooms. Excel offers robust functionality for data manipulation, pivot tables and formula writing. Excel mostly secures data on your system or local servers rather than in cloud-based applications. This is considered comparatively safer for keeping data. You can start working with a 'blank workbook' as a new file, or you can choose a relevant sheet from multiple templates - such as Business, Personal, Planners and Trackers,

Lists, Budgets, Charts, Calendars, etc.
Google Sheets
A cloud-based alternative that offers many of the same functions as Excel. Google Sheets has advantages in terms of collaboration--multiple journalists can work on the same spreadsheet simultaneously from different locations. Google Sheets is particularly useful for training and for collaborative projects within news organisations that have adopted cloud-based workflows. A Google Sheet file can be downloaded into your system in multiple formats, including Excel.
Apple Numbers
This is a spreadsheet app by Apple Inc. for its own ecosystem (Mac, iPad, and iPhone). But it is compatible with other spreadsheets, including Microsoft Excel, and also allows online collaborations. Like Excel, this too offers many pre-built templates such as Basic, Personal Finance, Personal, Business, Education, etc.
Zoho Sheets
This is a cloud-based spreadsheet application, "powered by an automated data processor, an AI- assisted data analyst, and 1,000+ integration possibilities" (Zoho Corporation, 2025). Like others, this too helps analyse, visualise, and publish data while also allowing real-time online collaboration. Check Your Progress: 1 Note: 1) Use the space provided below for your answers.

13.5 WORKING WITH SPREADSHEETS FOR BETTER
REPORTING
As a data journalist, you essentially need two core skills: critical thinking (treating numbers sceptically, like any other source) and basic familiarity with spreadsheets. These two skills can help you find stories within different kinds of datasets such as crime statistics, property records or school results. To understand spreadsheets, what one needs is familiarity with its key features, which are as follows:
1. formulas (for automatic calculation)
2. sorting and filtering (for data organisation)
3. charts and graphics (for visualisation)
4. conditional formatting (for highlighting data)
5. pivot tables (for advanced summaries)
Now let us understand how reporters must use spreadsheets and their different elements.
13.5.1 Different Types of Data

Data entry involves inputting desired information, which can include text, numbers, dates or formulas, into individual cells within a spreadsheet. You can simply select a cell and type the information directly into the spreadsheet. Spreadsheets handle different types of data, and you need to understand these to analyse information correctly. Numbers: Numbers or numeric data are the values you calculate with--either as whole numbers or decimals. In journalism, you work with numbers constantly: population figures, budget amounts, vote counts, crime statistics, etc. Spreadsheets recognise numbers as data that you can add, subtract and calculate with. They line up numbers on the right side of the cells. Text: Text data includes words, names and addresses--anything that's not a number. These could be people's names, place names, event or item lists, etc. Your spreadsheet lines these up on the left side of the cells. Remember, you cannot do calculations with text. If you type "100" with quotation marks, the spreadsheet treats it as text, not a number. So, you will not be able to do calculations, though you will still be able to do sorting and filtering of the text. Figure 5: Spreadsheets line up numeric data on the right-hand side and text on the left-hand side of the cells. Dates: Date data is crucial for journalism, as you may need to sort out events chronologically and calculate time periods. Dates need to follow a consistent format like DD-MM-YYYY (e.g. 05-12-2025) or YYYY-MM-DD (e.g. 2025-12-05). Mixing date formats can create chaos and may not yield the correct results, so always maintain one date format throughout one dataset. Currency Data: This involves numbers presented with currency symbols (Rs or $) and decimal places (Rs100.00). Though these are just numeric data, using currency signs makes it clear to the reader that you are talking about money. Boolean Data: Boolean data simply means there are only two possible values - 'True' or 'False'; 'Yes' or 'No'; '1' or '0' (used for coding purposes). It helps journalists decide what to publish, flag or investigate further. For example, to check if a story is fact-checked, the column would say "Fact-Checked" and the answer would be either 'True' or 'False'. If the answer is 'False', it means the story needs review' before publication. Similarly, for "Legal Clearance" if the response is 'False', this means 'do not publish'.
13.5.2 Basic Calculations for Journalists
Spreadsheets contain many pre-made formulas that help to perform calculations on the entered data. These include SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT, MAX, MIN, etc. These functions help perform calculations rapidly and automatically using formulas, saving time that would otherwise be spent doing manual calculations. Let us look at some of these functions. Addition/Summation: Figures across rows and columns can be easily added using functions like SUM().When creating a formula, you should click on a cell and type your formula beginning with =. For instance, =SUM(B2:B6) will add all the numbers in cells B2 through B6. To use the SUM feature, select an empty cell where you want the result to be displayed and type "=SUM(" or just hit the "SH AutoSum" button. Then highlight the cells containing the figures to be added and close the brackets, like this =SUM(B2:B11). Alternatively, you can also add individual cells without the

SUM function by typing the equals sign followed by the cells you wish to add (e.g., =A1+B7+C4+D9). Difference/Subtraction: The same principle as addition applies here, the only difference being using the "-" sign. For example, subtract the original value (e.g., last year's wage in cell B2) from the new value (this year's wage in cell C2) using this formula, =B2-C2. Calculate the Percentage: Divide the resulting difference by the original value (the old value). For example, if a journalist is looking at salary changes, they would calculate the percentage difference by subtracting last year's wage from this year's wage, and then dividing that total difference by last year's wage. Take that difference and divide it by the original value. This calculation allows journalists to quickly assess the actual impact or growth between two figures. Average: Mean, median, and mode are fundamental ways to understand the central value or "average" of a dataset. Functions like average can help determine the mean of a column or row. Journalists should also be able to calculate the median (the number in the middle when sorted) and the mode (the number that appears the most times within your data) to identify central tendency. These can act as a lie detector to correct for outliers that distort the average. See how you can use this in the figure below. Figure 6: An example of calculating Mean, Median and Mode on an Excel Sheet. Notice the formulas given in the Rows: 6B, 7B, and 8B.
13.5.3 Key Features in Spreadsheets
In addition to formulas, pivot tables and visualisations, there are other significant features used in spreadsheets as well. These include the following: Sorting: Sorting allows you to re-arrange data - either alphabetically or numerically - making it easy to spot extreme values in any given information. This enables identification of extreme values such as the highest salary or lowest crime rate. Sorting data can instantly bring meaning to information. Filtering: This is essential for finding specific data by narrowing down the information to only its sub-parts that a journalist is interested in. For example, viewing only certain age groups, specific regions or other unique records within a large dataset. Paste Special: This allows you to link data from one part of your spreadsheet to another, even across different sheets or tabs. To use it, simply copy the desired cell(s), go to the destination, and

choose 'Edit' > 'Paste Special'. This creates a formula that references the original cell (e.g, =Sheet1!B1), ensuring that the data remains dynamically linked. Any change in the source cell will automatically update in the linked location. Formula Wizard: If you are not confident about typing formulas manually, most spreadsheets offer help via built-in formula tools. The 'Formula Wizard', often represented as 'fx' and typically located under the 'Formulas' button, can come in handy. It guides you step-by-step through selecting the right function by entering the required inputs and making formula-creation easier for beginners.
13.6 IMPORTING DATA AND DATA CLEANING
Data Journalism relies heavily on structured data. Raw data can be sourced from government records, institutional databases, publicly available statistics, etc. However, it may not be of immediate use unless imported carefully - knowing what data you want - and then cleaning for it to become usable. For this, reporters adopt a "data state of mind" and proactively ask for information in a structured format (such as an Excel file) rather than documents or PDFs.
13.6.1 Tools for Data Extraction
Today, there are many tools for journalists to find, scrape and transform data from PDF tables to spreadsheet-friendly formats for easy analysis. Some of these tools are as follows: Excel: Microsoft 365 Excel is a quick and no-code tool, and can import tables directly from multiple sources. It works well for simple, digitally-generated PDFs but struggles with files with complex layouts or scanned documents. Tabula: It is a free, open source tool that is used to turn PDFs into Excel spreadsheets and Comma-Separated Vales (CSV) files for analysis. Tabula is used to power investigative reporting at news organisations the world over. It is also considered a safe tool for journalists as it runs locally (instead of data being uploaded online to third-party applications), thus protecting sensitive data. Online converters: Web-based converters like Small PDF (https://smallpdf.com/pdf-converter) and I Love PDF (https://www.ilovepdf.com/pdf_to_excel) also offer a convenient online conversion solution, especially for non-sensitive information like publicly available datasets.
13.6.2 Importing Data from Different Sources
As discussed above, importing data involves acquiring information, which often requires the transformation of unstructured data into a structured format like a spreadsheet or database. Excel can import data from a variety of sources, including Access Databases, existing Excel files, and data copied and pasted from websites or documents. The formats of data that are acquired can be as follows: CSV format: CSV (Comma Separated Values) files are a commonly-used text file format where the comma typically separates each field. Excel can automatically open and display data from a CSV file. Docs and PDFs: Journalists often need to obtain data by extracting it from documents like PDFs or image documents. Tools like Tabula are designed to find data tables inside PDFs and scrape them out into an Excel-compatible format for analysis. API Data: Journalists may pull data from an API (Application Programming Interface), which is a set of tools and documentation that developers allow others to use. Web Scraping: Web scraping is the technique of extracting data from websites, documents and images. The focus of scraping is the transformation of unstructured data (such as HTML) into structured data (such as spreadsheets or databases).
13.6.3 Basic Data Cleaning

Raw data often requires cleaning to ensure it is in a single format, has no duplicate values, and is free of inconsistencies or errors. On average, a data journalist's 80% time is spent in data cleaning, while the rest 20% is used for analysis, storytelling and visualisation. This is called the 80/20 rule. This clearly establishes the importance of data cleaning in journalism. Two popular tools used for data cleaning in journalism are: OpenRefine (a free, open-source tool) is commonly used by journalists to clean and format datasets. It aids data teams in merging clustered data sets and checking for inconsistencies to make sure a "raw" dataset is ready for analysis. Pandas (an open-source tool) is utilised to manage large datasets, including removing empty cells and duplicated data points. While basic spreadsheet skills are sufficient for most everyday operations, large or highly complex datasets require specialised technology, which will be discussed in the next unit.
13.6.4 Data Integrity and Verification
Journalists need to learn to use their data responsibly, ensuring its accuracy as well as security. To this end, they should always bear the following in mind: Documentation and Metadata: To ensure data integrity, journalists must document the data thoroughly. This includes noting the original file, its source and the methods used to handle and analyse it. This documentation explains the formulas and data sources. It helps keep everything consistent and reliable. Protecting Data: Journalists should keep a copy of the original raw data in case of errors, corruption, or if the source is no longer available. For sensitive data, they may need to withhold it or store it in restricted access locations. Verification and Fact-Checking: Fact-checking needs dedicated time when working with data. To verify results, another person should reproduce the analysis easily. Regular reviews of spreadsheets and calculations can help correct errors and keep accuracy high. Transparency for Readers: Using data sources and web technology helps journalists be transparent. They can share raw data and calculations, allowing readers to check the work and verify conclusions. This kind of transparency is seen as the "new objectivity."

You must always calculate rates per capita (per lakh population) rather than using raw numbers, as population differences make direct comparisons misleading. For example, a journalist is analysing NCRB's data on crimes against women to understand state-wise patterns beyond headline numbers. State Population Total Crimes
Uttar Pradesh 20.4 Cr 56,011 Rajasthan 6.9 Cr 40,738 West Bengal 9.1 Cr 30,394 Madhya Pradesh 7.3 Cr 26,604 Here, a) Crime Rate = Total Crimes/Population in lakhs. So, in Rajasthan, the crime rate is 590 per lakh while in Uttar Pradesh, it is 274 per lakh. b) Rate Comparison: Rajasthan's crime rate is 2.1x higher than UP despite fewer total crimes being committed there.
13.8 SPREADSHEETS AND DATA VISUALISATION
Now, let us turn to one of the most advantageous aspects of using spreadsheets for data journalism. Data visualisation is about turning numbers into visuals, such as charts, graphs and maps, which are quicker for our brains to process. Instead of looking at rows of raw data, visualisations let us see patterns, trends and outliers more easily. They simplify complex datasets and make them quicker for our brains to process. Data visualisation and storytelling, especially when starting with spreadsheets, are important parts of modern-day journalism. They help reporters share complex data in a clear and trustworthy way. This process involves turning raw data into engaging visual formats and narrative structures. Some key benefits of visualisation are: Identifying Trends and Patterns: Visualisation helps quickly identify patterns, trends and outliers in large data sets. Quantification and Scale: Visualisation techniques, such as maps (e.g., Choropleth maps for aggregated data) or scatter plots, enable journalists to show the scale of a problem and the distribution of data across demographics or geography.

Interactivity: Visualisation tools support the creation of interactive dashboards, allowing readers to engage with the data while also fostering transparency and accountability.
13.8.1 Types of Visualisations
Spreadsheets are used for the foundational work of organising, calculating and analysing data before visualisation. Almost all spreadsheets like Excel, Google Sheets and Apple Numbers, allow visualisation of data in their software itself. In Excel, you will find most of these under the "Insert" button on the ribbon, listed as "Charts". Here are some commonly used visualisations: A Column chart is used to compare values across categories. A Line chart is used to display trends over time. A Pie chart displays the contribution of each value to a total, and can be used when values can be added together. A Bar chart is best for comparing multiple values. Area charts emphasise differences between several sets of data over a period of time. Scatter chart, also known as XY chart, compare pairs of values which are not in X axis order. It can be used when the values being charted represent separate measurements. Other charts include stock surface, doughnut, bubble and radar chart. Beyond a spreadsheet, if you have clean data, you can use any third-party apps for generating visuals. Tableau, Power BI, Flourish, Datawrapper, etc. are some such apps. However, to craft an effective visualisation, you must always start with clean data that is well-sourced and complete. Check Your Progress: 2 Note: 1) Use the space provided below for your answers.

Function: Pre-made formulas that help to perform calculations rapidly, such as SUM, AVERAGE, etc. Sorting: The process of arranging data in a specific order (like A-Z, smallest to largest, or by date) to make it easier find information quickly. Filtering: A feature that temporarily shows only the information you need for quick analysis, reporting or printing, without deleting any data. 14.0 INTRODUCTION
In this unit, we are going to learn about Grassroot Communication, which constitutes Grassroot and Social PR. Grassroots Communication is an approach to communication wherein, ideas, messages, information etc are shared and advocacy is practiced in order to drive positive changes in the society with the help of the local community. It generally depends upon interpersonal networks, community media and lately digital platforms to amplify voices that might otherwise be unheard, fostering collective action and empowerment.
14.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After reading this unit, you will be able to:

* Understand the meaning and concept of Grassroots Communication * Understand the Process of Communication * Associate Grassroots communication with communication theories * Design communication strategy for grassroots communication
14.2 CONCEPT, MEANING, AND DEFINITION
The concept of grassroots communication revolves around the engagement of the common people with issues, ideas, activities, and programs of the government. It is an understood fact that development cannot be ushered from the outside. Therefore the propelling force of ushering in transformation has to be within the community. This is possible when there is clarity of objectives and mutual benefits for the common masses. To make this compliance possible, there are stages of exchange of information of ideas, knowledge, the building of consensus to learn new skills needed, and acceptance by the people involved. This leads to the sustainability of development programs even when support organizations like NGOs have left the scene. Grassroots communication is a bigger umbrella under which includes all communication done at the level of the general masses belonging to a certain community, district, or region, to lobby, appeal or persuade by using self-organization and collective action by the community or by the public officer, NGO or government organization to communicate directly with the community, in an attempt to pressure into endorsing a particular opinion.
14.2.1. Functions of Grassroots communication
Grassroots communication is used for lobbying by both parties, the government/ NGO/corporate with the community and vice versa that is community lobbies through grassroots communication to build up movements like Narmada Bachao Andolan. Grassroots movements and organizations use collective action from the local level to effect change at the local, regional, national, or international levels. Grassroots movements are associated with bottom-up, rather than top-down decision-making. Similarly, when initiated by governments the grassroots communications involve the engagement of the community with the advocacy. Grassroots advocacy includes organizing, mobilizing, and engaging the public to advocate for themselves. The other important function deeply linked to advocacy is persuasion. Persuasion is a precursor to advocacy. Deliberation and advocacy both allow for facts and statements to be shared, but persuasion pushes these facts and statements, trying to sell them to those who don't already agree with their views.
14.3 Importance of Grassroots communication
The significance of grassroots communication is linked with the issues it represents. In rural development which envelops 29 subjects under Panchayat Raj like education, health, power, agriculture, minor irrigation, and so on. All these issues are linked with the quality of life of the community like livelihood, skilling, gender-related issues, education, health, etc. To be able to achieve good governance, local governments have to work together with communities and ensure community welfare. For any sustained effort to be able to bring a fruitful local solution, it is important to grant the community a certain amount of responsibility. This is possible only through grassroots communication. A successful example is Meena Radio Programme by UNICEF, in Bihar, launched in 2010 as part of its broader communication initiatives to promote girls' education and gender equality. Owing to its success, it was expanded to different regions for several more years.
14.3.1 Relevance of Grassroots communication
The world has witnessed the Covid-19 pandemic which has taught us the relevance of communication in the post-pandemic era. The relevance of Grassroots and word-of-mouth communication is that it can cut through the clutter, make messages stick, and persuade people to take action on behalf of organizations and issues of all sorts. When the first and second waves of the pandemic happened in 2020-21, several lives were lost worldwide. In such a situation where

people were confined to their homes, several daily wage earners and laborers were struggling for survival, millions of migrants walked barefoot to their villages, the only way communication from the government about the One Nation One Ration Card, about schemes for orphaned children under which ten lakhs Rupees was being provided to surviving children was possible as several youth clubs, NGOs, PRIs worked together to spread the word and provide information.
