14.4 GRASSROOTS COMMUNICATION AND COMMUNICATION
THEORIES
The genesis of all communication practices is linked to the context of theory. Numerous communication theories can be associated with grass-root communication. Prominent among them are diffusion and innovation theory, two-step flow theory, personal influence theory, development media theory, participatory approaches in communication theory, strategic communication theory, and so on. A standard example is to view the farmers' protest to the agriculture bills through these theories. Communication theories such as the `diffusion of innovations', implies `that the role of communication was (1) to transfer technological innovations from development agencies to their clients, and (2) to create an appetite for change through raising a `climate for modernization' among the members of the public. Similarly, two- Step Flow (Lazersfeld, Berelson, & Gaudet, 1948), stipulates that the mass media informs certain people, who in turn influence the meanings perceived by others. There is also the personal influence model of Katz and Lazersfeld (1955), which considers that responses to media messages are mediated by interpersonal communication between members of one's social environment. All these theories remain applicable to grassroots communication. In interpersonal communication theory, interaction is usually seen from the angle of person-to- person interaction or group interaction. This is closely associated with grassroots communication. Development Media theory requires the mass media to join the government in the task of nation-building and development "in the interest of national objectives." When communication impetus comes from government initiatives, then this theory is used to generate acceptance. The knowledge of traditional channels and strategies of communication used in the various environments where the interventions are made to induce the people to take responsibility for the communication process has also been identified for the enhancement of local knowledge, to allow both for the bridging of modern knowledge and the valorization of community knowledge. This method is media-oriented but derives its strength from the democratic participant media theory applicable to grassroots communication. As grassroots communication is omnidirectional, there is continuous up-gradation of meaning and interpretation that forms part of the development process itself. Hence, interactions are seen as a dynamic interplay between various stakeholders, which influences the consequences of the communicative transactions at a fundamental level. This ambit of definition circumscribes several theories under development communication and participatory communication by the likes of Everett Rodgers and Rosengren, Melkote, and so on. The importance of participation is increasingly being understood as an alternative grassroots approach to development (Craig & Mayo, 1995). Participatory communication is an approach based on dialogue, allowing the exchange of information, perceptions, and opinions among the various stakeholders thereby creating awareness, providing community-based solutions, strengthening community voices, and facilitating the empowerment of vulnerable and marginalized communities. Participatory

approaches aim to put decision-making in the hands of the people. By employing participatory approaches the capability of communities is strengthened to confront their ideas about development projects with planners and technical staff working for aid agencies. In addition, the participatory approach strengthens an internal democratic process within the communities. Such communication determines if the communication process is adapted to each community or social group in terms of content, language, culture, and media, rather than the tendency to use the same communication strategies in diverse cultural settings, and for different social sectors of society (Gumucio-Dagron, 2001). Rosengren (2000) suggests that, above all, communication concerns the process of meaning creation: questions concerning how people create meaning psychologically, socially, and culturally; how messages are understood intellectually; and how ambiguity arises and is resolved. Hence grassroots communication is an umbrella term under which several communication theories remain applicable. For the development of society, participation in concerned communities is important. Participation of people is based on interpersonal communication for providing freedom of expression, building a sense of ownership, and strengthening local-level planning and implementation of programs. By dialogue and consensus-building it enables people to expand their capabilities to negotiate with influence, control and hold accountable institutions that affect their lives (Narayan, 2006). Thus community participation has been recognized as an important aspect of development and is grouped under the ambit of grassroots communication. Also, this process has the potential to enable people to act as protagonists in leading their development. This applies to involvement and use of media tools. In this way, people were empowered
14.5 Grassroots communication Planning
The planning means recording in minute detail, the sequential, hierarchical, supervisory, and specific order of activities as assigned with responsibilities for different members. In the case of Grassroots communication, if the development impetus is top-down, it follows the pattern of development communication planning. If it is from below, that is as advocacy or mobilization, it follows a fountain approach led by local leadership. For Example development approach was used under SwamitvaYojna, initiated by the government, for using drone photography for gathering real-time images of land and identifying ownership in rural areas, this being a development approach to resolve land ownership disputes and also ensure that land taxes are levied on the right measurements. On the other hand, the advocacy done by the farmers under their leader against the three farm laws forms the example under advocacy.
14.5.1 Levels of grassroots communications taking place
Communication between two people occurs on numerous levels simultaneously, each with its nuances and complexities. These levels of communication are verbal, physical, auditory, emotional, and energetic. In terms of grassroots communication, when the communication happens as a development initiative with a top-down approach, it takes a different route and when it occurs as advocacy its path is different. Human communication per se follows six levels. Mass Communication, Organizational or societal/ community Communication, Small Group, Interpersonal, and Intra-personal. In the case of development communication, intrapersonal and interpersonal communication start at the policymaker's end and reach the general public as a means of mass communication. In the case of advocacy, the independent leaders initiate the thought process as intra-personal communication, and it trancesdents into the inter-personal, group, community, and with the aid of various tools and techniques into mass communication.

14.5.2 The stakeholders of Grassroots communication
Individuals and organizations who are actively involved in the project, or whose interests may be positively or negatively affected as a result of program/project execution are stakeholders. The primary stakeholders in a corporation are its investors, employees, customers, and suppliers. Then there are secondary stakeholders and tertiary stakeholders. In the case of grassroots communication the community is always the primary stakeholder along with the government- at the Panchayat level, state level, or central level which may implement the program/act/law affecting the community. Within the community, there may be primary and secondary stakeholders depending on the objective of the program. It is essential that whether developmental/advocacy communication, grassroots communication means engaging with localized stakeholder groups at the grassroots level using a language they understand best. Corporate social responsibility has also brought companies and corporates as primary or secondary stakeholders in development issues and programs. The concept has been extended to include communities, governments, and trade associations.Stakeholders can also be internal or external to an organization. Internal stakeholders are people whose interest in a company comes through a direct relationship, such as employment, ownership, or investment. External stakeholders are those who do not directly work with a company but are affected somehow by the actions and outcomes of the business. Suppliers, creditors, and public groups are all considered external stakeholders. In a professional setting, stakeholders may be as shown in the figure.

14.6 Designing communication strategy for grassroots communication
A communication strategy is a preconceived plan of action to be implemented throughout the length of the program cycle. It involves all decisions of what to communicate and how to communicate at different levels with different stakeholders. It specifies the plan through which the communication objectives have to be met and align these objectives with the production of messages in a meaningful, coherent, and cohesive manner. One must remember that communication being dynamic and flexible must ensure a malleable communication strategy as well. For example, during the Covid pandemic, the use of caller tunes was a very relevant and intelligent approach of the government. All communication strategies in grassroots communications emanate from the target audience which in most cases is the community. For Narmada Bachao Andolan or farmers' protest on farm

bills of 2020, the communication was twofold. One to highlight the points of cohesion between farmers and the other to highlight the points of discord with the proposed laws. On the one hand, it enlightened the farming community on why the protest mattered, and on the other hand, it raised the issues of discontent with alternative solutions to the government. Once the points of clarity on what has to be communicated and to whom emerge, then the important segment is the creation of appropriate messages in the right context and language. The third step is to choose the right media vehicle to take the message forward. Most grassroots protests whether against the CAA or the farm laws are difficult to sustain due to the wrong choice of media vehicle. When development communication tools are used then it is only the community and the geographical area that becomes relevant for use of media vehicles. In the case of advocacy, the idea is to build public opinion in favor of an argument. In such cases, the media vehicles and the appropriate timeliness to advocate matter the most. Last, once the messages are delivered, the revert or rebuttal has to be addressed with modified messages without wasting any time. Thus, the entire strategy is an ongoing process of back and forth communication between stakeholders. Activity 1 Identify two problems in your locality which need immediate attention and ideate a grassroots communication campaign to tackle them.
14.6.1 Grassroots communication
Strategies The communication strategies are identified based on the geographical area of impact. They can be bracketed as National, state, or local level communication strategies. The local level is the predominant type of communication that is seen in grassroots communication. Mostly such protests, Andolan, and demonstrations phase out at a small level through negotiations and settlements. Whether it is re-settlement due to dam construction, inundation of villages or road widening, putting up of a commercial plant, etc. These are local problems sought to be dealt with by local interventions. These local problems escalate to the state level when they spread across districts. The recent Karnataka ban or hijab row in which school authorities sought to impose the uniform strictly and retrain the wearing of hijabs to school resulted in such an escalation that people had to seek the intervention of the High court. The national-level campaigns are low and occur rarely. We can say that the nationalist movement in the 1940s in India was one such movement that connected the grassroots to the epitome of power in India to win the freedom movement. Strategies once determined by geography can further be divided into the use of media platforms for negotiation, external and internal environmental factors, and budget.
14.6.2 Establishing objectives
The setting up of communication objectives is of primary importance in grassroots communication. The objects not only follow the 7 Cs approach of clarity, correctness, conciseness, courtesy, concreteness, consideration, and completeness. But they must also adhere to the SMART which is a mnemonic acronym, giving criteria to guide in the setting of goals and objectives. SMART is an acronym for the five elements of specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-based goals. S - Specific goals have a significantly greater chance of being accomplished. It stresses specifying a specific goal . Measurement means a meaningful and quantifiable aspect that can work to motivate and propel the strategy towards achieving the objective. A stands for achievable or realistic targets. R stands for something relevant that is significant to the attainment of the set goal. T stands for the time-bound attainment of the objective which is the base of any successful strategy.

14.6.3 Identifying stakeholders
As specified above the two primary stakeholders are the community and the government. In grassroots communication, whether the case relates to the establishment of a new order or corporation or implementation of the law. The state comes sharply into the picture. The people who get affected by such implementations are the community and they form the primary stakeholders in the process. The secondary stakeholders are generally the parties affected as a consequence of the implementation of a program or project on the primary stakeholders. In the case of the Vedanta- Foxconn Semiconductor project (2022), the secondary stakeholders would be the builders and the other people who would have contributed in building the project. The tertiary stakeholders would have been the local political parties but in this case, the politicization of the issue led to the withdrawal of the project. The project was shifted to Gujarat from Maharashtra due to various political and bureaucratic hurdles.
14.6.4 Developing & Implementing Grassroots communication Planning
The next step involves identifying the proper messages through the proper channel or medium. These messages when received may ignite new reactions hence senders of the message have to be prepared with probable assessment and management of the social environment. Many-a- times, the media plays the role of adversary and creates problems. Hence, the messages must address the 5 Ws namely what, where, when, who and why very carefully. The H or how of the process has to be explained envisaging what role each stakeholder is expected to play and duties thereof. Once the message designed as per need is proliferated and reactions assessed, it must immediately follow up with a battery of explanations on possible reactions. The more crisp and clear the message, the less the chance for it to be manipulated by other stakeholders including the media. The media vehicles used in the campaign include Print Media- Newspapers, Magazines, and Direct mail; Broadcast Media - Radio, Television, Narrow Cast Media; Outdoor Media; Transit Media; Direct Marketing; Internet; Mobile; Specialty Media like T-shirts, mugs, etc as done in LGBT marches.
14.6.5 Evaluation and Follow-up.
The effectiveness of grassroots communication can be gauged at two levels -1) the communication effect it has created and 2) the attainment of the communication objective. Several times grassroots communications that spring up like advocacy of small groups may not be able to sustain. But if an amicable solution is reached, the government is made to reconsider its allocation or earlier decisions in favor of the community then it is deemed to have been a successful campaign. At times, court interventions are sought to resolve the issue. Likewise, the development initiatives of the government even after showing initial success may register a failure if the project and its outcome are not sustainable. It is always the primary responsibility of the community who are the prime stakeholders to be able to sustain fruitful results of interventions. In the recent campaign by the government to make several Gram Panchayats open defecation free, the government gave a monetary incentive of rupees one lakh to the Panchayat. In earnestness to get the reward, several panchayats set vigil and strictness. But once the Gram Panchayats were awarded the money, the Panchayat loosened their control, and old habits re- emerged. Hence follow-up must be done to ensure adherence to successful practices.
14.7 THE MEDIA MIX FOR GRASSROOTS COMMUNICATION
The communication campaign may use a single media or develop a creative media mix which depends entirely on whether the approach is top-down (development communication) or bottom to up (advocacy by the community) for delivering the campaign messages. The former case generally uses an allocated budget hence has the privilege of using media vehicles used in the advertising campaign including Print Media- Newspapers, Magazines; Broadcast Media - Radio, Television, Narrow Cast Media; Outdoor Media; Transit Media; Direct Marketing; Internet; Mobile; Specialty Media - Tshirts, caps, buttons, badges, etc. and finally digital media

through the use of voice SMS, WhatsApp, automatic call, etc. The more the use of a vehicle, the stronger the probability of delivery of the message and consequently the effectiveness of the persuasive message. When using an allocated budget, attention must be given to the opportune audience, with the apt message at the appropriate time through the right medium. Selecting a media that meets the requirements of the selected target audience is an essential step for a successful media mix selection.
14.7.1 Coverage and Reach
Grassroots communication is a part of the integrated approach to communication. As defined by the American Association of Advertising Agencies, "Integrated marketing communication recognizes the value of a comprehensive plan that evaluates the strategic role of a variety of communication disciplines including advertising, public relations, personal selling, and sales promotion and combines them to provide clarity, consistency and maximum communication impact." Integrated communication campaigns bring different channels together to deliver a message in a way that is effective and persuasive. Frequency and Reach are said to be important for Grassroots communication. Frequency refers to the number of times the communicated message reaches the same person. Reach refers to the total number of people covered. The greater the frequency with which you touch the same person through media selection, the smaller the reach will be and vice versa (assuming a limitation in the size of the budget).
14.7.2 Persuasive Grassroots Communication
The success of messages in general and grassroots communication, in particular, depends on the pressure the message can generate for its acceptance. Grassroots communication whether done for development or by the community for advocacy needs to generate interest, importance, and an adequate amount of stress to follow the desired outcome. For this, although government communication is directed towards pacifying the needs of the community and directional/ instruction in case of awareness campaigns, the community is generally more volatile and disruptive to convey their point of view. Hence it is witnessed that most peaceful protests are marked with violence instigated from either side as keeping the issue alive in the eyes of the media supposedly demands a certain propaganda approach. The farmers' sustained protest against farm bills in 2020 which was marked by violence was more or less peaceful and a very good example of advocacy. 14.7.3 Advantages and disadvantages of Grassroots Communication
The use of grassroots communication is basically for effectiveness. This purposive or strategic approach makes it the very foundation of positive interaction. Like all communications, this will have an emotional impact, actual effect on the ground situation, and factual spread of the message. At the same time, all communications suffer from side effects of wrong interpretation, misinformation, fake news, and consequently result in violence and hatred. The best way forward to prevent such spread is in the clarity and simplicity of the messages and ongoing negotiations.
14.7.4 Media Planning in Digital Age
The digital age has increased the multiplicity of Media along with options of convergence through android phones. There are different digital platforms, networks, syndicated, along with the traditional cable television. This added mix of media not only gives an adequate opportunity of spreading and generating content but at the same time raises the challenges of deep fake and

spread of misinformation. The availability of cheap Android smartphones makes it possible for a community to stay connected through apps like WhatsApp and telegram in exchanging pictures, audio, and video through smartphones. This makes it easy to segment their receivers and targeted population in receiving persuasive messages. Customization, ease of access, and speed are making digital mediums more popular means of reaching the desired public. Search Engine Optimisation (SEO) is one of the most prevalent marketing tools used today. Viral campaigns, reviews, and social media campaigns are fast replacing traditional campaigns. Digital technologies are further enhancing the customer experience by enabling direct interaction between the community, government, corporates, and media. As advocacy or bottom-up communication depends to a great extent on the public opinion hence online surveys can be conducted through survey sites that help gather data from multiple audiences within a limited time frame. Google Analytics can also be used to know the amount of traffic being received on your site/ tweet, in other words, the number of people visiting your site or page. Online keyword search also helps understand the interest and inclination of the general public. A lot of narratives are evolved online through posting on Instagram, tweets, blogs, vlogs, podcasts, reviews, resolve queries and comments. This helps the communication bandwagon to strengthen the direction and orientation of the stakeholders. Another important aspect of digital media is that it is measurable when compared to traditional media. Therefore the exact number of people reached can be gauged successfully. Moreover, it is cheaper compared to traditional media.
14.8 BUDGET CONSIDERATIONS
A choice of media will depend to a large extent upon the size of the media campaign budget. In the case of development communication, there is an inbuilt budget allocation for IEC campaigns by using media and getting the needed involvement and engagement of the community. But in the case of advocacy, there may not be any formal mode of allocated funds. Certain media types may be too expensive for the funds available. For example, the cost of national transmission over Doordarshan may be too high. The cost of maintaining a neon sign cannot be afforded by a small budget. The promotional efforts of the advocacy need banners, pamphlets, and slogans that are made by people who lead such movements at no cost low-cost basis. In the case of developmental projects that affect many geographies, for example, programs executed by Jal Jeewan Mission (JJM), calculated costs as per budgets and pricing of different media and media vehicles, a lot of softwares is used. Media planners are engaged in number-crunching all the time. In such a situation, big budgets are allocated for promotion and public relationship- building exercises.

14.9 LET US SUM UP
Grassroots communication is an umbrella term used to denote development communication and advocacy and mobilizations that arise at the community level. The primary stakeholders in such communications are the community that is affected, the government, and the implementing agency which can be either an NGO or a Corporate. The secondary stakeholders are the middlemen, small businesses, and others who may get affected due to the implementation of a program and finally, the tertiary stakeholders are political parties, groups, media, etc. There are three levels at which communication strategy is operated in grassroots communication-national, state, and local. Generally, it is the local level where discussions happen the most. There may be an allocated budget for communication campaigns mostly if it has a developmental orientation and is being done by the government. In the case of advocacy, the local community may pool in and the slogan making, use of media, etc is more local and voluntary. Sadhguru's Esha Foundation is one such example where a lot of his videos and messages are generated and forwarded by volunteers. There are several growth opportunities in the development sector as urban spaces are saturated. Well-meaning and passionate people can pursue careers in such areas.

14.0 INTRODUCTION
Data is everywhere. Seemingly simple tasks such as deciding which train to take to get home in time for Diwali celebrations involves a series of data-based decisions (when does the train reach its destination, what is the ticket price, how many hours does the journey take, and if tickets are available or not). Now imagine the amount of data journalists need to analyse to write in-depth news reports. They either use data to understand basic patterns to find stories (for example, using government data on education to highlight neglected areas, such as villages with no schools) or to build stories around the data itself (such as a comparison of reading proficiency scores among middle school students from different states in India). But if there is all this data in the world, it obviously needs to be managed, and that too, efficiently. Especially in a field like journalism, where data needs to be processed, analysed and stored in quick, organised and accessible ways. In this unit, we will learn about the tools and systems that are used to create, maintain and manage databases that store the precious commodity we call data.
14.1 LEARNING OBJECTIVES
After going through this unit, you will be able to: understand the connections between databases and database management systems (DBMS); identify various types of DBMS and their uses;

describe how journalists use data and DBMS in their work; apply learnings about data in your own work with information sets in the public domain; and learn how to use literature reviews and referencing software.
14.2 WHAT IS DATABASE MANAGEMENT?
Let us begin by flagging three key terms--database, database management systems (DBMS) and query. Database: A database is simply an organised collection of data. Imagine a dump of books in the library. If these books are sorted as per author name or alphabetically or as per subject, it becomes easier for readers to access the book they want. This book dump is a database or dataset. Database Management System (DBMS): It is simply the mechanism used to sort this data. While a database is essentially a storehouse of all data ever used, DBMS is a system that sorts and organises this data neatly. Query: This is a command we use to obtain the neatly sorted data from a DBMS. According to the tech website GeeksforGeeks.com, a query is a formal request to retrieve or manipulate data stored in a database. Queries let users and applications communicate with the DBMS to fetch, insert, update or delete records. Think of these terms and this process as a Google search, which can help you look for the exact information you need. For example, you wish to know the name of the book written by author Ayn Rand in 1957. In this case: the database is all the books ever written by all authors, the DBMS is the author's name and year of publication, and the query is 'Name of the book written by Ayn Rand in
1957. '
14.3 HOW DIGITAL JOURNALISTS USE DBMS
Now that we have understood the basics of DBMS, let us see how journalists use them to tell their stories. Depending on their need, journalists select the source of data, such as government records, legal documents, annual reports, websites, etc. This could be data from a single source or a cross pollination of data points from diverse sources. They ensure that all data is cleaned and standardised. This forms the database. Thereafter, a DBMS is used to pull data from the database. Once the final data points are collated, journalists analyse it for discrepancies and errors, and to capture trends. Data is then presented through visualisations in the form of bar graphs, pie charts, etc.
14.3.1 Application of Data-Driven Journalism
The use of data is particularly important while reporting on topics that involve using large-scale information. During the Covid-19 pandemic, live dashboards on the CoWin App allowed the authorities to monitor vaccination updates and deploy vaccines quickly and accurately. Many journalists also plugged into public datasets on the availability of beds, oxygen cylinders, etc., to verify the authorities' claims of adequate arrangements. Science journalists use data generated by scientists to comment on current trends and issues. DBMS allows them to avoid duplication, redundancies and inconsistencies in data. Similarly, environment reporters not only use data to understand issues, gaps and challenges, but also develop easy-to-understand graphics and visualisations. We know weather charts on TV make it easy to present large amounts of data. Other important domains where data is used often include crime, business and solutions journalism. This type of reporting requires accessing multiple datasets and efficient DBMS.
T. Sukumar, a Mint data journalist (2025), analysed the Time Use Survey 2024, to study sleep
patterns and gender disparities in labour and leisure activities. The dataset included 10.2 million rows from 454,192 respondents. It logged 24-hour activity diaries, including sleep episodes, bedtime routines and disruptions. Queries grouped data by age, gender and location to reveal

trends. It was found that women in their 30s sleep around 29 minutes less than men. Pre-bedtime activities differ too: women often clean kitchens, while men watch TV or use phones, and childcare disrupts women's sleep far more than men's. This is a good example of how journalists can use DBMS to tell their stories.
14.3.2 Integrating Databases into Storytelling
Telling stories using data is not as easy as it sounds. Journalists need to adhere to strict protocols when working with data. Data can be confusing, complex or sometimes irrelevant. Therefore, one needs to adopt a systemic approach. Let us look at some of the steps involved in integrating database into news reporting. Step 1: A journalist must first define their data needs. What is the purpose of the investigation, the answers they are seeking, and the type of information required, such as crime or health statistics. Step 2: Collect and combine raw data from different sources. Convert this data into a DBMS-friendly file. You will need to clean and standardise it - file formats may need to be changed, columns and rows may need headers, etc. Step 3: The core data to be analysed is picked up from the dataset. It is classified based on entities (e.g., "State," "Literacy rate," "Year" and their attributes (name, percentage, year). This data is now structured, based on which visualisations can be done. Step 4: The data is now loaded into a suitable DBMS such as MySQL, MongoDB, and others, which we will discuss later in the unit. Using queries, we retrieve specific information and perform complex operations to find patterns and anomalies in it. Step 5: Now, the results of the queries are analysed to uncover the narrative and identify key findings. The story angles and points of interest are decided as per editorial requirements. A storyline is created using information from the data and breaking it down into smaller, understandable bits. Step 6: The story is published using a combination of texts, videos, graphs, charts, maps, etc. for easy understanding. Data visualisation is supported by text inputs that explain the significance of the data and how to connect it to existing information. Some data stories evolve daily and use comparison charts to highlight changing trends, such as in elections as different phases of polling are completed. 14.4 OVERVIEW OF DATABASE MANAGEMENT IN
DIGITAL MEDIA
So far, we have discussed what DBMS is, and how journalists integrate it into the process of storytelling. Now, we will delve deeper and explore the technical aspects of DBMS, including its types and how they are optimally utilised. To reiterate, DBMS is software that helps organise, store and manage data so it can be easily accessed, updated and shared. A film song may be organised in a DBMS as per names of the singer, music director or film. You can access the song using any of this information. The results will be same regardless of who or how many people are searching for the data. Here's another example. A list of villages with number of toilets constructed as part of the Swachh Bharat Mission (SBM) is a dataset. When this list is sorted and organised as per fields such as State> District> Block> Village, and into categories such as dry and wet latrines, year and month of construction, this becomes a database. As a journalist, one can command the system to pick the number of toilets built under SBM per district in any month of any year in the database. It can also be used to compare data from two districts within the same time frame. This data is maintained using specialised DBMS software categorised as Relational DBMS (RDBMS) where data is structured and filed into rows and columns. Conversely, another DBMS type, Not Only SQL Database Management Systems (NoSQL DBMS) have data that is unstructured but quickly identifiable. There are also cloud-based systems which are the most advanced versions available today. All of these will be discussed at length later. Given below is a basic step-by-step guide on how a DBMS system works: Step 1: The User/Application sends a query (e.g., using a SQL command, which is simply an instruction used to communicate with a database to perform specific tasks). Step 2: The Query Processor, which is a sequence of steps to translate the SQL command, interprets the request. Step 3: The Transaction Manager ensures consistency and manages simultaneous operations. Step 4: The Storage Manager retrieves or updates data from the Database, and Step 5: Results are returned to the User/Application.
14.5 TYPES OF DATABASES
Although there are different types of DBMS, here we will focus on three types. Let us discuss these in detail.
14.5.1 Relational Database Management Systems (RDBMS)
RDBMS is a software system that organises data into tables (rows and columns), making it easy to store, search and analyse structured information. It is especially useful for managing large datasets, tracking sources, archiving articles and analysing trends. Relational databases, such as MySQL, PostgreSQL, and SQLite, are the most common type used in data journalism. Here are some advantages of using RDBMS: RDBMS supports ACID (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability).The ACID principle means that the entire dataset moves as one unit. If changes are made to any dataset, then all connected files in the system automatically reflect that change. It is very useful in cases where data needs to be accurate. For example, for health records of patients. Data is stored in tables which represent a specific entity. Relationships between tables are defined using keys. RDBMS such as MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL and Microsoft SQL Server store information in structured formats, and provide tools to create, update, delete and query data using languages

like SQL. They control access, enforce rules to maintain consistency, and protect data from unauthorised use. But they also allow multiple users to work with the same database simultaneously. The data is available, backed up, and optimised for fast queries. This allows journalists to work from different locations and collaborate on cross-border investigative themes. In addition to tracking journalists' work, it can be used to compile all interviews with a politician or celebrity, and manage list of sources, contacts, interview transcripts, etc. It is important to note that SQL is not a software -- it is just the set of rules and syntax. It is often considered same as MySQL. However, MySQL is a type of RDBMS that uses SQL. SQL is like the English language used in many tools (Word, Google Docs, Notepad).
14.5.2 NoSQL DBMS
NoSQL is a class of non-relational databases designed to store, process and scale large volumes of unstructured or semi-structured data. NoSQL DBMS is not always accurate as it prioritises the ability to integrate wider access more than the accuracy of data. It also allows us to easily add columns, headers, etc., in comparison to RDBMS. Here are some advantages of using NoSQL DBMS: Its ability to use multiple query languages makes it more user-friendly. A large amount of data can be saved as infographics, posters, etc., here. It is used to manage live updates from social media, sensors or public dashboards (e.g., Covid-19 vaccination data). The most frequent use of NoSQL DBMS is to collate audience metrics, meaning it is useful for storing and analysing user interactions, comments and engagement metrics from websites and apps. This type of DBMS allows us to use flexible formats such as key-value pairs, documents, graphs or wide-column stores. The key is a label or name that helps you find information quickly, and the value is the actual data linked to that key. For example, in a database of images, the key might be "photo_20251124_001" and the value could be details of the photo, such as its filename, caption, date and tags. This allows journalists to quickly retrieve, update or search for images based on tags, dates or captions--without needing a rigid table structure. The choice to use RDBMS and NoSQL depends on the needs of the newsroom and the type of information to be stored.
14.5.3 Cloud-based DBMS
Cloud-based DBMS is a system that operates on cloud infrastructure, providing scalable, on-demand access to database services over the internet. It allows users to create custom tables to manage articles, sources, multimedia assets and project workflows. Since cloud-based versions include features like automated backups, keeping multiple copies of the same information to facilitate quick retrieval and faster processing, and failover mechanisms, they are preferable when we need to work with large datasets. They are usually compatible with all query languages and are therefore easier to integrate. Among the more popular cloud-based DBMS are Google Sheets, Airtable, etc. Some key advantages of cloud-based DBMS are: This system allows you to access data from anywhere. This helps journalists to access documents and databases from the newsroom or from the field, enabling faster story production. It is best for collaborations across newsrooms. Reporters, editors and fact-checkers can all access and analyse the data real-time. This improves coordination, especially in large-scale and cross-border collaborations. Cloud-storage can offer enhanced data security. Not only does it enable backup, it can help in handling sensitive data effectively using encryption and strong security measures.

These systems do not require onsite presence and therefore are often preferred by smaller newsrooms with limited budgets.
14.6 DBMS TOOLS POPULAR IN JOURNALISM
14.6.1 MySQL
This is a type of RDBMS that organises information in tables with rows and columns, like a spreadsheet. It is ideal for keeping track of articles, interviews, contacts, etc. A newsroom uses MySQL to quickly find articles by author or topic, or to compile interviews with a politician. Social media networks, user profiles, activity data, etc. can be easily analysed by APIs or web scraping. This type of information is useful in investigating the spread of misinformation. It also helps news organisations to connect with readers, understand their preferences and serve custom content.
14.6.2 MongoDB
It's a type of NoSQL DBMS that is good for handling various information formats. Its features make it easy for teams to group, sort, access and change information quickly, so reports can be made faster and searches work well. Newsrooms use MongoDB to manage thousands of images, each with captions, dates and tags, making it easy to search and organise without strict rules.
14.6.3 Airtable
This is a cloud-based DBMS that supports real-time collaboration between teams, allowing members to update records of their stories, attach files, and track progress from anywhere. It is used frequently for data-oriented collaborations. It is also useful to track audience engagement, surveys and impact analysis. While Google Sheets is used as a basic go-to tool, Airtable is being adopted for its advanced features and workflows.
14.7 REFERENCING AND LITERATURE REVIEW IN
DIGITAL MEDIA
So far, we learnt about DBMS - what they are, how they work, their types and tools. Now, let us turn to the concept of referencing. Journalists are constantly referring to sources in the course of researching their stories. How do they navigate and acknowledge these sources in their work? In this section, we will talk about two intertwined processes: literature review and referencing. Let's get started.
14.7.1 Purpose and Process
Literature reviews are foundational to the work journalists do. It is essential for them to understand what has been already published, what facts are debated, where and what type of gaps exists in knowledge. As a journalist, a good literature review will give you ideas about sources to reach out to, organisations to contact for quotes, data required to strengthen the story and decide story angles. Poor literature review makes the reporter look incompetent and might cause important issues to be overlooked. Here are some tips to do a literature review efficiently: Decide the broad area of your work, but narrow it down to small, searchable goals. Refer to multiple sources for the same search topic. Information from different sources may indicate discrepancies and anomalies. Always keep your goal in mind. Check bibliographies. These are found at the end of the story/article and could lead you to other important resources. While searching for information, you might find it hard to keep track of information. However, using Excel sheets or referencing software such as EndNote and Zotero can help you save the references.

Remember to keep neat summaries of each page you visit, essentially, one paragraph notes on what that resource was about. This is very useful in the long run as you may need to revisit the resource over the years.
14.7.2 Reference Management Tools
As mentioned above, Zotero and Mendeley are two reference management tools that help journalists and researchers organise, store and cite sources efficiently. They work by capturing metadata, which is information that contains details about other data or digital assets such as keywords, tags, filetype, author name, etc. Using these software makes it easy to save articles, books and webpages directly into libraries, add notes, and sort sources by tags or keywords. The metadata makes it easy to search and retrieve references later. Zotero and Mendeley also integrate with word processors, allowing users to insert citations and build bibliographies in various styles. They streamline data collection and help in acknowledging textual and other sources, which plays a big role in maintaining journalistic integrity.
14.8 EVALUATING SOURCES AND CREDIBILITY
All information you find online may not be useful. It may not even be authentic or credible. Journalists follow some tricks to check claims quickly. Begin by checking the source: The first stage is always 'who said this?' Is there an official declaration or statement available on the website of the concerned organisation? Is there video or audio evidence? But this too can be manipulated using AI. If the statement is true, does the person stating it have any knowledge about it? For example, celebrities tweet about health benefits of potential alternative cancer treatments, but oncologists say these are not proven. Is the information being shared merely for publicity, or as part of propaganda? All these factors should be checked. Independent verification of facts: You must fact-check claims by triangulating information. Using multiple sources, talking to experts, referring to archives and public data sources help in this verification. Objective of information: Sometimes information is published or presented to spread misinformation or disinformation or serve some political or economic interests. Consider the purpose of the source and look for potential biases or conflicts of interest. Transparency: Journalists often seek accountability and transparency from governments. And they, in turn, are transparent about their own sources, unless the source wants to remain anonymous. This helps readers verify if the conclusion drawn by the journalist is accurate. Critical Thinking: Reporters must analyse the relevance of a piece of information to the story, question assumptions, and strive for balanced reporting by including multiple perspectives. Ultimately, journalism rests on facts, not opinions and assumptions. So, journalists need to ensure that digital and human systems are incontestably trustworthy so they can deliver stories that serve public good. 14.9 LET US SUM UP
In this unit, we learned about database, DBMS and referencing software. A database is a collection of data from one or more sources. This could be in various formats such as scanned files, excel sheets, infographics, etc. We then discussed DBMS or database management system, which is used to make sense of this data, and explained how journalists use databases and DBMS to organise, analyse and present information in digital media. We also covered the basics of cleaning and preparing data, different types of databases (like MySQL and MongoDB), and how these tools help manage articles, images, and multimedia content. Examples from newsrooms were discussed o illustrate how technology and teamwork help uncover complex stories. In the final section of the unit, we discussed ways to do a quick, efficient literature review, and referencing software which journalists can use to manage sources and references.
14.10 KEYWORDS
DBMS: A database management system is a software that helps organise, store and manage data in a database so it can be easily accessed, updated and shared. RDBMS: Relational database management system organises data into tables (rows and columns), making it easy to store, search, and analyse structured information. NoSQL: NoSQL is a class of non-relational databases designed to store, process and scale large volumes of unstructured or semi-structured data. Key Pairs: Each piece of data has two parts: a "key" and a "value." The key is like a label that helps you find the information quickly, and the value is the actual data or content linked to that key. Cloud-based DBMS: It is a DBMS that operates on cloud infrastructure, providing scalable and on- demand access to database services over the internet. Metadata: Metadata is a set of information that contains details about other data or digital assets such as keywords, tags, filetype, author name, etc.

15.2 SOCIAL MEDIA AND ITS IMPORTANCE FOR BRANDS
15.2.1 What is social media?
Social media is where your brand goes to interact with its online audience. It is also where your customers and fans introduce your brand to their friends and followers through their comments, likes, posts, retweets, reels, videos, and more. Thus, brands can receive rich unmediated customer insights faster than ever. This action initiated by customers leverages their brand and adds credibility. The idea of the brands is to reach a considerable audience and create awareness about their brand. This will attract more traffic and engagement which will help generate more leads. The objective is to bring the customers to your website and pull them to purchase. There is also the negative side of the exponential exposure that brands get on social media- the trolls. Trolling is when you respond to online content or comments in a purposely disruptive fashion. It happens when a brand puts up something controversial on social media intentionally or unintentionally, the post draws the attention of the same people, and the brand gets beat up. Brands need to understand the social media dynamics and stay up to date with the trends popular amongst people. This is how they can use social media to their advantage.
15.2.2 How Is Social Media Useful For Branding?
Social media has challenged brands to explore newer ways of reaching out to their prospects. Thus, it is quite different from the traditional approach of placing advertisements on mass media. It is not linear. Social media interaction is more divergent and two-way. The idea is to compete against multiple brands using social media platforms. Although the cost-effectiveness of social media in comparison to traditional media, makes it more attractive. But the volatility and short attention span pose a big challenge. To create customer-connect you need to build relationships, and open-up, thereby building trust gradually. You cannot buy authenticity; brands need to win customers through the ways they reach out to them. Social media acts as an effective tool for promoting brands as: * engaging content across various platforms to help attract and reach out to the new audience. * Social engagement helps to reflect your brand personality. This helps build authenticity and thereby trust and authority. * endless opportunities for customer service and support are provided * other marketing activities are complemented * platforms for networking are provided * feedback and engagement on platforms are encouraged * traditional and social media platforms may be rightly mixed to engage customers for contests and rewards schemes * exclusive offers for fans on social media are provided Activity - 1 Go through the social media platforms of Coca-Cola and make a note of the various efforts they are making to engage customers on their platform

15.5 DO's AND DON'Ts OF SOCIAL MEDIA BRANDING
Brands use different social media platforms based on their business and the characteristics of the platform.
15.5.1 Do's of Social Media Branding
* Choose the social media platform-specific to your business needs. Though you might want to have your presence on all social media platforms, you need to see whether it caters to your business objective. Also, it is not feasible to manage all social media platforms and do justice to them. * Evaluate from time to time in terms of which part of the content is helping you maximize your profits or the part of the content which is not able to pull in the expected crowd. Use social media tools to analyze it. * You must know how to use search engine optimization (SEO) to your advantage. In simple terms, it is extremely important for you to be known by people if you wish to increase your sales. * Post the right content at the right time. Make efforts to find out your target audience and the time when they are online, depending on this you can decide to post. * Give a human touch to your content. Engage with your audience at a personal level and build connections. They should get a feeling that they are interacting with humans and not robots. * Images, Infographics, and videos are more appealing than plain text. * Appreciate your followers for subscribing or following you and incentivize them. Give them rewards or discounts or lucky draw entries and giveaways to join. * Maintain professionalism in your posts. Do not give individual opinions * Learn to face the trolls * Your followers must look forward to your updates. * Make your content easy to share. * Interact with users who share your posts * Familiarize yourself with the guidelines of the platform. * You must have customer involvement if you wish to become a popular brand. You must get customers to promote your brand and make them your brand ambassador. You must conduct competitions to get the customers involved in your business and visit your pages on a regular basis. * Be prepared for the worst and have a plan in place that will allow you to quickly act and save the day. * You must try and reinvent yourself from time to time and give your audience something new to experience. If you do all these then rest assured, your company would do well in the social media marketing field.
15.5.2 Don'ts of Social Media Marketing
* Know your boundaries while interacting with your audience. You will see that it is possible for you to connect with your audience in a better way if you keep it professional. * Explore all the features of the social media platform and make sure that you are using everything to your advantage. * Do not repeat the same content on all your different platforms. You must keep the same tone but present the products in a different way. * You must update your account from time to time. Brands need to be careful of their social media acts to avoid any controversy which leads to Online vigilantism.

(Note: Online vigilantism started from the action of doxing, which is the publishing of personal information of a particular subject on the internet (mainly on social media such as Facebook and Twitter), with malicious intent. The main idea of online vigilantism is to publicly shame their target to get a response from the authorities or in the lack of any response from the authorities.)
15.6 CHOOSING SOCIAL MEDIA PLATFORM FOR YOUR BUSINESS
Brands need to know that each social media platform has its own benefits, limitations and the way it interacts with content and the users. Brands need to have a look at the following aspects before deciding on a social media platform for their business. * It is based on the nature of your business whether it is business-to-business (B2B) or Business to consumer (B2C). B2C companies can prefer Facebook and Instagram when they want visual engagement, gaining visibility, or interaction with customers. LinkedIn is better for B2B companies as it helps in reaching out to current and potential clients and helps build personal connections. YouTube can attract an audience irrespective of the nature of the business due to its audio-visual appeal, secondly, it's Google-friendly and adds authenticity. * Research to find out who your target audience are i.e., their demographics. * Research to find out on which platform your target audience will be available. * Master the platform where your target audience is available. * Research your top competitors to find out the social media platforms they are engaged in, the content they are posting there, the frequency of posting the content, and number of users engaging with the content. Based on this research, choose the social media for your brand which can yield the best results. * Keep your website up to date as you need to direct traffic from all social media platforms to your website. * Build a consistent strategy across the platform. * Participate in discussions or forums, engage with the audience. With its 10 million monthly viewers and over 500,000 followers on the IKEA USA page alone and they have established a global presence. One example of a successful campaign of IKEA was the one that ran in 2019. IKEA furniture realized that back to school was the peak time when school students look for furniture options. IKEA thought to address the requirements of the college-going students with a limited budget and limited space in their dorm/hostel. They devised a compact and small-space-friendly design and floated it on Pinterest to keep the target audience in

mind. They used Pinterest and Promoted Pins and keywords like "dorm ideas" and "dorm room organization" to push traffic in the right direction. As a result, their click-through rate increased by 72%, and the Cost Per Click decreased by 37%. Starbucks made a dramatic launch of a neon-colored pink-and-purple fruity drink, Unicorn Frappuccino, that changes color as you consume it. Starbucks created hype and generated curiosity among the younger generation. Millennials were aroused by feelings of FOMO (fear of missing out) as this beverage was served for a limited time only. This attractive and colorful beverage was suitable for posting pictures on Instagram, as well as Facebook, Pinterest, and Twitter. The customers went ahead and shared their pictures with the drinks. With the marketing gimmick of creating a scarcity of the Frappuccino's availability, a craze for the beverage was ignited. When paired with constant social media campaigns of the Unicorn Frappuccino and its hashtag #unicornfrappuccino Starbucks attracted customers' attention. The campaign went viral in no time. It was successful in generating a 'Call to Action'. People queued up in large numbers outside physical stores to purchase the drink before it was out of stock.

15.0 INTRODUCTION
The present unit has covered various dimensions of environmental governance, ranging from global initiatives to national policies, economic drivers, political ideologies, public engagement, media influence, and the crucial process of Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA). Understanding environmental governance is essential in the face of pressing global challenges such as climate change, biodiversity loss, pollution, and resource depletion. The interconnectedness of these issues necessitates collaborative efforts at local, national, and international levels. Economic drivers and their impact on the environment have been explored, including case studies on industries affecting natural ecosystems. Public engagement and activism have been highlighted as catalysts for positive environmental change, showcasing the power of collective action. The role of media in shaping environmental narratives, influencing public perception, and contributing to policy responses has also been examined. Additionally, the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) process has been discussed.

15.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After working through this Unit, you will be able to: * understand the concept of environmental governance * know about the various case studies * examine the impact of public engagement and activism on environmental issues * gain an insight into media framing and public perception of environmental issues
15.2 OVERVIEW OF MAJOR ENVIRONMENTAL
CHALLENGES
The global community faces a multitude of urgent environmental challenges stemming from both human activities and natural processes. Chief among these challenges is climate change, driven by the accumulation of greenhouse gases from activities like fossil fuel burning and deforestation. This phenomenon leads to widespread impacts on weather patterns, sea levels, and ecosystems. Another critical concern is the rapid loss of species and ecosystems, driven by habitat destruction, pollution, climate change, and resource overexploitation. Deforestation remains a pressing issue, contributing to climate change and habitat loss. Pollution in various forms--air, water, and soil--poses pervasive threats to both the environment and human health. Water scarcity, unsustainable fishing practices, improper waste disposal, and soil degradation further compound the environmental challenges. Addressing these interconnected issues requires collaborative efforts from governments, industries, communities, and individuals, emphasizing sustainable practices, eco-friendly technologies, and effective policies to safeguard the environment.
15.2.1 Interconnectedness of Economic and Political Factors With
Environmental Problems
The intricate relationship between economic and political factors and environmental issues forms a complex web that necessitates a nuanced understanding for effective strategies in addressing environmental challenges. Swift economic growth tends to fuel resource consumption, industrialization, and urbanization, contributing to environmental degradation and biodiversity loss. Political decisions and policies, especially economic ones like subsidies and tax incentives, play a pivotal role in shaping environmental outcomes; for instance, subsidies for fossil fuels may impede the shift to cleaner energy sources. Environmental externalities, wherein the costs or benefits of economic activities are not reflected in market prices, can lead to overuse of resources and pollution. Global economic interdependence, driven by international trade and supply chains, contributes to a globalized environmental impact as the production of goods in one region may result in resource depletion and pollution elsewhere. While economic growth and technological advancements can offer solutions through cleaner technologies and sustainable practices, they also pose risks if environmentally harmful technologies are prioritized. Political power distribution influences that how environmental policies are crafted and executed, often disproportionately affecting economically disadvantaged communities. Addressing trans-boundary environmental issues necessitates international cooperation, with political collaboration and economic agreements facilitating coordinated efforts to combat global challenges like climate change, biodiversity loss, and marine pollution.
15.3 ECONOMIC DRIVERS: EXPLORATION OF ECONOMIC
INTERESTS IN ENVIRONMENTAL ISSUES

Economic drivers significantly shape societal interactions with the environment, with pursuits of development and prosperity often giving rise to environmental challenges. Many of these issues stem from the extraction and exploitation of natural resources driven by economic demands for raw materials, minerals, and energy sources. Activities to meet the demand for goods and services, such as deforestation, habitat destruction, and resource depletion, are common practices. Economic growth and development involve industrialization and urbanization, contributing to pollution, habitat fragmentation, and ecosystem pressure. Agricultural practices, responding to economic demands for food, can lead to deforestation, soil degradation, water pollution, and biodiversity loss. The pursuit of energy, often linked to economic growth, results in fossil fuel extraction, deforestation for bioenergy, and large-scale energy infrastructure, contributing to air pollution and climate change. Economic systems encouraging consumerism and overconsumption drive increased production and resource use. While economic interests drive technological innovation, profit-focused motives may prioritize short-term gains over long-term environmental sustainability. Economic globalization and international trade contribute to the movement of goods and resources across borders, potentially leading to environmental exploitation in one region to meet consumption demands elsewhere.
15.3.1 Case Studies on Industries Affecting the Environment
Several industries have left significant environmental footprints, exemplified by specific cases: * Deepwater Horizon Oil Spill (2010): Among the largest environmental disasters, the spill in the Gulf of Mexico released millions of barrels of crude oil, causing extensive damage to marine ecosystems and coastal areas. Long-term effects on the Gulf's ecosystem are still under study. * Ok Tedi Mine (Papua New Guinea): Operating since the 1980s, the Ok Tedi mine's waste disposal into the Ok Tedi River has led to deforestation, heavy metal contamination, and disruption of local ecosystems. Mitigation measures are being implemented to address environmental concerns. * Amazon Rainforest Deforestation (Linked to Agriculture): Agricultural expansion drives deforestation in the Amazon, contributing to biodiversity loss, ecosystem disruption, and significant carbon emissions. * Water Pollution in Textile Manufacturing (Various Locations): Textile manufacturing, especially in developing countries, involves water-intensive processes, discharging pollutants into rivers. Untreated wastewater harms aquatic ecosystems and poses risks to human health, prompting efforts for sustainable practices. * Deforestation in the Amazon (Linked to Timber Industry): The timber industry, often associated with illegal logging, contributes to deforestation, leading to biodiversity loss and ecosystem disruption in the Amazon.
15.4 Environmental Economics - Introduction to concepts like
externalities Environmental economics is a branch of economics that examines the economic impact of environmental policies and seeks to provide solutions to environmental challenges. One key concept within environmental economics is the notion of externalities, which plays a crucial role in understanding the interplay between economic activities and the environment. Externalities refer to the unintended and unaccounted-for side effects of economic activities that affect third parties, either positively or negatively, without corresponding compensation. These effects are not reflected in the market prices of goods or services and can lead to inefficiencies in resource allocation. Understanding externalities is fundamental to addressing environmental challenges within an economic framework. Environmental economics provides valuable insights into how policy interventions can

correct market failures, promote efficient resource use, and contribute to sustainable development. By internalizing externalities, societies can strive for economic activities that balance individual interests with broader societal and environmental considerations.
15.4.1 The Role of Economic Policies in Environmental Conservation
Economic policies play a pivotal role in environmental conservation by shaping the behavior of individuals, businesses, and governments. Their goal is to align economic activities with environmental sustainability objectives, internalize externalities, and encourage the efficient use of natural resources. Measures such as taxes on environmentally harmful activities, like pollution or resource extraction, discourage such behavior by incorporating associated costs. Government incentives, such as subsidies or tax credits, promote renewable energy production, reducing reliance on fossil fuels. Standards and regulations set by governments limit industries' environmental impact, covering areas like emissions, water quality, and waste disposal.
15.5 POLITICAL IDEOLOGIES AND POWER STRUCTURES
Political ideologies and power structures are interconnected elements that shape the organization and governance of societies. These concepts influence how governments operate, allocate resources, and interact with citizens. Political ideologies are sets of beliefs and values that guide political thought and actions. They provide frameworks for understanding the role of government, individual rights, and societal organization. Power structures refer to the distribution and exercise of authority within a society.
15.5.1 Role of Political Institutions in Shaping Environmental Outcomes
The role of political institutions in shaping environmental outcomes is significant, as they influence the creation, execution, and enforcement of environmental policies. Government bodies, legislative entities, regulatory agencies, and international organizations collectively establish rules and incentives guiding societal interactions with the environment. Legislative bodies formulate laws related to environmental protection, creating a legal framework, while specialized agencies focus on policy development and research. Regulatory agencies, empowered by political institutions, monitor compliance, investigate violations, and enforce penalties. International negotiations result in environmental treaties, and organizations like the United Nations Environment Programme facilitate global cooperation. Political institutions employ economic tools, such as environmental taxes and subsidies, to incentivize or discourage specific behaviors, exemplified by carbon taxes encouraging emission reduction. Cap- and-trade systems allocate emissions allowances, providing economic incentives for emission reduction. Public participation in decision-making is facilitated, enhancing transparency and legitimacy. NGOs influence political institutions, providing expertise and advocating for stronger environmental protections. Local political bodies impact land-use planning and zoning, influencing ecosystems. Environmental impact assessments are required for projects, and certification programs encourage sustainable practices. Funding for research and development of eco-friendly technologies is allocated, supporting innovation for sustainability. Understanding the role of political institutions is crucial for effective environmental policy development and strategy implementation, involving policy design, regulation enforcement, and international cooperation.
15.5.2 International Agreements and Treaties Addressing Environmental Issues
Several international agreements and treaties have been instituted to tackle global environmental challenges and foster sustainable practices. Noteworthy examples encompass the Paris Agreement (2015), uniting 196 nations to curb global temperature rise and mitigate greenhouse gas emissions. The Montreal Protocol (1987) successfully strives to phase out substances detrimental to the ozone layer, contributing to its recovery. The Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) (1992) focuses on

conserving biodiversity, ensuring sustainable usage, and advocating equitable sharing of genetic resource benefits. The UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) (1992) lays the groundwork for international climate collaboration, encompassing pivotal agreements like the Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement. The Kyoto Protocol (1997) pioneers legally binding emission reduction targets for developed nations, setting the stage for subsequent climate accords. The Ramsar Convention on Wetlands (1971) concentrates on conserving and sustainably utilizing wetlands, designating them as internationally significant. Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES), 1975 addresses the threat of trade to the survival of wildlife by regulating and monitoring the trade of listed species.
