2.4 TYPES OF INTEGRATED COMMUNICATION STRATEGIES
In today's scenario when the number of publications is in lakhs, TV channels in thousands and radio channels in hundreds in our country and not to forget about millions of websites, blogs, easily accessible social media networks and chatting apps, it becomes a challenge for the communication planners to create and design any communication strategy for any organization. In this complex communication scenario, it requires a lot of hard work in understanding data related to media consumption patterns of consumers. With the advancement of analytics tools integration of communication channels in strategy planning and its measurement becomes effective. Even social listening and feedback surveys provide vital inputs that help to understand their audiences better. They can use these insights to determine what messages and which channels will create awareness, interest and lead to the action.
2.4.1 Relationship Communication Strategy
Communication is not only a tool of information, but participatory communication is a social phenomenon. Interactive communication creates meaningful relationships amongst organisations and communities. Maintaining good relations within the organization and with the external publics is an important aspect which is important in image building. Integrated communication can be helpful in maintaining relations in following ways:
i) Maintaining Relations Through Dialogue
Monologues in organisations are things of the past as new media has created new avenues for participatory and instant communication. Using interpersonal communication to maintain goodwill is the key to successful and effective communication. With the usage of Information and Communication Technologies it has become easier for the organisations and brands to communicate with their target audience frequently and easily. Dialogue boxes on websites, chatbots and responses through feedback play a crucial role maintaining relationships with the existing and potential buyers. ii) Maintaining Relationship using Public Relations Tools Public Relations is a communication method to maintain good relations and project a good image in front of stakeholders. There are publics of the organization/brand/government like employees,

dealers, retailers, customers, regulatory bodies, funding institutions, investors etc. To maintain goodwill a combination of various communication tools is used like House Journals, newsletter, Open houses, Bulletins, Websites, social media, meetings etc are used. All the students of IGNOU pursuing this course are the most important internal public of IGNOU. To communicate to you, the university uses emails, websites, letters, chats etc to keep you updated about the admissions, registration, study material, exams and results etc. Besides you, faculty members and admin staff of university are also internal publics. University Grant Commission, Ministry of Human Resource Development, Department of Higher Education, media organisations and other regulatory bodies of various programmes are important external publics for IGNOU. To maintain good relations with them, the university uses Newsletters, Annual Reports, Meetings, press releases, Press conferences and Institutional advertising.
2.4.2 Integrated Brand Promotion
The purpose of promotions is to create meaningful relationship with the target audience and make communication effective which adds more value to the brand. Its promotion is done through various communication channels in such a way that publicises the brand, consequently, increases the net profit. Although the term 'promotion' seems more related to marketing, yet the communication aspect of this tool creates a positive brand reputation that helps in more visibility of the brand. Communication with all the stakeholders with each other and with the brand helps in the promotion of the brand, making it more recognisable. This recognition creates the visibility of the brand in consumer's top of the mind recall. A consistent message from various communication channels makes the brand more trustworthy.
2.4.3 Positioning Communication Strategy
According to noted authors Al Ries and Jack Trout "Positioning is not what you do to the product. Positioning is what you do to the mind of the prospect." Position of a brand/individual/place/organization is not created unless consumers perceive its image in their minds. Effective communication messages promote only one central image that reflects one positioning idea. Positioning may be communicated on the basis of product, benefit, usage, attribute, price, quantity, quality or competitor. For example, in cosmetics Olay advertises its beauty products for 'middle aged women' whereas Elle18 positions itself for 'teenagers'. Digestive biscuits are positioned as healthy biscuits whereas Monaco positions itself as light biscuits. Lux is a beauty soap whereas Dettol is antiseptic soap.
2.4.4 Push and Pull Communication Strategy
All the communication by the organisation/brand is not always directed to the end users of their product/services. The communication is directed towards other stakeholders like retailers, distributors, influencers, investors, regulators etc. In the 21st century, most of the communication is directed towards stakeholders in electronic form i.e., through email, social media, websites and mobile etc. Communication through e-means is fast, customised and cost effective and may be sent to millions of receivers instantly. The target audiences are pulled towards products, services or ideas by creating awareness, attraction, interest and desire. The information about promotions on products pulls the customers towards distributors and retailers to buy the products. You must have observed while buying essential items for your household when you ask for a particular brand from the shopkeeper, he refuses to give the brand apparently because of unavailability, high price or low quality and you end up buying any other brand suggested by him with assurance of quality, quantity or low price. This strategy is pushed through communication by the brand for the retailers or distributors. They get more incentives or profit margins by the manufacturer for pushing their brand towards customers. Even aesthetically displayed new products in hypermarkets and departmental stores are pushed by the visual appeal and customers buy new/undesired products due to visual appeal.

Organisations and brands use both push and pull communication strategies to increase brand awareness and market share.
2.4.5 Advertising Strategy
Advertising is the most important paid form of communication used by brands irrespective of the size of the company. From small retailers to conglomerates, advertising is used as a means of communication with the target audience. Advertising strategy and its budget allocation depends upon marketing strategy and financial health of the organisation. Leiss et al. (1986) identify two approaches to the use of advertising as a tool of integrated marketing communication:
1. Hard sell approach: This type of advertising approach communicates a reason to buy for a
specific need satisfaction, recommends a unique selling proposition to buy a particular brand in the product category, uses a rational or fear appeal to create desire and persuades the buyers for prompt action.
2. Soft sell approach: Advertising may not always depict any rationale to buy a brand or take
action, at times stories of consumers with emotional appeal get imprinted into the audience and he;ps in the top-of-mind recall. The emotions take consumers to their near and dear ones in imagination. Dhara Refined Oil TV commercial with little kid who leaves the home, Dairy Milk 'Kuchh Khas Hai Hum Sabhi Me' the girl dancing in the cricket ground are examples of the unforgettable commercials based on emotional appeal. Consumers love such advertisements and some of the long TV commercials became popular like 'soap opera'. Advertising strategies can be categorised on the basis of motivation to create interest or purchase by customer. For example- I-phone's sleek looks created a storm in the market and the motivation to buy an IPhone was 'buy world's sleekest i-phone". In case of apparels, shoes and even cars, all sell on 'Looks Strategy' where appearance of the product is motivation for the customer to buy a product. Same way the "utility strategy" emphasises on how beneficial a product is to the consumer. For example, Moov's focus is always on pain relief in all the advertisements in various media.
2.4.6 Message Strategies
Message is the most important aspect and central idea of any communication strategy. Message strategy is the key approach for any integrated communication strategy. There are three types of message strategies include cognitive, affective, and conative approaches: Cognitive Message Strategies - For a product which can explain its benefits based on consumers' needs uses cognitive message strategy. It presents rational arguments or facts about the brand/place/individual/organisation. The message delivered to the audience requires cognitive processing. The message reflects the product's attributes/benefits to the buyers after purchasing the product. A rationale based on cognitive message strategy, the advertisement targets the buyer's beliefs and knowledge by communicating product benefits satisfying a particular need. Maggie noodles focuses on the benefit of time saving (2 minutes), taste and health. So, the benefit is crystal clear to mothers in terms of time saving and healthy food and taste for kids. Cognitive Message strategy may be used in three different ways: * Generic Messages- At times, the brand does not mention the product's attributes or benefits as any claim of superiority is known as generic message strategy. This approach is best suited for the market which works best for a market leader i.e., a brand with the largest market share. It has been observed that in a few product categories the brand becomes synonymous with the product category.e.g. Xerox copier, Cello tape, Dalda Ghee. These household brands in India did not use any superiority claim but when Indian consumer go for photocopy, they ask to get xeroxes, when they want to buy transparent adhesive tape, they ask for Cello tape and in the decades of 80s and 90s whenever they bought vegetable oil, they always asked for Dalda ghee even while buying Gagan or Rath brands of vegetable oil. The advertisements of these brands did not contain any information about the product's attributes, yet the brands got established on buyers' cognitive memory.

* Pre-emptive Messages-Brands with a Unique Selling Proposition or different feature from their competitors make claims of superiority based on a product's ingredient, originality or benefit so that other brands can't make the same claim in any advertising message. Dove has always claimed to be a cream soap; no other soap in the Indian market had ever claimed it. So, a different type of claim helped Dove retain a position in the mind of the consumers which no other soap was able to establish. Grofer was a delivery app which established itself earlier as a cheap and convenient option for home delivery of groceries but when competition increased in the market and it was renamed as Blinkit, it conveyed its Unique Selling Proposition as delivery in 10 minutes. This message on digital media advertisements further helped it to gain larger market share. So, if a brand has a unique and testable claim it is remembered by the target audience. * Comparative Advertising- A very popular approach used for cognitive message strategy is comparative advertising. It may be used by an advertiser directly or indirectly; a brand may compare itself with the brand positioned for the same market segment while conveying its attribute or benefit. The advertisement mentions the competitor by name or presents a fictional or generic set of competitors as direct comparison. You must have seen that many Indian National Dailies mention their readership or circulation figures with other newspapers. It's factual and direct comparison. But sometimes, brands don't get into controversy of direct comparison, and they compare the product attribute indirectly i.e., without giving direct reference. Most of the Detergents use an indirect approach while mentioning the cleanliness attribute of their detergent. Comparative ads gain more attention of the consumers leading to brand and message awareness Affective Message Strategies - in some of the product categories when most of the brands offer almost the same product attributes with no product differentiation, advertisements evoke feelings or emotions through interesting messages. These messages are simple and memorable which help in brand recall. This evocation of emotions leads to purchase of the product. The jingles played in various advertisements like Hamara Bajaj evoke emotions in the heart of the audience and create connection with them. Retro music as background score helps in recall of the brands which get imprinted in memory forever. Conative Message Strategy - The purpose of advertising is fulfilled when we persuade buyers to take desired action. The journey of consumers from being aware to taking action is a long and challenging task for the advertiser. A conative message strategy leads consumers to elicit consumer responses. Many methods to persuade consumers for quick action are mentioning 'Offer till stock lasts, win exciting prizes, redeem coupons, cash back, sale for three days, Buy Now, Pay Later and Buy One Get One Free' etc. Such offers motivate consumers for quick action. Point of purchase display is also a conative strategy where buyers make impulsive decisions of purchase. Making the sale constitutes the goal, with cognitive knowledge and affective feelings forming as the product is used. The decision of using any of these message strategies depends upon marketing objectives, business environment, positioning, USP and the market share of the brand. Cognitive, affective, and conative strategies can be understood with the hierarchy of effects model. The strategies are applicable on various stages from awareness to knowledge, liking, preference, conviction, and purchase/action. The choice of the right message strategy results in better return on investment. Activity
1. Select any marketing campaign around you and try to identify the 4Cs of Integrated
Communication strategy, there in.
2. To promote the usage of helmets, Posters of Ganesha with the message: NOT EVERYONE IS
AS LUCKY were floated across various cities. Discuss the meaning and interpretation of this sort of social advertisement.

2.5 LET US SUM UP
The integrated communications strategy should be devised on the basis of situation analysis, customer research and the set objectives. Before developing any strategy, one needs to understand the target audience, a clear positioning statement, unique selling proposition and the media available to reach the target audience. This communication planning and execution involves the development of a creative strategy, message design, methods and media which caters the audience's needs. The integrated communication strategy will go through various stages of awareness, liking, interest, preference, conviction and purchase. The evaluation of Integrated Communication Strategy should be on the basis of results of pretesting, mid-term testing and post testing against Return on investment. The criteria to choose any of the above-mentioned strategies should be based upon message differentiation from its competitors. The media has wide reach and accessibility to the target audience. The optimum reach of media and message is the key to the successful integrated communication strategy.

Internal communication - information and ideas exchanged within the organization itself. Pay Per Click - An advertising payment model where advertisers pay the host based on how many users click on their advertisement. Structure

2.0 INTRODUCTION
Research is the process of creating new knowledge. Every discipline, whether it is science, history, geography, sociology, psychology or journalism, depends on research to produce new knowledge, verify existing ideas, and find solutions to the problems. However, not all research is the same, and thus it is not a single, uniform process. It is as important to understand the methods of research as it is to understand its findings or results. Research methods are the different techniques that help in designing research projects to systematically carry out all the different steps in the research. These methods can be classified based on different aspects, such as the type of data and sources of data, the nature of inquiry, and the purpose of the research, etc. Classification helps in choosing the best suitable method for a research project. This unit will explore all the types of research methods classified based on above mentioned aspects. It will help learners understand these classifications, and know when and how to use each research method. The goal is to make learners familiar with these methods so that they can understand how the same can be applied to journalism, which we will discuss in subsequent units.
2.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After going through this unit, students will be able to: understand the different types of classification of research methods, learn how data sources, nature of inquiry, and research purpose determine their selection, and understand the characteristics of each research method and their appropriate use.

2.2 CLASSIFICATION BASED ON DATA TYPE
The most common way for classifying research is based on the type of data you take under study. Does your data consist of numbers and is countable, or does it describe qualities and attitudes and is expressed in words? Based on this, the classification is of the following types:
2.2.1 Quantitative Approach
Quantitative approach collects data that involves numbers, has fixed values and is measurable, such as frequencies, percentages, scores, ratings, etc. It relies on large samples because it aims for objectivity and generalisability. Generalisability means how much the results of a study can be applied to people or situations other than the ones studied. For data collection in this approach, tools like surveys, structured questionnaires, experiments, etc, are used. These tools primarily consist of closed-ended questions. Close-ended questions are questions that have a set of fixed answer options for respondents to choose from. Such questions help maintain objectivity and make responses easy to count and analyse. For data analysis, statistical tools such as averages, regression, correlation, etc, are used. Quantitative approach is very useful for testing hypotheses and determining relationships or effects. For example, to understand the media consumption habits of users across different age groups, a quantitative approach would be most appropriate. A large-scale structured survey will help in data collection, while statistical methods such as the 'average' or 'mean' will help in calculating the daily time spent on various media platforms. You can then apply a correlation test to understand if age is correlated with consumption habits. However, this method usually lacks depth because the data is collected in numbers via closed-ended questions, which does not allow participants to give detailed responses and share their experiences or feelings.
2.2.2 Qualitative Approach
Unlike quantitative approach which focuses on quanitifed answers, qualitative approach focuses on understanding deeper meanings, perspectives, experiences, opinions, and social context. It deals with non-numerical data that consists of words, images, text, observations, etc. This usually consists of a small and targeted sample size of the population. The focus is on understanding the deeper meaning for better contextual understanding. For data collection, it uses unstructured or semi-structured tools, like focus group discussions, open-ended interviews, content analysis, direct observations, case studies, ethnography, etc. Since the sample size is usually small and analysis is also subjective, this kind of research approach lacks generalisability. A good example of qualitative approach in research would include observing the daily life of a tribal community to understand their daily experiences, struggles and cultural practices. For this purpose, a researcher would live and spend time with members of the community and take part in their daily activities and cultural practices while also observing and taking notes of their interactions and behaviour. These observations and notes are the qualitative data that the researcher later analyses and interprets to identify themes and patterns to explain their lives, struggles and culture.
2.2.3 Mixed-Method Approach
The mixed-method approach uses both quantitative and qualitative techniques of research. In practice, most researches adopt a mixed-method approach to have a deeper contextual understanding and also generalisability. The mixed-method approach consists of both numerical and non-numerical data, and is beneficial in understanding trends and patterns, and also motives and contexts. The results and findings are far more comprehensive and convincing. Since it combines both quantitative and qualitative approaches, the research design is complex and requires more time, money and planning. For example, to assess the success rate of a newly launched government scheme, a mixed- method approach would be most appropriate. First, in its quantitative component, large-scale data can be collected from the scheme beneficiaries. In the second, qualitative component,

small-scale interviews can be conducted with a number of participants to understand their challenges and suggestions better.
2.3 CLASSIFICATION BASED ON NATURE OF INQUIRY
Another way classification of research is done is based on the nature of the inquiry, i.e., whether the focus is on theories and concepts, or on real-world observations.
2.3.1 Theoretical versus Empirical Research
Theoretical research, also known as conceptual research, involves developing and analysing new theories and concepts, or reformulating already existing theories and frameworks. It relies on existing literature and logical reasoning, and does not involve collecting new data, as it uses secondary data to build new frameworks. For example, a communication researcher is analysing the news on social media platforms and how well it fits with the traditional Gate Keeping Theory (editors decide which news reaches the audience) and Agenda Setting Theory (media tell people what to think about). He studies the Instagram handles of major news organisations and finds that certain political parties or individuals are shown more often. He then relates these findings to the aforementioned theories to explain how these theories are still very much relevant in today's digital media context. Empirical research, on the other hand, uses 'real-world' data collected through surveys, tests, observations, etc. It involves collecting and analysing primary data to test a hypothesis, or to find an answer to research questions. The findings and results are entirely evidence-based. For example, to explore if there is any correlation between the use of social media platforms and increased teenage self-image consciousness, a large-scale sample survey of teenagers is required to test this hypothesis. The researcher collects data from 100-200 teenagers using a survey method, which includes questions related to their daily social media use and how they feel about their looks, body and behaviour. He then statistically analyses this data to explore this correlation. This would be empirical research because it includes 'real-world' data.
2.3.2 Basic versus Applied Research
Basic research, also known as pure research, does not have direct practical application. This kind of research is carried out to know and understand a topic or idea better. It is dominantly theoretical and explanatory in nature as it aims to answer 'why' and 'how' questions. The goal here is not to solve any problem, but to discover, develop and test theories. The findings and results contribute to building new theories. Applied research is built upon the foundation built by basic research. But unlike basic research, it has direct practical application. It is context-specific and aims to find a solution to a specific and immediate problem using existing knowledge. Simply put, applied research uses the insights from basic research and puts them to practical use. For example, a researcher explores why people remember certain advertisements and the reasons behind 'ad recall' (basic research), the findings of this study can be utilised to design more effective ad campaigns (applied research). 2.4 CLASSIFICATION BASED ON DATA SOURCES
Another classification of research methods is based on the source of the data. This can be determined in two ways - whether the data is first-hand and comes directly from the field or from an original source, or is it already available to the researcher from some other source.
2.4.1 Primary Sources
A source is called a primary source when information or data is collected from original documents or records, or from people in the field. These sources provide first-hand, raw and unfiltered data relevant to a specific topic and problem. The collected information is presented as it was first recorded, and allows researchers to form their own conclusions. The data collected via primary sources is tailored to the researcher's needs. With primary data, the researcher has more control over measurement accuracy and consistency. However, collecting data from primary sources is very time-consuming and requires a lot of planning and resources. One can use different research methods to collect primary data, such as interviews, surveys, questionnaires, focus group discussions, observations, experiments, etc. In journalism, journalists primarily use original and first-hand raw data to develop stories and reports, such as conducting interviews with eyewitnesses or conducting surveys for opinion polls during elections, etc.
2.4.2 Secondary Sources
Secondary sources refer to second-hand data that has already been collected and analysed. After data is collected via primary sources and analysed, evaluated, interpreted, and summarised, it becomes a second-hand record, and therefore, a secondary source. Since data obtained from secondary sources has already been collected, filtered and analysed by others, it is less time-consuming and cost-effective for the researcher. Although secondary sources may be useful in providing a broad, historical and comparative perspective, the researcher does not have control over measurement quality, accuracy and consistency, because that depends on the source they refer to. Secondary sources can include government documents, books, newspapers, magazines, company annual reports, archival records, statistical databases, etc. For example, a journalist can use Press Information Bureau (PIB) reports and releases to analyse the governments' communication strategies. Or, they can use WHO's World Health Statistics Report to report on mortality rates.
2.5 CLASSIFICATION BASED ON RESEARCH PURPOSE
Another way for classifying research methods is based on their purpose and goal. Some research may explore a topic, another might describe it in a detailed manner, while yet others may focus on explaining a phenomenon. The following are the classifications of research based on their purpose:
2.5.1 Exploratory Research
As the name itself suggests, the main goal of exploratory research is to 'explore' a topic or problem that is new or unclear and under-researched. It does not aim to answer any questions, but it is the first step when a researcher wants to explore a new area of study. Exploratory research is helpful in gaining preliminary insights and precisely defining a problem, in order to develop hypotheses or theories that will further guide future studies. The research design is very flexible and usually qualitative in nature because it aims to understand and identify key issues, variables and questions related to the problem. The methods used for exploratory research are in-depth interviews with open-ended questions, focus group discussions, case studies, expert interviews, observations, literature review, etc. For example, researchers exploring how young people use AI (Artificial Intelligence) technologies to understand its possible influences, before designing a detailed and targeted study to be conducted at a later stage.

2.5.2 Explanatory Research
Explanatory research focuses on explaining a phenomenon. It is also known as 'causal research'. The main aim of explanatory research is to understand and identify the cause-and- effect relationship between two or more variables. This research answers the 'why' questions: Why is this happening? The research design is structured and quantitative in nature. By understanding the cause-and-effect relationship, it helps to predict future outcomes. It aims to test hypotheses, and the findings and results are used to build, test and refine existing theories. Such studies have high generalisability. The most commonly used methods in explanatory research include experiments, statistical analysis like correlation and regression, and so on. For explanatory research, a researcher explores why short videos on platforms such as YouTube and Instagram get more engagement than longer videos. The focus here is to explain the reasons behind higher engagement, so the researcher can examine factors like instant entertainment value, visual appeal, shorter duration, storytelling style, trends and hashtags, and algorithmic promotions.
2.5.3 Descriptive Research
Descriptive research aims to describe a problem, event, or phenomenon in a detailed manner. It answers all the HOW, WHERE, WHAT, WHO and WHEN questions. The focus of descriptive research is on presenting related facts systematically. In a detailed way, it describes the characteristics, behaviours, and conditions of a population, event or community. It does not involve the manipulation of any variables; instead, the researcher observes the variables in their natural environment without any intervention. Descriptive research does not aim to predict any future outcomes; it simply describes and deals with present facts, trends and patterns. It can be both qualitative and quantitative in nature, depending on the nature of the data collected. Methods that are used in descriptive research include surveys, case studies, observation, content analysis, etc. For example, evaluating the speech of a political leader to determine the frequency of specific words can help understand the patterns or popular themes addressed by said leader. 2.6 LET US SUM UP
This unit explored the different types of research methods classified based on data approach, nature of inquiry, data sources and purpose of the research. Based on a data approach, we explored three methods: qualitative, which deals with non-numerical data, quantitative, which deals with numerical data, and a mixed-method approach, which includes both qualitative and quantitative elements. In terms of the nature of inquiry, research methods are classified into theoretical, empirical, basic and applied research. Furthermore, the unit also explored the primary and secondary data sources used in research. Lastly, based on the purpose and goal

of research, we also understood the difference between exploratory, explanatory and descriptive research. As research is useful in exploring new areas, explaining the relationship between two or more variables and in describing situations, it is essential to understand these methods to create an effective research design, suitable and relevant for the study. Each research method is different from the other, and is used as per the needs of the researcher, their unique subjects, questions and purposes.
2.7 KEYWORDS
Quantitative Research: It includes numerical data and uses large samples because it aims for objectivity and generalisability. It is used for determining relationships or effects. Qualitative Research: It includes non-numerical data and focuses on understanding deeper meanings, perspectives, experiences, opinions, and social context related to a problem. Mixed-Method Research: It uses both quantitative and qualitative approaches in a single study, and provides a more comprehensive understanding of a complex problem. Theoretical Research: It involves developing and analysing new theories and concepts, and uses secondary data to build new frameworks. Empirical Research: It is based on observations and real-world evidence and involves collecting and analysing primary data. Basic Research: It is theoretical and explanatory in nature, and is used to understand a topic or idea better. The goal is to discover, develop and test theories. Applied Research: Unlike basic research, applied research has a direct practical application and aims to find a solution to a specific and immediate problem. Exploratory Research: It is used to explore a new or unclear topic. It is essential in gaining preliminary insights and precisely defining a problem. Explanatory Research: Explanatory research aims to understand and identify the cause-and- effect relationship between two or more variables. Descriptive Research: It is used to describe a problem, situation, or event in a detailed way, without manipulating the variables.

3.0 INTRODUCTION
In the previous two units of this block, we have discussed the meaning, types and importance of research, and the classification of research methods in social science. Research, as we have learned, is broadly classified into two categories: quantitative research and qualitative research. We know that qualitative research deals with non-numerical data because the focus here is on understanding the in-depth meaning, experiences and perspective of the population or the context being studied. In contrast, quantitative research works with numerical data, data that is countable and measurable. It aims to find the relationship between variables and to explore trends and patterns. As it involves a large sample size, it has high generalisability compared to qualitative research. In journalism, quantitative research is used in numerous ways, for instance, to analyse trends and patterns in a dataset, to evaluate the impact of policies, programmes, and to understand

the audience and their media consumption habits. This unit will introduce learners to quantitative research, its types and methods, data analysis and interpretation techniques, and its applications in the field of journalism and mass communication.
3.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After going through this unit, learners will be able to: understand the key features of quantitative research and its different types, learn about the important tools and techniques used for data collection, analysis and visualisation, and understand the importance of quantitative research and its application in journalism.
3.2 WHAT IS QUANTITATIVE RESEARCH?
Quantitative research works with data that is expressed in numbers and has fixed values. The aim is to measure the behaviour, habits, and opinions of a group in a way that is countable and can be expressed in numbers. It relies on a large sample size because the goal is to generalise the findings or results in order to apply them to a larger population. The research design is not flexible, as it follows a predetermined and structured plan. Here, research tools such as surveys, questionnaires, experiments, etc., are used. For data collection, analysis and interpretation, researchers employ mathematical tools like percentages, frequency, standard deviation, regression, and correlation. Objectivity is high in quantitative research because it aims to minimise the researcher's bias by following a structured plan and by focusing on precise measurements. Replicability is also high in quantitative research compared to qualitative research.
3.3 TYPES OF QUANTITATIVE RESEARCH
3.3.1 Descriptive Research
Descriptive research does not focus on cause-and-effect relationships between variables; it aims to accurately and systematically describe features of a problem, event, or phenomenon as it is, or in a detailed manner. The goal is to answer WHAT, WHERE, WHEN and HOW something happens. Common research methods that are used are surveys, questionnaires, observation (quantitative), etc. For example, a researcher wants to know how much time teenagers spend using social media. The entire process of gathering related data, and presenting it in numbers and percentages will be considered descriptive research.
3.3.2 Correlational Research
The purpose of correlational research is to understand the strength and direction of the relationship between two variables. It does not establish a cause-and-effect relationship, rather it determines if an increase or a decrease in one variable is related to another. The correlation coefficient (r) ranges from +1 to -1, and indicates a positive and negative relationship among variables. For example, a researcher trying to understand if there is any relationship between hours spent studying and exam scores would find the co-relational research method helpful.
3.3.3 Experimental Research
Experimental research is also called 'true experiment'. The main goal of experimental research is to establish a cause-and-effect relationship between two variables. It tells how the change in one variable brings about change in another. Experimental research involves random selection and manipulation of the independent variable and observing its effect on the dependent variable. The research design is very rigorous and structured, and the experiments are performed in a controlled environment. For example, as part of a research, two groups of people are shown two different kinds of advertisements, one with an emotional appeal, the other being informative. Using experimental research, the researcher can evaluate which advertisement has more product recall.

3.3.4 Quasi-experimental Research
Quasi-experiments also try to establish the cause-and-effect relationship between variables. Unlike experimental research where participants are placed into random groups in a controlled setting, quasi-experiments are usually conducted in real-world settings where randomly assigning participants into groups is not possible or ethical. Here, the researcher studies pre-existing groups or conditions, and so they have less control over the environment. Because of this lack of randomisation and limited control of the researcher, quasi- experimental research has lower internal validity.
3.4 KEY FEATURES OF QUANTITATIVE RESEARCH
The following are some key features of quantitative research:
3.4.1 Variables and Measurements
A variable is defined as a phenomenon or event that can be measured or manipulated. Variables are characteristics or factors like age, income, gender, audience behaviour, scores, etc, that can vary or change. There are several kinds of variables, some of which are: Discrete variable: It includes a finite set of values and cannot be divided into subparts. Example: the number of players in a team, the number of students in a class, etc. Continuous variable: It does not have a finite set of values and can further be divided into subparts. Example: height, time, etc. Dependent variable: It is the value being tested in a study, and it depends on the independent variable. Independent variable: It is the variable that researchers manipulate to observe its effect on the dependent variable. Control variable: These are variables that are kept constant or under control to avoid any confusion or influence. Measurements provide numerical values to variables and allow precise measurement and analysis. For example, on a rating scale, 1 refers to strongly agree, and 5 refers to strongly disagree. In this way, the scale allows us to quantify the variables that are not represented in numbers or finite values. In quantitative research, there are four scales of measurement: Nominal: It is the most basic level of measurement. It is used to label or classify people, objects or characteristics. Example: Male = 1, Female = 2, and Other = 3. Ordinal: This scale is used to rank the objects in some order; however, the interval between these ranks or orders is not clear or meaningful. Example: strongly agree, agree, neutral, disagree, strongly disagree. Interval: This scale has properties of both a nominal and an ordinal scale. The data can be categorised, ranked, and measured with equal intervals. The interval between values is meaningful; for example, the difference between 40 and 45 is the same as between 75 and 70. However, the interval scale lacks a true zero point, which means that a researcher is not able to make statements of a proportional nature. For example, 0degC does not mean that there is no temperature. Ratio: Ratio scale has the properties of all the above scales, along with a true zero point. A true or absolute zero point shows the complete absence of an attribute. All kinds of advanced arithmetical and statistical applications are possible here.
3.4.2 Hypothesis Testing
Quantitative research involves testing a hypothesis. A hypothesis is a tentative statement, predicting a relationship between two or more variables, which is then tested using empirical data. There are two types of hypotheses: Null hypothesis: It suggests that there is no relationship between the variables. Alternate hypothesis: It suggests the existence of a relationship between the variables.

The goal is to accept or reject the null hypothesis. Hypothesis testing is important in quantitative research because it provides an objective basis for supporting or rejecting a theory.
3.4.3 Reliability and Validity
Reliability and validity are the two most important features of quantitative research. Reliability refers to consistency; it means that if a study is repeated under the same conditions, it should produce similar results. Validity refers to the accuracy, which means how accurately a tool measures something that it is supposed to measure. Both these elements are essential for quality and trustworthy research.
3.4.4 Sampling and Generalisation
Sampling is the process of selecting a sample or subset or group that is representative of a population or universe. There are two kinds of sampling: probability sampling and non- probability sampling. Quantitative research relies on probability sampling, which involves the random selection of participants to make sure that the sample is representative of a larger population and reduces biases. It is like a lottery system where every participant has an equal chance of being picked whereas in non-probability sampling all the members of a population do not have an equal chance of being selected. Here, the researcher selects participants as per his/her convenience, judgement or some specific criteria. For example, if a researcher wants to know the buying behaviour of customers, they would survey people available at a shopping mall. Generalisation is the ability to relate the findings and results of a research from a small group of people (sample) to a larger population. If a research has high generalisability, it means that the results are applicable for a larger population other than the ones directly studied. Quantitative research uses large and randomly selected samples to collect data. It represents a wider range of people and random selection helps reduce bias, hereby increasing its generalisability.
3.5 QUANTITATIVE RESEARCH TOOLS
For data collection purposes, quantitative research uses structured tools, some of which are discussed below:
3.5.1 Surveys
Surveys are one of the major tools of quantitative research. Surveys include sets of questions to gather data from the respondents. In quantitative research, the data is collected using closed-ended questions to ensure that all the responses are in the same way, which allows consistency in measurement. Surveys can be of several kinds, such as field surveys, telephonic surveys, online surveys, etc.
3.5.2 Experiments
In quantitative research, experiments are conducted to test a hypothesis. They are essential to establish a cause-and-effect relationship among variables. It involves the manipulation of the independent variable and observing its effect on the dependent variable.
3.5.3 Content Analysis
According to Kerlinger, "Content analysis is a method of studying and analysing communication in a systematic, objective and quantitative manner for the purpose of measuring variables." This tool aims to accurately represent the body of the message, the trends and patterns and frequency of the key variables. For this purpose, researchers create coding categories to count and report how frequently certain themes, words or pictures appear in the content.

3.6 DATA ANALYSIS AND INTERPRETATION
In quantitative research, the next step after data collection is analysing and interpreting the data. This is done using statistical techniques, and data visualisation tools. Let us discuss these at length.
3.6.1 Statistical Techniques
Quantitative research uses statistical techniques for analysing and interpreting data to find the patterns and test relationships among variables. These techniques are mathematical methods that help determine whether a relationship exists between variables and how strong it is. They allow hypothesis testing and give strong evidence to support conclusions. Descriptive and Inferential statistics are the two widely used techniques in quantitative research. They both have different methods and purposes in analysing and interpreting numerical data. Descriptive statistics describe and summarise the general features of a dataset. Using statistical methods such as mean, median, mode, percentage, frequency, etc., it presents data in a simplified form. Inferential statistics help in predicting a future outcome based on the collected data. It generalises the findings and makes inferences about an entire population based on the findings of the representative sample of that universe. It involves testing the hypotheses to determine if the relationship among variables is statistically significant or not. It uses advanced statistical applications such as regression, t-test, ANOVA, chi-square test, correlation, etc.
3.6.2 Visualising Data (Tables, Charts, Graphs)
Once the data is analysed and interpreted, it is shown using tables, charts, graphs, etc., for a better and easier understanding of trends, patterns and relationships. Tools such as charts, plots, maps, and infographics can effectively and interactively communicate the findings. Each of these are designed for specific purpose: tables are useful in presenting the numerical data, bar charts are useful in comparing two categorical groups, pie charts are useful in presenting the proportion of each category, line graphs are useful in showing trends over time, while histograms are best suited for showing frequency distribution of the continuous variable.
3.7 SOME QUANTITATIVE APPLICATIONS IN JOURNALISM
Quantitative research is important in the field of journalism and mass communication as it provides objective data to analyse and report stories. In this era of data, news stories are based on facts, figures and evidence rather than opinions or experiences. Journalists use data

to identify trends and patterns and report how things are changing over time. Such data- backed stories are more clear, credible, accurate and trustworthy.
3.7.1 Data-driven stories
Today more than ever, journalism is data-driven because everything can be calculated and digitally represented in 'ones and zeros', whether it's sports, politics, environment, tourism, crime, traffic, or disease. In data journalism, journalists use datasets, government databases, conduct their own surveys, apply statistics to analyse and interpret trends and patterns, and visualise the findings to create factual stories. Such kind of data-driven reporting decodes complex numbers, enabling journalists to understand patterns and follow leads, promoting transparency and accountability.
3.7.2 Election Coverage and Opinion Polls
You must have seen that during elections, media houses conduct exit polls and opinion polls to understand the opinion of the public and voting trends. This process of data collection involves structured questionnaires to collect data from respondents. Media houses conduct polls and surveys with a large and accurate representative sample of the population to generalise the findings and predict the voting trends. After that, the findings are presented using visualisation tools such as tables, bar charts, pie charts, graphs, etc.
3.7.3 TRP ratings and Audience Analytics
In the media, understanding your target audience and their preference is essential. Target Rating Point (TRP) measures the popularity of a show by quantifying how many people watch it and for how long. This data further helps in planning and scheduling the content. It also influences advertising decisions, for instance, shows with higher TRP get more advertisement and more revenue, while shows with lower TRP get less advertisement. Understanding the demographics of the audience, like age, gender, region, interests, etc., and their engagement patterns, helps tailor the content according to their preferences. Contemporary media use quantitative data such as Click-through Rate (CTR), time spent on a page, bounce rate, location, etc., and use it to optimise the content for different audiences.
3.7.4 Social Media Analytics
Today, each media house, whether big or small, has a social media presence. Every activity on these platforms generates quantitative data. Journalists collect this data and further analyse it to understand audience behaviour, attitudes, interests, viral trends, etc. Metrics such as share, like, comment, repost, retweet, hashtag, etc., which generate reach and impressions, show how the audience interacts with the content. This helps journalists in identifying new topics and understanding what kind of posts and content get more likes and engagement to further plan their strategies. 3.8 LET US SUM UP
This unit is helpful for learners in understanding the basic concepts and methods of quantitative research, especially in journalism and mass communication. Quantitative research deals with numbers, measurements and statistical analysis for data analysis and interpretation. It supports fact-based reporting in journalism. In this unit, we discussed the different types of quantitative research, key elements and important tools for data collection. Data analysis and interpretation is done using descriptive and inferential statistics and findings are presented using visualisation techniques like tables, charts, and graphs. Furthermore, we also discussed some key areas in journalism where quantitative research is used extensively, such as data-driven reporting, election coverage and opinion polls, TRP ratings and audience analytics, etc. As the unit explains, journalists, whether early-career or veterans, use quantitative research to foster objectivity, credibility and accuracy in their work.
3.9 KEYWORDS
Variable: It is a characteristic, number or quality that can be measured or counted, and varies among individuals, objects or situations. Hypothesis: A hypothesis is a tentative statement that needs to be tested to understand the relationship among variables. Sampling: It is defined as the process of selecting a group of people from a larger population to make inferences about the whole population. Reliability: It refers to the consistency of a research result. Validity: It refers to the accuracy of a measurement tool, telling us how accurately it measures what it is supposed to measure. Data Visualisation: It is the process of presenting data using a graphical representation for clear and easier understanding.

4.0 INTRODUCTION
In this unit, we will learn about advertising campaigns. Advertising campaign is a series of coordinated advertisements designed to promote products or services across different media platforms. These ads carry the same theme, message, tagline and hashtags to ensure consistency and to enforce brand identity. For instance, you must be familiar with different advertising campaigns of Cadbury's Dairy Milk, which the brand launches on every other festival. In 2024, it launched # Creating Memories Never Clicked campaign for Raksha Bandhan celebrations, wherein it aimed to transform uncaptured moments into cherished memories. It encouraged siblings to celebrate their bond by focusing on genuine interactions rather than just posed photographs. This campaign went viral and created the buzz which was intended by the brand.
4.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
* To develop understanding of advertising campaigns among learners. * To acquaint them with various nuances of campaigns' types, planning stages * To aid them in designing an advertising campaign of their own.
4.2 ADVERTISING CAMPAIGN: AN OVERVIEW
4.2.1 Origin and Genesis of a Campaign
The word campaign was arguably first used in military organizations to indicate a series of planned activities to achieve a predetermined goal at the time of war. The word campaign finds its roots in the Latin word "Campania" meaning field or open countryside. It was attributed to the eastern French city "Champagne" because of its wide open countryside. The English too used "Champaign" in around the 14th century noting to describe open fields. Institutionally it was applied in the 17th Century for the military officers conducting a series of well coordinated

activities in "the field" to upstage the enemy. Later various institutions adopted it to represent a specific form and typology. Key characteristics that remain common irrespective of the nature and form of campaigns are: a) Series: Campaign are a series of activities, highlighting the multiplicity and rhythm (repeatedness). b) Goal : Campaigns are designed to achieve certain objectives . These objectives are preset as required by an organization at that point in time. c) Planned : To conceive and execute a campaign, a structured planning process based on strategy and tactics is a must. Evolution of various forms of campaigns Etymologically, campaigns are commonly referred to as used to denote political/election campaigns, advertising/marketing communication campaigns and public communication campaigns. Political Campaigns are interrelated communication and on ground efforts by a political party or an electoral candidate to create an identity or to redefine an image. Political campaigns can be short term campaigns, characterized by heightened intensity in a period where the people have to make a political choice with the aim to win an election or a long term strategy to gain acceptance for its ideological base. The aim of the campaign is to influence the audience's voting decisions, salience of issues and the perception of a political party regarding the issues.
Communication Campaigns
Several researchers including Roger and Shorey (1987) identified 4 major elements in all communication campaigns a) It employs series of communication activities (both personal and non personal) b) It aims to achieve specific outcomes c) It is targeted at large number of audiences d) It is time bound On the basis of purpose, communication campaigns can be classified as a) Commercial b) Non Commercial. Commercial Campaigns are Advertising and Marketing Campaigns are done by business enterprises with the purpose to gain a favorable advantage for their brand or organization to accentuate the profitability of business. The primary intent of these campaigns is profit making and competitive differentiation. Broadly, an Advertising Campaign can be defined as a series of interrelated and interrelated and interconnected advertisements across mass media vehicles to achieve certain objectives in a specific time frame. According to Dunn &Barban "An advertising campaign includes a series of ads, placed in various media that are designed to meet objectives and are based on analysis of marketing and communication situations". The legendary 'Welcome to the Marlboro Country' campaign for Marlboro cigarettes by Ogilvy and Mather and Think Small for Volkswagen by BBDO are amongst the most recalled advertising campaigns in the world. Some popular Indian

advertising campaigns are "Daag Ache Hain" by Lowe Lintas for Surf Excel,"Fevikwik and Zoozoos by O&M for Vodafone, Happy & Pinky by makemytrip.com, Incredible India! By O&M for Ministry of Tourism, Govt. of India and Lets Get Started#Stay Started by McCann Worldwide for Nescafe.
4.2.2 Types of advertising campaigns
On the basis of time period and ad spend, advertising /marketing communication campaigns can be of two types: a) Burst Campaigns: also referred to as disruptive campaigns, they focus on getting audience attention by using above the line media (Newspapers, TV, Radio, OOH etc.), below the line media ( pamphlets, brochures, specialties etc.) , interactive marketing , event sponsorships in short bursts of three to four weeks. The primary aim of the campaign is to create visibility and instant impact. b) Drip Campaigns: also referred to as nurture campaigns, they are long term campaigns, continuous in nature aimed to achieve brand building objectives for long term effects. One or two media vehicles (web mailers, emails) are carefully selected to spread the message bit by bit in an ongoing manner. The primary aim of the campaign is to secure a final purchase decision or change in attitude of the consumers.
Non Commercial Campaigns
Non commercial campaigns are done 'in public interest' with the purpose of serving a community or benefiting the society at large. Non commercial campaigns are done by the governments(s), public institutions, and non-profit organizations driven by the social responsibility function of mass media. Profit making companies make non commercial campaigns to fulfill their CSR mandate and requirements. According to Atkin and Rice (2013) public communication campaigns are : "purposive attempts to inform or influence behaviors in large audiences within a specified time period using an organized set of communication activities and featuring an array of mediated messages in multiple channels generally to produce noncommercial benefits to individuals and society" (p. 3). Forms of Non Commercial Campaigns: a) Public Service Campaigns: are aimed to spread awareness about a good cause. These campaigns inform, educate and motivate the audiences vis-a-vis adoption of a new technology or a drug, causes and effects of a disease, ideas on better health and sanitation, advantages of training and skill development. eg: The Swachh Bharat Abhiyan, The Pulse Polio Campaign etc. b) Advocacy campaigns: are especially designed to set or reset the agenda on a key issue or policy .These campaigns aim to inform, persuade and mobilize public support to create a climate of change in policy on political, social, economic and technological issues. These campaigns frame a particular issue in manner that it generates mass conversation to push for a new policy or change in existing one. Eg: Dark is Beautiful campaign by Women of Wonder (WOW) in Chennai to mobilize support against beauty prejudices created by the Fairness industry in India.

4.2.3 Salience of Campaigns
Companies that make one ad at a time are not able to create flow in communication rooted in the multiple identities of products. Its cross associations become feasible with campaigns. Since campaigns include a series of advertisements, it is able to extend to inform beyond mere brand existence. Through multiple ads across media platforms, the messages provide different types of information regarding its attributes, use, benefits, unique properties, availability etc. Unlike a single summative ad, a campaign gives the opportunity to the advertiser to inform the target audience about various facets of a brand. Campaigns are ideal to tell a brand story. People respond strongly to narrative, drama and tales. They are most suited to the games of persuasion. Advertising must remind the audience as 'out of sight is out of mind' Since campaigns showcase ad messages in a rhythmic manner, it has the potential to create memories , thus hammering the message home repeatedly. Activity 1 Opt for your favourite brand, find two of their successful ad campaigns and compare & contrast them on the basis of their key message and theme.
4.3 PLANNING A CAMPAIGN
4.3.1 Factors Affecting Campaign Planning
a) The Product Life Cycle: Before campaign development and design it is important to ascertain the phase of the product life cycle. If the product is at the introductory stage, a launch ad campaign, especially often a teaser campaign is created with the purpose to create buzz and hype. If the product is growing in sales and units of consumption, then a competitive ad campaign to spread awareness and knowledge about the features, strengths , benefits and unique salience of the product is preferred. If the product is at maturity stage i.e. steady in its sales curve, established in the market implicit comparative advertising or corporate advertising campaign can serve in the consolidation of the brand. When the product is saturated in the market meaning there is no increase in sales or consumption, and no further growth explicit comparative (combative) ad campaigns are often resorted to. At the decline stage when the product is losing ground and the sales are continuously decreasing, it is time to do a reminder advertising campaign. Hence we see at various stages of the PLC that different types of advertising campaigns are required. b) The Overall Business Environment: The overall business environment also affects the type and duration of the campaign. If the business especially in your product category is facing issues pertaining to tax structures, trade policies or new laws, the advertising expenditure will be directly affected. This in turn shrinks the scope of the campaigns. Periods of boom in the business cycle encourage the advertisers to invest more in campaigns and periods of depression scales down advertising expenditure. c) The Political Climate: Advertising campaigns are a marker of a market driven, consumption milieu. A stable ruling government with the requisite representation in the parliament creates a facilitating effect on business. The industry feels hopeful about the growth agenda and believes that a stable government will formulate policies to make businesses sustainable. It leads to expansion of business across product genres and

classes. On the other hand, a speculative political environment causes entropy thereby making business entrepreneurs passive and cautious. d) The Social System: Since advertising campaigns have the potential to affect a large heterogeneous mass audience it is also thought of as social communication to create a perceptual shift. A social system is the organization of relationships and roles within a primary or secondary group. For eg: roles played by mother, father and child w.r.t a or the representative identities and position of men, women and others in institutions of marriage. e) Digital Disruptions: Campaign planning is most affected by the disruptions caused by digital technologies in the brandscape (A motley of brands as cultural products, coined by John Sherry,1986). Digital disruption means how owing to the new media technologies business models change thereby disrupting the existing market systems. It provokes the business to re-evaluate the current market practices and change the value propositions of the brand. Changing value propositions and technological interventions stimulate the advertising agencies to create novel campaign themes and new media innovations customized to the current value propositions.
4.3.2 The Campaign Planning Cycle
Stephen King's planning cycle enlists the key questions that can serve as the broad guidelines for conceiving, designing and evaluating an advertising campaign. It illustrates the need for research in campaign planning. The Here five questions are arranged in a cyclical manner to indicate a circular relationship loop. While it indicates an interaction of various elements (questions), the process is flexible and adaptable to circumstances. a) Where are we? : An inquiry into the current brand equity and value status addresses the lead question. It is a data driven understanding of the market position of the brand in the brand playground. b) Why are we here? : Requires an investigation into the reasons behind the current position of the brand in the market. PEST (Political, Social, Economic and Technological) reasons need to be found out. c) Where could we be? : Requires a cogent assessment of the present in order to forecast the potential growth of the brand in a given time frame. From research to prediction, it displays the capability of the brand in the near future. d) How could we get there? : Results in a proposal to illustrate the key strategies and formats in integrated marketing communications to be able to achieve the potential position. It is largely about visualizing the right ideas, writing memorable copies and visuals and placing them on the best suited media platforms. e) Are we getting there?: Requires an ongoing system of review and checks to oversee once the plan has been put in place . It is monitoring the progress of the campaign in order to find gaps and digressions.
4.3.3 Stages of an Advertising Campaign
An advertising campaign is prepared by an advertising agency on the behalf of the advertiser to be consumed by the audiences. There are various stages involved in this process of the interaction between Advertiser-Agency-Audiences for a particular product, and are listed below:

a) Securing an agency brief: After successfully pitching in for a client(advertiser) and bagging the account , the account executive asks for an agency brief from the advertiser. The agency brief is a document containing information on advertisers' company, mission statement, vision, product, competition, consumers, management and past campaigns. b) Briefing the agency teams: The account planning executive studies the brief and shares the detailed information with the various departments such as creative, media planning, client servicing etc. The account planning team updates the members on the advertising budget for the campaign or the total ad spend fixed by the client in one year. c) Creative head prepares the creative brief: The creative head in turn prepares the creative brief outlining the goal of the campaign, message strategy and executions to his team of copywriters and artists based on the target segment selected and the campaign goal ascertained. d) Ist Plans Board Meeting: In the first plans board meeting, the creative and media planning teams come together in an extensive session for brainstorming. After the creative brief is given to the copy and art teams, they ideate to develop the campaign theme, the verbal and visual cues elements. e) 2nd plans board meeting: In the second plans board, comprehensive rough layouts, storyboards etc. are presented by the creative team and the media planner's layout the entire media plan and schedule. The ads are contextualized in view of their adaptations as per media selection. Final round of discussions on creative -media integration takes place. f) Producing the ads: Now the final artworks and ready to shoot storyboards are prepared. Radio, television and digital ads are recorded, shot and edited by a production house. Vendors are selected for printing of outdoor, transit ads and POP advertising. g) Presenting the campaign to the client: The client servicing team now takes the advertising campaign to the client. The entire ad campaign is shown to the client for approvals. The corrections or changes if any suggested by the client may be carried out in the ad campaign at this stage. Client's nod of consent for the campaign is imperative. h) Rolling out a campaign: Media booking is now done to roll out the campaign. The ads are published on various print ad media, broadcast on various television channels or uploaded on the web. The campaign is now presented to the audiences. i) Monitoring a campaign: It is important to check on the progress of a campaign especially for drip campaigns. Keeping tabs on the campaign will also create possibilities for remedial action at the earliest. j) Evaluating a campaign: The campaign effectiveness is gauged either internally by the research and development teams in large ad agencies or by outsourcing it to research affiliates to know the objective and outcome relationship w.r.t. the campaign. Steps in creating an advertising campaign
1) Review of the marketing plan: Campaign planning begins with the review of the
marketing plan. At this stage careful study of the situational analysis, marketing mix, the marketing strategies and tactical approaches is done. Primarily, we assess the situation of the industry with regards to its practices, regulatory frameworks, taxes and growth

patterns. We also do a product review in terms of its current market share, its strengths and weaknesses, demand, supply and price, labeling and packaging. It is followed by a detailed review of existing channels of product distribution and modes of transport. Then all the previous campaigns are examined to know the target marketinging, creative and media mix used.
2) Understanding consumer behavior: The next step is to understand the consumer
behavior and buying process. Through secondary sources (consumer databases) various personal, psychological and socio-cultural factors are looked into that influence the consumers while making purchase related decisions are looked at. It includes categorization of consumers into various segments.
3) Identifying the target audience: Determining the target audience is deciding to whom
this advertising campaign addressed. The process of TA selection starts with zeroing in the type of market followed by segmenting the diverse heterogeneous mass of audiences on the basis of geo-demography, lifestyle, consumption, socio-cultural identity etc. and forming homogeneous clusters. Measures like propensity to consume, size of the segment, return on consumer investment, sales potential form a criteria to select the most germane cluster or groups most relevant to the brand. Set against these criteria, the target audience segment is identified.
4) Setting the objective(s): Foremost attempt is to define a goal and set clear specific,
reliable, measurable objectives to achieve the goal (DAGMAR approach by Colley, 1961 quoted in Aaker & Batra (1995). An advertising objective is a brand communication task to be completed in a given period of time. An advertising campaign can have any of the following objectives: a) To introduce a new product development b) To increase the frequency of consumption of a product c) To introduce a new line extension d) To suggest alternative /new use of the product e) To encourage additional use/consumption of the product f) To underline a comparative advantage g) To create curiosity around a product or a brand h) To dispel rumors and false impressions
5) Campaign theme : Ad campaigns must find a theme that will remain consistent in all
ads across media vehicles. The theme of the campaign is often a keyword or phrase that sums up the strategic way by which the brand will do the communication task. Eg: the theme of Uber's #Isseapnihigaadisamjho campaign is apnapan (belongingness)
6) Formulate the creative strategy and executions: Shah and D'Souza (2008) described
the creative process in advertising campaigns in a pyramidal structure. Advertising Strategy (at the base) -Big Idea (thematic message) -Creative Executions(form of the ads) -Tactics (appearance on the media) form the creative process. The Creative strategy is about what is the message and how will this message be presented in various ads. The creative process begins by finding the big idea that encapsulates the campaign theme. The creative execution process will continue further as we identify the nature and type

of advertising appeal to be used, the ad format in print, radio or TV and the elements in the ads.
7) Develop a media Strategy and plan:The campaign objectives are translated into media
objectives. Media plan proceeds with the comparative analysis of the strengths and weaknesses of available media options in terms of their reach, frequency, continuity and impact. After understanding the media environment, audience estimation and allocation of budget the broad media categories are selected from which specific media vehicles, innovations and forms are arrived at. A media mix i.e. proportionate combination of the selected media options is made. Using media scheduling strategies, the campaign is put to timelines w.r.t choice of media type, vehicle, frequency of insertions, cost of the ad, days/dates, position/placement and day parts.
8) Releasing the campaign: The campaign is presented to the target audience either in an
integrated manner or in a cross mediated mode. Ads are now visible to the audience to see, read, opine, comment and act upon. The campaign continues as planned for the fixed time frame from start to finish. For eg: The Big Billion campaign was released on 4th October 2018 to inform about the big billion days sale at Flipkart, the e-commerce provider from 10th October to14th October 2018.9) Campaign review: After the campaign has run its course or has completed its cycle, it
is time to review the response of the audience towards the message, the media and their ability to achieve the campaign goal. .Hierarchy of effects in consumer decision making are assessed for the campaign. Check Your Progress 1 Note: 1) Use the space provided below for your Answers.
