4.4 TESTING A CAMPAIGN
Testing a Campaign: Even though success of a campaign cannot be guaranteed, evaluation of advertisements gives the advertiser and the agency much needed insights. Testing an advertising campaign is done both before the campaign is released and after it is presented to the audience.
4.4.1 Pretesting Methods
Both Quantitative and Qualitative testing methods are used to pretest Print and Electronic advertisements. Pretesting is done to gauge the likeability of the ads; whether the elements are able to convey the campaign theme; if the audience is able to appreciate the visual and verbal

elements; if the ads are believable and above all if the audience can comprehend the message. William Arens (2008) presents a summary of pretesting methods (p.221) Pretesting methods for print advertising Direct Questioning: two or three alternative ads are tested through interviews (structured or semi structured) or a set of forced choice questions during early stages of ad creation. It is an effective measure to know the likeability of cues, elements, choice of ad appeal and creative format. Focus groups: It is a qualitative technique in which a moderator carries forward a relatively freewheeling discussion with 6-8 people on the advertisements. The results give useful insights into the overall comprehension of an advertisement. Order of merit test: In this test two or more ads are shown to the respondents and are asked to arrange them in rank order from 0 to 10. Paired Comparison Method: In this method the respondents are grouped together and they compare the two binary ads. Portfolio Test : In this test two groups are created . One group sees a portfolio of test ads (ads being pretested) interspersed with the editorial content and real ads. The other group sees the portfolio of editorial matters and real ads without the test ads. The groups are given a feedback form or a questionnaire after the exposure. It measures the visibility and the unique salience of the test ads. Mock Magazine Test: In this test, test ads are stripped into a magazine. The magazine stays with the respondents for a stipulated period of time and then asks questions. Direct mail Orders: Here two or more alternative ads are mailed to different prospective buyers in the consumer database. It is used to know which advertisement generates orders for the advertised product. Pretesting audio-visual ads Central Location Projection Test: In this test, the respondents watch the test ads in a central location like a shopping mall. The response are asked to fill a questionnaire after seeing the ads. Trailer Test: Here the researcher shows the television commercials to a sample of respondents. The same respondents are given coupons of the product for redemption. The difference in coupon redemption is measured to know the purchase intent or use related potential of the ads. Theatre Test: Respondents are taken to a theatre and shown the ads. Through electronic devices like pointers, they indicate what they like and dislike in an advertisement. Live Telecast Test: In this test, the ads to be pretested are shown on Cable TV. Post exposure, the respondents are interviewed on phone along with sales audit at the local retail stores in that area. Sales Experiment: In order to identify right markets for the ads, two separate ads are shown in two markets. Psychological testing : Various measures of psychological research are used to find out about the buying prospects' personality, emotions, motivations, feelings and attitudes. It asks the respondents to tell the metaphors for feelings they cannot describe in words. This technique is able to elicit honest associations' w.r.t. consumer feelings.

Pretesting ads through laboratory experiments: these tests are also referred to as Physiological tests. a) Galvanometer Test: A mild electric current is passed through the respondents on exposure to the advertisement. The activity of the sweat glands is noted through a device called the Psycho Galvanometer. It records the degree of sweating (level of emotional arousal) caused by the advertisement. Exact points in the ad and amount of sweating are recorded. High emotional arousal signifies greater connection with the advertisement. b) Eye Movement Camera Test : In this test , the movement of the eye while watching the ad is noted. How much time is being spent on a visual or verbal element is recorded. c) Pupillometry test : it is also known as the eye observation camera test. In this test, the dilation of the pupil of the respondents is measured in relation to his/her interest points on visual cues in the ad. A direct relationship between dilation of the pupil and interest in the ad is assumed. d) Voice Pitch Analysis: The prospects' response of the prospects to the advertisements is recorded and later through voice pitch analysis softwares, changes in voice pitch caused by emotional responses are recorded. e) Projective tools: Word association tests and sentence completion tests are used to measure top of mind recall. TAT (thematic apperception tests) are done to gain insight into the hidden feelings stored in the repository of the unconscious mind of the respondents.
4.4.2 Post testing Methods
a) Aided Recall: This test can be used to know the effectiveness of the ad media use decision. Here the respondents are shown real campaign ads and asked to describe the broad media class, media vehicle, placement or programme association of the ad.. Questions on their previous exposure w.r.t. reading, viewing or noticing the ads are asked. b) Unaided Recall: Attitude scale based tests are used to measure the affective (emotional) feelings of respondents to the advertisement. They measure whether there is a creation of a favourable attitude after the campaign. Various measurement tools like forced choice options questions, semantic differential scales or even open ended unstructured questions are posed to know the message and behavioral variables and their interrelationship with each other. c) Inquiry Tests : In this test ,those who have seen the campaign ads will be given additional samples , coupons, premium incentives . Ads generating maximum response are noted to be most effective. It tests an ads attention getting value, its understandability and reader/viewer action. d) Sales tests: Various types of sales tests are conducted after the campaign. Consumer Purchase tests measure volume of sales generated from a particular campaign. Secondly, the sales of the product before and after the campaign are compared. Sales audits are also done eg: store inventory audits before and after the campaign are done to know the increase or decrease in stock w.r.t the campaign.

Now evaluate the result of these tests as per the objectives that you have set for your ad.
4.5 CASE STUDY OF PREGA NEWS' #SheCanCarryBoth
Fig 1: Prega News' #SheCanCarryBoth campaign Prega News, a leading pregnancy detection brand in India, had launched #SheCanCarryBoth campaign (2024), which proved to be quite effective. Following are the finer points, which ensured that the creatives of this ad came out as a winner: While doing a situation analysis, they recognised that the societal challenge faced by working mothers, the brand aimed to address the issue of women exiting the workforce post-childbirth, which stands at a significant 73%. This prompted them to decide their campaign goal, which was 'To highlight and challenge the societal pressures and biases', that lead to "mom guilt" and to celebrate the resilience of working mothers who balance both professional and personal responsibilities. The campaign goal helped them in choosing their communication objectives, which turned out to be: * To initiate conversations about societal perceptions and treatment of working mothers. * To position Prega News as a supportive ally for women navigating the challenges of motherhood and career. * To empower and inspire confidence among working mothers. For this campaign, their Target Audience were people of urban and semi-urban regions across India (geographic profile), working women, especially those in the teaching profession, aged 25- 40 (demographic profile), who are striving to balance career aspirations with motherhood, seeking societal acceptance and support (psychographics) & professionals contemplating career decisions post-childbirth, facing societal judgments (behavioural).

When it comes to creative strategy, the brand used emotional storytelling by depicting real-life scenarios of working mothers, balancing their dual roles. It emphasized their resilience and challenged societal stereotypes, urging a cultural shift in recognizing and appreciating working mothers. To disseminate this campaign they used digital platforms, social media channels, and collaborations with influencers to maximise reach and engagement among the target audience (Media Strategy). We can trace the effectiveness of this campaign by the fact that the campaign sparked crucial conversations about societal views on working mothers, reinforcing Prega News's commitment to supporting and celebrating women who challenge stereotypes. 4.0 INTRODUCTION
Research is broadly classified into two categories: Quantitative Research and Qualitative Research. In Unit 3, we discussed the foundations of quantitative research, which aims to measure and quantify phenomena. It tries to shed light upon the cause-and-effect relationship among variables to generalise the findings to a larger population. However, not everything can be counted and measured in numbers, especially the complexities of human experiences. This is where the quantitative research falls short. Thus, qualitative research takes a fundamentally different approach. Qualitative research is important when you want to know how people interpret and make sense of their worlds. The goal here is to explore and understand human experiences and realities, and cultural meanings through rich, in-depth explorations within a specific context. In this unit, we will explore the fundamental concepts, key features, methods and data analysis and interpretation techniques in qualitative research.
4.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
This unit will cover the broad concepts and methods of qualitative research. After going through this unit, students will be able to:

understand the meaning and different types of qualitative research, learn about the key features of qualitative research, like subjective experience, thick description, contextual understanding, and so on, understand different qualitative research methods, understand data analysis and interpretation techniques used in qualitative research, and learn about the importance of qualitative research and its application in the field of journalism and communication.
4.2 WHAT IS QUALITATIVE RESEARCH?
Qualitative research is rooted in the interpretivism research paradigm. Interpretivism states that our realities are socially constructed and subjective; because of this, understanding subjective experiences and perceptions of people is important, rather than simply seeking objective truths. Qualitative research focuses on understanding deeper meanings, perspectives, experiences, opinions and social context. It studies a phenomenon in its natural context without manipulating or controlling the variables. It deals with non-numerical data, which consists of words, images, text, and observations. This usually consists of a small and targeted sample size. The data is collected using interviews, focus groups, observations, case studies, textual analysis, and so on. It consists of open-ended questions as the focus is on understanding the deeper meaning for better contextual understanding, rather than generalising the findings to a larger population. For example, a researcher wants to understand the audience reception of political reels on Instagram. In a quantitative study, she would collect 400-500 surveys from respondents, asking them to rate the persuasiveness on a Likert scale from 1 to 5, and then correlate it. But in a qualitative study, she would conduct focus group discussions by showing reels to the respondents, facilitating a discussion, and making observations.
4.3 KEY FEATURES OF QUALITATIVE RESEARCH
The following are some key features of quantitative research:
4.3.1 Subjective Experience
Unlike quantitative research, which records only factual data and has high objectivity, qualitative data focuses on recording a phenomenon from people's perspectives, experiences, and beliefs. The researcher tries to make sense of these subjective experiences and understand the world from a human angle.
4.3.2 Inductive Approach
Qualitative research follows an inductive or bottom-up approach. This means that theories and themes emerge from the data itself. The researcher collects the data via interviews, observations, etc., and then analyses and interprets it to understand the hidden trends and patterns to create hypotheses. This is used as a springboard to build new theories and frameworks.
4.3.3 Contextual Understanding
Context is important in qualitative research. The focus is on exploring an event or phenomenon within a specific cultural or social context. A situation is incomplete without a context; if the context changes, the meaning and interpretation may also change.
4.3.4 Flexibility
Quantitative research follows a structured research design where everything is pre-planned, while the qualitative research design is flexible. However, while a researcher does have a planned research process, she does not necessarily need to stick to it. In this way, qualitative research offers flexibility, and the researcher may modify objectives and research questions, or refine the research design as the research progresses. Flexibility allows for more responsive research.

4.3.5 Thick Description
Qualitative research collects rich and in-depth data. The sample size is small, but it produces enormous data as it tries to collect information from all possible angles. It includes a detailed description of the facts as well as the event, meaning, context, intention, implications, and so on. Thick description increases the external validity of the study. 4.4 QUALITATIVE RESEARCH METHODS
Qualitative research focuses on exploring people's experiences, perspectives, emotions, and social context. It collects non-numerical data using unstructured or semi-structured techniques like interviews, focus group discussions (FDGs), observation, case study, semiotics, and the like which allow flexibility to gain deep insights into human behaviour.
4.4.1 Interviews
The word interview comes from a French term 'entrevue', which means 'a meeting' or 'to see each other'. It is one of the most widely used research methods for collecting in-depth information on a topic. It is a one-on-one conversation between an interviewer and an interviewee, but with the use of technology, interviews can be conducted remotely or online via telephone, video conferencing, online surveys, etc. Online interviews are relatively cheaper and easier to conduct as one can sit in the comfort of one's home, office or library while interacting with the interviewee. Interviews are broadly classified into: structured, semi-structured and unstructured interviews. Let us explore these one by one. a. Structured Interviews Structured interviews are highly rigid and follow a predetermined, fixed set of questions. They dominantly consist of closed-ended questions, and there is no scope for flexibility. These are useful when one needs to collect data from a large number of people. As the questions are highly structured, a structured interview does not provide in-depth insight into how people feel about the issues involved. Such interviews can be completed quickly and are relatively economical in terms of cost and time; they can be conducted via telephone or through online surveys. b. Semi-Structured Interviews Such interviews are neither structured nor unstructured but placed somewhere in between, and consist of elements of both. They offer some scope for moderate flexibility. Like structured interviews, they have a predetermined set of questions, but they also allow the interviewee to dive deeper. They differ from structured interviews because alongside closed-ended questions, they consist of some open-ended questions as well. Here, the researcher has the freedom to respond to any situation that emerges during the interview.

c. Unstructured Interviews These are in-depth and intensive interviews. Unstructured interviews are very useful in collecting complex information on opinions, beliefs, attitudes and personal experiences of the respondents. These are the most flexible kind of interviews, which consist of open-ended questions and allow free-flowing conversation. The sample size is small but it generates more data because there is no predetermined set of questions; the goal is to get information in the most detailed manner. Here, the interviewer has the most freedom and can ask follow-up questions and seek clarification on any point. However, such interviews are time-consuming, and the collected data can be difficult to analyse.
4.4.2 Observation Methods
The observation method involves observing people in their natural environment. Berger (2000) mentioned that the observation method is useful to study what "people actually do rather than what they say they do." This method explores the 'why' and 'how' of an issue or event. It allows researchers to explore and understand contexts, different cultures, rituals and lived experiences of individuals or communities. The observation method is used to collect primary data by observing and recording some real-life situations. It requires long periods of direct observation and fieldwork, allowing the researcher to see a topic from the subject's frame of reference. However, one major limitation of this method is that the observer's presence may influence the behaviour of the participants. Let us now discuss different types of observations: Participant Observation: In this type of study, the observer becomes a part of the phenomenon or community being studied, and the participants are aware of his/her presence. Here, the observer can decide to observe the participants from a distance and not actively indulge in their rituals or activities, or he/she can fully be a part of the culture or community under observation by living with them and participating in their activities or practices. By doing so, he/she not only observes the situation but also experiences it. Non-Participant Observation: Here, the researcher observes a situation from a distance. The group or community that is being observed is not aware of his/her presence. The researcher simply observes and records the observations without any interaction with the people. Here, the observer also takes help of different media like video cameras to record the observations to watch and analyse them later.
4.4.3 Focus Group Discussion Method
A focus group discussion (FDG) is a research method that involves gathering a group of individuals or experts (around 6-10 people) from a field of study, and engaging them in a conversation. The discussion is guided and moderated by a moderator. FGDs are useful in knowing the group's opinion and differences, as they motivate participants to build on each other's opinions and ideas. It helps in understanding the social dynamics even better. The discussion among the participants provides richer and more interactive data than interviews. Mostly, this method is used for exploratory studies and is quite cost-effective. However, conducting FGDs without proper training might be challenging; thus, the role of a moderator in conducting successful FGDs is very crucial. He/she needs to actively facilitate the discussion and make sure to include everyone in the discussion while not losing track.
4.4.4 Case Study Method
The case study method is one of the most popular qualitative research methods. It involves an in-depth and intensive investigation of a specific case. It allows a deeper and detailed understanding within a social context. The case can be any individual, institution, group or community, etc. This method is time-consuming but collects an enormous amount of data from multiple sources, taking into account necessary and related factors to understand how these are related in a specific context. This method particularly focuses on a single case, so it lacks generalisability. Some key features of the case study method are:

Case studies are heuristic; they allow researchers to explore, discover new insights, and gain an in-depth understanding to develop theories and hypotheses. Case studies are inductive; they try to identify patterns and relationships to develop theories and hypotheses from the collected data rather than verifying the already existing ones. Case studies are particularistic; they primarily focus on a particular event, situation or phenomenon. Case studies are descriptive; they use multiple sources to collect information on all the possible related factors, and aim to provide an elaborate description of the topic being investigated.
4.4.5 Semiotics
Semiotics is the study of signs, symbols and meanings. Let's understand this using an example. Rose is a flower, but it is also a sign of love; similarly, white is a colour, but it is also a symbol of peace. Similarly, in our day-to-day life, activities we participate in and the media content we consume are shaped by cultural and social codes. Analysing and understanding these codes is important to understand how these codes are socially- constructed and agreed upon. Semiotics is useful in decoding and encoding these cultural and social codes. Media content is also heavily influenced by cultural and social codes. For example, advertisements for detergents always portray women as primarily responsible for household chores while car ads depict women as passengers or accessories, instead targeting men as their primary audience. Another place semiotics play an important role is films. Think of all the Bollywood films and songs that objectify women. Semiotics analysis is essential to analyse visuals, texts, colours, language, and other symbolic forms in order to understand the representation of social codes and ideology in media content.
4.5 DATA ANALYSIS AND INTERPRETATION
So far, we have discussed what qualitative research is, what its key features are, and what are some methods that are used to conduct it. Now let us understand another aspect of qualitative research. Data is collected in the form of images, words, field notes, and documents, which are raw and highly unstructured. A researcher needs to put this massive data in order and make sense out of it. This process is called data analysis. There are several methods that are used to analyse data. Let us now discuss some of these.
4.5.1 Pattern and Theme Identification
When working with qualitative data, the researcher first needs to arrange it in a chronological order. Then, he/she needs to carefully go through all the descriptive responses and try to make meaning out of them. The aim is to identify recurring themes or patterns within the data relevant to the research questions. Once this is done, for the easy classification and analysis of data, the researcher develops some broad themes and categories. The researcher counts the number of times a theme occurs in the responses and then assigns a code to each of them using numbers and keywords.
4.5.2 Coding
Codes are short descriptors that capture the meaning of the data, and coding is the process of labelling that data. Coding makes massive data manageable and interpretable. There are three types of coding: Open coding: It is the initial stage to identify and label ideas from raw data. The researcher reads the data several times, line by line, creates summaries, and generates preliminary labels. For example, a researcher is studying why people are not trusting news on social media. In the initial stage of coding, the raw data generates open codes like trust issues, misinformation, fake news, bias, etc.

Axial Coding: Axial coding is used to group open codes into broader themes and categories. Axial coding for the above-mentioned open codes would be Perceived Media Credibility. Axial coding provides an organised set of categories. Selective Coding: Many open codes collapse into axial codes, and many axial codes collapse into selective codes. Selective codes are useful in identifying and assigning core themes that integrate all other categories. Following the same example used above, the core category would be Audience Negotiation of trust in social media.
4.6 QUALITATIVE RESEARCH APPLICATIONS IN JOURNALISM
Data in journalism is mostly qualitative in nature, as the focus is on crafting compelling stories and approaching them from all aspects. Journalism uses certain applications of qualitative work that you might see in daily news production such as feature stories or narrative driven stories that explore people, places and social issues in detail. Human interest stories which focus on emotions and personal experiences to reveal larger social realities. In this section, we will focus on some major interesting applications used in journalism.
4.6.1 Long Form Journalism
Long-form journalism is the detailed and in-depth reporting of news stories. It goes beyond daily news reporting. Such stories are longer and deeply researched. Journalists spend a considerable amount of time collecting information from multiple sources, such as interviews and field visits, to understand the complete picture. These stories are structured like narratives, with causes, background and human experiences. They often take weeks and months to complete. In India, print and online publications such as The Caravan. The Wire, and Scroll features long reports and articles on politics, elections, agriculture, governance, education, etc. The aim is not just to provide information to the public but also to build interpretation that supports public debate.
4.6.2 Profiles
Profiles are qualitative journalistic studies that focus on one individual. The individual can be a politician, an artist, a social worker, an activist, or an ordinary person doing something inspiring. A detailed profile story helps readers understand the life of the person, their work, experiences, challenges, achievements and the social impact of it. For the same, journalists conduct structured or unstructured interviews with the person, observe their daily life, and also talk to others who are related to them. A profile balances positive and negative aspects fairly and helps connect individual experiences to larger social, cultural and political themes. For example, a profile story of Nobel Laureate Kailash Satyarthi explains his work on child rights while also revealing the condition of child labour in India.
4.6.3 Sting Operation
A sting operation is a covert investigation. Journalists use hidden methods or techniques like undercover work, using fake identities, false setups, and secret recordings to uncover issues in society, such as crime, bribery, corruption, etc. However, it raises many ethical concerns,

whether it is right to record someone secretly without their consent. Thus, it is expected of sting operations that they should always serve public good and not any personal or political motives. A good example of a sting operation in the Indian media space was India TV's expose of the 'casting couch' phenomenon in India in 2005. Activity: Select two news articles on a similar issue from different newspapers of your choice and perform a semiotic analysis, focusing on symbols, structure, language, tone, images, and overall message. 4.7 LET US SUM UP
This unit explores the basic concepts and methods of qualitative research, especially in journalism and mass communication. Qualitative research is an interpretive approach that tries to understand the world through human experiences. Data is collected in the form of words, images, observations and focuses on understanding deeper meanings, perspectives, experiences, opinions and social context. The unit further expands on the key characteristics of qualitative research, tools and methods used for collecting data, and data analysis and interpretation techniques. Qualitative research is important in journalism and communication, as it allows journalists to go beyond facts and helps create detailed stories and uncover information that may not appear in daily reporting.
4.8 KEYWORDS
Inductive Approach: It is a reasoning process that leads to the development of theories from empirical data. Interpretivism: It is a philosophical approach according to which our realities are socially constructed and subjective. Semiotics: It is the study of signs and symbols, and to understand how meaning is created. Coding: The process of assigning categories to qualitative data for analysis and interpretation. Subjectivity: It is when both researchers and participants bring their personal perspectives and opinions into the research process.
4.9 FURTHER READINGS

Bryman, A., & Burgess, R. G. (Eds.). (1994). Analyzing qualitative data (Vol. 11). London: Routledge. Rojek, C. (2009). Stuart Hall on representation and ideology. Media/cultural studies: Critical approaches, 49-62. Chandler, D. (2022). Semiotics: the basics. Routledge.

5.0 INTRODUCTION
Welcome, my dear learners, to this new Unit. You might wonder, why is it important to learn about the classification and critique of advertising? Well, this knowledge is not only valuable for aspiring advertising professionals but also essential for anyone working in different spheres of the media industry; By understanding how advertisements are classified and critiqued, you will gain a comprehensive understanding of the strategies, techniques, and impacts of advertising campaigns. To make our journey through this unit more organised and comprehensive, we will divide it into two parts: classification of advertisements and. We all are consumers of media and in this era of social media one has to be a vigilant consumer. We will try to understand how advertising works in the Indian market. I hope you will be able to relate to these famous campaigns. Let's dive in and discover the exciting world of advertising together!
5.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After going through this Unit, learners would be able to: * Understand the fundamentals of advertising. * Able to distinguish between different kinds of advertising. * Evaluate the influence and impact of advertising in today's world.

5.2 THE WORLD OF ADVERTISING
We live in a world where any information is just a click away. Today we are not only aware about the Indian brands but the global brands as well. From the moment you wake up, you are constantly being pursued to buy into a product or service or to follow a trend. You may think its what you need but it might be possible that you have been influenced to feel that way by advertisements. It may sometimes be so subtle that you do not even realise that you are targeted to believe in an idea.
5.2.1 Where do you see Advertisements
Advertisements are everywhere. Whether you are traveling or sitting at home listening to your favorite music, whether you are enjoying ice-cream with your friends or you are learning from a youtube tutorial, you will find advertisements or it can be said that advertisements will find you. You are of course familiar with advertisements on the Television and Newspapers or the Hoardings on roadside and Banners on web pages But, the persuasion attempts do not end here. The communication experts are leaving no stone unturned to reach you - from the apps in your phone to the stepney covers on scooters, from the radio playing in the background to the polybag you carry your lunchbox in, from the car your favourite Hero drives in a movie to the little logo on your cap - you are witnessing some form of advertising.
5.2.2 The Definition
Advertising is a paid form of message that is generated to promote an idea, goods or services. It can be through text, photograph, video, sketch, audio etc. Today there are many innovative methods used for advertising by creating curiosity in the minds of people. Advertisements are messages paid for by those who send them and are intended to inform or influence people who receive them.
5.2.3 History of Advertising
India has witnessed many historic marks like industrialization, globalization and several economic reforms. With this growth comes the need to aware and inform people about the products and services that can be utilized in life. Although Advertising is a relatively recent phenomenon in ancient and medieval times, word of mouth was the source of information i.e. people talking to each other and spreading the information around. Traditional media was also a good medium of spreading a message like drama, puppetry, painting etc. India being a diverse nation consists of many forms of traditional media in different regions of the country. This changed after the knowledge of printing blended with industrialized mass production. Economy of scale and the Gutenberg revolution transformed the way markets functioned. Advertising agencies surfaced and their messages were very creative and effective in delivering the product information. The qualities of a product or service was communicated in attractive (usually exaggerated) formats fueling the aspirations of the audience, which were not always necessarily true. A tongue-in-cheek example of the power of advertising is the market for razors for women that Gilette created because they were unable to get men to buy the requisite quantity of blades. Advertising grew with innovative modes and methods, with the focus shifting from print to electronic media, which lasted well over the better part of the twentieth century, and then came the Internet and social media. The latter transformed the manner in which production and consumption occurred. Today, Digital advertising occurs in many ways. Entire revenue models are built to gauge the results in real time. Social media like Instagram, Facebook, X, WhatsApp are reigned by Influencers who are akin to celebrities of the good old days. And then there is Affiliate Advertising in which a third party is also involved in the process of advertising. Along with these emerging formats, the traditional method of advertising co-exists on the Web, when a mere ad copy is placed on the Website. The organic reach and hyper targeting abilities of the AI coupled with huge data has revolutionised the field of advertising. More budgets are being allocated to online promotions and specialised agencies have emerged to handle digital marketing.
5.2.4 Indian Market and Advertising
Indian is home of a vast variety of products and services to cater to the needs of its diverse population.In addition to it Indian markets attract many global brands. Being the youngest

country in the world, India is a market of over 140 crore people that no brand can afford to miss. It is diverse in its language and cultural preferences, in its income brackets and religious beliefs. The communication to the Indian audience thus, cannot be the same as the international audience. The content, its presentation has to be different and acceptable by the audience of multiple castes and creeds. To be effective it must understand and cater to the mindset that is 'uniquely' Indian. An advertisement is not limited to sponsoring a marketing campaign across platforms or placing an announcement. It involves understanding your audience, targeting the product and advertisement to the correct audience, and then ensuring that the call to action is fulfilled. Some advertisements are made directly to increase sales while some work on the image building of the brand. Ask yourself which advertisement do you remember first? Is it an advertisement of face serum you have seen on television or your favorite influencer making a video of his/her skincare routine and introducing you to a new face serum. Similarly, advertisements of a local convenience store promoting its latest sale offers are more likely to spread faster on a radio channel than an instagram account posting it, which might not even be followed by all age groups and categories of people. The brands may also use an integrated approach where more than one medium is used to advertise its products or services. Advertising can make 'wants' seem like 'needs'. It has few immediate impacts that reflect in sales and positioning of a brand and some deep rooted impacts that can change the notions of people. For example advertisements of different edible oils where the mother is cooking and worrying about her family's health. Then swoops in the brand of particular oil and now the mother seems happy and relieved. Through this advertisement the image of a healthy family has been attached to using that particular brand's oil. There are several such examples that you may notice that have impacted your life choices. 5.3 OBJECTIVES OF ADVERTISING
Advertising industry is blooming as the market is getting flooded with the increase in competition between brands. There innovative products and services, new business launched as India is a developing nation and one of the fastest growing economies. There are umpteen opportunities but at the same time it is a highly crucial job. There are several objectives of advertising, Let us read and understand. * When a new brand is launched, the advertising creates its brand image. It answers the most common curiosities about the product and also generates faith on the product among its target audience, * In a highly competitive market scenario, advertising helps a brand to stay in the minds of the people. It establishes top of mind recall. For example - if someone asks you to name 3 cold drink names, then the top three hitting you mind immediately are the ones who have managed to have a recall value in you mind. The first brand you name might be because of your loyalty towards a certain brand or might be a favorite one but the other two are stuck in your mind most likely because of the brand's advertising. * Advertising aims to increase sales. Sometimes it sends a direct message to influence the target audience to purchase the product. * It promotes a brand and creates its brand image. For example Tata steel has a brand image of reliability or Amul has a brand image of authenticity. * It also creates a better and bigger market for the brand. * Advertising establishes The USP i.e Unique Selling Point of a brand. * Advertising introduces the T.A.to the specifications of a product or service. It also highlights the new changes being done in the product. For example you must have seen advertisements like an old face wash now has honey and aloe vera.

5.4 CLASSIFICATION OF ADVERTISEMENTS
So far we have understood that the world of advertising is huge and it impacts our smallest decision like choosing a toothpaste to biggest ones like buying a car. Now that we have an idea of what and why we need ads, let us see what kinds of these ads exist. Let us look at some basic types advertising
5.4.1 Classification Based on Objectives
Above we understood the objectives of advertising. Now let us try to read the classification of advertisements on the basis of its objectives.
Informative Advertising
These advertisements aim to provide information to the target audience about a product or service, its features, benefits, and usage. For example, the advertisement campaign of stayfree sanitary napkins talks about its effectiveness, its usage, comfort and hygiene.
Persuasive Advertising
Prepare to be convinced! Persuasive ads are all about stirring emotions. If you recall the advertisement series of LIC policy you will instantly remember its tagline "Zindagi ke sath bhi aur zindagi ke baad bhi". It makes you emotional for your family and leads you to make a decision for them. These advertisements seek to persuade and influence consumer behavior by tapping into emotions, aspirations, and desires. This kind of advertising not only targets the sad emotions but the happy ones too.
Reminder Advertising
There are some advertisements whose mere purpose is to remind you of its USP or effectiveness or sometimes just its name. Few advertisements leave such a great impact that you cannot forget the brand name for years. For example advertisements of "mentos" there is an entire generation who can always remember "yeh hai aam zindagi aur ye hai mentos zindagi" these advertisements don't suggest any benefits of the product or make you emotional but they hammer the brand name mentos into your brains. Reminder advertisements serve as gentle prompts to keep a brand or product top-of-mind among consumers. Reminder advertisements maintain brand presence and loyalty.
Social Advertising
In this type of advertising. Brands associate themselves with some social welfare message. They create awareness campaigns, help society to grow and prosper in some manner. For example P&G created a campaign "Like a girl". They showed the difference between how girls and boys are raised differently and how doing something like a girl becomes a weak way of doing something. This kind of advertisement aims to impact the people's consciousness.
5.4.2 Classification Based on Geography
* National Advertising: These are the campaigns that target the entire country. Think of campaigns like Madhya Pradesh Tourism, its catchy tagline "Hindustan ka Dil Dekho". These advertisements promote the tourism of that state to the entire nation.It highlights the famous spots to visit and the culture of MP. ' * Regional Advertising: Regional advertising is the art of connecting with diverse cultures. This kind of advertising may be focused on one or two state audiences. For example, advertisement of 'Mukhymantri Rajshree Yojna" by Rajasthan Government. It is promoted in mostly rural regions of Rajasthan where a girl child gets a certain amount of money at different stages of life. * Local Advertising: Navigating the dynamics of local markets. Down to the grassroots! Local advertising speaks the language of neighborhoods. Think about the 'Kirana Store' promotions - simple, relatable, and deeply rooted in the local community.

5.5 MEDIA OF ADVERTISING
Advertisements are designed to impact the Target audience in the most effective way possible but it becomes very important to understand which media they are using to promote their brand. The content, the length, the elements involved, the presentation everything changes with the choice of media. In the ever-evolving world of advertising, understanding the different media channels used is crucial for effective communication with the target audience. In the ever evolving age of the internet, you may only think of Social media and OTT mediums as effective advertising mediums, but the traditional mediums still remain pivotal and are converging in the world of Internet. Don't underestimate the power of traditional channels. Flip through a magazine, switch on the radio, or watch a classic TV ad. These timeless mediums still weave magic. Remember the 'Doodh Doodh Doodh' jingle on television? Let us try to understand how advertisements are classified based on the Media.
5.5.1 Print Media
Print media has always been a preferred medium when it comes to trust and authenticity. We can understand its power from the role it played in India's freedom struggle. Advertisements like Flipkart's big billion sale or shampoo advertisement with a sample attached to the paper are few examples of Print advertising. Print advertising has the power to reach a massive number of audiences at relatively low costs. It includes instruments like newspapers, magazines, and brochures. Newspapers: newspapers are a form of print media managed by publishers that offer advertising space for display advertisements. Magazines: magazine advertising is generally used to focus on a specific target audience. They are published in intervals and offer relatively more attractive advertisement options than other print advertisements. Brochures, Pamphlets, and Information Booklets. You must have seen brochures of a college or received pamphlets of a new food joint opened nearby. Direct Mail: also known as letterbox advertising, is a form of print media in which the advertising entity sends customised messages through mail to a specific audience. It is the only medium which helps in building a direct relationship with the audience. The advertisement is sent only to the 'right people' (the audience segment most likely to respond). The pros and cons of Print Media * The strengths of print media lie in its tangibility, credibility, and the ability to target specific audiences through niche publications. For instance, a luxury watch brand may choose to advertise in high-end lifestyle magazines to reach their target audience effectively. * People trust a printed message more than an online one specially in the era of fake news and false advertising, * One can attach a sample of perfume or shampoo sachet for the audience to try the product, with the print media. This cannot be done in other medias * Print media faces limitations in terms of limited reach. * There is a challenge of capturing the attention of readers amidst the vast variety of content available. * It has a shortcoming that it can only cater to the educated audience. * It has a short shelf life
5.5.2 Broadcast Media

Who amongst us can ignore the profound impact of television and radio. Television and radio - the dynamic duo. Indian households have been serenaded by unforgettable jingles. Close your eyes and recall the catchy 'Washing Powder Nirma' tune. That's the magic of broadcast advertising. Television: Appealing to both eyes and ears; audio-visual advertisements are effective in communicating a message. It offers an extensive reach. Television advertisements offer a visually captivating and immersive experience, allowing brands to engage viewers through storytelling and creative visuals. The pros and Cons of Advertising on Television * The strength of television lies in its broad reach and the ability to convey emotions effectively. * Television is watched by family together. So the advertiser can reach all the members of the family at the same time which is difficult for other mediums. Like print media is read by one person at a time, not full families surf the internet together. * Television advertising can be costly, and with the rise of streaming services and ad- skipping options, it is essential for advertisers to strategically target their audience. * Television is highly challenged by OTT platforms today. With viewership being captured by OTT platforms, viewership of advertisements declines too. Radio: Radio advertising, another prominent media channel, utilizes audio to reach listeners. Audio advertisements are the quickest mode of communication. They are flexible and repetitive. The pros and Cons of Advertising on Radio * The strength of radio lies in its ability to target specific demographics and engage listeners through catchy jingles and memorable advertisements. * Radio advertisements can be particularly effective for local businesses or for campaigns targeting specific regions. For example, the opening of a local store can be advertised on the radio. People who are traveling to their work or at home will get the required information. Another example would be an event happening at the mall or a mela taking place in the city. People will know the essential details like timings, dates, place and exciting details like any celebrity visiting or offers available etc * The limitation of radio lies in its lack of visual elements, as advertisers need to rely solely on audio to capture attention and convey messages. * In audio medium you cannot demonstrate a product and lure the audience with its look.
5.5.3 Outdoor Media : also known as the OOH platform, is a form of communication that takes
place only when the audience is out of their homes. It gains a broad appeal and helps in creating brand awareness. Instruments of outdoor advertising include: Posters: a print promotional tactic used by sellers to invite attention and awareness. It uses colours, graphics, and slogans that attract the audience. Hoarding: a large structure usually placed near posh localities and busy roads to gain passer's attention. Other instruments: Electric displays, Transit advertisements on buses and trains, Sandwich Board Advertising, Window Display.
The pros and Cons of Advertising on Outdoor Media
* Outdoor advertising offers high visibility and exposure to a wide audience, making it effective for brand awareness campaigns. In the Indian market, you can witness vibrant and creative outdoor advertisements on busy streets and highways. * Clever one-liners, grand photographs, other creative inputs leave an everlasting image in the minds of the audience. * Outdoor advertising faces limitations in terms of limited message length and the potential for distractions amidst a visually crowded environment.

* Sometimes the weather conditions affect the outdoor advertising, leaving a part of it gone with the wind or even the whole banner destroyed.
5.5.4 Digital Media In the present times, we have all navigated the digital landscape, and of
course you have come across ads in this space. The advertisements propels you to notice them like random popups or brands like 'Blink it' commenting on a recipe video. Some brands use interesting events like a runout done by a famous cricketer and connect it to the brand. How many times have you found yourself humming an online jingle?. With the rapid advancement of technology, digital advertising has gained significant prominence. Digital media channels include online platforms, search engines, social media platforms, and mobile applications. The pros and Cons of Advertising on Digital Media * The strengths of digital advertising lie in its ability to target specific audiences. You can track campaign performance, and provide interactive experiences for users. * In the Indian market, we have witnessed the rise of digital advertising through engaging campaigns on platforms like YouTube, Instagram, and Facebook. * There is space for everyone on digital media. You are not limited to a few papers or particular time slots. You can be creative and even small businesses can promote themselves on digital media platforms. * Cost of advertising is highly variable. You can advertise with zero amount of money and invest big money to promote your brand on high end websites. * The digital landscape is highly competitive, and advertisers need to constantly adapt to evolving algorithms and user preferences to stay relevant. * Market is very competitive. Sometimes ideas are copied and reused by some Meetoo Brands, you have to be careful about it. You would recognize the following of Digital Advertisement formats: Display advertising conveys its advertising message visually using text, logos, animations, videos, photographs, or other graphics. Web banners are graphical ads displayed within a web page. Banner ads can use rich media to incorporate video, audio, animations, buttons, forms, or other interactive elements. Pop-ups/pop-unders: A pop-up ad is displayed in a new web browser window that opens above a website visitor's initial browser window. A pop-under ad opens a new browser window under a website visitor's initial browser window. Floating ad: is a type of rich media advertisement that appears superimposed over the requested website's content. Expanding ad: is a rich media frame ad that changes dimensions upon a predefined condition, such as a preset amount of time a visitor spends on a webpage, the user's click on the ad, or the user's mouse movement over the ad. Trick banners: ad where the ad copy imitates some screen element users commonly encounter, such as an operating system message or popular application message, to induce ad clicks. News Feed Ads/ Sponsored Stories/ Boosted Posts: typically exist on social media platforms that offer a steady stream of information updates in regulated formats (i.e. in similar sized small boxes with a uniform style). Interstitial ad: displays before a user can access requested content, sometimes while the user is waiting for the content to load Text ads: gives text-based hyperlinks. Text-based ads may display separately from a web page's primary content, or they can be embedded by hyperlinking individual words or phrases to the advertiser's websites. Some among many other familiar online advertising formats and types are: Mobile advertising Email advertising

Chat advertising Online classified advertising Adware Chat bots As advertising professionals, it is crucial to select the most appropriate media channels based on target audience demographics, campaign objectives, and budget considerations.
5.6 ADVERTISEMENTS AND THEIR TARGET AUDIENCE
The term "Target Audience" refers to the group of people for whom the product or service is created. For example the target audience for a newborns essentials supplying brand like 'Firstcry Cry' are new mothers, the pregnant women. It is important to understand the TA for making strategies and getting the desired impact of an advertisement.
5.6.1 Segmentation of Target Audience
Segmentation involves dividing the broader market into smaller, distinct groups based on shared characteristics. These segments are then targeted with tailored messages and offerings that cater to their specific needs. Through segmentation, advertisers can create more relevant and impactful advertisements. Now, let's explore different target audience classifications commonly used in advertising. * Demographic segmentation categorizes consumers based on demographic factors such as age, gender, income, and education level. An example of demographic targeting is "hero honda bike" which targets men belonging to middle class families who look for good mileage, usable features, good look. comfort, and trust. * Psychographic segmentation focuses on consumers' lifestyles, values, beliefs, and attitudes. By understanding the psychographic profile of the target audience, advertisers can create messages that align with their aspirations and values. An example of psychographic segmentation could be of "zouk bags". They target office going, career oriented women They underlines the feature of bags as spacious for keeping items like laptops, bottle, wallet etc and also establishes the bags as trendy and sophisticated for today's women to carry while going to office. * Behavioral segmentation examines consumers' purchasing behaviors, brand loyalty, usage patterns, and benefits sought. By understanding how consumers behave and make purchasing decisions, advertisers can tailor their messages to target specific behaviors. For example, an advertisement for a health and fitness app like Cult Fit or Healthify Me might target individuals who are already interested in leading a healthy lifestyle, highlighting features such as personalized workout plans and nutrition tracking. By examining these target audience classifications, we gain insights into how advertisers strategically position their messages and products to capture the attention and interest of specific consumer groups. Can you think of some advertisements that exemplify the effective targeting of different audience segments? Let's see: Advertisements for luxury car brands like "Mercedes- Benz" often focus on aspirational values, targeting consumers who desire prestige and status. On the other hand, advertisements for budget-friendly products like "Patanjali Ayurved" cater to consumers seeking affordable and natural options. By analyzing these advertisements and understanding the target audience classifications, we can witness how advertisers use different strategies, language, imagery, and appeals to connect with specific consumer groups. This targeted approach ensures that advertisements effectively reach and resonate with their intended audience. Check Your Progress: 1 Note: 1) Use the space below for your answers.

5.6.2 Be a vigilant Target Audience
It is crucial to remain vigilant and develop a critical eye when it comes to the advertising world. Here are a few tips to help you to be aware and protected. * Watch for Advertorials: There are published editorials which are purely promotional, they are called Advertorials. They are often required to disclose the information. Look for small printed words and phrases like "sponsored content" or "paid advertisement" to identify advertorials more easily. * Know the source of Advertising: The credibility of the publication, website, channel where the advertisement appears is very important. Is it known for unbiased reporting and reliable information? Assess the reputation and track record of the source to determine the level of objectivity. * Analyze the Content: Read the content critically and look for any biases or overtly positive language that just seems to promote a specific product or service. Be mindful of excessive praise without any strong ground. * Read, discuss and gain knowledge: If you come across an advertorial that piques your interest, or a reel talking about the benefits of a brand. Then seek out other sources and compare the information provided. By gathering diverse viewpoints, you can gain a more balanced understanding of the product or service. * Check for reviews: Look for independent reviews and opinions from reputable sources before making any purchasing decisions. Consumer review websites, expert forums, or recommendations from trusted individuals can provide valuable insights beyond the advertorial's messaging. Remember, hidden ad strategies are marketing tools designed to influence consumer behavior. By staying informed, critically evaluating the content, and seeking unbiased sources of information, you can protect yourself from being swayed solely by such content. By being aware of these advertising techniques and their potential side effects, you can protect yourself from falling victim to misleading or deceptive practices. Remember to critically evaluate advertisements, seek reliable information, and make informed decisions based on your own needs and preferences. Here, let me mention to you, a concept that is gaining momentum among media scholars and practitioners - Advertising literacy is the ability to critically analyse and interpret advertisements, understand their persuasive techniques, and make informed decisions as consumers. It empowers individuals to navigate the complex landscape of advertising, distinguish between truthful and misleading messages, and resist undue influence. As consumers, it is essential to be vigilant, ask questions, and stay informed. Together, we can foster a more transparent and ethical advertising environment.

5.0 INTRODUCTION
Information is a journalist's lifeblood. In the digital age, a journalist has to deal with a constant stream of data, videos, official reports, and expert chatter. The hardest part of being a journalist is no longer finding information; it is putting that information together in a way that makes sense. A journalist is no longer just a reporter, but a 'sense-maker' trying to find clarity. In this landscape, a disorganised journalist is an ineffective one. A forgotten source, a misplaced quote, or a failure to vet a viral claim can completely undermine a story and a journalist's credibility. This is why mastering source management is probably the most important skill you can build.

Things were not always this complicated. A journalist's world once revolved around a physical rolodex, a stack of notebooks, and a sturdy filing cabinet. Their power came from the exclusive contacts they would spent years cultivating. The digital age, with its citizen journalists and 24/7 news cycles, changed that. The tools we need now have to do more than just store things; they need to be dynamic systems for capturing, vetting, connecting, and protecting information. In this unit, we will learn how to manage sources like professionals. We will talk about how to make a modern "digital rolodex," how to tell good sources from bad ones, and how to sort through all the information to find what you need.
5.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After working through this unit, you will be able to: * explain why organised source management is a non-negotiable skill for any journalist today, * distinguish between different kinds of digital sources, from raw data to historical archives, * confidently select and use digital tools to capture, sort, and save your research material, and * develop a personal, repeatable workflow for handling sources on any given project, and
5.2 THE MODERN INFORMATION LANDSCAPE
To really understand why source management has become such a big deal, you have to understand the strange new world we journalists find ourselves in. The ground has shifted under our feet, changing not just our tools but the very nature of what "information" is.
5.2.1 How Sources Have Changed Over Time
Talk to a reporter who started their career before the internet, and they will likely tell you about their rolodex. That little rotating file of contacts wasn't just a desk accessory; it was their career, their most prized possession. Research meant long days at the library, digging through dusty archives, and making endless phone calls. Good information was a scarce commodity, and a reporter's value was often directly tied to their exclusive access. The digital revolution blasted those gates wide open. First, search engines and email made finding people and documents easier. Then the second wave hit: social media and smartphones, which effectively turned every single person into a potential publisher. The sources are now scattered everywhere: on X (formerly Twitter), encrypted chats on Signal, public databases, academic journals, and Reddit communities. This demands a completely new way of thinking about organising sources and information.
5.2.2 The Challenge of Information Overload
Today, the problem with information is not scarcity; it is that we are all drowning in information overload. We are faced with an abundance of data, opinions, and outright lies. For a working journalist, this creates some very real problems: * Filtering: Amidst a digital haystack of millions of posts, how do you find the one credible needle? The sheer volume can be paralysing. This leads to what is called "filter failure", a state where you either miss what is important or get distracted by what is loud. * Cognitive Load: Trying to juggle dozens of browser tabs, email chains, and social media feeds is a recipe for burnout and simple, preventable mistakes. Without a system, vital details will inevitably get lost in the shuffle.

* Verification: Social media rewards speed above all else. The pressure to be first is in constant conflict with the duty to be right. Being able to distinguish a real eyewitness from a clever bot is now a fundamental, everyday skill. * Confirmation Bias: When you are overwhelmed with information, it is natural to want to grab onto things that confirm what you already believe. This is confirmation bias. A good journalist must actively fight this impulse by building a diverse network of sources that consistently challenges their assumptions.
5.2.3 Why Source Management Matters
In this new world, having an effective source management system is more than just a good habit; it is a skill that will help you sustain your career as a journalist. You can think of good source management as a way to shield yourself. It lets you: * Work faster and smarter: You don't have time to look through old emails for a phone number when you have a deadline. An organised system makes it easy to find all the facts, quotes and contacts you need. * Accuracy: To make sure everything is correct, you should keep a clear, written record of every piece of information. It makes it easy to check facts and gives you confidence in your story when people ask questions. * Maintain lasting records: Your well-organised database of sources is a private intelligence network that grows in value over time. It helps you see patterns, link stories, and find new ways to look at things that others might miss. * Keep your sources safe: It is much harder to keep secret sources safe in a time when digital surveillance is common. When you take a systematic approach, you make sure that sensitive information is safe and not just left open in your inbox or a random cloud folder. ethically.

5.3 TYPES OF DIGITAL SOURCES
So far, we have discussed what today's information landscape looks like, understanding its benefits and challenges from the perspective of a journalist. Now, let us zoom in. Knowing how to organise is pointless if you don't know what you are organising. You can think of digital sources in terms of levels of reliability. Each level has its own strengths, weaknesses, and rules.
5.3.1 Primary Sources
Think of primary sources as the raw and unfiltered ingredients of your story. They are the bedrock of original reporting and the closest you can get to an event without being there. Some key examples of primary sources are as follows:

* Government databases: Public portals like data.gov.in, the National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB), and global sources like the World Bank's Open Data. * Peer-reviewed academic studies: You can find these on Google Scholar, PubMed, and JSTOR. They are vetted by other experts, which gives them weight and credibility. * Raw datasets: This could be financial data from a company, or scientific data from an organisation like ISRO. * Court documents: These could include documents like First Information Reports (FIRs) and judgments, which are often available online. * Eyewitness media (User-Generated Content): Photos, videos, and social media posts by people who were present on ground too can constitute primary sources for journalists today, subject to verification. Let us now discuss how a journalist can use primary sources optimally for their story: * For Data Stories: Instead of just basing your story on a summary provided on an organisation's website, download the raw data yourself. Analysing NCRB data on your own might reveal a trend in cybercrime that no one else has spotted. * For Breaking News: Eyewitness content is powerful, but you must verify it vigorously before you use it in your story. We will go into that later in the unit. * For In-Depth Features: Don't just read the summary of an academic study. Dig into the methodology. Who was studied? How big was the sample size? Who paid for the research? That is where the real story is. Primary sources provide your strongest evidence, but they demand the most work. It is your job to analyse them, verify them, and give your audience the context they need to understand them.
5.3.2 Secondary Sources
These sources build a bridge from raw data to your reporting. They analyse, interpret, or comment on primary sources, giving you that first layer of context and expert opinion. They are absolutely essential for efficient research. These include: Reports from other reputable news outlets: A solid article from a trusted media organisation is important in terms of research, and it makes for a credible source of information. * Expert analysis from think tanks: Organisations like the Centre for Policy Research (CPR) in India publish reports that analyse complex issues, making for a rich secondary sources. * Academic review articles and books: A book or an article that synthesises years of research on a topic is a classic secondary source. * In-depth articles and documentaries: Long-form journalism that pulls together many primary sources into a single story again makes for a secondary source. The same can e said of well-researched documentary films. Secondary sources can save you days of work by summarising the key points of a complex topic. They provide the history, the politics, and the social context. A good secondary source is also a roadmap to the primary sources you need and a list of experts you should call. However, they also pose some risks. If a secondary source got a fact wrong, you will too. Every source also has a perspective. A think tank might have a political slant. You should know who is behind the source and why they might be saying what they are saying. You should use secondary sources as a jumping-off point. Your job is to find a new angle, a new source, or a new piece of data to move the story forward. The idea is to use secondary sources for context and leads, not for your final story.

5.3.3 Tertiary Sources and Aggregators
These sources compile and summarise information from many other places. They give you a broad overview, but they are not very deep. In journalism today, tertiary sources can include encyclopedias like Wikipedia, fact-checking websites (like Alt News or BOOM Live), and news aggregators like Google News. Let us now look at some ways in which journalists can use tertiary sources: For initial research: Use Wikipedia to get a quick grasp of the key players, dates, and jargon for a new topic. Then, scroll down to the "References" section. That is your real starting point. To debunk falsehoods: See if a fact-checking site has already tackled a viral claim. To gauge coverage: Use a news aggregator to see who is covering a story and what their angle is. You should never cite a tertiary source in a final story. Think of them as a compass that points you where to go. Your real work begins where the Wikipedia article ends.
5.3.4 Digital Archives and Libraries
These are your time machines. Like their names suggest, they are huge digital collections of websites, books, newspapers, and more. They are a goldmine for journalists because they give you access to information that has disappeared from the live internet. They are absolutely vital for any serious investigation. Some important examples of digital archives and libraries a journalist can use today are: Internet Archive and Wayback Machine: You can use it to see what a website looked like a year ago or ten years ago. It is great for finding a deleted policy page or catching a famous person changing their story. Newspaper Archives: Reading the original news articles is the best way to get a sense of history. You can find these in India at places like the Nehru Memorial Museum & Library (NMML) or in The Times of India Archives. These articles show you events as they were first reported. National Digital Library of India (NDLI): This is a huge government project that gives you access to a lot of academic papers, reports, and historical documents. It is great for doing specialised research. An archive is a snapshot in time. Always note the date of the record and check it against other sources to get the full picture. A deleted webpage is a clue, not a conclusion.
5.4 THE DIGITAL TOOLKIT FOR SOURCE MANAGEMENT
Let us now learn about tools that will allow you to manage your digital sources and streamline all the information you have obtained. These are as follows:
5.4.1 Note-Taking and Research Hubs
This is your digital brain, your notebook and filing cabinet rolled into one. It is where you store and organise everything. You need a place to clip articles, save PDFs, write interview notes, and store photos, and then be able to find it all later. These include Evernote, Notion, Microsoft OneNote, and the like. Example: Imagine you are investigating water pollution. You can create a dedicated notebook where every scientific paper, government report, interview transcript, and photo goes, tagged with keywords like "Ganges" or "industrial waste." Six months later, you can find anything in seconds.

5.4.2 Social Media and Real-Time Sourcing
Social media is essential for breaking news, but it is also a minefield. Therefore, you need tools to manage it; for instance, to create curated lists of experts and officials to cut through the noise. Or to use advanced search to find people on the ground. These include X Lists, and TweetDeck. For example, during a cyclone, you can switch to your pre-made X List of meteorologists and local emergency services. This gives you a clean, verified feed of real-time information, separate from the public panic and speculation.
5.4.3 Curating Your Information with RSS
RSS (Really Simply Syndication) is an old-school tech that is more valuable than ever because it lets you escape the "filter bubble." You subscribe to sites directly, and you see everything they publish, in order. They combine updates from hundreds of blogs, news sites, and journals into one organised feed that you control. Applications like Feedly and Inoreader can be used to do this. For example, a health reporter can use Feedly to pull in updates from the World Health Organization, the ICMR, and key medical journals. They see every press release and new study the moment it is out, without an algorithm deciding what they should see.
5.5 A MODERN WORKFLOW: FROM DISCOVERY TO ARCHIVE
The right tools are useless without a process. What we need is a workflow that combines smart technology such as the tools we discussed in the previous section with your journalistic judgment. The process is simple but very helpful, as you will learn:
1. Discovery and Capture: This is where you cast your net. You are using your RSS feeds,
X List, and alerts to find new information. The moment you find something useful, you can use a web clipper to save a copy to your research hub. Don't just bookmark it, save it. Links die and posts get deleted.
2. Organisation and Annotation: Raw information is just clutter. You have to give it
context immediately. As you save an item, tag it with relevant keywords. More importantly, write a short note to your future self: "Why did I save this? What is the main point? Who is the source?" This takes 10 seconds but will save you hours later.
3. Verification and Triangulation: This is the core of journalism, and you can't automate
it. Every new piece of information must be treated with suspicion. Triangulate it by confirming the fact with at least two other independent sources. Vet the source themselves: who are they and what is their angle? Use tools like reverse image search to check photos.
4. Integration and Storytelling: Now you are ready to write. Your research hub is your
private, verified library of facts, quotes, and data. Because you know where everything came from, you can write with confidence and attribute everything properly.
5. Secure Archiving: Your work isn't over once the article is published. Archive your
research. This creates a permanent record you can use for follow-up stories, or to defend your work if challenged. And if your notes contain sensitive source information, make sure they are stored securely and, if necessary, encrypted.
5.6 POPULAR SOURCE MANAGEMENT TOOLS
5.6.1 Evernote
Evernote is a powerful tool for taking notes and clipping web pages. Its best feature is its search, as it can even find text inside PDFs and images. It is a workhorse for capturing information and finding it again fast.

5.6.2 Notion
Notion is more like a set of Lego bricks than a simple notebook. You can build interconnected databases. For a journalist, this means you can create a master database of sources with their contact info, expertise, and a history of your past interviews. It is great for managing complex, long-term projects.
5.6.3 Zotero
Zotero was built for academics, but it is a secret weapon for journalists. It is free, and fantastic for collecting, organising, and citing sources. It is especially good at grabbing all the metadata from academic studies and reports, which makes it perfect for any story that requires precise citation.
5.6.4 Feedly
Feedly is the best RSS reader out there. It is the most effective tool for monitoring your beat without getting manipulated by social media algorithms. You can even train its AI assistant to flag articles with specific keywords, helping you manage the daily flood of information.
5.7 THE ETHICAL DIMENSIONS OF DIGITAL SOURCING
Using these tools well is a technical skill. Using them ethically is your professional duty. The digital world is an ethical minefield, and you have to tread carefully. Let us discuss some key issues confronting journalists today:
5.7.1 Misinformation, Disinformation, and Verification
Misinformation is false information spread by people who don't know it is false (e.g., sharing an old video of an accident, thinking it is from today). Disinformation is false information that is deliberately created to deceive, often as part of an organised campaign. A journalist's primary job is to be a trustworthy filter for their audience. That means you must treat everything you find online with skepticism until you can prove it is true. If you don't, you become part of the problem. Always ask: "How does this person know this?"
5.7.2 Protecting Sources in the Digital Age
Protecting a confidential source is one of the most sacred duties in journalism. In the digital world, that means more than just not naming them. Every action you take online leaves a digital footprint, or metadata (the data about your data, like when and where a photo was taken). You must: * Use Secure Channels: Talk to sensitive sources using end-to-end encrypted apps like Signal. It collects far less metadata than services like WhatsApp or regular text messages. * Understand Your Footprint: Be aware that your search history, location data, and call records can be tracked. * Practice Good Digital Hygiene: Use strong passwords and two-factor authentication. Be paranoid about phishing scams trying to get access to your accounts.
5.7.3 Attribution and Digital Plagiarism
The internet makes it incredibly easy to copy and paste. Don't. Journalistic ethics require you to give credit where it's due. Clearly credit the original source, whether it's another news outlet or a person who posted a video to social media. Link back to the original report or dataset. This is good "link journalism." It respects the work of others and gives your readers a path to more information. Never pass off someone else's work as your own. There is a difference between aggregation and plagiarism. Don't cross that line.
5.7.4 The Ethics of Using User-Generated Content (UGC)

A video from an eyewitness can be a powerful primary source, but the person who shot it is not just a content creator; they might be a victim or a witness to a traumatic event. Before you use their content, you must ask yourself a series of questions: * Is it real? Have I done everything I can to verify its authenticity? * Do I have permission? Have I contacted the creator and received their explicit consent to use this? * Could I be putting them in danger? Broadcasting their content could expose them to harm. Should I blur their face or anonymise their name? * Am I being respectful? This person may have just gone through something terrible. Approach them with empathy, not as if they owe you something. * Have I given proper credit? Attribute the work exactly as the creator wants you to. Check Your Progress 2
1. What is source triangulation and why is it important?
