for news gathering.

5.8 LET US SUM UP
In this unit, we have dug into the vital skill of managing sources in the digital age. We can see how the job has changed from one where there wasn't enough information to one where there is too much, and how that makes things harder. We have divided the digital world into primary, secondary, tertiary, and archival sources to show how each one is important for good reporting. We also looked at the tools of the trade: note-taking hubs, social media monitors, and RSS readers. But more importantly, we have stressed that tools are nothing without a process. A systematic workflow grounded in the timeless principles of verification, triangulation, and ethics is what truly matters. In the end, source management isn't about the tools. It is about developing a critical way of thinking. You can cut through the noise and make journalism that is useful, accurate, and really valuable to the public if you learn to be a disciplined curator of information, a skeptical interrogator of sources, and an ethical user of content.
5.9 KEYWORDS
* Source Management: The system of collecting, organising, vetting, and archiving information and contacts for journalism. * Primary Source: Direct, uninterpreted information or data (e.g., a report, a video from the scene). * Secondary Source: A source that interprets or analyses primary sources (e.g., a news article about the report). * Tertiary Source: A source that compiles and summarises other sources (e.g., an encyclopedia). * Digital Archive: An online collection of historical documents, websites, or other media. * Wayback Machine: A service that archives old versions of websites.

* Source Triangulation: The practice of confirming information with at least two, preferably independent, sources. * User-Generated Content (UGC): Content created and posted by the public on online platforms. * Metadata: Data that provides information about other data (e.g., the time and location a photo was taken). * Filter Bubble: The intellectual isolation that occurs when algorithms personalise your online experience, showing you only content you are likely to agree with.

6.0 INTRODUCTION
Advertisements are the messages paid for by those who send them and are intended to inform or influence people. One of the most fascinating ways to communicate with the masses among the several forms of persuasive communication is advertising. Although considered a marketing tool, it is highly regarded as the most effective means of communication when approaching a consumer and making a decisive impact on their choices. Advertising is impersonal and persuasive, transmitted via mass mediums, consisting of tangible and intangible products, services and ideas. For an advertisement to succeed, the right message must reach the right people at the right time. Strategy is the most essential thing, requiring careful planning

and action. Various theories and models explain the process of advertising as a means of communication. Understanding these basic postulates will help you frame effective advertisements. Advertising is a powerful tool that companies use to promote their products and services. In India, a country with diverse cultures and a rapidly growing economy, advertisements play a crucial role in shaping consumer behaviour. At the heart of effective advertising are "advertising appeals" - strategies used to grab attention and persuade the audience. This chapter will explore various advertising appeals and how they are applied in Indian advertisements. We'll look at real examples from Indian brands to understand how these appeals work.
6.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After working through this Unit, you should be able to: * Recognise the importance of appeals in advertising. * Analyse how various appeals are used in Indian advertisements. * Interpret the appeals made to the intended target market in advertising.
6.2 ADVERTISING APPEALS
Advertising is a form of non-personal communication by an identified sponsor about a product, service, organisation, or idea. At its core lies advertising appeal, which is used to grab the attention of consumers, effectively influence their feelings, and change their attitude in favour of the advertised product/service. The appeal is concerned with the context that consumers feel with the ad. Creating such an appeal encompasses understanding what the consumers want or need and what excites them. Advertising appeals are communication strategies that marketing and advertising professionals use to grab attention and persuade people to buy or act. In rhetorical theory, the concept of an "appeal" dates to Aristotle, who identified the three main appeals of communication (also known as the rhetorical triangle): ethos, pathos, and logos, or, in modern language, credibility, emotion, and logic. The central concept was that if something can project itself as credible (ethos), it may persuade people. Also, if emotions (pathos) or logical reasoning (logos) are attached, people can be persuaded to act. Advertising appeals to people because it is credible, affects the consumer's emotions, or makes logical sense.
6.2.1 Importance of Advertising Appeals
Appealing to a consumer's rational or emotional buying behaviour, appeals in advertising play an essential role in persuading people to want a particular commodity or changing their wants from one to another. They act as a bridge between consumers' wants and the product or service. Appeal is the central idea around which the advertisement is created. Salient features of the product or service are called appeals in advertising. M. Satyanarayan defines advertising appeals as 'the earnest representation made by an advertisement about a certain quality, service or feature or fact which forms the keynote or theme in advertisements. Often called the unique sales proposition (USP), appeals ignite the will of prospective buyers to purchase and acquire the product or service. They can arouse desire and induce action on the part of customers. Advertisement appeals are usually directed towards consumers' buying motives. A theme or appeal is usually selected through consumer study and research. Generally, advertisements appeal to human emotions, feelings, sentiments, needs, etc.
6.3 TYPES OF ADVERTISING APPEALS
There are numerous appeals. As many emotions, that many measures to trigger them and those many advertising appeals. Let us discuss, with examples, some of the most used appeals by advertisers:
6.3.1 Favourable Price Appeal
The message is about the price, which takes the central stage in the advertisement. This is used extensively during any sales promotion, e.g., end-of-season sales, special offers, festivals, or any other occasion. It can

even revolve around a particular time of the day when sales are usually low, and the demand is low. For example, Big Bazaar, a popular retail chain in India, regularly runs a campaign called "Sabse Sasta Din" (which translates to "The Cheapest Day").
6.3.2 Feature Appeal
The significant traits or attributes of the product/service dominate the persuasion message. These advertisements are highly informative and build a favourable attitude of the target product towards the product. For example, Tata Motors used Feature Appeal extensively to promote their electric vehicle, the Nexon EV, by focusing on range, fast charging, safety, technology, and low running costs.
5.3.3 Competitive advantage appeal
The promotional message in the advertisement directly or indirectly compares competitors' products/services and their specific attributes. For example, E-commerce sites like Snapdeal.com and Flipkart.com remain competitors, which is visible even in their advertisements.

6.3.4 Emotional Appeal
Emotional appeals target the audience's feelings and sentiments. They aim to create an emotional connection between the brand and the consumer. Example: Surf Excel's "Daag Acche Hain" (Stains are Good) Campaign. This long-running campaign by the detergent brand Surf Excel uses the emotional appeal of parental love and childhood innocence. The ads typically show children getting their clothes dirty while doing good deeds or playing. The tagline "Daag Acche Hain" (Stains are Good) appeals to parents' emotions by suggesting that it's okay for children to get dirty while learning and growing. This emotional appeal works because it taps into the universal parental desire to nurture their children's development, even if it means extra laundry. By associating their brand with positive childhood experiences, Surf Excel creates a warm, fuzzy feeling beyond the product's functional benefits.
6.3.5 Health and Wellness Appeals
Health and wellness appeals focus on a product's benefits for a person's physical or mental well-being.
Example: Horlicks' Campaigns
Horlicks, a popular malted milk drink in India, often uses health and wellness appeals in its advertising. Their campaigns frequently focus on how Horlicks can help children grow taller, stronger, and sharper. One of their campaigns, "Badne ki Bhookh" (Hunger to Grow), showed how Horlicks could support children's growth and development. By appealing to parents' desire for their children's health and success,

Horlicks positions itself as more than just a tasty drink - it's presented as an essential part of a child's nutrition.
6.3.6 Fear Appeal
Fear appeals use the audience's fears or anxieties to motivate them to take action or buy a product. Lifebuoy Soap's Hand Washing Campaigns are an example. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Lifebuoy soap launched several campaigns promoting hand washing. These ads used fear appeals by highlighting the risks of not washing hands properly, especially during a pandemic. One of their ads showed how germs can spread through everyday objects like doorknobs and mobile phones. By creating awareness about these invisible threats, Lifebuoy tapped into people's fear of illness and positioned their soap as a solution to this fear. While fear appeals can be effective, they must be used responsibly and provide a straightforward solution to the fear being invoked.

6.3.7 Humour Appeal
Humorous ads are often the best remembered as they can hold consumers' attention and put them positively toward the product. Humour appeals make consumers laugh and create an emotional link with the product. A well-executed humour appeal enhances recollection, evaluation and the intent to purchase the product. Advertisers link the product with the humour. For example, Fevikwik's "Todo Nahi, Jodo" (Don't Break, Join) Campaign. Fevikwik, an instant adhesive brand, is known for its humorous advertisements. Their "Todo Nahi, Jodo" campaign features a series of funny situations where Fevikwik saves the day by fixing broken objects. One memorable ad shows a fisherman using Fevikwik to stick a coin to his fishing rod, tricking fish into thinking it's food. The absurdity of the situation and the clever use of the product creates a humorous appeal that makes the ad memorable. Humour appeals work well because they entertain the audience, making them more receptive to the brand message. However, ensuring that the humour is appropriate and doesn't overshadow the product itself is crucial.
6.3.8 Rational Appeal
When the advertisement focuses on the consumer's need for practicality and functionality in a product, rational and logical appeals work best. Advertisers relay this message by focusing on product features and cost. These ads tell consumers the benefits of purchasing a product and, to add credibility, provide proof. For example, Tata Salt uses a combination of rational and emotional appeals in its "Desh Ka Namak" campaign. The sensible part of the appeal focuses on the iodine content in the salt, which is crucial for preventing iodine deficiency disorders. In their advertisements, Tata Salt often mentions how it's "Desh Ka Namak" because it contributes to the nation's health by providing iodised salt. They use facts about iodine's importance and how their salt meets national standards. This rational appeal targets health-conscious consumers who want to make informed choices about their food.

6.3.9 Social Appeals
Social appeals tap into people's desire to be accepted, admired, or part of a group. Example: Tanishq's "Remarriage" Advertisement Jewellery brand Tanishq created a groundbreaking advertisement featuring a woman's second marriage. The ad showed a dark-skinned bride with a daughter from her previous marriage, preparing for her wedding. This ad challenged social norms and celebrated progressive values. By showcasing a scenario that's often taboo in Indian society, Tanishq appealed to consumers who value social progress and inclusivity. This social appeal positioned Tanishq as a forward-thinking brand that celebrates diverse forms of love and family.
6.3.10 Lifestyle Appeals
Lifestyle appeals associate a product with a desirable way of life or social status.
Example: Raymond's "The Complete Man" Campaign
Raymond, a textile and apparel brand, has long used the slogan "The Complete Man" in advertising. These ads typically show sophisticated, well-dressed men in various situations - successful at work, caring for family, or enjoying leisure activities. By associating their brand with this idealised image of a modern Indian man, Raymond appeals to consumers who aspire to this lifestyle. The lifestyle appeal works by suggesting that using Raymond products is a step towards becoming "The Complete Man."

6.3.11 Sensuality Appeal
Sex and romance capture the eyeballs and gain the attention of the people. Fragrance products like deodorants and perfumes very often use sex appeal to convey romance to women, indicating that the use of the product will help them find the man of their dreams. They are generally done by showing the woman spraying the fragrance and capturing the attention of an attractive male who passes her on the street. Sometimes, sensual messages capture attention but may fail to generate turnover owing to stiff competition and many ads with similar storylines. Example: Wildstone Deodorant Advertisements Wildstone, an Indian deodorant brand, often uses sensuality in its ads. Their commercials typically feature attractive men using the product, followed by women being irresistibly drawn to them. These ads show that the fragrance can enhance one's sensual appeal.
6.3.12 Bandwagon Appeal
A bandwagon appeal makes consumers believe that they are missing out on something by addressing the consumer's need to belong. For example, Airtel's "Jo Tera Hai Wo Mera Hai" Campaign Airtel, a telecom company, used the bandwagon appeal in its "Jo Tera Hai Wo Mera Hai" (What's Yours is Mine) campaign. The ads showed people freely sharing their Airtel data with friends and family, implying that everyone is part of the Airtel network and you should be, too. This appeal suggests that everyone uses a product or service, encouraging others to join in to avoid feeling left out.
6.3.13 Adventure Appeal
Many people love adventure and excitement. The adventure appeal aims to make people feel that this excitement, action, entertainment, and adventure will be enhanced if they purchase or use the endorsed product or service. This appeal associates a product with excitement, risk-taking, and thrilling experiences to attract adventure-seeking consumers. Example: Royal Enfield often uses adventure appeals in its advertising. Their campaigns frequently show their motorcycles being ridden through challenging terrains like the Himalayas, appealing to those who seek adventure and exploration.

6.3.14 Brand Appeal
Some people are brand-conscious and like to associate themselves with the name. Appealing to brand- conscious people with particular inclinations towards brands is the most pertinent way to establish a long- term consumer base. The brand appeal aims to make people buy a product because the brand itself is a statement that the person hopes to associate with. This appeal relies on the reputation and prestige of the brand itself to attract consumers. For example, Tata Group often uses its brand name as the primary appeal. Their "Trust" campaigns emphasise the Tata name and its long-standing reputation in India, using the tagline "Tata for India" to leverage their brand appeal.
6.3.15 Endorsement Appeal
This appeal uses recommendations from experts, celebrities, or satisfied customers to build credibility and trust. The endorsement appeal encourages people to buy a product or service or act in a certain way because people they know, respect, admire, and recognise also use that product or service. Trust is built by using recognisable people. For example, As a leading actress known for her style and beauty, Kareena lends credibility to a hair care product. Her association implies that Head & Shoulders can help consumers achieve beautiful, healthy hair like hers. Kareena's long-standing career and relatively controversy-free public image make her a trustworthy figure for many Indian consumers.

6.3.16 Masculine/ Feminine Appeal
This appeal is particularly gender-specific. Consumers are made to feel that if they use this product, they will appear more attractive, sexier, or stronger. This appeal targets gender-specific desires, roles, or stereotypes. Masculine Appeal Example: Imperial Blue Whisky's "Men Will Be Men" Campaign This long-running campaign plays on stereotypical male behaviours and fantasies. The ads often show men daydreaming about attractive women or trying to impress them, always ending with the tagline "Men will be men." It appeals to a particular notion of masculinity, though it has faced criticism for promoting outdated gender stereotypes. Feminine Appeal Example: Titan Raga Watches Titan Raga, a women's watch brand, often uses feminine appeal in its advertising. Their ads typically showcase successful, independent women and celebrate femininity. One of their campaigns, "#theallnewbold," highlighted women making unconventional life choices, appealing to modern Indian women's desire for self-expression and independence. The campaign features Alia Bhatt, one of Bollywood's leading young actresses known for her versatile roles and outspoken personality.
6.3.17 Topical Appeal
This appeal connects the product or brand to current events, trends, or popular topics. Example: Amul Butter's Topical Cartoons. Amul Butter is famous for its topical cartoon advertisements that comment on current events. These ads, featuring the Amul girl, cleverly incorporate butter-related puns into commentary on everything from politics to sports to entertainment. For instance, when India's Chandrayaan-2 mission reached the moon, Amul released an ad with the tagline "Moon meetha Karo," showing the Amul girl on the moon.

These appeals demonstrate the diverse strategies used in Indian advertising to connect with consumers. Each appeal targets different aspects of consumer psychology, from desires and aspirations to social trends and current events. The effectiveness of these appeals often depends on how well they resonate with the target audience and align with the brand's overall identity and messaging.
6.3.18 Patriotic Appeal
Patriotic appeals use national pride and love for one's country to create a connection with the audience. For example, Tata Tea has incorporated the "Desh Ka Kulhad" theme into its broader marketing strategy, which already has a strong foundation of patriotic appeal. It emphasises the traditional Indian method of serving tea in kulchas by associating the brand with a nationwide movement to revive traditional practices. 6.4 CASE STUDIES
6.4.1 Amul's Long-running Ad Campaign
Amul, one of India's largest dairy brands, provides an excellent case study on the effective use of multiple advertising appeals over a long period. Amul's cartoon advertisements featuring the Amul girl have been running since 1966. These ads comment on current events, from politics to sports to entertainment, always with a witty tagline that incorporates Amul's products. Appeals Used:
1. Humour Appeal: The ads use wordplay and visual jokes to entertain the audience.
2. Topical Appeal: Amul keeps its ads fresh and relevant by commenting on current events.
3. Emotional Appeal: The Amul girl character, with her distinctive polka-dot dress and blue hair,
evokes nostalgia and affection among Indians who have grown up seeing these ads.
4. Patriotic Appeal: The ads often celebrate Indian achievements or comment on issues of national
importance, fostering a sense of shared identity with the audience. Why It Works: * Consistency: The format has remained essentially unchanged for decades, creating a sense of familiarity and tradition. * Versatility: The campaign can adapt to any current event, keeping the brand constantly in the public eye. * Subtlety: While the ads comment on various topics, they always incorporate Amul's products without seeming forced. * Cultural Connection: The ads have become a part of Indian popular culture, with people looking forward to Amul's take on current events.

Amul's campaign demonstrates how a brand can use multiple appeals in a cohesive, long-term strategy to build strong brand recall and emotional connection with consumers.
6.4.2 Cadbury Dairy Milk's "Kuch Accha Ho Jaaye, Kuch Meetha Ho Jaaye" Campaign (2023-2024)
Cadbury Dairy Milk, a leading chocolate brand in India, launched a campaign with the tagline "Kuch Accha Ho Jaaye, Kuch Meetha Ho Jaaye" (which translates to "Let something good happen, let something sweet happen"). This campaign was notable for its focus on social responsibility and emotional appeal.
Key Appeals: Emotional and Social Responsibility
1. Emotional Appeal:
* The campaign tapped into the feelings of kindness, generosity, and community spirit. * It associated eating chocolate with doing good deeds, creating a positive emotional connection.
2. Social Responsibility Appeal:
* It positioned Cadbury as a socially conscious brand, resonating with increasingly socially aware Indian consumers. * The campaign encouraged consumers to act kindly and support local businesses. Why It Works: * Cultural Resonance: It taps into the deeply ingrained Indian cultural values of kindness and community support. The campaign aligns with "mithai" (sweets), which is associated with positive moments in Indian culture. * Emotional Connection: Linking chocolate consumption with acts of kindness creates a positive emotional association with the brand. It makes consumers feel good about their purchase, associating it with virtuous behaviour. * Universal Appeal: The message of kindness and community support resonates across different age groups and demographics. * Storytelling Approach: Using relatable, everyday scenarios makes the message more impactful and memorable. It creates mini-narratives that viewers can easily connect with and remember.
6.5 APPLYING ADVERTISING APPEALS EFFECTIVELY
While understanding these appeals is essential, applying apoeal effectively requires careful consideration of several factors:
1. Know Your Audience: Different appeals work better for different demographics. For example,
rational appeals work well for high-involvement products like cars or insurance, while emotional appeals are more effective for FMCG products.
2. Align with Brand Identity: The chosen appeal should align with brand identity and values. A
luxury brand might use lifestyle appeals, while a health food brand might focus on wellness appeals.
3. Cultural Sensitivity: In a diverse country like India, it's crucial to ensure that the appeals are
culturally appropriate and don't offend any group.
4. Combine Appeals: Many successful ads combine appeals. For example, a patriotic appeal might be
combined with a rational appeal to create a more compelling message.
5. Timing and Context: The effectiveness of an appeal can depend on current events or social trends.
For instance, health appeals became particularly relevant during the COVID-19 pandemic.

6. Regulatory Compliance: Ensure that the appeals used to comply with advertising standards and
regulations, especially when using comparative appeals or making health claims. Check Your Progress : 2 Note: 1) Use the space below for your answers.

6.6 LET US SUM UP
Advertising appeals are potent tools for marketers, especially in a diverse and dynamic market like India. From the emotional tugs of Surf Excel's "Daag Acche Hain" to the patriotic fervour of "Hamara Bajaj," from the humor of Fevikwik to the lifestyle aspirations of Raymond, Indian advertisements provide a rich tapestry of how these appeals can be applied effectively. The key to successful advertising is understanding and applying these appeals thoughtfully and creatively. As the Indian market continues to evolve, with changing consumer behaviours and new media channels, the application of these appeals will also need to adapt. However, the fundamental principle remains the same--to connect with the audience in a way that resonates with their needs, desires, and values. By mastering the art of using advertising appeals, brands can create messages that sell products and become a part of the cultural conversation, leaving a lasting impact on consumers and society.

6.8 GLOSSARY
Advertising Appeal: These are strategies for grabbing people's attention to persuade them to purchase your product or service. The approach can be a marketing or advertising strategy. Many advertisers commonly use appeals to influence their customers. Brand Identity: The visible elements of a brand, such as colour, design, and logo, that identify and distinguish the brand in consumers' minds. FMCG: Fast-moving consumer goods, which are products that are sold quickly and at relatively low cost. Target Audience: The specific group of consumers most likely to want your product or service, and therefore, the group of people who should see your ad campaigns.

6.0 INTRODUCTION
Imagine a journalism student working on her first news report. She observes people in a busy market, asks a few shopkeepers about rising prices, checks a government website for official figures, reads old news articles, and looks at what people are posting online about the same issue. Unbeknown to her, she is already using several data collection methods that professional journalists rely on every day. For journalists, data refers to pieces of information collected from different sources to understand an event or issue. This information may include facts, numbers, opinions, documents, photographs, or digital traces. Proper data gathering enables journalists to present accurate stories, prevent misinformation, and build public trust. Today, much of this data collection is no longer limited to notebooks and field visits. Journalists must keep up with the changes taking place in the media landscape and adopt new methods and tools accordingly. Reporters now rely heavily on online databases, social media analytics, and real-time digital tools to gather and verify information. In this unit, we will explore the basic methods journalists use to collect data and understand how these practices are evolving with new technological and digital developments.

6.1 LEARNING OBJECTIVES
After studying this unit, learners will be able to: * understand the meaning of data and its significance in journalism, * identify different sources and methods of data collection used in traditional and digital journalism, * understand the process of planning data collection for news stories, * develop basic skills required for effective and responsible data collection, and * recognise ethical considerations related to data collection, especially in the digital media environment.
6.2 WHAT IS DATA IN THE CONTEXT OF JOURNALISM
In journalism, data refers to raw facts, figures, statistics, and information that journalists collect, analyse and use to tell stories and report news. Data is described as the "new oil," which basically connotes that whoever controls this precious resource controls the world. Data can be either the tool used to tell a story, the source upon which a story is based, or both. Furthermore, in journalism, it involves the use of statistics, design, charts, graphs or infographics to present information to audiences. For instance, a reporter studying election vote shares across different phases to explain the final outcome works directly with data. She can then use graphs and infographics to explain this complex story to the audience in a simple way.
6.3 IMPORTANCE OF ACCURATE DATA COLLECTION
Accurate data collection is fundamental to journalism because it ensures that the stories reported are based on reliable and truthful information. Gathering data and distinguishing between reliable and unreliable sources of data is one of the building blocks of data journalism. Journalists need to develop an understanding of the public domain and the techniques to access publicly available data to ensure accuracy. Without accurate data, conclusions reached will be quite useless, and the credibility of the journalist will be compromised. Accurate data collection also helps journalists to create deeper insights into what is happening around us, allowing them to see patterns and trends that the naked eye cannot detect. Modern-day mass media cannot fulfill its watchdog function without harnessing and analysing data, making accurate data collection essential for demanding transparency and accountability in governance. An incorrect report based on unverified figures can quickly damage public trust when facts are later proven wrong.
6.4 THREE KEY TERMS: RELIABILITY, VALIDITY AND BIAS IN DATA
Each profession has its own tenets that serve as both principles and guide. For a medical professional, the four key tenets are respecting patients' choices, acting in their best interest, doing no harm, and fairness. For a journalist, these tenets include truth, independence, fairness and humanity. Every time a journalist sets out to work on a story, these tenets should be her guiding principles. Right from the data collection stage, she should question her own methods and the trustworthiness of the material she encounters. In this process, she must gauge her data against three key tests: Is this data reliable? How valid is it? What are the biases it may entail? Let us look at these three terms in greater detail. Reliability: It means the audience can trust that information is accurate, credible and complete. Reliability comes from rigorous fact-checking, transparent sourcing, accountability and strong editorial integrity. One must use correct names, dates and figures in a story for it to be credible. It also requires adherence to ethical codes that prioritise truth and minimise harm. Reliable reporting focuses on getting the story right and offering balanced perspectives, rather than simply being fast. In doing so, it builds

public trust through consistent, dependable practices, even as digital media continues to challenge traditional norms. Validity: This refers to the extent to which an enquiry gives the correct answer or provides a true reflection of social reality. Validity is about the truth-value of a story. It means that the data collected accurately reflects the thoughts, views, actions and experiences of the subjects. For data to be judged as objective, it has to be both reliable and valid. Validity ensures that the investigation reveals what it is supposed to reveal without distortion. If a news story on student issues truly captures their problems, the data used is valid. Bias: According to Oxford dictionary, bias means a strong feeling in favour or against a person or a group of people. Everyone should have the same opportunity to make their case in an investigation, meaning there should be freedom from bias. Bias can occur when data is collected in a manner that systematically favours certain outcomes, or when journalists impose their own views and interpretations rather than reflecting the true responses of their subjects. Collecting opinions only from one section of society can lead to a biased understanding of public opinion. Check Your Progress 1 Note: 1) Use the space provided below for your answers.
2) Compare your answers with those given at the end of the unit.

2. Why is accurate data collection important for journalists?

3. Differentiate between reliability and validity.

6.5 METHODS OF DATA COLLECTION IN JOURNALISM
Data collection is the most crucial component of research for journalists. This is because the credibility and accuracy of news reporting depend on the quality of information gathered. In contemporary journalism, the process of data collection has expanded beyond traditional methods and now includes digital platforms that generate large volumes of information. Journalists collect data using multiple methods, depending on the nature of the story, the availability of sources, and the urgency of reporting. Broadly speaking, the methods of data collection in journalism can be categorised into primary data collection, secondary data collection, and open source data collection, all of which are increasingly shaped by digital technologies. In the previous unit, we touched upon the different information sources available to journalists. Here, we will discuss these sources in greater detail and also discuss the methods reporters use to access information from them.
6.5.1 Primary Data Collection
Primary data collection refers to the process of gathering information directly from original sources. Primary data is first-hand data and allows journalists to capture real-time information,

human perspectives, and ground-level realities. In digital journalism, primary data collection is often supported by digital tools such as smartphones, online communication platforms, and digital recorders, which make the process faster and more flexible. Now, let us explore some of the sources from which journalists collect primary data. Interviews: These are among the most commonly used methods of primary data collection in journalism. Through interviews, journalists interact directly with sources such as officials, experts, eyewitnesses or members of the public to gather opinions, explanations and factual details. In the digital media environment, interviews are no longer limited to face-to-face interactions. Journalists frequently conduct interviews via video calls, emails or messaging applications. This allows them to access sources across geographical boundaries and report quickly, especially during breaking news events or developing stories. Surveys: This involves collecting information from a group of respondents through structured questionnaires. This method helps journalists understand public opinion, behaviour patterns or trends within a specific population. In digital journalism, surveys are increasingly conducted using online forms and social media platforms, enabling journalists to collect responses instantly from diverse audiences. The numerical data generated through digital surveys can be easily organised and analysed, making surveys particularly useful for data-driven reporting. Field visits: This involves journalists visiting locations related to a news event to observe situations directly, and to collect factual and visual information. Despite the growing use of digital tools and digital spaces, field visits remain essential for verifying information and understanding local contexts. Journalists often use mobile phones, digital cameras, and live- streaming applications during field visits to document events and share real-time updates with audiences through digital platforms. Beat reporting: Information from journalistic beats refers to data collected through continuous coverage of specific subject areas such as health, education, politics, crime or the environment. Beat reporters develop regular contacts and gain domain expertise, which helps them identify important developments quickly. In the digital era, beat-related information is frequently gathered from official websites, email alerts, online press releases and social media accounts of institutions, enabling journalists to track updates and policy changes efficiently. Right to Information Act: Information from RTI is an important source of primary data in journalism, especially for investigative and accountability reporting. The Right to Information Act allows journalists to access official records, documents, and data maintained and stored with public authorities. With the digitisation of governance systems, journalists increasingly file RTI applications through online portals and receive digital responses, which can be organised and analysed more easily using digital tools.
6.5.2 Secondary Data Collection
Secondary data collection means gathering information that has already been collected and published by other sources. As discussed in the previous unit, journalists use secondary data to provide background information, historical context, and comparative analysis for their stories. In digital media, secondary data is readily accessible through online databases and digital repositories, making research more efficient. Now, we will learn about some important methods using which secondary data collection is done. Government datasets: These are a major source of secondary data for journalists and include census records, economic surveys, crime statistics, and policy documents published on official digital portals. These datasets help journalists analyse social and economic trends, evaluate the impact of government policies, and support evidence-based reporting. Since government data is increasingly released in digital formats, journalists can download, organise, and visualise this information using software tools.

Media archives: These consist of previously published news articles, television broadcasts and digital content. Journalists rely on media archives of different organisations to trace the development of an issue, verify earlier claims, and compare past and present reporting. Digital archives allow journalists to quickly search and retrieve information, which strengthens follow- up reporting and long-term investigations. Academic reports: Research studies conducted by universities and research institutions are an important source of data collection. These reports provide verified data, theoretical perspectives, and methodological insights that help journalists add depth to analytical and explanatory stories. With academic journals and research papers available online, journalists can access scholarly work easily and incorporate research-based findings into their reports. Institutional reports: These are reports published by government bodies, international organisations, and non-governmental organisations. Reports of organisations such as WHO, UNESCO, NITI Aayog, and the like often include indicators, evaluations, and sector-specific data. Journalists use institutional reports to support reporting on issues such as development, public health, education and environmental change, with digital access making such data more timely and searchable. Corporate data: In additional to data accessed from government sources, corporate data is another important information source as it provides annual reports, financial disclosures, and performance statements released by companies. This data is essential for business and economic journalism. Journalists analyse corporate information using spreadsheets and digital visualisation tools to explain financial trends and corporate accountability.
6.5.3 Open Source Data Collection
Open source data collection refers to the process of gathering information from publicly and freely available digital sources. With the growth of the internet and digital platforms, open source data has become an important resource for contemporary journalism and digital media research. These 'open' sources allow people to collaborate and share of information, thereby promoting transparency, cost-cutting and innovation. Give below are some methods journalists use to collect open source data. Web scraping: This process involves extracting data from websites using automated tools or software. Journalists use web scraping to collect large volumes of publicly accessible data from government portals, public listings or online databases. This technique enables journalists to identify patterns and trends that may not be easily identified through manual data collection. Social media mining: This involves collecting and analysing data generated on social media platforms. Journalists study posts, comments, hashtags, and engagement metrics to understand public reactions, emerging narratives and audience behaviour. API data, which refers to data exchanged between different applications, allow journalists to access structured social media data for research and analysis, supporting digital storytelling and trend reporting. Open Source Intelligence (OSINT): This involves collecting information from publicly accessible sources such as satellite imagery, fact-checking platforms and investigative databases. In digital journalism, OSINT tools help journalists verify claims, check visual evidence and support investigative reporting using 'open' digital data. Collaborative databases: These are shared platforms where data is contributed and maintained by multiple organisations or individuals. OpenStreetMap, Wikidata and Global Fishing Watch are some examples of collaborative public databases. Journalists use such databases for cross- verification and collaborative projects, especially in large-scale investigations that involve digital data sharing across newsrooms.

Citizen journalists' reports: Such reports include photographs, videos and eyewitness information shared by ordinary citizens through digital platforms. With the rise of smartphones and social media, reports like these often provide early information during breaking news events. Journalists incorporate citizen-generated content after verification to supplement professional reporting in the digital media environment.
6.6 PLANNING THE DATA COLLECTION PROCESS
Planning the data collection process helps journalists organise their work, avoid errors, and ensure that the information gathered is relevant and accurate. For students of journalism, careful planning makes it easier to handle multiple digital and offline sources in a systematic and responsible manner. Let us look the process of how journalists should go about planning the collection of data.
6.6.1 Identifying the Needs of the Story
The process of data collection begins with understanding what the story actually requires. A journalist must clearly identify the purpose of the report and the type of information needed to tell the story accurately. This involves thinking about the main issue, the people involved, and the context in which the event is taking place. For students of journalism, this step helps in separating relevant information from unnecessary details, especially in a digital environment where information is available in abundance.
6.6.2 Formulating the Central Question
Once the needs of the story are clear, the journalist formulates a central question that guides the entire reporting process. This question acts as the backbone of the story and gives direction to the data collection efforts. A well-framed central question ensures that the journalist remains focused and collects only the data that contributes directly to answering that question.
6.6.3 Choosing a Suitable Data Collection Method
After defining the central question, the journalist must decide which data collection method will be most effective. Depending on the nature of the story, this may include interviews, surveys, field visits, official records, digital databases or open source platforms. Journalists often combine traditional methods with online tools to gather comprehensive and timely information.
6.6.4 Creating a Plan for Data Collection
Creating a plan helps organise the data collection process in a systematic manner. This involves deciding the sources of data, the sequence of collection, the time required, and the tools to be used. For journalists, planning also includes managing digital resources such as online documents, cloud storage and verification tools to ensure smooth and efficient data handling.
6.6.5 Verifying Data
The final step in the planning process is data verification, which ensures accuracy and reliability. Journalists must carefully check collected data for factual errors, inconsistencies, or misleading information. Triangulation, or cross-verifying information from multiple sources, is especially important in the digital media environment, where misinformation can spread rapidly and unverified data can harm journalistic credibility. Verification can include cross-referencing, expert consultation and source evaluation.
6.7 SKILLS FOR DATA COLLECTION
Effective data collection in journalism requires a combination of analytical, interpersonal and technical skills. It requires a blend of traditional reporting with digital abilities in order to find, analyse and tell stories. Some broad prerequisites for any journalist should be: critical thinking, accuracy and adaptability. Let us look at some more such skills a reporter must possess when trying to collect and work with data.

Identify relevant facts: One of the most important skills for data collection is the ability to extract useful data from a large amount of available information. Journalists, especially in the digital media environment, are often exposed to vast quantities of data from online platforms, official websites and social media. The ability to identify relevant facts and ignore unnecessary information helps in maintaining focus and accuracy. Assessment of the data: Another essential skill is evaluating the credibility of the information. Journalists must be able to assess whether a source is reliable, authentic and trustworthy. This involves checking the source of the data, understanding its context, and verifying it with additional sources when required. In digital journalism, this skill is crucial for dealing with online misinformation and unverified content. Technical ability: Know-how of software systems is also increasingly important for journalists. Familiarity with digital tools--spreadsheets, data visualisation tools, survey platforms and content management systems--helps journalists organise, analyse and present data effectively. Even basic technical competence can significantly improve efficiency and accuracy in reporting. Fostering trust of the source: Finally, winning the confidence of sources is a vital journalistic skill. Whether interacting with people during field reporting or communicating through digital platforms, journalists must build trust so that their sources feel comfortable sharing accurate and honest information. Together, these skills enable journalists to collect data responsibly and produce credible, effect and evidence-based stories.
6.8 ETHICS AND LEGAL ISSUES IN DATA COLLECTION
Ethics play a crucial role in data collection for journalists because the information they gather and then disseminate directly affects people's lives. Ethical practices ensure that journalism remains fair, responsible and trustworthy, especially in the digital media environment. Given below are some ethical considerations for every journalist vis-a-vis the data collection process. Consent in data collection: Journalists should take permission before collecting or using personal information. For instance, informing a person that their interview will be recorded or their photo will be used, or how and why data related to their yearly spending will be used is basic ethical practice. Protecting sources: Journalists must protect the identity of sources if revealing their identity can cause them harm. For example, when a whistleblower shares information about wrongdoing at their workplace, the journalist should not reveal their name. Handling sensitive information: Care must be taken while reporting sensitive matters such as health, family issues or financial problems. Reporting a person's medical condition without consent is unethical unless it serves a clear public interest. Data security: Journalists should store collected data safely, especially when it is in digital form. Keeping interview recordings and documents password-protected is a simple way to prevent misuse. Avoiding bias and manipulation: Journalists must collect data in a fair manner and not twist facts to support a personal opinion. For instance, collecting views from only one group while reporting public opinion will lead to biased reporting. Following these ethical practices can help journalists maintain credibility and public trust while carrying out responsible data collection.

6.9 LET US SUM UP
This unit explained the meaning of data and its importance in journalism. We discussed three key terms that each journalist should hold as sacred, i.e., reliability of data, validity of data and bias in data. Various data collection methods used by journalists were discussed in the unit. These include primary data collection methods such as interviews, surveys, field visits, and information collected via RTI; secondary data collection methods include collecting data from government datasets, media archives, academic and institutional reports, etc; and finally, open source data collection methods which include web scraping, social media mining, Open Source Intelligence, citizen journalists' reports, etc. The unit also highlighted the importance of planning in the data collection process, beginning with identifying the needs of the story, formulating the central question, creating a data collection plan, and finally verifying and triangulating that data. Skills required in the data collection method were also discussed, wherein the significance of identifying relevance, data assessment, technical ability and fostering trust were flagged. We rounded off with a discussion about the ethical considerations in the data collection, which include privacy, consent, data security and prevention of bias. In the digital media environment, responsible data collection is essential for producing accurate, credible, and trustworthy journalism; this unit was geared to guide the learners about that process.
6.10 KEYWORDS
Data: Raw information collected from different sources for reporting and analysis for the creation of engaging news stories. Reliability: It means the audience can trust that the information is accurate, credible and complete. Validity: This refers to the extent to which an enquiry gives the correct answer or provides a true reflection of social reality. Bias: When data is collected in a manner that favours certain outcomes, or when journalists impose their own views rather than reflecting objective facts. Open Source Data Collection: It refers to gathering information from publicly available digital sources.

OSINT: This involves collecting information from publicly accessible sources such as satellite imagery, fact-checking platforms and investigative databases. Web Scraping: This process involves extracting data from websites using automated tools or software. Social Media Mining: This involves collecting and analysing data generated on social media platforms. API (Application Programming Interface): A set of protocols that allows softwares to communicate and exchange data. Triangulation: The process of verifying data using multiple sources to cross-reference facts, reduce bias, and enhance a story's credibility.
6.11 FURTHER READINGS

1. Data in journalism refers to pieces of information collected from different sources that
help us understand an event or issue, and then report it. This information may include facts, numbers, opinions, documents, photographs or digital traces.
2. Accurate data collection ensures that news reports are reliable, credible and based on
truthful information, helping to maintain public trust. Without accurate data, conclusions reached will be useless, and the credibility of the journalist compromised.
3. Reliability means the audience can trust that the information is accurate, credible and
complete. It comes from rigorous fact-checking, transparent sourcing, accountability and strong editorial integrity. One must use correct names, dates and figures in a story for it to be credible. interviews, surveys, ssfield visits, beat reporting and RTI, while secondary data is obtained from already published sources such as government reports, media archives, academic and institutional reports, corporate data and the like.
2. Open source data collection involves gathering information from publicly available
digital sources such as websites, social media platforms, online databases and projects that are collaborative in nature. These 'open' sources allow people to collaborate and share of information, thereby promoting transparency, cost-cutting and innovation.
3. Data verification helps identify errors, ensures accuracy, prevent misinformation and
build public trust by cross-checking information from multiple sources. This can include cross-referencing, expert consultation and source evaluation.

7.0 INTRODUCTION
The American Association of Advertising Agencies (AAAA) defines an Ad Agency as an independent business organisation, composed of creative and business people, who develop, prepare and place advertising media for sellers for their goods and services. Hence advertising agencies understand the requirements of an advertiser which is then converted into an advertising campaign. The agency creates, plans, executes and manages this campaign through print, TV, radio, online, outdoor advertisements and mobile marketing. Agencies may also handle other forms of promotion and marketing for its clients which can include individuals or businesses, corporations, non-profit organizations and other agencies. The first acknowledged advertising agency was that of William Taylor in 1786. Initially the advertisement including copy, layout and artwork was done by the client with the agency doing the ad- space brokerage (Wlosik,2024).He adds that this model was followed until the 19th century when N.W.Ayer& Son, founded in New York, started providing a full range of services including planning, creating and executing complete campaigns for its customers like De Beers, AT&T etc. Kushwaha (2023) writes that "The Indian Advertising Agency" was the first ad-agency of India. It was the outcome of two events i.e. the swadeshi movement of 1907 which gave rise to indigenous industries and the installation of the first rotary linotype machine by "The Statesman" newspaper of Calcutta(Kolkata) in 1907. Madison Avenue, in the city of New York, USA is regarded as the Mecca of Advertising, because a number of renowned world ad agencies are located in this area. In India, Mumbai -considered to be the financial capital, has a concentration of a number of ad agencies, followed by metropolitan cities like Delhi, Chennai, Bangalore, Pune, Hyderabad, Kolkata, Gurugram etc. Some of the leading ad agencies in the world are Ogilvy and Mather, a New York based advertising and marketing company which was started in 1948 by David Ogilvy; Mullen ;McCann World groupwhich was formerly known as McCann Erickson; Publicis Group a French company founded in the year 1926 by Leo Burnett; Dentsu a Japanese ad agency; Havas; Grey Global which was founded in 1917 etc. Some of the leading Indian ad agencies are DDB Mudra Communications which was founded in the year1980, by A.G. Krishnamurthi, initially in Mumbai; Grey India a part of the Grey Global Group is

situated in Mumbai; Rediffusion (Y&R) ; McCann -Erikson India Ltd; Ogilvy and Mather; JWT; Triverse etc.
7.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES

7.2 ORGANISATIONAL STRUCTURE OF ADVERTISING AGENCIES
The functioning and organising of advertising agencies across the globe have evolved over the years. A lot of changes have happened in the typical set up of an ad agency for carrying its day-to-day activities. It performs its functions as a team as team work is very much needed to take the task forward as the student will see in the way the client-servicing is done. The organizational structure with the number of people employed depends on the type of work an agency does. An agency could be a "full-service" agency dealing in all stages of advertisement and will thus need different expertise for different stages of the advertising cycle; it could be an "interactive" agency specializing in digital media; a "creative boutique" which only creates advertisements; a media buying agency which only books slots in various media channels or it could be an "In House" agency such as ones used by very large corporations. The core activities of an agency remain the same. There are ad agencies which operate globally while some operate at the national level and a few which operate only at the local level. Ad agencies usually have various departments headed by concerned heads. Large ad agencies like any large organisation have a senior management team which takes up the responsibilities for the business and financial operations. The management team includes a chief executive and a finance director, a group of account officers, account planners, media planners, creative team, administrative team, the sales team and a production team. Usually, a member of the management team takes up the responsibilities of maintaining relationships with the Board of Directors in case there is one. Advertising agencies today mainly fall under two categories: full-service agencies and specialised agencies. Full-service agencies are those which offer the complete range of activities related to media and market sectors. On the other hand, specialised agencies have three categories of service, that of - independent agencies offering only limited services such as media planning and buying, secondly agencies specifically focusing on internet related activities and thirdly agencies working in a narrow market sector such as business-to-business advertising. 7.3 DEPARTMENTS OF AN AD AGENCY
Like any other organisation, ad agencies too have different departments that function according to their nature of activity, but are closely related to one another.

The various departments in an ad-agency are as follows: * Accounts * Client-Serving * Creative * Production * Media Planning Let us now look at these departments in detail.
7.3.1 Accounts
One of the major departments of an ad agency is the accounts department. In advertising parlance, an 'account' means a client. Usually, the accounts department is headed by an accounts director who is also the member of the board in case if it is a private limited company. He/She will be assisted by account executives or account planners who will assist him/her in carrying out the further activities. The main duty of these account executives is to understand the needs and requirements of a client. Popovic (2023) writes that the objective of account teams is to develop overall advertising strategies which will help the client achieve their advertising goals. He adds that these teams are responsible for holding the "creative briefs" (a one/two-page document outlining the strategy, objectives, and details of a project) which help the creative teams do a good job for the client. Apart from this, these teams will also be more or less responsible for holding creative briefs or meetings that help creative teams perform their best jobs. These briefs usually include client background information, main advertising objectives, target audience identification, and other facts/metrics/insights that will get the project more familiar with the customer, i.e., help with advertising and marketing tasks. Creative briefs typically include a set of specific deliverables and a deadline by which the teams have to "deliver" or achieve the set advertising goals. The major responsibility of getting the clients to the agency lies with the team of the accounts department. They need to coordinate with all the other departments so that ad campaigns are created in tandem. Clients approach an agency based on an agency's past and current assignments and popularity in the advertising market. The advertising term for account planning is called "client servicing", which means that the account planner takes care of the needs and requirements of the clients who have approached the agency for their advertisement needs. An account planning personnel in turn performs a number of activities as follows: * Planning the main objectives of the advertising * Selecting and evaluating the feedback received in the form of research, so that it becomes easy for the team to make further decisions and judgements. * They see to it that the objectives and the feedback are relevant and stimulating to the rest of the team members especially the creative team. * Responsible for acting as a bridge between the client and the agency and solving all the queries raised by the clients and finding suitable solutions for them. * They also assist in getting effective messages to their target audience by creating desired responses.
7.3.2 Client Servicing
Client servicing refers to providing all the necessary assistance for a client in terms of planning, designing, budgeting, production and media placements. Some clients spread their budget across more than one agency while some prefer the appraisal system too. Clients move out to a new agency when there is monotony, difference in ideas, difference in opinions or if the creative team quits an agency to move to another agency.

7.3.3 Creative
The heart and soul of an ad agency is the creative department which contributes by the virtue of its work in attracting as well as retaining the clients of an ad agency. This is the department which visualizes all the ideas and packages the bundle into a presentable product for its target audiences. The creative department is headed by a creative director who will be assisted by a group of creative members which include, copy chief, copy writers, visualiser, layout artists, typographers, freelancers and a full-time artist. These team members work together to develop the concepts of an advertisement campaign. In bigger and larger agencies, a creative director manages various teams who work on different accounts. Whereas, in smaller firms, these creative directors work with freelance writers to finish the tasks. * Copy Writers are the creative backbone of an agency. Their main responsibility is to give shape to the ideas in the form of words. Their content adds more life and vibrancy to the advertisements. They are responsible for creating and designing the promotional content for their clients. They are the ones who create the taglines, jingles, content texts which makes the ad linger in the minds of the consumers. They are the brains behind the billboards, catalogues, emails, websites which are extensively used by the advertisers. * Graphic Designers role is to create designs, logos, characters which suit the copy content, by identifying the colour textures, the fonts, the background, and the animation to convey the message in a stronger way. Graphics make an advertisement more attractive and effective. * Art directors are the individuals who are responsible for the visual images and styles in newspapers, magazines, product packaging, television and movie productions. Their main role is to create the overall design and direct others to develop art work and layouts. They are the individuals who need to have a thorough knowledge about the typography, photography and printing techniques. They work as a part of a team, so that they can create a campaign which can instantly have a positive impact on the consumer regarding the product and the brand. Their list of activities includes: discussion with the creative team, planning a budget, working with artists, photographers, maintaining on and off location shoots, presentation of the final draft to the clients. Most of the art directors work under the supervision of a creative director. Thus the activities of the creative department include :conceptualise the idea for the client ; copywriters do the copy and create storyline for the ad and contribute to the theme of the advertisements ; the copy is then converted into various forms by the visualiser ; visualiser with the help of layout artists designs the ad ; the typographers and the final artists prepare the final artwork and the creation of logo, selection of colour, using appropriate fonts etc.
7.3.4 Production Department
Is responsible for the delivery of the approved ad copy..The production department is headed by a production manager, who is assisted by several assistants. The responsibilities of these assistants are to do typography, making blocks, lettering, stereos and electros (the production process). It is in this department where the work gets organised in the form of copy, artwork proofs, corrections and then the final output in the form of final copy as per the schedule. In bigger agencies the work is supervised under traffic controller (who has a say for the finished final copy) but, in smaller agencies the work can be done by using freelancers in production. Ad makers are one who prepare the end product. Ad agencies might have in-house ad makers who do this work or some agencies outsource this work to other agencies or freelance ad makers who give the finished product. They assist in doing the ad production, by identifying the artists, musicians, jingle makers, voice over artists, set designers, editors who finish the ad as per the requirement of the clients. There is a huge demand for visual ads nowadays due to the medium of TV and social media. This is also done under the supervision of a production manager but exclusively for visual media communication. Hence this department's work areas include: manage the schedules of the clients; responsible for managing the campaign budgets; coordinate the work with creative and media departments; coordinate with external suppliers such as videographers, photographers, artists and printers and are responsible for all the final output requirements of clients of the agency.

Many times, ad agencies have to depend on outsourcing to finish their services. Many of the bigger agencies have in-house teams, but smaller agencies have to depend on freelancers to get the work done. They hire creative people according to their requirements. Freelancers can include: directors for planning; camera persons working under the guidance of the director; graphic designers; copy writers etc.
7.3.5 Media Planning
Another important department in an ad agency is the Media Planning department. The finished end product (advertisements) has to be sent to different media. The Media planning department is headed by a Media Controller or Planner, who is usually assisted by a number of sales executives and marketing executives. The marketing team, which consists of a research team, works very closely with these media planners to give a better idea about the market and its demands. Thus, giving a clear picture as to how the plan can be executed in favour of their clients. Their main role is to coordinate with the media houses and the agency. The very first question which arises is the allotment of budget for this process. Budget plays a very crucial role, because depending upon the budget availability, the clients are guided to position their ads in the various media outlets such as Print, Digital, TV, radio, outdoor etc. Not only the media but also the decision of which media to be selected, what should be the frequency, size of the ad, when to get it published/displayed - all these major decisions lie with the media planners. The sales executive acts as a bridge in getting the allotment of space in newspapers and magazines, time in Television and Spots in radio and digital media for their clients. The clients have to depend on these media planners to get their ads in the public domain. All the media planners have to maintain a very good rapport with the media outlets. Majority of the ads reach the media through ad agencies. Both media and these agencies are interdependent on each other, one can't survive without the other. The chances of getting the ads published and broadcasted is more if the clients go through any of the reputed ad agencies. The main activities performed by a Media planning department are :identifying a proper medium for their client; suggesting ideas and helping to place their ads at the right time; helping the clients get a good deal in terms of budgeting; buying space / time /spots for a client in various media; conducting periodic market research for their clients and coordinating all the activities between clients and media in terms of billing, commission, consent and getting the final approval. The media department completely works on a commission basis. The amount is shared between the ad agency and the media houses in the ratio of 70-30, which is universal in nature. The primary principles followed in a media and agency relationship are: the agency is responsible for all the payments to media; there is no cut in commission by the agency which is received from the clients to the media; uniform policy is followed by the media for all the agencies and the media does not alter any material without prior consent of the agency. There are a number of media planning agencies across the globe who take up the responsibilities of assisting and guiding the clients in all way. Some of the noted ones are: Vowels Advertising, The Media Ant, Grey, Adver labs, Good Apple Digital, YoYo Media, Seagull Advertising etc. As Popovic writes, advertising agencies are the most efficient companies that handle their client's advertising, marketing and promotional requirements using the latest and most appropriate strategy and technology and hence have a knack for meeting industry needs and keep evolving with technology. The ad agencies of today have been using various software's for the purpose of remaining relevant in the era of digital media and digital marketing. Some of the noted software's which are extensively used because of their user friendly and easy adaptability are Marketo, Vocus, Hubspot, Sailthru, Yesware, Localvox, Mailchimp. These software's are used for various activities such as customising emails, increasing user engagement, providing marketing solutions, customer acquisition and retainment, to launch marketing campaigns.

7.4 DIGITAL AD AGENCY STRUCTURE
Popovic (2023) writes that there is an intricate and complex nature involved in the world of digital advertising which changes the standard advertising structure of ad agencies in the digital ad arena. The digital ad agencies may also do the work of digital marketing for the clients to engage customers and drive revenue through online channels for example search engines, social media, advertising platforms and email. As digital is extremely technology centered, experts and teams need skills on a variety of software and digital tools. The Digital agencies or separate experts/teams/departments in standard ad agencies catering to digital advertising/marketing as per Popovic will have the following people or teams in them. The agencies could also outsource part of the work to expert freelancers or specialized agencies. * Marketing Strategist or the marketing team are the ones who understand how different digital channels work, what the target audience segment looks for and the overall impact and thus they manage the overall digital strategy including creating marketing plans and budget allocations * Data Analysts or the analyst team interpret Key Performance Indicators (KPI's) and other key metrics which determine whether the ad campaign is efficient or needs refinements. They are also the ones producing reports for tracked metrics. * Web Designers and Graphic Designers or the web design team design how websites and web apps look to represent a client's brand using a brand design language and brand identities or creating the feel and look of a brand. Working with content specialists and strategists they find best ways to visually represent a client's vision, mission and voice. * Developers and the development team are responsible for building websites and other digital solutions for example a custom blog or web application development. * SEO Experts or the SEO team specialize in helping websites and brands become visible to the target audience considering that all visibility is based on searches by target audiences on search engines and other sites. Thus, handling keywords, on-page optimization and link building ensure a higher ranking for the website built. * Content Marketing Specialists or the Content team to forge the client's content strategy which includes copy, site content, blogs, infographics etc. which helps a business with online visibility, credibility and reliability. * Social Media Managers or social media team takes care of the various social media channels and related tasks like creating content for different channels and even doubling for customer support in cases. This also includes optimizing client's social profile, social media marketing campaigns, using social tools and providing a meaningful engagement. * Paid Media Experts or the PPC (payment per click) experts/team are the ones who do paid digital advertising including its planning and running of paid media campaigns on platforms like Facebook Ads, Google Adsense etc. This is markedly different from the free campaigns on social media. They work with the social media department and content department to ensure an optimised social media ad strategy and ad copies that align with clients advertising needs. * Project Managers or the project management team are the people who connect all the above- mentioned experts/teams so that the project is effective and deadlines met. They also mediate between clients and other teams making sure there is a synergy between the client and the client-servicing teams. Examples of Digital agencies include 3 Media Web, Digital Silk, SmartSites, Mirum India, WATConsult, Webchutney etc. Activity - 2 Interact with some professionals from various departments in the agency you visit and enquire about their roles. This will give you a practical input to the theoretical knowledge you have gained in this Unit.

Ad agencies work closely with the client to gather information and pitch their campaign ideas, followed by the creative process of actually making and distributing both print, radio, TV , outdoor, digital and other media ads. Advertising agencies use a wide range of advertising strategies to create marketing campaigns tailored to their clients' needs. These days, the trend of specialised boutique agencies is picking up. 7.7 GLOSSARY
Account: A business relationship between the advertising agency and its client, including the management of marketing activities and campaigns. Commission: The fee an advertising agency charges for their services, usually a percentage of the total advertising spend. Collaterals: Supplementary advertising materials such as brochures, flyers, posters, and other printed or digital assets used to support a campaign.

Dailies: The raw, unedited footage from a day's shoot, reviewed to assess the progress and quality of the production.
