7.0 INTRODUCTION
Imagine you are sitting in your hostel room. You are scrolling through Instagram stories. Suddenly, one of your friends starts a poll: "Do you trust news shared on social media?" Y N You click an option almost instinctively. Within seconds, your response joins hundreds of others. Your friend created one tiny dataset. Tiny but powerful, reflecting real public opinion. Welcome to the world of online surveys. Surveys have been one of the oldest tools of human inquiry. From journalists in the 19th century collecting information door-to-door to newspaper editors in the 1980s mailing feedback forms to subscribers, surveys have always been about listening to people's voices systematically. But

what has changed dramatically in the 21st century is how these voices are collected. Smart phones, cloud computing and social media have replaced traditional mediums of data collection for surveys. Today, online surveys are faster, cheaper and much more easily accessible. Whether you want to know what kind of news people read, which OTT shows are trending among adolescents or how audiences respond to animated films, online surveys make it possible to collect opinions quickly and efficiently. As future journalists, communicators or researchers, understanding how to design, distribute and interpret online surveys will help you conduct your own projects, from class assignments to professional newsroom work. This unit will take you through the process step-by-step, with examples drawn from your own digital lives.
7.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After completing this unit, you will be able to: * understand the evolution and significance of online surveys, * learn about their advantages and scope in journalism, * apply principles of designing effective online questionnaires, * identify popular online survey platforms and their features, and * analyse and report survey data effectively.
7.2 BASIC UNDERSTANDING OF SURVEY
Survey is a primary method of data gathering from a specific population to study opinions, knowledge and behaviour trends. Traditionally conducted in person, by telephone or through mailed questionnaires, today almost all surveys are conducted online. Not only is this method faster, cheaper and far-reaching, it also allows us to track responses in real-time. However, this change has also meant there are new requirements in terms of its planning, distribution and analysis, especially in journalism. Today, media outlets use surveys to insert multimedia components in their work, make decisions based on automated skip logic, and have their data integrated directly into software for analysis, which will be discussed at length later in the unit.
7.2.1 Evolution from Traditional to Online Surveys
The survey method began to be used in the early 20th century when social scientists introduced standardised instruments for measuring public opinion. Over the years, surveys conducted via mail and telephone became popular because they could reach large sample groups at a relatively low cost. The internet revolution of the 1990s, which brought email and web-based platforms, opened new channels for conducting surveys, and today, online surveys have become the main choice for survey-based data gathering. A major change in the field has been the coming of open-source and freemium tools like Google Forms, which made survey-creation easy and accessible. These have been embraced by government, academic, corporate and nonprofit organisations for gathering audience feedback or programme evaluations. From the point of view of the media, such a transition implies the emergence of more participatory models of inquiry in which respondents express themselves through interactive polls and web-based response mechanisms.
7.2.2 Advantages of Digital Survey Methods

Online surveys offer considerable methodological and logistical benefits. In addition to cost- efficiency, they are characterised by fast circulation, automatic data capture, and built-in analytics that significantly cut down the time spent on gathering and processing data. Respondents can fill out questionnaires whenever it is suitable for them, making the process flexible in terms of time, reach and geography. There is also a certain amount of freedom in the way questions can be put to respondents. By using pictures or videos, you can ensure respondent's comprehension as well as interest. Moreover, automation can help in the reduction of human error in data entry and coding. Finally, and not the least, online surveys provide anonymity, which encourages more honesty in responses.
7.3 ONLINE SURVEY DESIGN PRINCIPLES
Survey designing simply means constructing a questionnaire. However, this involves choosing the types of questions and the form of answers very carefully so that there is a smooth flow. The design of an online survey influences the quality and trustworthiness of the data collected, as well as the degree of user-interaction. Good design principles make the survey understandable and capable of measuring variables accurately. Let us discuss some of these.
7.3.1 Questionnaire Construction for Digital Platforms
When converting a questionnaire into an online format, its construction principles remain the same, but its manner of presentation changes. It is important to adjust a questionnaire to a mobile and digital environment. Let us look at some important elements. Every questionnaire is preceded by an introduction, which gives the respondent the necessary information like the survey purpose, and the approximate time needed to complete it. It guarantees confidentiality and voluntary participation, and contact details that can be used if the participant has any questions or concerns. The initial message is vital in creating trust. The questions need to be formulated in a way that they do not have more than one interpretation and are unbiased. The wording has to be simple, clear and direct. It should not contain complex language or use words that the respondent may not understand. Questions should be based on single concept only. Double-barreled questions, which ask about two things at once, should be avoided, as they decrease clarity and can give invalid answers. The layout of the questions should be based on the logical order of topics, starting with the general or less sensitive ones to the more specific or sensitive topics. A pre-test or pilot test of the survey should be conducted as it helps in determining whether technical features and their adaptability to different devices and browsers are operational. Testing also points out issues like long wait times, unclear instructions or difficult navigation that could result in a higher dropout rate.
7.3.2 Question Types and Response Formats
Online surveys employ a variety of question types, which are as follows: Closed-ended type questions offer respondents a limited number of response choices. They are simpler to carry out and quantify, since straightforward coding and statistical analysis is possible. Some formats examples are: multiple choices, yes/no dichotomies, Likert scales (which represent a degree of agreement or frequency on a scale normally from 1 to 5), semantic differential scales (e.g.,

evaluating a service from "Excellent" to "Poor"), and ranking questions where the items are graded in order of preference. Open-ended type questions give respondents the liberty to express themselves in their own words and thus, provide more detailed and less standard data. However, for this, qualitative coding is needed for analysis. These types of questions are appropriate if you want detailed explanations, suggestions or opinions, which are not accounted for by the closed responses. The choice of using different question types depends solely on the journalist's objectives. For instance, scales (close-ended question type) can be used to measure attitudes or perceptions quantitatively. Meanwhile, open-ended questions can be employed for capturing new ideas and personal experiences. Often, a well thought-out questionnaire employs both formats to get structured data and exploratory insights. As for formats, in an online setting, response formats should be simple. The user interface should contain intuitive buttons, checkboxes, dropdown lists and sliders that are suitable for touch devices. The size of text-entry boxes should be adequate, and only short answers should be permitted to prevent respondents from tiring themselves with a small screen.
7.3.3 Survey Flow and User Experience
Survey flow means the order and way in which questions are presented to participants. This has a great influence on user-experience and the chances of the survey getting completed. A logically-arranged questionnaire reduces the mental effort required and contributes to obtaining more accurate responses. Remember the following when designing the survey: Questions: Normally, surveys start with screening or demographic questions, which are easy and straightforward. This serves as a warm up for the respondents. Onwards, the questionnaire moves toward thematic questions, which is where you will seek their engagement. It is advisable to place sensitive or difficult questions at the end of the questionnaire when the trust of the respondent has been won. Skip logic: Also known as branching, this feature allows the respondent to skip parts of the questionnaire that are irrelevant for them. For instance, if a person states that he/she does not have a car, questions related to the use of a car can be skipped. This helps in customising the flow to the respondent's needs, shortening the time needed for completion. User Interface: The survey's 'look' must be 'clean' so that the respondent's attention is not diverted from the questions. For this, you must use sufficient white space and consistent fonts. Buttons used for navigation should be unambiguously labeled so that the user can move forward, backward or save his/her progress without any difficulty. Progress bars which indicate the completed portion of the survey can be a source of motivation for respondents to carry on till the end.
7.3.4 Mobile Responsive Design Considerations
Since most online activity happens on mobile phones, mobile responsivity has become a must in designing a questionnaire. This allows a survey to be automatically adjusted to various screen sizes and orientations, without compromising the content or ease of navigation. Mobile optimised surveys must have bigger buttons for simpler tapping, should need less scrolling, and must be shorter. Answer options should be clearly visible, even if no zooming is done, and the pages should load quickly. Testing on a few mobile devices before the actual launch of the survey can be helpful in locating and fixing problems.

7.4 SURVEY PLATFORMS AND TOOLS
Survey platforms are the primary enablers of effective online surveying. They are internet- based systems that empower users to create, share and analyse surveys without necessarily having programming skills. The most popular ones used today are Google Forms, SurveyMonkey and Typeform. The choice of platform is dictated by goals, features and funds. Good-to-go tools are perfect for small-scale or pilot surveys, while paid platforms are feature-rich. This makes them suitable for media work that is large-scale, needs multiple languages and requires high-level security for respondent confidentiality. Let us briefly look at the following tools: Google Forms: It is very popular because it is a user-friendly, free tool. It makes the tracking of responses easy through its direct integration with Google Sheets. SurveyMonkey: It is feature-rich as it provides functions like creating intricate survey-type branching, branding the survey with one's logo, and producing reports that simplify complex survey projects. Typeform: It is credited with having the most interactive and conversational survey format, which motivates respondents to engage more deeply with the survey. Here are some key pointers you should keep in mind when choosing survey platforms are: It should allow you to download data in commonly used formats like CSV or Excel for further processing. The survey should be user-friendly and accessible, and should be easy to use on both computers and smart phones. Features like progress bars, the option to save a partially-completed survey, and skip logic enhance user-experience and data quality. These should be used. You must put in place safeguards that encrypt data. The survey platform must be in compliance of data privacy laws and ethical frameworks.
7.5 SAMPLING AND DISTRIBUTION STRATEGIES
SIn research, sampling means selecting and studying a small group from a larger population because it may not be possible to speak to everyone. The findings obtained from this group are then

generalised and applied to the larger population. Sampling in web surveys essentially resembles traditional surveys. A detailed discussion of these methods is beyond the purview of this unit, but some fundamentals of sampling, especially in the virtual context, are as follows: Methods: The two key methods used in sampling are a) probability sampling, in which the respondents are randomly selected, and b) non-probability sampling, in which respondents are selected based on certain criteria. Sample size: In online surveys, a good sample size could be anywhere between 5000 to 10,000, depending on the population size. The larger the sample size, the more accurate the result. Bias: The goal is always to reduce bias, as much as possible. Therefore, the more random the sample, the better the chances of reducing bias. Probability sampling methods are better is this regard. Now, let us look at how online surveys come to be spread among sample groups. This process of using digital technologies to circulate surveys is called Distribution. Email lists, online communities and social media platforms are great sites for sampling and distribution. Social media platforms like Facebook, Twitter, Instagram or LinkedIn can be excellent tools as they help to cover both broad and narrow audiences rapidly. One merely has to share the survey and it begins to circulate around. The only drawback of using these platforms is that the samples here are usually self-selected, meaning they volunteer to be in the study. This might lessen representativeness. Email campaigns are the most suitable option in professional or academic areas, where direct and personalised contact is responsible for a higher response rate. The content of the email invitation must consist of a brief introduction, information on confidentiality, and a survey link which is easy to access. You can send a gentle reminder to the respondent after some time, and boost their motivation without being intrusive. Surveys on websites - either in a pop-up form or as a sidebar widget - enable site visitors to give their immediate impressions. It is effective in gathering instant feedback but at the same time, they hardly ever serve as a substitute for thorough sampling strategies. Through the use of these distribution channels, journalists can extend both the scope of their work and the quality of their responses. This ensures that the data obtained is good both in terms of analysis and further decision-making.
7.6 DATA QUALITY AND VALIDITY
Data quality and validity are the main factors that determine the success of an online poll. Low- quality data can result in inaccurate conclusions, making the whole effort useless. In this section, we will discuss two key issues which ensure that the gathered data is reliable as well as representative of the target population.
7.6.1 Response Rate Optimisation
Response rate refers to the proportion of completions in relation to all the invitations sent. The higher the response rate, the less sampling bias, because the representativeness gets better. To make response rates higher, surveyors must make questionnaires that are simple, concise, target-oriented, have instruction clarity, motivate the respondents, and given them a sense of value and trust. This will, in turn, ensure wider distribution and participation.
7.6.2 Identifying and Preventing Survey Fraud
While deceptive responses are a major concern in any survey, online surveys are particularly vulnerable to deliberate manipulation. This could happen in the form of technological manipulation

such as automation, or by controlling programmes and devices. It can also occur due to manipulation through multiple attempts. These kinds of responses lower the quality of data and bias the calculations. Many digital measures are available to prohibit fraudulent behaviour. The use of CAPTCHA allows the responder to be tested if it is a human and not a robot. Some platforms limit entries to one per IP address or browser by using cookies to prevent them from submitting twice. Survey administrators generally use filter questions or include check questions to weed out those who give inconsistent or illogical answers. The amount of time spent on the survey may also be used to indicate that a bot conducted the task (e.g., if it was finished extremely fast). Fraud can be detected also through a thorough inspection of data post-collection. Data patterns like the same answers for a vast majority of the responses or repeated text might signal towards fraud. The elimination of suspicious entries from data before analysis is a must to protect the dataset's sanctity. This combination of automatic filtering and manual reviewing is a compromise between the depth and the possibility of the wrongful exclusion of legitimate participants.
7.7 ANALYSIS AND REPORTING
Once data has been collected and collated, it is now time to analyse it. This process begins with summarising responses through two types of statistical methods: descriptive statistics and inferential statistics. Descriptive statistics: This technique summarises and describes the characteristics of a dataset. It gives a snapshot of the data through measures like mean, medium and mode. Simply put, it offers an overview of the respondents' views or behaviours. Here are some technical pointers to keep in mind: Tools: These include frequencies, percentages, averages, and measures such as mean, median and mode. They help provide a clear picture of how respondents have answered each question. Visualisation: Once calculations are done, simple graphical presentations such as bar charts, pie charts, and histograms are used to illustrate these patterns visually. This makes the results easier to interpret at a glance. Automated dashboards: Many online survey tools provide these dashboards which show these data summaries in real time, enabling journalists to monitor collection progress and preliminary results as they come in. Inferential statistics: These methods allow journalists to draw conclusions about the larger population based on sample data. Here are some features of inferential statistics: Tools: These methods test hypotheses and examine relationships between variables - through tools such as correlation analysis, chi-square tests, t- tests, or regression analysis - depending on the data type and research questions. Cross- tabulation: This facilitates comparison between different groups, such as demographic segments, to identify significant differences or associations. Advanced data visualisation tools and interactive dashboards: These enable clear communication of complex findings, supporting evidence-based decisions. Proper reporting involves not only presenting statistics but also explaining their implications, limitations, and potential applications in a systematic and transparent manner to ensure the overall integrity of the survey findings.

7.8 CASE STUDY: RATE MY GOVERNMENT SURVEY
The "Rate My Government" survey on MyGov platform is probably one of the best examples of an online survey in India. It was conducted with the objective of encouraging citizens to provide feedback on various government initiatives. The survey design was short, simple and easy to understand, making it a perfect case study. In 2016, Indian citizens were invited to rate the performance of different government programmes such as Digital India, Swachh Bharat Abhiyan, Make in India and Startup India. Respondents were asked to rate these initiatives on a simple 1 to 5 scale where 1 was the lowest and 5 the highest. The MyGov platform was a registration-based one where participants had to sign up, therefore limiting the chances of multiple and fraudulent responses. Additional measures such as IP restrictions and response monitoring were also put in place to prevent bogus feedback from distorting the results. The questionnaire had two distinct parts: the first part contained 'yes/no' questions meant for understanding awareness of government schemes; the second had weights where people had to rate the progress of the selected initiatives. For instance, questions like: "Please rate the progress of the Digital India initiative?" and "Please rate the government's efforts to establish a transparent and predictable taxation system" were asked. This combination of question types enabled the collection of awareness and evaluative feedback in an uncomplicated and user-friendly manner. Sample Questions from "Rate My Government" Survey
1. Are you aware of the following government initiatives? (Respond 'Yes' or 'No' for each)
* Digital India * Swachh Bharat Abhiyan * Make in India * Startup India * Skill India
2. How would you rate the progress of the 'Digital India' initiative?
* 1: Very Poor * 2: Poor * 3: Average * 4: Good * 5: Excellent
3. Do you think the government is promoting entrepreneurship effectively through
'Startup India'? * Yes * No * Don't know

4. What improvements would you suggest for these initiatives? (Open-ended)
* [Text box for free response] The survey witnessed the submission of hundreds of thousands of responses through the web, IVRS (Interactive Voice Response System), and missed calls, thereby indicating lively citizen engagement. The results were displayed live on the MyGov website, enabling public scrutiny and hence, strengthening trust. This survey is a great instance of how online surveys can be used to collect large-scale, meaningful and inclusive data in a manner that is accessible and easy for people to participate in. It is also a lesson in the application of survey design, sampling and data quality principles discussed in this lesson. Check Your Progress 2 Note: 1) Use the space provided below for your answers.

8.0 INTRODUCTION
Research helps us explore the unexplored, find the unknown and gives us new directions or alters old ones. Advertising research helps to find out how advertising would work effectively and guides in making meaningful advertising decisions.

Advertising research is a highly specialised field that involves using statistical techniques to interpret qualitative and quantitative data. The data so collected aids to understand the customer preferences and plan the campaigns accordingly. Prominent agencies like Indian Market Research Bureau (IMRB) and ORG - MARG undertake marketing research that generates data which is useful for advertisers. Research also helps to conduct surveys and audience measurement. The National Readership Survey (NRS) conducted by National Readership Survey Council collects information on various parameters like the reach of the medium, demographic profile of audience, geographical spread of the readers and also their product consumption patterns.
8.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After working through this Unit, you should be able to: * Describe the meaning and importance of advertising research * Decipher the various techniques of conducting advertising research * Discuss the role of advertising research in the digital era.
8.2 IMPORTANCE OF RESEARCH IN ADVERTISING
The Indian advertising industry has grown tremendously from being a small-scale business to a full-fledged industry. Today, India is projected to be the second fastest growing advertising market in Asia after China. Advertising is a complex business. From initial positioning and development of the theme to the final copy and media planning, it involves numerous resources, hours of work and huge amounts of money. And thus, it is important for advertisers to make sure that it reaches the right audiences, resonates with the target audience and gets them to take action. As advertising practices in India continue to evolve, it is no more possible to make an advertising decision simply based on personal choices. Today's business environment is metrics driven and most advertising decisions need to be based on necessary measures and external validation. Most advertisers believe that research encourages creativity. It provides an opportunity to interact with the customers and gain an insight into the habits, attitude and lifestyle of the consumers which helps the advertisers and agencies to come up with more impactful ideas of advertising.
8.2.1 Growth of Advertising as a Business
Advertising in its various forms has always been an accepted way of promoting and selling products to potential buyers. Different forms of advertising have been existing for thousands of years. The Egyptians used papyrus to offer rewards for return of runaway slaves while picture, mosaic and wall paintings were used in ancient Rome by merchants and businessmen to sell their wares. Ancient Greece introduced Town Criers or Bellmen to the world of advertising who would go about the streets singing praises of the merchant's wares and making public announcements about the arrival of trade ships. The invention of movable types by Johannes Gutenberg in 1445 led to the development of printing technologies, thereby causing an upsurge in advertising. Newspapers started appearing in different parts of the world giving rise to competition and struggle for survival. This gave a major boost to the advertising industry. However, in the beginning, most ads carried in the newspapers were in the form of announcements. But since then, over the next few centuries, there have been such significant and positive upheavals in the Advertising industry, that the entire blood and soul of this field of Behavioural science have been transformed.

By the end of 1920's, colour printing was excessively used in newspaper advertisements Radio rapidly became a powerful advertising medium during the same time. This was also the era when marketing research entered the world of advertising. Advertising thereafter started focusing on the outcomes of consumer purchases. Advertisements now targeted qualitative aspects of the buyers like status, happiness, ego, love etc. rather than quantitative demographics like age, income, gender etc. Specialists in market research were hence appointed to run the advertising show.. It was also during this time that the potential of television as an advertising medium started being harnessed. The sight and hearing combination offered by television, made it the most powerful medium of advertising for several years that followed.
8.2.2 Need for Advertising Research
Advertising research is a specialised research conducted to improve the efficiency of advertising. It involves systematic gathering, recording and analysis of data to help design and evaluate advertising strategy or gauge the effectiveness of print advertisement or audio video commercial and media campaigns. The data gathered through research tells the marketer about its present and prospective customers, their needs and expectations from the product, their buying behavior, their attitude towards product characteristics and qualities, when and where are the products bought, the competitors, extent of competition. Advertising research is conducted both before and after the advertising campaign to evaluate its effectiveness on various grounds. Different techniques of pre- and post-testing are used to measure advertising effectiveness.
8.2.3 Chronology of Conducting Advertising Research
There are primarily five major steps involved in advertising research. Each stage involves a specific set of activities to be performed and decisions to be taken with respect to advertising.
1. Identifying the Objectives of Research:
The primary step in advertising research is to identify the objective/objectives for which the research is being conducted. It may be undertaken to evaluate the awareness of the consumers, changing their attitudes, changing their predisposition to buy or not to buy a product.
2. Developing the Research Plan: After identification of the problem, the next major activity is
developing the advertising research plan. This may be formally termed as advertising research design. This gives a detailed outline of the data to be collected during the research and also enumerates the tools to be used for collecting the required data.
3. Data Collection: This stage consists of physically collecting research data through pre-testing
or post-testing techniques. This process also involves preparing questionnaires, feedback forms, rough layouts, comparative tables and other such tools for gathering data for advertising research.
4. Analysis and Interpretation: After collecting the data, the last and final step is to derive
interpretation from the data. Check your Progress: 1 Note: 1) Use the space below for your answer.

8.3 PRE-TESTING TECHNIQUES OF ADVERTISING RESEARCH
Pre - Testing is the process of testing the advertisement before running it commercially, so as to detect and improve upon any flaws detected in the ad. It provides an indication of the likelihood of acceptance of a particular advertisement or campaign by its target audience. Results obtained may be further used to improve, alter or change the advertisement. Let us discuss some of the commonly employed pre-testing research methods:
8.3.1. Consumer Jury Method
Firstly a 'Jury' composed of customers or prospective customers. Then they are shown various forms of the advertisement copy. Then they are asked to rank the ads with reasons.
8.3.2 Dummy Test
This is a technique that can be applied to both print and electronic media. It involves placing the test ads in a dummy vehicle which resembles the actual media. The print ads may be placed in a Portfolio or a dummy magazine and shown to the respondents and television commercials may be tested by showing respondents actual TV programmes containing these test commercials. The respondents are then asked to recall what they noticed in the advertisement. The advertisement with the greatest recall is considered to be most effective in communicating the message desired by the advertiser. This test offers an opportunity to compare different ads.
8.3.3 Direct Questioning
This method is used to obtain direct responses of the respondents to a range of questions. A consumer jury may be formed and either the whole ad or its specific elements are tested by asking direct questions. Sometimes there might be a single question which enquires about the most important aspect of the ad and in other cases there might be an elaborate questionnaire aimed to understand the physical and emotional effect of the ad. Based on the responses, researchers can evaluate the effectiveness of advertising messages in communicating the key points.
8.3.4 Binocular Rivalry Tests
In these tests two different images are presented on the same screen in a way that each eye witnesses a different image at the same time. Two competing advertisements are presented simultaneously and given an equal chance to dominate attention and the one which has greater attraction is considered more appropriate.
8.3.5 Focus Groups
This is another commonly used method, which helps test the ad in its conceptual and finished stage. In this method, a small group of people from different backgrounds assemble to participate in a moderated discussion about a particular product, service or campaign. This technique is a quick and inexpensive method of gaining insights of selected members before launching the ad or campaign or to evaluate and guide after it has been executed.
8.3.6 Storyboard Tests
This method is used for testing TV advertisements. It involves developing a storyboard into film strips and recording the audio section on a tape. These are then synchronised to give the look of a TV commercial. Respondents are usually shown 8 - 10 of such experimental advertisements. After the screening, measurements of recall (how much the respondents remember), retention (how much is retained in their memory) and comprehension of the message (what meaning was made out of the contents of the advertisement) is made through interview and assessment.

8.3.7 Trailer Tests
Two groups of customers are selected for this test. Both groups are invited to the display of a product ad and given discount coupons to purchase the product. One group is shown the test ads related to the product while the other group is not. The redemption rate of the coupons is then evaluated for both the groups to find out the impact of advertisement in promoting sales.
8.3.8 Mechanical/Laboratory Pre Test Measures
These measures record the respondent's physical reactions to the ad messages usually in a controlled environment. Though these tests require specific equipment and machinery and are more expensive, they are considered more reliable because unbiased reactions of the respondents are recorded.
8.3.9 Eye Tracking Tests
Eye tracking systems are used to record the amount of time volunteers spend looking at the ad and also to track the movement of the eye from one element of the ad to another. This is done either with a beam of infrared light that reflects the eye movement or with goggles connected to the computer to record eye movements. Pupillometric devices may also be used to analyse eye dilation. It has been proved that the eyes dilate when they notice something pleasant or interesting and constrict when they witness something unpleasant or distasteful. Recent researches have also stated that more Pupil dilation indicates greater emotional response.
8.4 POST TESTING TECHNIQUES OF ADVERTISING RESEARCH
Post-Testing is done after the advertisement has been run on the media. It is usually undertaken to find out the impact of the advertisement on the audience. It is conducted either during the time when the ad is being run or a few weeks after the ad has been run. The purpose of post-testing is to provide an insight on the performance of the ad and to draw some conclusions about future advertising.
8.4.1 Recognition Tests
These tests are also known as Readership/Viewership Tests. It is designed to find out which advertisements have been read by the respondents. Daniel Starch, a pioneer in advertising research, started collecting audience exposure data for selected publications in the 1930's. He developed the popular Starch Test that focuses on the extent to which an ad is noticed by the customers. In this method, an ad is shown to a selected group of people and asked whether they recognise the ad. The respondents are shown issues of magazines which they claim to have read and they are asked to point out the advertisements they have noticed.
8.4.2 Recall Tests
These tests help measure the proportion of a sample audience that can recall an advertisement. The recall may be aided or unaided. In aided recall, the respondent is given prompts to remember the advertisement or brand. Unaided recall requires mental reproduction of the advertisement by the respondent without any prompts.
8.4.3 Persuasion Tests
Persuasion test helps determine the effectiveness of an ad in changing attitudes and preferences of the buyers. It analyses brand attitude before and after the ad exposure. Before seeing the proposed advertisements, the participants answer a series of questions about the product and the company and after being exposed to the advertisement they go through a second test which assesses whether the advertisement has changed their attitude and preferences.
8.4.4 Inquiry Test
This test is designed to measure the advertising effectiveness on the basis of the number of enquiries generated by the advertisement. The number of enquiries generated may be calculated

by the number of phone calls received, the number of coupons used or direct personal enquiries. Inquiries indicate that the respondents not only read the advertisement but also took some action which is a relatively stronger indicator than recall or awareness.
8.4.5 Attitude Tests
These tests measure the extent to which the advertisement has been successful in generating favourable opinion about the product. It helps to measure qualitative attributes like brand loyalty, acceptance, preference, image etc. Techniques commonly used to measure this are: * Semantic Differential Technique: It measures the attitude by bipolar adjective statements about the product like useful - useless, tasteful - distasteful, known - unknown * Likert Scale: It is a five-point scale through which the respondents show the degree of their agreement or disagreement with the statements. * Ranking Technique: Products and brands are ranked by the consumers in order of their preference. Activity - 1 Select three volunteers (preferably from three different age groups) and show them three different advertisements of the same product/brand. Perform an aided recall test and unaided recall test by asking them pertinent questions [after two hours of break] to see how much they could remember of the ads they saw/heard, and particularly what aspects (logo, jingle or illustration/character/text/message/meaning etc) they could recollect. 8.5 ADVERTISING CAMPAIGN
A campaign is an organised effort or course of action undertaken to achieve the objectives of an organisation. Advertising campaign is a process through which a series of ads are placed in different media based on audience segmentation through systematic planning. Throughout the campaign a common theme is promoted through different media platforms. It can be centered around long term or short-term goals of the company. Campaign is a part of the strategic marketing process. It incorporates creative strategy, advertising strategy and marketing strategy. Campaign planning involves a series of steps undertaken to meet the desired goals of the organisation. A well-designed plan helps to coordinate different advertising activities and enables optimum utilisation of the resources. A campaign may be undertaken for the fulfillment of an immediate goal or a long-term objective broken down into a series of milestones. This process often begins with the assessment of the situation in context of the goal to be achieved. Advertising campaigns may be undertaken to accomplish a particular objective or a set of objectives. Russel H. Colley (1961) pioneered the DAGMAR concept - Defining Advertising Goals for Measured Advertising Results. He identified 52 advertising goals classified under nine major categories. The objectives of the campaign are determined after complete analysis of the

market and the buyers. They are formulated in the light of the short term or long-term goals of the company. Let us now go through the steps of Campaign Planning in the following section.
8.5.1 Identification of Target Audience
A target audience is an identified group of consumers within the predetermined target market, identified as recipients of a specific advertising message. The process of defining target audience for a campaign involves the process of subdividing the market on the basis of geographical, demographic, socio - economic, psychographic and market situation. Once the target audience is identified their physical and psychological characteristics are analysed for better message delivery. The communication objectives of the message emerge from the analysis of the target audience.
8.5.2 Designing Advertising Message
Creating an impactful advertising message is the most important part of a campaign. A creative message can contribute massively towards the success of the campaign. While the primary aim of the message is to communicate information, it plays a key role in influencing the opinion of the buyers. The success and failure of an advertising message depends greatly on the marketers offering and the psychological predisposition of the target audience and also their needs and requirements. The key components of an advertising message are - a) Meaningful: The target audience must find the message meaningful or useful. It must cater to some need or desire. b) Distinctive: To capture the attention of the consumer the message should have some distinctive quality. c) Believable: The message should make the customers believe that the claims made in the advertisement are trustworthy. The product's USP - Unique Selling Proposition must be highlighted in the message.
8.5.3 Budgeting
Deciding upon the amount to be spent on the campaign is important for giving final shape to the campaign. The budget mainly depends on the duration of the campaign. Several techniques may be adopted for allocating budget for the ad campaign: a) Competitive Parity Method: This refers to allocating the budget which is at par with the budget of the competitors b) A fixed percentage of the turnover: In this method a fixed percentage of the annual turnover of the company is allocated for ad campaigns. c) Affordability: This is the best suited option for firms with limited budgets. In this case the company allocates the limited additional fund available after meeting all necessary expenses, for campaigning. d) Budget as per the services provided: In this method, the company may hire different agencies. e) The task or objective approach: This refers to determining the budget on the basis of the tasks/objectives achieved.
8.5.4 Developing Media Plan
The campaign may use a single media or develop a creative media mix for delivering the campaign messages. The media vehicles used in the campaign include Print Media- Newspapers, Magazines and Direct mail; Broadcast Media - Radio, Television, Narrow Cast Media; Outdoor Media; Transit Media; Direct Marketing; Internet; Mobile; Specialty Media - T shirts, caps, buttons, badges etc.

Effectiveness of advertising message, largely depends upon informing the public about the right product, at the right time, through the right medium. A media plan largely includes: a) Matching Media and Market: Selecting a media that meets the requirements of the selected profile of target audience. b) Reach: The number of individuals or households reached by a given medium over a period of time. c) Frequency: The average number of times different individuals or households are reached by a medium in a given period of time. d) Media Cost and Media Ability: The cost incurred on the media must be proportionate to the ability of the media to carry the message to the target audience. e) Media Scheduling: This involves deciding upon the number of advertisements to appear in each medium and the time and date on which they are to appear.
8.5.5 Evaluating Effectiveness of Campaign
The evaluation of an advertising campaign focuses on the following area: a) Communication Effects: Whether the intended message has been communicated effectively to the target audience. b) Sales Effect: Whether the campaign generated an increase in sales. c) Attainment of objectives: Whether the objectives laid down for the campaign have been achieved successfully.
Case Study: KFC India
KFC, a global restaurant chain, achieved huge success in India, through campaigns like Radio KFC RK Hunt and Design Your Own Bucket, targeting the youth with mobile apps. The Radio KFC RJ Hunt Campaign attracted over 3000 participants from 30 Indian cities. The "Design Your Own Bucket" initiative garnered nearly 5500 colorful entries, while special buckets featuring Sachin Tendulkar's image on his retirement day added an extra touch of excitement. KFC's "Currycature" campaign invited participants to select a character with an ethnic Indian twist and upload their pictures. The campaign received an impressive response, with fans creating around 17,000 Currycatures. This initiative provided fans with a unique and engaging experience with the brand. Results Achieved by KFC's Social Media Campaigns: * Facebook page engagement increased significantly from 6.2% to an impressive 93.8%, three times higher than the sector average. * Recognized among the five fastest-growing social media brands in India.
8.6 ADVERTISING RESEARCH AND CAMPAIGN PLANNING IN THE
DIGITAL ERA
The digital onset has brought tremendous change to the advertising research methods and techniques. Artificial Intelligence (AI), Internet of Things (IOT), Augmented Reality (AR), Virtual Reality (VR) have contributed to help marketers in advertising research as well. It has become easier today for marketers to segment their buyers on the basis of the mobile applications they access on their smartphones and place relevant ads to them through apps. Customisation, ease of access and speed are making the digital platform all the more popular ways to reach the customers. Search Engine Optimisation (SEO) is one of the most prevalent marketing tools used today. Viral campaigns, reviews and social media campaigns are fast replacing the traditional campaigns. The digital technologies are further enhancing the customer experience by enabling the company to directly interact with the customer and create a user profile on the basis of the information provided.

Advertising research can be easily carried out online with the help of technology. Online surveys can be conducted through survey sites that help gather data from multiple audiences within a limited time frame. Google Analytics can also be used to know the amount of traffic being received on your site, in other words, the number of people visiting your site. It also helps to understand the geography, interest and demographics of the people visiting the site. Online keyword search also helps understand the interest of the buyers and the kind of language being used to search for a particular product. This helps marketers to use these keywords on their pages. The interactive web pages of the companies also enable customers to post reviews, resolve queries and suggest improvements. This helps the brands to strengthen their relationship with the customers. Looking at social media accounts and websites of the competitors can also provide insights on the success and pitfalls of the competitors which can be taken advantage of. Activity - 2 Find out details of how the Italian brand Nutella became Nutella Unica (Unique) with the help of AI. It created 7 million different packaging designs/styles using Artificial Intelligence, to suit the choice of every Italian, which would otherwise be impossible for even the biggest of the big brands. The 7 million jars manufactured for this campaign were sold out almost instantaneously. Collect the images of some of the packages and try to interpret the preference patterns of the target audience.
8.7 LET US SUM UP
In this Unit, we discussed the origin of advertising research and its growing importance over the years. We also discussed the various pre-testing and post testing techniques used to evaluate advertising. Each of these techniques has its own relevance in the field of advertising. We then also talked about advertising campaigns, their needs and the different types of campaigns. We also understood the importance of market segmentation in the process of advertising and learned the different techniques through which we can segment the market and identify our buyers. While examining advertising campaigns, we also elaborated the process of campaign planning which involved - defining advertising objectives, identification of target audience, designing of advertising message, budgeting, media planning and evaluating the effectiveness of campaign. To sum up, it can be said that the Indian advertising industry is growing rapidly. New techniques and technologies are being used to make advertising more effective and impactful. Research plays a vital role in helping advertisers analyse ROI (return on investment) they will get from advertisements. Digital technologies have greatly impacted advertising research and campaigning. Many companies are now using online platforms to conduct research and run campaigns. The future of the advertising industry will greatly depend on how the advertising agencies and marketing companies make use of the massive audience data available online.

8.9 GLOSSARY
Advertising campaign is a series of advertisement messages to promote a product or service. An ad campaign is designed around a specific and unique theme to create brand awareness. Media Campaigns: A media campaign uses several different types of media to influence or inspire people to inculcate an idea, a belief, a practice or a brand. The objectives of such campaigns are to increase awareness, inform or change previous habits of the target audience. Post-Testing: The process undertaken after the advertisement has been run on the media. It is usually undertaken to find out the impact of the advertisement on the audience. It is conducted either during the time when the ad is being run or a few weeks after the ad has been run. The purpose of post testing is to provide an insight on the performance of the ad and to draw some conclusions about future advertising Pre-Testing: The process of testing the advertisement before running it so that there is a greater likelihood of preparing the most effective ad and also an opportunity to detect and improve upon any flaws detected in the ad. It provides an indication of the likelihood of acceptance of a particular advertisement or campaign by its target audience. Results obtained may be further used to improve, alter or change the advertisement.

8.0 INTRODUCTION
Digital media tools enable journalists to gather information from varied sources - government databases, corporate websites, social media posts and even videos uploaded by citizen journalists from remote areas. The use of digital technologies to gather and analyse huge data, and to

explore socio-cultural, political and geographical perspectives has helped to improve the quality, quantity and reach of news today. However, at the heart of it all, a good news story is one that is based on solid information that is presented to the public in a coherent way. As we know, this information is gathered from many sources, among which the most important is the interview. An interview is a 'focused and purposive conversation' between a journalist and their respondent. It involves asking questions, listening to individuals, and recording their responses. Although one may think it is something one can do on the fly, its objective and focus are much more systematic and scientific in nature and approach. Interviews fall under qualitative research, meaning they yield information that is subjective and linked to the interviewee's opinions attitude and statements, as we discussed in Unit 4. Like pretty much every aspect of human activity, interviews have moved into the digital space. Today, interviews can be conducted in real-time through audio-video applications, or through emails. The focus of this unit will be virtual or online interviews, where the journalist and respondent are present on an online platform, going back and forth on their questions and answers. The unit will guide you on how you can conduct interviews by using a good mix of framing, technology and method, which are foundational learning for aspiring media professionals.
8.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After studying this unit, you will be able to: * understand the transformation of the 'interview' in a digital world, * apply best practices to plan and conduct interviews, and build rapport in virtual settings, * manage technical considerations and contingency planning, and * implement appropriate data management and analysis procedures.
8.2 ONLINE INTERVIEW
For a journalist, the internet has become a primary site for data collection. But what if you want to connect with a source more personally? Of course, you can always choose online questionnaires and social media. But an interview is always so much more personal, and so much more rewarding. Here, we will discuss this very important aspect of internet-mediated journalistic work, which has transformed journalism. There was a time journalists had to run down to the offices or homes of their sources to conduct interviews, or spend a considerable amount of time conducting interviews remotely on the phone. While the former required time, resources and patience, the latter took away the personal touch. With the coming of the internet though, it is possible to have the best of both worlds. You can conduct an interview in a way that is time and cost efficient, but also personal. So, the best of both worlds. Now let us discuss the different types of interviews the internet has made possible for journalists.
8.2.1 Types of online interviews
Online interviews can be broadly classified based on their mode of interaction and the level of structure applied. The main types include: Synchronous Interviews: These are interviews where questions and responses are conducted simultaneously. In the case of online synchronous interviews, both interviewer and interviewee are present at the same time. The interviewer can base their questions on the responses garnered from the respondent. There is more spontaneity in the process, thus eliciting more candid data. Asynchronous Interviews: These are interviews where interviewer and interviewee can participate as and when they wish. Both do not have to be present for the interview at the same time. For example, in an email interview, you can send in your questions to which the respondent

can answer at a later time. These interviews give the interviewee time to respond to the questions after giving them due thought. These interviews elicit more formal data, as deliberation and thought have been put into the conversation.
8.2.2 Different Mediums for Online Interviews
Journalists usually face a shortage of resources in terms of both money and time, and therefore, online interviews make a lot of sense for many of them. Sometimes, respondents may not want to open up about specific issues in face-to-face interactions, but might feel comfortable doing so in a mediated communication set-up. Online interviews make it easier to accommodate the needs of different kinds of potential respondents. Online interviews can be conducted through various mediums, which will be discussed at length in later in the unit. Let us flag these here: * Video conferencing (real-time audio-video) * Telephonic tools * Instant Messaging or Chat * Email correspondence * Text-only chat platforms * Voice chat applications The choice of interview type depends on several factors, including the nature of the project, the sensitivity of the topic to be discussed, the availability and comfort level of respondents with technology, and the resources available to the journalist.
8.3 INTERVIEW TYPES AND FORMATS
Online interviews provide journalists flexibility in utilising various types and formats, depending on work requirements and the kind of information they wish to acquire. The main advantages and disadvantages of each format differ, and consequently affect the ways interviews are planned and conducted. Knowing which type and format of interview to use is key to collecting significant and dependable data. Let us discuss these below:
8.6.1 Structured Online Interviews
Structured online interviews are based on a tightly-controlled questionnaire with predetermined questions, mostly closed-ended ones. Using this type of interview, journalists are able to get numerical or categorical data that are easily comparable, and can be subjected to statistical analysis. The method is particularly popular in surveys where response uniformity is a must. On the one hand, web-based surveys or mailed questionnaires make the implementation of structured interviews very simple. So, this method is not only cost-effective but also scalable. But on the other hand, due to the method's inability to catch participants' nuanced viewpoints or further develop the dialogue based on the respondents' answers, the level of understanding may be limited.
8.3.2 Semi-structured Digital Interviews
Semi-structured interviews entail a set list of topics or themes to be discussed, thus ensuring coverage of all relevant areas. But at the same time, they allow the flexibility of going deeper into a certain topic. By employing this approach, the interviewer is able to respond to the participant's gestures and expressions, follow out unexpected lines of inquiry, and interpret clarifying questions. Semi-structured interviews are appropriate for studying people's perceptions, attitudes, or experiences, and at the same time allowing both comparability and depth of investigation. The role of moderators is to encourage participants to express themselves freely, as well as to guide

the discussion. For instance, a semi-structured format is ideal for interviewing a doctor during a health crisis - you always keep key questions ready but allow space for more detailed insights.
8.3.3 Unstructured Virtual Conversations
Unstructured interviews allow the interviewees to express their points of view freely, without the constraints of specific questions or a strict format. These are similar to natural conversations and they aim to learn about participants' perception of the world and their detailed experiences. Even though this method provides a wealth of valuable qualitative data, in order to successfully handle the flow, avoid bias, and effectively document complicated data, you must have excellent interviewing skills. The final transcripts, in most cases, are quite lengthy, and therefore, detailed coding and thematic analysis will be necessary.
8.4 PLANNING ONLINE INTERVIEWS
Planning an interview is a simple but important process, and as a reporter, you should attend to each aspect of the process to ensure the interaction is fruitful and smooth. Let us look at some basic yet significant steps that you must take before scheduling a virtual interview.
8.4.1 Vetting the Source
This means ensuring that your source is what they claim to be. As a journalist, you must verify their credentials and expertise, research potential conflict of interest, and cross-reference their information with other sources. You must ensure the source is credible and not impersonating someone. For example, before interviewing someone claiming to be a protest eyewitness, you must verify their location, identity, and association with the event. Moreover, clear communication regarding consent, procedure, and time of the interview should be given to the source before the actual interview.
8.4.2 Technology Selection and Setup
First and foremost, to conduct a virtual interview, it is very important to choose the right technology. Video conferencing tools such as Zoom, Skype and Teams offer features such as live interaction, recording and sharing of screen. The decision should be based on factors such as accessibility, bandwidth requirements, privacy/security, and the convenience of the journalist and the interviewee.
8.4.3 Structuring the Interview
Regardless of the type of interview - structured, semi-structured or unstructured - it is important to have a logical flow, and to cover topics that are relevant to your story. The questions should be designed in a way that they start from general and then become more specific. They should not contain leading words, and must be verified for their clarity. Moreover, the structure of the interview should have provisions for probing, follow-ups, and the ease of the respondent. Start with open-ended questions like 'What did you see?' before moving into specific fact-based questions.
8.4.4 Pre-interview Technical Testing
Before the interview, check your equipment - computer, camera, microphone and internet connection - so that there are no technical glitches during the interview. Conduct technical tests to ensure all devices and software work. Schedule a brief pilot or a set-up check with the interviewee to identify any glitches, and have simple troubleshooting guidance ready in case of connectivity issues or device failures.
8.5 CONDUCTING ONLINE INTERVIEWS
An interview is just an interview, one would think, so why all this fuss about mediums and forms? This is because each medium brings its own set of challenges, which the interviewer must

be able and prepared to tackle. Let us now discuss how online interviews must be conducted over different mediums.
8.5.1 Video Conferencing Interview Techniques
Video conferencing allows face-to-face communication. This means we can establish a 'connection' with the interviewee -we can see them, comprehend their body language, and most of all, encourage their involvement. After introducing yourself and your project, you can begin the interview, recording it if the interviewee gives consent. Be there, show attention, and encourage the participant to talk. Your friendly and neutral attitude will help the interviewee to relax and speak freely. With the help of multipoint conferencing, you can include more than one interviewee in the discussion.
8.5.2 Telephone and Voice-only Interviews
Telephonic interviews are simple and less expensive, and so are good for interviewees who have no access to the internet or video devices. First and foremost, make sure there are no connectivity issues. You should use direct, close-ended questions, which may encourage the source to give quick and sharp responses, but also offer you the opportunity for follow-up questions. The lack of visual cues can diminish the context and the subtlety of the exchange, and some respondents may feel disinterested, but you can make up for it by keeping the exchange engaging with well- framed questions and alert follow-ups.
8.5.3 Chat-based and Asynchronous Interviews
Text-based interviews (via email or instant messaging) offer an opportunity to discuss sensitive topics, especially to respondents who may be hesitant to face the camera. First and foremost, clearly tell the interviewee what you are looking for in the interview. Frame your questions in a clear and coherent language and structure, and check with the interviewee whether they have received your questions. It is important that you set a clear deadline for the answers, but in a polite way. Though the written format may appear more attractive as it provides time for thought, it also loses the spontaneity of an instant exchange. Non-verbal communicative signs and visual cues also remain undiscovered, but the answers are more focused since the interviewee takes the time to write them down.
8.5.4 Building Rapport in Virtual Settings
Let us now discuss some ground rules that apply to all virtual interviews, irrespective of the medium. Remember to start interviews with cordial but professional welcomes, and give an overview of what will be done during the session. Using the interviewee's name, demonstrating empathy, and confirming facts may help gain their trust. If it is a video conference, you must keep eye contact and use positive and affirming words such as "Thank you for your insights," "Can you please explain that again?" Interactions in chat or email can be more personal if interviewees receive gentle guidance. Show respect, avoid stereotyping, and always be sensitive to different customs, cultural mores and contexts. Check Your Progress 1 Note: 1) Use the space provided below for your answers.
2) Compare your answers with those given at the end of the unit.

Now, let us discuss some technical aspects which can help you decide which platform is ideal when and for which type of interview. These considerations can range from the kind of features a platform has to offer, issues concerning stability and security, recording and documentation abilities, and the like. 8.6.2 Recording and Documentation Methods
In the above table we highlighted how most communication platforms have a built-in recording feature. Now let us discuss the etiquettes of using this feature. Remember, interviews should be recorded only with the consent of the interviewee. You must respect their privacy at all times. Moreover, you must facilitate accurate presentation of their statements, claims and opinions through a thorough analysis of their recorded statements. You can always use an external recorder or a video camera. Field notes and digital logs can also serve as a supplement to the recordings by providing additional observations. Always make sure to tell the participants how the recordings will be stored and how they will be used.
8.6.3 Backup Systems and Contingency Planning
Be ready for delays and emergencies by having off-the-clock methods, spare gadgets, and extra batteries and power sources at hand. Emergency contact information along with rescheduling procedures should be communicated to participants. Also, keep telephone options handy just in case the internet breaks down.
8.6.4 Internet Connectivity and Quality Management
A reliable internet connection is what makes online interviews possible. So, the journalist as well as the interviewee must use stable internet connections, close unnecessary background applications, and pick a place where the signal is good. To ensure the connection remains uninterrupted in case of low bandwidth, one can lower the video quality or switch to audio-only. Think of an online interview as a meeting with a source in person; the only difference being, this meeting is mediated by digital technologies, which require as much attention as the interview itself.
8.7 DATA MANAGEMENT AND ANALYSIS
Without proper data management and thorough data analysis, it can get hard to get insights from online interviews, especially lengthy ones. Digitally collected data provide many pros for journalists, such as easily available transcripts of the interviews, and analysis of those transcripts based on keywords. Another key benefit is that it is much easier finding information with the 'find' button on text rather than the 'find' toggle in an audio or video recording. At the same time, there are some cons such as the need for coding, qualitative analysis, and secure data storage. These data management tools are mainly helpful in lengthy interviews or in collaborative news stories between different newsrooms. Let us take a brief look at this process of managing and analysing the data collected during an interview:
8.7.1 Transcription and Data Preparation
Transcription means converting data that has been recorded via audio, video or chat into words, thus creating a textual format that can easily be analysed and circulated. Newly developed AI- powered automatic transcription tools make the whole thing easy. However, the final result should be checked to ensure the text is accurate.
8.7.2 Coding and Thematic Analysis
The next phase of the post-interview data work involves using software for qualitative data analysis. This helps in better organisation, facilitation of coding, and interpretation of vast amounts of data in the form of text. Such instruments allow the unlocking of new patterns and themes that serve as evidence for journalists in developing interpretations of their questions. Another plus of this collaborative feature is that it extends the capacity of teamwork to handle complex projects.

Data coding and thematic analysis involve repetitive tasks that require journalists to pay close attention not only to the context but also the meanings coming from the interviewees' words. They take pieces of data, put them in groups, make codes, and when new insights pop up, they change the codes accordingly. This procedure does more than simply implementing descriptive coding, it also interprets and recognises patterns in the data.
8.7.3 Ethical Data Storage and Security
Finally, data security and the use of proper storage methods that are in line with ethical standards ensure confidentiality and journalistic integrity. Data should be encrypted, access to it should be limited, and it should be stored in multiple locations. When it is no longer needed, it should be destroyed in a proper way. Following all legal and institutional requirements safeguards the interviewee and interviewer, and also maintains trust among them. 8.8 LET US SUM UP
This unit explored online interviews as a crucial tool in online journalism today. We discussed different interview types such as synchronous and asynchronous, and also its different formats that include structured, semi-structured, and unstructured interviews. Learners were taught how to plan and conduct online interviews, focusing on both the technological and human aspect of the process, such digital literacy and technical seamlessness. The importance of rapport, ethics, technical setup, and data management were also emphasised. We also did a comparision of different online platforms that can be used to conduct virtual interviews such as Zoom, Google Meet, Microsoft Teams and WhatsApp. As communication technologies evolve, online interviewing continues to bridge geographical gaps. This unit offers learners new insights into this new face of journalism today.
8.9 KEYWORDS
Synchronous Interview: Real-time digital conversation between journalist and interviewee. Asynchronous Interview: Time-flexible interaction allowing delayed responses. Thematic Analysis: Identifying recurring ideas or themes from qualitative data. Data Management: Organising and securing data obtained from a source ethically, including interviews. Rapport-building: Establishing trust and comfort with interviewees in virtual settings. Vetting the Source: The process of research and fact-checking information about a sources, and evaluating potential biases and conflicts of interest.
