9.0 INTRODUCTION
Big data is the buzzword of our times, a term encapsulating all manner of "hype and hope," as Crawford et. al (2014) put it. It begins with a single human action, let us say on a mobile phone, before eventually snowballing into a mind-boggling collection of all kinds of digital actions and interactions. Today, everything is a piece of data that can be stored, processed and analysed. By its very virtue of being capable of touching each aspect of human life, big data has come to reshape how we live, work and think. It is as ubiquitous as the media, and together these two create a media landscape in which numbers and narratives blend into a stimulating synthesis. In this unit, we shall learn about big data and its nature, before moving on to the influential role it has come to

play in journalism today. The idea is to reflect on the changes being wrought upon news-making and the media sector, and understand the dynamics of big data and its meaning for journalism.
9.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After going through this unit, you will be able to: understand what big data means, and its key concepts; understand the significant role it plays in journalism today; learn about its different applications in the media sector; and understand some issues and concerns surrounding it.
9.2 WHAT IS BIG DATA?
Big data refers to the vast amount of structured and unstructured data that is generated in the digital domain every day. It encompasses every aspect of human activity, from health, education, transportation and businesses to the media. As the name suggests, big data is mind-bogglingly voluminous, and only getting more voluminous every day. Myriad sources keep adding to it on a daily basis. It is generated in things we post on social media platforms like Facebook, Instagram, YouTube, etc., e-commerce platforms and companies such as Amazon, Zomato, etc. in the form of customer and financial data, and data produced by a whole range of devices from mobile phones to cars, among others. Simply put, big data is data that is truly Big. When thinking of big data, two components are critical: data storage and data analysis. Raw and unprocessed data is collected by organisations and machines in the form of huge datasets. The information contained in these datasets is then classified and analysed to understand patterns and make discoveries about our daily activities in our digital lives, producing a new kind of knowledge. However, big data is too large and too complex to be processed by traditional data processing applications. Therefore, the coming of big data has necessitated a whole new ecosystem for the processing of huge volumes of data. In this unit, we will be learning about these systems, beginning with how these first came to be.
9.3 THE BIG DATA MOMENT
In order to understand how big data was able to grow to this extent, it is important to understand its evolution from a historical perspective. Big data as a concept and as a reality is embedded within the Digital Turn, which began in the late 20th century. The increasing availability of data stemming from digitalisation, connecting people and machines, created vast amounts of data from various sources. It is not surprising then that the term 'Big Data' has been in use since the early 1990s, the thick of the Digital Turn. Big data emerged from a knowledge domain that combined the traditional domain of statistics with the relatively new domain of computer science. One can say that the 'Big Data moment' was a coming together of mathematics, statistics, data analysis and digital technology in general. However, this 'moment' is not merely a technological episode. It is a sociotechnical phenomenon with cultural, economic, and political origins and implications. The continuous growth of big data has been fuelled by the generation of social data (from social media and online platforms), machine data (generated by devices, machines and sensors), and transactional data (from purchases and other financial activities). The collection of such varied information has led to innovation and efficiency, but it also has pitfalls of its own, laying bare the complexities these technologies give rise to. For now, let us delve into three key aspects of understanding the 'big data moment'
9.3.1 Data Deluge

The emergence of big data has led to an exponential growth in the global volume of data. Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt argued that from the very beginning of humanity to the year 2003, an estimated 5 exabytes of information was created. Ten years later, in 2013, that amount of information (5 exabytes) took only two days to create. In the intervening period between 2013 and the present, this growth has been mindboggling According to a Statista report, the total volume of global data generation, which was projected to reach 182 zettabytes in 2025, will reach 394 zettabytes by 2028, almost doubling in three years. To put this in context, one zettabyte is equal to 1,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 (1021) bytes. Simply put, each advancement in the field of big data has been centred on dealing with this tsunami of data, whether in terms of technology, analysis or developing ethical frameworks.
9.3.2 Paradigm Shift
Paradigm shift simply means a fundamental change in approach, when the usual way of thinking about or doing something is replaced by a new and different way. A good example of a paradigm shift is Charles Darwin's theory of natural selection which shifted our understanding away from traditionalist views to explain the evolution of life on earth. Darwin's theory paved the way for significant scientific advancements. In the big data paradigm shift, the most important change has been a shift away from treating data as a byproduct and viewing it as a core asset. Rather than products or services, the focus is now on insights and outcomes that the collection and analysis of vast amounts of data provides. These insights come to have direct influences on our lives, such as enabling data-driven decision-making to improve services like healthcare and transport. This has the potential to lead to increased transparency and accountability, and better decision-making.
9.3.3 Advanced Analytics
Analytics simply refers to the process of discovering patterns in data. This is done using a combination of computing, statistics and machine learning. Older applications were limited in terms of their capacity to store, process, and analyse large datasets. The coming of big data created the need for far more advanced technologies and systems than were used earlier. These advanced systems are what we call advanced analytics. Big data analytics has been shaped by several key developments. Here are the most important ones:
1. Real-time Analytics: Earlier, data was processed and analysed in batches, and over a certain
period of time. However, real-time analytics does these processes in milliseconds. This has allowed organisations to make more informed decisions based on up-to-date information that is delivered speedily.
2. Edge Computing: Edge computing allows data to be processed locally, rather than sending it
to a centralised server or cloud. For example, a smartwatch collects and processes your data locally, giving you real-time updates on your fitness, rather than sending that information to a cloud. This trend is gaining traction in industries such as healthcare and transportation, where real-time insights are critical.
3. Cloud-based Analytics: Cloud-based analytics allows data to be processed on cloud
platforms. This makes the process of analysing data cost effectiveness, accessible and flexible. Cloud platforms such as AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud Platform offer a range of big data tools and services.
4. Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning: Machine learning and AI are becoming
increasingly important in big data analytics, as they can help automate data processing and analysis, and provide more accurate insights.
5. Natural Language Processing (NLP): NLP is a field of AI that involves analysing and
interpreting human language. NLP is becoming increasingly important in big data analytics,

as it can help get insights from unstructured data sources such as social media and customer feedback. Trends such as these are shaping the future of big data analytics and will continue to influence the development of new tools and technologies in this field.
9.4 CHARACTERISTICS OF BIG DATA
Big data can be characterised by several distinct features, often referred to as "5 Vs", which are volume, velocity, variety, veracity, and value. Volume: This refers to the sheer amount of data generated by businesses, individuals, and machines every day. With the increase in the use of electronic devices and social media, data volumes continue to grow at an unprecedented rate. Velocity: This refers to the speed at which data is generated, processed, and analysed. Big data requires rapid processing of data, including both streaming and batch processing. Variety: It refers to the diverse types of data generated by businesses, individuals, and machines, including structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data. Big data requires the ability to manage and analyse various data types. Veracity: This refers to the accuracy and reliability of the data, which may vary due to data quality issues, noise, and other factors. Big data requires careful consideration of data quality and data cleansing techniques to ensure accurate analysis. Value: This refers to the usefulness of data. The end goal of any big data analytics system is to extract value from the data. This value is also related to its veracity or accuracy. For some applications, value also depends on how fast we are able to process the data.
9.5 THE IMPACT OF BIG DATA ON JOURNALISM
Information is the essence of journalism. Right from its earliest known origins in ancient Rome's daily gazette 'Acta Diurna' to its dynamic digital avatar in the age of Web 3.0, journalism's primary concern has been the dissemination of information. With the onset of the digital turn, data has become the building block of the structure that is information. While the term big data might conjure up images like industry, corporate, number crunching, and target audiences, today it lies at the heart of journalism. Big data has equipped reporters to explore public and private databases to tell their stories. Journalists can collect vast volumes of data from varied sources, analyse these treasure troves of information, and break things down for audiences to understand and engage with. The following are some of the key ways in which big data is impacting journalism today.
9.5.1 Quantification of Journalism
Today, big data has quantified jounrnalism, making data and numbers the real story. While earlier, too, journalists relied on revelations that numbers and statistics could offer, the coming of big data has meant a giant leap in that direction. The use of computational tools for analysis has greatly impacted news gathering and the uncovering of new stories. This approach is what we called data journalism. It uses statistical and computational analysis to uncover patterns and create data-driven narratives.
9.5.2 Knowledge Production
Big data allows journalists to analyse massive datasets from public and private databases, social media, and other sources. These datasets almost often contain patterns and trends that reveal newsworthy stories that may not be visible through traditional reporting methods. Examples of such a knowledge production would include journalists using advanced analytical tools to identify emerging trends, or even predict future events in areas like public health, climate change or

elections. Another key area where journalists use data science tools is verification - fact-checking claims, identifying misinformation, and cross-referencing information from other reliable sources.
9.5.3 Narrative Science
In the digital age, journalism is no longer simply about narrative. It is a narrative science - meticulous, objective and systematic. This means, in addition to being hard-nosed reporters, journalists need new skills in data analysis, interpretation, and programming. They must combine traditional storytelling with data insights. Working with large, complex datasets is often painstaking. It requires patience, attention to detail, and the ability to 'see' hidden stories within large volumes of raw data. Once narrativised, this data can become a weapon for public interest.
9.5.4 Automation
It takes years of training before journalists get published and earn their bylines. But today, computer programmes are writing articles and creating videos for audience consumption. This practice of using big data tools used to produce news is called automated journalism. Algorithms are fed data, template articles, and prompts about key details, and voila, they produce news stories! However, automated journalism is a two-edged sword - while some see it as a chance for freeing up journalists for more complex and nuanced tasks, others see it as a threat to the integrity of news, and even to the very jobs of human journalists. 9.6 APPLICATIONS OF BIG DATA IN MEDIA HOUSES
So far, we have learned about big data, its advent in the digital age, and its characteristics. We also discussed how the coming of big data has affected modern-day journalism. Now, let us turn our attention to the various ways in which media houses utilise big data today. These applications of big data empower media houses in not just telling the stories they want to tell but also how they can tell them. It has opened up new sources for journalists, and provided media houses new ways to engage with their audience. Let us discuss some ways in which media houses use big data:
9.6.1 Data Mining
As discussed, big data benefits the media industry in many ways, and so media houses are always keen on utilising it in their operations. This is perhaps most true in news-making. Although journalists today are well-equipped in ICT skills, big data and advanced analytics are a little technical even for them. Data mining helps in this, playing the role of a mediator between journalists and big data. It helps to extract useful information from large datasets, decode it, and break it down into a more understandable form. The integration of these innovations with traditional journalism has brought the profession into head-on into the new information age.

9.6.2 Data Journalism
The media industry as a whole recognised early on that data is a source as a well as a tool. Data journalism follows the same principles as reporting, investigative journalism, and the like. What sets it apart is that now the story is based on information that comes from big data and not only from traditional sources. This way of writing is characterised by complex computing work, and a collaboration between specialists and reporters. In journalism, communication should be open and transparent. Data journalism promotes both open journalism as well as open data. This in turn allows the upholding of journalistic principles such as accountability and accessibility.
9.6.3 Data Visualisation
Data visualisation is one of the key applications of big data within the media industry. News articles today are pretty much centred around data visualisations to reproduce large amounts of data in a meaningful way. This enriches the articles, allowing journalists to explain data and statistics through easy-to-understand diagrams, charts and maps. Visualisations can be static or interactive. In the former, there is only one view of data, so one may sometimes need more than one visualisation to convey the information. Interactive visualisations, on the other hand, are dynamic because they use animation, and have eye-catching interfaces. This encourages readers to use the tools for discovering details.
9.6.4 Target Marketing
The process of analysing and interpreting data, in terms of readership/viewership and profit, is becoming more widespread in the media industry. Although data such as ratings have always played an important role in the TV industry, big data is forcing innovative responses from the media sector. Media organisations study content consumption in platforms like Facebook, X, and YouTube - i.e., what and when their readers or audience are consuming - and design publishing strategies according to that. Like the corporate, media organisations use big data to optimise content, to ensure effective advertising and placement, and to improve user and advertiser experience. The idea is to deliver the right content to the right audience at the right time, and on the right device.
9.7 ISSUES AND CONCERNS
Technological progress in journalism has helped create new opportunities and cost efficiency. But like all new technologies, big data comes with its fair share of issues and concerns. While it offers benefits like deeper insights and new storytelling methods, it also presents challenges. Let us look at some potential pitfalls of the use of big data in journalism:
9.7.1 Reliability of Data
The credibility of data journalism hinges entirely on the reliability of data. Large datasets can contain biases, and if journalists are not careful, they may carry forward these biases in their reporting. Therefore, every effort should be made to test the reliability of the data you are working with.
9.7.2 Lack of Effective Systems
In this age of data-abundance, data journalism is still struggling with ineffective systems. Information overload and lack of access to quality data become major hindrances. As do lack of training, and time constraints on journalists. The possible solutions to these problems are better training, collaborative approaches and prioritising quality.
9.7.3 Regulations
Every country has different regulations applying to big data, particularly around data privacy, consent, and the use of information. In India, regulations like Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, require journalists to obtain consent for personal data, which can be impractical for

investigative work. However, used alongside the Right to Information Act, this can empower reporters to uncover information that might otherwise be hidden.
9.7.4 Privacy Concerns
With the increasing amount of data being collected and analysed, data privacy and security are becoming major concerns. There are ethical issues surrounding privacy, the use of personal data, and the potential for data to be misinterpreted or misused. Organisations must ensure that they follow data protection regulations, and that they are taking steps to protect sensitive data.
9.8 CASE STUDY: THE TRIBUNE'S AADHAAR
INVESTIGATIONS
In January 2018, Rachna Khaira of The Tribune investigated and exposed a massive breach in India's Aadhar programme overseen by UIDAI (Unique Identification Authority of India). This news report makes for a good case study on how journalists can use their skills to uncover the abuse of technological systems and their human manipulation. In her report titled, "Rs 500, 10 minutes, and you have access to billion Aadhaar details," Khaira exposed how she and other journalists were able to access personal data of millions of Indians for a small fee to 'agents,' including names, addresses, and phone numbers. Khaira's investigation revealed significant security vulnerabilities in the system and led to government action. This investigative report is the perfect example of the coming together of big data, media, and technological systems. Khaira exposed major flaws in the management of a database that contains the demographic and biometric data of over a billion Indian citizens. The report sparked widespread public concern and highlighted the serious risks associated with the security and privacy of the Aadhaar database. The fact that a journalist was able to find loopholes in the system and bring them to light showed just how vulnerable these systems can be. As Bradshaw (2010) has argued, "Data can be the source of data journalism, or it can be the tool with which the story is told, or it can be both." In Khaira's story, big data became both the tool and the story. It is up to journalists to use their skills to doggedly and effectively find stories that fight for the greater public good Check Your Progress: 2 Note: 1) Use the space provided below for your answers.

9.0 INTRODUCTION
Climate change is a recurring phenomenon in Earth's history, with seven glacial cycles over the past 650,000 years. The last age ended 11,700 years ago, marking the start of modern climate and civilization (NASA, 2020). While past changes were driven by natural orbital variations, current climate change is overwhelmingly linked (95-100% probability) to human activities (IPCC, 2014). Since the Industrial Revolution, greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions have risen sharply, correlating with global temperature increases (Petit et al.,2013). Studies show that over 97% temperatures rose by 7degC--ten times faster than post-ice age warming (NASA, 2020). Presently, global temperatures are 0.8degC above pre-industrial levels, with 1.5degC warming already inevitable (World Bank, 2014). Without intervention, warming could reach 2degC by mid-century and 4degC century's end posing serve threats to ecosystems, human livelihoods, and global stability.
9.1
LEARNING OUTCOMES
After studying this unit, you should be able to: * define climate change; * explain the mechanism and causes of climate change; * explain the extent and intensity of climate change through some case studies; * explain the impacts of climate change and; * explain the implications of climate change on the policies.
9.2
DEFINITION OF CLIMATE CHANGE
As per the UNFCCC, climate change is referred to as "any change in climate which is attributed directly or indirectly to human activity that alters the composition of the global atmosphere and which is in addition to natural climate variability observed over comparable time periods" (UNFCCC 1992). However, according to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), an international entity of United Nations (UN), climate change refers to "a change in the state of

the climate that can be identified (e.g., by using statistical tests) by changes in the mean and/or the variability of its properties and that persists for an extended period, typically decades or longer" (IPCC 2015, p. 120). So, climate change is "any change in climate over time, whether due to natural variability or as a result of human activity" (IPCC 2014). There is a difference between the usage of the term climate change in the UNFCCC and IPCC. Though the definition given by UNFCCC talks about only human-induced climate change, we find that the IPCC has adopted a broader definition that includes both natural and human-induced climate change.
9.3
CAUSES OF CLIMATE CHANGE
Now, there is categorical research evidence to prove that climate change is real and that human interventions are the major contributing factors to such changes (IPCC, 2014, p4). Though there has been natural climate variability due to natural internal processes within the climate system, there is an overriding impact of alterations in the atmosphere due to human or anthropocentric activities. In a report published in 2015, IPCC had emphasised the impact of human influence saying that "Human influence on the climate system is clear, and recent anthropogenic emissions of greenhouse gases are the highest in history. Recent climate changes have had widespread impacts on human and natural systems" (IPCC 2015, p. 2). Another recently published IPCC report highlights that "human influence has become a principal agent of change on the planet, shifting the world out of the relatively stable Holocene period into a new geological era, often termed the Anthropocene" (Allen et al. 2018, p. 53) Response to climate change has changed both in definition and scope. Though initially, the focus was on reducing and stabilising human-induced GHG emissions in the atmosphere, it has subsequently become broad-based (UNFCCC 1992). In addition, the scope of climate actors has also started involving non-state actors like the private sector, cities, civil society, and multilateral development institutions among others (UNFCCC 2018).
9.4
DRIVERS OF CLIMATE CHANGE
Fig. 9.1 Energy Budget of Earth and its atmosphere: A Schematic representation Source: UKOU website The schematic diagram as shown in Fig. 9.1 displays the energy budget of the earth and atmosphere. The figures are global annual averages expressed as a percentage of the rate per unit area at which solar radiation is intercepted by the Earth; i.e., 100 units are equivalent to 342 W m-2. Fig. 9.1 demonstrates that the entire Earth-atmosphere system is in a dynamic equilibrium. However, as we can see from this figure, energy circulates within the system at a higher rate

compared to the rate of input or output at the top of the atmosphere. Therefore, we find the earth's surface to be warmer than it otherwise would be. We also observe from this figure that there is no net accumulation of thermal energy in any specific part of the earth-atmosphere system. Therefore, Global Mean Surface Temperature (GMST) cannot change in this scenario. It is however interesting to find out what might cause Earth's GMCT to change? If we look at the energy budget as depicted in Fig.9.1, we can easily understand that any disturbance in the radiation balance at the top of the atmosphere has the potential to force the global climate to change. Such a disturbance can either warm-up or cool down till a balance is reached. This kind of energy perturbation in the energy balance of the entire earth-atmosphere system (expressed in W m-2) is called radiative forcing. Starting from its first major report published in 1990, IPCC has used the concept of "radiative forcing" as the potential mechanism for climate change. There could be several ways in which the energy balance can get disturbed.
1. Change in Solar Constant
For instance, we can work out the effect of change in the solar constant. Let us assume that planetary albedo remains unchanged (at 31%). Under these circumstances, an increase in the solar constant will lead to a positive radiative forcing. It means that the earth-atmosphere system will absorb solar radiation at a higher rate than the rate at which it emits. It will have a warming effect. Similarly, a reduction in solar constant will create a negative radiative forcing thereby leading to a cooling effect.
2. Volcanic Eruptions
The energy balance can also be disturbed by volcano eruptions which generally discharge a huge quantity of gases and volcano ash into the atmosphere. Sometimes these eruptions are so powerful that they inject materials up to the stratosphere. At such high altitudes, these materials gradually spread around the world and bring about a widespread cooling effect for a long time. The sulphur dioxide emitted during the eruption has a far-reaching impact as chemical reactions convert this gas into droplets of sulphuric acid. These sulphate aerosols are persist in the stratosphere for several years and enhance the backscattering of solar radiation. However gradually these aerosols come down to the troposphere and get washed away by rain. 9.5
IMPACT OF CLIMATE CHANGE
Climate change has widespread impacts extending well beyond an increase in temperature. It has an implication for almost everything which we depend upon, for example, water, energy, transportation, wildlife, agriculture, ecosystems, and human health. Anthropogenic activities have already caused major climatic changes and have set in motion, still more changes. Moreover, carbon dioxide, the predominant Greenhouse Gas (GHG), continues to linger in the atmosphere for hundreds of years and it takes a while for the planet to respond (for example oceans). As a result of this, the impact persists for at least several more decades, even if we stop emitting. In the

absence of major action to reduce emissions, global temperature is on track to rise by an average of 6 degC (10.8 degF), according to the latest estimates (NASA Global Climate Change). The temperature of the earth's surface does not react instantaneously to the rising carbon dioxide levels. It happens because a sizable amount of excess energy is stored in the ocean (large heat capacity). Even if all emissions were to stop today, some further warming will be unavoidable before temperatures stop rising. Therefore, we cannot afford to wait to control GHG emissions till it becomes intolerable. The warning signs of climate change have started impinging upon the lives of people (Please see Box 9.4). The battle against climate change will have to be fought on two major fronts 1) "mitigation" - reducing the flow of greenhouse gases into the atmosphere; and 2) "adaptation" - learning to live with, and adapt to, the climate change that has already been set in motion. It will require both a globally-coordinated response (such as international policies and agreements between countries, a push for cleaner forms of energy) and local efforts on the city- and regional level (for example, public transport upgrades, energy efficiency improvements, sustainable city planning, etc. (NASA Global Climate Change).
9.5.1 Impacts of climate change on Atmosphere
All these anthropogenic changes have the potential to modify the chemical composition of the atmosphere. Changes in atmospheric temperature also affect the rates at which chemical reactions take place (World Meteorological Organization, 2009). Climate warming is expected to enhance the release of biogenic hydrocarbons into the atmosphere which in turn contributes to the worsening of regional air quality (World Meteorological Organization, 2009). Emissions of nitric acid by bacteria in soils are sensitive to temperature and soil moisture and are affected by climate change (World Meteorological Organization, 2009). An increasing number of wildfires and droughts will lead to larger emissions of combustion products like carbon monoxide, nitric oxide, soot and other compounds, affecting the regional and global air quality. Changes in ocean temperature affect the ocean-atmosphere exchanges of compounds such as dimethyl sulphide, which are a source of sulphate aerosols. Just like greenhouse gases, aerosols can have profound impacts on the earth's radiative and energy balance. By controlling the amount of energy that reaches the earth from the sun, aerosols can create a cooling effect by reflecting the sun's energy into space. However, there is one aerosol soot (also known as black carbon), that can create a warming effect and thus contribute to global warming. Climate models have predicted that aerosols have masked about 50 per cent of the warming that would otherwise have been caused by greenhouse gases (NASA, 2009). The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change has concluded that industrial aerosols have acted as a significant brake on the increase in global temperatures over the last 30 years or so. Although aerosols have limited the warming, they also have detrimental effects on human health such as lung damage. Aerosols also affect rainfall patterns, some areas like India and China can experience reduced rainfall. They can also alter the pattern of wind and atmospheric circulation. Aerosol as air pollutants cause tens of thousands of premature deaths every year in the UK alone (the University of Leeds, nd).
9.5.2 Heat Waves and Extreme Temperatures
Climate change also leads to more extreme weather events for example more intense hurricanes, more droughts, and more floods, with all the devastation to life, livelihood and property that accompanies them. The past two decades have witnessed a greater occurrence of extreme heat waves leading to heat-related deaths, forest fires, and harvest losses. Such events include the European heatwave of 2003, the Greek heatwave of 2007, the Australian heatwave of 2009, the Russian heatwave of 2010, the Texas heatwave of 2011, and the U.S. heat wave of 2012. Quite often referred to as 3-sigma events, these events involve monthly and seasonal temperatures typically more than 3 standard deviations (sigma) warmer than the local mean temperature. Normally the frequency of such events is only once in several hundreds of years. If we count the five hottest summers in Europe since 1500, we surprisingly find that all of them took place after
2002. The European heatwave of 2003 and the Russian heatwave of 2010 took the exceptional
death toll of 70,000 and 55000 respectively. Extreme summer temperatures are gradually affecting an increasing proportion of the land area. They can be attributed to growing climatic warming since the 1960s. In the 1960s, three-sigma events were practically absent and affected less than 1

per cent of the Earth's surface. However, the area affected by such extreme events has grown to 4-5 per cent by 2006-08, and 6-13 per cent of the land surface by 2009-11. The studies have now predicted that such events typically cover about 10 percent of the land area now. It certainly could not have happened in the absence of global warming.
9.5.3 Socioeconomic Impacts
Climate change can have far-reaching socio-economic impacts. Societies that are most at risk are close to physical and biological thresholds. Ocean warming for example can reduce fishing catch, affecting 650 million to 800 million people relying on fishing for their livelihoods. In Ho Chi Minh City, direct infrastructure damage from a 100-year-old flood could increase from $200 million to $300 million today to $500 million to $1 billion by 2050. The average share of annual outdoor working hours lost due to extreme heat and humidity could increase from 10 per cent today to 15 to 20 per cent in 2050. Socioeconomic impacts of climate change can have non-linear impacts as system thresholds are breached and knock-on effects. Poorer regions often have climates that are closer to physical thresholds therefore, they rely more on outdoor work and natural capital and have fewer financial means to adapt quickly. Therefore, these regions are most at risk. However, the impact of climate change has been devastating even for developed countries like the USA which lost some 1.5 percent of GDP to such weather-related events in 2017 alone. But some regions are likely to gain from climate change, for example Canada where crop yields are expected to increase. Also, the rising temperature can boost tourism in northern Europe.
9.5.4 Climate Change Impacts on Health
Climate change affects many of the social and environmental determinants of health such as clean air, safe drinking water, sufficient food and secure shelter. Extreme heat can contribute directly to deaths from cardiovascular and respiratory disease, particularly among elderly people. High temperature raises the levels of ozone and other pollutants in the air that worsen cardiovascular and respiratory disease. Increased levels of pollen and other aeroallergens in high temperatures can trigger asthma affecting around 300 million people. Rising sea levels and extreme weather conditions can destroy homes and other essential medical facilities. Also, variable rainfall patterns can affect the availability of freshwater thus compromising hygiene and increasing the risk of diarrheal disease, which kills over 500 000 children aged under 5 years, every year. BOX 9.4: Some Emerging Warning Signs of the Climate Change
1. Glaciers are contracting at an average rate of 15m per year in the central and eastern
Himalayas. If this trend continues, these glaciers are expected to vanish by 2035. This can have serious impingements on the population depending on the glaciers for drinking water supplies etc. Khumbu Glacier, on the popular climbing route to the summit of Mount Everest, has retracted by 5km. The swelling of glacial lakes in Bhutan and the increasing risk of catastrophic flooding is another example of such a phenomenon (ICIMOD, 2019).
2. The thawing of Permafrost in the Arctic region poses a serious threat to the critical
infrastructure of the region. This can also pose a threat to the utilisation of natural resources and sustainable development of the region. Around 70 per cent of the infrastructure located in permafrost is at high risk of being thawed. One-third of Pan- Arctic infrastructure and 45 percent of hydrocarbon extraction in the Russian Arctic are located in high hazard regions (Hjort et al., 2018).
3. Sundarbans are the natural walls for some coastal areas of India and Bangladesh against
climate change. But with rising waters and illicit logging, these mangrove trees are nearing their extinction. Therefore, many local people and local species are losing their habitat. Coastal areas are losing their natural defence against extreme climate change phenomena such as floods and cyclones. In 1998 a large flood occurred in Bangladesh, which covered about 70 per cent of the country (Schwartzstein, 2019).
4. Advancement in flowering time for around 385 British plant species by 4.5 days has been
observed. This reflects the serious effects of temperature change on the ecosystem, as

flowering is a phenomenon that is sensitive to temperature (Fitter & Fitter, 2002).
5. In Monteverde, Costa Rica, twenty out of fifty species of Anurans disappeared during a
population crash in 1987. These crashes are expected to be the result of demographic changes that affected communities of birds, amphibians etc. These changes are associated with dry mist frequency, which is negatively correlated with sea surface temperature (Pounds, Fogden, & Campbell, 1999).
6. Antarctic peninsula Adelie penguin populations have shrunk by 33%, in the past 25 years
population has declined by 33 per cent owing to their declining winter sea ice habitat. Adelies depend on sea ice as a resting and feeding platform. They are being replaced by gentoo penguins (a sub-Antarctic species that has begun to migrate towards the pole) which thrive in open water. Source: Compiled from different Sources
9.6
POLICY IMPLICATIONS OF CLIMATE CHANGE
Complex and policy sensitive issues like climate change can evoke conflicting responses from interest groups and policymakers who tend to adopt a "pick n mix" approach to the available scientific evidence, promoting research that reinforces their existing arguments and beliefs, and neglecting or criticising more uncomfortable findings. Even today, quite often we come across people who deny the climate crisis. It has seriously affected the global fight against climate change. Quite often the facts of climate change come in conflict with people's values, ideologies and political allegiances. Cooling or warming is not necessarily bad for some areas. For example, Siberia might get warmer in a few decades and this could be profitable for the local population. On the other hand, the impact of climate change may force others to leave their homes because of changing environmental conditions. For instance, in the Sahel region of Africa, for example, declining agricultural productivity has driven people out of their homes for the past 30 years; this is expected to continue as a result of climate change, putting the lives of 60 million people who live in the Sahel region at risk (Goosse, 2005). Further, the opinions of individual scientists are often influenced by decision- makers or the media than the reliability of their knowledge. It has created a scenario where the disputes within the scientific community are often extensively reported by the media and become a matter of public debate. The politicisation of climate change-related issues which have seriously undermined the scientific pieces of evidence has often been observed. For instance, 2001 shortly after he assumed office, President George W. Bush withdrew the US from the Kyoto Protocol specifying that it would harm the US economy. It was seen across the world as the influence of business-backed lobby groups in government. The allegations were reported in the media that officials of the white house had tried to interfere with a report from US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to downplay the seriousness of climate change. Similarly, in 2019 President Donald Trump, who had mocked climate science as a hoax, decided to withdraw from the Paris Climate Change Declaration. Though a clearer picture of American participation in the agreement will emerge after the 2020 election, it has created a worldwide concern for the future of global efforts to prevent climate change. 9.7
LET US SUM UP
Climate change is a complex, borderless, and intergenerational challenge with wide-ranging impacts on development. As Mike Toman of the World Bank notes, it involves scientific, economic, and ethical complexities, deep uncertainties, and even disagreement on the nature of the problem. It is considered a "super wicked problem" with four traits: time is running out; those causing it also seek solutions; central authority is weak or absent; and policies often undervalue the future (Levin et al.,2012). Humanity now faces limit imposed by dwindling natural and social capital (Hawken, 1997). National prosperity is inseparable from global well-being, making collective, simultaneous action across social, economic, and environmental dimensions essential. For the first time, humans can determine Earth's Habitability. Strengthening capacities at all levels has become central to the development agenda. Only coordinated global efforts, supported by innovative and out-of-the-box strategies can effectively address the scale and urgency of the crisis.
9.8
KEY WORDS
Climate System: The climate system is a highly complex system consisting of five major components: the atmosphere, the hydrosphere, the cryosphere, the lithosphere and the biosphere, and the interactions between them. The climate system evolves in time under the influence of its internal dynamics and because of external forcings such as volcanic eruptions, solar variations and anthropogenic forcings such as the changing composition of the atmosphere and land-use change.

1.0 INTRODUCTION
At present, audio-visual media is the most popular. Media industry statistics also confirm it. If you observe your daily routine carefully, you will find that you use a large amount of audio- visual content every day. We use them on television, in cinemas, on computers and even on smartphones. Audio-visual content is also considered to be the strongest in terms of impact. In this unit, we will discuss in detail the concept and nature of audio-visual media.
1.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After reading this unit, you will be able to: * understand the meaning of audio-visual medium; * explain the main elements of audio-visual medium; * describe the characteristics and limitations of audio-visual medium; * compare audio-visual medium with other media; and * understand the production process of audio-visual content.
1.2 AUDIO-VISUAL MEDIUM
In this section we'll discuss the various dimensions of audio-visual medium in detail. First we'll discuss the meaning of audio-visual medium, then various elements of audio-visual content, then types, then strengths and limitations, and finally various uses of audio-visual content.

1.2.1 Meaning of Audio-Visual Medium
All the means through which audio-visual content is delivered to the people are called audio- visual media. As the name suggests, audio-visual material is made up of two elements. First, visual and second, audio. Visual are those elements which can be seen and audio are those which can be heard. It is true that audio-visual material includes both visual and audio elements but the visual element always remains dominant. Film and television have traditionally been audio-visual media but modern information and broadcasting technology has also included online platforms in it. With the help of internet, today we are able to watch audio-visual materials on our computer, laptop or smartphone.
1.2.2 Elements of Audio-Visual Content
As we have discussed above, audio-visual material is made up of two elements - visual and audio. In this subsection, we will discuss both these elements in detail.
Visual Elements
It is obvious that visual elements are those elements that we see. Many types of visual elements are used in audio-visual content. Some of the major ones are as follows: i. Video footage: Any visual material that is recorded by video cameras comes under the category of video footage. Although video cameras record audio as well as visuals, here we will discuss only visuals. A large part or say the largest part of the various types of content distributed through audio-visual media is made up of video footage. Today, different types of cameras are being used to record video footage. These include expensive professional video cameras as well as smartphones. ii. Film footage: Film footage is mainly moving visual material that is recorded with traditional film-based cameras. Such cameras record only scenes and use light-sensitive strips, also called film. Film cameras are mainly used in cinema production and in the production of high-budget television programmes. Their quality was better than video cameras but now their use has reduced considerably. They have now been replaced by high-quality electronic cinema cameras. iii. Photographs: Unlike video footage or film footage, photographs are still. Photography cameras are used for these. Sometimes you may see audio-visual material which is based only on photographs. These are created by combining photographs with some audio elements (background music, voice over, etc.). Photographs are also used in the production of news and documentaries. iv. Graphics and Animation: These are visual elements which are also used extensively in the production of audio-visual content. If you watch news programmes on television carefully, you will find that graphics are used in large quantities. Many types of texts seen on the screen of television news channels, such as news and advertisements on the ticker in the lower third, name and introduction of the person giving the byte, cricket score, information related to the stock market, temperature, breaking news plate etc. come under the category of graphics. Apart from this, charts, graphs, maps, tables and other infographics used in news programmes also come under the category of graphics.

Animations are broadly computer-made visual elements that are dynamic. Let us take a simple example. Suppose you drew a picture of a tree with the help of some computer software, now if you make it dynamic with the help of some software, it will be called animation. Television news channels also keep using them. Many times, if there is no video footage of any important news, it is presented to the viewers with the help of animation. You must have seen the use of animation in news related to any major accident (train, road, air, etc.). Here, with the help of animation, the process and causes of the accident are presented to the audience. The use of animation in audio-visual content is not limited to television or video news only. Animation is also an independent big industry. A large part of audio-visual material related to children is based on animation. We are all familiar with cartoon programs which are very popular among children. Many television channels broadcast only cartoon based programs. Animation can be both 2D (two-dimensional) or 3D (three-dimensional). v. Visual effects: Visual effects are also an important visual element. They are used to make audio-visual material attractive and to create such visual elements which are not real. Now with the use of computer software, the creation of many types of visual effects has become relatively easier. Audio elements Audio elements refer to such elements which can be heard. Audio elements also play an important role in the creation of effective audio-visual material. They tell the audience those things which are not known or are not clearly known by looking at the visual elements. If you want to know the importance of audio elements in any audio-visual material, then you should watch it by turning off its audio. If you watch it by turning off the sound or audio, you will have difficulty in understanding that content properly or that audio-visual material will not seem as attractive as it was with audio. This is the importance of audio elements in audio-visual material. Now we will discuss about some important audio elements. These are as follows: i. Spoken words ii. Music ii. Background music iii. Ambience iv. Sound effects i. Spoken words: Spoken words mean words that are spoken by mouth. Spoken words are used extensively in audio-visual material. They are used in many ways. If you take the example of television news channels, what the anchor says, what the people say in the bytes, the voice over that goes along with the scenes or what the visiting experts say in programs like discussion, all are spoken words. In documentary films, the voice over and the audio parts of the interview are also spoken words. The dialogues spoken by the characters in films and serials also fall in the category of spoken words. Hence, it is clear that spoken words are used as the most important audio element in audio-visual material. ii. Music: Many audio-visual programs are based on music, for example music videos, television programs based on music, songs in films, live telecast of a musical stage shows, etc. Music is the main audio element in these types of audio-visual programs.

iii. Background music: You must have often noticed in films, television programs, online video content that music keeps playing in the background along with the visual elements. The sound level of this music keeps changing, sometimes very low, sometimes loud but it never dominates the dialogues in the scenes nor does it reduce their clarity. This music is called background music. It makes the visual elements attractive and impressive. The background music in a funny scene and a scary scene is different. Choosing the right background music makes the scenes more impressive. iv. Ambience: Ambient sound is necessary to make any scene natural. Ambience sound means the sound normally present at a particular place. Suppose if you are standing on a road, then some sounds are normally available on the road, such as the sound of vehicles coming and going or the sound of their horns from time to time, etc. These sounds are called ambience. Without ambience, the scenes do not look natural, so they are used in audio-visual materials. iv. Sound effects: Sound effects are sounds that are added separately to the audio-visual material. These are not actually present at the time of shooting. These are recorded separately either in the studio or outside the studio. Let us understand this with an example. Suppose there is a morning scene in your film in which many birds are seen flying from the trees and the chirping of the birds is also heard. When you shoot this scene, such chirping of the birds is not normally recorded. This chirping is recorded separately and added to that scene. In this example, the sound of birds chirping added separately would fall under the category of sound effect. Let us take another example. In films, you must have often seen that a villain or hero breaks a door and a loud sound of the door breaking is also heard. This sound of the door breaking is not real; it is a sound effect which is recorded by Foley artists in the studio and later added to that scene. 1.2.3 Types of Audio-Visual Media
We have discussed that all the communication mediums used to deliver audio-visual content to the audience come under the category of audio-visual media. We have also talked about audio-

visual content in detail. In such a situation, if we look carefully, we find many types of audio- visual media around us. These are as follows: i. Film ii. Television iii. Video Player iv. Online Medium i. Film: This is the oldest audio-visual medium and also very effective. The specialty of this medium is - the audience goes to the cinema hall only to watch the film. The features of the audio-visual content, the big screen, the dark atmosphere of the movie theatre and the attention of the audience only on the film, all these together increase the impact of this medium to a great extent. ii. Television: This is a popular audio-visual medium which even today delivers a large amount of audio-visual content to the people. Television has travelled a long journey with technological inventions. From terrestrial broadcasting to satellite broadcasting and now smart TV, this medium has kept itself in demand as an audio-visual medium, constantly changing with time. iii. Video Players: Video players have also been a popular audio-visual medium. Their format has also changed with changing technology. The television monitor and VCR/VCP combination was quite popular. In those days, video cassettes were used to store audio-visual programmes and television monitor and video cassette player were used to view them. Later, CDs (Compact Discs), DVDs (Digital Versatile Discs) and Blu-ray Discs came into the market to store video content and so did their players. Pen drives and many types of memory cards fall under the category of flash memory and are used to store video content. Computers have many types of media players that can play these video content. Cloud storage is internet-based storage in which a video file can be stored, such as Google Drive, One Drive, etc. Whenever required, this file can be downloaded with the help of internet and viewed through media players. In this, internet is required only to download the file, then the video content can be viewed offline. iv. Online medium: The use of audio-visual content through online mediums is continuously increasing. With the help of internet, we are able to watch audio-visual content on computer, laptop or smartphone. OTT (Over the Top) platforms are becoming increasingly popular for audio-visual content. Audio-visual programs of OTT platforms like ZEE 5, JioHotstar, Sony LIV, Amazon Prime, Netflix, etc. are being liked a lot by the audience. Programs of almost all television channels are broadcasted live on their websites and their old episodes are also available there. YouTube has brought a revolution in this field. A large number of people are creating audio-visual content and making it available to people through YouTube. Old films and episodes of old serials can also be seen on YouTube. Due to the expansion of high-speed internet services and reduction in data prices, it is possible that in the coming times, online medium will become the most popular medium for dissemination of audio-visual content.
1.2.4 Audio-Visual Medium: Advantages and Limitations

Every medium has some advantages and some limitations. The same is true for audio-visual media. In this section, we will discuss the advantages and limitations of audio-visual media.
Advantages of Audio-Visual Media
Audio-visual media is considered popular and effective. Some of its main Advantages are as follows: More effective: Audio-visual media is considered to be relatively more effective. Since, while using audio-visual content, we use two senses (eyes and ears), hence the content transmitted through it has a greater impact. Interesting: Audio-visual content is quite interesting. The success of audio-visual media in the field of entertainment is proof of this. Even today, they dominate the field of entertainment. Films, television programs and online videos are its main examples. Ability to explain complex material: Due to the presence of both visual and audio elements, audio-visual media can explain complex things in a better way. For this reason, they are being used successfully on a large scale in the field of education. Many complex topics of science can be presented in a very interesting and clear manner with the help of animation. For example, if the motion of an electron in an atom has to be shown, then there can be no better medium than the audio-visual.
Limitations of Audio-Visual Medium
Audio-visual medium also has some limitations. Some of the major ones are as follows: Demand complete attention: We have already discussed that in using audio-visual media, two of our senses (eyes and ears) are used. The use of eyes limits the flexibility of audiences doing other works simultaneously. Just as we can use radio while driving, working in fields and gardens, audio-visual media cannot be used in the same way. Negative effect on eyes: In the present times, our screen-based activities have increased a lot. We constantly look at the screen, whether it is the screen of a mobile phone or a computer or laptop or television. Our studies, our office work, our shopping, our entertainment, everything is becoming screen based. Whenever we look at a screen, the rays coming out of it hit our eyes and looking at the screen for a long time is harmful for our eyes. Audio-visual media is also screen based and the negative effects on the eyes are one of the major drawbacks of these media.
1.2.5 Uses of Audio-Visual Media
We know that mass communication tools are mainly used for three purposes - information, education and entertainment. The same is applicable to audio-visual media too. We can classify the use of audio-visual media in these three following areas: i. For information: Audio-visual media is being used on a large scale to provide necessary information to a big section of the society. We all are seeing that audio-visual media are being used with great success in the field of news and current affairs. The rise of television news channels had changed the entire world of news. Instant information about events and watching the events happen on your own television screen, both these facilities had greatly influenced people. At present, apart from television, audio-visual news content is also being used

prominently on online platforms. The ability to show the events greatly increases the credibility of these media in the field of news. Apart from journalistic organizations and government institutions, the general public is also using audio-visual material to convey important information to the people. Online media has made the communication platform accessible to everyone. Suppose you have witnessed some incident about which it is necessary to inform the general public and government institutions, you can make a video of that with the help of your phone and bring it to the notice of the people and government institutions through social media. The availability of video cameras in almost every hand and social media have given a great power to the general public, but it also brings a great responsibility too at the same time. Misuse or irresponsible use of this power can create big problems for the society. The whole world is fighting the problem of tampering of audio- visual materials and their use in wrong contexts. ii. For education: Audio-visual media are considered very useful for education. In many developing countries like India, television has been seen as an important medium of education since the beginning. Here education means both formal and informal. Currently, the Government of India is operating many educational DTH television channels under the name of Swayam Prabha. These channels are broadcasting programs ranging from school education to technical and higher education. Online medium has also emerged as an important means of dissemination of audio-visual content. And if we talk about educational audio-visual content, then their highest availability is also on online platforms. Audio-visual content (video lectures) is the main component of online courses. The Corona epidemic led to an unprecedented increase in the use of audio- visual educational content provided through online platforms. iii. For entertainment: Entertainment is a major area of use of audio-visual media. If we look at the data of the media industry, we will find that audio-visual media are being used the most in the field of entertainment, whether it is the film industry or the television industry or internet- based OTT (Over the Top) platforms. Entertaining audio-visual content dominates all. We can consider the beginning of audio-visual media from the early days of films when moving pictures were shown with sound. Then came television and then online media. Audio-visual media completely changed the way society entertained. Many traditional means of entertainment disappeared or were in serious danger of extinction. Television in particular affected the way society entertained the most. Now the screen of the mobile phone is emerging as a popular means of using audio-visual entertainment content. iv. Other uses: Audio-visual content also has many mixed uses. You must have heard words like infotainment and edutainment. Content which is a mixture of information and entertainment is called infotainment and where there is a mixture of education and entertainment, it is called edutainment. Many television channels, for example - Epic, Discovery, History, Animal Planet, etc. broadcast audio-visual content based on infotainment and edutainment. Such content is also available in large quantities on online platforms.
1.3 CREATION OF AUDIO-VISUAL CONTENT

A general principle is followed in the production of audio visual content - if you can show, don't tell, if you can't show, tell, but you must show and tell everything. The visual element dominates. The more of the message that can be conveyed by showing, the better it is. Just as written language has a grammar and many rules, similarly visual language also has a grammar and some rules. In the production of quality audio-visual content, a deep understanding of the visual language and the skill of successfully combining it with the audio element is very important. The entire process of production of audio-visual content can be divided into the following three stages: pre-production, production and post-production. Pre-production includes all the work before shooting, such as script writing, arranging necessary equipment, selection of actors, selection of location for shooting and construction of sets etc. During production, shooting takes place using cameras and then the audio-visual material is finalized through editing in post-production. 1.0 INTRODUCTION
A brand is much more than its physical attributes; it is an experience and is responsible for building a relationship with the consumers. In today's marketplace, customers do not just buy any product; they buy brands. Companies use branding to create a different identity in the minds of customers so that they can associate with it. Brand identity is how companies want their brand to be represented, and brand image is what customers think of your brand. Brand identity and brand image lead to customers' trust and are important for long-term equity. This unit will explore the foundational concept of branding and how a brand and a product are different. Why brand identity matters and how it is beneficial in marketing. Understanding these concepts is crucial for people in the field of marketing and communication.
1.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After working through this unit, you should be able to: * Understand the difference between a product and brand; * Define brand and know the process of branding; and * Comprehend the dimensions of brand identity and Brand image.

1.2 DIFFERENCE BETWEEN PRODUCT AND BRAND
A product is the basic solution for the problem of a need. It is the bundle of benefits provided by marketers to satisfy a need. But all products are not brands. Can we differentiate a product from a brand? Is there a difference between an ordinary product and a branded product? Generally, people use products and brands interchangeably. But a product is a mere commodity offered in the market by a company with certain benefits, promises, and assurance. For buying products like bathing soap, one can buy brands like Lifebuoy, Dove, or Dettol; for clean water, brands like Livpure, Eureka, Aquaguard and many others are available. Let us just put down our thoughts on the products related to personal hygiene offered by the brand Dettol. The core benefit is to 'provide protection against germs which can cause infection and illness' and 'Be 100% Sure'. It is, thus, an assurance, a commitment to the customers. These taglines may define the brands by words, but a brand is built by actions and whatever it does and all the knowledge it delivers. There are three aspects of a brand: * The first aspect is when the product carries a logo, colour, look, feel, the packaging known as the visual identity of the brand. * Another aspect is the promise, commitment, and assurance known as the core benefits offered by the brand; for example, the brand Lifebuoy provides "99.9% germ-free protection." * The third aspect is the core-value-based mission such as to alleviate diseases from lack of hygiene in developing countries. These three aspects assist in giving a product a different story in comparison to its competitive brands selling the same product.
1.3 DEFINING A BRAND
A product can become a brand when it has a compelling story to tell which may inspire the customers to get associated with it. Consequently, it may also result in expansion of business through further acceptance of the other products that fall under the same brand. According to Tom Goodwin, "Brands are essentially patterns of familiarity, meaning, fondness, and reassurance that exist in the minds of people." Brands build up a "set of complex symbols that represents a variety of ideas and attributes" (Gardner & Levy, 1955) . A brand, thus, can be a set of distinct features which provide relevance, mental and emotional connections in the mind of the customers. A brand is meant to give a shortcut to the buyer by having a distinct name, logo, design, and packaging as well as the overall experience in terms of its presence in different media and activities. American Marketing Association (AMA) defines brand as a "name, term, sign, symbol, or design, or a combination of them, intended to identify the goods and services of one seller or group of sellers and to differentiate them from those of competition."
1.3.1 Characteristics of Brand
A brand is what can differentiate itself from the crowd. According to Kotler and Lee (2005), There can be six levels of meaning that a brand is able to deliver. They are attributes, benefits, values, culture, personality, and the user known as the primary target, the consumer. According to Kochan (1996), a brand can differentiate itself based on three forms of values. They are: functional values that define the product performance and the rationale behind making a purchase; expressive values that explain the self-image customers see with that brand; and central values which define the belief system of the brand as being honest, ethical, etc. A brand thus is the powerhouse that strengthens the position of the product in the market.
1.4 WHAT IS BRANDING?
Branding can be defined as the process of researching and analysing your product, defining its key characteristics, and highlighting its unique selling proposition (USP) to distinguish a product from its competitors. It is a way to form a true representation of a brand to be perceived in the same way by its customers. So, when you buy a Coca-Cola drink, you "open happiness" and "taste the feelings."

Figure 1: Branding: creating a unique identity using name, packaging and marketing When one makes a purchase decision, brand plays a key role as the deciding factor. Branding can give the colour, tone, and look to give a face to the product. It builds an identity of the products, services and organisations, which is known as Brand identity.
1.5 BRAND IDENTITY
Think of yourself as a person with a certain identity. What do you think your identity gives you? Does it provide you with a purpose and meaning in your life? What are your core values? How do you want the people to perceive you? What are the personality traits that you need to project to be accepted by the people? What relations are important to you? An identity can provide a structure and meaning to a brand. Customers associate with a particular brand over other products and when that brand is able to live up to the promise and expectations of its customers, may be in terms of quality, quantity, or any other intangible benefits that can help in developing an identity of its own. Thus, an identity can "help to establish a relationship between the brand and the customer by generating a value proposition involving functional, emotional or self- expressive benefits" (Aaker, D. A., 2002). A brand is different from a product and encompasses the values, promises, or commitments that are made. To build or maintain a brand, firstly it is important to define its identity. For this, we should start asking the brand who are you? What can define you? Answering these questions can help in giving a shape to a brand's identity, giving it direction, meaning, and uniqueness. Put simply, brand identity is a set of unique associations in terms of values and beliefs that are defined and created by the brand owner who wants to answer the question 'who is the brand' so that he/she can establish the right relationships with the right customers. So, brand identity is who the brand is if seen as an independent identity. Let us analyse all the non-alcoholic beverages offered by the Coca-Cola company: these include Thums Up, Fanta, Sprite, Coke, Diet Coke. They all are brands from the same company, yet each of these brands are uniquely presented by the company. What distinguishes one from another is known as its brand's identity.
1.5.1 Brand Identity Structure
Brand identity can be seen in two facets. Facet one is known as the core identity, and facet two is known as the extended or visual identity. Core identity signifies the core, the central fundamental principle of the timeless essence of the brand. It can also be called the DNA of the brand. It defines the brand as it is. This part consists of values, principles, and associations that do not change even with the changing times, or when the brand explores new product lines or regions. Let's take the example of popular antiseptic brand Savlon. The immediate thought that comes to our mind is that of an antiseptic liquid that does not hurt while healing wounds and has a better smell which is its core identity. A core identity, thus, forms the foundation of a brand. However, without the second facet, a brand identity is incomplete. Facet two is known as the extended or visual brand identity. This part includes the logo, the colour, the look and feel of the brand. Even if there are two products from the same company, they can still have two different core and visual identities. For example, Fanta and Sprite are both beverages from the same company Coca-cola. Fanta, an orange-coloured drink

presents a sense of playfulness, and the current logo is 'More Fanta Less Serious' whereas Sprite, the green colour one wants you to stay simple, honest, and straightforward and the slogan is Seedhi Baat, No bakwaas. This difference between their core identities is extended through their visual identities via the logo and packaging. Check Your Progress: 1 Note: 1) Use the space below for your answers.
2) Compare your answers with those given at the end of this unit.
