11.1 INTRODUCTION
The idea of gender and performativity emerges from an analysis of how cultures construct ideas around the idea of what is male and what is female. More often than not our understanding of men and women is completely different from the general idea of biological differences. Gender identity is created and sustained through multiple ways of being and doing. The two main strands of analysis in the anthropology of sex and gender look at ideas and practices that create differences, on the one hand--and remove or confuse those differences, on the other. This unit will try to unfold these differences. Later the discussion will move the way gender and performance are connected to each other in an extensive manner. The theorists who have influenced the analysis of gender from the perspective of performance will be discussed. We will look at examples and instances from India, in order to understand the subject matter better.
11.2 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After going through this unit, you will be able to: * Define and explain the connections between gender and performance; * Critically analyse gender from the perspective of performance; * Discuss the ambiguity of gender roles in rituals; and * Distinguish the differences and discrepancies in the gender and performance.

Gender and
11.3 DEFINING SEX AND GENDER
Performativity You have already read in detail about the sex and gender dichotomy in unit
2 Block 1 of MWG 002. Let us briefly look at these terms again in the
context of performativity. The terms sex and gender pertain to the spheres of biology and society, respectively. Sex lies in the domain of biological and anatomical differences, and gender is a socially constructed identity, that is to a large extent influenced by sex. The biological uncertainty created by the existence of hermaphrodites, posed newer questions regarding the identification of sex as binary or divided into two. Hermaphrodites are born with both the male and female sexual organs. The gender they belong to becomes an issue. The fact that sex and by extension gender is seen in terms of a binary division is based on the difference in sexual organs, orientation, socialization and also differences in division of labour. Yet, a lot of people do not fall into either the male or female category, on the basis of various social markers, such as clothing and mannerisms. This presupposes that most individuals are therefore seen not only as male and female, but that to be recognized as male and female an individual has to exhibit certain characteristics. These characteristics, particular the kind of walk, dressing, talking are socially endowed or recognised as masculine or feminine. From the World Health Organization website, ' "Sex" refers to the biological and physiological characteristics that define men and women "Gender" refers to the socially constructed roles, behaviours, activities, and attributes that a given society considers appropriate for men and women.' The website of the organisation goes on to list the sex and gender characteristics that distinguishes male and female as sex categories; and masculine and feminine as gender categories. In terms of sex characteristics, males have testicles that females do not have; females have developed breasts that are capable of lactating--that males do not possess. Gender characteristics however are listed in terms of cultural differences. So, 'In the US (and most other countries) women earn significantly less than men for the same work; in Viet Nam, many more men than women smoke as female smoking has not traditionally been considered appropriate; in Saudi Arabia, men are allowed to drive cars, while women are not; in most of the world, women do more housework than men.' These are often identified with what is known as gender roles. According to West and Zimmerman (1987), gender roles are related to behavioural aspects of being a man or a woman. Now this might be prescribed by cultures and be played out as per a prescribed format. In this sense there are many who do not follow a prescribed gender role because of ambiguity regarding their sex or gender. It is therefore important to note the different

Gender and Performance social categories of genders and identities before we go further into the unit. It may also be helpful for you to review similar categories in Unit 4, Block 3 of MWG 001. Transgender is an umbrella term used to refer individuals who do not conform to the gender role expectations of their biological sex. Also used by persons who may identify their gender as being the opposite of their biological sex. Under this category, and contiguous to it are others that cannot be placed under the strict demarcation of men and women. Transsexuals are persons with the biological characteristics of one sex who see themselves as the opposite gender and have had some type of surgical alteration and/or hormone treatment that changes their bodies' appearance in alignment with their identity. Cross dressers or Transvestites on the other hand wear clothes usually worn by people of the opposite biological sex. They do not however identify themselves as having a gender identity different from their biological sex or gender role. The motivations for cross- dressing vary. Intersex people are those born with aspects of both female and male physical features. This is usually understood to be congenital, involving chromosomal, morphologic, genital and/or gonadal anomalies, such as diversion from typical XX-female or XY-male presentations, e.g., sex reversal (XY female, XX male), genital ambiguity, or sex developmental differences. An intersex individual may have biological characteristics of both the male and the female sexes. Earlier, reportedly, doctors would often decide the sex of the infant at birth without consulting the parents (from the Boulder County advisory to understanding queer communities. Available on the website: www.bouldercounty.org). By and large, people who conform to different gender roles and expectations. They also challenge the established definition of sex and gender. West and Zimmerman believe that gender is performed--they call it the 'doing' of gender. So, ' "doing" of gender is undertaken by men and women whose competence as members of society is hostage to its production' (Zimmerman, 1987, p. 126). This means that people act out their 'natures' as belonging to either the masculine or the feminine as per socially prescribed rules. They usually act them out as per socially prescribed rules, which are more often than not dictated by the social context in which they find themselves. West and Zimmerman note how this context is an amalgamation of various social arrangements and relationships. The doing of gender as per gender roles therefore becomes a kind of performance. Let us examine this idea in a theoretical context in the next section.
11.4 THEORETICAL BACKGROUND
Gender performativity according to Judith Butler, refers to the process by which difference and identity are constructed in, and through the discourses

of sexuality (Morris, 1995). In an insightful study by Foucault, the idea of Gender and Performativity gender and performance becomes clearer. Foucault published the memoirs of an eighteenth century French hermaphrodite named, HercuMlianneg aBia Arbrainsu. In the memoirs Barbin talks of the predicament of forcibly taking on a male identity after having lived as a female for most part of 'her' life. The male identity is an imposition by medical and legal authorities who want to assign one particular 'sex' to Barbin. Through the memoir Foucault tries to recount the history of sexuality in pre-modern Europe wherein certain ideas of sex and gender were privileged over others. The most dominant amongst these ideas was that of the binary quality of sex and gender, i.e. there are only two types of gender and sex--man and woman, and male and female. This also resulted in a view that discriminated against those who did not fall into either category, or worse had sexual preferences for those belonging to the same sex. In Foucault's analysis history bears testimony to how sexuality comes to be seen in relation to sex and gender. Therefore homosexuality was seen as abnormal or going against nature. Interestingly the theoretical and academic work in the area of gender and performativity tries to do away with the binary division of sex and gender, and attempts to analyse it from a more dynamic perspective wherein the idea of gender and sex is ever changing. Performance theory is therefore seeking to place both gender and sex within multiple layers of understanding and practices. Rosalind Morris (1995) notes that the theory of performance emerged as a critique of structuralism within socio-cultural anthropology. Structuralism, as a theory and form of anthropological analysis espouses the importance of social structure in the mental life of individuals who make up society. According to structuralists, society and its structure condition individual actions as well as social rules and norms. Performance theory combines anthropology and a feminist perspective to arrive at a substantial critique of structural theory. Here, thinkers such as Pierre Bourdieu, Michel de Certeau and others are very important, even though a gendered perspective is not overtly present in their work. Yet, the influence they have exercised on performance theorists has been very important. Bourdieu's (1995, 1998) study of practice has been very influential in performance studies. Through the idea of the habitus, or a set of structuring structures that produce and are produced by specifically embodied subjects, Bourdieu wishes to place the idea of structures that recreate themselves through the acts of individuals who are socialized into reproducing the very same structures. Let us take the idea of acts and structures and then the idea of the embodied state.

Gender and Performance Practical logic, according to Bourdieu, creates the illusion that all acts are geared towards a model, knowing fully well that the model and its rules will be violated. Take for instance, the idea of the 'feel of the game'. To be successful, or good at what one does, one needs to have a feel of the game--a sentence we have heard often, in different contexts, but conveying the same meaning--that in order to win one must know how the game operates. So even though the football player enters the match with no hidden intentions or motivations, he still knows that they exist and the rules can be manipulated in order to win the match. This is how individuals act to subvert, go against established models and rules. We work out strategies to get over rules. A strategy, according to Bourdieu, is a way of calculating practice which is not previously thought out, nor mechanically determined by the rule. They are on-the-spot in a way and yet not completely devoid of some kind of idea of the consequences that will follow. Strategies are context-specific, and a very important aspect of practice and practical logic. For Bourdieu the importance of time cannot be discounted in practice. The way it is presented is often removed from how it really happens in real time. As models the representation of a practice hides many layers within it. For instance, in gift exchange one is unable to see the motivations of the actors involved or what repercussions a delayed gift might invite. All one sees is the process removed from its reality, in a way. This is how, for Bourdieu, most structuring structures operate. In this way the collective representation of the body, self and person come to be represented in material terms--that can be valued. In Bourdieu's idea of embodiment, the body comes to be seen as a result of social processes rather than in terms of abstractions. What we therefore call 'body language' is a carefully constructed set of codes and rules that are understood by others because they too are aware of, and practice the same rules. Tual gives the striking example of Iranian women, who must never let men be aware of their presence in public (Tual, 1986 ). For this they must be fully covered in the hijab or veil, they should avoid looking into the eyes of a stranger, and they should basically be invisible. Men, in turn, must treat them as if they are invisible. According to Tual, in Iran both men and women have embodied the habitus. Michel de Certeau looks at practice as a form of meandering, improvisational acts of the individual, who must move through the systematized world (Morris, 1995). Individuals therefore indulge in 'creative gestures' that cannot be seen within the perspective of structural principles. De Certeau is known for his approach that looks at the everyday negotiations that individuals go through in order to subvert and overturn established rules. And even though the individual is completely socialised into believing that he/she is an objectified product of society and its rules--there is indulgence, often unconscious and in small acts, in the overturning of structures.

In the everyday approach, the most cited example is de Certeau's reading Stage and Theatre of walking in the city (Certeau, 1984). Individuals often take shortcuts to navigate through routes in a city and to save time. Interestingly, for de Certeau, it is these shortcuts that defy established routes, which are often set down in maps and route guides. By taking the unidentified routes individuals create their own paths--a creative gesture--to go against the established and the given. Many gender theorists have been influenced by both de Certeau's and Bourdieu's approaches to look at everyday subversions of gender norms, as well as place practice within a dynamic, ever-changing perspective. Judith Butler (1999), has been influenced by Bourdieu's theory and sees gender as a set of non-normative practices. Butler, as one of the primary proponents of the gender and performativity theory, finds Bourdieu's idea of embodiment as relevant to understanding how even though the body assumes its sex as per culturally mandated practices, it is in the aberrations or deviations that gender and sex roles are really played out. So, as a set of acts gender 'derives its compulsive force from the fact that people mistake the acts for the essence--and come to believe that they are mandatory' (Morris, 1995). It is this very idea of the essence or essential nature that influences the next theoretical stance in the understanding of gender and performance.
11.4.1 Doing of Gender
Another key thinker, Erving Goffman (1976), theorised that 'doing' gender is a part of every individual's negotiations with her/his gender identity and role. Goffman mentions that it is during social interaction with others in the latter's environment that individuals exhibit, what he calls, their 'essential natures'. This essential nature is representative of their social situation and basic character--and it is relevant to give an idea to the other person the social context from which the individual is coming from. Often as expressive acts, essential natures get represented in the form of 'displays'. For Goffman, "If gender be defined as the culturally established correlates of sex (whether in consequence of biology or learning), their gender display refers to conventionalized portrayals of these correlates" (West & Zimmerman, 1987, p.130). These gender displays however come to represent the personalities of the individuals, more than their essential natures. In this form they become to be dramatizations of the cultural ideals of masculinity and femininity. As an important part of everyday interactions, individuals may not want to express the conventional ideas associated with their gender. That is when the doing of gender becomes very important for us to study and understand. Influenced by Goffman, West and Zimmerman base their analysis of doing gender by looking at how individuals negotiate in their everyday gender

Gender and Performance displays. They formulate and define three categories that form an important part of one's sex and gender identity. Sex is defined as the "determination made through the application of socially agreed upon biological criteria for classifying persons as females or males" (West & Zimmerman, 1987, p.127). This classification may be on the basis of genitalia, or chromosomal typing before birth. Sex category is defined as when "placement...is achieved through application of the sex criteria, but in everyday life categorization is established and sustained by the socially required identificatory displays that proclaims one's membership in one or the other category" (West & Zimmerman, 1987, p.127). The authors note that even though ostensibly sex and sex category go together, the two can be different. Finally, Gender "is the activity of managing situated conduct in light of normative conceptions of attitudes and activities appropriate for one's sex category" (West & Zimmerman, 1987, p.127). Gender activities emerge from membership to a particular sex category. Through a definition of the three concepts above the authors wish to point out how certain roles are played out in terms of one's sex-gender. However, they are unlike contextualized roles like that of a doctor, teacher, patient, which have an organizational base that is absent in sex and gender roles. In order to understand how individuals negotiate through the three categories defined above, West and Zimmerman draw on Harold Garfinkel's study of Agnes (1967). Agnes was a transsexual raised as a boy, who after the age of 17 took a female identity--and some years later underwent surgery to make herself 'permanently' into a female. Pre and post surgery, Agnes enacted the sex, sex category and gender of a female and a woman. Despite having male genitalia, Agnes undertook what Garfinkel calls--being a 'practical methodologist'. This implies that she did not fake being a woman but tried to negotiate her everyday interactions by presenting herself the way a woman would--as part of a calculated, preconceived design and assessment of herself. In their analysis, West and Zimmerman note that when it comes to negotiating with her 'sex', Agnes manages very well. She insists that she has a penis by mistake--a fault that has to be corrected, and is eventually corrected through surgery. She is able to camouflage her genital difference through clothes. At the cultural level therefore the identification of sex remains restricted--so while clothes may help identify one's sex, they may camouflage it too. In the case of sex categorisation it is slightly different, for in the absence of clothes as symbolic markers, recourse is taken to aspects such as voice and facial hair--again variable in character. Some men have less facial hair, while some women may have a deep voice--again a terrain that can be negotiated with ease. Agnes made her adjustments to convincingly portray her sex category. It is when gender comes into the question that the authors note that Agnes finds the performance of being a woman challenging. In trying to be a 'woman' Agnes takes recourse to her fiancee's assessment of other women. She follows his

guidelines to try and 'acceptable' gender performance. The fiancee's advisory Stage and Theatre is of course loaded with the unequal power relations between men and women--but in following the same Agnes conforms more to her advantage. The doing of gender therefore emerges from a mix of the prevailing social context and the kind of social relationships the individual is embedded in. In that sense, no particular social code with reference to gender display can be uniformly in practice. Variability is the most important characteristic of the ways in which gender plays itself out in different settings. Check Your Progress 1:
1) How would you describe the difference between sex and gender?
How does performance theory view this difference?
2) Summarise the ideas of Goffman and Garfinkel regarding the
'doing' of gender.
11.5 MARKING AND DILUTING GENDER THROUGH
PERFORMANCE
Rosalind Morris identifies two main strands of analysis in the anthropology of sex and gender. One strand looks at the way cultural orders construct gender and create subjects. This involves focusing on ideological and symbolic representations that further exacerbate the difference. For instance, rites of passage or life cycle rites (marriage, death, birth, initiation) that are an important area of analysis, combining performance and the explicit creation of a gender identity. The second strand decomposes difference and focuses on those institutions that create ambiguity in terms of transgendering institutions, especially those found in non-Western societies. This approach looks at subversion and agency through established and covert spheres such as theatre or marginalised groups. In the next section we look at both these spheres of analysis. In the first anthropological analyses of life cycle rites in Bengal are discussed to look at how cultures construct and socialize people into the idea of gender, through performance of rituals. With regard to the anthropology of decomposing difference, we look at a study on the Hijras of India.
11.5.1 Rituals and Sex Role Display
Rituals have always been important social markers of gender. There has been much anthropological analysis of the ways in which the rites of passage or life cycle rites play an important part in many non-Western cultures in

Gender and Performance social identification of sex and gender. Rites such as marriage and initiation use symbols and practices to stress the change in social status for individuals. The symbols often focus on the body, especially genitalia, in an attempt to highlight sexual relationships. Morris notes that in many cultures, for instance, virginity is made visible through its destruction--both symbolic and real. And the ambiguity surrounding the rites is often meant to fulfil the dual task of pointing out not only the difference between men and women, but between men as husbands and women as wives. Below we look at the analysis of traditional initiation rites prevalent in the Bengali community to see how virginity and purity are notions employed symbolically to identify a young girl as a woman at the time of her menstruation. In traditional Bengali kinship, the woman belongs to her husband's clan and family after marriage. This change in membership is important because she will bear her husband's children in future--children belonging to her husband's clan. It is for this reason that on attaining puberty the initiation ritual marks her transition to the status of a woman who is ready to be a wife and mother. In traditional Bengali culture women are also associated with ideas of auspiciousness (sumangali) and inauspiciousness (amangali). On attaining puberty, the girl stops being auspicious for her father's family-- and becomes auspicious for the family that will accept her as their daughter- in-law. All these aspects, the change in status especially is reflected in the ritual--as are the references (in the ritual) to the impending sexual union that will seal the girl's fate as wife and mother. Before puberty, a polluting state amongst most upper-caste Hindus in India, the girl is auspicious for her family and is worshipped as a goddess (the Gouri Puja is an example). Ostor and Fruzzetti (1984) look at the initiation ritual as an example of how the women's domain was ritualised and hierarchically placed in an inferior position --away from the public domain of men and power. In the Bengali menstruation rites the primary objects used in the ritual are the stone pestle and mortar (nora/sil) which women use in the kitchen to grind spices. The nora or pestle symbolises the penis (linga), while the sil or mortar symbolises the vagina or yoni. The two are together and can never be separated. The pure, virgin in the form of the goddess is the mortar, but with menstruation she must take the nora as an inseparable part of her. Interestingly, the pestle symbolises both the child and its father. Similarly the mortar is a symbol of the virgin, mother and wife--the latter two in relation to the pestle. These two objects, along with others appear through other rites specifically related to women, called stri acars. Even at the time of marriage they are essential to show the transition in status from an ambiguous, androgynous being to one who is now established in her role as woman and wife. The repetitive aspect of the rituals, according to Morris, is important in understanding gender performativity. In the above rite, not only the stress

on the use of the symbols, but their meaning as well is emphasized over Stage and Theatre many other rituals to stress on the importance of the purity of the bride before marriage. Interestingly, the virgin must be married off once she undergoes puberty. Earlier, in these communities where child child marriage was practiced, child brides would live in their parental home till their menstruation after which they would be formally transferred to their husbands' home for the consummation rite--establishing her firmly in her in-laws family and as a woman with procreative powers. Yet, in many rites in North India there are provisions to subvert the institutionalized mechanisms within which the ritual operates. These occasions become the source of rebellion against established cultural norms regarding gender and gender practices. Raheja and Gold (1994) have looked at women's rites during the marriage ceremony in North India to show how women use songs and dance to jokingly get the message across to mothers- in-law and other members of the patriarchy that their suppression of the former's desires are not forgotten, or will be taken lightly. The songs are laments by women against their husband's family, and even their fathers and brothers for having forgotten them after giving them away in marriage. These songs enabled women to use the rituals, to vent, and air their grievances against and unjust social and familial structure where patriarchy treats them as inferior. However some of these rites are clearly part of the ritual structure and may serve as only an avenue of protest without really impacting the nature of hierarchical relations already present. Yet, the festival of Tij which is traditionally celebrated by women for the welfare of their husbands has been analysed as a subversive movement amongst women, in the garb of tradition (Skinner, Holland and Adhikari, 1994). By looking at various types of Tij songs the authors trace their importance in women's lives as a medium through which they give voice to their grievances. So, for instance the dukha (sad) songs primarily deal with themes of marital unhappiness. The struggles that a young wife has to go through vis-a-vis her husband, mother-in-law, parents and society as a whole. The songs are often written and composed by the women themselves and form a part of their ritualised protest against the unfair treatment women are subjected to in society. The authors' analysis clearly places the Tij songs as subversive rather than a ritual overturning of otherwise dominant structures.
11.5.2 Ambiguity in Gender And Performance
In many cultures the idea of a third sex, not male or female, is neither seen as an aberration nor as something to be celebrated. The three sexes often live within the same social structure without necessarily threatening the structure. Hijras in India form a particularly interesting field of study. They are marginalized, and yet a necessary part of Indian culture. Serena Nanda

Gender and Performance (1990) undertakes a detailed account of the Hijra community to understand who they are and what place they occupy in mainstream Indian society. Nanda contests that simply defining Hijras as eunuchs would be incorrect. They have many definitions attached to the multiple ways in which they are perceived in society. Most of these definitions are either in opposition or in disjunction with each other. So while even though in India, Hijras are identified in their traditional role of performers--in reality many of them rarely fulfil their traditional roles and have been reduced to the status of prostitutes or sex workers. However, the understanding of Hijras as neither man nor woman can primarily be seen in the following ways. As hermaphrodites the Hijras are found in very few numbers; as genetically belonging to the male gender, but who prefer to be women; and as emasculated or those who have gone through the castration ceremony from being men to Hijras. The other understanding of who or what of Hijra is emerges from their rejection or renunciation of male sexuality in favour sexual relations with other men. Through the castration ceremony or even without it, most Hijras see themselves as impotent or unable to be men, both in the sexual and the social sense of being a man. Again as 'incomplete' men they are seen as lacking the appropriate genitals--and wishing to be like women. In this sense they are defined as in-between, or both men and women. Nanda notes that the desire to be like a woman is seen to be predominant amongst the Hijras, as seen in their clothings, gait, behavior and mannerisms. Even their names are feminine. Incidentally, many Hijras try to get themselves registered as women in the national population census in India. Yet in trying to be women, Hijras also believe that they are not like 'real' women. For real women do not behave in public as they do (loud, solicitious of male attention, often threatening to expose genitalia in public if not given alms, often threaten with curses, but also bestowing blessings), Hijras do not menstruate and do not have the ability to bear children. This is an important marker of why Hijras think they are not really women. Their public performances and gestures are both a sign of their lack of being a woman, and a man. However the lack of a male organ bestows on the Hijras special powers (Hindu mythology testifies to the same). Nanda describes this as creative asceticism wherein the castrated phallus is also the source of tapasya or meditation. Thus, a negative cultural feature of being without the male organ is turned into a source of positive energy. This energy is seen to be important especially during many Hindu life-cycle rites, where the Hijras blessings are actively sought. Especially after childbirth Hijras are known to provide blessings to the child. Their curse is regarded as equally strong as per cultural notions --and most people invoke their blessings rather than incur their wrath.

The emasculation ceremony is seen as a big sacrifice for those who are not Stage and Theatre born hermaphrodites but do not see themselves as male. The Hijras invoke the blessing of the Goddess Bahuchara to help smoothen the process of castration. In this way a Hijra enters the order and becomes the chela of a guru within the community. The Hijra community has an intricate set of caste relations governed by the guru-chela (teacher-student) relationship. The Jamat is the larger body amongst the Hijras headed by a few influential gurus. The Jamat as an umbrella organization includes in it other smaller groups, each headed by a particular guru. The gurus train, house and feed the chela in return for monetary compensation from them. The Hijras, as a community, are symbolic of how cultures assimilate groups with different identities. Even though marginalised, the Hijras draw from their marginal status to show how idea, regarding sex and gender are variable. Through their performance during key life-cycle rites the Hijras are able to show that those very rituals that reinforce social identities of men and women are open to interpretation. 11.6 LET US SUM UP
In this unit we embarked upon the study of sex and gender and their relationship to performativity. Along the way we learnt that it is very difficult to precisely define sex and gender especially when the two often intermingle and create identities that may be different from established ideas. Thus we learnt that: * gender is subject to negotiations in the way it is represented and performed in particular contexts and relationships; * gender and sex displays are often manipulated against established social codes; * while certain practices magnify sex and gender differences, others help hide them; and * different cultures have different understandings of sex and gender.

11.0 INTRODUCTION
There have been many changes in how people get their news and information today. With the rise of digital media, social media platforms, online news websites, and interactive news apps, news delivery is as innovative as it is speedy and exciting. New media has altered our very perception of the world. New media is not just about new devices but also about the combination of different technologies, and their content coming together. When media mixes text, sound, pictures, and allows interaction, it is called new media. This type of media is affordable and popular, so almost every media organisation has an online presence now. People want news quickly and they want it fresh, and new media is best at providing updates even as events are unfolding. In this unit, we will look at the new digital environment where digital public relations (PR) grew and became important. We will also discuss some popular digital PR practices and explore more opportunities created by new media.
11.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES

After completion of this unit, you will be able to: * Get an overview of the new media industry in India; * Understand various trends and practices existing within digital PR with the use of new media; and * Explore new possibilities in digital PR due to the advancements in new media.
11.2 AN OVERVIEW OF NEW MEDIA IN INDIA
This section provides an overview of how new media developed in India, from its beginnings to how things stand today. It highlights the key phases of its emergence and expansion, along with the significance of internet growth in the country.
11.2.1 Emergence of New Media
India's tryst with the internet started in 1987 with the launch of ERNET (Educational and Research Network), developed through cooperation between India's Department of Electronics and the UNDP. Initially, this network linked science and technology institutions, universities, and research organisations across India, primarily serving the needs of government agencies. Early uses of the internet included administrative planning, satellite data retrieval, and railway ticketing and scheduling through specialised networks like NICNET, Indonet, and Railnet.
11.2.2 Expansion of New Media
The internet began to be used commercially in India around 1995 when Videsh Sanchar Nigam Limited (VSNL) introduced the Gateway Internet Access Service (GIAS) with a pay-per-use model. This shift allowed various media outlets, organisations, and government bodies to develop websites, marking the start of widespread online presence. The development of computer technology was also crucial. Although India's first computer was installed in 1955, rapid expansion in the sector in the 1980s and 1990s culminated in the installation and use of over five million computers by 2000.
Importance of Internet Growth
As internet access expanded, so did the demand for high-quality, sophisticated media content. Today's users are knowledgeable and expect the media to fulfill their preferences for speed and interaction. This rising demand accelerated the growth of new media, which depended heavily on the internet's continued expansion in India. The rapid development of new media today reflects increasing digital literacy and technological demands of Indian audiences. Let us see the figure below to understand some key statistics pertaining to media use in India. Source: (Indian Readership Survey Q2 2019, 2019)

As seen in the above figure, the growth of consumption of the internet is much more than any other segment. This enables the internet to be used as the most viable medium of content consumption for audiences. The growth of new media depends upon two factors - the internet and smartphones. The consumer base of the smartphone is also rising at a high pace in India. Source: (Indian Readership Survey Q1 2019, 2019) With 142.3 million smart phones till 2018, the access to content online for consumers has been easy. Moreover, cheap data plans and deep internet penetration further impact this trend. 50% people in rural India are active internet users, while every second person in urban India consumes the internet proactively. Source: (Indian Readership Survey Q1 2019, 2019) Source: (India's Digital Future: Mass of Niches, 2019) Thus, it is no surprise that people owning smartphones and using internet data plans are exploring online content for personal and professional use - from news and entertainment to sharing files and conducting online meetings. 11.2.3 Importance of New Media in Today's India
People today do not just read text online; they also watch videos and listen to audio. Mobile phones are designed to provide good video quality, and with more phones in India, many people are watching videos online. The number of online video viewers in India was about 225 million in 2018 and was expected to reach 550 million by 2023. India is becoming one of the top 10 countries for Over-The-Top (OTT) video services, and the market was expected to reach about 5 billion US dollars in 2023. These expectations have since been surpassed. This growth has been possible due to better and more affordable internet data plans, cheaper smartphones, and creative video content available online. Source: (India's Digital Future: Mass of Niches, 2019)

In the digital media domain, revenue is earned in two ways: through advertising and through subscriptions. Currently, about 90% of digital media revenue comes from advertisements, but the subscription revenue model is growing due to the proliferation of paid video streaming services. The digital revenue projection for FY20 - FY24 is as shown below: Source: (India's Digital Future: Mass of Niches, 2019) The Indian OTT video market was expected to grow fast, from about Rs. 4,464 crore in 2018 to Rs. 11,976 crore in 2023. Subscription video-on-demand services too were expected to grow significantly, from Rs. 3,756 crore in 2018 to Rs. 10,708 crore in 2023. India's large population means its OTT market could become the eighth largest in the world, overtaking countries like South Korea. Experts have different views on this growth: some think it could threaten traditional TV, while others believe it offers opportunities for digital content to grow because more people are using digital media. Many believe that the quality of content will decide which digital platform succeeds. Among the types of content, sports are expected to be very popular. Content will also be more personalised, based on people's age, culture, economic status, and preferences. These changes happen fast due to new technology, making the media market very dynamic. 11.3 ROLE OF NEW MEDIA IN DIGITAL PR
Digital media's rapid growth in India has also allowed digital public relations (PR) to become stronger and more effective. Because it allows one to seamlessly tie together different types of content such as text, audio, and videos on the same platform, people can respond and comment quickly, making it interactive and more engaging. This makes it ideal for its role in PR.

Moreover, unlike traditional media like TV and newspapers, new media does not require the sender and receiver to be present at the same time. You can watch or read content from anywhere in the world at any time. For example, K-pop and Korean dramas are very popular in distant parts of India, and in fact the world, because new media allows easy access no matter where you live. This power of new media to quickly reach millions of people is very useful for public relations. PR needs to reach many people fast to build a good image, fix misunderstandings, or handle crises for organisations. New media serves as a powerful tool for digital PR because of its reach and speed.
11.3.1 Understanding Digital PR
Public Relations (PR) helps organisations build and protect their image, improve their reputation, and manage any problems or crises. It also ensures smooth communication between the management, employees, and other important people connected to the organisation like shareholders and government bodies. A well-known definition says PR is a planned way to influence public opinion by communicating clearly and fairly with all people whose support is necessary for the organisation to succeed (Cutlip, Center, & Broom, 1994). PR not only protects an organisation's image but also defends it from legal, political, economic, or social challenges by using communication effectively. With new technology changing how people get information, PR has also changed. The traditional ways of PR are now combined with new media tools like websites, blogs, social media, and smartphones. This updated form is called digital PR. Through digital PR, companies plan how to interact with their audience to show they are trustworthy and credible. All organisations--big and small, government or private--use digital PR. They maintain websites where they update their activities, achievements, and contact details. Digital PR needs people with creative and technical skills who can work fast and produce good results at lower cost.
11.3.2 Ecosystem of Digital PR
In the past, public relations (PR) mainly depended on traditional media like newspapers, TV, and radio, and often used celebrities to reach out to people. PR communication tools included press releases, press conferences, events, flyers, and newsletters, all mostly related to these media channels. This was called a mediated ecosystem because mass media was the main way to reach large audiences. The media acted like a "magic multiplier," helping messages reach many people. However, the digital revolution changed everything. Digital media is both collective (reaches many people) and personal (can speak directly to individuals). It allows customised communication but also creates a lot of information which can be overwhelming. The relationship between PR and media became complicated because both had to adjust quickly to new ways of communication without much preparation. People's behavior and how they consume information changed very fast. Now, the ecosystem includes both traditional media and digital presence like websites and social media pages. Organisations must keep these digital platforms updated with positive information to create a good image. This needs fast work, creativity, and expert professionals. Digital PR is effective in today's competitive business world because it can do all PR tasks more efficiently with just a click or swipe. Digital PR is growing in India and depends on a digital, internet-based ecosystem.
11.3.3 Reasons for Adopting Digital PR

It made sense for organisations to switch to digital PR because people spend a lot of time engaging with content online , which allows companies to reach a huge number of people in seconds. Yet, if we were to identify two big shifts that made digital PR possible, they would be as follows: * Media Shift: The digital revolution changed the media industry completely. Many traditional media workers weren't sure if they should stay with old media or move to digital. Suddenly, everyone could be a publisher on social media and there was no strict checking of information. New digital media platforms became popular because they were cheaper and reached more people faster. Some of these platforms made enough profit to survive and grow, causing a big shift toward digital media. * Social Shift: The revolution also gave birth to social media, where millions build their digital identities by regularly posting and interacting. Digital PR took advantage of this to influence people through social platforms. Online habits changed, not only how people get information but also how they shop and make decisions. People started using electronic communication like emails and social media instead of letters. Because of this, PR had to adapt and move to digital PR.
11.3.4 Importance of New Media in Digital PR
Digital Public Relations (PR) depends heavily on new media, which has changed and improved PR over time. We can think of PR evolving from version 1.0 to 4.0 (Arief, 2019). In the 1.0 era, PR mostly used print media like newspapers because that was the main way to communicate with many people at once. When Web 2.0 started, media became more interactive, marking the beginning of digital and online media. Then social media was invented, creating even more possibilities for PR. This was called the 3.0 era of PR. Social media got a lot of attention because it's easy to track results and measure impact. Now, we are in the 4.0 era, where big data and artificial intelligence (AI) are important. Many social media platforms are run by both people and automated bots, so PR now has to compete with both. PR in the future will be more demanding and will need advanced new media skills. Media has not only moved in a linear way, from traditional to digital, it has also evolved in many other ways at the same time. PR teams must understand and use these new tools well to build and protect their organisation's reputation. For an organisation interested in deployed digital PR, new media offers the following benefits: * It reaches out to, and sometimes even creates, new audiences * It creates new communication channels, or reinvents old ones. * It produces exciting content that connects with the audience, and * It crafts new and creative ways of delivering content To this end, it uses tools like Search Engine Optimization (SEO) and social media analytics to feel the public pulse and reach people directly and personally. PR, like so many functions of the media, has been reinvented, with the arrival of new media. Check Your Progress: 2 Note: 1) Use the space below for your answers.

11.4 POTENTIAL OF NEW MEDIA IN DIGITAL PR
As we have discussed in the previous section on the importance of new media in digital PR, its potential should also be explored to see how it is shaping public relations and where it is headed. This is why this segment of the unit is divided into three important sections dealing with different components of digital PR. Let us now discuss them in detail:
11.4.1 Digital Content Creation
The way content is made, shared, and used has changed a lot with new media. People today start their day by checking WhatsApp, Facebook, Instagram, and other platforms, before moving on to newspapers, radio, or emails. There is so much content available that it can be overwhelming. The saying "content is king" is as valid in digital PR as in any other media form and function. Thanks to digital media, anyone can create and share stories easily without gates controlled by a few big media companies. A single story can be turned into many forms, like a news article and social media posts, reaching different audiences in different ways. PR professionals need to be skilled in many areas and work well with strategy, content design, and creative work. Because there is so much information available, PR content must stand out by being creative, clear, and relevant to the main story. Digital content must also be flexible enough to work on new platforms, and use technologies like artificial intelligence, augmented reality, or virtual reality.
11.4.2 Digital Marketing
Digital marketing has changed how companies promote themselves online. Terms like e-commerce, digital advertising, and digital analytics are common now. Perhaps someday soon, "advertising" may come to mean mostly digital advertising. Digital PR uses digital marketing to create successful campaigns. Some important digital marketing tools used in PR include: * Search Engine Optimization (SEO): This helps brands show up first in internet searches by using keywords and relevant content. A press release, for example, can be optimised with keywords and links to increase visibility. * Digital Services and PR Campaigns: Digital marketing tools like blogging, social media posts, press releases, and email marketing are combined in campaigns. For instance, a consumer might

see a company's ad on Facebook with a link leading to the company's website for more information. This integration makes PR campaigns effective and reaches people directly.
11.4.3 'New Media' Relations
With the rise of new media, the way public relations (PR) connects with media has changed a lot. PR professionals must understand how the new media world works to build good relationships with media people. Today's journalists are very different from before. They are now 'byte reporters' who quickly share short news updates, and they do many jobs at once. They face pressure to be fast because of social media, breaking news, TV ratings (TRPs), and the need to collect news quickly. In legacy media, journalists had deadlines and time to research, but in digital media, everything happens instantly. Journalists today compete with machines and have limited resources. Moreover, journalists are also seen as social media influencers or brand promoters for their organisations, so they usually cannot share opinions different from their company's view. They must create many multimedia stories every day, which is very stressful. Because of this pressure, PR people cannot expect journalists to always have time to listen. The friendly informal relationship between PR and journalists is rare now. Also, there are many other new media players like bloggers, young influencers, and citizen journalists who have their own style and rules and are hard to manage. PR professionals have the challenge to maintain good relationships with all these different media types in today's changing environment.
11.5 VISIBLE TRENDS IN DIGITAL PR
In the backdrop of trends and potential of new media and the emergence of digital PR, there are some trends visible in digital PR as well, which are shaping the way digital public relations (PR) works today: * Media Bubble: Traditionally, PR and media had a close relationship. But now, both have become much more diverse and complex. PR professionals have to work with many different types of media at the same time, sharing similar messages. Since some media channels are not very effective, PR experts need good judgment to choose the right ones carefully. Using all media channels without focus can create too much noise and reduce the impact. * Social Media: Social media is the biggest trend in digital PR. It changed communication from one-way to interactive and engaging. Platforms like Facebook and Twitter became places to build communities and talk directly with customers. Although social media has some problems like privacy and fake news, it allows companies to understand what consumers want better than any other media. It has become essential for PR and marketing but also makes companies depend on a few big social media giants. * Influencer Marketing: Influencing people is the heart of PR. Nowadays, social media has made it possible for many people, even young individuals, to influence large audiences. Influencers help build trust because when someone else supports a company's product or idea, it seems more real and believable. Influencer marketing has become very important not only in digital PR but in many other fields as well. * Emerging Technology: Technology is deeply changing digital PR. Instead of paper press releases, emails and social media posts are common. Techniques like search engine optimization (SEO) help brands get noticed online. New technologies like artificial intelligence (AI), bots, augmented reality (AR), and virtual reality (VR) are also starting to be used in PR, and who knows what future technologies will bring.

11.6 USE OF NEW MEDIA IN DIGITAL PR: SOME
EXAMPLES
New media brings many new formats for digital public relations (PR). Some of these are: * Short and vertical videos: These are quick videos often with text captions, popularised by news outlets like AJ+ and NowThis. * Horizontal stories: Swipeable cards like stories on Snapchat and similar apps. * Longform scrollytelling: Longer stories presented in a way that scrolls smoothly, first used by The New York Times with their "Snowfall" story. * Structured news: News presented in small, reusable cards, like on Vox.com. * Live blogs: Real-time updates used during big events. * Listicles: Articles in the form of lists, popularised by Buzzfeed. * Newsletters and briefings: Regular emails summarising news or updates, very trendy now. * Timelines: Visual displays showing events over time. * Bots and chat: Automated chat apps that answer questions or deliver news, like Qz's chat app. * Personalised content: Content tailored to users' interests, often helping choose what stories to see. * Data visualisation: Using graphs and interactive charts to explain information clearly. * Virtual Reality (VR) and Augmented Reality (AR): Immersive formats pioneered by big publishers like The New York Times. In this unit, we learned about the rise and growth of new media in India and how it is changing the media and communication landscape, reaching millions of people through many digital platforms. We explored digital public relations (PR) and saw how new media is a key force behind its development. 11.8 GLOSSARY
New Media: A type of media which is new in technology and provides better access as well as content at our own convenience. It is free from time and space constraints and mostly convergent in nature. Digital Media: Everything which is not analogue is digital. This media is also dependent upon internet-based technology because the digital system complements the online system. ICT: Information and Communication Technology is a new emerging technology which allows us to interact, react and get any content anywhere such as Web 2.0, Web 3.0, smart phones etc. Digital PR: The public relations practices dependent upon digital and new media is called digital PR.

UNIT 12: PRODUCTION MANAGEMENT
Structure

12.1 Learning Outcomes
12.2 Understanding Production Management
12.3 Production Management at Pre-production Stage
12.4 Production Management at Production Stage
12.5 Production Management at Post-production Stage

12.0 INTRODUCTION
The function of Production Management in TV or film production is very similar to planning and executing a wedding. A Production Manager is the first to enter the set to check if everything is ready before shoot and is the last to leave the set to make arrangements for the next day. S/he oversees all the processes of television production - pre-production, production and post-production and ensures that the TV programme is delivered to the broadcasters on time and within the specified budget. For production management, co- ordination is the key word. While the creative art of producing TV programmes is appreciated by one and all, the logistical skills of a Production Manager often go unacknowledged. In this unit, we'll discuss the role and functions of Production Management in audio-visual content creation.
12.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After completing this unit, you will be able to: * understand what is production management; * describe the role and responsibilities of production management team at all the three stages - pre-production, production and post-production; and * explain the professional and personal skills required for production management.

12.2 UNDERSTANDING PRODUCTION MANAGEMENT
Production management, whether in television or in films, is the skilful craft of coordinating with various departments in a production unit to ensure that a TV programme is made within budgetary constraints, utilizing optimum resources and delivered on time. The size of a production management team generally depends upon the size of the production house and budget of the programme. Big production houses can have more people, while small budget productions may have to work with few. A production management team in a production unit generally consists of a production manager who is assisted by few production coordinators and production assistants. Unlike the creative processes of script-writing or direction that have clearly defined boundaries, the role of a production manager extends to supervising every aspect of production process from pre-production to post-production stage. Scouting talents, finalizing shoot locations, shortlisting production crew, seeking permissions to shoot in specific locations, managing budgets, overseeing the supply and proper functioning of technical equipment, arranging props required for the shoot, supervising the costume department, legalities and compliance, maintaining proper documentation, arranging transport and accommodation for artistes (performers) and crew, confirming safety of every individual on the set and providing medical aid, following timelines of production in terms of shoot, edit and timely delivery of episodes, ensuring availability of food and beverages to keep the unit going and also settling personal conflicts between the crew members of the show are a handful of tasks involved in production management. In other words, a production manager is a taskmaster who must possess an amalgamation of professional skills to conduct his/her day-to-day production duties and personal qualities to tactfully deal with individuals. It requires extraordinary organizational skills to deal with each and every department involved in the production process and get them to do their work on time. The production manager is a supervisor of sorts who ensures that the show must go on irrespective of any hindrance. The duties of a production manager also change depending on the genre that is being produced. In this unit, you will learn about the responsibilities of production management in both fiction and non-fiction genres. Let us now discuss the role of production management at different stages of production process.
12.3 PRODUCTION MANAGEMENT AT PRE-PRODUCTION STAGE

The major tasks in television or film production are accomplished even before the actual shooting process begins. A good pre-production preparation leads to a smooth and timely shoot. Although the stage of concept development and research are primarily managed by the creative team but the views of production manager must be considered and an outline of the programme must be provided to him to understand the execution of creative ideas. At this stage the production manager must ask questions like - Is the programme logistically doable within the specified time? Do we have enough resources to complete a production task like this? Can this production be completed within the specified budget? If the answer to all these questions is yes, the production commences to the pre-production stage. Let us now look at some important areas to be considered at the pre-production stage.
1. Budgeting : Budgeting is the most important aspect of production management. After an
overall allocation of the production budget, the Production Manager needs to carefully breakdown the budgetary components under different heads and allocate budget accordingly. The main areas that require attention are expenditure on technical equipment, remuneration of the cast and crew, location rent, travel costs, cost of edit suites, costumes, travel, accommodation etc. amongst multiple things. Every penny that is utilized must be accounted for by the production management team. There are moments when the creative team wants to add an extra day of shoot or additional equipment for better results but the production manager must allow these additions keeping check on the budgetary constraints. Addition of an equipment, increasing a shoot day or adding manpower all result in extra money that may or may not be accommodated in the budget. This is also a reason why ensuring timely start and finish of shoot is a primary task of production management as any spill overs in time will lead to extra costs. Also, sometimes there maybe unexpected constraints beyond the control of production team, for instance, bad weather or an actor falling ill that may result in the cancellation of a shoot. In such instances, the production manager must keep some amount of funds as contingency. If the cost under one head has shot up, the Production Manager can cut down cost from another head to avoid exceeding the budget. S/he must also provide for some petty cash on location for small expenses that may not be paid via online transfer or bank cheques. Maintaining excel-sheets of expenses and documenting all the bills is a key responsibility of production management. To monitor expenses and remain within the budget and deliver quality and timely production is essential in good production management.

2. Scheduling: Scheduling is another crucial factor in production management that enables a
production manager to smoothly execute shoots. It involves the detailing of shoot location; call times of cast and crew members and the total number of shoot days. Budget also influences scheduling as lesser the budget more work needs to be done in lesser number of days and vice-versa. But the shoot schedules must be prepared on realistic and achievable grounds in consultation with the creative team. A typical shoot day involves ten to twelve hours of shoot time. While preparing the schedule the production manager should not change too many shoot locations in a single day as travelling between locations and setting up light, camera also wastes a lot of time. Most shoot schedules are prepared keeping in mind the availability of an artiste on a given day. If you are shooting fiction, always keep a copy of script with you to prepare the schedule. Many a times, you may shoot scene-wise where only selected artistes/artists/performers are required on a given day. Try to schedule all their scenes on that particular day and do not schedule other artists on that day. An important thing to remember while preparing shoot schedules is to give a break day in between to the artists and crew that may also be utilized to make arrangements for future production needs. A continuous shooting schedule results in an exhausted and uncreative crew that directly impacts the quality of production.
3. Recce: Recce, a term commonly used in TV and film production deals with scouting for an
appropriate shoot location and is an essential pre-production task. There are many aspects that need to be accounted for before finalizing a shoot location. First, the location should be feasible in terms of daily commute and must be available for the duration of the shoot. Second, it must be visually in synchronization with the story and the plot of production. The production manager must also look at the space keeping in mind how the set will be built in that space, how the cameras and lights will be set up and what are the acoustic conditions of the place for recording sound. S/he must also check the supply of electricity, water, air conditioning in the location. S/he should also seek prior permission to shoot in that location for the specified dates. The production manager also needs to take into account the space available in the location where s/he can set up vanity vans, food stalls, press meets with journalists, parking vehicles etc. While shooting reality shows the sets are mounted for a period of three months to six months

but for shooting soap operas, the set is mounted for as long as eight to ten years. So, the production manager should confirm in advance the lease duration of the location. To check if the space has proper mobile network and internet connection is also a primary requisite in today's times since half the work is done via emails.
4. Contracts & Hiring: Although contracts and hiring is not an area that the production
manager directly deals with, s/he should be aware of the contractual agreements that take place between the crew and the company. To begin with, s/he may provide sanctions for the number of production crew and their remuneration depending on the budget allocation. The contracts often mention the working hours of artists and their specifications in terms of dos and don'ts during the shoot. For instance, if there is an artiste who refuses to shoot beyond eight hours while his contract may mention ten hours, the production manager can revisit the contract and request the artiste/artist/performer to shoot for extra hours. Or, if an artist's contract mentions eight hours and he has already shot for ten hours, the Production Manager may have to allocate the budget for extra hours as per the contract. For every production, crew or artistes that shoot beyond their contractual terms, in most cases, need to be financially compensated and the production management must take these issues into account. Also, if any artiste's contract clauses have special requests like not working on a Sunday, no nudity, special food requests then those must also be taken into consideration by the production manager.
5. Health & Safety Issues: Health and safety issues are also a major concern in television
production. All crew members work under tremendous work pressure in an environment that can be dangerous. The light man, for instance, literally walks through a catwalk, a raised platform several feet above the ground, to switch on a specific light for a shot. There are open wires all over the set that bear electric current. Heavy cameras, lights, props, trolleys and cranes are all mounted inside the set that if dropped down may cause severe injuries. In dance reality shows, participants often get injured while practicing. The crew members also work continuously day and night resulting in a lack of sleep that may cause other health effects like high blood pressure, insomnia etc. For all such reasons, risk assessment and the subsequent health and safety management is a prerequisite in production to ensure the safety and well- being of every individual on the shooting location. Large production companies have policies in place to comply with health and safety of the employees. Having a first aid box, a nurse and a doctor on the set could be the basic steps taken in the direction of health and safety.

6. Other Responsibilities: On the creative front, all audio-visual equipment like cameras,
lights, audio consoles etc. required for production must be booked in advance. The Production Manager must make sure that the script for the shoot is ready at least two days in advance and is provided in soft copies to all the stakeholders. The prop requirements as suggested by the creative team are also handed over to the Production Manager who ensures their availability on the shoot day. The requirement of props can range from day to day objects like umbrellas, flowers, table etc. to more obsolete objects like vintage clocks, gramophones, bullock carts etc. In case of a reality show, the Production Manager should also facilitate technical rehearsals and dress rehearsals a day before the shoot. Since reality shows are largely shot in a continuous mode unlike shot-by-shot mode used in fiction, the chances of technical glitches should be kept at minimum. Therefore, a technical rehearsal involves the technicians rehearsing along with the artistes to track exact camera movements, sound and light requirements suggested by the creative team. Production management team must also ensure that all the costumes for the artistes are ironed and ready for the shoot day. Check Your Progress: 1 Note: Use the space given below for your answers. Compare you answers with those given at the end of the unit.
1. Define the term "Production Management".

12.4 PRODUCTION MANAGEMENT AT PRODUCTION STAGE
The quote "well begun is half done" is apt to discuss television production management. If the pre-production of a TV programme is done in great detail, the burden of the production process is halved. The day of production or the shoot is full of chaos wherein both the crew and cast are under tremendous pressure to finish the shoot as per the schedule. The production managers, as discussed earlier are the first to enter the sets and ensure that everything is set before the artistes/artists and other crew members come. The primary task of the Production Manager and his team on the day of the shoot is to confirm that all the cast

and crew reach the set on time and the shoot begins and finishes as per the schedule. We shall now discuss some aspects that must be addressed during the production stage.
1. Transport and Other Activities: First and foremost, the production managers ensure the
availability of fully functional vanity vans for all artistes and senior crew members. They also make sure that transport facilities are provided for senior crew members and artistes. The production assistants who work under the production manager often have to make wake-up calls to artistes and follow up with everyone to ensure that they reach the set on time. Amongst other tasks, the production managers also make arrangements for security, especially in the case of a big celebrity coming for a shoot or if there is a prior warning of an untowardly incident that may occur. At this stage coordination with every department - technical team, graphics, sound engineers, costumes, hair and make-up is essential to make sure that everything runs smoothly. To make sure that the technical equipment hired from a third-party are delivered on time, sound-checks and video checks are conducted, appropriate setting of studio lights etc. are some initial duties of the production management team.
2. Food & Beverages: Providing food and beverages is a special task at this point. Producing
a show requires as much of physical labour as creative. Shooting for long hours requires that the cast and crew are well fed from time to time. Production managers should make available healthy and hygienic breakfast, lunch and dinner for all crew members. An ample supply of tea and coffee is also a prerequisite. In fact, the shoot schedule should allocate specific breaks for lunch and dinner so that the crew gets its meal on time. A healthy and sumptuous meal is a must for the crew members to work with greater efficiency. If the artistes or senior crew members give any special request in advance related to preferred food choices, the production managers make sure that it is made available.
3. Managing On-set Press Meets: At times, the journalists also arrive at the sets to interview
celebrities or artistes involved in the production. From the viewpoint of promotions, these are essential for the success of the show. The production managers make sure that the artistes are made available to the press and that there is a separate space allocated to the journalists where they can conduct their interviews. Separate media kits and snacks are also made available for the journalists. But these media interactions, at any point, must not hinder the primary task of shooting the programme. Additionally, the production managers also make provision for a

still photographer who may have to click pictures for social media platforms and news organizations. In case of fiction shoots, stills also help to track continuity in between shots.
4. Managing Junior Artistes/Artists/Performers: Junior artistes often referred to as
'extras' are an important component of TV production. In Reality TV shows, the huge gathering of audiences inside a set comprises of the junior artistes. In fiction shows, they constitute the insignificant crowd in public spaces. The production manager ensures that a desired number of junior artistes, who mostly belong to a union or association, are present on the day of the shoot. S/he also ensures that they are paid their compensation and are also provided with food and beverages from time to time. If there are any disputes between the crew members or any interference by a third party, the production manager has also to settle such disputes so that it does not become an obstacle and consume the already limited shooting time.
5. Other Responsibilities: From the creative perspective, the production manager ensures
that the shoot is being followed as per the script and it is completed on time. In non-fiction shows, if there are anchor links and sponsor related information, which is mostly shot at the end of the shoot, s/he confirms that these are done. In case of the requirement of specific props to be used in the episode, the production manager makes arrangements for them in the pre-production stage. After the completion of the shoot, the production manager makes sure that the recorded footage is transferred to hard disks and is immediately sent to the editors for the commencement of post-production. The pack up of shoot also includes returning the rented equipment back to the vendors, ensuring all cast and crew are provided transport for their return and making all meagre cash payments before the production manager leaves the set.
12.5 PRODUCTION MANAGEMENT AT POST-PRODUCTION STAGE
So far, we have discussed the responsibilities of a production management team during pre- production and production stage. The job of the production manager does not finish after the end of the shoot as s/he has to then follow-up with the post-production department which is an integral part of television production. Unlike film production, television programmes are usually made in extreme time crunch with a constant pressure of daily telecast falling on the

shoulders of producers and broadcasters. The editors of television programmes do not have the luxury of time and have to mostly edit episodes within a day or sometimes even overnight. Timely delivery of the shoot footage at the edit can fasten the process of post- production. The post-production usually consists of arranging the shots sequentially as per the script, dubbing, adding music wherever required, inserting graphics, programme logos etc. and delivering the episode to the broadcaster. In many big production houses, there is usually a separate production manager to oversee post-production. Let us now look at the contributions made by the production management team at the post-production stage.
1. Ensuring Log Sheet Creation: Logging of shots is a vital task of post-production that is
followed as a standard practice across television industries. During the shoot, a junior assistant director is often given the task of creating log sheets, wherein he/she makes a record of shots by entering time codes of beginning and end of shots along with small remarks. This helps the editor to capture only those time codes that are useful and not the entire footage. If the shots are logged properly, the editor will not waste time in searching through the entire footage for a specific shot as it will already be marked. Logging of shots helps to eliminate NG (Not Good) shots and put the rest of the shots sequentially on a timeline.
2. Arrangement for Dubbing: Dubbing is another aspect of post-production that the
production manager has to supervise. In many cases editing and dubbing is done in-house but there are instances when a specialized agency is hired that provides a dubbing studio. In such a scenario, the production manager has to book a dubbing suite in advance and if required, also make requisition for dubbing or voice over artists. Dubbing is mainly done in cases where the on-location sync sound lacks clarity due to external disturbances or if a voice over narration is needed.
3. Coordination with Special Effects & Graphics Teams: Special effects, graphics and
credits are also integral elements of post-production. Though special effects are not very frequently used in TV shows, graphics find an important place and may include the show logo, coming-up windows, name astons, end credit formats etc. and are mostly prepared by the broadcasters. The Production Manager has to ensure that these elements are made available to the edit team on time.
4. Compliance: Compliance is an umbrella term that refers to the duty of the production
management team to make sure that it complies with the law, with broadcast regulations and with agreements related to intellectual property usage. A production manager must ensure

that the programme to be broadcast does not go against the law. Any content that may lead to communal disharmony, indecency or showing a specific cast or religion in an inappropriate light must be avoided. The broadcast related complaints in India are addressed to the Broadcasting Content Complaints Council that ensures that any content that hurts the moral and communal sentiments of the audiences must go off air. The production manager should ensure in advance that no such issue is created by a programme broadcast. The production management team also ensures that no artistes or production crew's labour rights are violated by making them work beyond the regular working hours or by asking them to cover up for extra duties. Licenses or clearances also need to be taken in advance for the usage of any video material like archival footage or film footage. Music logging sheets need to be properly maintained by the post-production team. It is also important to get legal clearances from music companies. The time code at which a music piece is used, the duration for which the music is used and the music company name need to be mentioned clearly in the music log sheet which is then sent to the broadcasters. Most of the broadcasters have tie-ups with some music labels that allow free usage of music to certain extent. In cases where the broadcasters do not have permission to use a specific music label, they need to take permission from the music company and pay royalty to use that piece of music.
5. Paperwork: At the end, the production management team should ensure that the final
episode with all edit changes reaches the broadcasters in advance so that they carry out checks on technical specifications and content monitoring before the episode goes on air. The Production Managers must also do a compilation of all the paperwork and correspondences from the pre-production to the end stage. A coherent compilation of all documents is useful when one wants to use it for future references. Check Your Progress: 2 Note: Use the space given below for your answers. Compare you answers with those given at the end of the unit.
1. Write any three tasks of production management team at the production stage of a
television programme?

12.6 LET US SUM UP
We discussed the role of the production management team in television production, and talked about the functions of production management in all three stages - pre-production, production and post-production. The main responsibility of the production management team is to coordinate with every department and ensure that TV programs are produced within the prescribed budget and deadline.
