13.4 ANIMATION TECHNIQUES
Animation offers a free space for alternatives, for constructing motion by creating a series of hypothetical impressions. An imaginary world, which an animator creates is based on a set criterion of visual systems based on time, distance, value, shape, form, sound, and words in some sort of narrative or non-narrative format. Now we will be discussing types of animation categorized on the basis of techniques, genre and it's use in films for special effects before the use of computer for visual effects. Types of Animation techniques We can broadly categories animation into three different types: * Traditional 2D Animation * Stop Motion * Mechanical Animatronics The traditional method is hand-drawn often called 'Cel' animation, where artists drew and then colour each picture or frame by hand on a sheet of transparent plastic sheet called 'cels'. This enabled the animators to place their character animation frames onto a background and photograph the sequences. The last film Disney released which used only traditional cel animation was Oliver and Company (1988). Since 1989, Disney switched to a colouring system called CAPS (Computer Animation Production System). This computer-based system was developed by Pixar and The Walt Disney Company.

Stop motion (also known as stop action) is an animation technique to make a physically manipulated object appear to move on its own. The object is moved in small increments between individually photographed frames, creating the illusion of movement when the series of frames is played as a continuous sequence. Stop motion animation has a long history in films. It was often used to show objects moving as if by magic. Stop motion animation has several sub-categories based on the technique and material used with one thing in common that the object is manipulated physically frame by frame: * Claymation: Puppets of clay or plasticine on an articulated armature are set-up and photographed. Nick Park is one of the most successful animation director to use this technique. He has won four Academy Awards for his short films. His characters Wallace and Gromit are probably the most famous Claymation characters. * Sand animation: Sand is manipulated using tools or fingers on a backlit surface. This technique was pioneered by Caroline Leaf while she was working at the National Film Board of Canada. Her short film The Street (1976) was nominated for Academy Awards. * Paint-on-glass: This technique utilizes slow-drying oil paints often mixed with glycerine. Some of the finest work created using this technique is by Aleksandr Petrov. He has produced several films using this technique. The old man and the Sea (1999) won Academy Award for Animated Short Film and Grand Prix at the Annecy International Animated Film Festival. * Direct Animation or Scratch on Film: this process involves painting, scratching, pigmenting, etching and pasting on a 16mm or 32mm film. It is called Direct animation too as there's no camera involved. This technique was used extensively by Norman McLaren and Len Lye with a central theme of movement and sound. * Pixilation: This technique involves using a live actor or actors as a stop motion puppet and is often combined animated objects. Norman Mclaren's pixilation film Neighbours (1952) won the Academy award for Best Documentary Short Subject. Jan Svankmajer often uses this technique, his films Food (1992) and Conspirators of Pleasure (1996) are worth mentioning. Mechanical Animatronics: Mechanized puppets with life-like covering were developed as long ago as 1933 for use in museums. Mechanically driven characters and prosthetics have been used in films since 1950's.
Experimental Animation

Experimental animation as a term and genre is hard to categorise due to its heterodoxies of what the form is and has been defined and categorised under several descriptors such as: independent, alternative, avant-garde and artistic. This heterodoxy has become more prominent with the digital revolution. Through the course of history, the term experimental animation has been associated with numerous visual moving image innovations, both in terms of innovative forms and techniques such as painting and scratching directly on celluloid, pixilation, stop- motion, hand-rendered and computer-generated imagery. Experimental animation films usually are categorized under non-industrial productions. Experimental animation is a unique form of art, which is on the same level as other serious arts such as painting and music. The pioneer animators took abstract animation to a level where it received a much-deserved positive response from its audience. Most of whom were artists adapting this new form of art. It was the Dadaists, Surrealists and artists from other modern art movements who adapted the possibilities of cinematography and animation and used it for experimentation and self- expression. The work of these artists proves that 'Experimental animation' is an extension of art. Leopold Survage (a Dadaist) was one of the first artists to theorize abstract animation through his paintings. In 1921, Walter Ruttmann released his short film Lichtspiel Opus 1 in Frankfort and Berlin in Germany; it is considered as the first abstract animation screened for the general audience.
13.5 Technical Advancements in the Field of Graphics & Animation
13.5.1 Graphics: Definition
The term Graphic is derived from a Greek work 'graphikos' which means belonging to drawing. Traditional definition of graphics would be visuals or design on a surface, such as wall, canvas, paper, stone with the purpose to entertain or inform. Although in contemporary scenario especially when mentioned along-with animation and visual effects 'graphics' means visual representation of data as design, typesetting and digital art for entertainment, education and experience. Common examples would be: typography, symbols, maps, images, photographs and a combination of all these to create books, websites, animation, visual-effects and user-interface, a graphic can serve artistic or functional purpose or both. A sub-category of graphics which is most apt for this chapter is Computer Graphics. Computer graphics can be divided into two types: Rastor Graphics: these are made of several pixels; more pixels would mean more resolution and thus can be enlarged easily or used for visual effects. For visual effects, higher bit depth is crucial, also known as colour depth (number of bits used for each colour component of a single pixel) as higher bit-depth gives better results while compositing virtual elements with live action footage.

Vector Graphics: these are based on mathematical expressions and are sharper compared to rastor. Vector are usually smaller in size but more complex vector graphics are large in size. These are used for text, billboards, logos, artwork and commercial printing.
13.5.2 Brief History of CGI/ VFX
When graphics are used as a series of images for animation or visual effects using computer, then they are referred to Computer Graphic Imagery. The first CGI character was created by Pixar studio for the film Young Sherlock Holmes (1985), it was a knight composed of peices from a stained-glass window pane. In 1993 film Jurassic Park, dinosaurs created with CGI were seamlessly integrated into live action scenes, which transformed the movie industry forever. It marked the transition from stop-motion animation effects to digital techniques. In 1995, the first fully computer-generated feature film, Pixar's Toy Story was released and was one of the top grossing feature film of that year. Additional digital animation studios such as Blue-Sky Studios, Omation Studios, Sony Pictures Animation, and many went into 3D production, even The Walt Disney Company began to make a shift from traditional animation to digital animation.
13.5.3 Different Types of VFX
Visual Effects are the various processes by which graphics are created and manipulated outside the context of a live action, often involving integration of live-action footage and computer- generated imagery (CGI) in order to create hyper-realistic environments and life-like characters. four broad categories of Visual Effects: Models: miniature sets and models, animatronics. Matte painting: digital or traditional paintings or photographs which serve as background for compositing virtual elements. Live-action effects: keying actors or models through blue-screening and green-screening. Digital animation: modelling, computer graphics lighting, texturing, rigging, animating, and rendering computer-generated 3D characters, particle effects, digital sets, backgrounds. 13.0 INTRODUCTION
Consumers today are bombarded with messages from different sources, across different media, and on different devices. Brands specially are relentless in this, marketing their products and services to customers through diverse social media platforms. In the process, platforms like Facebook and Instagram have accumulated a wealth of personal information from their users. In fact, one might argue that these platforms might know your best friend's likes and dislikes better than you--that is the level of personalised targeting these platforms enable. By doing so, they provide more options and freedom to the consumers, and in one sense, empower them to make the right choice. Although half of the world's population is present on social media, brands are in a state of constant struggle to seek the consumer's, and the public's, attention. In this Uni, we will learn how brands achieve their commercial goals effectively using social media branding, allowing consumers to get genuine and useful content.

13.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After working on this Unit, you will be able to: * Understand the significant role social media plays in branding today; * Learn how to best use the strength of various social media platforms such as Facebook,
Instagram and Snapchat;
* Understand the best practices and potential pitfalls when branding on social media.
13.2 SOCIAL MEDIA AND ITS IMPORTANCE FOR BRANDS
13.2.1 What is social media?
The notion of social media needs no introduction. This collection of platforms are where we create and share content, interact with each other, and participate in online communities. With half the world's population present on them, it is a space where countless conversations are taking place even as you read this. And so, it is naturally the place where brands go to interact with their online audience. It is also where customers and fans introduce your brand to their friends and followers through their comments, likes, posts, retweets, reels, videos, and more. Thus, a brand can receive rich, unmediated customer insights faster than ever before. These actions initiated by customers gives a brand leverage and adds to its credibility. The goal of any brand is to reach a considerable audience and create awareness about itself. This will attract more traffic and engagement which will help generate more leads. The objective is to bring the customers to your website and reel them in to make a purchase. But there is also a negative side to the potential exposure a brand can get on social media--and that is dealing with 'trolls'. Trolling is when one responds to online content or comments in a purposely disruptive fashion. Controversial (but sometimes even harmless) posts will most likely draw negative attention and get 'trolled'. Brands may also get bashed, or lose followers, when they start using social media for pitching and selling, rather than interacting with fans and followers. Worse still, a brand can sometimes lose its grip on their message, promise, personality, character, or even common sense; then, the backlash would most certainly be brutal. Thus, brands need to understand the dynamics of the social media space, and stay up to date with the popular, and unpopular, trends. This is how they can use social media to their advantage.
13.2.2 How is social media useful for branding?
Social media has challenged brands to explore newer ways of reaching out to their prospects. It is quite different from the traditional approach of placing advertisements on mass media. Unlike traditional media, social media is not linear, and the nature of interactions it facilitates are more divergent. The idea is to compete against multiple brands using social media platforms. Although it is cost-effective and hence more attractive for brands, its volatility and the very real problem of short attention span pose a big challenge. To create customer-connect, you need to build relationships and foster openness, thereby building trust. One cannot buy trust, nor can one buy authenticity. To establish these, one needs genuine interaction and consistent action. Let's look at some ways social media is used for branding: Engagement: Social media allows brands to disseminate engaging content across various platforms. This helps them connect with new customers through targeted marketing, and hence fulfill business goals. This engagement helps in reflecting a brand's personality, thereby building trust and authenticity.

Support: These platforms provide a very important space for customer feedback. It is where they can voice their concerns, report issues, and make requests. Brands, on their part, should see these spaces as providing them the opportunity to improve customer service and support. Attractions: Brands may use social media to attract customers through exclusive offers, deals, contests, and the like. But rather than 'marketing gimmicks', these instances can be used to build lasting relations with customers. Networking: Brands can use social media to encourage the creation and nurturing of communities centred around their product or service, encouraging customers to connect and communicate with each other and with them. Benefits for brands: * Facebook encourages users to engage via comments, likes, and shares from followers, seamlessly integrating text, image, and video posts in a user-friendly design. * Brands can promote their campaigns on the platform, which can go viral very quickly. Brands also connect with other businesses on the platform to foster ties and collaboration within the industry.

13.3.5 WhatsApp
WhatsApp started as a messaging app for personal chats, but it has turned out to be a great hub for branding. Brands use WhatsApp for a direct and quick engagement with their target audience. They answer questions, make sales, provide follow up customer support, and product recommendations. Its commercial version, WhatsApp Business, is used to create dedicated business profiles with information about the product or service, contact information, as well as catalogues and showcases. What started as a place where one could forward memes and share viral videos, is today a great platform for expanding business through branding.

Due to less saturation in this area, podcasts are an excellent tool for branding. They also help to humanise companies through easy going conversations and personal reflections in authentic and long-form content. 13.4 REVIEW AND RATING SITES
Customer feedback on review or rating websites is a testimony to your brand. It greatly impacts buying decisions of potential customers, who like to make informed decisions; in this time and age, reviews and ratings are an important part of their research. For instance, if you want to order a watch online, you will check reviews and ratings given by other customers on rating websites. If that watch has a got a 2/5 rating, you will be dissuaded from buying it. Thus, reviews and ratings are a social proof, giving evidence of users' and customers' experience and satisfaction level with a brand. Popular review and ratings websites include Tripadvisor, Yelp, Amazon, and the like

For example, TripAdvisor is the world's largest travel site that enables travelers to plan a perfect trip. Users get Trip Collective points in exchange for reviews, tips and comments, forum posts, and photos. You can earn badges at every level to showcase travel expertise and be more recognised in the travel community. Brands must learn how to manage their presence on review sites. Some ways of doing so are as follows: * Keep abreast with the review sites related to your business. Learn which sites customers visit before making a purchase decision and claim your presence there. If you're in the travel business, your customers or those who influence them most likely use TripAdvisor (www.tripadvisor.com). * Encourage customers to give their reviews by displaying review site logos in your business and on your web pages making it convenient for customers to share their experiences. Personally reach out to the best customers to share their opinions. * Be mindful that customers give reviews on a regular basis. The spurt of reviews on the site creates doubt about the authenticity of reviews. In case you receive any negative comments or poor ratings, do not get defensive or show displeasure on the site. It is wiser to find out the truth in the complaint or criticism and try to fix it. You can also use your blog, review comment box, Facebook page, X page, etc. to describe how you have addressed the issue and highlight the changes made. People are watching your behavior on social media, so politely handle the disgruntled customer and show care for his comments. Try to negate one negative review or rating by earning several positive reviews and ratings.
13.5 DO's AND DONT'S OF SOCIAL MEDIA BRANDING
Brands use different social media platforms based on their business and the characteristics of the platform.
13.5.1 Do's of Social Media Branding
* Choosing the right platform: Choose the social media platform-specific to your business needs. Though you might want to have your presence on all social media platforms, you need to see whether it caters to your business objective. It is not feasible to manage all social media platforms and do justice to them. Furthermore, familiarise yourself with the guidelines of the platform. * Evaluate your content: Post the right content at the right time. Make efforts to find out your target audience and the time when they are online, depending on this you can decide to post. From time to time, reevaluate your content, find out which parts are helping you maximise your profits, and which parts are not able to pull in the expected crowd. Use social media tools to analyse it. Go through all the content that you have used before and if it is possible repurpose and use it. * Manage tools well: It is extremely important for you to be known by people if you wish to increase your sales. So, you must know how to use search engine optimization (SEO) to your advantage. * Give a personal touch: Engage with your audience at a personal level and build connections. They should get a feeling that they are interacting with humans and not robots. Appreciate your followers for subscribing or following you and incentivise them. Give them rewards or discounts or lucky draw entries and giveaways to join. * Customer is king: You must have customer involvement if you wish to become a popular brand. You must get customers to promote your brand and make them your brand ambassador. You must conduct competitions to get the customers involved in your business and visit your pages on a regular basis.

* People skills: One is bound to encounter all kinds of people on social media platforms, and must learn how to deal with different people differently. Maintain professionalism in your posts, and . Do not give individual opinions which might not sit well with your audience. Learn to face the trolls. Be prepared for the worst and have a plan in place that will allow you to quickly act and save the day. You must try and reinvent yourself from time to time and give your audience something new to experience. If you do all these then rest assured, your company would do well in the social media marketing field.
13.5.2 Don'ts of Social Media Marketing
* Know your boundaries while interacting with your audience. You will see that it is possible for you to connect with your audience in a better way if you keep it professional. * Explore all the features of the social media platform and make sure that you are using everything to your advantage. * Do not repeat the same content on all your different platforms. You must keep the same tone but present the products in a different way. * You must update your account from time to time. Brands need to be careful of their social media acts to avoid any controversy which leads to online vigilantism. Online vigilantism started from the action of doxing, which is the publishing of personal information of a particular subject on the internet (mainly on social media such as Facebook and X), with malicious intent. The main idea of online vigilantism is to publicly shame their target to get a response from the authorities or in the lack of any response from the authorities.
13.6 CHOOSING SOCIAL MEDIA PLATFORM FOR YOUR
BUSINESS
Brands need to know that each social media platform has its own benefits, limitations and the way it interacts with content and the users. Brands need to have a look at the following aspects before deciding on a social media platform for their business. * It is based on the nature of your business whether it is business-to-business (B2B) or Business to consumer (B2C). B2C companies can prefer Facebook and Instagram when they want visual engagement, gaining visibility, or interaction with customers. LinkedIn is better for B2B companies as it helps in reaching out to current and potential clients and helps build personal connections. YouTube can attract an audience irrespective of the nature of the business due to its audio-visual appeal, secondly, it's Google-friendly and adds authenticity. * Research to find out who your target audience are i.e., their demographics. * Research to find out on which platform your target audience will be available. * Master the platform where your target audience is available. * Research your top competitors to find out the social media platforms they are engaged in, the content they are posting there, the frequency of posting the content, and number of users engaging with the content. Based on this research, choose the social media for your brand which can yield the best results. * Keep your website up to date as you need to direct traffic from all social media platforms to your website. * Build a consistent strategy across the platform.

13.7 SUCCESS STORIES OF SOCIAL MEDIA BRANDING
Nowadays, brands are majorly investing in social media marketing. Facebook, X, Instagram, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Snapchat, and YouTube have grabbed a major share of marketing for brands. But with the arrival of an increasing number of social media applications, digital marketers are looking for different ways to broaden their scope of marketing. Brands are also exploring to make their content unique and different. Some of the companies have managed to create quite an impression on some social media platforms or others. Let us learn about some of the brands that have used social media successfully to their advantage. TOMS is a shoe company that pioneered the 'buy one give one' charitable model. They set a goal that for every pair of shoes they would manage to sell, they would donate a pair of shoes to the destitute and needy children. This philanthropic campaign of TOMS was showcased on Instagram. TOMS's mission was quite noble. Whenever someone would post a picture of their bare feet with the hashtag #withoutshoes, TOMS would donate a pair of shoes to the needy. They wanted to demonstrate the dedication their company had towards the cause they had committed to. They had managed to donate 296,243 pairs of shoes altogether. IKEA is one of the best examples of a global company that has used social media to its advantage in innovative ways. With its 10 million monthly viewers and over 500,000 followers on the IKEA USA page alone, they have established a global presence. One example of a successful campaign of IKEA was the one that ran in 2019. IKEA furniture realised that back to school was the peak time when school students look for furniture options. IKEA thought to address the requirements of the college- going students with a limited budget and limited space in their dorm/hostel. They devised a compact and small-space-friendly design and floated it on Pinterest to keep the target audience in mind. They used Pinterest and Promoted Pins and keywords like "dorm ideas" and "dorm room organization" to push traffic in the right direction. As a result, their click-through rate increased by 72%, and the Cost Per Click decreased by 37%. Starbucks made a dramatic launch of a neon-colored pink-and-purple fruity drink, Unicorn Frappuccino, that changes colour as you consume it. Starbucks created hype and generated curiosity among the younger generation. Millennials were aroused by feelings of FOMO (fear of missing out) as this beverage was served for a limited time only. This attractive and colorful beverage was suitable

for posting pictures on Instagram, as well as Facebook, Pinterest, and X(Twitter). The customers went ahead and shared their pictures with the drinks. With the marketing gimmick of creating a scarcity of the Frappuccino's availability, a craze for the beverage was ignited. When paired with constant social media campaigns of the Unicorn Frappuccino and its hashtag #unicornfrappuccino Starbucks attracted customers' attention. The campaign went viral in no time. It was successful in generating a 'Call to Action'. People queued up in large numbers outside physical stores to purchase the drink before it was out of stock.
13.8 LET US SUM UP
In this Unit, we discussed social media and its benefits for branding. We also discussed the strengths of dominant social media platforms such as Facebook, X, LinkedIn, Instagram, Pinterest, Snapchat, Tik Tok, Blog, Podcast, and YouTube. We learned the importance of studying customer demographics and the importance of knowing the strengths of social media platforms before deciding on a social media platform for branding. To sum up, we can say that social media platforms are the key to the success of brands primarily that work on shoestring budgets. The tip for learners is to explore each social media platform for personal branding to understand its nuances before starting to use it for business purposes.
13.9 GLOSSARY
SEO (Search Engine Optimization): It means the process of improving your site to increase its visibility when people search for products or services related to your business in search engines. Branding: The process of creating a unique identity and image for a product or company in the minds of consumers. Social Media: Online platforms that allow users to create, share, and interact with content to connect with others and build communities. Engagement: The level of interaction and participation that users show with a brand's social media content. Metaverse: A virtual 3D space introduced by Facebook's parent company Meta, where users can interact, work, play, and socialise through digital avatars.

14.0 INTRODUCTION
An audio-visual program takes its final shape after editing. Whether it is news programme or entertainment programme, editing plays a major role in all types of television production. But it is also true that the time available for editing in different types of television programmes may vary. For example, you will get significantly less time to produce a news package than an entertainment television show. Therefore, in this case, editing should be very fast. You will certainly find difference in editing a news programme and editing a documentary or a short film or a film. Generally, news programmes are produced in a hurry and their main focus is on providing information to the audience as quickly as possible, instead of the aesthetic aspects of the presentation. Therefore, the speed is more important than aesthetics in TV news editing.
14.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After going through this unit, you will be able to: * explain the importance of video editing in audio-visual content production; * describe the process of non-linear video editing;

* discuss the different techniques and guidelines of video editing; and * understand the user interface and tools of a video editing software.
14.2 UNDERSTANDING EDITING
Editing takes place in all the mediums but in this unit, we are discussing editing in the context of audio-visual programme production. In simple words, we can say that selecting, combining and trimming various audio and visual elements to convey the intended message effectively is called editing. You can compare editing with cooking. Just as in cooking, we prepare a final dish using various ingredients; similarly in video editing we create a final programme using various audio and visual elements. If you take the example of a documentary film, we have many materials such as recorded footage, voice-over, interviews, graphics, background music, audio and video effects, etc. During editing, we use all these components in such a way that finally an effective documentary comes out. Figure (1) explains this process clearly. Figure (1): Editing Writing with Images: We have already discussed in previous units that audio-visual media use both audio and visual components, but the visual always dominates. Thus, for a good editor, it is necessary that s/he knows the art of storytelling with images. It is basically the art of writing with images. Different shots interact with each other and create meaning. Shots should be arranged in such a way that they can convey the desired meaning. Just like different arrangements of the same words can give different meanings, similarly different arrangements of same shots can create different meanings. See the following example: Shot 1: A college student enters his house.

Shot 2: He opens his bedroom's door and comes into it. Shot 3: He is shocked after looking towards his bed. Shot 4: A black cobra is sitting on his bed. Now we put these shots in two different sequences. Case A: Here we shall put all four shots in following sequence: shot 1 - shot 2 - shot 3 - shot 4 So, in case-A, suspense will arise after shot-3. After shot - 3, viewers will think why that college student was shocked. Case B: Here we shall put the same four shots but in a different sequence: shot 1 - shot 4 - shot 2 - shot 3 Here too, the same four shots are used, but they are arranged in a different sequence, so it will also have an impact on the meaning. In this case, after seeing shot 4, there will be a mixed sense of fear and suspense in the audience. They have already come to know that there is a snake on the bed. Now they are thinking that there is a snake on the bed and this college student is going there, what will happen to him? We shall discuss it with one more example. The following figures (2) and (3) will explain it further in detail.

Figure (2) The figure (2) has a total of six shots in a particular arrangement (1,2,3,4,5,6). After watching this arrangement, one may think that the child is sitting on the couch and thinking something. He then calls someone on the phone. Meanwhile, his elder sister arrives and asks him to disconnect the phone. He follows his sister's instructions and listens to her. Now look at the Case 2 in figure (3). This case also has the same six shots but in different arrangement (6,5,1,2,3,4).

Figure (3) Here in the case-2, different arrangement of the same shots creates different meaning. In this case, one may think that the boy is sitting on the couch and his sister is asking him to call someone. He thinks something and then follows the sister's instruction. We can clearly see that if the same six shots are arranged in different ways, almost opposite meaning may be derived. Therefore, a good editor should know the art of storytelling with the help of images. An Invisible Art: Editing is often called an invisible art. It is a unique process, particularly in film and video productions, where multiple motion pictures are combined to create a story. This 'cutting and joining' process is often referred to as 'invisible art' because, as in any well-edited film or programme, the viewers are so deeply involved and so engrossed in watching it that they cannot even think about the editor's efforts. Editing: Technology and Role of Editor: Basically the job of any video editor is to simply put different pieces of motion pictures together, cut off unwanted footage, and edit dialogue sequences along with balancing their audio. It is just like joining the pieces in a linear way. An editor has to handle lots of images, motion pictures, dialogues, music and other elements. S/he mixes all of them in such a way so that when it is played before the viewers, they assume the

whole film or programme as a single piece. It is very challenging for any editor to maintain the pace, continuity and rhythm. Until the 1990s, editing was very challenging and a highly specialized job. After the expansion of computer technology and digitization of photography and videography, it moved out from the limited expert hands to the common masses. Simultaneously, it now opens up the new challenges for video editors to utilize and experiment with these tools for crafting new stunning and mesmerizing visual effects to attract the viewers. Traditional analogue film editing process had lots of limitations. But now, technology offers various digital editing tools in form of both commercial and open source software. Software like, Adobe(r) Premier Pro(r), Sony Vegas(r), Final Cut Pro(r) etc. are some professional high-end digital editing software. These are commercial software, and can be used after purchasing their licenses. Some open source software are also available which are free for use. These free open source software are - HitFilm Express(r), Openshot(r), Shotcut(r) etc. Along with these, editors also need photo editing and special effects compositing software such as Adobe Photoshop(r), Adobe After Effect(r) etc. Both are commercial software and require valid license to use them. Here, you can also use open source digital photo editing software such as Krita(r). These new digital tools not only help to perform fast and quality editing but are also helpful in controlling colors, lights, image resolution and basic motion jerks, keying and overall balancing etc. Here, one important thing you may note is that these software will enable you to finish the job effectively, but do not expect magic from them. Technology can only help in functioning or execution; it is the human brain and creative skills that transform any piece of edited film into an extraordinary production.
14.3 TECHNIQUES OF VIDEO EDITING
Whether it is linear (conventional) or non-linear (digital) editing, both serve the same purpose, i.e. to narrate a saga by developing drama to engage the audience. It is only the change of tools and techniques. Basic concept to edit any given story in an interesting order remains same in both methods. While linear technique of editing was difficult and had limited tools, non-linear editing has vast number of tools and effects that help in finishing the task more effectively. It gives the flexibility to re-edit a film/TV programme at any point of timecode by adding, manipulating or removing the shots. Here, we shall discuss the process of video editing. The ultimate aim of any editing process is to create a final product i.e. film or any video programme. The final product should be smooth and engaging. We can divide the editing process

into two stages : rough edit and final edit. Rough edit is just putting relevant videos or visuals with the audio track. These are fine-tuned later on by trimming/expanding as per the requirement of the story. Adding the suitable VFX and transitions to any film/programme makes the entire production crisp, meaningful and attractive. The main job of an editor is to engage the viewers and keep their attention uninterrupted. Some useful editing techniques and rules have been developed by the old masters. Understanding and following those will help you in learning editing. Now, we shall discuss some important video editing techniques.
1. Continuity Editing Approach: Continuity editing approach supports the logical, smooth and
seamless progression of the story. According to this approach, viewers should not feel any jerk or distraction while watching a film or any television programme. The most accurate continuity can be maintained by presenting the footage without any editing. It will present the real happening with complete continuity, but it is not possible. We need editing to compress the time and space otherwise, it will not be possible to tell the whole story in the short duration of a film or television programme. So, as an editor we have two major challenges. First, to tell the whole story within the time limit of the film or programme, and second, to present the story in such a way that viewers should find it seamless without any visual or psychological jerks or distractions. In editing, we combine different shots taken at different times and places, audio elements and other visual components to produce a whole complete film or programme. We have to combine them in such a way that they appear smooth and seamless. Continuity editing creates the sense of continuous and logically smooth action. It generally presents the action in a logical and chronological sequence. Even though the time and space of a sequence may be manipulated, it has the appearance of real time to the audiences. While editing a film or a programme, we should take care of different types of continuity, for example - space and time continuity, props and costume continuity, acting continuity, audio continuity, etc. The direction in which things move on screen is important in continuity editing. If a bus exits the screen on the right, it will be expected in a following shot to reappear on the left, otherwise the bus will be perceived as a different bus coming from the opposite direction. The relative positions of the characters are also important for maintaining continuity. In this context, 180 degree rule is very important. We have already discussed this rule in the unit-13. If you will break the 180 degree rule, relative positions of your characters will change and it will cause confusion in viewers' mind which is not good for the continuity. Following figure (5) shows the result of breaking 180 degree rule.

Figure 5: Breaking 180 degree rule In the above figure, we can clearly see that violation of 180 degree rule has changed the relative position of the two characters. It disturbs the continuity. For maintaining continuity, we should follow few more rules given below: i. Always remember that cut should be seamless and smooth. It is treated as a good edit point if the viewer does not notice any distraction. ii. Cutting on action: Always cut at action. When you cut a shot at any action point, viewer assumes or expects the next logical shot, because his/her brain anticipates the result of previous shot. Figure (6) explains it properly. Figure (6) Here the long shot of kicking the ball near goal post has been cut at action (Clip A), in between the shot of a trophy (Clip B) inserted (for showing winning goal) before next close up of the football in goal post (Clip C). It makes the sense of match winning moment.

iii. Match cut: When we cut from one shot to another and match the two shots by the action or subject to create a seamless reality-effect, it is called match cut. We use this technique to maintain the continuity while combining two shots of different activities. iv. Invisible cut: These types of cuts are used to create the effect of continuous take. Invisible cut joins two shots with similar frames together. It is used to hide the transition from the viewers. Here, you have to be more creative by using certain momentary shots very cleverly.
2. Parallel Editing: This is sometimes also termed as cross-cutting. It is an editing technique
which is used to cut between shots of two or more actions or events. It suggests that these actions are going on at different places, generally at the same time. Cross-cutting includes more than one shot which are used simultaneously to link the story together. It can be used to show the two sides of a story. It may also be used to build suspense and excitement in the story and sometimes contradict the other scene. We can make the sequence more interesting with the help of parallel editing. Following figure (7) explains the parallel editing in which shots of two different actions are used. Figure 7: Parallel editing
3. Montage Editing: In this editing technique, a series of different types of short shots are put
together in a sequence, generally to compress the time and space. Montage Editing is almost opposite to the continuity editing. It may also be used to give viewer a sense of overall summary of the story with different shots/cuts. Montage can be used to create dynamic rhythm in a scene. This technique may be used with loud music.
4. Video Transitions: We use video transitions to connect two shots one after the other. They
provide the viewers with a seamless and smooth visual experience that is the base of continuity editing approach. Cut is the most basic but most powerful and maximum used transition. Fade, dissolve, wipe, slide, page peel, iris, etc. are other popular transitions. Transitions are used in audio also. You should always use video transitions with a purpose. Figure (8) explains the transition with a diagram.

Figure 8: Video transition
14.4 GUIDELINES FOR EDITING
We have discussed some important editing techniques. Now we will talk about some basic guidelines of video editing. If you follow them, you can be a better editor. These guidelines are as follows: * The interaction between the two shots creates meaning. An editor must understand this principle and focus on the meaning emerging from the interaction between two juxtaposed shots. * Do not cut without any positive reason. * Reaction shots are important for logical and smooth progression of the story. So, use the reaction shots suitably. * Close-ups enhance emotional impacts. * Always keep it in mind that - A picture is worth a thousand words and action speaks louder than words. * Television is an audio-visual medium and a good editor should always remember this principle - If you can show, do not tell. * As a general rule, avoid jump cuts. But jump cuts can also be used creatively. * Using different shots such as long shot, medium and close-up helps to create a more effective sequence. They provide pace to the story. * Use only the required length of a shot which is appropriate to convey the information. In a dialogue scene, length of shot can be as long as the conversation going on. If it is getting lengthier then relevant insert (reaction) can be used at a certain point to avoid monotony. * The different pacing of shots (fast cuts and slow cuts) create different mood and atmosphere. For example, fast or rapid pacing (fast cutting) can create excitement, passion and thrill

whereas slow pacing (slow cutting) shows thoughtfulness and relaxation. Slow cutting can also be used to create suspense. * Use cut-ins and cutaways appropriately. Do you know about cut-ins and cutaways ? Let us discuss them briefly. Cut-ins: As the name suggests, cut-ins mean, first cut the main scene and then go inside it. The cut-ins are the close-up shots of something visible in the main scene. Take the example of a television interview. Your guest is explaining something and you interrupt that shot by placing closeup shots of her finger movements or leg movements or facial expressions and then return to the original shot. Here, these closeup shots will be called cut-ins. You can use the cut-ins to add additional information coming from the guest's body language. Cut-ins are also used to correct jump cut issues and break the monotony of lengthy shots. Cutaways: Cutaways mean, cut a shot and go away from that scene and return again to that scene. It is the interruption in a continuously recorded action by putting a shot of something else. It is generally followed by a cut back to the first shot. Just take one more example of a television interview. You have taken an interview of a doctor on COVID-19. You recorded the whole interview. Now, you are editing it. Just take an example of a shot in which your expert is describing the trial phases of a vaccine. If you will keep that shot as it is for a long duration, it will become boring. So, after the shot of doctor in which he is describing trial phases, you put the shots of vaccine trials and again return to the previous shot of the doctor. Here, the shots of vaccine trail will be called cutaways. With the help of cutaways, you can make your interview more interesting and informative. Cutaways can also be used to correct jump cuts. So, keying is a special compositing effect in which we take a part of a video and make it transparent. This part of the video may also be selected on the basis colour. And then we superimpose some other visual on it. As a result superimposed visual appears on the transparent portions of the video. You can see the examples of keying in figure 22 and 23. 14.0 INTRODUCTION
In today's digital-first world, every click, search, and scroll you make contributes to something much larger than you can see, a vast pool of digital information called Big Data. From online shopping and food delivery to watching reels and sharing memes, everything you do online leaves behind data trails. Now imagine billions of such trails being collected and analysed every second, that's Big Data at work! But what does this mean for brands?

For any brand to succeed today, knowing its audience deeply is crucial. Gone are the days when companies relied only on intuition or simple surveys. Today's brands listen to their customers through data, understanding what they buy, when they buy, how they feel, and what they expect next. This deep understanding, powered by Big Data, helps brands make smarter decisions, build stronger identities, and maintain meaningful relationships with their customers. This unit takes you behind the screens of modern branding to explore how insights drawn from Big Data are quietly shaping everything you see online: the ads you notice, the recommendations you get, and even the conversations brands start. You will learn how data fuels creativity, strategy, and reputation management in the digital ecosystem. And, we'll also look at the fine line between smart data use and misuse, privacy, ethics, and the evolving laws that protect you as a digital citizen. By the end, you'll appreciate data not just as a tool, but as a powerful storyteller in brand communication.
14.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After completing this Unit, you will be able to: * Define and explain the concept, characteristics, and scope of Big Data in the context of digital branding and communication. * Analyse how Big Data helps in understanding consumer behaviour and shaping brand strategies through data-driven insights. * Evaluate the ethical, legal, and professional implications of using Big Data for branding and digital public relations.
14.2 UNDERSTANDING BIG DATA
If you've ever wondered how Netflix seems to know exactly what you'd like to watch next or how Amazon recommends products you didn't even realise you needed, the answer lies in Big Data. Every online action you take: a "like," a "share," a "view," or even the time you spend on a post, contributes to a growing pool of data that tells stories about your habits, choices, and preferences. Big Data is more than just "a lot of data." It's a powerful collection of large, complex, and dynamic data sets that cannot be managed using traditional tools or manual analysis. For brands and communication professionals, Big Data acts like a treasure chest filled with clues about audiences, what they think, what they do, and what influences them.
14.2.1 Definition and Characteristics of Big Data
There are many definitions of Big Data, but one of the most widely accepted is given by Gartner: "Big Data is high-volume, high-velocity, and high-variety information assets that demand cost-effective, innovative forms of information processing for enhanced insight and decision-making." Simply put, Big Data refers to huge amounts of structured and unstructured data generated from digital activities: social media interactions, search queries, online purchases, GPS tracking, app usage, and more. In media and communication, this data helps us understand audience behaviour and predict what kind of messages or campaigns will work best. For instance: * When you scroll through Instagram, the app tracks what you pause to see, giving marketers clues about your interests. * News websites analyse which stories get the most clicks to decide what topics readers prefer.

* Streaming platforms use your watch history to personalise recommendations. What makes Big Data unique is not just its size but its speed, diversity, and usefulness. That's where the concept of the 5 Vs of Big Data comes in.
14.2.2 The 5 Vs of Big Data
To understand how Big Data operates, let's break it down into five defining dimensions often called the
5 Vs:
1. Volume: This refers to the enormous quantity of data being generated every second. Think of
millions of YouTube views, tweets, or Google searches happening simultaneously. For instance, every minute, Indians upload thousands of Instagram reels generating a massive volume of user- generated content.
2. Velocity: This is the speed at which new data is created and shared. In the digital world,
information travels instantly. For brands, this means that trends, customer feedback, and public opinion can shift within hours.
3. Variety: Data comes in many forms: texts, videos, photos, emojis, tweets, comments, and even
voice notes. The diversity of data allows brands to understand emotions, tone, and intent; not just facts and numbers.
4. Veracity: Not all data is accurate or reliable. Veracity deals with data quality, ensuring that what
you analyse reflects real consumer behaviour, not fake or misleading inputs. For example, bots or fake accounts can distort analytics on social media.
5. Value: Ultimately, all the data in the world is meaningless unless it provides value. The real
strength of Big Data lies in turning raw information into actionable insights. Brands use analytics to extract meaningful patterns that guide their marketing strategies. These 5 Vs help us see Big Data not as a messy flood of information but as an organised system that can reveal patterns, relationships, and predictions if we know how to interpret it.
14.2.3 Importance of Big Data in Media and Communication
The media and communication industry thrives on understanding people, what they watch, read, share, and talk about. Big Data gives professionals a magnifying glass into these audience behaviours. It helps them: * Identify trends in real time (like viral hashtags or breaking stories). * Measure audience engagement with precision (likes, shares, dwell time). * Design targeted messages for specific groups of people rather than "one-size-fits-all" campaigns. * Evaluate campaign performance instantly, seeing what's working and what needs improvement. Let's understand with an example. During the 2023 ICC Cricket World Cup, brands like Dunzo and CRED used Big Data analytics to track conversations on X (formerly Twitter) and Instagram. They could spot trending memes, fan emotions, and match reactions to release quick, witty social media responses that went viral within minutes. That's Big Data in action, fast, responsive, and insight-driven communication. For public relations professionals, Big Data allows listening at scale, tracking what people say about a brand across thousands of online spaces. Whether it's a new product launch or a controversy, PR teams use data to manage reputation and craft the right messaging.

Thus, Big Data is the new currency of communication. It helps brands move from guesswork to evidence-based storytelling, building stronger and more personal connections with audiences. Activity 1 Find and Reflect: Think of a brand you follow on social media (like Nykaa, Zomato, or Swiggy). Observe its posts for a week. Now ask yourself: * What kind of content gets the most engagement (likes, shares, comments)? * What might this data tell the brand about its audience? Write your reflections in 100-150 words.
14.3 BIG DATA AND CONSUMER INSIGHTS
Imagine standing in a crowded shopping mall, thousands of people around you, each with their own choices, habits, and moods. Now imagine you could "see" what each person wants to buy, how they decide, and what makes them pick one brand over another. That's exactly what Big Data enables brands to do: digitally. In today's world, where most interactions happen online, understanding consumer behaviour is no longer guesswork. Every like, click, search, and purchase creates a data point that tells a story. By collecting and analysing this information, brands can draw consumer insights, deep understandings about what people value, how they think, and how they make decisions. These insights are what turn marketing into meaningful communication.
14.3.1 How Data Reflects Consumer Behaviour
Consumer behaviour is shaped by a mix of emotions, habits, social influences, and personal needs. Big Data helps marketers decode these patterns by turning online activities into meaningful signals. For example: * When a user searches for "eco-friendly detergents," it reflects their environmental concern. * When someone repeatedly watches travel vlogs, it indicates an aspiration for exploration. * When thousands of users order biryani on Sunday nights through food apps, it signals a cultural pattern. Brands collect such data through multiple sources: social media interactions, e-commerce platforms, customer feedback forms, web cookies, and app analytics. These datasets, when analysed together, help companies understand the "why" behind the "what." Sugar Cosmetic, the beauty and wellness brand, uses consumer browsing and buying data to recommend personalised product bundles. If a customer frequently checks skincare content and reviews, Sugar highlights new serums or organic products in that category. This data-backed recommendation not only boosts sales but also enhances customer satisfaction by giving users exactly what they want. So now you get it, Big Data makes it possible for brands to move from mass communication to micro communication, talking to individuals, not just audiences.
14.3.2 Data Analytics and Market Segmentation
Once data is collected, the next step is to make sense of it and that's where data analytics comes in. Data analytics is like a microscope that helps brands observe patterns within large numbers.

Through analytics, marketers can segment their audience, that is, divide them into smaller, meaningful groups based on shared traits such as age, interests, location, or behaviour. For instance: * Netflix divides its audience based on genres they watch most: thriller lovers, comedy fans, or documentary viewers. * E-commerce platforms like Ajio or Myntra use purchase history and browsing behaviour to create categories like "bargain seekers," "fashion trend followers," or "festival shoppers." By identifying such segments, brands can design customised messages and personalised offers that appeal to each group differently. Traditional marketing segmentation relied on surveys or focus groups, which gave limited insights. Big Data analytics, however, analyses millions of digital footprints in real time. This enables dynamic segmentation, where consumer groups can change or evolve as new data comes in. For PR professionals, this means that media outreach and influencer collaborations can be tailored to each audience type, ensuring that the right message reaches the right people at the right moment.
14.3.3 Predictive Analytics and Trend Forecasting
Wouldn't it be amazing if brands could predict what consumers are going to want next month or next season? That's exactly what predictive analytics does. Predictive analytics uses algorithms and historical data to forecast future trends. It looks at past behaviour patterns to anticipate what might happen next. For example: * During festive seasons like Diwali, e-commerce giants such as Amazon India and Flipkart use predictive analytics to forecast product demand stocking up on categories likely to see higher sales. * Streaming platforms like Spotify and Gaana predict what kind of music will trend based on current listening patterns and regional preferences. * PR professionals use predictive analytics to monitor social media chatter and foresee possible reputation risks or crises before they escalate. These insights allow brands to prepare marketing strategies in advance and stay ahead of competitors. In a fast-moving digital world, being predictive rather than reactive gives brands a huge advantage. At the same time, predictive analytics helps brands build emotional connections. If data suggests that consumers are becoming more health-conscious or sustainability-focused, a brand can craft communication around those evolving values showing empathy and relevance. In this way, Big Data not only supports business goals but also helps brands stay in tune with social change. 14.4 BIG DATA IN BRAND MANAGEMENT
In today's digital marketplace, brand management is no longer just about creativity or intuition. It is about decisions guided by data. Big Data has transformed the way brands plan, communicate, and grow. It tells brands who their audiences are, what they want, and how to reach them most effectively. From small start-ups to large corporations, every successful brand today uses data as a compass to guide its direction, measure performance, and adjust its strategy in real time. In this section, we will explore how data helps in shaping brand strategy, enhancing customer experiences, and building loyalty through personalised communication.
14.4.1 Data-Driven Brand Strategies
A brand strategy defines what a brand stands for and how it wants to be perceived by its audience. Traditionally, brand managers relied on intuition, market surveys, and advertising feedback. But with Big Data, they can make decisions based on real-time insights rather than assumptions. Data-driven brand strategies are built on three key pillars:
1. Understanding the audience deeply: using analytics to know who your customers are, what they
value, and how they behave online.
2. Measuring brand performance: tracking engagement metrics, sentiment scores, and conversion
rates to understand how people feel about your brand.
3. Optimising campaigns continuously: testing, analysing, and improving based on data feedback
rather than waiting for post-campaign reports. For example, when a brand launches a new product, Big Data allows it to track reactions instantly across multiple platforms: social media mentions, website traffic, reviews, and even chat queries. If negative comments appear, the brand can act immediately, addressing issues before they escalate. A good case is Swiggy's data-driven marketing. Swiggy analyses user data to determine eating habits, time preferences, and even regional food choices. This data guides their promotional strategy, showing breakfast offers in the morning, snack deals in the evening, and biryani combos on weekends. Each communication is timely and relevant, reinforcing the brand's promise of convenience and satisfaction. Through such strategies, Big Data enables brands to stay agile, responsive, and deeply connected with consumer expectations.
14.4.2 Personalisation and Customer Experience

If you think about the brands you love most, chances are they make you feel seen and understood. That's what personalisation does. It transforms customer experience from generic to meaningful. Big Data is at the heart of this shift. By analysing browsing patterns, purchase history, location, and even sentiment, brands can tailor messages that feel personal. For instance: * Blinkit shows "Recommended for You" products based on past browsing and purchase behaviour. * Zomato sends push notifications around lunchtime or dinner hours, using your order history to suggest dishes you love. * YouTube creates personalised thumbnails and recommendations, ensuring no two users see the same homepage. This level of personalisation is only possible because of Big Data. Behind every "You might also like..." suggestion is an algorithm trained on thousands of data points. But personalisation isn't just about sales. It's also about emotional connection. When customers feel that a brand "gets" them, loyalty grows naturally. A user who receives relevant suggestions, timely reminders, and helpful responses is more likely to trust the brand. However, with personalisation comes responsibility. Brands must respect privacy and use data ethically. Many companies now highlight their data protection policies and offer users control over what data is collected. This transparency enhances trust, which is an essential element of long-term brand success.
14.4.3 Case Studies: Indian Brands Using Data
Let's now look at some brands that prudently use Big Data in their brand management practices.
1. BigBasket
BigBasket leverages Big Data to forecast demand, manage inventory, and personalise user recommendations. By studying customer purchase cycles--such as when households restock essentials--it predicts future orders and suggests relevant add-ons. During festive seasons, data analytics helps the brand anticipate surges in specific product categories, ensuring smoother supply-chain management.
2. Ola Cabs
Ola uses real-time data analytics to optimise ride allocation, pricing, and driver incentives. The app analyses traffic conditions, location demand, and customer feedback to minimise waiting time and improve service reliability. Its surge-pricing algorithm, based on predictive data modeling, helps balance demand and supply efficiently--especially during events, festivals, or bad weather.
3. Amazon India
Amazon's recommendation engine is a textbook example of Big Data in action. The brand analyses every customer's past behaviour--searches, purchases, ratings, and even browsing duration--to suggest what they're most likely to buy next. This creates a seamless, personalised shopping experience that feels intuitive.
4. Plum Goodness
Plum Goodness, a vegan beauty and skincare brand, uses data insights from its e-commerce platforms and social media engagement to track emerging beauty trends. It analyses product reviews, search queries, and influencer content performance to fine-tune marketing messages and product development. Data-driven insights also guide its decisions on new product launches and inventory management.

These examples show that Big Data is not limited to large corporations; even home-grown Indian brands are using it creatively to connect, engage, and grow. By now, you can see how Big Data is not just about technology or analytics; it's about creating experiences that matter. When used thoughtfully, data gives brands the power to be more human, understanding emotions, anticipating needs, and building trust that lasts.
14.5 BIG DATA AND DIGITAL PUBLIC RELATIONS
In the age of digital media, public relations (PR) has moved far beyond press releases and newspaper clippings. Today, conversations about brands unfold across millions of online spaces from tweets and blogs to YouTube comments and review sites. Managing a brand's reputation in this complex digital environment requires more than human intuition, it demands data intelligence. Big Data helps PR professionals listen, analyse, and act with speed and precision. Let's explore how Big Data is shaping two major PR functions -- sentiment analysis and crisis communication.
14.5.1 Sentiment Analysis and Online Reputation Management
Every post, tweet, comment, or review about a brand contributes to its digital reputation. With Big Data tools, PR professionals can now track these conversations in real time and decode how people feel about the brand -- whether positive, negative, or neutral. This process is called sentiment analysis. Sentiment analysis uses natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning to scan vast volumes of text and categorise opinions. For example: * If many users say "Love the new packaging by MamaEarth!", the algorithm marks it as positive sentiment. * If others post "Delivery delays ruined my Zepto experience," it flags negative sentiment. * Mixed or uncertain comments get labelled as neutral. This continuous analysis forms the foundation of Online Reputation Management (ORM). It helps PR professionals:
1. Measure public mood - knowing whether the sentiment is improving or declining.
2. Identify influencers and critics - recognising who shapes public opinion most.
3. Respond strategically - thanking satisfied customers or addressing complaints before they
escalate. For instance, Uber and Cred actively monitor Twitter, Reddit, and Instagram for customer feedback. When a negative experience trends, their PR teams respond within minutes, often with humour or empathy -- turning potential backlash into brand goodwill. Big Data tools like Brandwatch, Talkwalker, Sprinklr, and Hootsuite Insights make this possible. They visualise data on dashboards showing spikes in mentions, trending keywords, and sentiment ratios -- giving PR managers a "pulse" of public perception at any moment.
14.5.2 Real-Time Feedback and Crisis Communication
Crises can strike suddenly -- a product recall, data breach, insensitive ad, or viral complaint. In such moments, speed and accuracy of response determine whether a brand's image survives or collapses. Big Data analytics provides real-time feedback, enabling PR teams to act fast and with context.

For example, if a negative hashtag starts trending, PR teams can: * Track its origin -- where and when it began. * Identify key amplifiers -- who is making it viral. * Analyse engagement velocity -- how fast it's spreading. * Prepare data-backed statements and FAQs to control misinformation. A well-known case is when Maggi noodles faced a major safety controversy in India in 2015. Although the brand was temporarily banned, Nestle used continuous monitoring of social media data to understand consumer emotions, rebuild trust, and plan a comeback campaign once the product returned. Similarly, during the COVID-19 pandemic, several companies, from airlines to e-commerce platforms, used data analytics to track customer sentiment about safety measures, refund policies, and delivery reliability. The insights helped them adjust their messaging and reassure anxious customers. Today, many PR teams rely on AI-based dashboards that alert them instantly when brand mentions spike unusually = often the first sign of a brewing issue. This predictive function allows brands to move from reactive to proactive crisis management. Beyond crisis control, Big Data also helps in strategic storytelling. By understanding what people are already talking about, PR professionals can craft campaigns that resonate emotionally and socially. For instance, Sirona's campaigns during Women's Day or Dream 11's IPL-based humour posts are rooted in social media trend data, showing how insights can drive positive engagement as well. Big Data has revolutionised PR by turning the internet's chaos into meaningful intelligence. It enables professionals to listen better, understand faster, and respond smarter. Whether it's managing a crisis, protecting reputation, or simply knowing what customers feel -- data ensures that PR strategies are grounded in truth, not guesswork. As media options grow more complex, tomorrow's PR professionals must become fluent in data interpretation -- blending the heart of communication with the precision of analytics. 14.6 ETHICAL AND LEGAL DIMENSIONS OF USING BIG
DATA
As Big Data continues to power digital marketing and brand management, it also brings with it an important question -- how do we use data responsibly? In the race to understand customers better, brands often gather enormous amounts of information -- from browsing habits and purchase histories to location patterns and even emotional responses. But with great data comes great responsibility. Let's explore the ethical and legal aspects that guide this space.
14.6.1 Data Privacy and Protection (Indian Context: IT Act & DPDP Act 2023)
In India, the first step toward regulating digital data came with the Information Technology Act, 2000, which set the foundation for cyber laws, including provisions for data security and privacy. However, as data usage became more sophisticated, a stronger legal framework became necessary. This led to the introduction of the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023. The DPDP Act aims to protect citizens' personal data and ensure that organisations handle it responsibly. Some of its key provisions include: * Consent-based Data Collection: Companies must seek clear consent from individuals before collecting their personal information. * Purpose Limitation: Data can only be used for the purpose for which it was collected. * Right to Access and Correction: Users have the right to know what data is stored about them and can request corrections. * Obligation to Delete: Once data is no longer needed, companies must delete it. * Penalties for Violations: Heavy fines can be imposed for unauthorised sharing, misuse, or data leaks. For media professionals and brand managers, this means that data cannot be treated as a free commodity. Whether it's collecting email IDs for newsletters or tracking social media behaviour for targeted ads: transparency and consent are non-negotiable.
14.6.2 Responsible Data Use in Branding
Beyond laws, there is also an ethical side to how brands use data. Consumers today value trust and authenticity as much as innovation. Brands that misuse personal data risk not just legal penalties but also long-term damage to their reputation. Responsible data use involves: * Anonymising sensitive information to protect individual identity. * Avoiding manipulative targeting, such as exploiting emotional vulnerabilities or fear-based marketing. * Ensuring inclusivity, so data-driven branding does not stereotype or exclude certain communities. * Communicating openly with users about why data is collected and how it benefits them.

For example, when Hotstar or Audible recommend your next watch or listen, users feel comfortable because they've opted in knowingly, thus they see it as a service, not surveillance. But if users feel they're being watched without permission, the same data practice becomes unethical. Thus, digital branding today is not just about creativity and analytics; it's also about integrity. Ethical data use builds trust, and trust builds lasting brands. Activity 2: Look for the privacy policy of any Indian brand's website (for example, BookMyShow, BigBasket, or Reliance Retail). * Identify how they describe data collection and usage. * Does the policy align with the DPDP Act's consent-based principles? * Write a short paragraph on whether you find the brand's approach transparent and ethical.
14.7 CHALLENGES AND FUTURE OF BIG DATA IN
BRANDING
As powerful as Big Data is, it's not without its pitfalls. Every marketer or brand manager who uses data for decision-making soon realises that numbers can tell us a lot--but not everything. Let's look at some of the challenges we face today and the future trends that will shape how Big Data continues to influence branding.
14.7.1 Limitations and Risks of Data Dependence
In recent years, companies have become increasingly data-dependent. From designing ad campaigns to predicting what consumers will buy next, data seems to drive every decision. But this dependence brings its own set of problems.
1. Data Overload: The sheer volume of data can be overwhelming. Not all data is relevant, and
filtering useful insights requires time, money, and skill.
2. Quality vs. Quantity: A brand might have a million data points, but if they're outdated, biased,
or incomplete, the insights drawn from them can be misleading.
3. Loss of Human Touch: Brands that rely only on algorithms risk losing emotional connection with
their consumers. Data can tell you what people are doing, but not always why they are doing it.
4. Security Risks: More data means more vulnerability. Breaches and leaks can harm both customers
and brand reputation.
5. Ethical Concerns: Predictive targeting can sometimes cross moral lines, such as manipulating
consumers' behaviour or invading privacy. For instance, during India's 2019 general elections, several digital campaigns were accused of using consumer data to micro-target voters in ways that blurred the line between persuasion and intrusion. Such incidents highlight the thin boundary between smart marketing and unethical manipulation.
14.7.2 Emerging Trends: AI, Machine Learning, and Predictive Branding
Despite these challenges, the future of Big Data in branding is exciting. The next decade belongs to AI- driven analytics, machine learning, and predictive branding.

* Artificial Intelligence (AI): AI tools are now capable of scanning millions of consumer conversations online and identifying emerging trends in real time. Brands can act quickly to adapt their messaging. * Machine Learning (ML): ML algorithms continuously learn from consumer interactions, refining recommendations and improving personalisation. For example, Netflix's content suggestions or Spotify's playlist curation are powerful examples of ML in action. * Predictive Branding: This is where Big Data truly becomes futuristic. By analysing years of behavioural patterns, brands can forecast what consumers might want next, before they even know it themselves! In India, companies like Tata Neu, District, and Paytm are already experimenting with predictive analytics to anticipate customer needs and offer hyper-personalised experiences. As we move forward, the key will be balance -- blending technology with empathy. Big Data can tell you the direction, but human creativity and ethics will always steer the journey. Activity 3: Pick any Indian brand that you think uses AI or predictive analytics (for example, SonyLiv, MilkBasket, or Gullak). Write a short note (100-150 words) on how the brand uses data to predict customer needs and improve experience. Reflect on whether you think this makes the brand more efficient or more intrusive.
14.8. LET US SUM UP
In this unit, you explored how Big Data has become the driving force of modern brand management. We began by understanding what Big Data is, its key features, and why it matters to communication and media professionals. You learnt how data reveals consumer behaviour, enables market segmentation, and helps forecast trends. We also discussed with case studies, how brands are using analytics to build stronger connections with their audiences. The unit also helped you understand how Big Data supports digital PR, shapes brand reputation, and guides crisis communication in real time. Finally, we reflected on the ethical and legal concerns of data use and the emerging trends like AI and predictive branding that define the future of digital brand management.
14.9 GLOSSARY
Big Data: Extremely large data sets analysed to reveal patterns and trends. Predictive Analytics: Forecasting future behaviour based on existing data. Sentiment Analysis: Assessing emotions expressed in online text. Data Privacy: Protecting personal information from misuse. Machine Learning: AI systems that learn and improve from experience without explicit programming.
