18.1 INTRODUCTION
As Internet and new media grows, concerns about a possible gender digital divide in use of these new media technologies have also emerged. In the Indian context, where mobility largely determines access to new media technologies - be it through accessing cyberworld through mobile /gaming cafes or through affording new technologies - young women may very well find it more difficult to use computer-based new media than young men, either teenagers or adolescents. But more than the gender division of digital knowledge, the divide is between the rural and urban region or location. The positionalities of individuals are now more to do with their location than with their genders. New media technologies have recently

Visualising Gender outgrown human intelligence and artificial and emotional intelligence are occupying the human mind of thinking. The basic process of comprehension has been taken over by the AI voice of either Google or Wikipedia to provide the required knowledge. This may right now raise a cause for alarm. Some scholars, particularly a branch of cyber feminists, are of the view that women regendering the new media technologies because these media might not serve the purposes they value and trying to turn it to their own privileges. Such writing, in turn, has been attacked by other feminists as furthering an idea of essential gender difference and hindering equality. It is important to note that in certain parts of the world, the hetronormative cisgendered use of a range of new media is at par with or has even surpassed that of homonormative people and, of late, has also been accompanied by significant shifts in attitudes through prevalent individual cyberspace and traits of self-objectification and commodification. These are some of the issues which we will discuss in this unit.
18.2 LEARNING OUTCOMES
On completing this unit, you will learn to: * Describe and differentiate new media from what is now termed as traditional media; * Describe the early history of cultural responses to technology; * Discuss the different responses to women's relationship with technology; and * Critically analyse the cyber world and its relationship with the gender.
18.3 UNDERSTANDING NEW MEDIA AND GENDER
While the question of inclusion is an important part of understanding new media and gender, there is another important frame within which the question of gender in relation to new media technologies has been asked. This is the question of how new media technologies necessarily break the very idea of binary gender difference i.e. the idea that there are necessarily only two sexes from which the two respective genders emerge naturally and universally. To some of you this may be a traditional argument that binds the gender into binary process. It is quite validating when we talk about cyberspace, gender encompasses the normativity into both the cisgender and non-cisgender. Furthermore, it is significant here that cyberworld is constantly creating a fluidity of gender identity. The comprehension of body is complicated through gendered performativity and this is well seen in social media accounts, for instance boys behaving like girls or girls behaving like boys. In fact, the whole notion of gendered behavior has been overtaken with performativity and thus locationality of any gender becomes more significant. Obviously then questions rise how does our immersion into

these new technologies change our very understanding of how we experience Engendering New Media: Cyberspace our own body as gendered body? Does the idea of technology break our simplistic ideas of binary thoughts of female as nature and technology as male? Or as Donna Haraway claims in her work on Gender and Technology, have we, in our immersion into technology, been transformed into Cyborgs, with no fixed male and female gender identities but with multiple and fluid gender positions. But, before we begin to understand the relationship between gender and new media we will first have to unpack the term New Media, a broad and often confusing term that refers to many historical and technological processes.
18.4 GENESIS OF NEW MEDIA TECHNOLOGIES
Before the emergence of New Media in the latter part of the last century, communication used to take place through an analogue form of broadcasting, either on television or on print. About these, you have already read in the first two units of this block. But with the invention of digital computers, communication became synchronous or much easier. Crossing all geographical barriers, huge volumes of messages and information could be transferred at a much higher speed. Communication also became much more interactive than the analog media. Thus, with the birth of New Media, and its primarily interactive synchronous digital media technology, a digital shift in human relationships also took place. For instance, service providers, like Microsoft, Google, made individualized accounts opening plethora of unknown accompaniment of cyber communities, through their chatrooms. In India, Yahoo and Indiatimes came up first to create cyber communities of like- minded people, through their chatrooms, where the account holder has to have an account either in Yahoo, or Hotmail, or Rediffmail. Most of them are platforms where the comminucations are encrypted into words, numbers and signs/symbols (emojis). These interactions with the unexplored cyberworld made the technocrats create social media platforms for better communications through images, videos and calling. Orkut.com and Outpersonals.com are two big giants at the turn of the century to build up a wide social media platform for interactions. But after Facebook came into existence, outpersonals.com faded away, while orkut tried to survive for few years, but in vain and soon died. These are good examples of new media phenomena that combine digital text, images and video with web- links, creative participation of contributors, and interactive feedback of users and formation of various networked communities. Other examples include CD-ROMS, DVDs, Internet, websites, blogs, computer multimedia, computer games and interactive mobile technologies. Unlike popular misconception, what differentiates new media from traditional media is not digitizing of media content. The difference has more to do with the shifts in ideas of production, distribution and importantly, interactivity that began

Visualising Gender with digital media. According to Vinaya Nayak, the differences between the traditional media and new media are as the following.
Traditional Media New Media
Broadcasting: Mass Audience Narrowcasting: Segmented Audience
Single or Few Channels of Flow Multiple Channels of Flow
Zero or Little Feedback More Feedback
Mostly Analog and Not Compressible Mostly Digital
Not Networked Networked
Separate Integrated
Active Gate Keeping Less Gate Keeping
Passive Receiver Active Receiver
Less Interactive More Interactive
For example, a high definition digital T.V receiving digital broadcast signals is still traditional media but graffiti that advertises a website like Orkut, where users are actively creating and shaping content, is digital media. But soon digital TV got replaced by Smart TV and Orkut by Facebook. The new digital world had something better to offer technologically. Social media became popular through WhatsApp, Twitter or X TikTok, and Instagram. What distinguishes the two is the dynamic nature of the content and flow of media. With new media the consumers have the opportunity to transform themselves into producers and distributors of content through digital technologies, whereas with traditional media the consumer is merely a receiver and the ability to create content is minimal. The following would all fall into traditional media: films screened in theatres, books, newspapers and magazines printed solely on paper and television programs. In the Box gives you the key characteristics of traditional and new media. The dynamic features of New Media allow for active participation and feedback thus making it truly democratic.
18.5 GENDER AND NEW MEDIA TECHNOLOGIES
In many of the third-world post-colonial nations like India, technology has been simultaneously represented as both positive and negative. This relationship to technology is also something that one sees in the way gender work in India has progressed. Early responses to science and technology from nationalist thinkers like Gandhi and Tagore still inform cultural attitudes to technology, of which new media technologies are the latest. Asha Achutan (Achutan, 2010) in her work on women and technology notes "four responses to technology - presence, access, inclusion, resistance. Reflected from the vantage point of women as one of the disadvantaged

constituencies with respect to technology, these are voiced as the demand Engendering New Media: Cyberspace for presence of women as agents of technological change - either through presence in production or through incorporation of their 'native' wisdoms into the system; sometimes as the demand for improved access for women to the fruits of technology; at other times the demand for inclusion of women as a special constituency that must be specially provided for by technological amendments. And then again, the demand for a need to recognize technology's ills particularly for women, and the consequent need for resistance to technology on the same count becomes quite pivotal. This inclusion model can be seen today, for instance, in the aims of the Dynamic Coalition on Gender Equality, which is a part of the Internet Governance Forum (IGF) which states on it's website that it "aims to ensure gender perspective is included in the key debates around internet governance issues, such as content regulation, privacy, access, freedom of expression among others. Among others, the coalition wants to promote women's visibility at the IGF and related fora; to conduct research and input on the main topics of IGF debates; to support capacity building of gender advocates and to promote more effective linkages between local, regional and global initiatives on gender and information society" (IGF, 2010, 22-23 November). But soon the Indian government took initiatives to change the whole idea of internet and citizens of this country. In 2011, Bharatnet project was initiated with the thought that digital knowledge could be disseminated all acroos the country. It rather wanted the rural population to be equipped with internet and cellular services through the Gram panchayats. Gradually, in 2014 National Digital Lietrary Mission and in 2015 Digital Literary Mission were launched to make at least one in each family digitally educated in the rural India and provide high speed internet connectivity. The main purpose of all these schemes and missions were to make the rural india digitally literate and skilful, along with create safety and secured affordable internet services for all citizens in the country. Check Your Progress 1: Do you usethe cyberspace? Discuss how you use it, and the advantages and disadvantages of the cyberspace.

18.6 PARADIGMS OF DEVELOPMENTS
The Women in Development Paradigm: The presence, access and inclusion responses to new media world come under the Women in Development (WID) approach to building gender just models of development. WID emerged in the early 1970s to increase women's presence in development related work, particularly through increasing access to the latest development technologies and inclusion of women in the process of achieving economic growth. The goal of WID was economic growth through investment in women. Even though these efficiency-based arguments proved to be effective as a political strategy for having women's issues taken up by development work in the third world, it also entailed a number of debatable results. Because of the WID model, emphasis was placed on how women could contribute to economic development, while their own demands from development (including gender equity) became secondary and conditional upon showing positive economic growth. The WID paradigm gave way in the early 1980s for the Gender and Development (GAD) paradigm. Gender and Development Paradigm (GAD): A major flaw noted in the WID analysis was that women were assumed to have common, homogeneous interests simply because of their sex. This ignores that women have varied and often conflicting interests depending on their class, race, ethnicity, religion, and sexual orientation and the GAD approach with its focus on gender and not women, sought to correct this imbalance and recognized that a woman's interests will vary depending on a complex interplay of her social, political and cultural contexts. We can see that there is still a connection between these two approaches, which is that both of them see technology as separate from the human who is either in control of such technology or its victim. The gender and technology relationship therefore is caught in an endless argument between the benefits and damages that accrue to women from the use of new technology. One way out of this debate can be seen in the cyborg theories of Donna Harraway and other feminist scholars. Accessibility ot internet services widely spread all across the country mainly collapsing the digital divide between urban and rural sphere of the country. These educational platforms really helped the educational system to function more smoothly during the pandemic. facilitators are being trained to facilitate financial transactions for rural Engendering New Media: Cyberspace people who fail to use the banking transactions. They help everyone workers in the informal sector to women working at home to our ageing parents receiving a pension. 18.8 GENDER AND CYBER LAWS IN INDIA
Cyberspace has always admonished the gender-neutral characteristics, but failing to do so Indian Government has made the jurisprudence of the cyber world functioning in the Indian domains more strict, yet open for modifications. But the legal systems have tried to make amendments to incorporate cybercrimes against women, men, students, teachers, children, government (including police, and other government employees). To understand what cybercrime is, you need to probe into the cyberspace more deeply. Cybercrimes in India is almost gender-neutral; all genders get trapped into the web world, and become victims of such virtual or digital crimes. The five most committed cybercrimes in India are phishing, spoofing, ransomware, malware and IoT (Internet of Things) hacking. Gender based cybercrime that takes place is our country is mostly phishing, ransomware, trolling, cyberstalking, and sextortion are other forms of gender based cybercrimes.
18.8.1 Phishing
Phishing is the most common type of cybercrime, and it is the practice of deceiving, pressuring or manipulating people (victim) into sending information or assets to the wrong people (attacker). The attackers manipulate the victim to reveal sensitive information. Phishing attacks are most sophisticated and often transparently mirror the site being targeted, allowing the attacker to observe everything while the victim is navigating the site, and transverse any additional security boundaries with the victim. There are several kinds of phishing practiced, like the email, SMS, voice, whaling, and calendar phishing to name a few. The data of the NCRB suggests that women are more susceptible than men to phishing and participants between the ages of 18 and 25 are more susceptible to phishing than other age groups.
18.8.2 Spoofing
Spoofing attack is a situation in which a person successfully identifies as another by falsifying data, to gain an illegitimate advantage of the victim. The attacker poses as a known to the victim and uses the data to transfer financial benefits from the victim, like the detailed information in the email account of the victim. Spoofing can happen through email, IP addresses, poisoning (destroying) files, caller ID/voice and domain spoofing. But among all these, geolocation spoofing is the most authenticating and dangerous among all spoofing. In this fake GPS address is used to hack the account of a victim. Most of the spoofing are done through hacking the information and network security of the victims. It is important to note that falling prey to attacker's spoof may overpower personal details and hack the entire information collected in victim's profile. In this kind of attack, all genders fall prey to such spoofing, as the vulnerability of the victim is not very

technologically expert, rather technologically challenged. It is often seen Engendering New Media: Cyberspace through that people who are not literate to some extent or not a frequent user of technological gadgets or devices fall prey, especially older people.
18.8.3 Ransomware/Malware
Ransomware is a type of malware (malicious software) that locks a victim's data or device and threatens to keep it locked--or worse--unless the victim pays a ransom to the attacker. According to the IBM Security X-Force Threat Intelligence Index 2023, ransomware attacks represented 17 percent of all cyberattacks in 2022. There are two types of ransomware are very popular, they are as follows: Locker ransomware: This type of malware blocks basic computer functions. For example, you may be denied access to the desktop, while the mouse and keyboard are partially disabled or may not function as you want it to. This allows you to continue to interact or follow the instructions popping up in your window containing the ransom demand in order to make the payment. Apart from that, the computer becomes almost inoperable. But this kind of malware doesn't usually target critical files saved in your desktop/laptop; it generally wants to lock you out. Complete destruction of your data is unlikely to happen. Crypto ransomware: The aim of crypto ransomware is to encrypt your important data, such as documents, pictures and videos, but not to interfere with basic computer functions. Encryption is basically using a secret code or ciphertext from seeing, looking or understanding your details. This spreads panic because victims can see their files but cannot access them. Crypto developers often add a countdown to their ransom demand, like "If you don't pay the ransom by the deadline, all your files will be deleted." and due to the number of users who are unaware of the need for backups in the cloud or on external physical storage devices, crypto ransomware can have a devastating impact on the victim's mental health. Consequently, many victims pay the ransom simply to get their files back. It is often seen that this kind of attack is also victimizing all genders.
18.8.4 IoT Hacking
IoT hacking is controlling the victim's physical objects through attackers' control. The Internet of Things (IoT) describes the network of physical objects--"things"--that are embedded with sensors, software, and other technologies for the purpose of connecting and exchanging data with other devices and systems over the internet. Smart TVs, smart watches, cars, heating and cooling systems, fitness machines, dishwashers, refrigerators, trackers, etc. are examples of IoT-enabled products with which you may have personal experience or they recognize your voice only. But when the hacker hack these devices, you feel trapped and lose the personal rapport

Visualising Gender that you developed with this objects. Even Alexa, Siri and Cortana can also be hacked. So this kind of attack is also not any particular gender based.
18.8.5 Trolling
Trolling is posting inflammatory, abusive, controversial, offensive, irrelevant messages against you to upset or provoke you to lash out or display emotional responses. It can start off a heated battle of words among the members in the group against each other while the person who started it enjoys the frustrated responses. Inflammatory, attacking, agitating or provocative or derogatory posts target a specific individual or subject or group. Sometimes posts on controversial topics may also incite anger and reactions from the followers, viewers, or fans. Trolling is frequently associated with Internet discourse or the cyber structure of everyday functioning. Media attention in recent years has equated trolling with online harassment, which is cyberbullying or online bullying or cyber harassment. This is a form of bullying or harassment using electronic means. It has become increasingly common, especially among teenagers, as the digital sphere has expanded and technology has advanced encompassing the genZies and millennials to emphasis their existence. Cyberbullying is when someone, typically a teenager, bullies or harasses others on the internet and other digital spaces, particularly on social media sites, like Instagram, Twitter or X Facebook or other SNS platforms.
18.8.5 Cyberstalking
Cyberstalking, or the stalking or harassing a person or an individual, group, or organization by electronic means (often the internet), is a kind of electronic harassment. It may include false accusations, defamation, slander (voice/video messages) and libel (written or documented messages). It may also include monitoring, identity theft, threats, vandalism, and solicitation for sex, doxing, or blackmail. Doxing is the act of publicly providing personally identifiable information about an individual or organization, through the cyberworld. It may be carried out for reasons such as online shaming, extortion, and vigilante aid to law enforcement. Such kind of harassment takes many forms and might include monitoring someone's online behavior, making threats, stealing their identity or data, or even faking their data. Cyberstalking is often accompanied by realtime or offline stalking. Such cybercrimes are motivated by a desire to control, intimidate or influence a victim. A stalker may be an online stranger or a person whom the target knows. They may be attack as an anonymous and solicit involvement of other people online who do not even know the target. In this kind of cybercrimes, the most vulnerable are women and LGBTQ+ people.

18.8.7 Sextortion Engendering New Media:
Cyberspace Sextortion is a form of extortion of sexual favors from the victim employing non-physical forms of coercion. Sextortion refers to the broad category of sexual exploitation in which abuse of power is the means of coercion. Abuse of power is just that the accused have certain digital information of the victim which if exposed may cause harm to the victim. It is mainly a category of sexual exploitation in which threatened release of sexual images or information is the means of coercion, and is considered as a form of corruption in which people entrusted with power - such as government officials, judges, educators, law enforcement personnel, and employers - seek to extort sexual favors in exchange for something within their authority to grant or withhold. For example, a teacher might ask for sexual favor in trade of good marks/grades, or a government official may ask for sexual favors to issue licenses or permits, or an employer may ask sexual favors to provide a job or promotion. Sextortion also refers to a form of blackmail in which sexual information or images are used to extort money or sexual favors from the victim. Social media and text messages are often the source of the sexual material and the threatened means of sharing it with others. For instance, people in dating apps fall prey to such sextortion, where the victim may have shared some nude images of themselves through sexting. They are later coerced into giving money, or perform sexual acts with the person doing the extorting or are coerced into posing or performing sexually on camera, thus producing a hardcore pornography. It is important to note that most of the victims trapped in this kind of cybercrimes are from LGBTQ+ community and young women who are on dating applications. Such extortion many a times takes away the human dignity for survival, or may lose jobs, and in extreme cases, the victims die by suicide (especially the closeted LGBTQ+ individual).

of the victim of certain offences, two years and fine. etc.
18.8.9 IP (Intellectual Property) laws in accordance with
Gaming in India
We are mentioning here these laws so that you have some ideas how the laws in India function. But it is also important to note here, this may not be directly linked with the theme of this Unit. Still at many points, one can always argue that the coder, developer or the creator of the game may be segregated through gender lens. For example, due to the demand-supply gap in the current workforce, 20%-30% are female programmers and 70% - 80% are male programmers, or 23.7% of video game developers are women and 76.3% of video game developers are men.

Types of IP laws in India related to Gaming
1. Cinematographic work: As far as India is concerned, no specific
regulations have been provided under the IP laws prevalent in our country which have thereby created several ambiguities for the game developers. The Copyright Act, 1957 ("CA 1957") provides for cinematograph film as a work of visual recording analogous to cinematography. According to the definition, video recording would imply recording in any medium of moving images or representations. Meaning, a video game may be presented in the form of a movie but will still be created through computer programming codes which cannot be considered as video recording. Even if a game gives the perception of being a video, it is the action of the player caused through the pressing buttons which runs the game, thereby questioning whether a video game can be a cinematographic work at all. It can thus be summaries that video games cannot be presented as a movie but rather require the interaction of the player with the console for it to function at all.
2. Author: A developer can either be an individual or it could be a
team of a group of people who develop the game. According to the CA 1957, an author is defined with respect to literary, dramatic, musical, artistic, photographic and cinematographic works. Further, section 2(o), defines literary work to include computer programmes, tables and compilations including computer databases, which implies that the author, with respect to a video game can be assumed to be either its developer, producer or whosesoever has caused the work to be created.The interpretation of the above definition can only cover the coder, programmer or any other person using a computer to run the game. The producer, game animator, creative director, etc. will not be covered under the definition of an author. This means that their contribution may not necessarily get the monetary reward they deserve through royalties which, assuming the eventual success of the game, may be significant to say the least. Further, a contract of service and a contract for service create ambiguity in the rights of the developers. Under the former, an employer is the owner of the copyright created in the course of employment unless any contract is signed contrary to the same and is also entitled to the royalties. In the latter, the contractor or developer who is specifically hired to create all or the varied components of a game ought to be the first owner of the copyright. A contract for service would give both the employer and the contractor royalties created during the course of work. It would include outsourcing done by the employer for getting the game created and developed by a person or a company which has the

required skills and expertise. The issue here would be when both Cyberspace the employer and contractor have a joint IP right over the game. As seen from the act itself, the CA 1957 does not specify the clear definition of an author when there are multiple developers in the gaming industry and which invariably has the potential of creating ambiguities regarding the allocation of royalties.
3. Computer Programme: Section 2(ffc) of the CA 1957 explains the
concept of computer programmes and the copyright protection attributed to it. It is primarily a set of instructions in the form of codes which causes a computer to perform a particular task or achieve a particular result. A gaming console or a particular game does not provide instructions to the computer or any other electronic device for performing any tasks. It is the software which performs such functions. A game and a gaming console only receives instructions from the player who is playing the game.
4. Patents: The very essence of a game lies in its game play i.e. how
a person reacts to the various aspects like the controls, story, video, audio, etc. Section 3(m) of the Patents Act, 1970 ("PA 1970") provides that the method of playing a game does not count to be an invention. However section 2(l) provides that any invention or technology which does not exist in the country can be patented. Moreover, section 2(ja) provides that an inventive step which leads to technological advancement and having economic significance shall attribute towards an invention. Therefore, the method of playing a game should be allowed to be patented since it is a technological advancement with economic significance. Compared to the 1970's, games have developed a lot, play methods have changed and there is a lot of economic significance on account of the revenues that gaming can generate. Thus, whether the players like or dislike it, depends upon the particular method created by the developer enabling the player to carry out various stunts, actions, character selection etc. to perform its personalized qualities.
5. Designs: A game consists of various designs. This means that creating
various levels within a game, designs for the location, where it is played, the natural environment, etc. However, the Designs Act, 2000 ("DA 2000") does not cover this under the definition of a design. Section 2(d), provides that a design includes the features of shape, configuration, patterns, composition of lines applied to the article in two or three dimensional forms by any industrial process etc. No design created through technology has ever been covered by the statute, which only provides for designs created through an industrial process.

18.9 LET US SUM UP
New media offers users a certain level of freedom from the realm of 'bodies' and the anonymity of cyberspace offers a forum unhindered by hierarchies of sex and gender. It can therefore be an enabling and politically charged space. It is very intriguing to see how the technological advancement has widened the digital divide in accordance to gender. Whether it is the dating applications, or the OTT platforms or the online gaming in India, the gender digital divide is either diffusing or creating further stringent divisions between all genders. The Indian legal systems are trying to cope up with the changing nature of gender based cyber violence or cybercrimes. In recent times, the internet has been used by women's and feminist groups as forums for both discussion and activism -allowing for a plurality of discourses that may have otherwise not been possible.

18.0 INTRODUCTION
In this unit, we will explore the various aspects of perception management, focusing on its significance in public relations. We will explore the perception process, the role of perception in public relations, strategies for effective perception management, and the tools and techniques used in the field. Additionally, we will examine real-life case studies and discuss the challenges faced in perception management, particularly in the Indian context.

18.1 LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of this Unit, you would be able to: * Analyse the fundamental concepts and significance of perception management in the context of public relations * Evaluate the role of media, social media, and public events in shaping public perception * Apply various tools and techniques for effective perception management in practical scenarios
18.2 MEANING AND IMPORTANCE
Welcome to the fascinating world of Perception Management! Before diving into the details, let's first understand what perception management actually means. Perception management is the process of influencing how people perceive information, events, or organisations. It involves carefully crafting messages and utilising various communication channels to shape the audience's perceptions in a way that aligns with specific goals. This is especially crucial in public relations, where managing public perception can make or break an organisation's reputation. Imagine you are working for a well-known company like Tata. Your job in public relations would be to ensure that the public views Tata as a trustworthy and innovative brand. This involves strategically planning how information about Tata is presented to the public, handling any negative news that may arise, and constantly monitoring public opinion. Perception management is not just about presenting positive information; it's also about managing negative perceptions effectively. For instance, if Tata faces a product recall, it's the job of the PR team to handle the situation transparently and efficiently, ensuring that the public's trust in the brand is maintained.
18.3 UNDERSTANDING PERCEPTION AND ITS PROCESS
18.3.1 What is Perception?
Perception is the process by which individuals interpret and organise sensory information to make sense of their environment. It involves selecting, organising, and interpreting information from the world around us. Perception is subjective and can vary significantly from person to person based on their experiences, beliefs, and cultural background. In the context of public relations, perception refers to how the public views an organisation, event, or individual. For example, consider how people perceive the Indian government's Digital India initiative. Some may see it as a significant step towards modernisation and inclusivity, while others may view it sceptically, focusing on issues like data privacy and internet access. Understanding perception is crucial for PR professionals because it helps them tailor their communication strategies to influence public opinion effectively. By understanding how people perceive information, PR professionals can craft messages that resonate with their audience and achieve their communication goals.
18.3.2 The Perception Process
The perception process involves several stages: sensation, selection, organisation, and interpretation. * Sensation: This is the initial stage where our senses (sight, sound, touch, taste, and smell) detect stimuli from the environment. For instance, when you see an advertisement for a new product, your eyes are sensing the visual elements of the ad. * Selection: In this stage, we select which sensory information to focus on and which to ignore. This selection is influenced by factors such as interest, motivation, and relevance. For

example, if you are interested in technology, you are more likely to notice ads for the latest smartphones. * Organisation: After selecting the information, our brain organises it in a meaningful way. This involves grouping the information based on patterns, similarities, and other organising principles. For instance, you might organise the features of a new smartphone into categories like design, functionality, and price. * Interpretation: Finally, we interpret the organised information to form a coherent perception. This interpretation is influenced by our past experiences, cultural background, and personal beliefs. For example, your perception of the new smartphone will be shaped by your previous experiences with similar products and your expectations. Understanding these stages helps PR professionals create messages that can effectively influence public perception. For example, a PR campaign for a new healthcare initiative would need to consider how the target audience senses, selects, organises, and interprets information about healthcare to ensure the campaign is successful.
18.3.3 Factors Influencing Perception
Several factors influence how we perceive information. * Personal Factors: These include individual characteristics such as age, gender, personality, and past experiences. For instance, a young tech-savvy individual in India might perceive a digital banking app as convenient and essential, while an older person might find it confusing or unnecessary. * Situational Factors: These are external factors related to the context in which the perception occurs. For example, the time and place of a message can significantly affect how it is perceived. A PR message about environmental conservation will be perceived differently if it is delivered during an environmental crisis compared to a time of environmental stability. * Social Factors: These involve the influence of society and culture on perception. Cultural norms, social expectations, and group affiliations play a significant role. For example, in a diverse country like India, cultural background can greatly influence how people perceive social media campaigns. By considering these factors, PR professionals can better understand their audience and craft messages that effectively manage perceptions. For instance, a PR campaign aimed at promoting women's education in rural India must consider the cultural and social factors that influence how education is perceived in these communities. Hope, by now, you have an understanding of perception and its critical role in public relations. 18.4 ROLE OF PERCEPTION IN PUBLIC RELATIONS
18.4.1 Building and Managing Perceptions
In public relations, building and managing perceptions is a fundamental task. The perception that the public holds about an organisation can significantly impact its success or failure. PR professionals have the role to create a positive image and manage any negative perceptions that may arise. Consider the case of Amul, one of India's leading dairy brands. Amul has successfully built and maintained a positive public perception through consistent messaging and strategic communication. Their advertising campaigns, often featuring the iconic Amul girl, are not only humorous but also timely and relevant, addressing current events in a light-hearted manner. This has helped Amul build a strong, positive perception as a brand that is both trustworthy and relatable. Managing perceptions involves several steps:
1. Identifying Target Audiences: Knowing who you need to influence is crucial. For example,
Amul targets a broad audience, including families, health-conscious consumers, and even children.
2. Crafting the Message: The message should be clear, consistent, and aligned with the brand's
values. Amul's messaging emphasises quality, tradition, and fun, which resonates well with their target audience.
3. Choosing the Right Channels: It's important to use the appropriate communication channels
to reach your audience. Amul effectively uses traditional media like print and billboards, as well as digital platforms like social media, to reach a diverse audience.
4. Engaging with the Audience: Interaction with the audience helps build a strong relationship
and manage perceptions. Amul engages with its audience through social media, creating a sense of community and loyalty.
5. Monitoring and Responding: Continuous monitoring of public perception and timely
response to any issues are essential. Amul's PR team is quick to address any negative feedback or misconceptions, ensuring the brand's image remains positive.
18.4.2 Perception and Media
The media plays a crucial role in shaping public perception. In today's digital age, where information spreads rapidly, the media's influence is more significant than ever. As PR professionals, understanding the media landscape and its impact on public perception is vital. Let's take the example of the Swachh Bharat Abhiyan (Clean India Mission), a nationwide campaign launched by the Indian government. The media has played a significant role in promoting this initiative, shaping public perception, and encouraging participation.
1. Media Coverage: Extensive media coverage can amplify a message and influence how it is
perceived by the public. The Swachh Bharat Abhiyan received widespread coverage across print, television, and digital media, highlighting its importance and generating public interest.
2. Framing of Messages: How the media frames a message can significantly impact public
perception. Positive framing of the Swachh Bharat Abhiyan, focusing on its benefits and successes, helped build a favourable perception of the campaign.
3. Media Relations: Building strong relationships with media professionals can help in
managing perceptions. By providing timely and accurate information about the Swachh Bharat Abhiyan, the PR team ensured that the media conveyed the campaign's objectives effectively.

4. Social Media Influence: Social media platforms have become powerful tools for shaping
public perception. The Swachh Bharat Abhiyan utilised social media to engage with the public, share success stories, and encourage citizen participation, thus creating a positive perception. Media's role in shaping perception is evident in these examples. For PR professionals, leveraging media effectively involves understanding the media scenario, crafting messages that resonate with the audience, and maintaining strong media relations.

18.5 STEPS AND STRATEGIES FOR EFFECTIVE
PERCEPTION MANAGEMENT
18.5.1 Research and Analysis
Effective perception management starts with thorough research and analysis. Understanding the audience and their perceptions is crucial for crafting successful PR strategies.
1. Audience Analysis: Identify and understand your target audience. This involves
segmenting the audience based on demographics, psychographics, and behaviour. For example, if you are working on a PR campaign for a new educational app, you might target students, parents, and educators. Each segment may have different perceptions and needs, which should be considered in your strategy.
2. Perception Analysis: Assess the current perception of your organisation or campaign.
Tools like surveys, focus groups, and social media listening can provide valuable insights. For instance, if a telecom company wants to launch a new service, they need to understand how customers currently perceive their brand and what expectations they have.
3. Competitive Analysis: Analyse the perception of competitors to identify opportunities and
threats. This can help in positioning your brand effectively. For example, if you are promoting an eco-friendly product, understanding how competitors are perceived regarding sustainability can help you highlight your unique selling points.
18.5.2 Message Crafting
Crafting the right message is essential for influencing public perception. The message should be clear, consistent, and resonate with the target audience.
1. Key Messaging: Develop core messages that convey the essence of what you want to
communicate. These messages should align with your organisation's values and objectives. For instance, if you are working on a PR campaign for a healthcare initiative, your key messages might focus on accessibility, affordability, and quality of care.
2. Storytelling: Use storytelling techniques to make your message more engaging and
relatable. Stories can humanise your brand and create an emotional connection with the audience. For example, sharing success stories of individuals who have benefited from your healthcare initiative can make your campaign more impactful.
3. Cultural Sensitivity: Ensure that your message is culturally appropriate and resonates with
the audience. In a diverse country like India, it's important to consider regional differences and cultural nuances. For instance, a PR campaign promoting a new food product should consider regional tastes and preferences.

18.5.3 Media Channels
Choosing the right media channels is crucial for effective perception management. The channels you select should align with your target audience and campaign objectives.
1. Digital Media: Digital platforms like social media, websites, and email newsletters are
effective for reaching a wide audience quickly. For example, a PR campaign for a new smartphone in can leverage social media platforms like Instagram and Twitter/X to reach tech-savvy young consumers.
2. Traditional Media: Traditional media like newspapers, television, and radio are still
influential, especially for reaching older audiences or rural areas. For instance, a government PR campaign on healthcare awareness might use television and radio to reach a broad audience across India.
3. Integrated Approach: Combining digital and traditional media can maximise reach and
impact. For example, a PR campaign for a new movie release can use television ads, social media promotions, and influencer partnerships to create a buzz across multiple platforms.
18.5.4 Crisis Management
Handling negative perceptions during a crisis is a critical aspect of perception management. A well-managed crisis can even strengthen an organisation's reputation.
1. Preparedness: Have a crisis management plan in place. This includes identifying potential
risks, preparing response strategies, and training spokespersons. For instance, an airline might have a plan to handle crises like flight delays or safety incidents.
2. Transparency: Communicate openly and honestly during a crisis. Acknowledge the issue,
provide accurate information, and update the public regularly. For example, during a product recall, an FMCG company should inform consumers about the issue, the steps being taken to resolve it, and how they can return or replace the product.
3. Swift Response: Act quickly to address the crisis and prevent it from escalating. A timely
response can mitigate negative perceptions and demonstrate the organisation's commitment to resolving the issue. For instance, when faced with a social media backlash, a brand should promptly address the concerns and take corrective actions.
Example: Maggi Noodles Crisis
A notable example of effective crisis management is the Maggi noodles crisis. In 2015, Nestle faced a major crisis when allegations of excessive lead content in Maggi noodles surfaced. The company promptly recalled the product, conducted extensive testing, and communicated transparently with the public. By taking swift action and being transparent, Nestle managed to regain consumer trust and successfully reintroduced Maggi noodles to the market. These strategies for effective perception management, when applied thoughtfully, can help PR professionals build and maintain a positive image for their organisations, even in challenging situations. 18.6 TOOLS AND TECHNIQUES FOR PERCEPTION
MANAGEMENT
18.6.1 Media Relations
Building strong relationships with journalists and media outlets is crucial for ensuring favourable coverage and managing public perception. The commonly used tools to do this are:
1. Press Releases: A well-crafted press release can effectively communicate important news
and shape public perception. For example, when Infosys launches a new service, a detailed press release highlighting the benefits and innovations can generate positive media coverage.
2. Press Conferences: Hosting a press conference allows for direct interaction with the
media, enabling PR professionals to convey key messages and answer questions. For instance, during a product launch, companies like Tata Motors often hold press conferences to provide in-depth information and generate media interest.
3. Media Kits: Providing media kits with comprehensive information about the organisation,
including press releases, fact sheets, and backgrounders, helps journalists write accurate and positive stories. For example, a State tourism board might create media kits for journalists covering a major tourism campaign.
4. Media Monitoring: Regularly monitoring media coverage helps PR professionals
understand how their messages are being received and make adjustments as needed. Tools like Meltwater and Google Alerts can track mentions and sentiment, providing valuable insights.
18.6.2 Social Media
Social media has revolutionised perception management, offering direct and immediate channels for communication with the public.
1. Content Creation: Creating engaging content that resonates with the target audience is
key. For example, Zomato's witty and relatable social media posts have helped build a strong, positive perception of the brand among young Indians.
2. Influencer Collaborations: Partnering with influencers can amplify messages and reach
a broader audience. For instance, beauty brands like Nykaa collaborate with popular beauty influencers to promote their products, leveraging the influencers' credibility and reach.
3. Community Engagement: Actively engaging with the online community fosters a
positive relationship and builds loyalty. For example, Amul regularly interacts with its followers on social media, responding to comments and sharing user-generated content.
4. Crisis Management: Social media can also be a powerful tool for managing crises.
Addressing negative comments promptly and transparently helps mitigate damage. For instance, when a restaurant faces a food safety issue, promptly addressing the concern on social media and outlining corrective measures can help maintain trust.
18.6.3 Public Events
Public events offer opportunities to engage directly with the audience and shape perceptions through personal interaction and experiential marketing.

1. Product Launches: Hosting an event for a product launch allows the organisation to
showcase its offerings and create a buzz. For example, smartphone companies like OnePlus often organise grand launch events to introduce new models, attracting media and consumer attention.
2. Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) Events: CSR events demonstrate the
organisation's commitment to social causes, positively influencing public perception. For instance, Infosys Foundation's initiatives in education and healthcare highlight the company's dedication to societal development.
3. Trade Shows and Exhibitions: Participating in industry-specific trade shows provides
opportunities to network, display products, and enhance brand visibility. For example, Indian tech companies participating in events like the India Mobile Congress can position themselves as industry leaders.
4. Community Outreach Programs: Organising community outreach programs helps build
a positive image and strengthen relationships with local communities. For example, companies like ITC organise health camps and educational programs in rural areas, enhancing their reputation as socially responsible organisations.
18.6.4 Content Marketing
Content marketing involves creating valuable, relevant content to attract and engage the target audience, ultimately shaping their perception of the brand.
1. Blogs and Articles: Publishing informative and engaging blog posts and articles
establishes the organisation as a thought leader. For instance, HCL Technologies regularly publishes articles on emerging tech trends, positioning itself as an industry expert.
2. Videos and Webinars: Creating video content and hosting webinars provide a dynamic
way to share information and engage the audience. For example, Flipkart's behind-the- scenes videos and webinars on e-commerce trends help build a strong connection with consumers and industry professionals.
3. E-books and Whitepapers: Offering in-depth resources like e-books and whitepapers
adds value and demonstrates expertise. For example, a financial services company like HDFC might publish whitepapers on investment strategies, enhancing its credibility and trustworthiness.
4. Infographics and Visual Content: Utilising visually appealing content like infographics
makes information more digestible and shareable. For instance, UNICEF uses infographics to communicate key messages about child health and education effectively.

18.7 CASE STUDIES
Let us now look at some of the popular cases that illustrate how effective perception management can lead to successful outcomes and shape public perception, even in challenging situations. * Swachh Bharat Abhiyan The Swachh Bharat Abhiyan (Clean India Mission) is a notable example of a successful perception management campaign in India. Launched by Prime Minister Narendra Modi in 2014, the

campaign aimed to eliminate open defecation and improve solid waste management across the country. Background and Objectives: The primary objective of the Swachh Bharat Abhiyan was to promote cleanliness and sanitation. The campaign sought to change public attitudes towards hygiene and encourage active participation from all sections of society. Strategies and Execution:
1. Media Campaigns: The campaign utilised mass media extensively, including television,
radio, and print advertisements featuring prominent personalities like Amitabh Bachchan and Sachin Tendulkar, to spread the message of cleanliness.
2. Social Media Engagement: Social media played a crucial role in engaging with the
younger generation. Hashtags like #SwachhBharat and #MyCleanIndia were used to create a buzz and encourage citizen participation.
3. Public Involvement: The campaign involved the public through initiatives like Swachh
Bharat Runs, cleanliness drives, and competitions among cities and states for cleanliness rankings.
4. Partnerships: Collaborations with corporates, NGOs, and celebrities helped amplify the
campaign's reach and impact. For instance, partnerships with companies like Hindustan Unilever brought in additional resources and expertise. Outcomes: The Swachh Bharat Abhiyan successfully changed public perception about cleanliness and sanitation. It led to a significant increase in toilet construction and usage, particularly in rural areas. The campaign also heightened awareness about waste management and personal hygiene. By effectively managing perceptions, the Swachh Bharat Abhiyan became one of the most recognised and impactful public health initiatives in India. * Maggi Noodles Crisis The Maggi noodles crisis is an exemplary case of crisis perception management. In 2015, Nestle India faced a major crisis when allegations of excessive lead content in Maggi noodles emerged, leading to a nationwide recall and a significant blow to the brand's reputation. Background and Objectives: The crisis began when food safety regulators in Uttar Pradesh reported that samples of Maggi noodles contained high levels of lead. The objective for Nestle was to manage the crisis effectively, restore public trust, and reintroduce Maggi noodles to the market. Strategies and Execution:
1. Transparency: Nestle adopted a transparent approach by acknowledging the issue and
cooperating with regulators. They provided regular updates and detailed information about their actions to address the problem.
2. Product Testing: The company conducted extensive testing of Maggi noodles in
independent laboratories both in India and abroad to verify the safety of the product. The results were shared publicly to reassure consumers.
3. Public Communication: Nestle communicated openly with the public through press
releases, media briefings, and social media. They addressed consumer concerns, clarified misconceptions, and provided a timeline for the product's return.
4. Rebranding and Relaunch: Once the product was cleared by authorities, Nestle
relaunched Maggi noodles with a strong emphasis on quality and safety. The relaunch campaign included new packaging, marketing messages highlighting the safety of the product, and promotional offers. Outcomes: Despite the initial setback, Nestle successfully managed the crisis and rebuilt consumer trust. Maggi noodles made a strong comeback, regaining its market position within months of the

relaunch. The case demonstrates the importance of transparency, proactive communication, and rigorous quality control in managing public perception during a crisis.

18.8 CHALLENGES IN PERCEPTION MANAGEMENT
18.8.1 Negative Publicity
Negative publicity poses a significant challenge in perception management. It can arise from various sources, including media reports, customer complaints, or social media backlash. Addressing negative publicity requires a strategic and proactive approach.
1. Monitoring and Response: Continuous monitoring of media and social platforms is
crucial for identifying negative publicity early. Tools like Mention and Hootsuite can help track mentions and sentiments. For example, if a leading airline faces customer complaints about delayed flights, timely monitoring allows the PR team to respond quickly and address the issues.
2. Transparent Communication: Being transparent and honest when dealing with negative
publicity helps build trust. For instance, if a pharmaceutical company faces allegations of adverse effects from a new drug, providing clear, factual information about the situation and the steps being taken to resolve it can mitigate negative perceptions.
3. Addressing Root Causes: It's essential to address the underlying issues that led to negative
publicity. For example, if an e-commerce company receives negative reviews about delayed deliveries, improving logistics and customer service can help resolve the problem and restore the brand's image.
4. Positive Content: Balancing negative publicity with positive content can help shift public
perception. Highlighting positive stories, achievements, and testimonials can counteract the negative impact. For instance, after facing a data breach, a tech company can focus on sharing stories about their improved security measures and customer support efforts.
18.8.2 Managing Misconceptions
Misconceptions about an organisation or its products can lead to unfavourable perceptions. Addressing and correcting these misconceptions is a key challenge in perception management.
1. Educational Campaigns: Launching educational campaigns to inform the public and
clarify misconceptions is effective. For example, a food company might run a campaign to educate consumers about the health benefits of its products and dispel myths about ingredients.
2. Engaging Influencers: Collaborating with influencers who can credibly address
misconceptions and provide accurate information helps reach a broader audience. For instance, a fitness brand might partner with nutritionists to counteract false information about diet products.
3. Direct Communication: Engaging directly with the audience through social media, Q&A
sessions, and public forums allows organisations to address misconceptions head-on. For example, a telecom company facing misconceptions about network quality can host live sessions where experts explain the technical aspects and improvements made.

4. Utilising Data and Facts: Presenting data and information helps correct misconceptions.
Sharing statistics, case studies, and third-party endorsements can reinforce the message. For example, a renewable energy company can use data to demonstrate the environmental benefits and efficiency of their technology.
Example: Ola's Ride Safety Measures
Ola, a popular ride-hailing service in India, faced misconceptions about ride safety. To address this, Ola launched a comprehensive campaign highlighting their safety measures, such as driver background checks, real-time tracking, and in-app emergency features. They used social media, influencer partnerships, and direct communication to educate users and correct misconceptions, successfully improving public perception of their safety standards. Check Your Progress 3: Note: 1) Use the space provided below for your answers.
2) Compare your answers with those given at the end of this unit.
1. What strategies can be used to handle negative publicity?

2. How can organisations address misconceptions?

18.9 THE FUTURE OF PERCEPTION MANAGEMENT
18.9.1 Technological Advancements
Technological advancements are shaping the future of perception management, offering new tools and techniques to influence public perception.
1. Artificial Intelligence (AI): AI is revolutionising perception management by enabling
advanced data analysis and predictive modelling. AI can analyse vast amounts of data from social media, news, and other sources to identify trends and sentiments. For example, AI- powered tools can help a fashion brand understand consumer preferences and tailor their marketing strategies accordingly.
2. Big Data Analytics: Big data analytics allows organisations to gain deeper insights into
public perception and behaviour. By analysing data from various sources, PR professionals can identify patterns and trends, making informed decisions. For instance, a retail company can use big data to understand shopping trends and personalise marketing campaigns.
3. Virtual Reality (VR) and Augmented Reality (AR): VR and AR are emerging as
powerful tools for engaging audiences and shaping perceptions. For example, real estate companies can use VR to offer virtual tours of properties, enhancing the buying experience and influencing perceptions positively.
4. Blockchain Technology: Blockchain technology offers transparency and accountability,
which can enhance public trust. For example, a supply chain company can use blockchain to provide verifiable information about product origins and processes, building trust with consumers.
18.9.2 Changing Consumer Expectations

As consumer expectations evolve, PR professionals must adapt their perception management strategies to meet these changes.
1. Demand for Authenticity: Today's consumers value authenticity and transparency.
Organisations that are honest and open about their practices tend to be perceived more positively. For example, a cosmetics company that transparently shares information about ingredient sourcing and manufacturing processes can build stronger consumer trust.
2. Personalisation: Consumers expect personalised experiences and communications.
Leveraging data and technology to deliver tailored messages and offers can enhance perception. For instance, an e-commerce platform can use personalised recommendations and targeted marketing to improve customer satisfaction and loyalty.
3. Social Responsibility: Increasingly, consumers expect organisations to demonstrate social
responsibility. Companies that actively contribute to social and environmental causes are perceived more favourably. For example, ITC's sustainability initiatives and community development programs enhance its reputation as a socially responsible organisation.
4. Engagement and Interaction: Consumers expect to engage with brands directly and
receive prompt responses. Organisations that effectively engage with their audience on social media and other platforms can build stronger relationships and positive perceptions. For instance, brands like Swiggy and Zomato actively interact with customers on social media, addressing queries and feedback promptly.
Example: Tata's Sustainability Initiatives
Tata Group has consistently adapted to changing consumer expectations by focusing on sustainability and social responsibility. Tata's initiatives in renewable energy, education, and healthcare demonstrate their commitment to societal development. By aligning their business practices with consumer values, Tata has maintained a strong and positive public perception. Embracing technological advancements and understanding evolving consumer expectations will be crucial for the future of perception management. PR professionals who stay ahead of these trends will be better equipped to shape public perception and drive organisational success.
18.10 LET US SUM UP
Perception management is a vital component of public relations, involving strategic efforts to influence how the public views an organisation. This unit covered the definition, importance, and key principles of perception management. It discussed various tools and techniques, such as media relations, social media, public events, and content marketing. Through real-world case studies, we learned how effective perception management can drive success. Challenges in perception management, such as negative publicity and misconceptions, were also explored, along with strategies to address them. The future of perception management, shaped by technological advancements and changing consumer expectations, was highlighted.

18.12 GLOSSARY
Perception Management: Strategies and actions taken to influence how the public perceives an organisation or individual.

Media Relations: Building and maintaining relationships with journalists and media outlets. Crisis Management: Strategies used to handle and mitigate the impact of a crisis on an organisation's reputation. Social Responsibility: Ethical framework suggesting that entities, whether government, corporate, or individuals, have an obligation to act for the benefit of society at large.

2.0 INTRODUCTION
If we look at our media habits, we will find that we consume a large amount of AV (audio- visual) content. The same is happening in the field of news. Audio-visual news reaches us through television or online media. Broadcast-based television is a relatively old medium. The rise of the Internet, its expansion and increase in its speed have changed the world of news a lot. A large number of people are getting news through internet-based platforms. In this unit, we'll discuss different aspects related to the production of AV (audio-visual) news.
2.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After going through this Unit, you will be able to: * describe the characteristics of audio-visual news; * explain the stages in production of audio-visual news; and

* discuss the fundamental rules of audio-visual news writing.
2.2 AV NEWS
AV (audio-visual) news has two components - audio and visual. Visual component dominates. As far as audio is concerned, it supports and compliments the visuals. Many a times the audio plays very crucial role in AV news. It helps in explaining the message, setting the mood of the scene and expressing the emotions of the characters. It is really very difficult to produce an effective AV content without the audio component. Different types of audio elements are used in AV programmes, for example - voice-over, characters' voice, background music, ambience and various sound effects. Now we shall discuss the most important component of AV, i.e., visuals. Visuals are the core component of AV news used to convey the message primarily. The term visual encompasses various elements, like - recorded video, photographs, animations and graphics.
2.3 AV NEWS FOR TELEVISION
As we discussed earlier that audio-visual news is mainly delivered to the people through two types of media - first television and second online platforms. Television news channels use only AV news content. So, in this section we will discuss various aspects of TV news only
2.3.1 What is News for Television
We all know that television is an audio-visual medium with dominance of visuals. Keeping this in mind, we can say that news with visuals is television news. But it does not mean that news without visuals is not fit for TV. Presently, if any important event happens and there is no possibility of immediate visuals, then that piece of news is put on 'air' with the help of graphic plates containing texts. In this scenario, the TV behaves like a speaking newspaper. Though news is always news, yet visually rich events and happenings are considered more suitable for television due to the inherent nature of this medium. Hence at times, you can observe that news which is played big on TV, does not even find a mention in the newspapers. Yet another important factor related to TV is TRP (Television Rating Points). It emerged as one of the most important factors in deciding news for television in India. Desire to grab big commercial market after economic liberalization and the resultant cut-throat competition among news channels completely changed the definition of news and the whole gamut of news. Crime stories are still considered important in news channels because there is a separate dedicated audience for this genre. But, in recent times, news channels have developed a self- regulatory body which keeps eyes on their content.
2.3.2 Characteristics of TV News

We know that television news is quite different from other media i.e. print and radio. We shall now discuss the main characteristics of television news.
Audio-Visual Medium
Let us start with the critical and most significant characteristics of TV- it is an audio-visual medium. You can hear the description of any happening or event and at the same time you can also watch visuals of the same. You would agree that without visuals TV is nothing more than a radio, so visuals are indispensable elements for TV. Television tends to select those stories which have visuals and dramatic content like fire, crime, natural disasters, embarrassed politicians etc. In the early stages of evolution of the TV news, only recorded visuals were put on 'air'. Visuals used to be brought to the news rooms usually on tapes. But, newer technologies have changed the whole scenario. With the help of satellites, 'live' elements began to be added and gradually visuals started coming on 'live' also. With more developments on the technology front, there are now many ways to bring the visuals to the news rooms and put them on 'air'. The two elements, audio and visuals make TV news very special. You would have certainly watched the video of 9/11. Just think, if television was not there, you would have only read about that gruesome terrorist attack. Now, recall 26/11 as many of you might have watched every detail of it, be it small or big, on the TV sets sitting at your home. If TV had not been there, you would not have seen brutality of terrorists, bravery of our soldiers and endurance of our citizens. It has the potential to change your perception of the event. Hence, the strength of this medium to show each and every development live should be utilized judiciously in many contexts.
Quicker Delivery
Now tell us one thing. What would you do to satisfy your curiosity if you hear that there was a bomb blast in a big city of some other country? Tune in to Radio? Wait for newspaper to be delivered next morning or switch on your TV to watch any news channel? You would certainly watch a TV news channel because you will get each and every detail of what has happened and at the same time you will be able to see the activities at the scene of crime. You will see the damage, rescue works, how the police are investigating the matter, who took the responsibility, information about suspects, it means whole lot of information within minutes. In another words, news is delivered quickly through television. This is an important characteristic of TV news. Distance does not matter for television. You will get the comprehensive news within minutes even if the event happens thousands of kilometers away. As soon as the news comes in, it is delivered through graphic plates of 'Breaking News'. And later visuals are inserted either 'live'

or recorded. Meanwhile, the reporter or any witness on the spot is connected through phone who provides all the information.
Wider Reach
You will certainly agree that a significant part of our population is still illiterate. There are millions of people who cannot read and write but they can be made aware of news by seeing it on TV or in other words even those unable to read newspapers can watch TV news and easily comprehend. Apart from this, there are many people who do not find time to read newspapers. They can watch TV news at least when they are sitting in their drawing room for entertainment and surf TV channels for news. This shows that TV news has a wider reach than any other news medium. So news through TV reaches more people than newspapers. Moreover, there is no need to allocate a separate budget for TV news as TV has already reached most of the houses in our country. In fact, TV has almost become a necessity in our day-to-day life because it is one of the cheapest medium of entertainment. And when you subscribe to any cable service provider or DTH, you certainly get news channels also.
Greater Impact
Yet another characteristic of TV News is its impact on an individual as well as on the society as a whole. If a crime happens at any nook or corner in your city and the local media start covering it then the whole government machinery begins to act swiftly. This is not to undermine the impact of the print media but in comparison the impact of TV is much greater, quicker and more penetrating. A newspaper may carry an exclusive report about corruption in any government department, but that story will reach out to a large segment of the society only if that story is carried by the TV news channels also. And when that story reaches the masses in a short time period, the government and ruling class tend to be anxious and conscious of their image. At the same time, in order to score brownie points and create favorable impression about their political party, the attacks from other political opponents begin. The whole matter gets escalated within a few hours and forcing the government or the department under question to take action. TV news not only helps build images but also destroys them quickly. There are numerous examples where the power of TV news has helped to mobilize people and create movements.
