2.0 INTRODUCTION
Public health plays an important role in disease prevention efforts in both the developing world as well as in developed countries, through local health systems and non-governmental organizations. The focus of a public health intervention is to improve health and quality of life through prevention, treatment and management of diseases, injuries and other physical and mental health conditions through surveillance of cases and the promotion of healthy behaviors, communities and environments. The World Health Organization (WHO) is the international agency that coordinates and acts on global public health issues. Most countries have their own government public health agencies, sometimes known as ministries of health, to respond to domestic health issues. The public health system in India is managed by the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare of the government of India with state-owned health care facilities.
2.1 OBJECTIVES
On completion of this Unit, you should be able to: * understand the history of medicine, * explain the background of public health, * describe what public health is, * explain the changing concepts of public health, and * describe the health care revolution of curbing the public health issues.
2.2 HISTORY OF MEDICINE
In the evolution of medicine, medicine has drawn richly from the traditional cultures, biological and natural sciences and also from social and behavioural sciences. In ancient times, health and illness were interpreted in a cosmological perspective. Thus, medicines were heavily dominated by magical and religious beliefs. The primitive people attributed disease, calamities and all human suffering to 'evil spirits'; people used different means to drive away evil spirits such as appeasing gods by prayers, rituals and sacrifice, using charms and amulets, etc. At present in India, such practices are still continuing in the form of black magic. Indian medicines are mainly Ayurveda and Siddha. Ayurveda is traced back to the Vedic times about
5000 B.C. (Park 2015). The medical history was associated with mythological figures, sages and
seers. Ayurveda by definition implies the "knowledge of life" witnessed tremendous growth and development during the Buddhist times. King Ashoka and the other Buddhist kings patronised Ayurveda as the state medicine and established schools of medicine and public hospitals. Disease was explained as a disturbance in the equilibrium of the three humors such as vata (wind), pitta (gall)

and kapha (mucus). This theory of disease is similar to the theory of Greek medicine of four humors. In ancient Indian medicine, hygiene was given an important place. It was also mentioned that the Indus Valley revealed advanced knowledge of sanitation, water supply and engineering. Likewise, the other indigenous system of medicines namely, Unani- Tibb and Homoeopathy were introduced into India by the Muslim rulers during 10th century A.D. Today, Unani-Tibb and Homoeopathy have become part of Indian medical treatment options.
2.3 EVOLUTION OF PUBLIC HEALTH
The period from 1453-1600 A.D. was the vital period for medicine in the world. The 17th and 18th centuries were the period of discoveries of circulation of blood by Harvey in1628, Leeuwenhoek's microscope in 1670 and vaccination against smallpox by Jenner, 1796 who had founded a new area in evolution of public health. During the industrial revolution of the 18th century, there were several problems like creation of slums, overcrowding with all its ill-effects, accumulation of filth in cities and towns, high rates of sickness and death especially among women and children, infectious diseases like tuberculosis, industrial and social problems which deteriorated the health conditions of the people. The 'great sanitary awakening' in the mid- nineteenth century which took place in England was another historic milestone in the evolution of public health. It had a tremendous impact in modifying the behaviour of people. The great cholera epidemic of 1832 led Edwin Chadwick to investigate the health of the inhabitants of the large towns with a view to improve their conditions. Thus, 'The sanitary conditions of the labouring population in Great Britain' a landmark in the history of public health, set London and other cities on the way to improve housing and working conditions. In19th century, cholera which was often called the 'father of public health' appeared time and again especially in the western world. John Snow (1848), an English epidemiologist studied the causes of cholera and established the role of polluted drinking water in the spread of cholera. William Budd, in1856 observed the outbreak of typhoid fever in the rural north of England which spread due to polluted drinking water. After these two discoveries, legislation was brought into force in England namely, the Public Health act of 1875. Sir John Simon (1816-1904) was the first medical officer of health of London and was one of the prominent sanitary reformers. His efforts were directed entirely towards general cleanliness, and disposal of garbage. His system of public health in England was admired and followed in different countries. This early phase (1880-1920) of initiative in public health is addressed as "the disease control phase'. The development of the public health movement in America closely follows the English pattern. France, Spain, Australia, Germany, Italy, Belgium and the Scandinavian countries subsequently developed their public health. By the beginning of the 20th century, there was a broad foundation of public health- clean surroundings; clean water, proper housing conditions, control of offensive trades, etc., were laid in all the countries of the western world. The concept of "Germ Theory of Disease" breakthrough came in1873, when the French bacteriologist Louis Pasteur (1822-1895) demonstrated the presence of bacteria in air. He advanced the 'germ theory of disease'. In 1877, Robert Koch (1843-1910) showed that anthrax was caused by bacteria. Thus, the discoveries of Pasteur and Koch confirmed the germ theory of disease. It was the golden age of bacteriology. Microbes were also discovered in quick succession-gonococcus in 1847; typhoid bacillus, pneumococcal in 1880; tubercle bacillus in 1882; cholera vibrio in1883; diphtheria bacillus in1884, etc. All attention was focused on microbes and their role in disease causation. Thus, it stopped the dogma and superstition and put on robes of scientific knowledge.
2.4 WHAT IS PUBLIC HEALTH?
Public health refers to "the science and art of preventing disease, prolonging life and promoting human health through organised efforts and informed choices of society, organisations, public and private, communities and individuals" (Winslow, 1920). The WHO Expert Committee on Public Health Administration, adapting Winslow's earlier definition has defined " the science and art of preventing disease, prolonging life, and promoting health and efficiency through organised community efforts for the sanitation of the environment, the control of communicable infections, the education of the individual in personal hygiene, the organisation of medical and nursing services for early diagnosis and preventive treatment of disease, and the

development of social machinery to ensure for every individual a standard of living adequate for the maintenance of health, so organising these benefits as to enable every citizen to realise his birthright of health and longevity". Public health is an approach to concentrate on what we can do collectively, as a society to assure the conditions in which people can be safe and healthy. The perception of preventive, promotive, curative and rehabilitative is seen as an integrated existence and a just division of medicine. It is a tool to understand the health status of a population by using different disciplines, for example- epidemiology, bio-statistics, social sciences, demography, etc., as a basic science of public health and consequently help in influencing the policy and programmes in health sector of a state helping to prioritize relevant issues. So, multidisciplinary is a characteristic of public health. With the adoption of the goal of "Health for All" by members of WHO in 1981, public health is redefined as "the organised application of local, state, national and international resources to achieve "Health for All" i.e., attainment by all people of the world by the year 2000 of a level of health that will permit them to lead a socially and economically productive life". According to Park (2015), there are four distinct phases of public health: a) Disease Control Phase (1880-1920) During 19th century, public health was largely focused on sanitary legislation and sanitary reforms aimed at the control of man's physical environment like water supply, sewage disposal, etc. Thus it was not focused on controlling any specific disease; however, such measures had improved the health conditions of people and controlled infectious diseases. b) Health Promotional Phase (1920-1960) A new concept of 'health promotion' began to take shape at the beginning of 20th century. During the previous phase, individuals were neglected, it was realised that the State had a direct responsibility for the health of an individual. Thus, health promotion of individual was added to public health. It was further initiated as personal health services such as mother and child health services, school health services, industrial health services, mental health and rehabilitation services. Later public health departments began expanding their programmes towards health promotional activities. They promoted a provision of "basic health services" through the medium of primary health centres and sub-centres for rural and urban areas. The Bhore Committee,1946 of India recommended the establishment of health centres for providing integrated curative and preventive services. Later "Community Development Programme" was also introduced to promote village development through the active participation of the whole community and on the initiative of the community. But it failed to reach out to the people due to inadequate resources and limited time. c) Social Engineering Phase (1960-1980) Due to advances in practices of public health, the pattern of disease began to change both in developing and developed countries as many of the acute illnesses have been brought under control. But new health problems in the form of chronic diseases such as cardiovascular diseases, cancer, diabetes, etc., began. The concept of 'risk factors' as determinants of these diseases came into existence that gave a chronic burden on the society. Thus, public health entered into a new phase called 'social engineering' which needed reorientation towards the society. Public health moved into the preventive, behavioural change and rehabilitative aspects of chronic diseases. d) Health for All Phase (1981-2000AD) In this phase, it is seen that most people in the developed countries and elite of the developing countries are enjoying all the health determinants such as education, adequate income, nutrition, safe drinking water, sanitation and comprehensive health care. Unfortunately, only a small percentage of the population in developing countries had access to health services of any kind. Thus, there was a global awakening that the health gap between rich and poor within countries and between countries should be narrowed and ultimately eliminated. So, the neglected world's population too has an equal claim to healthcare, to protect themselves from the killer diseases of childhood, to primary health care for mothers and children, etc.

2.5 CHANGING CONCEPTS OF PUBLIC HEALTH
The two major branches namely, curative medicine, and public health/preventive medicine were evident at the close of the 19th century. The pattern of disease began to change to non- communicable diseases, the so called modern diseases such as cancer, diabetes, HIV/AIDS, cardio vascular disease, mental illness and accidents came into prominence and have become the leading causes of death in developed countries. The realization began that there are other factors or causes in the etiology of diseases, namely social, economic, genetic, environmental and psychological factors which are equally important. Most of these factors are linked to a man's life style and behaviour (Park, 2015). The germ theory of disease gave place to a newer concept of disease i.e., multi factorial causation. Epidemiologists have significantly contributed to the concept of multi factorial causes of diseases and risk-factors in the etiology of disease. The developments in modern medicine are conceptualised broadly under the following heads: a) Curative Medicine In mid 20th century, a profound revolution brought allopathic medicine which has been defined as 'treatment of disease by the use of drug which produces a reaction that itself neutralises the disease'. The primary objective of curative medicine is the removal of disease from the patient (rather than the mass). Hence, to accomplish this objective, it employs diagnostic techniques, and treatment. The medical technologies have developed due to advancement in the science, technology, understanding of human body, which further helped in coming up with specialization. Some of the specializations that have emerged are- surgery, radiology, anaesthesia, ENT, ophthalmology, cardiology, gynecology, pediatrics, geriatrics and obstetrics, etc. Specialisations have raised the standards of medical care but it has simultaneously increased the cost of medical care and placed specialist medical care beyond the affordability of an average citizen. Specialisation has further contributed to the decline of general practice and the isolation of medical practitioners at the periphery of the medical care system. b) Preventive Medicine Although the term 'public health' has lost its original meaning the terms like preventive medicine, social medicine and community medicine are used as synonyms for public health. The term preventive medicine comes from United States where public health was almost exclusively concerned with the prevention of infectious disease and was dominated by the medical profession. Preventive medicine is applied to healthy people, customarily by actions affecting large numbers of populations. Preventive medicine includes health promotion, treatment and prevention of disability. It is not only to prevent the occurrence, progression of disease, disability, mental and physical but also the timely application of all means to promote the health of individuals and of the community as a whole, including prophylaxis and health education. Initially preventive medicines were in the field of bacterial vaccines and antisera which helped in declining the morbidity and mortality from diphtheria, tetanus, typhoid fever and others. After the discovery in the field of nutrition such as recognition of the role of vitamins, minerals, proteins and other nutrients, a new dimension have been added to Preventive medicine. New strategies have been developed for combating specific deficiencies such as nutritional blindness and iodine deficiency disorders. Further the discovery of synthetic insecticides such DDT, HCT, malathion and others have brought fundamental changes in the strategy to control the vector- borne diseases which have been among the most important world-wide health problems for many years. The discoveries of anti- malarial drugs, anti- tubercular drugs, anti-leprosy drugs and antibiotics have all enriched preventive medicine. Later in 20th century, the development of screening for the diagnosis of disease at preliminary stage has become an important part of preventive medicine. But preventive medicine is currently faced with the problem of population explosion in many developing countries like India where uncontrolled growth of population is causing social, economic, political and environmental problems. It has further branched into new areas such as screening for disease, population control, environmental control, genetic counselling and prevention of chronic diseases. Scientific advances, improved living standards and education of the public have opened up a number of new avenues to prevention. There are three levels of prevention, i.e., primary prevention, secondary

prevention and tertiary prevention. The primary prevention is intended to prevent disease among the healthy people; secondary prevention is attempted towards those in whom the disease has already developed; and tertiary to reduce the prevalence of chronic disability consequent to disease. Thus, preventive medicine is a kind of anticipatory medicine. c) Social Medicine The term 'Social medicine' was first introduced by Jules Guerin, a French physician in 1848. The background of the idea came from the French Revolution which broke out in France and spread to Italy, Austria, Bohemia and Hungary. The revolution was aimed at establishing a new order and new society based on socialism. In 1911, the concept of social medicine was revived by Alfred Grotjahn of Berlin who stressed the importance of social factors in etiology of disease known as social pathology. Social medicine can be defined as "the study of man as a social being in his total environment". Social medicine reflected a concern with role of social factors in the etiology of disease and the need for government intervention in the areas of disease prevention and medical care. It is concerned with all factors affecting the distribution of health and ill health in populations including the use of health services. It is an extension of the public health idea reflecting the strong relationship between medicine and social sciences. Social medicine is an expression of the humanitarian tradition which includes care of patients, prevention of disease, and administration of medical services. Thus, social medicine is not a new branch of medicine but rather a new orientation of medicine to the changing needs of man and society. d) Community Health The terms public health, preventive medicine and social medicine have been replaced by community health in some countries. A EURO symposium in 1966 defined community health as including "all the personal health and environmental services in any human community, irrespective of whether such services were public or private ones". e) Family and Community Medicine The emergence of Family and community medicine has been a rediscovery of the human, social, local and cultural aspects of health and disease, and of the recognition of family as a focal point of health care and the right place for integrating preventive, promotive and curative services. Family oriented medicine is applied to the care of patients and their families; it becomes the speciality of practice. Likewise community medicine has also shared common ground. Community medicine implies activity at the local level rather than the national action abhorred by the conservative leadership of the medical profession. 2.6 HEALTH CARE REVOLUTION
The standard of health services was not catering to the real needs of a large section of people. A very high proportion of the population in many developing countries, especially those living in rural areas

does not have ready access to quality health services. Rather the health services favoured only the privileged group and urban dwellers. It is considered that health is a fundamental human right but there is a denial of this right to millions of people who are caught between poverty and ill health. Therefore, there are marked differences in health status between people in different countries as well as between different groups in the same country. To improve the health conditions of all sections of the population, an increasing importance is being given to social justice, equity, recognition of role of community participation, changing ideas about the nature of health and development.
Primary Health Care in India
Government of India launched a Rural Health Scheme, based on the principle of placing people's heath in people's hands in1977. The health care delivery has developed three tier system based on the recommendations of the Shrivastav Committee in 1975. As a signatory to the Alma-Ata Declaration, the Government of India was committed to achieving the goal of Health for All through primary health care approach which seeks to provide universal comprehensive health care at a cost which is affordable. Thus, the Government of India evolved a National Health Policy based on primary health care approach and was approved by Parliament in 1983.The National Health Policy laid down a plan of action for reorienting and shaping the existing rural health infrastructure with specific goals to be achieved by1985, 1990, and1995 within the frame work of the Sixth (1980-85) and Seventh (1985-90) Fiver Year Plans and the new 20 point Programme. Likewise, National Health Policy 2000, National Population Policy 2002, National Rural Health Mission 2005, National Health Mission 2013 with formulation of Indian Public Health standards have been taken up to curb the public health problems in India.
Millennium Development Goals
In September 2000, representatives from189 countries met at the Millennium Summit in NeYork, to adopt the United Nations Millennium Declaration. The goals in the area of development and poverty eradication are now referred as "Millennium Development Goals" (MDGs). The goals are an integral part of the road map towards the implementation of the UN Millennium Declaration. The health related Millennium Development goals in India are: Goal 1: Eradicate extreme poverty and hunger MDG 2: achieve universal primary education MDG 3: promote gender equality and empower women Goal 4: Reduce child mortality Goal 5: Improve maternal health Goal 6: Combat HIV/AIDS, malaria and other diseases Goal 7: Ensure environmental sustainability Goals 8: Develop global partnership for development. 3.0 INTRODUCTION
A brand represents the relationship customers have with an organisation. But not all brands are able to sustain or evoke long term commitments in their customers. This is where the concept of brand equity comes in. Simply put, brand equity is the commercial value of a brand, derived from customer loyalty, their awareness of the product, and their perception of it. This concept helps one understand why some brands have more customer loyalty and more market value than others. Any good company will include strong brand equity as part of its long-term marketing strategy. In this unit, we will explore the foundations of brand and brand equity. Here, we shall try and understand the four major components of brand equity - brand identity, brand meaning, brand response and brand resonance. Furthermore, we will learn how to measure and manage brand equity over time.
3.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After working through this unit, you will be able to: * Identify the different perspectives on brand equity; * Outline the components of brand equity marketing communications to build brand strategy; and * Comprehend how companies have managed their brands over time.

3.2 CONCEPT OF BRAND AND BRAND EQUITY
At times, when we see a symbol, a logo, an alphabet or a name, a term, or some specific features, we can identify a particular product associated with it. That product may be a good or service. For example, if you see a blue washing powder, the first thing that comes to our mind is, this is Surf. According to the American Marketing Association (AMA), a brand is a "name, term, sign, symbol, or design, or a combination of them, intended to identify the goods and services of one seller or group of sellers and to differentiate them from those of competition". These brand names can come in different forms. Sometimes they are based on names of people like Haldiram's Snacks, and at times they are based on a geographical location like Bikanerwala. Suppose you are at a shop to buy a detergent bar to wash your white shirt. There are so many detergent bars available at the shop and yet you ask for Rin. There might be other detergent bars which are better than or cheaper than Rin, still, you buy Rin because you know the product, you have been using this product, you are satisfied with the product, and you do not want to change. That is Brand Equity. As a business, when your products have positive brand equity, your brands' products are easily recognisable by the customers. They are memorable, impactful, and leave a positive impression on your consumers. This results in financial benefit for the company and allows the company to charge a premium for its products. The concept of Brand Equity has three perspectives: * Financial-based perspective * Employee-based perspective * Customer-based perspective The financial-based perspective defines brand equity as the "total value of a brand which is a separable asset
- when it is sold or included in a balance sheet" (Feldwick, 1996). An alternative definition considers brand
equity as "the incremental cash flows which accrue to branded products over unbranded products" (Simon & Sullivan, 1993). So, when we measure brand equity from this perspective, it is expressed purely in monetary terms. The employee-based perspective defines brand equity as the value a brand provides to a firm through its effects on the attitudes and behaviors of its employees (Tavassoli, Sorescu, & Chandy, 2014). This perspective is significant as many 'strong brands' today are services or products with an important service component, in which employees play an important role in the delivery of the brand experience. Employees who understand and committedly endorse the organisation's objectives deliver value to their customers and thus serve as a base to build customer-based brand equity. The customer-based perspective approaches the concept of brand equity from a customer's viewpoint. The customer can either be an individual or an organisation, an existing customer or a prospective customer. According to David Aaker, brand equity is a set of brand assets and liabilities linked to a brand, its name, and symbol, that add to or subtract from the value provided by a product or service to a firm and/or to that firm's customers (Aaker, 1991) . This perspective is based on the idea that to create a strong brand, a business should understand how the customers think and feel.
3.3 COMPONENTS OF BRAND EQUITY
As we discussed above, customer-based brand equity is based on creating positive experiences for your customer. For achieving this, the company has to understand the needs of its customers and provide them with appropriate products and maintain relationships with them. One needs to focus on various components which lead to building brand equity. Let us now look at an established model which discusses the components of brand equity.

According to Keller's Pyramid Model, there are four different levels of brand building where companies have to understand their customers and design strategies as per their needs. This model is shown in figure
3.1.
Figure 3.1: Keller's Brand Equity Pyramid Model Source: Keller (1993)
3.3.1 LEVEL 1: BRAND IDENTITY
In this stage, the company needs to create brand awareness. You have to communicate to your customers about who you are. At this stage the customers do not know your brand, they cannot differentiate between your brand and other brands in the market. It is necessary to ensure that your brand stands out, and it is recognisable by the customers and they are aware of it. You also have to make sure that brand perceptions are "correct" at all the significant stages of the buying process. At this stage, you will use target marketing and advertising campaigns to make the customers aware of your products and identify the brand.
3.3.2 LEVEL 2: BRAND MEANING
To find brand meaning, customers would want to know the features of the products, their reliability, durability, and other features which will provide them value for money. This level is made up of two major building blocks of brand associations that define the meaning of brands in customers' minds: brand performance and brand imagery. Brand performance: The performance of your brand is important for the customer and this can make or break your brand's position. This refers to how well your products can meet your customer's needs. This includes : * Primary characteristics and features of the product * Product reliability, durability, and serviceability * Service effectiveness, efficiency, and empathy * Style and design of the product * Price of the product Indian companies like Mahindra, Bata, Hero Honda, Jio, Titan, Lakme, Raymonds have built great brand equity because they have delivered what they have promised to the customers and sometimes even more than their promises. Brand imagery: This refers to the image that customers perceive about the brand. Customers have a picture of a brand in their minds which is shaped by various factors. For example, when we think of a car, what do we expect? We expect a mode of transport that is comfortable as well as safe. Similarly, for a fast-food brand, we expect it to be delivering the eatables fast with less waiting time. Brand image can be built through target marketing and word of mouth.

3.3.3 LEVEL 3: BRAND RESPONSE
Customers have specific expectations from a brand and when those expectations are met by the brand, the customer is happy and shows positive behavior. If the brand exceeds the customer's expectations, the customer will be delighted and he/she will recommend your brand to others in the market. Customers get "feelings" as a result of such favorable experiences. On the other hand, if customer expectations are not fulfilled by the brands, then he/she is left with negative feelings which can be termed as "judgments". It is critical for the brand to strike a balance between "Judgements" and "Feelings" in order to establish brand equity. If there are too many customers who have negative opinions about your brand, your products will not be sold in the market. So, in order to be successful, your customers must have a greater number of positive feelings rather than the negative judgements.
3.3.4 LEVEL 4: BRAND RESONANCE
This level is the most important and desirable level of brand equity but it is equally difficult to achieve hence this level is at the top of the pyramid. This is the stage where the brand has built a strong social and psychological relationship with the customer and the customer is highly engaged with the brand. A buyer is devoted to the brand, believes it is superior, and will not buy anything else. The customer also advocates the merits of the brands to others. For example, a person who has once ridden a Royal Enfield motorcycle will not switch to another brand as he/she feels deeply associated with it, even though there are cheaper motorcycles available in the market. Customers may be willing to take part in online forums or social media, or any other event related to the brand. Customers respond to a variety of factors, including lifetime experience, customer service, products, and value. Very few brands are able to reach this level. Some of the examples of such brands are Harley-Davidson, Apple, and Amazon. Activity: 1 Choose one of your favorite brands and analyse its four components of brand equity. 3.4 INTEGRATING MARKETING COMMUNICATIONS TO
BUILD BRAND STRATEGY
To be successful in the market, companies need to inform, persuade, and remind consumers--directly or indirectly--about the brands they sell. For this, companies use marketing communications to establish a dialogue and build relationships with consumers.These marketing communications not only represent the voice of a brand but also create a brand image and build brand awareness among the consumers. Besides establishing the point of similarity, marketing communications at times explain the points of difference with

competition, making an impression on consumers' minds. This leads to the development of strong consumer-based brand equity as well as long-lasting relationships. While designing and implementing brand-building communications in today's evolving environment, companies need to be careful as well as creative in reaching their customers. The companies need to ensure that their communication is reaching the right people at the right time and at the right pace and place. To judge the effectiveness of its marketing communication, companies need to follow a three-step model. You as a company could answer the following questions stepwise to judge the effectiveness of your marketing communications: Step 1: Current Brand Knowledge: What is my customers' current knowledge about my brand? Have I created a detailed map in their minds? Step 2: Desired Brand Knowledge: What is the brand knowledge of customers that I desire for? Have I defined the ideal points of parity and difference and my brand mantra? Step 3: Communication: How does the communication option help the brand to achieve the desired brand knowledge of consumers? Have I clarified the specific effects on knowledge created by communication? Knowing the answers to these questions will help you to know whether your communication contributes to brand awareness or if it helps in creating, maintaining, or strengthening certain brand associations. The answers will also help you to know whether these communications have resulted in positive favorable brand feelings or negative brand judgements. You will also get to know whether the communications have enhanced consumers' knowledge and encouraged them to buy more of your products or not. Traditionally, companies have been using audiovisual and print media along with promotions to communicate with their customers. But over time these mediums underwent a change. Communication avenues like television advertisements have undergone subtle changes. Marketing research revealed that the consumer tends to watch their favourite shows on various platforms after their telecast. Marketing research also revealed that the consumers tend to skip the advertisements during the recorded programs. In this case, the companies are unable to communicate with consumers despite spending resources on creating the advertisements. Research also reveals that consumers today are tech and information savvy and like to spend more time on their mobile screens for playing games and surfing on social media. Keeping in view the changing tastes and preferences of consumers, companies are progressively using multiple avenues to reach their customers along with the traditional means. In the era of the internet, social media and big data companies are increasingly using means like websites, blogs, applications (apps), in-app advertising, and social media handles to reach out to their customers. These modern means of communication not only have faster reach but have a boundary-less and timeless appeal to customers. Figure 3.2 Marketing options used by companies

3.5 DEVELOPING A BRAND EQUITY MEASUREMENT AND
MANAGEMENT SYSTEM
A brand equity measurement system is a system designed to effectively measure the source and outcome of branding strategies. It provides a set of up-to-date and relevant information, which can then be used effectively for tactical and strategic decision-making. There are two methods that can be used in designing measurement systems. While the indirect method sorts and records emotional level changes in consumers, direct measurement method measures and analyses consumer response towards brand in terms of sales, revenues, etc. A brand equity measurement system is composed of three key components. These components are as follows:
3.5.1 Conducting Brand Audits
A brand audit is a customer-centered exercise that examines your market position in comparison to competitors and evaluates the overall efficacy of your approach. While conducting a brand audit, besides taking a closer look at the situation within your company, you also take a closer look at your branding and brand values. You undertake a SWOT analysis and analyse your strengths and weaknesses to determine the direction in which your company should develop. Brand audit is like a full health check-up of the company to identify its target market and needs, produce products as per those needs, and ultimately increase the return on investment (ROI). Brand audit is used to set the strategic direction of the brand and consists of two steps: brand inventory and brand exploratory. While brand inventory provides detailed information about the marketing and branding of the company's products, brand exploratory helps to identify what the consumers think and feel about the brand.
3.5.2 Designing Brand Tracking Studies
After conducting brand audits, companies design brand tracking studies. These studies are quantitative in nature, and help in knowing the current performance of brands based on key dimensions identified by brand audit. These studies involve collecting information from the customers on a routine basis to provide valuable tactical insights of the short-term effectiveness of marketing programmes and activities. By tracking its brand, a company can monitor its own health with respect to the competitive landscape and obtain information that facilitates its marketing team's decision-making. This exercise also helps to know whether the marketing programmes have been able to deliver the intended effects. To achieve desired results, the companies should know who, what and when to track, and how to interpret the results gathered by this exercise. The information gathered will lead to the generation of a brand equity report and creating responsibility centers, which can oversee the development of an efficient marketing department. Thus, this process can help create a perfect brand equity measurement and management system.
3.5.3 Establishing Brand Equity Management System
In order to set up a brand equity management system, the company should follow three major steps as shown in figure 3.3. Figure 3.3: Steps in establishing a brand equity management system

For establishing an efficient and effective brand management system, the company should first emphasise on formalising its view of brand equity in a document, and prepare the brand charter. This document will not only account for the company's general philosophy with respect to brand equity, but it will also summarise the activity and outcomes of brand audits, brand tracking, and related studies. An updated charter will assist in identifying new opportunities and emerging risks, while also reflecting information gathered from the brand inventory and brand exploratory exercises. Furthermore, it will also assist in laying out the guidelines for brand strategies and tactics for proper brand treatment. After formulating the brand charter, the company should assemble the results of tracking studies and other relevant outcomes to prepare a brand equity report. This report will not only provide descriptive information on what is happening to a brand, it will also provide diagnostic evidence on why it is happening. These reports should be updated and distributed to management on a regular basis. For ease of review, these reports could be displayed in marketing dash boards. Lastly, the senior management must oversee the treatment of brand equity within their own company. These senior executives in charge of overseeing the brand charter and brand equity reports should make sure that product and marketing actions are carried out in such a way that the spirit of the charter and the substance of the report are reflected across divisions and geographic boundaries to maximise the brand's long-term equity.
3.6 MEASURING SOURCES OF BRAND EQUITY
It is very important for the companies to know the level of brand knowledge of its products among the consumers. For measuring the sources of brand equity, the companies should have in-depth understanding of why and how customers buy and use their products, what customers know, think, feel and how they act towards its brands. It is important to gather this information not only to build the strategies for marketing communication, but also for measuring the change in the consumers' buying patterns due to implementation of marketing programs. Unearthing this information is challenging because this crucial brand knowledge resides in the customer's mind. Companies need to unravel this emotional information and convert it into data for analysis using quantitative and qualitative approaches. Qualitative approaches are relatively unstructured approaches and permit a range of questions along with their answers. They help to identify the possible brand associations and brand equity. These techniques are the first step in exploring the perceptions of brands and products among the consumers. Because of their unstructured nature these measures are appropriate to provide an in-depth glimpse of what brands and products mean to consumers which might be otherwise difficult to decode. However, due to the qualitative nature of data, the interpretations of answers may differ from person to person. Generally, these techniques are applied to a small sample size, so the results obtained from these qualitative techniques cannot be generalised to a larger population. While quantitative measures are useful to identify the range of associations with a brand and some initial insights into the brand's strength, favorability, and uniqueness, quantitative techniques provide a definite and precise portrait of the brand that allows the companies to make strategic and tactical decisions. The data gathered from these quantitative techniques is often represented by numerical summaries and charts. Besides providing important information about the depth and breadth of brand awareness, these techniques provide useful insights into the strength, favorability, and uniqueness of brand associations. They also help to understand the negative judgments and positive feelings along with the extent and nature of brand relationships. Basically, these techniques are used to measure the brand awareness and its image amongst the customers.
3.7 MANAGING BRANDS OVER TIME
The markets in which the companies operate today are highly dynamic due to constant change in consumer lifestyle, tastes and preferences, government regulations, introduction of technology, etc. As the brand moves in its life cycle, it faces saturation at some point in time. At this point in time, companies must focus

on expanding awareness and look for ways to generate more consumption. Consumption can either be increased by highlighting instances of consumption or by highlighting the diverse ways and occasions where the brand can be consumed. For the survival of a brand, it is necessary that brand equity is strengthened by developing marketing programs, which express brand knowledge consistently and do not confuse the consumer. Brand knowledge is derived from brand attributes and brand association. If the company tries to fiddle these sources, the customers will be confused, and the resulting effects can be devastating. For example, Koutons - the apparel retailer, frequently used temporary price reductions (50% to 50%+40%) to promote the sale of its apparel. This created and strengthened a "discount" association to the brand and had negative effects and responses from customers when the company implemented non price-oriented marketing communication efforts. So, when the company stopped offering the discounts for which it was known, the customers did not buy its products. The company which was incorporated in 1991ultimately filed for liquidation. For survival of their brands, companies should not only be active in managing brand equity over time by reinforcing the brand meaning, they must also be proactive in adjusting their marketing programmes to identify fresh sources of brand equity. For example, Wipro launched Santoor soap in the mid1980s as a sandal and turmeric soap. This soap was priced attractively and achieved little success against well- established brands like Lux, Hamam, and Cinthol in the popular segment of India's soap market. Very soon, the brand lost momentum and its growth slowed down. In order to revitalise the brand, the company moved away from emphasis on ingredients - sandal and turmeric - to a promise of skin care and younger-looking skin. This change in approach brought in instant results, brought the brand back to the growth track, and attracted a whole new set of users. For this, Wipro not only adjusted, revitalised and strengthened the Santoor advertising over time; it also modified and improved the product and its packaging. 3.9 GLOSSARY

Brand Audit: It is the process of examining the market position of your product in comparison to competitors and evaluating the overall efficacy of your approach. ROI: Return on Investment is a financial ratio used to calculate the benefit an investor will receive from the investment cost. SWOT: Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities and Threats (SWOT). It refers to strategic planning and management techniques used by companies to identify internal strengths and weaknesses and external opportunities and threats.
