3.1 INTRODUCTION
There are four major activities of any media organization - news gathering, editorial decision making, converting selected news material into presentable formats and disseminating it to the public. You can consider newsroom as the most important part of any news organization as raw news content reaches here from various sources, editorial decisions are taken here, after gatekeeping process the raw news content is converted into presentable formats and then it is finally sent to the public. All of these activities take place in the newsrooms of both television

and online news organizations. In this unit, we will discuss the structure and functioning of television and online newsrooms.
3.2 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After going through this unit, you should be able to: * describe the structure of a television newsroom; * explain functioning of a TV newsroom; and * discuss the roles and responsibilities of different components of a TV newsroom.
3.3 NEWS PRODUCTION IN A TV NEWS CHANNEL
To understand the functioning of a newsroom, it's imperative to first take a look at the production process of news bulletins or a news programme in a news channel. Let us have a glimpse. We have already stated that newsroom setups are not similar in all the channels, and there also differences in the nomenclature of desks and personnel. For example, in some channels, the people who are in-charge of news bulletins are called Producers, whereas in some other channels they are called Output Editors. In the same manner what is termed the Assignment Desk in some channels, in the other channels, it is known as the Input Desk. As in any news media, there are two branches for the production of news in a channel. First is the news gathering and second is to make the raw news presentable for the viewers. Newsroom comes into the picture in the second stage. When a reporter has done his/her job of news gathering, which here means shooting of the story, the work goes forward. First the reporter comes back to the newsroom and writes his/her script. These days it is done on computer, which is connected to all computers of the office through local area network (LANs). In fact, these days, computers are connected through wide area networks (WANs) as well, so the senior officials of the news channels also remain connected to the office systems from anywhere. After the script is written, it goes to the script desk, where it is checked by a senior person. When the script is cleared, reporter takes it and goes for the voice over and video editing. Video editing is a technical process. In every channel now, reporters are required to edit their stories themselves. A video editor, who is a technical person, checks the edited story before it is published for telecast. As the story is published, the reporter hands it over to the production/ output desk. Production/output desk can then include that story in a Rundown; in some channels it is also known as a Run Order. A Rundown or a Run Order is a sequence of Headlines and stories, which are to be played. Then, the Production/output person goes to the PCR (production control room) with the Rundown. From there, the final telecast takes place which is entirely a technical process executed by engineers and other technological experts. However, a newsroom person or a journalist always remains there, because, s/he understands the News, and it is his/her

responsibility to keep the bulletin or the programme in order. If there is breaking news, only a journalist can decide how to go into it, how long to stay on that news, what is the need of the coverage, i.e., whether any live interview or graphics are needed, it is s/he who feeds the latest information regarding that news to the anchor. Actually, it is the news producer / output editor, who editorially or you can say, content-wise controls the show. Here we mentioned three main functions of the newsroom- scripting, making rundowns and executing the rundowns. But there are other functions as well which are performed by senior journalists. These are mainly related to conceptualisation, planning and execution. In any channel, the news takes shape from here. It is at this level, that the policies are formulated and the whole newsroom gets its guidance. As we now understand the main functions of a newsroom, we are in position to know its structure, for the simple reason that the structures are made to perform the functions and achieve the targets. Electronic media newsrooms mainly consist of three desks. These are: Assignment or Input desk, Output desk and Script desk. These desks are additional to the sitting arrangements of reporters/ bureaus, as well as other journalists/ functionaries of the channel.
3.4 ASSIGNMENT/INPUT DESKS
As the name suggests, the responsibility of this desk is to arrange and give input to the channel. In practical terms, it means feeding the channel with news items and information, which can be produced and presented to the viewers. This desk consists of many input editors, who work under the guidance of their in-charge and have many functions to perform. Let us look at the job of assignment/ input desk.
3.4.1 Overseeing Reporters
The reporters of the channel come under the assignment/ input desk. From there, they get their work assigned. They have to report to this desk. The reporters are expected to keep the assignment/input desk informed about the status of their stories. If they come to know about any new information or breaking news, they first pass it to the assignment/ input desk. It is this desk, which decides what to do about that information, how much importance it is to be given, and how it is going to be played up. This is the desk which is responsible for whatever news and information you watch on a channel. So, input editors keep an eye on whatever is happening in the world. They continuously keep track of the news agencies, other news channels and news web sites. They are expected to flash all the information that they think would be useful for a channel and the journalists there.
3.4.2 Arranging Visuals
TV being a visual media, visuals are of prime importance there. Every news channel wants to be the first to air the visuals. They also want to air the best visuals available. You can get an idea of this race only by being in a TV newsroom. It is the duty of the assignment/input team to fulfil this need of the channel and they keep pressurising reporters on the spot, to send the visuals as soon as possible. As the visuals are uplinked, they immediately inform the output team and as the visuals arrive they give all the related details to them.

In addition to channel's own sources, the assignment/input team have to continuously track the agencies, like APTN, REUTERS and ANI. Most of the channels subscribe to the services of these agencies and are dependent on these agencies for the visuals of the events and the developments happening in the foreign countries. The assignment/input desk is also expected to keep an eye on the foreign broadcasters, so that they are aware of the events taking place in the areas or countries of interest of the viewers of that particular channel. By overseeing these channels, they also get an idea of the visuals that might be available in due course to their channel.
3.4.3 Arranging Phone-in interviews
When news breaks in, generally the information first comes through phones. If the news is big, then the channels try to stay on it for many hours. It takes time to show the visuals or bytes of the eye witnesses or authorities, due to a simple reason that the reporters or the technical infrastructure can't be present everywhere. As they try to reach there as soon as possible, the channel has to give the latest information to its viewers. So, here come in phone-in interviews. These interviews are called Phonos in newsroom parlance. The assignment/input team first lines-up all their reporters, who can give any piece or type of information or perspective regarding the development. A competent assignment/input team keeps an updated phone directory of important persons from every walk of life, so that they can be approached for information or their perspective in case that a big event or a development occurs in their field. The aim is to keep the viewers engaged, so that they don't switch over to any other channel. Continuing with the latest and new information, new elements, and new perspectives, the newsroom tries to achieve their aim. And providing all these NEW information is the duty of the assignment/input desk. Phonos are not required only in the case of breaking news. During normal coverage also, Phonos are required to get updates or for getting reactions of the concerned parties or persons. It is the assignment/input team that arranges these.
3.4.4 Monitoring Other Channels
The assignment/input desk is required to continuously monitor the other channels, which are its competitors. After all, there is a cut-throat competition to attract more and more viewers. News channels are vying for snatching viewers of the other channels. So the most important thing is to know, which channel is showing what, and in what manner. Based on this information and its analysis, channels prepare their strategy. Generally, the assignment/input desk keeps flashing headlines of other channels every hour on an intra-mail system of the organisation. They also tell the whole team, if some other channel has any exclusive story or extra information/input regarding a running story.
3.4.5 Story Planning
Story planning is a major responsibility of the assignment/input desk. They have to assess the different angles of a story, what elements are required to present the full picture, from where these elements will come, and which reporter is best suited to do that story. After assessing all these aspects, the story is assigned to a reporter; s/he is given a detailed guideline to proceed with, and is also told the deadline. Then the assignment/input desk informs the newsroom about the Expected Time of Arrival (ETA) of the story. It is duty of the assignment/ input desk to

follow and make reporters follow the timetable. Sometimes, a single story needs input from many places. For example, if a story is being done on a controversy regarding an advertisement featuring a cricketer, it might be the case that the player at that time may be in Bangalore and the ad company officials are in Mumbai. Naturally, the bytes will have to be taken in those cities. In addition, it may be imperative to give voice of the fans of the player. These have to be brought from different places. Coordinating and collecting all these inputs and handing it over to the story packaging team are the responsibilities of the assignment/input desk.
3.4.6 Forward Planning
Forward planning implies planning for the near future. Many dates fall in the coming weeks or month, which may be important for news coverage. For example, festivals, birthdays of celebrities, elections, sports tournaments, and release of big budget/ multi-starrer films. It comes under forward planning to prepare a calendar of these events and suggest how the channel should cover it. Providing background material of each and every such event is also the job of the assignment/input desk. The day, every channel will play up the event, your channel should not lack in any aspect or look dull. The assignment/input desk also has to shoulder this responsibility. From above discussion you would have understood that the assignment/input desk of the newsroom is very important. It is the provider of the information, story and perspectives. How other parts of the newsroom perform is totally dependent on the assignment/input desk. In fact, their roles begin after this desk has done its job. Check Your Progress 1 Note: 1) Use the space below for you answers.
2) Compare your answers with those given at the end of this unit.
1. Discuss the role of input desk in a television news channel.

3.5 OUTPUT DESK
The Assignment/input desk gives raw material and the Output cooks it up as `digestible food' for the news hungry audience. To keep the audience engaged, the 'food' should be tasty enough. It's the duty of the Output desk to ensure that the raw information is produced in a presentable format, in the shortest possible time frame and put on air. Output persons have many functions to perform. One should always keep it in mind that the job at the output desk is half journalistic and half technical. If you aspire to work at the output desk, then you must be conversant with modern information and telecast technologies and computer savvy. You must have the knowledge of video editing, news publishing in technological terms, making published stories ready for telecast and all technological nuances of telecast that come across when a news bulletin or a news programme is being aired. You must be aware of the vocabulary of all these processes.

Nowadays, all output persons are expected to (in fact in many channels required to) know video editing. As visuals and bytes arrive, the output team has to edit it in a way that it is available for telecast within minutes. Sometimes when reporters are not present in the office, output persons have to make the full story themselves, so that they fulfil the duty of a reporter as well. Thus, the job of output person is like an all-rounder who performs different functions at different times. Let us now have a look at the main functions of the output desk:
3.5.1 Preparing the Rundown
This may be considered as the foremost job of the output team. In some channels, a Rundown is called as a Run Order. It's the order or the sequence in which the news is planned to be aired. Before every bulletin/programme, an output editor is assigned to make the rundown. S/he prepares it as per the directions of the news editor/executive producer. Generally, a set pattern is followed while making rundowns but nowadays, breaking patterns are in vogue. For example, earlier, headlines had to be the first item in a news bulletin. But now, to present a surprise element to the viewers, channels sometimes begin the bulletin with impressive visuals or interesting bytes. In conventional terms, these things are called teasers, and now often, teasers are becoming the first thing in a news bulletin. The pattern of a Rundown is given below -- * Headline * Anchor Link giving a glimpse of what is special or interesting in his/her kitty * News stories * Discussion with guest or reporter (if it is planned) * Teaser before going for a commercial break * Commercial break * Come back * Headlines (optional) * News stories * End of the bulletin. News bulletins or programmes may be of half an hour or an hour's duration. This pattern continues if the bulletin or the programme is of an extended duration.
3.5.2 Executing the Rundown
It is the duty of Output Editor (OE) / producer to execute the rundown and for doing this s/he has to go to the PCR (production control room). The OE/ Producer works there with a team of technical persons. The OE/Producer is expected to be present in the PCR much before the actual telecast begins. The person has to line-up the OBs and Phonos. If the anchor is doing continuous bulletins and cannot find time to go through the Rundown, s/he has to tell the anchor the whole plan of the bulletin.

While the bulletin is in the progress, the OE/Producer is the point person and is answerable for all content related matters. Thus it is a job of responsibility and a job of journalistic as well as technical competence. In case of breaking news, skills of the whole team of a news channel are tested, but it's a special test for the OE/Producer. S/he has to take decisions then and there and has to feed the anchor with the latest information and also direct the PCR team to go where, how and to whom. S/he has to coordinate with reporters, keep a track on coming visuals and bytes and get them played according to importance and novelty. The job of making and executing rundowns is given to capable and experienced people. On a news heavy day or during the breaking news situations, they are assisted by other people at the output desk as well.
3.5.3 Getting Stories on Air
As discussed above, the input desk arranges stories and raw materials and hands it over to the output desk. Now it is the duty of the output team to put it on air. The edited or prepared stories could be included in the rundown at once, as they are ready for telecast. The output team is expected to know about the full content, the visual sequence and the bytes details etc. of the story, therefore they first have to watch it. If they feel that story is lacking somewhere they ask the input desk to get that corrected by the concerned reporters. In case the story has come from out station or the reporter is not available, this has to be done by the output team itself. Working in a television news channel is a very fast affair. The reporters are expected to write scripts and edit their stories themselves, but sometimes they have to remain in the field for long time, as they have to cover minute to minute detail of a developing story. Obviously they can't return to the office just for filing their story. In those cases, they give information regarding the story on phone and explain the visual and bytes details to the input desk. Then the input desk tries to get that story by some other reporter, but if there is a shortage of human resource at that front, then the output desk has to do that job.
3.5.4 Information on Screen
When you are watching news, you see many written information on the TV screen. In that information you will find the gist of the story, the name and the designation of the person whose bytes have been used in the story, the information about the location, which means the place where the incident has taken place or the place where the concerned person has given the bytes. In TV news parlance, this information is called a SUPER. Putting supers is also the output team's responsibility. Thus, command on the language is necessary to work at the output desk. Whatever you write, it goes on air, appears at the TV screen and is seen by the viewers. So, there is no scope for any mistake and you have to be foolproof. In western countries, the trend of the cluttered screen is decreasing, but in India it is on the rise. Here TV news channels are cluttering their screen with more and more information. It is believed that some studies have reinforced this thinking that cluttered screens are helpful in keeping viewers remain at the channel. Even though watching visuals being covered by text information can be agonising for the enlightened viewers, the channel officials think otherwise. Anyway, supers are a very important part of a news story, and writing these has its own demand. Having command on the language is not enough; you must be innovative as well. Supers are written in a very limited number of words. There is a limit to accommodate the numbers of letters on the screen. You are asked to write 'catchy' supers, i.e., such words which

will appeal to the viewers and which leave them amused. Their aim is to create curiosity; keep the viewers occupied, and tell the story in such a manner that it synchronises with the visuals and the theme of the story.
3.5.5 Tickers
Whenever you watch a news channel, you see that the top headline stories are running in a written text form at the bottom of the screen. These are called Tickers. Putting tickers is also a job of the output team. Generally, in news channels, one person is specially assigned for this duty. His/her job is to keep information continuously updated. As we saw in the case of supers, this is also a specialised job. A person of deep news sense, having command on the language, and capable of writing correctly in hurried situations as well, is given this responsibility. Tickers are considered very important as many viewers go to a news channel just to scan the main news of the day or of that hour, and they get it from the tickers. As the tickers are running continuously, one does not need to follow the clock and hit the channel at the beginning of the hour. Secondly, tickers give an idea of the priorities of the selection of news in a particular channel. It attracts viewers of a particular taste, and it may distract other viewers if they find information running at the bottom of the screen intriguing. For example, if a channel runs a horoscope forecast in the ticker, then many viewers who take news seriously, may shift to some other channel. Similarly, if there is only serious news on the ticker, then the viewers of who prefer lighter news may shift to other 'location'. Thus, tickers are written according to the channel's policy. There are some simple rules for it. You have to put the information here in a very simple and communicative language. If you can create magic with the language without compromising on simplicity, then that is highly appreciated. Tickers are also used as programme promos. You must have seen that channels give information about their forthcoming programmes in tickers, with the objective to inspire people to watch those programmes at the scheduled time. From above analysis you would have understood that working at the output desk is full of responsibilities. If you want to get a job at output desk, you must have a sound news sense, technical competence and you should be a good team person. In addition, you must know video editing, have command on the language and patience to handle the breaking news situations, because at that moment things are very fluid and decisions have to be taken quick and fast. 3.6 SCRIPT DESK
In television, apart from the visual element, the act of listening also plays an important role. Therefore, if camera person is an integral part of TV news presentation, so is the script writer. Script Desk consists of senior and highly experienced persons as writing a script is a job of responsibility. Only those persons are considered for writing scripts, who have in-depth knowledge about social, political, economic, and legal issues as well as have excellent command on the language. In news channels, in normal situations, reporters write their scripts themselves. After that they go to the script desk to get their scripts checked. Outstation reporters send their scripts through mail, then they inform it to the input desk, and the input desk asks the script desk to check the script. The script editor goes through all the facts written in the scripts carefully. If s/he has doubt anywhere, s/he asks for clarification from the reporter. Only after being fully satisfied, s/he clears the script. It is also expected from the script editor that s/he will do necessary corrections in the language of the script and make it more simple and catchy. At times, script editors have to write the full script when the story is being prepared on desk only. A news channel telecasts many special programmes of half an hour's duration and scripting of these programmes is done on the desk. The script person goes through all the visuals and bytes available, and writes the script for the planned programme. These days, stories of short duration are in vogue and in some television channels, scripts for news stories are written in not more than 90 words which is a challenging task. Moreover, since scripts are written to the pictures; visuals get priority over the words. In fact, it is said that the words are written according to the available pictures - to explain and match the visuals. They should enhance the impact and the effectiveness of the pictures. A script editor is required to learn these qualities to fulfil the specific demands of a news channel They have to develop a visual sense and for the NEWS part of the story, the information is also significant which comes from reading. If you wish to work as script writer; you must develop the habit of reading a serious newspaper thoroughly on a regular basis and develop a visual sense.
3.7 FUNCTIONING OF A TV NEWSROOM
On a normal day, when there is no breaking news or it is not a big news day like elections, newsroom functions in a set pattern. Every morning, there is phone conferencing with all the bureaus, reporters, and input desk persons. Executive Editors and other bosses or in-charges of different departments also take part in it. In this very meeting, the agenda of the day begins to take shape. Bureaus and reporters inform what they have to offer that day - if they have some special story or information, what events or developments are going to or are expected to happen in their area. Decisions are then taken which development or event or news has to be given how much importance. Accordingly, a plan of coverage is chalked out and guidelines given to the reporters.

After this meeting, the input desk follows up and implements the decisions and keeps the office informed about the progress regarding the stories. Meanwhile, whatever information is received, the input desk keeps forwarding to the output desk and the output as per its news sense, the policy of the channel and the orders from the bosses, keeps putting that information on air. This sequence breaks only when there is breaking news. During breaking news situation, a new style of working comes into operation. In a professional news channel, a special breaking news drill is organised occasionally to keep the staff prepared. In this situation, only that news and the information relating to it go on air. two most popular social media sites.

In this unit, we tried to discuss the structure and functioning of newsrooms of television and online news organisations. It is important to understand the role of different components and workflow. We talked about the various important departments of a television newsroom and discussed how a television newsroom works. Apart from TV newsrooms, we discussed in detail the structure and functioning of the newsroom of online news platforms.

3.0 INTRODUCTION
Welcome to the Unit on Market Segmentation, a crucial aspect of persuasive communication strategies. In this Unit, we'll explore how dividing a market into distinct segments can enhance the effectiveness of advertising and media efforts. By understanding your audience better, you can craft messages that resonate deeply, ensuring that your campaigns are more impactful. Market segmentation is the backbone of successful marketing strategies. It allows advertisers to identify and target specific groups of consumers who are more likely to respond positively to their messages. This Unit is designed to equip you with the knowledge and skills needed to segment markets effectively.

Throughout this Unit, we'll explore various types of market segmentation, the process involved, and how to implement these strategies in real-world scenarios. We'll use examples to illustrate key points, making the concepts more relatable and easier to understand.
3.1 LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of this unit, you would be able to: * Understand the fundamental concepts and importance of market segmentation in advertising and media. * Identify and differentiate between the various types of market segmentation, including demographic, geographic, psychographic, and behavioural segmentation. * Analyse the steps involved in the market segmentation process and evaluate the criteria for effective segmentation. * Apply targeting and positioning strategies to select appropriate market segments for different products or services.
3.2 UNDERSTANDING MARKET SEGMENTATION
3.2.1 Definition and Concept
Market segmentation is the process of dividing a broad consumer or business market into sub-groups of consumers (known as segments) based on some type of shared characteristics. These segments can be defined by various criteria, such as demographics, psychographics, behaviour, or geography. The main goal is to identify and target groups of consumers with similar needs or preferences. What is Market Segmentation? At its core, market segmentation is about recognising that different consumers have different needs and preferences. Instead of trying to appeal to the entire market with a single marketing approach, businesses can develop specific strategies tailored to each segment's unique characteristics. This targeted approach increases the likelihood of meeting the needs of each segment more effectively. For example, consider a company that sells beauty products. Rather than marketing all its products to everyone, the company might segment its market into groups like young women, older women, men, and teenagers. Each group has distinct needs and preferences, so the company can create specific marketing messages and product offerings for each segment.
The Role of Market Segmentation in Advertising
Market segmentation plays a vital role in advertising and media by enabling advertisers to deliver more relevant and personalised messages. By understanding the unique characteristics of different market segments, advertisers can create campaigns that resonate more deeply with their target audiences. This relevance increases the likelihood of capturing the audience's attention and driving desired behaviours, such as making a purchase or engaging with the brand. For instance, a fast-food chain might use market segmentation to target health-conscious consumers with ads promoting their healthier menu options, while simultaneously targeting budget-conscious consumers with ads highlighting value meals and discounts.
3.2.2 Importance of Market Segmentation
Why Do Businesses Segment Markets? Businesses segment markets to better understand and meet the needs of different consumer groups. This understanding allows them to develop products, services, and marketing strategies that are more likely to appeal to specific segments. The primary benefits of market segmentation include:

* Increased Relevance: Tailored messages are more likely to resonate with the target audience. * Improved Customer Satisfaction: By addressing specific needs and preferences, businesses can enhance customer satisfaction and loyalty. * Efficient Use of Resources: Segmentation allows businesses to allocate their marketing resources more effectively, focusing on the most promising segments.
Benefits of Market Segmentation
In the context of advertising, market segmentation offers several key benefits: * Targeted Advertising: Advertisers can create ads that speak directly to the needs and interests of each segment. * Higher Conversion Rates: Tailored messages are more likely to convert viewers into customers. * Better ROI: By focusing on the most receptive audiences, businesses can achieve better returns on their advertising investments.
Real-World Examples
Let's look at some examples from the Indian market to illustrate the importance of market segmentation: * Britannia: Britannia segments its market based on consumer preferences and health consciousness. It offers a variety of biscuits, from affordable Good Day and Marie Gold for mass consumers to NutriChoice for health-conscious buyers. * Dabur: Dabur uses demographic and psychographic segmentation for its personal care and healthcare products. For instance, its premium ayurvedic skincare line caters to urban professionals, while its economy-range hair oils target rural consumers. * Tata Motors: Tata Motors segments its market based on geographic and demographic factors. It targets urban consumers with its compact cars and rural consumers with more rugged, utility- focused vehicles. By understanding these segments and tailoring their marketing efforts accordingly, these companies can effectively meet the diverse needs of the market.
3.3 TYPES OF MARKET SEGMENTATION
Market segmentation is crucial for marketers to effectively target their audience by dividing a diverse market into manageable segments based on specific characteristics. This section explores different types of market segmentation strategies used by companies to tailor their marketing efforts and products to meet the unique needs and preferences of consumers.
3.3.1 Demographic Segmentation
Demographic segmentation divides the market based on variables such as age, gender, income, education, and occupation. This type of segmentation is one of the most common and straightforward methods used by marketers because demographic information is relatively easy to obtain and analyse.

Age Different age groups have different needs, preferences, and buying behaviours. For instance, a cosmetic brand might target younger audiences with products like bright-coloured makeup, while offering anti- aging creams to older consumers. Example: Lakme, a leading cosmetics brand, has different product lines targeted at teenagers and young adults with vibrant, trendy colours, while also offering anti-aging and skincare products for older women. Gender Gender segmentation involves creating different marketing strategies for men and women. Products and advertising messages can be tailored to cater specifically to the preferences and needs of each gender. Example: Many brands, such as Gillette and Dove, create separate product lines and advertisements for men and women. Gillette focuses on men's grooming products, while Dove has a range specifically for women's skincare. Income Income segmentation targets consumers based on their economic status. Companies can offer premium products for high-income consumers and more affordable options for those with lower incomes. Example: Hindustan Unilever offers a wide range of products from premium brands like Dove and TRESemme to more affordable options like Lifebuoy and Sunsilk, catering to different income groups in India.
Education and Occupation
Education and occupation can influence consumer preferences and buying behaviour. Professionals might prefer products that are convenient and time-saving, while students might look for budget- friendly options. Example: Laptops and gadgets are often marketed differently to students and professionals. Dell, for instance, offers budget-friendly models for students and high-performance laptops for professionals.
3.3.2 Geographic Segmentation
Geographic segmentation involves dividing the market based on geographical boundaries such as region, city, or neighbourhood. This type of segmentation is particularly useful in a diverse country like India, where consumer preferences can vary significantly from one region to another.
Regional Preferences
Different regions may have unique cultural, climatic, and economic conditions that influence consumer behaviour. Example: Amul, known for its dairy products, tailors its marketing strategies and product offerings to different regions in India. For instance, it markets lassi and buttermilk more heavily in North India, where these products are more popular. Urban vs. Rural Markets Urban and rural consumers often have different needs and preferences. Urban consumers might prioritise convenience and brand image, while rural consumers may focus on affordability and practicality. Example: Coca-Cola India has distinct strategies for urban and rural markets. In urban areas, the focus is on branding and lifestyle, while in rural areas, the emphasis is on affordability and distribution.

3.3.3 Psychographic Segmentation
Psychographic segmentation divides the market based on consumers' lifestyles, values, attitudes, and interests. This type of segmentation helps marketers understand the deeper motivations behind consumer behaviour. Lifestyle Consumers with different lifestyles may have varying needs and preferences. Lifestyle segmentation can be based on activities, interests, and opinions. Example: Royal Enfield, the iconic motorcycle brand, targets adventure enthusiasts and those with a passion for biking. Their marketing campaigns often emphasise the lifestyle of freedom and exploration.
Social Class
Social class segmentation involves targeting consumers based on their socioeconomic status. Products and marketing messages can be tailored to appeal to different social classes. Example: Titan Watches, a popular Indian brand, offers a wide range of watches from luxury models for the upper class to more affordable options for the middle class.
Personality Traits
Personality-based segmentation focuses on the individual characteristics that influence consumer behaviour. Brands can develop products and messages that resonate with specific personality traits. Example: Harley-Davidson appeals to consumers who value individuality and a rebellious spirit. Their marketing emphasises freedom and non-conformity, resonating with the personalities of their target audience.
3.3.4 Behavioural Segmentation

Behavioural segmentation divides the market based on consumers' behaviours, including their purchasing patterns, usage rates, and brand loyalty, providing insights into consumer preferences and decision-making processes.
Purchase Behaviour
This involves segmenting consumers based on their buying patterns, such as frequency of purchase, occasion of purchase, and benefits sought. Example: Reliance Smart and D-Mart, popular retail chains in India, target frequent shoppers with loyalty programs and special discounts, encouraging repeat purchases. Reliance Smart offers personalized discounts through its digital platform, while D-Mart focuses on everyday low pricing to retain cost-conscious customers.
Usage Rate
Consumers can be segmented based on how often they use a product. This includes heavy users, moderate users, and light users. Example: Telecom companies like Airtel and Jio segment their customers based on data usage. They offer different plans for heavy data users, moderate users, and occasional users.
Brand Loyalty
Loyal customers are a valuable segment for any business. Companies often create special programs and offers to reward and retain loyal customers. Example: Starbucks India has a loyalty program that rewards frequent customers with points that can be redeemed for free

3.4 THE PROCESS OF MARKET SEGMENTATION
3.4.1 Steps in Market Segmentation
Market Research and Data Collection
The first step in market segmentation is gathering relevant data about the market and consumers. This involves conducting market research to understand consumer behaviours, preferences, and trends. Various methods can be used, such as surveys, focus groups, interviews, and analysing existing data. Example: A company looking to segment the Indian market for a new beverage might conduct surveys to understand consumer preferences regarding flavours, packaging, and pricing. They could also analyse sales data from existing products to identify trends and patterns.
Identifying Segmentation Variables and Segmenting the Market
Once the data is collected, the next step is to identify the variables that will be used to segment the market. These variables could be demographic, geographic, psychographic, or behavioural. Example: For a skincare brand, variables might include age, gender, skin type, and purchasing behaviour. The company could then segment the market into groups such as young women with oily skin, older men with dry skin, and so on.

Developing Profiles of Resulting Segments
After identifying the segments, it's essential to develop detailed profiles for each one. These profiles should describe the characteristics, needs, and preferences of each segment. This helps in understanding each segment better and tailoring marketing strategies accordingly. Example: A detailed profile for a segment of young urban professionals might include their average income, preferred communication channels, key motivations for purchasing skincare products, and preferred product attributes (e.g., natural ingredients, quick absorption).
3.4.2 Criteria for Effective Segmentation
Measurable The size, purchasing power, and profiles of the segments should be measurable. This means there should be enough data available to quantify these aspects. Example: For an e-commerce platform targeting fashion products, measurable segments could be based on the frequency of online shopping, average spending per purchase, and preferred categories (e.g., casual wear, formal wear). Accessible The segments should be reachable and serviceable through marketing channels and distribution networks. Example: If a company segments its market based on geographic regions, it should ensure it has the distribution channels to reach customers in those regions. An FMCG company targeting rural areas in India needs an efficient supply chain to deliver products to remote locations. Substantial Segments should be large and profitable enough to justify targeted marketing efforts. Small or insignificant segments may not provide a good return on investment. Example: A luxury car manufacturer may focus on high-income urban professionals because this segment is substantial and profitable, even if it is smaller than the middle-income segment. Differentiable Each segment should respond differently to different marketing strategies. If segments do not show distinct responses, it may not be worthwhile to treat them separately. Example: If both teenagers and middle-aged adults respond similarly to a particular advertising campaign for a smartphone, it might indicate that these segments are not sufficiently differentiable for targeted strategies. Actionable The company should be able to develop effective programs for attracting and serving the segments. This includes having the necessary resources and capabilities to implement segmentation strategies. Example: A small local bakery may segment its market based on dietary preferences (e.g., gluten-free, vegan) but must ensure it has the resources to create and market these specialised products.

3.5 TARGETING AND POSITIONING

3.5.1 Selecting Target Segments
Evaluating and Selecting Target Segments
Once the market is segmented, the next step is to evaluate each segment's attractiveness and select the ones to target. This involves considering factors such as segment size, growth potential, competition, and alignment with the company's strengths and resources. Example: An electronics brand might evaluate segments based on the demand for smartphones and tablets. If the youth segment shows high growth potential and aligns with the brand's innovative image, it may be selected as a primary target.
Strategies for Targeting Multiple Segments
Businesses often target more than one segment, employing different strategies for each. This can be done through differentiated marketing, concentrated marketing, or a mix of both. Example: Maruti Suzuki, an automobile manufacturer, uses differentiated marketing to target various segments. It offers budget-friendly models like Alto for the price-sensitive segment, and premium models like Baleno for the affluent segment.
3.5.2 Positioning Strategies
Differentiating Your Product or Service
Positioning involves creating a distinct image of the product in the minds of the target segments. Differentiation can be based on product attributes, benefits, usage occasions, or user categories. Example: Patanjali positions its products as natural and ayurvedic, differentiating itself from other FMCG brands that use synthetic ingredients.
Positioning Map and Value Proposition
A positioning map helps visualise the competitive landscape and identify opportunities for differentiation. The value proposition is the unique value a product offers to its target segment, making it stand out from competitors. Example: A positioning map for smartphones might plot devices based on price and features, highlighting gaps in the market. A brand like OnePlus might position itself as offering premium features at a mid-range price, appealing to tech-savvy consumers who seek value for money.
Case Studies: Successful Positioning Strategies in the Indian Market
Maggi: Maggi has successfully positioned itself as a quick and tasty meal solution for busy individuals and families. Its tagline "2-minute noodles" emphasises convenience, appealing to both students and working professionals. Tata Tea: Tata Tea's "Jaago Re" campaign effectively positioned the brand as a socially conscious and responsible choice. The campaign encouraged consumers to wake up to social issues, aligning the brand with a cause and resonating with socially aware consumers. 3.6 IMPLEMENTING SEGMENTATION IN ADVERTISING
3.6.1 Developing a Segmentation Strategy
Aligning Segmentation with Marketing and Advertising Goals
To develop an effective segmentation strategy, it's crucial to align segmentation efforts with the overall marketing and advertising goals of the business. This ensures that the segmentation strategy supports broader business objectives, such as increasing market share, improving customer retention, or launching new products. Example: A company like Cadburys may align its segmentation strategy with the goal of expanding its market presence among young adults. This could involve creating targeted campaigns around popular occasions like Valentine's Day or Friendship Day, which resonate with this demographics.
Integrating Segmentation into Marketing Plans
Segmentation should be an integral part of the marketing plan. This includes identifying the target segments, defining the marketing mix for each segment, and outlining how the segmentation strategy will be executed. Example: A clothing brand like FabIndia could integrate segmentation into its marketing plan by creating specific lines of clothing for different segments, such as ethnic wear for traditional occasions and contemporary fashion for young urban professionals.
3.6.2 Creating Segmented Advertising Campaigns
Crafting Messages for Different Segments
Once the segments are identified, the next step is to craft tailored messages that resonate with each segment. These messages should address the specific needs, preferences, and pain points of the target audience. Example: Airtel might create different messages for its broadband services targeting working professionals (emphasising speed and reliability for work-from-home setups) and families (highlighting entertainment options and parental controls).
Media Selection and Scheduling
Choosing the right media channels and scheduling the ads effectively is critical for reaching the target segments. Different segments may prefer different media, such as social media, TV, print, or digital platforms. Example: A brand like Amazon India may use social media platforms like Instagram and YouTube to target young adults, while using TV ads and newspaper inserts to reach a more mature audience.

3.7 EVALUATING AND REVISING SEGMENTATION STRATEGIES
3.7.1 Measuring Segmentation Effectiveness
KPIs and Metrics to Track Success
To evaluate the effectiveness of segmentation strategies, it's important to establish key performance indicators (KPIs) and metrics. These might include sales growth, market share, customer retention rates, and engagement levels. Example: A telecom company like Jio might track metrics such as new subscriber growth, average revenue per user (ARPU), and churn rate to assess the success of its segmentation strategy targeting different customer groups.
Feedback Mechanisms and Continuous Improvement
Collecting feedback from customers and analysing performance data helps businesses refine their segmentation strategies. Continuous improvement ensures that the strategies remain effective and relevant in changing market conditions. Example: Myntra, an online fashion retailer, might use customer feedback and purchasing data to refine its segmentation strategy, ensuring that product recommendations and marketing messages remain aligned with customer preferences.
3.7.2 Revising Segmentation Strategies
Adapting to Market Changes
The market is dynamic, and consumer preferences can change over time. Businesses need to stay agile and update their segmentation strategies to reflect these changes. This might involve re-segmenting the market, updating customer profiles, or changing the targeting approach. Example: During the COVID-19 pandemic, many companies had to adapt their segmentation strategies. For instance, Domino's shifted its focus to contactless delivery and safety measures, targeting health-conscious consumers.

Case Studies: How Indian Companies Revised Their Segmentation Strategies
Swiggy: Swiggy, a food delivery service, revised its segmentation strategy during the pandemic by introducing new services like grocery delivery and focusing on safety protocols. This adaptation helped Swiggy retain and attract customers who were concerned about health and safety. Hyundai Motors: Hyunai regularly revises its segmentation strategy to stay ahead in the competitive automobile market. For instance, recognising the growing demand for eco-friendly vehicles, it introduced hybrid and CNG models targeting environmentally conscious consumers.

Market segmentation is a vital component of persuasive communication strategies. 3.10 GLOSSARY
Market Segmentation: The process of dividing a broad consumer or business market into sub- groups of consumers based on shared characteristics. Demographic Segmentation: Segmenting the market based on variables such as age, gender, income, education, and occupation. Psychographic Segmentation: Segmenting the market based on lifestyle, activities, interests, and opinions. Behavioural Segmentation: Segmenting the market based on consumer behaviours such as purchasing patterns, usage rate, and brand loyalty. Positioning: The process of creating a distinct image and identity for a product in the minds of the target audience.

4.0 INTRODUCTION
In this unit, we will explore the concept of brand extension within the broader context of advertising, public relations, communication, and media. We live in a competitive marketplace where consumers have multiple choices; thus, companies try to use these media to expand their reach. Brand extension is a strategic market approach. Companies that have a reputable brand image and identity, and have a good consumer base, use it to launch new products and services under the same brand name. Nowadays, where everything is possible online, brands also utilise online platforms to connect to consumers and adapt to evolving consumer behaviour. Thus, it is essential to understand brand extension and how it functions in today's digital ecosystem.
4.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After working through this unit, you will be able to: * Understand the term brand extension with the help of case studies; * Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of brand extension; * Differentiate the types of brand extensions and their relationship with other brand properties;
4.2 BRAND EXTENSION: DEFINITION AND TYPES
The term 'Brand Extension' was coined by Edward M. Tauber in 1979. Kopp (2021) terms it as brand stretching and defines brand extension as 'the use of a company's established brand names on a new product or new product category.' Hence, in creating a brand extension, a company leverages the reputation, popularity and loyalty associated with earlier well-known product(s) to launch a new product or product categories. Kotler (1991) defines a brand extension strategy as 'any effort to expand a successful brand name to launch new or modified products or lines.' One of the major drivers of brand extension is when companies detect a new trend or need. Ambler and Styles (1996) were of the opinion that extension is strategy when a consumer's need is identified, and seen to be unfulfilled by the current brand or other brands in the category in question.

Brand extension is a marketing strategy like branding. It is brand stretching because once a brand helps consumers identify a product by making it different, there is opportunity for marketers to launch a new product under the same brand which can borrow a similar positioning as that of the existing product. Brand extension is used to create product differentiation, increase revenue, reign in niche segments, etc., which allows a brand to gain incremental market share. Let us understand this with an example. The brand Nike is associated with shoes as most consumers know about it. At the same time, by brand extension, Nike has moved into sunglasses, soccer balls, basketballs, golf equipment and clothing. Similarly, the Indian customer knows about Wipro as a computer brand, but it was originally a vegetable oil company, before eventually the brand 'Wipro' extended to Computers. Students must note that brand extension as a term also typically gets confused with another term called 'line extension'. When a brand extends its product line within the same product category as they currently are in, it is called a 'line extension' while brand extension involves new products under the same brand in new territories or markets. So Mother Dairy, a dairy company, launching cow milk will be a 'line extension' while its launching of wheat bread or ice cream will be a brand extension. Types broadly categorised under brand extensions are as follows:
1. Product Form Extension: In this type of extension, a branded product is launched in a different
form whereby the new form product competes in a totally different product category. For example, Amul milk available in a new form of 'condensed milk' or Real Juice available in a new form of 'juice concentrate'.
2. Companion Product Extension: This type of extension is one where the extension
compliments the original product i.e., it is directly related to the original product. For example, Pepsodent' toothpaste brand extending into Pepsodent toothbrush segment. This type of brand extension is the most popular as the extension promotes the sales and marketing of the parent brand.
3. Brand Distinction Extension: Brands that are unique based on attributes of benefits get strong
customer associations to such uniqueness. This allows the brand to extend into new products with the same uniqueness. For example, Parachute is the flagship brand of Marico associated with coconut nourishment. The brand extended from hair oil into hair care, body care and personal care, etc.
4. Customer Franchise Extension: When a brand extends into different product categories but
still focuses on a single market segment. For example, Johnson & Johnson, the American multinational, focuses on the market segment of babies and develops different products under the same brand name.
5. Company Expertise Extension: In this type, a company extends its expertise and brand name
to create a new product. For example, Honda brand extends from cars into 'scooters' and 'gensets' (generator sets).
6. Brand Prestige Extension: This type of extension is when, based on brand prestige, the brand
extends to new product categories unrelated to the original product. For example, the Tata brand has extended from steel to automobiles to salt to software while Godrej can be seen in almirahs to refrigerators to hair dyes.
7. Extension by Transfer of Component: Some brands get known for a particular component in
their product like flavour, ingredient, scent, color, etc. The brand may then capitalise on this property/properties and leverage in other product fields. For example, the brand Dr Scholl's, known for its orthopedic foot care insoles, extending into footwear.
8. Leverage a Celebrity Expertise: Some famous international examples of this include
celebrities who are also associated with the broad operational field of these brands, including Jack Welch Management Institute, Jane Fonda Workout DVD, Martha Stewart Bedding, Ralph Lauren Paints, etc.

9. Leverage a Celebrity Lifestyle: Brands utilise celebrity endorsements to attract consumers
who are fascinated by celebrity lifestyles. Examples like Cindy Crawford Jewelry, Donald Trump Signature Collection Apparel, Ritu Kumar apparel, Hrithik Roshan HR brand, etc.
10. Changing Brand Image: One can change brand image by creating a new product or by using
modifier words to change consumers' perceptions of the company's core product. For example, 'Vaseline Petroleum Jelly' to 'Vaseline lotion'. Check Your Progress: 1 Note: 1) Use the space below for your answers.

4.3 ADVANTAGES AND DISADVANTAGES OF BRAND
EXTENSION
Brand extensions can work to increase brand equity but it can also have the effect of diluting a brand if the extension is unable to prove its relationship to the existing brand in the eyes and minds of the customers. Amber and Styles (1996) opined that risks and benefits of brand extension can be divided into four categories - efficiency benefits, effectiveness benefits, risk to extension, and risk to the brand. Volckner and Sattler (2006) argued that the most important component of a brand extension's success is the fit between the brand and the extension. If consumers feel the extension does not fit with the parent brand, the new products under the extension have a greater risk of failure. An established brand has pre-established relationships with its customers. This relationship is because the customer trusts the brand and hence any extension will normally get the same trust from customers. Along with this, a brand extension can strengthen the existing brand by attracting new consumers who use the new product. An easy way to understand is the brand Dove, which has a wide range of products including personal care and hair care. However, there are risks associated with the brand extension strategy. Two of those described by Amber and Styles (1996) are: (i) Risks to the extension: Whereby the extension has a poor fit with the existing brand. For example, the brand Colgate, which was extended as 'Colgate beefy lasagna frozen dinner' (details for which are given later in this chapter under case studies). It could also be due to an overestimation of the benefits of the new product. A closer example is Pond's toothpaste stumbled after struggling for some time with brand extension. (ii) Risks to the brand: In an extreme case, an extension can lead to the dilution of a brand itself by reducing the favorable attribute customers have of the original brand. Let us summarise the advantages and disadvantages of brand extensions: Advantages

i) More visibility and increase of operating market: An extension increases a brand's visibility to a larger audience which has the effect of increasing brand equity as well as operating market. ii) Brand Image: An extension elevates the parent brand image. iii) Saving costs: Cost of developing a new brand, including its marketing and promotion, are saved. It also increases efficiency of marketing and promotion. iv) Reduces perceived risk for customers: As customers are acquainted with the parent brand, extension gives them confidence about the new product. Disadvantages i) Hurting parent brand: In case of a failure of the extension, it can hurt the parent brand. ii) Brand dilution: If by the extension the customer gets confused on what the brand stands for and what to expect out of it. iii) Wastage of resources and good will.
4.4 RELATIONSHIP WITH OTHER BRAND CONCEPTS/
PROPERTIES
4.4.1 Effect of Brand Extension on Brand Equity
Aaker (1991) defined 'Brand equity' as "a set of assets and liabilities linked to a brand, its name and symbol that adds to or subtracts from the value provided by a product or service to a firm and/or to that firm's customers." Simply put, brand equity can be described as the value brand name adds to a product. Also, brand equity is generally treated as a composite of brand-related beliefs, including brand awareness, brand image, and brand loyalty (ibid.) So, if the extension leads to a drop of any of the sub-components i.e., awareness, image or loyalty of the brand, then the brand extension will lead to a loss of brand equity.
4.4.2 Effect of Brand Extension on Brand Image
Martinez and de Chernatony (2004) found that there are two types of brand image: general brand image and product brand image. For strong brands like Nike or Sony, there is no negative impact on general brand image and any dilution due to extension would happen on the product image and not on the general image, with most customers sticking to their beliefs about the parent brand with respect to its attributes. However, their study also showed that with not very strong brands, an unsuccessful brand extension does lead to diluted brand image with beliefs and associations associated with a parent brand tending to get affected.
4.4.3 Effect of Brand Extension on Brand Loyalty
Many companies employ a brand extension strategy on their core product to enhance customer loyalty. This is done by introducing a complementary product having high synergy with the core product. This provides a more comprehensive solution to the existing customer base, thereby increasing loyalty. A successful extension can sustain, leverage, and revamp brand equity.
4.4.4 Effect of Brand Extension on Brand Personality
Brand personality is referred to as "a set of human characteristics associated with a brand" (Aaker,
1997) . Freling and Forbes (2005) found a strong and positive brand personality often leads to benefits
such as increasing consumer preferences, usage, trust, loyalty and brand equity, thereby creating a set of unique and favorable associations in the consumer's memory of the brand, thus building a differentiated offering.
4.5 CASE STUDIES ON BRAND EXTENSION
Titan, Snickers, Gillette, Colgate, Tide, etc. have all used brand extensions in the Indian market. Let us understand brand extension with the help of the case studies of the brand 'Maggie', and 'Colgate'.

i) The brand 'Maggie', as an instant noodle was launched by Nestle India Ltd. (NIL) in 1982. It was an entire new food category in India at that time. Due to persistent efforts of NIL, and being the first mover, 'Maggie' was the leader in instant noodle category for a long time till early 2000s. It was positioned as a '2-minute noodles' with a punch line 'Fast to cook! Good to eat' and was positioned as a snack between meals. This was because the wheat/rice consuming Indian households at that time would not have accepted 'noodles' as a wholesome meal as per various studies done. 'Maggie' has done various brand extensions over the years into a variety of culinary products like soups, sauces and cooking aids which saw a mixed success, not like the one NIL saw with the 'instant noodles' product category. Maggie today is still associated with the '2-minute noodles.' ii) Colgate has been in operation and an established brand for over 200 years. In fact, Colgate was the first company to put toothpastes in collapsible tubes. 'Frozen dinner entree' was becoming popular in the USA in the 1980s with students and housewives for its cost effective and time efficient way for preparing dinner. (Basically, prepared dinner which was frozen and sold and all one needed was to heat it to eat) Colgate, with their established brand in the oral hygiene sector, felt it could extend its brand to the food sector and make a connection in the minds of their customers with their extension product, the 'Colgate beefy lasagna frozen dinner'. The extension was a huge failure. The reason was simple as when customers thought about Colgate they thought about minty and fresh. People could not associate Colgate with anything outside oral healthcare and that led to a total failure of the extension.
4.6 EXTENSION IN THE DIGITAL WORLD
A brand is more than just a name and logo; it represents an emotion and a reputation. In digital branding and its extensions, it's the messaging which foregrounds everything else. As the online world is virtually being inhabited by anonymous users and communities, the messaging involves things like, 'what the company believes in', 'what is the company or brand communicating online,' and 'how the brand/company communicates that online.' The next important thing to understand in the online space is, consistency across all online platforms and online engagements are a necessity for the consumer/customer to feel connected even though the messaging may vary depending on the channel or the platform. For example, the message may be constructed differently for 'Instagram' and 'LinkedIn' platform users as the user profiles are very different and the usage is different. Digital branding highlights the underlying values of the company. Digital brand extensions can have two connotations in the online world: i) The first one begins with the creation of new products and/or services in a new category, and the subsequent messaging and communication of this extended product/s done in the online space through digital branding, online advertisement and online marketing. (Online advertising and online marketing falling in the realm of digital marketing). ii) However, brand extension has another connotation in the online world, whereby a physical product is extended into the online space as a new product. Brand extension strategy on the internet is a common and popular strategy in the media industry. Tarkiainen, Ellonen and Kuivalainen (2009) assert that the internet has been one of most widely used ways of extending an established brand. Let us understand this with a case study of a published magazine extended into the online world as a new product, a webzine. A monthly American food and entertainment magazine, Bon Appetit as shown in Fig.1, headquartered in New York had been in publication since 1956.

Figure 1: Cover of theBon Appetit magazine (source:https://www.newsstand.co.uk/issueimages/535x745/2652296.jpg) The magazine did a brand extension in the online world as shown in Fig.2. Figure 2: Website of Bon Appetit (Source: https://www.bonappetit.com/) Amber and Styles (1996) write that the consumer's acceptance of an extension increases if the following conditions are met: i. The parent brand is perceived to be of high quality. ii. A perception of 'fit' between the new product category and the parent. iii. Category is seen as 'difficult to make' and hence some expertise is needed by the brand. Johnson (2017), writing about this brand extension, was of the opinion that the webzine communication strategies centers on accessibility, convenience, surveillance and interaction in its online product. Extension into the digital involves various content and technological aspects. Dynamic, interactive content of a website versus static, single-dimension and non-interactive content of the printed magazine on the content side. Among technological issues, publishing dynamic web content and keeping in mind the accessing technologies used by customers like various browsers and

devices like mobiles, laptops, tablets, etc. This can hurt the brand if the extension is not thought of and executed well in both these above-mentioned cases. When a product or service extends into the online space for the customer a 'perception of fit' can take three distinct dimensions as per Aaker and Keller (1990). According to them, these dimensions are: i) Complementary whereby the extension is considered complementary to the parent, and both are consumed jointly to satisfy a need. Certainly, a magazine and a webzine might be complementary as a customer could consume a magazine in the lazy confines of her home and on a mobile device while off for work. ii) Substitute whereby the extension can substitute or replace the other in usage as well as satisfy the same need as the original. Certainly, for the younger audience interested in food and cuisines, the webzine will replace the magazine, as this segment is on the move and hates being pinned down at a place and with a habit. iii) Transfer is what the customer sees as a relationship in product manufacturing between the parent and extension. Obviously, a webzine manufacturing is different from a magazine though both deliver content on 'food and entertainment'. Even though the parent brand was of high quality with exceptional reputation, it had to convince the customer that the extension was sound and of value by being able to deliver high quality engagement online, as did the parent brand in the physical world. This 'perception of fit' is extremely important between a parent and an extension for the extension to succeed. In case of a 'fit', the customers incorporate the extension into their everyday lives or else the extension fails. This was the reason why the "Colgate beefy lasagna frozen dinner" didn't work as was shown above. One common strategy used by magazines and newspapers is what Bon Appetit did, which was to use its website as an anchor for all its social media channels, i.e., whenever a customer would come across any content in any social media platform, the content link would lead them back to the website. Based on his research on the Bon Appetit webzine, Johnson (2017) asserts that a combination of six brand extension strategies were used by the brand in its brand extension. This was done as follows: i) Shift the form: This involves changing the form of an existing product (magazine to webzine) by altering the delivery method as well as its retail placement. ii) Transfer a Component: Bon Appetit transferred the 'genre of food' as was showcased by tabs and content on the webzine. iii) Transfer a Benefit: The webzine transfers the brand benefit of the Bon Appetit brand. From the language used, which is relational to menu tips, cuisine tricks and outdoor suggestions like 'America's Best New Restaurants of 2016,' or 'Host a dinner party on a $50 budget,' were value additions to the customers of the brand extension. iv) Leverage a Special Expertise: Bon Appetit expertise of food is leveraged in the brand extension. For example, in 'Cooking Tips' under the 'Test Kitchen' tab, the webzine publishes content discussing the best cooking practices its staff discovered. v) Leverage your Consumer Base: As the brand has been around for long, it has a very loyal customer base, which was leveraged to guide them to the webzine, pulling newer customers. vi) Leverage a Lifestyle: Bon Appetit leverages a 'love of the food' lifestyle in its extension around which it has built its communication strategy. Earth to Echo MineCraft Plug-in: This is an extension by Relativity Media for their film "Earth to Echo". 4.8 GLOSSARY
Brand Extension: It is the market strategy when a company uses its established brand names on a new product or service. Parent Brand: It is the existing brand that is extended. All the brands created under the parent brand have some important features related to the existing brand, along with certain differentiated factors. Brand Dilution: It is when a brand loses its value or image because of a poor brand extension strategy. It confuses customers and reduces their trust in the company/brand. Brand Personality: It is defined as the set of human characteristics and traits associated with a brand. Line Extension: It is when a brand extends its product line within the same product category in which it currently is. Webzine: A publication usually in magazine format that exists solely on the World Wide Web.

4.1 INTRODUCTION
In the previous units of this block, you learnt how to critically analyze literary texts through a gendered lens. These units introduced you to alternative ways of reading, writing and criticism from feminist perspectives. Now that you have observed that there are various possible approaches to reading and appreciating literature, we will examine one particular approach which has been of utmost significance to feminist theorists in the last century. In this unit, you will read about the relations between feminism and deconstruction, and how feminists have been able to employ deconstructive strategies to advantage. We will begin by locating deconstruction within its historical literary context, and examine other movements, more specifically, Structuralism and Post-Structuralism, with which it is related. We will then try to explain the salient aspects of deconstruction and its relevance to feminism.
