6.5 STRUCTURES OF CINEMA AS ART
The most important structure of cinema is its narrative technique. Cinema is basically a medium of expression which tries to represent the realities of life. Every form of art has its own specific style of communication. Cinematic art is defined by structures like the language of the film. When a film is taken into consideration, the technique of its narrative structure, or Aristotlean opsis, depends much on the scientific technology used for making films. This includes image, sound, camera, cinematic apparatus and so on which involves not only the actors but the entire production team including every technician who contributes to the making of the film. The structure of language comprises Saussurean theory of major components
- semantics and syntax. You have already read about signs and their meanings.
Signs constitute the semantic structure of cinema. But the syntactical structure of cinema is very different from other forms of art because it includes image, sound and montage as its integral parts. The syntax of a film is basically the linear aspect illustrating the ways in which different techniques are put together to complete the form, like the camera, the images shot with it, the sound, the music, the editing, the locations where the images are shot (sets), the costumes, the lights, the dialogues, the performances, and above all, the direction, which we have discussed in the previous sections. Take for instance, the hero along with his male friends might try to find out the name of the heroine stay in the story, their sound is shot at such a decibel that as spectator you will be able to listen to it, but as other characters present in the same scene may not be able to decipher what they are discussing. Or take another example when a quarrel between hero and heroine takes place, it is mostly being accommodated or made hyperbolic by adding background score to it. Images seen in a film can be 'read' at two levels - the optic and the mental
- that is, what you see and what you perceive or think you have seen. This
occurs at three levels: the saccadic, the semiotic and the cultural (Monaco, 2009, 1977, p. 194). Saccadic images follow one another quickly to augment the sense of motion. This is easy to understand with the example of the animation film. One needs to draw one image at a time and then shoot

them. When each film formulates the reel and its motion taking place, you Gaze/Eye of the Camera see that a cartoon character is moving fast like any animate object. This is what saccadic structures are. Regarding semiotics, it has already been explained in the previous section that it is based on the relationship of signs, signifier and signified. The last level of cinematic construction is the cultural structuring. This focuses on the spectator. When watching a film, a spectator from a rural background may have very different expectations and experiences from that of another spectator who has grown up in a metropolitan city. Because of this basic difference in cultural experiences, each person would connote an image with a different meaning. Understanding the image of cinema is very different from reading it. Interpreting the Saussurean theory, Monaco comments that there are two ways of understanding any film, they are paradigmatic and syntagmatic. In a paradigmatic structure, one is guided by individual choices which are mainly denotative and connotative. In denotative choice, icon and symbols are important, whereas connotative choice has symbol, metonymy and tropes; symbol and metonymy produce the index of the film. For example in a scene picturising a song, the hero shows his dancing capabilities, say stretching the legs at 180 degrees. This becomes a symbol and you exclaim in wonder because you have never seen such a dancing pose before. Or take an example where the heroine is fighting masculine stunts with several men. The same awestruck feeling might envelope you as you may not even imagine that a woman can do stunts like that. This is what a paradigmatic structure of cinema means. For a syntagmatic structure, there are two categories of construction - space or the synchronic structure, and time or the diachronic structure. In space, the language of the film is descriptive or detailing takes place. In the diachronic structure, the language is historical, providing the information about the sequence in which the shot is taking place. In the narrative structure, one derives the meaning from the codes that the film portrays. Codes derive from certain aesthetics, like mise-en-scene and mise-en-shot. Mise-en-scene is a French word, which literally means 'putting on stage' or 'staging'. It has originated from the theatrical art that depicts Aristotlean opsis. But in cinematic terms, it means any given event that you as a spectator can see, the way it is filmed, the set design, the location, the lighting, and the portrayal of the character. Mise-en-shot is a cinematic term. It means 'putting into shots' or simply 'shooting (a film)'. The main parameters of mise-en-shot includes the position of the camera, the movement of the camera, the shot scale or distance from where is it being shot, the duration of single shot and the pace of editing. There are three ways of shooting any scene - the long take, deep focus photography and continuity editing. 'Long take' is a shot taken for a long duration, whereas deep focus photography keeps several planes of the shot -foreground, middle-

Gender, Film and Cinema ground and background --in focus at the same time. Continuity editing is something quite different and deals with the synthetic unity of space and time by breaking down a scene into a multitude of shots. We discussed earlier in this unit that in a commercial cinema a heroine is made to appear more beautiful through the usage of lighting and position of the camera. The camera will focus on her face and the light will be brighter while the back drop light will be faded so that her beauty is revealed perfectly. Or to understand the camera shots, take the example where in a scene the hero is trying to rescue the heroine from a hanging bridge. Note here that most of the time in commercial films, the heroine is placed in such circumstances so that the villain can be cast in a negative light and the hero's entry justifies him to be good-hearted and in true love with the heroine. You will notice that in some scenes their facial expressions are revealed in the most realistic way possible while in others the camera zooms out in order to make the spectator realise how dangerous or fatal is their situation. While you watch the film it will look that all the shots are happening simultaneously, this is because the film is edited in such a manner. But realistically these three camera shots -the close-ups, the long- distance shot, and the close up of the rope -are shot at different intervals. This comprises an example of narrative structure.
6.6 WAYS OF LOOKING AT CINEMATIC ART
Looking at cinema as an art form is important for anyone to appreciate its socio-cultural importance. A wide variety of factors interrelate to create the aesthetics of cinema. We will discuss them in three categories (i) spectrum of abstraction, (ii) modes of discourse and (iii) rapports de production.
6.6.1 Spectrum of Abstraction
According to Aristotle, art can be understood as a type of representation, or imitation of reality depending on a medium through which it is expressed, and mode, i.e. the way the medium is utilised. Being a form of art, cinema can also be understood to be practical, environmental, pictorial, dramatic, narrative and musical (Monaco, 2009, 1977, p. 31-32). Practical refers to the art of design, i.e. the props and sets used in a film, like what background should be in the focus of the camera, what furniture to be used, what costumes, what form of make-up, and everything that comprises the props of a set. Take for example, if the scene is of a palatial living room, the furniture would have to match the contours of the sets, the colours have to be rich and bright, and so on. In this case, if you think of a particular scene of Sanjay Leela Bhansali's film Devdas, you can see the detail used to create the opulence of Devdas' home, the costumes of the people in the home and the exquisitely matched furniture. At the same time, the female

characters are made to look gorgeous and affluent with heavy jewellery Gaze/Eye of the Camera and richly embroidered costumes. Designing, on the other hand, happens only with architecture of the designs. To some extent, architecture interacts with other categories that are environmental, and often depends on the immediate ambience. Architectural forms leads to the representation or imitation of a certain philosophy, and one such architectural form is the pictorial category of art of the set where a shooting of a film takes place. If you think of any film showing a destitute or a poor person's house, the clothes may be shown dirty, sometimes torn, and the characters will appear unkempt hairs, but it differs entirely if the hero or the heroine is portrayed in the same setting. Their costumes and architectural set will be same but not the make-up. It is always made perfect so that they differ from all the other characters in the same setting. Photography, although pictorial, can also be interrelated with practical and environmental like architectural set. Dramatic art has something to do with stage and theatre, which would inter-relate it to pictorial, environmental and practical category. The narrative category of art includes literary forms such as the novel, story, non-fiction and other forms. But when one thinks of musical form of art, some interrelation between literary art and music is clearly visible. Like poetry and dance are both literary and musical. But only music is typically the musical expression of art. Think of any song sequence of any film, you will note that the background score, the locations, the costumes, change at once. And the music is used to add appeal. All of these aspects together comprise a spectrum of abstraction that we see in cinematic art.
6.6.2 Modes of Discourse
The most important relationship for any art is with its modes of discourse -- what form is it, who is the creator or the artist and who observes the artistic form. We accept the fact that art is a form of communication, depending on the degree of abstraction it is being formulated in. Film theorist James Monaco defines this system of artistic communication through a geometric figure. He uses two axes - the axis of experience and the axis of transmission. The axis of experience has two poles -- artifact that is used to make the art and performance that modulates this artifact from within (Monaco, 2009, 1977, p. 33). Take for example, an action scene of any recently released movie. As a spectator, you will see cars rolling or crashing in the background, the music is harsh and sound effects are used to reinforce of every action taking place. Now if the axis of transmission is taken in this particular example, than the artefacts become the cars rolling or crashing, and the protagonists' action sequences are modulated according to the demands of the scene. The axis of transmission also has two poles --

Gender, Film and Cinema representation and the record of the representation. Now keeping the same example of an action scene, if the hero and the villain are both performing, the sound effect has a different note, while with other protagonists the sound effects used will be different. Both these axes meet at a point, which is you, the spectator, who observes the art or watches cinema.
6.6.3 Rapports de Production
You, as a spectator, are the centrifugal point of both the axes in the modes of discourse. What is important to be presented for you is the result of the production procedures and consumption techniques (Monaco, 2009, 1977, p. 34-35). For example, after watching a film, you might not like it so you may not refer it to anyone else; soon you realise that the movie flops because of similar word of mouth commentary that is being circulated widely. This is what is implied by 'rapports de production' or in simple terms, the relationships of production. There are certain determining factors for the production and its relationship with the spectator. They are socio- political, psychological, technical and economic factors, depending upon the function and system of criticism. In the socio-cultural context of any society, the determining factor for watching a film is based on its utility or the usefulness. When such a social system of utilitarian mindset for watching a film with some company is there, the psyche of entertainment from that specific film depends on the ethical and political reasons. For example, watching a film with your family would be different from watching it with friends. You might enjoy with your family a particular genre and with friends it may be a different one. By chance if you watch the same film with your family as well as friends at two different venue and time, the entertainment varies in both the context. In the psychological context, the determinant function is the expression that has several reactions upon you for the immediate ambience. Similarly in the technical category, the function of art is the philosophy 'art for art's sake' and the determining factor of criticism is aesthetic. For instance, you just went to watch a film because you didn't have any other choice of recreation, so you will take the film in a different way; or if you desperately want to watch a particular film and waiting anxiously for it, your reactions would be different. All these reactions are because your inclination for watching a particular film is different from that of socio-cultural reasons. The last determining factor is economic and this is very important in today's society. The interrelation between you as an observer of the film and the producers who make the film, is also an economic one. If a film becomes successful then the production unit gains a lot of money, the protagonists and the technicians get a break-through, just as Zanjeer was a breakthrough film for Amitabh Bachhan. But in the system of film criticism, this economic aspect might not be very significant as the film critics would be discussing not from then economic aspect but from the technical perspective: for

instance, how does the camera work, how is the music produced and such Gaze/Eye of the Camera other factors. These factors constitute this category of 'rapports de production' of looking at cinema as art. Activity 1 Watch a film either in a cinema hall or on television and try to test all the concepts you have studied. Try to interpret it with the help of the philosophies of the film you have read. You will soon realize that the film you watched can be discussed from many different angles.
6.7 GENDERING THE GAZE OR CINEMATIC EYE
After these discussions, you may feel more confident about reading and understanding a film. According to the film theorist Toby Miller interpreting Freud's psychoanalytical study of mental processes, he says that while viewing cinema exemplifies the cultural efforts to provide the viewer with paradigmatic and syntagmatic structures of images which according to the gaze of the viewer appear natural and automatic (Miller, 2000, p. 476). These images combine together to build a relationship between the film and the spectator, like what was the motive behind making a film like Deewar (1975). If you probe into the contemporary social scenario, you will find the relevance of making such a film, like migrating to big cities for better economic opportunities. So, we can conclude that everything you see in the film has some relevance and interrelation with your own experience in cultural or social life. In this regard, Miller interprets Freud's scopophilia or "the pleasure in looking" as the visual capture of something that seeks to make an object from the first and hold fast to it. This pleasure could be perverse if it is not the only means of obtaining sexual satisfaction (Miller, 2000, p. 477-478). This 'gaze' of the spectator has a significance in terms of the different types of responses to what is a film according to the attitude and temperament of the viewers, like exhibition, voyeurs, slaves, masters, victims and victimisers. The term 'exhibition' indicates that the viewer may be influenced by watching a film, say, by the physical appearance of the hero or heroine, and may begin to reflect certain characteristics in social or cultural life. Lacan's voyeurism is another type of response of the gaze. The film you watch may become an object of pleasure or displeasure and affects one's psychic internality. For example, when you watch a character undergoing pain and sorrow, you may shed tears or feel pity; in other words, the cathartic effect of fear and pity works upon you and your immediate reaction changes. Similarly, the other responses -like that of slave and master, victim and victimizer relationships -work in terms of similar paradigmatic structures.

Gender, Film and Cinema The film theorist Laura Mulvey in her essay "Visual Pleasure and Narrative Cinema" defines the psychoanalytical structure of a viewer's gaze from a gendered perspective. The paradox of phallocentricism depends on the notion of the castrated woman to give a structure or order and meaning to the world she exists in. Thus 'woman' becomes the mode of construction of a symbol that the society views, as for instance in a Bollywood film. Cultural concepts of respect and dignity (maan-maryada) are often thrust upon either women or the subordinates, who must bear the burden of protecting social values. So the symbol of a woman as a mother figure or a subordinate figure gains significance. In the case of males, there is a different structuring, for instance, a son is supposed to support his father as per the norms of a patriarchal society. Therefore, cinematic art is expected to replicate the same social structures. Mulvey further describes from a psychoanalytical perspective the pleasure one derives while watching a film, referring to this as Fascination with the Human Form and Woman as Image, Man as Bearer of the Look. She interprets the former phrase - 'Fascination with the Human Form' -- in the light of Freud's scopophilia on an erotic basis. She says that characters in the film become objects of a spectator's gaze. The spectator subjects them to a controlling and curious gaze and derives erotic pleasure in looking at the other person as object. Thus, the spectators in the cinematic world engage in surreptitious observation of the unknowing and unwilling victims, who are portrayed in a hermetically sealed world and unveiled in front of the spectator, producing a sense of separation from the surroundings and creating an intimate world of voyeuristic fantasy (Mulvey, 2000, p. 487-492). Simply put, this implies a certain level of identification with the characteristics on the cinematic screen. The concepts of Recognition, Figuration, Identification which you have already read about in the pervious sections, take place during this process too. In the context of the phrase, 'Woman as Image, Man as Bearer of the Look,' Mulvey discusses the sexual imbalances that exist in the pleasure of looking. She identifies two sexual roles, active and passive. In a heterosexual world, the active sexual role is usually performed by the male and the passive role by the females; but in the queer world, the active and passive roles may not be as clearly demarcated on gender lines and may have more to do with sexual desires. The traditional exhibitionist role assigned to women in mainstream cinematic production makes a woman an object for the patriarchal society. Her appearance is aimed at creating a strong visual and erotic impact in patriarchal phallocentric societies, where women are projected as objects of sexual gratification. The depiction of women in many sexist songs is aimed at producing voyeuristic pleasure through the objectification of women for sexual gratification. Women are displayed as objects to the male gaze which is invited to take on a position of control. We will examine similar concepts in the context of queer people in the last unit of this block.

Gaze/Eye of the Camera
6.8 LET US SUM UP
You may now understand why 'gaze' or the 'eye of the camera' becomes important in the context of the gender perspective of a film. Depending upon the orientation, attitudes and perspectives of the director, actors, actresses and spectators, the viewing experience may be 'gendered' in different and complex ways. The 'gaze' or 'eye of the camera' is thus inherently connected to both those who wield the camera, and those who view what the camera looks at, and reproduces as spectacle.

6.10 GLOSSARY
Auteur : In, the 1950s-era auteur theory holds that a director's film reflects the director's personal creative vision, as if he or she were the primary 'auteur', derived from the French word meaning 'author'. Despite -- and sometimes even because of --the production of the film as part of an industrial process, the author's creative voice is distinct enough to shine through all kinds of studio interference. In some cases, film producers are considered to exert an 'auteur' influence on the films they produce. But in legal terms, a film is treated as a work of art, and the auteur as its creator. Under European Union law, the film director is considered the author or one of the authors of a film. Hermeneutics : It is the study of interpretation theory, and can be either the art of interpretation, or the theory and practice of interpretation. Opsis : It is derived from Aristotle's Poetics meaning spectacle in theatre and performance. It is now used by theatre critics, historians and film theorists to describe the mise-en-scene of any performance, whether theatrical or cinematic. 103

Gender, Film and Cinema Bollywood : It is an informal popular term used for the Hindi- language film industry based in Mumbai, India. The name was modeled on USA's Hollywood. The term refers only to a part of the entire Indian film industry, which includes several regional film industries sorted by language of a particular state. Bollywood is the largest film producer in India and one of the largest centers of film production in the world. Phallocentrism : Phallocentrism or phallogocentrism is a neologism coined by Jacques Derrida to refer to the privileging of the masculine (phallus) in the construction of meaning.

6.0 INTRODUCTION
After going through the earlier unit of this block, you would have understood some important aspects related to online brand management. Both in traditional media and in online media, brand management involves two key players: The company that wants to market the brand, and the customer who needs to be persuaded to purchase the brand. In this unit, you will understand how technological convergence has facilitated greater online interactivity. You will also understand what kinds of advertising and marketing strategies are being used to improve consumer experiences of brands on online and social media.
6.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After going through this unit, you should be able to: * Understand the impact of media technologies and convergence; * Learn about the interface between convergence and interactive media; and * Know about the consumers' perceptions about interactive advertising, both on the internet and mobile phones.
6.2 MEDIA TECHNOLOGIES AND CONVERGENCE
The concept of 'convergence' emerged in the 1990s with the growth of Internet-based technologies. Baran (2009) defines convergence as 'the erosion of distinctions among media.' To put it simply, with the coming of the Internet, movies, music, advertisements, games, books, newspapers and TV shows can be viewed at the same time on several media platforms. For example, you can read the latest breaking news or view the current cricket score or watch a favourite video at the same time on your mobile phone or on your laptop screen. Convergence has facilitated and integrated our work, life and entertainment. All media have now converged on the Internet and are catering to diverse audiences with different tastes and likings. Convergence in mass communication implies the merging of different media, like print, television, radio, and the internet, along with portable and interactive technologies through various digital media platforms. Media convergence enables mass communicators like journalists, advertisers, PR professionals, broadcasters and other communication specialists to present news, advertisements,

information and entertainment through a variety of media simultaneously via the internet. Converged communication also provides multiple tools for sharing content, allowing consumers to select their level of interactivity, while controlling content delivery. Activity 1: Explain with the reference of your own experience how the convergence of media technologies has benefitted you?
6.2.1 IMPACT OF MEDIA CONVERGENCE ON ADVERTISING
The Internet and converging technologies have changed the nature of advertising. Traditional forms of advertising in print media, television or radio were non-personal in nature and controlled by brand sponsors. But in the present era, convergent technologies operating on the internet are enabling advertisers to create ads that are more targeted and more personal, in which the consumer can interact, participate and be more engaged. The control has shifted from the advertiser of the brand to the consumer, who is now given a range of options with regard to the product or service information. The consumer in today's world has greater interaction in the online advertising space, which was absent in the traditional media of advertising. Thus, we can now list the three characteristics of online advertising as: Interactivity, Personalisation and Engagement. Interactivity: In the digital or online media, interactivity implies 'a characteristic of a medium in which the user can influence the form and / or content of the mediated presentation or experience' (Lombard,
2001) . Interactivity involves giving the consumer the option to choose which pieces of information he
wants to learn more about, and in this way actively browse through any aspect of the product information which the advertisement provides. For example, the consumers can click a banner advertisement for more information and often enter a realistic experience where they feel that they are using the product. Interactive advertising is also beneficial for the advertisers because these ads promote positive attitudes towards brands and enhance the effectiveness of advertising. Personalisation: Online advertising provides the advertiser with the tools to tailor messages for consumers, and make the advertising message of personal relevance to them. New methods are available with the advertiser to assess the demographic characteristics of the consumer, their media habits, lifestyles, tastes, and use this information to personalise messages for them. The idea is to make the consumers feel that the advertisement is specifically meant for them. By tracking consumers online through the latest technologies, advertisers are able to adapt content such as the price, product specifications and variations at the very moment when the consumer interacts with the ad. For example, if you decide to do online shopping on Amazon, for say, a mobile phone, you will notice the range of options that the website provides you, relating to product range, brand names, price, speed of delivery, phone features, and so on. Engagement: In the context of online advertising, engagement refers to the consumer's interactions with brands in social media platforms through responses like clicking the 'like' button or by making a comment on the advertisers' section on Facebook or by posting a review about a product or downloading an app related to the brand on the mobile phone. By counting on the number of clicks, likes etc., advertisers can get insights into the kind of engagement that consumers are having with the brand, which includes information processing as well as emotional responses towards the brand. 6.3 CONCEPT OF INTERACTIVITY
The terms 'interactivity' and 'interactive media' became significant buzzwords during the late 1980s and early 1990s due to the vast developments in internet-based technologies. 'Interactivity' in sociological terms refers to the interactions that take place between human beings, but it also refers to interpersonal communication between two persons based on symbols and meanings. Computer science looks upon interactivity as the dialogue between humans and computers, through both hardware and software. Interpersonal communication via computers may be considered as an overlap between both the fields of sociology and computer science. Let us understand some of the features of online interactivity: Firstly, due to online interactivity users can send feedback on the device they are using, like say, a mobile phone or laptop via emails, SMS, or contact forms. However, for traditional media like TV, for example, the viewers would need to send a postcard or SMS for the purpose of sending feedback. Secondly, users can contact communicators or the source of information online easily through chats, discussions, email, etc. Thirdly, it is easy for advertisers and media professionals to respond to consumer queries instantly from online media. They can even join the online chat forums and user discussions. A big advantage for media professionals is that online media enables them to get a lot of data about users like their likings, record the number of visits to a website per day without incurring any costs and without letting the users know. Fourthly, in online media the distinction between the sources and receivers diminishes because even receivers or users can create content for it (as in the case of citizen journalism). Another example is that of Wikipedia where any user can feed information and thereby contribute to content creation. Pavlik and McIntosh (2010) note that 'Interactivity includes the following three elements: 1) a dialogue that occurs between a human and a computer programme, 2) the dialogue affects the content of the interaction, and 3) the audience controls what content it sees and when it sees it.'
6.3.1 CONVERGENCE & INTERACTIVE MEDIA
From the perspective of advertising, let us understand how convergence and interactive media function. This can be explained by means of an Interactive Advertising Model (IAM). Interactive Advertising Model: Rodgers and Thorson (2000) explain the IAM model as an integrative process based on three aspects: function, structure and information processing. Interactivity is the most significant advertising feature of online ads made possible by the Internet as it allows all users to be engaged in the persuasion process. The consumer responds to online advertisements in different ways, which helps the advertisers to understand consumer motives on whether they have any serious intent towards a specific goal to purchase or whether they are merely surfing without a specific purpose in mind. The advertisers respond to the consumer's internet activities by coming up with different kinds of appeals to influence them towards the purchase of the brand. The structure of the advertisement would be defined by the type of advertisement - whether it is for a product, service, social issue, political or corporate purpose. Structure also refers to the different formats of the ad like banners, interstitials (pop-ups), website, sponsorships, etc.
6.3.2 USE OF INTERACTIVE MEDIA IN ONLINE ADVERTISING &
MARKETING COMMUNICATIONS
Let us understand some of the key trends in interactivity in online advertising today. Online advertising has several categories, prominent among these being: banner advertising, video advertising, search advertising, mobile advertising, social media advertising, advergames, native advertising, interstitials and podcasts. Let us try and understand each of these categories.

Banner Advertising: A banner ad is usually a form of display advertising created with images or with animation within a website by an advertiser who pays for the advertisement's inclusion. The idea is to attract the attention of the consumer through eye-catching displays and communicate the desired message. Advergames: Advertisers often use this tactic of making consumers engage with games while going to specific websites to get more information about the advertised product. Brands like Coke and McDonalds have used advergames to get more online subscriptions to their websites. Video Advertising: Video ads are the most popular form and have become the mainstay of online advertising. Creatively made, short and long video ads are promotional tactics which are used by advertisers to target diverse consumers. The success of video advertising can be seen on YouTube which sells video ad space on a real time exchange. While video ads attain a high degree of viral presence on social media sites like Facebook, it does not guarantee that viewers will be converted into customers. Search advertising: User searches for products and services on search engines like Google are common. The search results are accompanied by advertisements offering consumers a variety of purchase options that match the search terms. Search advertising has become quite popular with advertisers due to its effectiveness. Mobile advertising: Mobile advertising refers to any form of advertising that appears on smartphones and mobile devices wherein the objective of the advertiser is to ensure continuous engagement with the consumers by means of different types of updates. Mobile advertising leads to customer retention through new offers, detailed information about a particular product or service by sending out the relevant news to the consumers, brand engagement activities such as quizzes and contests and more. These ads appear as pop-ups between news items or while browsing mobile websites and much more. Social media advertising: Posts, videos and product promotion are gaining popularity on social media. Advertising on social media is advantageous for advertisers because of the opinions generated through customer chats and forums resulting in the most influential form of recommendations. Advertisers succeed in building a loyal base of customers on social media sites like Facebook since a loyal fan base for a brand would see customers recommending the brand to others by sharing and spreading the word online. Native advertising: This form of advertising involves featuring sponsored content disguised in the form of editorials online, commonly known as advertorials in the print media. This kind of content seeks to reinforce the qualities of the brand. Interstitials: When a user is waiting for a website's content to download, the ads that appear on the screen are called interstitials. Podcasts: This is a medium that distributes radio-like files into iPods and MP3 players and is very popular with online advertisers. Advertisers are doing their best to offer a variety and wide range of choices and options for consumers online and users are able to actively control as per their choice of shopping trends. For example, be it Amazon or Flipkart and several other MNCs are able to 'micro-target' their advertising to meet the interests and needs of their consumers. Due to interactivity, the Internet has the benefit of increasing consumer involvement and satisfaction, and provides immediate feedback to both the advertisers and the consumers. Activity 2: Give examples of different kinds of online interactive ads which you have come across while surfing on your laptop or on your mobile.
6.4 INTERACTIVITY IN INTERNET ADVERTISING
Let us try to understand the various facets of interactivity in Internet advertising. The four facets are reciprocity, responsiveness, speed of response and non-verbal information. All these facets can be explained as follows:

1. Reciprocity: The term reciprocity can mean dialogue, two-way communication, actions and
reactions, etc. as opposed to monologue or one-way communication which does not permit a response. In online advertising this can be understood as the dialogue that takes place between the sender (the advertiser) and the receiver (the consumer) in response to the advertisement. If the online advertiser provides clickable buttons and links, it would be considered as high on reciprocity.
2. Responsiveness: The term responsiveness can be described as message contingency or the extent
to which an interface produces answers tailored to a user's queries, implying that answers need to be appropriate or relevant to the consumer's questions. Interactivity is grounded in responsiveness implying that there is a continuity in interactive dialogue wherein the advertiser immediately sends his response to the consumer's query. Another way of looking at responsiveness is that if the online advertisement provides highly appropriate and relevant responses to the consumer's actions online, then it is perceived to be highly responsive to consumer interests.
3. Speed of response: It is another aspect of interactivity. It refers to the extent to which a message
exchange occurs in real time or is delayed (Burgoon et al., 2002). The quicker the response from the advertiser to the consumer's feedback, the better would be the consumer's perception about the brand. Instant actions to the consumer's commands show sincerity on the part of the advertiser and improve consumer's perceptions about the brand.
4. Nonverbal communication on the Internet: This refers to the use of graphics, animation, pictures,
video, music, and sound. This is different from verbal communication which is in the form of text- based messages. Advertising communication that uses more of non-verbal information will be perceived to be more interactive by the consumer and would create a positive attitude towards the brand. Now let us understand the strategies used by brand advertisers for getting the best return on investment. This is done by using social media influencers to spread positive electronic word of mouth (e-WOM) reviews about their brands. This is explained further. Advertisers have realised that electronic word of mouth (e-WOM) can play an important role in influencing the consumer's purchase decision-making on the internet. By selecting the appropriate social media platform, designing appropriate messages and using the right influencers to spread the message, the brand company's social media advertising and marketing efforts can prove to be successful. Social media can be used to generate positive word of mouth reviews, spread knowledge about the brand, generate sales and increase return on investment. (Graph source: Kumar, V., and Mirchandani, R., 2012) The above graph shows the seven steps that advertising and marketing professionals can use through interactivity on social media to ensure better sales and best returns on their investment. Step 1: Monitor the conversations. Advertisers these days monitor conversations that take place between consumers about brands on social media. This enables businesses to get valuable information about influential persons as well as about the consumers' engagement with the brand. Step 2: Identify influential individuals who can spread messages. Brands are trying to look out for social media influencers who can help to spread the right message about the brand and influence the consumers' perceptions about the brand.

Step 3: Identify the factors shared by influential individuals such as the level of engagement with the brand; the number of times the message is forwarded by recipients to their friends; and the number of comments and replies received for each message. Step 4: A company tries to identify those influential social media users who show interest in the company's category of goods and services. The final steps are related to recruiting the right influencers to spread the positive e-WOM about the brand, and providing them with incentives to work for the brand. By constantly monitoring and tracking positive e-WOM, businesses can ensure brand growth, and develop more effective social media campaigns in the future. Activity 3: Have you been positively influenced by social media influencers towards any product or service brands? Give examples from your personal experience.
6.5 CHALLENGES OF INTERACTIVITY IN ONLINE
ADVERTISING & MARKETING COMMUNICATIONS
Since advertisers are constantly collecting data about consumers from social media websites and various online sources, there are several concerns about the accountability crisis in advertising and marketing in this digital era. A number of ethical issues need to be addressed by advertisers in this interactive online environment. Marketers need to take into account these current sources of concern and as they could face the challenges of any new government legislation, regulation or anti-trust actions on the industry. Privacy: Privacy is a major area of concern for consumers, since advertisers are using data about consumers from websites like Facebook without the consumers' consent. Consumer information is often being sold or supplied to a third party without permission. Advertisers need to operate within standards of regulation so that while using consumers' data they realise the importance of protecting the consumer against any misuse of their personal information. Fraud and Inappropriate Information: There is ample possibility of fraud in this age of speedy developments in online technologies. Most of the time consumers are forced to deal with unwanted calls, text messages and mails from advertising companies. Even higher prices are charged from them by passing on advertising costs to them. Fraudulent advertising schemes result in hacking addresses, and individual computers of consumers who are unaware of such malpractices. Misinformation, inappropriate content and fraud can lead to lowering of trust in the brand in the eyes of the consumer. Measurability and Reliability of research numbers generated on audience profiles, forecasts and other kinds of consumer data can vary between research providers. This can prove to be challenging for advertisers since different data organisations use diverse kinds of measurability metrics which makes the data that is generated unreliable. Advertising Clutter is a challenge for advertisers since interactivity gives power of control to the consumer to avoid ads that constantly appear. For example, on YouTube, users experience advertising intrusions all the time and exercise the option to skip ads. This is a challenge for advertisers and studies have shown that banner ads have lost their effectiveness for this reason. Advertisers need to deal with all the above-mentioned challenges of personalisation in interactive advertising and invasion of consumer privacy, if they want to get the best results from interactive advertising in the online media. 7.0 INTRODUCTION
Audio-visual content is produced in various genres and programme formats. Writing is important in all of them. The previous unit discussed audio-visual news writing. In this unit, we'll discuss writing of other audio-visual programmes.
7.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After going through this unit, you will be able to: * explain how to write a documentary; * describe the process of writing of travel shows, cookery shows, etc.; and * discuss the writing process of a film, web series, and TV serial.

7.2 WRITING FOR DOCUMENTARIES
Unlike fiction films, documentaries do not rely on actors or an imagined story line. However, this does not mean that scripting is any less relevant in documentaries. Structuring a documentary is a demanding process and writing plays an important part in this process. Different types of documentaries approach writing differently. While documentaries which use a voice-over narration will rely heavily on a script writer, even observational documentaries which do not use any voice-over might require an element of text to convey information or to move the story forward. The following sections will familiarize you with a few modes of documentary narratives and the role of writing in framing these narratives.
Story Arc
Most films have a beginning, middle and an end. Documentaries also use a similar narrative structure. In a documentary, we are dealing with non-fiction material and one has to work with the material that emerges out of the filming process. Just editing together the filmed rushes in a sequential manner will not yield a coherent narrative in the case of most documentaries. Instead, one needs to develop a story arc by placing the filmed material in an order that will allow the audience to form a meaningful engagement with it. Developing a story arc does not always need the involvement of a writer. In films that use a writer, this writer works very closely with the director and the editor to develop the story arc. If the film is a character based one, a story arc can be developed around the character or characters. For example, the film Sita's Family (Dewan, 2002) begins with a journey where we are introduced to the women in the filmmaker's family. The different life choices made by these women and the inner conflicts within the family are unravelled before the viewers through interviews and a personal voice-over by the filmmaker. The confrontation between the filmmaker, her sister and their mother is placed towards the end of the film. This confrontation is a high point in the film. It makes the characters in the film to face difficult questions that they have been avoiding. In this film, the filmmaker builds her story arc by beginning with a gentle introduction; the most dramatic moment in the film is placed towards the end. By the time the film finally ends, the viewer is able to get a sense of closure about issues within the family. Beginning with a gentle introduction and gradually moving towards the more dramatic moments in the film is just one way of developing a story arc. Keeping the key moments of the film towards the beginning can also be a way of structuring the story line. While there are no set rules about creating a story arc, the best possible way in which the audience's interest can be sustained could guide the formation of the narrative. Since writing is a key element in documentaries that use voice-overs, let us now examine the different steps involved in building a voice-over for a documentary.

Voice-Over in Documentaries
Voice-over is a very powerful tool for a documentary filmmaker. It allows the filmmaker to shape the non-fiction material that he or she has filmed in a structured manner. However, if not used carefully, voice-overs can become very boring for the viewers. So how can you write an interesting voice-over or onscreen narration? First of all, the writer should find an engaging style that will work well with the filmed material. For example, in a film which has potential for lighter moments, the voice-over could be humorous at the right places. Understanding the story line which emerges from the filmed material can help us to build a voice-over that will take the narrative of the film forward in an engaging manner. The dominant mode of the film is another factor that will determine the nature of its voice-over. The narration for an expository film about educational policy will be markedly different from a performative film about the educational system which is told from the perspective of a student from a marginalized community. However, despite the differences in style and perspective, a few essential points need to be kept in mind while writing any documentary voice-over. First of all, the writing should work together with the visuals and sound bites in the film. Since the audience can already see the visuals in the film, the voice-over can give the context or other information to add another layer of meaning. In the case of reflexive films, the narration can prompt the viewers to question the manner in which the visuals function within a documentary. Similarly, the writer should be aware that he or she is working with an audio visual medium and should avoid verbose narration. Unlike in the case of a book which can run up to several hundred pages, in a documentary film the entire story needs to be told within a matter of a few hours; in the case of shorter films, the time available is even lesser. So, the writer needs to be economical with words. The writing also needs to work well with the visual pauses of the film as well as its music. In short, voice-over should be able to work together with the rest of the elements in the film; it should not stick out like a sore thumb. In order to build a good voice-over, the writing process should be a part of the film from its initial stages onwards. In the next section, we shall discuss about how the writing should function through the different stages of the production of a documentary. Research Documentary films require a dedicated phase of research. This phase is often used to unearth in depth knowledge about the topic of the film as well as to find suitable characters or filming situations. In a film which intends to use a voice-over, this is a key phase. At this stage, relevant information for the narration can be collected and a tentative style can be decided. However, it is very important to be flexible at this stage. While the research during the pre-production stage can deliver important insights, the final film will depend on what emerges during the filming process. Often carefully laid out plans may not work. In the case of such scenarios, it is

important to follow the logic of the filmed material and the story that emerges from it. So, the plan for the voice-over will be reviewed after the production phase. So, how do we arrive at a first draft of the narration? The following section will examine this process.
Writing the First Draft
Once the initial phases of filming finish, the structuring process of the documentary can begin. The first draft of the voice-over can be written at this stage. Placing this initial voice-over with the filmed material will allow the filmmaker to ascertain whether the ideas for the narration which were developed during the research stage are workable. This process will help to finalize the narrative style of the voice-over. At this stage, it will be advisable to show the rough edits with the voice-over to a selected group of people to ensure that the narration is working well with the filmed material. Changes can be made using the feedback from such screenings. Narration can be used as the key device to structure a film. Finding the correct balance between the voice-over and interviews is a main task during the scripting process. The pace of the narration needs to work with the rest of the film's flow. Once the entire filming process is finished, the narration can be finalized.
Finalizing the Narration
The narration is generally finalized towards the end of the editing phase. Generally, it takes several drafts to arrive at the final narration for a film. An engaging voice-over should have a strong introduction, a cohesive structure which works well with the visuals as well as interviews and a suitable ending. Depending on the mode of the film, the narration can be first person or impersonal. In case there is an on-screen narrator, the writer will have to keep the personality of the narrator in mind while writing the voice-over. Since we are dealing with an audio-visual medium, special care should be taken to avoid verbosity. The narration should work together with the other elements in the film instead of drawing attention to itself. When written well, voice-over can enhance the emotional appeal of the film. Just like in other audio- visual formats, in documentary also it is important to write to the visuals. Since documentary is a longer format when compared with news packages, extra care needs to be taken to sustain the interest of the viewers throughout the narrative. Going through a few examples of engaging documentary voice-overs can help us to form an understanding about the way in which writing can be used to create a strong narrative.

7.3 WRITING FOR TRAVEL SHOWS
You can find many such television channels where travel shows are shown in large numbers. Apart from TV, a large number of such shows are also popular on the internet. But it is also true that travel shows have a niche audience. Therefore, while writing for a particular program format, it is essential to consider the expectations and needs of its target audience. A travel show usually contains many beautiful and interesting shots of a particular location. You can find some shows based entirely on voice-over and some travel shows have presenters who show and describe the features and specialties of the place. Along with this, s/he also talks to some people in between. In both these types, the role of writing is very important. Everything spoken as the voice-over or by the presenter is written in advance in the form of a script. Let us now discuss some of the important points for writing travel shows: * Audio-visual is the perfect medium to bring the beautiful sights and sounds of different countries and places to us. Good writing helps the audience to experience these beautiful scenes in a better way. * Travel shows usually have very beautiful and interesting visuals. The writer has responsibility to explain the context of these visuals as well as to provide the audience with more information about these scenes. * It is necessary to do adequate research on the place we are about to cover in our show. It helps us to improve our scripts. Let us understand this with the help of an example. Suppose we are showing an ancient tower located in a city. If we have done good research and we have some historical information related to that tower then we should include it in our script. This will give new and interesting information to the viewers and make the show better. * Travel shows may have one presenter or sometimes two presenters. In such shows, the writer must work with the presenters to develop a narrative that fits their personality. * If there are two presenters in the show, smooth conversation between them is also necessary. The writer should write it properly. Also, the audience gets new information from those conversations. * As discussed earlier, travel shows sometimes use pieces from interviews, but narration is still the main method through which most of the information is conveyed to the audience. In this case, the description should be interesting and full of information. * The conversational style of writing can be very useful in a travel show. This may help in making the show more popular among the viewers. Often a large section of the audience of such shows do not get the opportunity to travel to the beautiful places of the country and abroad

being shown on a regular basis. In such a situation, these shows become a means for them through which they can reach a world full of beautiful scenes and adventures. Hence, creating a connection with the audience through a script that makes them experience the journey alive can definitely increase the emotional connect between the show and its viewers.
7.4 WRITING FOR PUBLIC RELATION VIDEOS
The target audience should always be kept in mind while writing. Let us understand this with the help of an example. Suppose a new medical equipment manufacturing company has entered the market. They want to make a PR video for themselves. There can be ample use of technical language in this video as its target audience is not the general public. Through this video, the company wants to reach doctors and hospital management who can understand the technical language related to the subject very well. It is also true that writing for any type of audio-visual programs requires understanding and awareness of the characteristics of this medium. Now we shall discuss how writing can play a significant role in different non-fiction audio- visual (AV) programme formats.
7.5 WRITING FOR COOKERY SHOWS
Cookery shows are also popular audiovisual programs enjoyed by a certain section of the audience. Such shows are very popular on TV as well as on the Internet. There have been continuous new experiments with their format as well. The following points should be kept in mind while writing the script for a cookery show: * Cookery shows usually have a presenter who demonstrates the preparation of the dish as well as explains the whole process. The language of the script should be such that the audience feels that the presenter is explaining to them personally. * Sometimes there may be two presenters in a cookery show. One of them is a cook and the other keeps talking to the cook about the dish. In such a situation, the conversation between the two presenters should be made interesting and informative in the script. * If any process in making the shown dish is a bit complicated, then it can be shown again in detail. Therefore, special care should be taken in the script for those procedures which are a bit complex and where the audience may get confused. * Sometimes viewers of cookery show want to write down recipes. This need of the audience should be kept in mind while writing the script. So, the script should be written in such a way that the viewer gets time to write down the recipes. * You must repeat the steps of the recipe in your script.

* Many cookery shows are also competitive. Script writing is more complex for them. In the world of TV, many competitive cookery reality shows have become popular all over the world. * Research can also play an important role in script writing for a cookery show. Many cookery shows also go into detail about the history of the dish, which may make the show more interesting. Check Your Progress 2 Note: Use the space provided below for your answers. 7.6 WRITING FOR ENTERTAINMENT PROGRAMMES
The field of entertainment is very wide. Audio-visual entertainment content itself has a wide variety of programs and formats. But in this unit, we shall only focus on writing for films, web series and TV serials. Coming to India itself, films have been entertaining the common masses for more than a hundred years. After that came the era of television serials and then web series came in the internet era. These three are very important in the world of entertainment. There are many similarities in the writings for all three but some differences too. There should be a story in all the three, characters have to be created, scenes and dialogues have to be written. But there is a big difference in the time available to tell the story and it affects the writing as well. Here we'll discuss various aspects of film writing. Along with this, we shall also try to see the difference between film writing and writing for web series and TV serials.
7.6.1 Writing for Films: Different Steps
Screenplay writing is certainly a creative work, but it is also a technical one. It is a craft that has to be learned. Screenplays are generally not read by the general public. It is read by

important people associated with film making like directors, actors, cinematographers etc. There are many stages in this whole writing process - from idea to final draft. Now we shall discuss the various steps involved in it.
Idea and Its Expansion
Every film starts with an idea. Many ideas keep coming in your mind and they can come anytime. Always note them down. Now the question arises that where do these ideas come from? These can come from your studies, traveling to different places, talking to people, observing people, watching movies and documentaries or even reading newspapers. There can be many reasons. Suppose you read a news that the incidents of suicide among students preparing for competitive exams are on the rise. Now you got an idea that why not write a film on this. If after a lot of thinking you feel that a good film can be made on this idea, then the next step is to expand this idea. You should expand this idea so that it becomes the story of a film. Now you are expanding your idea and giving it the form of a film story. In this process, keep the following things in mind: i. In every good film, there are few characters that the audience remember for a long time. You also have to develop characters in your story that the audience can relate to. ii. Your story should be a journey of your main characters. And this journey should not be simple and straight. There should be ups and downs. There must be a lot of problems and obstacles. There should be enough struggle in this journey only then the story will be suitable for a film. iii. There should be logic in your story. Events must be intertwined in a chain of cause and effects. The audience should understand the reason for all the happenings. They should not be confused as to how something happened. iv. The end of the story is also very important. Sometimes the success or failure of the film depends on it. End must be logical. v. At the time of expanding the idea, you should be clear in your mind that what is the setting of your story? In what place and time is it set? Suppose you are writing the story of a film on the life of Swami Vivekananda, then this story will be set in the time period of 1863 to 1902 in India and USA of that time. Research Research is very important for film writing. If adequate research is not done, then there will be lack of logic and reality in the story, events and characters. Each film is set in a particular place

and time. Only after doing enough research on that place and time, we can create suitable characters and events. This research is also very important for dialogue writing. Now the question arises that how does the writer of a film do the research? Here are some ways to do it : i. All kinds of material available on the subject should be studied. This may include biographies, novels, memoirs, reports, etc. A study of the newspapers or magazines of that time can also be useful. ii. Make sure to watch films or documentaries made on your subject or similar subjects. iii. Spend some time visiting places related to the story. Things, people and general activities of these places should be observed minutely. Observe people's way of speaking, their way of behaving, their characteristics. This helps a lot in developing characters, writing dialogues etc. iv. Meet relevant people, talk to them and try to understand them. For example, if your story idea is related to students preparing for competitive exams, then you should meet such students, talk to them, spend time with them so that you can understand various aspects of their lives.
Character Development
Character development is a very important task in writing for films. Characters of many films get captured in our memory forever. Strong characters play an important role in making films successful. If we observe carefully, we can find different types of characters in the films. The protagonist is the character of the film whom we can consider the most important. The audience feels the most connection with this character. They rejoice in his/her happiness and the audience also feels pain in his/her sorrow. In popular language we also call him the hero of the story. This character can be male or female. The story of the film is mainly his/her life journey in which other characters play their respective roles. Many stories may have more than one protagonist. These are called dual protagonists or multiple protagonists. The second important character is the antagonist. The antagonist is a character who constantly creates difficulties in the protagonist's journey. This makes the hero's journey a struggle. And only such journeys full of struggle become interesting and successful stories. In a story it is necessary for the antagonist to be powerful. The more powerful it is, the more difficult the struggle of the protagonist. And the success of the protagonist at the end will be just as enjoyable. Apart from these two types of characters, there are many other types of characters who play an important role in taking the story forward. It is necessary for a good film writer to develop each and every character with utmost care. Many times, such characters, whose role in the film is very small, leave an indelible mark in our memories.

Structure The three-act structure is quite popular in film writing. In this, we divide the story into three parts - Setup, Confrontation, and Resolution. Let us discuss all three acts in detail. Setup (First Act) : This is the first act of the story which may constitute roughly twenty to twenty five percent of the entire story. In this act, we establish all our major characters and the story world. The inciting incident that calls the protagonist to act and gives the story a kick start comes in this first act only. The 'setup' mainly makes it clear to the audience what the film is about. Confrontation (Second Act) : Act two is the longest act in the script and may cover around fifty to sixty percent of the story. It is also referred to as rising action. We show struggle of the protagonist in this act. The ups and downs in the struggle of the protagonist should be depicted in this part of the script. Resolution (Third Act) : This final act may cover roughly twenty to twenty five percent of the story. It contains the resolution of the story. The climax is part of this act. The tension reaches its peak in this act and then the audience finally gets the answer to the dramatic question of the story.
Script Elements and Format
We should always try to write the script in the standard format popular in the industry. Following are some of the key elements of a script in this format : a. Scene Heading b. Action c. Character Name d. Dialogue e. Parenthetical a. Scene Heading : As the name suggests, scene heading comes first in scene writing. Mainly three types of information are given in scene heading - Is the scene indoor (Interior/Int.) or outdoor (Exterior/Ext.) ? Where is the location of the scene ? What time is the scene ?

b. Action: We write the description of what the audience will see on screen in 'action'. When we write scene actions, those activities keep getting visualized in our mind. Following example carries scene heading and action : c. Character's Name : After writing the action, we write the name of the character who speaks the dialogue. d. Dialogue : We write the words spoken by the characters here. e. Parenthetical : A parenthetical is a note or direction on how a particular dialogue is delivered by a character. Parentheticals often communicate emotion, action, or delivery within a screenplay's dialogue. Now we'll understand all these elements with an example - EXT. VILLAGE POND SHORE - DAY (Scene Heading) Two monks, Swami Vivekananda and Swami Brahmananda, are resting under a tree on the bank of a pond outside a village. Swami Vivekananda has a letter in his hands and both are talking to each other. (Action) SWAMI VIVEKANANDA (Character's Name) (with sadness) (Parenthetical) Brother, crores of people of our country are living a life worse than that of animals. I keep thinking what can we monks do for the progress of our countrymen ? (Dialogue) We have to write all these elements of the script in a standard format. Script writing software makes this task very easy.
First Draft
By dividing the entire story of the film into scenes and following a standard format, we prepare the first draft of the script. This is not final. We make a lot of changes and improvements, but the first draft is still a very important step in script writing.
7.6.2 Writing for Web Series
In comparison to a film, a web series gives more time to tell the story. Usually a movie gives you around 2 hours while a web series gives 8 to10 hours or more. Web series are divided into episodes. Web series writing has many common things with film writing as it is also a type of screen writing. In this also we develop the characters, divide the story into scenes and then the scenes

are written in the same format. We write the scene headings, the actions of the scenes, the names of the characters and their dialogues. Rajkumar Singh and Satyanshu Singh in their book "Idea Se Parde Tak" beautifully explain the difference between film writing, web series writing and TV serial writing. They compare it with cricket game and its three different formats - Twenty 20, One day and Test. Same bat, same ball, same wicket, same batting, same bowling and same fielding. But changing the format definitely brings some changes in the way of playing. Not all players are able to perform equally in all these three formats. Similarly, despite all the tools being almost the same, there is a difference between writing for films, writing for web series and writing for TV serials.
7.6.3 Writing for TV Serials
The beginning of TV serials in India dates back to 7 July 1984 when 'Hum Log' was telecast for the first time on Doordarshan. This serial was written by Manohar Shyam Joshi and it became very popular and thereafter this genre attracted a large section of viewers to television in India. Serials like 'Buniyaad', 'Ramayana' and 'Mahabharata' in a way created a television revolution in the country. Later, after the entry of private channels in the field of television entertainment, a large amount of work was done in this genre. They also did many experiments. Serials provide much more time for storytelling than films and web series. That's why its writing is also a little different. In fact, a good serial becomes a habit of the audience. And people want to see it every day. Since the time available here is relatively longer, the events are presented with more details. Visual Action and Dialogues: Less dialogues in films are usually considered an advantage. If a large part of the story is told through visual actions, then it is considered better but this is generally not the case in serials. There are much more dialogues in serials than in films. The main reasons behind it are - First, the scenes full of dialogues slow down the story a bit which is necessary for serials. So that they can take many hours to tell the story. The second aspect is related to the budget. The budget of serials is less compared to films. In such a situation, scenes full of dialogues can provide more run time at lesser expense. Use of Cliffhanger Moments: We have to write serials in such a way that the audience waits for the next episode. Attracting audiences to your show every day is essential. For this, it is necessary that we leave the story of each episode at such a point that the audience becomes curious to watch the next episode. This is called cliffhanger moment.
