7.0 INTRODUCTION
Technological innovations and the changing media environment have been offering the users opportunities to choose, select and control the amount of information available on the internet. Though traditionally, advertising has been a one-to-many communication medium, the role of advertising is being re-defined in today's changed landscape. The personalisation and customisation of content has made it possible for the creation of niche markets online. Moreover, online markets offer the consumers a sense of control. Thus, online environments help the advertisers to connect with the consumers meaningfully through personalised content. In this unit, we will trace the history of the changing trends of online advertising.
7.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After working through this unit, you should be able to: * Introduce the concept of online advertising;

* Familiarise the students with the development of online advertising; and * Understand the development of different pricing models used in the online advertising industry.
7.2 WHAT IS ONLINE ADVERTISING?
Online advertising is a form of marketing that is done using the internet as a platform to reach audiences. Both products and services can be promoted in this kind of advertising. It is somewhat similar to the traditional advertising occurring in electronic media and print as it involves the creation of videos and banners with interesting and innovative designs and taglines, but the difference lies in the personalisation of the ads for individual customers using automated software systems. In online advertising, a publisher integrates the advertising content into its online content, to reach potential consumers. Once the consumers click on the content, they can view the entire ad or can get redirected to the page of the company advertising the product or service. Online advertising helps in promoting information about a product across geographical boundaries, in vernacular languages, using the ad serving technology which helps the advertisers to serve ads, count and choose them while monitoring the reach of the advertising campaigns. Let us now look at the important features of online advertising:
1. Online advertising is inexpensive in comparison to traditional advertising.
2. Online advertising can reach a wider audience surpassing geographical boundaries
3. The reach of an ad can be tracked in online advertising.
4. Again, responses from users can be collected through surveys and questionnaires in order to make
the ads more interesting.
5. Online advertising can be personalised according to the needs and wants of the user.
7.3 EVOLUTION OF ONLINE ADVERTISING:
Online advertising initially retained some of the features of traditional advertising. However, with the rapid developments in the world of web characterised by user-generated content and interactivity, advertisers were compelled to take notice as the consumers now had a chance to write reviews of the product in the public domain as well as recommend, value or discard the product through his/ her profile or blogs. Thus, advertisers needed to be cautious about both the quality of the product as well as the message carried in the ad. Just like print, radio and television, the web too is primarily funded by advertising. If we look back at the history of online advertising, we find that in the initial stages, the internet was only used as a medium to provide information about products and brands to the consumer. This was done mainly to increase the credibility of the products and services in the offline spaces and to inform the consumers about the products. So, initially the traditional mass media approach of one-way communication was used.
7.3.1 Advertising via Emails
Online advertising began initially with emails when in May 1978, a man named Gary Theurk who worked at Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC) advertised an open house for a new model of DEC computer via an email sent to the users of ARPANET in the west coast of America. Electronic mail marketing expanded quickly to reach a wide range of audiences. However, soon unsolicited messages started crowding the users' inbox causing disturbance to the user. These kinds of unwanted advertisements sent via email came to be known as Spam. Nevertheless, advertising via email is still being used by advertisers to create brand awareness among users. Many companies have also entered into an opt-in email advertising known as permission marketing, to inform their users about the upcoming events or new product launches via their newsletters that were sent to the users after receiving their consent.

7.3.2 Banner Ads are Launched
During the early years, traditional methods of advertising like web versions of business directories or web versions of classified ads were used by the companies. Also, since less than one-third of the households in the USA had computers with proper internet connectivity, there was a lot of apprehension regarding online advertising. Despite these apprehensions, advertisers started using the web as a medium of advertising, and two issues became important topics of discussion among the advertising community
- the first being tracking the visits of users to the sites, while the second was in relation to the pricing of
ads which were published in the content sites. If we look into the history of online advertising, we will notice that banner ads were the first ones to make their presence felt digitally. On October 24, 1994, banner ads officially started to bring changes on the internet. A web magazine named Hot Wired sold a banner ad to the company, AT&T and displayed the ad on its webpage. For the first time, the digital publication adopted a model used traditionally in print advertising where space is sold for printing ads; similarly, some portions of the website were put aside to sell space to advertisers. These kinds of ads came to be known as banner ads. The ad remained on the site for a period of three months. Based on the number of impressions - viewers clicking and seeing the ad - the reach of the ad was measured. Later, 'cost per mile' or 'CPM', which refers to cost per thousand viewers, became the norm for measuring online ads. Banner ads became hugely popular among big companies and the advertisers sought to find sites leasing out banner spaces. Instead of using traditional media like magazines, newspapers and television, many companies started focusing on attracting clickers via the web itself. However, in those days many people visited the websites after finding out about them in a magazine or newspaper ad. So, in the year 1996, many companies published ads about their websites in the traditional media. Another approach that gained popularity in the year 1996 was the idea of Piggybacking, also known as affiliate marketing. Using this approach, ESPN became the first sports site to provide links for their partners on their site with an understanding that people will visit those links. Hence, by using the Piggybacking approach, business- to-business links with partners were created by the websites to increase traffic. Since users were primarily using the internet for the purpose of news and information, many advertisers started switching from entertainment-oriented ads to information-oriented ads. There were some ads which were published in the form of editorials and are now known as advertorials. In order to promote different kinds of music, CDNow was one of the earliest companies to use editorial content. The first affiliate marketing program on the internet was also created by CDNow.
7.3.3 Targeted Banner Ads
The next change in online advertising was in relation to banner ads where instead of placing them anywhere on the webpage, advertisers started taking an interest in targeting specific consumer demographics. 1997 was a breakthrough year in internet advertising as online advertising revenue continued to grow and advertisers started focusing their attention on personalisation of online ads. So, proximity and immediacy became important for the advertisers. This was mainly because some companies began providing specialised services targeting specific customers on the web. An ad agency named WebConnect started identifying potential websites that will help their clients to get a more targeted reach. This was an important development in the digital space as both the clients and the websites hosting the ads benefited. The benefit for the clients was in reaching the right audiences and the benefit for the websites was in hosting ads which were interesting for the visitors. To avoid 'banner fatigue', WebConnect also introduced the Custom View tool, which capped the number of times a single banner ad was shown to the user. This was done as the companies realised that users stop noticing the same banner ads after some time and thus, capping was the best option. A development which helped the advertisers to understand the performance of their ads was through the launch of DoubleClick, which was one of the world's first ad servers. In the domain of internet "ad-

serving", DoubleClick was one of the earliest Application Service Provider (ASP). DoubleClick helped the advertisers to measure the results of their efforts by offering Return on Investment (ROI) tools for ad campaigns. The CPM pricing model was developed by the search engines around this time due to the launch of DoubleClick. In 1996, the Interactive Advertising Bureau (IAB) was founded to provide legal support, create industry standards, and conduct research in online advertising. Throughout the year 1998, several developments took place in the domain of online advertising. Interstitial Ads became common during this period. These ads appeared on the users' screen while they were waiting to download something online. Nowadays, interstitial ads are mostly used in mobile applications.
7.3.4 Introduction of Pop-up Ads
The next development took place in the area of pop-up ads. Pop up ads help to open a new browser window showcasing the advertisement. While pop up ads appeared immediately while the user searched anything on the browser, interstitial ads depended on the users' actions and appeared mostly between content and at transition points. Pop up ads were created by Ethan Zuckerman who was a developer for Tripod.com. In the beginning pop-up ads seemed to be the most viable option in an age of shrinking banner ads' click-through rates, but in the long-run it didn't transform into real ROI. Moreover, users were often irritated by pop-up ads. The ads provided a bit of respite to the advertisers in the wake of decreasing click-through rates of banner ads, it did not last long as by the early 2000s majority of the web browsers incorporated a pop-up blocking feature. During the late 90s, ad server company, NetGravity, and market research firm, Abacus Direct, were acquired by DoubleClick, which helped DoubleClick to create a strong position in the online advertising sector as the acquisition helped the company to combine technology, reach and data. After that, the launch of the social media website, Facebook, in the year 2004, which was then known as The Facebook by Mark Zuckerberg and his friends at Harvard University can be considered as one of the most important developments in the history of online advertising
7.3.5 Hyper-Targeted Digital Ads
In the twenty-first century, companies like DoubleClick grew as they offered technology products and services to the advertising agencies and media companies. With the help of these services, the clients of the advertising companies were able to traffic, target and report on their advertising campaigns. This was also a time when we saw the growth and development of social media, and this stimulated the rise of online advertising. In order to improve its profitability, Facebook started to work with advertisers in
2006. Advertisers during this time wanted to create strategies which would be effective, and non-
intrusive for the users. As the young users spent most of their time on social networking sites, Facebook seemed to be the most viable option for advertising. In the beginning, Facebook started with small display ads and sponsored links; gradually they started incorporating ads targeting users' demographics and interests. So, rather than bombarding consumers with ads, targeting consumers with relevant ads has become the norm of online advertising. Other social media sites like Twitter, YouTube and Instagram also emphasise on providing the users with an experience that is not aggressive and impersonal.
7.3.6 Emergence of Native Advertising
With the emergence of companies like BuzzFeed and Mashable, advertisers found new ways to connect with the audiences. Advertisers started paying these companies to create videos, articles and other kinds of content for media sites and Google. These ads tried to supplement the online experience of the user by creating content that will look more like a regular piece of content on the website but will also promote the business interest of the company. This kind of advertising is known as Native advertising, and it has been quite successful in creating engagement with the users. Check Your Progress: 1

7.4 EVOLUTION OF THE PRICING MODELS USED IN
ONLINE ADVERTISING
In the early years, it was difficult for advertising managers to understand the value of online advertising as there were no proper industry norms or research available in measuring the effectiveness of online advertising. Except for programs like CD Now's Buy Web, there was no other way to understand the value of online advertising. This made it difficult for advertising managers to trust online platforms. But those who were willing to advertise adopted a flat-fee pricing model. In this model, the website charges the advertisers for a certain period during which the ad is displayed on its page. Some websites also guarantee the amount of traffic their site will generate. However, since all websites did not offer this option, the advertisers started requesting for information on traffic. This was essential for the advertisers because after having the accurate traffic information, they could convert the flat-fee prices into a CPM (cost per mille) model.
7.4.1 Performance Based Pricing Model
Since 2006, the performance-based pricing model has dominated the online advertising industry where payments are made based on the campaign measurement data accumulated through click-throughs and purchases. One of the earliest performance-based pricing models has been the cost-per-click (CPC) pricing model.
7.4.1.1 Cost-Per-Click Model
If we look back, then we find Proctor and Gamble negotiated a deal with Yahoo in 1996 where they paid the website only when a user clicked on the ad. The CPC model became the dominant model in paid search advertising and was adopted by both Google and Yahoo in 2002. Payment based on number of clicks became the standard as it not only exposed the visitor to the banner ad but also allowed the user to become exposed to the target communication if he/ she decided to click on the ad. Thus, the CPC model made it possible for the advertisers to pay for those exposures which attracted interested users. However, some website providers felt that sometimes the creativity of the ad helps in generating an interest in the viewers to click-through the ad and hence, the websites have no control over the user. Also, the unique, interactive nature of the web was something which the traditional-exposure based models for the web did not take into account. However, since responses from the consumer can be measured on the internet unlike the traditional media outlets, the web offered an opportunity to understand the potential customers.
7.4.1.2 Cost-Per-Action Pricing Model

In the next few years, it became important for the advertiser to understand whether the viewer who clicked on the ad actually liked the communication. This is something that the CPC model did not guarantee. So, it became important for the advertisers to create value around the ad on the basis of the degree of visitor's interactivity with the target communication. Hence, the time spent on the ad, the number of pages visited by the user through the ad, the number of times the user visits the ad, etc., were used to calculate the interactivity metric. The website providers however were not happy with the model as it was beyond their ability to create engagement around the ad and thus, in no way can they be held responsible for any activity or the lack of it related to the ad published on their sites. Many websites referred to the print ads mentioning their charges regardless of the sales but advertisers and advertising agencies stuck to the narrative of the web offering the affordance of accountability which should be used to create models to measure consumer behaviour. Hence, the cost-per-action (CPA) model offers the advertisers the opportunity to pay when an action like purchase, download, registration or subscription takes place.
7.4.1.3 Outcome-Based Pricing Model
As advertising depends on outcome, ads that can actually target the audiences to lead to an outcome like influencing attitudes, or motivating consumers to give personal information, or leading to sales, is considered to be more effective. Hence, it is essential for the advertisers to track and measure the effectiveness of an ad through integrated marketing campaigns conducted on the web. Banner ads create awareness among the consumer related to the product or service but after that what is essential is the action taken by the consumer in terms of his/ her intention regarding purchase. An example of this model can be the per-inquiry (PI) ads where the money is paid on the basis of actual sales.
7.5 THE CHANGING TRENDS OF ONLINE ADVERTISING
As online advertising keeps evolving due to rapid innovation in technology accompanied with the interest of the advertisers to be more creative and imaginative for the pleasure of the audience, this space is going to be dynamic in the future. A trend that is the norm today might not be important in the near future. The trend that is dominating the online advertising spend in recent years is online video advertising followed by influencers' branded content and social media marketing. Activity: 3 Find out about augmented reality campaigns of any two brands and note down the important points associated with their campaigning. However, over the years, the trends that can be observed in the online advertising space are:
7.5.1 Dominance of Content Marketing
As content becomes important, advertising companies are also trying to engage the audiences by offering them information in the form of articles and newsletters. Consumers are also being encouraged to give feedback on the product or service offered through the website.
7.5.2 Dominance of Image-Centric Content
In order to create engagement with the users, advertisers are creating content which is image-heavy. This is because people have a tendency to get attracted to images, and thus, putting up photographs or images of the product or service helps in creating connections with the consumers. As we see, in recent years, personalised mobile display ads and in-banner video ads are in trend. Also, advertisers are using the option of Remarketing whereby they are targeting those users who have been to their sites but haven't taken any action like clicking on the link or signing up. Remarketing is being done with the help of third- party cookies that collect information like demographic data, users' interests and preferences. Cookies help the advertisers to re-target the passive audiences with display ads that attract them to eventually buy the product.

7.7 GLOSSARY
Cost-Per-Action: It is a digital advertising metric that measures the total cost of achieving a specific user action such as a purpose, sign-up or form submission. Cost-Per-Click: It is the amount the advertiser pays for each click an ad receives. Pop-up Ads: These are new, often intrusive apps that literally 'pop up' that suddenly appear on a mobile or computer screen when one is browning the web. Interstitial Ads: An advertisement that appears on a screen during natural transition points when being used by the device user, appearing mostly when content is being loaded. Hyper-targeted Digital Ads: A marketing strategy that uses user data to deliver highly personalised ads to their customers

7.3 DEFINING REPRESENTATIONS
At the outset, we could begin by saying that a representation is a depiction or a sign that stands for, or takes the place of, something else. This could be the world around us or an abstract idea or for that matter even a political articulation. A representation could be conveyed through a variety of forms such as theatrical performances, cinematic narratives, literature, art, photography, digital encoding and so forth. These choices, however, are not random or politically innocent. Moreover, as there is no unmediated access to reality, representations are an essential component of our lives for they help us understand our world better and even from a different perspective. Nonetheless to treat a representation as politically neutral is a fallacy. This unit underscores the need to read representations in terms of their ideological effects, for even the earliest modes of representations which comprised theatrical performance and poetry dealing with the valour of kings, tales of war or the separation of lovers, were not devoid of the ideological mores of their age. Thus, the ancient Greek poet Homer sang ballads about the Trojan War and of the marvellous exploits of the Greek hero Odysseus mainly because he catered to an audience of courtly lineage. What really is a representation? Why do we use the term 'representation', when categories like art, literature, film or aesthetics would suffice? One would like to know why a bust of the Greek philosopher Aristotle falls well within the realm of representational art, while a rare satellite photograph of the moon does not? This is not to imply that photography is not a representational art form, but to draw attention to the difference between representation as a creative activity, distinct from the mechanical process of imitation. As re-creation, a representation must be filtered through the subjectivity of the artist, who in turn belongs to a certain historical context and cultural milieu. So, while Keats "Ode to Autumn" is brilliant poetry, it is nonetheless a depiction of an English autumn from the point-of-view of a subject called John Keats, who was located at a moment in time when industrialisation was first making its appearance in the English countryside. The "Ode" captures a fast disappearing pastoral activity - that of the hand operated cider press. Similarly, while the impressionist artist Claude Monet's masterpiece entitled The Water Lilies (http://www.moma.org/images/ dynamic_content/exhibition_page/31634.jpg) is a re-presentation of actual water-lilies, it has in turn inspired many more representations which, while simulating the original, are by no means servile copies of it. When seen as a representation, art cannot be abstracted from the conflicts of its age. It is no longer viewed as transcendental or as occupying a realm of pure beauty untouched by time or place; rather, it is very much a part of its times, of the mundane and politically inundated reality from which it grows. Therefore, as representation, art stands demystified and embedded

in the discourse of its time. Thus we can say that culture and ideology are Representations the salient factors that determine the study of representation. Let us look at some examples. While the sign of the Red Cross, for instance, represents medical and humanitarian aid, Edvard Munch's iconic painting The Scream attempts to re-present the angst of the post World War II generation; likewise, the Russian director Sergei Eisenstein's film Battleship Potemkin attempts to re-create the essence of a complex historical period - the Tsarist regime in Russia; and last, but not the least, is the diasporic Indian filmmaker Deepa Mehta's film Fire which attempts to re-presents gender taboos in the Indian society. The term 'attempt' used here, illustrates the difference between reality and its portrayal; for while reality is far too complex, rough, unclear and often diffuse, when it gets transformed into a piece of art it appears as an artistic product that has finesse, shape and form. In other words, reality has been re-constructed. The reality that art attempts to portray is therefore a construction and like all constructions it is not free of its politics or ideology. However, as no system of representation can ever encompass the entire gamut of reality, new modes and media of representation are constantly being invented/ constructed to signify reality in better ways. Newer media are forever being invented, as is evident in the trajectory of art forms beginning with cave paintings to movements such as Surrealism, Dadaism, Cubist art, and post- modernism, and various other art forms such as literature, cinematography, digital and electronic media and so forth. As a representational art form, literature, it has been stated perhaps naively, is a 'representation of life'. 'Naively', because while a novel like Charles Dickens' Hard Times for instance does represent life in the Victorian age or the gory aspects of industrialisation in Victorian England, it is instrumental in influencing opinion regarding capitalism in general and the Victorian age in particular. Likewise, the play Dance Like a Man by the contemporary Indian playwright Mahesh Dattani represents the effect of a normative, machismo culture on a protagonist who challenges the stereotypical definitions of 'masculinity'. Commenting on the play after watching the performance, the audience commended Dattani for presenting a departure from the regular stereotypes of dissidence. They admitted that the play had influenced and even changed their perceptions regarding gender. It is important to remember that mainstream Indian cinema exerts a strong influence on various aspects of Indian life including fashion, ethics, politics and especially gender and the social expectations of gender roles. The curious question is, if representations stem from life, what effect, if any, can representations have on life? In this regard the Victorian writer Oscar Wilde was not far from the truth when he made the controversial statement that life imitates art and not vice-versa. From the above discussion one can infer that representation and reality are in dialogue with one

Gender, Film and Cinema another and while it is an established fact that the former is not a mirror reflection of the latter, yet representations cannot be divorced from the culture and society that have produced it. Art as representation can mould society's attitudes, perceptions, behaviour and values. In the Indian subcontinent, media and cinema have proved to be the most influential modes of representation. However, before we embark on a full-fledged analysis of gender representation in film, certain theoretical aspects must be clarified. The two factors that stand established are: one, art is influenced by life and in turn exerts its influence over life; and two, all art is representation, which means that it is hardly ever neutral, unbiased or politically innocent. This is not to say that all art whether popular or elitist is no different from propaganda. But by describing art as representation, we foreground its ideological and political constructedness. In the next section, let us look at various attempts to theorise and debate representation through the ages.
7.4 DEBATING REPRESENTATION: PLATO TO EDWARD
SAID
The earliest attempts to theorise representation are found in the work of the Greek philosophers Plato and Aristotle. In their treatises, the word mimesis is used to define representation as a literal translation amounting to imitation. 'Imitation' is not viewed in a pejorative manner but treated more in terms of the layered ambiguity of representational art. As Aristotle saw it, 'imitation' is a natural aspect of the human condition and humans, far more imitative than other animals, learn their first lessons through imitation. It is thus the first step towards a performance. For instance in the Poetics, Aristotle uses the term mimesis to describe tragedy - the most performative and representative art form in ancient Greece: "An imitation of an action that is serious and complete, and which has some greatness about it. It imitates in words with pleasant accompaniments It imitates people performing actions and does not rely on narration. It achieves, through pity and fear, the catharsis of these sorts of feelings." (Butcher, 1974, p. 31-55). The aim of tragedy as an art form is to bring about catharsis or purgation. Aristotle insisted that tragedy, by arousing pity and fear, had a purging effect on individuals. Aristotle's statement was made in response to Plato's call for censorship in the arts. In Book X of The Rebublic, Plato had proposed banning imitative poetry in the ideal city-state as he claimed that it aroused emotions of baser and irrational nature and perversely affected the human mind. The performance of tragedy and comedy would therefore promote undesirable modes of behaviour among the citizens. Bolstering his argument

further, Plato insisted that imitative art being thrice removed from reality Representations was a falsehood and deserved to be banished. The argument goes as follows: while the original form, let's say of a chair, for instance, rests with the creator, it was in turn copied by the carpenter and the likeness of this was further reproduced by the poet or the painter. Art was thus thrice removed from the original idea (Allen, 2006). This argument can be better understood in the context of the present-day media which bear the charge of mediating reality and creating for the viewer a version of reality that may be far removed from the events that actually transpired. So, for Plato, art created illusions, in much the same manner as the present day media is accused of falsification of reality. Plato makes a strong argument regarding the potentiality of representational art to rouse emotion and influence opinion. It therefore had no place in his ideal republic. The only poetry that was allowed in the city state or in the nurseries of the young and impressionable was the kind which dwelt on heroic valour or the coronation of kings or didactic tribute to the state. While Plato was well aware and wary of the idea of art on the mind, Aristotle made a case for the same by drawing upon the catharsis or purgation. He argued that by re-presenting the more disturbing, volatile and irrational side of human nature, the viewer's experience was at best vicarious and this induced a purgation of those undesirable elements thereby cleansing viewer of negative emotions. Aristotle insisted that art and its performance led the citizen to leave the theatre completely purged of all that was base (Butcher, 1974, 1961). Moving from ancient Greece to the Romantic Period may appear to be a quantum leap but it was with the Romantics (Coleridge, Kant, Hegel among others), that the concept of aesthetics as the philosophy of art was first articulated. Speaking about this period, Terry Eagleton states "... the assumption that there was an unchanging object called 'art' or an isolable experience called 'beauty' or the 'aesthetic', was largely a product of the very alienation of art from social life " (Eagleton, 1983, p. 21). This was the time when industrialization was beginning to make its presence felt in the English countryside. Thus, for the Romantics, artistic creation transcended the vagaries of historical, material, social or political change. In other words, art was removed from the materiality of commercial activity and appeared absolved of the conflicts of its age rather than embodying them. The Victorian age with its emphasis on utilitarianism and progress welcomed this line of thought by insisting that imaginative endeavour was as an activity gloriously useless, and at best an end in itself. Attempting to make a case for the arts, Oscar Wilde insisted on the adage 'art for art's sake', implying that it was reductive to look for a message or purpose in a work of art. Paradoxically, Victorian art is extremely representative of the discourses of its times. Moreover, with the emergence of print culture in

Gender, Film and Cinema the Victorian age, artistic representation especially literature found wide dissemination. As the post-modernist philosopher Michel Foucault later pointed out, the Victorian age straitjacketed sexuality into discourses of the normative as opposed to that of the deviant or the dissident. Representation played no small role in this facilitation; rather, as Foucault writes in The History of Sexuality Volume II, it added to the proliferating discourses on sexuality. Typical representations of sexuality such as the normative family, the hysterical woman, the dissident, the deviant, the lady, the prostitute and so forth abound in the Victorian Age. The thrust of Foucault's investigation is why all this transpired in the Victorian age and not before or after it? He tries to show how discourse and the knowledge it produces and disseminates are connected to the power structures which in turn stand validated by that knowledge. Foucault relates this to the demands of the welfare state that was beginning to consolidate its position and shows how representations of normative sexuality were complicit with it. Using the Foucauldian framework, the post-colonial scholar Edward Said in his path-breaking study titled Orientalism (1978), analyses the way geographical territory of the Orient (Middle East) was depicted by the European imagination through the entire period of colonial expansion from eighteenth century onwards. He notes how these representations of the Orient focus on images of primitivism, despotism, cruelty, sensuality, superstition, exotic splendour and so forth to create certain stereotypical notions about the Orient and its inhabitants. For the European imaginary, the Orient, through its representations, stood for everything that they prided themselves on not being. In other words, the Orient was the uncivilized, barbaric 'Other' to the civilized West. Thus, Orientalism helped the West to define its self-image more than it did for the East. You have already come across Said's work in unit 3, Block 5 of MWG 001. It may be helpful for you to review the relevant section. The overarching question is why such representations of the Orient would be helpful to the Western power structures of the time in time and why would the West wish to propagate such representations? The answer lies in the economics of colonial polity which needed an ideology such as Orientalism to facilitate the project of colonial conquest. As Said says, Orientalism became: "...a western style for dominating, restructuring, and having authority over the Orient." (Said, 1978, p. 3). The ideology of Orientalism projected colonial expansion not as the exploitative mechanism it really was but as a civilizing mission of carrying the white man's [and woman's] burden - that is, of carrying the light of civilization and modernity to the darker and savage regions of the earth. In this regard, representations of the Orient by the Occident, worked to validate the altruistic aspect of colonial conquest. While agreeing that representations can never be exactly

realistic, for there is no Orient (except as a geographical location) out Representations there waiting to be realistically depicted, Said states: "there is no such thing as a delivered presence but a re-presence, or a representation" (Said, 1978, p. 21). Representations however cannot be dismissed as untrue, for as the text goes on to demonstrate, Orientalism, i.e., knowledge about the Orient produced by the Occident, deeply influenced colonial polity and therefore had vast implications for real people in real contexts. Our next point regarding the theory of representation deals with the politics of the viewer because besides the creating subject, the interpreting subject too imparts meaning to the piece of art in terms of her politics and ideologies. As the cultural critic Ella Shohat says: "Each filmic or academic utterance must be analysed not only in terms of who represents but also in terms of who is being represented for what purpose, at which historical moment, for which location, using which strategies, and in what tone of address." (Shohat, 1995, p.166-178). In other words, while studying representations we must be alert to the ideological work the representation accomplishes. So while liking or not liking a text/art may appear to be no more than a value judgment, it speaks volumes about how power operates in a society at any given point of time. Our critical responses, variable as they may be, are demonstrative not just of the vagaries of human nature but reflect deeper prejudices and beliefs, which as mentioned earlier on in this essay, shows how power operates in society. For instance, while the neo-classicists decried Shakespeare's plays as the products of a mind untrained in Latin, Greek and mathematics; the Romantics deified him but doubted the literary capabilities of the poet John Donne. As you have seen from the above discussion, representations are therefore deeply political and laden with ideological mores. This is particularly true of cinema and mainstream Indian cinema which is labelled as an escapist mode of mass entertainment. When studied in terms of representation, this cinema reveals the politics of its making. In the next section we will take a closer look at gender representation in contemporary Indian cinema. 7.5 GENDER REPRESENTATIONS IN INDIAN CINEMA
Gender representations in the mainstream contemporary Indian cinema (Bollywood) generally follow a set pattern or formula; for instance femininity is represented in terms of passivity, chastity and as the repository of traditional, ritualistic values, while controlled anger and violence are the characteristics of the virile male hero in his role as protector of the defenceless women. Their maschismo character makes them the hero, while gay men are often shown as effeminate, and lesbians are portrayed as exhibiting masculine traits. Films did evolve beyond such stereotypical depictions, about the gay men and lesbian portrayals we will talk in details in the last unit of this block. The nuances of such attempts will be explored in this section. We will look at representations of dissidence vis-a-vis their equation with heterosexuality, the manner in which they challenge the traditionally established and inviolable gender demarcations and how this relates to the homophobia of a heteronormative society.
7.5.1 Masculine Representations
In this section, we will begin by examining two important aspects of masculine representations in Indian cinema: homosociality and homoeroticism. The difference between the two terms lies in the social behaviour between two male protagonists in a film. Homosociality refers to a bonding between the two characters without any sexual connotations. For instance, either they are two heroes, or two brothers, or hero and a villain. Between the male hero and the male villain, certainly action and showing physical power of the two are evident, overlaying the fact that good (hero) always wins over evil (villain) whatsoever may be the incidental development in the movie. So this category might be seen through ethical and moral point of view; but the first two categories of two heroes/brothers are more prominent examples of homosociality. For instance, the bondage of friendship between two male protagonists is sometimes portrayed sharing their feelings and love for each other at plutonic level. Films like Dosti (1964), Sholay (1975), Yaraana (1981) and many more films where two protagonists turn out to be heroes of the films each having two different heroines. Not only such portrayals, but pairing up two male heroes with bondage of same profession or motive behind their acts, like Do aur Do Paanch (1980), Shaan (1980), and many others, is also quite common examples of homosociality. Still today such representations of masculine homosociality are acceptable by spectators widely. The other representation of two male actors is homoeroticism. Their amiability and bondages with other male protagonists in any given film sometimes depicts an erotic bondage beyond the parameters of sexual overtones. Take examples of films where, two heroes fall in love with the same girl and one sacrifices for the other, like Arzoo (1965), or Muqaddar

ka Sikandar (1978), or Qurbani (1980). Another example of homoeroticisms Representations in Bollywood Hindi cinema are camp readings. Camp readings see male spectacle as masculine. Camp readings combine the antithetical qualities of authenticity and theatricality. This can be seen as an oppositional reading of popular culture offering the identification and pleasure that dominant cultures deny to homosexuals. Camp emphasises the performativity of gender and shows that gender enacts a set of discontinuous, if not parodic, performances (Butler, 1990, pp. 163-80). Representations of gender matter because gender is a fiction disseminated by the prevailing power structures, which is in this case the welfare state. In being seen as natural, gender representation assumes dimensions akin to natural truth and can exercise the power to determine the destiny of the persons concerned. Particular acts and choices function as the markers of pathology typifying the deviant character type which expresses, as Foucault says, a degenerate constitution whose sexuality is governed by concepts of risk, danger and violence (Foucault, 1976, pp. 38-79). These groups are taken to be marginal but in their marginality function to determine the dominant, that is, they consolidate reproductive sexual relations as normative and healthy.
7.5.2 Feminine Representations
As you have read, femininity is often represented in mainstream commercial cinema in terms of passivity, chastity where woman becomes the repository of traditional, ritualistic values making her the carrier of maan-maryada of the family, community and nation, such as the figure of the pativrata (devoted wife and mother), the Sati-Savitri, and the portrayal of villainy through characterisations of vamps. The depiction of deviance on the Indian screen has followed a staple pattern too, with very few exceptions. The Pati- Parameshwar phenomenon has become a ritualistic tradition for representing women in cinema. Until the 80s of Bollywood there was an increase in the number of female-orientated movies. Masculine characteristics of action were depicted. Even, the roles of vamps or female villainy saw changes during this period. Vamps were no longer shown as docile feminine characters attached to the male villains, they rather were portrayed as over-powering and significant roles in most of the family dramas, for example like a torturous saas or nanad, like Sau Din Saas Ke (1979), Ghar Ek Mandir (1984), Biwi Ho To Aisi (1988), etc. Another significant factor can be seen in films, is the feminine homosociality. The plutonic bonding between two female protagonists is also represented in many films, like the male bonding. Two female protagonists may be involved in the same act, like stealing Parvarish (1977), or supporting the heroes to take revenge, like in Mawaali (1983).

Gender, Film and Cinema 7.5.3 Same Sex Representations: Lesbians
In Indian cinema, same sex love has often been used as stock situation for comedy. This is especially true in the depictions of male homosexuality which is often represented in terms of effeminacy or an inadequacy in terms of meeting the norm of masculinity typified by the figure of the hero. For instance, the blockbuster Kal ho Na Ho (2003) directed by Karan Johar was among the first films to portray camp reading gestures on screen. Yet when this was shown through sexual postures of the two male leads Shahrukh Khan and Saif Ali Khan, the camera focussed instead on the nervous agitation of the bai bringing the morning tea. Her reaction prompted hilarious comedy, thereby negating the possibility of making manifest the subversive sexuality observed by the viewer, who through the reaction of the bai is now encouraged to view the enactment as a comic misunderstanding rather than a conscious choice made by the protagonists. The subversive edge of the preceding shot -- enacting Camp (through gestures) -- was thus translated as a comic occasion. The film Dostana (2008) followed a similar theme but established heterosexuality of all the couples involved in the final sequence. The possibility of a committed and fulfilling homosexual relationship, in this case between the two male leads Abhishek Bachhan and John Abraham, was reduced to the level of farce. You will read more about such examples in Hindi and vernacular films in the last unit of this block. In this unit, you will learn about lesbian representations in Bollywood cinema, citing two examples only. Deepa Mehta's radical movie Fire (1996), despite the representation of a bond between the two main characters played by strong female lead of Shabana Azmi and Nandita Das, ultimately took recourse to explaining the desire between the two women as the outcome of a cloistered and lonely marriage. Female homosexuality was seen as demonic and threatening and needed to be erased to re-set familial and social balance. Depictions of homosexuality as in the films mentioned above strengthen the binary between the hetero and the homo, with normativity and health associated with the former. In this regard, Karan Razdan's film Girlfriend (2004) marks a departure from the set norm. At the outset, the 'Tanya' character in the film is depicted as a masculine woman or the mannish-lesbian; but she is so by choice. As the masculinised lesbian, the character of Tanya follows the stereotypical image of female homosexuality but it is through the inherent doubleness of her character, existing and partaking of both the realms of masculinity and femininity that she challenges established and exclusivist gender boundaries. Through her, the auteur is able to subvert the staid dichotomy of active male as opposed to the passive female - a binary that is foundational for defining gender in a patriarchal culture.

Narratives are often structured through opposition, thereby enabling the Representations spectator to identify with the point-of-view desired by the auteur. In this text the stereotype of the homicidal, psychotic butch Tanya, is foiled by the ultra feminine, victimised, 'normal' woman Sapna, who besides being a professional model is utterly incapable of taking care of either herself or her finances. Needless to say, she has to be rescued time and again by Tanya. While Sapna fits the stereotypical mould of the damsel in distress, Tanya on the other hand straddles a bike, makes money as a street fighter and becomes the menacing serial killer. Danger stalks her character. Following lesbian stereotypes, she too is cast in terms of the castrated female lesbian. She is in this regard the wild uncontrollable entity- the female homosexual, who by subverting societal mores now exists in a space that is taboo. Representations of female homosexuality, as is evident from the above example, do not serve the function of celebrating female desire but place it on display for the masculine spectator. Women's desire is a matter of curiosity, and it demands investigation simply because it is the 'other'. The spectator engages with the scene by seeing the lesbian as the 'other', a fit object of 'investigation-by-scrutiny' (Kuhn, 1985). This objectification of the images on screen imply a masculine subject position, which can be occupied by spectators, be they men or women. According to Sigmund Freud (Frued, 1905, pp. 387-90), homosexual women suffer from penis envy, therefore the homosexual female, as visualized in the dominant discourse, tries to overcome her castration by assuming a masculine role in life, cross-dresses and behaves through gestures and desire like a man. A significant part of the lesbian fantasy/myth is the origin of the lesbian. For Freud, a lesbian is a woman who has never recovered from her sense of phallic inequality. Ultimately, the cinematic text attempts to contain the unruly and deviant female body which threatens to confuse gender boundaries and disrupt the social order. Such an argument establishes heteronormative sexuality as the accepted sexual behaviour and dismisses homosexuality as a pathological deviation. However, the final method of containment is always lethal. The psychotic lesbian must die, which may not be the case with the male homosexual who by being effeminate and funny is rendered innocuous. As Michel Foucault iterates, the culturally sanctioned signifiers of the homosexual experience cannot go beyond casual encounters, the anonymous sexual act and the immediate albeit illicit pleasure (Blackman & Walkerdine, 2001, p. 168). Foucault argues that homosexual connections assume disturbing and disruptive positions when they translate into gentler modes of camaraderie, affection, friendship, passion, solidarity, companionship and tenderness (Blackman & Walkerdine, 2001, 168). The dominant stereotypes of gay men range from

Gender, Film and Cinema the sissy to the sad young man to the ageing queen and as mentioned earlier they are characteristically the source of comedy because they fail the norm of masculinity. These stereotypes are often introduced through visual, aural and descriptive iconography to typify male homosexuality, such as codes in dressing, certain gestures, stylistic decor or extended looks, all of which can invoke the homosexuality of the character. Typically in the Girlfriend, the male homosexual is a limp-wristed effeminate man. The representation of the male homosexual objectifies the male body and delivers to the gaze. But the image of the male body as an object of the gaze is fraught with ambivalences, repressions and denials. Like the masquerade, the notion of spectacle has such strong female connotations: for a male performer to be an object of display and desire, even if it means donning a mask, it threatens his very masculinity. But because the phallus is a symbol and signifier no male body can ever symbolise it completely and although the patriarchal male subject has a privileged relation to the phallus, he will always fall short of the phallic ideal. Jacque Lacan (Lacan, 1977, p. 291) notices this effect in his essay on the meaning of the phallus: "the curious consequence of making virile display in the human being itself seems feminine." Hence the male spectacle acquires a feminine position. While the theatricality of the performing male is aimed at arousing desire, sensuality is more a feminine trait. It is the female body that can legitimately be objectified as sensual and desirable thereby commanding the gaze, while the sensual masculine posturing, even in theatricality, easily becomes an object of laughter. 7.6 LET US SUM UP
Our analysis of gender representation in mainstream Indian cinema shows how representations are far from innocuous and stereotypes far from sterile. Their presence ensures that the hegemonic social gendering maintains and validates its position as the dominant, true and natural. However, it is the inherent ambivalence in the nature of representation that reveals the antithetical directions at one and the same time. The cinematic text discussed above, at one level solidifies the position of the heteronormative by playing on the homophobic notions of society but at the same time destabilises notions of gender by pointing to the 'performance' of gender. What this makes apparent is that 'gendering' is an ambivalent process and that identity, 116 specially gendered identity, is relational.

7.0 INTRODUCTION
Health journalism involves the spread of all types of health-related information through media outlets to the public. Like new medicines, health policies, the results of medical research, the benefits of immunization, disease outbreaks and how to stop them, and anything else that would keep people up to date and help them take smart decisions about their health. Health journalists can influence, educate, and change the attitude and belief of the public towards a particular health issue, encourage healthy practices, and also bring health related concerns to the attention of authorities. Through their reporting, they can get people to support health policies that are good for them. Hence, health reporters must work hard to give accurate, thorough, and reliable news because any of these things could mislead the public and force lawmakers to make laws and rules that may not work or are even harmful.
7.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
At the end of the course, you will be able to * Understand the significance of health reporting * Implement effective research techniques for factual health reporting. * Apply principles of ethical reporting.
7.2 BRIEF OVERVIEW AND SIGNIFICANCE OF HEALTH JOURNALISM
7.2.1 Significance of Public Awareness About Health and Related Issues

Understanding health issues and their causes can help people stay healthy by adopting the right attitudes, taking preventative measures, and using control strategies like vaccination, hygiene, and lifestyle choices. By showing how diet, sleep, and exercise prevent CVDs and diabetes, people may adopt them. Similarly, raising awareness of the dangers of smoking, binge drinking, and drug use may reduce their prevalence. Health awareness empowers people to make informed health decisions and be proactive by seeking consultations or screenings. In addition, it builds empathy and lowers stigma. For example, raising awareness busts myths about mental health and encourages support. Making people more aware of and knowledgeable about health issues can lower the cost of long-term and preventable illnesses. In fact, a key component of disease outbreak control is spreading accurate and reliable information during times of public health emergencies. Early awareness of the illness outbreak would help in understanding risk behaviour and enable the public to react swiftly to the outbreak. In addition to lessening the overall strain on healthcare systems, early detection and action can stop the spread of infectious diseases. All of us have witnessed the importance of this during the COVID-19 pandemic. The mass media, which are the main ways that health messages get out, were used to tell people how to prevent and treat diseases, as well as government rules they needed to follow during the pandemic. Public awareness and understanding of health issues and conditions can serve another crucial role, that of national health management, by aiding in effective healthcare resource allocations and focusing governmental attention on prevalent health problems and challenges. Further, it could also lead to the mobilization of support for advantageous public health policies. More about this will be discussed under subsection 7.2.2. Raising people's awareness of health issues would also lead to global health cooperation. Such as working together to solve health problems that many countries share. Sharing information will also make it easier to share the best ways to do things and build global health efforts.
7.2.2 Impact of Health Journalism on Public Health Policies
Studying how health journalism affects public health policies is a complicated and multidimensional field that touches on the relationship between the media, healthcare, and policymaking. Participation and public involvement are essential results of good health journalism. Through promoting public awareness and participation in health policy dialogues, health journalism enables people to make knowledgeable decisions about their health and supports neighbourhood-based projects. The effective execution of public health policy can be impacted by media coverage due to its ability to mould public attitudes, rally support, and encourage adherence. Social media, podcasts, and other emerging technologies have a significant influence on the narratives surrounding health and policy. Outside the sphere of information distribution, health journalism has a major role in influencing public opinion and establishing political agendas pertaining to health. By drawing attention to important issues and affecting how resources and attention are allocated in government, journalists have the ability to highlight certain health- related concerns through their reporting. In addition, health journalism is essential for assessing the effects of policies, holding decision-makers responsible for their actions, and offering insightful commentary for the creation of new policies. The influence does, however, come with obligations and difficulties, highlighting the significance of truthful information sharing, moral reporting, and the ongoing modification of journalistic techniques to fit the changing media environment. According to the Association of Health Care Journalists (AHCJ), professional standards of truth, accuracy, and context in every report are absolutely necessary for health- care journalists. To do this, health journalists need to be cautious when selecting their sources, investigate and record any relationships between information sources and proponents of novel ideas or treatments, understand how medical research functions so that they can report accurately, use television library or file footage sparingly, avoid using language that is unclear or sensational, and weigh the benefits and risks of the story. They should be responsible and check their facts before they write stories.

Spreading false information can hurt the public's trust in public health programs and make them less effective. In 1998, the Lancet published a poorly designed study that suggested a connection between autism and the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine. This link was later disproved. After the study came out, childhood vaccination rates dropped for years in the UK, Ireland, and the USA. This was because the study was widely reported in the media. This shows that false scientific information in the media can make people less trusting of vaccinations. The effects of using the media to disseminate scientific research when it contains false information, as in the case of the MMR can lead to public misunderstanding, distrust in science, and harmful health behaviours (Dempster, G., Sutherland, G., & Keogh, L., 2022). To help create public-resonant strategies, health journalists must work in tandem with legislators, health experts, and communication professionals. People are more likely to understand and act on health information that is presented in an interesting way, such as through stories, graphics, and other methods that make it easier for them to find and use. Further, health journalists must effectively navigate social media areas to guarantee that the public receives accurate and trustworthy health information because of the speed and scope of information transmission through these platforms. The impact of health journalism on public health policies varies depending on the nation and culture. The ways in which health journalism and its impact on policymaking are approached vary depending on the media environment, cultural perspectives on health, and the social role of journalism. 7.5 INTERVIEWING IN THE HEALTH CONTEXT
7.5.1 Developing Effective Interviewing Techniques for Health Journalists
If your aim is to become a health journalist, then you must learn how to effectively interview people to get accurate information, explain complicated health issues, and connect with your readers. Here are some important things health reporters should think about and do when they are interviewing people:
1. Know your subject, do a lot of research on the subject, and the person you will be interviewing
before the interview. Find out about their background, what they specialize in, and any new work or contributions they have made. With this information, you will be able to ask better, more relevant questions. It is also important to make the person you are interviewing feel at ease. Make sure they understand why they are being interviewed and how their answers will help the public learn about health issues.
2. Use open-ended questions to get detailed answers. Questions that start with "how," "why," or "tell
me about" would encourage a more detailed answer. As a follow-up to answers, ask probing

questions to make more specific or complicated ideas clearer. This will help you understand the subject better and bring out more details.
3. Pay close attention to what the person being interviewed says. Active listening not only helps you
understand what was said, but it also shows that you value the other person's point of view.
4. Keep an open mind during the interview in case something unexpected comes up. The most useful
information can sometimes be found in conversations that were not planned. Being flexible is important for capturing these moments.
5. Working as a health journalist often means talking to people and groups from different backgrounds.
Be aware of how cultural factors may affect health beliefs and practices, and be sensitive to them.
6. Use plain, easy-to-understand language when talking about technical matters. It is important for
health reporters to translate difficult medical or scientific terms into simple language so that their readers can easily understand what they are reading.
7. While discussing personal health related matters, it is important to be mindful of the individual's
privacy. You have to respect the boundaries set by the interviewee and clearly inform the person about how the information will be used
8. In health journalism, accuracy is very important. If you are not sure about something or need more
information, do not hesitate to ask the person you interviewed again.
9. After getting permission from the person being interviewed, record the conversation to make sure
the report is correct. This lets you go back and read what was said during the conversation, which lowers the chance of misquoting or missing important points.
10. Collect information from a variety of sources to make sure that the health issues you write about
reflect their complexity and variety accurately. This means looking at things from different cultural, socioeconomic, and demographic points of view.
7.5.2 Navigating Sensitive Topics with Empathy and Professionalism.
As health issues often involve personal and emotionally charged stories, it is important for health journalists to be able to handle sensitive topics with empathy and professionalism. To become a good journalist, you need to understand the feelings of people who are dealing with health problems. Finding a way to connect with interviewees through genuine interest, respect for their experiences, and a promise to accurately represent their points of view is essential for building trust. When writing about mental health, trauma, or sensitive medical conditions, health reporters must be very careful about the words they use. They must be respectful, empathetic, and free of words that stigmatize or judge. Communicating the interview or story's purpose and potential impact is essential to informed consent, which is an important ethical requirement while taking interviews. Getting consent makes sure that people being interviewed know how their stories will be shared and gives them control over how much information is shared. Trauma-informed reporting is crucial, and health reporters must note that discussing personal health experiences can cause trauma. Setting up a safe and supportive space for interviews and stories is part of this approach. Further, respecting privacy is very important. Journalists have to find a balance between the public's right to know and a person's right to privacy and stay out of people's personal lives unless they have to. Diversity and inclusion are important parts of sensitive reporting. For example, health journalists should be aware of and include different points of view. To present information objectively and without personal bias, journalists must stick to professional boundaries. Giving people information about support services is a kind thing to do, especially when the information is about mental health, addiction, or other sensitive topics. As part of this, information about support services, hotlines, or groups that can help should be

included. Journalists need to take care of themselves by recognizing the emotional toll that covering tough topics can have and getting help when they need it. Lastly, it is important to deal with concerns in a responsible way. Journalists should respond to feedback and corrections with care and honesty. Using these guidelines can help health journalists talk about issues more empathetically and responsibly.
7.6 MENTAL HEALTH REPORTING
7.6.1 Addressing the Challenges and Responsibilities of Reporting on Mental Health
The challenges of reporting on mental health must be discussed to maintain ethical standards and help people understand this sensitive topic. News about mental health can be hard, and there is a chance that it could spread stigma and false information. Media portrayals that are sensationalized can reinforce stereotypes and make it harder for people to get help. Concerns about privacy also come up, so reporters have to find a fine line between being open and protecting people's right to privacy. Another problem is that mental health problems are very complicated and need to be understood in depth so that they are not oversimplified or misunderstood. As a result of these problems, mental health reporters have some duties. It is important to spread accurate information, which means you need to make a commitment to keep up with the latest research, treatments, and developments in the field. Staying away from sensationalism is very important if you want to stop stigma and false information from spreading. It is very important to respect the privacy and dignity of people with mental health conditions. This means that journalists must get informed consent and put the well-being of those sharing their experiences first. Language and framing are very important. They must take special care to avoid using words that are degrading and must present stories in a kind, non-degrading way. It is also important for health reporters to offer helpful resources while spreading a message of hope and healing. For instance, a list of mental health resources, such as helplines and support groups, would be helpful for people who need them. It is important to continuously educate the audience by providing clear explanations of the complexities surrounding mental health conditions and dispelling any misconceptions. Working alongside mental health experts improves the precision and comprehensiveness of reporting, guaranteeing that information is well-researched and aligned with current advancements.
7.6.2 Destigmatizing Mental Health Through Accurate and Compassionate Journalism.
The stigma surrounding mental health has been around for a long time. This is usually because of false information, sensationalism, and negative media portrayals. Getting a clear and academic understanding of mental health problems is important to fight stereotypes and false beliefs that get in the way of open communication. Stigmatization can have serious repercussions, such as discouraging people from seeking help, fostering feelings of shame, and escalating the isolation that those with mental health issues experience. Using sensationalised or false information in the news about mental health issues reinforces this cycle and highlights the need for a shift toward more accurate and caring reporting. A more nuanced understanding of mental health can only come from accurate reporting that challenges these harmful stories. There is no doubt that journalists have a huge impact on how people think and feel. Recognizing this duty, there is an increasing demand for journalists to handle mental health reporting with sensitivity, compassion, and a dedication to precision. It is crucial to prioritize the welfare of individuals above sensationalism and to challenge stereotypes through thoughtful and well-informed storytelling. To accurately represent mental health issues, we need to go beyond one-dimensional portrayals. Being aware that mental health problems are complicated and affect people from all walks of life, journalists should try to include a wide range of experiences. Emphasizing the human aspect and highlighting the themes of recovery and strength can be effective in challenging stereotypes.

Language holds significant influence in shaping perceptions. It is important for journalists to be mindful of their language choices, refraining from using stigmatizing terms and instead opting for terminology that demonstrates a compassionate understanding of mental health. Promoting the use of respectful language plays a crucial role in diminishing stigma and cultivating a discourse that is more inclusive. Recognizing the difficulties at hand, journalists have the ability to shed light on success stories and positive results pertaining to mental health. Highlighting narratives of resilience, recovery, and the efficacy of treatment can serve as a source of inspiration and provide a counterweight to the predominantly negative stories prevalent in media coverage. Collaboration with mental health professionals and advocacy organizations is crucial for journalists to maintain accuracy and sensitivity in their reporting. Consulting with experts not only enhances the credibility of the reporting but also offers a more nuanced and informed perspective on mental health matters.
7.8 DIGITAL MEDIA AND HEALTH COMMUNICATION
7.8.1 Exploring the Impact of Digital Media on Health Communication.
Digital media has a huge effect on health communication, completely changing how information is shared in the healthcare field. Digital platforms make it easy for health information to get around quickly. This means that people all over the world can get news and advice almost instantly, which is especially important during health emergencies. People can now obtain more information about their health as a result of information democratization. This encourages patient engagement and shared decision-making. Social media plays a key role in building communities around health issues, making it easier for people to get involved, build support networks, and spread health campaigns to a wide range of people. Interactive websites, apps, and online communities can all be used to promote health and change people's behaviour. This can help people live healthier lives and stick to their treatment plans. Organizations now use social media to spread their message, rally support, and raise money for global health advocacy and awareness campaigns. The effectiveness of digital media in communicating intricate health information is further improved by personalizing health communication with targeted messages and interactive educational tools. Digital progress has made telehealth possible, which has changed the way healthcare is delivered by allowing remote consultations and more people to get medical help, especially in areas that do not have enough doctors.
7.8.2 Leveraging Social Media Responsibly in Health Journalism
In this age of instantaneous information sharing, it is imperative that health journalism responsibly utilizes social media. Before sharing information on social media, journalists should verify its accuracy and credibility by consulting reliable, evidence-based sources. Attributing data to reputable organizations or experts and being open and honest about where the information came from are two of the most important ways to build trust. Content should be balanced in its presentation of health information and should not be sensationalized or click-baited in order to inform rather than scare. Participating in meaningful conversations with your audience on social media helps build a community that values reliable health information by encouraging constructive dialogue. In order to promote health literacy, it is necessary to give background information, define medical terms, and simplify difficult concepts. Important factors to keep in mind include: adhering to ethical standards; protecting privacy; and getting informed consent for personal stories. In order to stop the spread of false information, it is crucial to verify user-generated content. Reporters must try to be inclusive by considering different viewpoints and cultural sensitivities when using social media to reach a wide range of audiences. The credibility of social media health journalism is enhanced by promptly publishing updates and corrections, working in tandem with experts, and guaranteeing responsible engagement.

Health journalism is the dissemination of health-related information to the public via media outlets in order to keep people informed and to assist in the development of some level of health literacy among the general public. To become a health journalist, one must first learn how to conduct effective interviews in order to obtain accurate information, explain complex health issues, and connect with readers. Honing interviewing skills would help health reporters produce more accurate, useful, and ethically and culturally sensitive news. Health journalists must be able to handle sensitive topics with empathy and professionalism. For example, mental health journalism necessitates a meticulous and accountable approach that considers the field's unique challenges as well as journalists' ethical obligations. In this unit we learn about the health journalists who want to write accurate and nuanced stories about health must build strong relationships with health professionals. Involving health experts in the story development process ensures that the finished product is accurate and comprehensive.

8.0 INTRODUCTION
Nowadays many health care programmes in most countries, particularly in developing countries, are using behavioural change communication (BCC) to improve the health status and well-being of its people. Generally speaking BCC is a process that motivates people to adopt and sustain healthy behaviours and lifestyle. A comprehensive BCC strategy would be helpful to effectively implement BCC activities in order to improve health status of the population. It is pertinent to mention here that BCC is one of the health care education strategies outlined in the Uttar Pradesh National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) to achieve the goals of reduction in mortality, fertility and morbidity.
8.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After reading this unit you should be able to: * explain the meaning and benefits of BCC in family health care; * discuss various channels of BCC; * how to formulate a BCC strategy; and * describe and follow guidelines for successful BCC.
8.2 BEHAVIOURAL CHANGE COMMUNICATION IN HEALTH CARE:
MEANINGAND BENEFITS
National Health Policy (1982) emphasised on appropriate communication strategies to provide health information in easily understandable form and to motivate formation of an attitude for healthy living. Communication is derived from a Latin word "Communis" which means common. When we communicate we are trying to establish commonness with someone. It is the way which provides a link between two individuals or an individual and the world outside himself / herself.
8.2.1 Meaning of BCC in Health Care
Some of the definitions of BCC are narrated below. * BCC in health aims at to improve people's health and well-being including education about

maternal and child health care, health care of adolescents and the elderly, family planning and communicable and non-communicable diseases. * The BCC in health care is customarily a process that motivates people to adopt and sustain healthy behaviours and lifestyle. A sustained BCC programme leads to improvement in the health status of people. Behavioural Change Communication strategy in health refers to systematic attempts to modify and influence behaviour or practices; and environmental factors related to that behaviour which directly or indirectly promotes use of healthy practices. * Behavioural Change Communication (BCC) is the strategic use of communication to promote positive health outcomes based on proven theories and models of behaviour change. * According to Bertrand and Becker- Benton, the main difference between IEC (Information, Communication and Education) and BCC is that while IEC stresses one-way communication focussed on "Messages", BCC is more "Outcome" oriented and also includes the role of participatory methods and motivation in the behavioural changes process. * Behavioural change communication is part of an integrated, multi-level, interactive process with communities, aimed at developing tailored messages and approaches using a variety of communication channels. * Behavioural Change Communication uses behavioural and communication theories and research to develop interventions that influences individual behaviours and the social contexts in which they occur.
What is Behaviour Change
Communication? BCC is about changing specific behaviours - "well defined actions at the household, community and health service levels". BCC approaches recognize that behaviour change is more about identifying the causes and barriers to behaviour change and overcoming the barriers. It is about understanding the communities, contexts and environments in which behaviours occur. BCC is also about using persuasive techniques to demand health rights and to make public sector health services available and accessible to the neediest. BCC is about integrating new practices into long standing social, cultural and communication systems.
Nandita Kapadia-Kundu
8.2.2 Benefits of BCC
Behaviour change communication (BCC) is the strategic use of communication to promote positive health outcomes, based on proven theories and models of behaviour change. BCC employs a systematic process beginning with formative research and behaviour analysis, followed by communication planning, implementation, and monitoring, evaluation and follow-up activities. Audiences are carefully segmented; messages and materials are pre-tested, and both mass media and interpersonal channels are used to achieve defined behavioural objectives. BCC aims to foster positive behaviour; promote and sustain individual, community and societal behaviour change and maintain appropriate behaviour. Some of the important benefits of BCC are as follows: * Increases knowledge, attitude and skill * Stimulates community dialogue * Promotes essential attitude change * Creates demand for information and services * Advocates for appropriate

* family health care policies * Enhances use of promotive, preventive and curative health care services * Is more appropriate for the illiterate and less literate group of audiences
