8.0 INTRODUCTION
In today's world, online advertising has become an essential part of marketing. It has changed the way businesses reach and communicate with people. With the growing use of the internet and social media, online ads allow companies to connect with customers more easily and effectively. Through online advertising, businesses can target specific groups of people, check how their campaigns are performing

instantly, and design personalised messages for their audience. It also helps brands reach a global market at a much lower cost compared to traditional advertising. In this unit, we will learn about different types of online advertising tools and explore examples from the Indian advertising industry.
8.1 LEARNING OUTCOME
After having read this Unit, you would be able to: * Understand the key concepts and principles of online advertising; * Analyse the evolution of online advertising in the Indian market; and * Evaluate the effectiveness of tools and platforms for online advertising.
8.2 UNDERSTANDING ONLINE ADVERTISING
Online advertising is a major part of modern marketing. It helps brands connect with people through digital platforms like websites, search engines, and social media, where most online activity happens today.
8.2.1 Definition and Significance
Online advertising, also known as digital advertising, means promoting products or services through the internet. This can be done by using ads on social media, emails, search engine results, or website banners. Its main aim is to reach people online, interest them in the business, and turn their interest into purchases. Compared to traditional marketing, online advertising is less costly, helps reach specific groups of people, and gives quick results and feedback through data.
8.2.2 Key Concepts and Terminology
To navigate the world of online advertising effectively, it is essential to familiarise ourselves with key concepts and terminology: * Digital Channels: The places where ads are shown online, such as social media sites, search engines (like Google), websites, and mobile apps. * Targeting: The process of picking certain groups (like by age, location, or interests) to show ads, so businesses can talk to those most likely to buy. * Ad Formats: The types of ads used online, including video ads, banners, or posts that fit in with other online content. * Campaign Metrics: Measurements used to see if ads are working, such as, how many times ads are seen (impressions), clicked, or if they lead to sales (conversion). Common metrics include click-through rate (CTR) and return on investment (ROI).
8.3 ONLINE ADVERTISING IN INDIA
Online advertising has grown rapidly in India over the past few years. More businesses are using digital channels to reach people, thanks to rising internet use and smartphones. The digital advertising market in India is now worth thousands of crores and keeps growing every year.
The Growth
Many factors have helped online advertising expand here: * More people use the internet on their phones. * E-commerce sites like Flipkart and Amazon are popular.

* Social media, with over 400 million users in India, lets brands target just the right audience. Platforms like Facebook, Instagram, and X help businesses connect easily, using data like age, interests, and location to show relevant ads. Earlier, online ads were basic banners and simple messages. Now, companies use new technology and creative campaigns to stand out. Social media sites such as LinkedIn, Facebook, and YouTube help brands engage with people in new and personal ways.
Famous Indian Campaigns
Some online ad campaigns have created big changes, not just for brands but for society, too. Examples include: * Ariel's 'Share the Load': This campaign challenged gender roles and made people think about equality at home. It got a lot of attention and inspired new conversations. * Dove's 'Stop the Beauty Test': Dove's ads asked people to change how they see beauty and accept themselves, making a positive impact on viewers. * Flipkart's Big Billion Days: Through online ads and social media, this huge sales event creates excitement and brings lots of shoppers to Flipkart's website. * Cadbury's #SayThankYou: Cadbury used video ads and posts to thank frontline workers during COVID-19, helping the brand connect with people emotionally.
8.4 TOOLS AND PLATFORMS FOR ONLINE ADVERTISING
8.4.1 SEM and SEO
Search Engine Marketing (SEM) and Search Engine Optimization (SEO) are two essential components of online advertising that play a crucial role in enhancing a brand's visibility and driving traffic to its website.
Definition and Importance
SEM uses paid ads to help websites show up more often in search engines like Google. For example, companies pay to have their ads appear at the top when someone searches for relevant words. SEO means improving a website so it appears higher in search results naturally, without paying for ads. This is done by making the site's content better, updating its structure, and getting trustworthy links from other sites. SEM is good for getting traffic and sales quickly because ads are shown right away to the people as they search for said goods or services. SEO is important for building steady, long-term website visits and trust with audiences over time.
Role of SEM in Online Advertising
SEM lets businesses pick keywords and set ad budgets. Their ads show up above regular search results and can be adjusted as needed. Many Indian companies use SEM tools, especially Google Ads, to target their audiences and check how well ads are working. This has become a common approach for businesses wanting quick results in the Indian market.
Cases of Successful SEM and SEO Campaigns
Successful SEM campaigns in India have demonstrated the power of paid advertising in driving traffic, conversions, and brand awareness. One notable SEM campaign is the 'Swiggy Super' campaign by Swiggy, a popular food delivery platform. By strategically targeting keywords related to food delivery services, and offering exclusive benefits to users, Swiggy was able to increase its customer base, drive app downloads, and boost sales significantly.

In the realm of SEO, the 'MakeMyTrip' campaign stands out as a successful example of optimising a website for organic search. By focusing on relevant keywords, creating high-quality content, and building authoritative backlinks, MakeMyTrip improved its search engine rankings, increased organic traffic, and enhanced its online visibility, leading to a significant growth in bookings and revenue.
08.4.2 Social Media Advertising
Social media advertising is now one of the main ways companies promote their products or services. It helps businesses reach the right audience, build brand image, and encourage people to buy or use their products.
Social Media Advertising Platforms
Social media platforms have changed how marketing works by giving businesses direct access to their audience. Popular platforms like Facebook, Instagram, Twitter (now X), LinkedIn, and Snapchat allow companies to design and run highly targeted ad campaigns. These ads can be customised according to people's age, location, interests, and online behaviour. * Facebook Ads: Facebook helps businesses reach a wide audience using advanced targeting tools. Companies can choose who sees their ads and then track how well they perform using Facebook's analytics. * Instagram Ads: Instagram focuses on visual content. Businesses use photos, stories, and short videos (reels) to display products attractively. With features like hashtags and influencer collaborations, businesses create stronger connections with users and gain more visibility.
Effective Social Media Advertising Campaigns
* Cadbury Dairy Milk Silk: Cadbury's 2024 'The Story of Us' campaign, which centred around Valentine's Day, encouraged the users to scan QR Codes on Instagram, to create personalised and interactive messages. This not only increased brand awareness, it also improved sales by showing the product in a fresh and engaging way. * Zomato: Zomato used Facebook to run interactive ads and personalised content, encouraging users to download the app and engage more. Their ad campaigns aligned with popular cultural events, for example its 'Zomato Premier League' campaign during the cricket season. The campaign succeeded because of its exciting visuals, connection with customers, and smart use of Facebook's targeting tools.
8.4.3 Display Advertising
Display advertising means using visual ads on digital platforms to catch the attention of specific audiences.
Understanding Display Ads
Display ads are graphical advertisements displayed on websites, mobile apps, and other digital platforms. They typically consist of images, text, and sometimes interactive elements, designed to attract users' attention, and drive them to take action, such as clicking through to a website or making a purchase. For example, banner advertising is a specific type of display advertising that involves placing ads in prominent positions on webpages, often at the top, bottom, or sides. These ads come in various sizes and formats, including leaderboard, skyscraper, rectangle, and square banners, each offering unique advantages in terms of visibility and engagement.
Impact on Brand Visibility
By strategically placing ads on relevant websites and targeting specific audience segments, brands can increase their visibility among potential customers, thereby strengthening brand recognition and recall.

Display ads allow brands to convey their messaging visually, capturing attention and conveying brand values and offerings effectively. Through eye-catching creatives and compelling copy, advertisers can leave a lasting impression on users, influencing their perception of the brand and driving engagement.
Display Ad Formats and Placements
Display ads come in various formats and placements, each offering unique opportunities to reach and engage target audiences: * Standard Banner Ads: Classic display ads in standard sizes, like leaderboard (728x90 pixels), skyscraper (160x600 pixels), and rectangle (300x250 pixels), usually placed near website content or in apps. * Rich Media Ads: These are interactive ads that include video, sound, animation, or other engaging elements to attract user attention and increase interaction. * Native Ads: These ads blend into the website or app's natural content and design, making them less disruptive and often more effective in engaging users. * Social Media Ads: Platforms like Facebook and Instagram offer display ads such as sponsored posts, carousel ads, and display banners, using social networks' large user base and targeting options to reach audiences well.
Examples of Creative Display Ad Campaigns
Indian brands have used creative display ads to grab attention and connect with audiences: * Amazon India's Great Indian Festival: This yearly shopping event features bright, attractive banners showing big deals, which help Amazon bring more visitors and increase sales during the festive season. * Tanishq's Ekatvam Campaign: Tanishq promoted unity and diversity by showing diverse models and touching stories through beautiful display ads, communicating the brand's values clearly. * MakeMyTrip's Travel Diaries: This campaign uses eye-catching pictures of travel destinations and special offers to inspire people to travel, boosting bookings and revenue.
8.4.4 Email Marketing
Email marketing offers a direct and personalised way to connect with audiences.
Importance of Email Marketing
In an era dominated by social media and other digital channels, email marketing continues to thrive as a powerful tool for engaging audiences and driving conversions. Here's why email marketing remains indispensable: * Direct Communication: Email provides a direct line of communication between brands and their audience, allowing for personalised messaging and targeted outreach. * High ROI: Email marketing offers one of the highest returns on investment (ROI) among digital marketing channels. With low costs and the potential for high engagement and conversion rates, email campaigns can deliver significant results for businesses. * Audience Segmentation: Email marketing enables precise audience segmentation based on demographics, behaviour, and interests. By tailoring content to specific audience segments, marketers can deliver more relevant and impactful messages. * Automation and Scalability: Automation tools allow marketers to streamline email campaigns, from subscriber onboarding to post-purchase follow-ups. This ability to change enables businesses to nurture leads and maintain customer relationships effectively.

Successful Email Marketing Campaigns
Indian brands have leveraged email marketing to drive engagement, promote products, and build lasting relationships with customers. Some noteworthy examples are as follows: * OYO's Personalised Offers: OYO, a leading hospitality brand in India, implements personalised email marketing campaigns to offer tailored promotions and discounts to its subscribers. By analysing customer data and preferences, OYO delivers targeted emails that resonate with the recipients, driving bookings and revenue. * Swiggy's Weekly Digest: Popular food delivery platform, Swiggy, sends out weekly email digests featuring curated restaurant recommendations, exclusive offers, and food-related content. These engaging emails keep subscribers informed and entertained while promoting Swiggy's services effectively. * Nykaa's Beauty Tips: Nykaa, an e-commerce platform specialising in beauty and wellness products, sends out regular emails with beauty tips, tutorials, and product recommendations to its clientele. These informative emails not only educate subscribers but also drive traffic to Nykaa's website and encourage purchases. Check Your Progress: 1 Note: 1) Write your answer in the space provided below

8.5 DATA ANALYTICS IN ONLINE ADVERTISING
Data analytics is the process of cleaning and interpreting raw data to identify trends and patterns that empowers businesses and marketers to make informed decisions, optimise campaigns, and drive better results. It uses several tools, such as softwares and visualisation tools, and techniques, such as statistics and machine learning to understand past behaviours, predict future outcomes and offer solutions.
8.5.1 Importance of Data-Driven Decision-Making
In today's digital world, people's interests and actions change quickly. Using data to make decisions is necessary to keep up, stay competitive, and get good returns on marketing. Among the key reasons marketers use it today are: * Understanding Consumers: Data analytics helps marketers learn about what people like, how they behave, and what they buy. By checking data from websites, social media, and sales, businesses get to know their audience better, and can aim their ads more effectively. * Improving Campaigns: Data analytics lets marketers see how their ads are doing while they run. By looking at numbers like how many people click on ads, how many make purchases, and how much profit is made, they can adjust ads to work better.

* Personalising Ads: With detailed data, marketers can send ads that match individual tastes and interests. Targeting with precision means ads are more relevant, engagement goes up, and more people end up buying.
8.5.2 Tools and Platforms for Collecting and Analysing Data
Marketers use different tools and platforms to collect and study data. The most popular among these are: * Google Analytics: This tool shows details about website visitors, their actions, and how ads are performing. * Social Media Analytics: Tools like Facebook Insights, Twitter Analytics, and LinkedIn Analytics help track how much users engage with content and ads on social platforms. * CRM Systems: Services like Salesforce, HubSpot, and Zoho CRM store customer details and track interactions, helping analyse customer habits. * Data Management Platforms (DMPs): These gather data from different sources such as mobile apps, websites, and even offline sources; they then build thorough customer profiles, and help target ads. Examples are Adobe Audience Manager and Oracle BlueKai.
8.5.3 Data Analytics Use Advertising Cases
Here are some examples that show how Indian brands use data analytics: * Cadbury's 'Real People, Real Stories': Cadbury used data to find touching stories and target the right people. This led to high engagement and better brand connection. * Flipkart's Retargeting Campaigns: Flipkart tracks people who have visited their site but didn't buy products. With data, they show these users ads for what they viewed, encouraging them to come back and shop.
8.6 AUDIENCE TARGETING IN ONLINE ADVERTISING
In online advertising, data and technology help advertisers reach the right audience. Traditional methods like demographic (age, gender, income) and psychographic (lifestyle, interests) targeting are still useful, but digital tools now allow more advanced and precise ways to reach consumers. Let's look at some common audience targeting strategies.
8.6.1 Behavioural Targeting
Behavioural targeting means showing ads to people based on their online behaviour such as the websites they visit, the links they click, or the products they buy. It helps advertisers show the right ad at the right time to people who are most likely to be interested. By studying users' past online activities, businesses can create personalised ads and place them where users are likely to notice them. This increases engagement, improves recall, and often leads to more sales. Common Techniques: * Retargeting: Showing ads for products users have already viewed or shown interest in. For example, if someone looked at a pair of shoes online, similar ads might appear later while they browse other sites. * Product Recommendations: Suggesting products similar to what a user has browsed or purchased earlier. This creates a tailored shopping experience and encourages repeat visits or purchases.
8.6.2 Geo-targeting and Contextual Advertising
Both these strategies focus on delivering relevant ads based on location or content.

Geo-targeting means showing ads to users according to where they are. It can be as broad as a country or as specific as a neighbourhood. Advertisers use it to connect with local consumers, adapt to regional interests, and promote location-specific offers. Contextual advertising means placing ads on websites that match the topic or theme of what a user is reading or watching. For instance, ads for travel insurance might appear on a travel blog. This makes ads feel more natural and increases the chances of user engagement. Examples: * Zomato's Local Campaigns: Zomato offers special deals based on where users live, like featuring nearby restaurants. * Google Local Search Ads: A bakery in Mumbai can appear at the top of search results when someone nearby searches "bakery near me." * HDFC Bank's Contextual Ads: HDFC promotes financial products on websites about money and investments, targeting readers already interested in finance.
8.7 CONVERSION TRACKING AND ROI MEASUREMENT
Conversion tracking and ROI (Return on Investment) measurement help advertisers know how well their ads are performing. A conversion happens when a user completes a desired action, such as making a purchase, filling out a form, or downloading an app. ROI shows whether the money spent on advertising is giving good returns. Advertisers use various online platforms like Google Ads, Facebook Ads, and Microsoft Ads to track conversions. These tools collect data such as which ad was clicked, where the user is located, and whether the user completed a purchase. This information helps advertisers understand which ads are most effective and where they can improve. Sometimes, advertisers also track offline conversions for example, when a customer calls a phone number or visits a store after seeing an ad online. Tools such as QR codes or call-tracking software (like Nimbata) help record these conversions by linking real-world actions to online campaigns. In India, many companies measure their advertising success using methods like retargeting ads, personalised product suggestions, and influencer marketing. These techniques help businesses attract interested customers again and get better returns on their advertising spends.
8.8 MOBILE ADVERTISING AND APPS
8.8.1 Mobile Advertising
Since people increasingly use smartphones and tablets to browse the internet, mobile advertising has become a major part of digital marketing. In India, the use of mobile devices for online shopping, entertainment, and communication has made mobile advertising an essential way for brands to reach their audiences. Mobile advertising means promoting products and services through mobile devices. During the Covid lockdown, people spent more time on their phones, leading many brands to increase their mobile ad spending. Today, almost half of India's digital advertising budget goes toward mobile advertising. Tips for Effective Mobile Advertising: * Keep ads short and clear so they fit well on small screens. * Use simple language and clear calls to action (like "Buy Now" or "Learn More"). * Make sure ads adapt well to all types of mobile devices. * Use location targeting to reach users in specific areas or cities.

Indian brands have successfully used mobile ads with features like retargeting and product recommendations to engage customers. These ads have not only increased clicks and sales but also built stronger brand connections with mobile users.
8.8.2 In-App Advertising
In-app advertising refers to showing ads inside mobile apps. This type of advertising is growing fast in India as more people use apps for shopping, music, payments, and video streaming. It gives advertisers direct access to users who are already engaged with the app. Common In-App Ad Formats: * Banner Ads: Small ads that appear at the top or bottom of an app screen. * Interstitial Ads: Full-screen ads that show up at natural break points, such as between game levels. * Native Ads: Ads that match the look and feel of the app content. * Rewarded Videos: Users watch short videos to earn rewards like coins or discounts. In-app ads work well because they hold the user's attention better than traditional mobile web ads. However, advertisers need to ensure these ads do not slow down apps or disturb users too often. In-App Purchases: Many apps, especially games, earn money through in-app purchases where users buy items or upgrades. While it's a good revenue source, too many purchase prompts can frustrate users. Successful Campaigns: Popular Indian apps like Airtel, JioSaavn, Paytm, and Flipkart use in-app ads and cross-promotion strategies to attract and retain users. Here are some examples of their noteworthy execution: * Coca-Cola's "Share a Coke" Game Ads: Coca-Cola partnered with some gaming apps to offer rewards and challenges linked to its campaign, increasing engagement and brand visibility. * Amazon India's In-App Offers: Amazon ran special in-app promotions to show personalised deals, driving traffic and boosting sales during festive seasons. * Swiggy's Sponsored Listings: Swiggy allows restaurants to pay for featured spots in the app, helping users easily find popular or local dining options.
8.9 VIDEO ADVERTISING IN ONLINE CAMPAIGNS
Video advertising means using video content to promote products, services, or brands on digital platforms. It is one of the most effective ways to attract attention because it combines visuals, sound, and storytelling to create a stronger emotional impact than plain text or images. In India, video advertising has grown rapidly. With hundreds of millions of internet users accessing content mostly through their smartphones, videos have become a main part of how people discover and interact with brands. Many businesses now focus on mobile-friendly video ads to reach wider audiences and increase engagement.
Benefits of Video Advertising
* Higher Engagement: Videos grab attention quickly and keep viewers interested for longer. They can show how a product works, tell a story, or make audiences feel emotionally connected. * Better Brand Recall: Because people remember visuals and stories more easily, video ads help build strong brand recognition. * Improved Conversions: Video ads often lead to more clicks, visits, and purchases than other types of ads. They encourage users to take action after watching. Examples of Successful Video Campaigns in India:

* Google India's 'Reunion' Ad: This ad tells the story of two childhood friends separated by the partition of India and Pakistan, reunited through the help of Google Search. It connects emotionally while showing the usefulness of the product. * Vodafone Zoozoos: These funny, animated characters became instantly popular for their creative and light-hearted storytelling. The campaign made Vodafone stand out as a fun and innovative brand.
8.10 EMERGING TRENDS IN ONLINE ADVERTISING
8.10.1 Native Advertising
Native advertising is a type of paid ad that fits naturally into the platform where it appears. It matches the design, tone, and format of the surrounding content, so it feels like part of the user's browsing experience rather than a typical advertisement. Because of this, it attracts more attention and creates a better connection with viewers. Some key features of native advertising are as follows:
1. Relevance: Native ads are related to the content around them, making them more meaningful to
the audience.
2. Seamlessness: They blend smoothly into the platform's layout and design, ensuring the user's
experience is not interrupted.
3. Transparency: Even though they look natural, native ads are marked as "sponsored" or
"promoted" to maintain trust and clarity.
4. Variety: Native advertising can appear in many forms, such as sponsored blog posts, social media
promotions, content recommendations, or in-feed ads. Now let us look at some benefits of native advertising: * Builds higher user engagement since the ads feel like regular content. * Improves brand reputation through non-intrusive storytelling. * Bypasses ad blockers more effectively than traditional ads. * Helps distribute content widely and organically. * Enhances credibility by aligning with user interests and providing value.
8.10.2 Influencer Marketing
Influencer marketing is a popular way for brands to reach their audience by partnering with social media personalities who have many followers. These influencers create authentic and relatable content that helps influence their followers' buying decisions. This strategy builds trust because it feels more personal than traditional ads. Let us look at two examples of successful influencer marketing in India. * Myntra's 'End of Reason Sale' with Hrithik Roshan: Myntra teamed up with Bollywood star Hrithik Roshan, who shared posts on Instagram and Twitter about the sale. His personal style and the deals promoted created excitement and increased website visits and sales. * Nykaa's Beauty Influencer Collaborations: Nykaa works with beauty influencers who review products, create tutorials, and promote the brand. This helps Nykaa reach more beauty lovers and encourages more purchases on their platform. Check Your Progress: 2 Note: 1) Write your answer in the space provided below

8.11 LET US SUM UP
Online advertising plays an important role in modern marketing. It helps companies reach people through different platforms like search engines, social media, and mobile apps. Common methods include Search Engine Marketing (SEM), Search Engine Optimization (SEO), social media ads, and video ads. In India, mobile and in-app advertising have become very popular for connecting with consumers. New trends such as native advertising and influencer marketing also help brands reach audiences in more natural ways. By using the right tools and strategies, businesses can attract more visitors, increase engagement, and achieve their marketing goals.
8.12 GLOSSARY
Ad Campaign: A series of coordinated advertisements designed to achieve specific marketing objectives. Content Marketing: A marketing strategy that involves creating and sharing valuable, relevant, and consistent content to attract and engage a clearly defined audience. Engagement: The level of interaction and involvement of users with advertising content. Conversion: The action taken by a user in response to an advertisement, such as making a purchase or filling out a form. ROI (Return on Investment): A measure of the profitability of an advertising campaign relative to its cost.

9.0 INTRODUCTION
Welcome to the fascinating world of Digital Influencers! In this Unit, we'll find out how ordinary individuals and niche creators have risen to become powerful voices in advertising and communication. As students of persuasive communication, it's essential to understand why brands and organisations are turning to these digital pioneers to connect with their audiences. We will explore what makes digital influencers effective, the unique ways they engage their followers, and how they build trust and loyalty through storytelling and authenticity. We'll also examine their critical role in the rapidly evolving advertising world. It would be apt to rename this unit as 'Digital Influencers: Powering Persuasive Communication' From this Unit, you'll have a clear understanding of how influencers shape perceptions, build brands, and persuade audiences. You'll be equipped with insights to strategically engage with influencers in your future roles in advertising, journalism, and public relations.

9.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
By the end of this unit, you would will be able to: * Define the role of digital influencers in modern communication and their influence on advertising and PR strategies. * Analyse the key traits and types of influencers and their effectiveness in different marketing campaigns. * Evaluate the ethical considerations and challenges in influencer marketing and suggest strategies to mitigate them.
9.2 ACQUAINTING OURSELVES WITH DIGITAL
INFLUENCERS
9.2.1 Who are Digital Influencers?
Digital influencers are individuals who capitalise social media platforms to build a strong personal brand and influence audience behaviour. Unlike traditional influencers such as celebrities or public figures, digital influencers gain trust through relatability and consistent interaction with their followers. Their role in modern communication goes beyond just promoting products--they create authentic content that aligns with the interests and preferences of their niche audiences. For instance, beauty influencer Ankita Chaturvedi (@Corallista) uses YouTube and Instagram to share makeup tutorials, establishing herself as a trusted voice in the beauty industry. Unlike traditional celebrities who rely on mass appeal, digital influencers often cater to specific interests or communities, like tech, travel, or fitness. For example, Gaurav Taneja (@FlyingBeast) combines travel and fitness to inspire his audience. Digital influencers are now central to advertising and public relations, helping brands connect with consumers in an engaging, authentic way.
9.2.2 The Rise of the Influencer Economy
The explosion of social media platforms has been instrumental in the emergence and growth of digital influencers. These platforms provide individuals with the tools to create, share, and promote content, enabling them to build substantial followings and influence public opinion. In India, the influencer marketing industry is experiencing significant expansion. According to 'The Influencer Marketing Report 2024' by Influencer.in, the industry is projected to reach Rs5,500 crore in 2024, accounting for 11% of the overall digital media sector. This growth trajectory is expected to continue, with estimates suggesting the industry will touch Rs6,875 crore by 2025 and Rs10,750 crore by 2027. (Campaign India: https://www.campaignindia.in/article/indias-influencer-industry-to-touch-rs-10-750-crore-by- 2027/498520?utm_source=chatgpt.com). Prominent Indian influencers represent this trend. Bhuvan Bam, known for his YouTube channel 'BB Ki Vines,' has amassed over 25 million subscribers, making him one of India's most popular content creators. Prajakta Koli, operating under the moniker 'MostlySane,' has garnered a substantial following with her relatable content, boasting over 7 million subscribers on Instagram. These influencers have taken advantage of the accessibility and reach of platforms like YouTube and Instagram to engage with diverse audiences. Their content resonates with viewers, leading to high engagement rates and substantial influence over consumer behaviour.

Brands recognise this impact, increasingly collaborating with influencers to leverage their reach and authenticity. The growing influencer economy in India is a clear reflection of how social media is reshaping the way we communicate and market today. With platforms constantly evolving and more people coming online, digital creators are becoming an integral part of India's digital ecosystem--shaping trends, driving conversations, and redefining brand-consumer relationships. Their influence is only set to grow in the coming years.
9.3 CHARACTERISTICS OF DIGITAL INFLUENCERS
9.3.1 Types of Influencers
Digital influencers can be classified into four categories based on their audience size and engagement levels. These categories help brands tailor their campaigns for specific goals, from mass visibility to targeted niche engagement.
1. Mega Influencers
Mega influencers have over a million followers and are often celebrities or public figures. They command extensive reach across platforms, making them ideal for high-visibility campaigns. Example: Cricketer Virat Kohli, one of India's most-followed personalities on Instagram with over 265 million followers, collaborates with brands like Puma, MRF, and Audi. His posts often receive millions of likes and comments, ensuring broad exposure for these brands.
2. Macro Influencers
Macro influencers typically have 100,000 to 1 million followers. They often gain fame as industry experts or social media creators, making them appealing for campaigns that require a blend of reach and credibility. Example: Tech reviewer Geeky Ranjit, with over 3 million YouTube subscribers, reviews gadgets and technology. His detailed and informative content influences purchasing decisions among tech enthusiasts.
3. Micro Influencers
Micro influencers, with 10,000 to 100,000 followers, specialise in niche areas like food, travel, or fitness. Their content is highly relatable, fostering a loyal and engaged audience. Example: Indian travel influencer Bruised Passports, with approximately 40,000 Instagram followers, focuses on budget-friendly international travel. Their recommendations often guide travel plans for young Indian audiences.
4. Nano Influencers
Nano influencers have fewer than 10,000 followers and cater to hyper-specific communities or local audiences. Their strong personal connection with followers makes them effective for promoting grassroots-level campaigns. Example: A local baker in Mumbai using Instagram to showcase homemade cakes and collaborating with ingredient brands like Weikfield for promotions. Each category offers distinct advantages, from mega influencers driving widespread visibility to nano influencers creating intimate and personal connections. Understanding these categories enables brands to select the right influencers for targeted campaigns, ensuring maximum impact.
9.3.2 Key Traits of Successful Influencers

Successful influencers share specific traits that make their content impactful and their presence influential. These traits help them build trust, grow their audience, and collaborate effectively with brands.
1. Authenticity
Authenticity is the essance of an influencer's appeal. Followers trust influencers who are genuine and transparent about their experiences. For instance, Malvika Sitlani, a beauty and lifestyle influencer, openly discusses her struggles and successes, creating a sense of relatability that endears her to her audience.
2. Storytelling
Influencers excel at weaving engaging stories into their content, making brand promotions feel natural and relatable. Fashion influencer Komal Pandey is a master storyteller. Her Instagram reels, blending outfit inspirations with humourous anecdotes, captivate her audience. Her 'getting ready' videos are not just about clothes but also a journey of self-expression, which resonates with her followers.
3. Niche Focus
Successful influencers often cater to specific interests, becoming authorities in their chosen domain. Tech influencers like Tech Burner focus on simplifying technology for everyday users, gaining credibility and trust in the tech space.
4. Audience Engagement
Interacting with followers through comments, Q&A sessions, or live videos fosters a strong sense of community. Fitness influencer Ranveer Allahbadia (@BeerBiceps) regularly responds to comments and shares follower success stories, creating a personal connection. 9.4 ROLE OF DIGITAL INFLUENCERS IN ADVERTISING
AND PR
9.4.1 Influencers as Brand Ambassadors
In today's digital-first world, brands are increasingly partnering with influencers to act as brand ambassadors. Influencers tap into their trusted relationships with audiences to promote products in ways that feel more authentic than traditional advertising.

Unlike traditional celebrities, digital influencers integrate branded content into their daily lives, creating a seamless experience for their followers. This approach not only boosts engagement but also drives action, such as product purchases or service sign-ups. Example: Amul, the iconic dairy brand, has embraced influencer marketing effectively. Collaborating with food bloggers and Instagram chefs, Amul promotes its wide range of products like butter, cheese, and cream. Influencers create recipes using Amul products and share step-by-step videos or posts, demonstrating how the products fit into everyday cooking. For instance, food bloggers like Archana's Kitchen frequently showcase recipes featuring Amul butter or paneer, blending the brand's identity with relatable content. This strategy highlights product utility and builds trust among followers who see these influencers as credible sources. Influencers also act as brand ambassadors by participating in live events, unboxing experiences, and Q&A sessions, fostering a direct connection between the brand and its audience. For brands like Amul, this partnership reinforces its position as a household name while reaching younger, digitally savvy consumers. By leveraging influencers as brand ambassadors, companies can effectively humanise their messaging, increase relatability, and achieve greater resonance with targeted demographics.
9.4.2 The Power of Storytelling in Influencer Content
Storytelling is one of the most powerful tools in an influencer's arsenal. By weaving brand promotions into compelling narratives, influencers make the content feel organic, engaging, and relatable, rather than overtly commercial. These stories resonate deeply with audiences because they are not simply about the product but about the experiences surrounding it. Influencers create stories that their followers can see themselves in, often positioning the brand as a key part of their daily lives. These narratives can range from personal experiences to shared community values, making the brand feel like a natural extension of the influencer's lifestyle. Example: Zomato, the popular food delivery platform, has successfully collaborated with food and travel influencers to tell engaging stories around food discovery. Influencers like Kunal Vijayakar and Radhika Agarwal share their food experiences while using Zomato to explore new restaurants or order in for a special meal. These influencers integrate Zomato's services within their personal adventures, whether it's exploring local delicacies or satisfying midnight cravings. This approach humanises the brand, builds emotional connections, and drives engagement, making the product more desirable by aligning it with real-life experiences. The power of storytelling allows brands to build a deeper connection with consumers, making the content feel less like an advertisement and more like an authentic recommendation.
9.4.3 Shaping Public Perception
Influencers play a crucial role in shaping public perception, especially in public relations (PR) campaigns. They are often seen as more relatable and trustworthy compared to traditional advertising, which is why brands and organisations increasingly rely on them to build credibility and raise awareness about important issues. Influencers can create powerful emotional connections with their followers, making them effective messengers for causes that require public trust and support. Their ability to humanise a message, share personal stories, and engage with audiences in a direct, conversational manner helps shift perceptions and drive social change. Example: In recent years, Indian influencers have used their platforms to promote mental health awareness, helping break the stigma surrounding mental health issues. Influencers like

Deepika Padukone and Kusha Kapila have been vocal about their struggles with mental health, using their influence to share personal stories and encourage followers to seek help. Deepika, through her organisation Live, Love, Laugh, and Kusha, via candid Instagram posts, have helped normalise conversations about mental health. Their stories resonate with millions of young Indians, fostering empathy and promoting mental health awareness. These PR campaigns not only enhance public understanding but also inspire individuals to take action-- whether it's seeking therapy or supporting mental health initiatives. Activity: Research a recent influencer marketing campaign in India (e.g., from brands like Nykaa, Myntra, or Zomato). Write a brief analysis (150-200 words) of how influencers were used in the campaign and how they shaped the brand's message.
9.5 STRATEGIES FOR ENGAGING WITH INFLUENCERS
9.5.1 Choosing the Right Influencer for a Campaign
When you're working on a campaign and thinking of collaborating with an influencer, choosing the right one is crucial for success. It's not just about the number of followers--they need to align with your brand and connect with your audience in the right way. There are a few important things to consider:
1. Relevance:
The influencer should fit with your brand's values and goals. For example, if you're promoting eco-friendly products, partnering with an influencer who supports sustainability is a natural choice. This ensures the promotion feels genuine to the audience.
2. Engagement Rate:
It's not always about the number of followers. An influencer with fewer but highly engaged followers is often more valuable. Look at the likes, comments, shares, and overall interaction on their posts. For instance, a fashion influencer with 50,000 followers who gets hundreds of comments on each post may have more impact than someone with 1 million followers who barely gets any engagement.
3. Audience Demographics:
Make sure the influencer's followers match your target audience. If your campaign is aimed at young adults, partnering with an influencer whose audience consists mainly of teenagers or older adults may not work. Example: Myntra, one of India's largest fashion e-commerce platforms, effectively uses fashion influencers like Komal Pandey and Dolly Singh for their youth-focused campaigns. These influencers not only promote Myntra's trendy clothing but also appeal to young, fashion- conscious consumers. Their style and relatable personality make them the perfect fit for Myntra's vibrant, youthful brand image. Choosing the right influencer is all about finding someone who feels like a natural fit with your brand and speaks to the right people in a way that feels authentic.
9.5.2 Co-creating Content with Influencers
One of the most powerful ways to work with influencers is by involving them in the content creation process. This approach helps maintain authenticity and ensures the final product resonates with their followers. When influencers help create content, it doesn't feel forced or

scripted. Instead, it reflects their personal style and voice, making the message more genuine and relatable. By co-creating content, influencers can integrate your brand in a way that feels natural to their audience, creating a seamless experience. This also gives influencers creative freedom to present the brand in a way that best suits their personality and their followers' interests. Example: Nykaa, a leading beauty and cosmetics platform, often collaborates with beauty influencers like Shreya Jain and Debasree Banerjee. Instead of simply asking them to promote products, Nykaa works with these influencers to create tutorials and product reviews that align with their unique content styles. These influencers not only showcase the products but also offer their honest opinions and tips, which builds trust with their audience. For instance, Shreya Jain's makeup tutorials featuring Nykaa products feel like a personal recommendation, not a paid promotion. Co-creating content helps both brands and influencers connect with their audiences in a more meaningful way, increasing engagement and building lasting trust.
9.5.3 Managing Influencer Relationships
When it comes to influencer marketing, building long-term relationships is the key. It's not just about one campaign or a short-term collaboration. Successful brands understand that trust is the foundation of any influencer partnership. The best results come when influencers feel valued and supported by the brand over time, rather than being treated as a one-off resource. This kind of relationship allows for more genuine content and better alignment between the brand and the influencer's audience. Over time, the influencer becomes a true advocate for your brand, and their followers will begin to trust your product more because it's coming from someone they already know and admire. For example, beauty brands like Nykaa and Mamaearth often collaborate with influencers over multiple campaigns, not just once. This consistency builds trust and helps create a more authentic connection between the influencer and the brand's target audience. At the end of the day, treating influencers as long-term partners rather than just promoters will lead to stronger, more successful campaigns. 9.6 CHALLENGES AND ETHICAL CONSIDERATIONS

Challenges in Working with Influencers
While working with influencers can be a game-changer for a brand, it doesn't come without its challenges. One major issue is the high cost involved, especially when partnering with mega or macro influencers. These influencers often charge hefty fees for their posts, which can strain a brand's marketing budget. It's important to weigh the benefits against the investment, ensuring the campaign will generate a return on investment (ROI) that justifies the cost. Another challenge is the issue of fake followers. Many influencers, especially those with larger followings, have been found to purchase fake followers to boost their numbers. This can make it difficult to gauge an influencer's true reach and engagement. Even more concerning is that some brands unknowingly work with influencers who have inflated follower counts, only to see little real impact from the campaign. To overcome these challenges, brands need to carefully vet influencers, check their engagement rates, and track performance more accurately to ensure they are getting real value from their partnerships.
Ethical Concerns in Influencer Marketing
As influencer marketing continues to grow, there are some important ethical concerns that brands and influencers need to address. One of the biggest issues is transparency--especially when it comes to paid partnerships. Many influencers promote products without clearly stating that they are sponsored. This can mislead their audience into thinking that the endorsement is based purely on personal opinion, rather than a paid promotion. Undisclosed sponsorships can lead to a lack of trust between the influencer and their followers. When followers feel that content is biased or doesn't come with full disclosure, it can damage the credibility of both the influencer and the brand involved. For instance, if a well-known beauty influencer promotes a skincare product without saying it's sponsored, their followers might feel deceived if the product doesn't live up to expectations. Another concern is misleading claims. Some influencers make exaggerated or unverified claims about the benefits of a product, leading to disappointment or harm to consumers. For example, a fitness influencer might promote a supplement that promises quick weight loss, but without proper evidence or scientific backing, it could lead to unrealistic expectations among their followers. In India, the Advertising Standards Council of India (ASCI) has set clear guidelines for influencer marketing to address these issues. The ASCI mandates that influencers must clearly disclose any paid partnerships or sponsored content. This disclosure should be made in a visible and understandable way--such as using hashtags like #ad or #sponsored. The guidelines also encourage influencers to avoid misleading or false claims about products and services. Activity: Look for an influencer marketing campaign that faced criticism or failure due to ethical concerns (such as undisclosed sponsorships or misleading claims). Summarise the situation in 150-200 words and suggest how the campaign could have been handled differently to maintain ethical standards.
9.7 THE FUTURE OF DIGITAL INFLUENCERS
Emerging Trends

The future of digital influencers is looking brighter than ever, with a few key trends set to shape the way they interact with audiences and brands. One of the biggest trends is the rise of AI influencers. These are virtual personalities created using artificial intelligence, with no human behind them. Brands are already experimenting with AI influencers to promote products in a more controlled and tailored way. For example, Indian fashion brand BIBA collaborated with an AI influencer named 'Shirley' in 2021 to showcase its collection on Instagram. While this trend is still in its early stages, it's something that could become more common in the future as AI technology improves. Another major trend is the growth of regional language content. With platforms like Moj and Josh seeing a huge rise in popularity, more influencers are creating content in regional languages to connect with audiences outside of major urban centres. These platforms are growing rapidly, particularly in tier-2 and tier-3 cities in India. In fact, Josh has seen more than 100 million downloads, tapping into the vernacular audience and providing influencers a platform to reach people who might not be as active on global apps like Instagram and TikTok. Focus on hyper-personalisation is increasing. Influencers are moving beyond general content to deliver niche, highly-targeted messages that resonate on a deeper level with their followers. This trend is fuelled by data and analytics, helping brands and influencers create content that is specifically tailored to the interests, preferences, and behaviours of their audience.
Impact on Careers in Advertising and PR
With these trends taking shape, the world of advertising and PR is also evolving. The rise of influencers has led to the creation of new roles, such as influencer managers and content strategists. Influencer managers are responsible for finding the right influencers for campaigns, negotiating deals, and ensuring that both the brand and the influencer are aligned in their messaging. They also handle influencer relationships and performance tracking, ensuring that the campaign goals are met. On the other hand, content strategists work closely with influencers to create engaging content that aligns with both the brand's identity and the influencer's voice. These strategists need to stay on top of trends, understand audience behaviours, and work on creating strategies that feel organic and not overly commercial. In India, with influencer marketing set to reach Rs5,500 crore by 2024, these roles are becoming increasingly vital. For instance, brands like Myntra and Nykaa rely on influencer managers to ensure that their campaigns connect with the right audience through the right influencers. The demand for such roles is only expected to grow as influencer marketing becomes a permanent fixture in the advertising and PR world. 9.8 CASE STUDIES FROM INDIA
A Successful Influencer Campaign
One of the most successful influencer marketing campaigns in India in recent years was Cred's campaign featuring Indian celebrities and digital influencers. Cred, a platform that rewards users for paying their credit card bills on time, has been using influencers strategically to boost its brand awareness. Cred's campaigns, such as '#CredDiwali', featured Bollywood stars like Kartik Aaryan and Madhuri Dixit, alongside popular digital influencers like Kusha Kapila and Barkha Singh. The blend of Bollywood celebrities and relatable social media influencers created a perfect balance of mass appeal and niche engagement. The campaign cleverly used humour and quirky ads to promote the idea of 'better spending,' while engaging viewers through relatable, fun content. What made this campaign stand out was the clever use of influencers from diverse backgrounds to showcase different aspects of the platform. Celebrities helped spread the message to a wider audience, while influencers connected with younger, digital-first users. This strategy not only generated massive engagement but also created a buzz on social media, making Cred a household name in the Indian fintech space. According to data from Influencer.in, Cred's influencer campaigns contributed significantly to the platform's growth, with a 40% increase in app downloads during the campaign period. By tapping into both established stars and rising digital influencers, Cred successfully blended traditional and digital marketing strategies. Lessons from a Failed Campaign On the flip side, there are campaigns that didn't go as planned due to poor influencer alignment. One such example is Bingo's campaign in 2019, which faced criticism due to poor selection of influencers and lack of proper audience targeting. Bingo, a popular snack brand in India, collaborated with several influencers for their campaign '#BingoTakaTak'. The campaign involved influencers promoting Bingo's chips through fun, lip-syncing videos on TikTok. However, the campaign faced backlash because the influencers chosen were not well-aligned with the brand's target demographic. Many of the influencers did not have a strong connection to food or snack-related content, and their audiences did not match Bingo's key consumer group--young adults interested in quick, tasty snacks. The lack of audience relevance led to low engagement rates and negative feedback from followers, who felt the campaign was forced and disconnected from the brand's identity. According to an article in Campaign India, the poor influencer alignment and mismatch in audience engagement led to the campaign failing to meet its goals of boosting brand awareness. This failure highlights the importance of aligning influencers with the brand's values and target audience. Influencer marketing is most effective when there is a natural fit between the influencer's personality, their content, and the brand they are promoting. In this case, Bingo's choice of influencers didn't resonate with their core customers, making the campaign feel inauthentic and ineffective. These two case studies--one successful and one less successful--demonstrate the critical importance of selecting the right influencers and ensuring alignment with your brand's message and target audience.

9.11 GLOSSARY
Influencer: An individual who uses social media platforms to impact the opinions and behaviours of others, often in exchange for brand partnerships. Engagement Rate: A metric that measures how much interaction (likes, comments, shares) an influencer's content receives relative to their audience size. Brand Ambassador: An influencer who regularly represents a brand, promoting its products or services. Co-creation: Collaborative content creation between a brand and an influencer to ensure authenticity in promotion.

9.0 INTRODUCTION
From Web 2.0 onwards, e-commerce, mobile-commerce, and now social media and mobile marketing have altered people's life significantly. The digital media has integrated into the powerful smartphone and other static digital devices. The integration of digital media is a recent phenomenon that has undergone evolutions, processes, designs and development to satisfy the users of digital platforms. In the process of integration, users of the digital media platform have been given the highest priority by the advertisers. This unit will help you to identify different digital media platforms and integration strategies. This can, then, be implemented for advertising using social media and digital marketing through various digital channels.
9.1 LEARNING OUTCOMES
After reading this unit, you will be able to: * Understand various aspects of hybrid advertising; * Locate it theoretically in social power theory and resource dependence theory; and * Understand the uses of hybrid advertising in various domain areas and recognise emerging trends.

9.2 DIGITAL MEDIA
Digital media may be described as any format of communication that is converted from waves to binary codes, stored, transmitted and transformed into 0s and 1s. Several devices use these formats for communication, for example, digital TVs and or Digital Versatile Discs (DVDs), mobile phones, MP3 players, digital recorders, and so on. In the process of using these formats of communication, these devices break signals, converting audio or video into binary digits. Smartphones and other such powerhouse devices have given birth to lots of social media applications. Today, we have several digital media types, with different user characteristics and limitations. It is a versatile space which can be customised to meet the needs of the user and the consumer. In one sense, it has become an extension of the human experience, a tool to communicate with each other in our social and non-social life, in terms of information, education and entertainment. Digital media has made erstwhile communication systems such as traditional postal systems and landline telephones redundant, giving way to countless digital means of communication. It is this versatility of digital media that has enabled it to be used in hybrid forms in the world of advertising and marketing. Digital media provides a variety of solutions to the world of digital marketing and hybrid advertising through its adoption in a customised manner through the integration of both traditional media and digital media content and techniques. According to Wymbs, digital marketing may be defined as "online channels, formed by the range of access platforms and communication tools" (Wymbs, 2011). However, in this unit, hybrid advertising focuses on the adoption and integration of traditional media content into the digital realm. These integrated techniques help capture attention, create interest, and persuade the consumer toward the act of making a purchase of a product or a service. Hence, it is a little different from pure digital marketing, which uses digital communication tools and platforms for marketing products and services. The difference lies in the fact that in hybrid marketing, traditional media is integrated with digital media content and techniques. For example, while digital marketing is done through social media platforms, hybrid marketing will involve traditional media, digital media, blending the two through effective marketing strategies.
9.3 TYPES OF DIGITAL MEDIA PLATFORMS
Digital media keep evolving according to the need and innovation in the world of technology. It comes in many different avatars and formats, including print media (e-books, e-magazines, e-newspapers), television, movies, video games, music, cell phones, various kinds of software, and the Internet. Digital media platforms also include social media. According to Kaplan and Haenlein (2010), "Social Media is a group of Internet-based applications that build on the ideological and technological foundations of Web 2.0, and that allow the creation and exchange of User Generated Content". However, each type of media involves both content and a device or object, through which that content is delivered. Some present-day digital media platforms can be categorised as follows:
1. Social media platforms like Facebook, WhatsApp, X (formerly Twitter), Instagram, and
LinkedIn.
2. Knowledge platforms like Stack Overflow, Quora, and Yahoo! Answers.
3. Media sharing platforms like YouTube, Spotify, and Vimeo.
4. Service-oriented platforms like Uber, Airbnb, and Grub Hub.

9.4 ELEMENTS OF DIGITAL MEDIA
The palpable shifts in communication processes with the advent of new media technologies evidence a decrease in the gap between the advertiser and consumer of products, programs, services and information. Consumers want everything, they want it quickly, and they want it at their doorsteps. It is this demand that has enhanced the usage of digital media in the hybrid mode. Traditionally, an advertisement is the integration of four basic elements - attention, interest, desire and action. In a similar vein, the three key elements of digital media are computing, communication, and content. A convergence of these two can lead to effective advertising through the merger of traditional media and digital technology. Some key elements of this entire domain of human activity and knowledge are as follows:
9.4.1 Networked
A key element that makes digital media superior to analogue media or traditional media is the quality of being networked. It can be produced, distributed and consumed through two-way networked infrastructure in a variety of ways such as the internet, mobile phone or WiFi networks, whereas traditional broadcast or telecast media tends to be consumed on one-way analogue infrastructures. In fact, by concept, digital media is more akin to the telephone than television telecasts or cinema screenings. Digital media is innovative, need-based and disruptive. Today, we have smartphones with internet connectivity to provide instant access to information. Customised content generation is evolving at an increasingly fast pace based on artificial intelligence (AI) and algorithm-based systems. Therefore, the various networked elements that constitute digital systems, too, are in flux and dynamic.
9.4.2 Interactive
Perhaps the simplest but most useful definition of interactivity in the context of digital media is provided by Jensen (1998), "A measure of media's potential ability to let the user exert an influence on the content and or form of the mediated communication" (Jensen, 1998, cited in Kiousis, 2002). We can say that while the traditional media pushes information, digital media pulls the user to be responsive to the piece of information, media object, needs or activities of the user. Moreover, it is sociologically-oriented and

relates to the context in which the communication occurs and the results of that communication among different groups or societies. It is this feature that connects digital media with its users but, it also calls upon them to unconsciously work for it in the process of providing them the chance to consume. In fact, Manovich (2001) proposes that 'interactivity' is a meaningless term since the ability to manipulate and customise information is the most basic fact about computers.
9.4.3 Hypertextual / Hypermediated
The elements of 'hypertextuality' and 'hypermediality' have enabled digital media in the interlinking of databases that allow us to navigate from one bit of content or web page to another . Hypertext is a form of text that is composed of nodes or blocks of text (or media in the case of hypermedia) which form the content, the links between these blocks of content, and the buttons or tags that enact the link from one node to another. For instance, the hyperlinks in Wikipedia. In digital media advertising, the choice rests with the viewer or reader, which means the hypertext by nature is a non-linear form of text, and it begins to blur the distinction between the 'creator/writer' and the 'reader/viewer'. Thus, hypertext combines traditional text with interactive branching to create a non-linear text which is different from 'traditional' printed page (Conklin, 1987). In this way, the digital media user is creating 'new works' by navigating their way through different hypertexts which makes content automatic, personal and customised.
9.4.4 Automated
It was Manovich (2001) who can be credited for suggesting 'automation' as one of the key elements of digital media. He proposed that the numerical constitution of digital media and communications means that such products can be easily manipulated through the use of automated templates and algorithms. This means that digital products and digital media can be automatically modified or even created through software and programs instead of being specifically created or modified by people. Digital products such as hybrid advertisements can be automatically modified or even created out of databases by machines as opposed to being the result of human action as in traditional media. The most significant way in which this happens is through the increasing personalisation of media. Thus, we can consider that it is this element of digital media that the internet and other forms of digital media use for their commercial value by collecting information about consumers' profile and targeting them with hybrid advertising more efficiently. It makes it clear that the automated processes of personalisation, which is often data-based profiling, are fundamental to the digital media environment.
9.4.5 Databased
Digital media uses databases continuously. When we travel by a vehicle and go to places or purchase a product, we use a satellite navigation system or one of the many online mapping services and route planners such as Multi-map, Google maps, and so on. For route planners, a database is created using information about starting points and destinations; even a speed camera database is maintained. These digitised pieces of information are elements of digital media. In the most general sense, a database can be defined as a 'structured collection of data' (Manovich 2001), or container of information (Paul 2007). The database system is essentially composed of three components; storage, retrieval and filter. They all together form part of digital media as a means to turn the database into meaningful information (Paul
2007) , even in hybrid advertisements.

9.5 INTEGRATION TECHNIQUES AND HYBRID
ADVERTISING
Hybrid advertising is a new mantra for success in digital and traditional media advertising. Hybrid advertising, as already explained, is a mix of traditional marketing strategies, and a more recent and innovative one. At its heart, advertising is a method of persuasion of the prospective consumer, irrespective of the channel, media or mode of communication, by which an organisation or company reaches out to its target audience. But for the more discerning eye, there is a difference between web and online content, and commercials and advertisements. We might be tempted to club hybrid advertising with integrated media techniques. But neither is the same, even though they share some common points. Both integration techniques and hybrid advertising involve the use of consistent brand messages throughout and all across traditional and new marketing channels and media, but they use different promotional methods to get them going.
9.5.1 Concept and evolution
The concept of 'hybrid advertising' is a recent phenomenon that has resulted from the usage of digital media technology and its management in the usage of advertisements to capture attention, create interest, cause desire, and lead the consumer to action. In this process of persuasion, hybrid advertisements' prospective customers and consumers of products or services are targeted through different modalities of communication, be it visual, text or audio formats. In recommender systems and advertising platforms, marketers always want to deliver products, content, or advertisements to potential audiences over media channels such as display, audio, video, or through digital social group platforms. The evolution of hybrid advertisements is the result of the need for customised and personalised services and product delivery systems that every consumer desires for the money they spend. So, there is an economy behind this evolution. Given a set of audiences or customers (seed users), the audience expansion technique (look-alike modeling) through the concept of hybrid advertisement is a promising solution to identify more potential audiences, who are similar to the seed users and likely to finish the business goal of the target campaign. In a way, we can find that media consumption across the globe is increasingly happening in digital formats. The increase in the number of devices and technology capable of supporting digital media along with increasing internet access speed, has provided consumers with an option to access the media content of his choice, be it information, entertainment or social activity anytime, anywhere. This is the result of the need for consumer base and technology usage.
9.6 TECHNIQUES FOR PRODUCING HYBRID
ADVERTISING USING DIGITAL MEDIA

There are several techniques for producing hybrid advertising using digital media. The technique is based on traditional advertisements and modern digital advertisement formats and modalities used for communication. The usage of translation facility for subtitles/captions used by YouTube video, in the form of closed captions (CC) is a clear example of hybrid advertising that targets global populations that use different languages. These techniques (for example, the usage of .srt file uploads in Google Translation engine in closed captions facilitation in multiple global languages) have slowly evolved and will continue to evolve in the future with the advancement of technology. Digital devices all around us, from smartphones and tablets to desktops and laptops, facilitate simultaneous procurement of products, services and programmes. A company's ads popping-up suddenly on the side panels of our TV screens during prime time, and then when we're reading news on handheld gadgets is also one example of hybrid advertisement. Another example is automated phone calls where we get messages from businesses, or are required to engage with an interactive voice response system (IVRS) that requests us to choose information step-by-step, for instance, while registering a complaint about a product or a service. Again, hybrid advertisements are seen on YouTube videos or news channels with Quick Response (QR) codes, leading the viewer to another link. The technique used in these hybrid advertisements is limited to smart usage of multiple tracks available on multimedia channels of the telecast, using an advanced video editing console or software such as Studio Pinnacle or Final Cut Pro (FCP). Besides, the usage of Chrome Color while making videos will enable us to tinker with the content, for instance to remove the background or change colour settings, as per the need of the target group.
9.6.1 SEO and Digital Media Design
Search Engine Optimization (SEO) is the basis of hybrid advertisement design. When we search in the digital space for information about a product or service, it is significant for the prospective customer to ascertain its details. He or she will do an initial search for the same in the digital space based on their needs and interest. When a customer searches for a service or product in the search engine, it would most likely be the first option to appear. This is what an SEO does. Hence, it is important to optimise the usage of SEO for any hybrid advertisements, based on the optimal techniques prescribed by the World Wide Web Consortium. This includes alternative text to visuals, captions or subtitles to videos and audio descriptions for multimedia programmes. Furthermore, norms of accessibility must be followed in hybrid advertisements to help optimise search engine results. The choice of terms and key words, too, play a significant role for any hybrid advertisement in order for the product or service to be the first in the search output.
9.7 BENEFITS OF HYBRID ADVERTISING
The benefits of hybrid advertising are manifold, depending on the customer base selected as the target in terms of its effect. They are as follows:
1. Wider audience: Using a mix of traditional and digital media, hybrid advertising helps
businesses reach a wider customer cluster who may be consuming media through different platforms.
2. Greater visibility: Since hybrid advertising appears across different platforms, it allows
businesses to reach customers more frequently and repeatedly.
3. Increased speed: Hybrid advertising can reach target audience faster as it may start rolling out on
digital platforms and be subsequently be carried on through traditional media.
4. Low-cost in the long run: Hybrid advertising helps lower costs by sending similar messages
across different media forms.
5. Tracking impact level: In terms of digital media, it is easy for businesses to track the satisfaction
level of customers through the application of analytics, which is difficult in traditional media alone.
6. 'Glocal' reach: Hybrid advertising helps reach both global and local audiences. Digital media can

target customers globally, while traditional media can reach local customers, benefiting a campaign. Check Your Progress: 2 Note: 1) Use the space below for your answers.

9.9 GLOSSARY
Digital Media: Digital media may be described as any format of communication that is converted from waves to binary codes, stored, transmitted and transformed into zeros and ones. Hybrid Advertising: It is a mix of traditional marketing strategies and the more recent and innovative digital media one. Traditional Media: This refers to media such as television, radio, newspapers, and the like, which are less dependent on the internet, and are also less interactive. Online Branding: It is a tool to interact and communicate with existing and potential customers using digital media.
